en: The Bhāvaprakāśa composed by the illustrious Bhāvamiśra, First Section:
[Salutation to] the elephant-faced one, the foremost of the immortals, the bestower of success, and the remover of obstacles.
I pay homage to the Guru, who bestows the eye of understanding, and to the chosen deity who grants all that is desired.
Having examined various treatises, I shall first set down here the manner in which the arrival of Āyurveda occurred upon the earth.
That in which the learned find information regarding the life-span, what is beneficial and harmful, the etiology of disease, and likewise its pacification, is called Āyurveda;
for by means of this, a person attains and understands his life-span (āyuḥ).
Therefore, this is remembered as Āyurveda by the best of sages.
Revealing Āyurveda, the entire essence of the Atharvaveda, the Creator composed a straightforward compendium in his own name consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
Then Vidhi, the ocean of intelligence, instructed Dakṣa Prajāpati— who was himself skillful in all undertakings— in the Ayurveda along with its auxiliary branches.
Then Dakṣa, who was proficient in action, [taught] the two physicians of heaven the science of longevity.
The two learned ones, the best of gods and sons of the Sun,
having studied under Dakṣa, composed their own blessed *Saṃhitā* for the sake of increasing the understanding of the entire world of physicians. (7–8)
Then, that head of Svayambhu was severed by Bhairava in his wrath;
it was restored by the two Aśvins, and therefore they were born as partakers of the sacrificial offerings.
In the battle between the gods and the asuras, those gods who were wounded by the Daityas—
Those [sacrificial cakes] were instantly made uncrushed by the two Dasras—this was a great wonder.
The paralysis of the arm of the wielder of the thunderbolt was treated by the two Dasras; the moon, which had fallen from Soma, was made well again by those very same two. 10–11.

The teeth of Pūṣan were shattered, the eyes of Bhaga were lost, and the Moon was afflicted with consumption; these were all treated by the Aśvins. Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu, being lustful and old, underwent a transformation.
Endowed with vigor, complexion, and voice, they were made young again by the two Aśvins.
Through these and many other deeds, the two best of physicians became highly honored by Indra and the other inhabitants of heaven.
Having observed these deeds of the two Aśvins, Indra,
the lord of Śacī, exerting himself, requested from them the Ayurveda free from affliction;
it is said that the two Nāsatyas were thus entreated by Śakra, who is true to his promise.

The two [Aśvins] imparted the Āyurveda exactly as they had studied it to Śatamanyu (Indra). Having studied the Āyurveda from the Nāsatyas, Śatakratu (Indra) then taught it to many sages, headed by Ātreya.
Once, beholding the world afflicted by disease here and there, the Blessed One Ātreya, the bull among sages, reflected:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may the worlds be free from affliction?"
I am unable to look upon these beings who have fallen into such a state;
I am exceedingly compassionate, for nature is difficult to overcome.
Because of their suffering, sorrow increases even more within my own heart.
Having resolved, "I shall study Āyurveda for the sake of the health of embodied beings," Ātreya went to the abode of the gods.
Having gone there to the palace of Indra, he beheld Śakra.
Seated upon a lion-throne, being praised by the celestial sages,
illuminating the quarters with his splendor like the sun in brilliance,
he was the great teacher of Ayurveda, to be held as a crown upon the heads of the dwellers of heaven.

But Śakra, upon merely beholding him, rose from his throne and stood before him; he honored him, who was exceedingly emaciated by intense asceticism, and inquired after his welfare as well as the reason for his arrival. (24)
That sage began to explain the reason for his arrival:
"O King of the Gods, you do not know that from heaven itself you were appointed by the Creator with great effort as the protector of the inhabitants of the three worlds."

The people on this earth are afflicted by diseases and their minds are overwhelmed with grief; have compassion for them and act to destroy their suffering. Out of mercy, grant me instruction in Āyurveda for the benefit of humanity.
Having said "So be it," the thousand-eyed Indra taught that sage.
Having studied the Ayurveda along with its auxiliary branches from the lord of sages, Indra,
he honored him with blessings and returned once more to the earth.
Then the venerable Ātreya, the best of sages and a mine of compassion,
composed a compendium (saṃhitā) under his own name out of pity for the class of men.
Then [he taught it] to Agniveśa, Bhela, Jātūkarṇa, and Parāśara.
He taught Āyurveda to Kṣīrapāṇi and Hārīta.
In ancient times, Agniveśa was the first author of a treatise (tantra); thereafter, Bhela and others composed their own respective treatises. 31–32.
They caused Ātreya, who is honored by the multitude of sages, to hear them;
and having heard those tantras, the son of Atri became joyful.
Seeing that they were properly composed as aphorisms (sūtras), the sages were delighted.
In heaven, the celestial sages and the gods, having heard this, exclaimed, "Excellent! (34).
Once, by chance, many sages gathered together on the slopes of the Himalayas; I shall now mention them by name. (35)
The eminent sage Bharadvāja arrived first;
after him came Aṅgiras, then Garga, Marīci, Bhṛgu, and Bhārgava;
as well as Pulastya, Agasti, Asita, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara. (36)
Hārīta, Gautama, Sāṃkhya, Maitreya, and Cyavana;
Jamadagni, Gārgya, Kaśyapa, and Kāśyapa;
as well as Nārada, Vāmadeva, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Kapiñjala. (37–38)
Śāṇḍilya, Sahakauṇḍinya, Śākuneya, and Śaunaka;
Āśvalāyana and Sāṃkṛtya, Viśvāmitra, and Parīkṣaka; Devala, Gālava, Dhaumya, and both Kāpya and Kātyāyana. 39.
Kāṅkāyana, Vaijapeya, Kuśika, Bādarāyaṇa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Laugākṣi, Śaralomā, Gobhila,
the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise other great ṛṣis.
Treasures of the knowledge of Brahman, and of self-restraint and discipline, they were radiant with the splendor of their asceticism like fires into which oblations are being poured;
seated there at ease, they all engaged in this conversation.
The body is said to be the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
and that [body] would serve for the accomplishment of all goals if it were free from disease.
(43) [It is the basis] of austerity, self-study, dharma, celibacy, vows, and longevity.
Diseases spread everywhere, carrying away [all] in every direction.
Diseases have been observed to cause emaciation, to destroy strength, to rob the body of its capacity for movement,
to diminish the power of the senses, and to inflict pain upon every limb.

"Since these [passions], which are the very nature of great obstacles to dharma, artha, all kāma, and mokṣa, forcibly and swiftly snatch away the life-breaths—if they exist, how can there be security for living beings?
Therefore, some method must be devised by you wise and capable ones for their pacification. Having spoken thus in the assembly, they addressed the sage Bharadvāja.
"O Blessed One, you are worthy; request from the Thousand-eyed One that Āyurveda which we have received through tradition, by studying which we shall be liberated from the fear of disease.
Thus entreated with humility by those worthy sages, Bharadvāja, the best of sages, went to the abode of the gods.
Having gone there to Indra’s abode, he saw the slayer of Vṛtra seated in the midst of the hosts of celestial sages, blazing like a fire.
Upon seeing the sage, the blessed Maghavan spoke with joy:
Then, he who knows the Dharma honored that sage, saying, "Welcome to you.
Having approached and greeted the Lord of the Gods with blessings of victory,
he related the words of the sages exactly as they were spoken.
For diseases have arisen that are terrifying to all living beings;
you ought to explain, according to the truth, the means for their pacification.
(51) Śatakratu taught the sage Āyurveda along with its auxiliary branches.
Having heard this, the embodied being shall live for thousands of years free from disease.
That great sage, with his mind fixed upon it, quickly and correctly understood in its entirety that Ayurveda, which is infinite, boundless, and consists of three sections.
By that [means], Bharadvāja obtained a very long and healthy life;
he also made other sages free from disease and long-lived.
All the seers, through the eye of knowledge produced by his system, [attained this]. 54.
Having observed the qualities, the elements, and the activities, and having relied upon their prescribed method,
they attained health and long life joined with happiness; by following the procedure taught in Āyurveda, others too may become like sages.
When the Veda was retrieved by Hari in his incarnation as the Fish, Śeṣa then obtained that very Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (sāṅga) right there;
he also properly acquired the Āyurveda contained within the Atharva Veda. 57.
Once, like a spy, he came to observe the state of the earth;
there he saw people seized by diseases, tormented by agony, distressed in many places, and even dying.
Seeing them, Ananta, filled with great compassion and pained by their suffering, reflected upon the means to alleviate their disease.
Having reflected, he himself became the son of that sage there.
Because he was renowned, pure, and a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas),
and because he arrived as if moving stealthily so that he was not recognized by anyone,
he became famous on the circle of the earth by the name Caraka.
That teacher of the Carakas shines like the preceptor of the gods in heaven;
he is a portion of the Thousand-faced One by whom the destruction of diseases was accomplished.
Agniveśa and others were the disciples of the sage Ātreya.
Many sages have each composed their own respective tantras. Having refined and compiled those tantras, the wise Caraka produced this work, named after himself as the *Caraka*.
Once, the gaze of the king of the gods fell upon the earth;
there he saw men who were severely afflicted by diseases. Seeing them, his heart was deeply pained with compassion.
With a heart moistened by compassion, Śakra said to Dhanvantari:
"O Dhanvantari, best of gods, O Blessed One, something is being said: you are worthy; be intent on the welfare of all beings."
For the benefit of the worlds, who has not performed what [was necessary] in the past?
Viṣṇu, the lord of the three worlds, assumed forms such as the fish and others.
Therefore, go to the earth and become a king in the midst of Kāśī.
"Reveal the Āyurveda for the remedy of diseases.
Having spoken thus, that tiger among gods, desiring the welfare of all beings, instructed Dhanvantari in the entire Veda of longevity.
In ancient times, having studied the Veda of Ayurveda from Indra and returned to the earth, Dhanvantari was born in Kāśī in the house of Bāhuja;
he became renowned on earth by the name Divodāsa.
Even as a child he became dispassionate and performed most intense austerities.
With great effort, Brahmā made him the king of Kāśī;
therefore, Dhanvantari is called "Kāśīrāja" by the worlds.

Then, for the welfare of embodied beings, he composed his own Saṃhitā; subsequently, he taught that Saṃhitā to people who were seekers of knowledge. Then, through the vision of wisdom, Viśvāmitra and others came to understand it.
"This is Dhanvantari; he is called Kāśirāja in Kāśī.
Among them, the sage Viśvāmitra said to his son Suśruta:
"O child, go to Vārāṇasī, which is beloved by Viśveśvara."
There, a king of Kāśī named Divodāsa, born of the Bāhu lineage, resides;
for he is Dhanvantari himself, the foremost among those who know the Āyurveda.
(78) You should study the Āyurveda for the sake of benefiting the world.
Compassion for all living beings is the sacred ford; doing good to others is the great sacrifice.
(79) Having heard his father’s words, Suśruta went to Kāśī; a hundred sons of sages went along with him to study together. (80)
Then, filled with humility, they all beheld the venerable Dhanvantari, the best of gods, who was established in the forest-dweller’s stage of life (vānaprastha), praised by many sages,
and who was Divodāsa, the king of Kāśī.
Then Divodāsa, whose wealth was his fame, said, "Welcome," and inquired after their welfare as well as the reason for their arrival;
thereupon, they gave their reply through the medium of Suśruta.
O Blessed One, seeing human beings tormented by diseases, crying out and dying, pain has arisen in our hearts.
We have come here to learn the means for the alleviation of these ailments. (84)
"May you diligently teach us the science of Ayurveda.
Having accepted their request, the king instructed them;
and those sages joyfully received what was explained by him with great effort.
Having greeted the King of Kāśī with blessings of victory, Suśruta and the others, filled with joy and having achieved their purpose, went each to his own home.
Among them, Suśruta first clearly composed an independent treatise.
Even the friends of Suśruta composed separate treatises; however,
because the treatise composed by Suśruta was [accepted] by many, it became renowned on the face of the earth by the name "Suśruta."
Thus ends the first section, the Chapter on the Manifestation of the Proponents of Āyurveda, in the Bhāvaprakāśa.
Now begins the second section, the Chapter on Creation, and the commencement of the work itself:

Having diligently extracted the jewels of yoga from the midst of the ocean of Āyurveda, the sages of supreme intellect have placed them in their respective compendia for the destruction of the diseases of all people.
With the jewels of well-spoken words gathered from various treatises and infused with his own insights, he composes this work to dispel the darkness of ignorance regarding the science of medicine.
By the grace of the feet of Śrīpati and through the blessings of the gods upon the earth,
may this work titled *Bhāvaprakāśana* be studied by all.
The Self is light, consisting of consciousness and bliss, eternal and free from desire;
though devoid of qualities, through union with Prakṛti it becomes possessed of qualities and creates the universe.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities of Prakṛti, which are originally in equilibrium.
Though she is insentient, she is the creator of the world due to her inseparable connection with the immutable consciousness of the Supreme Self;
she is called Pradhāna, Prakṛti, Śakti, Nityā, and Avikṛti— these are her names— and she rests upon the Puruṣa.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are to be known as the three qualities of prakṛti;
I shall describe all the qualities of the mind when it is joined with them:
faith, moderation in eating, freedom from remorse, and truthful speech.
Wisdom, intelligence, fortitude, patience, compassion, knowledge, sincerity,
blameless action, desirelessness, humility, and righteousness— these qualities are always praised by the wise as belonging to a mind endowed with the quality of *sattva*.
Anger, a habit of striking others, excessive suffering, a craving for pleasure, great deceit, lustfulness, falsehood, lack of composure, and egoism [are the marks of *tamas*].
Arrogance due to power, excessive joy, and constant wandering—

these are indeed the well-known qualities of the mind when it is associated with the quality of *rajas*. Furthermore, atheism, extreme despondency, excessive laziness, and a corrupt intellect [are its traits].
Delight in deeds that bring reproach, constant sleep day and night,
ignorance in every respect, and perpetual blindness through anger and delusion— these are indeed the well-known qualities of a mind possessed by the quality of darkness (tamas). 9.
In that regard, a person in whom the quality of *sattva* predominates is known as *sāttvika*; likewise, human beings are of three types—*rājasa* and *tāmasa*.
From that [unmanifest] arose the principle of *mahat*, which is also designated by the term *buddhi*.
The Great Principle (mahat), consisting of the three qualities and abounding in sattva, is stainless like crystal;
it is said to possess consciousness through the reflection of consciousness and to be composed of that [primordial] will.
From the three-guṇa Great Principle is born the ego (ahaṅkāra), which is likewise endowed with the three qualities.
It is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic.
From that [sattvic aspect] the sense organs were born, along with the rājasic;
they are the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and likewise the nose. 12–13.
Speech, hands, feet, the generative organ, and the anus, along with the mind as the eleventh—these they call the five organs of cognition (buddhīndriya) and the others [the remaining five].
The wise declare that there are exactly five organs of action (karmendriya). 14–15.

The wise have declared the mind to be both an organ of perception and an organ of action; indeed, it is only when presided over by the mind that this [group of] senses functions. Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell follow in their respective order.
The objects of the sense organs have been fully described by the great seers:

that which is to be spoken, that which is to be grasped, that which is to be gone toward, that which is to be experienced as pleasure, and that which is to be abandoned; these are the objects of the organs of action, while the heart is to be known as the object of the mind.

From the *tāmasa* ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) arise; from the *rājasa*, the five organs of action arise. Indeed, due to their connection with a small amount of *sattva*, they possess those respective characteristics. These are: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, and the subtle element of form.
The subtle element of taste and the subtle element of smell—these [along with sound, touch, and form] are the subtle elements (tanmātras).
From these subtle elements, in that same sequence, arise these five great elements (mahābhūtas): ether, air, fire, water, and the earth.
Sound, the faculty of hearing, and the cavities, as well as the distinctness of space— these are declared by those who investigate qualities and non-qualities to be the attributes of ether (ākāśa).
Touch, the faculty of touch, lightness, and the movement of the body [are the attributes of air].
The movement of the entire body is known as the qualities of wind (vāyu).
Form, the faculty of sight, digestion, heat, sharpness, as well as color, brilliance, impatience, and heroism—these are the qualities of fire (vahni). 23–24.

Taste, the sense of taste, coldness, unctuousness, heaviness, and the collection of all fluids—these are known as the qualities of water. Odor, the sense of smell, as well as hardness and weight [are the qualities of earth]. (25)
These qualities of the earth have been described by those who know its attributes.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are, in that order,
the specific manifestations of the subtle elements (tanmātras) once they have attained a gross state.
Because it is not possible for Prakṛti to be an effect, Prakṛti alone is considered that [cause];
the seven principles beginning with Mahat are traditionally known as modifications (vikṛti) of Śakti, since they are the causes of the sense organs and the elements, according to the great sages. 28.
The seven principles beginning with Mahat are also declared to be Prakṛtis.
The ten sense organs, the mind (citta), and the five great elements—these sixteen are known as the modifications (vikāras) by those who understand creation. 29–30.

Thus, when the house of the body has been established by means of the twenty-four principles (tattvas), the embodied soul (dehin)—subjected to the destiny of the individual self and accompanied by the messenger of its own mind—dwells therein;
he is described as such through his experiences of sin, merit, suffering, pleasure, and so forth. 31.
Pervaded and bound by the mind through artificial bonds of karma—
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the cognition of objects, effort, the mind, volition, deliberation, memory, as well as the intellect and the knowledge of arts.
The upward movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the downward propulsion of the wind through the anus,
and the exertion in performing the functions of opening and closing the eyes— these are the qualities of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Miśra Bhāva, son of the venerable Miśra Laṭakana.
The section on procreation is completed.
Now begins the third section, on the womb:
from the twelfth year onwards until the fiftieth year, women [are capable of conception].
Every month, the menstrual flow should naturally discharge through the birth canal. The period of sixteen nights following the day of the menstrual flow is known as the *ṛtu*;
that alone is considered the time suitable for conception.
From the day of the flow of menses, she shall observe non-violence and remain celibate;
she shall sleep on a bed of *darbha* grass and must not even look at her husband.
For three days, she should carry sacrificial food in her hand, in a shallow dish, or on a leaf.
Shedding tears, clipping the nails, oil massage, applying ointments,
collyrium for the eyes, bathing, sleeping during the day, running, listening to very loud sounds, laughing, and speaking excessively— [these should be avoided].
One should avoid physical exertion, digging the ground, and exposure to strong winds.
(5) Whether through ignorance, negligence, greed, or even by fate, if she should perform these forbidden acts, the embryo will then incur defects. (6)
From her weeping, the fetus will have deformed eyes (7).

From [her] cutting her nails, he will have diseased nails; from anointing [herself], he will be a leper; likewise, from applying ointments and bathing, he will be of a miserable disposition; and from collyrium, he will be blind (8).
One who is habituated to sleeping becomes restless by sleeping during the day;
from running about excessively, one indeed becomes deaf from hearing very loud sounds.
By laughing excessively, a dark discoloration occurs on the palate, teeth, lips, and tongue.
One becomes talkative from excessive speaking and insane from exhaustion;
one stumbles from digging the earth and becomes insane from exposure to the wind.
A woman who has bathed after her menses sees whatever kind of man she beholds first.

She shall give birth to such a son; thereafter, she will behold her husband as dear to her. Just as an object cast into flowing water sinks downwards, so too the semen, when cast into blood that is flowing, moves downwards.

Out of fear for the exhaustion of his own lifespan, a husband should avoid sexual union with his wife on the first day, and likewise on the second day, even when she is in her fertile period; furthermore,
any embryo conceived during those times does not survive once born.
He who was established [as a patient] on the third day, having a very short lifespan and impaired limbs—
therefore, on the fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth,
or even the twelfth night, one should attend to him according to the prescribed ritual.
In this regard, one should know that from approaching [the temple] in successive order, the results are longevity, health, progeny, good fortune, sovereignty, and strength (verse 16).
For women, there are three types of people among the womankind who stand at the entrance of the temple of the Mind-born One (Kāma).
I shall describe the specific characteristics of these: Samīraṇā, Candramasī, and Gaurī.
(17) Samīraṇā is the preeminent special channel on the parasol of Madana;
the Moon-crested Lord [Śiva] has declared that whatever semen falls into its opening shall be fruitless. (18)
Furthermore, the other channel, Cāndramasī, which resides in the house of Kandarpa, is preeminent;
that beautiful woman gives birth only to daughters, and she becomes suitable for festivals involving little sexual pleasure.
The channel called Gaurī, when it is naturally preeminent within the womb of the vulva, [produces sons].
That woman gives birth to a son, yet she is difficult to enjoy sexually when seated for lovemaking.
Sons are born from women on even nights, while daughters are born on odd nights.
[The husband should be] bathed, his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, and honored with fragrant flowers.
Having consumed aphrodisiacs, wearing fine garments, well-dressed, and fully adorned;
with his mouth flavored by betel-leaf, full of passion for her and with intense desire, a man seeking a son should approach the woman upon an auspicious bed.
One who has overeaten, one lacking self-control, one afflicted by hunger, one with aching limbs, one suffering from thirst,
a child, an elderly person, or one distressed by other morbid humors (doṣas) should abstain from sexual intercourse.
A moderate diet, endowed with the proper qualities, is prescribed for a man.

A woman desiring a son should unite with a man during her fertile period (ṛtu). However, she should not do so if she is menstruating, afflicted by disease— especially if she has a vaginal disorder— or if she is older than him, devoid of desire, unclean, or pregnant.
Indeed, from union with these women, defects arise in men. Through desire, in the conjunction of the couple, a fetus is produced in a woman from pure blood and semen; once born, it is called a child.
When offspring is born from a husband and wife who both suffer from an abundance of leprosy and whose blood and semen are corrupted, that child also should be known as leprous.
(28) During the union of man and woman in the fertile period, driven by the impulse of the god of love, [the embryo is conceived].
Due to the friction between the penis and the vulva, the semen residing throughout the man's entire body is liquefied by the bodily heat and wind; then,
the wind causes it to be discharged through the urinary passage into the female organ.
Having flowed there, it enters the opened mouth toward the womb;
there, it becomes united with the menstrual blood that has arrived like semen.
The womb is shaped like the whorl of a conch shell, and it is described as having three spirals.
In its third whorl, however, the bed of the embryo is established.
Just as the mouth of a rohita fish appears in form, so do the wise know the bed of the embryo to be shaped accordingly.
Indeed, at the very moment that the union of semen and ovum occurs, the *jīva* enters, joined within the semen and ovum;
just as [light] arises from the union of both the sun’s rays and the sun-gem. 34.
Just as fire is produced from [the friction of] wood, so too is the living being (jīva) born from semen, menstrual blood, and other factors.
This Self (ātman) is beginningless, endless, and unmanifest; it cannot be described, for its singular nature is consciousness and bliss, and it is not accessible even to the mind.
Even though he is thus [liberated], because ignorance has taken hold through the power of destiny, he enters the womb under the influence of karma (37).
He alone is the knower, the taster, the seer, the smeller, and he is the one who touches.
The listener, the speaker, the doer, the goer, and even the one who gives pleasure—
just as the lotus inevitably closes when the day has passed, so too does a woman's womb contract when her season has passed. (38–39)

When the seed is split by the internal wind, two living beings enter the womb; they are called twins, preceded by dharma and its opposite (adharma). If the semen is in excess, there is a son; if the menstrual blood is in excess, there is a daughter.
If there is an equality of the two, it is a neuter; as is the will of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvarī).
Having thus united with her, he should again enjoy her after a month.
Then, from the womb, there is an outflow of semen and blood, arising from exhaustion.
There will be weakness in the thighs, thirst, exhaustion, and a throbbing sensation in the vulva (42).
There will be blackness of the nipples and the appearance of hairlines on the breasts; furthermore, her eyelashes will especially tend to close together (43).

Vomiting even after eating wholesome food, revulsion toward pleasant fragrances, excessive salivation, and a sense of exhaustion are said to be the symptoms of a pregnant woman in her second month. 44. These signs occur in a woman carrying a male fetus during the second month.
The embryo is observable in the womb as a mass-like form; hear further [signs]:
there will be heaviness in the right eye, milk first in the right breast, the right thigh will be well-nourished, and the complexion of the face will be serene. (45–46)
One’s desire for substances with auspicious names is fulfilled even in dreams;
one obtains mangoes and other fruits in dreams, as well as lotuses and the like. A girl becomes pregnant, and in the second month, there is a *peśī* (a fleshy mass) within the womb.
One observes signs that are the opposite of those for a male fetus (48).
When a neuter being is in the womb, the fetus has the appearance of water;
both sides of the abdomen are elevated, and the belly is large in the front (49).
The *āsekya*, the *sugandhī*, the *kumbhīka*, and likewise the *iṣyarya*—these should be understood as possessing semen; the one designated as *ṣaṇḍha* is without semen.
Due to the paucity of virility in both parents, a man becomes an *āsekya*.
Having consumed semen, he undoubtedly attains the elevation of the banner (virility).
He who would be born from a putrid womb indeed becomes fragrant; having smelled the scent of the womb and the phallus, he gains strength. 51–52.
He who, out of a lack of celibacy, behaves toward women like a man toward his own anus, should be known as a *kumbhīpa*; he is remembered as one born from the anus.
He who, having seen the sexual union of others, engages in sexual union [with them]... [53]
He should be known as envious, and he is remembered as having a "view-born" origin.

He who, out of delusion, engages with his wife during her fertile period as if she were a woman, there arises a form characterized by feminine behavior; such a one is designated as a *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuch). 54–55.

If a woman should engage in intercourse during every season like a man, and if a daughter should be born there, she would possess the conduct of a man. When two women, desiring sexual union
When two people emit semen into one another without bones [i.e., without sexual union], no offspring is born there.
However, when a woman who has bathed after her menses engages in sexual intercourse even in a dream, the wind takes up her menstrual blood and produces a fetus in the womb. 57–58.
Month by month that embryo, characterized by the signs of gestation, increases;
the *kalala* is produced for it, devoid of paternal qualities.

(59) Those who are deformed, having the shapes of snakes, scorpions, or pumpkins— Please note: The provided text fragment appears to be part of a larger work discussing embryology and the nature of certain beings. Those women whose fetuses are lost should be known as great evildoers.
Due to the provocation of wind (vāta) or when pregnancy longings (dohada) are disregarded,
the fetus may become humpbacked, clawed, lame, mute, or even indistinctly speaking.

With whatever kinds of food, conduct, and activities the woman and man are endowed when they unite, their son will also be like that. The semen and the menstrual blood situated in the womb are known as "jīva" (the living soul).

Nature (prakṛti) along with its modifications— all that is designated as the embryo (garbha). When the embryo, having been developed by time, becomes endowed with major and minor limbs, it is then called "the embodied one" (śarīrin) by the sages.
Having understood its primary and secondary limbs from the Suśruta Śāstra, they are now described starting from the head; O disciples, listen with diligence.
The first limb is said to be the head, and its secondary limbs are the locks of hair.
Within it are the brain, the forehead, and the pair of eyebrows (66).
There are two eyes, and between them are the two pupils;
there are the two black globes [the eyeballs], the two white parts, and the two eyelids (67).
The eyelashes, the outer corners of the eyes, the temples, the two ears, the two earlobes, the two ridges, the cheeks, and the nose are thus proclaimed;
as are the upper and lower lips, the corners of the mouth, the mouth, the palate, and the two jaws. 68.
The teeth, the gums, the tongue, and the chin constitute the second limb;
the neck, by which the head is supported, is the third; and now I shall describe the pair of arms as its secondary limbs (upāṅgas). 69–70.
There, above the wrists are the two upper arms (skandhas), below which are the two forearms (pragaṇḍas);
below those are the two lower forearms (prakoṣṭhas), as well as the two wrists (maṇibandhas) and the palms (talas). And in those [palms] are ten fingers. 71.
The ten nails are to be established; they are proclaimed as the ten "to-be-cut" (daśacchedya).
The fourth limb is the chest; now I shall describe its secondary parts (upāṅgas): the breasts for both man and woman, though there is this distinction between the two. 72–73.
Upon the arrival of youth, a woman's breasts become full;
when she is pregnant and has given birth, those very same breasts become filled with milk. The heart, resembling a lotus, is turned downward.
It expands while one is awake and closes when one sleeps.
That *āśaya* is the supreme seat of consciousness for the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, indeed, when it is pervaded by darkness, living beings fall into sleep. (75–76)

The junctions of the two armpits with the chest are designated as the clavicles (*jatru*); both armpits are well-known, and their lower parts are the groins (*vaṅkṣaṇa*). The abdomen is considered the fifth limb, and the two sides (*pārśva*) are regarded as the sixth.
The entire back, including the spinal column, is recorded as the seventh [limb].
Now the secondary limbs (upāṅgas) are being described; learn them with diligence.
The spleen is born from the blood, located to the left and below the heart.
The great sages have declared that it (the liver) is the root of the blood-carrying vessels;
the lungs, born from the froth of the blood, are situated below and to the left of the heart,
while the liver is situated below and to the right of the heart.

That [organ], located below and to the right of the heart, is considered to be born from blood; it is the seat of the coloring bile (rañjaka-pitta) and is known as the kloman, which is rooted in the water-carrying vessels and is considered to cause the suppression of thirst. 81–82.
From the essence of the fat and blood, the pair of kidneys arises;
these two are said to nourish the fat situated within the abdomen. One should specify that the intestines of women are less by half a vyāma [than those of men]. 83.
The wise have stated that the three and a half *vyāmas* [of the body] consist of the male organs;
the *unduka*, the waist, the sacrum (*trika*), the bladder, and the two groins are the site of origin for the tendons (*kaṇḍarāḥ*), while the penis is the passage for semen and urine. (84–85)

That very [organ] effects the implantation of the embryo within the womb of the woman; the vagina is shaped like the navel of a conch shell and is described as having three folds (*triyāvartā*). In its third fold, however, the bed of the embryo is established.
The two testicles are the essence of phlegm, blood, muscle, and fat;
they are considered the repositories of the channels carrying semen and are the bringers of virility.
The measurement of the entire anus is four and a half finger-breadths. 87–88.
Therein, there should be three coils resembling the whorls of a conch shell;
the first is considered to be the *pravāhiṇī*, measuring one and a half finger-breadths (89).
Below that is the *utsarjanī*, which is likewise measured at one and a half finger-breadths.
Below that, the covering is considered to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) thick;
the opening of the anus is held by the wise to be half a finger-breadth in measure.
This anus is fashioned in the body as the path for the evacuation of waste.
The two nostrils of a man are known as the *protha*, while those of a woman are the *nitamba*.
Between these two, at the junction of the thighs, are the *kukundara* cavities; this is the eighth minor limb (*aṅga*).
We shall now describe its subsidiary parts (*upāṅga*): the two knees and the two calf-muscles (*piṇḍaka*).
The two calves, the two knees, the two heels, the two soles, and likewise the two foreparts of the feet; there are ten toes on the feet, and ten nails for them.
Now the defects (doṣas) will be explained, and immediately after that the constituent elements (dhātus). 93–94.

The course of food and other substances, as well as their transformation, will be described; likewise the menstrual flow, the tissues (dhātus), their impurities, the secondary humors (upadhātus), the receptacles (āśayas), the anatomical parts (kalās), the vital points (marmas), and the joints (sandhis). 95.

The veins, the ligaments, the arteries, and likewise the tendons; the numerous apertures, the channels, the networks, the tufts, and the cords; the sutures, the unions, the boundaries, and likewise the layers of skin. 96–97.
The body is considered to consist of these: the body hairs and the hair follicles.
Briefly stated, there are three humors (doṣas): wind (vāyu), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha).
When they are either disordered or in their natural state, they respectively destroy or nourish the body. 98.

Although these [vātas] are all-pervasive, they reside respectively in the heart, the navel, and below it; in the middle, and above; and they occupy the end, the middle, and the beginning of the three stages of life, the day and night, and the food consumed.
Because of this, the dhātus and the malas become vitiated by them.
These three—wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha)—are known as the humors (doṣas). They are also called "elements" (dhātus) by the wise because they sustain the body.
Wind is the swift conductor of the humors, elements, waste products, and so forth.
Consisting of the quality of rajas, it is subtle, dry, cold, light,
and mobile; [it is known] by its instigation of enthusiasm, exhalation, inhalation, physical exertion,
and forceful impulses, as well as by the proper movement of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and the sharpness of the sense organs.
Unmodified, it favors [the self] as the sustainer of the heart, senses, and mind.
104 Consisting of the quality of *rajas*, it is subtle, cold, dry, light, mobile, rough, soft, and pervasive; through its conjunction [with other qualities], it effects both purposes. 105
Fire, conjoined with heat, produces digestion; it produces coldness by relying on the moon; and wind is predominant in the collection of the *doṣas* due to its power of division.
[The seats of these are] the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), the waist, the thighs, the ears, the bones, and the sense organ of touch. 106.
The location of vāta is there as well, specifically in the receptacle of digested food (pakvādhāna).
Udāna, prāṇa, samāna, apāna, and vyāna—these are the names of vāyu according to the distinction of its locations. 107–108.

This wind, the best of breaths known as udāna, which moves upward, dwells successively in the throat, the heart, below that in the stomach and the fire, and in the entire body within the receptacle of waste. 109.
Through that [vitality], there occurs the activity of speech, song, and so forth; however, when it is provoked, it specifically produces diseases located above the clavicle.
That wind named *prāṇa*, which sustains the body, moves through the mouth.
It causes food to enter within and also supports the vital breaths (prāṇas);
yet when vitiated, it generally produces diseases such as hiccup and dyspnea.
The Samāna [vāyu], moving through the stomach and the large intestine, is associated with the digestive fire.
It indeed digests food and differentiates its various constituents.

This apāna wind, residing in the colon (pakvāśaya), causes disorders such as malabsorption, weak digestion, and abdominal tumors; furthermore, it draws [the contents] out at the proper time. (113–114)
When the *samīraṇa* (vāyu) is aggravated, it carries downward the feces, urine, semen, fetus, and menstrual blood, and produces terrible diseases localized in the bladder and the rectum,
as well as disorders of the semen and urinary disorders (*prameha*) arising from the provocation of *vyāna* and *apāna*.
The Vyāna wind, moving throughout the entire body, is intent upon circulating the nutritional essence (rasa);
it also causes the flow of sweat and blood, and performs five types of actions:
vibration, upward transport, filling, and evacuation.
Retention—these five activities of the wind (prāṇa) have been declared:
movement, contraction, upward lifting, closing the eyes, and opening the eyes;
indeed, almost all the actions of embodied beings are dependent upon it. 118
When provoked, it generally produces diseases that pervade the entire body;
if all three are simultaneously aggravated, they would undoubtedly shatter the body.
Bile (pitta) is hot, liquid, yellowish-green, and preponderant in the quality of sattva.
Pitta is liquid, pungent, light, unctuous, and sharp; it is sour upon digestion (pāka).
Furthermore, according to its different locations, the names of pitta are: pācaka, rañjaka, sādhaka, ālocaka, and bhrājaka. (120–121)
Pitta resides sequentially in the receptacle of fire (the stomach), in the liver and spleen, in the heart, in the two eyes, in the skin, and throughout the entire body.
Pācaka-pitta digests what has been eaten and increases the strength of the remaining digestive fires. 122.
It constantly purges the chyle, urine, and feces (verse 123).
Enough of this consideration of what is not relevant; let us return once more to the subject at hand:
that pitta known as *rañjaka* carries the chyle into the blood.
That which is known as *sādhaka* produces intelligence, fortitude, and memory;
that which is known as *ālocaka* is the cause for perceiving forms;
*bhrājaka* bestows luster and digests ointments, massages, and the like. (124–125)
Phlegm (śleṣman) is white, heavy, unctuous, slimy, and likewise cold;
it is characterized by a predominance of the quality of darkness (tamas), is sweet, and when transformed, becomes salty.
These are the names of phlegm: it is the moistener and the supporter.
Due to its location, phlegm (śleṣman) is respectively liquefying, lubricating, and adhesive;
it resides in these locations of human beings in succession: in the stomach, the heart, the throat, the head, and the joints. (127–128)
Furthermore, the supporting [tongue] maintains the threefold [union];
therefore, both remain gentle and close together, so that the tongue and the sense of taste, being equal, perceive the flavors. (130–131)
Through the application of oil, it provides lubrication, satisfies all the sense organs,
and acts as an adhesive, effecting the binding together of all the joints;
since these seven, by abiding within themselves, sustain the bodies of men.
Chyle, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the tissues (dhātus).
Nourishment, vitalization, lubrication, unctuousness, maintenance, filling, and the production of the embryo are indeed declared to be the functions of the tissues. 133–134.
The verbal root *ras* has the meaning of "to move"; therefore, this [fluid] is called *rasa*.
It is known as *rasa* because it flows (*rasati*) through the entire body along with the blood.
That which is the essence of food that has been properly digested is declared to be *rasa*.
That rasa, however, is mobile, white, cold, sweet, unctuous, and light.
Although it pervades the entire body, the heart is the site of rasa,
because it was first held in the heart by the equalizing wind (samāna-vāyu).
Having ascended and traveled through the channels (dhamanīs), this essence (rasa) nourishes all the bodily constituents (dhātus); subsequently, it pervades the body with its own qualities.
However, if the digestive fire (vahni) is weak, that rasa becomes pungent or sour.
It produces many diseases and even acts as a poison.
When the *rasa* reaches the liver (*yakṛt*), it undergoes coloring and digestion there through the agency of *rañjaka-pitta*, and thus it becomes known as blood (*rakta*). 138–139.

Blood, which resides throughout the entire body, is the supreme support of the life-force (*jīva*); it is unctuous, heavy, mobile, and sweet, and when vitiated, it becomes like *pitta*. The liver (*yakṛt*) and spleen (*plīhā*) are the primary seats of blood, wherein it is located.
For those who are attached and established elsewhere, it becomes a nourisher.
Blood, cooked by its own fire and thickened by the wind, one should know that very thing to be flesh; I shall now describe its various classifications. 141–142.
Just as wind, joined with heat, tears open the channels and,
having entered the flesh, divides it into muscle-fibers (peśīs), so too are there indeed five hundred muscle-fibers declared to exist in men. 143–144.

Four hundred of them are said to be in the branches; furthermore, sixty-six are said by the best of sages to be in the trunk; and those extending upward from the neck are proclaimed to be thirty-four. (145)
These same [muscles] exist in women as well, but they number twenty more:
in the uterus, the birth canal, the vagina, and also in the breasts.
As for the muscles of men that were previously mentioned as being located in the penis and the scrotum—

For women, they remain concealed; indeed, they possess the fruit within. (147) For embodied beings, the vessels, sinews, bones, joints, and articulations become strong only when enveloped by muscles. (148)
That flesh which is cooked by its own internal heat is called fat (*medas*);
it is extremely heavy, unctuous, strengthening, and highly nourishing.
Indeed, fat is situated within the bones in the bellies of all living beings. (149)
For this very reason, an enlargement of the abdomen generally occurs in those who are obese (150).
That fat which is digested by its own internal fire and excessively dried up by the wind (151) attains the designation of "bone"; it is the essential core (sāra) within the entire body.
Just as trees stand firm because of the pith located within,
so too are the bodies of embodied beings certainly sustained by the pith of bone;
therefore, even when the skin and flesh of living beings have long since perished, [the body remains].
Bones do not perish; these are their essential constituents in every respect.
(153) In the science of surgery (*śalyatantra*), three hundred fragments of bone have been described. (154) Those very bones are now being enumerated here, along with their locations.
The wise have stated that there are one hundred and twenty bones in the limbs;
a physician should know that among those in the two sides, the pelvic plates, the chest, the back, and the abdomen, there are one hundred and seventeen.
One should know that there are sixty-three bones extending upward from the neck;
these bones are of five types, which are as follows:
they are indeed the cartilages (taruṇa), the cranial plates (kapāla), and the sockets (rucaka).
These may be called *valaya* (wrinkles), and some are called *nalaka* (folds);
they occur on the eye-sockets, the ears, the nose, the neck, and in the young [parts], as well as on the head, the temples, the cheeks, the palate, the lips, and the knees. (157–158)
From these teeth, skull-cups (kapāla) and bracelets (rucaka) are formed;
on the two heels, the pair of sides, the back, the breasts, the belly, the anus, and the feet, there are bangles (valaya). Now I shall describe the anklets (nalaka). 159–160.

One should know that there are also nalakas in the hands, on the soles of the feet, in the hair of the body, at the wrists, and likewise in both the arms and the shanks; these are masses of flesh, entrails, and sinews bound together by veins. 161.
Taking the bones as their support, they neither break nor fall.
That which is cooked by its own internal fire is the bone; its solid essence becomes dense, and that which separates like sweat is called marrow. 162–163.
Marrow is specifically situated within the large bones (164).
From the nutrient essence comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat is produced; from fat, bone; from that, marrow; and from marrow, the production of semen occurs (165).
Impelled by the prāṇa-vāyu, food first goes to the āmāśaya;
though it possesses six tastes, it attains sweetness and a frothy state.
That which is proclaimed as the sixth constituent (kalā) is named pittadhara.
That which is situated between the stomach (āmāśaya) and the large intestine (pakvāśaya) is called the *grahaṇī*.

In that *grahaṇī*, food is digested by the fire known as *pācaka-pitta* (the digestive bile), which is located between the stomach and the large intestine; it becomes pungent (*kaṭu*). Thus it is said: "In the *grahaṇī*, within the abdominal cavity, food is cooked by the fire and becomes pungent."
The five heats—those of earth, water, fire, wind, and space—successively digest their respective qualities of food, such as the earthly and so forth, within the body composed of the five elements;
for food itself consists of the five elements. (169)
When fully digested, it correctly increases its own fivefold qualities. (170) A sweet taste is digested as sweet, while a sour taste is digested as sour;
the post-digestive effect (*vipāka*) of pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes is pungent. (171)
The essence of food is its *rasa* (nutritive fluid); that which is devoid of essence is the liquid waste (*maladrava*).
Carried by the vessels (*śirā*) to the bladder (*vasti*), that water attains the state of urine (*mūtra*).
Whatever remains of it as dregs (*kiṭṭa*) is called feces (*purīṣa*).
Carried by the samāna wind, it remains in the receptacle of waste (malāśaya). Then, urine is expelled through the urinary passage and feces through the anal passage,
cast out from the body by the apāna wind.
The rasa, impelled by the samāna vāyu, reaches the heart;
then, distributed by the vyāna vāyu, it nourishes all the bodily constituents (dhātus),
just as irrigation channels nourish various medicinal herbs in fields.
In the same way, the nutrient essence (*rasa*) increases all the constituent elements (*dhātu*) within the body.

That essence is threefold in each instance—gross, subtle, and its waste; the gross portion nourishes its own [subsequent] element, while the subtle portion becomes the waste, which in turn nourishes the waste of that [subsequent] element. (176–177)

Within each of the elements, beginning with *rasa* and ending with marrow, the *rasa* itself remains for five and a half *daṇḍas* during the course of a day and night. (178) This occurs as the elements, starting from *rasa* and ending with marrow, are being cooked by their respective internal fires.
The sages have declared that impurities arise within the six elements (dhātus).

Just as there is indeed no impurity in gold when it has been smelted a thousand times, so too there is no impurity in the vital essence (rasa) once it has been repeatedly cooked and reached the state of semen (śukra). 179–180.
Ojas, residing throughout the entire body, is considered to be unctuous, cold, stable, white, and of the nature of Soma; it provides strength and nourishment to the body.
It is likewise heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, dense, sweet, and stable.
It is known to possess ten qualities: it is clear, slimy, subtle, and vital energy (ojas).
Measuring eight drops in size, it is slightly red and yellow;
indeed, it is described as having two forms by virtue of its nature as both Agni and Soma. 182–183.
Ojas is considered the supreme essence of the elements ending with semen;
though situated in the heart, it is pervasive and the basis for the maintenance of the body.
Upon its increase, there arise satisfaction, nourishment, and the emergence of strength in the body. (184)
Upon the destruction of which destruction is certain, and in which life resides;
from which various states dependent on the body are produced—such as enthusiasm, genius, fortitude, grace, and delicacy. (185–186)
Then, after one month, the thickened portion of the *rasa* becomes semen (*śukra*) in men, while in women it becomes the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) and semen;
as it is stated in the Suśruta:
"In this way, after one month, the *rasa* becomes semen in men and the menstrual flow in women"—by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that women also possess semen.
For this very reason it is stated in the Suśruta:
"In women also, semen indeed flows during union with a man."
In that regard, it is not considered that [the medicine] does nothing at all for the embryo;
rather, it is universally agreed that the menstrual blood (*ārtava*) is necessary for women’s conception, and indeed, it strengthens their strength, complexion, semen, and nourishment. (187–188)
From the nutrient essence (rasa) comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat is produced; from fat, bone; from that, marrow; and from marrow arises semen.
Within the body, the nutrient essence flows in three ways, like sound, light, and a stream of water.

For this [sexual impulse] indeed always moves in accordance with the embodied beings (190). Erection-promoting herbs, by the excellence of their own inherent power and qualities, cause the semen of men to flow out, just like purgative substances (191).

Milk, black gram, the marrow of the marking-nut (bhallātaka) fruit, and impurities are declared to be the causes for the evacuation of semen. (192) Semen exists even in children, but it is not perceived due to its subtlety.
Just as the fragrance of flowers, though present, is not perceived while they are in bud (193),
that very same fragrance indeed attains manifestation in their youth due to fullness; for when flowers are in full bloom, their scent becomes manifest (194).
The line of body hair and other such features arise in men, and they also appear in women during youth; furthermore, the distinction between them should be understood from the detailed exposition.
In old age, due to the drying up of the vital essence (rasa) by the increasing wind (vāyu), [these signs disappear].
The increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus) does not occur in that manner; therefore, one should conquer the wind (vāyu) therein.
Semen is known to be lunar, white, unctuous, and a producer of strength and nourishment;
it is the seed of the embryo, the essence of the body, and the supreme refuge of the living soul.
The living soul (jīva) dwells within the entire body, yet especially in that [semen] which resides in the semen, blood, and waste;
when it is depleted, [the body] perishes in an instant.
It is crystal-like in appearance, liquid, unctuous, sweet, and has the fragrance of honey.
Some, however, desire semen, which resembles oil or honey;
for just as butter is hidden in milk and just as the juice is latent in sugarcane,
so indeed does semen reside within the entire body of embodied beings.
In men, semen is discharged through the urinary tract at a point two finger-breadths below the opening of the bladder on the right side;
likewise, the semen situated throughout the entire body flows forth when the mind is serene. (201)
And for one striving after women, that semen is discharged out of passion;
through desire for a lovely woman, it flows forth from seeing her, from touching her, from hearing her voice, or even from the mere thought of union. (202–203)
From *rasa* alone, the *rajas* of women flows for three days every month;
after the twelfth year, it reaches its cessation by the age of fifty.
That *ārtava*, accumulated over a month, [is discharged] from the vessels at the proper time.
The wind may lead [the blood] to the opening of the womb as slightly discolored or black;
that which resembles rabbit's blood or is like the juice of lac—such menstrual blood they praise, provided it does not stain the cloth. (205–206)
In blood, the qualities of fire predominate; in flesh, those of earth;
in fat, those of water and earth; in bone, those of earth, air, and fire; in marrow and semen, those of the moon (Soma); and in urine, the qualities of fire.
Likewise, O Agni, for the purpose of consumption, the impurities of the earth are phlegm; those of water are bile, excrement in the channels, sweat, nails, and hair;
and the impurities of the bodily constituents (dhātus) are, in order, oiliness in the eyes, feces, and unctuousness in the skin. (208–209)

In women who have given birth, milk arises from the very essence that has reached the breasts via the two vessels; it is produced within the pair of breasts. That which is the oily essence of pure flesh is designated as *vasā* (fat).
The fat of the body being heated becomes either oil or boiled muscle-fat (vasā). Breast milk,
menstrual blood, muscle-fat, sweat, teeth, hair,
and likewise vital essence (ojas)— these are the seven secondary constituents (upadhātu) corresponding respectively to the seven primary constituents (dhātu).
Below the seat of blood (the heart) is known to be the seat of phlegm (kapha), and below that is the seat of undigested food (āmāśaya); Caraka has stated its characteristic signs.
That membrane which lies below the seat of undigested food and above the seat of digested food (pakvāśaya) is [the seat of bile].
That very organ is called the grahaṇī and is described as the seat of digestion (pācakāśaya).
The seat of fire (agnyāśaya) is situated above the navel in its middle portion; one should know that the seat of bile (tila) is above it, and below that is the seat of wind (pavanāśaya). 214–215.

Below that is the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), which is indeed the receptacle of waste (malāśaya). Below that is said to be the bladder (vasti); for it is considered the receptacle of urine.
These are the receptacles of phlegm, undigested matter, bile, and wind, as well as of waste and urine.
In addition to those [organs] common to men, women have three other receptacles (āśayas).
The earth element is said to be the uterus (garbhāśaya), located between the receptacle of bile (pittāśaya) and the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya).
Those same two [elements], when they have increased as breasts, are considered by the wise to be the receptacles of breast milk (stanyāśayas). 217–218.

Those parts which are covered with sinews, pervaded by the fetal membrane (jarāyu), and enveloped by phlegm (śleṣman) are known as the kalās. Furthermore, that moisture of the constituent element (dhātu) which resides within the cavities of the bodily tissues (dhātv-āśaya) [is also known as a kalā]. 219.
And that which is cooked by the heat of the body is called *kalā*.
The first is said to be the sustainer of flesh, the second the sustainer of blood, the third the sustainer of fat, and the fourth the sustainer of phlegm. 220–221.
The fifth, however, bears impurity; the sixth is considered the bearer of bile;
the seventh should be the bearer of semen—thus are the seven *kalās* remembered.
The *sannipāta* (conjunction) arises from the channels (*śirā*), sinews (*snāyu*), joints (*sandhi*), flesh (*māṃsa*), and bones (*asthi*).
The vital points (marmas) reside within them, and the life-breaths (prāṇas) especially so. There are one hundred and seven vital points in the bodies of embodied beings;
eleven of these are located in the flesh, and eight indeed exist in the bones.
There are twenty joints; twenty-seven of these belong to the sinews.
Furthermore, there are forty-one vital points (marmans) among the vessels (śirās);
of these, twenty-two are in the pair of legs and an equal number in the pair of arms.
There are twelve vital points (marmas) on the chest and the abdomen, fourteen in the region of the back,
and thirty-seven are indeed considered to be in the neck and its upper portion; these marmas here are further classified into five types.
There are nineteen vital points (*marmas*) that take life instantly;
thirty-three vital regions cause death after a lapse of time;
and forty-four indeed produce deformity. (228)
The eight vital points (marmas) are considered to cause pain when injured, while the triad [of marmas] destroys the arrow-head (viśalyaghna).
The śṛṅgāṭakas, the adhipati, the two temples (śaṅkhas), the vessels of the throat, the anus, the heart, the bladder, and the navel— if these are struck, they kill instantly.
The vital points (marmas) of the chest, the sīmantas, the talas, the kṣipras, the indravastis, the two vṛhatīs at the joints of the sides, the two kaṭīkataruṇas,
and the two nitambas— these, however, are fatal after a period of time. 231.
The two red eyes, the two knees, the two thighs, the two heels, the two shoulders, the two elbows, the two hollows of the loins, the two armpits, the two temples, the two shoulder-blades,
the two corners of the eyes, the two dark-blue regions of the neck, the two collarbones, and likewise the two nape-of-the-neck muscles.
They say that the two *āvartas* likewise cause impairment;
a wise person should know that these eight—the two ankles, the two wrists, and the tendons of the heels—are the causes of pain. (233–234)
The two types of *utkṣepa*, *sthapanī*, and *viśalyaghna* are considered the three [types of] *trikarma*.
Indeed, those that kill instantly destroy life within seven nights;
those that kill after a lapse of time destroy life within a fortnight or a month. 235–236.

A wound inflicted at the end [of life] that takes away life immediately may kill by means of time; however, one that takes away life after an interval causes suffering at the end. Indeed, those various disorders that arise in the bodies of men, having taken hold of the vital points (*marmas*), become intensified. (237)
Generally, these [injuries] become most difficult to treat, even when managed by a physician with great effort.
(238) Now, as for the joints:
they are of two kinds, mobile and fixed.
Indeed, those in the branches [of the body], the jaws, and the hips are mobile;
all the remaining joints are declared by the experts to be fixed. Thus, two hundred and ten joints have been described in the bodies of embodied beings.
Sixty-eight [joints] are in the limbs (śākhās), while fifty-nine are in the trunk (koṣṭha).
Eighty-three are proclaimed to be in the region above the neck; among these, those located in the limbs are first enumerated here. 240–241.

The *korodūkhalasāmudga*, *pratara*, *tūṇasevanī*, *kākatuṇḍa*, *maṇḍala*, and *śaṅkhāvarta* are the eight types of bone joints (*sandhi*). These alone are declared to be the joints of the bones. (242)
There is no definite count for the joints of the muscles, ligaments, and vessels (243).
These vessels, which form the connections of the joints and carry the humors and tissues, are all attached at the navel and extend outwards in every direction (244).
This entire body is constantly nourished by its veins,
just as gardens are by canals or the crops in fields by irrigation channels (245).
Through activities such as extending and contracting, [the body] is perpetually [sustained] within the physical frame.
The vessels indeed provide assistance; they number seven hundred.
Just as veins are clearly seen spreading across the leaf of a tree, even so do the vessels exist throughout the entire body of a living being.
The vital breaths of living beings are situated in the navel, and the navel is supported by the vital breaths;
the navel is covered by the channels (nāḍīs) like the hub of a wheel by its spokes.
It is free from obstruction in its activities and free from delusion in its functions of cognition and action.
Moving through its own channels, the wind also produces other qualities.
But when the wind becomes aggravated and enters its own channels,
then various diseases arising from wind (vāta) are born in him.
Moving through its own vessels, pitta produces brilliance, a relish for food, digestive heat, freedom from disease, and other qualities as well;
however, when pitta becomes aggravated, it courses through its own carrying channels.

Then various diseases arising from pitta are produced in him. (252) However, phlegm (valāsa), circulating through its own channels, produces unctuousness in the limbs, stability of the joints, strength, health, and other qualities as well. (253)
But when the provoked phlegm enters its own channels, then various diseases arising from phlegm are produced in him;
[it also causes] the filling of the bodily constituents and the certain perception of color and touch. (254)
The blood circulating within one’s own vessels produces other qualities as well.
When, however, the provoked blood courses through its own carrying channels, then various diseases arising from blood are born in that person. (255–256)
In that regard, the vessels carrying wind (vāta) become reddish and are filled with air;
those from bile (pitta) are hot and blue; those from phlegm (kapha) are white, firm, and cold; and those carrying blood (asṛgdharā) are red and neither excessively hot nor cold. (257)
Taking the oiliness from the fat, it attains the state of vessels and sinews;
for the maturation of the vessels is soft, whereas that of the sinews is rough. The sinews serve as the bonds for the body’s flesh, bones, and fat.
The joints are known to be even more firmly fixed than the veins; just as a boat, when covered with planks and joined by many bindings,
becomes capable of carrying a heavy load when placed upon deep water.
In this very same way, however many joints are recorded in this body, bound together by numerous tendons, by that means men are able to bear weight. Nine hundred tendons arise in the bodies of men.
We shall provide an exposition of these; listen with diligence, O disciples!
(262) There are six hundred [ligaments] in the branches, two hundred and thirty in the trunk, and seventy ligaments are recorded in the region above the neck. (263)
The vessels (dhamanīs) arise from the navel, numbering twenty-four;
ten go upward, ten go downward, and the remaining are known to move transversely,
according to their natural disposition, like the channels within lotus stalks and reeds.

Likewise, there are the channels of the arteries through which the vital essence (rasa) circulates on all sides. Then, the five elements, being overcome five times over, nourish the five sense organs within the five [elements];
having nourished the five sense organs within the five, they return to the state of the five at the time of destruction.
The large sinews are called *kaṇḍarās*, and they are sixteen in number;
their function is observed to be extension and contraction.
Four of these are in the hands, and an equal number are recorded to be in the feet. (267)
In the neck as well, there are that many [vertebrae] joined to the back. 268.
Two apertures each are proclaimed for the eyes, ears, and nostrils; one aperture each is said for the mouth, the urethra, and the anus. 269.
The tenth is said to be at the head; men know these as the "apertures" (randhras), while for women there are three others: in the breasts and in the path of the womb.
[These are] the mind, the vital breaths, food, drink, the humors (doṣas), the primary constituents (dhātus), and the secondary constituents (upadhātus). 270.

The impurities of the bodily constituents, such as urine and other excretions, circulate through the body by means of certain paths; these are known as the channels (*srotas*). They are so numerous that they cannot possibly be enumerated or described in their entirety.
Indeed, networks (jālāni) arise from the veins, ligaments, flesh, and bones;
there are four of each, making sixteen in total.
There are two "brushes" (kūrcas) in the hands and likewise two in the feet.
One is at the neck, and one is at the penis; thus all six are recorded.
On both sides of the spinal column there are large muscular cords (māṃsarajju), whose purpose is the binding of the muscle masses (māṃsapeśī). 274–275.
There are seven suture-joints; of these, five are in the head, one in the penis, and one in the tongue—one should never pierce them.
There are fourteen clusters of bones; three of these are at the ankles, the knees, and the groins.
By this, the other two thighs and two arms are also explained; there is one each for the sacrum and the head.
Thus, exactly fourteen sīmanta-s have been described by the best of sages;
they are proclaimed as "sīmanta-s" because the joints (saṅghāta-s) are sewn together (sīvitā) by them.
Just as a film forms on milk being boiled, so too, as the *śukra* and *rajas* are being processed, the first layer of skin appears; that is known as the site of *sidhma*. (279)

The second is to be known as red, the place of origin for *tilaka* and *alaka*. The third would be white; it is the location of *carmadala*. The fourth is to be understood as copper-colored, the ground for *kilāsa* and *śvitra*.

The fifth, known by the name Vedinī, is five parts in measurement and should be known as the seat of visarpa (erysipelas) and kuṣṭha (skin diseases). The sixth, however, is celebrated as Rohiṇī; this sixth Rohiṇī is the site for granthi (nodules), gaṇḍa (tumors), and apacī (scrofula). 283
The seventh layer is known as the *sthūla* (gross) skin; it is also the site where abscesses and similar ailments reside.
Indeed, there are countless impurities and hairs [in the body]; for as many hairs as there are, so many hair-pores (*lomakūpaka*) exist. 284–285.
The formation of the major and minor limbs, as well as the configuration of the body parts, arises from inherent nature alone; no other cause exists here.
Regarding the qualities that arise during the formation of the major and minor limbs, they are likewise produced by nature.
These various states of the embryo should be understood as arising from the causes of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).

The falling out of teeth, their regrowth, and the impossibility of regrowth once they have fallen out; likewise, the non-emergence of body hair on the palms and soles—all this occurs by way of its own nature (svabhāva). 287–288.
In the first month, it remains as a liquid exactly like the semen and the menses that have fallen into the womb;
in the second month, it is being cooked by the wind, bile, and phlegm located therein. (289)
The collection of great elements situated in the *kalala* stage becomes solidified;
in the third month, the five protuberances of the head, hands, and feet are established, as well as the subtle limbs and members of the body. (290–291)
Indeed, all the primary limbs (aṅgas) and secondary limbs (upāṅgas) become manifest in the fourth month;
for consciousness is also revealed through the manifestation of the heart.
Therefore, in the fourth month, the embryo desires various objects.
Therefore, a woman who possesses two hearts is considered "dauhṛdinī" (one with pregnancy-longings).
By disregarding her pregnancy-longings, a woman gives birth to a son who is hunchbacked, crippled in the hand, impotent, or dwarfed; or one with deformed eyes, or even sightless. (293–294)

Since a woman, having attained her pregnancy-longing (*dauhṛda*), gives birth to a son who is powerful and long-lived, one should therefore grant her whatever she desires. (295) Whatever objects of the senses that pregnant woman wishes to enjoy, [those should be provided].

Out of fear of injury to the fetus, the physician should have various [desired objects] brought and given to her. Having obtained the pregnancy-longings (*dauhṛda*), she shall give birth to a son endowed with virtues;
but one who has not obtained the longings may suffer danger either to the fetus or to herself.
In whatever objects of the senses her pregnancy-longing (dauhṛda) is disregarded,
she gives birth to a son who suffers pain in those very same sense organs.
If a longing arises in a woman at the sight of a king, [she will likewise experience suffering].
She gives birth to a son who is meaningful and highly fortunate (299). Due to her pregnancy-longing for fine linen, silk, and ornaments, she gives birth to a graceful son who desires finery (300).
In a hermitage, one gives birth to a son who is self-restrained and virtuous;
in an image of a deity, however, one gives birth to one resembling a servant. In the sight of predatory beasts, one gives birth to a son of a violent disposition.
From a pregnancy-longing for buffalo meat, one gives birth to a son who is red-eyed, hairy, and brave;
from pork, a son who is sleepy and brave;
and from deer meat, a son who is fleet-footed, courageous, and a forest-dweller.
Therefore, whatever woman experiences a longing (*dauhṛda*) for things not mentioned here will give birth to a child equal in body, conduct, and character.
In the fifth month the mind [is formed], and in the sixth the intellect becomes fully awakened.
In the seventh month, all the primary and secondary limbs become clearly manifest.
In the eighth month, the vital energy (*ojas*) circulates repeatedly between the mother and the son in turn;
because of this, both may become emaciated or exultant, and the one born may not survive.

One born in the eighth [month] does not live, because the *ojas* (vital energy) therein is not stable; likewise, because it belongs to the region of Nirṛti, one should cause that *bali* offering to be given therefrom. Then, in the ninth or tenth month, a woman gives birth to a child.
In the eleventh or twelfth month, or otherwise due to some transformation, the head of the limb appears first;
thus says Śaunaka, because the primary sense organs arise in the head itself. (308–309)
The sage Kṛtavīrya said that the heart is born first,
because it is declared to be the locus of both the intellect and the mind.
Pārāśarya, however, stated previously that it originates from the navel.
Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) resides, joined with heat, it causes the body to grow.
According to the opinion of the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, the hands and feet must first be formed,
because all the movements of an embodied being depend upon the hands and feet.
First the abdominal cavity is formed, and from that the development of all the limbs occurs;
indeed, Gautama, the bull among sages, has declared that all the major and minor limbs arise simultaneously. 313.
They are not perceived because of their subtlety; this is the opinion of Dhanvantari.

(314) In the tiny fruit of the mango, the flesh, bone, marrow, and so forth exist simultaneously; they are not perceived individually due to their extreme thinness, yet when fully developed, they become clearly manifest.
Thus, when the embryo has arisen, all its parts become simultaneously perceptible; yet, due to their subtlety, they do not reach manifest visibility until they have attained growth.
Now, the portions of the body derived from the father, the mother, age, and the self are described therein.

The hair of the head, the beard, body hair, nails, teeth, as well as the veins, arteries, sinews, and semen—these indeed are derived from the father. Flesh, blood, marrow, fat, liver, spleen, intestines, and the navel [are derived from the mother]. 316.
The heart and the rectum—these originate from the mother;
the growth of the body, complexion, strength, and the maintenance of the physical frame arise from the nutrient essence (rasa); thus have the physicians and sages declared.

Knowledge, consciousness, life-force, as well as pleasure, pain, and the like, and all the sense organs—these belong to the self. Fire and moon, earth, wind, space, and the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas [also belong to it]. 319.
Indeed, the five sense organs and the elemental self (bhūtātman) vitalize the embryo. Through the umbilical cord of the embryo, however, a channel carrying nourishment from the woman is attached;
by that means, the growth of the embryo occurs constantly.
He experiences the agitation of inhalation and exhalation, as well as portions of dreams,
arising from the mother’s own inhalations, exhalations, agitations, and dreams. Furthermore, the fixed locus of light is traditionally held to be in the center of the umbilical cord of the embryo.
Then the wind blows through his body, and by that it increases;
moreover, the vital air (māruta), together with the internal heat (ūṣman), tears apart his channels (srotas) in every way—upward, sideways, and downward. (323–324)
"Vision and the well of Rāma never increase; these two are constant for mortals—such is the opinion of Dhanvantari. Even while the body is wasting away, these two always increase. (325)
Taking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as the fundamental state, the established order is as follows:

for sentient beings, the basis consists of the mind and the body together with its sense faculties, excluding the tips of the hair, body hair, and nails, as well as impurities, excrement, and bodily fluids. (326–327)
Due to the deficiency of wind and the lack of movement of the wind within the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya),
the fetus situated there does not discharge flatus, urine, or feces.
Its mouth is covered by the placenta (jarāyu) and its throat is enveloped by phlegm.
And because the passage of the vital air is obstructed, the fetus does not cry out.
From the first day [of her pregnancy], the pregnant woman should be joyful, adorned, and pure;
she should wear white garments and be devoted to the worship of the Guru and the Brahmins.
She should always consume food that is predominantly sweet, unctuous, pleasing, liquid, light, well-prepared, and digestive-stimulating (331).
However, a pregnant woman should avoid physical exercise and fasting.
One should not indulge in sexual intercourse, nor should one practice excessive satiation (332). Likewise,
one should avoid staying awake at night, grief, riding in vehicles, bloodletting, the suppression of natural urges, and sitting in a squatting posture (333).
Whichever part of the pregnant woman is afflicted by the assault of the humors (doṣas),
that very same part of the child within the womb is afflicted.
One should not touch a woman who is filthy, deformed, or deficient in limbs.
He should not smell even a foul odor, nor see anything unpleasant to the eyes; he should not hear words that are disagreeable to the ears,
nor should he eat food that is stale, dry, or boiled.
One should avoid shrines, cremation grounds, trees, and things that bring ill repute; one should also avoid going outside, anger, and empty houses.
One should not speak loudly, nor should one do anything by which the fetus might perish.
She should not excessively indulge in oil massages or dry body rubs;
she should not use a mattress that is not soft, nor should her bed or seat be too high.
A pregnant woman should diligently observe all these rules.
In the ninth or tenth month, a woman gives birth to her child;
in the eleventh or twelfth, or otherwise, it is due to some abnormality.
[The dwelling] is eight cubits in length, beautiful, and four cubits in width.
One should construct the maternity chamber with its door facing either east or north.
For when the womb has become relaxed and the bond of the heart is released,
and the pelvis is accompanied by pain, the woman should be known as eager for delivery.
For a woman whose delivery is imminent, there will be pain in the hips and back,
along with frequent urges to urinate and void feces. Her body should be anointed with oil and she should be bathed with warm water.
