One should have her drink lukewarm gruel mixed with ghee in the proper measure. Then, on a soft and spacious bed provided with a pillow, the woman, though afflicted by pain, should remain lying on her back with her thighs unbent. (344–345)
Four women who are capable, skilled, beneficial, elderly, with well-trimmed nails, should properly attend to her;
having anointed the birth canal all over with oil. (346)
Among them, O fortunate one, he should say to one: "Flow forth. [He should say:
"Flow without distress; do not flow with distress. If you were to flow with distress, you should flow slowly at first, and thereafter more forcefully. (347–348)

Then, when the fetus has reached the opening of the womb in its most intense state, the fetus—unsupported by another—falls to the ground; it may be mute, deaf, humpbacked, or afflicted with asthma, cough, and consumption. (349)
She gives birth prematurely to a child with a collapsed body due to excessive straining.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the womb, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the fourth chapter, on the child.
Now, when a child has been born, one should perform the rites in accordance with the traditional succession of the customs of the elders of the family and women. 1.
After giving birth, she should consume wholesome food and engage in wholesome conduct;
she should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, and exposure to cold.
Whatever disease arises in the woman who has recently given birth due to improper conduct [should be treated].
Whether that condition be curable with difficulty or incurable, one should follow this wholesome regimen:
she should remain entirely pure, eat wholesome and unctuous food in small quantities,
and constantly devote herself to sudation and massage for a month without weariness.
Dhanvantari’s opinion is that a woman who has given birth should remain under the care of those attending women for at least one and a half months, or until the next menstrual period is observed;
provided she is free from complications and her bodily humors have been purified, O fair-complexioned lady.
After four months, one should relax the restrictive regimen. The sweet essence of the fluids, produced from the consumption of digested food,
reaches both breasts from the entire body and is designated as "breast milk."

The milk of women flows forth after three nights, or alternatively after four nights; the channels situated in the heart, having been opened, cause it to flow. This milk [is produced] through contact with, the sight of, or even the remembrance of one's son.
Even from the extraction of breast milk, a continuous secretion flows like semen; this constant flow is said to be caused by [the following factors]:
lack of maternal affection, fear, grief, anger, and excessive depletion.
The breast milk of women becomes scanty due to the obstruction caused by another pregnancy (10).
[One should avoid] rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, meat, small fish, black spinach, bottle gourd, coconut, and *kaseruka* (11).

A woman who consumes śṛṅgāṭaka, varī, vidārī-kanda, and garlic will increase her milk and become cheerful. She who drinks a paste of *kalama* rice grains ground with milk [will obtain the same result].

She becomes exceedingly youthful, with a pair of high breasts as if filled with milk. That rice known as *kalama*, famous in the Kali age, is produced in the great lake of Kashmir; it is said to be called *mahātaṇḍula*.

One should drink the juice of *vidārīkanda* for the increase of breast milk, or one should drink its powder mixed with milk for that same purpose. [This occurs] due to the mother's consumption of heavy foods and likewise due to unwholesome activities that aggravate the bodily humors (*doṣas*). 15.
The bodily humors (doṣas) become aggravated, and consequently, the breast milk becomes vitiated.
When the wind and other humors of a woman who indulges in improper diet and lifestyle are corrupted, they pollute the milk; by that means, diseases afflict the body of the infant.
If the breast milk is vitiated by vāta, it is astringent and floats on water;
from pitta, it is sour and pungent, and yellow streaks appear in the water.
However, that which is vitiated by kapha sinks in the water and is slimy.

That which arises from two [doshas] should have two genders, while that which arises from the combination of all three (sānnipātika) should have three genders. For the purification of her breast milk, the wet nurse should eat mung bean soup and meat broth, and she should drink a paste of bhārgī, dāru, vacā, and ativiṣā.
A decoction made from pāṭhā, mūrvā, abda, bhūnimba, dāru, śuṇṭhī, kaliṅgaka,
sārivā, and matsyapittā purifies the breast milk.
[21] One should likewise take paṭola, nimba, asana, dāru, pāṭhā, mūrvā, guḍūcī, and kaṭurohiṇī.
For the sake of purifying the breast milk, one should drink āmalakī boiled in water with ginger.
When the milk in the water becomes tasteless, discolored, stringy, pale, thin, and cold, one should declare that milk to be pure.
If one would provide a wet-nurse for the child, one should first carefully examine her virtues and defects; then, one should appoint such a nurse as this:
one of the same caste, middle-aged, of virtuous character, and always cheerful. (24)

She was a cow yielding pure milk in great abundance, accompanied by her calf and exceedingly affectionate toward it; she was self-controlled, content with little, of noble breed, and the offspring of virtuous parents—
yet she had been abandoned through deceit because her calf resembled her own son.
With eyes agitated by grief, she was distressed, exhausted, and perpetually afflicted by illness;
she was exceedingly tall and extremely short, and both excessively stout and very thin. She was pregnant, suffering from fever, and possessed pendulous, elevated breasts.
Furthermore, one who eats while suffering from indigestion, likewise one who avoids wholesome food (pathya),
one who is attached to trivial matters, one who is afflicted by suffering, and one who is fickle— the infant becomes ill by drinking their breast milk. (28–29)
There, the mother— possessing auspicious limbs and wearing beautiful garments— sitting on a seat facing the east, having properly washed her right breast with water and allowed it to drain slightly,
consecrates it with the two mantras.
Having gently placed the infant, facing northward, upon one's lap, one should feed it.
(31) If the child drinks from a breast that has not been expressed, its channels become excessively filled with milk; consequently, the child suffers from vomiting, cough, and labored breathing. (32)
May you be an ocean of milk for your breasts, always filling them with milk; may this child be ever fortunate and possess great strength.
O lady of auspicious countenance, having drunk milk like nectar, may your son [attain his desires].

"May he obtain long life, O gods, just as you have attained immortality. (34) Considering the suitability of milk, one should give goat's or cow's milk to children in the proper measure until they reach the age of weaning. (35)
According to the prescribed method, one should have the infant taste a little food in the sixth or even the eighth month; thereafter, one should gradually increase that amount.
One should hold the child comfortably on one's lap and never frighten him at any time.

One should never hastily seat an unfit person for the sake of awakening (37). One should not pull someone onto one's lap, nor cast them suddenly onto a bed; one should never cause anyone to weep, except when it is required by an essential rule (38).
One should follow that child's mind and always rejoice in his company;
one must diligently protect the child from lightning, thunderbolts, rain, smoke, fire, water, and the like, as well as from low and high places. 39.
Oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, as well as collyrium for the eyes,
soft clothing, and likewise a mild unguent— all these are beneficial for the child in every respect from birth onwards. (40)
Gargling [with medicinal decoctions] should begin from the fifth year, the administration of food from the eighth, purgation from the sixteenth year, and sexual intercourse from the twentieth.
Furthermore, there are three stages of life: childhood, middle age, and old age.

A man under sixteen years of age is called a child (bāla). He is also of three kinds: one who subsists on milk, one who subsists on milk and rice, and one who subsists on solid food. One who subsists on milk remains so for up to one year; one who subsists on milk and rice for two autumns (years).
Beyond that, one who eats food is considered a child; thus the child is known to be of three types.
Between the ages of sixteen and seventy, the middle stage is described by the wise as being fourfold, consisting of growth, youth, fullness, and decline. (44)
Up to twenty years there is growth; one is considered a youth until thirty.
Until forty years of age, one remains filled with vigor and other qualities;
thereafter, one gradually declines until reaching seventy.

Thereafter, beyond seventy years, with his vital essence and other fluids diminished, his sensory faculties and strength wasting away day by day, and his semen depleted, he becomes afflicted by wrinkles, grey hair, and baldness, and is incapable of performing actions.

A person becomes afflicted by cough, dyspnea, and other ailments as he grows old. Phlegm increases in childhood, bile is predominant in middle age, and wind increases in old age; having considered this, one should apply the appropriate treatment. 48–49.
Childhood, growth, complexion, intellect, skin, vision, semen, prowess, understanding, the organs of action, the mind, and vitality— these ten diminish with each decade.
Furthermore, there are seven constitutions (prakṛti) for men, arising from wind, bile, and phlegm.

According to the opinion of physicians, [these] arise from combination (saṃsarga) and from the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta). Whatever humor becomes predominant at the time of the union of semen and blood, by that the constitution (prakṛti) is produced; its characteristics are now described. 51–52.

The constitution (*prakṛti*) is said to be of seven types according to whichever *doṣa* is predominant during the following conditions: [the state of] semen, blood, pregnancy, food, activity, and the pain of the womb.
(53) One who is wakeful, has sparse hair, cracked hands and feet, and is emaciated...
One who moves swiftly, speaks much, and is harsh, and who travels through the sky in dreams—
such a person is to be known as one of a vāta constitution (vātaprakṛti). Now, the nature of a person of a pitta constitution is described.
One who is prematurely grey-haired, fair-complexioned, prone to anger, perspiring, and intelligent;
55 one who eats much, has copper-colored eyes, and sees lights in dreams—such a person is of a pitta constitution. 56

A man with dark hair, who is patient, stout, very vigorous, and possesses great strength, who observes reservoirs of water in his dreams, is one of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) constitution. Wherever the characteristics of two humors (doṣas) are observed in a person's nature, [he is considered to have a dual constitution]. 57.
One should recognize that which arises from the combination of two [doṣas] by their respective signs, and that which arises from all three doṣas by all their signs.

Because of its pervasiveness, its rapid action, its strength, its provocation of other [doṣas], its independence, and its causation of many diseases, vāta is the most powerful among the doṣas. (58–59)

For this very reason, humans dwelling in windy regions are generally of a *doṣa*-dominated nature; their hair and bodies are cracked and grey, they loathe the cold, and their fortitude, memory, intellect, physical exertion, affection, vision, and gait are unstable;
they engage in excessive chatter, possess little bile, strength, vitality, sleep, and speech that is faltering, incoherent, wavering, and broken. (60)
They are atheists, gluttonous, and full of amorous dalliance; they are addicted to song, laughter, hunting, and gambling (61).
They crave foods that are sweet, sour, pungent, hot, and agreeable to their taste; they are thin and tall in stature, and their gait is noisy.
They are neither firm nor have they conquered their senses; they are neither noble nor beloved by their wives, nor do they have many offspring (62).
Their eyes, ashy-grey, round, and unlovely, resembling those of the dead, seem to open even while they sleep; thus they go toward the mountains, trees, and the sky.
Unfortunate, puffed up with envy, and thieving, their calves are held tightly bound.
Dogs, jackals, camels, vultures, rats, and crows are of the wind (vāta) temperament.

Bile (pitta) is fire, or that which is born from fire; therefore, one whose pitta is predominant has intense thirst and hunger, fair and warm limbs, copper-colored hands, feet, and face, and is brave, proud, with reddish-brown hair and sparse body hair.

One who wears beloved garlands, ointments, and ornaments, who is well-conducted, pure, and affectionate toward those who depend on him, and who is endowed with wealth, daring, intelligence, and strength, becomes a refuge even for his enemies in times of fear.
(66) One who is intelligent, whose joints and flesh are loose, who is disliked by women, and who has little semen and little desire— [he is likewise so described].
His dwelling is among the dark-blue waves of grey hair; his food consists of that which is sweet, astringent, bitter, and cold.
He hates righteousness, perspires, and has a foul odor. He is prone to frequent excrement, anger, drinking, eating, and envy.
When asleep, he sees karṇikāra and palāśa trees, as well as forest fires, firebrands, lightning, and the fire of the sun.
Their eyes are thin, tawny, and restless; they have sparse lashes and are fond of cold.
Through anger, intoxication, and the brilliance of the sun, their eyes quickly turn red.
They possess middling lifespans and middling strength, are learned, and are fearful of suffering.
Those of a bilious (paittika) temperament resemble tigers, bears, monkeys, cats, and wolves.
(70) Phlegm (śleṣman) is like the moon; one of a phlegmatic (śleṣmala) temperament is therefore lunar (saumya). His joints, bones, and flesh are hidden, smooth, and well-knit.
He is not tormented by hunger, thirst, suffering, affliction, or heat; he is endowed with intelligence, possesses the quality of goodness (sāttvika), and is true to his word. (71)
Having the complexion of priyaṅgu, dūrvā grass, śara stalks, darbha grass, gorocanā, and the color of gold lotuses;
with long arms, a broad and full chest, a large forehead, and thick, dark hair;
with soft limbs and a well-proportioned, beautiful body; he possesses abundant vigor, intense passion, semen, sons, and servants.
Virtuous in nature, he never speaks harshly; he conceals his enmity firmly and for a long time.
(73) His gait is like that of a lordly elephant in rut; his voice is like the roar of clouds, the ocean, a drum, or a lion.
Possessing mindfulness, diligent, and humble, he did not cry excessively even in childhood, nor was he fickle. (74)

He eats bitter, astringent, pungent, hot, dry, and small quantities of food; yet he is strong, with eyes that have red corners, are very glossy, large, long, well-defined, and possess white and black parts with beautiful lashes.
He speaks little, is free from anger, drinking, eating, and envy; he possesses abundant longevity and wealth, is far-sighted, and is generous.
One who is faithful, profound, munificent, patient, noble, free from sleepiness, not procrastinating, grateful, upright, wise, fortunate, modest, devoted to his teachers, and firm in friendship;
such a person sees in his dreams reservoirs of water filled with lotuses and flocks of birds, as well as clouds. (76–77)

Those whose nature is dominated by phlegm (śleṣma) are equal to Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, Tārkṣya, the Swan, and the Lord of Elephants; likewise, they are like the lion, the horse, the cow, and the bull.
Just as an insect born from poison is not afflicted by poison, [so too is one of phlegmatic temperament].
In the same way, the primary constituents (*prakṛtis*) are unable to afflict a mortal;
neither their provocation, nor their transformation, nor their pacification arises by their own nature, but rather they arise for one whose life has reached its end. (79–80)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Child, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the fifth chapter, on Daily Regimen (*dinacaryā*) and so forth.
The terrain of the land is of three kinds: marshy (anūpa), arid (jāṅgala), and characterized by a mixture of both.
The marshy land is rich in rivers, ponds, and mountains, filled with clusters of blooming lotuses, and frequented by swans, cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, ruddy geese, and other such birds.
It was teeming with hares, boars, buffaloes, ruru deer,
and roe deer; it was rich with abundant trees and flowers, endowed with dark crops and fruits, and adorned with many fields of rice, plantains, and sugarcane.
One suffering from diseases of wind and phlegm should know this as the Anūpa region.
It is level like the sky, high-lying, with very few waters or trees,
and is crowded with *śamī*, *karīra*, *bilva*, *arka*, *pīlu*, and *karkaṇdu* plants.
A region crowded with deer, antelopes, bears, spotted deer, gokarṇa deer, and wild asses, abounding in sweet fruits, and characterized by windy conditions is known as *jāṅgala*.
A region with abundant water and trees is called *anūpa*, which is prone to diseases caused by phlegm and wind.

The Jāṅgala region has sparse water and vegetation, and is dominated by pitta, blood, and vāta. That region which possesses characteristics of both is considered Sādhāraṇa (temperate), because in it cold, rain, heat, and wind are balanced.
Therefore, there is an equality regarding faults;

thus, one who abides in what is appropriate is not subject to the fear arising from an unfavorable location, provided that his food, sleep, movements, and so forth are conducted in accordance with that place. (8–9)
Whatever creature belongs to a particular region, medicine produced from that same region is beneficial for it;
however, medicine possessing similar qualities when used elsewhere than its native land may provoke the humors.
Defects that are latent in one’s own region become aggravated when one resides in another.
Likewise, aquatic and terrestrial creatures would not possess such strength;
therefore, by whatever method a human being remains always healthy, that very method the physician should employ, since health is always desired. 11–12.

A person who practices the daily regimen, the nocturnal regimen, and the seasonal regimen as prescribed remains healthy at all times; it cannot be otherwise. He possesses balanced humors, balanced digestive fire, and balanced constituents, wastes, and bodily functions.
One whose self, senses, and mind are serene is said to be "established in well-being" (svastha). One should wake up during the *brāhma-muhūrta* for the sake of preserving one's health and longevity;
at that time, for the pacification of all sins, one should indeed remember Madhusūdana.
One who is awake should perform the sight and touch of curd, clarified butter, a mirror, white mustard, the bilva fruit, gorocana, and a garland, as these bring auspiciousness.
If one desires long life, one should look at one's own face reflected in clarified butter.

The evacuation of waste and other impurities at dawn is said to promote longevity; it prevents intestinal rumbling, flatulence, heaviness of the abdomen, distension, colic, cutting pain, constipation, and upward movement of wind (urdhvavāta). (17)
Or else, when the urge for feces is suppressed, the feces may even exit through the mouth of a man.
From the suppression of wind, there occurs the retention of flatus, urine, and feces, as well as distension, exhaustion, pain in the abdomen, and other diseases born of Vata. (18–19)
Pain in the bladder and penis, difficulty in urination, headache,
bending of the body, and distension of the groins are the symptoms of suppressed urine. One who feels the urge should not engage in other activities, nor should one forcibly suppress the urges.
One should restrain the impulses of the mind—desire, grief, fear, and anger.
(21) The purification of the channels of excretion and the like is declared to bestow beauty, strength, and purity; it removes misfortune, strife, and sin. (22)
Washing the hands and feet is considered the cause of purification;
it removes dirt and fatigue, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and subdues the quality of passion (rājas).
One should chew a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths in length.
With a brush that is as thick as the tip of the little finger, straight, without knots, and likewise free of sores,
one should rub each tooth individually with a soft brush using tooth-cleansing powder, taking care not to injure the gums.
One should daily clean the teeth with a powder made from honey and *trikaṭu* (the three pungents), or with a powder derived from sesame oil and salt, or from *tejovatī*.
Among sweet substances, *madhuka* is best; likewise, among pungent substances, *karañja* is best.

The nimba tree is the best among bitter substances, and likewise the khadira tree is the best among astringent ones. (27) Having carefully observed the season, the [patient's] doshas, and their constitution, one should employ medicinal substances endowed with appropriate tastes and potencies. (28)
Consequently, for such a person, disorders of the mouth, bad taste, and ailments of the teeth and tongue arise; furthermore, relish, clarity of the senses, and lightness of body do not occur.
(29) There is potency in the *arka* plant, radiance in the *vaṭa*, and victory in the *karañja*.
In the *plakṣa* tree there is the attainment of wealth; in the *vaidurya* tree, a sweet voice;
in the *khadira* tree, fragrance of the mouth; in the *bilva* tree, abundant riches; in the *udumbara* tree, perfection of speech; and in the *āmra* tree, health itself. (30–31)
In the *kadamba* there is fortitude and intelligence; in the *campaka*, a firm mind;
in the *śirīṣa*, fame, good fortune, long life, and indeed health.
In the *apāmārga* there is fortitude and intelligence; likewise, in the *āsana* there is wisdom and power.
A beautiful form [is attained] from the pomegranate, as well as from the *kakubha* and *kuṭaja*; by means of the *jātī*, *tagara*, and *mandāra*, bad dreams are destroyed.
The *gurvāka*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, *ketaka*, and *bṛhattṛṇa* [are likewise effective].

Date palm and coconut— these seven are the kings of grasses (tṛṇarāja). A man who uses for cleaning his teeth anything produced from these kings of grasses shall remain in the womb of a *caṇḍāla* until he beholds the Gaṅgā.
One should not consume it in cases of diseases of the palate, lips, tongue, or teeth; nor when there is inflammation or swelling of the mouth, nor in cases of dyspnea, cough, or vomiting (verse 37);
nor by one who is weak, has indigestion, has recently eaten, or is afflicted with hiccup, fainting, or intoxication.
One suffering from headache, one who is thirsty, exhausted, or afflicted by fatigue from drinking;
one suffering from facial paralysis, earache, eye disease, or acute fever; and even one afflicted with heart disease—these should avoid the tooth-stick. (38–39)
A tongue-scraper may be made of gold, silver, or copper;
likewise, it may be made of split soft wood or from soft leaves.
Ten finger-breadths long, soft, and smooth—one should comfortably scrape the tongue with such an instrument. 40.
One should repeatedly perform gargling with cold water, which removes impurities of the tongue, bad taste, foul odor, and numbness;
it dispels phlegm and thirst, and brings about purity within the mouth. 41–42.
A gargle of lukewarm water removes phlegm, anorexia, and impurities;
it also relieves numbness of the teeth and brings lightness to the mouth.
(43) It is [contraindicated] for those suffering from poison, fainting, or intoxication, as well as for those with wasting diseases or bleeding disorders.
It is not recommended for those with inflamed eyes, or who have thin and rough eyelashes.
Washing the face with cold water conquers *raktapitta* (bleeding disorders), dries up facial pustules, and destroys dark spots, blue marks, and blemishes.
One may also perform oral cleansing with lukewarm milk,
which alleviates kapha and vāta, is unctuous, and destroys dryness of the mouth (46).
One should employ substances such as *kaṭutaila* for nasal administration through constant practice.
In the case of phlegm, [nasal therapy] should be administered in the morning; in the case of bile, at midday; and in the case of wind, in the evening.
(47) Those who habitually practice nasal therapy shall have fragrant breath, smooth voices, and pure senses; they shall be free from weakness, wrinkles, graying hair, and freckles. (48)
One should therefore constantly apply *sauvīra* collyrium, which is beneficial for the eyes; by this, your two eyes will become beautiful and possess keen vision.
*Sroto'ñjana*, originating from the Indus region, is considered the most excellent and pure.
It removes itching and impurities from vision, and it cures burning, discharge, and pain; it brings clarity of form to the eyes and enables them to endure wind and heat.
Since eye diseases do not arise [otherwise], one should therefore practice the application of collyrium.
One who has stayed awake at night, one who is fatigued, one who has vomited, one who has just eaten,
one afflicted by fever, or one who has bathed his head should not apply collyrium to the eyes.
Every five nights, one should have one's nails, beard, hair, and body hair trimmed.

The cutting and grooming of the hair, beard, nails, and so forth, is nourishing, auspicious, life-prolonging, and supreme for producing purity and luster. (53) One should never pluck out the hairs of the nose.
From pulling that [hair] too quickly, weakness of vision may arise.
(54) One should perform the grooming of the mass of hair with a comb;
this grooming of the hair is beneficial for the hair and removes dust, insects, and impurities. (55)

Beholding one's reflection in a mirror is said to be auspicious, bestowing radiance, nourishment, strength, and longevity; it destroys evil and misfortune, and brings about lightness, capability in action, and well-proportioned limbs. 56.
The depletion of the humors (doṣas) and the increase of the digestive fire (agni) arise from physical exercise (vyāyāma).
For one whose limbs are strengthened by exercise, no disease ever occurs; moreover, food that is incompatible or improperly digested is quickly metabolized. 57–58.
In his body, looseness and other such symptoms do not quickly arise,
nor does old age suddenly and forcefully take hold of him; furthermore,
there is nothing equal to that for diminishing corpulence.
He always imparts strength to those who are powerful and eat wholesome food; he is considered especially beneficial during the spring and the cold season,
but at other times as well, it should be administered with half the dose according to one's strength.
When the wind residing in the heart quickly reaches the mouth and the mouth becomes dry, that is the sign of the loss of half one's strength.
Or [it may be felt] on the forehead, the nose, the joints of the limbs, or the armpits.

When perspiration arises, one should then prescribe half the [usual] strength. One who has eaten, one who has engaged in sexual intercourse, one suffering from cough, dyspnea, emaciation, consumption,
hemorrhaging, chest wounds, or wasting— [the physician] should never apply this to them.
From excessive physical exertion, cough, fever, vomiting, fatigue, exhaustion,
thirst, wasting, fainting, and internal hemorrhage (raktapitta) arise.
One should always apply oil massage (abhyaṅga) to all the limbs, as it bestows nourishment.
One should especially practice that [mantra] on the head, ears, and feet.
Whether it be mustard oil, scented oil, or oil perfumed with flowers, an oil mixed with other substances is never defiled.
Anointing the body removes wind and phlegm, relieves fatigue, and bestows strength, comfort, sleep, a healthy complexion, softness, and longevity; it nourishes the physique.
When practiced on the head, anointing gratifies all the sense organs.
It produces satisfaction through its appearance and destroys ailments located on the head.
It brings about an abundance of hair, as well as firmness, softness, length, and blackness; it likewise makes the head full. (69–70)
There shall be no ear diseases, no wax, nor pain in the neck or jaw; there shall be no excessive sensitivity to sound nor deafness, through the constant filling of the ears [with oil].
Filling the ears with liquids and other substances before eating is highly recommended.
Filling the ears with oil and other substances when the sun has set provides stability for those [ears], induces sleep, and clarifies the vision;
it also removes numbness, fatigue, stiffness, contraction, and cracking of the feet. (72–73)
Diseases do not approach one whose body has been worn out by physical exercise and likewise pressed by walking on foot, just as serpents do not approach Vainateya;
[this applies] to the body with its pores, network of veins, and arteries. 74.
An immersion bath combined with oil provides nourishment and bestows strength.
For just as the sprouts and other parts of trees whose roots are drenched with water flourish,
so too do the bodily tissues (dhātus) of men thrive when moistened with oil.
One suffering from acute fever, one with indigestion, as well as a person who has undergone purgation, emesis, or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), should by no means be anointed with oil.
In the case of the first two conditions, there may be difficulty in curing the disease or even its incurability.
Furthermore, for the remaining [doshas], diseases such as those caused by the impairment of digestive fire (vahnisāda) are described here.

(78) Udvartana (rubbing with medicinal pastes) alleviates kapha, destroys fat (medas), and is excellent for increasing semen; it is strengthening, promotes blood formation, clarifies the skin, and makes the skin soft. (79)
From applying this as a facial ointment, the eyes become firm, the cheeks and face plump, and the countenance becomes lovely, free from blemishes or pimples, resembling a lotus.
This bath is digestive, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and bestows vigor and strength.
It removes itching, impurities, fatigue, perspiration, drowsiness, thirst, burning sensations, and afflictions.
When oppressed by external sprinklings of cold water and the like, the internal heat recedes;
therefore, by the mere act of bathing, a man's digestive fire is kindled.
Bathing with cold milk brings about the pacification of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders);
that same bath with warm water is strengthening and removes *vāta* and *kapha*.
Bathing the head with excessively hot water is always detrimental to the eyesight.
Furthermore, that which has been proclaimed as beneficial when wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) are provoked is as follows:
bathing with water that is not cold, drinking milk, [union with] young women, and a diet that is unctuous and small in quantity—this, O men, is wholesome for you. (84–85)
The man who always performs his bath with *āmalaka* fruits will certainly be freed from wrinkles and grey hair and shall live for a hundred years.
Bathing [with them] is beneficial in cases of fever, diarrhea, and afflictions of the eyes, ears, and wind (*vāta*).
It is forbidden for those who are bloated, suffering from catarrh, indigestion, or who have just eaten (verse 87).
Immediately after bathing, the thorough wiping of the limbs with a cloth bestows luster upon the body and destroys itching and skin disorders (verse 88).
Silk, woolen cloth, and likewise dyed garments—these remove wind and phlegm; one should wear them during the cold season.
Garments that are pure, very cool, and astringent are said to destroy bile.

One should wear that during the hot season; even then, a light garment is recommended. A white garment, which bestows auspiciousness and wards off cold and heat, should be worn during the rainy season, as it is neither too hot nor too cold.
New, stainless clothing brings fame, fulfills desires, promotes longevity, increases prosperity and joy, is beneficial for the skin, exerts a captivating influence, and is pleasing to the eye;
never should people of integrity wear soiled garments. (92)
However, that [application] causes itching, worms, and extreme exhaustion and misfortune.
Saffron, sandalwood, and black agalloch mixed together are hot; they destroy wind and phlegm and are recommended for the cold season. 93–94.
Sandalwood mixed with camphor and musk is supremely fragrant and cooling; it is highly recommended during the hot season.
Sandalwood combined with saffron and joined with musk [is likewise excellent]. 95.
In the rainy season, that [ointment] is considered to be neither hot nor cold.
It overcomes thirst, fainting, foul odor, perspiration, and burning sensations; it increases good fortune, luster, the complexion of the skin, pleasure, vitality, and strength.
Even for those who are unworthy of bathing, this unguent is beneficial. 97.
Wearing fragrant flowers and leaves bestows luster, removes sins, demons, and malevolent planets, grants desires, and increases prosperity. 98.
One should adorn the body with ornaments as is appropriate according to the prescribed rules;
gold is traditionally held to bestow purity, good fortune, and contentment (99),
removing the malefic gaze of the planets, providing nourishment, and destroying evil dreams.
The wearing of jewel ornaments pacifies misfortune and ill luck: the ruby is said to belong to the Sun; the pure pearl, well-born, to the Moon; coral to Mars; and the emerald to Mercury. 100.
For the preceptor of the gods (Jupiter), a *puṣparāga*; for the teacher of the asuras (Venus), a *vajra*;
for Saturn, a pure *nīla*; and for the other two (Mercury and Mars), a *gomedaka* and *vaidūrya* respectively are prescribed.
Wearing garments and gems that enhance beauty increases one's affection.
It is a destroyer of demons, pleasing to the gods, bestowing vigor, and supremely conducive to good fortune (102).
Likewise, there is the constant wearing of perfected mantras, great medicinal herbs,
yellow pigment (*rocanā*), mustard seeds, and other auspicious items (103).
It bestows longevity and prosperity, removes demons, grants auspiciousness,
destroys fear of violence and other evils, and is a cause for subjugation.
(104) Therefore, at the time of eating, one should perform the rite of beholding auspicious objects.
The constant display of that [image] increases longevity and righteousness.
In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, the sacrificial fire, a garland of flowers, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth. (105–106)

One should wear sandals before or after eating; they remove diseases of the feet, are aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and conducive to longevity. (107) A fourfold desire constantly arises within the bodies of men.
Hunger, thirst, the desire to sleep, and longing for pleasure;

from the obstruction of the desire for food, there arise bodily aching, loss of appetite, fatigue, drowsiness, weakness of the eyes, burning of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and loss of strength. 108–109.

From the obstruction of thirst, there occurs dryness of the throat and mouth, obstruction of hearing, drying of the blood, and pain in the heart; from the obstruction of sleep, yawning, and heaviness of the head and eyes arise. (110)
There will be aching of the limbs, as well as drowsiness and indigestion.
For one who is hungry yet does not eat, the digestive fire of the body becomes weak due to the lack of fuel in the form of food, just like a fire without fuel.
The fire digests food; when devoid of food, it digests the humors (doṣas).
Upon the depletion of the humors, it digests the tissues (dhātus), and upon the depletion of the tissues, it even digests the vital breaths (prāṇas).
Food provides immediate gratification, generates strength, and sustains the body.
One should consume food endowed with the aforementioned qualities, which increases memory, lifespan, strength, complexion, vitality, courage, and beauty,
after having carefully considered the humors, the time, and other factors during both meal times. 114–115.
The scripture ordains that for human beings there is eating in the evening and in the morning;
one should not eat in between. This rule is equal in importance to the Agnihotra sacrifice. One should not eat during the middle watch of the day, nor should one skip two watches.
The production of rasa occurs within one watch (yāma), and the loss of strength occurs after two watches.
Hunger arises when the rasa, doṣas, and malas have been digested;
whether at the proper time or not, that is declared to be the time for food. 117–118.
Cleanliness of eructation, enthusiasm, timely evacuation of the urges, lightness of the body, and hunger and thirst are the signs that food has been digested.
(119) One should always take one's meals in private, and likewise, one should always evacuate in private.

One may possess fortune through both [means], yet in public one is deprived of splendor. (120) The activities of eating, excreting, and recreation should always be performed by the virtuous in private.
(121) [The qualities of] father, mother, friend, physician, cook, swan, and peacock...
The gaze of a crane or a cakora bird is excellent when it comes to food (122).
However, the gaze of those who are wretched, lowly, or overcome by hunger, as well as that of sinners, heretics, the sick, cocks, and dogs, is not auspicious at all regarding food (123).

A golden vessel for eating removes defects, bestows right vision, and is wholesome; a silver one is beneficial for the eyes, removes bile, and increases phlegm and wind. Bell-metal (kāṃsya) bestows intelligence, improves the appetite, and clarifies blood-bile (raktapitta).
Food prepared in a bell-metal vessel increases wind (vāta), is parching, hot, and destroys parasites and phlegm (kapha).
Food prepared in an iron or glass vessel brings about success [in its effects];
it removes swelling and anemia, is strengthening, and is excellent for curing jaundice (kāmalā). 125–126.

Eating from a vessel made of stone or clay wards off misfortune; that made of wood, especially, provides relish but increases phlegm; a vessel made of leaves is appetizing, stimulates digestion, and removes poison and sin. (127)
A water vessel made of copper is recommended, or in its absence, one made of clay.
A vessel fashioned from crystal is pure and cooling, as is one fashioned from glass or originating from lapis lazuli (vaidūrya). 128–129.
At the beginning of a meal, one should always consume salty and moist foods;
this kindles the digestive fire, stimulates the appetite, and cleanses the tongue and throat.
Brahmā is the food, Viṣṇu is the essence, and the consumer is the Lord Maheśvara.
Thinking thus, the defect of the glance does not afflict one who eats.
131 I remember Hanumān, the celibate youth born from the womb of Añjanā, for the destruction of the defect of the glance. 132
One should eat with a focused mind, beginning with sweet flavors,
followed by sour and salty in the middle, and finally bitter, pungent, and astringent ones.
A wise person should first consume fruits such as pomegranate and the like.
Likewise, the karkaṭī gourd must be avoided unless it has its seeds removed;
similarly, lotus stalks, lotus roots, tubers, sugarcane, and so forth should be eaten only when raw, and never after they have been cooked. 134–135.
One should never eat food made of flour, nor rice, nor flattened grains (pṛthuka); if hungry, one should eat only in measured portions.
One should eat soft food preceded by ghee, and hard food thereafter.
Furthermore, one who possesses the power of the "drava-śī" (the faculty of liquefaction) releases [the food] through the force of its potency.
Whatever is sweeter, that one should provide increasingly; that which is desired again after having eaten is called "sādu-bhojana" (delicious food). 137–138.

Food that is delicious produces cheerfulness, strength, nourishment, enthusiasm, and an increase in lifespan; however, food that is tasteless produces the opposite effect. (139) Food that is excessively hot destroys strength, while food that is cold or dry is difficult to digest.
Food that is excessively moist causes illness; indeed, food should be eaten according to the proper method.
One who eats too quickly does not perceive the virtues or the defects of the meal, and for one who eats too slowly, the food becomes cold and unpalatable. (140–141)
A person with a weak digestive fire should avoid substances that are heavy by measure, as well as those that are heavy by nature and those that are heavy by processing.
Mudga and other such legumes are heavy by measure; Māṣa and others are heavy by nature. (142)
It is stated that food made from flour is heavy due to its processing; this is merely an illustration.
One should know that among the six kinds of food—namely, that which is sucked, drunk, licked, eaten, chewed, and bitten—they become increasingly heavy in the order mentioned. 143–144.
For heavy foods, half-satiation is desired; for light foods, full satiation is intended.
Furthermore, a liquid or predominantly liquid food is not considered "heavy" by measure.
Dry food, when consumed habitually, does not undergo proper digestion. (145–146)
Dried, obstructed, or constipating barley-meal (saktu) causes injury to the digestive fire.

One should not eat it after having already eaten, nor by chewing it with the teeth, nor at night, nor in large quantities, nor when mixed with water, nor without being mixed with liquids, nor alone. 147–148.

One should avoid giving [the medicine] again, drinking it separately, taking it with meat, at night, with milk, while the teeth are chattering, or when it is hot; these seven [conditions] are to be avoided regarding roasted barley flour (*saktu*).
(149) Because of its softness, the barley flour taken as a linctus is digested quickly. (150)

That which is eaten in excess at the proper time, or that which is eaten in too small a quantity or at the wrong time, should be known as irregular eating (viṣamāśana). It excessively produces lethargy, heaviness, flatulence, and indigestion. (151)
Even a slight deficiency in the body causes emaciation and loss of strength.
For a man who eats at an improper time, his body becomes incapable, he contracts various diseases, and meets with death. 152–153.
When time has passed and the digestive fire of a person has been impaired by wind (vāyu),
what is eaten is digested with great difficulty, and there is no further desire to eat.
One should fill two parts of the stomach with food and the third part with water.
One should leave a fourth part remaining for the purpose of circulating the vital air (vāyu).
Just as the tongue, when satiated by the first taste of food, does not perceive its flavor so well, it must therefore be cleansed with water in between. 155–156.
Food is not properly digested from drinking excessive water, and that same fault arises from not drinking water at all;
therefore, a person should drink water frequently, but not in great quantity, in order to increase the digestive fire.
Water drunk before a meal causes emaciation and the disorder of weak digestion.
Drinking water during the middle of a meal is best for stimulating the digestive fire; drinking at the end causes corpulence and increases phlegm.
Those who are of normal build, stout, or thin should drink water during the middle, at the end, or at the beginning of their meal, respectively.
One who is thirsty should not eat, and one who is hungry should not drink water.
One who is thirsty becomes afflicted with gulma (abdominal tumors), and one who is hungry suffers from jaḷodara (ascites).
Therefore, having become single-minded, one should eat first the sweet taste, then the sour and salty in the middle, and finally the pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes. (160–161)
Milk is sweet-tasting, unctuous, strengthening, and increases the bodily tissues (dhātus);
it alleviates wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, increases phlegm, and is heavy and cold.
(162) Indeed, whatever foods and drinks that cause internal burning (vidāhin) a person consumes, [milk counteracts them].
To pacify that burning sensation, one should drink milk at the end of the meal (verse 163).
One should take food ending with milk, but never ending with curd; nor should one consume salty, sour, pungent, hot, or burning substances.
To remove that fault, one should conclude the meal with something sweet (verse 164).
Just as the exhaustion of a slayer of enemies is seen through the destruction of a powerful foe,
so too does one become exhausted by the destruction of an adversary oneself.
Water may indeed destroy the heat of iron heated by fire.
(165) Now, if it is argued that pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes employed at the conclusion of a meal will pacify phlegm and cause an increase in wind, that is not so.
Because the power of pungent and other [tastes] has been exhausted, how could that which destroys one humor (doṣa) increase another?
For in the destruction of one humor, its power is indeed diminished. (166)
All tastes, even when consumed, come under the control of strength,
just as provoked humors (doṣas) come under the control of one who possesses superior strength.
Having eaten in this manner, one should rinse the mouth with water, preceded by the intake of dry food.
After removing food particles stuck between the teeth, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana).
One should slowly extract food stuck between the teeth using a cleaning tool; for if it is not removed, it will cause an unpleasant odor in the mouth. 168–169.
One should regard a coating stuck to the teeth that cannot be removed as being like the teeth themselves;
one should not exert great effort toward its removal.
Having sipped water, one should touch the eyes with both hands moistened with water.
If, after eating, one rubs the palms of the hands together and applies that water to the eyes, it will dispel cataracts (timira) in no time at all.
Furthermore, after eating, one should always remember Agastya and other such deities who bring about happiness. 171–172.
Viṣṇu is the Self, and likewise is food and its transformation;
by that truth, may this food eaten by me be digested.
May Agasti, Agni, and the Vaḍavānala fire digest all the food I have eaten without exception.
May they grant me that happiness arising from its transformation, and may my body be free from disease.
One should constantly remember these five—Aṅgāraka, Agasti, Pāvaka, Sūrya, and the two Aśvins; for such a person, what has been eaten is quickly digested. 174–175.

Having recited this and rubbed his belly with his own hand, he should perform tasks that cause no fatigue, remaining free from sloth. When food is digested, the wind (vāyu) increases; when it is improperly digested (vidagdha), the bile (pitta) increases.
Immediately after eating, phlegm may also arise;

this sequence following a meal [should be managed] by clearing it away with smoke, or with pleasant, astringent, pungent, and bitter substances, such as betel nuts, camphor, musk, cloves, and jasmine flowers. 177–178.
A wise man [should offer betel] with fruits that are pungent or astringent, which produce clarity of the mouth, or with fragrant betel leaves;
likewise during sexual intercourse, upon waking from sleep, after bathing, after eating, after vomiting, and in battle.
In an assembly of learned men and kings, one should chew betel leaf (tāmbūla).
Betel is said to be sharp, hot, appetizing, astringent, laxative, bitter, alkaline, pungent, light, and it causes passion and blood-bile (rakta-pitta). 180–181.
It is effective for subjugation; it removes phlegm, foul breath, impurities, wind-disorders, and fatigue;
it produces clarity, fragrance, luster, and excellence in the mouth;
it destroys impurities of the jaws and teeth, and purifies the faculty of the tongue. 182.
It alleviates mouth-rinsing needs and destroys diseases of the throat.
That same [vegetable] when fresh is sweet with an astringent aftertaste, heavy, and generally known to produce phlegm; such are the qualities of leaf-vegetables. 183–184.
The leaf originating from Vaṅgadeśa is extremely pungent, laxative,
digestive, provocative of pitta, hot, and is known to alleviate kapha. (185) A leaf that is old, not pungent, small, thin, and pale— [is of inferior quality].
Specifically, that which possesses excellent qualities is known as *anvaddhīnaguṇa*.
Pūga (betel nut) is heavy, cold, dry, and astringent; it subdues *kapha* and *pitta*, induces stupor, stimulates digestion, improves the appetite, and eliminates bad taste in the mouth. (186–187)
Betel nut (pūga) that is firm in the center, when steamed, alleviates the three doṣas; however, that which is succulent, heavy, and causes secretions is extremely destructive to the digestive fire.
The powder of khadira destroys kapha and pitta, and increases the strength of vāta.
Through their combination, it destroys the three *doṣas* and produces mental well-being;
it brings about clarity, fragrance, luster, and excellence of the mouth.
Betel nut (*pūga*) is most effective in the morning, while *khadira* is likewise so at midday.
One should always consume more lime and betel leaf during the nights.
Longevity resides at the tip, fame at the base, and prosperity is situated in the middle;
therefore, one should avoid the tip, the base, and the middle of the leaf.
A leaf from the base of the stem causes disease; one from the tip of the leaf brings about sin;
a leaf from the middle of the leaf takes away life; and a leaf with a vein destroys the intellect.
The first type of leaf, when drunk, is like poison; the second is purgative and difficult to digest.
On the third day, one should partake of the elixir (rasāyana) which is equal to nectar.
One should not consume betel-leaf when one has been purged or when one is hungry;
[otherwise] there occurs a wasting away of the body, eyes, hair, teeth, digestive fire, ears, complexion, and strength.
Excessive chewing of betel leaf causes consumption (śoṣa) due to the provocation of pitta, vāyu, and blood.

Betel is not beneficial for those with weak teeth, those suffering from eye diseases, those afflicted by poison, fainting, or intoxication, nor for those with wasting diseases or bleeding disorders (raktapitta). (195–196)
After eating, one should walk slowly for a hundred paces; by this, the mass of food becomes loosened in the neck, knees, and waist.
If one sits after eating, drowsiness arises, but if one lies down, there is nourishment.

Death runs after life as it moves along, even as one runs. (198) One should lie on one's back and take eight breaths; then twice that number on the right side, and then double that again on the left, after which one may sleep as comfortably as desired. (199)
In the left direction from the navel, there is fire (anala) in living beings;
therefore, one should lie on the left side for the sake of digesting what has been eaten.
A cotton mattress (tūlī) alleviates the three humors (tridoṣa) and removes wind and phlegm (vāta-kapha).
Sleeping on the ground is nourishing and aphrodisiac, whereas sleeping on a wooden plank increases vāta.
Sleeping on the ground increases vāta, is extremely parching, yet destroys pitta and blood disorders.
Sleeping on a good bed is pleasing to the heart and bestows nourishment, sleep, and fortitude.
It removes the wind of fatigue, is aphrodisiac, and the opposite of this is otherwise [harmful]. 202.
Massage is supreme for clarifying the flesh, blood, and skin;
it produces pleasure and sleep, is aphrodisiac, and removes phlegm, wind, and fatigue. 203.
A breeze causes dryness, discoloration, and stiffness, yet it alleviates burning sensations and pitta;
it destroys perspiration, fainting, and thirst. A non-breeze has the opposite effect. Therefore, one should enjoy a pleasant breeze during the summer and autumn, or at intervals between them.
One should always resort to a windless place for the sake of longevity, health, and well-being.
(205) The eastern wind is heavy, hot, unctuous, and it aggravates pitta and rakta;
it causes a burning sensation and increases vāta, yet it is beneficial for those suffering from fatigue, phlegm, and wasting. (206)
Sweet, sharp, and causing secretions, it aggravates skin diseases, hemorrhoids, poison, worms,
the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta), fever, dyspnea, and rheumatism (āmavāta).
The southern wind is sweet, removes bile and blood disorders, and is light.
By its vigor, it is cooling, strengthening, beneficial for the eyes, and not provocative of wind (vāta). 208.
The western wind is sharp, drying, strength-depleting, and light; it destroys fat, bile, and phlegm (kapha), while increasing the wind (prabhañjana). 209.
The northern wind is cool, unctuous, provocative of the *doṣas*, moistening, beneficial to those in their natural state, strengthening, sweet, and mild.
The south-eastern wind causes burning and is parched; the south-western wind does not cause burning.
The wind from the northwest is bitter, while that from the northeast is known to be pungent.
The wind blowing from all directions (viṣvagvāyu) is detrimental to longevity and causes many diseases for living beings;
therefore, one should never resort to it, for when resorted to, it does not lead to well-being.
The breeze from a fan removes burning sensations, perspiration, fainting, and fatigue;
the air produced by a palm-leaf fan is considered to pacify the three *doṣas*.
However, that produced by a bamboo fan is hot and aggravates *rakta-pitta*.
Fans made of yak-tail hair, cloth, peacock feathers, or cane—
when pure, free from defects, smooth, pleasing to the heart, and well-maintained— bring forth wholesome winds. One should not sleep during the day, for that leads to an increase of phlegm (kapha).
Sleeping during the day is prohibited at times other than the summer season.
(216) For those embodied beings for whom daytime sleep is a constant habit, the bodily humors such as wind (vāta) and the others become aggravated if they do not sleep during the day. (217)
Those engaged in physical exertion, sexual indulgence, travel, or riding vehicles; those who are exhausted;

those suffering from diarrhea; those afflicted by colic, dyspnea, or thirst; those oppressed by hiccups or wind-disorders; those who are emaciated; children with diminished *kapha*; the elderly overcome by intoxication; and those with indigestion of *rasa*—[these should not be given emetics].
One may, at will, cause those men who have remained awake at night and fasted to sleep during the day (218).
For those by whom sleep has been made habitual, whether by day or by night, no fault arises for them whether they are sleeping or waking (219).
Sleep following a meal removes wind (vāta), alleviates bile (pitta),
produces phlegm (kapha), and indeed extends the nourishment and comfort of the body. Lying down [after a meal] serves to destroy bile, while massage destroys wind.

Emesis is for the destruction of *kapha*, while fasting (*laṅghana*) is for the destruction of fever. That which is taken while sitting and causes dizziness is neither obstructive (*abhiṣyandi*) nor drying (*rūkṣaṇa*).
[One should consume] sounds, touches, forms, tastes, and smells that are pleasing to the mind.
Even after eating, one should consume [these]; by that means, the food remains well-digested.
(223) Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell that are loathsome, as well as food that has been eaten by one who is impure, and excessive laughter—one should vomit these up. (224)
One should not indulge excessively in sleeping or eating, nor in water; one should avoid fire, sunlight, swimming, vehicles, and even riding animals (225).
One should also avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, running, and travel.

One should abandon fighting, singing, and reciting for a muhūrta after eating. Even if eaten at the proper time, food that is light and suitable to one's constitution does not undergo digestion in a person due to excessive drinking of water, irregular eating, suppression of natural urges, and the reversal of sleep patterns.
Food consumed by one possessed of envy, fear, or anger; by one who is greedy; by one afflicted by disease or dejection; or by one filled with hatred, does not reach proper digestion.
That which is eaten when the previous meal is undigested is called *adhyashana* (overeating). 228–229.

When the digestive fire is weak after a previous meal, one should not take food twice in a day. Eating while the previously consumed food is still undigested destroys the digestive fire. Furthermore, eating in the morning when the evening meal has not yet been digested is like consuming poison.

If there should be a suspicion of indigestion in the morning, then one should eat a small amount of food at the mealtime after consuming *abhayā* (harītakī) powdered with ginger and rock salt along with cold water; furthermore,
out of fear of the loss of longevity, a wise man should not indulge in a woman during the day.
If one should practice [the path] involuntarily, then during the summer and spring seasons:
sitting bestows complexion, phlegm, stoutness, delicacy, and happiness;
walking destroys complexion, phlegm, stoutness, and delicacy. 234–235.
Furthermore, walking that does not cause excessive strain to the body bestows longevity,
strength, intelligence, and digestive fire, and awakens the senses.
(236) Wearing a turban produces luster, benefits the hair, and removes dust, wind, and phlegm.
Therefore, that which is light is recommended; heavy footwear causes pitta disorders and eye diseases.
Wearing shoes is declared to be beneficial for the eyes, longevity, and the feet; it facilitates easy movement, bestows ojas, and is aphrodisiac.
Constant walking on foot without shoes always leads to ill health, shortens life, impairs the senses, and obstructs one's vision;
whereas carrying an umbrella wards off rain, heat, wind, and dust. (239)
Carrying a staff is said to destroy cold, to be beneficial for the eyes, and even auspicious;
it increases one's courage, energy, strength, stability, fortitude, and splendor, provides support, and destroys fear. 240–241.
A palanquin that is provided with an upper covering is dear to all;
mounting it is considered to pacify the three *doṣas* for men. However, it is harmful to those afflicted by diseases of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*), and it causes vertigo. (242)
An elephant causes an increase in bile and wind, and promotes prosperity, longevity, and nourishment.
Riding a horse is considered to produce wind, bile, digestive fire, and fatigue;
it destroys fat, complexion, and phlegm, and is most beneficial for those who possess strength. 243–244.
Sunlight causes perspiration, fainting, hemorrhagic disorders, thirst, exhaustion, fatigue, a burning sensation, and discoloration; shade relieves these.
Rain is aphrodisiac, cold weather is strengthening, and sleep induces lethargy.
It is terrifying, causes delusion, is deceptive, and increases phlegm and wind.
(246) Fire destroys wind, phlegm, stiffness, cold, and shivering; it pacifies undigested matter (*āma*) and occlusion (*abhiṣyanda*), but provokes blood-bile (*raktapitta*). (247)
Smoke immediately produces phlegm and is extremely harmful to the eyes;
it causes heaviness of the head and also agitates the wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
One should cultivate friendship with the virtuous and maintain affection for the good in every way.

One should associate with the virtuous and abandon the company of the wicked. (249) One should serve the gods, the brahmins, the elders, physicians, the king, and guests; one should not turn away those who seek help, nor should one despise anyone at all. (250)
One should always remain endowed with humility in the presence of gurus;
one should never engage in such acts as stretching out one's feet there.
A man should be intent on doing good even toward one who is intent on doing harm.
One should view all beings as oneself and dwell far away from enemies.
One should not reveal any enemy of one's own, nor oneself as an enemy to anyone; one should not disclose insults received, nor one's lack of affection for the master. (252–253)
One should not look at one's own reflection in water, nor should one enter the water naked;
likewise, one should not enter water whose depth is unknown, nor that inhabited by predatory creatures.
(254) One should speak at the proper time words that are beneficial, measured, truthful, consistent, and sweet.

One should eat food that is predominantly sweet, unctuous, wholesome, and moderate in quantity at the proper time. (255) One should not eat curd at night, nor should it be entirely saltless; likewise, it should not be without mung-bean soup, nor without honey, nor without ghee and sugar. (256)
Observing the disposition of people, one who is skilled in winning over others should accommodate each person exactly as they find satisfaction;
for no one is happy alone, nor is anyone entirely trusting or entirely suspicious in every situation.
One should never desist from exertion when there is a cause, but one should not envy the fruit;
one should never suppress the impulses of the vital breaths, yet one should restrain the impulses of the mind; one should not torment the senses, nor should one indulge them excessively.

In rain, heat, and similar conditions, one should protect the body by carrying an umbrella; at night or in times of danger, one should wear shoes. One should walk while looking only a yoke’s length ahead.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms, nor should one walk directly across a mass of fire.
One should not board a doubtful boat, nor climb a tree, nor mount a defective vehicle (261).
A wise person should not, while in an assembly, make a sound with an uncovered mouth,
such as coughing, laughing, belching, yawning, or sneezing (262).
One should not pick one's nose, nor should one ever sit with the buttocks raised high; one should not stand for long with the knees raised, nor should one scratch the ground with the fingernail.
One should never allow the dust from a broom to fall upon the body.

One should not cut grass with one's fingernail, nor should one touch a Brāhmaṇa while impure from food remnants. 264 One should never look at the sun when it is eclipsed, nor when it is rising, nor when it has set, nor when it is reflected in water. 265
One should never constantly look at minute things, nor at blazing objects, impurities, or unpleasant sights;
one should never show the rainbow (the bow of Indra) to anyone at any time.
One should not desire battle with the powerful, nor should one carry a burden upon one's head.
One should not strike one's limbs, nor should one shake one's hair with the hand (267).
One should not walk between two venerable persons, nor between a husband and wife; one should never eat the food of an enemy, nor even the food of a courtesan (268).
One should never act as a guarantor, nor should one serve as a witness in vain (269).
One should never hold a pawn, and one should abandon gambling from afar (270). One should not place trust in women, nor should one allow them to act independently.
They must always be protected with effort, especially during their youth.
One should not sleep on a broken bed, nor even on one with many gaps; nor alone in a temple, nor indeed at night beneath a tree.

Thus, a man devoted to right conduct should always pass his days; thereafter, he should perform the duties prescribed for the night. (273) Thus has conduct been briefly described; whoever should practice it...
He obtains long life, health, joy, righteousness, wealth, and fame.
(274) A wise man should avoid these five activities during the twilight hours: eating, sexual intercourse, sleep, recitation, and traveling on the road. (275)
From food arises disease; from sexual intercourse, deformity of the fetus; from sleep, poverty; from study, the loss of life; and from travel, fear.
(276) Moonlight is cool, bestows the bliss of love, and removes thirst, bile, and burning heat.
Then, when its qualities are diminished, it necessarily produces wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha).

Darkness (tamas), which brings about fear, becomes the cause of delusion and disorientation regarding the directions; it increases bile (pitta), heart-disease, phlegm, and desire, and causes lassitude. (277–278)
One should eat at night during the first watch, consuming a meal that is slightly less than full; one should avoid there food that is difficult to digest.
For the embodied being, a constant desire for sexual pleasure arises within the body.
Due to the absence of sexual intercourse, there is an increase in urine and fat, as well as flaccidity of the body;
a woman is called a "child" (bālā) until she reaches sixteen years of age, and thereafter she is known as "young" (taruṇī) up to thirty-two years. 280–281.

Ascending beyond that, she may remain so until the age of fifty; thereafter she is known as "old" (*vṛddhā*), devoid of the festival of sexual pleasure. A young girl (*bālā*) is considered beneficial for those seeking sensual enjoyment during the summer and autumn seasons. (282)
A young woman should be resorted to during the cold season, and a mature woman during the rainy and spring seasons.
A girl, when constantly resorted to, always increases one's strength; a young woman diminishes one's vitality, while a mature woman brings on old age.
Fresh meat, new food, young women, a milk-based diet, ghee, and bathing in warm water—these six are immediately life-sustaining.
Putrid meat, old women, young girls, and fresh curd [are immediately fatal]. 285.
Sexual intercourse at dawn and sleep [during the day]—these six immediately take away life.
(286) Even an old man attains youth by approaching a young woman; but by approaching a woman older than himself in age, a young man becomes like an elder. (287)
Venerable sirs, those who are restrained with women possess youthfulness, free from the decrepitude of old age, endowed with beauty and strength, and have firm, well-developed muscles;
even when rendered virile by *vājīkaraṇa* treatments in winter, they may indulge in desire according to their will. (288)
One may indulge in sexual intercourse at will during the onset of the cold season;
however, during spring and autumn one should do so every third day, and during the rainy season and the heat of summer, every fifth day.
Indeed, a man should approach his wife once every three days.
In all seasons, however, during the heat, the wise man should go every fortnight;
in the cold season at night, in summer by day, in spring both day and night, during the rains when the clouds roar, and in the autumn from the lake—thus one should remember [the practice]. 291–292.
A man should not approach his wife during the two twilights, nor on the sacred festival days (parvan), nor at the time of cow-releasing (gosarga), nor at midnight, nor even at midday.
He should engage in dalliance with his wife in a place that is well-concealed.
A woman should not take delight in a place that is pleasant, where the singing of women is audible, which is fragrant with a gentle breeze,
yet situated near elders, exposed,
and causes great embarrassment; nor should she take delight when hearing words that are a cause of distress.
Having bathed, his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, fragrant and adorned with fine flowers, having eaten aphrodisiacs, well-dressed, elegantly attired, and beautifully decorated;
with a mouth full of betel, devoted to his wife, and overflowing with passion. (296)
A man desiring a son should approach his wife on an auspicious bed (297).

One who has overeaten, one lacking self-control, one who is hungry, one with aching limbs, one who is thirsty, a child, an old man, one afflicted by other morbid urges, or one suffering from disease should avoid sexual intercourse (298).

One who is desirous, being himself joyful and strengthened by aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*), should appropriately enjoy his wife— who is endowed with beauty and virtue, of similar character, born of a noble family, full of desire, joyful, and adorned— provided she is a young woman. (299)
One who is menstruating, one who is unwilling, one who is soiled, and likewise one who is unpleasant;
one advanced in caste, one advanced in age, and likewise one afflicted by disease;
one with missing limbs, one who is pregnant, one who is hateful, and one possessed of a vaginal disorder. (300–301)
From that, there would be a loss of sight, lifespan, and vigor, as well as unrighteousness (303).

Furthermore, for one who approaches a woman wearing ascetic marks, the wife of a guru, a woman of the same lineage, an elderly woman, or [approaches them] during the sacred festivals or at the two twilights, there is a depletion of life-force (304).
If she is pregnant, there will be pain for the fetus; if she is diseased, there will be loss of strength.
For one who approaches a woman who is deficient in limbs, dirty, disliked, emaciated, or barren, in an uncovered place, his semen becomes diminished and his mind becomes despondent. (305–306)

One who is hungry, agitated in mind, thirsty at midday, or weak experiences the loss of semen and the provocation of wind (vāyu) while standing. For one who is diseased, pain, enlargement of the spleen, fainting, and even death may arise.

At dawn and at midnight, wind and bile are aggravated. Likewise, in the case of birth as an animal, in a non-vaginal birth, or in a deformed birth canal, there occurs venereal sores (upadaṃśa), the provocation of wind, and the depletion of semen and pleasure. 308–309.
By suppressing urine, feces, and semen, and by remaining in a supine position, the formation of seminal stones (śukrāśmarī) occurs quickly;
therefore, one should avoid all of this, as it is detrimental to both worlds. 310.
When semen has been discharged due to delusion, it must never be retained.
Bathing, milk with sugar, food prepared with sugarcane products, meat broth, wind-inducing [diet], and sleep—these are beneficial at the conclusion of sexual intercourse. (311–312)
Diseases such as pain from spears, cough, fever, dyspnea, emaciation, anemia, consumption,
and convulsions arise from excessive sexual indulgence.
Staying awake at night is parching and overcomes disorders of phlegm (kapha), as well as poison and affliction.
Sleep, when indulged in at the proper time, indeed brings about equilibrium of the bodily constituents, freedom from fatigue,
nourishment, complexion, strength, energy, and a brightening of the digestive fire—
for he who licks the powder of *bījapūra* petals mixed with honey at the time of retiring to bed.

But he sleeps happily because the spreading of the shameful wind is obstructed. He who drinks eight mouthfuls of water at the time of sunrise shall live for more than a hundred years, freed from disease and old age. 316–317.
Hemorrhoids, swellings, dysentery, fever, abdominal enlargements, old age, leprosy,
disorders of fat, urinary obstructions, internal hemorrhaging, diseases of the ears, throat, head, hips, and eyes—
whatever other diseases exist in living beings caused by wind, bile, injury, or phlegm.
Just as milk drunk at the end of the night removes various [impurities] through the practice of repeated application; so indeed,

the man who rises every morning during a clear night and drinks water through the nostril becomes full of wisdom, his eyes become equal to those of Tārkṣya, and he is freed from wrinkles, grey hair, and all diseases.
Water should be inhaled through the nose in a measure of exactly three *prasṛti*s.

This practice destroys deformities, wrinkles, and graying hair; it removes chronic rhinitis, hoarseness, cough, and swelling; and when practiced as a nasal therapy at the end of nightfall, it acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that restores sight. (320–321)

One should avoid that water when oil has been drunk, in cases of injury, after purification (emesis/purgation), in abdominal distension, in a stiff abdomen, in hiccups, and in diseases arising from kapha and vāta,
for it indeed causes the aggravation of the humors and the destruction of the body's essence.
That which is declared as the six seasons [is determined] by the Sun’s transit through the zodiac signs: 323.
Aries and Taurus are said to be summer; Gemini and Cancer are the rainy season (prāvṛṣ); Leo and Virgo are remembered as the autumnal rains (varṣā); and Libra and Scorpio are autumn (śarad). 324.
The two bow-holders (Dhanurgrāhau) are Hemanta and Vasanta;
Śiśira, Puṣpasamaya, Grīṣma, Varṣā, Śarad, and Himā are the six seasons, corresponding respectively to the pairs of months beginning with Māgha. 325–326.

In the region south of the Gaṅgā, because of the abundance of rain, both seasons are designated by the sages as *prāvṛṭ* and *varṣā*; whereas in the region north of that very river, due to the great prevalence of snow... [327]
These two are declared to be the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira (328). By the former [seasons] there is the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), and by the latter the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
The former is hot and robs one of strength; the other is cold and bestows strength (329).
The Hemanta season is cool, unctuous, sweet, and stimulates the digestive fire;
the Śiśira season is exceedingly cold, dry, and increases wind and digestive fire.
The Vasanta season is sweet, unctuous, and causes an increase in phlegm.
Summer is dry, extremely pungent, generates pitta, and destroys kapha.
(331) The rainy season is cold, causes a burning sensation, diminishes the digestive fire, and increases vāta.
Autumn is warm, generates pitta in men, and brings about moderate strength. (332)

The accumulation, provocation, and pacification of *vāyu* occur during the three seasons beginning with summer; those of *pitta* during the three beginning with the rainy season; and those of *śleṣman* during the three beginning with winter.
During the [seasons] beginning with autumn, the wind (*samīraṇa*) is accumulated by means of light and dry medicinal substances.

In such a body, that same [pitta] does not become aggravated by the heat of the season. (334) Through water and medicinal herbs that have an acidic post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*), that same pitta undergoes accumulation and aggravation, but not due to the coldness of the season. (335)
Kapha is accumulated by water and medicinal herbs that are unctuous and cold;

when the season and the body are similar [to its own nature], it does not become aggravated due to its state of being congealed. Pitta subsides in the cold season, while Vāyu and Śleṣman (Kapha) are accumulated.
That wind indeed becomes provoked in the early winter (śiśira), just as accumulated phlegm does;
phlegm, which was stored during the late winter (hemanta), increases excessively in the early winter,
yet it does not become provoked because its coldness is suppressed by substances that are cold, unctuous, and heavy.
Thus, this is the nature of time: by the power of food and other factors, the *doṣas* undergo accumulation (*caya*) and so forth even instantaneously, yet especially at specific times.
Through lifestyle, diet, and habits, the *doṣas* undergo accumulation, provocation (*kopa*), and pacification (*praśama*).
When the humors (doṣas) move with those of their own kind, even at an improper time, they lead to a state of equilibrium; when they move with those of the opposite kind, the reverse occurs.
When a humor increases while remaining in its own location, there is stiffness and swelling, a yellowish appearance, weakness of the digestive fire, and heaviness of the limbs.
Laziness is the cause of accumulation, while aversion is the characteristic of accumulation.
When the faults are removed during this accumulation, they do not attain further development;
however, in subsequent states, they become even more powerful. (342–343)
In the rainy season, the wind is particularly strong; therefore, the three tastes beginning with sweet (sweet, sour, and salty) should be consumed especially for the pacification of the wind (vāta).
This is because, during the rains, the body specifically becomes moistened.
To pacify that moisture, even the three [tastes] beginning with pungent (kaṭu) should be used;
likewise, sudation, massage, curd, warm meat from wild animals, *śāli* rice, barley, wheat, well water, and rainwater should be employed. 345–346.
One should avoid the east wind, rain, heat, cold, fatigue, riverbanks, sleeping by day, dry food, and constant sexual intercourse (347).
One should consume ghee and that which is sweet, astringent, or bitter in taste, as well as what is cool and light.

Milk, clear white sugarcane juice of sharp flavor, a small amount of lean meat from wild animals, wheat, barley, mung beans, and rice, river water, fine rice-gruel, moonlight, sandalwood, camphor, turmeric, garlands, and a spotless garment. (348)
That which is filled with rays of the moon at night is known as *aṃśūdaka*; it is unctuous and removes the three *doṣas*. [The remedies for fatigue are:
resting among groups of friends, sweet words, and sporting in a lake.

For those with pitta disorders, purgation is appropriate, as is bloodletting for the strong; these are the wholesome regimens during the period of the rainy season's end. One should avoid curd, physical exercise, sour, pungent, hot, and sharp foods, daytime sleep, cold things, and sunlight.
Sugarcane, *śāli* rice, mung beans, spring water, and boiled milk [are recommended].
In autumn, these are wholesome: the rays of the moon at dusk;
breakfast consisting of sour food, desired salts, ointments, heat, and physical exertion;
wheat, sugarcane products, rice, beans, meat, flour, fresh grain, and sesame seeds.

In the winter season, one should use musk combined with excellent saffron and agallochum, perform cleansing with warm water, enjoy the company of women, wear heavy and warm clothing, and partake of unctuous food (351).
In the early spring, there is excessive cold and dryness born of the pre-winter season; therefore, the regimen prescribed for winter is especially recommended for that time (352).
In the spring, one should employ emesis, nasal medication (nasya), and *abhayā* with honey; one should practice physical exercise and use massage (udvartana).
One should consume a gargle (kavala) that subdues *kapha*, as well as pungent meat from wild animals (*jāṅgala*), wheat, various types of rice, mung beans, barley, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice.

A wise person should avoid in the springtime unguents made of sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, and aloe-wood; as well as dry, pungent, or hot foods, light meals, sweet and sour foods, curd, oily substances, daytime sleep, and even dew, for these are difficult to digest. (353–354)
