On hot days, one should consume substances that are sweet, unctuous, cold, and light; liquid preparations such as *rasālā*, sugar, flour, milk, and the meat of wild animals; rice-soup with sugar and meat; moonlight, daytime sleep, sandalwood paste, cool water, and refreshing drinks. However, one should avoid pungent, alkaline, and sour foods, as well as heat and physical exertion. (355)
The man who conducts himself according to these rules during these seasons never incurs any defects caused by the seasons.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa.
The fifth chapter on the daily regimen and so forth is concluded.
Now begins the sixth chapter, the Miscellaneous Chapter (Miśraprakaraṇa). Disease is the imbalance of the humors (doṣa); the equilibrium of the humors is health.
For diseases such as fever and the like are indeed the givers of suffering;
some of them are said to be innate, while others are known to be adventitious;
some are declared to be mental, and some are described as physical.
Some diseases are said to be born of karma, others are born of the bodily humors (doṣas), and still others arise from both karma and the humors; thus, diseases are remembered as being of three types.
Those caused by karma are eliminated through the exhaustion of karma, while those born of the humors are cured by their respective medicinal remedies.

Those [diseases] arising from the defects of karma reach their end through the exhaustion of those karmic defects. Diseases are traditionally classified as threefold: curable, manageable, and incurable.
The curable type is said to be of two kinds: easily curable and difficult to cure.
One should know that [the disease] is palliable (yāpya) when it is sustained by treatment; for it is treatment that maintains it.
However, that which perishes immediately once treatment has ceased is incurable.
Treatment, when applied, sustains the patient who is palliable and brings them comfort.
Just as a pillar, though carefully erected, might fall as if the house were collapsing;
likewise, curable diseases turn into palliable ones, and palliable ones turn into incurable ones.
Furthermore, incurable diseases take away the lives of men who do not undergo treatment.
That other disorder which arises from the provocation of the doṣa that initiated the disease is called a complication (upadrava) by the wise.
Since the death of the patient is observed to be inevitable because of it, [it is so designated].
A tallakṣaṇa is called *ariṣṭa*, and it is also described as a sign of impending death (*ariṣṭa*). That action which removes disease is designated as *cikitsā* (therapeutics);
that which establishes the equilibrium of the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and *malas* is indeed the destroyer of disease.

Those actions by which the bodily constituents (dhātus) are restored to equilibrium constitute the treatment of disorders; that is considered the work of physicians. For it is that [treatment] which pacifies an aggravated [dosha] and does not produce another disease.
That is true action which removes disease and does not provoke another;
a disease should be treated as soon as it arises and must not be neglected because of its smallness,
for even in its slightest form, it is like fire, an enemy, or poison— it causes great harm.
First, the physician should examine the disease; immediately thereafter, the medicine;
and subsequently, he should perform the treatment preceded by knowledge.
But that physician who undertakes treatments without having understood the disease [is to be condemned].
Even if one who knows the application of medicines achieves success by mere chance,
if he only knows how to prepare the remedy and does not understand the disease, he deserves punishment from the king if he performs such medical treatment. 16–17.

But he who knows only the disease and is unskilled in medicines—having obtained such a physician, the patient will be like a boat without a sailor. And he who knows only the scriptures but is unskilled in practical procedures; [is likewise lost]. (18)
He becomes bewildered upon encountering the afflicted patient, just as a coward does upon reaching the battlefield.
But for one who knows the specific nature of diseases, is skilled in all medicines,
and understands the distinctions of place and time, there is success without a doubt.

At the beginning and at the end of diseases, the physician should strive for knowledge; thereafter, he should perform the best medical treatment by means of the application of medicines. One who is unskilled in the names of diseases should never feel ashamed.

Indeed, there is no permanent stability for any morbid transformation (vikāra) by name alone. Since there is no disease without the humors (doṣas), therefore the physician should treat the disease even if it has not been explicitly mentioned, by means of the signs of the humors.
Those who do not provide medical treatment for those whose conditions are incurable are the best of physicians;
therefore, physicians should exert effort in examining what is curable and what is incurable.
(24) In cold, one should apply a remedy against the cold; in heat, one should provide protection against the heat.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should perform the rite that has been reached; one must not let the time for the rite pass by.

Whether the time for the rite has not yet arrived or has already passed, a rite that is not performed, or one that is deficient or excessive, does not succeed even when the goals are to be accomplished.
To perform a great treatment for a minor disorder, or a mild treatment for a severe one—these two constitute lack of skill; skill consists in the appropriate application of treatment.
Furthermore, if the desired result is not obtained from the treatment, one should employ another treatment.
In the eastern [quarter], at Śāntavegā, no confusion of ritual acts is beneficial.
(28) No confusion of ritual acts is beneficial when the acts are of a similar form; however, there is no fault in such confusion when they are of different forms. (29)
Moreover, a wise physician does not rely exclusively on a prescribed treatise; he must himself exercise critical judgment in his medical practice,
for a particular condition may arise in relation to the strength of the humors and the time.

In which [action] what ought to be done becomes what ought not to be done, and action is devoid of its proper function; where at times there is wealth, at times friendship, at times dharma, at times fame, and at times the mere habit of action—in such a case, medical treatment is not fruitless. (31–32)
Those who practice the methods taught in Ayurveda for the sake of others' welfare become endowed with merit, long life, and increase [of prosperity], and remain free from disease.
One should never, out of greed, sell the merit of one's medical treatment.
If one seeks wealth from lords of great riches for the sake of a livelihood,
that foolish person who does not repay the body’s medical treatment by giving its value— the physician shall enjoy all the merit that person performs. (34–35)
There was no land devoid of men, nor were there men free from disease;
consequently, everywhere the livelihoods of physicians were well-established.
(36) A patient, a messenger, a physician, long life, wealth, and a good servant—[these are the six requisites].
The wise have declared that these are the constituent factors of medical treatment, beginning with the medicine itself.
(37) Listen now to what will be explained regarding the nature of the disease, the patient who possesses that disease, the kind of patient who is curable, and likewise the kind who is incurable. (38)

A patient who possesses his own natural constitution and complexion, who is endowed with mental strength (*sattva*), who is devoted to his physician, and who has conquered his senses, is curable by physicians; likewise, one who is long-lived, courageous, wealthy, and has friends is also curable. (39)
A patient who is treatable by physicians is one who follows the doctor’s instructions and possesses faith.
(40) One who is fierce, reckless, timid, ungrateful, or agitated; one overwhelmed by grief, desirous of death, or deprived of his sense organs—such a person is not to be treated. (41)

An enemy, one who is cleverly deceptive regarding his medical knowledge, one devoid of faith, one who is suspicious, and one who is not obedient to the physicians—these types of patients should not be treated by physicians.
By treating these individuals, a physician may incur many faults. (42-43)

The messenger who goes to fetch the physician is now described, as well as the kind of messenger who is appropriate for this purpose. (44) Messengers should be of noble birth, free from physical defects, capable, and dressed in clean garments.
Happy people mounted on horses and bulls, endowed with white flowers and fruits,
of the same caste, well-behaved, and gathered in the direction of life (the east), reach the physician at the proper time for the sake of the patient's well-being. 45-46.
For a messenger going to summon a physician on behalf of a patient,
an auspicious gentle omen is not favorable, whereas a "blazing" (dīpta) omen brings happiness. For instance, one should not go empty-handed to see a king, a physician, or a teacher.
One should predict the fruit from its fruit regarding an astrologer, a deity, and a friend.
He who performs medical treatment is called a physician; and he is described as being of such a kind as is truly proficient. 48–49.
One who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures, has observed the practical application of the work, is self-reliant,
light-handed, pure, brave, equipped with ready implements and medicines,
possessed of presence of mind, wise, industrious, and pleasant of speech— 50.
And a physician who is devoted to truth and righteousness—such a one is praised.
(51) One who is poorly dressed, harsh, stubborn, rustic, or merely self-referential—these five types of physicians are not honored, even if they are equal to Dhanvantari himself. (52)

Thorough knowledge of the nature of the disease and the suppression of the pain—this constitutes the medical expertise of a physician; however, the physician is not the master of life. At the outset, the physician should diligently examine the patient's lifespan.
Then, when the lifespan is extensive, medical treatment becomes fruitful.
He whose gaze is gentle, and likewise whose ears and mouth [are so], who perceives sweet fragrances—he is curable; of this there is no doubt. (54–55)

He whose hands and feet are warm, whose burning sensation is very slight, and whose tongue is soft— that patient does not perish. (56) He whose fever is devoid of perspiration and whose breath passes through the nostrils [is likewise saved].
If the throat becomes free of phlegm, that patient will certainly live.
He whose sleep is easy and whose body becomes radiant, and whose sense organs are clear—that patient does not perish. 57–58.
Learn from me, both in brief and in detail, the signs of impending death (ariṣṭa) for one whose body or character undergoes a transformation from their natural state:
They say that one who suddenly cannot hear sounds has reached the end of his life.
He who perceives cold as if it were warm, and warmth as if it were cold, or whose body becomes excessively hot and trembles violently from even slight cold, [is likewise near death].
He who does not perceive a blow, nor even the severing of a limb, and who regards his limbs as if they were merely covered with dust;
indeed, for him, there may be changes in complexion or streaks upon the body. (62)
Furthermore, he whom female bees attend while he is bathed and anointed,
or he who perceives tastes in a distorted manner, or he who no longer discerns tastes at all— he is declared to be one whose life has departed.
One who perceives fragrance as foul odor, or grasps foul odor as fragrance,
and perceives scent otherwise— such a person is free from disease when the lamp has been extinguished.
Or one who sees the sun blazing at night, or the moon shining with brilliance during the day.
He who sees the celestial lights during the day as if they were ablaze; he who sees dark, dense clouds charged with lightning in a cloudless sky;
and he who sees the atmosphere crowded with celestial chariots, vehicles, and palaces—66–67.
And he who beholds the wind personified in the atmosphere,
as if the earth were shrouded in garments of smoke and mist; or who sees the world as if ablaze, or as if submerged in water.
He who sees the earth marked with lines in the shape of a chessboard (aṣṭāpada),
he who does not see the stars, nor the goddess Arundhatī, nor the Pole Star (dhruva), nor the celestial Gaṅgā— of him they say that his life has come to an end. (69–70)
He who does not see his reflection in a mirror, in water, or in fire;

or who sees it with a missing limb, or deformed, or as belonging to another being—such as a dog, a crow, a *kaṅka* crane, a vulture, a *preta*, a *yakṣa*, or a *rākṣasa*—[is one whose death is near]. (71)

The sick man meets death, and the healthy one may fall ill. (72) He whose modesty and prosperity perish, and whose splendor, vitality, memory, and radiance suddenly desert him—he has undoubtedly lost his life. (73)
If his lower lip has fallen away or is turned upward, and likewise his upper lip,
or if both lips have the appearance of a *jāmbava* fruit, his life is difficult to preserve. (74) If his teeth are reddish, or dark-brown, or are falling out;
Or if there is a reflection like that of a wagtail, one should declare his life to have reached its end. Indeed, he whose tongue is black, smeared, empty,
or rough, shall soon abandon his vital breaths.
A man whose nose is crooked, cracked, or dry, or which quivers or is broken, does not live. Likewise,
one whose eyes are narrowed, distorted, fixed, parched, or tearful [does not survive].
He whose ears become swollen is certainly a man whose life has reached its end. He whose hair parts at the crown, whose eyebrows are drawn together and drooping,
and whose eyelashes roll upward, goes soon to death.
He who does not swallow food remaining in his mouth, nor supports his head,
being of deluded mind with one-pointed vision, immediately abandons his life-breaths;
he who, though being raised up many times, falls into a state of total stupor.
Whether strong or weak, the physician should declare that patient to be ripe for death. He who has constant sleep, or who stays awake at all times,
or who faints when wishing to speak— he should be rejected by the wise man as one whose life is ended.

One who licks his upper lip, one who makes spitting sounds, or one who converses with ghosts at night—one should designate him as having the form of a ghost. Furthermore, one from whose pores and hair-follicles blood flows— [he is likewise to be known]. 83.
In a person not afflicted by poison, that [poison] would cause him to lose his life instantly;
however, when a disorder increases despite being properly treated in one whose strength and flesh have wasted away, that is the sign of one whose life has departed. 84–85.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and various types of rākṣasas constantly approach the living being who is facing death,
and with intent to kill, they counteract the potencies of those medicines. (86)

Therefore, all actions of one whose life has ended become utterly futile. (87) Since all those such as the sick depend upon material resources, there is no medicine without wealth; thus, wealth is a constituent part of medical treatment. (88)

An attendant who is affectionate, free from disgust, strong, diligent in protecting the patient, compliant with the physician’s instructions, and tireless is fit for service. (89) A substance by which a physician removes disease is called medicine.
Therefore, I shall describe that which is necessarily disease-destroying:
produced in an auspicious place, extracted on an auspicious day, small in quantity yet possessing many qualities, and endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste. (90–91)
Medicine that destroys the doshas, does not cause exhaustion, and does not produce adverse effects when administered at the proper time after due consideration brings about beneficial results.
(92) The Vindhya mountains and others are known to be fiery (āgneya), while the snowy mountain (Himalaya) is considered lunar (saumya).
Therefore, those medicinal herbs should be gathered according to their specific causes [and requirements]. They grow in other forests and groves as well;
one who is pure and of good mind should collect them in the morning on an auspicious day. (93–94)

Facing the sun, observing silence, and having bowed to Śiva in his heart, he should take earth from a common site located in the northern direction. [He should avoid earth] born from anthills, desolate places, marshy lands, cremation grounds, salty soil, or roads. 95.95–96ab.
Plants pervaded by insects, fire, or frost are not effective for their intended purpose.
In autumn, one should collect medicinal herbs that are full of sap for the sake of all therapeutic actions;
however, for the purpose of purgation and emesis, one should gather them at the end of spring.
One should certainly take the bark of those plants whose roots are very thick;
a wise person should also take all those whose roots are fine. As for those whose large roots are entirely filled with wood on all sides, [one should take their bark]. 98.

Of those [plants], the bark should be taken, with the roots all cut short. The bark of the *nyagrodha* and others should be taken; the heartwood (*sāra*) comes from the *vījakā* and so forth; the leaves from the *tālīsa* and so forth; and the fruit from the *triphalā* and so forth. (99–100)
In some places the root, in some the bulb, in some the leaf, in some the fruit, in some the flower, in some everything, in some the pith, and in some the bark;
Citraka, Sūraṇa, Nimba, Vāsā, and Triphalā respectively. 101.
Dhātakī, Kaṇṭakārī, Khadira, and milk-exuding trees (102); in some cases one may take the leaves of Nimba, or even its bark in the absence of leaves;
likewise, the tender fruit of Bilva and the ripe fruit of Āragvadha (103).
If a specific part is not mentioned, the hair (jaṭā) is to be taken; if a portion is not mentioned, the whole is divided equally;
if a vessel is not mentioned, it should be made of clay; if a time is not mentioned, it is the break of dawn. Indeed, only fresh substances are to be employed in all ritual acts.
Except for *viḍaṅga* and *kṛṣṇā*, [these substances] should be used with jaggery, grain, ghee, and honey.
Old betel leaf is highly recommended, as is sour gruel (*kāñjika*); furthermore, dried substances should be employed in all ritual acts. 105–106.
One should employ double the amount of Ādra-raṅga; this is the rule for all cases.
Guḍūcī, kuṭaja, vāsā, kūṣmāṇḍa, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, sahacara, śatapuṣpā, and prasāriṇī—107.

O King, these should always be employed; one must never cause them to be used in double measure. (108) Vāsā, nimba, paṭola, ketakī, balā, kūṣmāṇḍaka, indīvarī, varṣābhū, kuṭaja, along with kanda, pūtigandhā, amṛtā, indrī, nāgabalā, kuruṇṭaka, puracchatrā, and amṛtā—these are always [to be used].
However, those [liquids] that already contain salt should never be used twice over in various tasks by the wise.
(109) Ghee, oil, water, decoctions, condiments, and so forth—once cooked and then cooled, all of them become like poison if reheated. (110)
The *pathyā* (harītakī) that has fine bones and flesh is honored for all medical procedures;
likewise, those *bhallātakī* fruits which sink when thrown into water are considered the best.
The tuber known as *vārāhī-kanda* has a root shaped like the head of a boar.

Sauvarcala salt has the appearance of glass, while saindhava has the luster of crystal; the excellent svarṇamākṣika is known to have the hue of gold. Manohvā is considered excellent when it resembles the flower of the oḍra plant.

The best *śilājatu* is known to be that which, when thrown into a bell-metal vessel filled with water, does not disintegrate, but instead increases by spreading out. Camphor is cooling and unctuous; small cardamom is excellent.
White sandalwood is exceedingly fragrant and highly honored by the gurus.
Red sandalwood is considered most excellent when it is intensely crimson.
That which resembles the beak of a crow, being glossy and heavy, is regarded as the best and most venerable.
Devadāru is considered excellent when it is fragrant, light, and dry;
sarala is highly beneficial when it is very fragrant and exceedingly unctuous.
Furthermore, the wood known as dāruniśā should be understood by the wise to be most praiseworthy when it is intensely yellow.
Jātīphala (nutmeg) that is heavy, unctuous, symmetrical, and bright within is excellent.
Mṛdvīkā (raisins) should be known as the best when they resemble the udder of a cow;
those shaped like the fruit of the karamarda are declared to be middling. 118–119.

The finest *khaṇḍa* is pure and excellent, with a luster like that of moonstone (*candrakānta*), resembling cow’s clarified butter (*gavyājya*), and possessing a pleasing fragrance; it is considered the best honey.
Among the *śāli* rice varieties, the red *śāli* is the best, and among the *ṣaṣṭika* varieties, the *ṣaṣṭika* itself is the best. (120)
Among awned grains, barley and wheat are considered the best;
among legumes, mung bean, lentil, and pigeon pea are likewise excellent.
Among tastes, the sweet is the most superior, and among salts, rock salt (saindhava) is the best.

Pomegranate, emblic myrobalan, grapes, dates, *parūṣaka*, *rājādana*, and citron are recommended among the groups of fruits. Among leafy vegetables, *vāstūka*, *jīvantī*, and *potikā* are excellent. 123.

Among leaf-vegetables, the *paṭola* is recommended; among bulbous vegetables, the *sūraṇa*. Among animals of the arid regions (*jāṅgala*), the black antelope (*eṇa*), the spotted deer (*kuraṅga*), and the *hariṇa* are praised.
Among birds, the partridge (*tittiri*) and the quail (*lāva*) are excellent; among fish, the *rohita* is the best. (124–125)
The *hariṇa* deer is copper-colored, while the *eṇa* is considered black;
the *kuraṅga* is described as copper-colored and large, having the form of a *hariṇa*.
Among waters, [cow's milk] is divine; among milks, that of the cow; and among clarified butters, that produced from a cow.
Among oils, sesame oil is beneficial; among products of sugarcane, white sugar is wholesome.
One should avoid mung beans among pulses during the summer season, and salt from saline soil among salts.
Among fruits, the breadfruit (lakuca) is not recommended, and among leafy vegetables, mustard is considered unwholesome.

Among the meats of domestic animals, beef is not beneficial; buffalo fat, ewe’s milk, safflower oil, and molasses should be avoided. One should also refrain from fish and the meat of marshy animals when combined with milk.
One should avoid pigeon meat fried in mustard oil;
likewise, one should avoid fish with milk products or honey;
one should avoid roasted grain flour (saktu) combined with meat or milk, and one should avoid curd with anything that is not hot.
One should avoid honey with warm rainwater, milk-rice mixed with *kṛsarā*, plantains accompanied by buttermilk, curd, or *bilva* fruit;
likewise, ghee that has stood for ten days in a bronze vessel, and honey and ghee in equal parts. (132)

One should discard cooked food that has turned sour and has been reheated. (133) Many types of meat mixed together in one place are mutually incompatible, as are honey, clarified butter, fat, oil, water, and milk. (134)
Rock salt is said to be *saindhava*, and sandalwood is *raktacandana*.
Powders, electuaries, fermented liquors (*āsava*), and medicated fats should be prepared with white sandalwood;
however, for decoctions and medicinal pastes, *raktacandana* is generally employed. 135

Ajamodā and yavānikā are to be known for internal cleansing; that same ajamodikā is to be understood for external cleansing. In applications involving milk and clarified butter, only those derived from the cow are indeed to be taken.
Cow dung that has been recently excreted is called *gomūtra* (cow urine). 137.
In the absence of *citraka*, *dantī* or alkaline salt from *śikhari* may be used; or, in the absence of *dhanvayāsa*, *durālabhā* should be added. 138.
In the absence of *tagara*, however, the best of physicians should give *kuṣṭha*;
in the absence of *mūrvā*, the wise should take the bark produced from *jiṅginī*. In the absence of *ahiṃsrā*, *mānakanda* is prescribed.

In the absence of *lakṣmaṇā*, however, the crest of the peacock (*nīlakaṇṭhaśikhā*) is prescribed. In the absence of *vakula*, one should offer *kahlāra*, blue lotus (*utpala*), or red lotus (*paṅkaja*).
In the absence of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), it is desired that the night-lotus (*kumuda*) be offered. 140–141.

If *jātī* flower is not available, clove (*lavaṅga*) is offered there; indeed, in the absence of the juice of *arka* leaves and other such items, its resin is considered a substitute. In the absence of *pauṣkara*, costus (*kuṣṭha*) is used, and likewise in the absence of *lāṅgalī*.

In the absence of *sthauṇeyaka*, physicians prescribe *cavikā* and *gajapippalī*; these two are considered equivalent to the root of *piplī*. In the absence of *somarājī*, the fruit of *prapunnāḍa* is regarded as a substitute.
If *dāruniśā* (Indian berberry) is not available, then *niśā* (turmeric) should be given by the wise.

In the absence of *rasāñjana*, a decoction of *dārvī* (daruharidra) is employed; in the absence of *saurāṣṭrī* (borax), *sphaṭikā* (rock salt) possessing those same qualities should be given by people. 145–146.
In the absence of *tālīsapatraka*, *svarṇatālī* is recommended;
in the absence of *bhārṅgī*, however, one may use *tālīsa* or the root of *kaṇṭakārī*.
In the absence of *rucaka* salt, one should give salt derived from sand (*pāṃśu*). 147.
In the absence of licorice (madhuyaṣṭī), one should employ dhātakī;
in the absence of amlavetasa, cukra is prescribed to be given;
and if grapes (drākṣā) cannot be obtained, the fruit of kāśmarī should be administered. 148–149.
In the absence of those two, the wise consider the flower of the *madhūka* tree to be appropriate; furthermore, in the absence of *nakha*, the flower of the clove (*lavaṅga*) should be given.
In the absence of musk (*kastūrī*), the wise know that *kaṅkola* should be cast [into the mixture].
In the absence of kaṅkola, however, jātipuṣpa is offered. (151) In the absence of camphor, fragrant mustaka should be given by the wise;
in the absence of camphor, granthiparṇa should especially be given. (152)
In the absence of saffron, one should offer fresh kusumbha flowers;
in the absence of śrīkhaṇḍa sandalwood, camphor is desired to be offered.
However, in the absence of these two, the physician should instead employ red sandalwood.
In the absence of red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), the wise know that fresh *uśīra* is to be used.
In the absence of *mustā*, *ativiṣā* is prescribed; in the absence of *śivā*, *śivā* is considered acceptable.
In the absence of *nāgapuṣpa*, the filaments of the lotus (*padmakeśara*) are desired. 154–155.
In the absence of Medā, Ājīvakā, Kākoli, and Ṛddhi—these pairs—or even if they are unavailable, one should add Darī, Vidārī, Aśvagandhā, and Vārāhī in sequence;
and likewise, in the absence of Vārāhī, Carmakārāluka is considered a substitute. 156.
That which is known as *vārāhīkanda* is found in the west; it is also called *gṛṣṭi*.
Another variety of *vārīhīkanda* is considered to be *carmakārāluka*, which grows in marshy regions and is hairy like a boar (*varāha*). 157–158.
If bhallātaka is unavailable, red sandalwood is prescribed;
in the absence of bhallātaka, citra is used, and in the absence of nala, ikṣu. In the absence of gold, the wise man should add svarṇamākṣika. 159.
White honey (mākṣika) should certainly be known by the wise as being like silver.
In the absence of even honey, one should provide gold-ochre;
or else, where dead gold or silver cannot be obtained, [one should use it]. 160–161.
In that regard, a wise physician should perform the procedures using a magnet;
in the absence of a magnet, the best of physicians should employ sharp iron.
Even in the absence of a pearl, one should employ a pearl-oyster shell.
Where honey is not available, aged treacle is considered the substitute (163).
In the absence of granulated sugar, physicians should give white sugar; however, if white sugar is unavailable, sugar-candy should be used by the wise (164).
In the absence of milk, the juice of mung beans or black gram may be given;
among the various substances prescribed here, a knowledgeable physician should substitute one for another when any particular item is unavailable. 165.

Having carefully considered a substance in terms of its taste, potency, post-digestive transformation, and so forth, one should employ it; likewise, one who knows the tastes and other qualities of substances may employ another substance of a similar nature.
In a formulation, however, that which is not the primary ingredient is considered eligible for substitution.
Even that which is the primary ingredient may not be perceived as similar [to the disease];

one should discard a substance that is unsuitable for the disorder even if it is mentioned among the group of drugs, and one should employ a substance not mentioned there if it is appropriate, for one who knows the tastes and other qualities. 168

In a substance, five categories— taste, quality, potency, post-digestive transformation, and power— reside and perform their respective functions. (169) The tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
These six substances are dependent upon the [six] tastes, and they bring about strength in the same order as previously mentioned.
Among them, the first three—bitter and the others—subdue Vāta; the three beginning with astringent, bitter, and sweet subdue Kapha; while the others produce Pitta. (170–171)

If those tastes which pacify vāta lack dryness, lightness, and coldness, they will not subdue the wind. If those tastes which pacify pitta [lack heat and sharpness]... 172. If those tastes which pacify pitta... [lack coldness and heaviness], they will not subdue it.
Sharpness, heat, and lightness—these qualities do not perform those functions [of pacifying phlegm].
(173) If those tastes which pacify *śleṣman* (phlegm) were indeed devoid of oiliness, heaviness, and coldness, then they would not destroy *kapha*. (174)
The sweet taste is cooling, nourishes the bodily tissues and breast milk, is beneficial for the eyes, and subdues Vāta and Pitta; however, it may cause obesity, impurities, and worms.
It is an antidote to poison, slimy, unctuous, and conducive to pleasure and longevity. (175)
It is considered beneficial for children, the elderly, those emaciated by disease, and those with impaired complexion, hair, senses, or vitality.
It is praised as nourishing, good for the throat, heavy, and a promoter of healing.
However, when used in excess, it causes fever, dyspnea, goiter, tumors, and worms.
It causes obesity, sluggish digestion, urinary disorders, and diseases arising from fat and phlegm.
Juice (rasa) is sour, digestive, appetizing, increases pitta, phlegm, and blood, is light,
scraping, hot internally, cold externally, moistening, and subdues vata.
It is unctuous, sharp, mobile, and it destroys semen, constipation, abdominal distension, and vision;
it causes exhilaration and the contraction of the hair, teeth, eyes, and eyebrows.
When applied excessively, it produces vertigo, thirst, burning sensations, cataracts, and fever.
It causes itching, pallor, erysipelas, swelling, eruptions, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Salt is purifying, appetizing, digestive, and increases kapha and pitta; it removes impotence and vāta, and produces looseness and softness of the body. (181)
It destroys strength; it is a cloud for the mouth and causes a burning sensation dripping from the cheeks (182).
When consumed in excess, it causes ophthalmia, hemorrhagic disorders, abscesses, wounds, and the like, and brings about wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, leprosy, erysipelas, and thirst (183).

Pungent, hot, sharp, and clear, it generates wind and bile, subdues phlegm, is light, and possesses fiery qualities; it destroys worms, itching, and poison; it diminishes semen and breast milk, and reduces obesity and fat. (184)

It is considered to cause dryness of the ears, nose, mouth, eyes, and tongue; it is an irritant (udvejanaka), an inflamer (dīpana), a digestive stimulant (pācana), and an appetizer (rucya). It causes extreme drying of the nose and dries up the moisture, fat, muscle-fat, marrow, feces, and urine. (185–186)
It is a purifier of the channels, parching, promotes intellect, and causes obstruction of feces.
(187) When used in excess, it causes vertigo, burning sensations, and dryness of the mouth, palate, and lips;
it afflicts the throat and other parts, induces fainting, internal burning, and destroys strength and luster. (188)
Bitter [taste] is cooling; it conquers thirst, fainting, fever, pitta, and kapha.

It removes worms, skin diseases, poison, excessive secretions, burning sensations, and blood disorders. It is appetizing, though itself lacking in relish, and it purifies the throat and breast milk. (189)
It increases wind (vāta), stimulates the digestive fire, dries the nose, is parching, and light. When used in excess, it causes headache, stiffness of the neck, exhaustion, and distress;
it induces trembling, fainting, and thirst, and leads to the depletion of strength and semen. (190–191)
Astringent (kaṣāya) is considered healing, absorbent, styptic, purifying, scraping, compressive, mild, desiccant, and provocative of vāta;
it destroys kapha, blood, and pitta, and is dry, cold, and light. 192.
The *āma* (undigested matter) is considered to be clear when it acts as a purifier of the skin, but it is regarded as a cause of stiffness and obstruction;
when located in the tongue, it causes numbness and creates blockages in the channels of the throat.
When excessively accumulated, it produces seizures, flatulence, pain in the heart, convulsions, and other such disorders. (193–194)
Sweet food is generally phlegm-increasing, with the exception of aged *śāli* rice, barley,
mung beans, wheat, honey, sugar, and the meat of wild animals.
Sour food generally increases bile, with the exception of the *dhātrī* fruit and the pomegranate.
Salt is generally harmful to the eyes, with the exception of *saindhava* (rock salt).
Likewise, pungent and bitter substances are generally non-aphrodisiac and aggravate *vāta*,
with the exceptions of ginger, black pepper, garlic, *paṭola*, and *amṛtā*.
Long pepper and ginger are said to be aphrodisiacs, while pungent substances are generally declared to be non-aphrodisiacs;
astringent substances, with the exception of *abhayā*, are described as generally being styptics.
Thus, the qualities arising from the six tastes have been indicated here in a general manner.
Through the combination of tastes, however, there arises an entirely different manifestation of qualities.
By contact with clarified butter,
honey— which is poisonous— becomes equal to nectar, just as the venom of one bitten by a snake turns into immortality [for the one who consumes it].
Lightness, heaviness, unctuousness, dryness, and sharpness—these are traditionally known as the qualities of ether, earth, water, air, and fire, respectively.
Lightness is declared to be supremely wholesome; it subdues phlegm and is quickly digested.
The heavy [variety] removes wind, promotes nourishment and phlegm, and is slow to digest;
it is unctuous, alleviates wind, increases phlegm, is aphrodisiac, and brings strength.
The dry [variety] is considered to increase wind and is a supreme remover of phlegm. (203)
Sharp [rasa] generally produces pitta, is scraping, and removes kapha and vata;
however, in the Suśruta, these twenty qualities are mentioned—listen as I name them:
heavy, light, unctuous, dry, sharp, smooth, stable, and mobile.
Stickiness, clarity, coldness, heat, softness, hardness, grossness, subtlety, fluidity, dryness, quickness, and slowness are known as the qualities (guṇas).
(205) Smoothness may exist even without oiliness, and indeed, even a hard object can be slippery. (206)

It is firm, obstructs wind and feces, causes the flow of urine, is slimy, fibrous, strengthening, promotes healing, increases phlegm, is heavy, dries up moisture, is known to be clear, and heals wounds. 207.
Cold [substances] are refreshing, cause a state of numbness, and alleviate fainting, thirst, perspiration, and burning sensations.
Hot [substances] are the opposite of cold and act as digestive stimulants (pācana). A thick [substance] produces bulk in the body and causes the obstruction of the channels. 208–209.
That which enters the subtle apertures of the body is called "subtle" (sūkṣma).
It is liquid and moistening, pervasive, and dry in its opposite state.
It acts swiftly, moving rapidly through the body like oil upon water.

That which is sluggish in all its functions is called "mild" (manda), even if it is slightly [active]. (211) That which digests the undigested (āma) but does not stimulate the digestive fire is called "dīpana" (stimulant); for example, fennel (misi).
(212) That which digests the undigested (āma) but does not [directly] stimulate the digestive fire is indeed "pācana" (digestive).
One should know that like *nāgakeśara*, it is a diverse stimulant and digestive;
that which purifies the humors (*doṣas*) without aggravating them when they are balanced, and equalizes them when they are disordered—that is pacification (*śamana*), such as *amṛtā*. (213–214)
Having matured the impurities and broken their bond, one should lead them downward;
that is to be known as *anulomana* (facilitating downward movement), just as the *harītakī* has been described.
Whatever impurities and such are stuck in the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*) should be brought to maturity even without being cooked [by fire].
That which causes downward discharge is called *sraṃsana* (laxative), such as kṛtamālaka.

That which is unbound, like feces and so forth, or that which is bound and consolidated by impurities, it causes to break down and fall downward; this is *bhedana* (purgative), such as kaṭukī. (216–217)
That which brings to a liquid state what is either matured or immature, such as impurities and the like, and also causes it to be expelled, should be known as a purgative (recana), such as *trivṛt*.
That which forcibly carries upward immature bile, phlegm, and food is [an emetic]. (218)
That indeed should be known as emesis (vamana), just like the fruit of the madana plant;
it expels the accumulation of impurities from its place, either upwards or downwards,
and serves as a purification of the body, just like the fruit of the devadālī plant.
That which is illuminating (dīpana), digestive (pācana), and dries up fluids due to its heat is also constipating (grāhi); such as ginger (śuṇṭhī), cumin (jīraka), and elephant pepper (gajapippalī).
Furthermore, that which results from dryness (raukṣya), coldness (śaitya), astringency (kaṣāyatva), and light digestion (laghu-pāka) [is likewise constipating].
That which causes stiffness through the action of wind (vāta) is *stambhana*, such as *vatsaka* and *kaṭuṇṭuka*.
That which forcibly uproots the accumulated humors (doṣas), such as phlegm (kapha),
is *chedana*, such as alkalis (*kṣāra*), black pepper (*marica*), and bitumen (*śilājatu*).

That which cleanses and scrapes away the impurities or the humors (dhātus) of the body is called *lekhanam* (scraping); for example, honey, warm water, *vacā*, and barley. That substance from which sexual arousal arises in women is indeed *vājīkaraṇam* (aphrodisiac).
Just as *aśvagandhā*, *musalī*, sugar, and *śatāvarī* (225)—
because they cause the increase of semen, they are indeed called *śukrala* (semen-promoting);
likewise, *nāgabalā* and others, as well as the seed of *kapikacchu* (226).
Milk, black gram, the marrow of the marking-nut (bhallātaka) fruit,
and impurities— these are the generators and the expellers of semen.
A woman in her courses causes the emission of semen, as does the fruit of the *bṛhatī*.

Jātīphala (nutmeg) is a styptic, and kāliṅga causes the wasting away [of phlegm]. That which destroys old age and disease should be known as a *rasāyana*, such as harītakī, dantī, guggulu, and śilājatu. (228–229)

That which first pervades the entire body and subsequently undergoes digestion is called *vyavāyin* (pervasive), such as hemp (*bhaṅgā*) and the foam arising from the ocean. Furthermore, that which causes the bonds of the joints to become loose is called *vikāśin* (expansive). 230.
That substance which, having dried up the vital energy (ojas) from the bodily constituents (dhātus) in due order— just as the betel nut and kodrava grain do— is said to be intoxicating;
it is characterized by a predominance of the quality of darkness (tamas), such as wine, liquor, and the like.

That which is pervasive (vyavāyi), expansive (vikāśi), a destroyer of phlegm (śleṣmacchedi), intoxicating (madāvaha), fiery (āgneya), life-taking (jīvitahara), and acting as a vehicle for combination (yogavāhi) is known as poison (viṣa).
By its own potency (nijavīryeṇa), that substance [expels] the accumulation of humors (doṣasañcaya) from the channels (srotobhyaḥ).

That which expels [impurities] by force is *pramāthī*, such as black pepper (*marica*) and sweet flag (*vacā*). (234) That substance which, by means of its sliminess and heaviness, obstructs the nutrient-carrying channels (*rasavaha-śirāḥ*) and thereby produces heaviness is *abhiṣyandi*, such as curd (*dadhi*). (235)
A burning substance causes belching, acidity, and thirst, as well as a burning sensation in the heart; it undergoes digestion only after a long time.
A synergistic substance, however, adopts the qualities of the substances with which it is combined.

Just as honey, water, oil, clarified butter, mercury, iron, and so forth, when being processed, [attain different qualities], the wise consider potency (*vīrya*) to be twofold due to the predominance of either hot or cold qualities;
for the entire three worlds are seen to consist of both fire and moon. (237–238)
Heat destroys wind and phlegm, but it increases pitta and promotes aging.
Cold generates afflictions of wind and phlegm, yet it is supreme for removing pitta.
Among these, heat causes dizziness, thirst, exhaustion, perspiration, burning sensations, and rapid digestion. (239)
The cold [season] pacifies wind and phlegm; furthermore, it provides refreshment, sustenance, stabilization, and clarity for blood and bile.
That other taste which arises from contact with the digestive fire is [the post-digestive taste]. 240.

That which occurs at the end of the transformation of tastes is known as *vipāka* (post-digestive effect). A sweet (*madhura*) taste and a salty (*paṭu*) taste are digested as sweet; a sour (*amla*) taste is digested as sour; and the digestion of pungent (*kaṭu*), bitter (*tikta*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*) tastes generally results in a pungent effect.
That which is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka) is considered to produce phlegm (śleṣman) and alleviate wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
The sour taste, however, produces bile but removes diseases caused by wind and phlegm.
The pungent taste increases wind and destroys phlegm and bile. (243)
Thus, the distinction among the results [of karma] has been demonstrated by way of their flavors.
Even when the flavor and other qualities are identical, that action which is distinguished arises from its specific power (*prabhāva*).
For example, *dantī* is a purgative because of its power, even though it is equal to *citraka* in terms of flavor and the rest. (244–245)

Madhūka, grapes, ghee, and milk are digestive stimulants; however, the specific potency of the lakucha fruit, like that of the āmalakī, destroys the three doshas even when present in equal proportions through its juice and other constituents. (246–247)
In some cases, a substance may act as a medicine by its own power alone;
for example, the root of *sahadevī* tied to the head cures fever.
When substances of opposing qualities are combined, the one that is more abundant overcomes the one that is less. (248)
Taste, post-digestive effect, potency, and specific action— these [latter] set aside those [former].
Thus ends the first section on miscellaneous topics within the Miscellaneous Chapter of the Bhāvaprakāśanighaṇṭu.
The Aśvins spoke these words to the self-composed Prajāpati Dakṣa:
"From where was the harītakī born, and how many species does it have?
How many tastes are declared for it, and how many secondary tastes (uparasa) are recorded?"
How many names have been stated, and what is their definition?
What are their colors and qualities, and which one is employed where?
With what substance is each associated, and which diseases does it dispel?
"O Blessed One, you ought to explain this question just as it has been asked.
Having heard the words of the Aśvins, Dakṣa spoke these words:
"A drop of Śakra’s nectar fell upon the earth as he was drinking it."

Then, born from the divine, there arose the seven-fold *harītakī*: *harītakī*, *abhayā*, *pathyā*, *kāyasthā*, *pūtanā*, *amṛtā*, and *haimavatī*; it is also called *avyathā*, *cetakī*, *śreyasī*, and *śivā*.
Vayasthā, Vijayā, Jīvantī, and Rohiṇī; furthermore,
Vijayā, Rohiṇī, Pūtanā, Amṛtā, Abhayā, Jīvantī, and Cetakī— these are the seven varieties of Pathyā.
Vijayā is known to have the shape of a bottle-gourd; Rohiṇī is said to be round; Pūtanā is bony and slender; Amṛtā is described as fleshy;
Abhayā is said to have five lines; and Jīvantī is golden-colored.
The *cetakī* is known to have three lines; this is the appearance of these seven [plants].
Vijayā is for all diseases, Rohiṇī for healing wounds, Pūtanā should be applied as a paste, and Amṛtā is beneficial for purification. 11.
Abhayā is recommended for eye diseases, and Jīvantī removes all diseases;
Cetakī is recommended for use as a powder and should be administered according to the specific requirements.
Cetakī is said to be of two kinds according to its color: white and black.
It is remembered as being six finger-breadths long and white, while one [variety] is one finger-breadth black.

One [type] may distinguish [the poison] by its mere taste, another by its smell, another by touch, and yet another by sight; thus the auspicious goddess [of medicine] distinguishes it in four ways. 13–14.
Those men who approach the shade of the *cetakī* tree are instantly torn apart, as are beasts, birds, deer, and other creatures. Indeed,
as long as the *cetakī* remains in the hand of a living being smeared with clarified butter, [it continues its lethal effect].
It may even be broken by forceful means through its potency; of this there is no doubt.
For kings who are delicate, emaciated, and averse to medicine, Cetakī is highly recommended as a beneficial and pleasant purgative. 16–17.
Among all seven species, Vijayā is remembered as the foremost; it is easy to administer, easily obtained, and is recommended for all diseases.
Harītakī possesses five tastes, is devoid of salt, and is not astringent. It is supreme.

It is dry, hot, digestive-stimulant, intellect-promoting, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and an elixir (rasāyana). It is beneficial for the eyes, light, life-prolonging, nourishing, and carminative.
It cures dyspnea, cough, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, edema, abdominal enlargements, and worms.
It cures disorders of voice,

diseases of the digestive tract, constipation, and irregular fevers; as well as abdominal tumors, flatulence, thirst, vomiting, hiccups, itching, heart disease, jaundice, colic, abdominal distension, splenic enlargement, and liver disease.
It destroys urinary calculi, dysuria, and urinary obstruction.
(22) Because it is sweet, bitter, and astringent, it removes pitta and kapha;
because it is pungent, bitter, astringent, and sour, the śivā fruit removes vāta. (23)
Since *śivā* (harītakī) produces pitta due to its pungent and sour qualities, why does it not produce vāta?

(24) Its capacity to destroy the doṣas is established through its specific potency (*prabhāva*); that which is thus proven is now elucidated by means of logical reasons for the sake of the student's understanding, rather than something entirely new being created here. (25)

The difference in action and the equality in quality are observed due to the distinction of their substrates; therefore, one should not conclude that they are identical, just as in the case of the *dhātrī* and the *lakucha* fruits.
(26) In the marrow of the *pathyā* fruit it is sweet, while in its fiber it is established as sour.
The juice is bitter in the stalk, pungent in the skin, and astringent when residing in the pith.
Fresh, unctuous, dense, round, heavy, and which sinks when thrown into water—that is declared excellent and bestowing of many virtues. (27–28)
Possession of the nine qualities and likewise a weight of two karṣas in the fruit of the *harītakī*—where both these conditions exist, it is called the best.
When chewed, it increases the digestive fire; when ground into a paste, it purifies the waste products.
Haritaki, when steamed, is constipating and wholesome; when fried, it is said to alleviate the three *doṣas*.
When taken with food, Haritaki awakens the intellect, strength, and senses; it eradicates *pitta*, *kapha*, and *vāyu*; and it eliminates urine, feces, and impurities. (30–31)
Harītakī, when administered after a meal, quickly removes the disorders caused by food and drink that arise from vāta, pitta, and kapha.
With salt it destroys kapha; with sugar it destroys pitta. (32)
One should consume *abhayā* with ghee to cure diseases born of wind (*vāta*), and with jaggery to cure all diseases.

Desiring the qualities of a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), one should consume *abhayā* with rock salt, sugar, ginger, long pepper (*kaṇā*), honey, and jaggery, respectively, during the rainy season and the other seasons.

One who is exhausted by travel, devoid of strength, coarse, emaciated, weakened by fasting, one with a predominance of *pitta*, a pregnant woman, and one who has bled after childbirth should not eat *abhaya*.
The *vibhītaka* has three genders; it is called *akṣa* and its fruit is a *karṣa* in weight.

The *vibhītaka* tree—known as *kalidruma*, the abode of spirits (*bhūtavāsa*), and the dwelling place of the Kali age—is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), astringent (*kaṣāya*), and it subdues phlegm and bile.
It is hot in potency (*uṣṇavīrya*) yet cold to the touch (*himasparśa*), acts as a laxative (*bhedana*), and destroys cough. (36)
The kernel of the *vibhītaka* is parched, beneficial for the eyes, good for the hair, and destroys worms and discoloration;
it removes thirst, vomiting, phlegm, and wind, and is light, astringent, and intoxicating. Furthermore, the kernel of the *dhātrī* possesses these same qualities. (37)
The *vayasyā* is *āmalakī*, which is aphrodisiac; the juice of *jātīphala* is auspicious.
The fruit of *dhātrī*, *śrīphala*, and likewise *amṛtaphala* are recorded [as synonyms].
Among these three, *āmalaka* is declared to be *dhātrī*, *tiṣyaphalā*, and *amṛtā*. (38)
The āmalaka fruit is equal to harītakī, but it is especially an excellent rasāyana that cures raktapitta and prameha, and is highly aphrodisiac;
it destroys vāta due to its acidity, and pitta due to its sweetness and coolness. 39.

The dhātrī fruit conquers the three doṣas because of its dry and astringent nature; it subdues kapha. Whatever kind of potency each fruit possesses here, one should indicate that the same applies to its marrow as well.
The three fruits—pathyā, vibhītaka, and dhātrī—in equal parts, constitute triphalā;
it is also called phalatrika and is celebrated as varā.
Triphalā destroys kapha and pitta, cures urinary disorders and skin diseases, and is laxative.

Ginger (śuṇṭhī), known as viśvā, viśva, nāgara, viśvabheṣaja, ūṣaṇa, kaṭubhadra, śṛṅgavera, and mahauṣadha, is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, improves the appetite, and destroys irregular fevers. 43–44.

Ginger (śuṇṭhī) is appetizing, destroys Vāta, promotes digestion, is pungent, light, unctuous, hot, and sweet in its post-digestive effect; it removes the obstruction of Kapha and Vāta, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the voice, and cures vomiting, dyspnea, colic, cough, and heart disease. 45.
It destroys elephantiasis, edema, hemorrhoids, flatulence, abdominal enlargement, and wind disorders (46).
That which possesses a preponderance of fiery qualities and dries up the watery element,
thereby absorbing the waste products, is called *grāhin* (astringent/absorbent), such as ginger and other similar substances (47).
But how could that which breaks through obstructions be "grasping"?
For the power to break through obstructions does not consist in the falling away of impurities. (48) There may be fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), as well as *kaṭubhadra* and *adrikā*.
Ārdrikā is considered to be digestive, heavy, sharp, hot, and a stimulant of the digestive fire (49).
It is pungent, sweet in its post-digestive effect, dry, and it removes wind and phlegm;
all the qualities that have been described for ginger (śuṇṭhī) are also present in Ārdrikā in their entirety (50).
At the beginning of a meal, the consumption of salt and moist foods is always wholesome;
it kindles the digestive fire, stimulates the appetite, and cleanses the tongue and throat.
It is beneficial in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), anemia (pāṇḍu), urinary disorders (kṛcchra), internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), ulcers, and fever.
In burning, heat, and autumn, the moist *ārdraka* is certainly not honored [as a remedy].
(52) Pippalī, māgadhī, kṛṣṇā, vaidehī, capalā, kaṇā, upakulyā, uṣaṇā, śauṇḍī, kolā, and tīkṣṇataṇḍulā are synonyms for long pepper. (53)
Pippalī is digestive, aphrodisiac, sweet in its post-digestive effect, a rejuvenative (rasāyana),
non-heating, pungent, unctuous, light, and it alleviates vāta and kapha.
Pippalī is purgative and cures dyspnea, cough, abdominal diseases, and fever.
It cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, colic, indigestion, and wind disorders.
When fresh, it increases phlegm, is unctuous, cold, sweet, and heavy;
it pacifies pitta, whereas when dried, it aggravates pitta.
Pippalī combined with honey destroys fat and phlegm;
it alleviates dyspnea, cough, and fever, and is aphrodisiac, intellect-promoting, and increases the digestive fire.
Guḍapippalī is recommended for chronic fever and weak digestion. (57)
This [medicinal preparation] cures cough, indigestion, loss of appetite, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, and worm infestations;
it is considered by physicians that in this case, the jaggery (guḍa) should be twice the amount of the powdered long pepper (pippalī).
Black pepper (marica), vella, kṛṣṇa, ūṣaṇa, and dharmapattana [are also used]. 58–59.
Black pepper (marica) is pungent, sharp, digestive, and subdues phlegm and wind;
it is hot, increases bile, is dry, and removes asthma, colic, and worms.
When fresh, it is sweet in its post-digestive effect, not excessively hot, pungent, and heavy.
A substance possessing some degree of sharpness (tīkṣṇa) and that causes excessive salivation (śleṣmapraseki) is apittala (non-bile-producing).
61. Viśva (ginger), upakulyā (long pepper), and marica (black pepper)—these three are called trikaṭu;
it is also termed kaṭutrika, trikaṭu, tryūṣaṇa, and vyoṣa. 62.
Triyūṣaṇa is a digestive stimulant; it destroys asthma, cough, skin diseases, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, phlegm, obesity, fat-related ailments, elephantiasis, and chronic rhinitis.
Granthika, pippalīmūla, trikaṭu, and the head of a sparrow [are also used].
Pippalīmūla is digestive-stimulant, pungent, hot, a digestive aid, and light (64).
It is dry, increases pitta, is laxative, and cures kapha and vāta-type abdominal enlargements;
it destroys flatulence, splenic disorders, and tumors, and removes worms, dyspnea, and consumption (65).
Trikaṭu (the three pungents) together with kaṇāmūla is called catūrūṣaṇa;
the qualities of catūrūṣaṇa are said to be even greater than those of tryūṣaṇa. Cavya is called cavikā, and it is likewise described as uṣaṇā.
Kaṇāmūla-guṇa and cavya are especially effective in curing hemorrhoids (gudaja).
The fruit of cavikā is called gajapippalī by the wise; it is also known as kapivallī, kolavallī, śreyasī, and vaśira. (67–68)
Gajakṛṣṇā is pungent; it increases the digestive fire and alleviates vāta and kapha.
It is hot and cures diarrhea, asthma, diseases of the throat, and worms.
Citraka is also named anala, pāṭhī, and vyāla; it is likewise hot.
Citraka is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), stimulates the digestive fire, is a digestive aid (pācana), and is light.
It is dry and hot; it cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema, hemorrhoids, worms, and cough.
It alleviates vāta and kapha, is astringent, subdues vāta, and removes both kapha and pitta.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara—
these five, when measured at the size of a kola fruit each, are called "Pañcakola.
Pañcakola is considered pungent in taste and digestion, and it stimulates the appetite.

The five spices (pañcakola), together with black pepper, are declared as the "six pungents" (ṣaḍūṣaṇa). It is sharp, hot, an excellent digestive, a stimulant of the appetite, and it subdues phlegm and wind; it destroys abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, flatulence, and colic, though it provokes bile. (73)
It possesses the five qualities of *kola*, is dry, hot, and destroys poison (74).
*Yavānī*, *ugragandhā*, *brahmadarbhā*, and *ajamodikā* (75)—
this same plant is called *dīpyaka*, *dīpyā*, and likewise *yavasāhvayā*.

Yavānī is digestive, appetizing, sharp, hot, pungent, and light (76). It is also a stimulant of digestion, bitter, and increases bile; it removes seminal pain and cures wind, phlegm, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, gulma, splenic disorders, and worms (77).
Ajamodā, kharāśvā, māyūra, dīpyaka,
as well as brahmakuśā, kāravī, and locamastakā are said [to be synonyms].
Ajamodā is pungent, sharp, digestive, and it subdues phlegm and wind.
It is hot, causes a burning sensation, is pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, strength-promoting, and light;
it removes eye diseases, worms, vomiting, hiccup, and the pain of enemas (79).
Pārasīkayavānī, however, is similar to yavānī in its properties.
Jīraka (cumin) is especially digestive, appetizing, astringent, exhilarating, and heavy. Ajājī is also called kaṇā and dīrghajīraka; kṛṣṇajīra is fragrant and likewise cleanses the eructation.
Kālājājī, suṣavī, kālikā, and upakālikā;
pṛthvīkā, kāravī, pṛthvī, pṛthukṛṣṇā, upakuñcikā, upakuñcī, kuñcī, and also bṛhajjīraka—these are synonyms for black cumin. 82–83.
The triad of cumin (jīrakatritaya) is parching, pungent, hot, digestive, light, astringent, increases bile, improves the intellect, purifies the uterus,
destroys fever, promotes digestion, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, appetizing, and removes phlegm. (84)
Coriander (dhānyaka), also known as dhānaka, dhānya, dhānā, and dhāneyaka, is beneficial for the eyes and cures disorders caused by wind (vāta), abdominal distension, gulma, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Kunaṭī, dhenukā, chatrā, kustumburu, and vitunnaka are likewise [described].

Coriander (dhānyaka) is astringent, unctuous, non-fecundating, diuretic, light, bitter, and possesses pungent-hot potency; it is known to stimulate digestion, promote digestion, alleviate fever, improve appetite, be constipating, have a sweet post-digestive effect, and pacify the three doṣas. 87.

It cures thirst, burning sensations, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, emaciation, and worms; when fresh, it possesses these same qualities, being sweet and especially a destroyer of pitta. (88) Śatapuṣpā, śatāhvā, madhurā, kāravī, and misi [are synonyms].
Atilambī, sitacchatrā, and saṃhitacchatrikā; chatrā, śāleya, śālīnī, miśreyā, madhurā, and misi;
śatapuṣpā is light, sharp, generates pitta, stimulates digestion, and is pungent. (89–90)

Miśreyā is hot and is said to remove fever, wind, phlegm, wounds, colic, and eye diseases; it possesses those same qualities [as the preceding], with the specific distinction of curing pain in the female reproductive tract (yoni-śūla).
It alleviates weak digestion, is pleasing to the heart, and removes constipation, worms, and semen disorders.
Rūkṣoṣṇā is digestive and removes cough, vomiting, phlegm, and wind.
Methikā, methinī, methī, dīpanī, bahupatrikā, bodhinī, bahubījā, and likewise jyotirgandhaphalā [are synonyms]. (92–93)
Vallarī, candrikā, manthā, miśrapuṣpā, kairavī,
kuñcikā, bahuparṇī, pītabījā, and municchadā (94)— methikā pacifies wind, destroys phlegm, and cures fever.
Then there are others with slightly lesser qualities, yet they too are honored:
Candrikā, Carmahantrī, Paśumehanakārikā, Nandinī, Kāravī, Bhadrā, Vāsapuṣpā, and Suvāsarā. 95–96.

Candrasūra is beneficial for those suffering from hiccup, wind-disorders, phlegm, and diarrhea; it counteracts diseases of blood and wind, and increases strength and nourishment. (97) Methikā, candrasūra, kālā, ajājī, and yavānikā—
This group of four, when combined, is known as the "four-seed" formulation (caturbīja).
When this powder is consumed daily, it destroys wind-related diseases, indigestion, colic, flatulence, pain in the flanks, and pain in the waist. 98–99.
Sahasravedhī, jaṭuka, bāhlīka, and hiṅgu (rāmaṭha) [are the names for asafoetida]. 100.

Hiṅgu is hot, digestive, appetizing, sharp, and it overcomes wind and physical weakness; it destroys colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, and worms, while increasing bile. 101.

Vacā, ugragandhā, ṣaḍgranthā, golomī, śataparvikā, kṣudrapattrī, maṅgalyā, jaṭilā, ugrā, and lomaśā—these are synonyms for *vacā*. Vacā is pungent, bitter, and hot; it induces vomiting and stimulates the digestive fire.

Pārasīka-vacā, which is white and called Haimavatī, destroys constipation, flatulence, and colic; it purifies the feces and urine, and removes epilepsy, phlegm, insanity, possession by spirits, parasites, and disorders of Vāta. (103)
Likewise, that which originates from the Himalayas especially destroys wind (vāta).
It may be fragrant or pungent-smelling; it specifically cures phlegm and cough, improves the voice, produces healthy skin, is appetizing, and cleanses the heart, throat, and mouth. 104–105.
The *sthūlagranthi* variety is fragrant; it is considered to have slightly inferior qualities [compared to the previous]. 106.
*Vaca* from another island is somewhat bitter and hot; it stimulates the digestive fire, destroys constipation, flatulence, and colic, and purifies the feces and urine. 107.

It specifically dispels wind-related diseases, epilepsy, insanity, and bodily pain, and is a destroyer of syphilis (phiraṅgāmaya). Hapuṣā, habuṣā, and visrā are considered synonyms for aśvatthaphalā. 108.
Hapuṣā destroys fish-smell, splenic disorders, poisons, and the affliction caused by crows;
it stimulates digestion, is bitter, mild, slightly heating, astringent, and heavy.
It removes pitta, abdominal enlargements, vāta, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, gulma, and colic.
These qualities are said to belong to the other [variety] as well; there is a difference in form between the two.
In the masculine and neuter genders, it is *viḍaṅga*, *kṛmighna*, and *jantunāśana*; it is also called *taṇḍula*, *vellam*, *amoghā*, and *citrataṇḍula*. (110–111)
Viḍaṅga is pungent, sharp, hot, dry, digestive, and light; it cures colic, flatulence, abdominal disorders, phlegm, worms, and wind-obstruction.
Nāḍī, hiṅgu, palāśākhyā, jantukā, and rāmaṭhī are synonyms for asafoetida.
Vaṃśapatrī, piṇḍāhvā, suvīryā, hiṅgunāḍikā,

tumburu, saurabha, saura, vanaja, sānuja, and andhaka (113)— these are the names for tumburu. It is renowned as bitter, and though it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), it is also pungent [in taste].
It is dry, hot, digestive, sharp, appetizing, light, and causes a burning sensation;
it destroys disorders of wind and phlegm, diseases of the eyes, ears, lips, and head, heaviness, worms, skin diseases, colic, loss of appetite, asthma, splenic disorders, and dysuria. (114–115)
Syādvamśarocanā, vāṃśī, tugākṣīrī, tugā, śubhā,
tvakkṣīrī, vaṃśajā, śubhrā, vaṃśakṣīrī, and vaiṇavī are synonyms for bamboo-manna (vaṃśalocana).
That which is born of bamboo is nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, sweet, and cooling.
Decoctions [of these] remove thirst, cough, fever, dyspnea, consumption, hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), and jaundice; they also cure leprosy, ulcers, anemia, and alleviate vāta-related dysuria.
117 Samudraphena, phena, hiṇḍīra, and abdhikapha are likewise [used]. 118
Sea-foam is beneficial for the eyes, scraping, and cooling;
it is astringent, destroys poison and bile, and alleviates earache, kapha, and hemorrhoids.
(119) Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, the two Medās, the two Kākolīs, Ṛddhi, and Vṛddhi—(120)

The group of eight (aṣṭavarga) is described by Caraka and others as consisting of eight substances. This group of eight is cooling, sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and heavy; it heals fractures, increases sexual desire, and enhances strength against phlegm (kapha).
It destroys wind, bile, blood disorders, thirst, burning sensations, fever, urinary diseases, and consumption.
(122) Jīvaka and Ṛṣabhaka are known to originate from the peaks of the Himālaya mountains; their bulbs are like those of garlic, devoid of pith, and possess fine leaves. (123)
Jīvaka is shaped like a tuft of hair (kūrcaka), while Ṛṣabha has horns like those of a bull.
Jīvaka is sweet, horned, short-limbed, and has a head resembling a tuft of hair.
Jīvaka and Ṛṣabha are strengthening, cooling, and increase semen and phlegm.
Sweet, it removes bile, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, emaciation, wind disorders, and consumption.
(125) The bulb known as Mahāmedā grows in regions such as Moraṅga.
(126) The lords of sages have stated that Mahāmedā is also called Vanīmedā. (127)
A tuber resembling white, moist *kanī* (white mustard), grown on a creeper and very pale-white, is to be known by the name *mahāmedā*; the characteristics of *medā* are now described.
A white tuber that can be cut with the fingernails should exude a substance like the bodily element of fat (*medas*).
That which is known as *medā* should be recognized by people intent on inquiry [as follows]:
*śalyaparṇī*, *maṇicchidrā*, *medā*, *medābhavā*, *adhvarā*, *mahāmedā*, *vasucchidrā*, *tridantī*, and *devatāmaṇi*. (129–130)

Medā-yuga (the pair of Medās) is heavy, sweet, aphrodisiac, increases breast milk and phlegm, nourishing, cooling, and cures pitta, blood disorders, vāta, and fever. Kṣīrakākolī grows in the same place where Mahāmedā is found. 131–132.
Where *kṣīrakākolī* is found, there *kākolī* is born;
its bulb is like that of *pīvarī*, milky, and possessed of a pleasant fragrance.
That is called *kṣīrakākolī*; the characteristics of *kākolī* are now described. 133.
Just as there may be *kṣīrakākolī*, so too may there be *kākolya*. This [latter] may be slightly black; this is the distinction between the two.
Furthermore, *vāyasolī* is *kākolī*, and likewise *vīrā* is *kāyasthikā*. 134–135.
That white variety is called *kṣīrakākolī*, *vayasthā*, *kṣīravallikā*,
*kathitā*, *kṣīriṇī*, *dhīrā*, *kṣīraśuklā*, and *payasvinī*.
(136) The pair of *kākolī*s is cooling, semen-enhancing, sweet, and heavy.
It is nourishing and removes wind, burning sensations, blood disorders, consumption, and fever.
(137) *Ṛddhi* and *vṛddhi* are two bulbous roots found on the Kośala mountain; the bulb is covered with white hair, grows from a creeper, and possesses many pores. (138)
That very [state] is both *ṛddhi* (prosperity) and *vṛddhi* (growth); yet I shall describe the distinction between these two:
*ṛddhi* is like a knot of cotton, and its fruit is counter-clockwise;
while *vṛddhi* is said by the great sages to have a clockwise fruit. (139)
Ṛddhi, yogya, siddhi, lakṣmī, and vṛddhi—these are its names.
Ṛddhi is strengthening, it subdues the three doṣas, increases semen, is sweet and heavy;
it bestows vitality and sovereignty, and destroys fainting and blood-bile (raktapitta). 140–141.
Vṛddhi is known to be cooling, nourishing, sweet, aphrodisiac, a pacifier of pitta and blood disorders, and a remover of chest wounds, cough, and consumption;
it is indeed very difficult to obtain even for kings, which is why this group of eight is so highly regarded. 142.
Therefore, the physician should take a substitute for this that possesses its qualities.
Even in the absence of the pair *medā* and *jīvakā*, one should add *kākolī* and *ṛddhi*;
likewise, one should add *vārāhī*, *vidārī*, *aśvagandhā*, and *vārāhī* respectively. 143–144.
Yaṣṭīmadhu, as well as yaṣṭīmadhuka, klītaka,
and another variety called klītanaka, is known as madhūlikā when found in water.
Yaṣṭī is cooling, heavy, sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and promotes strength and complexion.
It is very unctuous, promotes semen and hair, is beneficial for the voice, and conquers pitta, vāta, and blood disorders;
it removes wounds, swelling, poison, vomiting, thirst, exhaustion, and consumption.
(146) Kāmpilla is also known as karkaśa, candra, raktāṅga, and rocana.

Kāmpilla destroys phlegm, bile, blood, worms, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, and ulcers; it is purgative, pungent, and hot, and it cures urinary disorders, flatulence, poisons, and stones.
(147) Āragvadha, Rājavṛkṣa, Śampāka, and Caturaṅgula are synonyms for the same plant.
Ārevata, vyādhighāta, kṛtamāla, and suvarṇaka;
karṇikāra, dīrghaphala, svarṇāṅga, and svarṇabhūṣaṇa; āragvadha is heavy, sweet, cooling, and the best among purgatives. 148–149.
Its fruit relieves fever, heart disease, hemorrhaging from pitta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and colic; it is laxative, appetizing, and cures skin diseases, pitta, and kapha.
It is always wholesome in cases of fever and is an excellent cleanser of the digestive tract. 150
Kaṭvī, kaṭukā, tiktā, kṛṣṇabhedā, kaṭaṃbharā, aśokā, matsyaśakalā, cakrāṅgī, śakulādanī, matsyapittā, kāṇḍaruhā, rohiṇī, and kaṭurohiṇī are synonyms for the plant known as *kaṭurohiṇī*. (151)

Kaṭvī (kaṭukā) is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), bitter, dry, cold, and light; it is a purgative, a digestive stimulant, and beneficial for the heart; it removes phlegm, bile, and fever, and it destroys urinary disorders (prameha), dyspnea, cough, burning sensations, skin diseases, and worms. 152
Kirātatikta, kairāta, kaṭutikta, and kirātaka (153);
kāṇḍatikta, anāryatikta, bhūnimba, and rāmasenaka; another kirātaka is naipāla, which is addhatikta and jvarāntaka (154).
Kirāta is astringent, parching, cooling, bitter, and light;
it cures fever caused by the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), dyspnea, phlegm, bile, and blood, as well as burning sensations;
it also destroys cough, swelling, thirst, skin diseases, fever, ulcers, and worms. 155
It has been stated that *kuṭajabīja*, *yava*, *indradyava*, as well as *kaliṅga* and *kāliṅga*, and also *bhadrayava*—
in some instances, the name of Indra itself may serve as its designator. 156.
Indrayava and bhadrayava are its fruits.
(157) Indrayava destroys the three doṣas, is astringent, pungent, and cold;
it cures fever, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, vomiting, erysipelas, and skin diseases. (158)
It is an illuminant and overcomes hemorrhoids, dysentery, blood disorders, phlegm, and pain.
(159) Madana is emetic; it is also called piṇḍa, naṭa, piṇḍītaka, karahāṭa, maruvaka, śalyaka, and viṣapuṣpaka. (160)

Madana is sweet and bitter in taste, hot in potency, scarifying, light, emetic, and a destroyer of abscesses, coryza, and wounds; it removes dryness, skin diseases, phlegm, abdominal distension, swelling, tumors, and ulcers. 161
Rāsnā, yuktarasā, rasyā, suvahā, rasanā, rasā, elāparṇī, surasā, sugandhā, and śreyasī are synonyms.
(162) Rāsnā is unripe, bitter, heavy, and hot; it conquers kapha and vāta. (163)

Nākulī, surasā, nāgasugandhā, and gandhanākulī remove swelling, dyspnea, wind-blood disorders, vāta-śūla, and abdominal diseases; they also cure cough, fever, poisons, the eighty wind-related ailments, sidhma, and other skin diseases. 164.
Nakuleṣṭā, bhujaṅgākṣī, sarpāṅgī, and viṣanāśinī are synonyms for nākulī.
It is astringent, bitter, pungent, and hot; it destroys the venom of snakes, spiders, scorpions, and rats, as well as fevers, worms, and ulcers. (165–166)
Mācikā, prasthikā, ambaṣṭhā, ambālikā, ambikā,
mayūravidalā, keśīsahasrā, and bālamūlikā— these are the varieties.
(167) Mācikā is sour in taste and post-digestive effect, astringent, cooling, and light.
It cures chronic diarrhea, blood-bile disorders, and diseases of the throat.
(168) Tejasvinī, tejavatī, tejohvā, and likewise tejanī;
tejasvinī removes phlegm, asthma, cough, diseases of the mouth, and wind disorders. (169)
Pācanī is hot, pungent, and bitter; it stimulates the appetite and kindles the digestive fire.
(170) Jyotiṣmatī is also known as kaṭabhī, jyotiṣkā, kaṅgunī, pārāvatapadī, piṇyā, latā, and kakundanī. (171)
Jyotiṣmatī is pungent, bitter, laxative, and subdues kapha and vāta;
it is extremely hot, emetic, and sharp, bestowing strength of digestive fire, intellect, and memory.
(172) Kuṣṭha is also known as roga, vāpya, pāribhadraka, and utpala.
Kuṣṭha is hot, pungent, sweet, aphrodisiac, bitter, and light; it destroys wind-blood disorders, erysipelas, cough, skin diseases, and the humors of wind and phlegm.
Pauṣkara, puṣkara, and puṣkaramūla are said to be synonyms for this.
They say that *padmapatra* and *kāśmīra* are varieties of *kuṣṭha*. 174.
*Pauṣkara* is said to be pungent and bitter; it destroys wind, phlegm, and fever, as well as swelling, loss of appetite, and asthma, and specifically relieves pain in the flanks. 175.
Kaṭuparṇī, haimavatī, hemakṣīrī, himāvatī,
hemāhvā, and pītadugdhā— its root is called uka.
Hemāhvā is purgative, bitter, a laxative, and causes nausea.
It cures worms, itching, poison, abdominal distension, phlegm, bile, blood disorders, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Śṛṅgī, Karkaṭaśṛṅgī, Kulīraviṣāṇikā, Ajaśṛṅgī, Cakrā, and Karkaṭākhyā are its synonyms. 177–178.
Śṛṅgī is astringent, bitter, and hot; it removes disorders of kapha and vāta, wasting diseases, fever, dyspnea, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), thirst, cough, hiccups, anorexia, and vomiting.
Kaṭphala, somavalka, kaiṭaryya, and kumbhikā are also [similar]. 179.
Śrīparṇikā, Kumudikā, Bhadrā, and Bhadrapatī;

Kaṭphala is astringent and bitter, and being pungent, it destroys wind (vāta), phlegm (kapha), and fever, as well as dyspnea, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, throat diseases, and loss of appetite. 180–181.
Bhārgī, bhṛgubhavā, padmā, phaṃjī, brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā,
brāhmaṇyaṅgāravallī, kharaśāka, and hañjikā are synonyms for Bhārgī (182).
Bhārgī is dry, pungent, bitter, appetizing, hot, digestive, and light.

Dīpanī (Pāṣāṇabheda) is astringent and certainly destroys abdominal tumors, internal hemorrhaging, edema, cough, phlegm, asthma, chronic rhinitis, fever, and wind disorders; it is also known as aśmaghna, giribhid, and bhinna-yojinī. 183.
Aśmabheda is cold and bitter, astringent, and cleanses the bladder.
It is a laxative and destroys disorders of the humors (doṣas), hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary calculi, gravel, heart disease, and pain in the hips;
it also cures gynecological diseases, urinary disorders (prameha), splenic enlargement, colic, and ulcers. 184–185.
Dhātakī, dhātupuṣpī, tāmrapuṣpī, kuñjarā,
subhikṣā, bahupuṣpī, and vahnijvālā are recorded as its names.
Dhātakī is pungent, cooling, softening, astringent, and light.
It conquers thirst, dysentery, bile, blood disorders, poison, worms, and erysipelas (visarpa).
(187) Mañjiṣṭhā, vikasā, jiṅgī, samaṅgā, and kālameṣikā;
(188) maṇḍūkaparṇī, bhaṇḍīrī, bhaṇḍī, and yojanavallī as well.
Rasāyanī, aruṇā, kālā, raktāṅgī, raktayaṣṭikā,
bhaṇḍītakī, gaṇḍīrī, mañjūṣā, and vastrarañjinī—
these are synonyms for mañjiṣṭhā. It is sweet, bitter, and astringent, and it improves the voice and complexion.
Gurūruṣṇā cures poison, phlegm, swelling, diseases of the female reproductive tract, eyes, and ears;
it also cures bloody diarrhea, skin diseases, hemorrhaging, erysipelas, ulcers, and urinary disorders.
(191) Kusumbha is also known as vahnīśikha and vastrarañjaka.
Safflower increases wind and alleviates dysuria, hemorrhagic disorders, and phlegm.
(192) Lac—known as palankaṣā, alakta, yāva, vṛkṣāmaya, and jatu—is a coloring agent;
it is cooling, strengthening, unctuous, astringent, and light. (193)
Brihmana, Angaravalli, Kharashakha,
and Hanjika are not hot; they destroy kapha, pitta, blood disorders, hiccups, cough, and fever (194),
and they remove wounds, chest injuries, erysipelas, worms, and skin diseases.
Similarly, lac-dye (alaktaka) is distinguished by its qualities as a destroyer of bodily defects. 195.
Haridrā, kāñcanī, pītā, niśā, varavarṇinī, kṛmighnī, haladī, yoṣitpriyā, and haṭṭavilāsinī are synonyms for turmeric. 196.

Haridrā (turmeric) is pungent, bitter, dry, and hot; it subdues kapha and pitta, improves the complexion, and cures skin diseases, urinary disorders, blood disorders, swelling, anemia, and wounds. (197) Dārvī, medā, āmrāgandhā, surabhī, dāru, and dāru [are also mentioned].
Karpūrā is the same as padmapatrā; it contains *surī*, is fragrant, and possesses stars. 198.
That which is *āmragandhi* is *haridrā*; it is considered cooling and increases wind (*vāta*).
It removes bile (*pitta*), is sweet and bitter, and destroys all itching. 199.
*Aranya-haladī-kanda* destroys leprosy and gout.
*Dārvī*, *dāruharidrā*, *parjanyā*, *parjanī*, *kaṭaṅkaṭerī*, and *pītā* are synonyms; it is also known as *pañcampaṃcā*.

That very substance is called Kālīyaka, as well as Kāleyaka; it is also known as Pītadru, Haridru, Pītadāru, and Pītaka. Dārvī possesses the qualities of Niśā (turmeric), but it cures diseases of the eyes, ears, and mouth.
Having boiled milk equal in measure to a decoction of *dārvī* until it is reduced to one-fourth and thickened, that which is known as *rasāñjana* is produced; it is supremely beneficial for the eyes.
(203) *Rasāñjana*, *tārkṣyaśaila*, *rasagarbha*, and *tārkṣyajam* are its synonyms.
Rasāñjana is pungent, cures phlegm, poison, and eye disorders;
it is hot, an elixir (rasāyana), bitter, excising, and removes defects of wounds.
Avalguja, vākucī, somarājī, and suparṇikā are synonyms [for vākucī].
Śaśilekhā, kṛṣṇaphalā, somā, and pūtiphalī; it is also proclaimed as somavallī, kālameṣī, and kuṣṭhaghnī.
Bākucī is sweet, bitter, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and an elixir (rasāyana). 206–207.
It is constipating, increases the heart's strength, is appetizing, laxative, and removes phlegm and blood-bile (pitta).
It is dry, pleasant for the heart, and cures asthma, skin diseases, urinary disorders, fever, and worms.
(208) Its fruit increases pitta and is pungent, removing skin diseases, phlegm, and wind (vāta).

Cakramarda— also known as prapunnāṭa, dadrughna, meṣalocana, padmāṭa, eḍagaja, cakrī, and punnāṭa— is beneficial for the hair and skin, and cures worms, asthma, cough, swelling, indigestion, and anemia. (209–110)
The *cakramarda* fruit is light, sweet, dry, and alleviates pitta and vāta;
