it is pleasing to the heart, cooling, and removes kapha, asthma, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), ringworm (*dadru*), and worms.
Its fruit, however, is hot and destroys leprosy, itching, ringworm, poisons, and vāta.
Kaṭuka is known to destroy gulma, cough, worms, and asthma (212).
Viṣā, ativiṣā, viśvā, śṛṅgī, prativiṣā, aruṇā, śuklakandā, upaviṣā, bhaṅgurā, and ghuṇavallabhā [are synonyms]. (213)

Viṣā is hot, pungent, and bitter; it is digestive, stimulates the appetite, and removes disorders of phlegm and bile, dysentery, poisoning, cough, vomiting, and worms. (214) Lodhra, tilva, tirīṭa, śāvara, and gālava—these are likewise [used].
The second type is *paṭṭikālodhra*, also known as *kramuka*, *sthūlavalkala*,
*jīrṇapatra*, *bṛhatpatra*, *paṭṭī*, and *lākṣāprasādana*.
(215) Lodhra is astringent, light, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, and subdues phlegm and bile.
Kaṣāya removes blood-bile, hemorrhaging, fever, dysentery, and swelling. Laśuna is known as rasona, ugragandha, mahauṣadha, ariṣṭa, mlecchakanda, yavaneṣṭa, and rasonaka. (216–217)
When Vainateya carried away the nectar from the best of the gods, a drop fell from it to the earth, and that became garlic;
it was endowed with five tastes, being devoid only of the sour taste. 218.
Therefore, those who know the qualities of substances have called it *rasona*. It is pungent in its roots, bitter when located in the leaves,
declared to be astringent in the stalk, and known to be salty at the tip of the stalk.
The taste of garlic (rasona) is declared by those who know its qualities to be sweet in its seed;
it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, hot, digestive, and laxative; it is considered pungent in both its taste and its post-digestive effect, yet sweet in its potency. 220–221.

The *kaṇṭhya* (guttural) group of tastes heals broken joints, is heavy, increases pitta and blood, produces strength and complexion, is beneficial for intelligence, is good for the eyes, and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
It cures heart disease, indigestion, fever, abdominal pain, constipation, tumors, loss of appetite, cough, and swelling.
It destroys dyspnea, leprosy, fever, exhaustion, parasites, wind-disorders, asthma, and phlegm.
(223) Wine, meat, and sour substances are beneficial for those who consume garlic; however, one should avoid physical exercise, exposure to the sun, anger, excessive water, milk, and molasses. (224)
A person who does not eat garlic should avoid these [other items] continuously:
the onion (palāṇḍu) and the yavaneṣṭa, which are foul-smelling and corrupt the mouth;
for the onion should be understood by the wise as being similar to garlic in its qualities.
Sweet in digestion and taste, non-heat-producing, it increases *kapha* and does not excessively increase *pitta*;
it removes *vāta* alone, bestows strength and virility, and is heavy.
(227) *Bhallātaka* is declared to have three names: *aruṣka*, *uruṣkara*, and *agnika*.
Likewise, the Agnimukhī bhallī and the Vīravṛkṣa cause swelling.
228 The ripe fruit of the Bhallātaka is sweet in its post-digestive taste (pāka) and flavor (rasa), light, astringent, digestive, unctuous, sharp, hot, scarifying, and breaking up [obstructions]. 229
It is purifying, stimulates the digestive fire, and destroys phlegm, wind, ulcers,
abdominal enlargements, leprosy, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, abdominal tumors, edema, flatulence, fever, and worms.
Its marrow is sweet, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and alleviates wind and bile.
The stalk of the *āruṣkara* is sweet, pacifies *pitta*, promotes hair growth, and stimulates the digestive fire (231).
*Bhallātaka* is astringent, hot, aphrodisiac, sweet, and light;
it cures disorders of wind and phlegm, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the *grahaṇī*.
It destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), fever, vitiligo, impaired digestion, worms, and ulcers.
(232) Bhaṅgā, gañjā, mātulānī, mādinī, vijayā, and jayā are synonyms for hemp.
(233) Bhaṅgā removes phlegm (kapha), is bitter, constipating, digestive, and light.
It is sharp, hot, and increases bile (pitta), as well as delusion, intoxication, and the fire of speech. 234.
Tilabheda, khasatila, and khākhasa are known by these names;
the bark produced from the fruit of khākhasa is cooling and light. 235.

It is astringent, bitter, and astringent-tasting; it increases vāta, removes kapha and cough, dries up the bodily tissues (dhātus), is parching, causes intoxication, and enhances speech. It repeatedly induces delusion, improves appetite, and through habitual use, destroys virility. (236–237)

It has been stated that *khasaphala*, *kṣīra*, *āphūka*, and *mahiphenaka*— where *āphūka* is drying, constipating, destroys phlegm, and increases wind and bile— and likewise that which consists primarily of the bark produced from the *khasaphala* tree. (238)
These are called the *khasabīja* seeds; they are also known as *khākhasatilā*.
(239) The *khasabīja* seeds are strengthening, aphrodisiac, and very heavy;
they generate *kapha* and pacify *samīraṇa* (wind). (240)
Saindhava (rock salt) is not feminine; it is also called śītaśiva, maṇimantha, and sindhuja.
Saindhava salt is sweet, digestive, carminative, light, unctuous, appetizing, cooling, aphrodisiac, subtle, beneficial for the eyes, and a remover of the three doṣas. (241)
The varieties known as Śākambharīya, Gaḍa, and likewise Romaka have been described.
The variety called Gaḍa is light, subdues wind (vāta), is extremely hot, and is purgative (bhedī) and increases bile (pittala).
It is also sharp (tīkṣṇa), hot, subtle, causes secretions (abhiṣyandi), and has a pungent post-digestive effect (kaṭupāki).
That which is sea-salt (sāmudra), black salt (tula-lavaṇa), ox-bile salt (akṣīva),
and vasira— these are born of the ocean, produced from the sea, originating from the salt-water ocean.
Sea-salt is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), slightly bitter, sweet, and heavy.
Viḍa salt is not excessively hot, stimulates digestion, is purgative, alkaline, and non-burning; it increases phlegm, subdues wind, is sharp, non-dry, and not too cold.
It is prepared by cooking and is thus artificial, as are drāviḍa and āsura salts. 245.
Bida salt, when combined with alkaline substances, promotes the downward and upward movement of kapha and vāta;
it is digestive, light, sharp, hot, dry, appetizing, and pervasive, and it alleviates obstruction, flatulence, constipation, cardiac pain, heaviness, and colic. (246–247)
Sauvarcala is considered to be of two types: rucaka and manthapāka.
Rucaka is appetizing, purgative, a digestive stimulant, and an excellent carminative; it is unctuous, increases wind, greatly increases bile, is clear, and light. (248)
It purifies belching, is subtle, and conquers constipation, abdominal distension, and colic. 249.
Earth-born salt (*audbhida-pāṃśulavaṇa*), which arises spontaneously from the earth, is alkaline, heavy, pungent, unctuous, cooling, and destroys Vāta. 250.

Chana-kashaya (sour chickpea extract) is very hot, stimulates the digestive fire, and causes the teeth to tingle; it has a salty aftertaste, improves appetite, and cures colic, indigestion, and constipation.
Yavakshara, yava-shuka, and yavagraja are names for alkali produced by the fermentation of barley. 251.
Svarjikā is also known as kṣāra and kāpota; it is pleasant for the bowels.
Experts who know the distinctions have stated that suvarcikā is a variety of svarjikā.
Yavakṣāra is light, unctuous, very subtle, and an inflamer of the digestive fire.

It destroys colic from sharp pain (śūla-vāta), phlegm, dyspnea, diseases of the throat, anemia, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), flatulence, splenic disorders, and heart diseases.
Svarjikā is to be known as having slightly lesser qualities than that [sajjī], yet it removes abdominal tumors and colic.
Suvarcikā should be understood by people as being similar to svarjikā in its properties. Saubhāgya, ṭaṅkaṇa, and kṣāra are said to be the flux for metals.
Ṭaṅkaṇa stimulates the digestive fire, is parching, removes phlegm, and increases wind and bile.
Svarjikā and yāvaśūka are declared to be the two alkalis;

when combined with ṭaṅkaṇa, they are proclaimed as the three alkalis (kṣāratraya). When combined, they produce the aforementioned qualities, and specifically, they are supreme for gulma and heart disease.
Palāśa, vajrī, śikhari, ciñcā, akṛtila, nālaja, yavaja, and svarjikā— these are declared to be the eight alkalis (kṣāra).
These alkalis are equal to fire and are highly effective in removing abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic (śūla).
Cukra is known as sahasravedhi and its juice is called śukta; it is also sour.

Cukra is extremely sour and hot, an excellent stimulant of the digestive fire and a promoter of digestion. It alleviates colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, āma-vāta, and kapha, and is laxative. (260)
It removes vomiting, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, pain in the heart, and dullness of the digestive fire.
(261) Thus ends the second section, the Harītakyādi-varga, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the section on camphor and related substances:
Camphor (karpūra) is masculine and neuter; it is also known as sitābhra, himavāluka, ghanasāra, candra, and himanāman. (1)
Camphor is cooling, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, scarifying, light,
fragrant, sweet, and bitter; it destroys phlegm, bile, and poisons (2),
and it eliminates burning sensations, thirst, bad taste in the mouth, and foul odors from the fat.
Camphor is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being either processed (*pakva*) or unprocessed (*apakva*);
they say that the unprocessed camphor possesses superior qualities compared to the processed one.
Camphor known as *cīnāka* is traditionally held to cause the depletion of phlegm (*kapha*).

It is a destroyer of leprosy, itching, and skin eruptions, and it possesses a bitter taste (4). Mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, sahasrabhit, kastūrikā, kastūrī, and vedhamukhyā are recorded as synonyms for musk (5).

The musk originating from Kāmarūpa is black; that from Nepal possesses a blue color; and that from Kashmir has a tawny luster. Thus, musk is remembered as being of three kinds. The one originating from Kāmarūpa is the best, while that from Nepal is middling.
Musk produced in the land of Kaśmīra is indeed considered inferior.
Musk is pungent, bitter, alkaline, hot, aphrodisiac, and heavy;
it removes phlegm, wind, poison, vomiting, cold, foul odor, and emaciation.
Latā, kastūrikā, tiktā, svādvī, vṛṣyā, himā, and laghu are beneficial for the eyes, act as a depletant, and remove disorders of phlegm, thirst, and diseases of the bladder and mouth.
The properties of gandhamārjāra increase virility and alleviate kapha and vāta.

Śrīkhaṇḍa, Candana, Bhadra, Śrī, Tailaparṇika, Gandhasāra, Malajaya, and Candra-dyuti— these are names for sandalwood, which removes itching and skin diseases, is fragrant for the eyes, and dispels the odor of perspiration. 10–11.
Sandalwood that is bitter in taste, yellow when rubbed, red when cut, and white in its body, and which possesses knots and hollows, is said to be the best.
Sandalwood is cooling, dry, bitter, refreshing, and light.
It removes fatigue, emaciation, poison, phlegm, thirst, bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
(13) Kālīyaka is also called kālīya and pītābha; it is known as haricandana, haripriya, kālasāra, and likewise kālānusāryaka. (14)

Kālīyaka possesses red qualities and is especially effective in destroying facial spots (vyaṅga). Raktacandana is described as having red limbs; it is known as kṣudracandana, tilaparṇa, raktasāra, and pravālaphala.
Rakta is cold, heavy, sweet, and removes vomiting, thirst, and blood-bile (rakta-pitta);
it is bitter, beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and destroys fever, wounds, and poison.
(17) Pataṅga, raktasāra, suraṅga, and likewise rañjana [are similar].
Pattūrañja is said to be *paṭṭarañjaka* and *kucandana*.
Pataṅga is sweet and cooling; it cures bile, phlegm, wounds, and hemorrhages.
It should be understood as being like *haricandana*, with the specific distinction that it destroys burning sensations.
All types of sandalwood are similar in terms of their taste and other qualities, but there is a distinction in their fragrance; the former is the most excellent in its attributes.
Agallochum (aguru) is preeminent, as are the varieties known as loha, rājārha, and yogaja.
Agallochum (vaṃśika) may be produced from bamboo or from insects; that which is eaten by insects is considered ignoble.
It is heating, pungent, beneficial for the skin, bitter, sharp, and increases pitta.
It is light, cures diseases of the ears and eyes, and dispels cold, wind, and phlegm.
That which is black and superior in quality sinks in water like iron;
the resin produced from *aguru* is known as being equal to black *aguru*.
*Devadāru*, *dārubhadra*, *dārvīndra*, and *dāru* are synonyms for it.
Mastadāru, drukilima, kilima, and surabhūruha are synonyms for devadāru.
Devadāru is light, unctuous, bitter, hot, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka);
it overcomes constipation, flatulence, swelling, ama, drowsiness, hiccup, fever, and [vitiated] blood.
It cures urinary disorders (prameha), chronic catarrh (pīnasa), phlegm-related cough, itching, and wind disorders.
Sarala is known as pītavṛkṣa and also as surabhidāruka;
sarala is sweet, bitter, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and taste, and light.
It is known to be unctuous and hot, removing diseases of the ears, throat, and eyes, as well as demons;
it cures phlegm, wind, perspiration, burning sensations, cough, fainting, and wounds.
(27) Kālānusārya, tagara, kuṭila, nahuṣa, and nata [are synonyms].
Furthermore, *piṇḍatagara*, *daṇḍahastī*, and *barhiṇa*—these two types of *tagara* are considered hot, sweet, unctuous, and light;
they remove poison, epilepsy, colic, eye diseases, and the three *doṣas*. 28–29.
Padmaka is known as Padmagandhi and likewise as Padmāhvaya.
Padmaka is astringent, bitter, cooling, increases Vāta, and is light; it destroys erysipelas, burning sensations, eruptions, skin diseases, Kapha, and blood-bile (rakta-pitta). (30)

Guggulu is a stabilizer of the fetus, appetizing, and a remedy for vomiting, wounds, and thirst. Devadāru is also known as Jaṭāyu and Kauśika; it is called Pura, Kumbha, and Ulūkhalaka (in the neuter), and is also known as Mahiṣākṣa and Palaṅkaṣa.
Mahiṣākṣa, Mahānīla, Kumuda, Padma, and Hiraṇya as the fifth— these should be known as the five varieties of guggulu (bdellium).
That which has the color of bhr̥ṅgarāja or collyrium is remembered as Mahiṣākṣa.
The Mahānīla should be known by its characteristics corresponding to its own name;
the Kumuda has the luster of a white water-lily, the Padma resembles a ruby, and the one called Hiraṇya has the brilliance of gold—these are declared to be the marks of the five [gems]. 34–35.
Both the Mahiṣākṣa and the Mahānīla gems are beneficial for lordly elephants;
the Kumuda and Padma are the two others that bring well-being and health to horses;
and Kanaka is specifically proclaimed as being for humans. (36)
Sometimes even among men, Mahiṣākṣa is considered [a type of] Guggulu. It is clear, bitter, hot in potency, increases Pitta, and is laxative;
it is astringent and pungent, pungent in its post-digestive effect, extremely dry, and light.
It heals broken joints, is aphrodisiac, subtle, beneficial for the voice, and an elixir (rasāyana).
It is digestive-stimulant, slimy, strengthening, and cures disorders of kapha and vāta, wounds, scrofula (apacī),
fat, urinary disorders, calculi, vāta, moisture-related diseases, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and undigested toxins (āma) caused by wind.
It conquers pustules, glandular swellings, edema, hemorrhoids, scrofula, and worms (40).
Because of its sweetness it pacifies vāta, and because of its astringency it destroys pitta;
because of its bitterness it overcomes kapha; thus, guggulu is a destroyer of all the doṣas (41).

Fresh guggulu is nourishing and aphrodisiac, whereas old guggulu is excessively depleting. Fresh guggulu is said to be unctuous, resembling gold in color, comparable to the ripe jambū fruit, fragrant, and slimy.
That which is dry, foul-smelling, has abandoned its natural color,
and is old should be known as guggulu devoid of potency. Sour food, pungent food, indigestion, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, and exposure to the sun [are to be avoided].
One who serves the king and seeks merit should properly abandon intoxicants and anger.
(45) Śrīvāsa, Saralasrāva, Śrīveṣṭa, and Vṛkṣadhūpaka are synonyms for pine resin.
Śrīvāsa is sweet, bitter, unctuous, hot, astringent, and laxative. (46)
Rāla (Sal tree resin) cures diseases of bile, wind, the head, eyes, and voice, as well as phlegm;
it destroys demons and removes perspiration, foul odor, lice, itching, and wounds.
It is known as śālaniryāsa and sarjarasa. 47.
Devadhūpa, yakṣadhūpa, and likewise sarvarasa;
rāla, hima, and guggulu are bitter and astringent, absorbent, and remove disorders of the humors,
blood, sweat, erysipelas, fever, ulcers, and scabies.
It destroys those afflicted by planetary influences, broken limbs, and burns from fire; it is a destroyer of colic and dysentery.
(49) Kunduruka is known as Mukunda, Sugandha, and also Kunda.
(50) Kunduruka is sweet, bitter, sharp, beneficial for the skin, pungent, and removes [diseases].
Silhaka (benzoin) cures fever, obstruction of perspiration, Alakṣmī (misfortune), diseases of the mouth, phlegm, and wind; it is called turuṣka because it is born in the land of the Yavanas,
and it is also reckoned as kapitaila and named after the monkey (kapināmaka).
Sihlaka is pungent yet sweet, unctuous, and hot; it promotes semen and luster, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the throat, and removes perspiration, leprosy, fever, burning sensations, and seizures.
(53) Jātīphala, jātikośa, and mālatīphala are its synonyms.

Jātīphala (nutmeg) is bitter in taste, sharp and hot, appetizing, light, pungent, digestive, astringent, beneficial for the voice, and subdues *śleṣman* (phlegm) and *anila* (wind). It destroys bad taste in the mouth, as well as foul odor and blackness of the teeth. (54)
Worms, cough, dyspnea, consumption, catarrh, and heart disease [are cured by it].
(55) The bark of the *jātīphala* is called *jātīpatrī* by the best of physicians.
(56) *Jātīpatrī* is light, sweet, pungent, and hot; it improves appetite and complexion.
It removes phlegm, cough, vomiting, dyspnea, thirst, worms, and poison.
(57) Lavaṅga is known as devakusuma, śrī, and śrīprasūnaka.
Lavaṅga is pungent, bitter, light, beneficial for the eyes, and cooling. (58)
It stimulates digestion, promotes appetite, and destroys phlegm, bile, and blood disorders;
it quickly eliminates thirst, vomiting, flatulence, and colic, and certainly cures cough, dyspnea, hiccup, and consumption. 59
Elā, sthūlā, bahulā, pṛthvīkā, and tripuṭā;
also bhadrai lā, bṛhadelā, candrabālā, and niṣkuṭi.
Sthūlailā is pungent in digestion and taste, stimulates the digestive fire, and is light. (60–61)

Sūkṣmopakuñcikā, tutthā, koraṅgī, drāviḍī, and truṭi are dry and hot; they remove phlegm, bile, blood disorders, itching, asthma, and thirst, and they alleviate nausea, poisoning, abdominal distension, and pain in the mouth, head, and chest, as well as vomiting. 62.
Cardamom (elā) is subtle; it removes phlegm, asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, and dysuria.
Its taste is pungent, and it is considered cooling, light, and a subduer of Vāta.
(63) Cinnamon bark (tvak), cinnamon leaves (patra), varāṅga, bhṛṅga, coca, and utkaṭa are synonyms for cinnamon.
Bark (tvac) is light, hot, pungent, sweet, and bitter;
it is dry, increases pitta, and subdues kapha and vata.
It destroys itching, anorexia, diseases of the heart and bladder, vata-type hemorrhoids, worms, nasal catarrh, and [excessive] semen. 64–65.
Tvaksvādvī has a thin bark; likewise, Dārusitā is considered [a type of] sugar.
Dārusitā is said to be sweet and bitter, removing wind and bile, fragrant, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and it alleviates dryness of the mouth and thirst. (66–67)

Patra, tamālapatra, and likewise that which is named patra, as well as patraka, are slightly sweet, pungent, hot, slimy, and light; they destroy phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, nausea, anorexia, and chronic catarrh. 68.

Nāgapuṣpa is known as Nāga, Keśara, Nāgakeśara, Cāmpeya, Nāgakiñjalka, and it is called by the name Kāñcana. (69) Nāgapuṣpa is astringent, hot, dry, light, and it promotes the digestion of undigested matter (āma). (70)
It destroys fever, itching, thirst, perspiration, vomiting, and nausea;
it removes foul odors, skin diseases, erysipelas, phlegm, bile, and poisons.
(71) Equal parts of cinnamon, cardamom, and clove constitute the "three aromatics" (*trisugandhi*) and the "three spices" (*trijātaka*).
When combined with *nāgakeśara*, it is called *cāturjātaka*.

These two [groups] are pleasing, dry, sharp, and hot; they remove foul odors from the mouth, are light, stimulate the digestive fire (*agni*), improve the complexion, and destroy phlegm (*kapha*), wind (*vāta*), and poisons.
Kuṅkuma, ghusṛṇa, rakta, kāśmīra, pītaka, vara,

saṃkoca, piśuna, dhīra, bāhlīka, and śoṇita— these are the names for that which is produced in the field born of the Kāśmīra region. (74) Indeed, that which is produced in the land of Kāśmīra is called kuṅkuma.
That which has fine filaments, is slightly red, and possesses the fragrance of a lotus is considered the best.
Saffron produced in the Bāhlīka region that is pale white and endowed with the scent of the ketakī flower, though having fine filaments, is known as mediocre.
That Persian saffron which has a honey-like fragrance is described as being slightly pale in color; it is inferior and possesses thick filaments (sthūlakeśara).
Saffron is pungent, unctuous, and overcomes headaches, wounds, and parasites.
Bitter, it cures vomiting, improves the complexion, and removes the three types of skin defects (vyaṅga).
Gorocanā is auspicious, venerable, and known as Gaurī and Rocanā;
gorocanā is cooling, bitter, aphrodisiac, and bestows auspiciousness and luster.
It removes the afflictions of poison, ill fortune, planetary influences, insanity, miscarriage, and blood-wounds.
(79) *Nakha*, *vyāghranakha*, and *vyāghrāyudha* are its names; it is also called *cakrakāraka*.
(80) *Nakha* is said to be a small variety, while *nakhī* is [another name]; *hanu* is known as *haṭṭavilāsinī*.

The two types of *nakha* (claws/nails) remove seizures, phlegm, wind, blood disorders, fever, and leprosy; they are light, hot, aphrodisiac, complexion-enhancing, sweet, and destroy wounds and poisons; they remove misfortune and foul breath, and are pungent in both their post-digestive effect (*vīrya*) and taste (*rasa*). 81–82.
Bāla, hrībera, barhiṣṭha, udīcya, and keśāmbu—known as bālaka—are cooling, dry, light, and digestive-stimulating; they cure nausea, anorexia, erysipelas, heart disease, and diarrhea. (83)
Vīraṇa, vīrataru, and vīra are synonyms for the plant with many roots (bahumūlaka).
Vīraṇa is digestive, cooling, anti-emetic, light, and bitter; it is astringent, febrifuge, cures vertigo and intoxication, and removes kapha and pitta. (84)

It removes thirst, the poison of the *āsava* snake, erysipelas (*visarpa*), difficult fevers, burning sensations, and wounds. (85) The root of *vīraṇa* is known as *uśīra*, *nalada*, *amṛṇāla*, *sevya*, and also *samagandhika*. (86)
Uśīra is digestive, cooling, astringent, light, and bitter (87).
It is sweet, removes fever, vomiting, and diarrhea, and alleviates kapha and pitta; it cures thirst, hemorrhage, poison, erysipelas, burning sensations, and dysuria (88).

Jaṭāmāṃsī—also known as bhūtajaṭā, jaṭilā, and tapasvinī—is pungent, astringent, promotes mental clarity, and bestows beauty and strength. It is sweet, cooling, and alleviates the three doṣas, hemorrhaging, burning sensations, erysipelas, and leprosy. (89)
Śaileya is also known as śilāpuṣpa, vṛddha, and kālānusāryaka.

Śaileya is cooling, pleasing to the heart, light, and it alleviates kapha and pitta; it removes itching, skin diseases, urinary calculi, burning sensations, and poisons, and it cures blood disorders of the heart and rectum.
Mustaka is not feminine; musta is used in all three genders and is named after the water-giver (cloud).
Kuruvinda is also reckoned as another name, as is kroḍakaseruka.
Bhadramusta, gundrā, and likewise nāgaramustaka are also [names for it].
Musta is pungent, cold, constipating, bitter, and an appetizer and digestive;
it is astringent and removes phlegm, bile, blood disorders, thirst, fever, loss of appetite, and parasites.
That mustaka which grows in marshy regions is highly praised.
Among those as well, the sages have declared that *nāgara-mustaka* is the best.
*Karcūra*, *vedhamukhya*, *drāviḍa*, *kalpaka*, and *śaṭī* are also mentioned.
*Karcūra* is digestive, appetizing, pungent, and bitter. 94–95.
Sugandhi is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), cures leprosy, hemorrhoids, ulcers, and cough; it is hot, light, and removes asthma, abdominal tumors (gulma), wind, phlegm, and worms.
(96) Murā, Gandhakuṭī, Daityā, Surabhi, and Śālaparṇikā [are synonyms]. (97)

Murā is bitter, cooling, sweet, and light; it alleviates pitta and vāta, destroys fever, blood disorders, spirits, and demons, and cures skin diseases and cough. (98) Śaṭhī, palāśī, ṣaḍgranthā, suvratā, and gandhamūlikā [are synonyms].
Gandhārikā, Gandhavadhū, Vadhū, Pṛthupalāśikā,
and Gandhapalāśī are synonyms. It is astringent, absorbent, light,
bitter, sharp, pungent, non-heating, and it destroys impurities of the mouth.
Priyaṅgu—also known as phalinī, kāntā, latā, and mahilāhvayā—is the destroyer of swelling, cough, wounds, asthma, colic, sidhma, and demonic seizures (100).
Gundrā, also called gandhaphalā, śyāmā, and viṣvaksenāṅganāpriyā, [is likewise beneficial]. (101)

Priyaṅgu is cooling, bitter, astringent, and removes wind and bile; it cures bloody diarrhea, foul odors, perspiration, burning sensations, and fever; it destroys fainting, giddiness, and dysentery, and eliminates numbness of the mouth.
Gandhapriyaṅgu likewise destroys Gulma, thirst, poison, and delusion (103).
Its fruit is sweet, dry, astringent, cooling, and heavy; it relieves constipation and flatulence, provides strength, is constipating, and conquers Kapha and Pitta (104).
Reṇukā is known as the daughter of the king, Nandinī, Kapilā, the twice-born (dvijā),
Bhasmagandhā, the daughter of Pāṇḍu, Kauntī, and Hareṇukā.
Reṇukā is pungent in digestion, bitter, non-hot, acrid, and light.
Pittala is digestive, intellect-promoting, carminative, and causes abortion; it increases phlegm and wind, while also removing thirst, itching, poison, and burning sensations.
(106) Granthiparṇa, granthika, kākapuccha, and gucchaka [are synonyms].
The blue-flowered *tailaparṇaka* is said to be fragrant;
*granthiparṇa* is bitter and sharp, pungent and hot, digestive, and light, and it destroys phlegm, wind, poison, asthma, itching, and foul odors. 107–108.
Sthauṇeyaka, barhibarha, śukrabarha, kukkura, śīrṇaromaśuka, śukapuṣpa, and śukacchada—these are the names for the same substance.
Sthauṇeyaka is pungent, sweet, bitter, unctuous, and it alleviates the three doṣas. 109–110.
It promotes intelligence and semen, is appetizing, destroys demons, and conquers fever and parasites;
it cures skin diseases, hemorrhaging, thirst, burning sensations, foul odors, moles, and freckles.
(111) It is a night-stalker, a stealer of wealth, a gambler, and a source of laughter for the hosts.
Coraka is also known as Śaṅkita, Caṇḍa, Duṣpatra, Kṣemaka, and Ripu.

Coraka is sweet, bitter, and pungent; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), light, sharp, pleasing to the heart, and cooling. It destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), itching (kaṇḍū), phlegm (kapha), and wind (anila).
It destroys demons, misfortune, sweat, fat, blood, fever, foul odors, poisons, and wounds.
(113) Tālīsa is said to be rich in leaves along with dhātrī leaves.
(114) Tālīsa is light, sharp, and hot; it [cures] asthma, cough, phlegm, and wind disorders.
It destroys loss of appetite, abdominal tumors (gulma), indigestion, sluggish digestion, and consumption.
115 Kaṅkola is said to be kolaka, and it is likewise known as koṣaphala.
Kaṅkola is light, sharp, hot, bitter, beneficial for the heart, and provides relish.
Gandhakokilā removes foul breath, heart disease, disorders of phlegm and wind, and blindness;
it is unctuous, hot, pungent, fragrant, and alleviates phlegm. Gandhamālatī should be known as being identical to Gandhakokilā. (116–117)
Lāmajjaka is known as sunāla, amṛṇāla, lava, laghu,
iṣṭakāpathaka, sevya, nalada, and avadātaka.
(118) Lāmajjaka is cooling, bitter, light, and it conquers the three doṣas and blood disorders.

It cures skin diseases, excessive perspiration, difficult urination, burning sensations, and diseases of blood and bile (pitta). Elavāluka, maileya, sugandhi, and harivāluka are synonyms for elavāluka; it is also called elālu and kapitthatvac. 119–120.
Cardamom is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), astringent, cooling, and light;
it destroys itching, ulcers, vomiting, thirst, cough, anorexia, and heart disease, as well as phlegm (balāsa), poison, blood-bile (pittāsraka), leprosy (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders, and worms. 121
Kuṭannaṭa, dāsapura, bāleya, paripelava, plava, gopura, gonarda, kaivartī, and mustaka;
mustāvat, pelavapura, and śukābha are synonyms for bitunnaka. 122–123.
Vitunnaka is cold, bitter, astringent, and pungent; it bestows luster and destroys phlegm, bile, blood disorders, erysipelas, leprosy, itching, and poisons.
Spṛkkā, asṛg, brāhmaṇī, devī, marunmālā, and latā are light.
Samudrāntā, vadhū, koṭivarṣā, and laṅkopikā are synonyms for spṛkkā.
It is sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, bitter, and removes all the bodily humors (doṣas).
It cures leprosy, itching, poison, perspiration, burning sensations, eye diseases, fever, and blood disorders.
Parpaṭī, rañjanā, kṛṣṇā, jatukā, jananī, janī,
jatukṛṣṇā, agnisaṃsparśā, jatukṛt, and cakravartinī— these are the names of parpaṭī.
Parpaṭī is astringent, bitter, cooling, complexion-enhancing, and light.

Nalikā, vidrumalatā, kapotacaraṇā, naṭī, dhamanī, añjanakeśī, nirmadhyā, suṣirā, and nalī remove poison from wounds and cure itching, phlegm, bile, blood disorders, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 128–129.
Nalikā is cooling, light, beneficial for the eyes, and removes kapha and pitta; it cures dysuria, urinary calculi, vāta, thirst, blood disorders, skin diseases, itching, and fever.
Prapauṇḍarīka, pauṇḍarya, and pauṇḍarīyaka are beneficial for the eyes.
Pauṇḍarya is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it increases semen, is cooling, beneficial for the eyes, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), improves the complexion, and subdues pitta and kapha.
Thus ends the section on groups in the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The third section, the group beginning with camphor, is completed.
Now begins the group beginning with *guḍūcī*.
Then there was the proud Rāvaṇa, Lord of the Rākṣasas, the ruler of Laṅkā.
Afflicted by passion, he forcibly abducted Sītā, the wife of Rāma.
Thereupon, the powerful Rāma, surrounded by an army of monkeys, slew that enemy who had carried off his wife at the head of the battle.

When that enemy of the gods, Rāvaṇa, who was arrogant in his strength, had been slain, the thousand-eyed king of the gods was highly gratified with the descendant of Raghu. As for those monkeys there who had been killed by certain Rākṣasas in battle—
Indra restored them to life by sprinkling them with showers of nectar. Then, in those places where drops of ambrosia fell from the body of the monkey, the *guḍūcī* plant was born.
Guḍūcī, madhuparṇī, amṛtā, amṛtavallarī,
chinnā, chinnaruhā, chinnodbhavā, and vatsādanī are synonyms for it.
Jīvantī, tantrikā, somā, somavallī, and kuṇḍalī are also names for it.
The wheel-marked (cakralakṣaṇikā), the steadfast (dhīrā), the thorn-remover (viśalyā), the elixir (rasāyanī) [7],
the moon-laughing (candrahāsā), the age-stayer (vayasthā), the circular (maṇḍalī), and the god-fashioned (devanirmitā)—
guḍūcī is pungent, bitter, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and an elixir [8].
Astringent, astringent-tasting, hot, light, strengthening, and a stimulator of the digestive fire,
it removes the three *doṣas*, as well as indigestion, thirst, burning sensations, urinary disorders, cough, anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice,
skin diseases, blood disorders, fever, worms, and vomiting.
It cures primeha, dyspnea, cough, hemorrhoids, urinary distress, heart disease, and wind disorders.
Tāmbūlavallī, tāmbūlī, nāginī, and nāgavallarī are synonyms for betel.
Betel leaf is clarifying, appetizing, sharp, hot, astringent, and laxative.
Bilva (Aegle marmelos)—also known as śāṇḍilya, śailūṣa, mālūra, and śrīphala—is pungent, bitter, alkaline, light, and strengthening;
it increases blood and bile, and removes phlegm, foul breath, impurities, wind, and fatigue.
(12) Bilva, śāṇḍilya, śailūṣa, mālūra, and śrīphala are its synonyms.
The *śrīphala* (bilva fruit) is slightly astringent, bitter, constipating, dry, and it stimulates the digestive fire while increasing *pitta*.
It alleviates *vāta* and *kapha*, is strengthening, light, hot, and a digestive aid.
(13) It is also known as *gambhārī*, *bhadraparṇī*, *śrīparṇī*, and *madhuparṇikā*.
Kāśmīrī, kāśmarī, hīrā, kāśmarya, and pītarohiṇī (14),
as well as kṛṣṇavṛntā, madhurasā, and mahākusumikā—
these are synonyms for kāśmīrī. It is astringent, bitter, hot in potency, sweet, and heavy (15).
It is digestive, carminative, improves intellect, is laxative, and overcomes vertigo, wasting,

morbid humors (doṣas), thirst, indigestion, colic, hemorrhoids, poison, burning sensations, and fever. Its fruit is nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, beneficial for the hair, and acts as a rejuvenative elixir.
It alleviates wind, bile, thirst, loss of blood, and urinary obstruction (17).
It is sweet in its post-digestive effect, cooling, unctuous, slightly astringent and sour, and promotes purification;
it destroys burning sensations, thirst, vātarakta, pitta, chest wounds, and consumption (18).
Pāṭali, pāṭalā, amoghā, madhudūta, phaleruhā,
kṛṣṇavṛntā, kuberākṣī, kālasthālī, alivallabhā, and tāmrapuṣpī are said to be the names of the red pāṭalā; there is also another variety known as white pāṭalā.
Muṣkaka, mokṣaka, ghaṇṭāpāṭalikā, and aṣṭapāṭalā—these are synonyms for pāṭalā.
It is astringent, bitter, and not hot; it removes the three doṣas and cures anorexia, dyspnea, swelling, hemorrhage, vomiting, hiccups, and thirst.
The flower is astringent, sweet, cooling, pleasing to the heart, and subdues *kapha* and blood disorders;

it cures *pitta*-type diarrhea and is beneficial for the throat. The fruit removes hiccup and hemorrhagic disorders (*asrapitta*). (22) It is known as agnimantha, jaya, sasyaka, śrīparṇī, and gaṇikārikā.
Jayā, jayantī, tarkārī, nādeyī, and vaijayantikā—these are synonyms for agnimantha. It cures swelling, is highly efficacious, hot in potency, and removes kapha and vāta.
It cures anemia (pāṇḍu), is pungent, bitter, astringent, and sweet, and it stimulates the digestive fire.
Śyonāka is also known as śoṣaṇa; naṭa, kaṭvaṅga, ṭuṇṭuka, maṇḍūkaparṇa, patrorṇa, śukanāsa, kuṭannaṭa, dīrghavṛnta, aralu, pṛthuśimba, and kaṭambhara are its synonyms. (25)
Śyonāka is an appetizer; it is pungent in digestion, astringent, cold, constipating, bitter, and it destroys wind, phlegm, bile, and cough.
(26) The unripe fruit of Ṭuṇṭuka is dry and removes wind and phlegm. (27)
The mature fruit is pleasant to the heart, astringent, sweet, appetizing, light, and digestive;
it cures abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and worms, but it is heavy and aggravates the wind (vāta). (28) Śrīphala, sarvatobhadrā, pāṭalā, and gaṇikārikā [are synonyms].
Śyonāka along with these [other] five constitute what is known as the "Great Five Roots" (mahat-pañcamūla).
The Great Five Roots are bitter and astringent; they subdue kapha and vāta, are sweet, cure dyspnea and cough, are heating, light, and stimulate the digestive fire.
Śālaparṇī, sthirā, saumyā, triparṇī, pīvarī, guhā, vidārigandhā, dīrghāṅgī, dīrghapatrā, and aṃśumatī are synonyms.
(31) Śālaparṇī is heavy and conquers vomiting, fever, dyspnea, and diarrhea. (32)

Pṛśniparṇī—also known as Pṛthakparṇī, Citraparṇī, and Ahiparṇī—is bitter, sweet, and a rasāyana; it removes the three doṣas and wasting, is nourishing, antidotal to poison, and cures chest wounds, coughs, and worms. (33)
Kroṣṭuvinnā, Siṃhapucchī, Kalaśī, Dhāvanirguhā,
and Pṛśniparṇī destroy the three doṣas; they are aphrodisiac, hot, sweet, and non-diuretic, and they cure burning sensations, fever, asthma, bloody diarrhea, thirst, and consumption.
Vārttākī, kṣudrabhaṇṭākī, mahatī, bṛhatī, kulī, hiṅgulī, rāṣṭrikā, siṃhī, mahoṣṭrī, duṣpradharṣiṇī,
bṛhatī, grāhiṇī, hṛdyā, and pācanī remove phlegm and wind. (36)
Pungent and bitter, it destroys bad breath, bad taste in the mouth, impurities, and loss of appetite; it is hot and overcomes skin diseases, fever, asthma, colic, cough, and weak digestion.
(37) Kaṇṭakārī is also known as Duḥsparśā, Kṣudrā, Vyāghrī, and Nidigdhikā.
Kaṇṭālikā, Kaṇṭakinī, Dhāvanī, Bṛhatī, Śvetā, Kṣudrā, Candrahāsā, Lakṣmaṇā, Kṣetradūtikā,
Garbhadā, Candramā, Candrī, Candrapuṣpā, and Priyaṅkarī. (38–39)

Kaṇṭakārī is laxative, bitter, pungent, digestive-stimulant, and light; it is dry, hot, and promotes digestion. It destroys cough, dyspnea, fever, phlegm, and wind disorders, as well as chronic rhinitis, pain in the flanks, worms, and heart diseases. (40–41)
The fruit of these two is pungent in taste and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
It is a purgative for semen, a laxative, bitter, increases bile and digestive fire, and is light.
It destroys phlegm, wind, itching, cough, fat, worms, and fever. 42
In the same way, *sitā* (white) and *kṣudrā* (small) are said [to be varieties]; the latter is especially effective for conception.
43 *Gokṣura*, *kṣuraka*, *trikaṇṭa*, and *svādukaṇṭaka* are synonyms;
*gokaṇṭaka* and *vanaśṛṅgāṭa* are also names for *gokṣuraka*. 44
Palankaṣā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and likewise ikṣugandhikā, as well as gokṣura, are cooling, sweet, strength-promoting, and cleansers of the bladder;
they are sweet, digestive stimulants, aphrodisiacs, nourishing, and removers of urinary calculi. 45.
It cures urinary disorders (prameha), dyspnea, cough, hemorrhoids, painful micturition, heart disease, and edema.
Śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, vārttākī, kaṇṭakārikā, and gokṣura—these five constitute the *kaniṣṭha-pañcamūla* (the smallest group of five roots). 46–47.
The *pañcamūla* (small group of five roots) is light, sweet, strengthening, and subdues pitta and vāta;
it is not excessively hot, is nourishing, constipating, and cures fever, dyspnea, and urinary calculi.
The *daśamūla* (group of ten roots) is said to consist of both these *pañcamūlas*.
Daśamūla (the ten roots) destroys the three doṣas and removes dyspnea, cough, headache, drowsiness, edema, fever, abdominal distension, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.
(49) Jīvantī, jīvanī, jīvā, jīvanīyā, and madhusravā [are synonyms].

The *śāka* known as *māṅgalya* is excellent, milky, life-sustaining, cooling, sweet, unctuous, and it removes the three *doṣas*. It is an elixir (*rasāyana*), strength-promoting, beneficial for the eyes, constipating, and light. (50–51)
Mudgaparṇī, kākaparṇī, sūryaparṇī, alpakā, sahā,
kākamudgā, and mārjāragandhikā are said to be synonyms.
Mudgaparṇī is cooling, dry, bitter, sweet, and increases semen.

Māṣaparṇī (also known as Sūryaparṇī, Kāmbojī, and Hayapucchikā) is beneficial for the eyes, destroys wounds and swelling, is astringent, alleviates fever and burning sensations, removes the three doṣas, is light, and cures disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, and diarrhea. (54)
Pāṇḍulomaśaparṇī and Kṛṣṇavṛntā are the Mahāsahā group (55).
Māṣaparṇī is cooling, bitter, dry, and increases semen and strength;
it is sweet, constipating, and conquers swelling, wind, bile, fever, and blood disorders (56).

The group consisting of the eight drugs along with yaṣṭī, jīvantī, mudgaparṇikā, and māṣaparṇī is known as the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) group. It is proclaimed by name as both vitalizing and sweet. 57.
The group of vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs is said to be semen-promoting, nourishing, and cooling;
it is heavy, promotes conception, increases breast milk and kapha, and removes pitta and blood disorders.
It alleviates thirst, wasting, fever, burning sensations, and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). 58–59.
Śukla, eraṇḍa, āmaṇḍa, citra, gandharvahastaka,
pañcāṅgula, vardhamāna, dīrghadaṇḍa, vyaḍambaka, vātāri, taruṇa, and rubūka are also its names. (60)
Another variety is *rakta-urubūka*, while *urubūka* and *rubu* are also known as *vyāghrapuccha*, *vātāri*, *cañcu*, and *uttānapatraka*.
This pair of castor oils (*eraṇḍa*) is sweet, hot, and heavy; it destroys [certain ailments]. 62

Castor leaf destroys wind, destroys phlegm and worms, and cures colic, swelling, pain in the waist, bladder, head, and abdomen, as well as fever, vomiting, dyspnea, phlegm, flatulence, cough, leprosy, and diseases caused by aggravated wind. (63)
The leaf of Vātāri (Aragvadha) removes dysuria, though it provokes pitta and blood; it is supreme for curing abdominal tumors and pain in the bladder,
destroys kapha, vata, and worms, and cures all seven types of scrotal enlargement.
Castor seed is very hot; it cures abdominal tumors, colic, and disorders of Vāta (65).

It destroys liver and spleen enlargement, abdominal dropsy, and hemorrhoids; it is pungent, an excellent digestive stimulant, and likewise, its marrow is a purgative that removes Vāta, Kapha, and abdominal diseases (66).
The white *arka* is *gaṇarūpa*, while *mandāra* and *vasuka* are also [white];
it is also known as *śvetapuṣpa*, *sadāpuṣpa*, *alarka*, and *pratāpasa*.
Another, red in color, is named *arka*, and is also called *arkaparṇa* and *vikīraṇa*.
The red-flowered variety with white fruit is likewise proclaimed as Asphota (68).
The two types of Arka are laxative and destroy wind, skin diseases, itching, poisons, and ulcers;
they also eliminate splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, phlegm-related abdominal enlargements, and worms (69).
The flower of *Alarka* is aphrodisiac, light, and a digestive stimulant that promotes digestion;
it cures anorexia, salivation, hemorrhoids, cough, and asthma (70).
The red flower of *Arkapuṣpa* is sweet with a bitter taste, destroys skin diseases and worms, and subdues *kapha*.
It destroys hemorrhoids and poison, checks internal bleeding (raktapitta), and is beneficial for abdominal tumors (gulma) and edema (śvayathu).
(71) The milk of the Arka plant is bitter, hot, unctuous, slightly salty, and light;
it cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargement, and is an excellent purgative. (72)

Sehuṇḍa, siṃhatuṇḍa, vajrī, and vajradruma are synonyms for the sehuṇḍa plant. Sudhā and samantadugdhā are also names for it; furthermore, the feminine forms snuk, snuhī, and guḍā denote the same. (73) Sehuṇḍa is purgative, sharp, digestive, pungent, and heavy.
It cures colic, constipation, flatulence, kaphaja gulma, abdominal enlargement, and vāta disorders;
it also removes insanity, delusion, leprosy, hemorrhoids, swelling, obesity, urinary calculi, anemia, ulcers, edema, fever, splenic disorders, and artificial and natural poisons.
The latex of Snuhī is hot in potency, unctuous, pungent, and light;

it is beneficial for those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and likewise for those with abdominal disorders (udara). It is suitable for purgation, as well as for others who suffer from chronic illnesses.
Śātalā, saptalā, sārā, vimalā, vidulā,
as well as bhūriphenā and carmakaṣā— these are thus described.
Śātalā is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), increases vāta, is cooling, and light.
Bitter [kalihārī] conquers swelling, kapha, abdominal distension, pitta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and blood disorders.
Kalihārī, however, is also known as halinī, lāṅgalī, śakrapuṣpī,
viśalyā, agniśikhā, anantā, vahnivaktrā, and garbhanut.
Kaliṃhārī is astringent; it conquers skin diseases, swelling, hemorrhoids, ulcers, and colic (80).
It contains alkali, overcomes phlegm, and is bitter, pungent, and astringent; furthermore, it is sharp, hot, anthelmintic, light, increases bile, and causes the expulsion of the fetus (81).
Karavīra has white flowers and is called śatakumbha and aśvamāraka;
the second variety has red flowers and is known as caṇḍāta and laguḍa. Both types of karavīra are bitter, astringent, and pungent.
It lightens wounds, cures eye-inflammation, leprosy, and ulcers;
it is hot in potency, destroys worms and itching, and when eaten, is considered to be like poison.
Dhattūra, dhūrta, dhuttūra, unmatta, and kanakāhvaya are synonyms for the thorn-apple.
Dhattūra is known as Devatā, Kitava, Tūrī, Mahāmohī, Śivapriya, Mātula, and Madana; its fruit is called Mātulaputraka.
Dhattūra produces intoxication, complexion, digestive fire, and wind, and it cures fever and leprosy. (85–86)

Vāsaka, vāsikā, vāsā, bhiṣaṅmātā, and siṃhikā are synonyms for ādityabhaktā. It is astringent, sweet, and bitter; it destroys lice and nit-eggs. It is hot and heavy, and it removes wounds, phlegm, itching, worms, and poison. (87) ādityabhaktā vāsako vāsikā vāsā bhiṣaṅmātā ca siṃhikā | kaṣāyo madhurastikto yūkālikṣāvināśakaḥ || uṣṇo gururvraṇaśleṣmakaṇḍūkṛmiviṣāpahaḥ || 87 ||
Siṃhāsya has horse-teeth; āṭarūṣa and aṭarūṣaka are synonyms. Aṭarūṣa is also known as vṛṣa, tāmra, and siṃhaparṇa.
It is called vāsaka; it generates wind, is beneficial for the voice, and destroys phlegm, bile, and blood disorders. 88–89.
Pāṭalā (parpaṭa) is bitter, astringent, pleasing to the heart, light, and cooling;
it removes thirst and distress, and cures asthma, cough, fever, vomiting, urinary disorders, skin diseases, and consumption.
It is known as parpaṭa, varatikta, and parpaṭaka. (90)
The synonym for *pāṃśu* (dust) has thus been stated, as well as the name *kavaca*. 91.
*Parpaṭa* destroys bile-blood disorders, vertigo, thirst, phlegm, and fever;
it is astringent, cooling, bitter, a remover of burning sensations, increases wind (*vāta*), and is light. 92.
Nimba is known as picumarda, picumanda, tiktaka,
ariṣṭa, pāribhadra, and also hiṅguniryāsa (93).
Nimba is cooling, light, constipating, pungent in its post-digestive effect, and it subdues digestive fire and vāta.

The neem leaf (nimbapatra) is known to be unpalatable, yet it cures fatigue, thirst, cough, fever, anorexia, worms, ulcers, pitta, kapha, vomiting, skin diseases, nausea, and urinary disorders; it is also beneficial for the eyes and destroys worms, pitta, and poisons. 94.

The fruit of the *nimba* is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), increases *vāta*, and cures all types of anorexia, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), worms, and urinary disorders;
it is bitter in taste, digestive, sharp, unctuous, light, and hot. (95–96)
Mahānimba is known as Drekā, Ramyaka, Viṣamuṣṭika, Keśamuṣṭi, Nimbaka, Kārmuka, and Jīva.
Mahānimba is cooling, dry, bitter, astringent, and constipating. 97–98.

It conquers phlegm, bile, vertigo, vomiting, skin diseases, nausea, and blood disorders; it destroys urinary disorders, asthma, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and the poison of rats. (99) The Pāribhadra, Nimbataru, Mandāra, and Pārijātaka [are synonyms].
Pāribhadra destroys wind, phlegm, swelling, fat, and worms; its leaf cures diseases of bile and destroys ailments of the ear. (100) Kāñcanāra, kāñcanaka, gaṇḍāri, and śoṇapuṣpaka are synonyms. (101)
Kovidāra, marika, kuddāla, yugapatraka, kuṇḍalī, tāmrapuṣpa, aśmantaka, and svalpakeśarī (102),
as well as kāñcanāra, are cooling, astringent, and alleviate phlegm and bile.
It cures worms, skin diseases, prolapse of the rectum, scrofula, and wounds.
The *kovidāra* tree is similar to those two; its flowers are considered light, dry, and constipating, and they alleviate hemorrhaging, dysentery, consumption, and cough.
Śobhāñjana, śigru, tīkṣṇagandhaka, akṣīva, mocaka, its seed (tadbīja), śvetamarica, madhuśigru, and the red śigru are synonyms.
Śigru is pungent, pungent in digestion, sharp, hot, sweet, and light. (105)
It is illuminating, clarifying, dry, alkaline, bitter, and causes a burning sensation; it is astringent, aphrodisiac, and beneficial for the heart, yet it aggravates pitta and blood.
It is good for the eyes, destroys kapha and vāta, and cures abscesses, swelling, and worms. (106)
It removes fat, scrofula, poison, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, goiter, and ulcers.
White [Karkoṭaka] should be known to possess the aforementioned qualities, but it specifically causes a burning sensation;
it destroys splenic enlargement and abscesses, is a healer of ulcers, and removes pitta and blood disorders.
Madhuśigru possesses the qualities previously mentioned; it is specifically digestive and laxative (108).
The fresh juice of the bark and leaves of Śigru removes extreme pain (109).
The seed produced from Śigru is beneficial for the eyes, pungent, hot, and a destroyer of poisons.
It is non-aphrodisiac, destroys Kapha and Vata, and when used as a nasal drop (nasya), it cures headaches.
Āsphotā, girikarṇī, viṣṇukrāntā, and aparājitā are synonyms for aparājitā; it is pungent, promotes intellect, is cooling, beneficial for the throat, and provides excellent vision.
It destroys skin diseases, urinary disorders, the three *doṣas*, fever, swelling, ulcers, and poisons;
it is astringent and pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), bitter in taste, and promotes memory and intelligence.
(112) Sinduvāra, Śvetapuṣpa, Sinduka, and Sinduvāraka [are synonyms].
Nirguṇḍī is also known as nīlapuṣpī, śephālī, and suvahā.
Sinduka is astringent, bitter, astringent-tasting, pungent, and light; it promotes hair growth, is beneficial for the eyes, and destroys colic, swelling, indigestion, and wind disorders.
Nīlā also possesses similar properties for [treating] worms, skin diseases, loss of appetite, phlegm, and fever.
(114) The leaf of Sinduvāra removes parasites, wind, and phlegm, and is light [to digest].
(115) Kuṭaja, Kūṭaja, Kauṭa, Vatsaka, and Girimallikā are synonyms. (116)
Kāliṅga, śakraśākhī, mallikāpuṣpa, indra, yavaphala, vṛkṣaka, and pāṇḍuradruma are synonyms for the kuṭaja tree (117).
Kuṭaja is pungent, dry, digestive, astringent, and cold.
It cures hemorrhoids, diarrhea, bile, blood, phlegm, thirst, and leprosy (118).
Karañja, naktamāla, karaja, and cirabilvaka are synonyms;
there is another variety called ghṛtapūrṇakarañja, as well as prakīrya and pūtika (119).
That is called *pūtikarañja* and is also known as *somavalka*.

*Karañja* is pungent and sharp, hot in potency, and it removes disorders of the female reproductive tract; it cures skin diseases, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, ulcers, worms, and phlegm. 120
Its leaf is an excellent remedy for phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, worms, and swelling;
it is purgative, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), hot in potency (vīrya), increases pitta, and is light.
(121) Its fruit destroys phlegm and wind, and conquers urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, worms, and skin diseases.
The *ghṛtapūrṇakarañja* is also similar to the *karañja* in its qualities.
Another is the third, *udakīrya*; furthermore, there are the *ṣaḍgranthā*, *hastivāruṇī*, *markaṭī*, *vāyasī*, *karañjī*, and *karabhañjikā*.
Karañjī is astringent, bitter, slightly astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka);
it is hot in potency (vīrya) and overcomes vomiting, bile disorders, hemorrhoids, worms, skin diseases, and urinary disorders.
It is called śvetā, guñjā, uccaṭā, and is also known as kṛṣṇalā.
The red variety is known as *kākaciñcī*, *kākaṇantī*, and *raktikā* (125). It is also remembered as *kākādanī*, *kākapīlu*, and *kākavallarī*.
Two types of *guñjā* promote hair growth and alleviate wind, bile, and fever (126).
It destroys dryness of the mouth, vertigo, labored breathing, thirst, and intoxication;
it cures eye diseases, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and removes itching and wounds.
It also cures worms, alopecia, leprosy, and both red and white [skin] disorders. 127–128.
Kapicchu, ātmaguptā, and markaṭī are said to be aphrodisiacs;
likewise, ajaḍā, kaṇḍurā, vyaṅgā, duḥsparśā, prāvṛṣāyaṇī,
lāṅgalī, and śūkaśimbī are declared by the great sages to be the same.
Kapikacchu is highly aphrodisiac, sweet, nourishing, and heavy;
it is bitter, alleviates Vata, is strengthening, and destroys Kapha, Pitta, and blood disorders.
Its seeds are considered pacifiers of Vata and are an excellent aphrodisiac. 130–131.
Māṃsarohiṇī is also known as atiruhā, vṛttā, carmakaṣā, vasā, prahāravallī, vikaśā, and vīravatī.
Māṃsarohiṇī is aphrodisiac, laxative, and it removes the three doṣas. (132)
Cihlaka removes wind, destroys phlegm, nourishes the bodily constituents (dhātus), and is fiery; its fruit is like poison in that it destroys fish.
Taṅkarī conquers wind, is bitter, destroys phlegm, stimulates digestion, and is light.
It destroys swelling, abdominal pain, and is beneficial for those suffering from erysipelas (pīṭhavisarpa). 134.
Vetasa is declared to be namraka, vānīra, and vañjula; it is also celebrated as abhrapuṣpa, vidula, ratha, and śīta. 135.

Vetasa is cooling and cures burning sensations, swelling, hemorrhoids, vaginal disorders, and pain; it destroys erysipelas, dysuria, internal hemorrhaging, urinary calculi, and disorders of kapha and vata.
(136) Nikuñjaka, parivyādha, nādeya, and jalavetasa are synonyms for vetasa.
The aquatic *vetasa* is cooling, cures skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and aggravates *vāta*. 137.
*Ijjala*, *hijjala*, *nicula*, and *ambuja* should be understood as being like *jalavetasa*; furthermore, this *hijjala* removes poison. 138.
Aṅkoṭa is known as dīrghakīla, aṅkola, and nikocaka; it is also called aṅkoṭaka. It is pungent, sharp, unctuous, hot, astringent, and light.
It is a purgative and removes worms, colic, abdominal tumors, swelling, seizures, and poisons. (139)
It cures erysipelas, disorders of kapha, pitta, and blood, as well as the venom of rats and snakes.
Its fruit is cooling, sweet, alleviates kapha, is nourishing, heavy, strengthening, and a purgative; it conquers vata, pitta, burning sensations, wasting, and hemorrhagic diseases.
Balāvāṭyālikā, vāṭyā, and likewise vāṭyālakā;
mahābalā, pītapuṣpā, and sahadevī are recorded as such. Furthermore, there is another, atibalā, which is also called ṛṣyaproktā and kaṅkatikā.

Gāṅgerukī, nāgabalā, jhaṣā, and short gavedhukā constitute the fourfold *balā* group. They are cooling, sweet, and bestow strength and a beautiful complexion; they are unctuous, constipating, and destroy wind, blood-bile disorders, hemorrhaging, and wounds. (143–144)
The powder of the bark of *Balā* root, when drunk with milk and sugar, cures dysuria and excessive urination; this has been observed and there is no doubt.
*Mahābalā* removes *kṛcchra* (urinary distress) and facilitates the downward movement of *vāta*.
One should cure diabetes with milk mixed with sugar.
(146) The *lakṣmaṇā* plant, which produces sons, has leaves marked with small red spots shaped like the young of a crow; it possesses the fragrance of the *vasta* flower. (147)
The Lakṣmaṇā plant has been described by the best of sages as necessarily bestowing sons.
Svarṇavallī, Raktaphalā, Kākāyu, and Kākavallarī are synonyms for Svarṇavallī; it cures headaches, destroys the three doṣas, and provides milk. 148–149.
Kārpāsī, Tuṇḍakeśī, Samudrāntā,
and Karpāsakī are described as light, slightly warm, sweet, and destroyers of Vāta (150). Their leaves subdue wind, promote blood, and increase urine.
It destroys ear-eruptions, pain, and the discharge of pus.
Its seed provides breast milk, is aphrodisiac, unctuous, increases *kapha*, and is heavy.
Bamboo, *tvaksāra*, *karmāra*, *tvacisāra*, *tṛṇadhvaja*, and *veṇu* are synonyms for bamboo.
The bamboo (veṇu), which has a hundred joints and seeds like barley, as well as maskara and tejana;
the bamboo (vaṃśa) is cooling, sweet, astringent, purifies the bladder, is scarifying, destroys kapha and pitta, and conquers skin diseases, blood disorders, ulcers, and swellings. 153–154.
The fruit of that tree (the *karīra*) is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), dry (*rūkṣa*), heavy (*guru*),
laxative (*sara*), astringent (*kaṣāya*), increases phlegm (*kapha*), is sweet (*svādu*), causes a burning sensation (*vidāhin*), and aggravates wind and bile (*vāta-pittala*).
Its grains (*yava*), however, are laxative, dry, astringent, and pungent in their post-digestive effect.

Nala, poṭagala, śūnyamadhya, and dhamana increase vāta and pitta, are hot in potency, cause the retention of urine, and alleviate kapha. Nala is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it conquers kapha and blood disorders.
It is hot and removes pain in the heart, bladder, and vagina, as well as burning sensations, *pitta*, and erysipelas (157).
Bhadra, muñja, śara, bāṇa, tejana, and ikṣuveṣṭana are synonyms for muñja (158).
Muñja, muñjātaka, bāṇa, sthūladarbha, and sumekhala are also names for it.
The two types of muñja grass are sweet, astringent, and cooling;
they conquer burning sensations, thirst, erysipelas, hemorrhaging, dysuria, and eye diseases.
They alleviate the three doṣas, act as an aphrodisiac, and are used for waistbands. (159–160)
Kāsa is known as Kāsekṣu; it is likewise called Ikṣurasas, Ikṣvālikā, Ikṣugandhā, and is also remembered as Poṭagala.
Kāsa is sweet, bitter, has a sweet post-digestive effect (pāka), is cold, and is coarse.

It conquers dysuria, urinary stones, burning sensations, hemorrhage, and diseases born of the depletion of *pitta*. 162. *Gundra*, *paṭeraka*, *gulma*, and *śṛṅgaverābha-mūlaka* are synonyms for *gundra*.
It is astringent, sweet, cooling, and conquers *pitta* and blood disorders.
It purifies breast milk, semen, menstrual blood, and urine, and removes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
(163) Erakā, gundra-mūlā, śivi, gundrā, and śarīti—
erakā is cooling, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and aggravates vāta.
It destroys dysuria, urinary stones, burning sensations, and the disorders of bile and blood.
(164) Kuśa, Darbha, and Barhi are synonyms; it has needle-like tips and is an ornament for the sacrificial ground.
Another variety is the Dīrghapatra (long-leaved), and likewise the Kṣurapatra (razor-leaved). (165)
The two types of darbha destroy the three doṣas; they are sweet, astringent, and cooling, and they conquer dysuria, urinary calculi, thirst, pain in the bladder, menorrhagia, and hemorrhage.
Kattṛṇa, rauhiṣa, devajagdha, and likewise saugandhika [are also included].

Bhūtika, dhyāma, paura, śyāmaka, and dhūpagandhika (167)—as well as rauhiṣa and tuvara—are bitter and pungent in their post-digestive effect; they dispel diseases of the heart and throat, blood-bile disorders, colic, cough, phlegm, and fever. (168)
Guhyabīja is also known as bhūtīka, sugandha, and jambukapriya;
bhūtṛṇa is called chatrā and mālātṛṇaka as well.
Bhūtṛṇa is pungent, bitter, sharp, hot, purgative, and light.
It causes a burning sensation, stimulates digestion, is dry, harmful to the eyes, cleanses the mouth,
is non-aphrodisiac, produces excessive feces, and vitiates the pitta and blood.
(170–171) Nīladūrvā, ruhā, anantā, bhārgavī, and śataparvikā [are also mentioned].
Śaṣpa is known as Sahasravīryā and Śatavallī (172).
Nīladūrvā is cooling, bitter, sweet, and astringent; it removes phlegm, bile, blood disorders, erysipelas, thirst, burning sensations, and skin diseases (173).
White Dūrvā grass is called Golomī and Śatavīryā;
white Dūrvā is astringent, sweet, healing for wounds, and vitalizing.
It is bitter and cooling, and it removes erysipelas, hemorrhaging, thirst, pitta, kapha, and burning sensations. (174)
Gaṇḍadūrvā, also known as gaṇḍālī, matsyākṣī, and śakulādanī,
is cooling, laxative, astringent, light,
bitter, astringic, sweet, wind-increasing, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka). 175.
It removes burning sensations, thirst, *balāsa*, rheum, leprosy, and bile-fever.
(176) That which is known as *vārāhīkanda* is called *gṛṣṭi* in the West; it is also considered by others to be *carmakārāluka*. (177)
In a marshy region where lotuses grow, the plant known as *vārāhī* is hairy like a boar;
it is called *gṛṣṭi* and also *varadā*.
As for *vārāhī*, its taste is sweet, it is bitter, and its post-digestive effect (*pāka*) is pungent.

Vidarī, which has sweet tubers, increases semen, lifespan, voice, complexion, digestive fire, strength, and pitta; it removes kapha, skin diseases, wind disorders, urinary disorders, and worms, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana). It is known as kroṣṭrī and sitā. (179)
The *ikṣugandhā*, *kṣīravallī*, *kṣīraśuklā*, and *payasvinī*— also known as *vidārī*—
are sweet, unctuous, nourishing, and increase breast milk and semen.
They are cooling, beneficial for the voice, diuretic, vitalizing, and bestow strength and a healthy complexion.
Guru destroys pitta, blood disorders, vāta, and burning sensations; it is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
Tālamūlī is proclaimed by the learned as Muśalī.
Muśalī is sweet, aphrodisiac, hot in potency, nourishing, and heavy.
Bitter *śatāvarī* is a rejuvenative that destroys hemorrhoids as well as vāta disorders.
It is known by the names bṛhat-sutā, bhīru, indīvarī, varī, nārāyaṇī, śatapadī, śatavīryā, and pīvarī. (183–184)
Mahāśatāvarī, as well as śatamūlī, ūrdhvakaṇṭikā,
sahasravīryā, hetu, ṛṣyaproktā, and mahodarī [are synonyms].
(185) Śatāvarī is heavy, cooling, bitter, sweet, and a rejuvenative (rasāyana).

Mahāśatāvarī bestows intelligence, stimulates the digestive fire, promotes nourishment, is unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and overcomes abdominal tumors (gulma) and diarrhea. It increases semen and breast milk, is strengthening, and conquers disorders of wind, bile, blood, and swelling; it is intellect-promoting, pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative elixir. 186–187.
Cold in potency, it destroys hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and eye diseases; its sprouts destroy the three *doṣas* and are light, removing hemorrhoids and consumption. 188.
*Gandhāntā*, *vājināmādi*, *aśvagandhā*, and *hayāhvayā* are synonyms for *aśvagandhā*.
Varāhakarṇī bestows boons and strength; it possesses the fragrance of kuṣṭha.
Aśvagandhā removes wind, phlegm, leucoderma, swelling, and consumption; it is strengthening, an elixir, bitter, astringent, hot, and highly spermatogenic. (189–190)
Pāṭhā, ambaṣṭhā, ambaṣṭhakī, prācīnā, pāpacelikā,
ekāṣṭhīlā, rasā, pāṭhikā, and varatiktikā are synonyms for pāṭhā.
(191) Pāṭhā is hot, pungent, sharp, light, and it subdues vāta and kapha.
It destroys colic, fever, vomiting, skin diseases, dysentery, heart disease,
burning sensations, itching, poison, asthma, worms, abdominal tumors, internal abscesses, and ulcers.
(193) Śvetā, trivṛt, tribhaṇḍī, trivṛtā, and tripuṭā are synonyms for the same plant.
Sarvānubhūti, Saralā, Niśotrā, and Recanī (193);
Śvetā is Trivṛt-recanī; it is sweet, hot, wind-alleviating, dry, and removes pitta-fever, phlegm, bile, swelling, and abdominal enlargement (194).
Trivṛt, Śyāmā, Ardhacandrā, Pālindī, Suṣeṇikā, Masūravidalā, Kālī, Kaiṣikā, and Kālameṣikā— among these,
Śyāmā is inferior in quality to Trivṛt, yet it is a powerful purgative.
Udumbaraparṇī causes fainting, burning, intoxication, delusion, and the extraction [of darts] from the throat; it is also laghudantī and viśalyā.
Similarly, eraṇḍaphalā, śīghrā, śvetaghaṇṭā, and ghuṇapriyā are likewise.
Vārāhāṅgī is also mentioned, as well as Nikumbha and Makūlaka;
Dravantī, Śambarī, Citrā, Pratyakparṇī, and Ākhuparṇī;
Upacitrā, Śrutaśroṇī, Nyagrodhī, and likewise Vṛṣā. 198.
The two types of *dantī* are laxative, digestive, pungent in taste, and a stimulant of the digestive fire (199).
They cure hemorrhoids, urinary calculi, colic, blood disorders, itching, skin diseases, and burning sensations;
being sharp and hot, they destroy bile-blood disorders, phlegm, swelling, abdominal enlargements, and worms (200).

The small *dantī* fruit is sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (*pāka*), cooling, and it promotes the evacuation of feces and urine; it removes artificial poisons (*gara*), edema, and phlegm.
*Jayapāla*, *dantibīja*, and *tintiḍīphala* are well-known synonyms for it. (201)
Jayapāla is a mild guru (heavy), emetic, and it removes pitta and kapha. 202.
Now, indravāruṇī, mahendravāruṇī, aindrī, indravāruṇī, citrā, gavākṣī, and gavādanī [are described].
Vāruṇī is also said to be another [variety], as well as Viśālā and Mahāphalā (203).
Śvetapuṣpā, Mṛgākṣī, Mṛgairvāru, and Mṛgādanī— these two types of Gavādanī are bitter, pungent in digestion, laxative, and light (204).

Vīryoṣṇa removes jaundice, bile disorders, phlegm, and splenic enlargement; it cures asthma and cough, and destroys skin diseases, abdominal tumors, glandular swellings, and ulcers. It also eliminates urinary disorders, obstructed labor, scrofula, and poisons. (205–206)
Nīlī, nīlinī, tūṇī, kālā, dolā, nīlikā,
rañjanī, śrīphalī, tucchā, grāmīṇā, madhuparṇikā,
klītakā, kālakeśī, and nīlapuṣpā are recorded as its synonyms.

Nīlinī is purgative, bitter, beneficial for the hair, and removes delusion and vertigo. It is hot in potency and destroys abdominal enlargements, splenic disorders, vātarakta, kapha, and vāta; it also cures āmavāta, udāvarta, intoxication, and potent poisons. (208–209)
Śarapuṅkha resembles the nīlī tree in appearance; it is also known as plīhaśatru.
Śarapuṅkha removes disorders of the liver, spleen, abdominal tumors, wounds, and poisons;
it is bitter and astringent, cures cough, hemorrhage, dyspnea, and fever, and is light. 210
Vṛddhadāruka (also known as āvegī, chāgāntrī, vṛṣyagandhikā,
and vṛddhadvāru) is astringent, hot, pungent, and bitter; it is a rejuvenative (rasāyana),
aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of vāta, āmavāta, hemorrhoids, edema, urinary disorders, and kapha.
Yavāsa (Alhagi) promotes semen, longevity, strength, intellect, digestive fire, voice, and luster; it is a laxative.
It is known as yavāsa, duḥsparśa, dhanvayāsa, kunāśaka, durālabhā, durālambhā, samudrāntā, and rodinī. (211)
Gāndhārī, kacchurā, anantā, kāṣāyā, and harivigrahā are synonyms for yāsa.
It is sweet, slightly bitter, astringent, cold, and light;
it conquers phlegm, fat, intoxication, confusion, bile, blood disorders, skin diseases, and cough. (212)
It is known to remove thirst, spreading diseases, wind-disorders, hemorrhages, and fever.
Durālabhā is said by the wise to possess qualities equal to those of yavāsa.
Muṇḍī is also called bhikṣu, śrāvaṇī, and tapodhanā.
Śravaṇāhvā, Muṇḍatikā, and Śravaṇaśīrṣakā;
another is known as Mahāśrāvaṇikā, as well as Bhūkadambikā and Kadambapuṣpikā; and Avyathā is called Atitapasvinī. 215–216.

Muṇḍatikā is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), hot in potency (vīrya), sweet, and light; it is beneficial for the intellect and cures scrofulous swellings (gaṇḍa), apacī, urinary disorders (kṛcchra), worms, vaginal diseases, anemia, elephantiasis (ślīpada), aversion to food, epilepsy, splenic enlargement, obesity, and pain in the rectum. (217)
And Mahāmuṇḍī is said by the great sages to be equal to it in its qualities. Apāmārga, Śikharī, Adhaḥśalya, Mayūraka, Markaṭī, Durgrahā, Kiṇihī, and Kharamañjarī [are synonyms]. 218–219.

Apāmārga is very sharp, digestive, bitter, pungent, a promoter of digestion, appetizing, and it removes vomiting, phlegm, fat, and wind; it destroys heart disease, flatulence, hemorrhoids, itching, colic, abdominal disorders, and scrofula. (220)
Rakta, anya, vaśira, vṛttaphala, and dhāmārgava are synonyms; it is also called pratyakparṇī, keśaparṇī, and kapipippalī.
Apāmārga is reddish, causes constipation of the wind (vāta), removes phlegm (kapha), and is cooling.
Those who know its qualities have declared it to be dry and deficient in the aforementioned properties.
The fruit of the *apāmārga* is sweet in taste and digestion, yet difficult to digest;
it causes constipation, increases *vāta*, is dry, and clarifies *rakta-pitta*.

*Kokilākṣa* is called *kākekṣu*, *ikṣura*, *kṣuraka*, and *kṣura*; it is also termed *bhikṣu* and *kāṇḍekṣu*. *Ikṣugandhā* and *ikṣubālikā* are synonyms for *kṣuraka*. *Kṣuraka* is cooling, aphrodisiac, sweet and sour, and slimy.

Tikta (Piper chaba) conquers wind, vomiting, swelling, urinary stones, thirst, impaired vision, and blood disorders caused by Vāta. Granthimān (Cissampelos pareira), Vajrāṅgī, and Asthiśṛṅkhalā are said to dissolve bone tissue; they remove Vāta and Kapha and strengthen the bones.
It is known to be hot, laxative, anthelmintic, a destroyer of hemorrhoids, a conqueror of eye diseases, dry, sweet, light, aphrodisiac, digestive, and increases *pitta*.
(227) A stalk devoid of its skin is half the size of a chain-like bone; a fresh *māṣa* bean is two parts, while one without its husk is half of that.
O fair-limbed one, a *vaṭaka* (ball) made from sesame paste ground with its oil and cooked thoroughly is an excellent destroyer of Vāta. 228.
Kumārī, Gṛhakanyā, Kanyā, Ghṛtakumārikā, and Kumārī are purgative, cooling, bitter, beneficial for the eyes, and an elixir (*rasāyana*). 229.

Madhurā is nourishing, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of wind and poisons; it removes abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, liver enlargement, and fever caused by kapha; and it cures glandular swellings, burns from fire, eruptions, and diseases of the blood and skin caused by pitta. 230

Punarnavā (Boerhavia diffusa), known as śvetamūlā, śothaghnī, and dīrghapatrikā, is pungent with an astringent aftertaste; it is an excellent healer of jaundice, a digestive stimulant, and a remover of swelling, wind, poisons, and phlegm, while also curing hernia and abdominal enlargement. 231
Punarnavā is also known as aparā, raktā, raktapuṣpā, śilāṭikā,
śothaghnī, kṣudrā, varṣābhū, varṣaketu, and kaṭhillaka.
(232) Punarnavā is reddish, bitter, pungent in its post-digestive effect, cold, and light.
Prasāraṇī, rājabalā, bhadraparṇī, pratāninī, saraṇī, sāraṇī, bhadrā, balā, and kaṭaṃbharā increase vāta, are astringent, and destroy kapha, pitta, and blood.

Prasāraṇī is heavy, aphrodisiac, a binder of the joints, laxative, hot in potency, bitter, a remover of Vāta, and a destroyer of Vātarakta and Kapha. (235) Kṛṣṇā, Śārivā, Śyāmā, Gopī, and Gopavadhū are synonyms for it. (236)
Dhavalā, sārivā, gopā, gopakanyā, kṛśodarī, sphoṭā, śyāmā, gopavallī, latā, asphotā, and candanā—
these constitute the pair of sārivās. They are sweet, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and heavy.
It destroys sluggish digestion, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, and the poisons of *āmadoṣa*;
it also cures the three *doṣas*, menorrhagia, fever, and diarrhea. (238) *Bhṛṅgarāja*, *bhṛṅgaraja*, *mārkava*, and *bhṛṅga* are its names.
Aṅgāraka, Keśarāja, Bhṛṅgāra, and Keśarañjana—these are synonyms for Bhṛṅgarāja.
It is pungent, sharp, dry, and hot; it subdues phlegm and wind.
It is beneficial for the hair, good for the skin, and cures worms, asthma, cough, swelling, indigestion, and anemia.

Śaṇapuṣpī is known as Ghaṇṭā; it has a shape similar to the flower of the hemp plant (śaṇa). Śaṇapuṣpī is pungent and bitter, causes vomiting, and conquers kapha and pitta. (241–242) It is beneficial for the teeth, acts as a rejuvenative tonic, is strengthening, and cures skin diseases, eye disorders, and ailments of the head. (241)

Balabhadrā, trāyamāṇā, trāyantī, girijā, anujā, trāyantī, tuvarā, and tiktā are bitter and laxative; they remove pitta and kapha, and they destroy fever, heart disease, gulma, hemorrhoids, vertigo, colic, and poison. (243)
Mūrvā is known as madhurasa, devī, moraṭā, tejanī, sruvā, madhulikā, madhuśreṇī, gokarṇī, and also pīluparṇī.
(244) Mūrvā is laxative, heavy, sweet, and bitter; it cures pitta, blood disorders, and urinary diseases.
[These] remove the three *doṣas*, thirst, heart disease, itching, skin diseases, and fever.
(245) *Kākamācī*, *dhvāṅkṣamācī*, *kākāhvā*, and *vāyasī* are synonyms for *kākamācī*.
*Kākamācī* destroys the three *doṣas*, is unctuous and hot, and bestows voice and semen. (246)

Bitter, it is an elixir that conquers swelling, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, fever, and urinary disorders; pungent, it is beneficial for the eyes and destroys hiccups, vomiting, and heart disease. (247) It is known as *kākanāsā*, *kākāṅgī*, and *kākatuṇḍaphalā*. (248)
Kākanāsā is astringent and hot; it is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, destroys kapha, causes emesis, is bitter, and removes swelling, hemorrhoids, vitiligo, and skin diseases.
(249) Kākajaṅghā, Nadīkāntā, Kākatiktā, and Sulomaśā are synonyms.
The *pārāvatapadī* is also celebrated as *dāsī* and *kākā*.
The *kākajaṅghā* is cold and bitter, astringent, and it conquers phlegm and bile;
it destroys fever, hemorrhaging, ulcers, itching, poisons, and worms.

Nāgapuṣpī, also known as Śvetapuṣpā, Nāginī, and Rāmadūtikā, is pungent, bitter, sharp, and hot; it subdues phlegm and bile, destroys poison, colic, disorders of the female reproductive tract, worms, and parasites. (252)
Meṣaśṛṅgī is also known as viṣāṇī, meṣavallī, and ajaśṛṅgikā.
Meṣaśṛṅgī is bitter in taste, increases vāta, and cures asthma and cough.
It is dry, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and alleviates pitta, wounds, phlegm (śleṣman), and pain in the eyes. (253–254)

The fruit of Meṣaśṛṅgī is bitter; it cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), and phlegm (kapha); it stimulates digestion (dīpana), acts as a laxative (sraṃsana), and removes cough, worms, ulcers, and poisons.
(255) Haṃsapādī, Haṃsapadī, Kīṭamātā, and Tripādikā [are synonyms].
Haṃsapādī is heavy and cooling; it destroys blood disorders, poisons, and wounds, as well as erysipelas, burning sensations, diarrhea, spider-bites, spirit possession, and agnirohiṇī.
(256) Somavallī, somalatā, somakṣīrī, and dvijapriyā are synonyms for the same plant.
Somavallī destroys the three doṣas; it is pungent, bitter, and an elixir (rasāyana).
(257) Ākāśavallī is called Amaravallarī by the wise.
Khavallī is astringent, bitter, slimy, and removes diseases of the eyes. (258)
Tuvarā is digestive, beneficial for the heart, and destroys pitta, kapha, and ama.
(259) Chilihiṇṭa, also known as Mahāmūla and Pātālagaruḍa, is highly aphrodisiac, destroys kapha, and removes vāta. (260)
Vandā, vṛkṣādanī, vṛkṣabhakṣyā, and vṛkṣaruhā are synonyms for vandāka.
It is cold, bitter, astringent, and sweet in taste;
it is auspicious and destroys phlegm, wind, blood disorders, demons, wounds, and poisons. (261)
Vaṭapatrī is called Mohinī and Airāvatī by the wise;
Vaṭapatrī is astringent and hot, and it removes diseases of the female reproductive tract and urinary disorders.
Hiṅgupatrī, Kavarī, Pṛthvīkā, Pṛthukā, and Pṛthu are synonyms for asafoetida. 262–263.
Hiṅgupatrī is appetizing, sharp, hot, digestive, and pungent; it removes pain in the heart and bladder, constipation, hemorrhoids, phlegm, abdominal tumors, and wind.
(264) It is also known as vaṃśapatrī, veṇupatrī, piṇḍā, hiṅgu, and śivāṭikā.
The wise have declared that *hiṅgupatrī* is also known as *vaṃśapatrī*.
*Matsyākṣī* is also called *bāhlikā*, *matsyagandhā*, and *matsyādanī*.
*Matsyākṣī* is astringent, cooling, and it conquers skin diseases, bile, phlegm, and blood disorders.
Sarpākṣī is light, bitter, astringent, and sweet, with a pungent post-digestive effect (vipāka). It is also known as Gaṇḍālī and Nāḍīkalāpaka.
Sarpākṣī is pungent, bitter, hot in potency, and destroys worms.
It destroys the poison of scorpions, centipedes, and snakes, and heals wounds.
(268) Śaṅkhapuṣpī is also called Śaṅkhāhvā and Maṅgalyakusumā.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī is laxative, purifies the intellect, is aphrodisiac, and removes mental diseases. (269)
Rasāyanī is an astringent and hot; it bestows memory, luster, strength, and digestive fire, and it destroys the humors (doṣas), epilepsy, possession by spirits, leprosy, worms, and poisons.
Arkapuṣpī, Krūrakarmā, Payasyā, and Jalakāmukā [are synonyms]. 270.

Arkapuṣpī conquers worms, phlegm, urinary disorders, and diseases of the bile. 271 Lajjālu, svācchamīpatrā, samaṅgā, jalakārikā, raktapādī, namaskārī, and also known by the name khadirakā—[these are synonyms]. 272
Lajjālu is cooling, bitter, and astringent; it conquers kapha and pitta, destroys internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), diarrhea, and diseases of the female reproductive tract.
Alambuṣā, kharatvak, and likewise medogalā are so described.
Alambuṣā is light, sweet, and removes worms, bile, and phlegm.
(274) Dugdhikā is known as svāduparṇī, kṣīrā, and likewise vikṣīriṇī.
Dugdhikā is hot, heavy, dry, increases wind, and promotes conception. (275)

Tāmalakī, also called Bhūmyāmalakikā and Śivā, is sweet-tasting, pungent, and bitter; it promotes the evacuation of urine, removes impurities, causes constipation, is aphrodisiac, and destroys phlegm, skin diseases, and worms. (276)
Bahu-patrā, bahu-phalā, bahu-vīryā, ajaṭā, bhū-dhātrī, and vāta-kṛt are bitter, astringent, sweet, and cooling;
they destroy thirst, cough, hemorrhagic disorders, phlegm, itching, and wounds. (277–278)
Brāhmī, Kapotavaṅkā, Somavallī, Sarasvatī,
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, Māṇḍūkī, Tvāṣṭrī, and Divyā are the great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadhi).
Brāhmī is cooling, demulcent, bitter, light, moderately heavy, and cold.

The *kaṣāyā* is astringent, sweet in taste and sweet in post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), promotes longevity, acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), is beneficial for the voice, bestows memory, and conquers skin diseases, anemia, urinary disorders, hemorrhages, and cough;
likewise, *maṇḍūkaparṇinī* possesses these same properties and removes poison, swelling, and fever. (280–281)
Droṇā, droṇapuṣpī, and phalepuṣpā are thus proclaimed.
Droṇapuṣpī is heavy, sweet, dry, and hot; it generates vāta and pitta (282).
It is slightly pungent, salty, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), bitter, and a digestive stimulant.
It conquers phlegm, desire, jaundice, swelling, asthma, and parasites.
It is known as Suvarcalā, Sūryabhaktā, Varadā, and Badarā;
it is also called Sūryāvartā, Raviprītā, Aparā, and Brahmasudurlabhā. (283–284)
Suvarcalā is cooling, dry, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), laxative, heavy,
non-bile-producing, pungent, alkaline, and it overcomes constipation, phlegm, and wind.
Another variety is bitter, astringent, hot, laxative, dry, light, and pungent.
It destroys phlegm, bile, and blood disorders, as well as asthma, cough, anorexia, and fever;
it also cures eruptions, leprosy, urinary disorders, diseases of the female reproductive organs, pain, worms, and anemia.
It is known as Vandhyākarkoṭakī, Devī, Kanyā, and Yogīśvarī. (286)
The Nāgārī, Nakradamanī, and likewise the Viṣakaṇṭakinī;
the Bandhyākarkoṭakī is light, it subdues phlegm, purifies wounds, destroys the pride of serpents, is sharp, and removes the poison of erysipelas (visarpa). 287–288.
Mārkaṇḍikā, bhūmivallī, and mārkaṇḍī are mild purgatives (289).
Mārkaṇḍikā removes skin diseases, cleanses both the upper and lower parts of the body,
destroys poison, foul odors, and cough, and cures abdominal tumors and enlargement of the abdomen (290).
Devadālī is known as yuveṇī, karkaṭī, and garāgarī;
it is also called devatāḍa, vṛttakośa, and jīmūta.
The yellow variety is known as parā, kharasparśā, viṣaghnī, and garanāśinī.
Devadālī is bitter in taste; it destroys phlegm, hemorrhoids, swelling, and anemia.
It is emetic, sharp, and cures consumption, hiccup, worms, and fever.
The fruit of Devadālī is bitter and destroys worms and phlegm.
