It causes purging, destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and colic, cures hemorrhoids, and is supreme for conquering Vata.
Jalapippalī is called Śāradī, Śakulādanī, Matsyādanī, Matsyagandhā, and is also celebrated as Lāṅgalī. 293–294.
Jalapippalikā is pleasing to the heart, beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and light; it is astringent, cold, and parching, and it removes hemorrhaging, burning sensations, and wounds;
it is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect, appetizing, astringent, and increases the digestive fire. (295–296)

Gojihvā, also known as gojikā, gobhī, dārvikā, and kharaparṇinī, is heavy for the wind (vāta), cooling, constipating, and subdues phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta). It is pleasing to the heart, cures urinary disorders (prameha), cough, hemorrhages, wounds, and fever, and is light. (297)
Komalā is known to be astringent, bitter, and sweet in its post-digestive taste (vipāka).
Nāgadamanī should be understood as Balamodā, a destroyer of poison, and it is also called Nāgapuṣpī, Nāgapatrā, and Mahāyogeśvarī. (298–299)
Balāmoṭā is pungent, bitter, light, and it removes pitta and kapha;
it cures dysuria, wounds, and the disease jālagardabha, and it pacifies all grahas while destroying all poisons without exception. (300)
Bestowing wealth and long life, she brings victory everywhere.
(301) The *Vīrataru* tree is renowned in the world as *vellitara*. It has flowers that are white, black, reddish, crimson, and blue;
its blossoms resemble those of the *jāti* jasmine, and its leaves are like those of the *śamī*. This thorny tree grows only in waterless regions. (302)
Vellantara is bitter in taste and digestion; it removes thirst and phlegm, cures urinary obstruction and calculi, is astringent, and conquers disorders of the vagina, urine, and wind.
Chikknī causes sneezing, is sharp, and is known as chikkikā; it produces pain in the nose. 303

Chikkanī is pungent, dry, sharp, and hot; it increases digestive fire and pitta, removes vātarakta, and cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), worms, vāta, and kapha. (304) Kukundara, stāmracūḍa, sūkṣmapatra, and mṛducchada [are synonyms]. (305)
Kukundara is pungent and bitter; it removes fever, blood disorders, and phlegm.
Its fresh root, when placed in the mouth, removes dryness of the mouth. (306) Sudarśanā, Somavallī, Cakrāhvā, and Madhuparṇikā [are synonyms].
Sudarśanā is sweet, hot, and overcomes phlegm, swelling, hemorrhage, and wind.
Ākhukarṇī, ākhuparṇī, parṇikā, and bhūdarībhavā are synonyms for ākhukarṇī;
it is pungent, bitter, astringent, cooling, and light.

The peacock-crested plant (*mayūrāhvaśikhā*) is said to be bitter in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and it destroys urinary disorders, phlegmatic diseases, and worms (308). It is also called *sahasrāhi*, *madhucchadā*, and *nīlakaṇṭhaśikhā*; it is light and conquers bile, phlegm, and diarrhea (309).
Thus ends the fourth section, the Guḍūcyādi-varga, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Pūrva-khaṇḍa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭaka Natanaya.
Now begins the Puṣpa-varga (the Section on Flowers).
Or [these words] are masculine: *padma*, *nalina*, *aravinda*, *mahotpala*,
*sahasrapatra*, *kamala*, *śatapatra*, *kuśeśaya*,
*paṅkeruha*, *tāmarasa*, *sārasa*, and *sarasīruha*.
Bisaprasūna, rājīva, puṣkara, and ambhoruha;
the lotus (kamala) is cooling, praiseworthy, sweet, and it conquers phlegm and bile.
It destroys thirst, burning sensations, hemorrhages, eruptions, poisons, and erysipelas.
Specifically, the white lotus is known as *puṇḍarīka*;
the red one should be understood as *kokanada*, and the blue one is remembered as *indīvara*.
The white *kamala* is cooling, sweet, and conquers phlegm and bile.
Therefore, something else possessing only a few qualities, such as a red lotus, is not so called; rather,
that which is endowed with roots, stalks, petals, blossoms, and fruits is designated by the wise as "padminī" (lotus-pond), and it is also remembered as "bisinī" and so forth.

The lotus (padminī) is cooling, heavy, sweet, and salty; it subdues pitta, blood disorders, and kapha, is laxative, and causes wind (vāta) and constipation. The pericarp is the new leaf (saṃvarttikā), while the seed-vessel is the karṇikā.
The filaments are called *kiñjalka* or *kesara*, and the nectar is known as *makaranda*.
The lotus stalk is *mṛṇāla*, and it is likewise known as *bisa*.
The bud (*saṃvartikā*) is cooling, bitter, and astringent; it removes burning sensations and thirst.
It destroys dysuria, anal diseases, and hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta).
The pericarp of the lotus is bitter, astringent, sweet, and cooling; it clarifies the mouth, is light, and subdues thirst, blood disorders, phlegm, and bile.

The filaments (kiñjalka) are cooling, aphrodisiac, astringent, and absorbent; they conquer phlegm, bile, thirst, burning sensations, hemorrhoids, poison, and swelling. (11) The lotus stalk (mṛṇāla) is cooling, aphrodisiac, heavy, and conquers bile, burning sensations, and blood disorders. (12)

The lotus root (śālūka) is likewise characterized by these same qualities: it is difficult to digest, sweet in its post-digestive effect, increases breast milk, wind, and phlegm, is astringent, sweet, and dry.
The varieties of the lotus plant are padmacārinī, aticarā, avyathā, padmā, and śāradā.
The white lotus (padmā) is not hot, pungent, bitter, and astringent; it conquers kapha and vāta, cures dysuria and colic, and removes asthma, cough, and poison.
White water-lily is called kuvalaya, as well as kumuda and kairava.
The *kumuda* is slimy, unctuous, sweet, refreshing, and cold.
(15) It is called *kumudvatī*, *kairavikā*, and likewise *kumudinī*.
(16) However, when it is described by the wise as possessing all its parts, beginning with the roots, it is termed *samuditā*.

Whatever qualities are declared for the *padminī* lotus are remembered to belong to the *kumudinī* as well. The *saugandhika*, *kalhāra*, *hallaka*, and *raktasandhyaka* varieties of the *kalhāra* are cooling, constipating, heavy, drying, and cause flatulence.
Vāriparṇī is known as kumbhikā, vārimūlī, and khamūlikā; śaivāla is called jalanīlī, chaivala, and jalaja.
Vāriparṇī is cooling, bitter, light, sweet, laxative, and pungent.
It removes the three doshas, is dry, and causes blood disorders, fever, and emaciation.
(20) Shaivala, however, is astringent, bitter, sweet, cold, light, and unctuous;
it is an excellent remedy for burning sensations, thirst, pitta, blood disorders, and fever. (21)
The Śatapatrī is described as young, possessing a pericarp and beautiful filaments;
it is known as Mahākumārī, rich in fragrance, with flowers like lac, and exceedingly lovely.
The Śatapatrī is cooling, pleasing to the heart, absorbent, aphrodisiac, and light.
Kaṭvī is praised for conquering the three humors, blood disorders, and promoting complexion; it is digestive (pācanī).
23. Those who know it call Nepālī, Saptalā, Navamālikā, and Vāsantī by these names.
It is cooling, light, bitter, and conquers the three humors and blood disorders. 24.
Śrīpadī, Ṣaṭpadānandā, Vārṣikī, and Muktabandhanā—these are synonyms for Vārṣikī.
Vārṣikī is cooling, light, bitter, and removes the three doṣas;
it cures diseases of the ears, eyes, and mouth. Its oil is known to possess these same qualities.
Jāti, Jātī, Sumanā, Mālatī, Rājaputrikā, Cetikā, and Hṛdyagandhā—these are the varieties of jasmine; when yellow, it is known as Svarṇajātikā.
The pair of Jātīs is bitter, hot, astringent, light, and a conqueror of the bodily humors (doṣas).
It conquers pain in the head, eyes, mouth, and teeth, as well as poison, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), wind disorders (vāta), and blood disorders (asṛj).
Yūthikā, Gaṇikā, Ambaṣṭhā, and Hemapuṣpikā are synonyms for that [plant].
The pair of Yūthīs is cooling, bitter, pungent in post-digestive taste (pāka) and flavor (rasa), and light.
Sweet, astringent, pleasing to the heart, it subdues pitta and increases kapha and vāta;
it cures wounds, bleeding disorders, diseases of the mouth, teeth, eyes, and head, and removes poison.
(30) The *cāmpeya* is called *campaka*, and it is also known as *hemapuṣpa*.
Its buds are described by the wise as having fragrant fruit (gandhaphala).
Campaka is pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, and cooling;
it removes poison and worms, and conquers dysuria, phlegm, wind, thirst, and pitta.
Bakula, Madhugandha, and Siṃhakesaraka;
Bakula is astringent, not hot, pungent in post-digestive taste and potency, heavy, and it removes phlegm, bile, poison, vitiligo, worms, and diseases of the teeth. 33
Śivamallī, Pāśupata, Ekāṣṭhīla, Vaka, and Vasu (34).
Vaka is non-hot, pungent, and bitter; it destroys phlegm, bile, and poison, and cures vaginal pain, thirst, burning sensations, leprosy, swelling, and hemorrhages (35).
The kadamba, priyaka, nīpa, vṛttapuṣpa, and halipriya are synonyms for the kadamba tree.
It is sweet, cooling, astringent, salty, and heavy; it is laxative, causes constipation, is parching, and increases phlegm, breast milk, and wind. (36)
The *kubjaka* is auspicious, possesses young, rounded flowers, and has abundant filaments;
the *mahāsahā* is richly thorny and crowded with swarms of blue bees.
(37) The *kubjaka* is fragrant, sweet, and has an astringent aftertaste; it is laxative.
It is known to pacify the three *doṣas*, act as an aphrodisiac, and remove coldness.
(38) *Mallikā*, *madayantī*, *śītabhīru*, and *bhūpadī*—the *mallikā* is hot, light, aphrodisiac, bitter, and pungent; it removes [cold]. (39)
It cures diseases of wind, bile, mouth, and eyes, as well as leprosy, loss of appetite, poison, and wounds. (40) Mādhavī, vāsantī, puṇḍraka, maṇḍaka,
atimukta, vimukta, kāmuka, and bhramarotsava are synonyms for the same plant.
Mādhavī is sweet, cooling, light, and removes the three doṣas.
(41) Ketaka has needle-like flowers; it is also called jambuka and krakacacchada.
Another variety is suvarṇaketakī, which has small flowers and is fragrant. (42)
The *ketaka* is pungent, sweet, light, bitter, and dispels *kapha*.
The golden *ketakī* (*hemaketakī*) is known to be hot, bitter in taste, beneficial for the eyes, and golden-yellow.
The *kiṅkirāta* is golden-white, yellow, and known as *pītabhadraka*. 43–44.
Kiṅkirāta is cold and bitter, as well as astringent; it removes phlegm, bile, thirst, hemorrhaging, burning sensations, wasting, dysentery, and worms.
Karṇikāra is also known as parivyādha and pādapotpala.
Karṇikāra is pungent, bitter, and astringent; it is purifying, light, coloring, and provides comfort. It conquers swelling, phlegm, blood disorders, wounds, and skin diseases.
(46) Aśoka is also known as Hemapuṣpa, Vañjula, and Tāmrapallava.
Kaṅkeli, piṇḍapuṣpa, gandhapuṣpa, and likewise naṭa—these are known as aśoka. They are cooling, bitter, astringent, complexion-enhancing, and digestive;
they alleviate the humors (doṣas), thirst, burning sensations, worms, emaciation, poisons, and blood disorders.
Amlāta is said to be amlāṭana, and it is also called amlātaka. Kuraṇṭaka is varṇapuṣpa, and that same plant is also called mahāsaha.
Amlāṭana is astringent, hot, unctuous, sweet, and bitter.
Saireyaka is the white-flowered *sairaya*, also known as *kaṭasārikā*;
*sahācara* and *sahacara* are synonyms, and it is also called *bhindī*.
(51) *Kuraṇṭaka* refers to the yellow variety here, while the red one is known as *kurabaka*.
The blue variety is said to be the best of the two; it is called *dāsī* and *ārtagala*.
It destroys leprosy, wind-disorders, blood disorders, phlegm, itching, and poisons.
It is bitter, hot, sweet, non-sour, very unctuous, and a conditioner of the hair.
The *kunda* is said to be the *mādhyam*, and it is traditionally known as the ever-blooming flower (*sadāpuṣpa*).
The *kunda* is cooling, light, and removes phlegm, headache, poison, and bile.
(54) The *mucukunda* is the *kṣatravṛkṣa*, the *citraka*, and the *prativiṣṇuka*.
Mucukunda destroys headaches, disorders of bile and blood, and poisons.
Tilaka, Kṣuraka, Śrīmān, Puruṣa, and Chinnapuṣpaka are synonyms for it.
Tilaka is pungent in digestion and hot in taste; it is an elixir (rasāyana).
It removes phlegm, skin diseases, worms, and ailments of the bladder-mouth and teeth.
Bandhūka, bandhujīva, rakta, and mādhyāhnika are synonyms for bandhūka; it increases phlegm, is astringent, alleviates wind and bile, and is light.
Oḍrapuṣpa and japā are synonyms; that japā is of three colors—red, white, and [the others].
It is astringent, beneficial for the hair, and the trisandhyā variety conquers phlegm and wind.
Sindūrī, raktabījā, raktapuṣpā, and sukomalā are synonyms.

Sindūrī removes poison, bile, blood, thirst, and vomiting, and it is cooling. 59. Now, Agastya, Vaṅgasena, Munipuṣpa, Munidruma, and Agasti conquer bile and phlegm and cure quartan fever; they are cooling. 60.
Rūkṣa (rough) and bitter, it generates wind and wards off catarrh. Tulasī is known as surasā, grāmyā, sulabhā, bahumañjarī,
apetarākṣasī, gaurī, bhūtaghnī, and devadundubhi.

Tulasi is pungent, bitter, pleasing to the heart, hot, and causes burning sensations and pitta; it is digestive, and conquers skin diseases, urinary calculi, hemorrhage, pain in the flanks, phlegm, and vata.
Both white and black Tulasi are proclaimed to be equal in their qualities. (63)

This plant is known as māruta, marubaka, marunmaru, phaṇī, phaṇijjaka, prasthapuṣpa, and samīraṇa. (64) It stimulates the digestive fire, is pleasing to the heart, sharp, hot, increases pitta, and is light. (65)

Damanaka—also called Dānta, Muniputra, and Tapodhana—is said to destroy the poison of scorpions and the like, as well as phlegm, wind, leprosy, and worms; it has a pungent post-digestive taste (pākara), is appetizing, bitter, dry, and fragrant. (66)
Gandhotkaṭa, brahmajaṭa, vinīta, and kalapatraka—these are known as damana. It is astringent, bitter, heart-pleasing, aphrodisiac, and fragrant;
by its use, it conquers seizures, poison, leprosy, hemorrhages, moisture, itching, and the three doṣas.
Barbarī, tuvarī, tuṅgī, kharapuṣpā, ajagandhikā, and parṇāśa are synonyms;
however, when it is black, it is called kaṭhillaka and kuṭheraka. When it is white, it is called ajaka, and another name for it is vaṭapatra.
The three types of *barbarī* are dry, cold, pungent, and burning;
they are sharp, appetizing, pleasing to the heart, digestive stimulants, and light in digestion.
They increase *pitta*, and they destroy *kapha*, *vāta*, blood disorders, itching, worms, and poisons. (70–71)

Thus ends the fifth section, the Chapter on Flowers, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. Now begins the Chapter on the Vaṭa and other trees.
The *vaṭa* tree— known as *raktaphala*, *śṛṅgī*, *nyagrodha*, *skandhaja*, *dhruva*, *kṣīrī*, *vaiśravaṇa*, *vāsa*, *bahupāda*, and *vanaspati*—
is cooling, heavy, astringent, and cures phlegm, bile, and wounds.
The *varṇya* (color-promoting) decoction destroys spreading inflammation and burning sensations, and removes disorders of the female reproductive tract.
The *bodhidru* (Bodhi tree), *pippala*, *aśvattha*, *calapatra*, and *gajāśana* are synonyms for the *pippala*.
The *pippala* is difficult to digest, cooling, and conquers pitta, kapha, wounds, and blood disorders.
Gurūstuvaraka is parching, improves the complexion, and cleanses the female reproductive tract.
Pārīṣa, the other palāśa, kapicūta, kamaṇḍalu,
gardabhāṇḍa, kandarāla, kapītana, and supārśvaka [are similar].
The *pārīṣa* is difficult to digest, unctuous, and increases worms, semen, and *kapha*.

Its fruit is sour and sweet; its root is astringent and sweet, and its pith is likewise. (5) The *nandīvṛkṣa* is a variety of the *aśvattha*, characterized by its sprouting nature and known as the "elephant-foot tree."
The Sthālīvṛkṣa, Kṣayataru, Kṣīrī, and Vanaspati are synonyms for the Nandīvṛkṣa. It is light, sweet, bitter, astringent, and hot;
it has a pungent post-digestive taste (pāka-rasa), is constipating, and conquers poison, bile, phlegm, and blood disorders.
The Udumbara is known as Jantuphala, Yajñāṅga, and Hemadugdhaka (8).
Udumbara is cooling, dry, heavy, and it conquers pitta, kapha, and blood disorders;
it is sweet, astringent, improves the complexion, and cleanses and heals wounds (9).
Kākodumbarikā, phalgu, malayū, and jaghanephala—
known as malayu— are astringent, bitter, cooling, and constipating;
they conquer disorders of kapha and pitta, as well as wounds, vitiligo, skin diseases, anemia, hemorrhoids, and jaundice.
*Plakṣa*, *jaṭī*, *parkarī*, and *parkaṭī* are also feminine names for this tree.
(11) The *plakṣa* is astringent, cooling, and removes diseases arising from wounds;
it destroys burning sensations, pitta, kapha, and blood disorders, cures swelling, and alleviates *raktapitta*. (12)
Śirīṣa, bhaṇḍila, bhaṇḍī, bhaṇḍīra, kapītana, śukapuṣpa, śukataru, mṛdupuṣpa, and śukapriya (13).
Śirīṣa is sweet, not hot, bitter, astringent, and light.
It destroys defects, swelling, and erysipelas, and removes cough, ulcers, and poison. 14.
Now, the five milky trees and the five barks:
the trees Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Pārīṣa, and Plakṣa.

These five milky trees constitute the *pañcavalkala* (the pentad of barks). These milky trees are described as cooling; they cure gynecological diseases and wounds, are parching, astringent, reduce fat, and destroy erysipelas and hemorrhoids.
The five barks (tvak-pañcaka) destroy swelling, pitta, kapha, and blood; they are galactagogue and heal fractured bones. They are cooling, astringent, and conquer ulcers, swellings, and erysipelas.
Among them, the leaf is cooling, astringent, light, and does not increase kapha, vāta, or blood.
It overcomes constipation and flatulence, is bitter, astringent, light, and scraping. (18) Śāla, Sarja, Kārśya, Aśvakarṇaka, Śasya, and Śambara—
among these, Aśvakarṇa is astringent and [removes] wounds, sweat, phlegm, and worms.
It cures earache, deafness, and diseases of the ear caused by [vitiated] *dhātu*s.
Another variety is *sarjaka*, also known as *ajakarṇa*; it is the *śāla* tree with pepper-like leaves.
*Akarṇa* is pungent, bitter, astringent, and hot; it dispels [these ailments].

Śallakī, gajabhakṣyā, suvahā, surabhī, rasā, maheruṇā, kundurukī, vallakī, and bahusravā [are synonyms for the plant known as] kaphapāṇḍuśrutigada, which cures urinary disorders, leprosy, poisons, and wounds. (21–22)
Śallakī is astringent, cooling, and is said to conquer pitta, kapha, and diarrhea; it removes raktapitta and wounds, and promotes nourishment. Śiṃśapā is slimy, dark-colored, blackish, and heavy.
That very [wood] is called *kapilā* by the sages, as it contains ashes within.
The *śiṃśapā* is pungent, bitter, and astringent; it removes emaciation, possesses a hot potency (*uṣṇavīryā*), and destroys fat, skin diseases, vitiligo, worms, and parasites.
It causes pain in the bladder, ulcers, burning sensations, hemorrhage, and phlegm, and it induces miscarriage. 25.
That which is known by the names Kakubha and Arjuna is celebrated as Nadīsarpa; it is also remembered as Indradru, Vīravṛkṣa, Vīra, and Dhavala. 26.

The *kukubha* is cooling, pleasing to the heart, and conquers wasting diseases from chest wounds, poisons, and blood disorders; being astringent (*tuvara*), it destroys obesity, urinary disorders, and ulcers, and removes *kapha* and *pitta*.
It is also known as *bījaka*, *pītasāra*, and *pītaśālaka*. 27.
Bandhūkapuṣpa, priyaka, sarjaka, and asana are known as synonyms for āsana (28).

Bījaka destroys skin diseases, leprosy, erysipelas, leucoderma, urinary disorders, and intestinal worms; it subdues phlegm, blood, and bile, is beneficial for the skin and hair, and acts as a rejuvenative tonic (29).
The *khadira* tree has red heartwood; it is of the *gāyatrī* meter and serves as a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*).
It is thorny, possesses young leaves, has many thorns, and is fit for sacrifice (30).
The *khadira* is cooling, beneficial for the teeth, and removes itching, cough, and loss of appetite (31).
Bitter and astringent, it destroys fat and removes worms, urinary disorders, fever, ulcers, vitiligo, swelling, undigested matter, hemorrhaging, anemia, skin diseases, and phlegm.
(32) Khadira has a white pith; another variety is Kadara, also known as Somavalkala.
Which one is white, what is its description, and which cures diseases of the mouth caused by kapha and blood?
(33) Irimeda, vitkhadira, kālaskandha, and arimedaka—irimeda is astringent and hot; it conquers diseases of the mouth and teeth, as well as [excess] blood.

It destroys itching, poison, phlegm, worms, leprosy, toxins, and ulcers. (34) Rohītaka, rohitaka, rohī, and dāḍimapuṣpaka are synonyms for rohitaka; it cures enlargement of the spleen, improves the appetite, and clarifies the blood. (35)
Babbūla is called kiṅkirāta, and kiṅkirāṭa is the same as pītaka. Those who know it declare that this very plant is known as ābhāṣaṭpadamodinī;
babbūla alleviates phlegm, is astringent, and removes skin diseases, worms, and poisons.

The *ariṣṭaka* is auspicious, black in color, and a means of accomplishment; it has red seeds and yellow foam. It is foamy, causes abortion, destroys the three *doṣas*, conquers the planets, and induces miscarriage. (38)
Putrajīva produces conception, is a *yaṣṭīpuṣpa*, and is a means of accomplishment (39).
Putrajīvī is heavy, aphrodisiac, bestows pregnancy, removes phlegm and wind,
promotes the discharge of urine and waste, is parching, cold, sweet, pungent, and bitter (40).
The iṅguda is the charcoal tree (aṅgāravṛkṣa), the bitter tree (tiktaka), and the ascetic’s tree (tāpasadruma).

The iṅguda destroys skin diseases, spirits and other [supernatural influences], seizures, wounds, poisons, and worms; it is hot, cures leucoderma and colic, is bitter, and has a pungent post-digestive effect. 41
Jiṅginī, jhiṅginī, jhiṅgī, suniryāsā, and pramodinī.
(42) Jiṅginī is sweet, slightly warm, astringent, and purifies the female reproductive tract;
it is pungent, removes wounds and heart disease, and is sharp in curing dysentery caused by wind. (43)
Tamāla is called tāpiccha, kālaskandha, and amitadruma;
it is also known as lokaskandha, nīladhvaja, and nīlatāla.
Tamāla is to be understood like the śāla tree, and it further removes burning sensations and eruptions. 44
Tūṇī, tunnaka, āpīna, tuṇika, kacchaka,
kuṭheraka, kāntalaka, nandīvṛkṣa, and nandaka— these are the names [of this plant].
Tūṇī is red, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), astringent, sweet, and light.
Bhūrja (birch) is bitter, astringent, cooling, aphrodisiac, and it conquers wounds, skin diseases, and blood-bile disorders.
Bhūrja is known as bhūrjapatra, carmī, and bahulavalkala;
bhūrja conquers possession by spirits, seizures, phlegm, earache, and blood-bile disorders.
Kaṣāya destroys Rākṣasas and is supreme for removing fat and poison.
(48) Palāśa, Kiṃśuka, Parṇa, Yajñiya, Raktapuṣpaka, Kṣāraśreṣṭha, Vātapotha, Brahmavṛkṣa, and Samidvara are its names. (49)
Palāśa is digestive, aphrodisiac, laxative, hot, and overcomes wounds and abdominal tumors; it promotes the healing of fractures and removes disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, and worms.
Its flower is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), but pungent, bitter, and astringent.

The fruit increases wind, is astringent, cold, and alleviates disorders of kapha, pitta, and blood; it is highly effective in curing thirst, burning sensations, vātarakta, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). It is light, hot, and removes urinary disorders (meha), hemorrhoids, worms, wind, and kapha. 52.
It is bitter and astringent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and it cures leprosy (kuṣṭha) and abdominal tumors (gulmodara).
The Śālmali tree is known as Mocā, Picchilā, and Pūraṇī;
it has red flowers, is long-lived, abounds in thorns, and possesses cottony fibers.

The Śālmalī is cooling, sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, an elixir (rasāyana), increases phlegm (śleṣman), and removes pitta, vāta, and blood disorders; it conquers raktapitta. Its exudation is slimy, and it is also known as śālmalīveṣṭaka. 55.
It is also known as mocāsrāva, mocarasa, and mocaniryāsa.
(56) Mocāsrāva is cooling, astringent, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and slightly bitter;
it cures dysentery, diarrhea, ama, kapha, pitta, blood disorders, and burning sensations. (57)
The inferior *śālmali* is called *rocana* and *kūṭaśālmali*.
The *kūṭaśālmalika* is bitter and pungent; it subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, is purgative and hot, and removes splenic disorders, abdominal enlargements, liver diseases, tumors, and poisons. (58)
It removes the obstruction of the bodily elements (dhātus), wind, blood, fat, colic, and phlegm.
(59) Dhava is also known as dhaṭa, nanditaru, sthira, gaura, and dhurandhara;
dhava is cooling and cures urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, anemia, bile, and phlegm.
Its fruit is sweet, slightly astringent, and somewhat sweet.
The *dhanvaṅga* is the bow-tree, the clan-tree, and the excellent reed.
The *dhanvaṅga* alleviates phlegm, bile, and blood disorders, relieves cough, is astringent, and is light.
It is nourishing, strength-promoting, emaciating, a promoter of joint-healing, and a healer of wounds.
(62) Karīra, also known as krakarīpatra, granthila, and marubhūruha,
is considered pungent, bitter, sudorific, hot, and a purgative.
Śākhoṭa removes Durnāmaka (scrofula), phlegm, wind, worms, swelling, and ulcers.
Śākhoṭa— also known as Pītaphalaka, Bhūtāvāsa, and Kharacchada—
conquers internal hemorrhaging, hemorrhoids, wind, phlegm, and diarrhea.
Varuṇa, varaṇa, setu, tiktaśāka, and kumāraka are synonyms for the varuṇa plant.
It increases pitta, is purgative, and destroys kapha, dysuria, urinary stones, and vāta disorders.
Being hot and digestive-stimulant, it also cures abdominal tumors (gulma), vātarakta, and worms.
Kaṣāya is sweet, bitter, pungent, rough, and light.
Kaṭabhī has sweet flowers; it is also called madhureṇu and kaṭambhara.
Kaṭabhī [cures] urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, sinus ulcers, poisons, and worms.
It is declared to be hot, pungent, and dry, and it destroys phlegm and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
Its fruit should be known as astringent (tuvara), and it specifically removes phlegm and semen.
Mokṣa, mokṣaka, golīḍha, and goliha are its synonyms.
The best of alkalis is the *kṣāravṛkṣa* (alkali-tree), which is of two kinds: white and black.

Mokṣaka is pungent, bitter, astringent, heavy, hot, and it removes phlegm and wind; it cures poison, disorders of the blood, abdominal tumors, itching, pain in the bladder, worms, and [abnormal] semen.
Śirīṣikā, ṭiṇṭinikā, durbalā, ambuśirīṣikā,
and vāriśirīṣikā remove the three doṣas, poison, skin diseases, and hemorrhoids.
Śamī has seeds like barley, is called tuṅgā and keśahantrī, and its fruit is known as śivāphalā.
Maṅgalyā, Lakṣmī, and Śamīrā are considered to be varieties of the small Śamī (72).
Śamī is known to be bitter, pungent, cold, astringent, purgative, and light;
it conquers phlegm, cough, vertigo, asthma, leprosy, hemorrhoids, and worms (73).
Saptaparṇa (Alstonia scholaris) has broad bark, is found in autumn, and possesses uneven leaves. It conquers wounds, phlegm, wind, leprosy, blood disorders, and parasites;
it stimulates digestion, destroys asthma and abdominal tumors, and is unctuous, hot, astringent, and laxative.
The *tiniśa* tree—known as *syandana*, *nemi*, *rathadru*, and *vañjula*—is astringent;
it conquers phlegm, bile, blood disorders, leprosy, and urinary disorders (*prameha*), and destroys vitiligo, burning sensations, wounds, anemia, and worms. (76)
Bhūmīsaha, dvāradāru, varadāru, and kharacchada—
bhūmīsaha is cooling and clarifies blood and bile.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous substances in the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The sixth section, the group beginning with the *vaṭa*, is completed.
Now begins the group of fruits beginning with the mango (*āmra*):
the mango is called *cūta*, *rasāla*, *sahakāra*, and *atisaurabha*.
The mango (mākanda) is known as Kāmāṅga, Madhudūta, and Pikavallabha.
It cures diarrhea caused by *āmrapuṣpa*, as well as disorders of phlegm (*kapha*), bile (*pitta*), and urinary disorders (*prameha*).
It removes vitiated blood (*asṛgdūṣi*), is cooling, improves appetite, is constipating, and increases wind (*vāta*).
The unripe mango is astringent and sour, appetizing, and it increases wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
However, when very young, it is excessively sour, parching, and it aggravates all three humors (doṣas) as well as the blood.
Unripe mango that has been stripped of its skin and thoroughly dried in the sun [is likewise beneficial].
Sour, sweet, and astringent, it is laxative and conquers phlegm and wind.

When ripe, however, it is sweet, aphrodisiac, unctuous, and bestows strength and comfort; it is heavy, alleviates wind, is pleasing to the heart, improves the complexion, is cooling, and does not increase bile.
It has an astringent aftertaste and increases digestive fire, phlegm, and semen. That same fruit, when fully ripened on the tree, is heavy and an excellent alleviator of wind;
it possesses a sweet-sour taste and may slightly aggravate bile.
The mango that is artificially ripened becomes a destroyer of pitta;
it is deficient in sourness and especially in sweetness. When sucked, it is highly appetizing, promotes strength and virility, and is light.
It is cooling, quickly digested, alleviates vāta and pitta, and is laxative (8). That same juice, when strained, is strengthening, heavy, alleviates vāta, is laxative,
unpalatable, highly satiating, nourishing, and increases kapha (9).
Its kernel is heavy, highly nourishing, slow-digesting, sweet, bulk-promoting, strengthening, cooling, and a destroyer of wind (vāta);
it alleviates wind and bile (vātapitta), is appetizing, nourishing, and increases strength. (10)
The milk-mango is aphrodisiac, improves the complexion, is sweet, heavy, and cooling.

(11) Excessive consumption of mango causes weak digestion, intermittent fever, blood disorders, intestinal obstruction, abdominal enlargement, or eye diseases; therefore, one should not eat them in excess. (12)

This refers specifically to sour mangoes, which are characterized by sweetness and acidity; it does not refer to [sweet] mangoes alone, because the qualities such as being beneficial for the eyes belong to the former.
If one eats mangoes in excess, ginger water should be taken as an after-drink (anupāna).
Or cumin should be used together with sauvarcala salt. The juice of ripe mango spread upon a cloth,
dried by the heat and applied repeatedly, is known as *āmrāvarta*.
The mango-juice (āmrāvarta) is laxative, removes thirst, vomiting, wind, and bile, and is appetizing; it is indeed proclaimed to be light after digestion due to exposure to the sun's rays.
The mango seed is astringent and destroys vomiting and diarrhea.
Slightly sour and sweet, it likewise relieves heartburn. The sprout of the mango is appetizing and destroys kapha and pitta.
Āmrātaka, pītana, markaṭāmra, and kapītana are synonyms for it.
The unripe āmrātaka is sour, subdues vāta, is heavy, hot, appetizing, and laxative (19).
When ripe, however, it is astringent, sweet in taste and in its post-digestive effect, is considered cold,
refreshing, increases kapha, is unctuous, aphrodisiac, causes constipation, and is nourishing.
The *guru-balya* (the king of mangoes) conquers wind, bile, wounds, burning sensations, consumption, and hemorrhaging.
20. It is known as *rājāmra*, *aṣṭaṅka*, *āmrāta*, *kāmāhva*, and *rājaputraka*.
21. The *rājāmra* is astringent, sweet, clear, cooling, and heavy.
The *kośāmra* is said to be astringent and parching; it causes constipation, flatulence, and wind, while subduing *kapha* and *pitta*. It is also called *kṣudrāmra*, *kṛmivṛkṣa*, and *sukośaka*.
*Kośāmra* removes skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), swelling, hemorrhaging (*asrapitta*), wounds, and *kapha*. (22–23)
Its fruit is constipating, subdues wind, is sour, hot, heavy, and increases pitta.
When cooked, however, it is digestive, appetizing, light, hot, and alleviates kapha and wind.
(24) It is called panaśa, kaṇṭakiphala, palasa, and atibṛhatphala.
The ripe jackfruit is cooling, unctuous, and pacifies pitta and vāta (25).
It is nourishing, bulk-promoting, sweet, substantial, and highly increases kapha;
it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and cures hemorrhaging, chest wounds, and ulcers (26).
The unripe fruit of that same tree is constipating, wind-increasing, astringent, heavy,
causes a burning sensation, is sweet, strengthening, and increases phlegm and fat.
(27) The seeds produced from the panasa tree are aphrodisiac and sweet.
One should describe heavy fruits as those that cause constipation and the discharge of urine.

The marrow of the jackfruit is aphrodisiac and alleviates wind, bile, and phlegm; however, the jackfruit should especially be avoided by those suffering from abdominal tumors and those with weak digestive fire.
The lakuca, chudrapanasa, likuca, and also known as ḍahurī— raw lakuca is heating, heavy, causes constipation,
and is sweet as well as sour; it aggravates the three doṣas and increases blood.
It is also known to destroy semen and digestive fire, and is considered harmful to the eyes (31).
When well-ripened, it is sweet and sour, subdues wind and bile, increases phlegm and digestive fire, is appetizing, aphrodisiac, and causes constipation (32).
The plantain (kadalī), known as vāraṇā, mocā, ambusārā, and aṃśumatīphalā—its fruit is sweet, cooling, constipating, increases kapha, and is heavy;
it is unctuous and conquers pitta, blood disorders, thirst, burning sensations, chest wounds, consumption, and vāta. (33)

Ripe plantain is sweet, cooling, and sweet upon digestion; it is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and destroys hunger, thirst, eye diseases, heart ailments, and urinary disorders, while promoting appetite and increasing bodily mass.
There are many varieties of the plantain tree, such as Māṇikya, Martya, Amṛta, Campaka, and others.
The aforementioned qualities are present in them, but they possess superior merit, freedom from defects, and lightness.
(35) The citron, cow’s milk, and likewise the *gorakṣakarkaṭī* [are also mentioned].
(36) The citron is sweet, dry, heavy, and it removes pitta and kapha.

The coconut (nārikela)—also known as dṛḍhaphala, lāṅgalī, kūrcarśapaka, tuṅga, skandhaphala, tṛṇarāja, and sadāphala—is non-heating, constipating, and causes flatulence when raw; however, when ripe, it is heating and increases pitta. 37–38.
The coconut fruit is cooling, difficult to digest, and cleanses the bladder; it causes constipation, is nourishing, strengthening, and alleviates wind, bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
(39) In particular, the tender coconut destroys fevers caused by pitta and the disorders of pitta.
That same [gruel] when stale is considered by physicians to be heavy, provocative of pitta, burning, and constipating (40).
Its water is cooling, pleasing to the heart, digestive, aphrodisiac, light, sweet, a conqueror of thirst and pitta, and excellent for cleansing the bladder (41).
The fruits of the coconut (*nārikela*), the palmyra palm (*tāla*), and the date palm (*kharjūra*) are astringent,
unctuous, sweet, nourishing, and heavy.
(42) *Kālinda* has black seeds, while *kāliṅga* is perfectly round.
Kālinda is astringent, beneficial for eye disorders and bile, aphrodisiac, cooling, and heavy when raw;

when cooked, it is warm, alkaline, increases bile, yet conquers phlegm and wind. (43) Now, the ten-fingered cucumber (*daśāṅgula*) and the melon (*kharbūja*) are mentioned, and their qualities shall be described. (44)
The watermelon (kharbūja) is diuretic, strengthening, purifies the digestive tract, is heavy, unctuous, very sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, and alleviates pitta and vāta.
Among these [fruits], that which is sour-sweet and alkaline arises from its juice. 45.
That [fruit] causes blood-bile (raktapitta) and is highly provocative of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). 46.
Trapusa, kaṇṭakiphala, and sudhāvāsa are very cooling; blue trapusa is light, and when fresh, it conquers thirst, fatigue, and burning sensations. 47.
Sweet, cooling, and a remover of pitta, it is excellent for curing raktapitta;
when ripe, it becomes sour, hot, increases pitta, yet alleviates kapha and vāta.
Its seeds are diuretic, cooling, dry, and conquer pitta, blood disorders, and urinary calculi. 48
Ghoraṇṭa, pūgī, pūga, guvāka, and kramuka are synonyms for the betel nut tree;
its fruit is called pūgīphala and is also referred to as udvega.
Pūga is heavy, cooling, dry, astringent, and it conquers kapha and pitta.
It is intoxicating, digestive-stimulating, appetizing, and removes bad taste from the mouth.
When moist, it is heavy, causes secretions, and is known to diminish the digestive fire and impair vision;
when steamed, it cuts through the three *doṣas* and is firm in the middle—this is considered the best. (50–51)
The palmyra (tāla) has a leaf that can be written upon; it is the king of grasses and is very tall.
(52) Ripe palmyra fruit increases pitta, rakta, and kapha; it is difficult to digest, causes excessive urination, and produces drowsiness, ophthalmia, and semen. (53)
The tender palm-sap (tālamajjā) is slightly intoxicating, light,
increases phlegm, subdues wind and bile, is unctuous, sweet, and laxative.
The fresh water produced from the palm tree is considered to be highly intoxicating.
When it has become sour, however, it produces bile and removes the disorder of wind (vāta).
Bilva, śāṇḍilya, śailūṣa, mālūra, and śrīphala are its synonyms.
Young bilva fruit, bilva-karkaṭī, and bilva-peśikā are also names for it.
The pulp of the bilva fruit is astringent and cures disorders of phlegm, wind, and colic (śūla).
The young fruit of the bilva is astringent, digestive-stimulant,
carminative, pungent, astringent, hot, light, unctuous, bitter, and dispels wind and phlegm.
Overripe fruit is heavy, aggravates the three *doṣas*, is difficult to digest, produces putrid gas, causes a burning sensation, leads to constipation, is sweet, and weakens the digestive fire.
Among fruits, that which is fully ripe is said to possess these qualities. 58–59.
It should be understood that the unripe fruit of the *bilva* is superior in its qualities except in other cases;
indeed, the dried fruit of *drākṣā*, *bilva*, *śivā*, and others is superior in its qualities. Furthermore, the *kapittha* is known as *dadhittha* and also as *puṣpaphala*.
Kapipriya, dadhiphala, and dantaśaṭha are also [known by these names]. 61.
Raw kapittha is constipating, astringent, light, and scraping;
when ripe, it is heavy, alleviates thirst and hiccups, and conquers vāta and pitta.
It may be sour, astringent, a cleanser of the throat, constipating, and difficult to digest.
(62) The nāraṅga is also called nāgaraṅga; its rind is fragrant and pleasing to the mouth. (63) The nāraṅga is sweet and sour, appetizing, and a destroyer of wind.
Furthermore, it is sour, very hot, difficult to digest, aggravates wind (vāta), and is laxative. 64.
Tinduka, sphūrjaka, kālaskandha, and asitakāraka are synonyms;
raw tinduka is constipating, increases wind, is cold, and light.

When ripe, it destroys pitta-type urinary disorders, blood disorders, and phlegm; it is sweet and heavy. (65) The tinduka is also known as jalada, dīrghapatraka, kupīlu, kulaka, kākatinduka, and kākapīluka. (66)
Kākendu, viṣatindu, as well as markaṭatinduka, kupīlu, śītala, tikta, vātala, madakṛt, and laghu;
it is an excellent reliever of pain, constipating, and a destroyer of kapha, pitta, and blood disorders. 67–68.
The kings of fruits are said to be Nandī, Rājajambū, Mahāphalā, Surabhipatrā, and the Mahājambū is also remembered; the fruit of the Rājajambū is sweet, constipating, heavy, and appetizing. (69)

The small rose-apple (*jambu*) has fine leaves; it is known as *nādeyī* or *jalajambukā*. It is astringent, parching, and conquers phlegm, bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations. (70) In the masculine and feminine genders, it is called *karkandhū*, *badarī*, and *kola*. (71)
Phenila, kuvala, ghoṇṭā, sauvīra, and large jujube (badara);
ajapriyā, kuhā, and kolī—these have thorns on both sides that are poisonous.
When cooked, sauvīra and large jujube are very sweet.
Sauvīra (sour gruel) made from jujube is cooling, laxative, heavy, and increases semen;
it is nourishing and alleviates bile, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, wasting, and thirst.
Sauvīra made from kola (jujube), when well-cooked, is said to be light and sweet.

The *kolantu* is astringent, palatable, hot, and subdues wind (*vāta*); it increases phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*), is heavy, and is said to be constipating. The small jujube fruit (*badara*) is called *karkandhū* by the ancient scholars.

The small jujube (kṣudravadaraka) is sour, slightly astringent and sweet, unctuous, heavy, and bitter; it is known to pacify vāta and pitta. When dried, it is all [the varieties] are laxative, stimulate the digestive fire, light, and conquer thirst, fatigue, and blood disorders.
In the world, *prācīnāmalaka* is known as *pānīyāmalaka*; it destroys the three *doṣas* and cures fever.
*Lavalī* has fragrant roots, is pale, and possesses tender bark. (78–79)

The *lavalī* fruit removes urinary calculi, hemorrhoids, phlegm, and bile; it is heavy, clear, appetizing, dry, sweet and sour, and astringent in taste. (80) The *karamarda* is also known as *suṣeṇa* and *kṛṣṇapākaphala*.

Therefore, that which yields light fruit should be known as *karamardikā*. Two raw *karamarda* fruits are said to be sour, heavy, and thirst-quenching; they are heating, stimulate the appetite, and increase blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*).
When ripe, it is sweet, appetizing, light, and subdues pitta and vāta. (82) The priyāla has a rough trunk, is aromatic, and possesses thick bark;
it is known as rājādana, tāpaseṣṭa, sannaka, druda, and dhanuṣpaṭa. (83)
The bark destroys pitta, kapha, and blood; its fruit is sweet, heavy, unctuous, and laxative, and it removes wind, pitta, burning sensations, fever, and thirst.
The pulp of the priyāla is sweet, aphrodisiac, and subdues pitta and vāta.

The rājādana (the king of fruits), also known as phalādhyakṣa, rājanyā, and kṣīrikā, is pleasing to the heart, very difficult to digest, unctuous, causes constipation, and increases āma. The fruit of the kṣīrikā is aphrodisiac, strengthening, unctuous, cold, and heavy.
It conquers thirst, fainting, intoxication, delusion, consumption, and the three humors (doṣas).
It is called vikaṅkata, sruvāvṛkṣa, granthila, svādukaṇṭaka; it is also known as yakṣavṛkṣa, kaṇṭakī, and vyāghrapād.
The ripe fruit of the *vikaṅkata* is sweet and conquers all the *doṣas*.
(88) As for the lotus seed (*padmabīja*), the lotus-eye (*padmākṣa*), the *gāloḍya*, and the lotus-cucumber (*padmakarkaṭī*):
the lotus seed is cooling, sweet, astringent, bitter, and heavy. (89)

The food of Makha (makhananna) resembles the seed of a lotus and is also known as *pānīyaphala*. It is constipating, aphrodisiac, dry, and highly effective at stabilizing the fetus; it increases *kapha* and *vāta*, is strengthening, astringent, and alleviates *pitta*, blood disorders, and burning sensations. (90)
One should declare that the food of the *makha* (the month of Māgha) is equal in its qualities to the lotus seed (91).
The *śṛṅgāṭaka* is a water-fruit, also known as the "triangular fruit" (92).
The *śṛṅgāṭaka* is cooling, sweet, heavy, aphrodisiac, and astringent.

The seeds of the kumuda are said by the wise to be astringent, and they provide semen, wind, and phlegm; they alleviate bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations. The seeds of the kairaviṇī are known as kumudvatī seeds; they are sweet, dry, cold, and heavy. (93–94)
Madhūka is known as guḍapuṣpa, madhupuṣpa, and madhusrava;
it is also called vānaprastha and madhuṣṭhīla. Among those growing in water, it is called madhūlaka. Madhūka flowers are sweet, cooling, heavy, and nourishing.
It is said to increase strength and semen, and to destroy wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
The fruit is cold, heavy, sweet, aphrodisiac, and subdues wind and bile; it is unpalatable but destroys thirst, hemorrhaging, burning sensations, dyspnea, chest wounds, and wasting. 96–97.
The *parūṣaka* fruit is coarse, has small seeds, and is of various sizes; when raw, it is astringent and sour, increases *pitta*, and is light (98).
When ripe, it is sweet in digestion, cooling, causes constipation, and is nourishing.
It is beneficial for the heart and removes bile, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, fever, consumption, and wind.
Tūta, tūla, pūga, kramuka, and brahmadāru—
ripe tūta is heavy, sweet, cooling, and subdues bile and wind.
That very [fruit] is heavy, slimy, sour, and hot, and it produces blood-bile (raktapitta).
100 The pomegranate is called *dāḍima*, *karaka*, *dantabīja*, and *lohitapuṣpaka*.
Its fruit is of three kinds: sweet, sweet-sour, and purely sour. 101
It is sweet, pacifies the three doṣas, and destroys thirst, burning sensations, and fever; it removes foul odors from the heart, throat, and mouth, is satiating, increases semen, and is light (102).
It has an astringent aftertaste, is constipating, unctuous, and promotes intelligence and strength (103).
Sour and slightly acidic, it stimulates digestion, improves appetite, produces a small amount of pitta, and is light.
Raw sour [fruit] generates pitta and alleviates vāta and kapha.
(104) Now, regarding the *bahuvāra* (*ilisoḍāṃi*): its names are as follows.
The *bahuvāra* is cooling; the *uddāla* is also called *bahuvāraka*.
The *śelu*, *śleṣmātaka*, *picchila*, and *bhūtavṛkṣaka* are synonyms.
(105) The *bahuvāra* cures poison, eruptions, ulcers, erysipelas, and leprosy.
The unripe fruit is sweet, astringent, and bitter; it benefits the hair and removes kapha and pitta.
When ripe, it is sweet, unctuous, increases phlegm, is cooling, and heavy; it conquers pitta, kapha, and blood disorders. (106–107)

The *kataka* fruit, known as *payaḥprasādī*, clarifies water; it removes turbidity from water, like collyrium for the eyes. It alleviates wind and phlegm, and is cold, sweet, astringent, and heavy. (108)
Drākṣā is said to have sweet fruit, and it is also called Madhurasā, Mṛdvīkā, Hārahūrā, and Gostanī. (109) Ripe drākṣā is laxative, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, and heavy.
It has a sweet taste and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), is beneficial for the voice, is astringent, and promotes the discharge of urine and feces.
It stimulates the bodily wind (*vāta*) within the digestive tract, is aphrodisiac, nourishes the *kapha*, and bestows appetite.
It destroys thirst, fainting, dyspnea, wind disorders, internal hemorrhaging (*vātarakta*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*).

Undigested matter (āmā) causes difficult labor, hemorrhaging, delusion, burning sensations, emaciation, and alcoholism (madātyaya). That same matter, when heavy and sour, produces blood-bile (raktapitta).
The grape (drākṣā) from the cow's udder (gostanī) is aphrodisiac, heavy, and subdues phlegm and bile. 112–113.

Another variety, seedless and very small, resembling a cow's teat in its qualities, is the mountain-grown *drākṣā* (raisin); it is light and sour, and it produces phlegm and acid bile. As is the mountain-grown *drākṣā*, so too is the *karamardikā*. (114)
The *bhūmikharjūrīkā* is sweet, difficult to climb, and has soft leaves;
likewise, the *skandhaphalā* and *kākakarkaṭī* have sweet tops.
Furthermore, another variety, the *piṇḍakharjūrikā*, is found in the western region.
The date palm (kharjūrī), shaped like a cow’s udder, which comes here from other islands and so forth, grows in the western region; it is celebrated as *chohāra*.
The three types of date palm are cooling and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect. 116–117.
It is unctuous, appetizing, pleasing to the heart, heavy, nourishing, and cures wasting from chest wounds;

it alleviates hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), promotes nourishment, relieves constipation, increases semen, pacifies the bodily wind (vāta) in the digestive tract, provides strength, and removes vomiting along with wind and phlegm (kapha). 118
It wards off fever, diarrhea, hunger, thirst, cough, and asthma (119).
It is the destroyer of intoxication, fainting, wind-disorders, bile-disorders, and diseases arising from alcohol.
The small *kharjūrikā* is considered inferior to the two large varieties in its qualities (120).
The juice of the date palm (kharjūrī) produces intoxication and pitta;
it alleviates vāta and kapha, is appetizing, digestive, and increases strength and semen. The *sulemānī* is soft, and its fruit is without leaves.
Sulemānī (Sulaimani) removes fatigue, confusion, burning sensations, fainting, and blood-bile disorders.
122 Vātāda is an enemy of wind; likewise, netropama-phala is similar to it.
Vātāda is hot, very unctuous, subdues wind, generates semen, and is heavy. 123
The marrow of the *vātāda* tree is sweet, aphrodisiac, and alleviates pitta and vāta;

it is unctuous, hot, increases kapha, and is not desired for those suffering from disorders of *rakta-pitta*. (124) One should consume the *badara*, *sevya*, and *sivitikā* fruits in the measure of a handful. (125)
Sevaṃ (the fruit of *sevam*) subdues wind and bile, is nourishing, increases phlegm, is heavy in taste and digestion,
sweet, cooling, and promotes appetite and semen. Amṛtaphala is light, aphrodisiac, very delicious, and removes the three doṣas.
In the regions of the Mudgalas, that [fruit] is found in abundance by people.
The Pīlu has a sweet fruit, is laxative, and also possesses cool fruit;
Pīlu destroys phlegm and wind, increases bile, is purgative, and cures abdominal tumors (gulma).
The *pīlu* fruit, which is sweet and bitter, is not excessively hot and alleviates the three *doṣas*.
The *pīlu* is known as *śailaja*, *akṣoṭa*, and *karparāla*;
the *akṣoṭaka* is similar to *vātāda* and increases *kapha* and *pitta*.
Bījapūra, mātuluṅga, rucaka, and phalapūraka are synonyms for the citron.
The fruit of the bījapūra is sweet in taste, sour, digestive, and light;
it alleviates internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta) and purifies the throat, tongue, and heart. (130)
It is known to alleviate dyspnea, cough, and loss of appetite; it is heart-tonic and relieves thirst.
Another variety of Bījapūra is called Madhukarkaṭī.
Madhukarkaṭikā is sweet, appetizing, cooling, and heavy.

It removes blood-bile disorders, consumption, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, and vertigo. (133) Jambīra, Dantaśaṭha, Jambha, Jambhīra, and Jambhala are synonyms for the citron. The citron is hot, heavy, and sour; it alleviates wind and phlegm as well as constipation. (134)

The small citron (svalpa-jambīrikā) conquers colic, cough, phlegm, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and disorders of intoxication; it likewise removes bad taste in the mouth, cardiac pain, weak digestion, and worms, while acting as a remedy for thirst and vomiting. 135
The lime is called *nimbū* (feminine) and *nimbuka* (neuter); it is also known as *nimbūka*.
Lime is sour, destroys wind, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, and is light (136).
Lime destroys swarms of worms, is sharp and sour, and removes abdominal distress.
It is beneficial for those suffering from pain caused by wind, bile, and phlegm, and is the supreme stimulant for appetite lost through hardship.

The sages declare that it should be administered to those afflicted by the three humors, loss of digestive fire, and wind diseases; to those overwhelmed by poison, those with weak digestion, those with intestinal obstruction, and in cases of choleraic colic (visūcikā). 137–138.
Sweet lime fruit is sweet, heavy, and subdues wind and bile;
it destroys throat diseases and poisons, increases phlegm, removes blood disorders, and alleviates wasting, loss of appetite, thirst, and vomiting; it is strengthening and nourishing. (139–140)
Karmaraṅga is veiny and very sour, causing pain;
it is cooling, constipating, sweet-sour, and removes phlegm and wind.
(141) Amlikā, cukrikā, amlī, cukā, and dantaśaṭhā are synonyms for the tamarind tree.
Amlā, ciñcikā, ciñcā, tintiḍīkā, and tintiḍī are synonyms for the tamarind tree (142).
Amlā is sour, heavy, and alleviates vāta, while it increases pitta, kapha, and blood; however, when ripe, it is digestive, dry, slightly hot, and subdues kapha and vāta (143).
Amlavetasa is known as cukra, śatavedhin, and sahasranut.
Amlavetasa is extremely sour, a laxative, light, and a digestive stimulant (dīpana).
It destroys heart disease, colic, and abdominal tumors (gulma); it increases bile (pittala) and causes horripilation. 144.

The meat-juice (rasa) made from goat meat is parching, it destroys defects of feces and urine, and it cures splenic enlargement, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), hiccups, flatulence, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, indigestion, and vomiting; it is a destroyer of diseases caused by kapha and vāta. 145.
The properties of chickpeas (caṇaka) should be known as those of the *lohasūcī* plant; they cause the skin to contract. 146.
Vṛkṣāmla, tintiḍīka, cukra, and amlavṛkṣaka are synonyms for the tamarind tree.
Raw vṛkṣāmla is sour and hot; it destroys wind (vāta) and increases phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta). 147.
The ripe [fruit] is heavy, constipating, pungent, astringent, and light (148).
It is sour, hot, appetizing, dry, digestive, and increases phlegm and wind.
It conquers thirst, dysuria, malabsorption syndrome, abdominal tumors, colic, heart disease, and parasites (149).
The fourfold sour (caturamla) consists of *amlavetasa*, *vṛkṣāmla*, large *jambīra*, and *nimbuka*; it becomes fivefold sour (*pañcāmala*) when combined with *bījapūra*.
Among fruits, that which is fully ripe is declared to be the most excellent in quality.
In fruits other than the *bilva*, the unripe state should be understood as superior;
for that which is succulent among fruits is declared to possess the greatest qualities.
(151) The dried fruit of *drākṣā*, *bilva*, *śivā*, and others possesses even greater qualities.
One should indicate that all marrow possesses qualities equal to those of its fruit.
(152) One should not consume fruit that has been damaged by frost, fire, harsh winds, serpents, insects, and the like; nor that which is out-of-season, grown in poor soil, or overripe. (153)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, the section on fruits such as mangoes, in the *Miśra-prakaraṇa* (Section on Miscellaneous Substances) of the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.

Now begins the eighth chapter, titled the "Section on Metals and the Like," which is also known as the "Section on Metals, Sub-metals, Mineral Salts, Semi-metals, Precious Stones, Semi-precious Stones, Poisons, and Anti-poisons."
Gold, silver, copper, tin, zinc, lead, and iron— these seven metals are derived from the mountains.
[They ward off] wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, emaciation, debility, and the diseases of old age.
Having warded off the body, they sustain that of men; thus the elements (dhātus) are considered to be so named.

Long ago, seeing the wives of the self-controlled Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) dwelling in their own hermitages—women endowed with the beauty of loveliness and in the prime of youth— [the gods became enamored].
The semen of the Fire-god, whose mind was shattered by the pride of Kandarpa, fell upon the surface of the earth; that became gold,
and it also becomes artificial through the processing of mercury.
Svarṇa, suvarṇa, kanaka, hiraṇya, hema, hāṭaka;
5 tapanīya, gāṅgeya, kaladhauta, kāñcana, cāmīkara, śātakumbha, and likewise kārttasvara—these are its names. 6
Jāmbūnada, jātarūpa, and mahārajata—these are names for gold.
When heated it is red, white when cut, and has the luster of saffron on the touchstone;
free from silver and copper, it is glossy, soft, and heavy—this is excellent gold.
That leaf which is white, hard, rough, discolored, and dirty, which turns black when burned or cut, and white when rubbed, should be rejected; it is light and easily split.
Gold is cooling, aphrodisiac, strengthening, heavy, and a rejuvenative elixir.
Sweet, bitter, and astringent, sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and slimy;
it is purifying, nourishing, beneficial for the eyes, and bestows intelligence, memory, and intellect.
It is pleasing to the heart, promotes longevity, and produces luster, purity of speech, and stability of the skin.
It conquers the two types of poison, insanity, fever arising from the three *doṣas*, and wasting diseases.
It takes away the strength and vitality of men, nourishes the multitude of diseases in this body, and being a constant cause of unhappiness, this impure gold may even bring about death. (11–12)
Gold that has not been properly killed destroys strength and vigor, causes diseases, and leads to death; therefore, one should kill it with great effort.
For the sake of slaying Tripura, [the gods] gazed with unblinking eyes.
Filled with rage, Śiva gazed intently;
at that moment, fire suddenly fell from his eye,
and from it Rudra emerged, blazing like Vaiśvānara.
From the second eye, a tear-drop fell from the left; from that, silver was produced, which one should employ in rites for liberation.
Indeed, that [silver] may also be artificial, produced through the application of mercury and substances such as tin. 16–17.
Silver (rūpya), however, is known as rajata, tāra, candrakānti, and sitaprabha.
It is heavy, glossy, soft, white, capable of withstanding heating and cutting, rich in color, and as clear as the moon; thus silver possesses nine auspicious qualities.
Silver that is hard, artificial, rough, red, yellow-leaved, light, and destroyed by burning, cutting, or hammering is declared to be defective (19).
Silver is cooling, astringent and sour, sweet in its post-digestive taste, and laxative.
It stabilizes youth, is unctuous, acts as a depletive, and conquers vāta and pitta;
it certainly destroys diseases such as urinary disorders (prameha) and others without delay.
Silver (tāra) causes heat in the body, brings about emaciation, and causes the destruction of semen.

It destroys vigor, strength, and the nourishment of the body, and indeed nourishes great diseases when it is impure. (21) Those conversant with antiquity say that this copper originated from the semen of Kārttikeya which fell upon the surface of the earth. (22)
Tāmra, audumbara, śulva, and udumbara are also recorded as synonyms; it is known as ravipriya, mlecchamukha, and by names synonymous with the sun (sūrya).
It resembles the japa flower, is glossy, soft, and capable of bearing a dense [polish].
Copper that is free from iron and tin is recommended for the process of killing (māraṇa).
Copper that is black, rough, very hard, white, unable to withstand pressure, or mixed with iron and tin is proclaimed to be defective. 24–25.

Copper is astringent, sweet, bitter, and sour; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), strengthening to the vital tissues (sāraka), a subduer of pitta, a remover of kapha, cold, and it acts as a digestive stimulant (dīpana), light, and scarifying (lekhanā).
It cures anemia, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, fever, skin diseases, cough, dyspnea, consumption, chronic catarrh, and acid gastritis (amlapitta).
Others say it removes swelling, worms, and pain, yet this is considered a slight nourishment.
In the case of mercury (*tāmra*), there is one defect when it is not properly processed:
burning, sweating, loss of appetite, fainting, moistening, purging, vomiting, and giddiness. 28.
Ranga, vanga, trapu, as well as piccaṭa, kṣuraka, and miśraka—these are said to be the two types of vanga.
Among them, kṣuraka is considered superior, while miśraka is regarded as inferior. (29–30)

Ranga (mercury) is light, laxative, dry, and hot; it destroys urinary disorders, phlegm, and worms, as well as anemia and asthma. It is beneficial for the eyes, slightly increases bile, and just as a lion destroys a herd of elephants, so too does Vaṅga (tin) destroy the entire category of urinary disorders.
It certainly bestows physical comfort, strength of the senses, and nourishment upon a man.
Zinc is considered similar to tin and is a source of copper;
zinc is astringent, bitter, cooling, and removes phlegm and bile.
It is supremely beneficial for the eyes and destroys urinary disorders, jaundice, and asthma.
(33) Having seen the beautiful daughter of Bhogi, Vāsuki released his semen;
from that was born the Naga who removes all diseases of men. (34)
Lead (sīsa), brass (bradhna), zinc (vapra), and that which is desired for medicinal preparations (yogeṣṭa) are known by the name "nāga.

Lead should be understood as having the qualities of mercury (raṅga); it is especially effective in destroying urinary disorders. Nāga bestows strength equal to a hundred elephants, destroys disease, and extends life.
When consumed continuously, it kindles the digestive fire, increases the power of desire, and destroys death. 37.

Indeed, if tin and lead are deficient in their processing (*pāka*), they cause leprosy, abdominal tumors, as well as extremely painful itching, urinary disorders, exhaustion from wind, swellings, fistula-in-ano, and other such ailments when administered. 38.
Long ago, when the Lominas and Daityas were slain by the gods in battle, various types of metals were produced from their bodies.
"Loha" (metal) is not feminine; it refers to iron, steel, sharp metal, a lump of metal, black iron, and wrought iron. (39)
Heaviness, hardness, excessive moisture, foulness, a burning sensation,
the defect of stone formation, and a very foul odor are the defects of iron.
Iron is bitter, laxative, cooling, sweet, astringent, and heavy.
It is dry, beneficial for the eyes, scraping, and increases vata;

it overcomes kapha, pitta, artificial poison (gara), colic, swelling, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, anemia, fat, urinary disorders, worms, and skin diseases (kuṣṭha); its waste product (kiṭṭa) has exactly the same properties. 41–42.

Iron that is impure and unrefined certainly brings about impotence, leprosy, disease, and death; it causes heart disease and colic, as well as urinary stones, and likewise provokes various ailments, nausea, and anemia. It is life-destroying and intoxicating. (43)
It does not bestow vigor upon the body and inflicts a terrible pain upon the heart.
(44) One who serves iron should likewise avoid pumpkin, sesame oil, black gram, mustard seeds, as well as wine and sour juices. (45)

When iron is smeared with sour liquid, those parts which remain fine and resemble the peaks of mountains are called *sāra* (essence); this iron known as *sāra* cures malabsorption (*grahaṇī*) and diarrhea (*atisāra*). 46
It dispels wind (vāta) arising from all parts of the body, colic born of digestive disorders (pariṇāmaja),
vomiting, chronic catarrh (pīnasa), bile (pitta), dyspnea, and cough—
[that which does not spread upon a heated vessel, just as a drop of oil does not spread on hot water]. 47.

Aspeltum (hiṅgu) loses its own fragrance, and the bark of the neem tree its bitterness; heated milk takes on a peak-like shape and does not touch the ground; black-bodied chickpeas become filled with water, and that is said to be kāntaloha (magnetite). 48.
Gold removes gulma, abdominal enlargement, hemorrhoids, colic, undigested matter (āmam), āmavāta, fistula-in-ano, jaundice, edema, skin diseases, consumption, and anemia;
it also cures splenic disorders, acid gastritis (amlapitta), liver disease, and headaches. 49–50.
Kāntaloha (magnetite) undoubtedly conquers all diseases;
it bestows strength, virility, and nourishment of the body, and increases the digestive fire.
When iron is being smelted, its dross is called maṇḍūra.

Lohasiṃhānikā is called the dross (kiṭṭī) of metals and of lions; whatever metal possesses which quality, its dross likewise possesses that same quality. (52) There are seven minor minerals (upadhātus): gold pyrite (svarṇamākṣika), silver pyrite (tāramākṣika), and so forth.

Tuttha, kāṃsya, rīti, sindūra, and śilājatu (53)—in all these secondary minerals (upadhātu), the qualities of their respective primary metals are also present; however, in these [secondary minerals], those qualities are subordinate due to the small proportion of those [primary] elements. (54)

It is called *svarṇamākṣika* (golden pyrite) and *tāpīja* (born of the Tāpī river); it is also known as *madhumākṣika* (honey-pyrite), *tāpya*, *mākṣikadhātu* (pyrite ore), and *madhudhātu* (honey-ore).
Because it contains a small amount of gold due to its association with it, it is termed *svarṇamākṣika*.
An alloy (upadhātu) is that which possesses some of the qualities of gold;
likewise, in the absence of gold, gold-oxide (svarṇamākṣika) is given.
However, because it is a substitute (anukalpa), its qualities are slightly inferior to those of the former.
Not only do the qualities of gold exist in *svarṇamākṣika*;
because of its contact with other substances, there are also other qualities present, since *svarṇamākṣika* is sweet, bitter, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*). 59
It is beneficial for the eyes and destroys bladder pain, skin diseases, anemia, urinary disorders, abdominal poison, hemorrhoids, swelling, toxins, itching, and even the three doṣas.
It also cures weak digestion, loss of strength, severe constipation, eye diseases, and skin diseases including kuṣṭha.

Likewise, that which produces a garland and is preceded by a wound is impure *tāpīja*; 61. *Tāramākṣika* is another [type], which resembles silver; because it contains a small amount of silver, it is called *tāramākṣika*. 62.
Because it is considered a secondary substitute for that [silver], its qualities are remembered as being inferior;
for while it possesses the quality of silver,
tāramākṣika is somewhat sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, slightly bitter, aphrodisiac, and an elixir.

It is beneficial for the eyes and destroys bladder pain, skin diseases, anemia, urinary disorders, poisoning, abdominal diseases, hemorrhoids, swelling, consumption, itching, and even the three doṣas.
It also cures weak digestion, severe loss of strength, constipation, and eye diseases along with skin ailments.
In the same way, it produces a garland preceded by sores; this seed of *tāpī* acts likewise.
(65) *Tuttha*, *vitunnaka*, and *śikhigrīva*—the latter being peacock-green.
*Tuttha* is indeed a mineral of copper; it arises from copper in some measure. (66)
Possessing some of the qualities of copper, as well as those qualities which will be described hereafter,
tutthaka is pungent, alkaline, astringent, emetic, light,
scraping, fissuring, cold, beneficial for the eyes, and it removes phlegm and bile. (67)
Kharpara destroys poison, stones, skin diseases, and itching; it possesses qualities similar to those [of copper].
68. That which is known as tāmra, trapu, ja, kāṃsya, ghoṣa, and kaṃsaka is called an upadhātu (secondary metal); kāṃsya is produced from the two metals copper and tin. 69.
The qualities of bell-metal (kāṃsya) should be understood by people as being similar to those of its constituent elements;
however, other qualities are also traditionally attributed to it due to the power arising from their combination.
Bell-metal is astringent, bitter, hot, scraping, clear, and laxative.
Lead (guru) is beneficial for the eyes, dry, and is supreme in removing kapha and pitta.
Brass (ārakūṭa), however, increases pitta; it is also called āra, rīti, rājarīti, brahmarīti, kapilā, and piṅgalā.
Rīti may also be an alloy of copper and brass; its qualities should be known by people as being similar to those of its own source.
However, through the power of combination, other qualities are also recorded for it. (73–74)
Rītikā (bronze) is dry, bitter, and salty in taste;
it is a purifier, cures anemia, destroys worms, and is not excessively scraping. Sindūra, raktareṇu, and nāgagarbha are derived from lead.
Cinnabar (sindūra) is a derivative of lead; by its qualities it is considered similar to lead.
Due to the power of its combination [with other substances], other qualities are also attributed to it:
cinnabar is hot and destroys erysipelas, leprosy, itching, and poisons.
It promotes the healing of fractures and cleanses and heals wounds. In the summer heat, the mountains, scorched by the sun, exude a mineral essence like resin; that is celebrated as *śilājatu*.
That [metal] is fourfold: gold, silver, copper, and iron.
Śilājatu, adrijatu, and śailaniryāsa; likewise gaireya, aśmaja, girija, and śailadhātuja [are synonyms for bitumen]. 79.
Śilāja (bitumen) is pungent, bitter, and hot; it has a pungent post-digestive effect and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).

It is fissiparous, facilitates the administration of other drugs, and destroys kaphaja urinary disorders, urinary stones, gravel, dysuria, consumption, asthma, hemorrhoids caused by vāta, and jaundice.
It cures epilepsy, insanity, edema, skin diseases, abdominal enlargements, and worms.
Gold, which has the color of a hibiscus flower, is sweet, pungent, and bitter in taste; it is cooling and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
Silver is white, cool, pungent, and sweet in its post-digestive effect;
copper has the luster of a peacock's neck and is sharp and hot; iron has the appearance of a vulture's wing and is bitter and salty.

Because it is bitter in its after-effect yet cooling, mercury (pārada) is declared by those seeking elixirs to be the best of all; therefore it is called "Rasa," and it is also remembered as a mineral (dhātu). 85–86.

The semen fallen from Śiva’s body onto the surface of the earth became white and translucent because it was produced from the very essence of his body. This seed of Śiva is to be understood as fourfold, according to the distinction of its fields (*kṣetra*). 87.
White, red, yellow, and black—these indeed occur in sequence; by birth, they correspond respectively to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
White is commended for the destruction of diseases, while red is indeed used for rejuvenation (rasāyana).
In the science of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), however, that which is yellow when swallowed and black when in the sky [is mercury].
Mercury is the mineral of taste (*rasadhātu*), the lord of tastes (*rasendra*), the great elixir (*mahārasa*),
the volatile (*capala*), the seed of Śiva (*śivavīrya*), the essence (*rasa*), the progenitor (*sūta*), and he who is named after Śiva.

Mercury (pārada) possesses six tastes, is unctuous, pacifies the three doṣas, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana). It is a vehicle for other drugs, highly aphrodisiac, always bestows strength of vision,
cures all diseases, and is specifically said to destroy all forms of leprosy.
When the *rasa* is in its natural state (*svastha*), it is Brahmā; when bound (*baddha*), it is to be known as Janārdana;
when colored (*rañjita*) and desired (*kāmita*), it is the god Maheśvara himself.
When swooned (*mūrcchita*), it removes disease; and having experienced bondage, it brings about movement in the sky.

For who other than the Creator, the mine of compassion, can restore to youth one who is dead? (94) Whatever disease may be incurable for which no medical treatment exists, the Lord of Mercury (Rasendra) destroys that disease in men, elephants, and horses. (95)

They declare that impurity (*mala*), poison (*viṣa*), fire (*vahni*), and mountain-skin (*giritvaca*) are the natural defects (*naisargika-doṣa*) of mercury; while the lords of sages have stated that two adventitious defects (*upādhija-doṣa*), namely those produced by contact with tin (*trapu*) and lead (*nāga*), exist in the king of fluids (*rasendra*). (96) Through impurity comes fainting, through poison death, and through fire a most painful burning within the body.
The body suffers dullness from stone; from mercury, men experience instability and loss of virility;
from tin, leprosy; and from lead, impotence; therefore, this [mercury] must be thoroughly purified.
Fire, poison, and dross—these are the three primary defects in mercury.

These cause distress, death, and fainting in men in succession. (98) Even though other defects regarding mercury have been mentioned by physicians, nevertheless, these three defects must be removed with special care. (99)
Indeed, he who consumes the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*) devoid of processing (*saṃskāra*) suffers affliction;
it certainly brings about the destruction of the body and generates painful diseases for men. (100) [The substances are:
sulfur, vermilion, mica, yellow orpiment, realgar, antimony, and borax.
Rājāvartaka, cumbaka, sphaṭika, śaṅkha, khaṭī, gairika, kāsīsa, rasaka, kaparda, sikatā, bola, kuṅkuṣṭhaka,
and saurāṣṭrī— these are considered the minor minerals (uparasas) of mercury due to their slight similar qualities. 101
Hiṅgula, darada, mlecchamiṅgula, and cūrṇapārada are names for it;
darada is said to be of three kinds: carmāra, śukatuṇḍaka, and haṃsapāda as the third, each possessing superior qualities in successive order. 102–103.
The *carmāra* is white in color, while the *śukatuṇḍaka* is yellow;
the *haṃsapāda*, resembling the *japā* flower, is the most excellent of all.
*Hiṅgula* is bitter, astringent, and pungent; it cures eye diseases and removes phlegm and bile.
It destroys nausea, leprosy, fever, jaundice, as well as splenic disorders, flatulence, and artificial poisons (105).
Indeed, cinnabar processed in a *ḍamaru* apparatus by means of upward sublimation yields mercury that is already pure; one need not purify it further (106).

Formerly, on Śvetadvīpa, while the Goddess was sporting, her silken garment (dukūla) became covered with dust; from that dust which spread over the Ocean of Milk as she bathed, sulphur (gandhaka) was produced. 107.
Gandhaka, gāndhika, gandhapāṣāṇa, and also saugandhika are mentioned; it is also called bali and balarasa. Thus, gandhaka is said to be of four types: red, yellow, white, and black. 108–109.
Red sulphur is recommended for gold-making; yellow for rejuvenation (rasāyana);
white for the application of ointments on wounds and the like; and black is the best, though very difficult to obtain.
Sulphur is pungent and bitter in taste, hot in potency, astringent, and laxative.
Sulphur is bitter in taste, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and it conquers *jantu*, itching, and erysipelas (*visarpa*).
It destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), consumption (*kṣaya*), splenic disorders, phlegm, and wind; it is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
However, sulphur that has not been purified causes skin disease and irregular fever within the body.
It destroys happiness, beauty, strength, as well as vitality and semen, and indeed causes blood [to flow].
Formerly, for the sake of slaying Vṛtra, the thunderbolt was raised by the wielder of the thunderbolt; from it, sparks then scattered throughout the sky. 112–113.
They fell with a deep roar upon the peaks of the mountains;
from those very [peaks] arose the various ores of abhra upon the hills.
That was indeed *vajra* because it was born from *vajra*, and it was called *abhra* because it originated from the sound of *abhra*.
Because it has fallen from the sky, it is therefore considered to be the sky (gagana).
Due to the divisions of Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, it is fourfold; in order, it is white, red, yellow, and black by color. 115–116.
White [mercury] is praised for the purification of silver; red for alchemy (rasāyana);
yellow for gold; black for diseases and for liquefaction.
It is of four kinds: Pināka, Dardura, Nāga, and Vajra.
The Pināka bow, when thrown into the fire, releases its mass of bark;
eating it out of ignorance bestows the great leprosy.
But the Durdara, when thrown into the fire, produces the sound of the Durdara.
Having fashioned many small balls [of the aforementioned substance], he shall become a giver of death;
furthermore, when the snake emits a hiss repeatedly like a serpent,
that which is consumed by it will certainly cause fistula-in-ano.
The diamond (vajra) remains as firm as a diamond; it does not undergo transformation even in fire.
Among all types of meteoric iron (abhra), diamond is the best, for it removes disease, old age, and death.
Meteoric iron originating from the northern mountains contains many living beings and possesses superior qualities.

The Abhra (mica) originating from the southern mountains possesses little vitality and confers few qualities. It is astringent, sweet, very cooling, promotes longevity, and increases the bodily tissues (dhātus).
It destroys the three doṣas, as well as ulcers, urinary disorders, skin diseases, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, nodes, poisons, and worms.
It destroys diseases, strengthens the body, and brings about an increase in vigor;
it delights one with a hundred young women at all times and produces long-lived sons whose prowess is equal to that of lions.
When constantly consumed, processed mica (*mṛtābhra*) removes the fear of death;

however, unrefined and unprocessed mica causes various afflictions for men, such as leprosy, consumption, anemia, and swelling, and it produces pain in the heart and flanks—it is heavy and causes distress. (125–126)
Haritāla is known as tāla, āla, and also tālaka.
Haritāla is said to be of two kinds: that called *patra* (leaf-like) and that designated as *piṇḍa* (mass-like).
Of these two, the former is superior in its qualities, while the latter is inferior.

One should know that *tālaka* (realgar) called "leaf-like" (*patrākhya*) is gold-colored, heavy, glossy, and possesses leaf-like layers like those of a cloud; it is rich in qualities and an elixir for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*).
That which is leafless, resembling a solid lump, has little potency, and is likewise heavy [is of inferior quality]. (128–129)

The yellow orpiment (haritāla) found in the flowers of women is of little quality; that which is in the form of a mass (piṇḍatālaka) is pungent, unctuous, astringent, and hot. It removes poison, itching, skin diseases, diseases of the mouth, blood disorders, phlegm, bile, and hair-diseases. (130)
It takes away the natural luster born of the body,
produces excessive heat and pain from the contraction of the limbs, bestows phlegm and wind disorders, and may cause leprosy.
This [substance] has been eaten impurely and also improperly processed. 131.
Realgar (manaḥśilā), manoguptā, manohvā, nāgajihvikā, naipālī, kunaṭī, golā, and śilā are known as divine medicinal herbs (divyauṣadhi). 132.
Realgar (manaḥśilā) is heavy, improves the complexion, is slightly hot, scraping, pungent, bitter, and unctuous;
it cures poison, dyspnea, cough, possession by spirits, phlegm, and hemoptysis.

(133) Realgar certainly weakens the strength of a person unless it is properly purified; indeed, it causes the retention of waste products, urinary obstruction, gravel, and the disease of painful micturition (kṛcchra). (134)
There is collyrium from the Yamunā and also what is called kapotāñjana; that which is black is known as sroto’ñjana, while sauvīra is said to be white.
It has the appearance of an anthill’s peak and, when broken, resembles collyrium.
When rubbed, this [srotoñjana] has the appearance of red ochre (gairika); it is known as srotoñjana. Sauvīra is to be known as similar to srotoñjana, but it is pale white.
Srotoñjana is considered sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and a subduer of kapha and pitta.
Astringent, scraping, unctuous, absorbent, and a remedy for vomiting and poison;
it cures skin diseases (sidhma), consumption, and hemorrhage, and is cooling. It should always be used by the wise.
(138) All the qualities of *srotoñjana* are also considered by the wise to exist in *sauvīra*.
However, among the two types of collyrium (*añjana*), *sroto'ñjana* is considered the best.
