(139) *Ṭaṅkaṇa* kindles the digestive fire, is parching, destroys *kapha*, and increases *vāta* and *pitta*.
*Sphaṭī* is called *sphaṭikā*; it is white, bright, and imparts color. (140)
Dṛḍharaṅgā, raṅgadṛḍhā, and raṅgāṅgā are also mentioned [as synonyms].
Sphaṭikā is astringent and hot; it destroys wind, bile, phlegm, and ulcers, as well as vitiligo and erysipelas, and causes the contraction of the female genital tract. 141–142.
Rājāvarta, nṛpāvarta, rājanyāvartaka,
the gem known as āvartamaṇi, and likewise simply āvarta—
rājāvarta is pungent, bitter, cooling, and a destroyer of pitta.
Rājāvarta destroys urinary disorders (prameha) and wards off vomiting and hiccup.
Cumbaka, kāntapāṣāṇa, ayaskānta, and lauhakarṣaka are synonyms for the magnet stone.
Cumbaka is scraping, cooling, and removes fat, poison, and artificial poisons (garas).
Gairika, raktadhātu, gaireya, and likewise girija are synonyms;
however, suvarṇagairika is another variety, for it is indeed more red than the former.
This pair of gairikas is unctuous, sweet, astringent, and cooling.
It is beneficial for the eyes and removes burning sensations, bile, blood disorders, phlegm, hiccups, and poison (147).
Chalk is also called *kaṭhinī* and *lekhanī*;
it is cooling, sweet, cures burning sensations and hemorrhaging, and conquers poison and swelling (148).
From its application as a plaster, these qualities are declared; when eaten, it is equal to clay.
Khaṭī and Gaurakhaṭī are both proclaimed to be equal in their properties. Bālukā is called sikatā, and it is also known as śarkarā and retajā.
Vālukā (sand) and lekhani (chalk) are cooling and destroy wounds and chest injuries.
(150) Kharparī and tutthaka are known as rasaka; whatever qualities are proclaimed for tutthaka, those same qualities are recorded for rasaka. (151)
Kāśīśa, dhātukāśīśa, and pāṃśukāśīśa are names for that very same substance; when it is slightly yellow, it is called puṣpakāśīśa.
Kāśīśa is sour, hot, bitter, and likewise astringent. (152)

It is proclaimed to remove wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), to be beneficial for the hair, to destroy itching of the eyes and poisons, and to cure dysuria, urinary calculi, and vitiligo. (153) Saurāṣṭrī, tuvarī, kālī, mṛttālaka, and surāṣṭraja [are synonyms]. (154)
It is also known as āḍhakī, mṛtsnā, and suramṛttikā;
all the qualities of sphaṭikā are likewise proclaimed for saurāṣṭrī.
Mṛn-mṛdā, mṛttikā, mṛtsnā, kṣetrajā, and kṛṣṇamṛttikā are synonyms for clay.
Black earth (kṛṣṇamṛd) cures wounds, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, and disorders of phlegm and bile. Paṅka, jala-kalka, culuka, kardama, mala,
cikila, palita, drāpa, palala, and niṣadvara are synonyms for mud.
Kardama is cooling and laxative, and it destroys burning sensations, hemorrhaging, and swelling.
(157) Kapardaka, varāṭa, kapardī, and varāṭikā destroy ear discharge and weak digestion, and they eliminate pitta, rakta, and kapha. (158)
The conch (*śaṅkha*) is born from the ocean; it is a *kambu*, resonant with sound, and possesses a purifying tone.
The conch is cooling, cold, light, and conquers bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and blood disorders.
(159) Bol, gandharasa, prāṇa, piṇḍa, and goparasa are similar [in their properties].
Bola removes blood, is cooling, improves the intellect, stimulates digestion, and promotes digestion;
it is sweet, pungent, and bitter, and it conquers burning sensations, perspiration, and the three doṣas.
It destroys fever, epilepsy, and skin diseases, and effects the purification of the uterus. 160
Kaṅkuṣṭha is produced on the peaks at the foot of the Himavat mountains;
among these, one is red-black and the other is known as daṇḍaka.
The first type of kaṅkuṣṭha is considered the best when it has a yellow luster, is heavy, and is unctuous.
That which is dark, yellow, light, and devoid of essence is not desired, as is the case with the *aṇḍaka* variety.
Kaṅkuṣṭha, kākakuṣṭha, viraṅga, and kolakākulam [are the types].
Kaṅkuṣṭha is purgative, bitter, pungent, hot, and improves the complexion.
It cures worms, swelling, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, tumors, constipation, and phlegm.
Since all people who desire wealth take extreme delight in it,
it is therefore called a "ratna" (jewel) by those expert in the science of words.
The word *ratna* is neuter, while *maṇi* is masculine; it is also said to be feminine.
That [term] refers to a gemstone such as coral (*pāṣāṇabheda*) or pearl (*muktā*) and the like. Emerald (*gārutmata*), topaz (*puṣparāga*), and ruby (*māṇikya*) are also called *ratna*. 166.
Indranīla, gomeda, as well as vaidūrya, pearl, and coral—these are indeed declared to be the nine gems. (167) Pearl, diamond, vaidūrya, and ruby... (168)
Puṣparāga, gomeda, nīla, and likewise gārutmata, along with pravāla—these indeed are the nine great gems (mahāratna).
Hīraka is masculine, while vajra is used in all genders; it is also called candra and maṇivara.

That [mercury] is known as white when it is a Brahmin, red when it is a Kṣatriya, yellow when it is a Vaiśya, and black when it is a Śūdra; thus it consists of the four castes. In alchemy (rasāyana), the white variety is considered the best, bestowing all perfections (siddhis).
The Kṣatriya is remembered as the destroyer of diseases and the remover of old age and death;
the Vaiśya is declared to be the bestower of wealth and likewise the maker of the body firm; and the Śūdra destroys diseases and brings about the stabilization of youth. 171–172.
Now, since that [tree] is of three kinds—divided into male, female, and neuter—their characteristics as male, female, and neuter are to be defined here by their defining marks:
those that are well-rounded, full of fruit, endowed with luster, and very large. (173)

Those [triangles] devoid of lines and dots are declared to be males; those endowed with lines and dots and having six sides are known as females; and those that are triangular and very elongated are to be understood as neuter. 174.
Among them, there may be superior men who effect the binding of the *rasa*. Women bestow beauty upon the body and grant pleasure to women.
Neuters, however, would be devoid of virility, lacking desire, and bereft of vital essence (*sattva*).
Women should be administered to women; one should employ eunuchs for eunuchs. Men who increase virility should always be given to all [patients].
(177) It makes the *vajra* impure, as well as causing leprosy and pain in the sides.
Therefore, having purified it of its paleness and lameness, one should kill it;
for when consumed, killed diamond undoubtedly bestows longevity, nourishment, strength, virility, complexion, and happiness, and destroys all diseases. (178–179)
Gārutmata, marakata, aśmagarbha, and harinmaṇi are synonyms for emerald (180).
Māṇikya, padmarāga, śoṇaratna, and lohita are synonyms for ruby (181).
Puṣparāga and mañjumaṇi are synonyms for topaz, which is the favorite of Vācaspati (182).
Sapphire, as well as indranīla, and gomeda, which is a yellow gem; 183.
Vaidūrya is a gem from afar (dūrajam), beloved by the planet Ketu. 184.
Muktika is cool and bitter; it is called muktā and likewise muktāphala.

The oyster shell, the conch, the elephant, the boar, the serpent, the fish, the frog, and the bamboo—these are declared by the experts to be the sources of pearls. Pearl is cooling, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and bestows strength and nourishment. (185)
The word *pravāla* may be used for both masculine and neuter, whereas *vidruma* is masculine only. (186) Gems, when eaten, are sweet and laxative;
when worn, they are beneficial for the eyes, cooling, and destroy poison.

Regarding the question: "Which jewel is auspicious, pleasing, and a remover of the defects of the planets; and by bringing satisfaction to which planet does it become a remover of defects? the answer is given in the *Ratnamālā*: [187]
The well-born, pure ruby is for the Sun; the pearl is for the Moon; coral is said to belong to Mars; the emerald to Mercury;
the topaz to Jupiter; the diamond to Venus; and [the sapphire] to Saturn.
Sapphire and the stainless [emerald] are declared to be distinct from the other two, namely gomedaka and vaidūrya (188).
Secondary gems include glass, camphor-stone, as well as pearl-oyster shells, conch shells, and many others of this kind (189).

Just as the qualities of gems exist in semi-precious stones, so too do they exist in these [inferior gems], though they are somewhat inferior; this distinction has been illustrated. 190. Viṣa, gara, and kṣveḍa are synonyms for poison; now I shall describe its varieties.
Vatsanābha, along with Haridra, Saktuka, Pradīpana,
Saurāṣṭrika, Śṛṅgika, Kālakūṭa, Hālāhala, and Brahmaputra— these are the nine varieties of poison. (191)

That which has leaves resembling the *sinduvāra* and a shape like the *vatsanābha*, and where there is no growth of trees at its side, is declared to be *vatsanābha*. (192) That which has roots equal to turmeric is called *hāridra*. (193)
That which has a knot with its center filled with flour is called *saktuka*.
That which is red in color, radiant, and possesses the brilliance of fire, causing great burning, is described by the ancients as *pradīpana*. 194–195.
One who belongs to the region of Surāṣṭra is called a Saurāṣṭrika (196).
That [substance] to which, when a cow-horn is attached, milk becomes red is declared by those expert in the true nature of substances to be Śṛṅgika (197).
In the war between the gods and the asuras, from the blood of the Daitya Pṛthumālin who was slain by the gods, a tree resembling an aśvattha tree was born;
its resin is proclaimed by the sages to be kālakūṭa.
He may appear in Ahikṣetra, Śṛṅgavera, Koṅkaṇa, or Malaya. His fruit-cluster has the appearance of a cow’s udder, and its leaves resemble those of the palm tree;
by his splendor, trees and other plants situated nearby are consumed with fire.
This is to be known as Hālāhala; it grows in Kiṣkindhā, on the Himalayas, on the shore of the southern ocean, and also in the region of Koṅkaṇa.
That which is tawny in color is likewise so in its essence.
The son of Brahmā is to be known as born on Mount Malaya.
Among them, the Brāhmaṇa is white, the Kṣatriya has a reddish luster, the Vaiśya is yellow, and the Śūdra is black; thus poison is said to be of four kinds. (200–201)
One should give poison to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of elixir (rasāyana), to a Kṣatriya for bodily nourishment,
to a Vaiśya for the destruction of leprosy, and indeed to a Śūdra for execution. Poison is said to be life-taking, pervasive, and diffusive.

It is fiery (āgneya), removes wind and phlegm, is a vehicle for medicinal formulations (yogavāhi), and induces exhilaration (madāvaha). That same substance, when properly prepared with appropriate adjuncts, bestows life, acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana), is a vehicle for formulations, destroys the three doṣas, is nourishing, and increases virility.
Whatever defects exist in impure poison are eliminated by purification;
therefore, one should employ poison in its applications only after it has been purified. (205) [The substances used for purification are:
the milky sap of *arka*, the milky sap of *snuhī*, *lāṅgalī*, and *karavīraka*.
Guñjā, ahiphena, and dhattūra—these are the seven types of upaviṣas (secondary poisons).
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the section on Metals and other Substances, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. 8.
Now begins the ninth section on grains:
rice-grain, paddy-grain, awned grain as the third, podded grain, and small grain—these are said to be the fivefold group of grains. (1)

Rice includes red rice and the like; *vrīhi* includes the sixty-day rice and others; *śūkadhānya* (awned grain) includes barley and the like; *śimbīdhānya* (pulsed grain) includes mung beans and the like;
*kṣudradhānya* (minor grain) includes *kaṅgu* and the like; and *tṛṇadhānya* (grass grain) is recorded as being of that [last] kind. 2.
Winter rice (*śāli*) is known to be white and requires no threshing.
[The varieties are: *raktaśāli*, *sakalama*, *pāṇḍuka*, *śakunāhṛta*, *sugandhaka*, *kardamaka*, *mahāśāli*, and *dūṣaka*.
Puṣpāṇḍaka, puṇḍarīka, as well as mahiṣamastaka,
dīrghaśūka, kāñcanaka, hāyana, and lodhrapuṣpaka—
these and many other varieties of śāli rice grow in many different regions.
Fearing excessive prolixity, all [the varieties] have not been described here.
Śāli rice is sweet, unctuous, strengthening, constipating with slight fecal output,
astringent, light, appetizing, beneficial for the voice, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
Shali rice grown on soil scorched by fire is slightly cooling and slightly increasing wind and phlegm;
it is cold, pacifies pitta, promotes urination, is astringent, light in digestion, facilitates the passage of urine and feces, is dry, and reduces kapha. (7–8)
Rice grown in marshy fields (kaidāra) subdues wind and bile, is heavy, increases phlegm and semen,
is astringent, causes scanty feces, is purifying, and bestows strength.
Rice grown on dry land (sthalaja) is sweet, subdues bile and phlegm, and increases wind and bile.
Some are slightly bitter and astringent, and pungent in their post-digestive effect (vipāka).
When sown [as seeds], they are sweet, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and destroy pitta;
they increase kapha, cause scanty feces, are astringent, heavy, and cold. 10–11.
Those that have not been sown are said to be slightly inferior in qualities to those that have been sown.
Freshly planted [grains] are considered nourishing (*vṛṣya*), while old ones are known to be light.
Among these, those planted for a second time are even more so, being quick to ripen and superior in qualities.
Rice that has been cut and regrown is cold, parched, strengthening, and removes pitta and kapha;
it binds the feces, is astringent, light, and slightly bitter.
Among these, red śāli rice is the best; it is strengthening, improves the complexion, and conquers the three doṣas.

It is beneficial for the eyes, diuretic, improves the voice, increases semen, and removes thirst and fever; it alleviates poison, wounds, dyspnea, cough, and burning sensations, and bestows digestive fire and nourishment.
Therefore, rice varieties such as *mahāśāli* and others possess qualities that differ only slightly from it. (15–16)
The *vārṣika*, *kaṇḍita*, *śukla*, and *cirapākin* varieties of rice;
as well as *kṛṣṇavrīhi*, *pāṭala*, and *kukkuṭāṇḍaka* (17);
and *śālāmukha*, *jatumukha*, and so forth—these are recorded as types of rice.
That rice which has black husks and grains is to be known as *kṛṣṇavrīhi*.
The rice that is pale-red in color, like the hue of the *pāṭalā* flower, is called *pāṭala*.
The rice that has the shape of a hen’s egg is called *kukkuṭāṇḍaka*. 18–19.
The *śālāmukha* has black awns and is called *kṛṣ�ṇataṇḍula*;
that whose mouth is lac-colored should be known as *jatumukha*. These varieties of rice are said to be sweet when cooked and cooling in their potency.
Those that cause little internal obstruction and produce firm stools are equal to *ṣaṣṭika* rice; among these, black *vrīhi* is the best, while others are inferior in their qualities.
Those which reach maturity while still in the husk are considered *ṣaṣṭika*. 21–22.
The *ṣaṣṭika*, *śatapuṣpa*, *pramodaka*, *mukundaka*, *mahāṣaṣṭika*, and others are declared to be *ṣaṣṭikas*; these too are called *vrīhis* because they exhibit the characteristics of *vrīhi*. 23.
The *ṣaṣṭika* rice is sweet, cooling, light, and constipating;
it pacifies *vāta* and *pitta* and is equal to *śāli* rice in its qualities.
Among these, *ṣaṣṭika* is the best; it is light, unctuous, and conquers the three *doṣas*.

Sweet, soft, constipating, strength-giving, and fever-removing; it possesses qualities equal to red śāli rice, while other varieties have slightly fewer qualities. (26) Yava is that which has white awns, while the one without awns is known as atiyava.
Similarly, the *tokya* (rice) is green and is said to be very small;
it is astringent, sweet, cooling, scarifying, and mild.
Like sesame seeds, it is beneficial for wounds, dry, and increases intelligence and digestive fire. (27-28)

It has a pungent post-digestive effect (pāka), is non-obstructive to the channels (anabhiṣyandi), beneficial for the voice, strength-promoting, heavy, increases flatus and waste products, stabilizes the complexion, is slimy,
and destroys diseases of the throat and skin, as well as phlegm, bile, and fat. (29)
It cures chronic catarrh, dyspnea, cough, stiffness of the thighs, blood disorders, and thirst;
atiyava is inferior to this [yava], and tokya is even more inferior than that. Wheat (godhūma) is also known as sumana, and it is said to be of three types.
That which is called *mahāgodhūma* has come from the western region (31).
*Madhūlī*, however, is slightly inferior to that and is produced in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*).
The awnless long wheat is known in some places by the name *nandīmukha* (32).
Wheat is sweet, cooling, heavy, and alleviates wind and bile;

it increases phlegm and semen, is strengthening, unctuous, promotes healing, is laxative, vitalizing, nourishing, improves complexion, heals wounds, stimulates the appetite, and makes the skin firm. (33-34)

Madhūlī is cooling, unctuous, pacifies pitta, is sweet, light, increases semen, nourishing, and wholesome; Nandīmukha is known to have the same properties. (35) Those produced from the Śamī tree, those produced from pods, those originating from legumes, and those classified as pulses are called vaidala. (36)
Pulses (vaidala) are sweet, dry, astringent, and pungent in their post-digestive effect;
they increase vāta, destroy kapha and pitta, bind the urine and feces, and are cold. With the exception of mung and masūr, others cause flatulence. (37)

Mudga is dry, light, constipating, cold, sweet, slightly wind-increasing, beneficial for the eyes, and a destroyer of fever; the wild variety (vanaja) is likewise. Mudga is of many kinds, such as black, green, and yellow.
Among these, the white and the red varieties are traditionally held to be progressively lighter;
however, Suśruta declared the green variety to be superior in its qualities,
and Caraka and others have likewise stated that this very one possesses the greatest excellence of attributes.
The black gram (māṣa) is heavy, sweet in its post-digestive effect, unctuous, appetizing, and subdues Vāta.
It is laxative, nourishing, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and highly nourishing.
It increases urine and excrement, promotes breast milk, and increases fat, pitta, and kapha. (41)
It destroys hemorrhoids, dyspnea, indigestion, and colic.
(42) Black gram produces phlegm and bile; curd produces phlegm and bile;
fish produce phlegm and bile; and eggplant produces phlegm and bile. (43)
The rājamāṣa, mahāmāṣa, capala, and bala are thus remembered.
The rājamāṣa is heavy, sweet, astringent, satiating, and laxative; it is dry, increases wind, is appetizing, promotes breast milk, and bestows great strength.
It is proclaimed to be of three kinds: white, red, and black;
among these, that which is large is said to be superior in quality.
Niṣpāva is *rājaśimbi*, while *vallaka* is *śvetaśimbika*.

Niṣpāva is sweet, dry, sour in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), heavy, and laxative. It is astringent, and it obstructs breast milk, bile, blood, urine, and flatus. It causes a burning sensation, is hot in potency, and destroys poison, phlegm, swelling, semen, and [diseases of] the heart. 46–47.
Makuṣṭha is known as vanamudga, makuṣṭhaka, and mukuṣṭhaka.
(48) Makuṣṭha increases vāta, is constipating, alleviates kapha and pitta, and is light.
It stimulates the digestive fire, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, generates worms, and destroys fever. (49)
Maṅgalyaka is masūra, and maṅgalyā is masūrikā;
masūra is sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), constipating, cold, light, a subduer of phlegm (kapha), bile, and blood, parching, increasing wind (vāta), and a destroyer of fever. 50.
Āḍhakī is also called tuvarī and śaṇapuṣpikā.
Āḍhakī is astringent (tuvarā), dry (rūkṣā), sweet (madhurā), cold (śītalā), and light (laghu).
It is constipating (grāhiṇī), generates wind (vātajananī), improves the complexion (varṇyā), and conquers pitta, kapha, and blood disorders.
Caṇaka is known as harimantha and sakalapriya; furthermore, caṇaka is cooling, dry, light, astringent, constipating, increases wind, and destroys fever, while it removes pitta, rakta, and kapha. (53)
That [meat], when roasted on charcoal or fried in oil, possesses those same qualities;
however, it is proclaimed that meat roasted while moist bestows strength and is appetizing (rocanaka).
When roasted dry, it is extremely parched and aggravates wind (vāta) and skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

Steamed soup (svinna-sūpa) destroys pitta and kapha; it is considered to be agitating. 55 Fresh soup is light, soft, appetizing, cold, astringent, increases vāta, is constipating, and removes kapha and pitta. 56
The *kalāya* is said to be round, as are the *satīna* and the *hareṇuka*.
The *kalāya* is sweet, palatable, dry in digestion, and cooling.
(57) It may also be called *tripuṭa* or *khaṇḍika*; now its qualities are described.
Tripuṭa is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it is extremely parching, alleviates phlegm and bile, stimulates the appetite, is constipating, and is cooling.
However, it causes lameness and paralysis, and excessively aggravates the wind (vāta). 58–59.
Now, the qualities of *kulatthikā* and *kulattha* are described:

*Kulattha* is pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), astringent, provocative of *pitta* and blood, light, burning, hot in potency (*vīrya*), and it cures asthma, cough, phlegm, and wind disorders. (60–61)

It destroys hiccup, urinary calculi, burning of the semen, and flatulence along with catarrh; it is sudorific, astringent, and removes fat, fever, and worms. Black, white, and red sesame are known as wild sesame (vanya) and small sesame (alpatila).
Sesame is pungent and bitter in taste, yet sweet and astringent; it is heavy, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and sweet. It is unctuous, hot, and subdues kapha and pitta.
It is strengthening, beneficial for the hair, cold to the touch, wholesome for the skin, increases breast milk, and is beneficial for wounds.

The black sesame produces little urine, is astringent, subdues wind, stimulates the digestive fire, and is the best among them; the white is middling in its potency for generating semen; and other varieties such as the red, as declared by those who know the subject, are said to be inferior. (65)
Atasī is called nīlapuṣpī, pārvatī, umā, and kṣumā.
(66) Atasī is sweet, bitter, unctuous, pungent in its post-digestive effect, heavy, hot, and it destroys eye disorders, semen [disorders], and vāta, while destroying kapha and pitta. (67)
Tuvarī is said to be astringent, light, and a conqueror of phlegm, poison, and blood disorders;
it is sharp and hot, stimulates the digestive fire, and removes itching, skin diseases, abdominal ailments, and worms.
(68) Sarṣapa, kaṭuka, sneha, tuntubha, and kadambaka [are synonyms].
The white mustard seed is called *siddhārtha* by the wise.

Mustard is pungent in taste and post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), unctuous, slightly bitter, sharp, and hot; it destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, and increases blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and the digestive fire.
Rakṣohara conquers itching, leprosy, abdominal worms, and planetary afflictions;
it is red as well as pale-yellow, but the pale-yellow variety is considered superior.
Rājī, rājikā, tīkṣṇagandhā, kṣujjanikā, and āsurī are synonyms for black mustard.
Kṣava is that which produces sneezing; kṛṣṇīkā is black mustard (black sarṣapa).
Rājikā destroys kapha and pitta; it is sharp and hot, and it causes raktapitta. It is slightly dry, stimulates the digestive fire, and removes itching, skin diseases, abdominal disorders, and worms.
Black mustard (*rājikā*) is especially very sharp; it is likewise [sharp]. 73.

Small grain (*kṣudradhānya*), bad grain (*kudhānya*), and grass grain (*tṛṇadhānya*) are so remembered. Small grain is not hot (*anuṣṇa*); it is astringent (*kaṣāya*), light (*laghu*), and scraping (*lekhanam*). 74.
Sweet in taste and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), it is dry, dries up moisture, increases vāta, binds the feces, and removes pitta, blood disorders, and kapha.
(75) Among women, there are two types of kaṅgu and priyaṅgu: black, red, and likewise white.
Yellow grain is of four kinds; among them, yellow *kaṅgu* is considered the best.
*Kaṅgu* heals broken joints, alleviates *vāta*, is nourishing, heavy, dry, and excessively removes *śleṣman*; it greatly benefits horses. (76–77)
Cīnāka and kākakaṅgu are known as suślakṣṇa and ślakṣṇaka;
cīnāka is a variety of kaṅgu and should be understood to possess qualities similar to those of kaṅgu.
Śyāmāka, śyāmaka, and śyāma are synonyms for tribīja, which is not disagreeable to the digestive fire (avipriya).
Sukumāra is the royal capital [of grains]; that *tṛṇabījottama* (supreme seed of grasses) is *śyāmāka*. It is parching, dry, increases wind (*vāta*), and removes phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
(79) *Kodrava* is *koradūṣa*; *uddāla* is wild *kodrava*.
Kodrava is wind-increasing, constipating, cooling, and it subdues pitta and kapha.
Uddāla, however, is hot, constipating, and strongly increases vāta.
Cāruka is the same as the seed of śara; now its qualities are described.
Cāruka is sweet, dry, cooling, light, aphrodisiac, astringent, and it alleviates blood-bile and phlegm while aggravating wind.
Bamboo grains (yava) are dry, astringent, and pungent in their post-digestive effect.
They cause retention of urine, destroy phlegm (kapha), increase wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), and are laxative.
Kusumbha seeds are called varaṭā and also varaṭṭikā. Varaṭā is sweet, unctuous, and removes blood-bile (raktapitta) and phlegm (kapha).
Kaṣāya is cooling, heavy, non-aphrodisiac, and subdues vāta.
Gavedhukā is called gavedhu by the learned in the feminine;
gavedhu is pungent, sweet, causes leanness, and destroys kapha. 84–85.
Prasādhikā is known as nīvāra and tṛṇānna;
nīvāra is cooling, constipating, subdues pitta, and increases kapha and vāta.
Yāvanāla is cold, sweet, reddish, and conquers kapha and pitta.
It is non-aphrodisiac, astringent, dry, moistening when boiled, and light.
(87) All grain that is fresh is considered sweet, heavy, and increases phlegm; however, that which has been stored for a year is wholesome, for it is indeed much lighter. (88)
All grains that have been stored for a year lose their nutritional essence (*gaurava*), yet they do not abandon their own potency (*vīrya*); thereafter, they gradually release it.
Among these, barley, wheat, sesame, and mung beans are beneficial when fresh.
"Old, tasteless, and dry grains do not produce such beneficial qualities.
Thus ends the ninth section on grains, within the Section on Miscellaneous Items, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*. 9.90. 9. End.

Now, regarding the group of vegetables: leaf, flower, fruit, stalk, bulb, and likewise that which is born of moisture—vegetables are thus seen to be of six kinds; one should know them to be increasingly heavy in the order mentioned.
Generally, all leafy vegetables (śāka) are constipating, heavy, dry, cause excessive feces, and promote the discharge of stool and flatus.
Leafy vegetables break down the body, destroy the bones, harm the eyes, and ruin the complexion, as well as the blood and semen.

The experts declare that it causes the decay of wisdom, surely brings about graying hair, and destroys memory and intelligence. All diseases reside within leafy vegetables (*śāka*); they are the causes for the destruction of the body.
Therefore, a wise person should avoid leafy vegetables; the same defect applies to sour things as well.
Vāstūka and vāstuka are synonyms, as is kṣārapatra; it is the king of leafy vegetables (śākarāṭ).
That same variety with large leaves and red color is known as gauḍavāstuka.
Because it generally has a shape like a barley grain in the middle, it is remembered as yavaśāka.
The two types of vāstūka are sweet and alkaline, yet said to be pungent in their post-digestive effect (vipāka).
They stimulate the digestive fire, promote digestion, improve the appetite, are light, and bestow semen and strength.
They are laxative and eliminate disorders of the spleen, blood-bile, hemorrhoids, worms, and the three doṣas.
The potakī, upodikā, mālavā, and amṛtavallarī are cooling,
unctuous, increase *kapha*, and alleviate *vāta* and *pitta*.
The potakī is beneficial for the throat, slimy, induces sleep, increases semen, and conquers *rakta-pitta*.
It bestows strength, improves the appetite, is wholesome, nourishing, and produces satiety.
(9) Māriṣa is known as vāṣpaka and mārṣa; it is recorded as being both white and red.
Māriṣa is sweet, cooling, causes constipation, subdues pitta, and is heavy. (10)

It increases wind and phlegm, subdues blood-bile, and overcomes irregular digestion; it is heavy, not excessively alkaline, sweet, laxative, and increases phlegm; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect and is said to cause very little morbidity. (11)
Taṇḍulīya is also known as Meghanāda, Kāṇḍera,
Taṇḍuleraka, Bhaṇḍīra, Taṇḍulībīja, Viṣaghna, and Alpamāriṣa.
(12) Taṇḍulīya is light, cooling, dry, and it conquers pitta, kapha, and blood disorders.
It promotes the excretion of urine and waste, is palatable, stimulates digestion, and is a destroyer of poison. 13.
Kañcaṭa is declared to belong to the Pānīya and Taṇḍulīya groups;
kañcaṭa is bitter, light, and removes blood-bile and wind. 14.
The palakyā resembles vāstuka in appearance, and its leaves are cut with serrations (15).
Palakyā is wind-increasing, cold, phlegm-producing, laxative, heavy,
constipating, and it removes intoxication, dyspnea, pitta, blood disorders, and kapha (16).

Nāḍīkā, kālaśāka, and kālaka—the latter being the śrāddha-vegetable—are cooling, palatable, and increase vāta while removing kapha and swelling. They are strengthening, appetizing, intellect-promoting, alleviate raktapitta, and are cold in potency. (17)
Paṭṭaśāka is known as nāḍīka and nāḍīśāka;
nāḍīka destroys blood-bile (raktapitta), causes constipation, and aggravates wind (vāta).
Now, the qualities of kalambī and śataparvī will be described.
Kalambī is said to provide breast milk, being sweet and aphrodisiac (śukrakāriṇī). Loṇā and aloṇī are also mentioned; vṛhallōṇī is called ghoṭikā.
Loṇī is considered dry, heavy, pungent, and it alleviates vāta and kapha.
The sour *ghoṭikā* destroys hemorrhoids, stimulates digestion, and neutralizes poison; it is laxative, hot in potency, increases wind (*vāta*), and removes phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
It cures defects of speech, ulcers, and abdominal tumors, and alleviates asthma, cough, and urinary disorders (*prameha*). (21)
It is declared by those who know it to be beneficial in cases of swelling and eye diseases (22).
Cāṅgerī, cukrikā, dantaśaṭha, ambaṣṭhā, amlaloṇikā, aśmantaka, śapharī, kuśalī, and amlapatraka [are synonyms]. (23)
Cāṅgerī is digestive, appetizing, dry, hot, and alleviates kapha and vāta;
it increases pitta, is sour, and destroys disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids, skin diseases, and diarrhea.
Cukrikā is known as patrāmlā, rocanī, and śatavedhinī. 24–25.

The *cukra* is very sour, sweet, a destroyer of wind (*vāta*), and a producer of phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*); it is appetizing and lighter in digestion than the *vṛntāka*, and is highly stimulating to the appetite.
The *ciñcā*, *cañcu*, *cañcukī*, and *dīrghapatrā* are slightly bitter.
Cañcu is cooling, laxative, appetizing, sweet, and a remover of the three doṣas;
it is known to nourish the bodily tissues (dhātus), provide strength, improve the intellect, and be slimy.
(27) Brāhmī, Śaṅkhadharā, Acārī, Matsyākṣī, and Hilamocikā [are also included].
Hilamocikā removes swelling, skin diseases, phlegm, and bile.
(28) Śitivāra, śitivara, svastika, suniṣaṇṇaka, śrīvāraka, sūcipatra, parṇaka, kukkuṭa, and śikhī [are synonyms]. (29)
The *cāṅgerī* is said to resemble [the *cāṅgerī*] in its leaves and is described as having four petals;
this potherb is called *catuṣpatrī* in regions abounding in water.
*Suniṣaṇṇaka* is cooling, astringent, and removes the three humors including fat (*medas*). (30–31)
It is non-burning, light, sweet, astringent, drying, digestive, aphrodisiac, appetizing, and it cures fever, asthma, urinary disorders, skin diseases, and vertigo.
Fresh radish leaves are digestive, light, appetizing, hot, and pungent.
When prepared with fats, it pacifies the three doṣas; when unprepared, it increases kapha and pitta.
(33) The leaf of droṇapuṣpī is sweet, dry, heavy, and increases pitta;
it is a purgative and removes jaundice, swelling, urinary disorders, and fever, being pungent in taste. (34)
Yavānī-śāka is fiery (āgneya), appetizing, and subdues vāta and kapha;
it is hot, pungent, bitter, increases pitta, light, and removes colic.
Dadrughna-patra destroys the [three] doṣas, is sour, and removes vāta and kapha.
The leaf of *sehuṇḍa* (Euphorbia neriifolia) is light, sharp, digestive-stimulant, and purgative; it removes itching, cough, worms, dyspnea, ringworm, leprosy, and swellings.
It also cures flatulence, inguinal hernia, abdominal tumors, colic, edema, and abdominal enlargements.
Parpaṭa destroys bile-blood disorders, fever, thirst, phlegm, and vertigo;
it is astringent, cooling, bitter, a reducer of burning sensations, increases wind, and is light.
(38) Gojihvā removes skin diseases, urinary disorders, blood disorders, gravel, and fever; it is light. (39)
The leaf of *paṭola* destroys *pitta*, stimulates digestion, is digestive, light,
unctuous, aphrodisiac, hot, and cures fever, cough, and worms.
(40) The leaf of *guḍūcī* is fiery, removes all fevers, and is light.

Astringent, pungent, and bitter, yet sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), it is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) tonic; it is strengthening, hot in potency, and constipating. It destroys the three doṣas, as well as thirst, burning sensations, urinary disorders (prameha), blood disorders, jaundice, leprosy, and anemia. 41–42.
Kāsamarda, arimarda, kāsāri, and likewise karkaśa—the leaf of kāsamarda is appetizing, aphrodisiac, and cures cough, poison, and hemorrhage;
it is sweet, subdues kapha and vāta, is digestive, and cleanses the throat. (43)
In particular, the potherb of chickpeas (caṇaka-śāka) is a cure for cough, pacifies pitta, is astringent, light, and appetizing;
however, it is difficult to digest, increases kapha and vāta, is sour, causes flatulence, alleviates pitta, and removes swelling from the ears. 44–45.
The *kalāya* potherb is laxative, light, bitter, and a conqueror of the three *doṣas*.
(46) Mustard greens (*sārṣapa*) are pungent, increase urine and excrement, are heavy,
sour in post-digestive effect (*pāka*), cause a burning sensation (*vidāhin*), are hot, dry, and produce the three *doṣas*.
Vegetables that are salty, alkaline, or pungent are considered unwholesome, though those that are sweet are not. The flower of the *agasti* plant is cooling, wards off quartan fever,
destroys night-blindness, and is bitter, astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
The sages consider the flower of the plantain (kadali) to be unctuous, sweet, astringent, heavy, and a destroyer of catarrh, phlegm, bile, and wind;
it is cooling and cures hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta) and consumption (kṣaya). 48–49.

The flower of *śigru* is pungent, sharp, and hot; it removes swelling of the tendons, destroys worms, and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*. It conquers abscesses (*vidradhi*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
Honey from the *śigru* tree is beneficial for the eyes and clarifies *rakta-pitta*. (50)
Śālmalīpuṣpa-śāka, prepared with ghee and rock salt, undoubtedly destroys even difficult-to-cure pradara;
it is sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, astringent, cooling, and heavy. 51.
It is proclaimed to conquer phlegm, bile, and blood disorders, to be constipating, and to increase wind (vāta).
Thus end the leafy vegetables;
now follow the fruit vegetables.
The kūṣmāṇḍa has flowers and fruit; its flowers are yellow and its fruit is large (53).
Kūṣmāṇḍa is nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, and it alleviates pitta, blood disorders, and wind.
The young fruit removes pitta and is cooling; the middle-sized fruit generates kapha (54).
The ripe *kūṣmāṇḍa* is not excessively cold, is sweet, slightly alkaline, digestive, light,
purifies the bladder, removes mental diseases, and conquers all the *doṣas*. The *karkāru* is also said to be very light.
The *karkāru* is cooling, heavy, and removes *rakta-pitta*;
when ripe, it is bitter, stimulates the digestive fire, is slightly alkaline, and subdues *kapha* and *vāta*.
(56) The *alābū* is said to be the same as the *tumbī*, which is of two types: long and round. (57)

The sweet gourd fruit is said to be pleasing to the heart, pacifying pitta and kapha, heavy, aphrodisiac, appetizing, and a promoter of the nourishment of the bodily tissues (dhātus). (58) Ikṣvāku is the same as kaṭutumbī; it is also called tumbī and mahāphalā.
Bitter gourd (kaṭutumbī) is cooling, pleasing to the heart, and removes bile, cough, and poison;
it is bitter and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and it terminates disorders of wind and bile as well as fever.
(59) Ervāru and karkaṭī are now mentioned; their qualities shall be described hereafter. (60)

The karkaṭī (cucumber) is cooling, dry, constipating, sweet, and heavy; it is appetizing and removes pitta. When unripe, it causes thirst and increases fire and pitta; when ripe, it does so [less]. The ciciṇḍa is white-striped, very long, and is known as gṛhakūlaka.

Cicinda destroys wind and bile, is strengthening, wholesome, and provides relish; it is drying and highly beneficial, though slightly inferior in qualities to paṭola (62). Kāravella is also called kaṭilla; the female variety, kāravellī, is lighter than that.
Kāravella is cooling, laxative, light, and bitter; it does not increase vāta and destroys fever, pitta, kapha, and blood disorders. It cures anemia, urinary disorders, and worms.
Kāravellī possesses these same qualities, but it is specifically digestive and light.
Mahākośātakī is called hastighoṣā and mahāphalā;
it is also known as dhāmārgava, ghoṣaka, and hastiparṇa.
Mahākośātakī is unctuous and alleviates rakta-pitta and vāta.
Dhāmārgava, pītapuṣpa, jālinī, kṛtavedhanā,
and rājakośātakī are likewise called rājimatphalā.
Rājakośātakī is cooling, sweet, and increases kapha and vāta.
It destroys worms, stimulates digestion, and cures dyspnea, fever, cough, and parasites.
(68) Paṭola is also known as Kulaka, Tikta, Pāṇḍuka, Karkaśacchada, Rājīphala, Pāṇḍuphala, Rājeya, and Amṛtaphala. (69)
Paṭola possesses a seed-filled interior, is beneficial for the face, cures leprosy, and breaks up cough;
it is digestive, pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, light, and stimulates the digestive fire.
Being unctuous and hot, it destroys cough, hemorrhage, fever, the three doṣas, and worms. (70)

The root of the *paṭola* causes easy purgation; its stalk removes *śleṣman*, its leaf removes *pitta*, and its fruit is said to remove all three *doṣas*. Likewise, the bitter *paṭolikā* is [described] in the same manner. (71–72)
Bimbī, raktaphalā, tuṇḍī, tuṇḍīkerī, bimbikā,
oṣṭhopamaphalā, and pīluparṇī are said to be synonyms. The fruit of the bimbī is sweet, cooling, heavy, and it conquers pitta, blood disorders, and vāta.

It causes constipation, scraping of the bowels, improves the complexion, and produces intestinal obstruction and flatulence. (74) Both types of *śimbī*— namely *śimbī*, *pustaśimbī*, as well as *pustakaśimbikā*— are sweet in taste and digestion, cold in potency, and heavy.
It is said to be strengthening, a digestive stimulant, increases phlegm (kapha), and conquers wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
(75) Kolaśimbi has black fruits, as does paryaṅkapaṭṭikā. (76) Kolaśimbi destroys wind, is heavy, hot, and produces phlegm and bile.
The fruit of *śobhāñjana* is aphrodisiac, appetizing, heavy, and causes constipation;
it pacifies *kapha* and *pitta*, and is an excellent digestive stimulant that cures colic, skin diseases, consumption, asthma, and abdominal tumors. (77–78)
The eggplant is called *vṛntāka*, *vārttāku* (feminine), *bhaṇṭākī*, and also *bhāṇṭikā*.
Eggplant is sweet, sharp, hot, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and does not increase *pitta*.
It destroys fever, wind, and phlegm (*balāsa*); it is digestive, aphrodisiac, and light. (79)
Young eggplant destroys phlegm and bile; when old, it increases bile and is heavy.
Eggplant roasted over coals slightly increases bile, but it destroys phlegm, fat, wind, and undigested matter (āma), and is exceedingly light and digestive.
That very same [vegetable], heavy, oily, containing oil, and mixed with salt—
another variety of white eggplant (śvetavṛntāka) which is the size of a hen's egg— is especially beneficial for hemorrhoids, being superior to the previous one. 82
The *ḍiṇḍiśa* has hairy fruit and is also known as *muninirmita*.
It is said that *ḍiṇḍiśa* is appetizing and a purgative; it subdues *pitta* and *śleṣman*, is very cooling, increases *vāta*, is dry, diuretic, and removes urinary calculi.

Piṇḍāra is cooling, strengthening, a destroyer of pitta, and an inducer of appetite; it is especially known to be light in digestion and a pacifier of poison. (85) Karkoṭakī is called Pītapuṣpā and Mahājālī.
Karkoṭī removes impurities, cures skin diseases, vomiting, and loss of appetite;
it destroys dyspnea, cough, and fever, is pungent in its post-digestive effect, and stimulates the digestive fire.
(86) Ḍoḍikā, viṣamuṣṭi, ḍoḍī, and sumuṣṭikā are synonyms. (87)
Ḍoḍikā provides nourishment, is aphrodisiac, appetizing, stimulates the digestive fire, and is light;
it destroys pitta, kapha, hemorrhoids, worms, abdominal tumors, poisons, and diseases.
(88) The fruit of Kaṇṭakārī is bitter, pungent, digestive, and light.
Rūkṣa (dry) and uṣṇa (hot), it destroys dyspnea and cough, and removes fever, vāta, and kapha. (89) Thus ends the section on fruit vegetables.
The stalk of mustard is sharp and hot, and it removes vāta, kapha, and wounds.
It removes itching and worms, destroys ringworm and skin diseases, and promotes appetite.
(90) Thus end the leafy vegetables; now follow the bulbous vegetables.
Sūraṇa is known as kanda, ola, kandala, and aśoghna.
Sūraṇa is digestive (dīpana), dry (rūkṣa), astringent (kaṣāya), causes itching (kaṇḍukṛt), and is pungent (kaṭu).
It is constipating (viṣṭambhī), clear (viśada), appetizing (rucya), destroys phlegm and hemorrhoids (kaphārśaḥ-kṛntana), and is light (laghu).
It is beneficial for those with *viśeṣādarśa* (loss of vision) and destroys splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors.
Among all bulbous vegetables, *sūraṇa* is said to be the best;
however, it is indeed not beneficial for those suffering from ringworm, leprosy, or blood-bile disorders.
Sūraṇa, having attained the yoga of union, is most excellent in its qualities (93).
Ārūka, Vīrasena, Vīra, and likewise Vīrārūka, as well as Ārūka, Āluka, and that which is called Vīrasenaka—these are [the varieties]. (94)
The *kāṣṭhāluka*, *śaṅkhāluka*, and *hastyāluka* are mentioned;
the *piṇḍāluka*, *madhvāluka*, and *raktāluka* are also described.
All types of *āluka* are cooling, cause constipation, are sweet, and heavy. (95–96)

The *alukī*— which is red, bulbous, long, and slender— is laxative, purges urine and waste, is parching, difficult to digest, alleviates *rakta-pitta*, increases *kapha* and *vāyu*, is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and slightly increases the digestive fire.

Ālukī is strengthening, nourishing, unctuous, heavy, and destroys heart-disease and phlegm; when fried in oil, it causes constipation and bestows great relish. (98) Radish is said to be of two kinds, one of which is the small radish (*laghumūlaka*).
The *śālāmarkaṭaka* is foul-smelling; the *śāleya* originates from the desert.
The *cāṇakyamūlaka* is sharp, as is the *mūlakapotikā*. Another variety, the *nepālamūlaka*, is like an elephant's tusk. 99–100.
Laghumūla is pungent and hot; it is appetizing, light, and a digestive stimulant.
It pacifies the three doṣas, is beneficial for the voice, and destroys fever and asthma.
It cures diseases of the nose and throat and eliminates disorders of the eyes. (101–102)
That very same [substance], when dry and hot, is heavy and produces the three *doṣas*;
yet that same thing, when prepared with oil, becomes the destroyer of the three *doṣas*. Gṛñjana is said to be the carrot (*gājara*), as well as the orange-colored variety.
Carrot is sweet, sharp, bitter, hot, digestive, light,
astringent, and it conquers hemorrhagic disorders, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), phlegm, and wind.
(104) The root of the plantain is cooling, strengthening, beneficial for the hair, and it conquers acid bile (amlapitta).
Mānaka has large leaves; it generates digestive fire, removes burning sensations, is sweet, and stimulates the appetite. Now its qualities are described:
Mānaka removes swelling, is cooling, cures hemorrhaging and bile disorders (raktapitta), and is light. 105–106.
Vārāhī is heavy, strengthening, pungent, bitter, and a rejuvenative; it promotes longevity, semen, and digestive fire, and it cures urinary disorders, phlegm, skin diseases, and wind.
Gajakarṇā is bitter and hot, and likewise conquers wind and phlegm.
Its tuber is sweet in digestion and cures cold fevers; it removes anemia, edema, worms, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, flatulence, and abdominal enlargements,
and it destroys disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids, like the wild sūraṇa tuber.
Kemuka is pungent in digestion, bitter, constipating, cold, and light;
it stimulates the digestive fire, promotes digestion, is beneficial for the heart, and removes kapha, pitta, and fever;
it destroys skin diseases, cough, urinary disorders, and hemorrhages, is provocative of vata, and is acrid. (110-111)
Kaseru is of two kinds: the large one is called Rāja-kaseruka;
that which is small, resembling musta grass, is known as Cicoḍha.
Both types of kaseru are cooling, sweet, astringent, and heavy. (112)

It is known to destroy bile, blood, and burning sensations, to cure eye diseases, to be astringent, and to increase semen, wind, phlegm, appetite, and breast milk. (113) The bulbous root of the lotus and others is called śālūka and karahāṭa. (114)

The root of the lotus stalk (mṛṇālamūla), the bulb (bhissāṇḍa), and the water-lily bulb (jalālūka) are called śālūka; it is cooling, aphrodisiac, heavy, and removes bile, burning sensations, and hemorrhages.
It is difficult to digest, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and increases breast milk, wind, and phlegm. 115.

The bulbous root (bhiṣṣāṇḍa) is astringent, sweet, and dry, and it possesses the same qualities as that [of the plant]. One should avoid all bulbs that are young, out of season, old, diseased, infested by worms, or those damaged by fire and the like.

One should not eat any leafy vegetable (śāka) that is overcooked, grown out of season, prepared with dry ingredients, or grown in an unsuitable place; nor one that is too coarse, too soft, excessively cold, or tainted by snakes and the like; nor one that is completely dried out—with the exception of radish (mūlaka). (117–118)

Thus have been described the bulbous roots and vegetables; the moisture-born vegetable has been mentioned as the *bhūmicchatra* and the *śilīndhraka*, which grows upon earth, cow dung, wood, trees, and so forth. 119
All moisture-born fungi are cold, aggravate the humors (doṣas), and are slimy; they are heavy and cause vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and diseases of phlegm (kapha).
Those produced on white ground, wood, bamboo, or cow dung [are likewise]. 120.
Those [remaining ones] would not cause excessive harm; the rest are censured compared to them.

Thus ends the tenth section, the Vegetable Group (Śākavarga), in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Laṭakana. 10.121. The Section on Miscellaneous Items (Miśraprakaraṇa) is complete. 10.121.

Now begins the eleventh section on meat:
*māṃsa*, *piśita*, *kravya*, *āmiṣa*, *palala*, and *pala* are synonyms for meat.
All types of meat alleviate *vāta*, are nourishing, and promote strength and corpulence.
It is pleasing, heavy, heart-tonic, and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (1).
The category of meat should be known as twofold, distinguished by the wild (jāṅgala) and the marshy (ānūpa) types (2).
Within this category of meat, there are those that run on their legs (jaṅghāla), those that live in holes (bilastha), and those that dwell in caves (guhāśaya).
Likewise, the leaf-eaters (parṇamṛga), the scatterers (viṣkira), the peckers (pratuda), the snatchers (prasaha), and the domestic animals— these eight are the species of the *jāṅgala* category.
The *jāṅgala* meats are sweet, parching, astringent, and light.
They are strengthening, nourishing, aphrodisiac, digestive stimulants, and removers of the humors;
they likewise cure muteness, nasal speech,
stammering, facial paralysis, deafness, anorexia, vomiting, urinary disorders, and diseases of the mouth.
It cures elephantiasis, goiters, and diseases caused by Vāta.
Aquatic creatures that frequent the banks, those that float, those that dwell in shells, those that move with their feet, and fish— these are declared to be the five types of marsh-born species.

Meats from marshy regions are sweet, unctuous, heavy, and they diminish the digestive fire; they increase phlegm, are slimy, and greatly promote the nourishment of muscle tissue. Furthermore, because they cause internal secretions (abhiṣyandi), they are generally considered most wholesome. 8
The *hariṇa*, *eṇa*, *kuraṅga*, *ṛṣya*, *pṛṣata*, *nyaṅku*, *śambara*,
*rājīva*, *muṇḍī*, and others are known as the "swift-footed" (*jaṅghāla*) deer.
The *hariṇa* is said to be copper-colored, while the *eṇa* is proclaimed to be black.
The *kuraṅga* is slightly copper-colored, large, and has a form similar to that of a deer (*eṇa*);
in the world, the *ṛṣya*, which has a dark-blue body, is celebrated as the *rojh*.
The *pṛṣata* has spots like the moon and is somewhat smaller than the *hariṇa*.
Then there are the nyaṅku, the bahuviṣāṇa, the śambara, and the great gavaya.
The rājīva deer is to be known as one surrounded by stripes.
That deer which is devoid of horns is called the muṇḍī.
Almost all crawling animals (jaṅghāla) are considered to pacify pitta and kapha;
they slightly increase vāta, are light, and increase strength.
The hole-dwelling animals include the monitor lizard, rabbit, snake, rat, porcupine, and others.
Bile-dwelling animals (fish) are said to alleviate Vata, be sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, nourishing, constipating for feces and urine, and hot in potency.
Likewise, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, hyenas, and leopards [are similar]. 15.
The babhru, jambuka, mārjāra, and others are cave-dwellers (guhāśaya).
Cave-dwellers dispel wind (vāta), are heavy, hot, sweet, unctuous, and strengthening; they are always beneficial for those with disorders of the eyes and the anus.
Now, the leaf-eaters (*parṇamṛga*) are those animals that climb trees, such as the forest-dwelling bear (*vanaukā*), the tree-panther (*vṛkṣamārjāra*), the tree-monkey (*vṛkṣamarkaṭikā*), and others;
these are declared to be the leaf-eaters by the great sages such as Suśruta. 18
The leaf-deer (parṇamṛga) are considered aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and wholesome for those suffering from consumption;
they pacify dyspnea, hemorrhoids, and cough, and promote the evacuation of urine and feces.
(19) The quail, the common partridge, the grey partridge, the francolin, and the partridge are likewise [beneficial].
The *kuliṅga*, the wild cock (*kukkuṭa*), and others are declared to be *viṣkira* birds;
because they scatter [the grain] and then eat, they are therefore called *viṣkira*.
The *kapiñjala* is said by the wise to be the grey partridge (*gauratittiri*). 20–21.
Scattered-feeders (viṣkira) are known to be sweet, cooling, astringent, and pungent in their post-digestive effect;
they are strengthening, aphrodisiac, destroyers of blood disorders, wholesome, and light.
These include the kālakaṇṭhaka, hārītaka, kapota, and śatapatraka.
The pigeon, the wagtail, the cuckoo, and others are known as "peckers" (pratudāḥ). Because they eat by pecking with their beaks, they are called pratudāḥ.
These peckers are sweet, they destroy pitta and kapha, and they are astringent and cooling.
They are considered light, constipating, and slightly wind-producing.
The crow, the vulture, the owl, the hawk, the shashaghata, the blue jay, the bhāsa, the osprey, and others like them are known as the *prasaha* (pouncing) birds. 24–25.
These are proclaimed as the *prasahas* (forcible eaters), so called because they seize and devour their prey by force.
Indeed, the *prasahas* are powerful and hot in potency; those who eat their flesh certainly become afflicted with consumption, digestive disorders, insanity, and depletion of semen.
Goats, sheep, bulls, horses, and others are declared by the great sages to be domestic animals.
All domestic animals alleviate Vata, stimulate the digestive fire, increase Kapha and Pitta, are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect, are nourishing, and increase strength. (28)
The buffalo, boar, yak, elephant,
and others are declared to be "bank-dwellers" (*kūlecara*), because they frequent the banks of waters.
Bank-dwellers alleviate wind and bile, are aphrodisiacs, and bestow strength.
They are sweet, cooling, unctuous, diuretic, and increase phlegm (30).
The swan, crane, kāraṇḍava, duck, curlew, and sarārika (31),
as well as the nandīmukhī, the kādamba, the balākā, and others, are known as the plavas.
Because they float upon the water, they are known as *plavas*.
*Plavas* remove pitta, are unctuous, sweet, cooling, increase vāta and kapha, provide strength and semen, and are laxative. (32–33)
The conch, the small conch, the pearl oyster, the snail, and the crab—
these and other such creatures dwelling within shells are thus proclaimed.
Those dwelling in shells are sweet, unctuous, cold, and they alleviate wind and bile.
They are nourishing, produce abundant feces, are aphrodisiac, and increase strength.
The kumbhīra, tortoise, crocodile, iguana, makara, śaṅku, ghaṇṭika, and śiśumāra—these and others are known as the "pādinas" (animals that walk on feet). 35–36.
And furthermore, those that dwell in the water are equal in qualities to those that dwell in the treasury [of the earth]:
the Matsya, Mīna, Visāra, Jhaṣa, Vaisāriṇa, Aṇḍaja, Śakulī, Pṛthuromā, and also the Sudarśana. (37–38)
Those living beings beginning with the Rohita are proclaimed to be fish.
Fish are unctuous, hot, sweet, heavy, and increase phlegm and bile; they subdue wind, are nourishing, aphrodisiac, appetizing, and increase strength. (39)
They are highly esteemed for those addicted to wine and sexual indulgence, as well as for those with a keen digestive fire (40).
The hare is cooling, binds the feces and urine, stimulates digestion, is light,
sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, fragrant, and destroys the *sannipāta* disorder (41).
The ena deer is astringent and sweet; it is known to remove pitta, blood disorders, kapha, and vāta; it is constipating, appetizing, strengthening, and a pacifier of fever.
The kuraṅga is nourishing, strengthening, cooling, removes pitta, and is heavy.
It is known to be sweet, wind-alleviating, constipating, and slightly increases phlegm (43).
The rishya, the blue-testicled animal, the gavaya, and also the rojha—
the gavaya— is sweet, strengthening, unctuous, hot, and increases phlegm and bile (44).
The *pṛṣata* (spotted deer) is delicious, astringent, cooling, and light; it stimulates digestion, improves appetite, and overcomes asthma, fever, the three *doṣas*, and blood disorders.
(45) The *nyaṅku* (antelope) is sweet, light, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and removes the three *doṣas*. (46)

Sābara meat is known to be unctuous, cooling, and heavy; it is sweet in taste and in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), increases kapha, and subdues blood-bile (raktapitta). (47) The rājīva fish, however, should be understood by people as being equal in qualities to the pṛṣata deer. (48)
The *muṇḍī* rabbit removes fever, cough, hemorrhage, consumption, and asthma, and is cooling.
The long-eared rabbit (*lambakarṇa*), the rabbit with hairy ears (*lomakarṇa*),
and the burrowing rabbit (*bileśaya*) are cold, light, constipating, dry, sweet, and always beneficial.
It is known to stimulate the digestive fire, pacify kapha and pitta, and is considered neutral for vāta;
it also removes fever, diarrhea, consumption, hemorrhagic diseases, and asthma. Now, the sedhā, śalyaka, and śvāvidh are described, along with their qualities.
The śalyaka (porcupine) removes the three doṣas and cures asthma, cough, hemorrhage, and wasting. 51.
Pakṣī, khaga, vihaṅga, vihaga, vihaṅgama, śakuni, viḥ, patatrī, viṣkira, vikirā, and aṇḍaja are synonyms for bird.
The flesh of those creatures here that feed on grain-sprouts is considered light and excellent;
the flesh of marsh-dwellers (ānūpa) is known to be strengthening, unctuous, and very heavy.
The vartīka, the varttaka, the citra, and others are known as varttakas.

The quail (vartaka) produces digestive fire, is cooling, removes the three doshas of fever, is highly palatable, increases semen, and is strengthening; the female quail possesses slightly lesser qualities than that.
Lāvas are considered by the wise to be of four types among the group of forest-dwelling birds (viṣkira). 53–54.
The *pāṃśula*, *gauraka*, *pauṇḍraka*, *darbhara*,
*lāvā*, and *vahnikara* types are unctuous, destroyers of poison, catchers [of fish], and beneficial; however,
among these, the *pāṃśula* is phlegm-increasing, hot in potency, and a destroyer of wind (*vāta*).
Gaura rice is lighter, dry, stimulates the digestive fire, and conquers the three *doṣas*.
Pauṇḍraka rice slightly increases *pitta*, is light, and removes *vāta* and *kapha*.
Darbharu rice destroys *rakta-pitta*, cures heart disease, and is cooling. 56–57.
The *vartīka*, the *varticaṭaka*, and the *vārtīka* are recorded as such;
the *vartīka* is sweet, cooling, dry, and subdues *kapha* and *pitta*. The *tittiri* is black in color, while the *kapiñjala* is pale.
The partridge (*tittiri*) is strengthening, astringent, and removes the three *doṣas* such as hiccups;
it cures asthma, cough, and fever; therefore, the grey partridge (*gaura*) is superior in its qualities. (59) The sparrow (*caṭaka*) is also known as *kalaviṅka*, *kuliṅga*, and *kālakaṇṭhaka*. (60)

The *kuliṅga* bird is cooling, unctuous, sweet, and increases semen and *kapha*; it cures *sannipāta*. The house-sparrow (*veśmacaṭaka*) is exceedingly spermatogenic. (61) A cock is called *kukkuṭa*, *kṛkavāku*, *kālajña*, and *caraṇāyudha*.
The copper-crested cock (tāmracūḍa), as well as the dakṣa, yāmanādi, and śikhaṇḍika,
are nourishing, unctuous, hot in potency, subduing vāta, heavy,
beneficial for the eyes, increasing semen and kapha, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and astringent.
The wild jungle fowl (āraṇyakukkuṭa) is unctuous, nourishing, increases phlegm, and is heavy;
it destroys wind, bile, consumption, vomiting, and intermittent fevers. The *hārīta* bird is reddish-yellow and is also called *harita*.
The green parrot (hārīta) is said to be dry, hot, and a remover of blood-bile and phlegm;
it induces perspiration and improves the voice, though it slightly increases wind.
The parrot (pāṇḍu), however, is known to be of two kinds: the variegated-winged and the sweet-voiced. 65–66.
The second is said to be the white pigeon (*dhavala*); it has a clear call, variegated wings, removes phlegm, subdues wind, and cures malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*).
The white one is designated as pale (*pāṇḍura*); it removes hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*) and is cooling.
It is sweet in taste and digestion, constipating, and pacifies wind (vāta).
68 The peacock is called mayūra, candrakī, kekī, megharāva, bhujaṅgabhuk, śikhī, śikhāvala, barhī, śikhaṇḍī, and nīlakaṇṭhaka. 69
The peacock, with white outer corners of its eyes, dances to the sound of thunder;
it is sweet in taste and digestion, constipating, and a pacifier of wind (vāta).
The pigeon has a melodious call, and the red-eyed dove is likewise known as the *kapota*.
The pigeon is heavy, unctuous, and removes blood-bile and wind;
it is described by those who know it as constipating, cooling, and an increaser of virility.
It is not excessively unctuous, is aphrodisiac, and has a sweet post-digestive taste and flavor.
The eggs of birds are wind-alleviating, highly aphrodisiac, and heavy.
(72) A goatling is called a *barkara*, a *chāga*, a *basto*, an *aja*, a *chelaka*, or a *stubha*.
(73) A she-goat is called a *ajā*, a *chāgī*, a *stubhā*, or a *chelikā*, as well as a *galastanī*.
Goat meat is light, unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, and pacifies the three doṣas (74).
It is not excessively cold, does not cause burning sensations, is sweet, and destroys nasal catarrh.
It is supremely strengthening, appetizing, nourishing, and increases virility (75).
The meat of a goat that has not yet brought forth young cures nasal catarrh;
it is beneficial for dry cough, loss of appetite, and consumption, and it stimulates the digestive fire. The meat of a young goat is considered even lighter [to digest].
It is pleasing to the heart, excellent for removing fever, and provides great comfort and strength.
(77) The meat of a goat whose testicles have been extracted for a month increases phlegm and is heavy;
it cleanses the channels, is strengthening, nourishes the flesh, and subdues wind and bile. (78)

The head of a goat is beneficial for those who are aged or afflicted by wind-related (vāta) disorders, as well as for those who have died of disease; it cures ailments above the clavicle and provides a relish to the appetite.
Now, regarding the sheep (*meṣa*): its names are *mieḍhra*, *aiḍaka*, and it is also called *aṇḍavihīna*.

Meḍhra, meḍha, huḍa, meṣa, uraṇa, eḍaka, avi, vṛṣṇi, and ūrṇāyu are the names by which the sheep is known; now its qualities shall be described. The meat of the sheep (meṣa) is beneficial for nourishment, increases pitta and kapha, and is heavy.

The meat of that very [animal] when devoid of its testicles is considered slightly light. (81) Now, regarding the *eḍaka* (ram): *diuṃbā*, *meḍāi*, and so forth are its names; and for its variety, the ram with broad horns is the *eḍaka*, while the one with a fatty tail is the *dumbaka*.
The meat of a sheep (*eḍaka*) should be known as equal in its qualities to that of a ram (*meṣa*).
Fat derived from the tail is pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, and dispels fatigue;
it slightly increases bile and phlegm, and destroys wind-related diseases. 82–83.
A bull is called a *balīvarda*, *vṛṣabha*, *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣa*, *anaḍvān*, *saurabheya*, *gauḥ*, *ukṣan*, and also *bhadra*. (84) A cow is designated as *surabhi*, *saurabheyī*, *māheyī*, and *gauḥ*.
Beef is very heavy, unctuous, increases pitta and kapha, is nourishing, subdues vata, is strengthening, unwholesome [for those with certain conditions], and cures chronic rhinitis (pīnasa). 85.
Regarding the horse: ghoṭaka, aśva, turaga, turaṅgama, and turaṅga.
Bājī, vāha, arvā, gandharva, haya, saindhava, and sapti are synonyms for horse (86).
Horse meat is astringent, stimulates the digestive fire, increases kapha and pitta,
removes vāta, is nourishing, strengthening, beneficial for the eyes, sweet, and light (87).
The buffalo is called *mahiṣa*, *ghoṭakāri*, *kāsara*, and *rajasvala*.
It has thick shoulders, a black body, and is known as *lulāya* and the vehicle of Yama.
The meat of the buffalo is savory, unctuous, hot, and destroys wind (*vāta*). 88–89.
Sleep induces semen, is strengthening, provides firmness to the body, is heavy, aphrodisiac,
promotes the discharge of feces and urine, and destroys Vāta, Pitta, and blood disorders.
(90) Maṇḍūka, plavaga, bheka, varṣābhū, dardura, and hari are synonyms for the frog.
The frog is phlegm-increasing, not excessively bile-producing, and a provider of strength.
(91) The tortoise—known as *kacchapa*, *gūḍhapāt*, *kūrma*, *kamaṭha*, and *dṛḍhapṛṣṭhaka*—is strength-giving, subdues wind and bile, and promotes virility. (92)

The meat of an animal killed immediately after death is like nectar; it destroys diseases, promotes youthfulness, is nourishing, and is wholesome. Otherwise, one should avoid it. The meat of an animal that died of itself causes debility, induces diarrhea, and is heavy.

The meat of old animals is aggravating to the *doṣas*, while that of young animals is light and strength-giving. (95) The meat of a snake-bitten animal and dried meat (*śuṣkamāṃsa*) aggravate all three *doṣas*. The meat of an animal bitten by a wild beast (*vyāla*), when dried, is the supreme cause of colic (*śūla*). (96)

A corpse that has died from poison or water, which causes the defects of death and disease, is putrid, produces nausea, is emaciated, and aggravates vāta; one filled with water and showing prominent veins, or one that has died in water, causes the three doṣas. 97
Among birds, the male is considered superior; among quadrupeds, the female is superior.

For males, the latter half [of the body] should be known as light, while for females, the former half should be so designated. The middle of the body is traditionally held to be predominantly heavy for all living beings. (98)

For birds, that very [body] is said to be light due to the flapping of their wings; yet for all [other creatures], the eggs are heavy, as is the neck of birds. Likewise, the chest, shoulders, belly, flanks, feet, hands, and hips [are heavy]. 99.
The back, skin, liver, and intestines are progressively heavier in this order.
The meat of birds that feed on grain is light and increases wind (vāta);
that of fish-eaters is said to increase bile (pitta), suppress wind, and be heavy.
It is declared that among those who eat fruits, those who eat the leaves produce phlegm, are light, and dry;
whereas those same leaf-eaters are nourishing, heavy, and subdue the wind.
Among those of the same species, those with smaller bodies are considered superior to those with large bodies.
Likewise, those with small bodies are praised, as are those with large bodies.
A fish with a red belly, a red mouth, red eyes, and red fins, having a black tail, is declared by the wise to be the best Rohita fish. 104

The Rohita is the best of all fish; it is aphrodisiac, removes distress, has an astringent aftertaste, is sweet, subdues Vata, and does not excessively increase Pitta. The Rohita-muṇḍaka destroys diseases located above the clavicle. 105
Śilīndhra is phlegm-increasing, strengthening, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), heavy,
a subduer of wind and bile, beneficial for the heart, and it produces undigested matter (āmavāta).
Bhākhura is sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, phlegm-increasing, and heavy.
It is also known to cause constipation and to alleviate *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic disorders).
107 *Mocikā* removes *vāta*, is strengthening, nourishing, sweet, and heavy;
it removes *pitta*, increases *kapha*, improves the appetite, is aphrodisiac, and is beneficial for those with a stimulated digestive fire. 108
The pāṭhīna fish increases phlegm, provides strength, induces sleep, and is a flesh-eater;
it vitiates the blood and bile, and causes leprosy.
The śṛṅgī, however, pacifies wind, is unctuous, and provokes phlegm.
In taste, it is bitter and astringent; it is considered light, appetizing, and is known by the wise [to possess these qualities]. 110.
The *illīsa* fish is sweet, unctuous, appetizing, and increases the digestive fire (*vahni*);
it removes *pitta*, produces *kapha*, is slightly light, aphrodisiac, and subdues *vāyu*. 111.
Śaṣkulī is considered to be heart-pleasing, sweet, and astringent.
Gargara increases bile slightly, overcomes wind, and provokes phlegm.
Kavikā is sweet, unctuous, destroys phlegm, and promotes relish.
The *varmimatsya* (scaleless fish) generates bile, destroys wind (*vāta*), increases digestive fire,
removes wind, and is light and appetizing. The *daṇḍamatsya* is bitter in taste and removes bile, blood, and phlegm (*kapha*).
It is said to be compatible with wind (vāta), aphrodisiac, and strength-promoting.
(116) Eraṅga is sweet, unctuous, constipating, cold, and light.
(117) That known as Mahāśaphara is bitter and removes pitta and kapha.
It is considered cooling, sweet, appetizing, and a general pacifier of the bodily winds (vāta).

118 It destroys poison, is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it removes wind and bile, destroys phlegm (kapha), promotes appetite, is light, stimulates digestion, and increases strength and virility. 119
The Madgura fish is light, alleviates wind, is strengthening, aphrodisiac, increases phlegm, and promotes intelligence;
it reduces fat, increases wind and bile, and is considered the best for creating appetite. 120–121. It is even more so when accompanied by half-fish (sapādamatsya).

The *proṣṭhī* fish is bitter, pungent, and sweet; it bestows semen, conquers *kapha* and *vāta*, is unctuous, cures diseases of the mouth and throat, is appetizing, and is considered light. Small fish have a sweet taste and destroy the three *doṣas*.
They are considered beneficial as they are easy to digest, stimulate the appetite, and bestow strength (123).
Extremely fine grains destroy virility, though they are appetizing and alleviate cough and wind disorders (124).
Matsyagarbha is highly aphrodisiac, unctuous, nourishing, and light.
Fresh fish increase phlegm and fat, provide strength, cause lassitude, and cure urinary disorders. Dried fish are strengthening but are difficult to digest and cause constipation.
Fish that have been roasted are superior in quality; they promote nourishment and increase strength.
Fish from ponds increase semen, urine, skin diseases, and phlegm;
those born in lakes are sweet, unctuous, strengthening, and destroy wind;
and river fish are nourishing, heavy, and destroy wind.
Water from ponds causes blood-bile (raktapitta), is aphrodisiac, unctuous, hot, and produces scanty feces;
water from wells causes pitta, is unctuous, sweet, light, and cold;
while water from tanks (taḍāga) is heavy, aphrodisiac, cold, and increases excrement and urine.
Fish born in ponds are beneficial for strength, longevity, intellect, and vision during the autumn;
those born in wells are beneficial in the winter; those from lakes are beneficial in the early spring;
those from rivers are beneficial in the spring; and those originating from marshes are beneficial in the summer. (128)
Water born from ponds is unwholesome during the rains; that from rivers is likewise [unwholesome] then; water from springs is best in autumn—this distinction has been declared.
Thus ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The eleventh section on meat in the Miscellaneous Chapter is completed. Now begins the twelfth section on prepared foods:
regarding the qualities enumerated by the sages when the cause is present as a combination.
Even in the case of prepared food, all these are declared by technical convention to be "unfit to be known" (impure).
Since a difference in quality may arise from a difference in processing— for instance,
old śāli rice is light when cooked, whereas flattened rice (ciṭiṭī) is heavy— [the distinction must be understood accordingly].
In some cases, by the power of yoga, it depends upon another quality; for instance, coarse food is heavy, yet when combined with ghee, it becomes easily digestible.
Similarly, *bhakta* is called food, as is *andhas*, and in some instances, *kūra* is also so designated.
*Odana* is not feminine; the feminine form is *bhissā*. *Dīdivi* is said to be masculine. One should cook well-washed, plump grains of rice in five times their measure of water.
That which is thus cooked is called *prasruta*; when it is warm, clear, and possesses excellent qualities, it is considered superior.
Cooked grain (bhakta) kindles the digestive fire, is wholesome, satiating, appetizing, and light;
however, when it is unwashed, unstrained, cold, heavy, unpalatable, and increases phlegm (kapha).
Split pulses are called *śamīdhānya*; the words *dālī* and *dālī* (both feminine) denote the split pulse itself.
Pulse cooked in water and combined with salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida is known by the name *sūpa*; its qualities are now described:
*sūpa* causes flatulence, is parching, and is especially cold in potency.

Parched rice that has been husked and thoroughly prepared attains an extreme lightness. Rice grains mixed with split pulses (*dālī*), combined with salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and cooked in water, are called *kṛśarā* by the wise. (8–9)

Kṛśarā (rice and pulse porridge) is considered semen-enhancing, strengthening, heavy, and a producer of pitta and kapha; it is difficult to digest and is known to cause dullness of intellect, constipation, and retention of feces and urine.
(10) One should fry a ball made from black gram flour in ghee mixed with turmeric. (11)
One should also roast well-washed rice grains together with them;
then, the skilled practitioner should add water suitable for cooking and cook it,
adding salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida in the proper measure.
This Siddhi has arrived and is declared by the wise to be a remover of distress (13).
It removes distress, is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and increases phlegm;
it is nourishing, satiating, appetizing, heavy, and is known to remove bile (14).
Pāyasa is supreme rice-milk, and it is also called kṣīrikā.
When milk is half-cooked and pure, one should cook rice grains smeared with ghee;
once cooked, they are known as kṣīrikā, which is excellent when combined with sugar and clarified butter.
Kṣīrikā is said to be difficult to digest, yet it is nourishing and increases strength; it causes constipation, removes bile, and cures internal hemorrhaging, impaired digestion, and wind disorders.
(16) One should cut a coconut into thin slices and place them in cow’s milk.
One should cook that in cow's milk mixed with sugar and clarified butter over a gentle fire. The coconut-derived *kṣīrī* is unctuous, cooling, highly nourishing,
heavy, very sweet, aphrodisiac, and it alleviates blood-bile and wind disorders.

Having made very fine coils of *samitā* stalks resembling barley, dried them, and prepared them with milk, they should be eaten with sugar; they are digestive, satiating, strengthening, heavy, and they pacify *pitta* and *vāta*. (19)
One should eat that, which is adhesive, promotes digestion, and is pleasing to the taste, but not in excess.
(20) Wheat that is white, washed, ground, dried, then sprinkled with water, processed in a mill, stirred, and tempered is known as *samita*. (21)

Having made it soft with water and well-kneaded, one should thoroughly knead it with the movement of the hands; then, one should properly extend the core of the lump. This should be cast outside, spread out over the mouth of an upside-down jar. 22.
Prepared with a mild fire, it is called *maṇḍaka* when cooked.
A person should eat this *maṇḍaka* with milk mixed with ghee and sugar-candy,
or else with prepared meat, or with buttermilk and *vaṭaka*.
Maṇḍaka is nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and highly appetizing;
it is sweet even after digestion, constipating, light, and removes the three doṣas.
Samita is extremely thin, and parpaṭikā is even thinner than that. (25-26)
The wise have said that one should steam that *polikā* over a heated vessel;
one should eat it accompanied by *lapsikā*, for its qualities are like those of *maṇḍaka*.
(27) One should fry *samitā* in clarified butter and throw it into milk with sugar.
When that has been thickened, one should add cloves, black pepper, and other such ingredients; this is known as *lapsikā*. I shall now describe its qualities:
*lapsikā* is nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and it pacifies pitta and vāta.
It is unctuous, increases phlegm, heavy, appetizing, and highly nourishing.
(29) Having slightly enriched a *polikā* with the flour of dry wheat, one should steam it over hot coals and then bake it on a bed of charcoal. (30)
This *aroṭikā* is declared to be perfected; we shall now describe its qualities:
*Aroṭikā* provides strength, is appetizing, nourishing, and increases the bodily tissues (*dhātus*).
It subdues wind (*vāta*), increases phlegm (*kapha*), is heavy, and is highly esteemed for those with a stimulated digestive fire. (31–32)
One should thoroughly knead the flour of dry wheat with water,
form it into the shape of balls (vaṭaka), and cook them slowly over a smokeless fire;
this is indeed Aṅgārakarkaṭī, which is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and light.
Dīpanī stimulates digestion, increases phlegm, provides strength, and conquers chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough.
(34) Yavajāroṭikā is appetizing, sweet, clear, and light;
it promotes feces, semen, and wind, provides strength, and destroys diseases of phlegm. (35)
The flour of dried black gram (māṣa) is called *camasī*;
a cake (*roṭī*) made from *camasī* is known as *balabhadrikā*.
It is dry, hot, increases wind (*vāta*), provides strength, and is highly esteemed for those with a stimulated digestive fire. 36
The husks of black gram (māṣa), having been soaked in water and stripped of their skins, dried in the sun and ground in a millstone, are known as *dhūmasī*.
And that which is fashioned from *dhūmasī* is called *jharjharikā* by the wise. (37)
Jharjharī is known to destroy kapha and pitta, while slightly increasing vāta (38).
A flatbread made from chickpea flour (caṇakyā roṭikā) is dry, heavy, and subdues phlegm, pitta, and blood;
it causes constipation and is not beneficial for the eyes. Śaṣkulī possesses qualities similar to those [of the former] (39).
The dālī is placed in water, then its husk is removed; it is thoroughly ground upon a stone, and this paste is thus described by the wise.
(40) Its interior is filled with a paste of black gram (*māṣa*) mixed with wheat flour (*godhūma-cūrṇa*).
That very *roṭikā* (flatbread) prepared [in this manner] is called *beḍhamikā* by the wise.
*Beḍhamikā* is strengthening (*balyā*), aphrodisiac (*vṛṣyā*), appetizing (*rucyā*), and subdues wind (*anilāpahā*).
It is hot (*uṣṇā*), nourishing (*santarpaṇī*), heavy (*gurvī*), highly bulk-promoting (*bṛṃhaṇī*), and supremely semen-generating (*śukralā*). 41–42.

When combined with soot, resin, asafoetida, turmeric, and salts, it breaks up urine and impurities, provides breast milk, fat, bile, and phlegm, and destroys hemorrhoids, afflictions, dyspnea, and colic in the digestive tract. (43)
When cumin and sarsaparilla are ground thin and rolled out, they become *parpaṭas*.
These, when always roasted on live coals, are highly appetizing, digestive stimulants, and carminatives; they are described as being somewhat dry and heavy.
Maudga (mung bean) preparations are said to possess those same qualities, but they are specifically lighter and more beneficial.
(46) Parpaṭas made from chickpeas share the qualities of the chickpea;
however, when all of these are fried in oil or ghee, they become moderate in their properties. (47)
One should fill [the dough] with a paste of black gram (māṣa) mixed with salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida;
a *polikā* made by filling it with that paste and sealing it is then cooked in oil, and is called *pūrikā* by the wise. 48.
