It is palatable, sweet, heavy, unctuous, strengthening, and a corrupter of the blood and bile (pitta).
It diminishes the luster of the eyes, is hot, and destroys Vata in its post-digestive state (vipāka).
Likewise, even when cooked in ghee, it is beneficial for the eyes and removes blood-bile (raktapitta).

Alternatively, one may prepare dry or juicy *vaṭakas* (balls); having mixed a paste of black gram (*māṣa*) with salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida, one should form those *vaṭakas* and cook them slowly in oil. 51

Dried Vaṭakas are strengthening, nourishing, and increase virility; they alleviate diseases caused by Vāta, improve the appetite, and specifically cure facial paralysis (ardita). They break up constipation, increase Kapha, and are highly esteemed for those with excessive digestive fire.
Having crushed [the ingredients] and added cumin and asafoetida fried in buttermilk (53), one should immerse all the salted *vaṭaka* balls therein;
this *śukrala-vaṭaka* is aphrodisiac, strength-giving, appetizing, and heavy. (54)
One should consume those [fruits] that are free from blemishes, exceedingly lustrous, ripening, and which cause obstruction, burning of the heart, increase phlegm, and alleviate wind;
a fresh churning-vessel should be kept, smeared with pungent oil.
Having filled it with pure water, one should throw into it a powder made of mustard, cumin, salt, asafoetida, dry ginger, and turmeric (56).
One should drop the *vaṭaka* balls into it and seal the mouth of this vessel.
After three days, the vaṭakas will certainly become non-acidic (57).
Kāñjikā-vaṭaka is appetizing, subdues wind, increases phlegm, relieves colic, cures indigestion and burning sensations, but it is not beneficial for eye diseases (58).
Having steamed the *amlikā* fruit, one should grind it with water; people should then immerse the *vaṭaka* balls in that water which has been duly prepared.
Those *amlikā-vaṭakas* are indeed appetizing and stimulate the digestive fire.
These [other] vadas also possess the same qualities as those previously mentioned. Mudga-bean vadas, soaked in buttermilk, are light and cooling;
by virtue of their processing, they pacify the three doṣas and are beneficial.
A paste of black gram (māṣa) prepared with asafoetida (hiṅgu), salt, and fresh ginger,
is formed into pills on cloth and thoroughly dried;
these are then either fried in hot oil or treated with water.
The *rocanā* (yellow myrobalan) should be known as being endowed with the qualities of the *vaṭaka*;
it is called *kūṣmāṇḍaka-vaṭī*. It possesses the qualities of the previously mentioned pills, but is specifically said by the wise to destroy bile and blood disorders and is light. 63–64.
Likewise, a pill made of mung beans prepared in that same manner is wholesome, appetizing, light, and is known to possess the qualities of mung bean soup (65).
A large betel leaf smeared with black gram flour [is also beneficial] (66).
One should steam that [fish] with the proper method upon a layer [of leaves] in a pot;
then, having removed it and cut it into pieces, one should fry it in oil. This method for cooking the *alīkamatsya* has been described by those skilled in culinary arts.
One should eat that eggplant with *bhaṭitra* and *vāstūka*.
In a pot, one should fry turmeric and asafoetida in either ghee or oil;
then, one should add buttermilk mixed with an electuary (*avalehana*) into that very same [mixture].
This *samarica* (black pepper) is declared by the wise to be perfected when boiled.
When boiled, it is digestive, appetizing, light, and a stimulator of the digestive fire;
it destroys phlegm, wind, and constipation, while slightly aggravating bile. 69–70.
Whether dried or boiled, false fish (alīkamatsya) are nourishing,
appetizing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and a remedy for diseases caused by vāta;
they cleanse the digestive tract, though when dried, they slightly aggravate pitta.
These are especially remembered as beneficial for Ardita (facial paralysis) accompanied by stiffness of the jaw. 72.
One should properly crush with the hand the *vaṭakas* (balls) prepared from ground mung beans and fried in oil, and then sprinkle the powder into that [mixture]. 73.
One should properly fry asafoetida, fresh ginger, fine black pepper, cumin, and likewise lemon juice and yavānī; then, one should skillfully mix all these together.
One should cook the ground mudga beans thoroughly on a plate placed over the mouth of a cooking pot.
One should make balls (*golaka*) from that [mixture], and one should place a filling in their center (75).
Having cooked those balls in oil, one should immerse them in boiling [oil];
these are called *pācaka-golaka*, and they are also known as *ārdra-ka-vaṭa* (76).
Fresh mudga-gram cakes are appetizing, light, strength-promoting, digestive, nourishing, wholesome, and highly esteemed for their efficacy against all three doṣas.
Likewise, dehusked chickpeas (caṇaka) that have been ground in a machine are beneficial.

That powder is called *vesana* by those expert in the science of cooking (78). A *vaṭikā-vesana*, when immersed in boiling [liquid], is known to be appetizing, non-obstructive to digestion, strengthening, and nourishing (79).
One should place ghee in the cooking vessel, or oil if that is unavailable;
then, one should fry asafoetida and turmeric therein. Next, one should certainly add the boneless meat of a goat or similar animal, cut into pieces. 80.
One should slowly fry that [meat] in the clarified butter after it has been washed and strained;
then, having added water suitable for cooking, one should cook it with salt.
Once cooked, one should grind it with water and add *veśavāra*.
The ingredients are, in brief, dried meat (veśavāra), betel leaves, rice, cloves, and black pepper;
prepared according to this method, it is known as *śuddhamāṃsa* (pure meat). 83–84.
Pure meat is supremely aphrodisiac, strengthening, appetizing, nourishing,
an excellent pacifier of the three doṣas, digestive, and increases the bodily tissues (dhātus).
[85] Furthermore, the meat of goats and the like, or of sheep and the like, should be minced and then cut into pieces.
One should cook this together with *sahadāraka* according to the procedure for pure meat;
it is recorded that *sahadāraka* possesses the same qualities as pure meat in the context of medical formulations.
Having placed ghee in the cooking vessel, one should fry turmeric and asafoetida.
One should also fry the pieces of all [meat], such as goat and so forth (87).
Having added water suitable for cooking, one should cook them very gently; likewise, one should marinate the pieces of meat in buttermilk mixed with cumin and other spices (88).
Buttermilk with meat (takramāṃsa) subdues Vāta, is light, appetizing, and bestows strength;
it slightly subdues Kapha, increases Pitta, and acts as a digestive for all types of food. One should place pieces of meat into a large cooking vessel.
Abundant water, copious ghee, asafoetida, cumin,
turmeric, fresh ginger, salt, black pepper, rice, wheat, and plenty of the juices of jambīra fruits. (90–91)
Just as all things are indeed well-cooked, so should the skilled cook prepare them with an abundance of thick sauce (maṇḍa).
This *harīśā* is strength-giving, subdues wind and bile, and is heavy [to digest].
It is cooling, heating, semen-provoking, unctuous, laxative, and promotes healing.
When meat is properly prepared according to the method for pure meat and then fried in ghee, it is called *talita* by the wise. (93–94)

Fried meat increases strength, intellect, digestive fire, muscle mass, vitality, and semen; it is satiating, light, very unctuous, appetizing, and promotes firmness. (95) Pieces of meat such as the *kālakhaṇḍa* should be threaded together on a skewer.
Having added ghee and salt, one should cook it in a smokeless fire;
that is called *śūlya* by those skilled in the art of cooking.
*Śūlya* meat is equal to nectar, appetizing, digestive, and light.
It indeed pacifies kapha and vāta, is strengthening, and slightly increases pitta.
(98) Pure meat, cut into thin strips, minced, and steamed in water, combined with cloves, asafoetida, salt, black pepper, and fresh ginger— (99)
When elā, jīraka, dhānyaka, and lime juice are combined and fried in fragrant ghee, it is called *pūraṇa* by the wise.
A *śṛṅgāṭaka* (water chestnut) prepared with sugar and filled with this *pūraṇa* [is known as *pūraṇapūrita*].
Furthermore, one should mention meat and *śṛṅgāṭaka* fried in ghee (verse 101).
Meat and *śṛṅgāṭaka* are appetizing, nourishing, strength-promoting, heavy,
pacifiers of wind and bile, aphrodisiac, destroyers of phlegm, and increasers of virility (verse 102).
The prepared meat broth is appetizing, it removes fatigue, dyspnea, and consumption;

it is nourishing, subdues wind and bile, and is beneficial for those who are emaciated, those with diminished semen, those with dislocated or fractured joints, and for those who have been purified or desire purification. 103

It is recommended for those deficient in memory, vitality, and strength; for those emaciated by fever or with a wounded chest; for those with impaired voices; and for those desiring improvement in vision, longevity, and hearing.
(104) Many varieties originating from meat have thus been described.
Fearing excessive prolixity, I have not described them here.
(105) One should throw well-chopped vegetables into oil mixed with asafoetida and cumin.
(106) Once the salt, spices, and so forth have been added and the dish is cooked, one should add water infused with asafoetida.
Thus, the procedure for the preparation of all medicinal herbs has been declared. (107) One should grind the *samit* with clarified butter and also mix it with water;
having formed a pill (*vaṭikā*) from that, one should cook it in ghee until it is dry.
Having immersed [the substance] in a white syrup (sitāpāka) adorned with cardamom, cloves, camphor, black pepper, and other ingredients, one should then extract it;
this method for successful accomplishment is called *maṇṭha*. 108–109.
Maṇṭha is nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, very sweet, heavy, pacifies pitta and vāta, is appetizing, and is highly esteemed for those with a stimulated digestive fire (dīptāgni).
Other varieties, such as those prepared with sugar and ghee, are also [recommended]. 110.
If those varieties are considered to possess qualities equal to this one:
parpaṭyas, prepared with ghee and fuel-sticks, fried in clarified butter, crushed, stirred, and kneaded with pure sugar. (111-112)
There, one should scatter powder consisting of cardamom, cloves, black pepper, coconut, camphor, and various types of *cāra* seeds;
then, one should prepare nourishing *roṭikās* (flat cakes) smeared with ghee and provided with sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*).
The wise person should fill its interior with that [mixture] and form a firm seal (mudrā).
A skillful person should cook it well in abundant ghee; this method, known by those who understand the methods, is celebrated as *sampāva*. 114–115.
The *sampāva* should be known by people as equal to *maṇṭhaka* in its qualities (verse 116).
Then, having formed a hollowed-out packet (*puṭa*) with a stick rich in ghee, it is combined with cloves,
black pepper, camphor, and sugar (verse 117).

This *karpūranālikā* is known to be prepared with clarified butter; it should be understood as being similar to *sampāva* in its qualities. One should prepare long wicks from *samitā* mixed abundantly with ghee.
One should hold those long, adjacent [threads] upon the seat; by shaking them with a shaking motion, one should make them into a single layer like a *parpaṭī* leaf,
and then one should cut that [layer] with a knife while it is still attached.
Then one should roll it again and smear it with *saṭṭaka*;
*saṭṭaka* is said to be rice flour mixed with ghee and water. Then, having covered it, one should apply those medicinal pastes separately.
Then one should roll it again so that it takes the shape of a circle (122). Next, one should fry it well in clarified butter until they become crisp and crisp;
then one should sprinkle it with fragrant sugar (123).
This [preparation] named *phenikā* has been perfected; it is equal to *maṇṭhaka* in its qualities, yet this one is slightly lighter—this is the distinction that has been illustrated.
(124) Having made two small balls (*loptra*) of sugar-candy (*samitā*) smeared with ghee, one should roll them.
One should fry that [dough] in clarified butter; once cooked, it is a *śaṣkulī* possessing the qualities of a *phenikā*.
Having made threads from that dough enriched with ghee and sugar, the skillful person should fry them in clarified butter and combine them with a preparation of candied sugar.
One should prepare sweetmeats (modaka) with these ingredients so that they possess qualities like those of the maṇṭhaka;
one should properly stir the smoke-seed of mung beans with pure water.
Then, one should place a jharjhara [filter] above the ghee in the cauldron.
When it has become fluid while being stirred, one should pour it over a *jhajhara* sieve (128).
As the drops fall from it, one should collect them once they are well-cooked;
then, having combined them with the cooking of sugar, one should form *modakas* with the hands (129).

The *mudga* pulse-bead (*mudgamodaka*) is light, easily digestible, a destroyer of the three *doṣas*, sweet, cooling, appetizing, beneficial for the eyes, a remover of fever, strengthening, and nourishing. (130) In this very same manner, *vesana* pulse-beads should be prepared. (131)
They are light, cooling, slightly increase vāta,
cause constipation, destroy fever, and remove pitta, rakta, and kapha.
(132) [This is prepared] with thickened flour paste mixed with rice powder and milk that has been removed.

One should prepare a firm small jar and cook it thoroughly with clarified butter (133). Then, having filled its interior with thickened milk and placed it within a *saṭṭaka* (a sealed vessel), one should cook its mouth until well-baked in hot clarified butter.
Then, one skilled in the art should bathe it in a pale-colored decoction perfumed with camphor;
that milk-well is strengthening, pacifies bile and wind, is aphrodisiac, cooling, heavy, semen-provoking, satiating, and appetizing. 134.

A skillful person, having brought a new jar, should coat its interior with sour curd measuring half a *prastha*. This brings about nourishment for the body and ensures that one's vision remains far-reaching for a very long time. 135–137.
Having mixed two *prasthas* of equalized *samitā*, one *prastha* of sour curd (*dadhyamla*), and half a *śarāva* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in a jar,
one should place it in the sun until it reaches a state of acidity. 138.
Then, one should place that [substance] into a vessel with holes;
having repeatedly swirled it, one should cast it again and again into well-heated ghee.
By repeating this process, one should fashion it into the shape of a mandala.

Having taken that well-cooked [substance] mixed with ghee, one should bathe it in a thin syrup of sugar-candy flavored with camphor and other fragrant ingredients; then, having removed it from there, this is known by the name Kuṇḍalinī, bestowing nourishment, beauty, and strength. 141.
It increases the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), is aphrodisiac, appetizing, and satiates the sense organs.
First, one should take an *āḍhaka* measure of buffalo curd that is sour and free from water;
then, one should gradually add two *prasthas* of bright sugar to it on a clean cloth, little by little.
One should cause milk from half a jar to flow steadily into a new earthen pot;
then, one should add to it appropriate cardamom, cloves, camphor, and black pepper.
This, prepared by Bhīma as a favorite dish, is known by the name Rasālā. 143. It is a delight in itself.

This [vāsantī] was repeatedly tasted with affection by Śrī Kṛṣ�ṇa in the past; for him who constantly partakes of it on days other than those of spring, there shall be a perpetual increase in great virility and the strength of all the senses. 144

This Rasālā quickly provides nourishment to the bodies of those whose limbs have been withered by the sun in summer or autumn, those exhausted by sexual union with intoxicated women, and those whose bodies are worn out from wandering along the road. (145) It is aphrodisiac, strengthening, pleasing, appetizing, and it conquers wind and bile. (146)
White sugar, when dissolved in cold water, is illuminating, nourishing, unctuous, sweet, cooling, and laxative; it destroys bleeding disorders, thirst, burning sensations, and catarrh. (147)
Combined with cardamom, cloves, camphor,
and black pepper, it is known by the name *śarkarodaka* (sugar-water) from the mouths of the learned.
This *śarkarodaka* is said to increase semen, be cooling, and be laxative.

Raw mango, when soaked in water and crushed with a firm hand, is strengthening, appetizing, light, sweet, and a destroyer of wind and bile; it is supreme for alleviating fainting, vomiting, thirst, burning sensations, and fever. (150)
This excellent beverage, prepared by Bhīmasena, is mixed with white sugar and cool water, and seasoned with camphor and black pepper;
it is immediately appetizing, strengthening, and quickly satiates the senses. 151–152.
The ripe fruit of *amlikā*, thoroughly crushed with water and mixed with sugar and black pepper, well-scented with cloves and camphor—
this beverage produced from the *amlikā* fruit destroys wind disorders. (153)
It slightly increases bile and phlegm, is very palatable, and stimulates the digestive fire.
One part of lime juice mixed with six parts of sugar water, combined with cloves and black pepper, is an excellent drink known as *pānaka*. (154–155)
A drink made from the fruit of the *nimbūka* is extremely sour, destroys wind (*vāta*), kindles the digestive fire, improves appetite, and digests all types of food.
Cumin (*dhānyaka*) that has been well-ground on a stone and filtered through a cloth [is likewise beneficial]. 156.
Sugar-water combined with camphor and other ingredients, kept in a new earthen vessel, is an excellent remedy for removing bile (pitta).
Fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika) is appetizing, improves the sense of taste, acts as a digestive, and stimulates the digestive fire. 157–158.
Kāñjika (fermented rice water) destroys colic, indigestion, and constipation, and is supreme for purifying the digestive tract;
it should not be administered here and there without [proper consideration].
Raw mango fruit, ground and mixed with black mustard and salt, [is used as follows]: 159.
When purified with refined asafoetida and melted, it is called *jālī*.
*Jālī* removes the dullness of the tongue and cleanses the throat; when drunk even in small amounts, it is appetizing and stimulates the digestive fire. (160–161)
One should strain very thick curd— preferably buffalo curd— that is mixed with a fourth part water, is quite sour, and has been fried with asafoetida,
cumin, salt, and a small amount of black mustard, into a clean earthen vessel.

One should mix flour into it; that buttermilk becomes pleasing to whom? (162) Buttermilk is appetizing, stimulates the digestive fire, is a supreme digestive aid, destroys diseases of the abdomen, and produces satiety. (163)

Whatever heating foods and drinks a person consumes, he should drink milk at the end of the meal for the purpose of pacifying that heating effect. (164) Grains roasted in a pan and ground in a mill are called *saktu* (barley meal). (165)
Barley-based parched grain flour (saktu), when cold, is said to be digestive-stimulant, light, laxative, alleviator of kapha and pitta, dry, and scraping.
When drunk, it bestows strength, is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and likewise a purgative. (166)
They are satiating, sweet, appetizing, and provide strength upon digestion (167).
They remove phlegm, bile, fatigue, hunger, thirst, and diseases of the wounds and eyes;
they are highly recommended for those whose bodies are afflicted by heat, burning sensations, travel, or physical exertion (168).

Barley meal made from roasted, husked chickpeas mixed with one-fourth part of barley, combined with sugar and ghee, is highly esteemed even in the summer. Barley meal derived from *śāli* rice is light and cooling, yet it kindles the digestive fire.
They are sweet, astringent, appetizing, wholesome, and bestow strength and semen.
(170) One should not eat *saktu* after having already eaten, nor by biting it with the teeth, nor at night, nor in large quantities, nor separated from water, nor without mixing it with water. (171)

One should avoid drinking separately, giving [food] again, food mixed with meat, [drinking] milk at night, chewing with the teeth, and [eating] hot [food]; these seven [practices] are to be avoided regarding roasted barley flour (saktu).
Barley that is husked and fried is known as *dhānā* in the feminine.

Parched grains (dhānāḥ) are difficult to digest, parching, heavy, and cause thirst; likewise, they are proclaimed to destroy urinary disorders, phlegm, and vomiting. Those grains which have their husks removed are called taṇḍulas.
The wise say that parched grains which have burst open are called *lāja*.
These *lāja* grains are sweet, cooling, light, and digestive stimulants;
they produce little urine and feces, are dry, strengthening, and destroy *pitta* and *kapha*.

They alleviate vomiting, diarrhea, burning sensations, blood disorders, urinary disorders, obesity, and thirst. (175) Rice grains with their husks still attached, when moist, roasted, and not split, are then crushed flat;
they are called *cipiṭa* and are also known as *pṛthuka*. (176)
Pṛthuka grains are heavy, pacify vāta, increase kapha,

and when mixed with milk, they are nourishing, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and promote the elimination of waste. Holaka is prepared from half-cooked śamī-grains that have been parched on a grass fire.
The *holaka* (roasted grain) removes wind, fat, and the three *doṣas*;
whatever kind of *holaka* one consumes, it will possess those respective qualities.
The *mañjarī* (ear of grain), whether half-ripe or otherwise, may be made from barley or wheat.
When roasted with a grass fire, it is known by the wise as *ūcī*.
*Ūcī* increases *kapha*, is strengthening, light, and removes *pitta* and *vāta*.
(179) Wheat, chickpeas, and other such grains should be half-steamed. (180)

In the treatises on grammar, they are called *kulmāṣa* by the learned; *kulmāṣas* are heavy, dry, increase wind, and cause loose stools. *Palala*, however, is defined as sesame paste mixed with molasses.
Palala (sesame paste) is purgative, aphrodisiac, subdues Vāta, increases Kapha and Pitta,
is nourishing, heavy, unctuous, and cures excessive urination.
Tilakiṭṭa, piṇyāka, and tilakhali are considered synonyms for sesame cake.
Oil-cake is scraping, dry, constipating, and harmful to the eyes (183).
*Tuṇḍulī* destroys urinary disorders and parasites; however, when fresh, it is very difficult to digest (184).
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous substances in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The twelfth chapter, the Section on Prepared Food, is completed. Now begins the Section on Water:
*pānīya*, *salila*, *nīra*, *kīlāla*, *jala*, and *ambu*.
Āpaḥ, vār, vāri, kam, toya, payas, pāthas, as well as udaka, jīvana, vanam, ambhas, aṇas, amṛta, and ghanarasa;
also pānīya, śramanāśana, klamahara, and mūrchā-pipāsā-paha.
It is said that [milk] causes drowsiness, suppresses vomiting and constipation, strengthens the heart, removes sleeplessness, provides nourishment,
is pleasing to the heart, possesses a hidden flavor, pacifies indigestion, is always beneficial, cooling, light, clear, the source of vital essence, and like nectar, it sustains life. 2.
Water has been declared by the sages to be of two kinds: celestial and terrestrial.

Celestial water is said to be of four types: that which falls as a stream, that which originates from hail, that which is frost-born, and that which is snow-born; among these, the water falling as a stream possesses the greatest qualities.
Water fallen in streams is caught by a large cloth;
and that which falls upon a stone or on cleansed ground,
as well as into vessels made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or glass, [is pure].
Water kept in an earthen vessel is called *dhāra*.
This *dhāra* water destroys the three *doṣas*, has an indescribable taste, and is light, soothing, an elixir (*rasāyana*), strengthening, satiating, refreshing, and life-sustaining.
It is digestive, clarifies the intellect, and removes fainting, drowsiness, burning sensations, fatigue, exhaustion, and thirst; it is wholesome and is especially recommended during the rainy season.
Water from mountain torrents is of two kinds, distinguished as being from the Ganges or from the sea. 8–9.
The saying of the wise is that the elephants of the quarters, having taken water from the celestial Gaṅgā, bring about rain through clouds when they are concealed; thus,
in the month of Āśvayuja, the cloud generally pours down the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In every respect, that water should be known as such; likewise is the statement of Caraka:
when placed in a vessel made of gold, silver, or even clay, the śāli rice moistened by it remains free from moisture and retains its color. (11-12)
That water from the Gaṅgā should be known as destroying all defects; the oceanic is otherwise.
It is salty and alkaline, it destroys semen, vision, and strength, is foul-smelling, aggravates the humors (doṣas), is sharp, and is not beneficial for any medical procedure. 13.
One should describe the ocean water in the month of Āśvina as being equal in quality to that of the Gaṅgā;
for, due to the rising of the divine sage Agastya, all its water becomes stainless, free from poison, sweet, aphrodisiac, and devoid of defects.
By the wind of their poisonous breath, the sky-dwelling nāgas release poisonous water during the rainy season— even celestial water— except for that of the month of Āśvina;
for it is they who cause the clouds to discharge unseasonable rain.
That is proclaimed as beneficial for all embodied beings in the three seasons.
Those [drops] which fall from the sky, gathered together through the conjunction of divine wind and fire, are like fragments of stone; they are called *kārakyas* and are like nectar. 17–18.

Water from a well is dry, clear, heavy, stable, harsh, cold, and thick; it subdues pitta while increasing kapha and vāta. Even at the edge of the ocean, the waters of a river are like fire compared to those born from the sea.
Those [clouds] which are devoid of smoke-particles are known as *tuṣāra*;
they are generally unwholesome for living beings, yet beneficial for trees.
*Tuṣāra* water and snow are parching, increase *vāta*, and do not increase *pitta*.
It cures diseases such as phlegm, stiffness of the thighs, throat ailments, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders, and goiters.
The wise call that very water "Haima" (snow-water), which falls from the peaks of the Himalayas and other mountains after having turned into liquid.
Snow-water is cold, it subdues pitta, is heavy, and increases vāta.
That water of the ocean which was driven by the smoke of the submarine fire (aurvānala), solidified, and brought to the north by the wind, is called "snow" (hima) by the wise. 22–23.
The winter season is cold, dry, harsh, and subtle; yet it does not vitiate the wind, nor the bile, nor the phlegm.
Earthly water is said by the wise to be the first of three kinds.
Jāṅgala, supreme Ānūpa, and then Sādhāraṇa are the regions in sequence.
25. That region should be known as Jāṅgala which has little water and few trees, and is afflicted by diseases of bile and blood; the water found there is Jāṅgala water. 26.

A region that has abundant water and many trees, and is afflicted with diseases of wind and phlegm, is known as *anūpa*; the water produced there is likewise *ānūpa*. A region that possesses mixed characteristics is indeed considered *sādhāraṇa* (ordinary).

In that region, whatever water there is, it is considered common (sādhāraṇa). Jāṅgala water is dry, salty, light, pacifies pitta, stimulates the digestive fire, removes kapha, is wholesome, and cures many disorders. 28–29.
Water from marshy lands (ānūpa) is moistening, sweet, unctuous, thick, heavy,
increases digestive fire, the heart, and phlegm, is beneficial for the heart, yet produces many disorders.
On the other hand, ordinary water is sweet, stimulates digestion, is cooling, and light.

It is nourishing, appetizing, and removes thirst, burning sensations, and the three *doṣas*. (31) Water from a river or a stream is known as *nādeya* (river water). (32) River water is parching, increases *vāta*, is light, and stimulates digestion.
[Water] that does not cause secretions, is clear, pungent, and subdues phlegm and bile [is light].
All rivers that flow swiftly are light, as are those with pure water;
whereas those that are covered with moss, flow slowly, and are turbid are heavy.
The rivers originating from the Himavat mountains— such as the Gaṅgā, Śatadru, Sarayū, Yamunā, and others— have waters struck by stones and are excellent in quality;
likewise, there are the rivers arising from the Sahya mountain, headed by the Veṇā and Godāvarī.
These generally cause skin diseases (kuṣṭha), though they slightly increase vāta and kapha.
One should observe the qualities and defects of water found in rivers, lakes, ponds, wells, and springs according to the differences between regions. 36–37.
The great seers say that water which flows from a large stream after breaking through the low-lying ground is called *audbhida*;
this *audbhida* water destroys bile, does not cause a burning sensation, and is extremely cooling.
It is pleasing, sweet, strengthening, slightly increases vāta, and is light.
(49) A mountain stream flowing from a ridge is called a *nirjhara*, a *jhara*, or a *prasravaṇa*; the water found therein is *nairjhara*. (40)
The water of a waterfall (nairjhara) is pleasing, destroys phlegm, stimulates digestion, is light, sweet, pungent in its post-digestive effect, increases wind, and does not increase bile.
[41] This refers to the water of a river obstructed by mountains and the like, which remains after flowing forth.
That lake is covered with water-lilies, and its water is known as *sārasa*.
*Sārasa* water is considered strengthening, thirst-quenching, sweet, light, appetizing, astringent, dry, and it binds the urine and excrement. (42–43)

A reservoir situated on a commendable plot of land and filled with water for many years is called a *taḍāga*; its water is known as *tāḍāga*. The water of a *taḍāga* is sweet, slightly astringent, and pungent in its post-digestive effect.
It increases wind (vāta), binds feces and urine, and removes blood, bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha).
A large well constructed with stones or bricks and provided with steps is called a *vāpī*; the water from such a place is known as *vāpya*. 45–46.
If the water in a pond is alkaline, it generates pitta and removes kapha and vāta;
yet that same water, when sweet, produces kapha and alleviates vāta and pitta.
(47) A pit dug in the ground, small in width but deep, circular in shape—
That well may be either dug or natural; its water is called *kaupa* (well-water).
If well-water is sweet, it alleviates the three *doṣas*, is wholesome, and light;
however, if alkaline, it destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, stimulates digestion, and excessively increases *pitta*. 48–49.
A natural cavern strewn with stones, its water resembling black collyrium,
and covered by a canopy of creeping vines is called *auñjya*; others, however, maintain that what is not bound together by stones and such materials is also termed *auñjya*.
The sages have declared that water from that place is *cauñjya*.
*Cauñjya* water is known to be fire-stimulating, parching, alleviator of phlegm (*kapha*), light, sweet, pacifier of bile (*pitta*), appetizing, digestive, and clear.

A small lake or pond is called a *palvala* where, when the sun is situated among the constellations of the Moon (Citrā) or the Sun (Puṣya), no water remains; that water belonging there is *pālvala*. *Pālvala* water is moistening, heavy, sweet, and causes the three *doṣas*.
The ground near a river or similar body of water that consists of sand, from which water is drawn forth—that they know as *vikira*.
*Vikira* is remembered as being cool, clear, free from defects, and light. 55.
Tuvara is sweet, pacifies pitta, is alkaline, and slightly increases pitta. (56) A *kedāra* is defined as a field; its water is known as *kaidāra*.
*Kaidāra* water is obstructive to the channels (*abhiṣyandi*), sweet, heavy, and produces the *doṣas*. (57)
In the rainy season, the water that has fallen on that day and remained on the ground is unwholesome;
however, after having stood for three nights, it becomes clear and like nectar.
In the winter, the water of lakes or ponds is considered wholesome.
Water prescribed for the winter season is also recommended for the cool season (śiśira).
During spring and summer, water from wells, ponds, mountain springs, or rivers is used;
however, wise men advise that river water should not be consumed during spring and summer.
Since water from forest trees is considered poisonous due to their leaves and other parts,
water from springs, from the atmosphere, or from wells is prescribed for the rainy season;
in autumn, river water is recommended, provided it is free from insects and is of the highest quality.
Water that is warmed by the rays of the sun during the day and by the rays of the moon at night should be known as *aṃśūdaka*; it is unctuous, removes the three *doṣas*,
does not cause secretions, is free from defects, and is like atmospheric water.
It is strengthening, an elixir, beneficial for the intellect, cooling, light, and equal to nectar (sudhā).
All water that is clear in autumn is wholesome after the rising of the star Agastya.
In the month of Pauṣa, water born from lotuses is recommended, while in Māgha, that which comes from a pond is so.
In the month of Phālguna, water from wells is considered beneficial; in Caitra, water from springs is held to be wholesome.
In Vaiśākha, water from mountain torrents is recommended, and likewise, water from natural springs is praised in Jyeṣṭha.
In Āṣāḍha, well-water is commended, while in Śrāvaṇa, celestial water (rainwater) alone is best.
In the month of Bhādrapada, well water is recommended; in Āśvina, water from a spring is likewise advised;
and in Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, any kind of water is praised.
Generally, the collection of terrestrial waters is desired in the morning.
Since coolness and purity are considered their inherent qualities;
(68) one does not suffer from indigestion by drinking excessive water, nor is that same fault incurred by abstaining from water;
therefore, a person should drink water repeatedly, but not in large quantities, in order to increase the digestive fire. (69)

Cold water is recommended for fainting, bile disorders, heat, burning sensations, poisoning, blood disorders, alcoholism, exhaustion, vertigo, indigestion, fainting spells, vomiting, and for upward-moving hemorrhaging and bile. (70)
In cases of pain in the flanks, catarrh, wind diseases, constriction of the throat, flatulence,
a sluggish digestive tract, immediate purification, and acute fever;
in loss of appetite, malabsorption syndrome, abdominal tumors, asthma, cough, and abscesses.

In cases of hiccups, during the administration of medicated fats (sneha), and in conditions of anorexia, catarrh, weak digestion, edema, wasting, excessive salivation, abdominal enlargement, skin diseases, eye disorders, and fever, one should strictly avoid cold water. (72)
One should drink water only in small quantities in cases of ulcers and diabetes mellitus (madhumeha).
Water is the life of living beings and the very soul of the world; since everything is permeated by it, water is never to be prohibited absolutely, nor at any time.
Thirst is heavy, terrible, and instantly destructive of life;
therefore, water that sustains life should be given to one overcome by thirst. One who is thirsty falls into delusion, and through delusion, he abandons his life.
Therefore, in all circumstances, one should never obstruct water anywhere.
(76) Water that is odorless, with unmanifest taste, very cold, and quenching of thirst; which is clear, light, and pleasing to the heart—such water is said to possess excellent qualities. (77)
Water that is slimy, infested with worms, putrid, discolored by moss and mud, faded in hue, tasteless, thick, and foul-smelling is not beneficial.
Water that is turbid and covered with lotus leaves, blue-green algae, grass, and the like [is likewise unsuitable].
It is difficult to touch and cannot be touched by the rays of the sun or the moon.
It is not seasonal, yet it is the first [rain] that falls upon the earth during the monsoon; this corrupted water must be avoided, as it aggravates all the bodily humors.
One should use that [water] for bathing and drinking to cure thirst, flatulence, chronic fever,
cough, weak digestion, ophthalmia, itching, swellings, and the like; likewise,
even condemned water may be used if it has been boiled or heated by the sun.
Gold, silver, iron, stone, and even sand,
having been intensely heated and quenched seven times, and likewise thoroughly perfumed with camphor, nutmeg, punnāga, pāṭala, and other fragrant substances.
Pure water flows from a thick, clean cloth, is free from tiny insects, is transparent, and is purified by gold, pearls, and the like; it should be flawless and devoid of defects.
[It is further purified] by leaves, roots, lotus stalks, knots, pearls, gold, and moss. 84.
One should clarify water using either *gomedaka* (agate) or a cloth. Water that is drunk [raw] is digested after two *yāmas*; that which has been boiled and cooled is digested in one *yāma*;
and that which was boiled while lukewarm is digested in half a *yāma*. Regarding the cooking of milk, there are only three stages of time. 85–86.
Thus ends the thirteenth section, the Chapter on Water (*vārivarga*), in the *Miśraprakaraṇa* of the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the Chapter on Milk (*dugdhavarga*).
Milk is known as *dugdha*, *kṣīra*, *payaḥ*, *stanya*, and also as *bālajīvana* (the sustainer of children).
Milk is very sweet, unctuous, pacifies *vāta* and *pitta*, and is laxative. It immediately produces semen, is cooling, and is wholesome for all living beings.
It is life-sustaining, nourishing, strengthening, intellect-promoting, and supremely aphrodisiac;
it stabilizes youth, promotes longevity, heals fractures, and acts as a rejuvenative (rasāyana). It should be used after purgation, emesis, and enemas, and it increases the vital essence (ojas).
In chronic fever, mental disorders, consumption, fainting, and vertigo;
in malabsorption syndrome, anemia, burning sensations, thirst, and heart disease;
and in colic, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary bladder diseases, and hemorrhoids.
It is remembered by the best of sages as always beneficial in cases of internal hemorrhage, diarrhea, gynecological disorders, fatigue, exhaustion, and miscarriage;
it is also suitable for children, the elderly, those emaciated by chest wounds, those suffering from hunger, those exhausted by sexual indulgence, and those who are lean.
Among these, cow's milk is declared to be always the most excellent for promoting well-being; it is especially sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (rasa-pāka), slightly moistening,
heavy, and it nourishes the doshas, dhātus, malas, and channels.

The milk of a black cow is cooling, nourishing to the breast, unctuous, and destroys wind, bile, and blood; it always brings peace to all diseases for those who consume it. (8) The milk of a black cow removes wind and is superior in its qualities. (9)

The yellow cow's milk removes bile (*pitta*) and likewise alleviates wind (*vāta*); the white cow's milk increases phlegm (*śleṣman*) and is heavy; while the red and variegated cows' milk remove wind. The milk of cows whose calves are very young or whose calves are absent causes all three *doṣas*. 10–11.
The milk of a cow that has recently calved (vaṣkayinī) destroys the three doṣas, provides nourishment, and increases strength.

Among cows roaming in arid (jāṅgala), marshy (anūpa), and mountainous (śaila) regions, the milk becomes progressively heavier and more oily according to the order of the habitats, following the nature of their food.
Milk produced from the consumption of very little food is heavy and increases *kapha*;
however, it is highly strengthening, aphrodisiac, and beneficial for those in good health.
Milk derived from straw, grass, or cotton seeds is wholesome for the sick. (14)
Buffalo milk is sweet, more unctuous than cow's milk, aphrodisiac, heavy,
induces sleep, causes secretions (abhiṣyandi), alleviates excessive hunger, and is cooling (15).
Goat's milk is astringent, sweet, cold, constipating, and light.
It cures hemorrhaging, bilious diarrhea, consumption, cough, and fever.
(16) Because goats are small-bodied, because they consume pungent and bitter foods, because they drink little water, and because they exercise, their milk removes all diseases. (17)
The milk of deer originating from arid lands possesses the qualities of goat’s milk.
Sheep’s milk is salty, sweet, unctuous, and hot; it cures urinary calculi, is unwholesome for the heart, is nourishing, beneficial for the hair, and increases semen, pitta, and kapha.
In cases of cough arising from *kāsa* and *anila*, or when *anila* alone is the cause, [the following] is excellent: 19.
Mare’s milk is dry, hot, strengthening, and cures wasting (*śoṣa*) and wind disorders;
likewise, all one-hoofed animals' milk is sour, pungent, light, and sweet. 20.
Camel’s milk is light, sweet, salty, and digestive;
it cures worms, skin diseases, phlegm, abdominal distension, edema, and ascites, and is laxative. (21) Elephant’s milk is nourishing, sweet, astringent, and heavy.
Cow's milk is aphrodisiac, strengthening, cooling, unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and promotes stability.
Human breast milk is light, cold, digestive-stimulant, and subdues wind and bile;
it cures eye pain and facial paralysis, and is excellent for use as nasal drops or eye-drops. 22–23.

Cow’s milk that is warm from the udder is strengthening, light, cooling, equal to nectar, digestive, and pacifies the three doṣas; however, one should avoid it when it is cooled by being poured in a stream.
Cow’s milk is recommended when warm from the udder, whereas buffalo milk is recommended when cooled by being poured in a stream.
Sheep's milk is wholesome when boiled and warm; goat's milk is wholesome when boiled and cooled.
Raw milk causes secretions, is heavy, and increases phlegm and undigested matter (āmavardhana).
All other types of milk, with the exception of that from cows and buffaloes, should be known as unwholesome.
Raw human breast milk is beneficial, but boiled milk is not;
milk that is boiled and then warmed destroys kapha and vāta, whereas milk that is boiled and then cooled subdues pitta.
Milk remaining after half has been replaced with water is lighter than raw milk.
Just as milk that has been deprived of its water and is thoroughly cooked becomes increasingly heavy, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and strength-increasing; so too,
the thick milk produced at the time of birth is called *pīyūṣa*.
The solidified mass of cooked milk that has turned sour is called *kilāṭaka*.
That which has turned sour while still uncooked is indeed *kṣīraśāka* (sour milk-vegetable).
Milk that has turned sour [and been processed] with curd or buttermilk, when bound with a fine cloth, [is known as *navanīta*].
That which is mixed with the essence of curd is called *takrapiṇḍa*.
Jejjaṭa stated that *moraṭa* is water produced from spoiled milk;
likewise, there are *pīyūṣa*, *kilāṭa*, and *kṣīraśāka*. 31–32.
These balls of buttermilk are aphrodisiac, nourishing, and strength-increasing; they are heavy, increase phlegm, are pleasing to the heart, and destroy wind and bile.
They are highly recommended for those with a stimulated digestive fire, for those suffering from insomnia, and for those with abscesses. (33)
Moraṭa, when combined with sugar, alleviates dryness of the mouth, thirst, burning sensations, blood-bile disorders, and fever; it is light, strength-promoting, and appetizing.
Santānikā (the cream on the surface of boiled milk) is heavy, cooling, aphrodisiac, and cures blood-bile disorders and wind.
Milk is nourishing, bulk-promoting, unctuous, and increases phlegm, strength, and semen.
(35) Milk combined with sugar generates phlegm and subdues wind;
when joined with white or black sugar candy, it promotes semen and removes the three humors.

Milk with jaggery destroys dysuria and is highly beneficial for increasing pitta and kapha. Furthermore, because of the moon's superior qualities at night and the absence of physical exertion, milk from the early morning is generally heavier and colder than that from the evening.

Milk consumed in the morning is light, removes wind and phlegm, is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and stimulates the digestive fire; however, milk from the evening until the following morning becomes heavy due to the impact of the sun's rays and the exposure to the winds of physical exertion. (38)
At midday, it is strengthening, alleviates *kapha*, removes *pitta*, and stimulates digestion;
in children, it promotes growth; in those with wasting (*kṣaya*), it prevents further decline; in the elderly, it maintains virility;
and at night, it is considered wholesome, pacifying many disorders and beneficial for the eyes. 39

They say that at night one should drink milk alone; no food such as boiled rice should be taken with it, for otherwise indigestion occurs. One should not sleep during the night [with undigested milk], nor should one leave any remainder of the milk that has been drunk. For a man who eats foods and drinks that cause a burning sensation during the day, [the milk serves as a remedy].
To pacify that burning sensation, one should always drink milk at night;

for milk is considered most beneficial for a man with a stimulated digestive fire who is emaciated, as well as for children and the elderly, since it is pleasant to them and provides immediate semen. 41–42.
One should drink cow’s milk or goat’s milk, slightly warm and stirred with a stick; it is light, aphrodisiac, fever-alleviating, and removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
(43) Whether derived from cow’s milk or produced from goat’s milk.

Phenā (foam) destroys the three doṣas, is appetizing, increases strength, stimulates the digestive fire, is aphrodisiac, provides immediate satiety, and is light; it is highly recommended in cases of diarrhea, weak digestion, and chronic fever. 44–45.

One should avoid milk that is discolored, tasteless, sour, foul-smelling, or clotted, as well as that which is mixed with sour or salty substances, since such milk causes skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and other ailments.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The fourteenth chapter, the Section on Milk, in the Miscellaneous Section, is completed. Now begins the Section on Curd:
Curd is hot, digestive, unctuous, has an astringent aftertaste, and is heavy.
It is sour in its post-digestive effect (pāka), constipating, and increases pitta, blood, swelling, fat, and kapha.
It is recommended for dysuria, catarrh, cold conditions, irregular fever, diarrhea, anorexia, and emaciation; it bestows strength and promotes semen.
First it is "mild" (manda), then "sweet" (svādu), then "sweet-sour" (svādvamla); after that, "sour" (amla) is the fourth, and "extremely sour" (atyamla) is the fifth; thus curd is of five kinds.
(3) The "mild" variety is like milk, with an unmanifested taste, and becomes slightly thickened.

That which is slow to digest, causes the discharge of feces and urine, and produces a burning sensation in the three *doṣas*, is [considered] *manda*. That which has attained perfect density and possesses a distinct sweet taste,
yet has an unmanifestly sour taste, is described by the wise as *svādu* (sweet).
It is sweet, excessively unctuous, aphrodisiac, and increases fat and phlegm;
it subdues wind, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, and clarifies blood and bile.
It is sweet and sour, thick, and possesses a sweet-astringent aftertaste.

The qualities of the sweet-sour (svādvamla) should be understood by people to be generally like those of curd (dadhi). That which has its sweetness concealed and possesses manifest sourness is called *amlaka*;
sour (*amla*) [taste], moreover, stimulates digestion and increases bile, blood, and phlegm.
That which is excessively sour causes horripilation of the teeth and a burning sensation in the throat and other areas;
excessive sourness is a digestive stimulant (dīpana), but it is supreme in producing blood disorders, wind, and bile.
Cow’s curd, in particular, is sweet-sour and provides a relish for food.
Among all types of curd, that produced from cow's milk is said to be superior in its qualities; it is purifying, digestive, beneficial for the heart, nourishing, and a subduer of wind (vāta).
Buffalo curd is very unctuous, increases phlegm (kapha), and alleviates wind and bile (pitta).
Goat curd is sweet in digestion, causes secretions to flow, is aphrodisiac, heavy, and impairs the blood; it is excellent, constipating, light, and removes the three *doṣas*.
It is recommended for asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, consumption, and emaciation, and acts as a digestive stimulant.
Curd produced from matured milk is appetizing, unctuous, and possesses the highest qualities;
it pacifies pitta and vāta, and increases the strength of all the dhātus, the digestive fire, and physical vigor.
(13) Curd that is insubstantial is constipating, cooling, increases vāta, and is light.
[Ordinary] curd is constipating, digestive-stimulant, appetizing, and a destroyer of diseases of the *grahaṇī*. 14.

Strained curd is very unctuous, subdues wind (*vāta*), increases phlegm (*kapha*), is heavy, promotes strength and nourishment, is appetizing, sweet, and does not excessively increase bile (*pitta*). 15.
Curd with sugar is excellent; it conquers thirst, pitta, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
Alternatively, curd with jaggery alleviates vāta, is aphrodisiac, nourishing, satiating, and heavy.
One should not eat curd at night, nor should one consume it without ghee and sugar.
It is not recommended without mung beans, nor without honey, nor when hot, nor without *āmalaka* fruits (17).
Curd is praised during the late winter, the cold season, and the rainy season;
it is generally censured during autumn, summer, and spring (18).
One who is fond of curd, having transgressed the prescribed rule, may suffer from fever, hemorrhagic disorders, bile-related diseases, erysipelas, leprosy, anemia, vertigo, and severe jaundice.
That portion of the curd which is thick on top and endowed with oiliness [is known as *moraṭa*].
In the world, it is called *sara*; the scum of curd is known as *mastu*. *Sara* is palatable, heavy, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of wind and fire (digestive heat).
It is sour, pacifies the bladder, and increases bile and phlegm.
Buttermilk (mastu) removes fatigue, is strengthening, light, and creates a desire for food;
it cleanses the channels, is refreshing, and alleviates phlegm, thirst, and wind.
It is non-aphrodisiac, nourishing, and quickly breaks up the accumulation of waste matter.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Section on Curd, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the Section on Buttermilk (Takravarga).
*Ghola* is churned curd; *takra*, *udaśvit*, and *chacchikā* are also [types of] buttermilk.
*Ghola* with water is *sasara*; *mathita* is churned [curd] without water.
*Takra* is said to have one-quarter water, while *udaśvit* has half water.
*Chacchika* water is clear and abundant in water but lacks essence;
*ghola*, however, when mixed with sugar, should be known to possess qualities similar to those of *rasālā*.
*Mathita* (churned milk) removes wind and bile, is refreshing, and subdues phlegm and bile.

Buttermilk (takra) is constipating, astringent-sour, sweet in its post-digestive taste (pāka), light, hot in potency (vīrya), digestive-stimulant, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and a destroyer of wind (vāta).
It is wholesome for those suffering from disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and the like; due to its lightness, it is also astringent. 4.
Furthermore, because it has a sweet post-digestive effect (vipāka), it does not aggravate pitta.
Being sour and hot, it stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, nourishing, and destroys vāta.
Due to its astringent, hot, and expansive qualities, as well as its dryness, it also removes kapha.
One who consumes buttermilk never suffers, nor do diseases prevail over one scorched by buttermilk;
as nectar is for the happiness of the gods, so they say that buttermilk is for men on earth.
Buttermilk is considered the best for alleviating phlegm, providing strength, and destroying undigested matter (āma).
Chacchika is cooling, light, removes bile, fatigue, and thirst, alleviates Vāta, increases Kapha, and when combined with salt, it is digestive.
But buttermilk from which the ghee has been extracted is especially wholesome and light. (8–9)
Butter with only a small amount of cream removed from it is heavy, aphrodisiac, and alleviates *kapha*.
Butter that has not had its cream removed is thick, heavy, nourishing, and increases *kapha*.
For *vāta*, buttermilk combined with ginger and rock salt is recommended, especially when it is sour.
In cases of pitta, it should be combined with sweet and sugar; in kapha, with trikaṭu and alkali.
Whey mixed with asafoetida, cumin, and rock salt is an excellent destroyer of vāta and is supreme for curing hemorrhoids and diarrhea.
It provides relish, nourishment, and strength, and destroys pain in the bladder;
when taken with jaggery, it cures dysuria, and with *citraka*, it cures anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
Raw buttermilk destroys phlegm in the stomach but causes it to accumulate in the throat.

In cases such as chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough, only the fermented buttermilk (pakva-takra) is employed; likewise, during the cold season, in cases of weak digestive fire, in disorders of Vata,
and in loss of appetite or obstruction of the channels, buttermilk is like nectar.

That [medicine] destroys poison, vomiting, excessive salivation, and irregular fevers; it cures anemia, edema, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, urinary retention, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, colic, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, and anorexia.

One should never administer buttermilk in cases of leucoderma, abdominal diseases, skin disorders, edema, thirst, or worms; nor when there is wasting (kṣaya), nor during the hot season, nor in those who are weak,
nor in cases of fainting, vertigo, or burning sensations, nor in diseases born of blood and bile (raktapitta).
One should declare that buttermilk possesses the same qualities as those eight types of curd previously mentioned (verse 18).
Thus ends the sixteenth section on buttermilk in the Chapter on Miscellaneous Substances within the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, the son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. 16.
Now begins the section on fresh butter (*navanīta*):
*mrakṣaṇa*, *saraja*, *haiyaṅgavīna*, and *navanītaka* are synonyms for fresh butter.
Cow’s fresh butter is beneficial, aphrodisiac, and promotes complexion, strength, and digestive fire. (1)
It is constipating and removes wind, bile, blood disorders, consumption, hemorrhoids, and cough;
it is beneficial for children and the elderly, and is especially like nectar for infants.
However, buffalo butter produces wind and phlegm and is heavy.

But butter produced from milk relieves burning sensations, pitta, and fatigue; it increases fat and semen, is beneficial for the eyes, cures raktapitta, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, very unctuous, sweet, constipating, and cooling. 3–4.
Fresh butter is delicious, constipating, cooling, light, and beneficial for the intellect;
it is slightly astringent and sour due to the slight transfer of curd particles.
However, because of its alkaline, pungent, and sour qualities, it causes vomiting, hemorrhoids, and skin diseases.
Fresh butter increases phlegm, is heavy, and is fatty; old butter [is the opposite].
Thus ends the seventeenth section, the Chapter on Butter, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. 17.
Now begins the section on clarified butter (ghṛtavarga).
Clarified butter is called ājya, havis, and sarpiḥ; its qualities are now described:
clarified butter is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), sweet, beneficial for the eyes, and a stimulator of the digestive fire. 1.
It has a cooling potency and removes poison, ill fortune, sin, pitta, and vāta; it causes little obstruction (abhiṣyandi) and increases luster, vitality, splendor, and charm.
It improves voice and memory, is purifying, promotes longevity, and is heavy, yet bestows strength.
Cow's ghee specifically removes upward-moving wind (udāvarta), fever, insanity, colic, abdominal distension, and ulcers;
it is unctuous, increases kapha, protects against demons, cures consumption, erysipelas, and blood disorders,
and is beneficial for the eyes, aphrodisiac, and stimulates the digestive fire.
It is sweet, produces a sweet digestion, is cooling, and removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
It is supreme for increasing intelligence, saltiness, luster, vitality, and splendor;
it destroys misfortune, sin, and demons, stabilizes youth, and is heavy [to digest].
Buffalo ghee is strengthening, purifying, life-prolonging, highly auspicious, an elixir,
fragrant, appetizing, beautiful, and superior in quality among all types of clarified butter;
it is delicious and subdues pitta, rakta, and vāta.
Ghee from a goat is cooling, increases phlegm, is aphrodisiac, heavy, and sweet when digested. It stimulates the digestive fire, is beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength.
It is also wholesome in cases of cough, asthma, and consumption (wasting disease), though it becomes pungent upon digestion.

Camel ghee is pungent in its post-digestive effect; it cures wasting diseases, worms, and poisons, stimulates the digestive fire, subdues kapha and vāta, and removes skin diseases, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.
Sheep's ghee is light in digestion and destroys all diseases. 9–10.
It promotes the growth of bones, removes urinary stones and gravel,
is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates the digestive fire, and wards off disorders of Vata. It is also wholesome in cases of Kapha, Vata, disorders of the female reproductive tract, Pitta, and blood.
Clarified butter produced from the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time, or the ghee of women, may be like nectar.
It increases the digestive fire of the body, is light in digestion, and destroys poison.
Mare's ghee (vaḍavāghṛta) is nourishing, cures eye diseases, and alleviates burning sensations.
Ghee, derived from milk, is constipating, cooling, and removes eye diseases;
it destroys bile, burning sensations, hemorrhaging, intoxication, fainting, vertigo, and wind disorders.
(14) Ghee produced from yesterday’s milk is known as *dhāryaṅgavīna*.

Fresh butter (haiyaṅgavīna) is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, greatly increases appetite, provides strength, is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and especially destroys fever. Ghee that has been kept for more than a year is considered aged; it alleviates the three doṣas.
It removes fainting, leprosy, poison, insanity, epilepsy, and blindness.
(16) It has been declared that the older the clarified butter becomes, the more it is superior in its respective qualities. (17)
One should employ this very clarified butter in food, as a satiation, or during physical exertion,
in cases of loss of strength, anemia, jaundice, eye diseases, pulmonary consumption,
in children, in the elderly, and in diseases caused by phlegm (kapha). 18–19.
In certain diseases— namely visūcī, constipation (vibandha), alcoholism (madātyaya),
fever, and burning sensations— ghee is not highly regarded when [the digestive fire] is weak.
Thus ends the section in the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The eighteenth section on ghee in the Miscellaneous Chapter is completed.
Now begins the section on urine:
Cow’s urine is pungent, sharp, hot, alkaline, bitter, and astringent.
It stimulates the digestive fire easily, improves the intellect, increases pitta, and removes kapha and vata.
It conquers colic, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, flatulence, itching, and diseases of the eyes and mouth; it destroys leucoderma, gout, rheumatism, pain in the bladder, and skin diseases.
It cures cough and dyspnea, and removes edema, jaundice, and anemia.

Even when drunk alone, cow’s urine eliminates itching, vitiligo, diseases, colic, diseases of the mouth and eyes, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, wind-related ailments, urinary retention, cough, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal enlargement, worms, and anemia.
Among all types of urine, cow's urine is superior in its qualities;
therefore, when "urine" is mentioned without qualification, it refers to cow's urine. It cures enlargement of the spleen, dyspnea, cough, edema, and constipation.
It removes colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, jaundice, and anemia;
as a decoction, it is bitter and sharp, and when used as an ear-drop, it cures earache.
Human urine, when consumed, destroys artificial poisons (gara) and acts as a rejuvenative tonic.
It is known to be sharp, removing blood and scabies, and containing alkali and salt.
The urine of cows, goats, sheep, and buffaloes—specifically females—is recommended;
the urine of donkeys, camels, elephants, humans, and horses—specifically males—is considered beneficial.
Thus ends the nineteenth section, the Chapter on Urine, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the Chapter on Oils (Tailavarga).
The oiliness of substances such as sesame seeds is called *taila* (oil);
all of it alleviates *vāta*, but that derived from sesame is especially so.
Sesame oil is heavy, promotes stability, strength, complexion, and is laxative.
It is aphrodisiac, laxative, clear, and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka);
it is subtle, has an astringent after-taste, and is bitter; it subdues vāta and kapha;
it is hot in potency (vīrya) but cold to the touch; it is nourishing and increases blood and pitta.

It is laxative, binds stool and urine, cleanses the uterus, stimulates digestion, promotes intelligence, is beneficial for the intellect, pervades the body, cures ulcers and urinary disorders, destroys pain in the ears, genitals, and head, and produces lightness. 4.
It is beneficial for the skin, the hair, and the eyes when used as an unguent; otherwise, it is so when used in food.
[This applies] in cases of being cut, pierced, fallen out, crushed, churned, wounded, or smeared with pus;
and in cases of fracture, bursting, perforation, burning by fire, separation, or tearing.

Likewise, sesame oil is recommended for use on a body wounded by a struck or mangled deer, tiger, or other beast; for drinking; for seasoning food; for nasal administration (nasya); for filling the ears or eyes; and for affusion, massage, and immersion baths.
When the wind (pavana), vitiated by dryness and other factors, causes the channels to contract,
the nutrient fluid (rasa), flowing improperly and failing to nourish the blood, produces emaciation.
This [fluid] is able to enter those [channels] due to its mobility, subtlety, unctuousness, and softness.
Oil is capable of carrying the essence (rasa) to emaciated persons; therefore, it is nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa).
Because of its qualities of being pervasive, subtle, sharp, hot, and mobile, oil gradually causes the depletion of fat (medas); therefore, it is declared to be scraping (lekhanam).

Oil that binds the stool quickly and causes it to flow when obstructed is called *grāhaka* (binding) and *sāraka* (solidifying). Ghee that has been cooked for more than a year becomes deficient in potency.
Sesame oil, whether cooked or uncooked, becomes superior in its qualities when kept for a long time.
Mustard oil is digestive, pungent in both post-digestive effect and taste, light,
scraping, hot in touch and potency, sharp, and it vitiates the pitta and blood.
It destroys phlegm, fat, wind, and hemorrhoids; it removes diseases of the head and ears;
and it dispels itching, skin diseases, worms, vitiligo, koṭha, and malignant parasites.
Similarly, oil from the seeds of rājika specifically causes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). 14–15.

Tila oil is sharp and hot, astringent, light, and constipating; it conquers phlegm and blood disorders, stimulates the digestive fire, removes poison, and destroys itching, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), boils, and worms;
it also eliminates defects of the fat tissue and is an excellent remedy for wounds and swellings. 16

Linseed oil is fiery (āgneya), unctuous and hot; it increases kapha and pitta, has a pungent post-digestive effect (pāka), is harmful to the eyes, strengthening, alleviates vāta, and is heavy. It produces impurities, is sweet in taste, constipating, cures skin diseases, and is thickening. 17–18.

Kusumbha oil should be employed for massage, drinking, as well as for anointing, nasal administration, filling the ears, and as a vehicle for adjunctive drinks, in order to pacify Vāta. It is sour, hot, heavy, and causes a burning sensation.
Oil from *khasa* seeds is beneficial for the eyes, strengthening, and increases blood, bile, and phlegm (20). It is considered strengthening, aphrodisiac, and heavy;
it removes wind and phlegm, is cold in potency, and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (21).
Castor oil is sharp, hot, digestive-stimulant, slimy, heavy, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the skin, anti-aging, and bestows intelligence, luster, and strength.
It has an astringent aftertaste, is subtle, and purifies the female reproductive tract and semen. (22)
It has a fleshy-smelling, sweet taste, and is slightly bitter and pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka).
It cures irregular fevers, heart disease, and colic in the back, private parts, and other regions;
it destroys Vata-type abdominal enlargement, flatulence, abdominal tumors, prostate enlargement, and stiffness in the waist.

This single lion of castor oil is the sole slayer of the lordly elephant of *āmavāta* as it roams the forest of the body, destroying wind-blood disorders, constipation, ulcers, swellings, and abscesses. (25)
Oil derived from *sarjarasa* destroys eruptive boils and ulcers,
removes skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), scabies (*pāmā*), and worms, and cures disorders of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Vāgbhaṭa maintains that all oil produces qualities inherent to its own source.
Therefore, the qualities of the remaining oils should be understood as being like those of their own source.
Thus ends the twentieth section, the Chapter on Oils, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana. 20.
Now begins the section on fermented liquors (*sandhānavarga*).
The scum of grain and similar substances that have been fermented is called *kāñjika* by people.
*Kāñjika* is a laxative, sharp, hot, appetizing, digestive, and light.
That which is prepared with *māṣa*-pulse cakes (*vaṭaka*) is superior in its qualities; it removes burning fever through touch, cures wind and phlegm when drunk,
is light, alleviates *vāta*, and is highly appetizing and digestive.

Kāñjika is not recommended for those suffering from colic, indigestion, constipation, or dysentery; nor for those afflicted by wasting, fainting, or vertigo; nor for those whose bodies are parched by intoxication or itching; nor for those with skin diseases (kuṣṭha) or internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). It is, however, a destroyer of abdominal tumors, indigestion, and constipation, and a cleanser of the bladder. (3–4)

For those suffering from jaundice, consumption, and wasting diseases, as well as for those emaciated by chest wounds, the fatigued, and those afflicted by mild fever— sour gruel (kāñjika) is said to be unwholesome for these, as it aggravates the bodily humors. 5
Tuṣodaka is prepared from raw barley grains that have been husked and split; it is water mixed with the husks.
Tuṣāmbu stimulates the digestive fire, is pleasing to the heart, and cures diseases such as jaundice and worms.
It is sharp and hot, acts as a digestive aid, increases bile and blood, and alleviates pain in the bladder.
Sauvīra is prepared with raw or cooked, dehusked barley, or even with wheat;
some teachers have stated this regarding sauvīra.
Sauvīra destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids, and phlegm; it is a purgative and a digestive stimulant.
It is recommended for upward-moving wind (udāvarta), body aches, pain in the bones, and abdominal distension.
Āranāla, however, may be made from dehusked raw wheat or from cooked wheat mixed together; it is equal to sauvīra in its properties.
Fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and rice flour may be prepared from kodo millet and other grains;

because it originates from grains, dhānyāmla is nourishing, light, and digestive-stimulating. It is beneficial for loss of appetite, all wind-related diseases, and in the administration of non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana). 11.
Śiṇḍākī is prepared with black mustard (rājikā), radish,
and plantain juice, or else with the expressed juice of mustard seeds combined with rice flour.
Śiṇḍākī is considered appetizing, heavy, and a producer of pitta and kapha.

That liquid in which bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, along with fats and salts, have been fermented is called *śukta*. *Śukta* destroys phlegm (*kapha*), is sharp and hot, appetizing, digestive, and light.
It cures *pāṇḍu* and worms, is parching, causes purgation, and produces *rakta-pitta*.
That which is rich in bulbs, roots, and fruits should be known as *āsutam*; it is appetizing, digestive, dispels wind (*vāta*), and is especially light. 15–16.
Madya, sīdhu, maireya, irā, madirā, surā, kādambarī, vāruṇī, and hālā— these are also beloved by those with strength.
Whatever intoxicating drink is consumed by people is designated as *madya*.
Just as *ariṣṭa*, *surā*, *sīdhu*, *āsava*, and various other kinds of liquor— indeed, all intoxicants— are hot in potency, they generate *pitta*, destroy *vāta*, are purgative,
undergo rapid digestion, are dry, and are excellent for removing *kapha*. (18–19)
It is sour, digestive-stimulant, appetizing, carminative, and acts quickly;
it is sharp, subtle, clear, pervasive, and expansive. (20) That liquor which is prepared from decoctions of matured medicinal herbs is called *ariṣṭa*. (21)

Ariṣṭa is light in digestion and superior in its qualities in every respect; the qualities of ariṣṭa should be understood as being identical to the qualities of the substances used as its source. Wine (madya) made from the flour of śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, and other grains is known as surā.
Surā is heavy; it provides strength, nourishment for breast milk, and increases fat and phlegm.
It is constipating and cures edema, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, and dysuria.
Vāruṇī is known to be prepared from *punarnavā* and ground stone (mica).
That *vāruṇī* liquor, prepared with the juices of *tāla* and *kharjūra* fruits combined together, is like *surā*; it is light and cures chronic catarrh, flatulence, and colic.
*Sīdhu* is prepared from the ripe juices of sugarcane, and it is likewise known as *pakvarasa*.
That *sīdhu* which is made from those very same [grapes] when raw is known as *śītarasa*.

*Sīdhu* made from ripe juice is the best; it produces voice, digestive fire, strength, and complexion; it generates wind and bile, acts as an immediate unctuous agent, is appetizing, and removes [impurities]. 25–26.
It cures constipation, obesity, edema, hemorrhoids, abdominal swelling, and diseases of kapha;

therefore, the cold-tasting variety is known to be of minor therapeutic virtue and is considered depleting (saṃlekhanaka). That liquor which is prepared from uncooked medicinal herbs and water is called āsava. 27–28.
The qualities of fermented liquor (āsava) should be known as being similar to the qualities of the substances from which it is derived.
Fresh liquor is obstructive to the channels (abhiṣyandi), generates the three doṣas, is laxative (sara), unpalatable, nourishing, burning, foul-smelling, clear, and heavy. (29–30)
That same [substance], when aged, is lustrous, dispels worms, phlegm, and wind, is pleasing to the heart, fragrant, virtuous, light, and a cleanser of the channels.
(31) In the *sāttvika* [state], there is singing, laughter, and so forth; in the *rājasa* [state], there is joking and the like.
In the *tāmasa* mode, one should practice censurable acts, sleep, and the consumption of intoxicants (verse 32).

However, for him who drinks liquor according to the prescribed rule, in proper measure, at the right time, with wholesome food, and in accordance with his strength, while remaining joyful, it shall be like nectar (verse 33).
But wine is traditionally considered to be like food by its very nature:

when taken improperly it leads to disease, yet when taken properly it is like nectar. He who, chewing cardamom, costus, long pepper, cumin, coriander, and black cardamom, articulates his speech in the assembly— 34. He who, chewing cardamom, costus, long pepper, cumin, coriander, and black cardamom, articulates his speech in the assembly— 34.
One should certainly avoid natural bodily excretions, foul odors, the scent of liquor, garlic, and the like, as well as worldly existence itself.
Thus ends the twenty-first section, the Chapter on Mixing, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana. 21.
Now, the section on honey:
Honey is declared to be *mākṣika*, *mādhvīka*, *kṣaudra*, and *sāragha*;
it originates from the nectar of flowers and is vomited by flies, bees, and bumblebees. (1)
Honey is cold, light, sweet, dry, constipating, and scraping; it is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates digestion, improves the voice, and cleanses and heals wounds.
It produces delicacy of skin, is subtle, and is supreme for purifying the channels.
It has an astringent aftertaste, is refreshing, and produces supreme clarity; it improves the complexion, enhances intellect, is aphrodisiac, clear, and appetizing.
It removes skin diseases, hemorrhoids, cough, internal hemorrhaging (pittāsra), phlegm disorders, urinary disorders, exhaustion, and worms.

It cures obesity, thirst, vomiting, dyspnea, hiccups, diarrhea, and constipation, as well as burning sensations, chest wounds, and consumption; it is suitable for various formulations and does not increase vāta.
Honey is of five types: *mākṣika*, *bhrāmara*, *kṣaudra*, *pauttika*, and *chātra*.
Ārghya, auddālaka, dāla, and so forth—these are the eight varieties of honey. Large flies of a reddish-brown color are the honey-bees;
the honey produced by them, which has the color of oil, is celebrated as *mākṣika*.
Honey from bees (*mākṣika*) is the best among honeys; it is light, removes eye diseases, and destroys jaundice, indigestion, consumption, asthma, cough, and wasting.
It is collected by well-known bees that are somewhat small in size. (8)
That honey which is stainless and resembles crystal is known as *bhrāmara* (bee-honey).
*Bhrāmara* honey destroys *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders), causes heaviness of the urine and numbness,
is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), is obstructive to the channels (*abhiṣyandi*), and is especially slimy and cold.

The small, brown flies known as *kṣudrā* produce honey which is called *kṣaudra* by the sages; it is brown (*kapila*) because of its color. In its qualities, *kṣaudra* is like *mākṣika*, with the specific distinction that it destroys urinary disorders. 11.

Those which are black, resembling gnats, very small, and generally large stinging insects that reside within the broad hollows of trees and produce floral nectar, are called *puttikās* by those who know them; [the medicinal oil] made with their [fat] and clarified butter— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
That which is called *pauttika* honey by forest-dwellers is similar [to the other types].
(12) *Pauttika* honey is dry and hot; it produces *pitta*, burning sensations, and hemorrhaging.
It alleviates *vidāha*, urinary disorders (*meha*), and dysuria (*kṛcchra*), and it dries up abscesses (*granthi*) and other wounds. (13)
The *varaṭā* bees—tawny and yellow—are generally found in the forests of the Himalayas.
They produce a honey shaped like an umbrella, which is known as *chātra-madhu*.
This *chātra* honey is tawny-yellow, slimy, cooling, and heavy.

The exudate of the Madhūka tree, produced from the old hollows of its trunks, is sweet in digestion; it conquers worms, vitiligo, blood-bile disorders, and urinary diseases; it removes vertigo, thirst, delusion, and poisons; it is nourishing and possesses superior qualities. (16)
That [liquid] which flows is called *arghya*; furthermore, in Mālava, it is known as *śvetaka*.
Those yellow flies with sharp beaks that resemble bees are worthy of honor (*arghya*);
others have declared that what is produced by them is *arghya*.
Madhu-ārghya is highly beneficial for the eyes, an excellent remover of kapha and pitta,
astringent, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), bitter, and it promotes strength and nourishment.
Generally, these small reddish-brown insects reside within anthills.
When prepared with a small amount of *kapila* [mudga], it becomes *auddālaka* honey. *Auddālaka* is appetizing, beneficial for the voice, and removes skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and poisons;
it is astringent, hot, sour, pungent in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and increases *pitta*. (20–21)
That which has flowed down and fallen upon the leaves, such as flowers and the like,
being sweet, sour, and astringent, is called *madhudāla*. *Madhudāla* is said to be light, digestive-stimulating (*dīpanīya*), and a destroyer of *kapha*.
Fresh honey has an astringent aftertaste; it is dry, appetizing, and overcomes vomiting and urinary disorders (23).
It is exceedingly sweet, unctuous, nourishing, heavy, and burdensome to the system (24).
Fresh honey serves for nourishment, does not excessively alleviate *kapha*, and is laxative.
Old honey is astringent, dry, reduces fat, and is highly purgative.
Scholars maintain that honey, sugar, and especially jaggery (guḍa), attain the state of being "old" when one year has passed.

Even from poisonous flowers, venomous bees and other insects extract the nectar and produce honey; that honey is cool and possesses excellent qualities. However, due to its connection with poison, it may become hot if combined with a substance that is hot by nature.
Honey is considered equal to poison for one afflicted by heat during the hot season.
Wax is known as *mayana*, *madhūcchiṣṭa*, *madhuśeṣa*, and *sikthaka*; it is also well-remembered as *madhvādhāra*, *madanaka*, and *madhūṣita*. 28–29.
Madana is soft, very unctuous, a destroyer of evil spirits, a healer of wounds,
