a promoter of the healing of fractures, and a conqueror of vāta, kuṣṭha, visarpa, and blood disorders.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous substances in the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The twenty-second chapter, the Madhu-varga, is completed. Now begins the Ikṣu-varga:
the sugarcane is said to have long leaves and likewise to possess abundant juice.
Guḍamūla, asipatra, and likewise madhutṛṇa are recorded [among these].
Sugarcane varieties destroy blood-bile (raktapitta), are strengthening, aphrodisiac, and increase phlegm;
they are sweet in taste and post-digestive effect, unctuous, heavy, diuretic, and cooling.
Pauṇḍraka, Bhīruka, Vaṃśaka, Śataparvaka, Kāntāratāpasa, Ikṣu, Kāṇḍekṣu, Sūcipatraka,
Naipāla, Dīrghapatra, Nīlapora, and Kośakṛt.

And Manoguptā— these are the species mentioned therein. Pauṇḍraka and Bhīruka are sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect (pāka), pacifiers of wind and bile, very cold, nourishing, and strengthening.
The *kośakāra* sugarcane is heavy, cooling, and removes blood-bile (*raktapitta*) and wasting disorders.
The *kāntāra* sugarcane is heavy, aphrodisiac, increases phlegm (*śleṣman*), is nourishing, and is laxative.
The *dīrghapora* sugarcane is very hard; it is known as *vaṃśaka* and contains alkaline salts (*sakṣāra*).
The *śataparvā* is somewhat like the fibers of the silkworm cocoon;
it is specifically slightly warm, alkaline, and dispels wind (vāta).
The *tāpasekṣu* is soft, sweet, and increases phlegm (śleṣman).
It is nourishing, appetizing, aphrodisiac, and strength-promoting;
thus, by these qualities, the stalk-sugarcane (kāṇḍekṣu) is so described, though it does provoke vāta.
[The varieties are] sūcīpatra, nīlapora, naipāla, and dīrghapatraka.
Vātalā increases wind, destroys phlegm and bile, is slightly astringent, and causes a burning sensation.
Manoguptā alleviates wind, destroys thirst and disease, is very cooling, extremely sweet, and cures hemorrhaging from blood and bile (raktapitta). 12–13.
Young sugarcane produces phlegm and causes obesity and urinary disorders;
that which is young (middle-aged) removes wind, is sweet, slightly pungent, and subdues bile; and mature sugarcane cures hemorrhaging, heals wounds, and increases strength and virility. 14.

Sugarcane is known by people to be extremely sweet at the root, sweet also in the middle, and sour at the tips and joints. The juice of sugarcane pressed with the teeth destroys pitta and blood disorders.
It possesses a potency equal to sugar, is non-burning, and increases phlegm (kapha). However,
the oil produced by mechanical means undergoes transformation due to the crushing of roots, tips, insects, and knots, the admixture of impurities, and being held for some time.
Therefore, the juice from the intestinal tract (yāntrika-rasa) is burning, causes constipation, and is heavy.
Stale juice is not desired; it is sour, alleviates Vāta, is heavy, increases Kapha and Pitta, causes emaciation, is purgative, and excessively increases urine.
The ripe juice is heavy, unctuous, very sharp, and is known to pacify kapha and vāta, alleviate abdominal tumors (gulma) and distension (ānāha), and slightly increase pitta.
The products of sugarcane destroy thirst, burning sensations, fainting, and hemorrhagic disorders caused by pitta.

Sugarcane juices that are ripe, somewhat thick, and very fluid are heavy, sweet, strengthening, unctuous, wind-alleviating, laxative, aphrodisiac, delusion-removing, cooling, nourishing, and antidotes to poison.
(20) As for the juice of sugarcane which is ripe, slightly thick, and flows abundantly:
That very substance, when processed from sugarcane, is known by the name *phāṇita* (unrefined treacle).
*Phāṇita* is heavy, causes secretions, is nourishing, increases *kapha* and semen, destroys wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and fatigue, and cleanses the urinary bladder. 21.
The juice of sugarcane that has been fully cooked until it becomes thick and slightly moistened with liquid,
which flows slowly from it, is called *matsyaṇḍī*.
*Matsyaṇḍī* is purgative, strengthening, light, and it alleviates *pitta* and *vāta*.
It is known to be sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and a remover of blood disorders.
(23) That juice of sugarcane which becomes solidified like a clod of earth is called *guḍa*;
in the Gauḍa country, however, *matsyaṇḍī* is considered to be *guḍa*. (24)
Jaggery (guḍa) is aphrodisiac, heavy, unctuous, alleviates vāta, purifies the urine,
does not excessively pacify pitta, and bestows fat, kapha, worms, and strength.
(25) Matured jaggery is light, wholesome, non-obstructive to the channels, and promotes the digestive fire.
Fresh jaggery (guḍa) is sweet, aphrodisiac, pacifies wind, and clarifies the blood;
it increases phlegm, asthma, cough, and worms, yet stimulates the digestive fire.
When taken with fresh ginger, it quickly destroys phlegm; the same [jaggery] combined with harītakī fruits destroys bile.
Taken with ginger, it removes wind entirely; thus, salutations to jaggery (*guḍa*), which destroys the three humors. 28.
Sugar candy (*khaṇḍa*), however, is sweet, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, cooling, alleviates wind and bile, is unctuous, strengthening, and an excellent remedy for vomiting. 29.
Sugar candy (khaṇḍa) has the appearance of sand, is very white, and is like white sugar; it is sweet, appetizing, and removes wind, bile, blood disorders, and burning sensations.
Being very cooling, it destroys fainting, vomiting, and fever, and promotes semen. 30.
Sugar made from flowers (sitopalā) is cooling, light, and removes blood-bile (raktapitta). It is laxative, light, cold, and removes wind and bile.
Sugar derived from honey (madhuśarkarā) is dry, heavy, and removes phlegm and bile.
They alleviate vomiting, diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, and blood-related disorders; they are astringent and cooling.

To the extent that these [fruits] possess clarity and sweetness, and to the extent that they possess unctuousness, lightness, coolness, and so forth, as well as laxity, to that same degree [are their properties]. 32–33.
Thus ends the twenty-third section, the Chapter on Sugarcane, in the Miśra-prakaraṇa of the Bhāvaprakāśa composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
The word *akṣa* is recorded in eight senses: [it is used for] black salt (*sauvarcala*) and the *bibhītaka* fruit.
Karṣa, padmākṣa, rudrākṣa, śakaṭa, indriya, pāśaka; and likewise those called kākākhya, kākamācī, kākolī, kākaṇantikā,
kākajaṅghā, kākanāsā, and kākodumbarikā.
The word *kāka* is declared by the wise to have seven meanings; the word *nāga* is employed for snake, elephant, ram, lead, *nāgakesara*,
*nāgabalī*, and *nāgadantī*.
The term *rasa* exists in nine [meanings]: in meat, in wine, in sugarcane juice, in mercury, in the sweet and other [flavors], in borax, in passion, in poison, and in water.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous topics in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.

The twenty-fourth chapter, the Section on Multiple Meanings, is completed. 24. Thus, in the first part of the first section of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Bhāvaprakāśa, the sixth miscellaneous section—also known as the Section on Substances and Qualities—is completed. 6. And this portion of the Nighaṇṭu is now finished.
Bhāvaprakāśa, First Section, Second Part; therein, the seventh chapter on technical definitions and so forth. 7.
Without measurement, the determination of substances is never possible;
therefore, for the sake of practical application, I shall here describe measurement.
Since it was accepted by the ancient physicians as the doctrine of Caraka, [I follow] his view.
Setting aside all other measures, that which is called the *māgadha* is now described. Three hundred atoms (*paramāṇu*) are declared by the wise to be one *trasareṇu*;
furthermore, the *trasareṇu* is also designated by the synonymous name *vaṃśī*.
A *vaṃśī* is seen through the rays of the sun passing through a lattice;
six *vaṃśīs* constitute a *marīci*, and six of those make a *rājikā*.
Three *rājikās* are declared by the wise to be a *sarṣapa*.
A barley grain is said to consist of eight mustard seeds; four of those make one *guñjā*. Six *raktikās* make one *māṣaka*, which is also called a *hemadhānaka*.
Four *māṣakas* make one *śāṇa*, which is declared to be a *dharaṇa*.
That very [unit] is called a *ṭaṅka*; two of those are said to be a *kola*, and a small *kola* is indeed called a *vaṭaka*. That is declared to be a *draṅkṣaṇa*.
Two *kola*s, however, would be a *karṣa*; that is proclaimed as a *pāṇimānikā*.
An *akṣa*, a *picu*, a *pāṇitala*, a *kiñcitpāṇi*, and a *tinduka* (8); likewise, a *viḍālapadaka* and a *ṣoḍaśikā* are considered [measures];
as well as a *karamadhya*, a *haṃsapada*, a *suvarṇa*, and a *kavalagraha* (9).
An *udumbara* is said to be equal to one *karṣa* by way of synonyms;
two *karṣas* constitute half a *pala*, as do a *śukti* and an *aṣṭamikā*.
Two *śuktis* should be known as one *pala*, as well as a *muṣṭi*, an *āmra*, and a *caturthikā*.
A *prakuñca* is sixteen [māṣas], and a *bilva* is proclaimed here as being one *pala*.
Two *palas* should be known as a *prasṛti*, and it is also called a *prasṛta*.
From two *prasṛtis* comes an *añjali*, which is a *kuḍava* or half a *śarāva*. 11–12.
That should be known as eight mānas; two kuḍavas make a mānikā, and likewise, eight palas should be known by the wise here as a śarāva.
Two śarāvas make a prastha, and four prasthas make an āḍhaka.
The vessel is a bronze bowl (*kāṃsyapātra*), and it weighs sixty-four *palas*.
A *droṇa* consists of four *āḍhakas*. *Kalaśa*, *nalvaṇa*, *amaṇa*, *unmāna*, *ghaṭa*, *rāśi*, *droṇa*, and *paryāya* are synonymous terms.
Two *droṇas* make one *śūrpa* and one *kumbha*, and sixty-four *śarāvakas* make one *śūrpa*.
Two *śūrpas* are known as a *droṇī*, a *vāha*, and a *goṇī*.
Four *droṇīs* are declared by those of subtle intellect to be a *khārī*.

Four thousand and ninety-six *palas* constitute one *bhāra*; two thousand *palas* are proclaimed to be one *tulā*. A hundred *palas* should be known as a *tulā*—this is the certainty everywhere. (17–18)
A *māṣa*, a *ṭaṅka*, an *akṣa*, a *bilva*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*,
an *āḍhaka*, a *rāśi*, a *goṇī*, and a *khārī*— these increase fourfold in successive order.
(19) Starting from the measurement of a *guñjā*, this continues until the state of a *kuḍava* is reached.
For liquid, moist, and dry substances, that same measure is considered equal.
(20) Starting from the *prastha* and other measures, the measure for liquids and moist substances is double; however, for the balance (*tulā*), doubling is nowhere prescribed. (21)
A vessel made of soft wood, bamboo, metal, or other materials, which is four finger-breadths wide and likewise high, one should call that measure a *kuḍava*. (22) Thus ends the Māgadha measure.
Since in the Kali age men have weak digestion, short stature, and diminished strength, the dosage appropriate for them is therefore declared by the wise to be as follows:
twelve white mustard seeds are said by the learned to constitute one *yava*.
Two *yava*s make one *guñjā*; three *guñjā*s are called a *valla*.
A *māṣa* may consist of eight or sometimes seven *guñjā*s. Four *māṣa*s make a *śāṇa*, which is also known as a *niṣka* or a *ṭaṅka*.
Six *māṣakas* make one *gadyāṇa*, and ten *māṣakas* constitute a *karṣa*.
Four *karṣas* are declared by the wise to be a *pala*, measured at ten *śāṇas*.
Four *palas* make a *kuḍava*, and the *prastha* and subsequent measures are considered to follow as before.

There is no fixed measure [of dosage]; one should determine the dose after observing the time, the digestive fire, age, strength, constitution, the humors (doṣas), and the location. A medicine that is too small does not destroy the disease, just as a small amount of water cannot extinguish a great fire.
"Excess leads to harm, just as too much water does to a crop. (28) Thus ends the section on the Kāliṅga measure.
This concludes the section on technical definitions and so forth, composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*.
The first chapter, titled "Definitions of Measurement," is completed.
Now begins the second chapter, "The Formulation of Medicines": fresh juice, paste, decoction, cold infusion, and hot infusion.

These five types of decoctions (kaṣāya) should be known to become progressively lighter [in potency] as they follow one after the other. That which arises from a substance that has not been heated, or is freshly extracted, or is crushed,
or is squeezed out from a cloth, is called a "rasa" (expressed juice).
One *kuḍava* of powdered substance should be thrown into double the amount of water and left for a day and night; from that, an excellent juice (*rasa*) may be obtained.
Alternatively, when fresh juices are unavailable, one may take the dried substance itself.
The substance should be processed with eight times its weight of water, and one-fourth of that remaining liquid is taken;
because of the heaviness of the mercury (svara), one should employ half a *pala*,
and having dried it and processed it with fire, one should drink the juice in the measure of one *pala*.
One should add sugar, honey, jaggery, salt, cumin, and likewise rock salt,
ghee, oil, and the powders in quantities of one kola each into the broth.
Then, one pala of husked rice should be placed in eight times its quantity of water.
Having infused it, the water should be taken and used in all ritual acts.
One pala of the substance, properly crushed and thoroughly saturated with six palas of water, should be dried overnight; that is "frost" (hima), and likewise, it is a "cold decoction" (śītakaṣāya).
The wise consider two palas to be the measure for that drink.
One pala of the crushed substance should be added to four palas of cold water in an earthen vessel;
it should be stirred thoroughly, and from that, one should drink two palas.
When one pala of the powdered substance has been thoroughly crushed, one should properly pour in hot water measuring one kuḍava into an earthen vessel; then, having strained it through a cloth,
that liquid extract is called *phāṇṭa*, and its measure is two palas.
One should add one *karṣa* each of honey, sugar, jaggery, and so forth.
Whether a moist substance is ground on a stone with water or is already dry, it should be understood as a paste (*kalka*);
its measure is equal to one *karṣa*.

In a medicinal paste (kalka), honey, ghee, and oil should be added in double the quantity; sugar should be added in equal measure, and molasses in the same amount; liquids should be added four times the quantity.
Whatever substance is extremely dry should be finely ground and filtered through a cloth.
That powder, dust, or grind is measured by a *karṣa*;
in such powders, an equal amount of jaggery (*guḍa*) should be added, while sugar (*śarkarā*) is considered to be double that amount.
In these powders, fried asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) should be added so that it does not cause excessive moisture.
One should grind the powder with all types of syrups (drava) and ghee, etc., in double the quantity;
likewise, one should drink the powder thus stirred with four times the amount of syrups.
This is the vehicle for powders, electuaries, pills, and pastes.
In cases of disorders caused by pitta, vāta, and kapha, one should take three, two, and one pala [of the medicine] respectively.
Just as oil, when thrown into water, spreads instantly,
so too does the medicine pervade the body through the power of the after-drink (anupāna).
Indeed, the quantity for the saturation is such that the entire powder becomes completely soaked;
this measure for the saturation of the powder has been declared by the best of physicians.
(19) This is because the juice is extracted from the paste used for *puṭapāka*.
Therefore, the method for *puṭapāka* (sealed cooking) is now described by me here:
(20) This cooking of *puṭapāka* consists of the application of a paste until it attains the color of charcoal;
and one should apply the paste to a thickness of two finger-breadths, measuring exactly two finger-breadths. (21)
Wrapping [the vessel] with leaves of *kāśmarī*, *vaṭa*, *jambu*, and so forth is excellent.
One *pala* of juice should be taken, and one *karṣa* of honey should be added; as for pastes, powders, liquids, and the like, they should be given in the measure of one *kola* by the wise. 22–23.
With an eighth part remaining, or with a fourth, or even with a half,
or simply by boiling, the hot water becomes prepared;
it destroys phlegm, undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and wind, and it cleanses the bladder and stimulates the digestive fire.
Drunk at night with warm water, it destroys cough, dyspnea, and fever.
(25) Eight parts of milk and one part of the medicinal substance are boiled until four parts of milk remain; when drunk, that decoction conquers colic arising from undigested food (*āmadoṣaja*). (26)
One should add sixteen times the amount of water to one *pala* of the crushed substance and boil it in an earthen vessel; the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-eighth.
From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should provide sixteen times the quantity of water.
From one *kuḍava* up to the point where the water is eight times the quantity [of the drug], and from there upwards until it reaches a *prastha* or more,
the wise man should cause that water— warmed and prepared over a gentle fire— to be drunk.
That which has been boiled is called *kvātha*, *kaṣāya*, and *niryūha*.
Regarding the dosage for medicinal fats (*sneha*), decoctions (*kvātha*), and drugs: the maximum dose is one *pala*, the middling is three *akṣas*, and the minimum is half a *pala*. (29–30)
For one pala of medicinal substance to be boiled, sixteen times as much water is prescribed;
when reduced to one-fourth, four palas of water remain to be drunk.
One who has a blazing digestive fire and a large body may drink a handful (añjali) of water.

Other physicians, however, omitting half [of the water], desire that the decoction be reduced until one-eighth remains; by traditional instruction, the elder physicians [prescribe] two *pala*s [of the remaining liquid]. 32–33.
One should add sugar to the decoction in parts of one-fourth, one-eighth, or one-sixteenth; this is known as light [and beneficial] in cases of disorders of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha respectively.
[Add] cumin, guggulu, alkali, salt, and śilājatu.
One should add one *śāṇa* each of asafoetida and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) to the decoction (35).
Likewise, milk, ghee, jaggery, oil, urine, or other liquids,
as well as pastes, powders, and so forth, should be added to the decoction in the measure of one *karṣa* each (36).
Having sat there and rested, with a serene face and eyes,
he should drink the medicine placed in a vessel of gold, silver, or clay; having drunk it with a tranquil heart, he should turn the vessel face down.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should consume water and betel leaves and other such items.
Furthermore, that which attains a state of thickness through the subsequent cooking of decoctions and the like is called *rasakriyā*, *avaleha*, and *leha*; its dosage should be one *pala*.
Sugar should be made four times the amount of the powder, and jaggery twice the amount of the powder;
one should provide liquid four times the amount—this is the rule everywhere.
When well-cooked, the electuary (avaleha) should possess a fibrous consistency and sink in water.
Stability [of the medicine] is achieved when it is pressed; the resulting mudrā (sealing) produces fragrance, color, and taste.
41 Milk, sugarcane juice, vegetable broth, a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), or a decoction of vāsā are recommended as appropriate after-potions (anupāna). 42
Now, *vaṭakas* are described; they are called by the names *guṭikā*, *vaṭī*, *modaka*, *vaṭikā*, *piṇḍī*, *guḍa*, and *varti*. 43.
Or, like a *leha*, jaggery (*guḍa*) or sugar (*śarkarā*) is prepared over the fire.
One should throw powdered guggulu into that [mixture], or one may prepare pills made from it;
the wise man should make a pill with guggulu processed by fire, either with a liquid or with honey. 44–45.
Sugar should be given four times the amount [of the other ingredients] in pills; in boluses, jaggery should be twice the amount;

in powders, guggulu should be made equal to the powder; honey should be equal to that; and in medicinal confections (modakas), excellent physicians should give liquid substances in double the amount. 46–47.
A dose of that size is administered after observing the patient's strength;
having added four times as much ghee or oil as the paste, it should be cooked with four times as much liquid, and its dose is measured at one pala. 48–49.
Having placed [the ingredients] into water four times the quantity of the substances to be boiled, one should take the decoction reduced to one-fourth and prepare the oil with that very [decoction].
Water should be fourfold for soft substances and eightfold for hard ones.
One should add eight times the amount of water for a combination of drugs that are soft and so forth;
for extremely hard substances, sixteen times the amount of water is prescribed. From one *prastha* up to a *khārī*, one should add four times the amount of water.
Where the preparation of a fatty substance (sneha) is done separately with water, decoctions, or juices, one should add a fourth, sixth, or eighth part of the paste (kalka).
In milk, curd, meat-broth, or buttermilk, the paste should be added as an eighth part.

For the sake of proper cooking with the paste, four times as much water should be used here. Indeed, when there are five or more liquids in these medicated fats (sneha), they say that each subsequent liquid should be equal in quantity to the fat, while the first liquid should be four times its amount.
If the cooking of the oil (sneha-pāka) is to be done with the medicinal substance alone,
then there should be a paste ground with water, and the water added here should be four times the quantity [of the paste].
In some cases, where it is prescribed that the cooking should be done with the decoction alone—
In that case, a paste (kalka) of the decoction ingredients is also employed in the oil.
However, an oil that is devoid of a paste should be prepared with the liquid alone. In the case of an oil where a flower-paste is used, four times as much water should be added.
The paste of flowers should be used at one-eighth the quantity of the oil (59). When the oil and paste, rolled together with the fingers like a wick,
can be cast into the fire without making a sound, then the oil is perfected (60).

When froth appears in oil, when the froth subsides in clarified butter (sarpiḥ), and when color, smell, and taste arise, then the unctuous substance (sneha) is perfected. The cooking of unctuous substances is said to be threefold: mild, medium, and hard.
When the paste (kalka) is slightly moist, the cooking of the oil (sneha-pāka) is considered mild;
when the paste is moisture-free and soft, the cooking of the oil reaches the medium stage;
and when the paste is slightly firm, the cooking of the oil becomes hard.
Beyond that, it becomes overcooked (dagdhapāka), which causes burning and is useless;
undercooked (āmapāka) oil is devoid of potency, causes sluggish digestion, and is heavy.
For use as nasal drops (nasya), the oil should be soft-cooked (mṛdupāka), while for all other procedures, medium-cooked (madhyamapāka) is appropriate.
A rough substance is prescribed for the purpose of massage; one should employ these [substances] as is appropriate.
One should not prepare ghee, oil, jaggery, and so forth on the same day; rather, when these have been kept overnight, they especially produce a collection of beneficial qualities.

A substance that has been stored for a long time in vessels and has become concentrated is called *āsava* or *ariṣṭa*, depending on the medicinal ingredients used. That liquor which is prepared from uncooked medicinal herbs and water is known as *āsava*.

Ariṣṭa should be prepared by decoction; the measure of those two [drugs] should be one pala each (68). In cases where the measure is not specified for Ariṣṭas, there should be one droṇa of liquid and one tulā of jaggery;
one should add honey equal to half the amount of jaggery, and the additive ingredients should be one-tenth of the total. (69)
Sīdhu prepared with unripe, sweet, and sour fruits is known as having a cool taste;
sīdhu prepared with fully ripe, sweet, and sour fruits has a cooked (pakva) taste.
They say that *surā* is produced from the fermentation of fully cooked grains.
The scum of wine is *prasannā*; from that comes the thick *kādambarī*.
Below that is known as *jagala*, and the solid part of the *jagala* is *medaka*.
*Vakkasa* is the dregs from which the essence has been extracted; the fermenting agent for wine is *kiṇvaka*.
That which is blended with the juices of *yatta*, dates, and *kharjūra* is indeed called *vāruṇī*.
When bulbous roots, fruits, and the like, along with fats and salts,
are fermented in a liquid, that is designated as *śukta*.
Wine that has turned sour, or a sweet liquid that has gone bad, or that which has been spoiled and subsequently restored, is called *cukra*.
It may be prepared with jaggery water, oil, and various tubers, vegetables, and fruits. (75)
When fermented and turned sour, it is called *guḍa-cukra*; likewise, that which originates from *mṛdvīkā* (grapes) is known as *śukta*.
Similarly, water mixed with husks and split raw barley should be understood as *tuṣāmbu*.
Sauvīra is prepared from hulled and cooked barley; however, when made from hulled raw wheat, it becomes āranāla. When prepared from cooked [wheat], it is similar to sauvīra in its qualities.
They know *kāñjika* to be sour gruel (*kulmāṣa*) together with the scum of grain (*dhānyamanda*) and so forth;
*śiṇḍākī* is to be understood as a preparation made with radishes, mustard seeds, and the like.
Thus ends the section on technical definitions and so forth in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*, composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana.
The second chapter, on the preparation of medicines, is completed.
Now begins the third chapter, on the purification and killing of the metals and other substances.
When heated it is red, when cut it is white, and when rubbed on a touchstone it has the luster of saffron.
Pure gold is free from silver and copper, lustrous, soft, and heavy.
One should reject that which is hard, rough, discolored, and impure at its fracture; likewise, that which is white when burned, white when rubbed on a touchstone, and clearly light in weight.
One should heat gold leaves that have been made into thin strips in fire,
and then repeatedly pour them while still hot into oil, buttermilk,
sour gruel, cow’s urine, and the decoction of *kulattha* beans— three times each.
In this way, there occurs the purification of gold and other minerals.
[Otherwise,] it robs men of their strength and vitality, nourishes a multitude of diseases in this body, and like something always causing unhappiness, this impure gold brings about death. 4–5.

One should grind mercury twice the weight of gold together with acid; then one should place an equal amount of sulphur above and below it. Then, having sealed the pill within a firm casket of two earthenware bowls (śarāva), [one should proceed].
One should give fourteen *puṭas* in this manner using thirty pieces of wood;
thus, a residue-less ash (*niruttha-bhasma*) is produced. Fragrance should be added again and again.
When the gold has been melted, one should add lead in the sixteenth part [of its weight].
Having powdered it and rubbed it with acid, one should form a ball (golaka). Then,
having added an equal amount of sulfur (gandha) above and below the ball,
and having placed it within a closed crucible (śarāvasampuṭa), one should heat it with thirty pieces of vanopalas.
In this way, after seven coatings, the gold becomes ash-like residue (niruttha).
Having rubbed mercury and sulfur in equal proportions with the juice of *kāñcanāra*, one should smear the resulting collyrium onto the gold leaves in that same manner. 10–11.

One should prepare a pair of crucibles using the paste of *kāñcanāra* bark; having placed the pill within that crucible assembly, and having placed that assembly inside an earthen crucible, one should seal the joint and thoroughly dry the pill.
One should make the fire very intense; having thus applied [the process] three times in a sealed crucible (puṭa), the ash becomes "niruttha" (without residue) and may be employed in all ritual acts.
By means of the *kāñcanāra* method, *lāṅgalī* destroys gold. 13–14.
Likewise, Jvālāmukhī should kill [the poison] just as realgar does.
One should give seven saturations of a powder of equal parts of *śilā* and *sindūra* with the milky sap of the *arka* plant, drying it again and again. 15–16.
Then, once the gold has melted, this paste (kalka) is added in equal measure;
one should heat it intensely again so that the paste dissolves.
In this manner, one should add the paste three times, and the death of the gold [its transformation into pure essence] will occur. 17
Gold is cooling, aphrodisiac, strengthening, heavy, and a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
It is sweet, bitter, and astringent; it is sweet upon digestion, slimy, purifying, nourishing, beneficial for the eyes, and bestows intelligence, memory, and wisdom. 18.
Gold that is properly processed is beneficial for the heart, promotes longevity, and brings about luster, purity of speech, and stability of the skin;
it conquers the two types of poison, consumption, insanity, fever arising from the three *doṣas*, and wasting diseases. (19) Gold that is improperly killed destroys strength and virility.
It causes diseases and even death; therefore, one should destroy it with effort.

(20) The non-recurrence of iron and other metals, their acquisition of those qualities, and the richness of those qualities, as well as the ability to float upon water—that is its perfection, which arises from *puṭana* (encapsulation). (21)
In a deep and wide square pit measuring two cubits,
filled with thousands of pebbles and stones,
one should carefully place the medicinal powder for *puṭana* within a crucible and hold it over cow dung.
One should place five hundred pieces of forest stone upon the crucible;
one should cast fire therein—this is known as the *mahāpuṭa*.
[This is done] in a pit that is one and a quarter cubits in depth and likewise in length.
One should place it in the center of a vessel filled with a thousand pieces of wood; having sealed the mouth of a crucible joined with the substances for sealing,
one should place smaller vessels below and half-vessels above.
This is declared to be the gajapuṭa, renowned as the best of all puṭas.
A puṭa performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one aratni is called vārāha;
when the excavation measures one vitasti, it is described as the kaukkuṭa puṭa.
In a pit measuring sixteen finger-breadths in depth, a "cock's nest" (*kaukkuṭa-puṭa*) is formed for someone;
indeed, that which is given as a "nest" in a pit with eight forest stones is called a "pigeon's nest" (*kapota-puṭa*) by those expert in *puṭa* techniques. (28–29)

Dried and powdered cow dung, trampled by the hooves of cows within a pen, is known as *gobara*; it is declared the most excellent for the preparation of mercury (*rasa*). Where a *puṭa* (burial) is administered using *gobara* placed inside a large vessel, [it is considered superior].
That is declared by physicians to be the *gobarapuṭa* for the ash of mercury (31).
One should place a crucible in the center of a large vessel filled with husks;
having applied fire, one should seal the vessel—that is called *bhāṇḍapuṭa* (32).
In a vessel one span deep, with a small jar placed in the middle and filled with sand up to the neck of the jar,
the medicine contained within that jar is heated there by means of fire. 33.
This is indeed known by the wise as the *bālukāyantra* (sand-oven apparatus).
Having bound the medicinal mercury onto an excellent triple-layered birch bark,
one should then firmly tie the mercury-pouch to a wooden post with a cord.
Having secured the medicine suspended within a sealed full pitcher, one should ignite a fire from below according to the sequence prescribed for each case;
this is indeed declared to be the "swing apparatus" (dolāyantra), which is also known as "sweating" (svedana). 36.

Having placed the substance to be sweated inside a cloth tied over the mouth of a water-pot and having covered it, that apparatus in which it is cooked is known as *svedana* (the sweating apparatus). 37.
One should place mercury in a lower pot and [place another] upon its opening.
Having properly sealed the mouth of the lower vessel with soft clay (38),
and having poured water into the upper vessel, one should carefully place them on the hearth and kindle a fire beneath them for five praharas (39).
Then, once it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract the excellent mercury from the apparatus;
this is called the "Vidyādhara" apparatus by those who know it. (40) One should place the crucible containing the mercury into a pit filled entirely with sand.
One should cover the apparatus named *bhūdhara* with glowing stones;

the apparatus known as *ḍamaru* consists of that [same type of stone] with its mouth sealed by a pot. [The stone should be] heavy, unctuous, soft, white, and capable of withstanding burning and cutting.
Rich in color, clear like the moon, bright, possessing nine qualities, and auspicious—[such is the pure silver]. 43.
Hard, artificial, rough, red, with yellowish spots, light, and destroyed by burning, cutting, or hammering—silver described thus is declared to be defective. 44.
One should heat the leaves made into plates over a fire of *tāra* (silver) and,
when they are thoroughly heated, pour them three times each into oil, buttermilk, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), cow’s urine, and the decoction of *kulattha* beans. 45.
In this way, the purification of silver leaves is accomplished.

However, impure silver causes burning, acts as an obstruction, diminishes vigor and strength, robs the body of nourishment, and spreads diseases; therefore, one should perform its purification. 46–47.
One part of *tālaka* (orpiment) should be ground for one *yāma* with some acid;
with that [paste], one should coat three parts of silver leaves. Having placed them in a crucible and sealed it, one should roast them with thirty pieces of *vanopala* (fire-clay).
Having extracted it again, having added *tāla*, and having sealed it in a crucible (*puṭa*), one should cook it;
thus, by fourteen such *puṭas*, silver is reduced to ash.
[49] One should grind honey with the milky sap of *snuhī* and smear [the crucible] with that. [50]
A wise person should enclose silver leaves in the manner of a *tālaka* (copper sulfate) within fourteen folds; the silver is thus reduced to ash.
Silver is cooling, astringent, sweet in its post-digestive taste (*pāka*), and laxative.
It stabilizes the vital breath (*vāyu*), is unctuous, scraping, and conquers *vāta* and *pitta*;
it certainly and swiftly destroys diseases such as urinary disorders (*prameha*).
[Gold] resembles the *japā* flower, is unctuous, heavy, and capable of withstanding great weight.
Copper abandoned by iron-nāga (iron-ore) is recommended for the process of killing [the mercury].
Copper that is black, rough, overly translucent, white, unable to withstand heat, or mixed with iron-nāga is proclaimed to be defective. 53–54.
One should heat copper leaves that have been made into plates over a fire and repeatedly pour them while still hot into oil, buttermilk, sour gruel (kāñjika),
cow’s urine, and the decoction of horse gram (kulattha)— three times each.
In this way, the purification of copper leaves is accomplished.

(56) There is one defect in poison, but when copper is impure, there are eight: delusion, vomiting, purgation, sweating, excessive moisture, fainting, burning sensation, and likewise loss of appetite. (57)
They say that poison is not truly poison; it is copper that is called poison.
There is one defect in [ordinary] poison, but eight defects are proclaimed in copper.
Having made thin copper leaves, the wise man should subject them to sweating.

Then, one should place [the substance] in a mortar with lemon juice for three days; having added mercury amounting to one-fourth part, one should grind it for one watch (yāma) with lemon juice. Then, having extracted it, one should smear the leaves with double that amount.
Then, having rubbed sulphur with sour [juice], one should form a ball from it;
subsequently, having ground either *mīnākṣī*, *cāṅgerī*, or *punarnavā*,
one should smear the exterior of that ball with that paste to a thickness of two finger-breadths.
Having placed that *golaka* in a vessel, one should seal it with a shallow bowl (62). Then, having filled [the space] with sand, ashes, salt, and water,
and having applied a seal (*mudrā*) on the mouth of the vessel, one should subsequently cook it over a furnace (63).

Having properly heated it with fire in gradual increments for four watches (yāmas) until it is cool to the touch, one should remove it and grind it with the juice of *śūraṇa*. After one watch, that ball (*golaka*) should be placed inside a *śūraṇa* root.
A coating of clay, one thumb's breadth thick, should be applied on all sides;
once placed in a *gajapuṭa* [furnace] and heated, it certainly becomes dead (calcined).
It [removes] vomiting, purging, dizziness, exhaustion, and loss of appetite.
It never causes burning, sweating, or excessive moisture.

Copper is astringent, sweet, slightly bitter, and sour; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), strengthening to the body, and it subdues pitta and kapha. It is cold in potency, healing for wounds, light, and scraping (lekhana).
It cures anemia, hemorrhoids, fever, skin diseases, cough, dyspnea, consumption, chronic rhinitis, acid gastritis, edema, worms, and colic; the wise call this a mild tonic.
However, there is one defect in mercury: if it is not properly processed, it becomes like copper.
Burning sensation, perspiration, loss of appetite, fainting, moisture, purging, vomiting, and vertigo [arise from its improper use]. 70.
Realgar (gairika) is of two kinds: *khuraka* and *miśraka*;
of these two, *khuraka* is considered superior, while *miśraka* is regarded as harmful. 71.

Indeed, tin (vaṅga) that is impure certainly brings about convulsions and tremors, leprosy, abdominal tumors, skin diseases, colic, edema due to wind (vāta-śotha), anemia, urinary disorders, fistula-in-ano,
a multitude of blood disorders resembling poison, consumption, difficult dysurias, and diseases arising from phlegm (kaphaja). (72)
Lead also produces the aforementioned disorders, such as urinary calculi, fistula-in-ano, and scrotal enlargement (mūṣkara).
Tin and lead, having been heated and melted, should be poured [into water] three times each; thus their purification occurs, and they should likewise be processed three times with cow's milk.
Having ground the powder of the bark of *ciñcā* and *aśvattha* in an earthen vessel with tin (*vaṅga*) until it is dissolved, one should then stir it with a ladle;
after two watches (six hours), the tin is transformed into ash. 75.
Then, having added talc equal in weight to the ashes, one should grind it with acid;
thereafter, having cooked it in a *gajapuṭa* fire, one should again grind it with acid.
Then, adding talc in the tenth part [of the total weight], one should cook it for one *yāma*.
Thus, tin (vaṅga) becomes killed when cooked in ten layers;
it is light, laxative, and dry. It destroys leprosy, urinary disorders, phlegm, and worms, as well as anemia and asthma; it slightly increases bile and is beneficial for the eyes.
Just as a lion destroys a herd of elephants, so too does vaṅga destroy the entire class of urinary disorders;
it certainly bestows physical well-being, strength of the senses, and nourishment upon a man.
(79) Yaśada and girija are its [impurities]; they are used for purification and killing.
Indeed, its qualities should be understood as being like those of tin; now I shall enumerate them:
it is a white metal (yasada), laxative, bitter, cooling, and removes phlegm and bile.
It is highly beneficial for the eyes and destroys urinary disorders, anemia, and asthma. (80–81)
Its natural defects have been demonstrated as being like those of tin, and its purification has likewise been described by physicians of old;
it is repeatedly rubbed with the juice of betel and smeared with realgar paste. 82.
With thirty-two layers, the mercury (nāga) becomes ash that cannot be reconstituted.
One should add the powder of the bark of the *aśvattha* and *ciñcā* trees in a fourth part; when the mercury has been liquefied in an earthen vessel, it is stirred with an iron ladle. 83–84.
In one watch (yāma), it becomes ash; an equal amount of realgar (manaḥśilā) should be ground with sour gruel (kāñjika).
Having ground both together, one should cook them using the "elephant-seal" (gajapuṭa) method.
When cooled by its own heat, it should again be ground with realgar and sour gruel.
One should cook it again using two śarāvas; thus, by sixty puṭas, death [of the impurities] occurs.

Lead (sīsa) should be known as possessing the qualities of tin (vaṅga), and it is especially a destroyer of urinary disorders. Mercury (nāga), however, bestows strength equal to a hundred times its own weight, destroys disease, and extends life.
When consumed continuously, it kindles the digestive fire, increases the power of desire, and destroys death;
however, impure iron causes lameness, leprosy, disease, and death, as well as heart disease, abdominal pain, colic, urinary stones, the provocation of various ailments, and nausea. 88–89.
One should heat iron leaves that have been made into plates in fire, and pour them,
while they are repeatedly heated, three times each into oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, cow urine, and the decoction of *kulattha* beans. (90)
In this way, the purification of iron leaves is thoroughly accomplished.
(91) Having ground pure iron powder with the juices of *pātālagaruḍī*, one should roast it in fire; thus, one should administer three such roastings. (92)
One should give three *puṭas* with the juice of *kuṭhāra-cchinnikā* for the maiden [iron];
then one should give six *puṭas*. In this way, the sharp [iron] will die.
One should then add cinnabar (*darada*) in the twelfth part of the powder of the sharp [iron].
One should rub it with the juices of *kanyākā* and *drāvī*, then subject it to a *puṭa* (roasting) twice;
thus, by seven such *puṭas*, one attains the death [destruction] of the iron powder.
This sequence for the killing of iron has been truly experienced by the lords of yoga. There is another method for the killing of iron.
Now, King Rāmarāja speaks out of a spirit of curiosity:

Having added twice the amount of fragrance relative to the *sūtaka*, one should prepare a collyrium (*kajjalī*); then, one should grind an equal quantity of iron powder with the juices of the *kanyā* plant. (95–96)

Then, having formed a pill from the pair of *yāmas* and placed it in a copper vessel, the wise one should hold it over heat and cover it with castor leaves (97). After three *yāmas*, it becomes warm; he should then place it upon a heap of grain.
Having placed a shallow bowl on top, one should remove it at the end of three days;
then, having ground it and strained it through a cloth, it will become water-soluble. Likewise, having ground a leaf of pomegranate with four times its amount of water—99.

Having ground that iron powder with its own juice, one should soak it and dry it in the sun; one should then roast it in a *puṭa* in this manner repeatedly for one hundred and twenty-one times— it dies [is neutralized], of this there is no doubt.
In this manner, one should also process all metals, such as gold and the rest.
(101) Iron is bitter, laxative, cold, astringent, sweet, heavy, parching, rejuvenating, beneficial for the eyes, scraping, and increases wind; it conquers [diseases]. (102)
It cures phlegm, bile, artificial poison, colic, swelling, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, anemia, obesity, urinary disorders, worms, and skin diseases; its dregs (ash) have the same effect.
Starting from a single *guñjā* seed up to nine *raktikās*, [it is administered].
A person should consume iron for as long as is necessary according to their specific doshas and digestive fire (104).
One who uses iron should avoid pumpkin, sesame oil, black gram, black mustard, liquor, and sour juices (105).
All metals, such as gold and others, when smeared with the juice of *śilājatu* and the milk of *arka*, are killed by twelve *puṭa* applications; this is as true as the word of the Guru.
[106] It causes weak digestion, severe loss of strength, constipation, and eye diseases along with leprosy.

One should likewise prepare *mālā* and that which begins with *vraṇa*; indeed, honey is impure [in this context]. One should cook three parts of honey with one part of rock salt using the juices of *mātuluṅga* or *jambīra*. 107–108.
One should stir it in an iron vessel until the vessel becomes bright red; then it attains complete purification and becomes *svarṇamākṣika*.
Alternatively, having rubbed it with a decoction of *kulattha* or with oil, one should roast it in a *puṭa*.
Gold pyrite (svarṇamākṣika) is killed with buttermilk or goat’s urine.
The defects found in gold pyrite should be understood to apply likewise to silver pyrite (tāramākṣika);
therefore, its purification is described here for the purpose of neutralizing those defects.
One should macerate [the substance] for a day with the juices of *karkoṭī* and *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and with those of *jambīra*, in the intense heat of the sun; thus it certainly becomes pure and stainless.
Having rubbed it with a decoction of horse gram (*kulattha*) or with oil, one should roast it in a closed crucible (*puṭa*).
Or, by means of goat's urine and death [of the impurities], it attains the state of *tāra* (silver) and *mākṣika* (pyrite).
Not only are the qualities of gold and silver considered to belong to those born of the Tāpī river, but through contact with other substances, other qualities also arise in them. 113–114.
Honey is sweet and bitter, beneficial for the voice, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative (rasāyana).

It is good for the eyes and subdues pain in the bladder, skin diseases, anemia, urinary disorders, poisoning, abdominal enlargements, hemorrhoids, swelling, consumption, itching, and the three humors (tridoṣa). (115–116)
One should grind Tuttha with the excrement of a cat and a pigeon;
then, having added one-tenth part of Ṭaṅkaṇa, one should cook it in a small *puṭa*. Thereafter, for the purification of the Tuttha, a *puṭa* should be applied with curd and a *puṭa* with honey. 117.

Tutthaka is pungent, alkaline, astringent, emetic, light, scraping, fissuring, cold, beneficial for the eyes, and removes phlegm and bile; it destroys poison, urinary stones, skin diseases, and itching, and kharpura is considered to possess these same qualities. (118–119)
One should heat sheets of bell-metal that have been made into leaflets over a fire;
while they are repeatedly heated, one should quench them three times each in oil, buttermilk, sour gruel, cow’s urine, and in a decoction of horse gram (kulattha). 120.
In this way, the purification of bell-metal and brass is thoroughly accomplished.
(121) One should grind sulphur with the milk of the *arka* plant and smear it [upon] pure sheets of bell-metal that have been repeatedly washed with acidic juices. (122)
Then, having placed it in a crucible, one should cook it with a "gajapuṭa" (elephant-seal) firing;
thus, after two such firings, bell-metal and brass are certainly killed.
Bell-metal is astringent, sharp, hot, scraping, clear, and laxative.
Bell-metal (Guru) is beneficial for the eyes, dry, and is an excellent remover of Kapha and Pitta. 124.
Brass (Rītikā), however, is dry, slightly bitter, and salty in taste;
it is a purifier, cures anemia, destroys worms, and is not excessively scraping. 125.
Its purification is said by the wise to be achieved through the application of milk and sour gruel (126).
Vermilion (sindūra) is hot; it removes erysipelas, leprosy, itching, and poisons;
it promotes the healing of fractures and cleanses and heals wounds (127).
Iron that is black like the smell of cow's urine, unctuous, soft, heavy, bitter, astringent, and cold is the best of all;
it is found in abundance in the Vindhya mountains and other such places where iron is predominant. 128.
Without that purification, it is useless due to the accumulation of many impurities.
(129) Having brought the *śilājatu* and reduced it to fine pieces, the wise person should place it in very hot water and let it sit for one *yāma*. (130)
Having kneaded it, the wise one should then take the water and filter it through a cloth; having placed it in an earthen vessel, he should keep it in the sun.
Whatever thick substance remains on top, that he should pour into another vessel.
In this manner, having been processed again and again for two months, the *śilājatu* becomes fit for its purpose; when cast into the fire, it becomes like a phallus (*liṅga*),
smokeless, and thus pure, one should employ it in all rites.

Following the specific requirements of the disease and the patient's constitution, one should first macerate the iron [preparation] in water alone that has been washed and dried; thereafter, it should be macerated with decoctions.
The medicinal drug for maceration should be boiled in eight times its quantity of water together with an equal amount of *girija* (red chalk). 134.
When that decoction has been reduced to one-fourth its original volume, strained, and made lukewarm, one should add the mountain-born mineral (gairika).
Once it has reached a state of uniform consistency and dried, one should again throw it into the liquid;
in this manner, it should be processed with its respective decoctions for seven times.

Then, for one who has been lubricated and purified, one should administer ghee prepared with bitter herbs for three days; likewise, for three days each, one should use [ghee] processed with *girija*, with the decoction of the "three fruits" (*phalatrika*), with *paṭolī*, and with *madhuka*. 137.
Thus, *śilāja* (bitumen) becomes extremely beneficial for the body.
It should be properly infused with iron, nimba, guḍūcī, ghee, and barley to ward off the defects caused by *santānikā*, insects, moths, stinging insects, and corrupted medicinal herbs. 138–139.
In the hot season, when joined with the heat of the sun, on a cloudless and windless day,
one should place four vessels made of black iron on a level patch of ground in the sunlight; having focused one's attention there,
and having obtained the best *śilājatu*, one should cast it into a vessel along with twice as much water.

Having added that [substance] heated and boiled until it is warm, one should purify it by kneading it properly (141). Then, whatever black portion rises to the top like a film when heated by the rays of the sun, one should place that in another vessel and pour lukewarm water over it (142).

Furthermore, when the water has been moved from that vessel to another, and then from that vessel to yet another, until it is completely pure—so that all the black impurity has gone downward—then one should discard both that water and the impurity; thus the water becomes pure like bitumen (*śilājatu*). 143.
Śilājatu is known to be bitter, pungent, and hot in potency, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
It is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), a vehicle for other medicinal properties (yogavāhi), and cures phlegm disorders, urinary disorders (meha), stones,
gravel, dysuria, wasting, asthma, edema, hemorrhoids, and anemia.
It cures vātarakta, as well as leprosy, epilepsy, and abdominal enlargements.
(145) One should fill an earthen vessel with various grains obtained as available, stripped of their husks and mixed with water, and preserve it until it reaches an acidic state. (146)
In the midst of that are bhṛṅgarāja, muṇḍī, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā, mīnākṣī, sarpākṣī, sahadevī, śatāvarī,
triphalā, girikarṇī, haṃsapādī, and citraka.

Having pounded it together with its roots, one should place it as available into a previously used sour vessel; this is known as *dhānyāmlaka*. One should employ it everywhere in processes such as sudation for the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*).
In its absence, one should employ fermented rice gruel (āmlamāranāla) or sour gruel (trayūṣaṇa).
[One should also use] salt, cumin, turmeric, the three myrobalans (triphalā), fresh ginger, mahābalā, nāgabalā, meghanāda, and punarnavā. 149–150.
Take equal parts of *meṣaśṛṅgī*, *citraka*, and *navasāra*;
grind this entire mixture, or each individually, with sour gruel (pūrvāmla). Smear the cloth with this paste to a thickness of one finger-breadth. 151–152.
One should place the mercury (sūta) in the middle of that, seal it, and cook it for three days in a dolāyantra combined with acidic substances; thus the mercury becomes "sweated" (svedita).
[Then one adds] radish, fire-citron, rock salt, trikaṭu, ginger, and mustard.

One should add the medicinal substances individually, each in a quantity equal to one-sixteenth part of the mercury (154). Regarding liquids for which no measure is specified, this is the measure established by the wise.
Having placed the mercury in these [substances] wrapped in cloth, one should immerse them in sour gruel (155).
The wise practitioner should subject the mercury to sudation for one day using a *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus).
Through sudation, the mercury becomes intense, and through rubbing (*mardana*), it becomes perfectly pure.
First, the mercury should be rubbed with brick powder and lime powder. (156)
The mercury, having been rubbed for three days with curd, jaggery, rock salt, black mustard, soot from a house,
decoctions prepared from a maiden, red safflower, and white mustard mixed with *bṛhatī*, as well as with the three fruits (*phalatrika*), is liberated from all impurities. (157–158)

One should grind mercury seven times with a soup prepared from *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *vandhyākanda*, the two types of *kṣudrā*, *citraka*, *ūrṇā*, *niśā*, alkali (*kṣāra*), *kanyā*, *arka*, and *kanakadrava*. (159)
Thus, thoroughly congealed, the mercury abandons even the seven coverings (kañcukas).

Having reduced it to a state of "destroyed-powder" (naṣṭapiṣṭī) by means of *mayūragrīva* and *tāpya*, one should perform the upward sublimation (*ūrdhvapātana*) of the mercury in the *vidyādhara* apparatus. 160–161.
Having prepared a "rasa" (liquid extract) from triphalā, śigru, and śikhin, combined with lavaṇa and surasā, one should form it into a paste and smear it onto the upper vessel.
Then, one should cause it to undergo downward precipitation using heated stones placed beneath it. 162.
In the apparatus known as Bhūdhara, the mercury (sūta) is then purified;
when it has been cleansed by means of processes such as sweating (svedana), it then performs its functions and may be employed in all ritual operations.
The maiden of the house (gṛhakanyā) removes impurity; triphalā, agni, and citraka destroy poison.

Therefore, one should cause [the substance] to be thoroughly saturated seven times with these mixed together. (165) Using decoctions made from kumārikā, citraka, red mustard, and combined with vṛhatī—
The mercury, having been processed for three days even with the three fruits, is liberated from all impurities.
One should grind the mercury for one day with *kumārī* and the powders of the night-blooming flowers; thus tormented, the mercury certainly becomes emasculated (*ṣaṇḍha*). 166–167.
Sweated with a decoction of many medicinal herbs, it becomes strong;
sweated with *sarpākṣī*, *ciñcikā*, *vandhyā*, *bhṛṅga*, and *abdhi*, it then becomes strong;
thereafter, sweated with the juices of *pāvakadrā*, it shall become exceedingly radiant. (168)
One should grind equal parts of dhūmasāra, rasa, torī, gandhaka, and navasādara with acidic juices for one prahara; then,
having placed them inside a glass flask, it should be sealed with a soft cloth seal.
Having smeared the face all around with mudrā, one should let it dry.
(170) One should place the *kūpī* (small jar) inside a perforated cauldron (*piṭharī*) below, and having filled the cauldron up to the neck of the *kūpī* with sand. (171)
Having placed [the vessel] on the hearth, one should kindle a fire beneath it very slowly;
thereafter, one should gradually increase the flame slightly beyond that.
In this manner, after twelve *yāmas*, the excellent mercury is killed.
One should break [the vessel] once it has cooled to the touch of one's own body; one should discard that sulphur which has gone upwards, and take the mercury (sūta) situated below, which is now dead.
One should employ that [mercury) in all operations according to the appropriate dosage and suitable adjuncts. 173–174.

One should prepare a pair of crucibles from the seeds of *apāmārga*; within their joined cavity, one should place mercury mixed with the milk of *malayū*. [Then add] the flowers of *droṇapuṣpī*, *viḍaṅga*, and *arimeda*. 175.
Having applied this powder both below and above, the seal (mudrā) is placed;
one should then properly position that globule within a pair of earthen crucibles (mṛnmūṣā-sampuṭa) and heat it.
In this way, by means of a single firing (puṭa), the mercury is reduced to ash.
That [substance] should be applied in the proper place, in the proper measure, and according to the prescribed method (178).
One should slightly grind the juice with the milks of the *kākodumbarikā* and rub it with *hiṅgu* using that milk; then, one should prepare a pair of crucibles (179).
Having cast the mercury into that crucible, one should apply the seal;
then, holding that globule, the wise man should heat it in a superior pair of earthen crucibles by means of the *gajapuṭa* method, whereby the mercury is reduced to ashes. (180)
Rubbed with the juices of *nāgavallī* and filled with the core of *karkoṭī* root,
the mercury (*sūta*) cooked in a crucible made of two earthen lids indeed attains the state of ash (is reduced to *bhasma*).
In that process, a brief purification of the mercury must be performed.
The wise practitioner should prepare each of the following equal to pure mercury:
red ochre, brick, chalk, rock crystal, and rock salt; as well as anthill earth, alkaline salt, and the clay used for glazing earthenware.
Having pulverized all these together, one should also purify them with a cloth. (183) One should grind the mercury combined with these powders for the duration of one *yāma*;
then, that mercury along with the powder should be cast into the middle of a crucible. (184)
One should place another vessel of equal size upon the mouth of that vessel;
one should seal the mouths of these two with cloth and pounded clay.
Having dried it thoroughly, one should seal it again, and having dried it again, one should seal it once more.
Having dried it thoroughly with the *mudrā*, one should place that vessel upon the stove.
One should provide a continuous fire for four days, and one must guard that apparatus with effort day and night over the glowing embers. 186–187.
One should slowly open the apparatus and take the mercury contained in the upper vessel;
it is as pure as camphor and possesses excellent qualities. This [mercury] should be combined with divine flowers, sandalwood, musk, and saffron.
By eating it, one instantly removes the disease of syphilis along with its complications (189).
The consumer of *rasakarpūra* constantly attains the brilliance of fire, nourishment, virility, and great strength; he delights a hundred women (190).
The physician should take four parts of purified mercury, one part of purified sulfur, and an equal amount of artificial sulfur; or indeed, half as much purified sulfur as there is mercury. (191)
One should prepare a kajjalikā from those two and grind it for one day (verse 192).
Together with clay and cloth, one should pound it with great effort;
likewise, one should properly coat a glass flask (kācakūpī) three times (verse 193).
Having dried the clay, one should place the soot (kajjalikā) inside a flask;
having placed that flask in a sand-bath apparatus (bālukāyantra), one should cook the mercury.
One should apply continuous fire for four days. 194.
One should take the juice that is attached to the upper part and resembles vermilion (195).
Thus is the vermilion-juice mercury; it destroys worms and leprosy, bestows victory, improves vision, and is a vitalizing elixir.
It removes death, possesses great heroism, is a vehicle for yoga, and dispels fever (196).
It bestows memory, vigor, and beauty; it is aphrodisiac, promotes growth, and increases the bodily constituents.
It destroys impotence, is heroic, moves through the sky, and is the supreme bestower of spiritual accomplishments (197).

Mercury (pārada) is traditionally held to be the destroyer of all diseases; it possesses six tastes, acts as a vehicle for all medicinal formulations, and is proclaimed to consist of the five elements. Therefore, it shines forth with a multitude of such qualities.
When combined with whatever specific formulation is required for a particular disease, it cures that very disease.

The king of rasas (mercury) destroys that disease in men, elephants, and horses. (199) Cinnabar, processed with sheep’s milk and the group of sour substances (amlavarga) seven times with great care, certainly attains purity. (200)
Hiṅgula is bitter, astringent, and pungent; it destroys eye diseases, removes phlegm and bile, and cures nausea, itching, fever, jaundice, splenic disorders, āma-vāta, and artificial poisons (gara).
[It should be processed] for one prahara with lime juice or with the juice of nimba leaves. 201.
Having rubbed the cinnabar, one should cause it to fall upwards according to the method for mercury;
there, one should take the excellent *rasa* adhering to the upper vessel.
Indeed, that purified *rasa* alone should be employed in all operations. (202–203)

Impure sulfur causes leprosy, diseases of the bile, and vertigo; it destroys virility, strength, and complexion. Therefore, purified [sulfur] is employed. (204) Having placed it in an iron vessel, one should heat the ghee over a fire.
One should throw an equal amount of powdered sulphur into the heated ghee (205).
Seeing that the sulphur has melted, one should pour it onto a thin cloth so that,
having flowed out from the cloth, it all falls into the midst of milk.
Thus, that purified sulphur becomes suitable for all medicinal applications.
(206) Sulphur is pungent and bitter in taste, hot in potency, astringent, and laxative;
it increases bile, is pungent in its post-digestive effect, and conquers itching, erysipelas, and parasites. (207)
It is an elixir (rasāyana) that destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), consumption (kṣaya), splenic disorders, and disorders of phlegm and wind.

However, impure abhraka causes various pains to men and may produce skin disease, consumption, and jaundice (pāṇḍu); it also causes unbearable pain in the heart and flanks, being heavy and detrimental to the digestive fire and the heart.

One should heat black mica (kṛṣṇābhraka) in fire and then throw it into milk; having broken its leaves apart, one should then saturate it for eight yāmas with the juices of rice-gruel and sour gruel—thus the mica becomes purified. 210

Having prepared the *dhānyābhraka* and dried it, one should then grind it with the milky sap of the *arka* plant for one day in a mortar; one should then form it into the shape of a disc (*cakrākāra*),
wrap it with *arka* leaves, and cook it properly in a *gajapuṭa*.
It should be rubbed again and cooked again, seven times over and over.
Then, likewise, three *puṭa* applications should be given using a decoction of *vaṭa* roots.
It is killed; there is no doubt about this. It may be employed in all ritual operations.
One should cook an equal amount of ghee with mercury-saturated mica (mṛtābhra) in an iron vessel;
once the ghee is digested, that mica should be employed in all formulations.
Then, having bound the mica mixed with a quarter-part of śāli rice within a blanket, [one should proceed].
One should let it stay in water for three nights; once it is moistened, one should rub it with the hands.
That which has fallen from the blanket, being fine and free from sand, is called *dhānyābhra* (grain-like mica), for the purpose of the alchemical transformation (*māraṇa*) of mica.
Abhraka (mica) is astringent, sweet, very cooling, promotes longevity, and increases the bodily tissues (dhātus).
It destroys the three doṣas, as well as ulcers, urinary disorders, skin diseases, splenic enlargement, tumors, poisons, and worms.
It cures diseases, strengthens the body, and brings about an increase in virility.
When consumed, *mṛtābhra* constantly delights one with a hundred women endowed with youth,
produces long-lived sons possessed of power equal to that of lions,
and utterly removes the fear of death. (218)
Impure *tālaka* causes consumption, reduces lifespan, and produces phlegm, wind, and urinary disorders; it causes fever, eruptions, and contraction of the limbs; therefore, one should purify it.
(219) Having broken the *tālaka* into small pieces, one should boil that powder in sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
Then, for one *yāma*, it should be cooked in the *dolāyantra* with the juices of *kūṣmāṇḍaja*;
for one *yāma* in sesame oil, and for one *yāma* in water of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Thus, cooked in the apparatus for four *yāmas*, the *tālaka* becomes purified. (220–221)
One should grind pure *sadala* and *tālaka* with the juice of *punarnavā* in a mortar for one day, and thereafter purify them; then,
one should fill half of a vessel with the alkali of *punarnavā*.
Having formed a ball there, one should fill that vessel again with the same [substance] up to the neck;
one should place a lid over its mouth,
set the pot upon the stove, and gradually increase the fire.
One should administer the fire [of digestion] for five days with intervals in between;
in this way, that *tāla* dies. Its dose is one *raktikā*, and one should employ various adjuncts (*anupāna*) as appropriate. 225–226.
Haritāla (orpiment) is pungent, unctuous, astringent, and hot; it removes poison, itching, skin diseases, oral ailments, blood disorders, phlegm, bile, and hair loss.
Tālaka (realgar) likewise removes diseases and wards off leprosy, death, and fever.
When purified, it produces luster, increases virility, and likewise bestows longevity.
(228) There is indeed a distinction between *tālaka* and *manaḥśilā*;
*tālaka* is extremely yellow, whereas *manaḥśilā* is red. (229)
Realgar (manaḥśilā) certainly weakens the strength of a person if it is not purified;
indeed, by binding the impurities, it causes retention of urine, gravel, and the disease of painful micturition (kṛcchra).
One should boil realgar for three days in goat’s urine using a *dolāyantra* (swing-oven).
If processed seven times with the bile of a goat, it becomes completely purified.
(231) Realgar is heavy, described as being reddish-brown, hot, scraping, pungent, bitter, and unctuous;
it destroys poison, dyspnea, cough, spirits, phlegm, and catarrh. (232)
One should cook *rasaka* for seven days in human urine and cow urine using a *dolāyantra*; it will then become purified and may be employed in various applications.
*Kharpara* is pungent, alkaline, astringent, emetic, and light.

Sūryāvarta, Vajrakanda, Kadalī, and Devadālikā are considered excellent for scraping, causing emesis, cooling, being beneficial for the eyes, removing phlegm and bile, and destroying poison, urinary stones, skin diseases, and itching. (234)
Śigru, kośātakī, vandhyā, kākamācī, and bālaka—

[one should take] these together with a single decoction of them, along with the three alkalis (trikṣāra), salts, and the group of sour substances (amlavarga), and diligently macerate [the mercury] for one day. 235–236.
Then, the wise one should cook it for one day in that liquid within a dolāyantra (swinging apparatus).
In this way, all those secondary minerals (*uparasa*) mentioned are purified:
namely, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *gairika*, conch-shell, *kāsīsa*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Blue antimony, varieties of mother-of-pearl, small shells, and cowries—
these, when steamed with the juice of *jambīra* and washed with lukewarm water, attain purity and may be employed by physicians for the successful accomplishment of medicinal formulations. (238–239)

If impure, it causes disorders of the *vajra*, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), pain in the sides, jaundice, and lameness; therefore, one should purify it and then kill it. One should cook it in a *dolāyantra* in a decoction of horse gram (*kulattha*) and *kodo* millet (*kodrava*).
The *vajra* placed within the tuber of the tigress (*vyāghrī*) becomes purified after three days.
Having taken the *vajra* on an auspicious day, one should place it inside the tuber of the tigress, smear it with the dung of a buffalo, and cook it over a fire of dried cow-dung (*kārīṣa*). 241–242.
During the three watches of the night, one should sprinkle it with horse urine for a fourth watch at the end of the night and cook it in this manner; after seven nights, it becomes purified.
One should throw [the substance] into a decoction of horse gram (kulattha) combined with asafoetida and rock salt.
Heated again and again twenty-one times, the diamond (vajra) becomes ashes.

Having ground together the horn of a ram, the bone of a serpent, the back of a tortoise, *amlavetasa*, and the tusk of a rabbit in equal parts with the milk of a *vajrī* plant, one should form a ball (*golaka*).
Having placed a vajra in its midst, it indeed dies when smelted.
When consumed, it bestows longevity, nourishment, strength, vigor, complexion, and happiness; there is no doubt that the dead vajra destroys all diseases. (246–247)

One should purify all gems like diamonds and likewise destroy them; hear now the qualities of those that have been purified and destroyed. (248) Gems are cooling by their potency (*vīrya*) and astringent-sweet in taste (*rasa*).
They are beneficial for the eyes, act as purgatives, are strengthening, and are antidotes to poison; when worn, they are auspicious and even remove the ill effects of planetary influences.
(249) Its leaves resemble those of the *sindhuvāra*, and its shape is like that of the *vatsanābha* [poison].
That on whose side there is no growth of a tree is called *vatsanābha*.
Having kept the poison in cow’s urine for three days, it becomes purified;
likewise, it should be held in a cloth soaked with red mustard oil. 250–251.
Whatever qualities are attributed to poison would be diminished by purification;
therefore, one should employ poison only after it has been purified during its application.
Poison is said to be life-taking (*prāṇahara*), pervasive (*vyavāyi*), and diffusive (*vikāśi*).

Agni (ginger) removes vāta and kapha, acts as a vehicle for other drugs, and induces exhilaration. That same substance, when properly prepared with appropriate adjuncts, bestows life and serves as a rejuvenative (rasāyana);
it is a supreme vehicle for other drugs, conquers vāta and śleṣman, and cures the disorders of the three humors combined (sannipāta).
The milky sap of *arka*, the milky sap of *snuhī*, *lāṅgalī*, *karavīraka*,
*guñjā*, *ahiphena*, and *dhattūra*— these are the seven types of secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*).
A medicinal substance loses its potency after a year, even if it retains its original appearance.
Likewise, after two months, the powder loses its potency;
if the pills and electuaries remain deficient for a year, as do the ghee, oils, and other substances for more than four months, they likewise become inferior. (256–257)
Ghee that has been cooked for more than a year loses its potency;
however, oil—whether cooked or uncooked—remains effective for a long time and increases in quality. Herbs undergo light digestion and lose their potency after a year.
The ancient *āsavas*, *dhātus*, and *rasas* should be endowed with [excellent] qualities.

Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the purification and killing of *dhātus* and other substances, in the *Paribhāṣādi-prakaraṇa* of the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. 3.
Now begins the fourth chapter, on the procedure for drinking medicated fats (sneha).
Fats are said to be of four kinds: ghee, oil, muscle fat (vasā), and marrow.
A mortal should drink them when the sun has slightly risen. 1.
Fixed and moving substances are said to be of two origins regarding oil:
among fixed substances, sesame oil is best; among moving substances, ghee is best.
A large dose consists of two, three, or four *yamaka-trivṛts*.
One should drink it for three days, four days, five days, or six days;
having observed the humors, the season, age, digestive fire, and strength, the wise physician should administer a small, medium, or large dose of unctuous substance.
Through improper quantity, as well as at the wrong time, and from the consumption of unwholesome food and lifestyle,
oleation (sneha) causes edema, hemorrhoids, drowsiness, excessive sleep, and loss of consciousness.
For one with a stimulated digestive fire, a dose of one pala of oleation should be administered.
For one of medium constitution, it should be three karṣas; for one of inferior constitution, two karṣas. Alternatively, there are three other measures of oil agreed upon by all:
the large dose is digested in a day and night, while the medium dose is digested in a single day.
That which is digested within half a day is known as "mild" (alpā), and it brings about comfort.
The mild dose is digestive, aphrodisiac, and highly recommended when the humors are slightly aggravated.
The medium dose should be known as oleating, nourishing, and a remover of dizziness.

Jyeṣṭhā destroys skin diseases, poisons, insanity, planetary possession, and epilepsy. That dose which is digested when the first watch of the day has passed is praised for kindling the digestive fire in those with few bodily humors.

That dosage which is digested when half the day has passed is aphrodisiac and nourishing; it is highly esteemed when the bodily humors are moderate. That dosage which is digested when the final watch of the day remains...
That quantity should be known as the emulsive dose, which is highly esteemed for those with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas).

Pure ghee should be administered in cases of Pitta; in Vāta, it should be combined with salt; and in cases of excessive Kapha, it should be combined with fire-promoting substances, trikaṭu, and alkali.

The drinking of ghee is recommended for those afflicted by dryness, wounds, or poison; for those suffering from disorders of vāta and pitta; and for those with diminished intellect, memory, and mindfulness.
It is also beneficial for those possessed by worms, abdominal diseases, or wind, and for those with increased phlegm and fat.

Those accustomed to oil should drink oil, as should those seeking firmness; likewise, men who are emaciated by physical exercise, those with depleted semen and blood, those suffering from great pain, and those whose digestive fire, wind, and vital breaths are robust, are considered fit for muscle fat (vasā).
Those of cruel disposition, who endure afflictions, are afflicted by wind, or have a blazing digestive fire,
should drink marrow or ghee, which is beneficial in every respect.
One should drink unctuous substances during the day in the cold season, and at night during the hot season.
When vāta and pitta are predominant, [one should administer] at night; when vāta and kapha are predominant, during the day.

Having observed the relative strength or weakness of the doshas, one should employ oil or ghee for nasal drops (nasya), massage (abhyajjana), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and for the saturation of the head, ears, and eyes. 18–19.

When ghee is used, lukewarm water should be drunk; when oil is used, vegetable broth is recommended; for muscle fat and marrow, one should drink the scum of boiled rice as a pleasant after-drink (anupāna).
This applies even to those who dislike fats, as well as children, the elderly, the delicate, and the emaciated. 20.
During the dry and non-hot seasons, one should have the patient drink [the gruel] with food;
a gruel containing ghee and many sesame seeds, with very few grains of rice, when consumed lukewarm, produces an immediate unctuous effect. 21–22.

Having milked a cow into clarified butter mixed with powdered sugar and kept it in a milking vessel, a person suffering from emaciation should drink the milk; this is an excellent immediate unctuous therapy (snehana).
For one whose unctuous substance does not digest due to improper conduct or excessive quantity—
Or it may cause obstruction, or it may be digested; one should induce vomiting with warm water.
When there is a suspicion of undigested fat (sneha-ajīrṇa), a person should drink warm water;
by that, belching becomes pure and likewise an appetite for food arises.

When the digestive fire of one with a pitta constitution is further sharpened by the intake of unctuous substances, it then excites a violent thirst; for such a person, one should administer cold milk-rice (pāyasa), by which his thirst is pacified. 26

One suffering from indigestion should avoid unctuous substances (sneha), as should those with abdominal enlargement, acute fever, weakness, anorexia, obesity, fainting, urinary disorders, those who have received an enema, those purged, those who have vomited, and those afflicted by thirst or exhaustion. (27)
One should avoid administering [therapies] to a woman who gives birth prematurely, or during inclement weather (28).
Those whose minds are addicted to sweating therapies, purification therapies, wine, women, or physical exercise;
the elderly, children, the emaciated, those with a parched constitution, those with diminished blood, and those with diminished semen—[these should also be avoided]. (29)
For those afflicted by Vāta and those afflicted by Timira (visual disorders), oleation is the supreme remedy. (30) [The signs of successful oleation are:

downward movement of Vāta, stimulated digestive fire, unctuous and non-hardened stools, softness and unctuousness of the limbs, absence of fatigue, cessation of aversion to unctuous substances, and lightness.
When the senses are properly cleansed, [the patient is well]; in the case of excessive unctuousness (snigdha), the opposite occurs.
Aversion to food, salivation, burning in the anus, dysentery, drowsiness, diarrhea, and pallor are the signs of one who has been excessively unctuous. 31–32.
One who is dry should be treated with unctuous substances, and one who is excessively unctuous should be treated with drying measures,
using such things as *śyāmāka* grain, chickpeas, buttermilk, oil-cake, and roasted grain flour. Thus,
one whose digestive fire is kindled, whose bowels are purified, whose tissues are nourished, and whose sense organs are strengthened [attains health].

A person who consumes fats becomes free from wasting diseases, endowed with strength and a healthy complexion, and full of vitality. (34) In the consumption of fats, one should avoid physical exercise, exposure to cold, suppression of natural urges, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, foods that cause internal secretions, and dry foods.
