(35)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the procedure for the administration of medicated oils, in the section beginning with technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) of the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana.
Now begins the fifth chapter, on the procedure for the five purificatory therapies (*pañcakarma*).
First emesis, then purgation, and then unctuous enema—
these are the five procedures (pañcakarma), along with non-unctuous enema and nasal medication;
these should be administered to embodied beings during the autumn, spring, and rainy seasons.

A skilled physician should administer both emesis and purgation to one who is strong, afflicted by an excess of *kapha*, suffering from nausea and other such symptoms, accustomed to emetics, and possessed of a steady mind. (2–3)
It is used in cases of poisoning, disorders of breast milk, weak digestion, elephantiasis, scrotal enlargement, heart disease, skin diseases, erysipelas, urinary disorders, indigestion, and vertigo;
as well as in cases of vidārikā, apacī, cough, asthma, chronic catarrh, and hernia.
In cases of epilepsy, fever, insanity, as well as blood-dysentery;
in inflammations of the nose, palate, and lips; in ear-discharge, epiglottis, and diarrhea; and likewise in diseases of bile and phlegm.

The physician should administer emesis in cases of jaundice and skin diseases. However, one suffering from timira (visual impairment), abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargement (udara), or being emaciated,
nor one who is excessively old, a pregnant woman, one who is obese, or one afflicted by chest wounds, should not be subjected to emesis.
An infant afflicted by intoxication, one who is emaciated, hungry, or has undergone a non-unctuous enema (nirūha);
one suffering from upward movement of wind (udāvarta), upward discharge of blood, difficult vomiting, or pure disorders of vāta;
one with anemia, infested with worms, or whose voice is impaired by vāta—[these should not be given an unctuous enema]. 8–9.
These too should be vomited: those afflicted by indigestion, those suffering from poison, and those overwhelmed by phlegm; they should be made to vomit by drinking a decoction of Madhuka.
One should induce emesis in the delicate, the emaciated, the young, the old, and the timid.
Having caused [the patient] to drink gruel, milk, buttermilk, or curd,
and having provoked the humors (doṣas) of embodied beings by means of unwholesome, phlegm-inducing foods, emesis administered to one who has been oleated and sweated proceeds correctly. 11–12.
In all emetic procedures, rock salt or honey is beneficial;
one should administer an emetic that is loathsome to the patient, while the opposite is prescribed for purgation.
Having boiled one *kuḍava* of the decoction substance in one *āḍhaka* of water, [one should use it].
And one should administer [the remaining] half-portion in emetic therapies. (14) For the drinking of decoctions, nine *prasthas* is proclaimed as the maximum dose;
the middling is said to be six *prasthas*, and the smallest is three *prasthas*. (15)
In emesis, purgation, and likewise in bloodletting,
the wise say that thirteen and a half palas constitute one prastha;
for medicinal pastes (kalka), powders (cūrṇa), and electuaries (avaleha), three palas is the maximum dose.
One should know that two palas is the middling dose, while one pala is the smallest.
In emesis, there should be eight urges; those ending with bile are considered the best, six urges are middling, and four other urges are considered inferior.

One should conquer *kapha* with pungent, sharp, and hot substances, and *pitta* with sweet and cold ones; when *kapha* is combined with *vāyu*, one should conquer it with substances that are very sweet, salty, sour, and hot.
For *kapha*, one should drink long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), *rāṭhaphala*, and rock salt (*sindhu*) with lukewarm water.
In cases of Pitta, one should drink paṭola, vāsā, and nimba with cold water (20).
When afflicted by Kapha and Vāta, one should drink madana with milk.
In the case of indigestion, a wise person should vomit after drinking a little warm water mixed with rock salt (21).
Having administered the emetic, the physician should cause the patient, who is seated on a stool knee-high, to vomit while touching his throat with an eranda stalk.
Excessive salivation, cardiac oppression, skin eruptions, and itching occur when the emesis is improperly performed.
In one who has vomited excessively, thirst, hiccups, eructation, and loss of consciousness occur (23).
Furthermore, the protrusion of the tongue, retraction of the eyes, clenching of the jaw,
vomiting of blood, spitting, and pain in the throat arise (24).
In the case of excessive emesis, one should administer mild purgation.
When the tongue has been forced out by emesis, gargles prepared with unctuous, sour, and salty substances, along with ghee, milk, and meat broth, are beneficial. 25
Other men should eat sour fruits in front of him;

once the [displaced] lens has emerged, one should insert it after coating it with a paste of sesame and grapes (drākṣā). When the eye has turned back, it should be anointed with ghee and pressed very gently.
In the case of *hanumokṣa* (dislocation of the jaw), sudation and nasal medication (*nasya*) are prescribed; these remove phlegm and wind.

One should treat spitting of blood according to the procedure for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic diseases), using the juice of *dhātrī*, *añjana*, *uśīra*, parched rice (*lāja*), and water infused with *candana*.
Having prepared a churned drink (mantha) with ghee, milk, honey, and sugar, one should have it drunk;
by this, thirst and other diseases arising from vomiting are pacified, as well as the cleansing of the heart, throat, and head, along with stimulated digestive fire and lightness of body. 29.

The destruction of *kapha* and *pitta* is the characteristic sign of one who has vomited properly (verse 30). Thereafter, in the afternoon, one should feed the patient— who possesses a stimulated digestive fire— with *mudga*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and *śāli* rice,
along with wholesome meat-broths from wild animals and vegetable soups (verse 31).
Drowsiness, sleep, salivation, foul breath, itching, malabsorption syndrome, and poison—
these never cause affliction to one who has vomited well.
One should likewise avoid undigested food, cold water, physical exercise, and sexual intercourse.
A wise person should avoid oil massages and anger for one day.
Once the patient has been lubricated and sweated, and has undergone emesis, one should properly administer a purgative;
however, in one who has not vomited, the phlegm (kapha) may descend and obstruct the duodenum (grahaṇī).
It may cause weak digestion and heaviness, or produce dysentery; otherwise, one should digest the undigested matter (*āma*) and the phlegm (*valāsa*) by means of digestive (*pācana*) remedies.
During the spring and autumn seasons, for the purification of the body, one should administer purgatives.
On other occasions, when there is urgent business, the wise man should practice purification (śodhana).

One should employ purgation (virecana) in cases of pitta, as well as in diseases arising from āma, in abdominal enlargement (udara), in flatulence (ādhmāna), and especially for the cleansing of the digestive tract (koṣṭhaśuddhi).
The doshas sometimes become aggravated when they have been subdued by fasting (laṅghana) and digestive therapies (pācana);
however, for those that have been purified by cleansing therapies (śodhana), there is no further recurrence.
[This applies except in the case of] a child, an elderly person, one who is excessively oleated, one emaciated by chest wounds, or one overcome by fear.
One who is exhausted, afflicted by thirst, corpulent, pregnant, suffering from acute fever, a woman who has recently given birth, one with weak digestion, one suffering from alcoholism,
one afflicted by a foreign body, and one who is parched— these should not be purged by a wise physician. (39–40)
Those afflicted by chronic fever, those overcome by poison, those suffering from wind-diseases (vāta), fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids,

jaundice, abdominal enlargement, tumors, heart disease, and consumption; those tormented by gynecological disorders, urinary diseases (prameha), abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and ulcers.
Those afflicted with internal hemorrhaging, vomiting, eruptions, cholera, leprosy, and similar ailments;

those suffering from diseases of the ears, nose, head, mouth, anus, and genitals; those tormented by splenic enlargement, edema, and eye diseases; and those afflicted by worms, alkaline poisoning, and disorders of wind (vāta). 42–43.
Men afflicted by colic or suffering from urinary obstruction are considered fit for purgation (44).
One with an abundance of pitta has a soft bowel; one with an abundance of phlegm has a medium bowel;
and one with an abundance of wind is said to have a hard bowel and is difficult to purge (45).
A mild dose is prescribed for a person with a mild digestive tract (koṣṭha), a medium dose for one with a medium tract,
and a sharp dose is considered appropriate for one with a harsh tract, according to substances that are mild, medium, or sharp.
Even those with a mild digestive tract are purged by means of strong drugs, as well as by the milk of a she-goat and castor oil.
A person of moderate temperament is purged by trivṛt, atiktā, and rājavṛkṣa;
a cruel person is purged by the milk of snuhī, hemakṣīrī, dantī, fruits, and so forth.
The maximum dose for purgation consists of thirty urges that end with the elimination of kapha.
Those with twenty urges are called medium, while those with ten urges are said to be inferior.
Two *palas* is declared the best dose for purgatives, one *pala* is medium, and half a *pala* is the smallest dose of decoctions for purgation. 48–49.
One *karṣa* of the paste, bolus, or powder should be taken with honey and ghee as a linctus;
or two *karṣas*, or even one *pala*, depending on the age, disease, and other factors.
(50) In cases where *pitta* is predominant, one should drink the powder of *trivṛt* with a decoction of *drākṣā* and similar substances.

One afflicted by phlegm (kapha) should drink the three pungent spices (vyoṣa) with a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and cow’s urine. A person afflicted by wind (vāta), desiring purgation, should drink the powder of trivṛt, rock salt (saindhava), and ginger (śuṇṭhī) with sour liquids or with the meat broth of wild animals.
Castor oil, when drunk combined with double the amount of a decoction of triphalā or with milk, causes purgation before long.
Trivṛt, kuṭaja seeds, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja [are also used for this purpose]. 53.

The juice of *samṛdvīkā* (grape) mixed with honey is a purgative during the rainy season. During the end of the monsoon, [a purgative consisting of] *trivṛt*, *durālabhā*, *musta*, sugar, *udīcya*, *candana*,
*drākṣā*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*, taken with grape-water, should be administered when it is cool.
In the winter season, one should drink the powder of trivṛt, citraka, pāṭhā, ajājī, sarala, vacā, and hemakṣīrī with warm water.
[One should also take] pippalyādi, nāgara, sindhu, and śyāmā together with trivṛt.
In the cool season and spring, one should lick [the powder] with honey;
in the summer season, a purgative consisting of equal parts *trivṛt* and sugar is used.
Now follows the *abhayādi-modaka*.
Abhayā, marica, śuṇṭhī, viḍaṅga, āmalaka,
pippalī, pippalīmūla, tvak, patra, and musta—
these should be in equal parts, while dantī should be three times that amount. 59.
Trivṛt is known here to be eightfold [in quantity], and sugar sixfold;
having made boluses with honey, each weighing one karṣa in measure, one should eat them one by one in the morning and drink cold water afterwards. 60–61.
A person continues to purge only as long as they do not consume anything warm;
one should always remain unrestrained in matters of drink, food, and recreation. [This cures] irregular fever, weak digestion, anemia, cough, and fistula-in-ano. 62.
It cures leprosy, skin diseases, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, goiters,
swellings, and vertigo; it also treats burning sensations, splenic disorders, urinary diseases, consumption, eye ailments, wind-related diseases, flatulence, dysuria, and calculi.
One should conquer pain in the back, sides, thighs, hips, calves, and abdomen;
the wise person should avoid oil massage and anger for one day. By constant practice, one may even destroy premature graying of the hair.
For these are indeed *abhayāmodaka* pills, known as the best of elixirs (66).
Having drunk the purgative, the wise man should sprinkle his eyes with cold water, smell some fragrant scent, and then habitually use betel leaf (67).
Staying in a windless place, one should neither suppress natural urges nor lie down;
one should never touch cold water, but should repeatedly drink lukewarm water.
Just as the wind departs after vomiting out phlegm, drugs, and bile, [so does the disease depart]. 68.
Through proper purgation, the impurity (mala), bile (pitta), and the medicine (bheṣaja) should likewise be expelled along with the phlegm (kapha).
In one who has been inadequately purged, there occurs stiffness at the navel, pain from abdominal colic,
obstruction of feces and flatus, itching, circular eruptions (maṇḍala), and heaviness.
Burning sensation, loss of appetite, flatulence, giddiness, and vomiting arise;
having first treated that with digestive and unctuous therapies, one should then administer a purgative after the patient has been lubricated.
By this, his complications subside, his digestive fire becomes kindled, and lightness of body occurs. 71
From excessive purgation, there may occur fainting, prolapse of the rectum, and colic;
there may be an excess of *kapha*, and blood resembling the wash-water of meat, or like fat, or appearing like water, is discharged during purging. (72)
Having sprinkled his body with cold water and rice-water,
one should induce mild emesis using cold water mixed with honey;
or [one may use] a paste of mango bark with curd or sauvīraka.
Having ground sauvīra with either raw or parched, dehusked barley, one should apply it as an ointment to the navel; this destroys even severe diarrhea.
Likewise, goat’s milk, meat broth, and the meat of gallinaceous birds or deer [are beneficial].
The physician should feed the patient with equal portions of *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or lentils (*masūra*),
along with cooling and astringent substances,
once there is lightness of body, satisfaction of mind, and the downward-moving wind (*anila*) has returned to its natural course. (76–77)

Having recognized that the person has been well-purged, one should administer a digestive (pācana) medicine at night. Through the practice of purgation (virecana), there arises strength of the sense organs, clarity of the intellect, stimulation of the digestive fire, stability of the bodily tissues (dhātus), and stability of youth.
One who has undergone purgation should avoid exposure to strong winds, cold water, oil massages, indigestion, physical exercise, and sexual intercourse; instead,
one should be fed gruel prepared with *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, green gram (*mudga*), and other such grains.

Shali rice with the meat-broths of jaṅghāla or viṣkira birds is beneficial. 81 Enema (vasti) is of two kinds: that called anuvāsana and the nirūha; of these, that which is administered as an oily substance is known by the name anuvāsana. 82
That which is administered with decoctions, milk, and oils is called *nirūha*;
because it is given by means of a bladder (*vasti*), it is known as *vasti*.
Among these, that which is called *anuvāsana* (oil enema) is now described here.
The specific type of non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is called the "measured enema" (mātrāvasti). Its dose is two palas, or even half of that.
A patient suitable for this enema is one who is dry, possesses a sharp digestive fire, or is afflicted by wind alone.
One suffering from leprosy (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), obesity, or abdominal enlargement (udara) should not be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsya).

Furthermore, those afflicted by chronic insanity (unmāda), thirst, facial paralysis (ardita), edema (śotha), fainting (mūrchā), anorexia (aruci), fear, dyspnea (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), or consumption (kṣaya) should neither be given a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpya) nor an unctuous enema. 86
The eye [of the image] should be fashioned from gold and other metals, or from trees, bamboo, lotus stalks, ivory, the tips of horns, or gems;
its measurement is six finger-breadths for those ranging from one year to six years of age. 87.
From there, up to twelve [units], the measurement should be eight [units];
beyond that, the length of the eye is twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The hole for the bean (mudga) is like a chickpea (kalāya), and the hole for the jujube stone (kola) is shaped like a jujube kernel. 88–89.
The eye should be smooth and resemble a cow’s tail in proportion;
it is thick at the base like a cow’s tail and gradually tapers from there.
It is fixed at the base with a thickness equal to the patient’s thumb.
Its circumference should be like that of the little finger, with a globular opening at the tip;
at its base, two ear-like projections (*karṇika*) should be made, each measuring one-fourth of a unit.
Therein, one should apply the enema bag according to the two methods of fastening.
The bladder may be made from the urine-bladder of a deer, goat, pig, cow, or even a buffalo; if these are unavailable, it should be made from skin.
That bladder should be dyed with astringent decoctions, soft, unctuous, and firm; such is beneficial. (93–94)
For the treatment of ulcers, the nozzle (netra) should be smooth, measuring eight finger-breadths in length,
having an aperture the size of a mung bean, and a circumference equal to that of a vulture’s wing-bone tube;
it brings about the growth of the body, complexion, strength, health, and longevity.
A bladder [enema] that is properly administered brings about full growth and nourishment. (96) An unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) is administered during the cool season, winter, and spring;
whereas an oil enema (anuvāsana) should be given at night during the summer, the rainy season, and autumn. (97)
One should not administer an oil enema after having the patient eat food that is excessively unctuous;
for oil administered in these two ways may produce intoxication or fainting.
Furthermore, administering it to one who has eaten extremely dry food will cause a loss of strength and complexion.
Therefore, after feeding a person who possesses proper affection [for the treatment], one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
Both types of enemas administered in deficient doses are said to be ineffective; likewise, those administered in excessive doses cause abdominal distension, exhaustion, and diarrhea.

The maximum dose for an oil enema (anuvāsana) should be six palas; the medium dose should be three palas; and it is said that the minimum dose is one and a half palas less than that. To the oil, a powder of śatāhvā and saindhava salt should be added. 101.
The best, middling, and lowest doses of that [oil] consist of six, four, and two māṣakas respectively (102).
Once seven nights have passed since the purgation, for one who has regained strength and has eaten food, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) should be administered as an after-treatment (103).

Likewise, having performed an unctuous enema (anuvasana), well-anointed with oil, and gently sweated with warm water, one should feed the patient according to the scriptures; then, after he has walked about and voided flatus, feces, and urine, one should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-basti). 104
While the patient is asleep on his left side, with the left leg extended and the other leg drawn up, one should insert the nozzle into the lubricated rectum;
the mouth of the enema bag should be secured with threads and held by the left hand.
The wise practitioner should apply pressure with the right hand using moderate force.
At the time of administering the enema, one should not perform yawning, coughing, or sneezing.
The duration for pressing the enema is said to be thirty mātrās. 106–107.
Then, once the oil has been applied, one should lie flat on one's back for a hundred words;
with all limbs extended, it spreads according to its potency. One should then rotate the hands around one's own knees, snapping the fingers again and again.
This shall be one *mātrā*; this is the certainty everywhere.
The wise have declared that this *mātrā* may be the closing and opening of a man's eyes, or the snap of a finger, or the utterance of a long vowel. 109–110.
He should strike him gently on the palms three times each,
and likewise on the buttocks, the hips, and then lift him up from the bed.
Then the wise man should strike him on the buttocks with his own hands as before.
Then, after performing the ritual three times, one should lift his feet from the bed;
once the procedure is completed, he may sleep as comfortably as he desires.
For him whose oily substance, along with wind and feces, has been expelled, [the treatment is successful].
If there are no complications, he has been properly administered the unctuous enema quickly;
then, when the food is digested and the oil has returned in the evening, one should feed him light food at will, provided the person's digestive fire is strong. (114–115)

On the following day, lukewarm water or a decoction of coriander and dry ginger should be given to the patient who has undergone oleation; this destroys complications arising from the unctuous substances.
By this method, [the procedure] should be repeated six, seven, eight, or even nine times.
These enemas should be administered, and at their conclusion, a nirūhaṇa enema should also be given.
The first enema administered provides oleation to the bladder and the groin;
the second, when properly administered, conquers the vāyu located in the head.
When administered as the third [application], it generates strength and complexion;
when given as the fourth and fifth, they nourish the plasma (rasa) and blood (asṛj);
the sixth nourishes the muscle (māṃsa), and the seventh the fat (medas).
The eighth and ninth [days] are likewise for the marrow, in due order. (120) Thus, one who properly applies double the dose should thoroughly treat the defects residing in the semen.
(121) This applies to the man who consumes [the medicine] for eighteen-day periods, starting from the first day.
That physician, possessing the strength of an elephant, the speed of a horse, and the splendor of an immortal,
should administer an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) daily to one with dry and excessively windy constitutions, and likewise to others for three days out of fear of impairment of the digestive fire.

A small dose of unctuous substance administered over a long period is harmless for those who are dry; likewise, a small dose of non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is recommended for those who are already unctuous. Alternatively, it is also beneficial when the unctuous substance is expelled at that time as pure oil alone.

To that [patient] as well, a smaller dose should be given, for [the oil] does not remain in one who is ununctuous (snigdha). When the unrefined oil mixed with impurities does not reach its destination, then bodily exhaustion, flatulence, colic, and dyspnea arise. (124–125)

If there is heaviness in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should administer a sharp non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) combined with sharp medicinal substances, or even a medicinal suppository (phalavarti), so that the flatus,
feces, and unctuous matter are moved in their natural downward direction.
Likewise, one should administer a strong purgative, and a sharp nasal medication (nasya) is recommended. If an unexpelled oil enema (sneha-vasti) causes no complications,
it should be ignored by the wise physician, as all such cases— whether small in quantity, withdrawn, or due to dryness— are considered minor.
If the oil has not yet descended after a day and night, one should eliminate it with purificatory measures;
when the oil of an oil enema (snehabasti) has not descended, no other oil should be administered.
[One should instead use] guduchi, eranda, putika, bharangi, vrishaka, and rauhitsha.
One pala each of śatāvarī, sahacara, and kākanāsā,
and one prasṛta each of yava, māṣa, atasī, kola, and kulattha,
should be boiled in four droṇas of water until one droṇa remains. With that [decoction], 130–131.
One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with one pala each of all the jīvanīya (life-promoting) drugs; this indeed is an anuvāsana enema that cures all disorders of vāta.
Furthermore, seventy-six complications may arise from the administration of basti therapy.
These [disorders] arising from vitiation by the combination [of humors] should be treated according to Suśruta;
drinks, diet, and lifestyle, as well as all prohibitions, should be carried out exactly as in the administration of oleation therapy—there is no need for hesitation in this matter. 133–134.

The *nirūha* enema is divided into many types according to its various ingredients; the preeminent sages have assigned these very names to it. (135) Furthermore, another name for the *nirūha* has been declared by the wise as *āsthāpana*.

The stabilization of the humors (doṣas) and the tissues (dhātus) is considered to result from restoring them to their proper places. The dosage for a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is one prastha; the maximum is one and a quarter prasthas, the medium is specified as one prastha, and the minimum is three kuḍavas. (136–137)
One who is excessively unctuous, whose humors are not afflicted, who has chest injuries, or is emaciated;
one suffering from flatulence, vomiting, hiccups, dyspnea, cough, or asthma;
and one afflicted by swelling of the anus, diarrhea, choleraic disorder (visūcī), or leprosy (kuṣṭha). 138.
A pregnant woman, one suffering from diabetes (madhumeha), one with ascites (jalodara), and one who is unfit for non-unctuous enemas (anāsthāpya) [should not undergo this treatment].

[This applies] in cases of wind-diseases (vātavyādhi), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), gouty fever (vātāsṛj), irregular fever (viṣamajvara), fainting (mūrchā), thirst (tṛṣṇā), abdominal enlargement (udara), flatulence/distension (ānāha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and urinary calculi (aśmarī). 139–140.

A wise physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) according to the prescribed rules in cases of edema, menorrhagia, weak digestion, urinary disorders (prameha), colic, acid gastritis (amlapitta), and heart disease (141).
[The patient] should have his flatus, feces, and urine evacuated, be treated with oleation and sudation, and not have eaten before the procedure.

At midday, within the house, the wise physician should administer the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) appropriately according to the procedure for an unctuous enema (snehavasti). Once the nirūha has been administered, the patient should then sit in a squatting posture (utkaṭaka-āsana).
One may wait for just a moment with the desire for the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to come out; however,

if it has not arrived after a muhūrta, the wise physician should expel that non-emergent enema using purificatory measures consisting of further non-unctuous enemas containing alkali, sūtra, sour substances, and rock salt.
One should designate that patient as having been properly purged by non-unctuous enema (nirūha) when the feces, bile, phlegm, and flatus pass out in succession and a sense of lightness arises.
One whose bladder-enema (vasti) has very little force and has expelled only a small amount of waste and wind [is considered insufficiently administered].

One should diagnose [the condition] as fainting (mūrchā), extreme dullness, loss of appetite, and difficulty in administering the enema. 147. Serenity of mind, contentment, unctuousness, and the subduing of the disease are the signs of the correct administration of both the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and the unctuous enema (sneha-vasti). 148.
One who knows how to administer an enema should apply the nirūha according to this procedure—either a second, a third, or a fourth time as appropriate.
One enema with oil is indicated for vāta; two with milk are indicated for pitta.
Decoctions, pungent substances, and strong urines, as well as the three [types of oil], are beneficial when excessively hot in cases of Kapha.

Having administered a Nirūha-vasti to one afflicted by Pitta, Śleṣman, and Vāyu, and having fed them with milk, vegetable soup, and meat broth in that order, one should then administer an Anuvasana-vasti. 150–151.
For the delicate, the elderly, and the young, a mild and beneficial enema is appropriate; however, if a sharp one is administered to them, it may destroy their strength and lifespan.
First, one should administer a provocative enema, and thereafter, one that eliminates the humors.
Thereafter, the wise physician should administer a pacifying enema (saṃśamanīya-vasti).
Eranda seeds, madhuka, pippalī, rock salt, vacā, and the paste of hapuṣā fruit are known as the enema that relieves distension (utkleśana-vasti). 153–154.
A enema consisting of śatāhvā, madhuka, bilva, and the fruit of kauṭaja,
along with kāñjika and cow’s urine, is known to remove the doṣas.
Likewise, priyaṅgu, madhuka, mustā, and rasāñjana [are used for this purpose].
An enema containing milk is recommended and is known to pacify the *doṣas*.

Enemas combined with a decoction of *triphalā*, cow’s urine, honey, and alkali, along with the addition of *ūṣakādi* drugs as counter-irritants (*pratīvāpa*), are known as scraping (*lekhanā*) enemas. 156–157.

Enriching enemas (bṛṃhaṇa-vasti) are known to consist of decoctions of nourishing substances combined with the pastes of sweet drugs, along with ghee and meat broth. [The flowers and sprouts of] badarī, airāvatī, śelu, and śālmalī are also used. 158.
Those prepared with milk and mixed with honey are known by the name *picchila*.
Wise practitioners should administer them along with the blood of goats, sheep, and deer.
The dosage for *picchila* enemas is considered to be twelve *palas*.
First, having added one *akṣa* of rock salt and two *prasṛti*s of honey,
one should stir them together and then add three *prasṛti*s of oil.
Once the oil has become unified, one should then throw in one *prasṛti* of the medicinal paste (*kalka*).

When the mixture has become well-blended, the physician skilled in treatment should take four *prasṛta* measures of the decoction; or alternatively, he may take a smaller amount at the end measuring two *prasṛta*. Having added these and stirred them thoroughly, he should administer the non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*). 162–163.
Thus prepared, the enema (basti) should consist of twelve prasṛtas.
In the case of vāta, one should add four palas of honey and six palas of unctuous substance (sneha).
In the case of pitta, one should add four palas of honey and three palas of unctuous substance.
In the case of phlegm (kapha), however, one should add six palas of honey and four palas of oil;
[this] along with an equal portion of castor-plant decoction, eight palas of honey and oil combined,
half a pala of *śatapuṣpā*, and half a pala of rock salt.

This enema, known as Madhutailaka, when stirred with wood-apple (dāru), destroys fat, abdominal tumors, worms, splenic disorders, impurities, and upward movement of gases (udāvarta). It bestows strength and complexion, is aphrodisiac, and acts as a digestive stimulant and nourisher.
One *prasṛta* each of honey, muscle-fat, milk, and oil,
along with one *akṣa* each of *hapuṣā* and rock salt, constitutes an excellent *yāpana-vasti*.
A decoction of castor root, combined with honey, oil, and rock salt, [is likewise used].
This "Yuktaratha" enema consists of vacā, pippalī, and fruit;
with decoctions of the five roots (pañcamūla), oil, māgadhikā, honey, rock salt, and yaṣṭyāhva, it is known as the Siddha-vasti. 169–170.

One should bathe with warm water, avoid sleeping during the day, and abstain from indigestion; all other matters should be observed as in the case of an oil enema (sneha-vasti). Hereafter, I shall describe the enema known as the uttara-vasti.
Because it follows the *nirūha* enema, it is therefore designated as "uttara" (subsequent).
The nozzle should be twelve finger-breadths long, with a constriction (*karṇikā*) made in the middle;
it should resemble the stalk of a *mālatī* flower, and its aperture should allow a mustard seed to pass through.
The best of physicians have stated that for those under twenty-five years of age, the dose of oil should be two karṣas, and from that age upward, it should be one pala.
Now, for one who has been purified by non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) and has been satisfied with bathing and eating—
While standing in knee-deep water, once the penis has been anointed with oil and rubbed with a lubricated probe,
one should gradually insert the nozzle into the urethral passage— six finger-breadths deep— after it has been smeared with clarified butter.
Then one should squeeze the enema bag and slowly withdraw the nozzle;
once the oil has returned, the procedure for an oil enema (snehavasti) is beneficial.
For women, one should make the nozzle ten finger-breadths long and as thick as the little finger.
One should apply a fine tube four finger-breadths long for introduction into the vagina,
two finger-breadths long for the urinary passage,
and one finger-breadth long for children, in cases of disorders such as dysuria. 178–179.

The wise should slowly and steadily apply the subtle instrument; it is further described as being like the stalk of a *mālatī* flower. In the vaginal passages of women, the quantity of oil should be two *pālikās*.

In the urinary tract, the dose for children is one *pala*, and for those two years old, it is two *karṣas*. A wise physician should administer [the enema] with the patient lying supine, with the knees drawn upward; if the medicine does not return, the physician should proceed with the enema known as the *uttara-vasti*.
Furthermore, the physician should administer a vaginal enema (vasti) combined with purifying qualities,
or he should insert a firm medicinal suppository (phalavarti) into the vaginal canal,
fashioned from threads, lubricated, and compounded with purifying substances. 183–184.
When the bladder is thus being burned, the expert physician should administer an enema with a decoction of milk-exuding trees or with cold milk.
This enema cures seminal disorders in men and disorders arising from the menses in women. (185)
However, the uttaravasti (urethral/vaginal douche) should never be administered to one suffering from urinary disorders (meha).
The signs of correct administration, complications, and the sequential procedure for the bladder known as uttaravasti are identical to those of the oleation enema (snehavasti). 186–187.

A smooth wick, resembling one's own thumb, smeared with clarified butter and inserted into the anus to expel impurities, is known as a *phala-varti*. That medicine which is to be taken through the nose is called *nasya* by the wise. (188)
Nāvana and nasyakarman are considered its two names. (189) Nasya is declared to be of two types: recana and snehana. Recana is said to be depleting, while snehana is considered nourishing. (190)
Nasal therapy (nasya), which destroys phlegm, bile, and wind, is administered in the forenoon, midday, or afternoon; it may also be taken at night when the disease is severe.
One should avoid nasal therapy after a meal, on a cloudy day, or when one is suffering from insufficient nourishment.
Likewise, one suffering from acute catarrh, a pregnant woman, one poisoned by another,
one with indigestion, one who has received an enema, one who has drunk oil, water, or fermented liquor (āsava),
one who is angry, one overcome by grief, one afflicted by thirst, the elderly, and children [should not undergo purgation]. 192.
One who suppresses natural urges, one who is exhausted, and one who desires to bathe should avoid [nasal therapy].
(193) One should perform the administration of nasal drops for a child of eight years; beyond eighty years of age, nasal drops are never administered. (194)

Alternatively, for purgative nasal therapy (virecana-nasya), one should employ very sharp oils prepared with potent medicinal drugs, or likewise, medicated fats, decoctions, or meat broths. Eight, six, or four drops should be administered into each of the two nostrils. (195)
Each [dose] for evacuation is appropriate according to the primary, medium, or small measure.
In the administration of nasal therapy (nasya), one *śāṇa* of a sharp medicine should be given;
*hiṅgu* should be the size of a barley grain (*yava*), and rock salt (*saindhava*) is considered to be one *māṣa*. 196–197.

In the administration of nasal therapy (nasya), one should employ eight śāṇas of milk, three karṣas of water, and one karṣa of sweet substances. Two other types of nasal therapy are recognized: the pressed drop (avapīḍa) and the blown powder (pradhamana).

Now, those two [types of errhines] should be administered for head-purgation (śirovirecana) as appropriate. That juice which has been extracted by pressing the medicinal substance after it has been made into a paste is designated as an *avapīḍa*; it originates from sharp (pungent) substances.

A tube six finger-breadths long with two openings should be used to blow in a sharp powder; blowing in a dose of one kola-measure through the breath from the mouth is beneficial for diseases of the supraclavicular region caused by *kapha* and for the loss of voice. (201)
In cases of anorexia, catarrh, headache, and chronic rhinitis (202), as well as for swelling,
epilepsy, and skin diseases, purgative nasal therapy (nasya) is beneficial;
for those who are timid, women, the emaciated, and children, unctuous nasal therapy is recommended (203).

The Avapīḍana (nasal drops) is honored for use in diseases of the throat, in disorders of the three humors (sannipāta), in irregular fevers, in mental disturbances, and in cases of worms; it is also administered in those with extremely aggravated humors and in those who have lost consciousness. 204.
The wise should administer this as a powder for insufflation, since it is indeed very sharp.
An errhine (nasya) made from jaggery and ginger, or from long pepper and rock salt ground with water, cures diseases of the ears, eyes, nose, and head. (205–206)

Those [afflictions] arising from the neck, throat, and chest, as well as those born on the back of the arms, are destroyed by a nasal medication (nasya) consisting of the pith of *madhūka*, *kṛṣṇā*, *vacā*, *marica*, and *saindhava* salt, ground with lukewarm water; this should be administered to restore consciousness. 207.
In cases of epilepsy, insanity, fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), and facial paralysis, rock salt, white pepper, mustard seeds, and kuṣṭha,
ground together with goat’s urine and administered as nasal drops (nasya), remove drowsiness. (208–209)
Black pepper, *vacā*, and *kaṭphala* processed with the bile of a rohita fish— this powder should be administered as a nasal insufflation (*pradhamana*) by the wise.
(210) Now, the preparation for nourishing nasal therapy (*bṛṃhaṇanasya*) is described.
Enema (marśa) and after-enema (pratimarśa) are considered the two types of oleation therapy.
For an enema, the primary satiating dose is recorded as eight śāṇas;
the medium dose is four śāṇas, and the low dose is considered to be one śāṇa.
O Mātreya, this [medicine] should be administered by the wise into each nostril two or three times for a nasal drop (marśa),
after considering the strength or weakness of the humors; an expert should administer a nasal medication (nasya) every other day or every second day.
Whether for three days, five days, or seven days, one should remain well-restrained;
various complications are recorded to arise from massage and head-purgation (śirovireka),
which should be understood as resulting respectively from the provocation of the *doṣas* and from depletion.
In cases caused by the provocation of the humors (doṣas), one should employ purification through emesis;
however, in cases caused by depletion (kṣaya), nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) appropriate to the specific condition is beneficial.
This applies to diseases of the head, nose, and eyes, as well as sūryāvarta and arddhabheda.
In cases of dental disease, loss of strength, ailments arising from the neck, arms, and shoulders,
dryness of the mouth, ringing in the ears, as well as disorders of wind and bile, premature graying of hair, and the falling out of hair and beard. 218.
Nourishing nasal therapy (nasya) with unctuous substances or sweet juices is recommended.
Saffron ground with milk and sugar, fried in clarified butter (ājya),
when administered as a nasal application, destroys the pains arising from vātarakta.
For disorders of the eyebrows, temples, eyes, head, ears, sūryāvarta, and arddhabheda, nasal medication (nasya) should be administered using aṇutaila, or nārāyaṇa oil,
or ghee prepared with māṣa and other appropriate medicinal herbs.
In cases of kapha and in pure vāta, one should administer oil as nasal medication (nasya); in pitta, one should always give muscle fat (vasā), ghee, or marrow.
[One may also use] māṣa, ātmaguptā, rāsnā, balā, arubuka, and karoiṣa.
A decoction of *aśvagandhā* prepared with *hiṅgu* and rock salt,
when administered lukewarm as a nasal drop (*nasya*), overcomes hemiplegia accompanied by tremors, as well as facial paralysis, torticollis, and *avabāhuka*. (223–224)

The dosage for *pratimarśa* is considered to be two or three drops for each nostril; this is determined to be the measure for oleation. Once the oil has been submerged up to two knots [of the tube] and then withdrawn, it is ready. 225.
The index finger (tarjanī) should drip a drop; that measure is designated as a *bindu*.
Eight such measures, known as *bindus*, are called a *śāṇa*.
This [amount] is to be administered for the *marśana* [nasal drops], while the *pratimarśa* consists of two *bindus*.
The wise have declared fourteen times for self-reflection: at dawn, after using the tooth-stick, upon leaving the house,
after physical exercise, travel, or sexual intercourse, after voiding feces or urine, and after applying collyrium.
Pratimarśa is administered at the end of a mouthful of food, at the end of a meal, after waking from daytime sleep,
likewise after vomiting, and in the evening;
it is a lubricant that reaches the mouth by means of slight spitting.
One should know that when it is poured into the nose, it is measured according to the standard for *pratimarśa*.

One should not swallow what remains, nor should one spit out what has entered the mouth. This [practice] is highly esteemed for those who are emaciated, those suffering from thirst and dryness of the mouth, and for children and the elderly.
From its regular application, diseases arising above the clavicle do not arise;
there is the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair, and strength born of the senses is produced. (233) [The ingredients are: *bibhītaka*, *nimba*, *gāmbhārī*, *śivā*, *śelu*, and *kākinī*.
By the application of each oil as a nasal drop (nasya), gray hair is certainly destroyed.

(234) Now, I shall describe the procedure for nasal therapy (nasya-vidhi) for the purpose of administering the nasal drops: in a place free from wind and dust, having performed the cleansing of the teeth, (235)
The person should be purified by the inhalation of smoke, with the forehead and neck thus fomented;
he should lie on his back, with the head slightly extended and the hands and feet spread out, while his eyes are covered with a cloth. (236)
The physician, having raised the tip of the patient's nose, should administer the nasal medication (nasya) with a continuous stream of lukewarm liquid using a golden or silver shell-cup,
or by means of a mechanical device, or with cotton pads. (237-238)

While the nasal drops are being poured, one should not shake the head, nor become angry, nor speak, nor yawn, nor laugh; for if these [actions] are performed, the oil does not reach its intended end. (239)
Otherwise, there arises cough, catarrh, headache, and eye disease.
Having reached the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, one should hold [the oil] there and not swallow the liquid; the duration for holding the unctuous substance should be five, seven, or ten *mātrās*.
Having sat down, one should then spit out the liquid that has reached the nose and mouth;
one should spit from the left and right sides, but certainly not facing forward.
When the nasal medication has been administered, one should abandon mental distress, passion, and anger.
Having abandoned sleep, a person should lie down on their back and recite a hundred verses.
Likewise, at the conclusion of head-purification (śirovireka), medicinal smoke or gargling is beneficial.
Three signs are taught regarding the application of nasal therapy (nasya). 243–244.
Indeed, those who contemplate the scriptures should recognize the signs of deficient, excessive, and proper application:
lightness, purification of impurities, the subsiding of diseases in the channels, clarity of mind and senses, and the cleansing of the head are the characteristics of proper purification. (245)
Itching, a burning sensation, heaviness, and the discharge of phlegm from the channels are proclaimed as the signs of insufficient purification of the head. Furthermore,
the emergence of brain matter, the aggravation of wind (vāta), and the derangement of the sense organs [occur].

When the head has been thoroughly purged by means of *śirovirecana*, and the head is excessively cleansed, one should employ treatments that subdue *kapha* and *vāta*. In that case, once the head has been purified by mild nasal therapy (*nasya*), one should apply measures that subdue *vāta*. (247–248)
When the head is properly purified, medicated ghee is administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
Excessive salivation, heaviness of the head, and confusion of the senses are the signs of over-oleation; in that case, one should administer a drying (*rūkṣa*) treatment. (249)
One should feed [the patient] food that does not cause internal secretions; in the case of Vāta, one should prescribe nasal therapy (nasya).

Thus ends the fifth chapter, "The Procedure for the Five Medical Actions," in the section on General Principles and so forth, within the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by Śrī Miśra Bhāva, son of Śrī Miśra Laṭakana. 5.
Now begins the sixth chapter, on the procedure for smoking therapy (dhūmapāna) and so forth.
Smoking is said to be of six types: pacifying (śamana), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa), purgative (recana), cough-alleviating (kāsahā), emetic (vāmana), and wound-fumigation (vraṇadhūpana).
Furthermore, the synonyms for *śamana* (pacification) are *madhya* (moderate) and *prāyogika* (habitual);
the synonyms for *bṛṃhaṇa* (nourishing) are *snehana* (oleating) and *mṛdu* (soft);
and the synonyms for *recana* (purgation) are *śodhana* (cleansing) and *tīkṣṇa* (sharp).
Indeed, these individuals are unfit for smoking therapy: one who is exhausted, frightened, or suffering from pain;

one who has been administered an enema or undergone purgation; likewise one who has stayed awake at night, is thirsty, afflicted by burning sensations, suffers from dryness of the palate, or has abdominal disease.
One suffering from headache, blurred vision, vomiting, or abdominal distension;

one with chest injury, afflicted by urinary disorders (prameha), suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), or who is pregnant; as well as one who is dry, emaciated, or has recently consumed milk, honey, ghee, or fermented liquors (āsava)—[these should not be given purgatives].
Smoke used by one who has eaten food, curd, or fish, or by a child, an elderly person, or one who is emaciated,
as well as when used at the wrong time or in excessive quantity, produces complications.
In such cases, the drinking of ghee, nasal drops (nasya), collyrium (añjana), and eye-filling (tarpaṇa) are desired.
One should administer ghee, sugarcane juice, grapes, milk, sugar-water, or even sweet and sour juices for the purpose of inducing emesis.
Regarding medicinal smoking (dhūma), it is practiced from the twelfth year onwards and not beyond the eightieth year.
Properly administered, medicinal smoke (dhūma) destroys cough, dyspnea, coryza, pain in the neck, jaw, and head, as well as disorders of vāta and kapha; through its use,
a person’s senses, speech, and mind become clear.
One should have firm hair, teeth, and beard, and a fragrant face. There, the smoke-pipe should be three-segmented with three joints,
having a circumference equal to the little finger and a length reaching the space between the thumb and forefinger.
For the pacification of disease, the length of the smoking pipe (dhūmanetra) should be forty finger-breadths; likewise, it is considered to be thirty-two for mild cases,
twenty-four for sharp (tīkṣṇa) applications, and sixteen for the cure of cough.
For the treatment of emaciation (*vāmanīya*), the wound-channel (*vraṇanāḍikā*) should likewise be ten finger-breadths long,
as thick as a pea (*kalāya*) circle, with an opening the size of a horse-gram (*kulattha*). Then, one should smear a very smooth probe (*iṣikā*) twelve finger-breadths in length.
A plaster made from the paste of *dhūmadru* wood is prescribed for a length of eight finger-breadths (15).
Having applied one *karṣa* measure of the paste and allowed it to dry in the shade, one should then carefully remove the inner core (*īṣikā*) and prepare a wick soaked in oil (16).
Having ignited [the resin] with charcoal and held it at the opening of the eye,
one should inhale the smoke through the mouth and exhale it through the mouth alone.
Then, the wise person should inhale it through both nostrils and exhale it through the mouth.
Having placed the medicinal paste inside a hollowed-out earthenware cup and ignited charcoal within it, one should then apply the eye-salve to the opening and fumigate the ulcer with that very smoke.
For pacification, a paste of cardamom and other ingredients mixed with unctuous substances should be used; for mild cases, resin of the *sarja* tree is employed.
For evacuation, one should administer a sharp paste; for the destruction of dyspnea, minor *koṣaṇa*;
and for inducing vomiting, one should give a smoking preparation rich in sinews and skin.
For ulcers, fumigation with *nimba*, *vacā*, and other such ingredients is highly recommended.
Other incense-sticks should also be prepared in the houses for the pacification of disease:
peacock feathers, nimba leaves, bṛhatī fruit, black pepper, asafoetida, māṃsī, and seeds derived from cotton. (21–22)
The hair of a goat, the slough of a snake, the excrement of a cat,
and an elephant’s tusk— this powder, mixed with a small amount of clarified butter and applied as incense within houses, removes all infant-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*). (23)
By slaying the piśācas and rākṣasas, it shall become the remover of all fevers (24). It wards off mental anguish, passion, and anger during the practice of smoke-inhalation (dhūmapāna).
The eyes are said to be composed of the bodily constituents (dhātus), as well as substances derived from bamboo and other sources (25).

The procedure for holding a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣa) is as follows: one remains with the mouth filled with substances such as oils, milk, or decoctions until the excess phlegm is removed or the morbid humor (doṣa) is eliminated. (26)
One should hold the gargle (gaṇḍūṣa) for as long as it takes for the fluid to flow from the eyes and nose.
Remaining well-seated, with the forehead and neck perspiring, one should perform three, five, or seven gargles until the humors (doṣas) are eliminated. 27–28.
Gargling (gaṇḍūṣa) may be of four types: emollient (snehana), palliative (śamana), purifying (śodhana), and healing (ropaṇa); the mouth-rinse (kavala) is likewise of these same types.
The emollient type is prepared with unctuous and warm substances for [conditions of] Vāta, while the palliative type is prepared with sweet and cold substances.

In cases of pitta, purification is achieved with pungent, sour, salty, and hot substances; in cases of kapha, with astringent, bitter, and sweet substances. For a wound, one should apply a powder of these substances that is pungent and hot for healing.
One should administer a dose the size of a jujube fruit (kola) of these powders as a gargle.
A paste measuring one *karṣa* is administered by the wise as a gargle (*kavala*).
Gargles (*gaṇḍūṣa*), mouthfuls (*kavala*), and so forth, are to be held starting from the fifth year of age.
[The signs of success are: the reduction of disease, satisfaction, clarity, and lightness of the mouth.
When a mouthful is held, there occurs clarity of the sense organs.
Indeed, the gargle removes bad taste in the mouth, dryness, inflammation, ulcers, and thirst; it also relieves loose teeth and brings about clarity. (33-34)

The procedure for gargling (kavala) is as follows: having placed half a mouthful of a substance that subdues wind, bile, and phlegm in the mouth and chewed it well, one should spit it out. Gargling creates a desire for food and removes phlegm. 35. Kavalaḥ kurute kāṅkṣāṃ bhakṣyeṣu harate kapham.
It cures thirst, dryness, bad taste, and loosening of the teeth.
(36) Gently rubbing the teeth, tongue, and mouth with powders, pastes, or electuaries using a finger is called *pratisāraṇa*. (37)
Pratisāraṇa (rubbing with medicinal substances) cures a bad taste in the mouth, foul breath, dryness of the mouth, thirst, loss of appetite, and dental pain;
however, when applied insufficiently, it causes numbness, aggravation of kapha, and a lack of discernment regarding tastes.
From excessive application, there occurs inflammation of the mouth, dryness, thirst, vomiting, fatigue, and sweating.
Four types of sudation have been described: tāpa, ūṣma, and the one known as sveda;
the liquid sudation is called upanāha. All of these alleviate the afflictions of vāta.

Sweat induced by heat and warmth is generally said to destroy *śleṣman* (phlegm), while poultice (*upanāha*) destroys *vāta*. When there is an association with *pitta*, a liquid application is beneficial. In cases of great strength and severe disease during cold weather, a strong sudation is prescribed.
In cases of weakness, mild sudation is prescribed; in moderate cases, moderate sudation is considered appropriate.
For *balāsa* (phlegm), drying sudation is used; for the combination of *kapha* and *vāta*, sudation that is both drying and unctuous is indicated.
When *vāta* is obstructed by *kapha* and *medas* (fat), one should stay in a slightly warm room with the rays of the sun.
Wrestling, walking on foot, heavy upper garments, and constant exercise—these, along with worry and carrying weights, one should employ for the sake of freedom from disease;
indeed, for those embodied beings to whom nasal medication (nasya) and enemas (vasti) are to be administered, these practices are beneficial. 43–44.
Whosoever are to be purified should first be considered fit for sudation;
hereafter, those suffering from fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, and urinary stones—all three—should likewise undergo sudation before the surgical procedure. (45–46)
After the foreign body has been extracted, as well as in cases of obstructed labor or disease,
a woman— whether she has given birth at the proper time or prematurely— should be fomented later; indeed,
all types of fomentation should be administered in a windless place once the food has been digested.

In a person whose body has been moistened with oleation, the morbid humors (doṣas) residing in the tissues reach a state of liquidity through sudation; having entered the internal cavity of the abdomen, they undergo evacuation.
For one whose body has been anointed with oil, the eyes should be covered with cold substances.

One whose body is being fomented should touch the heart with something cool. (49) One suffering from indigestion, one who is weak, one with urinary disorders, one emaciated by chest wounds, one who is thirsty,
(50) one with diarrhea, one with hemoptysis, one with jaundice, and likewise one with abdominal diseases [should avoid this].
One who is obese and a pregnant woman should certainly not be subjected to sudation by a wise physician;
for through sudation, their bodies may meet with destruction, and their disorders may become incurable.
Even these individuals, if their conditions are treatable by sudation, should be treated with mild sudation therapies.
One should apply mild sudation to the heart, the scrotum, and the eyes (53).

From excessive sudation, there may arise pain in the joints, burning sensations, thirst, exhaustion, vertigo, and the provocation of pitta-blood pustules; in such cases, one should treat with cooling measures (54).
Among them, that which is called "Heat" (tāpa) is produced appropriately by means of sand, cloths, and hands, as well as by skull-balls and glowing embers;
it occurs when the body, wrapped in lac, is heated and sprinkled with sour liquids. (55)
Fomentation by heat (*ūṣmasveda*) should be applied using iron balls, bricks, and the like, or else with decoctions and juices of substances that destroy *vāta*.
Having filled a jar with hot [liquids] and having made a hole in its side... (56)
One should employ a tube that is unsealed, three-segmented, made of metal, wood, or even bone;
it should be six finger-breadths wide at the mouth, shaped like a cow's tail, and two cubits long.
[The practitioner] should be seated comfortably, well-anointed, and covered by the teacher’s upper garment.

One should apply sudation to a patient suffering from wind disorders using a tube shaped like an elephant's trunk (58). Alternatively, having cleared a patch of ground measuring one fathom in length, burned it with *khadira* wood, and then sprinkled it with milk, fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), and water (59).
One should cause a person lying down to undergo sudation by covering them with leaves that subdue vāta;
likewise, one should administer sudation to the person while they lie down using boiled beans and other such substances.
Then, one should apply poultice-sudation (upanāha-sveda) using drugs that alleviate vāta.
Having fomented the body afflicted by Vāta with milk, meat broth, and so forth, one should then apply a warm, comfortable poultice consisting of sour substances ground with salt and mixed with fats,
or else with the meat of domestic and marshy animals, along with the group of drugs known as the Jīvanīya-gaṇa.
With *dadhisauvīraka*, milk, and likewise with *vīrataru* and others,
as well as with horse gram (*kulattha*), black gram (*māṣa*), wheat (*godhūma*), linseed (*atasī*), sesame (*tila*), mustard (*sarṣapa*),
*śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, *śephālī*, and large cumin (*sthūlajīraka*). (63)
With castor root and cumin, with rāsnā root and śigru,
with miśī, black pepper, and kuṭhera, combined with salts and sour substances,
along with prasāraṇī, aśvagandhā, the various balās, and the ten roots (daśamūla).

One should cause a person to undergo sudation using guḍūcī and vānarī seeds, gathered as available, crushed, steamed, and bound in a cloth. This formulation, known as Mahāśālvaṇa, removes all afflictions caused by vāta.

Alternatively, one should apply fomentation using medicinal herbs ground with sour liquids, placed in a fine cloth, and applied while lukewarm; or else, using those same herbs already steamed, kept in a cloth, and applied while lukewarm. Furthermore, liquid fomentation (*dravasveda*) consists of a vessel filled with a decoction of Vata-alleviating substances.
Seated comfortably in a cauldron or even in a chamber, one should immerse [the patient].
One should construct a chamber there, made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or wood, with a height of twenty-six finger-breadths.
Or it may be of that same length, but four-cornered and smooth (70).
The man, whose body has been lubricated, should remain with his shoulders sprinkled by a lukewarm stream of decoction until he is submerged up to six finger-breadths from the navel (71).
Starting from a single *muhūrta* up until four of them have passed,
one should remain immersed in that [liquid] until health is certain;
in this manner, one should cause the person to undergo sudation with oil, milk, or clarified butter.
Oil used for immersion therapy is appropriate when applied at intervals of one or two days;
properly administered through the openings of the vessels, the pores of the skin, and the arteries, it nourishes the body and bestows strength. (73–74)
Just as sprouts and other growths increase at the root when it is moistened with water,
so too does the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātu) occur when they are nourished with unctuous substances (sneha).
There is no other means superior to this for the destruction of Vāta.

When the cold and pain have subsided, when stiffness and heaviness are restrained, when the digestive fire has been kindled, and when softness has arisen, cessation from sudation is prescribed. Then, in due order, follow massage, affusion, poultice, and enema.
Head oil (mūrdhataila) is of four types, each succeeding one being more powerful than the preceding;
as the first three, beginning with abhyaṅga, are well-known and prescribed for all [parts of the body],
here the procedure for head enema (śirovasti) is described according to the consensus of the wise.
The *śirovasti* (head-pouch) should be made of leather, having two openings and measuring twelve finger-breadths;
it should be the size of the head. Having bound it over the head and quickly secured the joints with a paste of *māṣa* beans, one should fill it with lukewarm unctuous substances.
It should be held for as long as there is discharge from the nose, ears, or mouth;
or until the sensation subsides, or for a thousand measures (mātrās).
One should perform the "hand-turning" (karāvarta) on one's own knee, accompanied by a snap of the fingers. 81–82.
This shall be the single measure in all cases; this is the certain conclusion.
Here, the application of a head-pouch (śirovasti) is recommended even without food.
The head-pouch should be applied for five or seven days.
Having released the enema from the head, one should apply it all around;
then, one should perform a bath in lukewarm water for the upper body.
By this, diseases born of Vāta that are difficult to conquer go to their destruction.
Therefore, shaking the head and other such actions are appropriate at all times.
One should cause the region of the ear to sweat while the patient lies on his side; one should fill the auditory canal with urine, unctuous substances, or warm meat broths. 85–86.
One should protect the ear when it is filled with one hundred, five hundred,
or even a thousand measures of substances, in cases involving the ear, throat, or head (verse 87).
Filling the ear with urine and other such substances is recommended before eating.

When the sun has set, one should fill the ear with oil and other substances. (88) In an ear afflicted by pain, one should pour lukewarm goat urine mixed with rock salt; by this, the pains arising from inflammation, suppuration, and so forth are pacified. (89)
Fresh ginger, licorice, rock salt, and oil— these, when applied lukewarm to the ears, shall alleviate pain.
A leaf of the yellow amaranth (pītārka), smeared with clarified butter, should be heated over a fire.
Applied to the ear, that essence is the supreme remover of earache (91).

Now, the names for an ointment (*ālepa*) are *lepa*, *lepana*, and *liptaka*; it destroys the humors (*doṣa*), removes poison, and improves the complexion, and that ointment is considered to be of three types (92).

Measuring three units [in length], it should be raised by one-fourth, one-third, or half an *aṅgula*; when moist, it removes disease, but when dry, it spoils the complexion—just as a medicinal paste destroys the *doṣas*. 93.
A plaster made from Śothaghnī, dāru, siddhārtha, śuṇṭhī, and the bark of śobhāñjana,
ground with *āranāla* and applied as a paste, destroys all types of swelling.
(94) Śirīṣa, madhuyaṣṭī, tagara, and red sandalwood—
Cardamom, spikenard, the two types of turmeric, costus,
and tagara— having powdered these together, this plaster, saturated with a fifth part of ghee and applied with water by the wise, is known as "Daśāṅga" (the ten-ingredient). 95–96.
It conquers erysipelas, poisonous eruptions, swellings, and malignant ulcers.
As for the anti-poisonous application:
an application of goat’s milk, sesame seeds, and fresh butter [is effective].
An application of *āruṣkara* (marking nut) cures swelling, or alternatively, an application of black clay (*kṛṣṇamārttika*) does so.
Furthermore, another application that destroys worms and poison consists of *lāṅgalī*, *ativiṣā*, *alābū*, seeds of *śālinī*, and *mūlaka*.
An ointment ground with rice-water destroys insect bites and eruptions (sphoṭaka).
An ointment that bestows beauty upon the face consists of red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, lodhra, kuṣṭha, and priyaṅgu. 99.
The sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree and *masūra* lentils destroy facial blemishes and bestow radiance upon the face.
Now, the procedure for medicinal pastes (*lepa*) is described according to the consensus of the wise;
two varieties of it have been spoken of: the *ālepa* (thin paste) and the *pradeha* (thick paste). 100–101.
The measure for those two is like that of moist buffalo hide when it is well-raised;
a cold application is considered a remover of pitta, while a thick, warm poultice (pradeha) is a destroyer of kapha and vāta.
102. Moist, dense, and likewise hot, it [the poultice] destroys phlegm and wind.

One should not apply an ointment at night, nor should one keep it on while it is drying; one should disregard a medicinal paste as it dries with respect to its application for compression. For the heat, being enveloped by darkness, remains at the openings of the hair follicles.
It comes out at night even without an ointment; therefore, one should not apply an ointment [during the day].
Even at night, an ointment and such should be applied to the ulcer by the wise, provided it is non-suppurating, very deep, and originated from blood and phlegm.
As for medicinal pastes: a paste of madhuka, candana, mūrvā, nalamūla, parpaṭa, uśīra, bālaka, and padma removes swelling caused by pitta. 106
A poultice made from the root-fiber of *bījapūra*, *hiṃsrā*, *devadāru*, *mahauṣadha*,
*rāsnā*, and *araṇi* is a destroyer of wind-induced swelling. (107)

A warm poultice made from black pepper, old oil-cake, *śigru* bark, sand, and *śivā*, ground with cow's urine, destroys swelling caused by *śleṣman*. Furthermore, one should cause the patient's blood to flow after carefully examining the disease.
In the autumn season, a person should naturally cause blood to flow in the measure of one *prastha*, or half a *prastha*, or even half of that;
by doing so, skin diseases, tumors, swellings, and other ailments arising from blood are destroyed. (109–110)
A wise person should cause blood to flow during the rainy season when the sky is cloudless, as well as in winter, summer, and autumn; it should be drawn at midday during the cold season.
Blood that is neither hot nor cold, sweet, unctuous, and red in color is healthy.

Blood is heavy and has a fleshy odor; its burning sensation is like that of pitta. Foul smell, liquidity, redness, mobility, and fluidity—these are recorded as the qualities of blood derived from the five elements, beginning with earth. (112–113)
When blood is vitiated, there occurs swelling, as well as red circular patches (raktamaṇḍala),
pain, burning sensation, suppuration, itching, and the eruption of pustules.
When blood is increased, there is redness of the body and eyes, as well as fullness of the veins.

Heaviness of the limbs, sleepiness, delusion, and a burning sensation arise when the blood is diminished (115). When the blood is depleted, there is a craving for sweet things, fainting, dryness of the skin, and flaccidity of the veins; furthermore, due to the wind (vāta), the vessels tend to deviate from their normal course (116).
Blood vitiated by vāta is reddish, frothy, dry, rough, thin, and flows rapidly; it leaps upward, pricks like needles, and is painful.
Blood vitiated by pitta is yellow, green, blue, or dark-brown, and has a fleshy odor.
That which is tasteless and hot is disagreeable to flies and ants;

that which is cold, abundant, unctuous, resembling water mixed with red ochre, having the luster of a piece of flesh, flowing in a stream, moving slowly, and vitiated by phlegm—[is known as *skandha*]. (118–119)
That which is corrupted by two humors is mixed; that corrupted by three is foul-smelling;
and that endowed with all [defective] characteristics becomes like sour gruel (kāñjika). That corrupted by poison becomes dark-brown and likewise flows through an abnormal path toward the nose.
Fetid and resembling sour gruel (kāñjika), it likewise causes all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
It should be known as having the luster of an *indragopa* insect when it is in its natural state and not congealed.
[This occurs] during swelling, burning, inflammation of the limbs, and redness upon the discharge of blood.

In cases of vātarakta, as well as kuṣṭha, in difficult-to-conquer vāta accompanied by pain, in anemia (pāṇḍuroga), elephantiasis (ślīpada), and blood vitiated by poison; in glandular swellings (granthi), tumors (arbuda), scrofula (apacī), minor diseases, and the condition known as adhimantha.
In cases of Vidari and diseases of the breasts, in the sinking and heaviness of the limbs (124),
in blood congestion, drowsiness, and the foul odor and burning sensation of the nose and mouth, in liver and spleen enlargements, erysipelas, abscesses, and the eruption of carbuncles (125).
In cases of suppuration or burning of the ears, lips, nose, or mouth, as well as in headache, venereal sores (upadaṃśa), and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), bloodletting is highly recommended.
For these diseases, one may also employ horns, leeches, or gourds (alābu).
Alternatively, one may effect the removal of blood through venesection (sirāmokṣa).

However, one should not perform venesection on those who are emaciated, those who have overindulged in sexual intercourse, the impotent, the timid, pregnant women, women who have recently given birth, or those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍuroga).

For those suffering from hemorrhoids, generalized edema, abdominal enlargement (udara), dyspnea, cough, vomiting, or diarrhea, as well as for those whose bodies have been excessively subjected to sudation, [this is indicated] after they have undergone purification through the five types of therapeutic procedures and have consumed oleaginous substances. 129
Venesection is not recommended for one who is less than sixteen years of age, nor for one who has reached seventy, nor for one from whom blood has already flowed due to a wound (130–131).
In these cases, if an urgent disease occurs, one should extract the blood using leeches.
Likewise, venesection is not recommended for those afflicted by poison (132).
A wise physician should drain blood vitiated by vāta, pitta, and kapha in three ways: by means of a cow’s horn, leeches, or gourd (133).
Blood that is vitiated by two doṣas or even corrupted by all three doṣas should be drained with skillful venesection at the appropriate sites; likewise,
a horn ten fingers long may forcibly extract the blood.
The leech (*jalaukā*) should be one *hasta* in length, while the gourd (*tumbī*) should be twelve *aṅgulas*.
A vein (*sirā*) measuring only one *aṅgula* purifies the entire body.
[Bloodletting is contraindicated] when it is cold, when one has fasted, or when there is fainting, pain, sleepiness, fear, intoxication, or exhaustion. (135–136)
In those who are properly constricted, blood does not flow out, nor does it do so for those whose bowels and bladder are obstructed.
However, when the bleeding has ceased, one should rub the opening of the ulcer with *kuṣṭha*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and rock salt; by this means, the blood will flow forth again.

Therefore, a wise physician should let blood from one who has been satiated after drinking gruel, provided it is neither cold, nor excessively hot, nor perspiring, nor over-heated; likewise, one should avoid bloodletting in one who is over-sweated, during the hot season, or from excessive venesection. (138–139)
If the blood flows excessively, one should apply a remedy;
indeed, when the blood is flowing excessively, one should treat it with *lodhra*, resin of *sarja*, and *añjana*,
along with the flour of barley and wheat, and with *dhava*, *dhanvana*, and *gairika*.
Alternatively, having bound the mouth of the ulcer with the powder of sloughed snake-skin or with the ashes of two linen cloths,
one should treat the ulcer with cold applications;
one should then pierce the superior vein and cauterize it with alkali or fire.
An astringent (kaṣāya) heals a wound; a cold substance (hima) causes the blood to congeal;
an alkali (kṣāra) ripens the opening of a wound; and cauterization (dāha) contracts the vessels. Even when the vitiated blood remains, the disease will not further aggravate.
Therefore, one should preserve some blood; excessive bleeding is not beneficial.
[If it occurs, it causes] blindness, convulsions, thirst, blurred vision, pain in the head, hemiplegia, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, burning sensations, and jaundice. (144)
It causes excessive hemorrhage or even death.
The body originates from blood, and by that very blood the body is sustained;
blood is the support of the living soul, therefore a wise man should protect the blood. 145–146.
When Vāta has become aggravated by cold treatments,

one should sprinkle the painful swelling with lukewarm ghee after blood has been let; for a patient who is emaciated, [the meat soup] produced from the flesh of deer, rabbit, sheep, antelope, or goat [is recommended].
Milk with *ṣaṣṭika* rice is beneficial as a drink; it is the appropriate flavor.

When blood has been properly extracted, the signs will be the alleviation of pain, lightness of body, the subsiding of the disease and its complications, and the restoration of mental composure. (148–149)

One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, cold baths, and strong winds; eating only once a day, sleeping during the day, and consuming alkaline, sour, or pungent foods; as well as grief, debate, and indigestion, until strength is restored. (150–151)

One should treat the eye with these formulations: *sekam* (sprinkling), *āścyotanam* (dropping), *piṇḍī* (pills), *viḍālaka* (cat-like application), *tarpaṇam* (satisfying), as well as *puṭapāka* (steaming) and *añjanam* (collyrium).
Among these, *sekam* is beneficial for the entire eye when administered as fine streams.
For a person with closed eyes, it should be applied at a thickness of four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula).
It should be oily in cases of vāta; it acts as a healer (ropaṇa) in cases of pitta and rakta, whereas it should be used for scraping (lekhana) in cases of kapha. Its dosage is now described. 153–154.

An irrigation for the purpose of soothing should be performed with six hundred applications of the liquid, four hundred for healing, and three hundred for scraping; this is for the clarity of the eyes.
Alternatively, the opening and closing of the eyelids by men may be measured by the snap of a finger.
The utterance of long syllables is considered by the wise to be mere speech. 156. However, sprinkling [with water] should be performed during the day, and at night in the case of a severe illness;
goat’s milk cooked with ground leaves of *eraṇḍa* is beneficial.
Warm water poured into the eyes, when lukewarm, destroys *vātābhiṣyanda* (ophthalmia caused by wind).

The beneficial procedure known as *āścyotana* (eye-drops) consists of pouring drops of decoction, honey, or fatty substances into the eyes while they are opened to a distance of two finger-breadths; this is said to be wholesome. 157–158.

Eight drops are prescribed for scarifying, ten drops for healing, and twelve drops are declared for oleation; these should be lukewarm when applied in cold weather, but cool when applied in hot weather—this is the rule in all cases. (159)
For vāta, bitter and unctuous [medicines] are beneficial; for pitta, sweet and cold;
and for kapha, bitter, hot, and dry—these are the appropriate āścyotana (eye-drops) applied in this sequence.
The dosage for all types of āścyotana should be one hundred and fifty drops.
Thereafter, no one should ever apply eye-drops at night for any reason when the eyes are afflicted by the improper application of medicinal substances (162).
[One may instead use] the five roots beginning with Bilva, along with Bṛhatī, Eraṇḍa, and Śigru.

A lukewarm decoction used as eye-drops destroys wind and ocular congestion (abhiṣyanda). A bolus made from a paste of properly prepared medicinal drugs, bound with a piece of cloth and applied in the measure of a mouthful, destroys ocular congestion when placed upon the eyes. 163–164.

An ointment ball (*piṇḍikā*) that is unctuous and warm is prescribed for *vāta*; it is considered cool for *pitta* and dry and warm for *śleṣman*. This procedure has been declared by the wise. (165) One made from castor leaf, root, and bark is a destroyer of *vāta*.
An external plaster made of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) is for [excess] *pitta*, while one made of *śigru* leaves is for *kapha*. The *viḍālaka* (cat-like) plaster, which excludes the eyelashes,
should have its dosage understood according to the procedure for facial plasters.
An external plaster made from equal parts of yaṣṭī, gairika, saindhava, dārvī, and tārkṣya,
ground with water, removes all eye diseases. [168] This should be applied while the patient lies supine in a room free from wind, sunlight, and dust.
The two eye-sockets should be made even, firm, and unobstructed by surrounding them with moistened bean flour (māṣa-cūrṇa) and kneading it together.
One should fill them with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) and lukewarm water.

One should fill the eyes with ghee washed a hundred times or with ghee produced from milk while the eyelashes are submerged; one should keep them filled for as long as they remain submerged, and once the eyes are closed, one should then slowly open them.
This is the renowned procedure for *tarpaṇa* (eye saturation) declared by physicians.
[It is indicated when] the eye is dry, exuding moisture, distorted, and turbid, accompanied by decayed eyelashes, hordeola (*sirotpāta*), and painful opening of the lids. (172–173)

A physician skilled in eye diseases should properly perform *tarpaṇa* (eye saturation) for that eye which is afflicted by *timira*, *arjuna*, *śukla*, and other disorders, as well as by *abhiṣyanda*, *adhimantha*, dry ophthalmia (*śuṣkākṣipāka*), swelling (*śotha*), and various disorders arising from *vāta*. (174)
In diseases of the eyelids, a wise person should retain the *tarpaṇa* for one hundred recitations;
when healthy, or in cases of *kapha* and joint diseases, for five hundred recitations;
for six hundred in *kapha*-related black eye diseases (*kṛṣṇaroga*); and indeed for seven hundred in other cases.
In cases of eye diseases (dṛṣṭiroga), eight hundred [drops] should be used; for adhimantha, one thousand;
and for diseases of the wind (vātaroga), one thousand [drops] of *tarpaṇa* should indeed be retained.
