Once the full measure has been reached, one should drain it through the outer corner of the eye and thus cleanse the eye.
Then, having applied steamed barley flour impregnated with the potency of fats,
one should purge his *kapha* using appropriate medicinal smoking (*dhūmapāna*).
One should administer nourishing therapy (*tarpaṇa*) for one day, three days, or even five days.
In the case of satiation by *tarpaṇa*, one should observe these signs of satisfaction in the eye:
pleasant sleep and waking, clarity, acuity of vision, contentment, the subsiding of disease, and lightness of function. (180)

One should designate as *atitarpita* (over-saturated) an eye that is turbid with heavy secretions, excessively unctuous, accompanied by tears, itching, and discharge, and characterized by friction and pain;
it is further abounding in diseases such as lacrimation and swelling, and is overwhelmed by a thick coating. 181.
The eye that is parched, non-exuding, and reddish is one that has been under-nourished (hīnatarpita).
Due to the abundance of these two types of defects, one should strive for medical treatment; the remedy for these two consists of dry and unctuous therapies respectively. 182–183.
Tarpaṇa is not recommended for the eyes during cloudy days, extreme heat or cold, when one is anxious or agitated, or when there is no subsiding of complications.
Two bilva fruits are considered equal to one pala of fatty meat.
One should grind all these ingredients together in a measure of one *kuḍava* (185);
having thoroughly mixed them into a single mass and wrapped it well with leaves,
the wise man should cook it according to the procedure for *puṭapāka* and extract its juice.
One should apply it correctly according to the procedure prescribed for *tarpaṇa*;
it should be poured into the eye of one who is lying flat on their back every day.
It is threefold: emollient (*snehana*), scraping (*lekhana*), and healing (*ropaṇa*). 187.

For one who is excessively dry, it is beneficial and unctuous; for one who is already unctuous, however, it is drying (lekhana). The other [type] is for the sake of strengthening the vision and alleviates pitta, blood disorders, wounds, and vāta.
It is prepared with fats, meat, muscle fat (vasā), marrow, bone marrow (medas), and sweet medicinal herbs.
The *puṭapāka* for oleation (*snehana*) should be retained for two hundred words;
it is prepared with the liver and meat of wild animals combined with scraping substances,
as well as with black iron powder, copper, conch-shell, coral, and rock salt.
A lekhana (scraping) enema prepared with sea-foam,
kāsīsa, srotoñjana, and curd-whey is desired for the supreme retention of a hundred words.
[192] A [mild] enema cooked with breast milk, meat of wild animals, honey, ghee, and bitter substances [is also used].
The healing *puṭapāka* should be maintained as three times the amount of the *lekhana*;
this group, consisting of nimba, amṛtā, vṛṣa, paṭola, and nidigdhikā, is renowned as the "Five Bitters" (*pañcatiktaka*). 193–194.
Upon the appearance of complications, one should perform the procedure prescribed for *tarpaṇa*.

Once the eyes have been treated with *tarpaṇa*, or by one who has undergone *puṭapāka*, one should not look at bright objects such as flames, the wind, the sky, mirrors, or any other luminous things. (195–196)
Now, for one whose humors have fully ripened, one should administer the appropriate collyrium (añjana).
That substance by which collyrium is prepared is also considered "añjana.
Each of these is said to be threefold: scraping (lekhanam), healing (ropaṇam), and likewise [palliative]. 197.
And emollience—listen now to their symptoms in detail.
Lekhana (scraping) is said to be the application of collyrium with alkaline, sharp, or sour tastes; it acts upon the eyelids, the network of vessels, and the *śṛṅgāṭaka* located in the ears. 198–199.
Having agitated the morbid humors (doṣas) through the mouth, nose, and eyes, one should cause them to flow out;
that [medicated oil] is considered healing when it is astringent, bitter, and unctuous.
Due to the coolness of the unctuous substance, it improves the complexion and increases the strength of the vision.
That collyrium, being sweet and containing a scum of oil, is a clarifying agent (prasādana);
it is beneficial for the purpose of clarifying defects of vision and for the purpose of oleation (snehana).
As for the scraping collyrium (lekhanī), its measure should be the size of a grain of *hareṇu*. 201–202.
A *ropaṇī* (healing) wick is desired to be one and a half *hareṇuka* in measure;
a *snehana* (oleating) wick is made with a measure of two *hareṇuka*. The measure of *rasāñjana*, however, is considered to be the amount that can be ground into a paste for a wick.
Physicians prescribe a powder for scraping with two sticks,
for healing with three sticks, and four sticks for an ointment used as an eye-salve.
The applicator should be shaped like a bud at both ends and be the size of a pea in circumference.
The probe (śalākā) should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) in length and made of stone or metal; a probe made of copper, iron, or stone is intended for scraping,
while one produced from gold or silver is prescribed for lubrication.
The finger, by virtue of its softness, is employed for application;
one should smear the collyrium starting from the black portion of the eye up to the outer corner.
In both the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons, the application of collyrium is desired at midday.
It is desired [to be applied] in the forenoon or the afternoon during summer and autumn (208);
during the rainy season when it is not cloudy and not excessively hot; and always indeed in the spring.
Or else, one may apply the collyrium at all times, either in the morning or in the evening (209).
It should be applied during a time when it is neither too cold nor too hot, nor when there is wind or clouds; however,
collyrium should not be applied when one is fatigued, weeping, frightened, has consumed alcohol, suffers from acute fever, or has indigestion or suppressed natural urges.
It cures redness, coating, darkness of vision, pain, irritation, sleepiness, and wasting; when contraindicated, collyrium is properly applied [as follows]:
conch-shell, the marrow of bibhītaka, harītakī, and realgar.
One should grind equal parts of pippalī, marica, kuṣṭha,
and vacā with goat’s milk and make a wick (varti) the size of a barley grain;
having ground [the same ingredients] with water in the measure of a hareṇu seed, one should prepare an ointment (añjana).
Timira, fleshy growths, cataracts, pterygium, tumors, night-blindness, seasonal ophthalmia, and pupillary dilation— these the Candrodya Varti removes.
Thus ends the Candrodya Varti, the scraping collyrium.
Eighty sesame flowers, sixty grains of long pepper (*pippalī*),
fifty jasmine flowers (*jātīpuṣpa*), and sixteen black peppercorns (*marica*)— having ground these finely with water, a wick called *kusumikā* is prepared. (216)
This collyrium is said to destroy cataracts (timira), arjuna, and śukla, and to remove the growth of flesh;
its measure is one part of hareṇukā with a half-part added. [The ingredients are] dhātrī, yakṣa, and pathyā seeds, taken in one, two, and three parts respectively. 217.
Having ground these with water, one should prepare a medicinal wick (varti) and apply it as a collyrium (añjana) containing two parts of hareṇuka;
this quickly removes eye discharge as well as the pain of vātarakta (218–219).
[The following ingredients are: tuttha, mākṣika, saindhava, sugar, śaṅkha, and manaḥśilā.
One should powder together red ochre, rock salt, and black pepper;
by mixing this with honey, one should prepare a medicinal extract (rasakriyā) for use as a collyrium, which is supreme for curing diseases of the eyelids, ama, timira, kāca, and śukra.
Rasāñjana, sarjarasa, jasmine flower, realgar, sea-foam, salt, red ochre,
and black pepper— these taken in equal parts and ground with honey [are used] for a moistened eyelid.
Collyrium (añjana) alleviates moisture and itching and promotes the growth of eyelashes. Having ground the fruit of the *kataka* tree with honey, one should apply it as an eye-salve;
when combined with a small amount of camphor, it is known to clarify the vision of the eyes.
An ointment made from *dakṣāṇḍatvak*, mica, glass, conch, sandalwood,
and rock salt constantly and powerfully removes all diseases of the eye.
Having ground *rasaka* on a stone slab, it should be thoroughly saturated with water.
One should take all that water and discard the powder that has settled at the bottom.
When that entire water has dried, it will become like thin wafers (parpaṭī).
Having pulverized it, one should properly saturate it three times with the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
One should add camphor powder there in the tenth part;
by applying it to the eyes, all defects are pacified.
This powder undoubtedly destroys all eye diseases. 228

One should heat sauvīra salt over fire and sprinkle it seven times with the juice of triphalā and likewise with the breast milk of women. Once it has been sprinkled and ground into powder, one should apply it as an ointment to the eyes daily; this is beneficial for the eyes.

This will undoubtedly destroy all disorders of the eye. Once the defects have subsided and the tearing has ceased, one should wash the eye thoroughly in water; thereafter, an ointment (añjana) should be applied according to the specific disorder.
Or, when there is no risk of wind-induced complications, one should employ eye-washing;
in that case, one should apply a counter-collyrium consisting of a sharp, clarifying powder.
When the mercury (nāga) has been purified and liquefied, one should cast pure *tuttha* (copper sulfate) and purified mercury into it.
One should grind black antimony equal in quantity to those two together into a single powder (233).
One should then add camphor amounting to one-tenth of that powder; this counter-collyrium (pratyañjana) conquers eye diseases and is an elixir for the eyes (234).
Likewise, a snake that has been heated and sprinkled with the juices of triphalā, bhṛṅga, and śuṇṭhī, along with ghee, cow’s urine, honey, and goat’s milk,
serves as a probe (śalākā) that indeed removes all diseases arising in the eye. 235–236.

Thus, regarding the various preparations of medicines, a wise person should generally take the medicine in the morning; however, decoctions (kaṣāyas) are especially to be taken then, as their specific distinctions have been shown therein. 237
The time for men to take medicine should be known as fivefold:
when the sun has slightly risen, at the time of the midday meal, at the evening meal, frequently during the day, and likewise at night. (238)
Generally, when there is an aggravation of pitta and kapha, one should administer medicine without food in the morning for the purposes of purgation, emesis, and scraping (lekhanārtha).
Medicine is recommended at the beginning of a meal when the downward-moving wind (apāna) is impaired.
In cases of lack of appetite, one should provide appetizing food mixed with various colorful delicacies (240).
When the Samāna Vāyu is deranged and the digestive fire is weak,
a skilled physician should administer a digestive stimulant during the course of the meal (241).

When the Vyāna Vāyu is provoked, one should administer medicine at the end of the meal; in cases of hiccups, convulsions, and tremors, it should be taken both before and after the meal. When the Udāna Vāyu is provoked, causing disorders such as loss of voice and so forth—
Medicine should be administered between morsels of food during the evening meal (243).
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is disturbed, medicine is generally given by the wise at the end of the evening meal; this is known as the third time. (244)

And in cases of thirst, vomiting, hiccups, dyspnea, and poisoning, one should administer medicine repeatedly; this is the fourth time for administration. In disorders above the clavicle, as well as in those requiring depleting or nourishing therapies, [the same applies].

Food and medicine administered at night for the purpose of digestion or pacification possess superior potency; such medicine and food, when not deficient, undoubtedly and swiftly destroy that disease. However, when consumed by children, the elderly, women, or those of delicate constitution, it quickly leads to extreme exhaustion and a loss of strength. (246–247)
It undergoes digestion quickly; it does not harm the digestive power when covered by food, nor does it repeatedly escape from the mouth.
This is beneficial for the elderly, children, the emaciated, and women; indeed, that which is eaten before a meal has the same effect.
When medicine is taken after a meal, or when a meal is taken after medicine has been drunk, [it is likewise beneficial].
It does not pacify the disease and instead provokes other disorders.
(249) Favorable wind brings about health, hunger, thirst, mental clarity, lightness, purity of the senses and eructations, and the characteristic signs of digested medicine. (250)
Fatigue, burning sensations, weakness of the limbs, vertigo, fainting, headache,
restlessness, and loss of strength— these are the signs that the medicine has not been fully digested.
(251) Having honored and bowed down to the gods, the preceptors, and the Brahmins, [one should proceed].
Having accepted these blessings with faith, one should partake of the medicine.
May this medicine be for you like the elixir of the sages, like the nectar of the gods, and like the excellent liquor of the supreme Nāgas. (252–253)
May Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, Earth, Moon, Sun, Wind, and Fire,
as well as the gods together with the multitude of medicinal herbs and the gods of the earth, protect you. (254) May the medicine, placed within a vessel of gold, silver, or clay, [protect you].
One should drink [the medicine] in the presence of trustworthy people, with a serene face and eyes;

then, having sat down in a state of tranquility and finished drinking, one should set the vessel face-down, perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with water, and then consume betel leaves and other such items. 255–256.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the procedure for smoking and other therapies, in the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana;
now begins the seventh chapter, on the examination of the patient. 7.
One should examine the patient through observation, palpation, and questioning;
for by observation one perceives longevity and so forth, by palpation coldness and so forth, and by questioning, one learns what follows.
Indeed, disorders that are wrongly observed or likewise incorrectly described [lead to error].
Likewise, physicians who have misdiagnosed may cause delusion;
in that regard, an examination of the eyes, tongue, urine, and so forth must be performed.
The eye, due to wind (vāta), becomes rough, smoke-colored, or reddish.
When the eye has entered as if into a hollow, with a fixed gaze,
and appears the color of turmeric pieces, or red, or likewise green,
and is constantly burning as if scorched by fire, it is due to the provocation of pitta.
Due to the predominance of the strength of the wind (vāyu), the eye becomes oily, as if submerged in water,
white in color, devoid of luster, yet endowed with strength. Due to the predominance of two doshas, the eye exhibits the characteristics of those two doshas.
By the combination of the symptoms of the three doṣas, it kills the patient (6).
The eye vitiated by the three doṣas becomes deeply sunken within;
it exhibits the three symptoms, exudes water, and can only be opened at the edge (7).
Due to Vāta, the tongue becomes rough like a leaf of the *śāka* plant and cracks;
due to Pitta, it becomes red or dark-brown; and due to Kapha, it becomes coated, swollen, and pale. When all three Doshas are predominant, it becomes scorched, rough to the touch, and black.
That same [condition], when there is an excess of two doshas, is characterized by those two doshas.
(9) Due to vāta, the urine is pale; due to pitta, it is red or blue;
due to blood, it becomes red; and due to kapha, it is white and frothy. (10)
Now, for the purpose of knowing the coldness, heat, and other qualities of the body, the sense of touch must be employed;
the excellent physician should examine the pulse located at the base of the thumb of the man’s right hand or the woman’s left hand. (11)
One who is skilled should touch the vein with three fingers; by its movement, he may know all about pleasure and pain.
[This applies to one] who has just bathed, or is asleep, or is accustomed to hunger, thirst, and heat.
The pulse of one whose body is exhausted by physical exertion is not properly perceived.

When Vāta is predominant, the pulse is clearly felt on the surface of the index finger; when Pitta is predominant, it is clear at the middle finger; and when Kapha is predominant, it is found at the third finger. 13–14.
When wind and bile (vāta-pitta) predominate, it is clearly manifest between the index finger and the middle finger;
when wind and phlegm (vāta-kapha) predominate, it becomes distinct on the ring finger and the index finger;
and when bile and phlegm (pitta-kapha) predominate, it is clearly manifest between the middle finger and the ring finger. 15.
It may also appear clearly on all three fingers due to the combination of the humors (sannipāta).

From wind (vāta), it moves in a crooked manner; from bile (pitta), it moves by leaping up; from phlegm (kapha), it is known to move slowly; and from the combination of all three (sannipāta), it moves very rapidly.
The pulse moves crookedly after leaping due to an excess of vāta and pitta;
it flows both crookedly and slowly due to a predominance of vāta and śleṣman. When pitta and kapha are excessive, the nāḍī leaps and moves slowly.
Flowing with force from desire or anger, diminished and overwhelmed by anxiety and fear,
that [pulse] which moves only after stopping repeatedly destroys the person when it falters from its place; likewise,
one that is extremely diminished and cold undoubtedly kills the vital breaths.
Due to the provocation of fever, the pulse becomes hot and forceful; in one with weak digestion and diminished bodily constituents, that same pulse is considered to be much slower.
It is rapid in one who is hungry, and steady in one who is satiated.
It should be known as stable even for those who are happy, and likewise it is considered powerful.
(22) Subsequently, the cause, the onset, the premonitory symptoms, the clinical signs, and likewise the therapeutic suitability—these five are the means for the diagnosis of disease. (23)
That which cannot exist without another is said in the treatise to be its cause for the sake of conventional usage; we shall now explain its synonyms:
nidāna, kāraṇa, hetu, nimitta, and nibandhana. (24)
The root-base (mūlāyatana) is there also designated as the condition (pratyaya).

Just as by means of a corrupted humor (doṣa), and just as by that which spreads along [the channels], so too is this the arising of disease; it is called attainment (samprāpti), birth (jāti), and arrival (āgati). 25–26.
It is differentiated according to the distinctions of number, variation, predominance, strength, and time, as will be stated right here: "there are eight fevers" (27).
Variation (*vikalpa*) refers to the conceptualization of the portions and parts of the combined *doṣas* (28).

One should determine the predominance of a disease by means of its independence or dependence [on other factors]. (29) One should distinguish between strength and weakness through the completeness or partiality of the causes and so forth. (30) The time of the disease is determined according to its nature by the portions of night, day, season, and mealtime. (31)
Vāgbhaṭa has stated that the provocation of Vāta and the other [humors] occurs during the respective parts of the night and so forth:
"Although they are pervasive, they reside respectively in the lower, middle, and upper parts of the heart and navel;
and they occur at the end, middle, and beginning of the three ages, the day and night, and the meal, respectively. (32)
The provocation of wind and the other humors occurs according to the seasons:
wind is provoked in the rainy season or the cold season, bile in autumn and summer, and phlegm in spring; this is the natural seasonal order. 33
The premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are those by which one may recognize a future disease;
they are described as being of two kinds: general and specific.
Among these, the general symptoms are those not yet determined by the specific characteristics of the doshas.

That which is distinguished, slightly manifest, and endowed with specific qualities is known as the "distinguished prior form" (pūrvarūpa-viśiṣṭa); its characteristics are remembered as configuration (saṃsthāna), mark (liṅga), sign (cihna), secondary characteristic (vyañjana), form (rūpa), and shape (ākṛti). 34–35.
One should know that the beneficial application of medicines, foods, and lifestyle activities which brings comfort to men is called *sātmya* (habituation).
[These include] sweet, salty, sour, unctuous, nasal drops, warmth, sleep, heavy food, exposure to sunlight, enemas, sudation, and massage.
Curd, ghee, sesame oil, massage, and nourishing therapies—these should pacify the aggravated *pavamāna* (vāta).
Bitter, sweet, and astringent tastes; cold winds, shade, night, fanning, moonlight, underground chambers, mechanical water-fountains, lotuses, and the touch of a woman’s body [are also beneficial].
Ghee, milk, purgatives, affusions, bloodletting, plasters, and the like— this regimen of drinks, food, conduct, and medicine will lead to the pacification of pitta.
38 Drying agents, alkaline substances, astringents, bitter and pungent tastes, physical exercise, and spitting [are likewise beneficial].
Fumigation, excessive heat, head-purgation, emesis, sudation, fasting, and so forth;
thirst, wind, walking on the road, wrestling, staying awake at night, playing in water, and sexual intercourse—this regimen of drink, food, recreation, and medicine removes even virulent *śleṣman*.
(39) Indeed, the aggravated *malas* are the primary cause of all diseases.
The causes for its provocation are said to be the consumption of various unwholesome things:
wild rice (*nīvāra*), *tripuṭa*, *satīna*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *śyāmāka*, green gram (*mudga*), *āḍhakī*, flat beans (*niṣpāva*), *makuṣṭhaka*, *cavaraṭī*, *maṅgalyaka*, and *kodrava*. (40)
Whatever substance is pungent, bitter, astringent, cold, and dry; eating in small quantities, irregular eating, fasting, or eating while the previous meal is undigested;

41 eating when the previous meal is already fully digested; exhaustion, the weight of disease, and other such causes; exposure to heat; [the consumption of] thick food; climbing a tree with one's arms, falling from it, walking excessively on the road, being struck by a staff or similar object, falling from a height, depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus), staying awake, obstruction of the channels, excessive sexual intercourse, and the suppression of the urges of wind and other humors; 42
Excessive emesis, purgation, excessive discharge, and loss of blood; depletion of muscle tissue, over-indulgence in sexual pleasure, anxiety, grief, and fear;
the rainy season, the winter, the third parts of the day and night, clouds, the easterly wind, and frost—these are the causes for the vitiation of the bodily winds (vāta). 43.
Through pungent, sour, hot, burning, sharp, and salty foods; through anger, fasting, exposure to the sun, sexual intercourse, thirst, hunger, physical blows, exercise, wine, and the like;
while the food being digested after a meal; and during autumn, summer, midday, as well as at the time of midnight—the provocation of pitta occurs for living beings. (44)
It causes a burning sensation, belching, and acidity, as well as thirst;
it produces a burning sensation in the heart and takes a long time to digest.
(45) [This occurs when consumed] with black gram, sesame, horse gram, fish, and mutton.

The *pitta* of men becomes aggravated by cow's curd and buttermilk (46). Furthermore, in the first part of the day and during the night, as well as immediately after eating in the spring season, there occurs an aggravation of *kapha* due to heavy, sharp, sweet, sour, and unctuous foods; mung beans, sesame seeds, liquid curd, daytime sleep, cold clarified butter, and excessive intake [of these] (47).
A disease that acts as the cause [of another] is also observed to be the cause of yet another disease.
(48) For some diseases, having become the cause of another disease, subside; (49) while others do not subside, even though they act as the cause. (50)
These two types of men—those who are always excessively stout and those who are always emaciated—are utterly contemptible.
The one with a medium build is the best; the stout man is not honored when he is wasted away, nor is the emaciated man honored when he is made fat.
Therefore, one should always cause the stout man to lose weight and the emaciated man to gain weight.
A skilled physician should also provide protection for those who are moderate;
the physician should diminish or augment the humors, tissues, and wastes in a person afflicted by disease until he becomes free from that disease. 51–52.

By whatever method an unwell person becomes well, that very method the physician should employ, since health is always desired. (53) One whose humors, digestive fire, tissues, wastes, and functions are in equilibrium [is healthy].
One whose self, senses, and mind are serene is said to be "established in health" (svastha).

There is equilibrium among feces, urine, all humors (doṣa), and bodily constituents (dhātu); there is a desire for food and drink, and what is eaten is digested for nourishment; digestion proceeds properly; sleep and waking are pleasant;
and one perceives objects as they truly are and adopts appropriate conduct through the functioning of the mind.
These fourteen types of characteristics have been described for a healthy person.

Indeed, the increase of the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and *malas* is said by the best of physicians to result from the excessive indulgence in food and activities that cause their respective increases. 55–56.
When Vāta is increased, there occurs emaciation, roughness, a desire for warmth, excessive excretion, diminished strength, a tingling sensation in the limbs, insomnia,
yellowness of the feces, urine, eyes, and body, and impaired sensory function.

When pitta is increased, there is a desire for cold, a burning sensation, fainting, and scanty urination (57). When kapha is excessive, there is whiteness of the feces and other excretions, coldness, heaviness, excessive sleep,
looseness of the joints, excessive moisture, and salivation from the mouth (58).
When the rasa-dhatu is increased, a distaste for food arises, along with heaviness of the limbs,
salivation, vomiting, fainting, exhaustion, vertigo, and phlegm (59).
An increased blood-dhatu makes the body reddish in color.
The blood, when increased, fills the eyes and the vessels as well;
it causes erysipelas, splenic enlargement, abscesses,
leprosy, gouty disorders, abdominal tumors, distension of the vessels, and jaundice.
Heaviness of the limbs, drowsiness, intoxication, and a burning sensation arise;
there is impairment of the sense organs, depression of the digestive fire, delusion, and redness of the skin, eyes, and urine.
Furthermore, there is suppuration of the anus, penis, and mouth, as well as hemorrhoids, pustules, and lice.
Indralupta (alopecia) destroys the limbs, while marda (pruritus), asṛgdara (menorrhagia), and astāpa (feverish exhaustion) affect the hands and feet.
One should pacify an increase of blood with blood-letting and purgatives.
However, when there is an increase of flesh in the cheeks, lips, buttocks, genitals, thighs, or arms, [it should be treated accordingly].
It causes an increase in the calves as well as heaviness of the limbs;

likewise, when there is an increase of fat (medas), there occurs an enlargement of the abdomen and the sides, along with cough, dyspnea, and other ailments, as well as foul odor and unctuousness of the body. (64–65)
When it is greatly increased, it produces fatness (medas), fatigue even with slight exertion,
and the onset of thirst, sweating, diseases of the throat, goiter, lips, and urinary disorders (meha),
as well as labored breathing and the sagging of the buttocks, abdomen, neck, and breasts. (66)
The aged bones produce other bones within the bones;
likewise, they produce large and formidable teeth.
When the marrow has grown old, it brings about heaviness in all the limbs and the eyes.

In the case of seminal calculi (śukrāśmarī), there is an increase in semen and excessive discharge of semen; when the waste products (malas) have increased, flatulence arises along with pain in the abdomen. When urine has increased, there is frequent urination, distension, and pain in the bladder.
When sweat increases, however, a foul odor arises along with itching on the skin.
There may be excessive discharge of the menses (ārtava), and a foul odor occurs in the menstrual flow;
body aches also arise—these are the signs when the menses are in excess.
Excessive fullness of the breasts, frequent discharge of milk, and a pricking sensation therein are the signs of an abundance of breast milk (72). Furthermore,
the enlargement of the abdomen and other such changes occurs when the fetus has grown large.
A pregnant woman may experience perspiration, and there is great distress at the time of delivery (73).
Indeed, the reduction of the humors (doṣa), tissues (dhātu), and wastes (mala) in humans is said to result from the consumption of various foods and behaviors that cause such diminution (74).
Each preceding [tissue] increases the succeeding one due to its own excessive growth;
therefore, the reduction of excessively increased *dhātus* is beneficial. [This occurs] through unwholesome food, constant anger, grief, anxiety, fear, and fatigue.

Excessive sexual indulgence, fasting, excessive purification therapies, the suppression of natural urges, reckless behavior, and lack of nourishment lead to the depletion of the *doṣas*, the *dhātus*, and the waste products (*malas*). (76–77)

In the depletion of Vata, there is a lack of physical activity, sluggish speech, and loss of consciousness; in the depletion of Pitta, there is an increase in Kapha, diminished digestive fire, and loss of luster (78);
in the depletion of Kapha, the joints become loose, and there is fainting, dryness, and a burning sensation.
In the depletion of *rasa* (plasma), there is pain in the heart, dryness of the throat, a sense of emptiness in the skin, and thirst.
In the depletion of blood (*asṛk-kṣaya*), the veins become flaccid, the skin becomes cold and rough, and [pain occurs] in the cheeks, lips, neck, shoulders, breasts, abdomen, and joints. 79–80.
In the case of wasting of the flesh (māṃsa-saṃkṣaya), there is swelling and nodules in the perineum, dryness of the limbs, pricking pain, and the vessels become flaccid.
There is enlargement of the spleen, a sense of emptiness in the joints, and dryness of the body. (81)
Longing for food is the sign of the wasting of fatty tissue (*medas*).
Pain in the bones, dryness of the body, and the breaking off of nails and teeth—this is declared by all physicians to be the sign of the wasting of bone (*asthi*). (82–83)
Scarcity of semen, fracture of the joints, and a pricking pain in the bones— these signs arise in men when the marrow is depleted. (84) In the depletion of semen,
there is an inability for sexual intercourse and pain in the penis and the testicles.
Emission of semen may occur with delay; when it does occur, there is a state of diminished semen due to blood.
Vital essence (*ojas*) is depleted by anger, anxiety, grief, fatigue, and the like, as well as by dry, sharp, hot, and pungent substances, and by other emaciating factors. (85–86)

A person with diminished *ojas* is constantly afraid, his senses are distressed, he is prone to rising up suddenly, dejected, rough, and emaciated (87). Upon the depletion of feces, there is pain in the flanks and the heart.
The upward movement of wind accompanied by sound, contraction of the abdomen, scanty urine during the depletion of urine, and a pricking pain in the bladder arise;
furthermore, there is the loss of perspiration, roughness of the skin, and dryness of the eyes. (88–89)
The hair follicles become stiff; these are the signs that occur upon the loss of sweat.
Furthermore, the absence or the paucity of menstrual blood at its proper time occurs, and pain arises in the vagina—these are the signs of the loss of menstrual blood (ārtavakṣaya).
There may be an absence or a slight amount of breast milk for you;
moreover, these are the signs of exhaustion and the depletion of breast milk:
the breasts become flattened, the abdomen does not swell, and likewise there is no movement of the fetus.

Thus have the wise declared the symptoms for the wasting of each [tissue] (garbhakṣaya). By strictly adhering to specific diets and lifestyles that promote the growth of each respective tissue, a person quickly attains those [nutrients] and wards off that particular wasting. 92–93.
The vital energy (*ojas*) of men increases through substances that are very unctuous, palatable, and aphrodisiac, especially through milk, meat broth, and the like.
Even a person whose humors (*doṣa*), tissues (*dhātu*), and wastes (*mala*) are depleted, as well as one whose strength (*bala*) is diminished, [is restored by these]. 94.
Whatever nourishment he desires for his respective growth—that very food and drink he longs for;
whatever kind of sustenance a person in a state of depletion seeks, by obtaining each of those, he dispels that particular deficiency. (95–96)
One whose *vāta* is diminished desires astringent, pungent, and bitter substances, as well as those that are dry, cold, and light;
likewise, barley, mung beans, *priyaṅgu*, and preparations made from the flour of sesame, black gram, horse gram, and the like. (97)

One whose *pitta* is diminished desires whey, fermented gruel, sour buttermilk, as well as sour rice-gruel and curd; pungent, sour, salty, and hot foods; sharp [substances], anger, and burning [foods]; and likewise a warm season and a warm country. (98–99)
One whose *kapha* is depleted desires sweet, unctuous, cold, salty, sour, and heavy substances, as well as curd, milk, and sleeping during the day (verse 100).
A man whose *rasa* is depleted repeatedly craves extremely cold water.

Nightly sleep, snow, the moon, and sweet flavors; sugarcane, meat broth, churned milk (mantha), honey, ghee, and jaggery-water; as well as grapes, pomegranate, and fermented vinegar, along with unctuous substances and salts. 101–102.
One whose blood is depleted desires meats prepared with blood;
one whose flesh is depleted desires foods prepared with curd, many kinds of *ṣāḍava* dishes, and the flesh of large carnivorous animals. (103–104)

One whose fat is diminished especially desires meat that has been prepared with fat, as well as the flesh of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, along with alkaline substances; likewise, one whose bone marrow is diminished desires meat combined with the fatty essence of bones.
One whose marrow is diminished desires substances combined with sweet and sour tastes (106).
One whose semen is diminished desires the eggs of the peacock, the cock, as well as those of the swan and the crane, and those of domestic, marshy, and aquatic birds (107).
One whose strength is diminished longs for barley-food, millet-food, and various kinds of vegetables, as well as soups of lentils and black gram;
he desires drinks such as sugarcane juice, milk, molasses, and jujube-water. (108)
One whose urine has been depleted desires cucumber and gourd;
one whose body has been depleted by sweating longs for oil massage, dry rubbing, wine, a sheltered bed and seat, and heavy clothing. (109-110)
Bitter, sour, salty, hot, burning, and heavy fruits, vegetables, and drinks—these a woman longs for when her menstrual flow has ceased.
Likewise, she desires wine, rice, meat, cow’s milk, and sugar. (111)
When her milk is diminished, she desires whey, curd, and heart-pleasing foods;
when her pregnancy has ended, she desires the prepared fetuses of deer, goats, sheep, and boars, as well as various kinds of roasted fat on spits and the like, to eat. (112–113)

That which causes the nourishment of the bodily constituents (dhātus), beginning from rasa and ending with semen, and which provides proficiency in physical activities, is designated as *bala* (strength).
[It is diminished] by trauma, fear, anger, anxiety, and exhaustion. (114)
Through the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and from grief, the strength of men is diminished. Heaviness, stiffness in the limbs, pallor of the face, discoloration,
drowsiness, sleepiness, and edema caused by Vāta are the signs of the destruction of strength.
That substance which brings about equilibrium of the humors (doṣas), brings about equilibrium of the digestive fire (agni),
and nourishes the tissues (dhātus) increases strength.
For it is observed that some who are emaciated are strong, while others who are corpulent possess very little strength.
Therefore, the wise know him to be strong by virtue of his physical agility. 118.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the examination of the patient, in the section on technical definitions and so forth, within the first part of the *Śrībhāvaprakāśa*, composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakana. 7.
Thus ends the first section;
now begins the middle section, the chapter on fevers (*jvarādhikāra*).
Therein begins the eighth section on therapeutics (cikitsāprakaraṇa).
Since fever is renowned as the king of all diseases, the chapter on fever is written by me first here. 1.

The fever born from the breath of Rudra, enraged by Dakṣa’s insult, is known to be of eight types: those arising separately from the individual *doṣas*, from combinations of two, from all three combined, and from external causes. Indeed, through improper diet and lifestyle, the *doṣas* take refuge in the *āmāśaya*.
Having cast the digestive fire (koṣṭhāgni) outward, the fever-inducing humors follow the bodily fluids (rasa). Fatigue, restlessness, discoloration, a bad taste in the mouth, watering of the eyes,
and frequent desire or aversion toward cold, wind, heat, and other such conditions [occur].
Yawning, aching of the limbs, heaviness, horripilation, loss of appetite, darkness of vision,
lack of joy, and coldness occur when fever is about to arise. Generally speaking, however, excessive yawning is caused by the wind (vāta).

From pitta, there is a burning sensation in the eyes; from kapha, a lack of desire for food. When the symptoms of any two [humors] are combined, they know it as arising from two [humors]. When all the symptoms are present together, it arises from the provocation of all three humors.
The obstruction of perspiration, a burning sensation, and a seizing pain throughout all the limbs occurring simultaneously in a disease— that is designated as *jvara* (fever). Furthermore,
because it obstructs the watery elements (*ap-dhātu*), the one afflicted by fever [is called *jvarātura*].
The patient's body becomes excessively hot and perspires not at all; where one is unable to distinguish even a portion from another among the humors (doṣas),
the physician should apply a general treatment.
In general, a person suffering from fever should first reside in a windless dwelling,
because a windless environment promotes longevity, health, and well-being.
The breeze from a fan removes thirst, perspiration, fainting, and fatigue.
Air produced from a palm-leaf fan is considered to pacify the three *doṣas*.
That produced from a bamboo fan is warm and aggravates blood-bile (*raktapitta*).
So too are those produced from yak-tail hair, cloth, peacock feathers, and cane.
These winds, which conquer the humors, are unctuous, heart-pleasing, and highly esteemed.
One suffering from acute fever should diligently clothe oneself in heavy, warm garments;
one should drink some water that has been boiled and cooled according to the season, while avoiding [certain things].
Even without medicines, disease is cured by wholesome diet alone;
however, for one who lacks a wholesome diet, it is not cured even by hundreds of medicines.
[One should employ] affusions, plasters, oleation, and purification therapies.
One suffering from acute fever should avoid sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, cold water, anger, exposure to drafts, and unwholesome food.
[Furthermore, one should avoid] wasting away, vomiting, intoxication, fainting, giddiness, thirst, and loss of appetite.
By the employment of affusions and similar treatments, one incurs these complications:

from physical exercise, there is an increase in fever; from sexual intercourse, stiffness, fainting, death, and [other disorders] from the intake of fats; and from [excessive] emesis, fainting, vomiting, intoxication, and loss of appetite. (18–19)

From eating heavy food and sleeping [after a meal], there occurs constipation, provocation of the humors (doṣas), loss of digestive fire, roughness, and the obstruction of the channels; likewise for one who has fever or is free from fever, [eating] burning and heavy foods [produces these same effects]. 20.
One should avoid unwholesome foods and drinks, incompatible or excessive meals, physical exercise, over-exertion, oil massage, and bathing;
by this, the fever subsides and, once pacified, does not recur. (21–22)
The dosha, located in the stomach (āmāśaya), destroys the digestive fire and obstructs the channels; therefore, it produces fever. For this reason, one should practice fasting (laṅghana).
Fasting is prescribed at the onset of fever, while digestive stimulants (pācana) are prescribed during the middle stage of fever.

One should administer medicine at the end of a fever, and purgation once the fever has been liberated. This [purgative] therapy, which is threefold, should be applied after considering the three types of *doṣas*:
fasting is beneficial when the *doṣa* is slight, and fasting combined with digestive treatment when it is moderate.

When the fever is severe, purification is required; this should uproot the impurities from their very root. However, one should first bring a fresh fever to exhaustion through fasting, or one should fast it according to the prescribed rules based on the signs of *āmadoṣa*.
O best among speakers, wind (vāta) undergoes digestion in seven days, bile (pitta) in ten days,
and phlegm (śleṣman) in twelve days. One who requires fasting should perform lightening therapy (laṅghana) according to the nature of the humors.
In cases of fever, for three nights, one night, or even a single day and night, one should avoid exposure to wind, apply sudation, practice fasting, and drink warm water;
once the fever caused by undigested matter (āmaja) has subsided, one should subsequently administer medicine. (28–29)
Fasting is prescribed at the onset of fever; during the middle stage of fever, digestive (pācana) treatment is indicated;

at the end of the fever, medicine should be administered; and once the fever has subsided, purgation (virecana) should be given for the sake of digesting the remaining morbid humors (doṣa) and for kindling the digestive fire.
If one has undergone leaping therapy (laṅghana) and remains free from complications, one should practice the drinking of gruel (yavāgū).
Alternatively, one should consume the soup of śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, and mung beans;
or, in the case of moderate fasting, one should take gruel prepared with pañcakola.
Seeing that he has excessively undergone fasting, a nourishing therapy (saṃtarpaṇa) is beneficial;
for one who requires nourishment, a satiating drink made from grapes, pomegranate, dates, priyāla, and parūṣaka should be administered for the pacification of fever. 33–34.
When the *doṣa* has been reduced by fasting (*laṅghana*) and the digestive fire (*agni*) has been kindled, freedom from fever, lightness, and hunger arise in the patient.
Fasting is the means for maturing the *doṣas* in one whose *doṣas* and digestive fire are unstable.
It destroys fever, stimulates digestion, and produces appetite, relish, and lightness of body (36).
When there is the discharge of wind, urine, and feces; lightness of the limbs; purification of the heart, eructations, throat, and mouth; and when drowsiness and fatigue have passed—(37).

When perspiration has arisen, when there is a relish for food, when hunger and thirst manifest together, and when the inner self is free from distress, the fasting regimen is declared to be accomplished.
Excessive secretion of phlegm, nausea, and frequent spitting [are signs that it is not yet complete].
Impurity of the throat, mouth, and heart, as well as drowsiness, occur when one has under-eaten (laṅghana).

There is also splitting pain in the joints, aching of the limbs, cough, dryness of the mouth, loss of appetite, loss of the urge to sneeze, anorexia, thirst, and weakness of the ears and eyes. (39–40)
Excessive mental agitation, frequent upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta), darkness in the heart,
and loss of bodily digestive fire and strength occur when fasting is performed to excess.
One should treat the patient with fasting that does not contradict their strength.
Health is the foundation of strength, for which this sequence of ritual actions is intended.
Indeed, it should not be performed by those suffering from wind-disorders, thirst, hunger, dryness of the mouth, or vertigo, nor by pregnant women, children, the elderly, the weak, or the timid.

One who suffers from wasting, fatigue from travel, anger, sexual desire, emaciation, or chronic fever (43) must certainly undergo fasting when the fever is associated with *āma* and the wind (*samīraṇa*) is predominant, for the purpose of digesting the *āma*; this is not to be done later on, as in the case of *kapha*. (44)

The essence and core of food that is not digested due to the weakness of the digestive fire receives the designation of "āma" (undigested matter), serving as the basis for many diseases. Some authorities call this undigested food-essence "āma," while others refer to it as a "collection of waste products."
Some declare the first type of vitiation of the doshas to be *āma*.
That which is undigested, unassimilated, foul-smelling, excessively slimy,
and causes a sinking sensation in all the limbs is designated as *āma*.

The doshas and the dushyas associated with that [amashaya], as well as the diseases arising from them, are known by the wise as "sāma. Vata accompanied by ama is characterized by constipation, loss of digestive fire, lassitude, and rumbling in the intestines.
It should afflict the limbs in succession with pain, swelling, and piercing sensations (verse 49),
and it may also move about or seize them all at once when provoked intensely;
its increase occurs through the application of unctuous substances and the like, during the rising of the sun, in the presence of clouds, and at night (verse 50).
Pitta that is *sāma* (undigested) is sour, foul-smelling, greenish, heavy, and associated with very slight pain;
it finds relief specifically through substances possessing opposite qualities, especially those that are unctuous (*snigdha*).
(51) Pitta that is *sāma* becomes sour, foul-smelling, green, and heavy.
Pitta devoid of Āma (nirāma-pitta) is described as sour, causing burning in the throat and heart, dark-brown, stable, copper-colored, extremely hot, pungent, laxative,
foul-smelling, appetizing, and an increaser of digestive fire and strength. (52-53)
The *sāma* (undigested) phlegm is turbid, thick, and remains in the region of the throat;
it is foul-smelling and causes great impairment of thirst and hunger.
(54) The *nirāma* (digested) phlegm is odorless, frothy, and consists of distinct fragments.
If that [undigested matter] becomes condensed, it produces paleness and a loss of the sense of taste.

They declare the disease accompanied by *āmā* (undigested toxins) to be characterized by laziness, drowsiness, impurity of heart, the onset of disorders, turbid urine, heaviness of the abdomen, loss of appetite, and excessive sleep. (55–56)

One should conquer undigested matter (āma) through fasting, lukewarm gruels, light food, soups, boiled rice, and bitter broths, as well as by means of drying, sudation, digestive treatments, and purification therapies (saṃśodhana) both upward and downward.
A person who is thirsty falls into delusion; from delusion, he loses his life-breaths.
Therefore, in all circumstances, one should never refuse water to anyone.
Thirst is a heavy and terrible affliction that instantly destroys life;
therefore, water, which sustains life, must be given to one overcome by thirst. 58–59.
In cases of acute fever, catarrh, pain in the sides, obstruction of the throat,
immediate purification [of the channels], flatulence, and diseases arising from Vāta and Kapha;
as well as in loss of appetite, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), asthma, cough, and abscesses (vidradhi).

In cases of hiccups and when drinking medicated fats (sneha), one should avoid cold water. When cold water is consumed, fever increases due to that cold liquid. However, [the water] should be boiled until it is free from agitation, devoid of foam, and clear.
The water that remains when half has evaporated is called hot water (uṣṇodaka).
Hot water is always wholesome; it destroys fever, cough, phlegm, asthma, bile, wind, and fat, and it acts as a digestive. 63–64.
In summer and autumn, water with three-quarters remaining is recommended;

likewise in the cold season (hemanta) and the rainy and spring seasons, it should have half remaining. However, in the heat of summer (nidāgha), it should be reduced by half a quarter, and in autumn, it should be reduced by one quarter.

Some wise scholars, based on the observation of Jejjata’s tradition, have declared that water remaining for half [the day] is recommended in the winter and spring, while during the rainy season, water remaining for an eighth part of the day is praised. (66–67)
In the two fortnights, the three Vedas, the five arrows, and the seven limbs—

of these, the remainder of the parts shall be the water [rains] in sequence during the rainy season and so forth. That [rainfall] diminished by one quarter cures bile, while that diminished by half cures wind.
Water that has lost three-quarters of its volume is light, subdues phlegm, promotes digestion, and is easily assimilated.
That water which remains as one-quarter is called "healthy water" (ārogyāmbu);
it is always wholesome and cures cough, asthma, and phlegmatic disorders.
Water from lakes or ponds is curative of acute fever, constipating, digestive-stimulant, carminative, light,
and it removes flatulence, anemia, colic, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, edema, and abdominal enlargement;
it should be used during the late winter and early spring seasons.
In the spring and summer seasons, water from a well, a pond, or a mountain spring is beneficial (verse 72).
A wise person should avoid river water during the spring and summer,
for its leaves, flowers, and so forth may be like poison due to contact with a contaminated stream (verse 73).
Water from wells or ponds is prescribed for the rainy season, while water from rivers is recommended in autumn; moreover, water that is free from impurities and devoid of silt is supreme.
By day it is graced by the rays of the sun, and by night by the rays of the moon. (74)
The water known as *jñeyamaṃśūda* is unctuous, removes the three *doṣas*, does not cause secretions (*anabhiṣyandi*), and is free from defects like rainwater;
it is strengthening, an elixir (*rasāyana*), promotes intelligence, is cooling, light, and equal to nectar (*sudhā*). (75–76)
From the rising of the month of Āśvina until autumn, all water is beneficial;
however, in the months of Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, only water is recommended for those suffering from burning sensations,
diarrhea, hemorrhaging, bile disorders, fainting, intoxication, or the effects of poison.
In cases of dysuria, anemia, thirst, vomiting, and fatigue,

as well as in diseases arising from the consumption of alcohol, those originating from Pitta, and those produced by the combination of all three humors (Sannipāta), water that has been boiled and then cooled is recommended. 79
Boiled water that has cooled by the condensation of its steam within the vessel destroys the three doṣas;
it is non-drying, non-obstructive, light for the heart, and cures worms, thirst, fever, and nausea.
Water that falls as a stream causes constipation and is difficult to digest, especially when struck by the wind.
Drunk at night, warm water breaks up accumulations of phlegm, draws away the wind (vāyu), and quickly digests indigestion.
Milk boiled during the day becomes heavy when consumed at night.
That which is boiled at night and drunk during the day becomes heavy; moreover, when it has stood overnight, its fiery qualities are lost, and it causes the three *doṣas*.
Being heavy, sour in digestion, and causing constipation, it is condemned in all diseases. (82–83)
Water that has been boiled and cooled, if heated again, becomes equal to poison;
likewise, a decoction that has been cooled, if heated again, is like poison. [This applies when it is reduced] to one-eighth part, or to one-fourth, or to half.
Alternatively, one may say that hot water is prepared simply by boiling;
when drunk at night, it destroys phlegm, wind, and fat, stimulates the digestive fire, cleanses the bladder, and removes asthma, cough, and fever. (85–86)

"One should drink hot water that has been heated at night," so it is said; "for that [water] generates fire, is light and clear, cleanses the bladder, and removes pain in the flanks, catarrh, flatulence, hiccups, wind, and phlegm. (87)
It is recommended for thirst, dyspnea, and colic; for immediate purification and in cases of acute fever (88);

for fainting, pitta disorders, heat, and burning sensations; for poisoning, blood disorders, and alcoholism; and likewise for those overcome by vertigo and fatigue, as well as for asthma and edema (89).
Cold water is recommended in cases of belching with a smoky odor, indigestion, dryness of the mouth and throat, and upward-moving hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
Raw water undergoes digestion within one watch (yāma), while once digested, it remains cool for half a watch.
After half that time, it becomes cooked and lukewarm; for three [parts], it is used in the cooking of well-purified water (91).
For those afflicted by bile, alcohol, or poison, [the water] should be boiled with bitter herbs and then cooled (92), using musta, parpaṭaka, uddīcya, chatrā, uśīra, and candana.
One should give boiled water that has cooled for the pacification of thirst, burning sensations, and fever. (93) One should not sleep during the day, because that brings about an increase of *kapha*.
Sleeping during the day is prohibited in seasons other than summer. (94)

For those embodied beings for whom daytime sleep is always appropriate, the [humors] such as wind (vāta) become aggravated if they do not sleep during the day. [This applies especially to those] who are exhausted from physical exercise, sexual indulgence, walking long distances, or riding vehicles, as well as those suffering from diarrhea. 95.1–2.
One should, at will, allow those afflicted by colic, dyspnea, vomiting, and thirst; those oppressed by hiccups and wind;
those who are emaciated or depleted of *kapha*; children; those overcome by intoxication; the elderly; those suffering from indigestion;
those kept awake at night; and those who have fasted, to sleep during the day. 96.
Indeed, a fever caused by Vāta reaches its peak (pāka) in seven nights, one caused by Pitta in ten nights, and one caused by Kapha in twelve days.
Wise men declare that a fever is "acute" (taruṇa) until the completion of seven nights.
One should administer medicine for twelve days, provided the fever has reached its middle stage by then; beyond that,
one should apply treatment for a fever caused by Vāta after seven nights, for Pitta after ten nights, and for Kapha after twelve nights.
The time for the administration of medicine for humans should be known as fivefold. When no specific time is mentioned therein, it should be taken at dawn, especially in the case of decoctions.
The administration of primary medicinal substances is prohibited during acute fever.
In that case, the medicine is rendered free from defects by means of processing with water, gruel, and so forth.
(102) In acute fever, the increased *doṣas* are arrested by astringent decoctions; they are suppressed and do not undergo maturation, thereby causing irregular fever. (103)
When the impurities (malas) are suppressed by astringents (kaṣāya), they do not pass downward nor are they digested;

moving along oblique or wrong paths, they cause a severe acute fever (navajvara) when the Vāta is involved. In the case of acute fever, emesis is indicated for those whose humors (doṣas) are not yet stabilized.
It causes heart pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and intense delusion.
Vāgbhaṭa stated that when fever arises immediately after eating, or when it is produced by over-nutrition (santarpaṇa), emesis is recommended for one who is fit for emesis. 105–106.

On the seventh day, one should administer a digestive (pācana) *sāma* [remedy] to the patient, or treat him with a pacifying (*śamana*) remedy once he is seen to be free of *āma*. Furthermore, one should treat a patient who is emaciated and has only a small amount of *doṣa* with pacifying measures. 107–108.
One should first administer this digestive (pācanaka) decoction, which removes fever, to those afflicted by fever: *nāgara*, *devadāru*, *dhyāmaka*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
Now, learn from me the pacifying (saṃśamanīya) decoctions.
Whatever remedies are to be administered for all fevers by a knowledgeable physician— bṛścīra, viśvā, varṣābhū, milk, and water itself—
one should boil these until only the milk remains; that should be drunk as a remedy that dispels all fevers.
Twice the amount of water relative to milk, along with *śiṃśapā* and *uśīra*, should be boiled down until only the milk remains; this decoction, when drunk, removes all fevers.
[Likewise,] *guḍūcī*, *dhānyaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *padmaka*, and red sandalwood [are used]. 112.
The decoction of these is well-known as a remover of all fevers;
it is an appetizer and cures burning sensations, nausea, thirst, vomiting, and loss of appetite,
as well as vomiting, fainting, intoxication, dyspnea, giddiness, thirst, and irregular fever.
By drinking a purgative, one suffering from acute fever attains recovery (114).
However, when a disease is curable by purification, the physician, having observed that the patient is weakened by the morbid humors (doṣas), should perform a mild evacuation of those humors (115).
One should administer it in cases of acute fever, poisoning, indigestion, weak digestive fire, abdominal diseases,
disorders of breast milk, heart disease, cough, asthma, and vomiting;
as well as in chronic fever, artificial poison, choleraic vomiting, abdominal tumors, and splenic enlargement.

One should administer purgation in cases of colic, swelling, urinary obstruction, and worm infestation (117). When the doshas are mobile and the digestive tract is soft, one need not consider the strength of the patients;
for in such a case, even a weak person will undergo purification without complications (118).
Even if it has been ripened, a morbid humor (doṣa) that remains in the body without being eliminated can cause a severe or irregular fever, or even the loss of strength.
A decoction prepared from āragvadha, granthika, mustā, tiktā, and harītakī [is recommended].

This decoction of Āragvadhādi (120) is beneficial for fever associated with *sāma*, *śūla*, and *kapha-vāta*, as it is digestive-stimulant (*dīpana*) and carminative (*pācana*). Water boiled with *pathyā*, *āragvadha*, *tiktā*, *trivṛt*, and *āmalaka* [is likewise beneficial].
The sages have declared that *pācanasāraka* and *mukta* are for chronic fever with residual *āma*;
thus ends the two groups of the "Fivefold Health-givers" (*ārogyapañcaka*). [The next group consists of:
*anantā*, *bālaka*, *musta*, *nāgara*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
Having ground the paste with lukewarm water, one should administer it in a dose of one akṣa.
This paste, in a very short time, destroys all diseases of fever; it effects the purification of the digestive tract and kindles the fire of digestion.

A person who has drunk [liquids], one emaciated by fasting, one whose food is digested, one who has just eaten, or one who is thirsty, should not drink medicine— whether it be for purification or otherwise. (124) Triphalā, the two types of turmeric, the two types of kaṇṭakārī, and śaṭī...
Trikaṭu, granthika, mūrvā, guḍūcī, dhanvayāsaka,
kaṭukā, parpaṭa, musta, trāyamāṇā, bālaka, nimba, puṣkaramūla, madhuyaṣṭī, and vatsaka. (125–126)
Yavānī, indrayava, bhārgī, śigru seed, surāṣṭrajā,
vacā, tvak, padmaka, uśīra, candana, ativiṣā, balā,
śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, viḍaṅga, and likewise tagara. (127)
Citraka, devakāṣṭha, cavya, and paṭola leaves;
jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, lavaṅga, and vaṃśalocana; puṇḍarīka, kākolī, patraka, and jātipatraka. (128–129)
One should powder these ingredients—tālīśapatra and the others—in equal parts; the wise person should then add one-half part of *kirāta* to the entire powder.
This powder, named Sudarśana, removes the three *doṣas*.
It destroys all types of fevers; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

It also annihilates those born of the humors (doṣas), as well as those that are exogenous (āgantuka), those situated in the bodily tissues (dhātus), irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), those arising from the combination of all humors (sannipāta), and even mental fevers. 131–132.
It wards off cold and other such conditions, as well as burning sensations, urinary disorders, drowsiness, vertigo, thirst,
cough, dyspnea, anemia, heart disease, jaundice, and pain in the sacrum, back, waist, knees, and sides. (133)
One should drink this with cold water for the cessation of all fevers.
Just as the Sudarśana discus is the destroyer of the Dānavas,
so too is this powder the destroyer of all fevers.

One should take equal parts of nimba leaves, varā, vyōṣa, yavānī, the three salts (lavaṇatraya), kṣāra, and ten, three, three, five, and three units [of the respective ingredients] in sequence; having combined all these into a powder, a person should consume it at dawn.

It undoubtedly destroys fever occurring on the first day, that of the second day, as well as that of the third day; the most terrible quartan fever, the constant fever, the daily fever, that which resides in the bodily constituents, and that arising from the three humors (doṣas). 137–138.
Thus is the powder of nimba and others: śaṭī, the two types of niśā, śuṇṭhī, dāru, puṣkaramūlaka,
elā, guḍūcī, kaṭukā, parpaṭa, and yavāsaka.
A person should drink a lukewarm decoction of Śṛṅgī, Kirātatikta, and likewise Daśamūlī, combined with powdered Saindhava salt;
it quickly destroys all fevers— of this there is no doubt.
Two palas each of harītakī, trivṛt, and vṛddhadāraka; one pala each of kaṇā, śuṇṭhī, guḍūcī, gokṣura, varī, sahadevī, and viḍaṅga. 141.
Having made pills with honey, one who eats them dispels fever;
it also subdues cough, dyspnea, constipation, and sluggish digestion.
(142-143) Ten *akṣas* of lac, six *akṣas* of *aruṇā*, along with sandalwood and red sandalwood.
Cinnamon bark, cinnamon leaves, water (liquorice), and *murā*, along with *mustā*—each of these [four] being one *pala* [in weight];
*kirātatikta*, *trivṛtā*, *satiktā*, *amṛtā*, *kaṇā*, *parpaṭaka*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *viḍaṅga*, *viśvā*, *āmalakāni*, *vāsā*, *rasāñjana*, *iṣu*, *vīraṇa*, and *sinduvāra*. (144–145)

All these medicinal ingredients should be given individually in the measure of half a *pala*; one should prepare a paste (*kalka*) of them with exactly one and a half *tulās* of cow's milk. Then, one should slowly cook one *tulā* of sesame oil with that very same paste.

This oil destroys all types of fevers and produces strength, virility, and extreme nourishment. Through massage, it quickly pacifies fatigue and dizziness, generates luster for the body, and likewise alleviates even pain arising from the bones; furthermore, it brings about the attainment of pleasant sleep.
Oil equal in measure to lac-juice, with four times as much whey as oil,
should be cooked with equal parts of aśvagandhā, niśā, dāru, kauntī, kuṣṭha, abda, candana, mūrvā, rohiṇī, rāsnā, śatāhvā, and madhuka.
The oil named Lakṣādika-taila, when prepared and used for massage and other applications, cures all fevers, consumption, insanity, dyspnea, epilepsy, and disorders of Vāta;
it destroys Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Bhūtas, and is highly recommended for pregnant women. (150–151)
Lākṣā, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, phenila, madhuka, balā,
lāmajjaka, candana, campaka, and blue utpala—
having boiled six handfuls of each of these in four times as much water; 152.
When the embryo has reached the fourth part [of its development], one should add these ingredients:
reṇukā, padmaka, vājigandhā, as well as vetasa, coraka, kuṣṭha, devadāru, nakha, and tvak. 153–154.

One should add an āḍhaka each of mastu, śukta, and āranāla, along with the paste (kalka) of śatapuṣpā, puṇḍarīka, māṃsī, and madhuka, which have been ground together with their decoction (kaṣāya). 155.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil combined with one *āḍhaka* of milk.
Indeed, by means of anointing with this oil, it quickly removes burning sensations as well as fevers arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*. (156–157)

This great *lākṣādika* oil pacifies the suffering of those children who suffer from delirious speech, thirst, dryness of the palate, and vertigo, as well as those possessed by planetary spirits (*graha*) or corrupted by *rakṣasas*. (158)

Take mercury, sulphur, and borax, along with an equal amount of sugar and fish bile; grind these together repeatedly for three nights. A dose of one *valla* should be administered with the juice of ginger.
During this period, the following regimen is prescribed as wholesome: cold food served with fans, and meals consisting of *takra* (buttermilk) and rice, enriched with eggplant (*vṛntāka*). 159.

It kills severe fever instantly; in cases of fever with a predominance of pitta, one should apply water to the head. 160. Mercury, rock salt, sea-foam, asafoetida, and *elā* should be rubbed together for one *yāma*; this "comet of fever" (*jvaradhūmaketu*), when applied with the juice of fresh *ambhaḥ* (water-lily) for three days, acts as a pair of fires against new fever. 161.
Pure mercury, poison, and sulphur—one *śāṇa* each;
*dhūrta* seeds should be three *śāṇas*, and twice as much as all of these combined.
One should carefully prepare a fine powder of these, known as "gold-named" (*hemāhva*). 162.
A powder measured at two *guñjā* seeds should be given with the pulp of *jambīra* fruit or even with the juice of fresh ginger;
it destroys fever born of the three *doṣas*, whether it occurs every day (*ekāhika*), every second day (*dvayāhika*), every third day (*tryāhika*), or every fourth day (*caturthaka*). (163–164)
This mercury, known by the name Mahājvarāṅkuśa (the Great Hook for Fever), destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara) in every way, whether recent or chronic; it is esteemed by all.
One part of purified mercury [is combined with] śailaja, pippalī, and śivā.
The *ākārakarabha* resin, purified with pungent oil (kaṭutaila), [is used];
these fruits of *indravāruṇī*, measured at one-fourth part, should all be ground together into a powder with the juices of *indravāruṇī*. 166–167.
Having prepared pills of one *māṣa* each, the wise physician should administer them for acute fever;
this pill is considered a destroyer of fever when taken with a decoction of *chinnā*.
[168] One part of mercury, one part of sulfur, one part of cinnabar, and one part of *jaipāla*, increased in that sequence...
Having ground it with the juice of *dantī*, a pill the size of a *guñjā* berry should be prepared.
Consumed in the morning with sugar and cold water, this [remedy] will eliminate acute fever (*navajvara*) in a single day. (169–170)

Take equal parts of juice, fragrance, poison, ginger, long pepper, black pepper, chebulic myrobalan, beleric myrobalan, emblic myrobalan, and purified seeds of *dantī*. Having made a powder of these, one should roast it with the juices of *droṇapuṣpī*.
One should prepare pills resembling a black gram (*māṣa*) in size and consume them during a fresh fever.
(172) One part of mercury, two parts of purified sulfur, three parts of poison (*garala*), and four parts of *himāvatī*. (173)
Five parts of *jaipālaka* (seeds of *Abrus precatorius*) ground with the juice of *nimbū* (citron) should be made into pills the size of a *kṛmighna* (mustard seed); these destroy all fevers.
One pill should be administered daily with *śṛṅgavera* (ginger).

In chronic fever, as well as in indigestion, or in fever with undigested toxins (āmaviṣa), or in irregular fever (viṣamajvara), this [medicine] destroys all fevers, just as a forest fire consumes a forest. Pure mercury, poison, sulphur, and thorn-apple seeds— these three in equal parts [should be used].
Take double the amount of each of the four [ingredients] to make a powder of trikaṭu (vyoṣa) in a dose of two guñjās; when combined with the juice of fresh ginger or the juice of jambīra,
it is known as Mahājvarāṅkuśa, the destroyer of all fevers.
It undoubtedly destroys fever that occurs every day, every two days, every three days, or every four days, as well as irregular fever or fever arising from the three *doṣas*.
[The ingredients are] mercury, sulfur, poison, borax, and realgar. (179)

These [ingredients] at the measure of one *ṭaṅka* each, with eight *ṭaṅkas* of black pepper (180), and six *ṭaṅkas* of the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), should be thrown into a mortar and ground into a powder.
This "Axe for Asthma" (*śvāsakuṭhāra*) is the supreme remedy that removes all fevers. 181.
Having taken one *ṭaṅka* each of *dārumukhā*, *śikhigrīvā*, and *rasaka*, separately, one should grind them with gold dust for three days; then pills the size of chickpeas should be prepared.
One should eat two pills made with twenty-one black peppers and seven *tulasī* leaves. As wholesome diet, one should consume rice with milk and sugar;
this certainly destroys all fevers—whether recent, chronic, or long-standing. (183–184)
One *karṣa* of *nāgara*, two *karṣas* of *ṭaṅkaṇa*,

one and a half *karṣas* of *marica*, and the same amount of burnt cowrie shells (*varāṭaka*), along with poison (*viṣa*) equal to a fourth part of a *karṣa*— one should grind all these together into a powder. (185)

The mercury, known by the name Hutāśana, should be consumed in a dose of one *guñjā* during fever. One *ṭaṅka* of pure *jaipāla*, two *ṭaṅkas* of *kaṭvī*, and one *ṭaṅka* of red ochre (*gairika*) should be ground together with the juice of *kanyā*. (186–187)
One should prepare a pill (vaṭikā) resembling a pea and consume it with cold water;
this pill removes chronic fever (jīrṇajvara).
[The preparation involves] copper struck with two parts of talaka, along with mercury, sulphur, and equal parts of mīna-māyu.

Equal parts of mercury and twice that amount of copper are rubbed together twenty-one times with the juice of *ariṣṭa* under the rays of the sun; this powder, when administered in a single *guñjā* dose along with sugar,
is called *Jvarāṅkuśa Ravisundara*, and it destroys all eight types of fevers.
One should grind pure mercury and likewise sulphur in a mortar until the mercury is no longer visible, but rather becomes like soot;
this is known as *kajjalikā*, which is nourishing and increases virility. 191.
By means of various applications of medicinal adjuncts, it destroys all diseases. [192] Furthermore,
by means of the juice of hibiscus leaves, the juice of *vardhamāna*,
the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, and the juice of *kākamācī*— [193]

One should purify the *rasa* with that [juice], and likewise purify the *bali* with it; having ground [the ingredients] with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, one should dry them in the rays of the sun seven times or even three times, and thereafter reduce them to powder.
Having powdered it, one should grind it evenly with that mercury.
When the powder has absorbed the mercury and becomes like collyrium,
one should diligently liquefy it over smokeless charcoal of the *badara* fruit.
There, one should place it upon a plantain leaf set over buffalo dung,
cover it with another leaf, and press it down;
then, having removed it from the leaf while it is cold, one should pulverize it.
Thus, the mercury-parpaṭī becomes perfected as a destroyer of diseases.
Having seen the universe pervaded by fevers and other ailments in the past, Hara, filled with compassion, fashioned this mercury-parpaṭī like nectar. 198–199.
One should consume *rasaparpaṭī* measuring one *raktikā*, combined with fried cumin, enriched with half a *guñjā* of fried asafoetida;
the wise person may also consume it along with medicines appropriate to the specific disease. (200)
Thereafter, one should drink three mouthfuls of cold water.
Every day, the physician should increase its dose by one *raktikā*,
but never should one consume more than ten *guñjās*.
Starting from the eleventh day, one may then reduce that [quantity];
in this manner, a man should consume it for twenty days, having worshipped and bowed down to Śiva, the gurus, and the brahmins. (203)
One should consume this with faith, subsisting on milk, meat, and broth. It cures fever, as well as dysentery (grahaṇī), diarrhea,
jaundice, anemia, colic, splenic disorders, and dropsy.
Having destroyed such diseases as these, the heroic man— joyful and robust— shall live for more than a hundred years, free from wrinkles and grey hair.
Now, regarding the time for giving food to one suffering from fever, Caraka says:
Hunger arises when the chyle, the humors, and the wastes have been digested, whether at the proper time or otherwise; this is declared to be the "time for food.
When digestion has occurred in men, there arises a longing for a meal.

Whether at the proper time or even at an improper time, that is declared to be the "time for food. In all fevers, one should feed the patient light meals in measured portions for seven days; otherwise, if this is not done when the paroxysms have subsided, it will cause the force of the fever to increase.
The wise should always practice the proper methods of eating, excretion, and recreation in solitude.
Even with slight exertion, fever and urinary disorders may arise;
therefore, one should feed the patient while he is seated and assist him in the evacuation of urine and feces.
A gargle (kavalagraha) should be prepared with substances appropriate to the specific disorder;
it removes anorexia, bad taste in the mouth, impurities, fetid secretions, and excessive salivation.
[It may also be made] with powdered fried cumin mixed with rock salt. 212.
Having rubbed the tongue against the teeth within the mouth, one should perform the *kavala* (gargling) practice.
Thus, impurities in the mouth, foul odors, and bad tastes are eliminated; the mind becomes serene, and there arises a great relish for food. (213–214)
One suffering from fever should eat what is wholesome even if there is a lack of appetite;
for by not eating at the proper time for meals, one wastes away and may even die.
Old red *śāli* rice and the like, along with *ṣaṣṭika* rice, are recommended.

For those suffering from fever, one should provide gruel, boiled rice, or parched grain flour as means to alleviate the fever; likewise, for those accustomed to soups, one should administer soups made from mung beans, lentils, chickpeas, horse gram, and wild kidney beans (makuṣṭhaka). (216–217)
Patola leaves, vārtāku, kulaka, kāravellaka,
karkoṭaka, parpaṭaka, gojihvā, and young radish (bālamūlaka),
as well as the leaves of guḍūcī, serve as vegetables that remove fever for those afflicted by fever. (218)
One should cause quails, grey partridges, antelopes, spotted deer,
hares, kuraṅgas, kālapucchas, and likewise mṛgamātṛkas to be given for the sake of meat to those suffering from fever who have a natural predilection for meat. 219–220.
Some authorities, established in this view, do not recommend cranes, curlews, peacocks, partridges, or roosters for those with fever, because they are heavy and hot;
however, when the wind (vāta) undergoes provocation in those afflicted by fever, [these may be used]. 221.
At that time, these too are recommended when prepared with the proper duration of fermentation:
one who desires sourness should be given nimbu, pomegranate, or the sour āmalaka fruit; or, for one accustomed to sour tastes, one should provide aged *kāñjika*.
A decoction made from well-cooked rice grains with fourteen times the amount of water, which is free of grains and scum, is called *maṇḍa*.
When combined with ginger and rock salt, it is digestive and promotes the digestion of food.
The successful preparation of food is to be known by the successful preparation of the *maṇḍa* (scum).
Among *peyā*, *yūṣa*, *yavāgū*, *vilepī*, and *bhakta*,
the *maṇḍa* is constipating, light, cooling, digestive-stimulant, and a balancer of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

Fever-destroying, nourishing, strengthening, and removing bile, phlegm, and fatigue—this is what is called *peyā* by the best of physicians: it is prepared from red rice and other grains with fourteen parts of water, containing a preponderance of liquid and few solid particles. (226–227)
It is known to be very light, absorbent, and a promoter of the nourishment of the bodily tissues (dhātus);
it destroys thirst, fever, wind-disorders, debility, and diseases of the abdomen; it generates perspiration and digestive fire, and facilitates the downward movement of flatus and feces. 228.
Combined with ginger and rock salt, it is digestive, carminative,

a remover of colic caused by undigested matter (āma), appetizing, and a destroyer of constipation. This is called *pramathyā*, prepared from one pala of the drug ground into a paste and boiled with water.
They say that two *pala*s of this [milk] should be drunk with eight times its amount of water;

it should be churned with the [usual] qualities and drunk like a *peyā* (thin gruel), for it is especially light. A broth boiled from leguminous grains (*śimbīdhānya*) should be prepared with eighteen times its amount of water.
A thick soup made from a small amount of grain is called *peyā*; that same preparation, when more substantial, is called *yūṣa*, which is especially appetizing. It is also called *niryūha*.
One *pala* of the paste-substance (*kalkadravya*) [is used], along with half a *karṣa* each of ginger and long pepper.
One should cook that with a *prastha* of water; this is called *bhava-yūṣa*.
This soup is strengthening, light in digestion, appetizing, beneficial for itching, and dispels *kapha*.
Two *palas* of *mudga* beans boiled in half an *āḍhaka* of water [is used as follows].
