That [mixture] should be placed in a foot-measure jar, crushed, and strained; it should then be combined with one *pala* of pomegranate, along with one-quarter part each of rock salt (*saindhava*), ginger (*viśvāhva*), and coriander (*dhānyaka*),
and finally sprinkled over with one *śāṇa* of the powder of long pepper (*kaṇā*) and cumin (*jīraka*).
This seasoned green gram soup (mudga-yūṣa) is considered to alleviate pitta and kapha.
It is the best among green gram soups; it stimulates digestion, is cooling, and light.
It conquers wounds, pain in the regions above the clavicle, burning sensations, kapha, pitta, fever, and blood disorders.

Soup made from green gram (mudga) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) is a laxative, it subdues pitta and vāta, alleviates thirst and burning sensations, is cooling, and removes fainting, fatigue, and intoxication. (238) Soup made from lentils (masūra) is astringent, nourishing, sweet, and cures urinary disorders (prameha). (239)
Gruel prepared with six parts of water, having thickened grains and combined with various thin liquid ingredients, is beneficial for a person suffering from fever.
This gruel stimulates the digestive fire, is light, quenches thirst, and cleanses the bladder. (240)
Pathyā (harītakī) removes fatigue and exhaustion, and is beneficial in cases of fever and diarrhea.
When prepared with four parts water, it becomes a *vilepī*—thick and with solidified grains—which, when free from separate liquids, is known as *śithilabhaktikā*. 241–242.
Vilepī (rice gruel) is digestive-stimulant, strengthening, pleasing to the heart, astringent, light, wholesome for those with wounds and eye diseases, nourishing, and it removes thirst and fever.
[It is prepared by] four palas of rice in fourteen times as much water. (243)
One should cook it until the scum is drained; that rice is sweet and light.
One should cook grain for *annam* in five parts of water, and for *yavāgū* in six parts of water. This rice is digestive-stimulating, wholesome, satiating, diuretic, and light. (244–245)
Well-washed, strained, and warm milk is clear and possesses superior qualities;
whereas unwashed, unstrained, and cold milk is aphrodisiac, heavy, and increases *kapha*.
Milk that is excessively hot diminishes strength, while that which is eaten with food, or is cold and dry, is difficult to digest.

Excessively moist [gruel] causes debility and is difficult to digest, whereas that made from fried rice (bhṛṣṭataṇḍula) is appetizing, fragrant, light, and subdues phlegm; it is recommended for those with wind disorders, constipation, weak digestion, and those who have undergone purgation. 247–248.
Four *pala* measures of the fleshy meat from the thighs of a partridge, likewise boneless and finely minced, washed in water,
[should be cooked] with *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, ginger, cumin, and coriander. (249)

In two śāṇas of water mixed with [the other ingredients] and boiled down until half an āḍhaka remains, one should add the juice of crushed pomegranate; this should be stirred together with asafoetida, roasted rock salt, and cumin. (250)
It is appropriate, well-smoked, wholesome, and purifying for those who are pure and desire purification.
(251) Rice cooked with meat broth is heavy, aphrodisiac, strengthening, and a remedy for wind-fever.
(252) Four *pala* of the medicinal substance should be boiled in sixty-four *pala* of water until it is reduced [to one-fourth].
With the decoction remaining after half has evaporated, one should prepare maṇḍa, peyā, and so forth. (253) Elderly physicians prescribe one pala of the medicinal substance for an āḍhaka of water;
however, due to the excessive quantity of the drug, there may sometimes be a lack of relish. (254)

Whatever gruels (maṇḍa) and other preparations have been prepared by the wise using various grains and medicinal herbs, one should describe their properties as being identical to the properties of those very ingredients, having carefully considered them. At the time of eating, a gruel made with appropriate digestive stimulants is beneficial.
It is digestive, carminative, light, and removes fever in those afflicted by fever.
(256) A decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla) is a carminative for vātika fever; for paittika fever, it should be prepared with musta, kaṭuka, indrayava, and yava, along with honey. (257)

A decoction of the *pippalyādi* group is a digestive (pācana) remedy for fever caused by *kapha*. [One may also use] with the light *pañcamūla*, along with *pippalī* and *dhānyaka*; or with the great *pañcamūla*, as well as *vyāghrī*, *duḥsparśā*, and *gokṣura*.
One should administer proven medicinal foods in their proper sequence for [diseases] arising from vāta-pitta, śleṣma-pitta, kapha-vāta, and the three doṣas combined;
or, in cases of pain in the bladder, the sides, or the head, one should give a gruel made of red śāli rice.

One suffering from fever with constipation should drink a decoction prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *kaṇṭakārī*, which removes fever. Or, the fever patient should drink a gruel (*peyā*) boiled with barley, *pippalī*, and *āmalaka*, mixed with clarified butter, which facilitates the downward movement of the humors.

One suffering from cough, dyspnea, or hiccups should drink gruel (peyā) boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī). Due to its medicinal combination and lightness, it kindles the digestive fire and promotes the downward movement of wind, urine, feces, and the bodily humors.
Because it is hot, it promotes sweating; because it is liquid, it quenches thirst;

because it serves as food, it sustains life; because it is mobile, it brings lightness; and because its properties are compatible with the causes of fever, it destroys fever; therefore, one should employ it first. (264)
Taking one handful each of barley, kola, kulattha, mung bean, radish, and ginger, one should boil them in eight times the amount of water;
this preparation, known as Pañcamuṣṭika, removes wind, bile, and phlegm.
It is praised for use in colic, abdominal tumors, cough, dyspnea, wasting, and fever.
For one whose urine and feces are obstructed, one should insert an enema-spoon (varti) into the anus prepared with long pepper,
long pepper root, yavānī, and cavya.

One should cause [the patient] to drink gruel (yavāgū) that promotes the downward movement of wind and other humors. However, in cases of alcoholism, in those habitually addicted to liquor, during the summer season, when fever arises from pitta and kapha, in upward-moving hemorrhage (raktapitta), and in fever, gruel is not beneficial.
One suffering from burning sensations and vomiting, who is emaciated, has abstained from food, and is afflicted by thirst;
likewise one distressed by heat or even a drinker of wine—
such a person should be made to drink parched grain flour (saktu) mixed with water, combined with sugar and honey, as a nourishing draught.
In certain cases, food combined with the juices of fever-alleviating fruits is beneficial. Water in which grapes, pomegranates, and dates have been crushed, mixed with sugar,
parched-rice flour, honey, and ghee, is declared to be nourishing (santarpaṇa).
Parched grain flour (saktu) mixed with honey and sugar is especially effective in removing vomiting,
diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, poison, fainting, and fever.
In that case, a nourishing drink (tarpaṇa) made from parched grain flour should first be administered.

Combined with the juice of fruits that alleviate fever, along with honey and sugar, this refreshing drink (tarpaṇa)—prepared with grapes, pomegranate, dates, priyāla, and parūṣaka—should be administered to one who requires refreshment; it destroys fever. (274–275)
Rice with meat broth (rasaudana) is always beneficial for fever arising from fatigue, fasting, or wind (vāta).
Rice with mung bean soup (mudgayūṣaudana) is beneficial when the fever originates from phlegm (kapha).
That same preparation, served cold and mixed with sugar, is beneficial for fever caused by bile (pitta).

One who is emaciated, has diminished doshas, whose kapha is depleted, and who suffers from chronic fever; one whose doshas are obstructed or not properly expelled, and who has dry pitta and vata fever; and one afflicted by thirst and constant burning sensations—he shall find relief through the use of milk. (278)
Goat’s milk mixed with jaggery should be drunk for the pacification of fever;
however, that same milk, if drunk [alone], destroys a person when the fever is acute.
But in a chronic fever where phlegm has been depleted, milk is like nectar.
That very [food], if consumed while the fever is acute, kills a person like poison (280).
One suffering from acute fever should never eat twice, nor in the forenoon, nor anything that causes secretions, nor anything sharp, nor anything predominantly heavy (281).
A wise man should never suddenly satiate one who is emaciated by fever.
Even if the fever has been pacified by that [treatment], it may arise once again;
burning sensation, perspiration, giddiness, thirst, trembling, diarrhea, loss of consciousness,
moaning, and extreme foul odor are the symptoms at the time of the fever's release.

Indeed, these are the signs in a fever born of the three *doṣas* when the internal impulse has reached the tissues (*dhātu*); at the time of liberation from the disease, there may be other signs, such as the appearance of perspiration.
(284) The body becomes light, exhaustion, delusion, and heat have departed, there is a sense of digestion in the mouth, excellence of the sensory organs, and absence of pain.
Perspiration, sneezing, a return to one's natural state, a desire for food, and itching on the head are the signs of one who has been freed from fever.
(285) Perspiration, lightness of the head, itching, a sense of ripening in the mouth, sneezing, and a longing for food are the characteristics of one released from fever. (286)

One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exercise, sexual intercourse, bathing, or walking about until he has regained his strength. (287) He should also avoid strenuous exertion, sexual intercourse, exposure to strong winds, and cold water.
One who has been freed from fever should not indulge [in bathing] until he has regained his strength.
For a person liberated from fever, bathing may cause the fever to return;
therefore, even when freed from fever, one should avoid bathing as if it were poison. (288–289)
As long as one's strength, complexion, digestive fire, and physical form have not returned to their natural state,
even though freed from fever, one should avoid things that ought to be avoided.
(290) Through wind-increasing food and activities, the *vāyu* [wind] takes refuge in the stomach (*āmāśaya*).
Having cast the digestive fire (koṣṭhāgni) outwards, the fever-inducing [poison] follows the bodily fluids (rasa).
There is shivering, irregular onset, dryness of the throat, lips, and mouth, loss of sleep, suppression of sneezing, and roughness of the limbs. (291–292)
In fever born of Vāta, there occur pain in the head, heart, and limbs; a bad taste in the mouth; constipation; colic; flatulence; yawning;
and various types of Vāta-related pains, as well as numbness. (293)

Constriction of the calves, tinnitus, astringency of the mouth, lassitude of the limbs, lockjaw, and loosening of the joints and knees; dry cough, vomiting, horripilation, tingling of the teeth, fatigue, and vertigo. (294)
Reddish discoloration of the urine, eyes, and other parts, along with thirst, delirium, and heat of the body [are the signs].
When six days have passed since the fever began, the physician should feed the patient light food and administer a digestive or palliative decoction.
One should administer medicine for fever caused by Vāta after seven nights, for Pitta after ten nights, and for Kapha after twelve days.
That very capacity of the Doṣas which allows them to endure fasting is what constitutes their power to tolerate it.
Indeed, when the doshas have been diminished, no one can tolerate great fasting (laṅghana).
While the liquid elements of kapha and pitta can tolerate much fasting, once the āma has been exhausted, even vāyu cannot tolerate it for even a moment. (298–299)
In that regard, the medicine consists of śrīphala, sarvatobhadra, kāmadūtī, śoṇaka,
tarkārī, gokṣura, kṣudrā, bṛhatī, kalaśī, and sthirā. (300)
A decoction of rāsnā, kaṇā, kaṇāmūla, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, kirātaka, mustā, balā, amṛtā, bāla, drākṣā, yāsa,
and śatāhvā (301) certainly destroys fever caused by vāta.
This yoga, along with its adjuncts, is remembered as the best of all yogas (302).
A decoction prepared with water from the roots of *triśatī*, *tarkārī*, *śrīphala*, *tuṇṭuka*, and *pāṭalā* is appropriate for digestion and removes fever produced by Vāta (303).

A decoction made from *kirātatiktaka*, *abhayā*, *amṛtā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *gokṣura*, *triparṇī*, *kālaśī*, and *bilva* removes fever caused by *vāta*. A boiled preparation of *guḍūcī*, *pippalīmūla*, and *nāgara* acts as a digestive (pācana).
Likewise, in vāta-fever, Kāliṅga should be drunk on the seventh day.

Water prepared with viśvā, amṛtā, and granthika—how could this fever remain for one who drinks it? Furthermore, a decoction of kustumburu, devadāru, and the two minor [bitters] is an excellent digestive (pācana) remedy here.

A decoction made from the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, rāsnā, kulattha, and puṣkara destroys head-shaking, pain in the joints, and fever caused by vāta (307). [Likewise, a preparation] with kaṇā, garlic, amṛtavallī, viśvā, nidigdhikā, rock salt, and bhūminimba...
This decoction prepared with *samustaka* and *kirāta*, when consumed by those who eat wholesome food, destroys these following ailments:
fever arising from the corruption of Vāyu, as well as that born of *balāsa* (phlegm), and weak digestion;
it also removes constriction of the throat, constriction of the heart, excessive perspiration, horripilation, coldness, and delusion. (308–309)

Then, one *tulā* (ten palas) of pure *kalpataru-rasa*, one *tulā* of the semen of Śaṅkara, and likewise one *tulā* of the menstrual blood of the wife of Mārāri; as much of the substance known as the clear saliva of Umāpati; as much pure *manaḥśilā*; and likewise *ṭaṅkaṇa* and *śuṇṭhī* each measured at two *akṣas* (two karṣas); *kaṇā* (Pippalī) and black pepper each measured at ten *akṣas* (ten karṣas);
and the poisonous substances and other items should be powdered upon a stone slab and purified within a cloth.
Then, indeed, mercury and sulphur, along with that powder, should be rubbed for two *yāmas*;
this excellent mercury named Kalpataru, which is true to its name, removes diseases caused by wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*). Its dose is recorded as one *guñjā*.
Taken together with ginger, this destroys fever arising from wind and phlegm;
it also cures dyspnea, cough, facial congestion, coldness, weak digestion, and cholera.
When used as a nasal drop (nasya), it quickly removes headaches born of phlegm and wind.
Even for great delusion and excessive talkativeness caused by the *kṣavathu-graha*,
the "Great Fever-Subduer" (*mahājvarāṅkuśa*), prescribed in the treatment of common fevers, should be administered here.
Now follows the *tripurabhairavarasa*.

This excellent *tripurabhairava* elixir— composed of *viṣama*, *auṣadha*, *māgadhika*, *uṣaṇa*, *dyumaṇi*, *raktaka*, and *mārdrika*, crushed together and increased in successive proportions— is the destroyer of fever.
(315) It is used for fever caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*, and for pain in the calves, sides, and bones, when accompanied by sweating.
One who knows the proper procedure should employ it for chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and deafness.
Having brought softness to the channels, having led the heat to its seat, and having destroyed the stiffness caused by Vāta and Kapha, sudation dispels fever. (316–317)

Sweating with sand sprinkled with sour gruel (kāñjika) heated in a frying pan and placed within a cloth-pouch pacifies diseases of wind and phlegm, as well as pain, breaking sensations in the limbs, tremors, and so forth; it is also effective for trembling, pain in the head, heart, and body, yawning, and numbness of the feet.
318. [It is indicated] in cases of trembling, headache, cardiac distress, bodily ache, yawning, and numbness of the feet.
When applied to the face,

the filaments of the *mātuluṅga* fruit combined with rock salt (*sindhujanman*) and black pepper, along with clarified butter, quickly destroy diseases of wind and phlegm located in the mouth, as well as facial paralysis, limb-lassitude, lockjaw, horripilation, dryness, numbness, and loss of appetite. (319–320)
One should hold in the mouth a paste made from sugar and pomegranate, or likewise from grapes and pomegranate; this destroys dryness and bad taste.
One should place a paste of grapes and emblic myrobalan with ghee in the mouth.
Having rubbed [the powder] with that, one should apply it as a local paste (pratisāraṇa) inside the mouth;
by this, dryness located within the palate and throat is pacified,
the mouth becomes pleasant-tasting, and there is a relish for food.

Sipping liquids, fasting, anxiety, physical exercise, grief, and fear— by these very means, sleeplessness occurs due to the extreme depletion of phlegm (śleṣman). One should consume fried powder of Vijayā with honey at night.

In cases of insomnia, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and diminished digestive fire, one should lick jaggery mixed with the powder of long pepper root; by this, even a person whose sleep has been lost for a long time regains it. (325–326)

The root of *vāyasajaṅghā* tied to the head, or the bark and root of *kākamācī* worn [on the body], produces sleep; likewise, the root of *kākamācī* boiled with jaggery [is effective]. Furthermore, the root of *kākamācī* tied to the head with a thread certainly [induces sleep].
One whose sleep has been lost should quickly practice this; it is proven effective.

One with diminished sleep should habitually consume milk, wine, meat broth, and curd, and should perform oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, and the pouring of liquids into the head, ears, and eyes. 328–329.
The embrace of a beloved’s creeper-like arms is bliss; objects of the senses that are agreeable to the mind grant the fulfillment of desires; and sleep provides happiness.
Ghee is found in the sauce, the vegetable, the soup, and likewise in the broth and the milk.
Onion, when consumed, quickly produces sleep.
Sugarcane, *potakī*, mung beans, liquor, meat broth, milk, wheat, sesame, and fish also induce sleep in embodied beings. (331–332)

One should apply a warm plaster made of *dāru*, *haimavatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and rock salt (*saindhava*), ground with sour liquids, to a belly afflicted by colic and flatulence (333).
[Also, one may use] mustard oil prepared with *kaṇā*, asafoetida, *vacā*, and garlic.
Warm [oil] applied to the ears destroys ringing sounds and pain.
334 Pippalī combined with fragrant vacā and yavānī, taken together with betel leaf and held in the mouth, destroys dry cough. 335
Rice with meat broth (rasaudana) is always beneficial for those suffering from exhaustion, fasting, or wind disorders;
however, a soup of mung beans and āmalaka is given to one whose stool is obstructed.
Or, in cases of pain in the bladder, the sides, or the head, a thin gruel (peyā) made of red śāli rice should be administered.

One suffering from cough, dyspnea, or hiccups should drink a decoction prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *kaṇṭakārī*, which removes fever; or one should drink a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūlī*). When there is a diet and lifestyle dominated by *pitta*, the *pitta* takes refuge in the stomach (*āmāśaya*).
When the digestive fire (koṣṭhāgni) has been expelled outward, it becomes the cause of fever and follows the bodily fluids (rasa).
A sharp impulse, diarrhea, diminished sleep, as well as vomiting, inflammation of the throat, lips, mouth, and nose, and perspiration arise. (338–339)
In the Pittaja fever, there is incoherent speech, harshness of the mouth, fainting, burning sensations, intoxication, thirst, yellow discoloration of the feces, urine, and eyes, as well as vertigo;
one should administer medicine for the Pittaja fever after ten nights have passed. (340-341)
Now, the decoction of Tikta and others:
water boiled with Tikta, Musta, Yava, Pāṭhā, and Kaṭphala, when drunk along with sugar, acts as a digestive (pācana) remedy in Pittaja fever. (342)
Now, regarding the decoction of parpaṭa and other herbs:
a decoction made from parpaṭa, vāsaka, tiktā, kairāta, dhanvayāsaka,
and priyaṅgu, combined with sugar, [is used].
This [decoction], combined with thirst, burning sensations, and pitta-related disorders, removes pitta-fever (pittajvara).
343 Now, the decoction of Drākṣā and others: Drākṣā, Harītakī, Mustā, Kaṭukā, and Kṛtamālaka.
A decoction prepared from these, including parpaṭa, removes fever caused by pitta;

it is considered to alleviate dryness of the mouth, delirium, pain, burning sensations, fainting, and vertigo, while pacifying thirst and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta) and acting as a laxative. 344–345.
Now, the decoction of *paṭola* and others:
*Paṭola*, barley, coriander, and licorice, combined with honey, destroy pitta-fever, burning sensations, and excessively tormenting thirst. (346)
Now, the decoction of *guḍūcī* and others:
*guḍūcī* combined with *āmalaka*, or *parpaṭa* alone, quickly removes pitta-fever accompanied by burning sensations, emaciation, and giddiness. (347)
A single *parpaṭaka* is excellent for destroying fever caused by *pitta*;
how much more so if it is combined with sandalwood, *uśīra*, and *bālaka* (348).
Now follows the decoction of *hrīvera* and other ingredients.
One should administer water prepared with *hrīvera*, sandalwood, *uśīra*, *ghana* (musta), and *parpaṭa*, well-cooled, which removes thirst, vomiting, fever, and burning sensations.
Now follows the decoction of *bhūnimbādi*.
A decoction of bhūnimba, ativiṣā, lodhra, mustaka, indrayava, amṛtā,
bālaka, dhānyaka, and bilva, when combined with honey,
removes dysentery, asthma, cough, and fever caused by raktapitta. (350–351)
Now, the decoction of grapes and other ingredients: grapes, sandalwood, lotus, musta, tikta, amṛtā, dhātrī, bāla, uśīra, lodhra, indrayava, and parpaṭa. (352)
Parūṣaka, priyaṅgu, yavāsa, vāsaka, madhuka, kulaka, kirāta, and likewise dhānyaka— 353.
A decoction of these indeed destroys fever arising from pitta.

It destroys thirst, burning sensations, delirium, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), vertigo, fatigue, fainting, vomiting, as well as colic, dryness of the mouth, loss of appetite, cough, dyspnea, and nausea; of this there is no doubt. (354–355)
Now, a decoction of coriander with sugar,
left to stand overnight and drunk in the morning, or a decoction of coriander and rice grains drunk in the morning, quickly pacifies internal burning and fever caused by pitta. 356
Now, *amṛtā* with *ahimavāsā* and *ahima*, or *amṛtā* with *himaprātaḥ* and sugar, conquers bilious fever; likewise, *vāsā* overcomes cough, hemorrhaging, and fever. (357)
Now, the second decoction, beginning with *guḍūcī*:
*guḍūcī*, *bhūminimba*, young *vīraṇa* root, small *musta*, *trivṛt*, *dhātrī*, *drākṣā*, *vāsā*, and *parpaṭa*. (358)

The decoction of these— either the tender leaves of *palāśa*, *badarī*, or *nimba*— when drunk in the morning with honey, quickly removes even fever accompanied by complications that has been caused by pitta. (359)

This plaster made from sour substances ground together destroys fever accompanied by burning sensations (360). Furthermore, while the patient lies on his back, a continuous stream of cold water falling upon the navel— which is placed in a deep vessel of copper, bell-metal, or similar material— quickly subdues both the burning sensation and the fever (361).
Now, the Pathyā electuary: by licking Pathyā with oil, ghee, and honey, one overcomes burning fever;
it also destroys cough, hemorrhagic disorders, erysipelas, dyspnea, and vomiting. (362)
Wrapping [the head] with a cloth moistened with sour gruel (kāñjika) destroys burning sensations; furthermore,
a gargle made from the paste of grapes (drākṣā) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), using a cloth that has been steamed with cow's whey and then cooled, is considered beneficial here.
Alternatively, one may use the seeds of ripe pomegranate or, in some cases, a paste of parched grain (dhānā).
For a patient afflicted by burning sensations and tremors, emaciated, abstaining from food, and possessed by thirst,
one should administer a satiating drink of parched grain (lāja-tarpaṇa) mixed with sugar and honey.
In a case of Pittaja fever, one should be given rice with mung bean soup mixed with sugar;
the patient suffering from Pittaja fever should sleep in a palace resembling a white cloud, cooled by the rays of the moon and sprinkled with sandalwood water. 366

The embraces of broad-hipped women, who are cooled by necklaces and sandalwood paste and adorned with fragrant flowers, garments, and ornaments, and who possess full breasts, quickly remove the burning heat.
Having recognized their gladdening effect, one should then remove those women from him.
One should eat wholesome food, for great pleasure does not arise from mere sensual gratification.
Ponds where lotuses bloom, auspicious water-machines,
and women whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste are considered the true removers of the misery of burning heat.
Thus ends the section on Pittaja fever;
now begins the section on Kaphaja fever:
indeed, through a diet and lifestyle that increases *śleṣman*, *kapha* takes its seat in the stomach (*āmāśaya*).
When the digestive fire (koṣṭhāgni) has been cast outward, the fever caused by it follows the rasa-dhātu;
there is numbness, a sluggish onset, lassitude, a sweet taste in the mouth, whiteness of urine and feces, stiffness, or even a sense of satiety. (370–371)
Heaviness, coldness, excessive moisture, horripilation, excessive sleepiness, coryza, loss of appetite, cough, and whiteness of the eyes occur in fever born of kapha;
one should administer medicine for kaphaja fever after twelve days. (372)
A decoction of the *pippalyādi* group, however, is a digestive (paripācana) remedy for [fever] caused by *kapha*.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, marica, gajapippalī, nāgara, citraka, cavya, reṇuka, elā, and ajamodā. (373–374)
Mustard, asafoetida, bhārgī, pāṭhā, indrayava,
cumin, mahānimba, mūrvā, viṣā, tiktā, and viḍaṅga—
this is indeed the pippalyādi group, which destroys kapha and vāta. (375)

This combination of honey and Pippalī relieves abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, and fever; it stimulates digestion and digests undigested matter (āma). It cures asthma, cough, and fever, destroys splenic enlargement and hiccups, and is recommended even for children. (376–377)
A person suffering from fever who licks equal parts of *pippalī* and *triphalā* with honey and ghee, or one suffering from cough and dyspnea, shall find relief.
(378) *Kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, and *kṛṣṇā* [should be taken] together with honey.
This linctus removes dyspnea, cough, and fever, and destroys phlegm.
(379) One should powder equal parts of kaṭphala, pauṣkara, śṛṅgī, yavānī, kāravī, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya). (380)
One suffering from fever caused by *kapha* should lick [the powder] with the fresh juice of *ārdra* or with honey;
it removes cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vomiting, hiccups, *kapha*, and *vāta*. (381) In fever caused by *kapha*, one should take a decoction of *sinduvāra* leaves enriched with *kaṇā*.
When strength in the calves has diminished and the ears are blocked, one should drink [this]; 382.
One should drink a decoction of *yavānī*, *pippalī*, *vāsā*, and the bark of *khākhasa* for cough, dyspnea, and fever born of phlegm. 383.
A decoction of vāsā, akṣudrā, and amṛtā taken with honey removes fever and cough.
(384) Marica, pippalīmūla, nāgara, kāravī, kaṇā, citraka, kaṭphala, kuṣṭha, sugandhā, vacā, and śivā— (385)

A decoction of *kaṇṭakārī*, *jaṭā*, *śṛṅgī*, *yavānī*, and *picumandaka* certainly removes fever accompanied by complications arising from *kapha*. Because it alleviates diseases of *kapha* and *vāta*, the "Kalpataru Rasa" mentioned in the section on *vāta* should also be employed.
A gruel made with mudga beans, along with *sindhuvāra*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and *rājī*, is beneficial for phlegm when moistened with *ārdra* [juice].
This should be administered in a fever arising from phlegm.
Thus ends the section on phlegm-fever (*śleṣmajvara*).
Now begins the section on fever caused by Vāta and Pitta:

Indeed, when Vāta and Pitta, provoked by factors that increase them, take refuge in the stomach (āmāśaya), they expel the digestive fire from the visceral cavity into the nutrient fluid (rasa) and thereby produce fever. (389)
In the premonitory stage of Vātapaittika [fever],
thirst, fainting, giddiness, burning sensation, loss of sleep, headache,
dryness of the throat and mouth, vomiting, horripilation, anorexia, and darkness before the eyes occur. (390)
Pain in the joints and yawning are the clinical features of fever caused by vāta and pitta (vātapittajvara).
On the fifth day, medicine for vātapittajvara should be administered;
[the ingredients are] kirātatikta, amṛtā, drākṣā, āmalaka, and śaṭī.
One should drink the decoction mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*) in cases of fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*.
(393) Gudūcī, parpaṭa, musta, kirāta, and viśvabheṣaja—this auspicious "Five-Fortunate" (*pañcabhadra*) compound should be administered in fever caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. (394)

Water boiled with triphalā, śālmalī, rāsnā, rājavṛkṣa, and āṭarūṣaka quickly removes fever arising from vāta and pitta. Madhuka, sārivā, drākṣā, madhūka, candana, and utpala [likewise act as a remedy].

One should crush the fruits of *kāśmarī*, *lodhra*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the filaments of *padmaka*, and *parūṣaka*, along with lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), and soak them in water overnight; then one should drink that liquid mixed with sugar, honey, and parched grain flour (*lāja*).

It pacifies fever caused by vāta and pitta, burning sensations, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and vertigo, as well as raktapitta, just as the wind disperses a cloud. (396) A soup of mudga and āmalaka is beneficial for fever caused by vāta and pitta.
In cases of severe burning sensations (mahādāha), a soup made from chickpeas (caṇaka) should be administered.
It is stated that a soup made from pomegranate (dāḍima), emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), and green gram (mudga) is indicated for vāta-paittika conditions;
likewise, green gram (mudga) and kāravellyādi plants alleviate kapha and pitta.
Generally, these [purgatives] should not be administered in a fever where wind (vāta) and bile (pitta) predominate;
for if given, they cause the suppression of the fever (jvara-viṣṭambha), colic, and upward movement of gases (udāvarta).
Thus ends the section on fever caused by wind and bile.
Now begins the section on fever caused by Vāta and Śleṣman:

When Vāta and Kapha, provoked by factors that increase Vāta and Śleṣman, are driven out from the stomach (āmāśaya) and enter the rasa-carrying vessels, they cause fever by displacing the digestive fire (agni) from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha). 399
In a fever arising from Vāta and Kapha, the premonitory symptoms of Vāta and Kapha occur:
stiffness, aching in the joints, drowsiness,
heaviness, stiffness of the head, coryza, cough, and the non-emission of sweat.
Fever caused by vāta and śleṣman has the symptoms of burning heat and moderate intensity (madhyavega);
on the ninth day, medicine for vāta-śleṣma fever should be administered.
Now, the *pañcakola*.
The group consisting of *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *nāgara* is known as the digestive stimulant (*dīpanīya*); it removes wind, phlegm, and fever.
Because it is used in the measure of five *kola*s, it is known as the "Five-Black-pepper" (*pañcakola*) group. 403

Sharp and hot, it is an excellent digestive stimulant, an appetizer, and a remover of phlegm and burning sensations; it destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, flatulence, and colic, though it provokes pitta. 404 Now follows the second decoction: Kirātādika-kvātha.

A decoction prepared from *kirātatiktaka*, *viśvā*, *amṛtavallī*, *siṃhikā*, *vyāghrī*, the root of *kaṇā*, *rasana*, and *sinduka* quickly destroys fever arising from wind (*vāta*) associated with phlegm (*kapha*). 405.
Now, the *pippalyādi* decoction:
One suffering from fever caused by vāta and kapha should drink a decoction of the pippalyādi group;
there is no better medicine for fever than this. 406.
Now follows the Bṛhat-pippalyādi-kvātha.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara, vacā, ativiṣā, ajājī, pāṭhā, vatsaka, reṇukā,
kirātatiktaka, mūrvā, sarṣapa, and marica.
Kaṭphala, puṣkara, bhārgī, viḍaṅga, karkaṭāhvaya (408),
arka-mūla, bṛhat-siṃhī, śreyasī, durālabhā, dīpyaka, ajamodā, śukanāsā, and hiṅgu (409).
These [drugs] taken in equal parts constitute one group of twenty-eight.
Their decoction, when drunk, removes fever caused by Vāta and Kapha;
it destroys Vāta, as well as coldness, excessive perspiration, and violent trembling. (410)
In cases of excessive talking, excessive sleep, horripilation, and loss of appetite (411),
as well as in great wind-disorders (*mahāvāta*), prolapse of the rectum (*apatrantra*), and emptiness of all limbs,
the great decoction of *pippalyādi* is honored in every type of fever (412).
Now, the decoction of the ten roots:
The juice of the ten roots, when drunk with an abundance of *kaṇā* (long pepper), cures fever born of phlegm and wind, indigestion, excessive sleep, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough. (413)
Now, the decoction of pippalī:
water boiled with pippalī is non-obstructive to the channels, stimulates digestion, cures fever caused by vāta and kapha when consumed, and destroys splenic disorders. 414
Now, for the Sūryaśekhara-rasa:
take equal parts of mercury (sūtaka), borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), roasted sulphur (gandha), and purified [mercury]; add twice the amount of mercury of *jaipāla* seeds, free from husks. 415

Saindhava salt, black pepper, the alkali of tamarind bark, and sugar— each equal in measure to mercury— one should grind these for one day with jambīra fruits. This elixir, named Sūryaśekhara, is to be taken in a dose of two guñjās.
When consumed with hot water, it removes disorders of wind (vāta), phlegm (śleṣman), and fever. 417.
They say that when perspiration arises, the application of fried horse-gram (kulattha) powder is recommended;
likewise, cow dung that has been digested [in fire], ground into a vessel, and used as a fine dusting-powder, removes perspiration. 418.
Now, the smearing with black pepper and other substances:
black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*pippalī*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), yellow myrobalan (*pathyā*), *lodhra*, and *pauṣkara*;
*bhūnimba*, *kaṭukā*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), *kacūra*, *liṅgikā*, and *śaṭī*. (Verse 419)

One should have these made into fine powders in equal proportions; this is the best dusting powder for the removal of perspiration through the channels. Now follows the *bhūnimbādyuddhūlana* (dusting powder beginning with *bhūnimba*).
Bhūnimba, kāravī, tiktā, vacā, and the powder of kaṭphala—
constant dusting with these is excellent for the continuous flow of sweat.
Now, the sand-sudation (vālukāsveda).
The previously mentioned sand-sudation (vālukāsveda) is also appropriate here,
as it has been stated: "In cases of rhinitis, dyspnea, deafness, and pain in the calves, flanks, or bones..."
A physician who knows the proper procedure should administer medicine for fever caused by vāta and kapha.

The filament of the mātuluṅga fruit, held in the mouth together with rock salt and black pepper, quickly destroys diseases of the mouth arising from vāta and kapha, as well as dryness, numbness, and loss of appetite.
On the seventh day, the physician should administer food that has been properly prepared with a large quantity of the five roots (pañcamūla) in cases of fever arising from Vāta and Kapha.
Thus ends the section on fevers born of Vāta and Kapha.
Now begins the section on fever caused by pitta and kapha:

Substances that increase pitta and kapha cause these two humors to leave their seat in the stomach (āmāśaya) and, having expelled the digestive fire from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), produce fever characterized by the essence of the body fluids (rasaugha). 425
In a fever arising from pitta and kapha, the premonitory symptoms of both pitta and kapha occur (426).
A coated and bitter mouth, drowsiness, delusion, cough, anorexia, thirst,
alternating heat and alternating cold— this is the clinical presentation of a pitta-śleṣma fever (427).

Medicine should be administered on the tenth day for a fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*. This decoction of *guḍūcī*, *nimba*, *dhānyaka*, *candana*, and *kaṭurohiṇī* is known as the *guḍūcyādi* group; it is considered digestive and appetizing.
It removes thirst, burning sensations, anorexia, vomiting, disorders of pitta and kapha, and fever.
(429) Amṛtā, kaṭukā, ariṣṭa, paṭola, ghana, candana, nāgarendra, and yava—this is declared to be the "Eightfold Amṛta" (Amṛtāṣṭaka). (430)
This decoction, prepared with powdered *kaṇā* (long pepper), cures fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*,
and wards off nausea, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations. 431 Now follows the decoction of *kaṇṭakārī* and others.
Having boiled together kaṇṭakārī, amṛtā, bhārgī, viśva, indrayava,
vāsaka, bhūnimba, candana, musta, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī,
one should administer the decoction, which removes fever caused by pitta and śleṣman. (432)

It alleviates burning sensations, thirst, anorexia, vomiting, cough, and colic (433). A decoction prepared with ginger, ushira, bilva, musta, coriander, and mocarasa, when mixed with water, is astringent and cures fever caused by pitta and kapha (434).
By drinking one akṣa-measure of sugar and kaṭukī with warm water, a person may conquer fever arising from pitta and śleṣman.
The juice of vāsā, along with its leaves and flowers, combined with honey and sugar [is likewise effective].
It destroys fever caused by pitta and kapha, as well as sour bile (amlapitta) and jaundice (kāmalā).
A decoction of ginger and paṭola, when thoroughly drunk, removes fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and itching arising from pitta and kapha.
The soup made from *paṭola* and coriander (*dhānya*) removes fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*.
(438) Thus ends the section on fevers born of *pitta* and *kapha*. Now begins the section on fevers born of the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*).
Vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, generated by the three doṣas, having reached the amāśaya and expelled the digestive fire from the stomach, enter the rasa-dhātu and cause fever.
There is burning at one moment and coldness at another, along with pain in the bones, joints, and head. (439)
The eyes are tearful, turbid, red, and even sunken;
the ears are ringing and painful; the throat feels as if covered with bristles; there is drowsiness, delusion, delirium, cough, dyspnea, loss of appetite, and vertigo. (440–441)
The tongue is parched, rough to the touch, and its extremities droop; there is excessive spitting of blood and bile mixed with phlegm,
rolling of the head, thirst, loss of sleep, and pain in the heart.
The infrequent appearance of sweat, urine, and feces after a long time; emaciation of the limbs that is not excessive; constant hoarseness of the throat;
and the appearance of dark-red patches and circular eruptions (maṇḍalas). 442–443.

Muteness, suppuration of the channels, heaviness of the abdomen, and the delayed maturation of the doshas constitute the clinical presentation of sannipāta fever. Among these, there are six types: those in which one dosha is predominant, and likewise those in which two are predominant. (444)
One should know that there is also one characterized by the predominance of all three [humors]; this is the seventh.
Thus, through the combinations of increased, moderate, and diminished *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, there are thirteen specific varieties of *sannipāta* fever. (445–446)
Visphāraka, Āśukārī, Kampana, the one named Babhru, Śīghrakārī, as well as Bhallu, the seventh being Kūṭapākala;
then Sammohaka, Pākala, Yāmya, and also Krakaca.
Then Karkaṭaka is mentioned, and then the one named Vaidārika (448).
Among them, the symptoms of Vātolvaṇa-visphāra are:
dyspnea, cough, vertigo, fainting, delirium, confusion, and trembling.
Pain in the sides, yawning, and a bitter taste in the mouth—
these should be recognized as the signs of a *sannipāta* dominated by *vāta*.
This extremely severe *sannipāta* is known by the name *visphāraka*.
Diarrhea, vertigo, fainting, as well as inflammation of the mouth, red spots on the body, and excessive burning sensation—
these should be recognized as the symptoms of *sannipāta* characterized by a predominance of *pitta*. (451)
Physicians declare this to be a rapidly acting *sannipāta* (combined derangement of the humors).
There is stupor, a faltering voice, sleep even at night, the eyes become fixed and motionless, and there is a sweetness in the mouth. (452–453)
One should recognize the symptoms of *sannipāta* characterized by a predominance of *kapha*;
this *sannipāta* has been termed "trembling" (*kampana*) by the sages. However, that *sannipāta* in which *vāta* and *pitta* predominate becomes aggravated.
Fever, intoxication, thirst, dryness of the mouth, drowsiness, flatulence, anorexia, torpor, cough, dyspnea, vertigo, and exhaustion— this condition,
named Babhru, has been described by the sages as a type of *sannipāta*.
In one whose *sannipāta* (combined derangement) is provoked by a predominance of *vāta* and *śleṣman*,
there occurs cold fever (*śītajvara*), fainting, hunger, thirst, pain in the flanks, colic in one who does not perspire, drowsiness, and dyspnea.
This *sannipāta* is called "swift-acting" (*śīghrakārī*) because it is incurable;
indeed, one whose body is possessed by it does not live for even a day and night.
That *sannipāta* in which *pitta* and *śleṣman* predominate becomes aggravated.
There is internal burning and external coldness; his thirst increases greatly (459). He suffers from piercing pain in the right side, as well as stiffness in the chest, head, and throat;
he spits out phlegm and bile with difficulty, and eruptions (koṭha) arise (460).
Diarrhea, dyspnea, hiccups, and pramīlaka (excessive sleepiness) increase;
this type of *sannipāta* is described by the sages as *bhallūna*. This *sannipāta* occurs when all the *doṣas* are aggravated and predominate.
One should observe the symptoms of all three doshas in him:
more terrible than diseases themselves, resembling a thunderbolt, a weapon, or fire;
with only breathing as his remaining function, his limbs are rigid and his eyes are fixed.
After three nights have passed, it takes away the life of this creature;
seeing him in that state, the deluded people say:
"He has surely been attacked by Rākṣasas who roam at improper times. (464)
Some say it was struck on the head by a mother-goddess, or by yakṣiṇīs, brahmarākṣasas, piśācas, guhyakas,
or others; or that he was overcome by his family deities because he had neglected the worship of his ancestral gods.
Some physicians call this *nakṣatrapīḍā*, others *garakarma*, and still others describe this *sannipāta* as *kūṭapākala* (467),
which arises from the excessive, moderate, or deficient states of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*).
Therefore, those very diseases have been described according to the strength of the respective *doṣas*:
delirium, exhaustion, confusion, trembling, fainting, restlessness, vertigo, and paralysis of one side; these [symptoms] are especially prominent therein. 468–469.

This very severe disorder known as Sammohaka is caused by a combination (sannipāta) of wind, bile, and phlegm that are moderate, increased, and diminished respectively. By this [combination], those very diseases are said to arise, depending on the relative strength of each humor (doṣa).
Delirium, incoherent speech, fainting, stiffness of the neck, rigidity of the head,
cough, dyspnea, vertigo, drowsiness, loss of consciousness, pain in the heart,
discharge of blood from the orifices, and reddishness with fixedness of the eyes may occur.
In that case as well, these specific features may occur, and death may happen within three days;
this type of *sannipāta* has been described by physicians as *pākalā*.
It is characterized by the diminished, increased, or moderate states of vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively.
Therefore, those very diseases have been described according to the strength of the respective doṣas:
his heart burns, and his liver, spleen, intestines, and lungs are excessively inflamed; there is an excessive discharge of pus and blood from both the upper and lower orifices. 474–475.

One with decayed teeth and death [occur] there as well; this particular condition is proclaimed by physicians as the "Yāmya" type of *sannipāta*. That which is characterized by the excessive, deficient, or moderate states of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*) [is also included].
Therefore, those very diseases have been described according to the strength of the respective doṣas:
delirium, exhaustion, confusion, tremors, fainting, restlessness, and vertigo;
in that case as well, death may occur specifically due to stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha). 477–478.

This saw has been proclaimed by physicians as being composed of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha). Those very diseases are said to arise from these [humors] when they are moderate, deficient, or increased, according to the strength of the respective doshas upon which they depend.
There is a specific internal burning here that cannot be described;
the circle of the face appears as if stained with red lac.
The phlegm, drawn upward by the bile, does not flow out from the heart.
The sides feel as if struck by an arrow, and the heart is pierced and excavated;
lethargy, labored breathing, and hiccupping increase day by day;
the tongue feels as if scorched and rough to the touch, and the throat is as if covered with bristles. 482–483.
He does not perceive the urge to defecate, and he coos like a pigeon;
being excessively filled with phlegm, his mouth, lips, and palate are parched.
Afflicted by excessive drowsiness and sleep, his speech is impaired and his luster is destroyed. (484)
He finds no pleasure at all and desires things that are contrary [to his nature]; he frequently strains excessively and spits out blood in small amounts.
This is the most dreadful disorder known by the name Karkaṭaka, a complication of the humors (sannipāta). 485–486.
Depending on whether the wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are diminished, moderate, or increased,
the diseases are said to arise according to the strength of those respective humors.
There is slight pain, piercing in the waist, burning in the middle [of the body], distress, and vertigo.
Excessive exhaustion, pain in the head, neck, heart, and speech;
drowsiness, dyspnea, cough, hiccup, stiffness, and loss of consciousness—these may sometimes cure the enema when it is first administered. (488–489)
When this [disease] has subsided, however, a most dreadful carbuncle arises at the root of the ear, by which the person lives only with great difficulty;
this is known as vaidārika, a most terrible disorder caused by the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).

Beyond three nights, the administration of medicinal preparations for this [fever] is useless. One whose limbs are cold, who suffers from a cluster of fevers arising from the three *doṣas*, who is drowsy and delirious, and who then spits blood— with eyes that are sunken— is counted among those [cases where treatment fails].

The *sābhiyāsaka* and *jihvaka* types are said to occur at the junction of the seasons; then there are the *antaka*, *rugdāha*, and *cittavibhrama*, as well as the two types involving the seizing of the ears and throat (492).
One afflicted by *sannipāta* fever has a body cold as ice and suffers from labored breathing, coughing, hiccups, delusion, trembling, and incoherent speech.

One who is afflicted by exhaustion, an excess of phlegm and wind, burning sensations, anointing, pain, and changes in voice; whose limbs are cold—he is so described. (493) Furthermore, there is excessive drowsiness, thirst, diarrhea, labored breathing, coughing, and a body pained by heat, along with itching and swelling in the throat and phlegm.
Where there is a darkish complexion, a parched tongue, exhaustion, deafness, and a burning sensation,
that is indeed declared to be the fever arising from all three humors (doṣas), known as tandrīka.
In that fever which is produced by the extreme provocation of all the humors, there is much delirium and the patient rises up suddenly.
Trembling, distress, falling down, burning sensations, and loss of consciousness occur; this condition is renowned on earth by the name *pralāpaka*.
There is spitting of blood, circular spots on the body resembling blood or black in color, redness of the eyes, thirst, aversion to food, vomiting, dyspnea, diarrhea, and vertigo.
In fever born of the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), there arise flatulence, loss of consciousness, falling down, hiccups, severe pain in the limbs, and the spitting of blood.
There is also extreme distortion of the eyes and face, labored breathing, cough, drowsiness, excessive delirium, intoxication, trembling, loss of hearing, and fainting.

In that fever where all the symptoms of every [aggravated] humor (doṣa) appear first, it is considered here by ancient physicians as Bhugnanetra. In that fever where all the humors become exceedingly intense and powerful,
there is extreme delusion, restlessness, agitation, heavy labored breathing, and muteness.
Burning sensation, a sticky mouth, weak digestion, and a loss of strength—this is proclaimed here as *abhinyāsa* by wise physicians of old.
It occurs in a fever born of the three *doṣas* where the tongue becomes excessively [parched]. 498.
Subsequently, being completely enveloped by stiff and sharp thorns, followed by profound muteness, impairment of hearing, strength, and complexion, and suffering from labored breathing and coughing—
the ancient, eminent physicians call this condition here "jihvaka. 499
Excessive pain accompanied by swelling in the joints,
excessive phlegm in the mouth, loss of sleep, and coughing—
these are proclaimed to be the complete set of symptoms present in this fever.

Indeed, that fever which is produced by the three *doṣas* is described by the wise as *sandhiga*. In that fever arising from all the *doṣas*, there is constant shaking of the head, coughing, and excessive pain in all the limbs. (500)
Hiccups, dyspnea, constant burning sensation, delusion, extreme heat in the body, physical impairment, and incoherent speech—these are proclaimed by the sages as that which is the Ender (Antaka).

501 Where there is excessive burning, intense thirst, and affliction from labored breathing, delirium, aversion to food, vertigo, and delusion; where there is pain in the neck and jaw, throat ailments, exhaustion, and a burning sensation—this fever arising from the three humors is called Rugdāha-saṃjña. 502

In the case of *cittabhrama-jvara* (delirious fever), a man sings, dances, laughs, prattles incoherently, stares with distorted vision, and becomes deluded; he is afflicted by the pain of burning sensations and fear. Indeed, this fever is produced by the three *doṣas*, and in the fever located at the root of the ear (*karṇamūla-jvara*), there occurs intense swelling and pain.
In the [fever] called Karṇika, there is seizing of the throat, deafness, labored breathing, delirium, perspiration, delusion, and burning sensations (504).
In Śatāvaruddha, there is extreme dyspnea, delirium, loss of appetite,
fever, bodily pain, thirst, lockjaw, and headache.

Delusion accompanied by trembling—where these constitute the complete set of symptoms in a fever arising from the three *doṣas*—that indeed has been described as *kaṇṭhakubja* by the ancient experts in therapeutics.
When it is localized in the joints (*sandhiga*), it may be curable; however, some cases involving lassitude and confusion are incurable.
Karṇika, jihvaka, kaṇṭhakubja, and the five types of kaṣṭaka— among these,
rugdāha is said to be cured only with great difficulty.
One who spits blood, has distorted eyes, cold limbs, and suffers from delirium [is incurable].
Abhinyāsa and Antaka— these six are proclaimed as incurable.
Kumbhīpāka, Prorṇunāva, Pralāpī, Antardāha, Daṇḍapāta, Antaka,
Eṇīdāha, and that known as Hāridra— these are the varieties of Sannipāta fever.
Ajaghoṣa, bhūtahāsa, yantrāpīḍa, saṃnyāsa,
and saṃśoṣī— these thirteen other specific types of his [breaths] are described elsewhere. [In one of these],
thick blood, black and red, flows profusely from the openings of the nostrils like a mountain stream.
One should know that he who rolls about with his head facing all directions and is tormented by *kumbhīpāka* [is in that hell].
510. One should recognize him as afflicted by *vicitrakṛcchra*, who, having lifted up his own limb, throws it down again and breathes heavily. 511.

Perspiration, vertigo, breaking pain in the limbs, trembling, feverish distress, vomiting, and a sense of oppression in the throat and body arise as signs of one afflicted by delirium (pralāpajuṣṭa). Internal burning, external coldness, swelling, restlessness, and dyspnea likewise occur.
His limbs are as if burnt, and he is tormented by an internal fever; 513.
the deluded-minded one finds no sleep day or night. Rising from his seat, he falls like a staff, and, afflicted by confusion, he wanders aimlessly in every direction. 514.
The body and the belly all around are filled with knots for one who is afflicted by labored breathing due to wind, constantly unconscious and tormented at the end;
in his limbs, which are like vessels of pain, the hosts of serpents, birds, and deer seem to run about. 515.
One who has trembling, constant burning sensations, and is afflicted by a fever with a burning sensation like that of a doe,

whose body is excessively yellow and whose eyes are even more soiled than that, and who experiences extreme coldness on the exterior despite the internal heat— such a person should be known as having *hāridraka* fever. (516–517)
A man whose body has a smell like that of a goat, who suffers from pain in the shoulders, whose throat-passage is obstructed, whose eyes are copper-colored due to a *sannipāta* caused by *ajaghoṣa*,
does not perceive his own objects such as sound through the collection of his sense organs. 518.
One who laughs and speaks harshly should be known as afflicted by *bhūtahāsa*.
He by whom the body is repeatedly crushed, as if by a mechanical press, due to the force of fever,
and who vomits blood and bile, should be recognized as suffering from *yantrāpīḍa*.
In the case of *sannyāsa-sannipāta*, the man passes stool, vomits, makes moaning sounds, and tosses his limbs about for a long time; he raves, and the circles of his eyes become intensely dark;
after voiding excrement, his body becomes dark blue and his pair of eyes becomes exceedingly black. 521.
In a fever characterized by drying up, white pustules, and circular patches, a person becomes like Nārāyaṇa himself;
the physician and the medicine for these conditions is the water of the Jāhnavī (Ganges), and for the sake of constant health, one should meditate upon Mṛtyuñjaya alone. 522–523.

At the end of a *sannipāta* fever, a most severe swelling arises at the base of the ear; by means of this, only some few are liberated. Others have declared that *sannipāta* fevers are difficult and incurable.

When the humors (doṣas) have increased excessively and the digestive fire (agni) has been destroyed, the fever characterized by all symptoms is a fatal *sannipāta* fever; otherwise, it is difficult to cure.
He who rescues a person submerged in the ocean of *sannipāta* [is truly a benefactor].

What dharma has not been performed by Kasta, and what worship does he not deserve? (527) One who treats a complication must fight with death; whoever emerges victorious therein is the victor in the turmoil of disease. (528)
In a disease arising from all three *doṣas*, one should first suppress the *śleṣman* (phlegm);

whichever *doṣa* is most predominant in a combined (*saṃsarga*) condition should be treated first. Where it is impossible to distinguish the respective portions of the *doṣas*, [one should treat them collectively].
In that case, the physician should employ general treatment:
fasting, sand-sweating (bālukāsveda), nasal medication (nasya), gargling (niṣṭhīvana),
electuary (avaleha), and collyrium (añjana) should be applied first in cases arising from the three doṣas.
The confusion of rituals is held to occur when the rituals are of identical form;
however, those [rituals] do not cause any fault when they are of distinct forms. Whether for three nights, five nights, or even ten nights—
In cases of *sannipāta* (combined humors), one should administer fasting until health is observed.
When the seventh, tenth, or even the twelfth day arrives,
the disease may become more violent again before subsiding or killing the patient.

Due to the increase of pitta, kapha, and vāta, it kills after ten days, twelve days, or seven days; or else, arising from the three doṣas, it releases [the patient] through the digestion of the bodily tissues and wastes (dhātumalapāka). There is loss of sleep, stiffness of the heart, constipation, heaviness, and anorexia.
Dislike [for food], loss of strength, and the symptoms of the maturation (*pāka*) of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) occur.

When the heart, the region of the navel, or the limbs—afflicted by the pain of maturation—are oppressed, the fever-stricken person rubs them with his fingers; this is described by physicians as *dhātupākin* (maturation of the constituents). 536–537.

If pain occurs when the area above the navel and below the heart is pressed, one should know that it is the digestion (*pāka*) of the nutrient essence (*dhātu*); otherwise, it is the digestion of waste matter (*mala*). Furthermore, there is a transformation of the humors (*doṣa*) and the natural state (*prakṛti*), as well as lightness of the fever and the body. (538)
The clarity of the sense organs and the ripening of the humors (malas) are characterized as follows:

where there is constant sharpness of the five senses and of the digestive fire, and the gradual subsiding of thirst and other symptoms along with the mildness of the fever, one should declare that to be the ripening of the humors.

Excessive pain in the heart and navel, diarrhea, high fever, thirst, intoxication, excessive dyspnea, loss of appetite, and restlessness— these constitute the manifestation of the digestion of the bodily constituents (dhātupāka).
This state lasts for seven days, doubling thereafter until the ninth and eleventh days.
This is the boundary of the three *doṣas*, leading both to liberation and to death.
(541) One suffering from *sannipāta* fever should first properly perform fasting (*laṅghana*);
one should drink boiled water that has cooled, and at the appropriate time, employ medicine. (542)
He who gives cold water to one suffering from thirst due to a *sannipāta* disorder, afflicted by pain in the sides and dryness of the palate, is death in human form.
In cases caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*, one should administer sudations prepared with dry substances.
Oily fomentation (sneha-sveda) is prohibited here, except in cases arising solely from Vata.

Fomentation with sand sprinkled with sour gruel (kāñjika) heated in an iron pan and placed within a cloth bag pacifies diseases of Vata and Kapha, as well as headaches, body aches, and other such ailments. (544–545)
By softening the channels, drawing [the heat] to the site of digestion,
and removing the obstruction caused by vāta and kapha, sudation dispels fever.
(546) Saindhava salt, white pepper, mustard seeds, and kuṣṭha—
Ground with goat's urine, this [mixture] used as a nasal drop (nasya) removes drowsiness.
(547) Equal parts of Madhūka-sāra, Saindhava salt, Vacā, Uṣaṇa, and Kaṇā, finely ground with water, should be administered as a nasal drop to restore consciousness. (548)
One should administer a strong nasal medication (nasya) consisting of lukewarm juice of *mātuluṅga* and *ārdraka* mixed with the three salts, or another preparation prescribed for success;
by this, the phlegm is broken up, and once broken up, it is discharged. (549)
Pain in the head, heart, throat, mouth, and sides is pacified.
(550) There is nothing else whatsoever capable of awakening one deluded by the disease of ignorance like the elixir named Kalpataru. (551)
When the tongue, palate, throat, and kloma are vitiated by wind and bile, then it causes dryness, a loss of taste in the tongue, and cracking;
at that time, one should smear the tongue with honey ground with [flour]. 552.
By means of that [mixture] with *drākṣā* and clarified butter, the tongue shall become succulent and soft.
(553) One should hold rock salt (*saindhava*), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), and fresh ginger juice in the mouth up to the throat, and spit it out again and again. (554)
By that [action], phlegm (śleṣmā), even though it is stuck within the palate, stomach, shoulders, neck, sides, head, and throat, is drawn out, and lightness arises for him.
[Otherwise, there occur] pain in the joints, fever, fainting, sleepiness, dyspnea, and diseases of the throat. (555)
Heaviness of the face and eyes, stupor, and nausea are pacified.
One should perform this once, twice, thrice, or four times, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the humors (doṣas).
Indeed, they declare this to be the supreme medicine for those afflicted by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
Thus is the gargle: one should lick a fine powder of *kaṭphala*, *pauṣkara*, *śṛṅgī*, *vyoṣa*, *yāsa*, and *kāravī* together with honey. (558)
This electuary destroys even the most severe *sannipāta* disorder;
it cures hiccup, dyspnea, cough, and throat diseases.
When there is an excess of phlegm (*kapha*), this powder should be administered with the juices of fresh ginger. (559)

One should lick the eight-ingredient formulation with honey or with the juice of *ārdra* (fresh ginger); this destroys severe delusion accompanied by drowsiness and cough. In all cases of *sannipāta*, however, one should not administer honey.
Honey is a cooling remedy, yet here it is contraindicated by coldness.
Having steamed and ground āmalaka fruit,
one should mix it with grapes and viśvabheṣaja (dry ginger), and have it licked with honey.
By this, his dyspnea, cough, fainting, and anorexia are pacified.
(562) A collyrium for awakening [the patient] should be prepared from śirīṣa seeds along with cow’s urine, kṛṣṇā, marica, saindhava, rasāñjana, sarala, manaḥśilā, and vacā. (563)
Iron filings, white *lodhra*, black pepper, and likewise collyrium (*añjana*),
combined with cow’s urine, are an excellent remedy for destroying drowsiness (*tandrā*).
Collyrium properly applied with honey, rock salt (*sindhūśilā*), and black pepper [is also effective].
The speech of Daṇḍapāṇi is delusive and hostile.
565 Thus, the ointment consists of mercury, poison, black pepper, tutthaka, and navasādara.
The powder should be ground with the fresh juices of *dhūrta* leaves and *rasoṇa*.
In cases of unconsciousness caused by *sannipāta*, one should apply this as a plaster over the feet;
likewise, for pain in the bones, one should apply the plaster over the feet using this same method.
Bilva, śyonāka, gāmbhārī, pāṭalā,
and gaṇikārikā constitute this "Great Five Roots" (mahat-pañcamūla), which destroys pitta and removes vāta and kapha.
Śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā [constitute the second group].
Gokṣura destroys vāta and pitta; this is the minor Pañcamūla (the five roots).
Both together constitute the Daśamūla (ten roots), which, when combined with powdered pippalī, cures sannipāta fever and eliminates afflictions of the heart and throat.
It cures drowsiness, the afflictions of Vāta and Kapha, dyspnea, and pain in the flanks.
One should take the bark of those roots that are large and have hard wood within them, as well as the entire roots of those that are small. (571–572)
A decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī), combined with long pepper (pippalī) and pauṣkara,
should be administered in cases of fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), accompanied by dyspnea and cough;
or it may be used in chronic fever characterized by a predominance of vāta and kapha, or in fever arising from all three humors when mixed with the ten roots.
The Kirātatiktādi group should be employed for one seeking purification, either mixed with Trivṛt, or [alone]. 574.
This group, consisting of Kirātatiktaka, Musta, Guḍūcī, and Viśvabheṣaja, is indeed called the Kirātatiktādi group, and it is also known as Cāturbhadra. 575.
Daśamūlī, śaṭī, śṛṅgī, pauṣkara, durālabhā, bhārgī, kuṭaja seeds, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī—
this is the eighteen-ingredient (aṣṭādaśāṅga) formulation, which destroys sannipāta fever. (576)

A decoction of *bhūnimba*, *daru*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *mahauṣadha* (ginger), *abhda* (musta), *tikta* (kuṭaja), *indravīja* (indrayava), *dhanika* (dhānyaka), *ibha* (musta), and *kaṇā* (pippalī) removes cough, cardiac distress, pain in the flanks, dyspnea, hiccup, and vomiting.
This decoction destroys drowsiness, delirium, cough, anorexia, burning sensations, delusion, dyspnea, and fever born from the three humors (*tridoṣa*). 577–578.
In the Rasapradīpa, for the fever caused by the combination of humors (sannipātajvara), the nine ingredients are recorded as:
poison, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), sulphur, borax, killed copper, seeds of *dhattūra*, and cinnabar as the ninth. 579

These [ingredients] should be taken in equal parts and ground for one day with *vijayā* and *drava*. Then, pills the size of chickpeas should be made; these are to be eaten and followed by a decoction of the root of the sun-plant (*ravimūlaka*).

The medicine named Mṛtasañjīvanī is a destroyer of sannipāta fever. One part of pure mercury, one part of sulphur, and one part of purified copper should be ground together with three parts of cow’s milk in the intense heat of the sun. (581–582)
One should rub [the substance] for one day with *nirguṇḍī*, *śigru*, and *jadrava*;

having formed that into a ball, one should cook that ball inside a sealed crucible (*andhamūṣā*) for three watches (*triyāma*) in a *bālukāyantra*, and then grind it into a fine powder in a mortar (*khalva*).
One should add one-eighth part of poison there and grind it with that as well. This mercury known as Trinetraka should be administered in a dose of two guñjās,
together with a decoction of the five-kola group or with goat’s milk.

When this decoction is consumed, even a great fever caused by the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) quickly goes to destruction; there is no doubt that this should be performed. Ash derived from forest stones (araṇyopala) should weigh sixteen niṣkas.
One *niṣka* of black pepper and one *niṣka* of poison should be finely powdered.
This elixir, named Bhasmeśvara, is the ender of *sannipāta* fevers;
it should be consumed in a dose of one *guñjā*, with the juice of *ārdra* (Solanum nigrum).

Two *karṣas* of *sūtaka* (mercury) should be taken, and likewise two *karṣas* of sulphur; both should be diligently ground for one day with the juice of *haṃsapadī*. Having formed a pill from this paste, one should place it in a glass vessel.
Having thrown one *karṣa* of *amṛta* into it, one should seal the opening (590).
One should fill the other two parts of the crucible with sand and cook it there for half a day and night (591).
One *yāma* (three hours) of fire should be applied; when it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract [the substance].

One should then add half a *tola* of nectar (*amṛta*) there, as well as an equal amount of heat (*uṣaṇa*). When consumed in a dose of one *raktikā*, this elixir is indeed the "Son of Fire" (*Agnikumāraka*).

It destroys fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipātajvara), as well as disorders of wind (vāta), weak digestion (mandāgni), colic (śūla), malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), consumption (kṣaya), and diseases of the supraclavicular region; furthermore, it shall annihilate all ailments such as asthma and cough. 593–594.

Gandha, ṭaṅka, marica, and viṣa should be ground for a day with the juices of dhattūra and dried; this becomes the Pañcavaktra rasa. This should be administered in a dose of one raktikā with the juice of fresh ginger.

In a terrible fever caused by the simultaneous aggravation of all three humors (sannipāta-jvara), a remedy that destroys those specific doshas should be administered. A pill composed of two parts of *amṛtā*, five parts of *varāṭaka*, and nine parts of *marica*,
prepared in the size of a mung bean, removes phlegm, the three doshas, and impaired digestion.
One should properly prepare one niṣka each of mercury, sulphur, yellow orpiment, and realgar, along with two niṣkas and likewise four niṣkas and five niṣkas, using the juices of *kāravelī*. 598.
One should smear equal pieces of copper leaf with that paste; having placed them inside a closed crucible (śarāva-sampuṭa), one should apply that same paste over them as well,
and subsequently cook them by means of puṭapāka.
Then, having thus pulverized it, the mercury, when consumed with honey in a dose of one *yava*, certainly destroys even a severe *śītajvara*.
[The ingredients are] mercury (*pārada*), sulphur (*gandhaka*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), cinnabar (*darada*), and poison (*viṣa*).
One should add eight parts of viṣa, along with marica and viśvabheṣaja (602).
Then, one should grind these powders together with the juices of aśvagandhā, vijayā, kāsamarda, and kaṭhillaka— these four (603).
Taken in a dose of one *raktikā* along with the leaves of *tulasī*,
this medicine named Śītakeśarī destroys even a severe chronic fever (*śītajvara*). Equal parts of powdered *tālaka* (antimony) and *śuktikā* (mica) should be used therein.
The ninth part should be equal [to the other ingredients]; one should macerate it with the juice of *kanyākā* (Marsilea quadrifolia).
When that has dried, one should cook it in a "Gajapuṭa" using wild stones.
Once cooled, one should powder it and take a dose of half a *guñjā*, combined with sugar.
If one consumes this at dawn, chronic fever (śītajvara) goes to its destruction;
though vomiting may occur for some, it does not occur for others.
[The ingredients are] calamine, blue vitriol, copper, mercury, sulphur, and borax.
All of this powder should be ground together for one day with the juice and decoction of *kāravellī*; then, with that resulting liquid paste,
one should smear the interior of a copper vessel to a thickness of half a finger-breadth.
That should be cooked in a sand-bath (*vālukāyantra*) until the barley grains burst; once it has cooled, the physician should extract it from the interior of a copper vessel.
This *śītabhañjī* elixir, taken in a dose of one *māṣa* combined with black pepper, [is effective].

When consumed with *parṇakhaṇḍa*, it destroys intermittent fevers (611). Arsenic (*tālaka*), mercury produced from cinnabar (*darada*), mercury (*pārada*), sulfur (*gandhaka*), and realgar (*śilā*)— each subsequent ingredient reduced by half a part— should be rubbed with the juice of *kāravelī* (612).
With this measure, one should smear a copper vessel;
having placed it face down inside a sturdy container, one should then seal it and fill [the space] with sand. One should then ignite a fire beneath it on the hearth for a full day.

One *māṣa* of this [medicine], having been finely powdered and placed upon a betel leaf, when eaten together with black pepper, destroys all types of irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*), such as those characterized by coldness and burning heat;
the wholesome diet consists of *śāli* rice and milk. (614–615)
One should boil one karṣa each of kaṭphala, triphalā, dāru, candana, parūṣaka, kaṭukā, padmaka, and uśīra in water;
this drink, esteemed for its mere consumption, destroys the three doṣas as well as burning sensations and thirst. (616)
For those afflicted by long-standing fevers, this [remedy] would be like nectar;
but as for one suffering from the burning heat of *sannipāta*, if one were to sprinkle him with cold water, how could that patient survive, and how could he be called a physician? (617–618)

The physician should administer a prepared diet containing *duḥsparśā*, *gokṣura*, and *kṣudrā* for one suffering from a fever caused by the three *doṣas*, in order to pacify the *doṣas* and restore strength and digestive fire. One should consume parched grain flour (*lāja-saktu*) combined with rock salt (*saindhava*).
These [medicines] digest without obstacle; then the fever patient will certainly survive.
Because parched rice flour (lāja-saktu) is beneficial for blood-bile (rakta-pitta), it is not at all considered beneficial here in cases of thirst, burning sensations, and fever. (620–621)
Since parched grain gruel (lājamaṇḍa) is known to be digestive, appetizing, and sudorific,
it is beneficial when prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla) and other herbs for fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of the three humors (saṃnipātajvara).
As for one suffering from saṃnipātajvara who trembles and even raves, [it should be treated accordingly].
If he does not know even a little [of this], medical treatment is prescribed for him:
one should first anoint him with aged ghee, and then sprinkle him with oils such as those prepared from balā, rāsnā, guḍūcī, and others. 623–624.
The quail, the female quail, the partridge, the vārttika, the francolin, the hare, and the *kuliṅga*— one should satisfy the digestive fire with their meat according to its intensity.
In a case of *sannipāta* fever where hunger has seized the patient, one should feed him rice mixed with meat.

How can that lowest of men obtain the title of "physician"? Now, for the treatment of a fever characterized by a predominance of Vāta and a combination of all three humors (sannipāta), one should administer a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī) in a fever where Vāta is predominant.
Having observed the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas*, [one should administer] either very hot or pleasantly warm [medicines].
Now follows the treatment for *sannipāta* fever characterized by a predominance of *pitta*:
*parūṣaka*, *triphalā*, *devadāru*, and *kaṭphala*.
Sandalwood, padmaka, as well as kaṭukarohiṇī,
and pṛśniparṇī— water boiled with these and then allowed to cool is a treatment for the derangement of pitta and for *sannipāta* in men. (628–629)

One should drink the decoction of kirātatiktaka, musta, guḍūcī, viśvabheṣaja, pāṭhā, uśīra, and mṛṇāla when pitta is predominant. Now follows the treatment for sannipāta fever in which kapha is predominant.
The *bṛhatyādi* group consists of the two types of *bṛhatī*, *pauṣkara*, *bhārgī*, *śaṭī*, *śṛṅgī*, *durālabhā*,
the seeds of *vatsaka*, *paṭola*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*;
it is recommended for *sannipāta* disorders where *kapha* is predominant.
It is beneficial for all types of dyspnea and other such conditions, even when accompanied by complications (verse 632).
Now follows the treatment for fever caused by the combined aggravation of Vāta and Pitta (Sannipāta):
the minor Pañcamūla (the five roots) is a tonic that alleviates both Vāta and Pitta.
The decoction of these [drugs], taken with honey, destroys fever characterized by a predominance of Vāta and Pitta.
Kirātatiktaka, Musta, Guḍūcī, and Viśvabheṣaja are called Cāturbhadra; it is used in fever where Vāta and Pitta are predominant.
Now, the treatment for fever caused by the predominance of pitta, kapha, or their combination (sannipāta):
parpaṭa, kaṭphala, kuṣṭha, uśīra, candana, water,
nāgara, mustaka, śṛṅgī, and pippalī— this decoction of these [drugs] is beneficial.
In cases of thirst, burning sensations, and low digestive fire (agnimāndya), when fever is dominated by pitta and kapha;
furthermore, regarding the treatment for sannipāta fever dominated by vāta, pitta, and kapha:
ginger, coriander, bhārgī, padmaka, and red sandalwood.
Paṭola, picumanda, triphalā, madhuka, balā, śarkarā, kaṭukā, musta, gajāhvā, vyādhighātaka,
kirātatikta, amṛtā, daśamūlī, and nidigdhikā. (636–637)
This king of formulations (yogarāja) destroys a derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) where all three are aggravated; it conquers even death that has arrived, arising from such a derangement.
Now follows the treatment for fevers caused by the aggravation of the three humors (sannipātajvara), categorized as severe, moderate, and mild.

The physician should diminish an increased humor (doṣa) and increase one that is diminished; this is the method of treatment to be applied for humors that are either aggravated or deficient. When the aggravated humor has been pacified, the moderate humor indeed subsides of its own accord.
Just as an animal to be sacrificed finds peace when it has been led to its tranquility, so too does the patient find relief.

A decoction prepared with *jīraka*, *vyoṣa*, *bhārgī*, *vyāghrī*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *puṣkaramūla*— using cow’s urine as the medium and boiled until the essence is radiant— immediately destroys the pain of cold limbs, delusion, dyspnea, an excess of phlegm, and cough.
In this case, an ointment consisting of the powder of *karkoṭikā* root, horse gram (*kulattha*), black pepper, *vacā*, *kaṭphala*, black cumin,
*kirātatikta*, *analaka*, *kaṭphala*, water, and *pathyā* is recommended.
[642] Also, with the ashes of mercury, *viṣama*, *rasa*, *māheśa*, *priyaphala*, one, earth, four, and eight [parts].
This medicinal paste (uddhūlana), measured in specific proportions, removes excessive perspiration and coldness.
(643) Kṣudrā, amṛtā, pauṣkara, and nāgara, boiled together and drunk with sugar (śivā), [cure fever].
A nasal medication (nasya) consisting of śuṇṭhī, kaṇā, agasti-juice, and uṣaṇa overcomes severe drowsiness (tandrā). (644)
When applied to the eyes, they certainly ward off both lethargy and sleep.

(646) Sattagara, varatiktā, revata, ambhodatiktā, nalada, turagagandhā, bhāratī, hārahūrā, malayaja, daśamūlī, and śaṅkhapuṣpī—when well-cooked together, these, when drunk, will shortly eliminate delirium. (647)

One should bring his mind, which is deranged in every way, back to its natural state through consolations, pleasing treatments, sharp nasal medications (*nasya*), and the application of darkness (*timira*).
[This is achieved] with *rohiṣa*, *dhanvayavāsa*, *vāsā*, *parpaṭa*, *gandhalatā*, and *kaṭukā*.

This decoction taken with sugar is a rising remedy for one who spits blood from a wound. (649) Water boiled with lotus, sandalwood, *parpaṭa*, and *musta*, along with *jātīka*, *jīvaka*, sandalwood water, *klītaka*, and neem, when fully cooked, shall here be a remover of blood. (650)
A cold decoction of *madhuka*, *madhūka*, *parūṣaka*, *pāṭhā*, along with the sprouts and wood of *candana*,
and the fruit of *śrīparṇī*, taken with sugar, shall lead to the conquest of hemorrhaging.
[651] With *turaṅgagandhā*, *lavaṇā*, *ugragandhā*, the essence of *madhūka*, *uṣaṇa*, and *māgadhī*...
