An errhine (nasya) prepared with goat’s urine, ginger, and garlic makes one who is emaciated and has sunken eyes regain their health.
[652] [An oil or preparation made from] śṛṅgī, bhārgī, abhayā, ajājī, kaṇā, bhūnimba, parpaṭa, devadāru, vacā, kuṣṭha, yāsa, kaṭphala, and nāgara [is used for this purpose]. [653]
Musta, dhānyaka, tiktendrayava, yava, pāṭhā,
hareṇu, hastipippalī, apāmārga, pippalīmūla, citraka,
viśālā, āragvadha, ariṣṭa, śaṭī, and the fruits of vākucī. 654.
A decoction prepared from equal parts of viḍaṅga, rajanī, dārvī, and the two types of yavānī, combined with hiṅgu and the juice of ārdra,
instantly destroys even a terrible abhinyāsa fever and drowsiness.

This [compound], combined with *kirātatikta*, *ākulaka*, *kuliṅgī*, camphor, and long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), along with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), cures urinary disorders (*prameha*), earache, the thirteen types of *sannipāta* fevers, hiccup, dyspnea, cough, as well as all secondary complications. (657)
Sour gruel pacifies the defects of speech, just as the son of Daśaratha did here; likewise,
śālūraparṇī, mālūra, mūlāmayā, and madhu,
combined with śaṅkhakapuṣpī, should be consumed for the purification of speech.
One should conquer the tongue by drinking a decoction of *kṣudrā*, *nāgara*, *puṣkara*, *amṛtalatā*, *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *suvratā*, *bhārgī*, *vāsaka*, *yāsa*, *toya*, and *surasa*;
or one may prepare it with *viśvā*, *varmā*, *vibhāvarī*, *yugavarā*, *vatsādanī*, *vārida*, *vyāghrī*, *nimba*, *paṭola*, *puṣkaramūla*, *jaṭā*, and *dāru*. (660)
Drink [a decoction] of *śaṭī*, the best of *surataru* trees, *asthaviradāru*, and *rāsnā*, equal parts combined with *nāgara*, *sudhā*, and *śatāvarī*,
cooked over a gentle fire along with *pura* (guggulu), for the relief of *sandhigraha*.

Do not undergo the useless practice of seeking relief through cold applications to remove your pain. (661) Vaca, kavaka, kacchurā, sahacara, amṛtā, bhaṅgurā, surāhvaya, ghana, nāgara, taruṇa, dāru, rāsnā, and purā—these, when combined with vṛṣā, taruṇa, and bhīru, form a compound that destroys joint-pain, stiffness, lassitude, vertigo, and hemiplegia. (662)
Suradāru, śaṭī, sudhā-latā, suvahā, śuṇṭhī, amṛtā, and purā, boiled together in water and consumed constantly, pacify *sadāgati* (asthma) located in the joints.
Mustā, eraṇḍa, prāṇadā, bāṇa, dāru, chinnā, rāsnā, bhīru, karcūra, and tiktā [likewise act as a remedy].

Vāsā, viśvā, pañcamūla, and aśvagandhā destroy manyāstambha, joint stiffness, and the pains of rheumatic seizures. Here, setting aside your vows, drink hot water and the fever-destroying soups and decoctions that remove disease;
constantly contemplate in your mind the conqueror of death (Mṛtyuñjaya), which cuts through fever and grants life.

Praise Him whose body is as white as a mass of camphor, who wears the *saṃyogamudrā*, who eternally cherishes His devotees, whose eye flashes upon His forehead, whose hand holds a vessel filled with the fullness of nectar, who bears a bright rosary, who is beautiful with a mass of high, tawny matted locks, and who has the crescent moon as His crest-ornament— He who has been determined by physicians to be the "Destroyer" (*Antaka*) in cases of *sannipāta* fever. 666.
The water of the Jāhnavī is indeed the medicine, and Govinda himself is the physician.
(667) One should administer water boiled with uśīra, candana, udīcya, drākṣā, āmalaka, and parpaṭa, and then cooled, for the alleviation of burning sensations, thirst, and fever. (668)
A decoction of *dhānyāka* and *taṇḍulaka* (rice) kept overnight and mixed with sugar, when drunk in the morning,
quickly pacifies internal burning and *paittika* fever.
One should lick *pathyā* (harītakī) combined with oil, ghee, and honey to destroy the burning sensation.
An application of jujube leaves mixed with curd quickly pacifies the burning sensation;
or alternatively, an application of sandalwood and neem leaves ground with buttermilk [is effective].
Furthermore, for one lying on their back, the navel should be placed over a deep vessel made of bronze or similar metal.
A profuse stream of cold water falling down quickly destroys burning sensations and fever.

Having smeared one suffering from fever with burning sensations with cow's ghee mixed with sandalwood and stirred a hundred times with cold water, and wearing garlands of lotuses and blue lilies, he shall quickly enter the water-chamber for a long time.
Wrapping [the patient] in a cloth moistened with sour gruel (kāñjika) destroys burning sensations.
Then, one who is afflicted by burning and fainting, emaciated, deprived of food, and possessed by thirst, should be treated with a cloth that has been steamed in cow's buttermilk and then cooled.
One should drink parched grain porridge mixed with sugar and honey. Furthermore,
lotus-bedecked ponds, auspicious water-machines (fountains),
and women whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste are considered removers of burning heat and dejection.

The embraces of broad-hipped women, who are cool as pearl necklaces and sandalwood and adorned with fragrant flowers, garments, and ornaments, and who possess beautiful breasts, quickly remove his burning heat.
Having perceived his refreshment, he should then have those women removed.
One should eat wholesome food by which one attains great happiness.

(678) [The following ingredients]—mustard, black pepper, pungent substances, excellent salt, *karañja* seeds, the impurities of women, *pathyā*, *akṣa*, white mustard, asafoetida, and ginger—mixed with goat’s urine [are used for this purpose]. (679)

Having ground these together, this pill should be applied to the eyes; it is renowned for restoring consciousness and is endowed with beneficial properties as the cause for destroying mental confusion, epilepsy, demonic afflictions, headaches, eye diseases, and vertigo. (680) [Take] lotus from the pitcher-born tree (the *udumbara*), jaggery, and *viśva* along with *kaṇā*.
Surely, if applied to the nose, it would destroy mental delusion— [a preparation] made from *mura*, *mūrdhaja*, *megha*, *madhūka*, and *malaya* flowers,
mixed with the honey of the *marutta* tree and the dust from the city-dweller’s fingernails. 681–682.
Incense made from *loha*, *lāmajjaka*, and *elā* removes mental confusion,
wards off the evil influence of planetary afflictions (*graha-doṣa*), bestows prosperity, and is the supreme means for bringing about good fortune.
(683) *Mṛdvīkā*, *amaradāru*, *matsyaśakala*, *mustā*, *āmalakī*, and *amṛtā*...

Haritaki combined with aravata, rāmasena, karaja, and rājīphala destroy diseases of the mind; furthermore, the decoction of dāruharidrā, pāṭhā, paṭolī, haritaki, parpaṭa, rājavṛkṣa, kaṭukā, and śambūkapuṣpī, when boiled together, [achieve the same]. 684.

A single application of this paste brings even a small amount of residual blood to an end, while combined it overcomes swelling; once the abscess has ripened, surgical intervention is appropriate, and that treatment is fit for when it has reached the state of an ulcer. (685) A paste made from niśā, viśālā, amaya, maṇimanthā, dārvī, and the root of iṅgudī [is likewise effective].
Prabhākara combined with milk, whether applied separately or all together, destroys the *karṇika* [ear-ache] by its power. Alternatively, equal parts of *kulattha*, *kaṭphala*, *śuṇṭhī*,
and *kāravī* should be used as a lukewarm plaster repeatedly at the base of the ear.
A plaster made of equal parts of red ochre, chalk, ginger, and the fruits of *kaṭphala* and *āragvadha*, ground together with warm *kāñjika*, destroys pain at the root of the ear (688).
One should apply a paste of *śigru* and black mustard to the base of the ear.

A swelling arising at the root of the ear is pacified by that ointment. Indeed, black pepper, *kaṇā* (long pepper), cumin, and rock salt, when rubbed with non-cold water and administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*), is said to quickly destroy pain in the ears and head. 689–690.

A decoction prepared with bhārgī, jayā, pauṣkara, kaṇṭakārī, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), ugrā, ghanā, kuṇḍalī, kulīraśṛṅgī, kaṭukā, and rasā is indeed a destroyer of ear-worms (*karṇika*). [Likewise, a decoction] made from the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *matsyaśakala*, *capalā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *mahauṣadha*, and *kirāta*— 691. [The verse continues: ...with these [ingredients], [a decoction is prepared]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)
Black pepper, when quickly boiled, forcibly overcomes all earaches. A decoction prepared with the three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (trikaṭu), musta, kaṭvī, kaliṅga, siṃhānana,
and śarvarī cuts through a goiter in the throat just as a lion swiftly destroys an elephant.
This group of medicinal herbs— consisting of *kirāta*, *kaṭukā*, *kaṇā*, *kuṭaja*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *śaṭī*,
*kalidru*, *kilima*, *abhayā*, *kaṭuka*, *kaṭphala*, and *ambhodhara*;
along with *viṣā*, *āmalaka*, *puṣkara*, *anala*, *kulīra*, *śṛṅgī*, and *vṛṣa*— together with the great medicine *mahauṣadha*, triumphs over throat-obstruction (*kaṇṭhakubja*).
Exogenous fever arises from injury, contagion, malevolent incantations, or curses; one should identify it according to its specific cause among the humors.
It may also arise from spirits, poison, wind, fire, wounds, fractures, and the like.
Furthermore, those adventitious diseases arise from passion, hatred, fear, and so forth.

Through lust, grief, and fear, the wind (vāyu) is provoked; through anger, the bile (pitta); and through possession by spirits, the three humors (malas) are disturbed, manifesting the common symptoms of such entities.
In poisoning by [animal] venom (viṣakṛta), there is a darkening of the face, as well as diarrhea,
aversion to food, thirst, piercing pain, and fainting.
In poisoning by the smell of medicinal herbs (oṣadhīgandhaja), there is fainting, headache, and vomiting.

From desire arises a derangement of the mind, characterized by drowsiness, laziness, loss of appetite, and pain in the heart; his body becomes parched, and there is fainting, bodily aches, and restlessness of the eyes, breasts, and face. (699)
In women suffering from fever of passion (kāmajvara), there may be perspiration and a burning sensation in the heart.
A decoction of bālaka, śatapatra, gandhasāra, uśīraka,
coca, dhānyeyaka, and māṃsī removes fever of passion.

At twilight, a bed should be prepared profusely with fragrant flowers; likewise, at night, a woman should enjoy herself with her beloved. (702) Out of fear there may be lamentation, and out of grief or anger there may be trembling. (703)
Agitation, laughter, weeping, and trembling arise from possession by spirits;
some declare such irregular fever to be caused by spirit-possession (bhūtābhiṣaṅga). Delusion and thirst are produced by malevolent magic (abhicāra) and curses (abhiśāpa).
A person suffering from an exogenous fever (āgantuja-jvara) should not undergo fasting (laṅghana).
Fasting is not beneficial in fevers born of desire, grief, anxiety, or loss; nor in a fever produced by fear, spirits, physical exertion, or anger.
However, when the digestive fire has been kindled there, one should administer meat-soup with rice;
in the case of fever caused by trauma (abhighāta-jvara), one should employ treatments devoid of heat,
as well as decoctions that are sweet and unctuous, according to the specific dosha involved.
Fever caused by trauma (abhighātajvara) is destroyed by the drinking and external application of clarified butter (sarpiḥ),
as well as by bloodletting, purifying treatments, and the consumption of meat broth with rice.
[This applies to fevers] arising from piercing, binding, exhaustion, excessive travel, breaking a fall, or falling down.
One should first treat fevers with milk, meat broth, and rice;
for those exhausted by travel, one should administer oil massage and induce sleep during the day.
Fevers caused by the smell of medicinal herbs or by poisons should be treated with remedies that subdue poison and pitta.
The wise physician should conquer [the afflictions] with all-fragrance preparations made from decoctions.
One should specify "all-fragrance" as consisting of the four products of the *jātaka* tree (*cāturjātaka*), camphor, *kaṅkola*, agallochum, saffron, and cloves.

In cases born of anger, one should employ remedies that conquer bile (pitta) and maintain virtuous speech; furthermore, the fevers of lust, anger, and fear are pacified through consolation, the attainment of desired objects, the alleviation of wind (vāyu), and acts of gladdening. 713

Fever arising from anger is pacified by means of objects that satisfy desire, treatments that alleviate bile (pitta), and well-spoken words. Fever born of anger is destroyed by desire, and likewise, fever born of desire is destroyed by anger.

By destroying both [lust and anger], one brings about the subsiding of the fever of desire and wrath. One should overcome the mental affliction arising from possession by spirits through the binding, entry, and striking prescribed in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā), and the mind itself through tranquility.
The root of *sahadevā*, tied around the neck according to the prescribed rite, removes the fever caused by malevolent spirits (*bhūta*) in men within one, two, three, or four days.
One should conquer fevers arising from sorcery (*abhicāra*) or curses (*abhiśāpa*) through fire-oblations (*homa*) and other such rites.
Through acts of charity, auspicious rites, and hospitality, one may overcome fevers arising from portents or the malevolence of planets.
(718) Thus ends the section on exogenous fevers;
[now follows] the fever where the humors are slight, arising from unwholesome conduct, or that which recurs in one who has previously been released from fever.
Having reached one of the bodily elements (dhātu), it produces irregular fever (viṣamajvara).

When the humors (doṣa) are provoked, they cause continuous fever when located in the lymph-chyle (rasa), constant fever when situated in the blood-element (rakta), and fever on alternate days (anyedyuḥ) when residing in the flesh (piśita). 719–720.
When it has reached the flesh on the third day, and having reached the bone and marrow again,
it produces the terrible quartan fever, a mixture of diseases that brings about death;
this occurs at irregular times and likewise through cold and heat.
Furthermore, that fever which is irregular in its onset is known as *viṣama* (irregular).
It is classified as *santata* (continuous), *satata* (daily), *anyedyus* (tertian), *tṛtīyaka* (quartan), or *caturthaka* (quaternian);
it may last for seven days, ten days, or even twelve days.
That which continues in an uninterrupted stream without cessation is called *santata* (continuous).
The *satataka* fever recurs at two times during the day and night. The *anyedyuṣka* fever, however, manifests at one time per day and night.
The *satataka* (daily) fever occurs on the first day, the *anyedyuṣka* (quotidian) on the second, the *tṛtīyaka* (tertian) on the third day, and the *caturthaka* (quartan) on the fourth day;
indeed, according to the division of the seats of *kapha*,
these produce the *satataka*, *anyedyuṣka*, *tṛtīyaka*, and *caturthaka* fevers respectively.
Day by day, from one location to another,
the *doṣa* reaches the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and produces irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*). Having subsided, it returns again on the fixed day, being irregular in its onset.
In this regard, the best of sages consider intrinsic nature (svabhāva) to be the cause.
Just as a seed sown upon the earth sprouts in due time,
so too does a disorder (doṣa), having resided within the bodily constituents (dhātu), become aggravated in its own time.
And that [wind], being unbalanced, never leaves the body, because one is not freed from its languor, heaviness, and emaciation; yet,
once its impulse has passed, it is perceived as having gone away.
Because it is dissolved within other bodily constituents (dhātu) and due to its subtlety, it is not perceived at all.

The tertian fever (tṛtīyaka) is of three types: that which seizes the sacrum (trika) arises from phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta); that which seizes the back consists of wind (vāta) and phlegm; and that which seizes the head arises from wind and bile. 732–733.
The quartan fever manifests its nature in two ways:
that arising from phlegm (ślaiṣmika) first affects the two shanks, while that born of wind (vātaja) first affects the head;
that which first seizes the middle part of the body is born of bile (pittaja).
The "reverse quartan" (caturthaka-viparyaya) is indeed another type of irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
When the morbid humor (doṣa) located in the bones and marrow produces the reverse quartan,
it should be known by physicians as that very same irregular fever.

It causes fever in the middle of the day and releases it at the beginning and the end. When kapha and vata are located in the skin, they first produce coldness in the fever; once those two have subsided, pitta produces internal burning heat.
First, the pitta located in the skin produces an excessive burning sensation;
once that has subsided, the other two [doṣas] subsequently produce cold.
These two types of fever, characterized by the onset of burning and cold, are known as those born from the combination [of doṣas].

Of these two, the one preceded by burning is difficult to treat, while the other is most easily cured. When the essence of food has been digested and the phlegm and bile are situated within the body, half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot.
When the bile (pitta) is deranged in the body and the phlegm (śleṣman) is situated at the extremities,
there is heat in the body and coldness in the hands and feet. When the phlegm is deranged in the body and the bile is situated at the extremities, [the opposite occurs].
By that [fever], there would be coldness in the body and heat in the hands and feet;
as if smearing the limbs with heat and heaviness, and being smeared by a mild fever, he is the *pralepaka* (the "smearing" type), which is characterized by coldness.
All irregular fevers (viṣama-jvara) arise from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta);

in these cases, the medical treatment should be administered according to whichever humor is most predominant. Even in irregular fevers, purification (śodhana) by means of emesis and purgation should be performed.
One should pacify irregular fever (viṣamajvara) with unctuous and warm foods and drinks. Kāliṅgaka, the leaf of paṭola, kaṭukarohiṇī,
paṭola, sārivā, musta, pāṭhā, and kaṭukarohiṇī [are used for this purpose].
Nimba, paṭola, triphalā, mṛdvīkā, musta, vatsaka, kirātatikta, amṛtā, candana, and viśvabheṣaja (748);
guḍūcī, āmalaka, and musta— these are the groups completed by half-verses.

The five astringent decoctions quickly pacify the five types of fever. Indeed, a decoction prepared from the roots of Mahābalā and Mahauṣadha destroys irregular fever; through its application for two or three days, it eliminates fever accompanied by chills, tremors, and burning sensations. (749–750)
A decoction of mustā, āmalaka, guḍūcī, viśvauṣadha, and kaṇṭakārikā,
drunk with powdered kaṇā and honey, destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
A paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil and salt, consumed in the morning, [achieves the same].

It removes the fever caused by poison and all disorders of wind (vāta). 752. Kālājājī taken with jaggery destroys irregular fevers; likewise, Abhayā licked with honey quickly kills irregular fevers. 753.
The juice of *tulasī* leaves mixed with black pepper powder,
or the juice of *droṇapuṣpī*, when drunk, destroys irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
Black cumin (*jīraka*) mixed with an equal amount of jaggery and a little black pepper, when consumed, [cures] immediately.
One should pacify it in a single day, just as Indra subdues the Dānavas in battles.
(755) Ginger, cumin, and jaggery ground together and drunk with warm water, or with buttermilk after consuming alcohol, will conquer even a severe cold fever. (756)
Now, the general treatment for continuous (*santata*) and other types of fevers:
one hundred parts of powdered *amṛtā* (guḍūcī) strained through a cloth, along with sixteen separate parts each of jaggery, honey, and clarified butter. (757)
Just as fire might consume this [mercury], so too a man who eats it while observing a wholesome and moderate diet will suffer no disease whatsoever, nor will he experience old age or graying hair;
there shall be no fevers, no irregular fevers, no delusion, and no blood-anemia caused by wind.
Furthermore, this is the supreme elixir for diseases of the eyes;
by its use, the wise man becomes endowed with intelligence, destroys the three *doṣas*,
and shall live for more than a hundred years, just like the son of Aditi.
One who consumes buttermilk with meat, milk with meat, curd with meat, or even black gram with meat is liberated from irregular fever; thus it was stated by Agniveśa.
761. Agniveśa said:
Surā with its scum (maṇḍa) for drinking, and for food,
the peacock, partridge, and other scattering birds (viṣkira), as well as the cock, are wholesome in cases of intermittent fever (viṣamajvara).
Water boiled with trāyamāṇā, kaṭukā, anantā, and sārivā [is also beneficial].

Water boiled with *paṭola*, *abda*, *vṛṣa*, *tiktā*, and *sārivā* should be administered in the fever known as *santata* for the alleviation of the [disturbances of] wind (*vāta*) and the other humors.
Water boiled with *paṭola*, *indrayava*, *anantā*, *pathyā*, *ariṣṭa*, and *amṛtā* [is likewise beneficial].
That water, once boiled, when drunk, conquers *satataka* (continuous) fever.
A person should quickly drink water boiled with *drākṣā*, *paṭola*, *nimba*, *musta*, *indrayava*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) for the swift pacification of *anyedyus* (quotidian) fever.
One should avoid common [contagious] diseases; the physician should treat the tertian and quartan fevers with specific prescribed therapies.
[The remedies are: uśīra, candana, musta, guḍūcī, dhānya, and nāgara.

Water boiled with [the aforementioned herbs] and mixed with sugar and honey should be drunk by men suffering from tertian fever accompanied by thirst and burning sensations. One should tie the root of *apāmārga* around the waist with seven red threads.
Bound on a Sunday, it quickly destroys tertian fever (769).
A decoction of sthirā, āmalakī, dāru, śivā, vṛṣa, and mahauṣadha,
combined with sugar and honey, is a supreme remedy for quartan fever (770).
An errhine (nasya) prepared from the juice of *agasti* leaves destroys quartan fever of fierce potency;
or alternatively, [it may be prepared] with a paste of *śirīṣa* flowers and the two types of *niśā* mixed with ghee.
As for one who suffers from fever while contemplating the timing of its paroxysms, [this remedy should be applied].

One should destroy that fever—whether it be continuous (*santata*), irregular (*viṣama*), constant (*satata*), or long-standing—by means of desired, wonderful, or even harsh treatments; furthermore, one should treat it with wholesome, beneficial, and pleasing foods. (772–773)
One should administer cooling treatments to a person overcome by cold,
but when overcome by burning heat, one should apply measures that destroy that heat.
[One should cover the patient] with many heavy coverings such as woolen blankets and the like.

One should remove great cold with cotton wool for those suffering from fever caused by cold and other factors. A young woman with full breasts, thick thighs, and broad hips should embrace him firmly; by that means, the cold is pacified.
When the cold produced by contact with the beloved’s body has been similarly dispelled, and having perceived his exhilaration, one should have that woman separated from him.
Then, when a burning sensation arises, [one should apply] leaves derived from the castor plant (eraṇḍa).
One should remove his burning sensation by applying cool substances held against the body.
To both of these [tālaka and śuktikā], one should add a ninth part of tuttha; having added these, one should grind them with the juices of kanyākā.
When that has dried, one should cook it with wild stones in a *gajapuṭa* fire;
once cooled, one should powder it. Taking a dose of one *guñjā* of this powder mixed with sugar at dawn, the chronic fever (*śītajvara*) is brought to an end.
Vomiting may occur for some, while for others it does not at all.
On the very same day, Śikhariṇī rice is most excellent for removing cold fever; it should be eaten as wholesome food at the time of midday.

Oil cooked with *kāyasthā*, *nākulī*, *tiktā*, *vayaḥsthā*, *pura*, *coraka*, *sahadevā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śītaghna*— along with sour substances— and used for massage (*abhyaṅga*), destroys coldness. (783–784)
One should place castor leaves on ground that has been smeared with [cow dung];
one suffering from fever accompanied by burning sensations and other symptoms should apply those leaves to the body.
By this, his burning sensation is destroyed and the fever is pacified.
When the burning has subsided, one should not by any means dispel that coolness;
for a woman afflicted by intense fever should envelop her body like a forest creeper—adorned with a jeweled girdle moving upon her hips and anointed with fresh sandalwood and moon-cream. (786–787)
When the burning has been relieved by the coolness produced from contact with her body,
and having recognized his relief, one should again remove that woman;
[then apply] Suvarcikā, Nāgara, Kuṣṭha, Mūrvā, Lākṣā, Niśā, and red Yaṣṭikā.
This oil, prepared by boiling with six times the amount of buttermilk, cures fever accompanied by burning sensations.
[It is prepared] with rāsnā, nāgara, kuṣṭha, candana, niśā, yaṣṭyāhva, kṛṣṇā, balā,
lākṣā, saindhava, sārivā, madhurasā, devāhva, and rohitaka.
One should cook oil with water from the Sośīra ocean, phenarohiṣa, and lotus stalks, along with six times its quantity of buttermilk;
this will conquer even the most stubborn fever, including burning sensations, coldness, and other such symptoms.
[One may also use] padmaka, utpala, kahlāra, mṛṇāla, bisa, and pauṣkara.
With *kumuda*, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *padmaka*, *gerika*, and *kaṭphala* (791),
along with the two types of *sārivā*, *lodhra*, *āhvā*, *kṣīrī*, the tops of *kharjūra* fruits,
and *dhātrī* and *śatāvarī*— these being employed as both a decoction and a paste (792).
This oil, cooked with lac-juice, milk, fermented gruel (śukta), whey (mastu), and sour gruel (kāñjika), is beneficial for the skin and is a supreme remedy for burning sensations and fever.
One should employ the treatment that removes phlegm-fever as an external application.
Rudrākṣa, matted hair, a cow’s horn, cat excrement, snake slough,
madana fruit, bhūtakeśī, bamboo bark, rudrākṣa remains from an offering, ghee, barley, peacock feathers, goat hair, and white mustard seeds along with vacā. 795.
Equal parts of asafoetida, cow bone, and black pepper, ground with goat urine,
certainly pacify all fevers by means of the fumigation method; this incense also [subdues] the disorders caused by grahas, dākinīs, piśācas, and pretas.
By worshipping with self-restraint the god Soma, together with his attendants, his mother-gaṇas, and the Lord (Īśvara), one is quickly liberated from chronic fever. [Likewise,
by worshipping] Viṣṇu, the thousand-headed, the all-pervading Lord of the moving and unmoving worlds.

By praising [the Lord] with the Thousand Names, one dispels all fevers. (799) Through visiting sacred fords, shrines, deities, fire, gurus, and elders, and by means of worship performed with faith, fever is also suddenly pacified. (800)
Thus ends the section on irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
When the fever is located in the rasa-dhātu, the symptoms that arise are heaviness, agitation of the heart, lassitude, vomiting, anorexia, and dejection. (801)
When that fever is located in the rasa-dhatu (plasma), one should administer emesis and fasting.
When the fever has reached the rakta-dhatu (blood) in men, there occurs spitting of blood, burning sensation, delusion, confusion from vomiting, delirium, pustules, and thirst. (802–803)
In fever located in the blood (raktaja), there is sprinkling (sekah), soothing applications (saṃśamanaḥ), and ointments (lepaḥ), as well as bloodletting (raktamokṣaḥ).

When the fever is located in the flesh (māṃsagaḥ), there is swelling of the limbs (piṇḍaka-udveṣṭanam), thirst (tṛṣṇā), discharge of urine and feces (mūtra-purīṣa-sṛṣṭatā), internal heat (ūṣmā), a burning sensation within (antardāhaḥ), restlessness (vikṣepaḥ), and exhaustion (glāniḥ). (804–805)
In fever located in the muscle tissue (māṃsa), one should likewise administer a strong purgative.
When the fever resides in the fat tissue (medas), there is excessive sweating, thirst, fainting, delirium, vomiting, foul odor, anorexia, exhaustion, and intolerance. (806–807)
If the fever is located in the fat (medas), the physician should effect its destruction from the fat.
One should recognize that when the fever has reached the bones (asthi), there is a breaking pain in the bones, creaking sounds, dyspnea, purging, vomiting, and a tossing about of the limbs. (808–809)
When fever resides in the bones, one should employ measures that destroy Vāta; likewise, enema therapy (vasti-karma), as well as oil massage and rubbing, should be applied.
Darkness before the eyes, hiccup, cough, coldness, and vomiting [occur when it resides in the marrow]. 810.
When the fever has reached the marrow, there is internal burning, labored breathing, and a cutting pain in the vital organs (marmans);
in that state, death may ensue. When the fever has reached the seat of the semen, there is stiffness of the penis and, specifically, the discharge of semen.
Thus ends the section on fevers arising from the seven *dhātus*. Now begins the section on chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*):
that which occurs after twelve days, and after the three *doṣas* have doubled.

When this fever remains in the body of men with a slow onset, it is called "chronic" (jīrṇa) by physicians. A man who constantly suffers from a mild fever, is emaciated, swollen, and has stiff limbs, and who is difficult to cure, is one in whom *vāta-balāsaka* (asthma-cough) predominates due to an excess of *śleṣman*.
A person suffering from chronic fever should never observe a fast;
for by fasting, he would become emaciated while the fever itself becomes more powerful,
especially since even in a chronic fever, the humors (doṣas) may be aggravated again by unwholesome things.
After that, one should leap over [the fever]; thereafter, one should perform the aforementioned treatment.

One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *āgaraka*, and *amṛtā* mixed with *pippalī*, in cases of chronic fever, anorexia, cough, colic, dyspnea, weak digestion, facial paralysis, and coryza. (815–816)

A decoction of *Chinnodbhava* (Guḍūcī) combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey generally destroys diseases arising from the upper part of the body; it is used in the evening. Alternatively, a decoction prepared from the five roots (*pañcamūla*) destroys chronic fever and phlegm.
The decoction of *amṛtā* (gudūcī), prepared cold and mixed with honey and other [sweeteners], when drunk, is said to be an excellent remedy for chronic fever;
one should drink the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* mixed with *pippalī* and honey.
It destroys chronic fever, phlegm, splenic enlargement, cough, and loss of appetite (818).
Guḍapippalī is recommended for chronic fever and weak digestion;
it also cures cough, indigestion, anorexia, asthma, heart disease, anemia, and worm infestations.
In this formulation, the physicians consider the jaggery to be double the amount of the pippalī powder.
Pippalī combined with honey destroys fat and phlegm;
it removes dyspnea, cough, and fever, and cures anemia, splenic enlargement, and abdominal dropsy.
Āmalaka, citraka, pathyā, pippalī, and likewise saindhava—
this group, known as a powder, is the supreme remedy for all fevers; it is a purgative, an appetizer, a destroyer of phlegm, and a digestive stimulant and carminative.
Drākṣā, amṛtā, śaṭī, śṛṅgī, mustaka, raktacandana,
nāgara, kaṭukā, pāṭhā, bhūnimba along with durālabhā,
uśīra, dhānyaka, padma, bālaka, and kaṇṭakārikā. (823)
Puṣkara and picumanda constitute this eighteen-ingredient formulation,
which is known to destroy chronic fever, anorexia, dyspnea, cough, and edema.
It may be prepared with an increase of three, five, or even seven units [of each ingredient].

One should indeed drink these ground with cow's milk for ten days; likewise, one should eliminate them over twenty days. For those drinking in this manner, there shall be relief from fever and the disease of jaundice (pāṇḍuroga) will be pacified.

Cough, dyspnea, impaired digestion, and an excess of phlegm are destroyed. The treatment prescribed for fever caused by vāta and kapha should be applied in vātabalāsaka, as well as in chronic fever (jīrṇajvara) when the phlegm is diminished and accompanied by burning sensations and thirst. 827–828.
Milk is like nectar, but when fresh it is like poison;
oils such as *candana* and others are beneficial, as described in the section on emaciation (*śoṣa*).
Likewise, *nārāyaṇa-taila* is the supreme remedy for chronic fever. 829
Thus ends the section on chronic fever (jīrṇajvara).
One should always consume the powder of these—harītakī, nimba leaves, ginger (nāgara), rock salt (saindhava), and citraka (anala)—for the pacification of fever caused by contaminated water. 830

A decoction prepared with one pala of dried ginger and honey quickly destroys loss of appetite, weakness of the digestive fire, catarrh, dyspnea, cough, abdominal diseases, and all disorders caused by water; it produces bodily luster and clarity of mind and eyes. (831) Two parts of burnt poison and five parts of burnt cowrie shells [should be used].
One should clean the powder of black pepper and dry ginger with a cloth; then, using the juice of fresh ginger, one should form pills resembling mung beans.
One should consume two pills with water in the morning and again in the evening. (832–833)

This decoction should be administered in cases of fever associated with undigested matter (āmaja), as well as that caused by contaminated water; it is also indicated for indigestion, flatulence, constipation, colic, asthma, and cough.
[The ingredients are: *paṭola*, *mustā*, *amṛtavallī*, *vāsaka*, ginger (*nāgara*), coriander (*dhānya*), and *kirātatiktaka*. (834)
A person should drink the decoction of these [drugs] with honey to ward off the violent affliction caused by contaminated water.

(835) The powder of kirātatikta, triphalā, ambu, pippalī, viḍaṅga, viśvā, and kaṭurohiṇī, when licked with honey, very quickly destroys even the most difficult fever born from the defects of contaminated water. (836)
If people eat at the beginning of their meal a paste made from ginger, cumin, and *abhayā*,
and regularly consume water originating from various regions along with *sahā*, *ārdraka*, and *kṣāra* (alkali), while drinking it with lukewarm water, [they will be cured]. 837.
It dispels the various defects of the water arising from different regions. (838) Fever that is strong but has few complications is curable;
[its complications include] dyspnea, fainting, anorexia, vomiting, thirst, diarrhea, and constipation. (839)
Hiccups, cough, aching limbs, and burning sensations—these are the ten complications (upadrava) of fever.
A disease that has developed complications should not be abandoned by physicians;
for when the primary disease is pacified, all the complications are immediately destroyed.
Therefore, a physician who is skilled in this matter should first conquer the disease with effort and afterwards the complications; however,
even among those complications, he should first eliminate those that act most rapidly when they are prevalent.

One should first conquer the primary disease, or whichever one is more powerful; the treatment for both should be carried out without conflict. (843) Siṃhī, vyāghrī, tāmramūlī, paṭolī, śṛṅgī, padmā, puṣkara, and rohiṇī.
Śāka, the seed of śaṭhyā and śailamallī, and [the other ingredients] constitute the ten-ingredient formulation (daśāṅga) which destroys dyspnea and sannipāta fever.
[844] Bhārgī, nimba, ghana, abhayā, amṛtalatā, bhūnimba, vāsā, viṣā, trāyantī, kaṭukā, vacā, trikaṭu, śyonāka, and śakradruma;
[845] rāsnā, yāsa, paṭola, pāṭala, śaṭī, dārvī, viśālā, trivṛt, brāhmī, puṣkara, siṃhikā, the two types of niśā, dhātrī, yakṣa, and devadruma.
This decoction indeed conquers, by its own power upon drinking, the thirty-two formidable types of *sannipāta* fevers— just as Garuḍa overcomes serpents—
and furthermore, it subdues asthma, phlegm, cough, anal pain, heart disease, hiccups, and wind disorders.
Even those afflicted by stiffness of the neck, diseases of the throat, indigestion,
and hernia, as well as those suffering from severe respiratory ailments, become happy after licking a powder made from *kṛṣṇā*, *kaṭphala*, and *karkaṭaśṛṅgī* with honey. (846–847)

The application of a heated blade—warmed over a forest stone or fire—to the front of the cage [of the nose] undoubtedly removes the disease of dyspnea; so it has been declared by the sages. (848) In cases of fainting, a person should administer nasal drops (*nasya*) using the juices of *ārdra* plants.
One should apply collyrium made from honey, rock salt, and long pepper;
there should be irrigation of the eyes with cold water, fragrant incense, scented flowers,
the breeze from a soft palm-leaf fan, and the touch of tender plantain leaves.
In case of loss of appetite, a gargle made of ginger and *jarasaka* with rock salt and warm water should be used;
likewise, holding rock salt, the seeds of *mātuluṅgī*, and saffron in the mouth [is beneficial].
A well-cooled decoction of *guḍūcī* mixed with honey, when drunk, brings about the cessation of vomiting.

A plaster made of honey, beeswax, sandalwood, and sugar, or else with *dantaśaṭha*, *bījapūraka*, pomegranate, and *badara* fruits mixed with *cukra*, applied to the mouth, overcomes thirst; furthermore, a silver pill placed inside the mouth has the same effect. (852–853)
Cold milk mixed with honey, when drunk to the throat, will cause one to vomit it up immediately;

it surely pacifies great thirst. Alternatively, holding honey, sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, and parched grain in the mouth [achieves the same]. For a strong person, there is no other remedy here than fasting alone.

It pacifies and even ripens the accumulated mass of aggravated humors (doṣas). Vatsādanī, vatsaka, vārivāha, viśvambharā, nimba, and viṣa, along with viśvā, quickly conquer fever and diarrhea; likewise, viśvā, amṛtā, vatsaka, and vārivāha [conquer them]. 855–856.
By boiling and drinking *pāṭhā*, *amṛtā*, *parpaṭa*, *mustā*, *viśva*, *kirātatikta*, and *indrayava*,

one forcibly overcomes all fevers and even those dysenteries that are difficult to cure (857). In cases of constipation, one should perform actions that overcome *vāta* and promote the downward movement of the bowels.
One should quickly induce purgation with sharp medicinal suppositories made from fruits (858).

Water boiled with *pathyā*, *āragvadha*, *tikta*, *trivṛt*, and *āmalaka* should be administered in chronic fever accompanied by constipation; thereby the retention of feces will be pacified, just as when a horse is relieved of its obstruction. (859)
Very fine sea-salt dust mixed with water, when administered as nasal drops (nasya), certainly destroys hiccup;
likewise, dry ginger combined with sugar, or incense derived from asafoetida, may be used by force [as a snuff].
In cases of cough, long pepper, the root of long pepper, and the powder of the fruit of the Kaliṅga tree [are effective].
One should lick Viśvabheṣaja with honey, or likewise Vṛṣādrasa (861). This electuary,
made from Puṣkaramūla, Kaṭutrika, Śṛṅgī, Kaṭphala, Yāsaka, and Kāravī,
mixed with honey, is indeed the enemy of cough and a destroyer of diseases caused by phlegm (862).
In the section on burning (dāha), it is written that one should apply treatment for burning;
however, that which is contrary to fever is not the appropriate treatment. Excessive external heat and a mildness of thirst and other symptoms [indicate this]. 863.
The external signs of *bahirbega* (outward-moving fever) are its ease of treatment.

In the rainy season, autumn, and spring, fevers caused by *vāta* and the other [doshas] are natural (*prākṛta*) in their sequence; such a natural fever arising from the fragrant season (*surabhi*) is easily curable.
The other type is *vaikṛta* (modified), which is difficult to cure; the *prākṛta* (natural) type arises from *vāyu*.
In the rainy season, the vitiated *vāyu*, conjoined with *pitta* and *kapha*, produces fever;
in autumn, *pitta* causes it, with *kapha* acting as its secondary force.
Due to its inherent nature and the seasonal excretion [of impurities], there is no danger from fasting during that time; however, in spring, even that [phlegm] may become aggravated by wind and bile.
Internal burning, excessive thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo [occur].
Pain in the joints and bones, absence of perspiration, suppression of the humors and the feces, and difficulty in cure are the signs of internalized fever (antarvega).
Furthermore, a fever that occurs in one who is emaciated or swollen, which is deep-seated and chronic, is difficult to treat. (869)
A fever that is incurable, powerful, and one that parts the hairline should be recognized as deep-seated (gambhīra) by internal burning, excessive thirst,
extreme distension, and the onset of cough and dyspnea. (870–871)

Whether occurring at the onset of fever, during its middle stage, or at its conclusion, inflammation of the root of the ear is declared by the sages to be, respectively, incurable, difficult to cure, or easily curable; for from it,
the patient's death is seen to be inevitable.
That which possesses the characteristics of *talla* is called *ariṣṭa*, and it is also designated as *riṣṭa*.
A fever that arises from many powerful causes, is accompanied by numerous symptoms, brings about the end of life, and swiftly destroys the sensory faculties, is likewise [an *ariṣṭa*]. (873–874)
The man who, unconscious, faints or even falls down while lying,
who is afflicted by cold yet feels internal heat, dies from fever; likewise, he whose hair stands on end, whose eyes are bloodshot, and who suffers from a piercing pain in the chest [shall die].
Fever destroys that man who breathes with his mouth open (876).
Fever brings about the end of a man who is afflicted by hiccup, dyspnea, and thirst, who is deluded, whose eyes are wandering, who breathes incessantly, and who is emaciated (877).
One should avoid treating a fever patient who has lost their luster and sensory power, who is emaciated and afflicted by anorexia, who suffers from deep-seated, sharp, and intense paroxysms;
such a person will meet with death when the fever has reached the seat of the semen (śukrasthāna). 878.
Erection of the penis and, especially, the discharge of semen;
that [fever] which is irregular from its onset, or which persists for a long duration, or which occurs in one who is emaciated and excessively dry—such a deep-seated fever kills him. 879–880.
Thus ends the first chapter on fever. Now begins the second chapter on diarrhea (atisāra).
[Diarrhea is caused by] heavy, excessively unctuous, dry, hot, liquid, bulky, or excessively cold substances.

Due to incompatible food, overeating, indigestion, and irregular meals; due to excessive application of oleation and other therapies, or their improper application; due to poisons, fears, grief, drinking contaminated water, and excessive consumption of alcohol; and due to the seasonal changes of things that were once habituated.
Diarrhea occurs in men due to excessive water-sports, suppression of natural urges, or from the presence of worms; its symptoms will now be described:
pain in the heart, navel, flanks, abdomen, and pelvic region, exhaustion of the limbs, and obstruction of the vital airs (vāyu).
Foul-smelling discharge, flatulence, and indigestion are the precursors of that which is about to occur.

When the watery element has subsided and the fire-element increases, it is then impelled by the wind and mixed with feces; this flows excessively as *atisāra*. They call this a terrible disease, and they describe it as being of six types.
It is said that diarrhea is caused by each of the [three] doshas individually, by all of them together, by grief as the sixth, and by ama (undigested matter).
(6) Since there is no treatment for atisara (diarrhea) that disregards the sequence of ama and paka (maturity), one should therefore examine both the ama and paka stages in every case of atisara. (7)
Feces that is mixed with undigested humors (āma), deposited in water, sinks;
it is extremely foul-smelling and slimy, and is designated as "āma. However, those very same symptoms, when reversed, belong to one who indeed possesses [proper digestion].

One should specifically indicate that the patient has been cured when there is lightness; however, one should not administer astringent (saṃgrāhaka) remedies at the outset to one suffering from acute diarrhea (āmātisāra),
for if administered at the wrong time, it produces many complications.
It cures fistula-in-ano, blackish boils, abdominal distension, malabsorption syndrome,
hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano with sinus tracts, edema, anemia, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, ascites, and fever;
as well as those caused by wind and bile in children and the elderly.
Furthermore, even undigested matter (āma) that has depleted the strength of the bodily constituents (dhātu), increased the humors (doṣa), and been excessively discharged, should be arrested;
for if it were treated with digestive measures (pācana), death would occur.
For a strong person, there is no other remedy in this world than fasting alone.
One should thus digest and pacify that accumulated mass of aggravated humors (doṣas).
Water boiled with coriander and rice-water should be given to one suffering from thirst, burning sensations, and diarrhea; or water boiled with hrivera and ginger, or with musta and parpaṭaka.

Water boiled with musta and uddīcya and then cooled should be given to one suffering from thirst. For a patient with diarrhea in its initial stage (pūrvarūpa), fasting is beneficial at first; or, at the conclusion of the fast, a light and liquid diet should be administered.

For the destruction of diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra), a person should drink a decoction made from pathyā, dāru, vacā, musta, nāgara, and ativiṣā. [16] One should also take the powder of pāṭhā, hiṅgu, ajamoda, ugrā, and the five spices (pañcakola).
Warm water drunk with rock salt overcomes undigested matter (āma) accompanied by pain. 17.
Having ground together harītakī, ativiṣā, asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, vacā, and rock salt, one should have it drunk with warm water. 18.
This application [of medicine] treats *āmātisāra* after it has been digested;
however, that *āmātisāra* which is not pacified by this application is not treated even by a physician with a hundred applications. (19–20)
Vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, mustaka, bālaka,
and śaṭī conquer diarrhea accompanied by undigested matter (āmātisāra), whether chronic or characterized by blood and pain.
Ginger (nāgara), ground with castor oil, likewise conquers both acute and chronic [diarrhea].
Water boiled with coriander, balaka, bilva, usira, and ginger is an excellent digestive, appetizer, and a supreme remedy for diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra) and colic.
Water boiled with coriander, balaka, bilva, usira, and ginger destroys colic and constipation due to ama, and is an excellent digestive and appetizer. (22–23)
In cases of pitta-type diarrhea, they say that the "four grains" (dhānyacatuṣka) should be used, excluding ginger;
for blood-type diarrhea as well, the four grains should be administered due to its similarity with pitta.
Thus ends the treatment for āma-diarrhea.
Now, the treatment for chronic diarrhea:
One should drink lodhra, dhātakī, bilva, mustā, the kernel of the mango stone, and kaliṅgaka with buffalo buttermilk; this destroys chronic diarrhea. (25)
Samaṅgā, dhātakī flower, mañjiṣṭhā, and lodhra;
śālmalīveṣṭaka, lodhra, the bark of the fruit of the pomegranate tree;
the pulp of the mango stone, lodhra, the pulp of the bilva fruit, and priyaṅgu. 26.
Madhuka, ginger, and the bark of dīrghavṛnta—
these four formulations are destroyers of chronic diarrhea (pakvātīsāra).
These formulations should be administered with honey and rice-water.
Kañcaṭa, pomegranate, rose-apple, water-chestnut leaves, wood-apple, barhiṣṭha,
along with musta and ginger, would even stop the swift-flowing Gaṅgā.
[29] With moca-resin, musta, ginger, pāṭhā, aralu, and dhātakī flowers...
Powder combined with *mathita* (churned curd) immediately stops even the flow of the Gaṅgā.
Mustā, seeds of *vatsaka*, *mocarasa*, *bilva*, *dhātakī*, and *lodhra*,
when joined with jaggery and *mathita*, would obstruct even the swiftly flowing Gaṅgā.
With Musta, Aralu, Śuṇṭhī, Dhātakī, Lodhra, Bālaka, Bilva, Mocarasa, Pāṭhā, Indrayava, Vatsaka,
Āmrabīja, Mañjiṣṭhā, and Ativiṣā— all these combined and powdered— 32.
Honey mixed with rice-water, when drunk, destroys dysentery (pravāhikā).
It overcomes all types of diarrhea and swiftly conquers malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī).
This "Vṛddhagaṅgādhara" powder would stem even the flow of the celestial river (Gaṅgā).
The paste of the root of *aṅkola*, drunk with rice-water and honey,
will instantly arrest diarrhea, just as a dam stops the rush of water.
(35) The physician should boil a handful of fresh *kuṭaja* bark in one *droṇa* of water.
Having brought it to one-quarter of its original volume, strained through a cloth, and boiled again,
one should add one *pala* each of the powder of *lajjālu*, *dhātakī*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *mocarasa*, *mustā*, and *ativiṣā*. (36–37)
Having cast [the ingredients] into it, one should cook it until the ladle becomes coated;
when drunk with water, goat’s milk, or gruel, it overcomes all terrible dysenteries of various colors accompanied by pain. 38.
It cures all forms of menorrhagia as well as dysentery.
Having prepared a very firm basin with ground *āmalaka* fruits, the physician should quickly fill the navel region with the juice of fresh ginger.
This king of formulations (yogarāja) instantly conquers and destroys severe diarrhea that has increased and become difficult for men to restrain, which is like the violent current of a river.
Pāṭhā ground with cow's curd, as well as the inner bark of the āmra tree, [is used]. 41.
It undoubtedly and quickly destroys diarrhea accompanied by pain and burning; there is no doubt.
When the stool is reddish, frothy, dry, scanty, and passed repeatedly, being undigested and accompanied by pain and sound, it is caused by Vāta. (42–43)
Vacā, ativiṣā, musta, and the seeds of kuṭaja—
this excellent decoction of these [herbs] is for the pacification of vāta-type diarrhea.
When caused by pitta, the stool is yellow, blood-stained, foul-smelling, green, and passes rapidly.
Accompanied by abdominal distension, thirst, fainting, and a burning sensation, [the diarrhea] sets in.
A decoction prepared from *bilva*, *śakrayava*, *ambhoda*, *bālaka*, and *ativiṣā* destroys diarrhea caused by pitta that is associated with undigested matter (*sāma*). 45–46.
One should administer *rasāñjana*, *ativiṣā*, the bark and fruit of *kuṭaja*, *dhātakī*, and *śṛṅgavera* with rice-water;
when drunk with honey, it destroys even severe *pitta*-type diarrhea. 47.
One should kindle the digestive fire; this will quickly alleviate the colic (śūla).
When one who suffers from a pitta disorder eats substances that excessively increase pitta, then a severe and frequent bloody diarrhea arises in him. 48–49.

One should boil the bark produced from the unripe fruit of the *vatsatvak* and *dāḍima* trees, along with a pair of barks [of other trees], measuring one *pala*, in water that is eight times their quantity; when the decoction is reduced to one-eighth part, a person should drink it with honey.
This will certainly destroy severe and excessive bloody diarrhea (raktātisāra).
A decoction of *kuṭaja*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bālaka*, *lodhra*, *candana*, *dhātakī*, *dāḍima*, and *pāṭhā*, taken with honey, [achieves this]. 52–53.

This decoction of *kuṭaja* and other herbs, which destroys all types of diarrhea, should be drunk for the alleviation of burning sensations and colic in cases of bloody diarrhea (*raktātisāra*). A paste of black sesame seeds with sugar added in a fivefold proportion [should also be used].
When drunk with goat’s milk, it immediately destroys diarrhea (54). A decoction prepared with vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, uśīra,
and musta is beneficial in cases of diarrhea that is accompanied by undigested matter (āma), pain, and blood, even when it has been chronic (55).
Black earth, madhuka, and lodhra, along with kuṭaja seeds, drunk together with rice-water and honey,
are an excellent remedy for checking hemorrhaging. One should eat bilva fruit with jaggery to destroy bloody diarrhea.
It destroys colic caused by undigested matter (āma-śūla) and constipation, and is supreme for curing diseases of the abdomen.
(57) One should crush fresh sprouts of the Jambu, mango, and Āmalakī trees;
when drunk with honey, it cures bloody diarrhea. (58)
Having properly boiled two *palas* of the pure root of *girimallikā* in four *śarāvas* of water until only one-quarter remains, that decoction should indeed be strained by the skilled;
One suffering from bloody diarrhea will quickly attain health by drinking that [milk].
By drinking the paste of *śatāvarī* with milk, or by drinking ghee prepared with it, a person who subsists on milk will conquer bloody diarrhea. (60–61)
Cow’s milk-butter (navanīta) licked together with honey and sugar is considered the supreme remedy for dysentery with blood.
Sandalwood mixed with honey and sugar, when drunk with rice-water, [is likewise effective].
It conquers bloody diarrhea and removes blood-bile, thirst, burning sensations, and urinary disorders.

(63) For one whose anus is scorched by pitta or undergoes suppuration due to excessive purgations, the treatments such as pouring [medicated liquids] and washing should be applied to those two conditions. (64)

Indeed, the anus should be washed with a cool decoction of *paṭola* and *yaṣṭimadhu*, and the anus should be irrigated with that same liquid. In cases of burning and suppuration, goat's milk mixed with honey and sugar is beneficial.
It is appropriate for washing and sprinkling the anus, as well as for use in drinks and food.
If severe pain occurs in the anus due to excessive discharge,
one should then apply fomentation to the anus with the flesh of a steamed rat.
Then, having formed a ball from wheat flour boiled with water and mixed with ghee, one should gently apply it as a fomentation to the anus.
For the prolapse of the anus, *cāṅgerī-ghṛta* (ghee prepared with *cāṅgerī*) is declared to be excellent.

In the case of prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), one should lubricate the rectum with unctuous substances and cause it to enter back inside. Once it has entered, one should apply mild fomentation using the flesh of a rat. Alternatively, well-steamed meat of a snail (śambūka), combined with oil and salt, may be used.
Having lightly anointed it with ghee, one should diligently apply fomentation;
this will quickly and completely cure prolapse of the rectum.
Furthermore, one should thoroughly smear the anus with the fat of a mouse.
The disease known as *gudabhraṃśa* (prolapse of the rectum) is undoubtedly destroyed.
Ghee cooked with *cāṅgerī*, *kola*, sour curd, alkali, and ginger should be drunk to remove the ailment of *gudabhraṃśa*. 72–73.
If one should eat tender lotus leaves mixed with sugar,
having ascertained this [remedy], it is declared that there shall be no further discharge from the anus.
[The stool] is white, unctuous, dense, formed, cold, and attended by mild pain.
In diarrhea caused by phlegm (kapha), the stool is passed with heaviness and a lack of relish;

first, fasting and digestive (pācana) treatments are beneficial, and the previously mentioned group of appetizing (dīpana) drugs that cure diarrhea with undigested mucus (āmātisāra) should be employed. 75–76.
Cavya, ativiṣā, musta, young bilva, nāgara, the bark and fruit of vatsaka, and pathyā cure vomiting and diarrhea caused by kapha.
So too do hiṅgu, sauvarcala, vyoṣa, abhayā, ativiṣā, and vacā.
The powder of these [drugs] taken with warm water cures diarrhea caused by *kapha*.
Now follows the general treatment for diarrhea arising from two *doṣas*; in that regard, there is a decoction of *kṛmiśatru* and other such [medicines].

The physician should administer a decoction of *kṛmiśatru*, *vacā*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *dhānyāka*, and *kaṭphala* in cases of diarrhea caused by two doṣas. (79) The treatment for these has already been stated, but a specific [treatment] is now being declared. (80)
Now, the treatment for diarrhea caused by Vāta and Kapha: in that regard, there is a decoction of Kaṭphala and others—
namely Kaṭphala, Madhuka, Lodhra, and the bark of the pomegranate fruit.
Rice-water with powdered [medicine] cures diarrhea caused by vāta and kapha.
Now follows the treatment for diarrhea caused by vāta and pitta; therein is the decoction of citraka and other ingredients.
Citraka, ativiṣā, musta, vālaka, bilva, nāgara, bark of vatsaka, its fruit, and harītakī cure diarrhea caused by vāta and pitta.
(82) Now follows the treatment for diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha.
In that regard, the decoction of mustā and others— mustā, ativiṣā, mūrvā, vacā, and kuṭaja taken in equal parts—
a decoction of these, when mixed with honey, cures diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha. (83)

When attended by drowsiness, delusion, exhaustion, and dryness of the mouth, it produces stools of various forms; when seized by thirst and arising from all [three] doshas, there is the manifestation of all symptoms. This condition is difficult to cure and is incurable in children, the elderly, and the weak. Now follows the treatment for diarrhea caused by the combination of all three doshas (sannipāta).
A decoction prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, nāgara, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, barhiṣṭha, kuṭaja bark, and kuṭaja fruit,
destroys diarrhea caused by all three doṣas, as well as fever and vomiting.
It also cures dyspnea accompanied by pain and cough that is difficult to overcome.

The common *pañcamūlī* (five roots) should be employed in cases of pitta, while the *kanīyasī* (smaller) *pañcamūlī* is considered appropriate for vāta, and the *mahatī* (larger) *pañcamūlī* for balāsa (kapha).

Abhayā, nāgara, and musta combined with jaggery constitute this "Fourfold" (catuḥsama) pill, which destroys all types of diarrhea, as well as diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātīsāra), flatulence with constipation, and choleraic disorders (visūcikā). 88.
It destroys worms and loss of appetite, and quickly kindles the digestive fire.
Having ground four palas of kuṭaja bark freshly harvested at that time with rice-water, it should be wrapped in a jambū leaf. 89–90.
Having bound it with thread and wrapped it in wheat flour,
one should coat it with thick mud and burn it in a fire of cow-dung. Once the clay has taken on the color of charcoal, one should remove it from the fire.
Then, having extracted the juice, one should drink it cold combined with honey.
This *puṭapāka* preparation of *kuṭaja*, taught by the son of Kṛṣṇātri, conquers all types of diarrhea, even those born of blood and those that have been long-standing. (92–93)
A decoction made from the bark of *kuṭaja*, strained through a cloth and cooled,
when licked while combined with *ativiṣā*, cures diarrhea caused by the three doṣas (tridoṣa).
In this case, they desire that the powder of *ativiṣā* be added at an eighth part of the weight of the decoction.
Some indeed say that one should add a fourth part [of the previous ingredients];
having ground one pala of aṅkoṭa root, along with an equal amount of pāṭhā and dārvī, in rice-water, one should prepare pills the size of an akṣa fruit. 95–96.

The physician should dry those [drugs] in the shade; having ground one of them with rice-water, he should administer it as a drink to the patient afflicted by diseases arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, those born of two doṣas combined, or from the combination of all three (sānnipātika). 97.
This medicinal bolus (vaṭaka), when administered, destroys all types of diarrhea. In a person who grieves over various circumstances and eats little, the heat of the vapors enters the digestive fire;
having reached the stomach (koṣṭha), it agitates the blood, which then appears at the lower orifice like the *kākaṇantī* plant.

When the stool is discharged mixed with fecal matter, or without feces, or odorless, or even fragrant, such diarrhea arising from grief is difficult to treat; this excessive disease is declared by physicians to be a painful one. (100) When the humors (doṣas), agitated by fear, vitiate the waste products (mala).
Then the person suffers from diarrhea, quickly passing warm, water-like stools (101).
It is generally endowed with the symptoms of vāta-pitta-type diarrhea; it is known as *bhaya* because relief occurs through fear and cessation [of the cause] (102).
Those [types of diarrhea] arising from fear and grief should be understood as being like wind-type diarrhea;

for them, treatment to alleviate wind should be administered through exhilaration and consolation. (103) When the humors, provoked by indigestion of food, agitate the collection of tissues and the waste products within the digestive tract, [diarrhea occurs].
They discharge various colors of stool many times; this sixth [type] is said to be accompanied by colic (śūla).
104 Now follows the treatment for diarrhea (atīsāra): in that regard, there is a decoction of *vatsaka* and other ingredients.
A decoction of vatsaka, ativiṣā, śuṇṭhī, bilva, hiṅgu, yava, ambuda, and citraka destroys āmātīsāra (diarrhea caused by undigested matter). 105.
Now follows the treatment for śothātīsāra (edematous diarrhea).
In that regard, a decoction of śothaghnī and the others— śothaghnī, indrayava, pāṭhā, śrīphala, ativiṣā,
ghana, and marica— when boiled and drunk, destroys swelling and diarrhea. (106)
Now, the treatment for vomiting and diarrhea: in that regard, there is a decoction of mango stones and other ingredients,
as well as a decoction of the pulp of mango stones and emblic myrobalan fruits, mixed with honey.
A decoction of fried mung beans, combined with parched grain (lāja), honey, and sugar, destroys severe vomiting and diarrhea;
it also cures thirst, burning sensations, fever, and giddiness. (107–108)
One suffering from *niḥsāraka* should eat with curd mixed with whey and honey;
or else, one whose digestive fire is blazing and who passes scybalous stools should eat with cold milk boiled with base metals (*kupya*) and saturated with honey. (109)
In cases of diminished feces, one should drink treacle, ginger, curd, oil, milk, and ghee;
or milk boiled with *balā* and *viśvā*, combined with jaggery and oil; this should be administered in the morning to one with a stimulated digestive fire, as it provides comfort. (111)
Having crushed one *tulā* of *bilva*, one should boil it until reduced to one-fourth;
then one should prepare oil with milk and these [following] ingredients ground finely in equal parts:
*bilva*, *dhātakī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rāsnā*, and *punarnavā*. (112)
Devadāru, vacā, musta, lodhra, and mocarasa—
cooked over a gentle fire with these ingredients, this oil known as Bilvataila, spoken by the son of Atri, cures malabsorption (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids (arśas), and diarrhea (atisāra). 113–114.

The unctuous substances (snehas) that have been demonstrated in the section on malabsorption (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids (arśas) should indeed be employed in cases of diarrhea as well, because the three [doshas] share common causes.
In one who consumes unwholesome food, the aggravated Vāyu pushes the accumulated phlegm (balāsa) downwards.
Experts declare that condition to be *pravāhikā* (dysentery) when the stool is frequently passed in small or large quantities and is smeared with mucus.

*Pravāhikā* caused by Vāta is accompanied by pain; from Pitta it is characterized by burning; from Kapha it is associated with phlegm; and that arising from blood is accompanied by blood. These are considered to originate from either unctuous (*sneha*) or dry (*rūkṣa*) factors. 116–117.
One should describe their symptoms, the sequence [of treatment], and the state of being undigested (*āmavipakvatā*) as being like those of diarrhea (118).
Now, the treatment for dysentery (*pravāhikā*):
a paste of *bilva*, jaggery, *lodhra*, oil, combined with black pepper.
Having licked [this], one afflicted by dysentery (pravāhikā) shall quickly attain ease.
One should drink dhātakī, the leaf of badarī, kapittha, honey, and lodhra together with curd to cure diarrhea from its onset. 119–120.
It resembles a ripe jambu fruit, or a piece of liver;
it is thin and has the appearance of ghee, oil, fat, marrow, vesavāra, milk, curd, or the water used for washing meat; it is black, or possesses a blue and reddish luster.
[The sputum] is variegated, dark, glossy, dense, and associated with the moon (candrakopagata).
It resembles a corpse, has the appearance of brain matter, is foul-smelling, and is putrid to a great degree.
It causes thirst, burning sensations, loss of appetite, dyspnea, hiccup, and pain in the sides and bones.

The physician should avoid treating a patient suffering from diarrhea who is characterized by fainting, aversion to food, and delusion; whose anal folds are sloughed and the rectum is protruded; who suffers from delirium;
who has an unrestrained anus; who is emaciated; and who is afflicted by colic and flatulence. (124)
One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea who has lost heat in the rectum and abdomen (pakvāśaya).
Diarrhea especially destroys an elderly man who is afflicted by asthma, colic, thirst, emaciation, and fever. (125–126)
Upon observing swelling, pain, fever, thirst, dyspnea, cough, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, and hiccup, one should abandon the patient suffering from diarrhea.
(127) Furthermore, suppuration at the joints of the fingers and toes and retention of urine [are signs of incurability].
Excessive heat in the stool indicates the imminent death of one suffering from diarrhea.

For a patient with diarrhea, one afflicted by a royal disease (rājaroga), or one suffering from malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), who is depleted of muscle mass, digestive fire, and strength— for such a person, life is difficult to sustain.

This [disease], when afflicted by these symptoms, is incurable in children and the elderly; even in the young, it may be incurable if the bodily constituents (dhātus) are excessively vitiated. It is incurable for one whose urine and flatus pass properly even without the urge to void.
For one who has a stimulated digestive fire and a light gastrointestinal tract, the abdominal disease may persist;
such a patient suffering from diarrhea should avoid bathing, immersion in water, oil massage, heavy or unctuous food, physical exercise, and exposure to the heat of the fire. (131–132)
Ten *gadyāṇas* each of pure mercury and sulfur,
having ground them for three days in a mortar,
one should then grind that collyrium-like mixture for three days with the milk of a *vajra* plant.
One should rub together fresh, variegated, white, and helpless *citraka* roots for three days, grinding them with their own juices until they form a collyrium-like paste;
then, twenty *gadyāṇas* of powdered yellow cowrie shells [should be added]. 134–135.
Twenty parts of conch powder mixed with forty [parts of mercury] should be rubbed in a mortar for three days according to the previously mentioned procedure;
[this should be done] for three days with the milk of the Arka plant and for three days with the milk of the Vajrī plant.
Having placed collyrium and other ingredients in the middle of that, one should grind them with the juice of fresh *citraka* in a mortar; then,
having formed pills of both substances the size of a *badara* fruit,
one should quickly burn them after coating the interior of a baked clay crucible (*kuhlikā*) with powder.

Having cast the pills into that [vessel], having placed a lid smeared with powder over it, and having covered it with cloth and plastered it with clay, one should place a *kuhlarī* (a small crucible) inside a pit measuring one cubit in size and apply the *puṭa* (roasting) using *śāṇaka* (cow-dung fuel). 139.
Afterwards, one should grind it with the juice of *citraka* until it is cool to the touch;
having formed pills according to the previous method, they should again be subjected to the *puṭapāka* process.
Once the pills have been burnt, their powder should then be placed in a vessel (*kūpaka*).

This perfected rasa, known as Śaṅkhapotalī, should indeed be administered in cases of fever with undigested matter (āmajvara), diarrhea, dyspnea, and cough; likewise in disorders of phlegm, bile, and wind, in weak digestion, and in malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī). 142.
In cases of the eighteen types of prameha and when the digestive fire and strength are depleted,
one should administer five vallas of this preparation along with thirty-two black peppers and ghee for all diseases, except in cases of fever where pepper and ghee are excluded. (143–144)
Rice, curd, milk, and other sweet foods are beneficial;
one should strictly avoid pungent, sour, alkaline, and oily substances.
According to this procedure, this *śaṅkhapoṭalī* elixir should be prepared. 145.
The aforementioned diseases are undoubtedly cured in due course.
(146) Taking two parts of *kaliṅgaka* equal to one part of *jātīphala* from the *Trailokyavijaya* formulation, this excellent electuary cures all types of diarrhea. (147)

A linctus composed of *bilva*, *mocarasa*, *lodhra*, *dhātakī* flowers, mango fruit, and seeds [of *madana*], combined with *ativiṣā*, will certainly destroy even the most difficult-to-restrain onset of diarrhea caused by *sindhu*.
(148) Thus ends the second chapter on diarrhea. 2.
Now begins the third chapter on fever-attended-dysentery (jvarātisāra).
Since the etiology of fever and dysentery has already been stated separately, the etiology of fever-attended-dysentery has not been mentioned again. 1.
The medicinal treatments that have been described separately for fever and diarrhea should not be administered when the two are combined, because they would aggravate one another; therefore,
one should treat them with specific therapies prescribed for their combination.
Except for fasting alone, there is no other medicine here [for this condition];
it digests the accumulated excess of the doshas in one who is strong and likewise pacifies them.
Fasting is prescribed for both; when they are combined, it should be performed especially after that.
One may drink the entire preparation of parched grain decoction (lājāmaṇḍa) and so forth, prepared with *utpala* as the sixth ingredient;
or, for fever and diarrhea, a man should drink the boiled decoction mixed with sour gruel, prepared with *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *bilva*, *dhanikā*, *nāgara*, and *utpala*.
A decoction of *kaṇā*, *akarika*, *kaṇāla*, and *lāja*, mixed with honey and sugar,
when drunk, quickly destroys thirst associated with fever and diarrhea (7). [A decoction] of *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *amṛtā*, *bhūnimba*, and *vatsaka*...
This decoction destroys all fevers and even most severe diarrhea (8).
[It is prepared] from guḍūcī, ativiṣā, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, bilva, abda, and bālaka;
along with pāṭhā, bhūnimba, kuṭaja, candana, uśīra, and parpaṭa (9).

One should drink this decoction with honey to destroy fever and diarrhea, and for the cessation of nausea, anorexia, thirst, burning sensations, and vomiting. [The ingredients are] blue lotus, pomegranate bark, and lotus stamens. 10.
Utpala, dāḍima-tvak, and padmakeśara.
Drunk with rice-water, it destroys fever and diarrhea.
(11) A decoction made from bilva, bālaka, bhūnimba, guḍūcī, musta, and vatsaka is digestive and destroys swelling, fever, and diarrhea. (12)
A decoction made from *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *bilva*, *guḍūcī*, *musta*, and *vatsaka* is digestive and destroys swelling, fever, and diarrhea.
One should drink one *makṣika* (two karṣas) of *viśva* with a decoction of *daśamūla*.
In fever, in diarrhea, in edema, and in disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
Thus ends the third chapter on fever and diarrhea.
Now begins the fourth section on the disease of *grahaṇī*.
Even when diarrhea has ceased, if the digestive fire is weak and the patient consumes unwholesome food,
the fire becomes further vitiated and may also afflict the *grahaṇī*.
Because it receives (*grahaṇāt*) the food, the seat of the digestive fire is considered the *grahaṇī*.
It retains undigested food and expels that which is digested downward.
The sixth constituent, which is proclaimed as the "pitta-dhara" (bile-holder), situated between the stomach and the large intestine, is called the *grahaṇī*.
For the strength of the *grahaṇī* is indeed the digestive fire (*agni*), and that fire is also dependent on the strength of the *grahaṇī*.

Therefore, when the fire is impaired, the *grahaṇī* also becomes disordered; consequently, one must observe dietary and behavioral restrictions in cases of diarrhea (*atisāra*) just as after a purgation. 4.
Completely overwhelmed by all the humors (doṣas), each acting individually or collectively,
that vitiated [vāta] frequently causes her to pass either undigested food or digested food that is painful,
foul-smelling, and alternately constipated or loose.
Those learned in Āyurveda call that disease *grahaṇī*;

it is caused by the consumption of excessively pungent, bitter, astringent, dry, and cold foods, as well as by eating in insufficient quantities, fasting, excessive physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, and sexual indulgence.
When the wind (māruta) is aggravated, it envelops the fire and produces disease;
food is digested with difficulty, becoming sour during digestion, and there is roughness of the limbs.
There is dryness of the throat and mouth, hunger, thirst, darkness of vision, and a ringing sound in the ears.
Pain in the sides, thighs, groins, and neck; frequent indigestion (visūcikā) [9];
oppression of the heart, emaciation, weakness, a bad taste in the mouth, cutting pain in the rectum, a craving for all flavors, and likewise depression of the mind [10].
When it is digested, there is flatulence, and after eating, the person returns to a state of health;
yet that man remains suspicious of vātagulma, heart disease, and splenic enlargement.
After a long time, he voids stool that is painful, liquid, dry, thin, scanty, accompanied by sound, and frothy.
Afflicted by cough and dyspnea due to vāta, one may repeatedly pass feces.
When pitta is aggravated by pungent, bitter, burning, sour, and alkaline substances,
it overwhelms the digestive fire (anal), just as hot water extinguishes a flame.

Afflicted by excessive acidity, eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, anorexia, and thirst, he passes undigested, liquid stools that are yellowish-blue in appearance, while he himself appears yellowish.
This occurs due to the consumption of heavy, excessively unctuous, or cold foods, as well as from overeating. (14)
In one who has just eaten, aggravated *kapha* destroys the digestive fire due to sleep;
his food is digested with difficulty, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, anorexia, coating of the mouth, sweetness in the mouth, cough, *ṣṭhīvana*, and chronic rhinitis (*pīnasa*). (15–16)
The heart feels constricted, the abdomen is distended, motionless, and heavy;
there is a foul, sweet eructation, lassitude, and a lack of sexual desire.
There is the discharge of stool that is broken up, mixed with phlegm, and heavy. (17)
In the kapha-type [fever], there is weakness and laziness even in one who is not emaciated (18).
When there is a combination of causes and symptoms individually specified for vāta and the other doshas, one should diagnose it as tridoṣaja; thus I shall describe their treatment (19).
The stool is watery, dense, white, and unctuous; it causes pain in the waist, is undigested, copious, slimy, noisy, and associated with mild pain.
It is discharged constantly, whether every fortnight, every month, or every ten days. (20)
There will be rumbling in the intestines, lethargy, weakness, and exhaustion.
Its provocation occurs during the day and it finds relief at night;
it is difficult to diagnose, hard to suppress, and persists for a long time. (21–22)
That condition caused by āmavāta is considered saṅgrahagrahaṇī (23).
Numbness in the flanks, pain, and a sound like that of a water-clock—
this they call ghaṭīyantra, an incurable form of grahaṇī disease (24).
One should treat a disease localized in the *grahaṇī* like indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), using fasting,
digestive stimulants, and the remedies always prescribed for diarrhea.
One should recognize the presence of *āmadoṣa* (undigested matter) or its absence in this condition just as one does in diarrhea.
Following the procedure prescribed for diarrhea (atisāra), one should digest that [undigested matter] with it;

the physician should administer thin gruel (peyā) and other light foods combined with pungent spices and the *pañcakola* group, as well as digestive stimulants (*dīpana*) and buttermilk (*takra*), in cases of malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*). 26–27.
A gruel prepared with wood-apple (kapittha), bilva, cāṅgerī, tamarind,
and pomegranate digests undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and also promotes the formation of feces.
Cow's curd is excellent, strengthening, sweet in digestion, and provides relish.
Among all types of curd, that produced from cow's milk is said to be superior in its qualities; it is purifying, digestive, unctuous, nourishing, and subdues the wind humor (vāta).
Buffalo curd is very unctuous, increases phlegm (kapha), and alleviates wind and bile (pitta).
Goat curd is sweet in digestion, causes secretions, is aphrodisiac, heavy, and impairs the blood; it is excellent for constipation, light, and removes the three *doṣas*.
It is recommended for asthma, cough, hemorrhoids, consumption, and emaciation, and acts as a digestive stimulant. (30–31)
Takra, ghola, mathita, and udaśvit—by these distinctions, the best of sages such as Suśruta and others have proclaimed four types of buttermilk.
Ghola is buttermilk with water added; mathita is buttermilk without water. 32.
Buttermilk (takra) is said to contain one-quarter water, while whey (udaśvit) contains half water.
Whey churned with buttermilk (ghola) removes wind and bile; it is churned [plain] buttermilk (mathita) alleviates phlegm and bile.
Whey (udaśvit) increases phlegm, is strengthening, and is considered the best for removing fatigue.
Buttermilk (takra) is constipating, astringent and sour, sweet, digestive, light, hot in potency, strength-giving, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and a destroyer of Vata.
One should understand that buttermilk possesses the same qualities as the eight types of curd previously described.
For those suffering from disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and similar ailments, buttermilk is wholesome because it is astringent and light.
