Freshly prepared buttermilk subdues wind (vāta) due to its acidity and density, and it does not cause a burning sensation;
furthermore, it is sweet in its post-digestive transformation (vipāka), though it eventually provokes bile (pitta).
Buttermilk (takra) from which the butter has been fully extracted is beneficial for phlegm due to its astringent, hot, and expanding properties, as well as its lightness;
however, that from which only a small amount of butter has been extracted is heavy, aphrodisiac, and increases phlegm. (38)
Freshly extracted ghee that is thick and heavy bestows nourishment and strength.
One should drink buttermilk (takra) mixed with sour substances and rock salt for vāta, sweetened with sugar for pitta, and combined with alkali and the three pungents (trikaṭu) for kapha. 39–40.
Gholam mixed with asafoetida and cumin, and sprinkled with rock salt, destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), hemorrhoids, and diarrhea; it is an excellent subduer of vāta.
It is appetizing, nourishing, strengthening, and a destroyer of bladder pain. 41–42.
Buttermilk destroys raw phlegm in the stomach and causes it to accumulate in the throat;
however, in cases such as chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough, only the matured (pakva) variety is specifically recommended.
One should never administer buttermilk to those with chest wounds, nor during the hot season, nor to those who are weak.
One does not suffer from fainting, vertigo, or burning sensations, nor from blood-bile diseases, when consuming *takra*.
Never does one who consumes *takra* experience affliction; diseases cannot prevail against one scorched by *takra*.
Just as nectar is for the happiness of the gods, so they say that *takra* on this earth is for the happiness of men. 44–45.
One should administer mudga-juice, meat broth, and buttermilk combined with coriander and cumin, along with rock salt; this is declared as the "six-fold seasoning" (ṣaḍyūṣaṇa).
Take one karṣa of sulphur and half a karṣa of mercury, and prepare them both into an auspicious collyrium (kajjala).

One who suffers from chronic diseases should eat two *karṣas* each of the two types of black pepper, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and the five salts, along with half a *karṣa* of fried asafoetida mixed with the two types of cumin and half that amount of *bhaṅgā*; this dose of one *ṭaṅka* should be taken with buttermilk or with *bilva* fruit. (47)
With nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, cinnamon bark, and nāgakeśara;
with camphor, sandalwood, sesame bark, kṣīrī, tagara, and āmalaka (48); and with tālīśa, plīha, harītakī, large cumin, and citraka.

Take equal parts of dried ginger (śuṇṭhī), viḍaṅga, and black pepper, and grind them into a powder. One should add as much hemp (bhaṅgā) as there is of all these combined, and having made it equal to the total weight of the powder, one should add white sugar. 49–50.

A person should eat this, measuring one *karṣa* and saturated with honey; it destroys *agrahaṇī*, cough, consumption-cough, and loss of appetite. [The ingredients are] *citraka*, long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), alkali, and the five salts.
One should grind together the three pungents (vyoṣa), asafoetida (hiṅgu), ajamodā, and cavya.
Made into pills with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga) or pomegranate (dāḍima),
this digests undigested matter (āma) and quickly stimulates the digestive fire.

The marrow of the unripe fruit of the *śrīphala* (bilva), mixed with powdered *nāgara* (ginger) and consumed with treacle while subsisting on buttermilk, overcomes even the most violent disease of *grahaṇī*.
[54] Four *palas* of the stem of *sudhā* (snuhī) and three *palas* of the three salts (*lavaṇatraya*)...
Having burnt one *kuḍava* of eggplant (*vārtāku*), one *bilva* of arka root, and likewise of *analā*, and having ground them with the juice of eggplant, a pill should be taken between meals;
it quickly digests whatever has been eaten and destroys the disease of *grahaṇī*.
Mustaka, ativiṣā, bilva, and kuṭaja, finely powdered and licked with honey, cure cough, dyspnea, as well as visūcī and heart disease;
it conquers all types of grahaṇī.
Whether it be white or red, a well-matured disease of the *grahaṇī* is quickly destroyed by consuming jaggery mixed with an abundance of *sarja* resin.
(58) He who drinks goat’s milk prepared with *bilva*, *arjuna*, *śakrayava*, *bālaka*, and *moca* for three days [is freed from the disease].
This [preparation] destroys even an incurable chronic disorder of the *grahaṇī* that has been excessively aggravated, provided it is accompanied by *sāma* and blood.

Having added three *prasthas* of pure *āmalakī* juice to half a *tulā* of jaggery, one should mix in the powders of *granthika*, *jīraka*, *cavya*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), along with *pippalī*, *hapuṣā*, and *ajamoda*. (59–60)

Having added one pala each of viḍaṅga, saindhava salt, triphalā, yavānī, pāṭhā, citraka, and dhānyaka, along with eight palas of trivṛt powder and eight palas of oil, one should cook it according to the prescribed method.
One should consume this in a dose of one akṣa (one pala), mixed with the three aromatics (trisugandhi), and may then engage in activities as desired.

By this, all disorders of the *grahaṇī*, along with dyspnea, cough, hoarseness of voice, and swelling, are pacified (62). Furthermore, it is the cause for the increase of long-suppressed internal digestive fire (*antaragni*) and virility;
in women, it shall be the destroyer of the diseases of sterility. This well-known jaggery preparation named Kalyāṇaka is thus established (63).
Having fried three palas of triphalā in a small amount of oil with trivṛt,
this should be added to the already prepared *kalyāṇaka-guḍa*.
[Then add] pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, and gajapippalī.
Coriander, viḍaṅga, yavānī, and black pepper;
triphalā, ajamodā, nīlinī, and likewise cumin; as well as rock salt, romaka, sea salt, rucaka, and viḍa salt. (65–66)
Āragvadha, bark, patra, sūkṣmailā, upakuñcikā, śuṇṭhī, and śakrayava—each of these should be measured at one karṣa;
four palas of mṛdvīkā are indeed prescribed for this preparation. 67.
Take eight palas of trivṛtā, half a tulā of jaggery,
eight palas of sesame oil, and three prasthas of āmalaka juice; cook all of this together slowly over a mild fire.
One should eat or consume this— Audumbara, Āmalaka, and Bādara— in appropriate quantities according to one's strength and digestive fire;
it cures all types of grahaṇī diseases as well as the twenty kinds of prameha.
It removes chest pain, catarrh, debility, and the diminution of digestive fire; it also cures all types of fever and bestows luster, intellect, and strength.
It quickly destroys anemia, as well as internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta) and constipation.

This "Great Auspicious Jaggery" (mahākalyāṇaka-guḍa) is beneficial for those whose bodily elements are depleted, those whose youth has faded, those who have lost their wives, and those suffering from consumption; it is also for the barren woman.
[It is prepared] from well-ripened kūṣmāṇḍa fruits that have been steamed, de-seeded, and peeled.
One should slowly cook one *prastha* of clarified butter with one hundred *palas* [of the following ingredients] in a copper vessel: long pepper, the root of long pepper, *citraka*, elephant pepper,
coriander, *viḍaṅga*, ginger, and black pepper.
One pala each of triphalā, ajamodā, kaliṅga, ajājī, and saindhava, eight palas of trivṛt,
eight palas of oil, and fifty palas of jaggery.
In this case, three *prasthas* of the juice of *āmalaka* are prescribed;
the physician should cook it over a gentle fire until a coating forms on the stirring ladle, at which point he should remove it from the heat. (77–78)
One should eat or consume this—whether it be udumbara, āmalaka, or badara—in such quantities according to one's strength and digestive fire;
and by this very method, it should be employed day after day. 79.
It destroys diseases of the duodenum (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara) (80),

fever, flatulence, heart disease, abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargements (udara), choleraic dysentery (visūcikā), jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha) (81).

One should treat all corrupted Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, as well as Vātaśoṇita (gout), Visarpa (erysipelas), Dadru (ringworm), Yakṣma (consumption), and Halīmaka (chlorosis), after first purifying them.
This applies to those men who are emaciated by disease, emaciated by old age, or emaciated by excessive sexual indulgence with women.

This jaggery (guḍa) is beneficial for them; it bestows sons even upon barren women, and it is aphrodisiac, strengthening, nourishing, and likewise stabilizes the vital age. (83) Furthermore, the Bilva oil described in the section on diarrhea is also beneficial here.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the diseases of the *grahaṇī*. Now begins the middle section;
therein is the second part.
Now begins the fifth chapter on hemorrhoids (arśas).

One should know that there are six types of hemorrhoids located in the three folds of the rectum: those caused by the individual doshas, those caused by all the doshas combined, those caused by blood, and those that are congenital. 1.
Astringent, pungent, and bitter tastes; dry, cold, and light qualities; eating in measured and small quantities; strong liquor; indulgence in sexual intercourse;
fasting; and cold regions, seasons, and physical exercise.

Grief, exposure to wind and heat, and touch [of cold] are the causes of wind-type hemorrhoids (vātārśas). Furthermore, pungent, sour, salty, and hot foods; physical exercise, digestive fire, and sunlight; the seasons of autumn and summer; anger, alcohol, and envy [are also causes]. (3–4)
All drinks, foods, and meals that are burning, sharp, and hot should be known as the cause for the provocation of hemorrhoids characterized by a predominance of pitta.
Sweet, unctuous, cold, salty, sour, and heavy [substances] [are the causes for those characterized by a predominance of kapha]. 5.
Delight in lack of physical exertion, daytime sleep, and the comfort of beds and seats;
indulgence in the morning breeze and cold things; and disregard for place and time—this is declared to be the cause of hemorrhoids caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika).
One should recognize the dual combinations through the association of their causal characteristics;
indeed, every cause of the three *doṣas* shares the same characteristics as those that are innate. Indigestion of food, weakness, and abdominal distension [are such signs].
Emaciation, excessive belching, weakness in the thighs, scanty stools,
suspicion of *grahaṇī* disorder, jaundice, and abdominal enlargement— these are declared to be the premonitory symptoms for the aggravation of hemorrhoids.
The *doṣas*, having vitiated the skin, flesh, and fat, produce various forms of fleshy sprouts in the anal region and elsewhere; these they call hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*).
Those hemorrhoids characterized by a predominance of *vāyu* are dry, located in the anus, and accompanied by a tingling sensation.
They were withered, dark-brownish-red, stiff, pale, rough, and harsh;
they were dissimilar to one another, crooked, sharp, split open at their tips,
and resembled the fruits of the *bimbī*, *karkandhu*, date palm, and *karkoṭī* plants.
Some resemble the kadamba flower, while others are like mustard seeds;
they cause excessive pain in the head, sides, shoulders, waist, thighs, and groins (14),
and produce sneezing, eructation, constipation, heart disease, and loss of appetite.
They bring about cough, dyspnea, irregularity of digestion, ringing in the ears, and vertigo (15).
Afflicted by these, the patient voids feces that are knotted, scanty, noisy, accompanied by tenesmus, and mixed with painful froth and mucus; the stool is obstructed (16).
The skin, nails, feces, urine, eyes, and face become black,
and from that very cause, there arises the occurrence of abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīha), and prostate-like growths (aṣṭhīlā).
Those [piles] dominated by pitta have blue faces and appear red, yellow, or black.
The ulcers are thin, exuding a foul-smelling discharge, soft, and flaccid;
they resemble the tongue of a parrot, a piece of liver, or the mouth of a leech,
and they cause burning, suppuration, fever, perspiration, thirst, fainting, restlessness, and delusion.
They are hot to the touch, with a liquid, blue, warm, yellow, or reddish-black appearance;
they are shaped like barley grains in the middle, and their skin, nails, and other parts are green, yellow, or turmeric-colored.
These piles, dominated by blood, are located in the anus and possess the characteristics of pitta.
Resembling the sprouts of the banyan tree and similar to guñjā berries or coral,
they are extremely painful and hot; oppressed by dense feces,
they suddenly discharge blood due to its excessive flow.
Resembling a frog, he is afflicted by sufferings arising from the loss of blood; his complexion, strength, and enthusiasm are diminished, his vital energy is destroyed, and his senses are clouded.
His stool is dark-brown, hard, and dry, and the downward wind does not flow.
The blood of those with hemorrhoids is thin, reddish in color,
and frothy; if there is pain in the waist, thighs, and anus, along with excessive weakness, that indicates a secondary involvement of Vāta, especially if the cause was a drying factor.
If the feces are loose, white or yellow, unctuous, heavy, and cold;
if the blood from the hemorrhoids is thick, stringy, pale, and slimy; and if the anus is slimy, numb, heavy, and unctuous—these are the causes [of the condition].
In those cases of blood hemorrhoids, the wise should recognize an association with phlegm (kapha).
[The hemorrhoids] are dominated by phlegm, have large roots, are thick, cause mild pain, and are white;
they are protruding, elevated, unctuous, stiff, round, heavy, and stable. (27–28)

They are slimy, motionless, smooth, abundant with itching, pleasant to the touch, resembling the seeds of the *karīra* or the kernel of the *panasa* fruit, and like cow's teats; they cause pain in the groin and afflict the anus, bladder, and navel. (29)
They cause cough, dyspnea, nausea, excessive salivation, loss of appetite, and catarrh; they produce urinary disorders, difficulty in urination, heaviness of the head, and cold-fever;
and they bring about impotence, weak digestion, vomiting, and various disorders characterized by undigested matter (āma).

Fat, semen, phlegm, chyle, and feces are discharged with straining, yet they do not flow freely nor are they broken apart; the skin and other parts are pale and oily—these are the signs. One should recognize the conditions where two doshas are aggravated by the combination of their respective causes and symptoms. 32–33.
They say that all [types of hemorrhoids] are present in their entirety along with their innate characteristics (sahaja).
Indeed, those hemorrhoids born together with birth are terrible;
they are difficult to look upon, pale, rough, and reddish.
With those [vital breaths] turned inward, one becomes afflicted, emaciated, and has a feeble voice;
his digestive fire is diminished, his semen is depleted, and his body is bent with prominent veins;
he has few offspring, is prone to anger, and possesses a voice like that of broken bell-metal.
Disease of the head, eyes, ears, and nose is treated with internal applications, ointments, and affusions (36).
However, hemorrhoids that have arisen on the external fold, which are aggravated by a single doṣa and have not been present for long, are easily curable (37).
Those born from dual causes (dvandvaja) located in the second layer (balī), as well as those that have persisted for more than a year, they say are curable only with great difficulty (kṛcchrasādhya).
Those that are congenital (sahaja), those caused by all three humors (tridoṣa), and those located in the innermost layer are likewise difficult to treat.
They arise by depending on the [remaining] portions; one should designate them as incurable (39).

Because some portion of the life-span remains and because of the presence of all four pillars of treatment, they may be palliated for one whose digestive fire is blazing; otherwise, they are to be rejected as hopeless. (40)
He in whose hands, feet, mouth, navel, anus,
or testicles there is swelling, and who suffers from pain in the heart and flanks, is indeed incurable.
Pain in the heart and flanks, delusion, vomiting, body ache, and fever— [these symptoms indicate a fatal prognosis].

Thirst, anal fistula, and inflammation of the mouth destroy those afflicted by hemorrhoids (42). Indeed, [these treatments] eliminate hemorrhoids accompanied by swelling and diarrhea, as well as those suffering from thirst, anorexia, pain, excessive bleeding, and diarrhea (43).
In the penis and other regions as well, they will be described according to their respective origins; they resemble earthworms or mouths, and are slimy and soft.
Vyāna, having seized the phlegm, produces hemorrhoids on the exterior of the skin.
They know that [condition] as *carmakīla*, which is firm, hard, and resembles a wooden peg (45).
From Vāta, there is pricking pain and roughness; from Pitta, excessive redness;
and from Śleṣman, its oiliness, nodularity, and coloration consistent with the skin (46).

Or else, whatever food, drink, or medicine is conducive to the wind (*vāta*) and increases the strength of the digestive fire (*agni*), all that should be constantly consumed by those suffering from hemorrhoids. (47) Rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, and barley, along with ghee— these foods [should be eaten].
Or with goat’s milk, or with the juice of nimba and paṭola (48),
or with juices extracted from the roots and stalks of vārttāku, or with meat broth,
or with the leafy vegetables of jīvantī, upodikā, taṇḍulīyaka, and vāstuka (49).
Furthermore, by means of other prepared drugs that stimulate the fire and promote the passage of flatus, feces, and urine,
one may cure hemorrhoids characterized by loose stools, as well as conditions involving Vata-pain and diarrhea.
One should administer buttermilk with salt to facilitate the downward movement of flatus and feces.

Hemorrhoids do not grow again when struck by buttermilk (51). One should practice the regular consumption of buttermilk to increase strength, complexion, and digestive fire; when the channels are purified by buttermilk, its essence flows properly through them (52).
By that, nourishment, satisfaction, strength, and complexion are produced, and a hundred disorders of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) are averted. [The ingredients are:
cirabilva, agni, sindhūttha, nāgarendra, yava, and aralu. 53.
For one drinking with buttermilk (*takra*), the hemorrhoids fall away along with the blood.
To effect the cure of the disease of hemorrhoids (*arśas*), the physician should apply an ointment made from powdered turmeric mixed with milk of the *sudhā* plant. (54–55)

A paste of long pepper (pippalī), rock salt (saindhava), costus (kuṣṭha), the fruit of the śirīṣa tree, along with the milky sap of the sudhā plant or the milk of the arka plant, removes hemorrhoids (gudajā).
Alternatively, a powder of turmeric (haridrā) and jālinī mixed with mustard oil [is effective].
This excellent ointment is declared to be a destroyer of hemorrhoids (arśas).
By eating one pala of black sesame seeds with cold water, hemorrhoids are pacified and the teeth become firm. 57–58.
Or else, with surgical instruments or leeches, a wise physician, having observed that blood has accumulated in a swollen and hardened hemorrhoid, should remove it repeatedly.
(59) Kāsīsa, Saindhava salt, Kṛṣṇā, Śuṇṭhī, Kuṣṭha, and Lāṅgalī—
The physician should cook oil with *śilābhida*, *aśvamāra*, *dantī*, *jantughna*, and *citraka* (60), along with *tālaka*, *kunaṭī*, and *svarṇakṣīrī*,
using the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, and four times the amount of cow’s urine (61).
One should prescribe this as an ointment; for it falls away like an alkaline solution, acting as an alkali-therapy (kṣārakarman), yet it does not damage the folds of the skin.

[The powder consists of] ginger, long pepper, black pepper, cinnamon bark, cardamom, and small cardamom, ground into a powder with each subsequent ingredient increased in quantity by one over the preceding.
One should consume this powder in equal parts for the treatment of hemorrhoids, sluggish digestion, abdominal tumors, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and diseases of the throat and heart.
(63) The three groups of three [aromatics], *vacā*, asafoetida, *pāṭhā*, the two types of alkali, the two types of turmeric, *cavya*, *tiktā*, *kaliṅga*, *śakrāhvā*, and the salts; (64)
Granthi, bilva, and ajamoda—this group is considered to consist of twenty-eight [substances].
One should have these made into fine powders in equal parts. One should drink this powder, known as *viḍālapadaka*, with warm water.
Or a person should lick this powder mixed with castor oil (eraṇḍa-taila).
It destroys all types of hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi), as well as asthma, emaciation,
fistula-in-ano, pain in the heart, pain in the flanks, wind-tumors (vātagulma), and abdominal enlargement (udara).
It cures hiccups, cough, urinary disorders (prameha), anemia (pāṇḍuroga) with jaundice (kāmalā), āmavāta, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), hernia (antravṛddhi), and worms in the rectum;
as well as other disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa) that have been described by physicians.
This powder named Vijaya shall quickly destroy all of those [afflictions].
It is indeed a beneficial medicine for those afflicted by high fever, those whose minds are possessed by spirits, and for women who are childless. (69–70)
Take one part each of *marica*, great *auṣadha* (*viḍaṅga*), *citraka*, and *śūraṇa*, with each subsequent ingredient being double the amount of the preceding one;
the portion of jaggery (*guḍa*) should be equal to the total weight of all these ingredients. This well-known medicinal bolus (*modaka*) should be consumed;
it kindles the digestive fire and uproots diseases such as colic (*śūla*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). (71)
It completely eliminates elephantiasis and quickly destroys hemorrhoids.
(72) There are sixteen parts of *śūraṇa* (mountain ginger), eight parts of *mahauṣadha* (ginger), half that amount of *marica* (black pepper), and half again of that. (73)
One part each of triphalā, kaṇā, along with its root, tālīsāru, ūṣakara, and kṛmighna;
an equal portion of mahauṣadha; one-sixteenth part of dahanāṃśā; and tālamūlī;
and portions of śūraṇa equal [to the others], as well as vṛddhadāraka—these should be given. 74.
One should prepare a powder by combining bhr̥ṅgarāja with a portion of marica;

this bolus (modaka), mixed with double the amount of jaggery, should be consumed by those possessing great wealth who are devoted to heavy and aphrodisiac foods. For others, it would cause complications. 75–76.
By this [root], the fire of Agastya was formerly produced; by the king of herbs (yogarāja), that of Bhīma Māruti as well. By it, those two great eaters were brought under control.
Not only is the Śūraṇa root of great potency, but it is also the cause of digestive fire, strength, and complexion.

This [remedy] is a destroyer of hemorrhoids even without the use of surgical instruments, alkaline caustics, or fire (78). It removes swelling, elephantiasis, intoxication, and dysentery caused by phlegm and wind;
it destroys wrinkles and graying hair, promotes intelligence, and removes old age (79).

This elixir quickly destroys hiccups, cough, dyspnea, royal diseases (jaundice), urinary disorders, and severe splenic enlargement for men. Trivṛt, tejovatī, dantī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, citraka, and śaṭī— [80]
Gavākṣī, mustā, viśvāhva, viḍaṅga, and harītakī— these eight substances, each weighing one pala, along with eight palas of aruṣkara,
eight palas of vṛddhadāru, and sixteen palas of śūraṇa; 81–82.
One should boil [the ingredients] in two droṇas of water until reduced to one-fourth; then,
having filtered that decoction and added treacle three times the weight of the boiled substances,
one should cook it until it reaches the consistency of a paste that adheres to the stirring ladle.
After having [the patient] dismount from that [vehicle], one should then cause him to take these powders:
three palas each of *trivṛt*, the root of *tejovatī*, and *citraka*;
and six palas each of *elā*, *tvak*, *marica*, and *nāgāhvā*. (84–85)
Having ground thirty-two palas of this [substance] here, one should store it;
then one should administer the dose to those who, once it is digested, subsist on milk and meat broth.
It destroys all types of hemorrhoids as well as all forms of abdominal enlargement (udara).
It cures abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, anemia, and chlorosis; it kindles a sluggish digestive fire and eliminates consumption.
It is considered beneficial for obesity-related wind disorders, catarrh, and chronic rhinitis.
By means of this, men become free from disease for a hundred years;
they attain long life, procreative vigor, and are rid of wrinkles and grey hair.
This excellent *rasāyana* known as Śrībāhuśāla-guḍa is considered the best.
For this [remedy] has been seen to be the ender of leprosy (*durnāman*) when applied a thousand times over.
(90) As long as the mixture remains as thick as a spoonful of paste, or until the molasses becomes stringy;
and when, thrown into a vessel filled with water, the molasses does not float; (91)
When thrown [into the vessel], it remains motionless; when fallen, it does not dissolve.
This is proclaimed as the method of cooking for all types of jaggery (guḍa). One should consume one and a half palas of the jaggery pieces.
The physician has declared that the dosage prescribed by the sages is threefold: superior, middling, and inferior.
(93) Equal parts of sesame, bhallātaka, pathyā, and jaggery [taken together] destroy hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough, and remove splenic disorders, anemia, and fever. (94)
Abhayā (myrobalan) taken with jaggery quickly pacifies pitta and kapha, removes itching and abdominal pain, and destroys hemorrhoids when consumed.
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, Rudra, the great lord who holds a staff in his hand—
Seeking long life and freedom from disease, Nārada questioned the Lord:
"O Protector, out of compassion, you ought to describe for the sake of men a treatment for hemorrhoids by an easy means, without the use of surgical instruments, caustic alkalis, or fire. (96–97)
Having heard the words of Nārada, Śaṅkara, desiring the welfare of men, spoke of the most excellent medicine for the destruction of hemorrhoids (arśas):
"Taking one of the auspicious metals, such as pāṇḍya, vajra, and others..."

Having first rendered it stainless with iron sulfate (kunaṭī) and honey, one should smear it with a paste of *pattūra* root mixed with its juice; then, having placed it in the fire according to the rules, one should blow out the smoke using charcoal from the heartwood of a tree. 99–100.
And its flame must be suppressed with the juice of *triphalā*; then, once the consciousness has dissolved, one should raise it upward by means of a peg.
Having drawn it out into the purified juice of *triphalā*, one should blow upon it.
That iron which has not been properly filtered should be melted again by that same method and then quenched in a decoction of triphalā;
that iron which is not yet dead (not fully processed) should be boiled once more as before.
That which has not died despite the administration of the "death" [process] must be discarded like impure iron;
then, having dried it according to the rules, one should grind it in an iron vessel.
One should likewise rub it with iron on a stone until it is finely powdered.
Having placed [the substance] in an iron vessel or one made of clay with its interior smeared [with wax],
and having made it like mud with liquid juices, one should cook it over a fire of cow-dung.
One should apply the *puṭa* treatments in succession, separately, according to these rules.
The wise [should employ] triphalā, ādraka, bhṛṅga, and keśarāja (106); as well as mānakanda, bhallātaka, vahnī, and śūraṇa,
along with hastikarṇapalāśa and likewise kuliśa (107).
Having powdered it leaf by leaf, one should take sixteen *palas* of iron and an equal amount—plus one *pala* more—of *triphalā*.
When the decoction of that [triphala] is reduced to one-eighth, the wise man should cook [the iron] in it. (108–109)
Having taken eight *palas* of clarified butter in a vessel of iron or copper, one should stir it with an iron ladle according to the prescribed method.
Then, the expert in the rules of cooking [should proceed] when the clarified butter has become clear and risen to the surface.

One who knows the procedure for its preparation, having performed the auspicious rites of *kautuka* at the commencement, should administer the medicine according to its mild, medium, and other grades, or otherwise determine the degree of digestion;
then, one should lick it mixed with clarified butter and honey, starting from the dosage of a single *raktikā*.
Cow's milk is considered the best after-drink (*anupāna*) for those who are emaciated;
in the absence of cow's milk, that of a goat is recommended, along with unctuous and aphrodisiac foods.
This immediately stimulates the digestive fire and subdues *bhasmaka* (hypermetabolism). 113.

It destroys wind (vāta), bile (pitta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and irregular fever (viṣamajvara); it also cures abdominal tumors (gulma), eye diseases, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), drowsiness, lassitude, anorexia, colic,
chronic dyspepsia (pariṇāma), urinary disorders (prameha), and apabāhuka.
It cures swelling, hemorrhaging, and especially piles; it bestows strength, is nourishing, grants luster, awakens the voice,
lightens the body, and increases health and nourishment.
It bestows longevity, brings prosperity, and is auspicious, increasing strength and splendor.
It ensures the birth of a fortunate son, destroys wrinkles and graying hair, and is the enemy of hemorrhoids; it has been seen [to be effective] thousands of times by this name. 117–118.
By this, hemorrhoids are burnt away just as cotton is by fire;
when a man who consumes liquor—due to his delicacy and small stature—should be administered [the treatment] together with food that includes digested liquor and similar substances. (119)
The common quail (*lāva*), partridge (*tittiri*), francolin (*varttīra*), peacock (*mayūra*), hare (*śaśa*), and so forth;
the sparrow (*caṭaka*), the *kalaviṅka*, the *varttakā*, the *haritālaka*, the hawk (*śyenaka*), the large quail (*bṛhallāva*), and other such forest-scatterers (*vanaviṣkira*). 120.

The meat of wild animals such as pigeons and deer is auspicious. Among fish, the madgura, rohita, and especially the śakula are declared to be the "kings of fish," beneficial for those who consume them.
The fruit of the eggplant (vṛntāka) is recommended, as are the patola, the fruit of the bṛhatī, the pralamba, the abhīru, the tips of vetra reeds, the tāḍaka, and the taṇḍulīyaka;
likewise vāstūka, dhānyaśāka, citraka, and cakramardaka.
Coconut, dates, pomegranate, and the fruit of the lavalī; śṛṅgāṭaka, ripe mango, grapes, and palm fruits; nutmeg, cloves, betel nut, and betel leaves.
These items are beneficial for those who consume this iron;
however, one should not eat lakuca, kola, karkandhu, badara,
jambīra, bījapūra, tintiḍī, or karamardaka.
Meats from marshy regions, the *krakara* bird, and *puṇḍraka* fish;
the *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, *dātyūha*, *cāṣa*, *krauñca*, and *balākikā* birds; *mānakanda*, *kaserū*, *karaka*, and *kaliṅgaka*. 127–128.
One should especially avoid the kūṣmāṇḍaka, the karkoṭa, and the kramuka; as well as the kaṭuka, the kālaśāka, the kuṇṭuru, and the karkaṭī (129).
One should avoid all items beginning with the letter 'ka' and all leguminous pulses (dvidala) (130).
This [mantra], the certain destroyer of Durnāma, was proclaimed by Śaṅkara out of compassion for the king of the Yakṣas for the benefit of the worlds;
even Mount Meru shakes from its place and the earth is tossed about by the wind. 131.
If I have spoken falsely, then let the moon and the stars fall.
Those who kill Brahmins, those who are ungrateful, the cruel, those who speak untruths,
and those who revile their teachers must be avoided by a physician who abides in righteousness.
Viḍaṅga ground with the juice of *muni* (Trichosanthes) and soaked in the juice of *muni*, kept for a long time in the heat,

dissolves the defects of iron just as fire melts a lump of butter. When the impurities have been expelled over time, there is lightness in the abdomen, purity in the eructations, and [freedom from] wind.

There is no depression in his limbs; rather, there is clarity of mind as it reaches its full maturity. (135) The powder of krimiripu, licked together with the juice of vaṅgasena, certainly and without delay destroys the colic arising from indigestion of iron. (136)
If diarrhea should occur, one may overcome it by drinking milk;
however, an increase beyond twelve *guñjās* of this [medicine] is dangerous.
In cases of bleeding hemorrhoids (*raktārśas*), the physician should initially ignore the flow of blood.
When the toxic blood has been expelled, colic, abdominal distension, and blood disorders will no longer occur.
(138) A decoction of sandalwood and others:
sandalwood, kirātatiktaka, dhanvayavāsa, and nāgara, boiled together—
The barks of *dārvī*, *uśīra*, and *nimba* pacify hemorrhoids characterized by bleeding (139).

Hemorrhoids involving the flow of blood are alleviated by the habitual use of fresh butter and sesame seeds, by the habitual use of saffron, fresh butter, and sugar, and by the habitual consumption of the liquid from churned curd (140).

By licking fresh honey and butter combined with lotus filaments and sugar, one suffering from hemorrhoids (raktārśas) shall find relief. [141] One should consume boiled milk along with soups made of *satīna*, mung beans (*mudga*), *āḍhakī*, and lentils (*masūra*).
One should eat rice— whether *śāli*, *śyāmāka*, or *kodo*— with sour substances,
along with the meat of rabbit, deer, quail, grey partridge, and antelope;
and [one should use] *samaṅgā*, blue lotus, *moca*, *tirīṭa*, blue water-lily, and sandalwood.
One should administer goat’s milk that has been prepared [with medicinal herbs] for hemorrhoidal growths caused by blood (143).
A thread that has been repeatedly impregnated with the powder of *rajanī* and the milky sap of *snuhī*,
when tied very tightly, cuts away the hemorrhoids and fistula-in-ano (144).

In the case of hemorrhoids arising from the nose, the navel, and likewise those originating from the penis and other parts— these three types— one should apply the appropriate treatment to each respective location.
As for a flesh-thorn (carmakīla), one should excise it and then cauterize it with either caustic alkali or fire.

One suffering from hemorrhoids should avoid riding on the back of a woman, suppressing natural urges, using vehicles, sitting in a squatting posture, and foods that aggravate one's specific bodily humor (doṣa).
Thus ends the fifth section, the chapter on diseases. 5.147.
Now begins the sixth chapter on disorders of the abdominal fire (*jaṭharāgni*).
Due to the predominance of *kapha*, *pitta*, and *vāyu*, or due to their equilibrium, the abdominal fire is of four types: dull, sharp, irregular, and even. (1)

Even a very small quantity of food eaten does not digest for one with weak digestion; instead, there may be vomiting, exhaustion, salivation, and heaviness of the head and abdomen. Even an excessive quantity of food eaten is digested easily by one with sharp digestion.
For this very reason, it is held by some that a sharp digestive fire is the best; indeed,
even a moderate amount of food eaten by a person with a diseased digestive fire may sometimes be properly digested, and sometimes it is not digested at all.
From that [disorder], flatulence, upward movement of wind, colic, heaviness of the abdomen, tenesmus, diarrhea, and rumbling in the intestines may occur.
When food is taken in a moderate quantity by one whose digestive fire is balanced, it is properly digested.

Among all these, the balanced digestive fire (*samāgni*) is said to be the best. That fire by which food is digested even when one eats excessively heavy food despite indigestion, or even while sleeping during the day, is the most excellent.
A sharp digestive fire produces disorders arising from pitta, while an irregular fire produces those caused by vāta;
likewise, a weak fire produces disorders originating from kapha.
This occurs in men who eat food that causes excessive pain and is dry, when kapha is diminished and vāta and pitta are increased.

Because this excessively aggravated fire, accompanied by wind, reduces consumed food to ashes in an instant, it is therefore known as *bhasmaka*; and if neglected, it consumes the bodily tissues (*dhātus*), producing thirst,
perspiration, burning sensations, fainting, and other symptoms arising from hypermetabolism.
Having quickly digested the food, it certainly and swiftly destroys the tissues (dhātus) and other elements.

Due to excessive drinking of water, irregular eating, suppression of natural urges, and the reversal of sleep patterns, even food that is timely, wholesome, and light does not undergo proper digestion in a person. (10–11)
Food consumed by one overwhelmed by thirst, fear, and anger; by one who is greedy; by one afflicted by disease and dejection; or by one possessed by hatred, does not reach proper digestion.
Those who lack self-control eat like animals, without moderation.
Indeed, indigestion (ajīrṇa) is the root of the host of diseases that afflict you.
For the most part, indigestion arises in humans from an imbalance of diet; it is the source of the multitude of diseases, and through its destruction, they perish. (13–14)

Malaise, heaviness, distension, vertigo, numbness from wind (māruta), constipation, or even the onset of movement—these are the general symptoms of indigestion (ajīrṇa). Undigested food (āma) is classified as threefold: fermented (vidagdha), obstructed (viṣṭabdha), and associated with phlegm, bile, and wind respectively.

Some maintain that there is a fourth type of indigestion (ajīrṇa) resulting from the residue of tastes; some say there is a fifth type of indigestion which is free from morbid humors and digests within a day;
and they speak of a sixth type of indigestion, which is natural and occurs every day.
In that condition, there is heaviness and nausea in the stomach, swelling in the cheeks and the eye-sockets,
and undigested food is expelled as eructations exactly as it was eaten (18). When [the food] is digested, there is vertigo, thirst, fainting, and various pains arising from pitta.
In Udāvarta, eructation accompanied by smoke and acidity occurs, as do perspiration and a burning sensation.
In Viṣṭabdha, there is colic, flatulence, various types of Vāta-pain, non-passage of feces and flatus, stiffness, delusion, and pain in the limbs. (19–20)
When the essence (rasa) remains undigested, there arises an aversion to food, as well as impurity of heart and heaviness.
Fainting, delirium, vomiting, excessive salivation, lassitude, and vertigo—
these complications arise from indigestion, and death may also occur.
The three types of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) described as *āma*, *vidagdha*,
and *viṣṭabdha* give rise to *visūci*, *alasaka*, and also *vilambikā*.
In *visūci*, the wind (*anila*) remains within, piercing the limbs as if with needles.
When this occurs due to indigestion, it is designated by physicians as *visūcī*. Those who eat in moderation and are learned in the scriptures do not suffer from it;
rather, it is the deluded, those who have no self-control, and those greedy for food who contract it.

Fainting, diarrhea, vomiting, thirst, colic, giddiness, cramps, yawning, burning sensations, discoloration, tremors, pains in the heart, and a splitting sensation in the head occur in that state; furthermore, there is loss of sleep, restlessness, shaking, suppression of urine, and loss of consciousness. (26)
These are the five terrible and dreadful complications of visūcī:
the abdomen becomes excessively distended, the patient faints and groans, and the obstructed wind courses upward within the belly. (27–28)
If one's flatus and feces are excessively suppressed,
that too is declared to be alasaka; furthermore, when one has thirst and eructations,
and food neither passes downward nor upward and does not undergo digestion.
Remaining in the abdomen and having become sluggish, he is therefore known as *alasa* (the sluggish one).

One who has dark teeth, lips, and nails; whose consciousness is diminished; who suffers from vomiting; whose eyes are sunken inward; whose voice is weak; and whose joints are all loosened—that man shall return again [to life]. (30–31)
When food that has been consumed by the deranged *kapha* and *vāyu* neither moves upward nor downward,
those ancient experts in the scriptures call that condition *vilambikā*, which is extremely difficult to treat.
(32) [The signs of cure include] clarity of eructation, energy, and the timely evacuation of natural urges.
Lightness of body and the absence of hunger and thirst are the signs that food has been digested (33).
Harītakī, as well as ginger, when consumed regularly with jaggery or combined with rock salt, serves to kindle the digestive fire (34).
One should always consume ginger, long pepper, and myrobalan as the third, or pomegranate with jaggery, in cases of undigested food (āma), indigestion, anal diseases, and constipation.
One should likewise take the powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa), danti, trivṛt, citra, and the root of kṛṣṇā.
One should eat that powder mixed with jaggery upon rising in the morning.

This preparation, known as Guḍāṣṭaka, increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire; it destroys edema, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and colic, and removes diseases of the spleen and anemia.
Cumin, ajamoda, rock salt, dry ginger, and black pepper, taken with sour buttermilk for seven days, produce fire in the digestive system and are supreme for destroying anemia and hemorrhoids.
In that condition, emesis is indicated when there is undigested matter (āma), while fasting is beneficial when the food is partially digested (vidagdha).

In the case of *viṣṭabdha*, sudation is recommended, and one should lie down when only the essence remains. In the case of undigested matter (*āma*), emesis with water mixed with *vacā* and salt is praised;
or alternatively, one may drink the paste of *kaṇā*, *saindhava*, and *vacā* with cold water.
Or the wise physician should administer water prepared with *dhānyaka* and *nāgara*,
which pacifies indigestion due to undigested food (*āmājīrṇa*), destroys colic, and cleanses the bladder.
When there is suspicion of indigestion in the morning, then [one should take] *abhayā* with *nāgara* and rock salt.

Having consumed this powder with cold water, one may eat food at the proper time without hesitation and in moderation. But for one whose food causes a burning sensation immediately after eating, and whose heart and throat burn intensely,
one shall find relief by licking a mixture of *abhayā*, sugar, and honey.
Equal parts of the three pungents (trikaṭuka), ajamodā, rock salt (saindhava), and the two types of cumin (jīraka), with one-eighth part of asafoetida (hiṅgu) added;

this powder, when consumed with ghee at the first mouthful of food, generates digestive fire and destroys diseases of wind (vāta). Two types of alkali (kṣāra), citraka, pāṭhā, karañja, and the salts [are to be used].
Sūkṣmailā, patra, bhārgī, kṛmighna, hiṅgu, pauṣkara,
śaṭī, dārvī, trivṛt, musta, vacā, indrayava, vṛkṣāmla, jīraka, dhātrī, śreyasī, and upakuñcikā. (45–46)
Amlavetasa, amlīkā, yavānī, and devadāru; abhayā, ativiṣā, śyāmā, hapuṣā, and aragvadha in equal parts (47);
along with tila, muṣkaka, śigru, kokilākṣa, and palāśa.

Having made fine powders of alkaline substances and iron dross (lauha-kiṭṭa) that have been heated and sprinkled with cow’s urine, one should prepare them in equal parts; then, using the juice of *mātuluṅga*, it acquires a radiance like a blazing fire. 48–49.

For three days, this powder—which generates intense digestive fire and possesses a radiance equal to a blazing flame—should be taken with fermented gruel (śukta) or fresh vegetable juice (ādrakarasena) according to the prescribed method; it quickly destroys all diseases. (50)
It cures indigestion, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids,
as well as hernia, abdominal enlargements, prostate enlargement, and gout; it dispels aggravated humors and kindles the extinguished digestive fire.
Having taken snuhī, arka, citraka, eraṇḍa, varuṇa, punarnavā, sesame, apāmārga, kadalī, palāśa, and likewise tintiḍī—
one prastha of these— burn them so that they become entirely ash. 53.
That which is to be cooked in one *laḍaka* [of liquid] until only a quarter remains, should be well-strained while still clear, then combined with one *prastha* of salt;
once cooked until firm and free of smoke, it should be ground again into a fine powder. (54–55)
One should mix that [powder] with half a *pala* each of powdered *yavānī*, *jīraka*, *vyoṣa*, *sthūlajīraka*, and *hiṅgu*;
then one should saturate it with the juice of fresh ginger and dry it again.
One should drink that powder in the morning with cold water in the proper dose; once it has been digested, one should eat food with soups made from the meat of wild animals,
slightly sour, salty, lukewarm, and digestive-stimulating.
By this, the digestive fire increases, as do strength and health;
for in that regard, buttermilk is recommended as a post-prandial drink and is beneficial in meals for those with weak digestion, hemorrhoids, and disorders of wind and phlegm. (59)
In cases of urinary calculi, gravel, and diseases of the feces, urine, and wind (vāta),
the wise should employ eight karṣas of sea salt (sāmudra-lavaṇa),
five karṣas of black salt (sauvarcala), and one karṣ each of biḍa salt, rock salt (saindhava), and coriander (dhānyaka).
The wise physician should prepare two karṣas each of these: pippalī, pippalīmūla, patraka, kṛṣṇajīraka, tālīśa, keśara, cavya, and likewise amlavetasa. (62)
Take one karṣa each of black pepper (marica), cumin (jīraka), and ginger (viśva); four karṣas of pomegranate (dāḍima); and half a karṣa each of cinnamon (tvak) and cardamom (elā).
All of this, when ground into a powder, is the salt known as Bhāskara. (63–64)
One should consume one śāṇa of this with buttermilk, whey, or sour gruel;
it cures gulma arising from vāta and kapha, as well as splenic enlargement, abdominal disease, consumption, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, skin diseases, constipation, and fistula-in-ano.
This [preparation] destroys colic, swelling, dyspnea, cough, intoxication-related disorders, and heart disease;
it also cures urinary stones, gravel, anemia, and worms, as well as weak digestion; it is an excellent digestive stimulant and carminative. (66–67)
Created by Bhāskara for the welfare of all the worlds,
this [formula] undoubtedly destroys all types of indigestion immediately upon ingestion.
It consists of saindhava, samūla, māgadha, kṣavī, anala, nāgara, and pathyā.
This powder, named Vaḍavānala, consists of [the aforementioned ingredients] increased in sequence as the fire increases.
(69) The powder made from Pathyā, Nāgara, Kṛṣṇā, Karañja, Bilva, and Agni, combined with an equal amount of sugar, digests even a heavy over-meal like the Vaḍavānala fire. (70)
Cardamom, cinnamon, and nagapushpa increase in quantity by one unit each;
black pepper, long pepper, and ginger increase by four, five, and six units respectively.
For as many units as there are of these ingredients, there should be the same number of white sugar. (71)
This powder should be employed as a supreme stimulant for the digestive fire (agni-sandīpana).
Take two palas of purified sulphur, one pala of mercury, and likewise two karṣas each of iron and copper, all of which have been processed with fire. 72–73.
Having pulverized everything and mixed it together, one should melt it thoroughly by means of fire; once it is completely liquefied, one should pour it onto the leaves of the *pañcāṅgula* plant (54).
Then, having pulverized all of that again, one should place it in an iron vessel.
One should add one hundred palas of strained jambīra juice to it;
having placed it on the stove, one should cook it carefully with a mild fire.
When that juice has become thickened, one should dry it and then grind it into a powder.
An infusion of *pañcakolaka* together with sour gruel (*cukra*) should be used for saturation (*bhāvanā*) therein; thereafter, one should dry it slowly.
Then, one should mix it with an equal amount of roasted *ṭaṅkaṇa* powder.
One should also process it seven times with equal parts of *marica* and half as much *viḍa*, using the acidic water of *caṇaka* beans; then,
having dried it and ground it finely, one should place it inside a sealed jar.
This elixir, named Kravyāda, was formerly taught by the yogi Bhairavānanda to the King of Siṃhala, who consumed much meat;
one should consume two māṣas of this elixir at the end of a meal.
After consuming the essence, one should afterwards drink buttermilk with rock salt (saindhava).
Whatever food has been eaten that is excessively heavy or even in excessive quantity—all that is digested quickly by the consumption of this essence. 81–82.
This juice named Kravyāda undoubtedly destroys colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, splenic disorders, and abdominal enlargement (83).
[One should take] the three alkalis, mercury, sulphur, and the five pungent spices (pañcakola) in equal parts.
Equal parts of *jayā* fried with all [the preceding ingredients], and half as much *jaṭā* produced from *śigru* (84)—
one should macerate all this for three days in the heat using only the juices of *jayā*, *śigru*, and *vahni*. Then, one should cook it in a mild *puṭa* (85).
The juice of *mārkava*, rubbed with the juices of *mārkava* itself, becomes *jvālānala*.
A *niṣka* of this, licked with honey and followed by a drink of jaggery and ginger, destroys indigestion, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and weak digestion. (86)
It conquers phlegm, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and loss of appetite.
(87) Take one part each of ṭaṅkaṇa, mercury, and sulphur, three parts of poison, and one part each of cowrie-shell, svarjikā-kṣāra, māgadhī, and viśvabheṣaja. (88)

Each one karṣa of these substances, ground for a day with the sour juice of *jambīra* fruits, is an effective remedy here; it becomes "Agnikumāraka" (the Fire-Child) for the pacification of *visūcī*, colic, wind disorders, and weak digestion. 89
Mercury, mercury-cinder, cloves, and sulphur—two parts each—mixed with black pepper;
to this, one-half part of nutmeg is added and ground with the juice of tamarind.
Taken in a dose of one *māṣa* as a post-digestive tonic, this Rāmabāṇa pill is a rejuvenative elixir.
When eaten with *bilva* leaves and black pepper, it immediately increases the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). Vata is destroyed by the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍikā*;
Pitta is destroyed by water boiled with coriander (*dhānyaka*); and *vāsā* removes the three humors (*tridoṣa*). 91.
A pill made from *śleṣmā*, *sindhuharītakī*, and a decoction of *paunarnava* destroys phlegm, abdominal disease, swelling, and anemia; it is a destroyer of the pain of those afflicted by disease.
The elixir known as *Rāmabāṇa* is renowned for curing weak digestion and the ten-mouthed [demon]—that is, consumption. 92.
One should conquer Saṅgrahaṇī, Kumbhakarṇaka, Āmavāta, Khara, and Dūṣaṇa [by this remedy].

When administered with black pepper as an after-drink (anupāna), it instantly kindles the digestive fire, improves the relish for food, destroys the host of phlegm disorders, and eliminates asthma, cough, vomiting, and parasites. 93–94.
One *pala* of tamarind alkali and these two types of five salts, each measuring one *pala*,
should be thoroughly ground with the juice of small lime fruits;
then, when that has been ground, one *pala* of conch-shell fragments [should be added].
One should cast it seven times here as well according to that same procedure.

(95) Three parts of the three pungents (*kaṭukatraya*) measuring one *pala*, half a *pala* each of *vacā* and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), mercury (*rasa*) and sulfur (*gandhaka*) joined with twelve parts of poison (*viṣa*) measuring half a *pala*—this is what has been stated. (96)
One should prepare pills of this [medicine] the size of a jujube stone;
by its regular consumption in equal doses, all types of indigestion are pacified, as well as all abdominal enlargements, colic, choleraic disorders, and various other ailments. (97)
Śaṅkhavaṭī is always beneficial for cases of weak digestion (agnimāndya) and abdominal tumors (gulma).
One should take the salts derived from snuhī, arka, ciñcā, apāmārga, rambhā, tila, and palāśa, taking one pala of each of these. 98–99.
Five different types of salts, each weighing one *pala*, should be taken;
along with *svarjikā* (sajji salt), *yavakṣāra* (barley alkali), and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax)—these three together weighing one *pala*.
Having thus prepared the entire mixture of thirteen *palas* as a fine powder, [one should proceed].
One should pour that [mixture] into a *prastha* measure of lime juice;
having heated a *pala* of conch-shell fragments in fire, one should quench them there seven times, whereby everything dissolves as follows. 101–102.
One should take three *palas* of ginger, two *palas* of black pepper,
one *pala* of long pepper, half a *pala* of fried asafoetida, and likewise *granthika*, *citraka*, *yavānī*, and cumin. (103)

Take two karṣas each of nutmeg (*jātīphala*) and clove (*lavaṅga*); likewise, one karṣa each of mercury, sulphur, poison, borax, and realgar. Having finely powdered all these, one should mix them together. (104–105)

One should have pills made for him with half a *śarāva* of fermented gruel (*cukra*), each weighing one *māṣa*; this is known by wise physicians as the *Bṛhacchaṅkhavaṭī*. (106) It pacifies all types of indigestion and wards off all colic pains.
It brings about the immediate destruction of visūcī, alasaka, and other such ailments.
(107) Equal parts of ṭaṅkaṇa, kaṇā, amṛtā, and hiṅgu, along with two parts of marica, should be made into pills with lime juice. (108)
One should consume one or two pills, resembling a pea,
for the certain alleviation of indigestion, for the increase of the digestive fire, and for the destruction of phlegm.
Drinking water with the root of *apāmārga* destroys *visūcikā*.
Water boiled with *kāravelī* and oil indeed destroys *visūcikā*.
A decoction of the root of *bāla*, combined with the powder of *pippalī*,
is the best destroyer of *visūcī* and an excellent stimulator of the digestive fire.
A decoction of *bilva* and *nāgara* destroys vomiting and *visūcikā*;
a decoction of *bilva*, *nāgara*, and *kaṭarī* is even more efficacious in its qualities.
Having added *vyoṣa*, the fruit of *karañja*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the root of *mātuluṅgī*, [one should prepare the remedy].
A pill made from these, dried in the shade, destroys visūcī when used as an eye-salve (113).
Equal parts of apāmārga leaves and black pepper, ground with the saliva of a horse and applied as an eye-salve, destroy visūcikā (114).
When *visūcī* has become excessively aggravated, one should employ buttermilk with an equal amount of water,
or coconut water, for the preservation of life. [Alternatively,
one may use] a paste made from cinnamon bark, *tvak*, *patra*, castor seeds, *kaśīśa*, *śigru*, and *kuṣṭha*, ground with sour liquids, along with *vacā* and *śatāhvā*.
Anointment (udvartana) destroys both khallī and visūcikā; likewise, oil cooked with those same ingredients serves the same purpose.
(116) A paste of kuṣṭha and saindhava, prepared in oil along with *śukra*, when used for massage during visūcikā, relieves the pain of khallī. (117)
Likewise, in cases of thirst or nausea, water infused with cloves or nutmeg is recommended;
or, O noble one, water boiled with *bhadradāru* or *musta* may be drunk.
When food is disturbed by excessive salivation and spitting, it does not pass through the body.

If his heart is oppressed, one should diagnose that as *utkleśa* (nausea/disturbance). Or, if there is pain with a distended abdomen, one should apply a plaster made of sour flour-paste along with *dāru*,
*haimavatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, *hiṅgu*, and rock salt.

Barley powder mixed with buttermilk, taken warm and containing alkali, destroys pain in the abdomen; or likewise, fomentation may be applied using jars filled with steam, or by other means such as heated boluses.
This same course of treatment applies to both Vilambikā and Alasaka.
For this very reason, no separate medical treatment has been prescribed for those two.
One should pacify that *bhasmaka* with food and drink that is heavy, unctuous, dense, cold, and stable, as well as with *pitta*-subduing purgatives. (122–123)
For the pacification of an extremely violent fire [in the body], one should consume buffalo curd, milk, and ghee;
likewise, one should repeatedly eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) prepared with ghee in milk mixed with ground barley,
which serves as a meal that removes bile.
One should administer milk boiled with *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* as a purgative (125).

Whatever food is sweet, intellect-promoting, phlegm-increasing, or heavy—all that is beneficial for those with excessive digestive fire; furthermore, sleeping during the day after eating such food [is likewise beneficial] (126).
Having eaten milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with goat’s milk and white lotuses along with white rice,
a person who has subsisted on meager food for ten days becomes fully satisfied by that.
The fruit produced from the plantain tree is sufficient for the ripening of a jackfruit.
For the ripening of plantain, ghee is beneficial even for the wise (128).
For the complete cooking of ghee, the juice of the citron is beneficial (129).
They know that rice is the immediate ripener of coconut fruit and palmyra seeds.
Milk itself is beneficial for ripening mangoes; likewise, alkali, marrow, and *harītakī* are helpful.

(130) For the ripening of *madhūka*, *mālūra*, *nṛpādāna*, *paruṣaka*, date palms, and *kapittha*, the seed of the *picumanda* tree should be drunk; it is equally wholesome when added to ghee or even to buttermilk. (131)
Date palms and water chestnuts are praised; likewise, the universal medicine (ginger) and *bhadramusta* are auspicious in certain cases.
Among the fruits of the sacrificial tree (*yajñāṅga*) and the Bodhi tree, those from the *plakṣa* tree are recommended when soaked overnight and well-drained.
With rice, milk is used; with milk-rice, *dīpyaka* (coriander) combined with long pepper (*kaṇā*) is employed. 132.

*Ṣaṣṭika* rice is digested with curd-water, and *karkaṭī* is digested among flowers. (133) Wheat, black gram, *harimanthaka*, *satīna*, and green gram are quickly cooked by means of *mātulapuṭraka*. For dates, lotus stalks, *kaśeru*, sugar, and *śṛṅgāṭaka*, as well as for sweet fruits, *musta* is recommended. (134)
Kaṅgu, śyāmāka, nīvāra, and kulattha grains digest without delay when taken with curd or water; however, pulses (vaidala) are digested with sour gruel (kāñjika).
One should cook flour-based foods with cold water, and kṛsarā with rock salt.
Black gram, *iṇḍarī*, nimba fruit, milk-rice, and mung-bean soup; 136. a *vaṭaka* with *vesavāra*, *lavaṅga*, and *phena*; *paparṭa* together with the seed of the drumstick tree (*śigru*);
from the root of *kaṇā* comes the cooking of *laḍḍuka*, *apūpa*, *saṭṭa*, and so forth, as well as *śaṣkulī* and *maṇḍa*. 137.
What is surprising in this? One who eats fish and meat would be happy from drinking sour gruel (kāñjika).
But it is truly wonderful that the fish reaches full digestion by means of meat cooked solely over fire!
Raw mango fruit is beneficial for the fish, while its seed is beneficial for the meat. 138.
Turtle meat indeed undergoes digestion quickly when treated with alkali from barley.
Having eaten the flesh of pigeons, doves, peacocks, and grey partridges, one who drinks the well-ground root of *kāśa* grass shall become comfortable; this has indeed been observed many times.
All types of meat are quickly cooked with milk and the juice of sesame stalks;
likewise, *cañcūka*, white mustard, and *vāstuka* are cooked with a decoction of *gāyatrīsāra*.
[The same applies to] *pālaṅkikā*, *kebu*, *kāravellī*, eggplant, bamboo shoots, and radish.

Upodika, alabu, and paṭola are digested by siddhārthaka; and megharava is likewise cooked with it. Śūraṇaka is digested with jaggery, and similarly, aluka with rice-washing water. Piṇḍāluka is digested by koradūṣa, and kaśeru is indeed said to be digested by nāgara.
Oil undergoes digestion quickly from salt, rice-water, ghee, sour jambīraka, and even from black pepper; likewise,
milk is digested by buttermilk, and that substance [is digested] by lukewarm *maṇḍa*.
Buffalo curd is digested by *māṇimantha* and conch-shell powder;
mango is digested by the three pungents (*vyoṣa*); sugar-candy by the consumption of ginger;
sugar by ginger and *musta*; and likewise sugarcane by the juice of *ārdrikā*. (145–146)

One should quickly apply jarāmarā and red sandalwood as prescribed by the sages; likewise, a collection of alkaline substances becomes digested by acids. Gold or silver, heated repeatedly in fire and then plunged into water seven times, [purifies] that water.
If there is indigestion after drinking water, one should take honey; *bhadramusta* is especially effective for that. 148.
Thus ends the sixth chapter on disorders of the digestive fire.
Now begins the seventh chapter on the disease of worms. 7.
Worms are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being external or internal.
The external ones are of four types, arising from impurities, phlegm, blood, and feces;
among them, those born from impurities are of twenty varieties by name.
In size, shape, and color they are like sesame seeds; they reside in the hair and on the skin.
Known by the names *yūka* and *likhya*, they are many-legged and minute.
These two types cause eruptions (*koṭha*), pustules (*piḍikā*), itching, and swellings.

One who eats while suffering from indigestion, consumes sweet and sour foods, is fond of meat, partakes of flour-based foods and molasses, avoids physical exercise, sleeps during the day, and eats incompatible foods, contracts worm infestations.
[The symptoms are: fever, discoloration, colic, heart disease, lassitude, and vertigo.
Aversion to food, diarrhea, and the symptoms of worms have arisen.
(6) Those born from phlegm arise from meat, black gram, molasses, milk, curd, and fermented gruel.
(7) Born from phlegm in the stomach, they grow large and spread everywhere.
Some resemble broad plows, some are like earthworms;
others have the shape of sprouting grain, or are thin and long, or minute.
They are white or have a coppery luster; thus, by name, they are of seven kinds.
The *antrādā*, *udarāveṣṭa*, *hṛdayādā*, *mahāguda*, *cyurava*, *darbhakusuma*, and *sugandha* [worms] cause nausea,
salivation, indigestion, and loss of appetite.
Fainting, vomiting, fever, constipation, cough, sneezing, and catarrh—
these indeed arise from blood when caused by incompatible foods, indigestion, leafy vegetables, and the like.
These minute creatures born of blood reside in the blood-carrying vessels.
Prapāda, Vṛtta, and Tāmra—some of these are invisible due to their subtlety.
Keśāda, Lomavidhvaṃsa, Romadvīpa, and Udumbara—these six share the same function as Kuṣṭha and have Saurasa as their mother. 13–14.
Those born from feces arise from black gram flour, sour substances, salt, jaggery, and leafy vegetables (15).
Originating in the colon, they spread downwards;
when increased, they may turn toward the stomach.
Then his eructations and breaths follow the odor of feces;
they are broad, round, thin, and thick, and are dark-brown, yellow, white, and black.
These five are known by name as the *kakeruka* and *makeruka* worms.
The *sausurāda*, known as *salūna*, and *lelihā* worms produce diarrhea,
colic, constipation, emaciation, roughness, pallor, horripilation, loss of digestive fire, itching of the anus, and movement along abnormal pathways.
A person should drink rice-scum (*anna-maṇḍa*) combined with *viḍaṅga* and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
This [diet] is for the destruction of worms and for the increase of the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni).
Daily food that is pungent and bitter destroys phlegm (kapha), eliminates worms, stimulates the appetite, and is supreme for kindling the digestive fire. 18–19.
Water boiled with *viḍaṅga* and sprinkled with *viḍaṅga* powder, when drunk,
is seen to destroy worms and conquer diseases born of worms. Alternatively, one should lick *viḍaṅga* powder with honey to destroy worms.

One should drink the juice of the palāśa seed mixed with honey, or one should drink the paste of that seed with honey; this destroys worms. Half a karṣa of kampilla powder, when consumed with jaggery, [achieves the same].
It will undoubtedly cause all the worms residing in the abdomen to fall out.
(22) A person should grind together the seeds of *viḍaṅga*, the seeds of the *kauṭaja* tree, and likewise the seeds of the *palāśa* tree, and eat them with sugar-candy to destroy the worms. (23)
One should drink the juice extracted from nimba leaves mixed with honey,
or likewise that produced from dhattūra leaves, which is an excellent destroyer of worms. When combined with mercury (rasendra), the juice of dhattūra leaves [becomes] a supreme remedy.
Alternatively, a paste made from betel leaves also destroys lice.
Oil cooked with the paste of *dhattūra* leaves and its juice, when used merely as an oil massage, destroys lice in an instant. (25-26)

This treatment has been described for worms arising from feces and phlegm; however, for those born of blood, one should effect their destruction through the treatment prescribed for skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Furthermore, [the authors] recommend milks, meats, clarified butters, curds, and vegetables.
One desiring to destroy worms should especially avoid sour and sweet tastes.
(28) Thus ends the seventh chapter on the treatment of worm diseases.
Now begins the eighth chapter on the treatment of anemia, jaundice, and chlorosis. (8)
Five types of jaundice (pāṇḍuroga) are recorded: three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha;
the fourth by the combination of all three (sannipāta); and the fifth from the ingestion of earth (mṛdbhakṣaṇa).
[The causes are: sexual intercourse, sour things, salts, wine, earth, sleeping during the day, and excessively sharp substances.

For one who indulges in [these], the humors (doṣas), having corrupted the blood, lead the skin to a pale-white condition. Skin eruptions, spitting, lassitude of the limbs, eating earth, abnormal vision, swelling of the eyelids, yellowness of the feces and urine, and indigestion are the precursors of that which is about to arise.
In the disease of Vāta-pāṇḍu, there is a rough, dark, or reddish-brown appearance of the skin, urine, eyes, and other parts, along with trembling, pricking pain, flatulence, giddiness, and so forth.
In [the Pitta-type], the skin, nails, feces, and urine are yellow, accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, and fever.
A person suffering from Pitta-type anemia (pittapāṇḍvāmaya) has loose stools and an excessively yellow complexion.
One with Kapha-type anemia has excessive salivation, swelling, drowsiness, lethargy, and extreme heaviness;
due to the Kapha, the skin, urine, eyes, and face become white.

In one who consumes all types of food, all the corrupted humors (doṣas) produce a form of anemia (pāṇḍuroga) arising from the three doṣas, manifesting the symptoms of all three and being extremely difficult to endure.
In one whose habit is to eat earth, any one of the humors becomes aggravated.

Astringent [tastes] aggravate wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), while sweet [tastes] aggravate phlegm (kapha). They disturb the soft tastes and others due to their dryness, and they dry up what has been eaten.
Furthermore, being undigested, they fill the channels and even obstruct them.
By destroying the strength of the sense organs, as well as their brilliance, vigor,
and vitality, [the consumption of earth] quickly causes anemia (pāṇḍuroga), which destroys strength, complexion, and digestive fire.
From eating earth, one becomes pale and afflicted by drowsiness and laziness.
Afflicted by cough, dyspnea, and pain, and constantly accompanied by anorexia; with swelling of the eye-sockets, cheeks, and eyebrows, and swelling of the feet, navel, and penis;
with worms in the abdomen, he suffers from diarrhea characterized by stool mixed with blood and phlegm.

A patient suffering from anemia (pāṇḍuroga) who is afflicted by fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and exhaustion due to the three doṣas, and who is emaciated with impaired senses, should be abandoned.
Anemia that has been long-standing and has become chronic does not succeed in treatment.

One whose body is swollen due to the long duration of the disease, or who sees yellow things; one who passes small amounts of feces that are greenish and mixed with phlegm while suffering from diarrhea;
one who is dejected, whose limbs are smeared with sweat and other secretions, and who is afflicted by vomiting, fainting, and thirst—[such a person is incurable]. (14–15)
One who has pale teeth and nails, whose eyes are pale,
and who perceives everything as a pale mass, perishes from jaundice.
One who is swollen at the extremities with a sunken middle, or likewise withered at the extremities with a swollen middle, [perishes].

One who desires fame should avoid a patient suffering from *pāṇḍu* (anemia/jaundice) who has swelling in the anus, mouth, penis, and scrotum; who is fainting and nearly unconscious; as well as one afflicted by diarrhea and fever.
Furthermore, a patient with *pāṇḍu* disease who excessively consumes *pittala* (pitta-aggravating) substances [will perish].
Having burnt his bile, blood, and flesh, it leads to disease. His eyes become intensely turmeric-yellow, as do his skin, nails, and face;
his feces and urine are yellowish-red, he takes on the color of a frog, and his sensory faculties are destroyed.

Afflicted by burning sensations, indigestion, weakness, exhaustion, and loss of appetite, this condition characterized by jaundice and excessive bile is considered to reside in both the visceral tract (koṣṭha) and the peripheral tissues (śākhā). When it becomes chronic over time, it is known as Kumbhakāmalā, which is difficult to cure.

Afflicted by vomiting, loss of appetite, nausea, fever, and exhaustion, one who suffers from asthma and cough perishes; likewise, one with diarrhea, jaundice (kumbhakāmala), blackish or yellowish feces and urine, and extreme swelling [perishes]. 22.22.120–121ab.
One whose eyes, face, vomit, feces, and urine are reddened, who faints,

and who is afflicted with burning sensations, loss of appetite, thirst, exhaustion, drowsiness, and delusion— having lost both digestive fire and consciousness— a patient suffering from jaundice (kāmalā) will indeed perish quickly. (23–24)
When, however, the complexion of the patient becomes greenish, dusky, or yellowish,
and there is loss of strength and enthusiasm, drowsiness, weak digestion, mild fever, lack of desire for women, body ache, dyspnea, thirst, anorexia, and vertigo; 25.
Then one should recognize that condition as *halīmaka*, arising from wind and bile (26).
For the purpose of pacifying *pāṇḍu* disease, a person should drink iron powder that has been processed with cow’s urine for seven nights, along with milk (27).
For one who eats iron filings processed with cow’s urine along with jaggery, jaundice and even severe digestive colic (paktiśūla) go to destruction.
Iron dross, well-heated and repeatedly processed with cow’s urine, [is likewise effective]. 28.
Having licked [this] combined with honey and ghee, one suffering from jaundice shall become well.
(29) Punarnavā, trivṛt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), viḍaṅga, devadāru, citraka, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, triphalā, dantī, cavya, and kaliṅgaka; (30)
Take one pala each of kaṭukā, pippalīmūla, musta, śṛṅgī, kāravī, yavānī, and kaṭphala; these should be equal in measure.
Add double the amount of maṇḍūra relative to the powder, and cook it in eight times the quantity of cow’s urine.
Having made balls (vaṭaka) with jaggery and mixing them with buttermilk, one should drink them.
This Punarnavādi-maṇḍūra-vaṭaka, prepared by Aśvin, quickly destroys anemia (pāṇḍuroga), jaundice (kāmalā), and chlorosis (halīmaka). 32–33.

By its regular use, it certainly destroys dyspnea, cough, consumption, fever, edema, as well as abdominal enlargement, colic, splenic disorders, flatulence, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, worms, gout, and leprosy. (34)
Trivṛt, Triphalā, mastu, viḍaṅga, and likewise citraka—
these [five] in nine parts each, along with nine parts of purified iron (hatāyasa).
This powder, all combined together, a person should take in a dose of eighteen raktikās.
One should lick it with honey and ghee, or drink it with buttermilk;
or one may drink it with cow’s urine, which will destroy anemia (pāṇḍuroga),
as well as edema, heart disease, abdominal worms, skin diseases, and fistula-in-ano.
One who has an abundance of phlegm should also lick [the powder] with the juice of Ārdra-ka to destroy weak digestion, piles,
and anorexia; or one may use the juice of Triphalā, Guḍūcī, Dārvī, or Marica.
A decoction mixed with honey, when cooled, removes jaundice (39).
For those afflicted by jaundice, the juice of *droṇapuṣpī* is beneficial as an eye-salve;
alternatively, one suffering from jaundice should drink the paste of *guḍūcī* leaves with buttermilk (40).
Myrobalan, iron filings, the three pungents (vyoṣa), turmeric, honey, ghee, and sugar,
when licked together, quickly ward off even severe jaundice. For the type of jaundice known as Kumbhakāmalā, however, the treatment prescribed for jaundice is beneficial.
One suffering from *kumbhakāmala* should drink *śilājatu* with cow urine (42).
The residue of burnt *akṣa* wood, cooled by immersing it eight times in cow urine, should be powdered and licked with honey; this quickly destroys the disease known as *kumbha-pāṇḍu*. (43)
The water of *kumārikā* instantly removes the affliction of jaundice when used as a nasal drop (44).
One should drink iron powder that has been processed (*mārita*) and combined with the powder of *mustā*, along with a decoction of *khadira*, to destroy *halīmaka* (chlorosis) (45).
One should lick iron powder mixed with honey and ghee, along with sugar, sesame, balā, yaṣṭimadhu, triphalā, and the two types of rajanī, for the cure of halīmaka (jaundice).
Ghee prepared with the juice and paste of amṛtalatā (gudūcī) and turagavidviṣ (mustā) [is also effective].
One should administer four times this amount of milk to those suffering from halīmaka and ārti;
one should treat him with sweet foods and drinks that alleviate vāta and pitta, and one should also apply here the therapeutic measures prescribed for jaundice (kāmalā) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga). 47–48.
A decoction made from triphalā, amṛtāvāsā, tiktā, bhūnimba, and nimba, when combined with honey, destroys halīmaka as well as the diseases of pāṇḍu and kāmalā.
(49) [The powder of] tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, musta, viḍaṅga, cavya, and citraka—
Take two palas each of the bark of *dārvī*, the mineral *mākṣika*, *granthika*, and *devadāru*. Having prepared these separately as powders,
add twice that amount of purified *maṇḍūra* powder, which resembles collyrium in appearance.

Having cooked it in eight times its quantity of urine, a person should add to that [mixture] balls (vaṭakas) shaped like udumbara fruits; these should be consumed with buttermilk according to one's digestive fire, and once digested, a wholesome meal should be taken.
These Maṇḍūra pills indeed bestow life upon those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu);
they pacify skin diseases, abdominal enlargement, edema, stiffness of the thighs, disorders of phlegm, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, and splenic enlargement.
Kirātatikta, devadāru, dārvī, mustā, guḍūcī, kaṭukā, paṭola,
durālabhā, parpaṭaka, nimba, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), the three fiery fruits (vahniphala-trika),
and the fruit of viḍaṅga— these in equal parts, along with iron powder equal to the total weight of all these ingredients. 55.
The physician should prepare pills with ghee and honey and administer them with buttermilk as an after-drink (anupāna).
These [pills] destroy anemia (pāṇḍu), chlorosis (halīmaka), edema, urinary disorders (prameha), diseases of the digestive tract (grahaṇī),
asthma, cough, hemorrhagic disorders, hemorrhoids, loss of speech, and rheumatism (āmavāta).
Through its application, it cures ulcers, abdominal tumors, phlegmatic abscesses, vitiligo, and leprosy (57).

For these conditions, the diet is recommended to consist of barley, wheat, and śāli rice, along with beneficial meat broths of wild animals and soups made from mung, āḍhakī, masūra, and other pulses (58).
Thus ends the eighth chapter on Anemia (pāṇḍuroga), Jaundice (kāmalā), and Chlorosis (halīmaka).
Now begins the ninth chapter on Hemorrhagic Fever (raktapitta): Through excessive indulgence in heat, physical exercise, grief, travel, and sexual intercourse, [the disease arises].
Pitta, aggravated by pungent, hot, alkaline, salty, sour,
and bitter substances, quickly burns the blood through its own qualities.
Thereupon, the blood flows upwards, downwards, or in both directions.
When aggravated, it flows upward through the nose, eyes, ears, and mouth; downward through the penis, vagina, and anus; and through all the pores of the skin.
[Its symptoms are] lassitude, a desire for cold things, a sensation of smoke rising in the throat, and vomiting.
In this [condition], the breath has the smell of iron;
it will be thick, pale, oily, slimy, and associated with phlegm (kapha).
That which is caused by wind (vāta) is dark-red, frothy, thin, and dry. 4–5.

The blood-bile (raktapitta) type has the appearance of a decoction, is black, resembles cow's urine, or has the luster of dark charcoal smoke and collyrium; the bilious (paittika) type possesses these characteristics. The combined (sānnipātika) type exhibits all three sets of symptoms due to the conjunction of their respective signs.
That which moves upward is associated with *kapha*, while that which moves downward follows *vāta*;
thus, it proceeds through two pathways by means of both *kapha* and *vāta*.
[Its complications include] debility, dyspnea, cough, fever, vomiting, intoxication, pallor, burning sensations, and fainting.

After eating, there is a terrible burning sensation, as well as constant instability and incomparable pain in the heart; thirst, a splitting sensation in the abdomen, a scorching heat in the head, spitting of pus, aversion to food, indigestion, and even morbid changes may occur—these are the complications of raktapitta. 8.
A disease following from a single doṣa is curable; one involving two doṣas is said to be palliable;
that which involves three doṣas is incurable, as is one occurring in a person with weak digestion or excessive force.
A disease moving upward is curable, one moving downward is palliable, and one that has reached both directions simultaneously is incurable.
