That which occurs in one who has a body emaciated by diseases, or in an old man who does not eat, is incurable; however, blood-bile (raktapitta) that arises from a single channel, is not excessively forceful, is newly manifested, and appears at a favorable time, may be curable provided there are no complications.
That which resembles the washing of flesh, or like boiled [meat], or like mud-water; that which is similar to fat, pus, or blood; or like liver, or with the luster of a ripe jambu fruit;
that which is black, or blue, or even intensely putrid—wherever these and other such morbid changes are described.
That hemorrhagic disease (raktapitta) which is free from distress and shines like the bow of the Lord of the Gods (Indra),
and that by which a person afflicted with raktapitta perceives both visible objects and the sky as red— that is undoubtedly incurable. 12–13.
One who vomits blood profusely, has reddened eyes,
and sees blood in his eructations, dies from a hemorrhage caused by pitta.
Since the flow of pitta-blood is strong when it has already set in, one should not attempt to arrest it at the very beginning in a patient who possesses strength.
It causes heart disease, anemia, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fever, and so forth.
For those suffering from *raktapitta*, the diet should consist of *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *nīvāra* wild grain, *koradūṣa* millet, *prasādhikā*, *śyāmāka* millet, and *priyaṅgu*. (15–16)
Masūra, mudga, caṇaka, along with kuṣṭha and the seeds of āḍhakī,
are recommended when prepared as soups or broths for those suffering from raktapitta.
Furthermore, the wise physician should also provide pomegranate and āmalaka for the purpose of providing sourness.

The tender leaves of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa* (18) are beneficial as vegetables for those accustomed to a vegetable diet; likewise, *taṇḍulīya* and other such greens are wholesome. Pigeons, doves, quails, and *raktākṣa* partridges (19) [are also recommended].
One should know that the juices of the śaśānka, piñjala, eṇa, hariṇa, and kālapuccha deer remove blood-bile (raktapitta); one should employ these juices,
slightly sour or non-sour, fried in ghee, and seasoned with rock salt.

If Kapha is the secondary humor (anuga), one should administer vegetable soups; if Vata is the secondary humor, one should give meat broth (rasa). As wholesome food, one may take rice with vegetable soup along with parched grain flour (saktu) mixed with sugar. A cold infusion (hima) made from coriander, emblic myrobalan, vāsā, grapes, and parpaṭa [is also beneficial].
It destroys internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fever, burning sensation, thirst, and emaciation. 23.
A decoction of hrībera, utpala, dhānya, candana, yaṣṭikā, amṛtā, uśīra, and trivṛt, taken with honey and sugar, [achieves the same]. 24.
One should have this drunk immediately, for by it hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta) is destroyed;
it conquers severe raktapitta, as well as thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
[The ingredients are] the filaments of lotuses and water-lilies, pṛśniparṇī, and priyaṅgu. (25)
In that juice, a gruel prepared with water should be given to those suffering from *raktapitta*.
The juice extracted from *vāsā* leaves, taken with honey and sugar—whether as a fresh juice or a decoction—when drunk, removes even the most severe *raktapitta*. (26–27)
The cold, sweet juice obtained from the *puṭapāka* method using ground leaves of the *vṛṣa* plant removes *raktapitta*, cough, fever, and consumption.
Blue water-lily, white water-lily, lotus, *kahlāra*, and red water-lily—

And Madhuka—this group [of drugs] removes pitta-blood disorders, thirst, and vomiting. (29) While Vāsā exists, and while there is hope for life, why should one suffering from internal hemorrhage, consumption, or cough despair? (30)
A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, combined with sugar, honey,
and clarified butter, destroys all types of dyspnea and *rakta-pitta*.
(31) [Likewise,] *dūrvā* grass, blue lotus stamens, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *sailavāluka*...

One should cook one *prastha* measure of ghee with one *karṣa* each of *śītā*, cool *uśīra*, *musta*, *candana*, and *padmaka*. One should add four times as much water as rice and goat’s milk. (32–33)
If that [medicine] comes out as blood from the mouth, one should administer it as nasal drops (*nāvana*); if it passes through the nostrils, one should fill the ears with it;
and if blood flows from the eyes, one should fill both eyes with it. (34)
If [the disease] manifests in the penis or the anus, one should employ enema treatments;
if it manifests in the pores of the skin, one should apply massage with that [medicated ghee].
Therefore, this ghee is the best remedy for all types of *raktapitta*.
One should powder grapes, sandalwood, *lodhra*, and *priyaṅgu*;
this powder should be drunk together with honey and the juice of *vāsā*.
It [removes] the forceful discharge from the nose, mouth, anus, vagina, penis, and so forth. (37)
This proven king of formulations stops the flow of *raktapitta*;
even blood that gushes forth with force as if from a wound inflicted by a weapon is brought to a halt when dusted with this powder. (38–39)
The central joints of sugarcanes along with the root-bulb, blue lotus,
the filaments of the white lotus, with *mocā*, *madhuka*, and *padmaka* (40),
as well as the shoots and sprouts of the banyan tree, grapes, and dates;
One should prepare a decoction from these [drugs] in equal parts;
having let it stand overnight, one should administer it mixed with honey and sugar.
This quickly subdues prameha and rakta-pitta. 41–42.
Milk boiled with *drākṣā*, *phalinī*, or with *priyāla*, *madhuka*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *śatāvarī* conquers [the disease] born of blood.
[Likewise, milk boiled with] ripe *udumbara*, *kāśmarya*, *pathyā*, *kharjūra*, and *gostana* [is effective]. 43.
When licked with honey, each of these separately destroys *raktapitta*.
Or, one whose blood has flowed excessively should drink blood mixed with honey;
or he should eat the liver of a goat, or meat combined with bile. 44–45.
Blood flowing from the nose is stopped by a plaster applied to the head consisting of *āmalaka* fruit ground finely and fried in ghee,
which acts like a dam against the force of water; or, when blood flows from the nose, one should quickly drink water with sugar through the nostril.
One should drink either grape juice with milk and ghee, or sugarcane juice with sugar, or a cold infusion [of grapes].
For nasal administration (nasya), the juice of pomegranate flowers, or that derived from dūrvā grass, or from mango stones, or from onions, conquers bleeding from the nose. 47–48.
Having taken a large, old, and thick fruit of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd,
one should render it empty of its seeds, receptacle, seed-skin, and fibers (verse 49).
Then, having weighed it, one should cook it in two *tulās* of water.
When that water is reduced by half and carefully cooled,
one should press those pieces of pumpkin with a firm cloth;
having diligently extracted that liquid, one should set it aside for cooking again.
One should dry the *kūṣmāṇḍa* in the heat of the sun and then place it in a copper vessel;
having poured a *prastha* of ghee into it, one should fry the *kūṣmāṇḍa* therein. Observing that it has taken on the color of honey, one should then pour water into it.
Having added an equal quantity of sugar there, one should cook it like a linctus (lehya).

When well-cooked, one should add two palas each of long pepper (pippalī), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and cumin (jīra), along with half a pala each of coriander (dhānyaka), cinnamon leaves (patra), cardamom (elā), black pepper (marica), and cinnamon bark (tvaca).

One should add the powder of these [drugs] there, and incorporate half a *pala* of ghee and honey; one should consume this in a dose of one *pala*, or according to the strength of one's digestive fire (55).
This *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍa-leha* destroys *raktapitta*.
It certainly destroys bile-fever, thirst, burning sensations, menorrhagia, emaciation,
vomiting, cough, dyspnea, heart disease, hoarseness of voice, chest wounds, and consumption;
furthermore, it is nourishing, strength-increasing, and promotes growth.
Having taken a large, firm, and mature fruit of the *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, one should remove its seeds, the inner lining of the seed-vessel, and the fibers until it is hollowed out.
Then, having cut it into very fine pieces, one should cook its pulp in a quantity equal to its own weight.
One should slowly cook one *tulā* of fresh cow's milk over a mild fire;
[add] one and a half *tulās* of sugar, one *prastha* of cow's ghee, half a *prastha* of honey, and one *kuḍava* of coconut. 59–60.
One should add two palas of the pulp of *priyāla* fruit, one pala of *tikhurī*,
and one [pala] of sugar; having cooked this well like a linctus (*leha*),
the physician, observing that it is properly prepared, should remove it from the fire.
When it has become lukewarm, one should throw the powder of these [substances] into it; I shall now state what they are:
one part each of akṣa, śatapuṣpā, kṣīrī, yavānikā, gokṣura, kṣuraka, pathyā, and the fruits of kapikacchu. (62–63)

The seventh [ingredient] is the bark of all [the trees]; then, separately for each pair of eyes, there are coriander, long pepper, nut-grass, ashwagandha, shatavari, talamuli, nagabala, balaka, patra, and shati. (64)
Jātīphala, lavaṅga, sūkṣmailā, bṛhadelikā, śṛṅgāṭaka, and parpaṭaka—one pala each of all these;
as well as candana, nāgara, dhātrīphala, and kaśeruka. 65–66.
One should add five *karṣas* each of these four, along with two *palas* of *uśīra*, *masana*, and *uṣaṇa*. This electuary of *kūṣmāṇḍa*, when consumed in a dose of one *pala*, [yields great results].
Or rather, by consuming it according to one's digestive strength, it destroys diseases such as internal hemorrhage (raktapitta),
cold-pitta (śītapitta), acid-pitta (amlapitta), loss of appetite (arocaka), weak digestion (agnimāndya) accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, and dysentery (pradara). 68–69.

This linctus is also supreme for treating hemorrhoids, vomiting, anemia, jaundice, venereal sores, erysipelas, and chronic or irregular fever; it is highly aphrodisiac, nourishing, and increases strength.
It should be carefully placed in a new earthen vessel.
One hundred palas of the fresh juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* (bottle gourd), an equal amount of cow’s milk, and eight palas of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) powder [are to be combined]. 71–72.
One should cook it over a mild fire until it becomes as solid as a ball;
then, one should add sugar equal to the weight of an emblic myrobalan (*dhātrī*) and lick half a *pala* of it afterwards.
Indeed, this *khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍaka*, when consumed regularly, removes [diseases].
Śatāvarī, chinnaruhā, vṛṣa, muṇḍatikā, balā, tālamūlī, gāyatrī, and likewise the bark of triphalā [cure] rakta-pitta, amla-pitta, burning sensations, thirst, and jaundice. (74–75)
Five *palas* each of *bhārgī* and *puṣkaramūla* should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-eighth;
this may be used for [the treatment of] a snake killed by a divine herb or even one killed by honey.
Twelve palas of powdered gold and iron should be given,
along with sixteen palas of ghee equal in quantity to the sugar-candy; the wise should cook this in a copper vessel until it reaches the consistency of jaggery.
Half a *prastha* of auspicious *aśmajatuka* (bitumen) should be given with honey; likewise, one *pala* each of *śṛṅgī*, *kṛṣṇā*, *viḍaṅga*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *ajājī*;
and [one *pala* each of] *triphalā*, *dhānyaka*, *patra*, *kaṇā*, *marica*, and *keśara*.

Having added the powder and thoroughly stirred it, one should store it in a greased vessel. One should administer it at the appropriate time in a dose the size of a cat's paw (biḍālapada), followed by cow’s milk as an after-drink; meat broth or milk may also be consumed. 80–81.

Guru (heavy), vṛṣya (aphrodisiac), and nourishing foods and drinks, as well as unctuous meat and other strengthening substances, [cure] rakta-pitta (hemorrhagic disorders), consumption (kṣaya), cough, and especially pain in the flanks (pārśva-śūla);

82 as well as vāta-rakta (gout/rheumatism), prameha (urinary disorders), śīta-pitta (chill-induced skin eruptions), vomiting, fatigue, swelling (śvayathu), anemia (pāṇḍu-roga), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and likewise splenic enlargement (plīhodara). 83
It destroys constipation, urinary discharge, and acid bile;
it is beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, aphrodisiac, auspicious, and increases joy.
It is the best for bestowing health and sons, and it increases desire, the digestive fire, and strength. 84.
Śrīkara, lāghava, and khaṇḍaka are thus proclaimed.
One should employ the meat of the goat, the pigeon, the partridge, the krakara, the hare, the kuraṅga, and the black antelope. 85–86.
Drinking coconut milk, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *vāstuka*, dried radish, *jīvā*, *paṭola*, the fruit of *bṛhatī*,
*vārtāka*, ripe mango, dates, and sweet pomegranate. 87.
Meat preceded by the letter 'ka' and that which originates from marshy regions (anūpa) must be especially avoided by one who consumes [the elixir], such as the *khaṇḍaka* and other varieties;
here too, processes such as smelting (*puṭana*) are desired, just as in the case of other metals.
Furthermore, killing [the mercury] is indeed not accomplished by honey alone nor by mica alone.

(89) One should take the paste of the root of *śatāvarī*, four times the amount of that paste of milk, and cow’s ghee equal in measure to the milk, along with sugar equal in measure to the paste. (90)
One should cook that remaining ghee and always administer half a *pala* of it as a linctus;
this indeed destroys *raktapitta*, *amlapitta*, consumption (*kṣaya*), and asthma (*śvāsa*). 91.
Thus ends the ninth chapter on *Raktapitta*. 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter, on Amlapitta and Śleṣmapitta.

Those who consume food and drink that is incompatible, corrupted, sour, burning, and provocative of pitta, have their pitta aggravated; the wise declare that to be Amlapitta, which was previously accumulated by its own specific causes.
The physician should declare *amlapitta* by its lack of digestion, fatigue, distress, bitter and sour belching, heaviness, burning in the heart and throat, and loss of appetite;
*amlapitta* is said to be of two types: that which moves downward and that which moves upward.

The wind (vāta), when accompanied by phlegm (śleṣman) and rasa, flows downward in various ways, appearing green, yellow, blue, black, or reddish-brown, exceedingly clear, resembling fish-water, or extremely slimy,
and it causes thirst, burning sensations, fainting, dizziness, and delusion.
It sometimes causes nausea, urticaria, internal heat, exhaustion, exhilaration, perspiration, and yellowness of the skin;

it may occur whether food has been digested or not yet eaten, and occasionally produces vomiting of bitter and sour matter, as well as belching of the same nature, along with burning sensations in the throat, heart, and abdomen, and pain in the head. 4–5.

It produces burning and heat in the hands and feet, great loss of appetite, and fever; it generates phlegm and bile, as well as a multitude of diseases including itching, circular rashes, pustules, and swellings.
One should recognize that [the condition] may be accompanied by wind, or by wind and phlegm, or by phlegm alone.
A wise physician should recognize that [condition] as being caused by the signs of the humors (doṣas), for it produces delusion.
Trembling, delirium, fainting, tingling sensations, exhaustion of the limbs, and piercing pains,
as well as visions of darkness, confusion, extreme bewilderment, and sudden joy— these occur when [the mind] is joined with Vāyu.

Excessive expectoration of phlegm, heaviness, lethargy, loss of appetite, coldness, exhaustion, a sense of being smeared, burning sensation, loss of strength, itching, and excessive sleep— these are the signs when Amlapitta is associated with Kapha.
These same signs, occurring together, would also be present when it arises from both Vata and Kapha.
This disease called *amlapitta* is successfully cured with effort if it is recent;
if it has arisen for a long time, it becomes palliable, and in some cases, it is difficult to cure.
It causes bitter, sour, and pungent eructations, as well as a burning sensation in the heart, abdomen, and throat.
Darkness, fainting, loss of appetite, vomiting, lethargy, headache,
salivation, and a sweet taste in the mouth are the symptoms of Śleṣmapitta (11).
In the case of Amlapitta, however, emesis should be induced using Paṭola, Ariṣṭa, and Vāsaka.
The physician should likewise administer purgatives with honey, sugar-cane products, and rock salt (saindhava).

The wise practitioner should remove [the humors] moving upward through emetics and those moving downward through purgatives, using a powder of *trivṛt* mixed with honey and the juice of *dhātrī* fruit.
One should drink preparations of barley and wheat, devoid of pungent seasonings,
along with parched grain flour (lāja) or groats (saktu), mixed with sugar and honey as appropriate;
or water boiled with dehusked barley, mung beans, and *dhātrī* (myrobalan), combined with the three aromatics (*trigandha*) and honey.
It very quickly removes the vomiting produced by *amlapitta*.
The leaves of *chinnodbhava*, *nimba*, and *paṭola*, mixed with honey and drunk in various forms, destroy that most dreadful *amlapitta* just as a thunderbolt destroys a fully grown palm tree. 15–16.
A decoction of vāsā, amṛtā, parpaṭaka, nimba, bhūnimba, mārkava, triphalā, and kulaka, taken with honey, destroys amlapitta (acid gastritis).

O Śivapāla, a linctus made from pāṭhā, paṭola, yava, candana, dhānyaka, dhātrī, vāsā, varāṅga leaves, nāgakeśara, and abhayā, combined with sugar, ghee, and honey, destroys amlapitta, as well as loss of appetite, fever, burning sensations, and emaciation. It also cures vomiting, nausea, burning sensations, fainting, alopecia, urinary disorders, cold sores, and defects of the semen caused by amlapitta.
By constantly consuming this with the juice of *āmalakī*, even an old man shall become youthful and full of desire for pleasure.
One hundred palas of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* juice should be taken, along with an equal amount of cow’s milk and eight palas of powdered *dhātrī*. 19–20.
One should add two *palas* of cow's clarified butter to an equal amount of black *dhātrī* (emblic myrobalan) and cook everything over a gentle fire until it becomes a solid mass.
One should consume half a *pala* or one *pala* of this daily.
Khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍaka is renowned as an excellent remedy for acid bile (amlapitta).
One should cook one kuḍava of coconut in water over a mild fire;
if coconut water is unavailable, one should cook it in cow's milk.
One should add one *ṭaṅka* each of powdered coriander, long pepper, musta, and the four aromatics (*cāturjāta*) to that [milk] once it has cooled; this,
when consumed daily by men in a dose of one *pala* or even half a *pala*, [yields great results].
This slice of coconut bestows virility, sleep, and strength.
It quickly destroys acid gastritis (amlapitta), hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), colic born of digestion (pariṇāma-śūla), and consumption (kṣaya), just as dry wood is consumed by fire.
One *prastha* of finely ground coconut, crushed on a stone,
along with half an *āḍhaka* of seedless pieces of pumpkin,
should be eaten together with meat in two *kuḍavas* of clarified butter. (27)
Then, one should pour one *āḍhaka* measure of pure cow’s milk into that, and likewise add two *prastha* measures of high-quality white sugar;
the physician should cook all these together over a gentle fire. (28–29)
When it is well-cooked and cooled, one should add the following ground ingredients:
small cardamom, coriander, āmalakī, parpaṭa, water-lily, and lotus stalks (30), as well as usīra, sandalwood, raisins, śṛṅgāṭa, and kaśeruka.
Two karṣas each of cinnamon bark, cardamom, and camphor should be taken separately;
one should mix them all together and preserve them in a new earthen vessel. One should consume one pala of this in the morning, according to one's digestive fire.
When consumed, this undoubtedly destroys these diseases:
acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), fever, bile disorders, hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), loss of appetite, gout (vātarakta), thirst, burning sensations, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and jaundice (kāmalā). 33.
It quickly destroys consumption and colic born of indigestion (pariṇāmaja).
This "Nārikela-khaṇḍa" was proclaimed of old by the Aśvins;
it bestows complexion, promotes corpulence, is aphrodisiac, and grants virility, sleep, and strength.

Abhayā, pippalī, drākṣā, sita, dhānyaka, and vāsaka, taken with honey, destroy burning in the throat and are excellent for removing pitta and śleṣman. Paṭola, yava, dhānyāka, pippalī, and āmalaka [likewise serve this purpose].
A decoction of these [drugs] combined with honey is supreme for removing pitta and kapha (37).
A decoction of ginger and paṭola is an excellent stimulant of digestion and digestive aid that cures vomiting due to pitta and kapha, itching, urticaria, eruptive boils, and burning sensations (38).

A bolus (modaka) prepared from equal parts of long pepper (pippalī), sugar-candy (khaṇḍa), and yellow myrobalan (pathyā), when consumed, removes pitta and phlegm (śleṣman) and destroys weak digestion (vahnimāndya).
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the section on Amlapitta and Śleṣmapitta. 10.
Now begins the eleventh chapter on consumption (rājayakṣmā).
Consumption, a disease arising from the three doṣas, is produced by four causes: suppression of natural urges, wasting away, reckless conduct, and irregular diet.
Because the physician strives with great effort against this disease on behalf of those afflicted by it,
it is called *yakṣmā* in the world by those expert in the science of grammar; and because this malady, they say, befell King Candramas.
Therefore, the wise call it *rājayakṣmā*;
because it causes the depletion of functions, it is called *kṣaya* by the learned;
and because it dries up the bodily fluids and so forth, it is designated as *śoṣa*.

When the channels of rasa are obstructed by doshas dominated by kapha, or when semen is depleted due to excessive sexual indulgence, all the other dhatus subsequently become depleted; consequently, the person withers away. (5)

In the case of impending consumption (śoṣa), there occur labored breathing, weakness of the limbs, expectoration of phlegm, dryness of the palate, vomiting, loss of digestive fire, intoxication, catarrh, cough, and excessive sleep; furthermore, that person has white eyes, is devoted to meat, and is full of lustful desire. In dreams, he sees crows, parrots, gallinules, peacocks, vultures, as well as monkeys and lizards.
They carry him away; he sees rivers devoid of water and trees withered, afflicted by wind, smoke, and forest fires.
Heat in the shoulders and sides, burning sensations in the hands and feet, and fever affecting the entire body—these are the symptoms of *rājayakṣman*.
Loss of appetite, aversion to food, fever, dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis,
and hoarseness of voice arise in the sixfold form of *rājayakṣman*. Hoarseness results from *vāta*, while pain and contraction of the shoulders and flanks also occur.

Fever, burning sensation, diarrhea, and the discharge of blood mixed with bile; a feeling of fullness in the head, aversion to food, cough, and hoarseness of the throat—these are to be recognized as arising from the provocation of phlegm (kapha). 10–11.
One who desires spotless fame should abandon a person afflicted by consumption, whether accompanied by these eleven symptoms, or even six, or three— namely, fever, cough, and diseases of the blood.

One who possesses all three types of swelling, or even two, when there is a loss of muscle mass and strength, should be rejected; however, one with all symptoms may still be treated if the condition is otherwise. One who eats excessively while wasting away and is afflicted by diarrhea [should also be rejected].
One should avoid a person with swollen testicles and an enlarged abdomen who suffers from consumption (yakṣman).
Consumption destroys a man in this world who has white eyes, who hates food, who is oppressed by upward-breathing (ūrdhvaśvāsa), and who voids urine copiously with great difficulty. (15–16)

If a young man afflicted by consumption, though treated by skilled physicians, should live for even a thousand days, he must be one who is free from persistent fever, strong, and capable of enduring medical treatment. 17.
One should treat a self-controlled man who has a strong digestive fire and is not emaciated (verse 18).
Now hear the characteristics of those suffering from consumption due to sexual excess, grief, old age, physical exercise, or travel, as well as those with chest wounds and ulcers (verse 19).
One emaciated by sexual excess is afflicted by the symptoms of seminal depletion;
his body becomes pale and his bodily tissues (dhātus) waste away as before. One emaciated by grief is likewise characterized by a tendency toward brooding and drooping limbs.
Not exhibiting any disorders caused by the loss of semen, he is characterized as one with wasting due to old age; he is emaciated, with diminished vigor, intellect, strength, and sense faculties;
he trembles, has swollen calves, and his voice is broken like that of a cracked bronze vessel. (21–22)
Afflicted by heaviness and loss of appetite, he spits out phlegm that is deficient [in quality]; his mouth, nose, and eyes are constantly discharging; his complexion is dry, parched, and withered.
His limbs are emaciated from the exhaustion of travel, and his skin is scorched and rough. (23)
With the limbs and parts of the body numb, with the *kloma*, throat, and mouth parched (24),
one who is excessively emaciated by physical exertion, and who possesses these very symptoms as well as those produced by chest-wounds— even in the absence of a wound (25).
From the loss of blood, from painful sensations, and likewise from the restriction of food, consumption (śoṣa) may arise in one who has been wounded; and that is considered most incurable.
[This occurs] in one who exerts himself with a bow or carries a heavy load.
While fighting with the powerful, or falling from a precarious height;
while restraining a charging bull, a horse, or another animal to be tamed; or while hurling blows of stone, wood, and rock at others and striking them down. (27–28)
For one who is reciting too loudly, or traveling a long distance quickly,
or crossing a great river, or running with horses, or suddenly leaping far away, or even dancing rapidly— 29. [In these cases, the breath is disturbed.]
Likewise, in one who is severely afflicted by other cruel karmas, or who is excessively attached to women, or who eats food that is rough, scanty,
or irregular, a powerful disease arises when the chest is wounded.
The chest is excessively pained, split, and torn asunder;
likewise, the sides are oppressed, the limbs wither, and one trembles.
Gradually, vigor, strength, complexion, appetite, and digestive fire decline. (32)
Fever, pain, mental depression, diarrhea, and likewise the suppression of the digestive fire; moreover,
as he repeatedly coughs, there flows forth a large amount of phlegm that is foul-smelling, dark-brown, yellow, clotted, and mixed with blood.
In the case of chest injury (kṣata), there is excessive wasting; likewise, due to the depletion of semen and ojas, there occurs pain in the chest, vomiting of blood, and specific cough.
In the case of general emaciation (kṣīṇa), there is the passing of blood-stained urine and stiffness in the sides, back, and waist.
Due to the obstruction of the wound, depletion, and likewise from the digestive tract (koṣṭha) being affected by morbid humors,

foul-smelling breath issues forth during the digestion of food in one with chest injury. This condition is curable when it is recent, occurs in a strong person with mild symptoms and a stimulated digestive fire.
One should treat [the patient] for a full year, yet one must avoid all [excessive] signs [of strength].
For a strong patient with abundant *doṣas*, one should administer the five procedures;
however, for a consumptive patient whose body is emaciated, those same procedures would be like poison. (37–38)

The strength of men depends on the waste products, and their life depends on the semen; therefore, one should diligently protect both the waste and the semen in a patient suffering from consumption (yakṣman).
Rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and others are beneficial.
For those who are emaciated, wines, meat of wild birds and animals, and wholesome foods are beneficial.
One should drink the unctuous goat broth, combined with long pepper (pippalī), barley, horse gram (kulattha), ginger (nāgara), pomegranate, and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka). (40–41)
By this, six disorders such as chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) and others are averted.

Meat weighing twice the quantity [of the grain], water eight times [the quantity of the meat] from all sides, and clarified butter (ājya) equal to one-fourth [the quantity of the meat], when prepared together, is called a six-ingredient broth (ṣaḍaṅga-yūṣa). 42–43.

The powder of *kakubha* bark, *nāgabalā*, and *vānari* seeds, drunk with milk along with honey, ghee, and sugar, cures consumption (*yakṣman*) and cough. Goat meat, goat’s milk, and goat’s ghee, combined with ginger, [are likewise beneficial].
One who consumes goat's meat and sleeps amidst goats overcomes consumption (yakṣman). 45.
Honey, sulphur, viḍaṅga, realgar, iron, ghee, and abhayā, when consumed by one who eats wholesome food, destroy even the most virulent consumption. 46.

A patient suffering from wasting (kṣaya) who licks fresh butter mixed with sugar and honey, while subsisting on milk, attains incomparable nourishment; likewise, when ghee and honey are combined with sugar-candy,
tugākṣīrī, long pepper, bahulā, and cinnamon.

Above the last [dose], one should double the quantity and powder it; mixed with honey and ghee, one should have the patient lick it at night if he is afflicted by consumption, cough, dyspnea, fever, pain in the flanks, weak digestion, numbness of the tongue, or loss of appetite.
In cases of burning sensations in the hands and feet, fever, blood disorders, and upward-moving hemorrhages (ūrdhvaga-rakta),
one should use nutmeg, viḍaṅga, citraka, tagara, sesame seeds,
tālīsa, sandalwood, ginger, cloves, and upakuñcikā. (49–50)
Camphor, abhayā, dhātrī, marica, pippalī, and tugākṣīrī—
each of these should be taken in parts equal to the bark (tvak), combined with cāturjātaka; seven palas of bhaṅgā are considered equal to the entire quantity of sugar.
This powder indeed destroys consumption, cough, asthma, disorders of the digestive tract, loss of appetite, catarrh,
and weak digestion— just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree. (52–53)

One should daily employ the *lākṣādi-taila* mentioned in the section on diseases of children for the massage (*abhyaṅga*) of a patient suffering from consumption (*yakṣman*), according to the instruction of elder physicians. One *prastha* of the juice of *vāsaka* and one *mānikā* of white sugar [should be used].

One should slowly cook two palas of long pepper (pippalī) with an equal amount of clarified butter (sarpiḥ). When it has reached the consistency of a linctus (leha), the physician should add eight palas of honey once it has cooled and remove it from the heat; this excellent linctus is ready to be licked.
It certainly destroys consumption (rājayakṣmā), cough, and severe dyspnea,
as well as pain in the flanks, pain in the heart, hemoptysis, and fever;
it restores one emaciated by sexual excess and depleted of plasma and muscle through the consumption of meat, ghee, and food.
One should treat [the patient] with fine, sweet, and pleasing *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) [drugs].
One should treat wasting due to grief (*śoka-śoṣa*) with exhilarating and comforting milks, unctuous, sweet, and cold [substances], and with digestive-stimulating and light foods. (58–59)
One should treat a patient emaciated by over-exertion with unctuous, cooling, and beneficial remedies for chest wounds and wasting,

using vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs according to the regimen prescribed for kapha disorders; furthermore, one should employ pleasant sedentary activities, daytime sleep, cold treatments, and sweet, nourishing foods.
One should treat dehydration from travel with food, meat, and meat-broth;
one should overcome dehydration from wounds with unctuous, digestive-stimulating, sweet, and cool substances, such as soups,
meat-broths, and the like, which may be slightly sour or non-sour.
Balā, aśvagandhā, śrīparṇī, bahuputrī, and punarnavā, when practiced daily with milk, pacify chest wounds and consumption. (63)
One should take half a pala each of cardamom, cinnamon bark,
and long pepper, along with one pala each of sugar, licorice, dates, and raisins; having powdered these, one should prepare pills by mixing them with honey.
Then, one should consume a single dose the size of an *akṣa* day after day.
It cures wounds, consumption, fever, cough, asthma, hiccup, vomiting, vertigo,
fainting, intoxication, thirst, emaciation, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.

The Elādi-guṭikā cures splenic enlargement, Āḍhyavāta, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and loss of voice; it is highly aphrodisiac and an excellent nourishing tonic. [One should take] one prastha of raisins and eight palas of madhuka.
When one *āḍhaka* of pure water has been boiled down to a quarter part,
one should add two *pala*s of ground *madhuka* and two *pala*s of black pepper,
along with one *prastha* of ghee and four times as much milk, and cook it.
When it has been proven efficacious and cooled, one should add eight *palas* of sugar;
this prepared *Drākṣā-ghṛta* brings comfort to those suffering from chest wounds and emaciation,
and it cures Vāta, Pitta, fever, dyspnea, eruptive boils, and *halīmaka*.
It cures menorrhagia and hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta) and bestows flesh and strength.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with milk, the juice of dhātrī, mañjiṣṭhā, and kṣīriṇī, along with one karṣa each of the "sweet" (madhura) drugs.

With half a *prastha* of honey added once cooled, along with half a *tulā* of sugar, [one should prepare a drink] using raisins, *dvicandana*, *uśīra*, sugar, blue lotus (*utpala*), *padmaka*, flowers of *madhūka*, *anantā*, *kāśmarī*, and the grass known as *tṛṇasaṃjñaka*. (73)
Having powdered half a pala each of cinnamon, cardamom, and lotus filaments, one should dissolve them therein and, being well-restrained, consume the appropriate dose daily;
this is proclaimed by the two Aśvins as "Amṛtaprāśa" (the consumption of nectar). 74–75.
It destroys bleeding disorders (raktapitta), chest wounds, and consumption; it subdues thirst, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and fainting.
It cures dysuria and fever, is strengthening, and increases sexual vigor. (76–77)
Whatever food and drink is refreshing, cooling, non-burning, wholesome, and light should be consumed by those suffering from chest wounds or emaciation who desire well-being.
One should abandon grief, women, anger, and envy, and one should enjoy noble sensory objects.
Likewise, one should listen to the twice-born, the gods, and the preceptors, and hear auspicious words from the twice-born.
Now, regarding pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman),
the medicinal juices consist of the ash of mercury (rasabhasma), amṛtā-sattva, and iron, combined with honey and ghee.
This [medicine] named Amṛteśvara is used for rājayakṣman (consumption) when six guñjas are administered.
(80) One part of processed mercury, one part of gold ash, one part of killed copper, along with realgar, sulphur, and orpiment; (81)
Each pair of parts should be taken; all of this should be powdered together.
One should fill cowrie shells with this powder and, having ground borax with goat's milk, one should seal the openings [of the shells] with it and place them inside an earthen vessel.
One should cook it in a *kūpyā* crucible within a *japupuṭa*; once cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should extract it.
This *Rājamṛgāṅka* elixir, in a dose of four *guñjās*, destroys consumption (*kṣaya*). It is prepared with nineteen black peppers (*marica*) and ten long peppers (*kaṇā*).
The physician should administer this juice with honey and clarified butter;
by this means, consumption born of Vāta and Kapha is quickly destroyed.
(85) One should prepare a kajjalī of purified mercury and sulphur in equal parts using a mortar and pestle.
One should grind the equal parts of the fine powder of those two with the juice of kanyākanda for two yāmas; having placed the resulting ball in a copper vessel,
one should cover it with castor leaves so that it becomes warm after two yāmas.
After eight nights, one should remove it from the heap of grain, grind it into a powder, and strain it through cloths; it will truly become water-clearing.
[Then add] the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three fruits (triphalā), cardamom (elā), nutmeg (jātīphala), and cloves (lavaṅga).
With these [ingredients] measured in equal parts, each being one-ninth [of the total], this elixir is prepared. One should daily lick it, measuring two *niṣkas*, along with honey.
This is the supreme elixir known as *Agnirasā*, which cures cough and consumption.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter on *rājayakṣman* (consumption).
Now begins the twelfth chapter on the disease of *kāsa* (cough):
[It arises] from injury by smoke, as well as from dust, and from the indulgence in physical exertion and dry food.
Due to the consumption of food on a wrong path, or likewise from the suppression of natural urges such as sneezing,

the *prāṇa* wind, following the *udāna*, becomes vitiated; it suddenly issues forth from the mouth with a sound resembling that of a cracked bell-metal vessel, accompanied by the morbid humors (*doṣa*), and is designated as "cough" (*kāsa*) by the wise.
The five types of *kāsa* (cough) are known to arise from vāta, pitta, śleṣman, chest injury (*kṣata*), and wasting (*kṣaya*).
If neglected, all of them lead to emaciation, each subsequent one being more severe than the preceding.
Their premonitory symptom is a sensation as if the throat and mouth were filled with awns of grain.
Itching in the throat and obstruction of food occur;

one suffers from pain in the heart, temples, sides, abdomen, and head; with a withered face and diminished strength, voice, and vitality, the patient coughs only dryly, with broken voice and constant urges caused by the wind (vāta).

Afflicted by chest pain, burning sensations, fever, and dryness of the mouth, with a bitter taste in the mouth and overcome by thirst due to *pitta*, one vomits yellow and pungent substances; such a person is pale and suffers from a burning sensation.
With a mouth as if smeared [with phlegm], sinking down, afflicted by headache, and with the body filled with *kapha*—[this describes the symptoms of vomiting due to *kapha*].
One afflicted by lack of appetite, indigestion, heaviness, and itching, may cough violently with thick phlegm due to the excess of *kapha*.

(7) In one who is dry from excessive sexual indulgence, carrying heavy loads, walking long distances, fighting, or being restrained while riding horses or elephants, the *vāyu* seizes the chest and brings about coughing. (8)
First he coughs dryly, and then he spits out blood;
with his throat excessively rasping and his chest as if shattered,
he suffers from piercing pain as if being pricked by sharp needles.
Afflicted by the touch of suffering, by piercing pain, and by the torment of splitting sensations, fever, dyspnea, thirst,
and loss of voice; he groans like a pigeon due to the force of coughing arising from internal injury.
Due to irregular or unwholesome food, excessive sexual indulgence, suppression of natural urges,
and in those who are loathsome or grieving, the three humors become aggravated when the digestive fire is impaired;
they then cause cough born of wasting (kṣayaja-kāsa), which brings about the depletion of the body.
One suffering from cough may experience body aches, fever, delusion, burning sensations, and loss of vitality (13).

Wasting away and devoid of strength, with emaciated flesh, the patient spits out blood mixed with pus; those who know medical treatment call this "kṣayaja" (arising from wasting), which exhibits all symptoms and is extremely difficult to cure (14).
Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja) destroys the bodies of those who are emaciated;
it may be curable for the strong, but that arising from injury (kṣataja) is merely manageable (yāpya).
Indeed, even when accompanied by one-quarter of its full symptoms, it is never cured.

In the elderly, all coughs caused by old age are declared to be palliable (yāpya). One should treat the three curable (sādhya) types with wholesome regimens, while one should manage the palliable types through supportive care.
Fever, anorexia, nausea, hoarseness of voice, wasting, and other such conditions [arise].
Since [these] arise through equanimity (*upekṣā*), one should therefore conquer them with the speed of reality (*tattvarayā*).
(18) The treatment for cough (*kāsa*) consists of *vāstūka*, *vāyasī* greens, radish (*mūlaka*), and *suniṣaṇṇaka*.
Oils and other unctuous substances, as well as foods made from sugarcane juice and molasses;
curd, sour gruel, sour fruits, clear wine (prasannā), and drink—these, along with sweet, sour, and salty items, are recommended for coughs caused by Vāta. (19–20)

The physician should feed [the patient] with *śāli*, barley, wheat, or *ṣaṣṭika* rice, along with the juices of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals, or with soups made from mung beans (*māṣa*) or *ātmaguptā*.
A preparation made from *daśamūlī* removes the afflictions of dyspnea, cough, and hiccups.
Barley gruel (yavāgū) is digestive-stimulant, aphrodisiac, and a destroyer of diseases of the hair.
Alternatively, the juice of *karkoṭaka* cucumbers fried in ghee with dry ginger (*nāgara*) pacifies wind-disorders and cough; or likewise, that of the *śṛṅgī* fish.

One should drink water boiled with *kaṇṭakārī*, the two types of *rāsnā*, *vāsā*, *karcūra*, *bālaka*, *nāgara*, and *pippalī*, combined with sugar and honey; this is an excellent remedy for curing *pitta*-type cough. 24
The treatment for cough born of phlegm (kaphaja-kāsa) consists of long pepper (pippalī), katphala, dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), karkaṭaśṛṅgī, bhārgī, black pepper (uṣaṇa),
kāravī, kaṇṭakārī, sinduvāra, and yavānikā. 25
One should drink the decoction of these— citraka and vāsaka— prepared according to the prescribed method and combined with the powder of kṛṣṇā, for the destruction of cough caused by kapha.
[Also beneficial are] sugarcane, ikṣuvālikā, lotus, lotus-stalk, blue lotus, and sandalwood.
Madhuka, pippalī, drākṣā, lākṣā, śṛṅgī, and śatāvarī [should be taken];
with twice as much tugākṣīrī and sugar four times the amount of all these, one should lick the mixture with honey and ghee for the cessation of cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa). 27–28.
The powder of *kākubha* (madana), repeatedly saturated with the juice of *vāsaka*, should be licked along with honey, ghee, and sugar; it removes wasting, cough, and blood disorders.
[29] When one suffers from coughing, nasal discharge, and hoarseness of voice while being tormented by consumption, [this remedy should be used].

In cases of sneezing and loss of the sense of smell, one should employ the inhalation of smoke (dhūmapāna). For three days, one should drink the smoke prepared with realgar (manaḥśilā), black pepper (marica), spikenard (māṃsī), nut-grass (mustā), and ingudi; thereafter, one should drink milk mixed with jaggery (guḍa).
This [remedy] will certainly cure coughs arising from individual, dual, or all three doṣas— even those incurable by hundreds of treatments—
when a leaf of the *badarī* tree has been smeared with [the aforementioned] stone and dried in the sun. 32.
That smoking [of the powder] with milk prevents severe cough (33). A decoction prepared from Kaṇṭakārī with Kṛṣṇā (Pippalī) cures all types of cough.
The powder of Kaṇṭakārī and Kaṇā (Pippalī) taken with honey destroys cough (34).
Having prepared one *akṣa* (24 g) each of the parts of *lavaṅga*, *jātīphala*, and *pippalī*, one should add half a *pala* of black pepper and four *palas* of ginger; then,
adding sugar equal in weight to the entire mixture, this powder quickly overcomes these diseases by its strength.
It cures cough, fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, dyspnea, weak digestion, and disorders of the *grahaṇī*.

(36) A linctus made from realgar (*kunaṭī*), rock salt (*saindhava*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, *āmalaka*, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), combined with ghee and honey, wards off cough, dyspnea, and hiccups. (37)

Harītakī, kaṇā, śuṇṭhī, and marica combined with jaggery are said to remove cough and phlegm, and are a supreme stimulator of the digestive fire (38). One karṣa, one-eighth of a pala, two palas, and half a karṣa [are the measures].

This is the supreme medicine for those coughs that are incurable by all other herbs and abandoned by physicians— even for those who vomit pus— consisting of *marica*, *pippalī*, pomegranate, molasses, and *yavaśūka*. (39–40)
One *karṣa* of black pepper (*marica*), one *karṣa* of long pepper (*pippalī*),
half a *karṣa* of alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), and two *karṣas* of pomegranate (*dāḍima*).
This should be powdered and combined with eight *karṣas* of jaggery (*guḍa*).
Having made pills of the measure of a *śāṇa*, one should hold them in the mouth;
by their power, all types of coughs indeed go to their destruction.
(42) Then, [one should take] a *tulā* of *kaṇṭakārī*, including its roots, bark, and leaves, along with two *droṇas* of water.
One should boil one hundred *harītakī* fruits in a single vessel until only a quarter of the water remains;

having strained that decoction through a fine cloth and mixed it with the *harītakī* fruits, one should add a *tulā* of jaggery and cook it until well-done, then remove it from the heat once it has become thoroughly cooled. 43–44.

Having powdered one pala each of the three pungents (kaṭutraya) and likewise one pala of the four aromatics (caturjāta), one should add six palas of flower-nectar (puṣparasa) and mix them together. This electuary (leha), when employed according to the prescribed method, [should be taken] according to one's strength and according to one's digestive fire. 45.

This Harītakī, as taught by Bhṛgu, destroys cough caused by Vāta, Pitta, Kapha, or all three Doshas combined; it also cures cough arising from chest injury, cough born of wasting, asthma along with chronic rhinitis, and even the fierce consumption (yakṣman) in its eleven forms. 46–47.
Having boiled one *tulā* of *kaṇṭakārī* in one *droṇa* of water until a decoction remains as one-fourth, one should take it and add the following powders,
each weighing one *pala*: *guḍūcī*, *cavya*, and *citraka*.
Musta, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, trikaṭu, dhanvayāsaka, bhārgī, rāsnā, and śaṭī—of each of these, one should take eight palas; twenty palas of sugar should be added, along with ghee and oil. 49–50.
Having cooked it and reduced it to the consistency of a linctus, once it has cooled, one should add eight palas of honey,
a fourth part [of that] of *tugākṣīrī*, and four palas of *pippalī*;
then one should place this auspicious preparation in a very sturdy earthen vessel.
This linctus destroys hiccup, excessive cough, and asthma completely. Thus ends the twelfth chapter on cough.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter on hiccup.
By foods that cause burning, heaviness, constipation, dryness, or excessive secretions;

by cold drinks, food, and baths; by dust, smoke, and likewise by the wind (vāyu); by lack of exercise, physical labor, carrying loads, walking long distances, suppression of natural urges, and fasting.
Hiccups, dyspnea, and cough arise in men.
Vāyu, accompanied by kapha, indeed produces five types of hiccups:
annajā, yamalā, kṣudrā, gambhīrā, and mahatī.

Again and again the wind arises with a sound, as if throwing out the liver, spleen, and intestines from the mouth; being thus afflicted by the humors, it quickly destroys the vital breaths, and for that reason it is called "hiccup" (hikkā) by the wise. There is also heaviness in the throat and chest, and an astringent taste in the mouth.
The premonitory symptoms of hiccup include distension of the abdomen (āṭopa).
When the vāyu, suddenly oppressed by food and drink consumed in excess, moves upward, it causes hiccuping; the physician should recognize this as annajā-hikkā (hiccup born of food).
That hiccup which occurs with double bursts after a long interval,
shaking the head and neck, one should designate as *yamalā*.
That which occurs with slow bursts at wide intervals is [designated as *vikṛṣṭakālā*].
That hiccup which has rushed to the base of the collarbones is called *kṣudrikā*. That hiccup which originates from the navel, being terrible, deep-sounding,
and accompanied by many complications, is known as *gambhīrā*.
That which proceeds constantly as if piercing the vital points (marmas),
causing all the limbs to tremble, should be known as Mahāhikkā.
He whose body shakes while hiccupping, and whose vision is perpetually fixed upward and distressed, [is lost].
One who is emaciated, one who hates food, and one who sneezes excessively— these two, when suffering from hiccupping, should be avoided.

[This applies to] one whose humors are excessively accumulated, one who is thin from aversion to food, one whose body is wasted by diseases, an elderly person, and one who has overindulged in sexual intercourse.
Hiccups arising from physical exertion quickly destroy life, as do those known as *yamikā*,
which are accompanied by delirium, distress, confusion, and thirst—
even in one who is not emaciated, who is not dejected, and whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and sense faculties (*indriya*) are stable. (13)

It can be cured by the Yamika treatment; otherwise, it kills. Whatever medicine, drink, or food subdues kapha and vata, is hot, and facilitates the downward movement of vata is beneficial in cases of hiccup and asthma.
For one afflicted by hiccup and dyspnea, sudation after anointing with oil is desired first;
purification (śodhana) via the upper and lower routes is recommended, while pacification (śamana) is considered appropriate for the weak.
[This is achieved] by means of breath-retention, threatening, causing alarm, and the sprinkling of cold water.
One should pacify hiccup through various narrative applications and by means of mental distractions. For one afflicted by hiccup, goat's milk prepared with ginger is beneficial;
one should drink the juice of mātuluṅga combined with honey and sauvarcala salt.
Madhuka mixed with honey, pippalī combined with sugar,
and ginger mixed with jaggery— these three nasal drops (nāvana) destroy hiccup.
Coral, conch shell, and the powder of triphalā, saturated with honey and ghee, [should be used].
A linctus made of long pepper (pippalī) and red ochre (gairika) is a remedy that wards off hiccup.

For the pacification of hiccup, one should inhale incense made from either the seeds of the *naipālī* plant, cow horn, kuṣṭha, resin of the *sarja* tree, or *kuśa* grass; or one should drink [the corresponding medicinal preparation]. 20–21.

Smoke produced from asafoetida, black gram flour, and the dust of charcoal that has been smothered so that it is smokeless, when inhaled, quickly destroys all five types of hiccups; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, a decoction of *hareṇuka* and long pepper, combined with asafoetida, [achieves the same].
This is the best remedy for pacifying hiccups, according to the words of Dhanvantari.
One should throw the seeds of *candraśūra* into eight times their weight of water; when they have become soft, one should crush them and then strain the liquid through a cloth. 23–24.
One whose hiccuping has been interrupted by forceful suppression should drink that water in a dose of one *pala*, and drinking it again, the hiccup will certainly be pacified.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter on Hiccup (Hikkā). 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter on the disease of asthma (śvāsa).
By those very same causes through which hiccough (hikkā) arises in embodied beings, that terrible disease known as asthma is produced by many of those same factors. 1.
That single major disease, *śvāsa* (dyspnea), is specifically divided into five types by way of its classifications: *mahā-*, *ūrdhva-*, *chinna-*, *tamaka-*, and *kṣudra-*.
Its premonitory symptoms are pain in the heart, colic, and flatulence.

When the wind (māruta), preceded by phlegm (kapha), obstructs the channels and moves in all directions while being constricted, it then produces breathlessness (śvāsa), characterized by a sensation of emptiness in the chest, a bad taste in the mouth, and a piercing pain in the temples. (3–4)
With his breath tossed by the wind, like a man suffering from a loud noise,
he pants loudly and incessantly like a rutting bull in its harness;
his knowledge and discernment are lost, and his eyes are wandering.
With eyes wide open and mouth agape, with urine and feces obstructed, and with speech failing;
the heavy labored breathing of one afflicted by mahāśvāsa is perceived from afar, and such a person perishes very quickly.
One who breathes excessively upward and cannot draw [the breath] downward, whose mouth and channels are obstructed by phlegm, and who is afflicted by the enraged wind;
looking upward and gazing about with eyes wandering here and there— 8. (This is the sign of the patient’s end.)
Bewildered, seized by pain, with a parched mouth and oppressed by restlessness (9),
when the upward breath (ūrdhva-śvāsa) becomes aggravated, the downward breath (adhaḥ-śvāsa) is obstructed; as he faints and gasps for air, that upward breath destroys his life-breaths (10).
But he who breathes with difficulty, interruptedly, oppressed by all his vital breaths,
or does not breathe at all, being afflicted by suffering and struck by the pain of the severing of his vital organs (marmans),
overcome by abdominal distension, perspiration, and fainting, with his bladder burning— 11. [He is one whose life is departing.]
With rolling eyes, emaciated, panting, and with one eye bloodshot (12),
the man— distraught, with a parched mouth, discolored, and delirious— is severed by broken breath and quickly abandons his life-breaths (13).
When the wind moves in a contrary direction and enters the channels,
seizing the neck and head and agitating the phlegm,
it thereby causes chronic catarrh as well as a rattling sound in the throat.
His breathing becomes exceedingly forceful and violent, afflicting his vital breaths; he faints with intensity, suffers from thirst, and is constricted;
while coughing, he repeatedly falls into a state of delusion.
When the phlegm is not being discharged, he becomes intensely distressed;
yet, upon its release, he obtains a moment of ease.
Likewise, his throat becomes parched, and he can only bark with great difficulty. (17)
Furthermore, afflicted by labored breathing, he finds no sleep even while lying down (18).
When he lies on his side, the wind seizes him;
only when sitting does he find comfort, and he welcomes warmth (19).
With eyes bulging, forehead profusely perspiring, and suffering intense pain, his mouth becomes parched; he breathes repeatedly and is frequently gasping for air.
This condition increases due to clouds, rainwater, cold, and eastern winds, as well as by factors that increase *śleṣman* (phlegm).
That *asthama* (obstructive) dyspnea, if it has recently arisen, may be curable;
however, one should recognize that *pratamaka* dyspnea as being accompanied by fever and fainting.
It is born from upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), menstrual blood, indigestion, or the obstruction of a body moistened by morbid humors.

One should know that the first stage of fainting is like sinking into darkness; it increases excessively with darkness and is pacified by cooling measures. Dryness arising from exertion excites the subtle vāta within the digestive tract (koṣṭha).
That minor dyspnea is not excessively painful, nor does it afflict the limbs;
it does not destroy the body parts, nor is it as distressing as other types, and it does not obstruct the normal passage of food and drink. 24–25.
That which does not cause any distress to the sense organs nor produce any pain is said to be curable; all those that are strong and whose symptoms are unmanifest are also curable.
O Kṣudra! Among them, Tamaka is the most easily curable, while [the others] are said to be difficult to treat.
Three types of dyspnea are incurable: that which is chronic, and that occurring in one who is weak.
(27) Indeed, although there are many diseases that take away life, they do not do so as quickly as dyspnea and hiccup truly deprive one of life. (28)
One should generally treat a patient afflicted by dyspnea and hiccups with unctuous sudations combined with salt and oil; by these means, the knotted phlegm within him dissolves,
the dyspnea comes to an end, and the wind (vāta) is pacified.
Knowing that he has sweated sufficiently, one should then feed him rice with meat broth (rasaudana).
One should cause him to drink the fresh juice of ginger mixed with honey; this destroys dyspnea and cough, and removes catarrh and phlegm.
One should prepare a paste from one *prastha* of *bibhītaka* fruits, excluding the seeds, in goat’s urine;
this electuary, when licked with honey, cures asthma and cough.
(32) Having ground *devadāru*, *balā*, and *māṃsī*, one should fashion a medicinal wick (*varti*).
One should drink that smoke, smeared with ghee; it destroys even the most severe asthma.
(33) [This is prepared] with the ten roots (*daśamūlī*), *śaṭī*, *rāsnā*, long pepper (*pippalī*), *viśva* (*śuṇṭhī*), and *pauṣkara*;
with *śṛṅgī*, *āmalakī*, *bhārgī*, *guḍūcī*, ginger (*nāgara*), and *agni* (*citraka*). (34)
A person should drink gruel prepared according to the prescribed method, or a decoction,
for the pacification of dyspnea, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, hiccups, and cough.
Alternatively, a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) mixed with the powder of ṣauṣkara [is recommended].
It pacifies dyspnea and cough and removes pain in the flanks.
(36) Having ground the flowers of the plantain, kunda, and śirīṣa together with long pepper, one should drink them with rice-water; this dispels dyspnea. (37)

A powder of śṛṅgī, mahauṣadha, kaṇā, ghana, and pauṣkara, along with śaṭī and marica, mixed with sugar and drunk with the decoction of amṛtā, vṛṣa, and the two pañcamūlis, indeed destroys even a severe form of dyspnea within three days.
However, the common (sāmānyā) pañcamūlī, specifically the smaller one (kanīyasī), should be employed when pitta is involved.

This same [preparation] should be administered when wind (vāta) is predominant, and it should also be given when phlegm (kapha) is excessive. The powder of the root of the kūṣmāṇḍaka gourd, drunk with lukewarm water,
quickly pacifies both asthma and even most severe cough.
By licking a paste of turmeric, black pepper, raisins, long pepper, rāsnā, śaṭī,
and jaggery with mustard oil, one may destroy even those breath-obstructing diseases that take away life.
(41) Having collected one hundred parts of bhārgī and likewise one hundred parts of daśamūlī, [one should proceed as follows].

One should boil one hundred *harītakī* fruits in four times their quantity of water; when that decoction is reduced to one-fourth and strained through a cloth, one should then dissolve one *tulā* of purified jaggery and [an equal amount of] *abhayā*.
One should cook it again over a gentle fire until it reaches the consistency of a thick syrup (leha).
When it has cooled, one should add six palas of honey,
and one pala each of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and the three aromatics (trisugandha), separately.
Then, having powdered two karṣas of barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), one should add it [to the preparation].
One should consume one abhayā (harītakī) as well as half a pala of the linctus;
this destroys even most severe asthma as well as the five types of cough.

It cures hemorrhoids, anorexia, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and consumption; it bestows clarity of voice and complexion and stimulates the digestive fire. This is renowned by all physicians as Bhārgī-guḍa by name. (47)
One should administer goat's milk combined with the powder of the eight ingredients;
this will undoubtedly destroy even severe asthma accompanied by cough.
The juice of the ten roots (daśamūla) should be given for the complete eradication and pacification of asthma.
A man who lives for a hundred years is inevitably destined for death. Take one karṣa each of mercury, sulphur, poison, borax,
and realgar, and eight karṣas of black pepper.
One should add two karṣas each of the three pungents (kaṭutraya) separately here;
this "Axe for Asthma" (Śvāsakuṭhāra) is the dispeller of all forms of asthma.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter on Asthma. 14.

The Fifteenth Chapter: On the Differentiation of Voice Disorders (Svarabheda) When the bodily humors— wind and the others— are aggravated by speaking too loudly, exhaustion, excessive study, trauma, or exposure to impurities, they enter the channels that carry the voice and destroy its stability.
Furthermore, that voice is indeed of six types:

1. Due to *vāta*, the eyes, face, urine, and feces become black; he speaks slowly with broken words and a voice like that of a donkey. 2. Due to *pitta*, the eyes, face, urine, and feces become yellow; he speaks with a throat accompanied by a burning sensation.

One should say that when the throat is constantly obstructed by *kapha*, a person speaks very little and slowly, especially during the day; when all [doshas] are involved, there is a combination of all symptoms, and the sages declare that such hoarseness of voice (*svarabheda*) is incurable. When caused by wasting (*kṣaya*), the speech becomes smoky and one suffers from emaciation; indeed, such a person who has lost their voice should be avoided by society.
Afflicted by thirst, with his throat coated with phlegm, he speaks after a long time with a hoarse voice that lacks clarity and distinctness due to the accumulation of fat.

A disorder of the voice that arises after a long time in one who is emaciated, aged, or thin, or one that is congenital, as well as one arising from all [three] humors in a person of great corpulence, never attains success in treatment.
The physician should employ here those formulations proclaimed as destroyers of dyspnea and cough born of wind (vāta) and other humors, according to the specific disorder:
oil with salt for vāta, and ghee with honey for pitta.
In cases of phlegm (kapha), honey mixed with alkali and pungent substances is desired as a gargle for conditions localized in the throat, palate, tongue, and roots of the teeth;
by this means, the phlegm is extracted and the voice quickly becomes clear.
In the first case, lukewarm water should be drunk after eating rice with ghee and meat broth;
in a disorder arising from pitta, one should diligently drink milk-water and ghee.
[The powder consists of] long pepper, long pepper root, black pepper, and ginger.
A wise person should drink [this] with urine in cases of loss of voice caused by kapha.
One *tulā* of *nidigdhikā* should be taken, half of that (*ardha-tulā*) of *granthika*, half of that again of *citraka*, and an equal amount of *daśamūla*. 10–11.
One should boil two *droṇas* of water down to one *āḍhaka*,
and once it is strained, one should add half of that amount of old molasses (*guḍa*). Having combined everything into one vessel, one should cook it thoroughly like a medicinal electuary (*leha*).
Eight palas of long pepper (pippalī), one pala each of the three aromatics (trijātaka),
and one pala of black pepper (marica)— all these ground together— should be mixed with one kuḍava of honey and consumed according to one's digestive fire. 13–14.
This *nidigdhikā-avaleha* (electuary of *nidigdhikā*) is considered by physicians and sages to be preeminent for curing hoarseness of voice,
as well as catarrh, cough, dyspnea, impaired digestion, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and diseases of the throat. (15)
This linctus,
consisting of musk, small cardamom, cloves, flower buds, and bamboo manna, combined with honey and clarified butter, destroys constipation, dysuria, and even glandular swellings and tumors.
It overcomes severe paralysis of speech accompanied by loss of voice.
By the use of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *abhayā*, *vāsā*, and *pippalī* combined with honey for seven days, one is sung of even by the *kinnaras*. 17–18.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter on the differentiation of voice tones (15).
The sixteenth chapter is on loss of appetite (16).
[Loss of appetite arises] from wind and the other [humors], as well as from grief, fear, excessive greed, anger, and from mental distress, improper food, or disagreeable sights and smells.
One should know that an averse to food with tingling teeth and an astringent mouth is caused by Vāta;
a mouth that is pungent, sour, hot, tasteless, and foul-smelling is caused by Pitta;
and a mouth characterized by sweetness, sliminess, heaviness, coldness, unctuousness, and foul odor is caused by Kapha.
Anorexia may arise from grief, fear, excessive greed, anger, and other such unpleasant or foul-smelling factors;
it may also be natural, or it may result from the three *doṣas*, in which case the taste is not uniform.

When caused by *vāta*, it is accompanied by pain and pressure in the heart; when caused by *pitta*, it is characterized by much thirst, burning sensations, a parching feeling, and excessive salivation with *kapha*.
One should know that another type [of anorexia] is characterized by phlegm (śleṣman), many pains, and various defects such as delusion and dullness.
Furthermore, when food placed in the mouth is not tasted by a person, that should be recognized as *arocaka* (loss of appetite); now hear about *bhaktadveṣa* (aversion to food).
Having reflected with the mind, or having seen or touched food,
the living being who develops aversion toward it is said to have "aversion to food" (bhaktadveṣa).
This applies to one who is angry, afflicted by fear, or likewise opposed to the food.
One who has no faith in food is called a person of non-devotional intent.
At the beginning of a meal, the consumption of wholesome, salty, and moist foods is always recommended;
it stimulates the appetite, kindles the digestive fire, and cleanses the tongue and throat.
One may also mix the juice of fresh ginger with honey;
this destroys loss of appetite, asthma, and cough, and removes catarrh and phlegm.
(9) Ripe tamarind, sugar, and cold water, filtered through a cloth— [this mixture is likewise beneficial].
Dusted with cardamom, cloves, camphor,
and black pepper, holding a mouthful of this *pānaka* repeatedly in the mouth certainly destroys loss of appetite and likewise pacifies bile (*pitta*).
One should prepare mustard seeds and cumin fried together, along with fried asafoetida, ginger, rock salt, and cow's curd; all of these should be strained through a cloth.
One should add just enough of this mixture there so that the flavor becomes excellent.

This buttermilk, when properly prepared, is immediately appetizing and increases the digestive fire. Milk that has been thoroughly churned and curdled into buffalo curd should be mixed with an equal amount of bright sugar and rubbed upon a cloth. 13–14.
One should prepare *śikhariṇī* by combining it with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and black pepper; this brings about a relish beloved by all.
One should take two *pala*s of sour pomegranate juice and add three *pala*s of sugar candy.
One should prepare a powder by combining one pala of the three aromatics (trisugandhi) together.

This powder, when consumed in the proper dose, is an excellent remedy for loss of appetite; it stimulates digestion, promotes the digestion of food, and overcomes chronic catarrh, fever, and cough. (16–17)
Lavaṅga, kaṅkola, muśīra, candana, nata, along with nīlotpala and kṛṣṇajīraka;
water [mixed] with kṛṣṇāguru, bhṛṅga, and keśara; kaṇā, viśvā, nalada, and sahelayā (18);
tuṣāra, jātīphala, vaṃśarocanā, and sugar in half-portion—all these should be ground together into a fine powder.
It is aphrodisiac, nourishing, a stimulant for the digestive fire, strength-bestowing, highly effective for subjugation, and a conqueror of the three doṣas.
It destroys chest congestion, asthma, throat obstruction, cough, hiccups, anorexia, consumption, chronic rhinitis,
malabsorption syndrome, diarrhea, chest wounds in men, as well as all types of urinary disorders.
One should prepare a compound consisting of four *śāṇas* each of *yavānī*, pomegranate, ginger, *tintiḍīka*, and *amlavetasa*,
along with two and a half *śāṇas* of black pepper and ten *śāṇas* of long pepper. (21)
Take two *śāṇas* each of cinnamon, *sauvarcala* salt, *dhānyāka*, and cumin;
to these, one should add sixty-four *śāṇas* of sugar. All these ingredients, ground together as a powder, constitute the preparation known as *yavānī-khāṇḍava*.
This powder conquers anemia, heart disease, malabsorption syndrome, and fever;

it also overcomes vomiting, emaciation, diarrhea, splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, constipation, loss of appetite, colic, weak digestion, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the tongue and throat. (23–24)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter on Anorexia (Arocaka), number 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter on Vomiting (Chardi), number 17.
[Caused] by excessive purgatives, excessively unctuous substances, unpalatable foods, and even salty ones...

Due to eating at the wrong time, in excessive quantities, or unwholesome foods; due to undigested matter (āma), fear, agitation, indigestion, or the presence of worms; and due to a pregnant woman or one who eats too quickly.
Food is forcibly provoked to vomit by other loathsome causes,
by corrupted humors (doṣas) individually or collectively, and by the sight of disgusting things and so forth;
these five types of vomiting are to be recognized, and their characteristics are now described.
Nausea, suppression of eructations, excessive salivation, a salty taste in the mouth,
and a strong aversion to food and drink are the premonitory symptoms of vomiting (vami).
Covering the face with its forceful onsets and afflicting the body with convulsive wrenches, [it manifests].
That which is called *chardi* (vomiting) is the morbid humor (*doṣa*) rushing forth from the mouth.
It is accompanied by pain in the heart and flanks, dryness of the mouth, and piercing pain in the head, navel, cough, and hoarseness of voice;
the vomitus is loud-sounding, frothy, broken up, blackish, thin, and astringent.
Afflicted by wind (vāta), one vomits with difficulty, in small quantities, and with great force, experiencing intense suffering as if vomiting against one's will.

Afflicted by bile (pitta), one vomits that which was previously drunk— excessively hot, green, bitter, and smoky— along with a burning sensation, accompanied by fainting, thirst, dryness of the mouth, heat in the head, palate, and eyes, darkness of vision, and giddiness.
Afflicted by drowsiness, sweetness in the mouth, excessive salivation, contentment, sleep, loss of appetite, and heaviness,
one vomits phlegm that is unctuous, thick, sweet, white due to the presence of *kapha*, accompanied by horripilation and little pain;
for such vomiting may arise from unwholesome food, from worms, from the womb, from loathsome sights, or from pregnancy-longings (*daurhṛda*).

One should discern that fifth [type] as well, which arises specifically from an excess of morbid humors (*doṣa*) as previously described; it is characterized by an abundance of piercing pain and nausea, and is marked by symptoms identical to those of *kṛmi-hṛd-roga* (heart disease caused by worms). 11–12.

Cough, dyspnea, fever, thirst, hiccup, mental confusion, cardiac pain, and tamaka-śvāsa are to be known as the complications (upadrava) of vomiting. Vomiting that is excessively persistent in a weakened person, accompanied by complications and mixed with blood and pus, [is fatal].
They declare that vomiting accompanied by fainting is incurable; however, one should treat that which is curable and free from complications.

Indeed, all types of vomiting are considered to arise from the agitation of the stomach (āmāśaya); therefore, fasting (laṅghana) is prescribed for all except that born of Vāta, for which purification (saṃśodhana) that removes Kapha and Pitta is indicated. 14–15.
Milk and water drunk together will destroy vomiting caused by Vāta;
or else, a soup of mung beans and āmalaka, prepared with ghee and rock salt [is effective].
Water boiled with guḍūcī, triphalā, nimba, and paṭola [should also be used].
One should drink that [mixture] combined with honey; by this, vomiting born of pitta is destroyed.
One should lick the powder of *harītakī* mixed with honey;
once the morbid humor has been expelled through the lower passage, the vomiting quickly ceases.
A powder of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and viśvā, combined with honey, overcomes vomiting born of kapha; or else, a powder of viḍaṅga, plava, and śuṇṭhī may be used for the same purpose.
Having ground one pala each of āmalaka fruit, parched grain (lāja), and sugar, [one should administer it].
Having added one pala of honey and a kuḍava of water, and having strained it through a cloth, drinking this destroys vomiting born of the three doṣas.
A cold infusion prepared from guḍūcī, combined with honey, likewise destroys it.
Even by force, one may overcome vomiting that is difficult to restrain and produced by the three *doṣas* (21),
by licking a powder composed of cardamom, clove, *gajakeśara*, the marrow of *kola*, parched grain, *priyaṅgu*, *ghanasāra*, sandalwood, and long pepper,
combined with honey and white sugar.
It destroys vomiting born of phlegm, wind, and bile.
(22) The bark of the *aśvattha* tree, dried, burnt, and extinguished with water—the mere drinking of that water conquers even invincible vomiting. (23)
By licking the powder of *pathyā*, the three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*), coriander, and cumin with honey, one destroys vomiting and anorexia caused by the three *doṣas*.
A decoction of either *bilva* bark or *guḍūcī*, combined with honey, [achieves the same].
Parpaṭa cures vomiting born of the three doṣas as well as that born of pitta. A decoction of mango stone and bilva, drunk with honey and sugar,
destroys vomiting and diarrhea just as fire consumes a sacrificial oblation.
Jambu and mango sprouts boiled together with parched grain flour, cooled and mixed with honey, pacify vomiting, diarrhea, and severe thirst;
[the latter] for vomiting born of loathing, and that for vomiting born of pregnancy-longing (dauhṛda) with pleasant and desired fruits. 27.

One should conquer vomiting born of undigested matter (*āmaja*) by means of fasting (*laṅghana*), and that born of unwholesome things by means of wholesome ones. One should treat vomiting arising from worms (*kṛmi*) like heart disease caused by worms;
in each case, the physician should apply the treatment according to the specific *doṣa*.
In cases of excessive vomiting accompanied by eructations, one should have the patient lick a powder of *mūrvā*, *dhānya*, and *mustā*, along with *madhuka* and *añjana*, mixed with honey (verse 30).
[One should also use] *sauvarcala* salt, *ajājī*, sugar, and black pepper.
When licked with honey, it immediately prevents vomiting.
(31) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter on vomiting.
Chapter eighteen: On thirst. 18.
Due to fear, fatigue, or the depletion of strength, or when accumulated by Pitta-aggravating factors,
the Pitta along with Vata becomes provoked in men and, having reached the palate, produces thirst.
Furthermore, when the channels carrying water are vitiated by the Doshas, thirst arises in a living being here in this world.
Three types are traditionally recognized; the fourth arises from wasting (kṣaya), another from raw matter (āma), and the seventh from food (bhakta). Learn now their symptoms in due order:
dryness and burning of the palate, lips, throat, and mouth, along with fever, delusion, vertigo, and incoherent speech.
At the time of its onset, all symptoms indeed manifest specifically;
in this fever arising from vāta, there is emaciation of the face, piercing pain in the temples and head,
obstruction of the channels, and a distaste for food, which increases when cold water is applied.
In the pitta-type [fever], there is fainting, aversion to food, lamentation, a burning sensation, redness of the eyes, constant emaciation,

a longing for cold things, bitterness in the mouth, and a smoky sensation. When the digestive fire is obstructed by kapha due to the suppression of vapors, thirst arises in the person through the action of phlegm (balāsa).

Excessive sleep, heaviness of the body, and sweetness of the mouth are its initial symptoms; furthermore, one becomes excessively emaciated. The fourth type of thirst is considered to be born of injury (*kṣataja*), arising from both pain and the loss of blood in a wound.
That which arises from the depletion of the bodily tissues (*rasakṣaya*) is known as being born of wasting (*kṣayasambhavā*); one who is overcome by it [suffers] throughout the nights and days.
Some say that one does not drink water with ease due to *sannipāta* (the simultaneous derangement of all three humors);
the physician should diagnose this condition by observing, in its entirety, the symptoms described for the depletion of *rasa*.
Arising from the three humors and from *āma*, it causes pain in the heart, spitting, and exhaustion. (8–9)
Likewise, consuming unctuous, sour, salty, or heavy food quickly produces thirst.
With a feeble voice, fainting, a dejected face, a distressed heart, and a parched throat and palate, that thirst indeed becomes accompanied by complications; it is emaciating and difficult to endure.
Thirst occurring in those whose bodies are afflicted by fever, delusion, wasting, cough, dyspnea, and other such conditions;
in those emaciated by chronic diseases; in those suffering from persistent vomiting; or when accompanied by severe complications—such thirst should be known as fatal. 12
In thirst arising from Vāta, food and drink that subdue Vāta—being mild, light, and cold—are recommended.
In thirst born of Pavana (Vāta), curd with jaggery is praised;
likewise, sweet, bitter, liquid, and cold substances are excellent for removing thirst caused by Pitta.
One should administer water cooled after being boiled with musta, parpaṭaka, uddīcya, chatrākhya, śīra, and candana for the alleviation of thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
Alternatively, one may give parched rice water (lāja-udaka) mixed with honey and cooled, or stirred with jaggery (guḍa).
A person afflicted by thirst should drink [water] mixed with *kāśmarī* and sugar.
By means of a moist bed, moist clothing, and a moist upper garment, the thirst and even the intense burning sensation of embodied beings will certainly be pacified. (16–17)
When the juice of the *gostanī* fruit, sugarcane juice, milk, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and *madhūtpala* are regularly inhaled through the nose, even severe thirst is pacified;
it produces clarity in the mouth and restores moisture to the oral cavity. 18.
