Holding a mouthful of honey allays the burning sensation of thirst (19). In cases of dryness of the tongue, palate, throat, and kloman, one should place the filaments of the mātuluṅga fruit, combined with ghee and rock salt, upon the head (20).
Having ground together pomegranate, jujube, *lodhra*, wood-apple, and citron, an application as a paste upon the head destroys thirst and burning sensations.
(21) Or, one who is thirsty may drink cold water mixed with honey up to the throat.
One should administer it as a purgative or emetic; by this, thirst is pacified.
(22) A decoction of coriander (*dhānyāka*) combined with sugar, taken in the morning, conquers thirst as well as burning sensations and serves to cleanse the channels. (23)

One should place a pill made from the powder of *āmala*, *kamala*, *kuṣṭha*, parched grain (*lāja*), and *vaṭarohaka* mixed with honey in the mouth; this destroys excessive thirst and severe dryness of the mouth. (24)
One should conquer pain arising from a wound by means of ghee and by drinking blood; that which arises from wasting (kṣaya) should be destroyed by milk-water, or meat-broth water, or sweet-water.
One should conquer that arising from suppuration with decoctions of bilva and vacā combined with digestive stimulants.
One should conquer wasting diseases (kṣaya) and all thirst caused by [excessive] eating by mentioning the food of the guru;
and one should quench with jaggery-water that thirst which arises after consuming unctuous food.
For those who are extremely weak from disease, milk quickly quenches thirst here in this world. 26–27.
Those suffering from fainting, vomiting, thirst, constipation, or those severely exhausted by women or wine,
as well as patients with internal hemorrhage (raktapitta) or alcoholism (madātyaya), should drink cold water.
Furthermore, one should overcome their thirst through the use of wholesome food, drink, and medicinal remedies.
When that [thirst] is conquered, any other disease can also be treated.
If a man, emaciated by a previous illness, should thirst and not obtain water, he would quickly meet with death or a chronic disease. (29–30)
One who is thirsty falls into delusion; from delusion, one gives up one's life.
Therefore, under no circumstances whatsoever should one withhold water.
Even without food, a living being can sustain its life for a long time.

Due to the absence of water, one afflicted by thirst is deprived of life in an instant. 32. Thus ends the eighteenth chapter on Thirst (tṛṣṇā). Now begins the nineteenth chapter on Fainting (mūrchā), Giddiness (bhrama), Sleep (nidrā), Drowsiness (tandrā), and Syncope (saṃnyāsa). 19.
In one who is emaciated, whose humors are greatly aggravated, who consumes incompatible food, or who suffers from the suppression of natural urges or physical trauma, or who is of weak constitution,
a violent [fever] arises in the sense organs, both external and internal.
When the humors (doṣas) settle [in the channels], then human beings lose consciousness.
When the channels carrying perception are obstructed by wind and the other humors,
darkness suddenly overcomes them, causing the cessation of both pleasure and pain.
And because of the removal of pleasure and pain, a person falls like a piece of wood;
they call that state "mūrchā" (fainting), which is proclaimed to be of six kinds:
[caused] by wind and the other humors, by blood, by wine, and by poison.
In all six of these [fevers], however, bile (pitta) predominates.
Heartache, yawning, exhaustion, loss of consciousness, and loss of strength are the premonitory symptoms of all of them; one should diagnose each according to its own specific characteristics.
Seeing the sky as blue, or black, or even reddish, he enters into darkness and awakens quickly;
there is trembling, aching of the limbs, and pain in the heart.
In fainting caused by Vata, there is emaciation and a dusky-red complexion;
seeing the sky as red, green, or yellow, he enters into darkness and awakens covered in sweat.
Thirsty, suffering from burning heat, with eyes turbid and reddish-yellow,
with loose stools and a yellowish complexion— these are the symptoms when fainting arises from Pitta.
The sky appears like a dark cloud or as if shrouded by dense darkness.
Seeing [nothing], he enters into darkness and awakens only after a long time;
with limbs covered by heavy [secretions] as if by the skin of a mountain, there is excessive salivation and nausea in fainting caused by phlegm. 11–12.
Taking on every possible form, like an epilepsy (apasmāra) that has arrived through a derangement of the humors (sannipāta), it quickly strikes down a living being even without loathsome movements.
Earth and water constitute its nature as darkness (tamas), and blood is its associated odor.
Therefore, human beings on earth faint from the scent of blood;
some say this is due to the very nature of the substance, for one becomes deluded upon seeing it.
One who has fainted has stiffened limbs and eyes, and breathes with shallow, suppressed gasps. (14–15)
The qualities of poison and wine exist in an even more intense degree;
therefore, from those two, the two types of delusion arise exactly as described.
One who has consumed wine lies down babbling, with a mind that is ruined and bewildered.
Until it reaches old age, one should toss the limbs on the ground;
trembling, sleep, thirst, and darkness occur when one is unconscious from poison.
This should be understood as more intense according to its own specific poisonous symptoms.

Fainting (mūrchā) consists primarily of pitta and tamas; vertigo (bhrama) arises from rajas, pitta, and vāyu; drowsiness (tandrā) results from tamas, vāta, and kapha; and sleep (nidrā) is born of kapha and tamas.
[19] There is a lack of perception regarding the objects of the senses, heaviness, yawning, and exhaustion.
One should designate as *tandrā* (lassitude) that state of one who is as if seized by sleep; 20.
that which is effortless fatigue in the body, increased and accompanied by labored breathing, is to be known as *klama* (exhaustion), which obstructs the objects of the senses. 21.
But when the mind is exhausted and the agents of action, overcome by fatigue,
withdraw from their objects, then the human being sleeps;
for the exceedingly powerful impurities seize the activity of speech, body, and mind.
The vital breaths, having resorted to the abode of life, abandon the weak creature.

He who has thus renounced through formal renunciation becomes like a piece of wood, resembling one who is dead; having abandoned his actions which yield immediate fruit, he is swiftly released from his life-breaths.
When the force of the humors (doṣas) such as intoxication and fainting has subsided, they subside in the embodied being of their own accord; renunciation does not occur without medicines.
Sprinkling, immersion, jewels along with necklaces, cold plasters, and the breeze from fans [are the remedies].
Cool, fragrant drinks are unrestrictedly beneficial in all types of fainting (mūrchā).
In the group of prepared sweet milks, as well as the juices of wild animals and pomegranate, barley, red rice, satīna, and mudga beans are wholesome in cases of fainting. 26–27.
Kola, majjā, uśīra, and kesara, drunk with cold water, will conquer fainting; or one may overcome it by licking *kṛṣṇā* mixed with honey.
One should lick *bisā*, *mṛṇāla*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *pathyā* with cold water and honey.
She should not obstruct her nose or mouth, nor should she drink the milk of human women.

She should drink cool decoctions containing grapes, sugar, pomegranate, and parched grain, as well as those containing white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses—those which bring fever to its cessation. (29–30)
An ointment for awakening [the eyes] should be made from śirīṣa seeds, cow urine, kṛṣṇā, marica, and saindhava; or with sarala, na, śilā, and vacā.
For it is said by the best of physicians that [this condition] arises from delusion (pramoha). 32.

Equal parts of *madhūka* essence, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *vacā*, black pepper (*uṣaṇaka*), and long pepper (*kaṇā*) should be finely ground with water and administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) to restore consciousness. 33.
In fainting caused by blood, cold treatments are beneficial;
in that caused by alcohol, one should drink alcohol or enjoy sleep at ease; in that caused by poison, one should administer anti-poisonous medicines. 34
One who has many morbid humors and, due to an excess of *tamas*, is so faint that he does not wake at all— having lost consciousness—
he is indeed proclaimed by physicians to be a man difficult to treat.
(35) [The treatments include] collyriums, nasal drops, medicated smokes, and insufflations.
Piercing with needles, burning, pain in the spaces between the nails,
plucking out the hair of the head and body, biting with the teeth, and rubbing with *ātmaguptā* (the castor-oil plant) are recommended for awakening him. (36–37)
In cases of fainting (mūrchā), the physician should administer mercury mixed with honey;
[he should also apply] cold sprinklings, immersion baths, and the like, as well as forceful pressure on all parts of the body.
[One should also use] copper powder, uśīra, and keśara with cold water.
When drunk, it quickly destroys fainting, just as Indra’s thunderbolt fells a tree.
(39) One should drink a decoction of durālabhā with ghee for the alleviation of dizziness;
or one may take ghee prepared with a decoction of pathyā or with the juice of dhātrī. (40)
Copper [powder] drunk with a decoction of *durālabhā* combined with ghee quickly wards off vertigo, just as Śambhu has declared.
(41) Horse saliva, excellent salt, camphor, realgar, and *māgadhikā* mixed with honey... (42)
When these are applied to the eyes and mixed together, they ward off drowsiness and sleep.
(43) White rock salt, white pepper, mustard seeds, and kuṣṭha, ground with goat's urine and used as a nasal drop (nasya), ward off drowsiness. (44)
45. By snuffing a preparation of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), *ugrā*, and the best salt (*lavaṇottama*), one overcomes excessive drowsiness (*tandrā*).
By drinking a decoction of *kṣudrā*, *amṛtā*, lotus-root (*pauṣkara*), ginger (*nāgara*), *bhārgī*, and *śivā*, [the same result is achieved].
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the section on fainting (*mūrchā*), vertigo (*bhrama*), sleep (*nidrā*), drowsiness (*tandrā*), and collapse (*sannyāsa*). 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter on the disorders of intoxication (madātyaya).
Wine, by its very nature, is considered by the wise to be just like food:
when used improperly it leads to disease, but when used properly it is an elixir (rasāyana). 1.

The vital breaths are the food of living beings; that which destroys the life-breaths through improper application is poison, yet that same [poison], when properly applied according to the prescribed method,
in the correct dose, at the right time, with wholesome foods, and in accordance with one's strength, becomes an elixir (rasāyana).
For one who drinks wine with great joy, it shall be like nectar.
One of a vāta constitution should drink [wine] after being treated with oil massage, rubbing, bathing, clothing, incense, and ointments, and after consuming similarly unctuous and warm foods.
A person of pitta constitution should drink [liquor] along with various cooling treatments— sweet, unctuous, and cold fruits and foods;
whereas one of kapha constitution should drink madirā liquor with the meat of wild animals and black pepper.

One with a predominance of phlegm (kapha) should drink wine before the meal; one with a predominance of bile (pitta) should drink it after the meal; one with a predominance of wind (vāta) should drink it during the meal; and one with balanced humors may drink as he desires.
Furthermore, a person with a predominance of wind generally drinks wine made from molasses or flour.

For one whose constitution consists of phlegm and bile (kapha-pitta), the drinking of *mādhvīka* or *mādhava* wine is prescribed; this is the rule for those possessing wealth as stated by Caraka and others,
or otherwise, one may drink wine in moderation according to what is available.
The heart is said to be the seat of the channels of rasa, vāta, and the other humors; of the vital essence (sattva), the intellect, and the senses; and of the primary ojas.
Alcohol, having entered the heart, [overpowers] the qualities of ojas by means of its own qualities.
Agitating the ten [faculties], these ten bring about transformation of the mind.
Alcohol is traditionally said to possess ten qualities: lightness, heat, sharpness, subtlety, acidity, pervasiveness, quick action, as well as dryness, expansiveness, and clarity.
Ojas is traditionally said to possess ten qualities: it is heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, thick, sweet, stable, clear, slimy, and subtle.
Its heaviness results from lightness [of other elements], its coldness from heat, and its sour nature from its own inherent character.

From sharpness (*taikṣṇya*), it produces sweetness (*mādhurya*) and softness (*mārdava*); from rapid transformation (*āśubhāvana*), clarity (*prasāda*); from dryness (*raukṣya*), unctuousness (*sneha*); from pervasiveness (*vyavāyitva*), stability (*sthiratva*) and subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*);
from expansiveness (*vikāsibhāva*), sliminess (*paicchilya*); and from clarity (*vaiśadya*), thickness (*sāndratā*). (13–14)
In this way, due to its subtlety, liquor destroys the qualities of *ojas* by means of its own qualities;

having quickly agitated the *sattva* and that which rests upon it, it produces intoxication. When the heart is permeated by the qualities of liquor, there arise exhilaration, thirst, passion, and pleasure.

Furthermore, various transformations—whether characterized by passion (rājasa) or darkness (tāmasa)—arise according to one's disposition, ending in the sleep of delusion; this is the definition of intoxication. Joy, vigor, strength, nourishment, health, and likewise manliness [are its signs].
When drunk with reason, wine quickly produces intoxication and happiness;
it is appetizing, digestive, pleasing to the heart, clarifies the voice and complexion, nourishing, bulk-promoting, strengthening, and removes fear, grief, and fatigue. (18–19)

It induces sleep for those who have lost their sleep, purifies the speech of the mute, destroys excessive sleep, removes obstructions, and brings an end to the suffering of execution, imprisonment, and affliction. 20. It also prevents the perception [of such things].
Even for the elderly, wine brings joy through its exhilarating effects;
for this world of living beings, which is wounded by many sorrows and afflicted by griefs, wine, when consumed with moderation, is a source of rest.

The first stage of intoxication is indeed declared to be exceedingly delightful; it brings joy through the recollection of the Buddha, is pleasant, increases the enjoyment of food, drink, and sleep, and enhances the quality of recitation and song.
(23) In the second stage, however, one's intellect, memory, speech, and movements become indistinct; one behaves like a madman and is not tranquil.

Stricken by sloth and sleep, and repeatedly intoxicated by the middle stage of intoxication, a man might go to one who should not be approached, fail to respect his teachers, eat what is unfit for consumption, and, with his senses lost,
speak the secrets held in his heart; in this third stage of intoxication, a man is no longer master of himself.
But in the fourth stage of intoxication, one is deluded and inactive like a broken log; no longer discerning between what should and should not be done, he is dead even beyond the dead.
Who would indulge in such intoxication, which is like another form of madness? (26)
Like one who is not deluded, a self-controlled and skillful man avoids a wilderness full of many dangers.

Those who are strong, who have eaten their fill, who consume large meals, who are unctuous, endowed with vigor and youth, and whose lineage is accustomed to intoxicants, do not become excessively intoxicated.

Those with an excess of fat and phlegm, mild vata and pitta, and strong digestive fires do not suffer from intoxication; however, those who are the opposite, or those who are constipated and have aggravated humors, become excessively intoxicated by wine that is sour and dry, or even by a large quantity when taken on an empty stomach. (29)

Those very qualities observed in poison which provoke the *sannipāta* [disorder] are seen in wine as well, though they are even more powerful in poison. Therefore, [the effects of wine are intensified] when it is drunk improperly or in excessive quantity.
Indeed,
through liquor that is unwholesome, impure, or consumed at the improper time, diseases such as alcoholism (madātyaya) arise.
When liquor is consumed constantly by a person, even if it has been completely digested, [it leads to these ailments].
It may produce most grievous disorders, and it may even cause the dissolution of the body—
[when the patient is] angry, terrified, thirsty, tormented by grief, hungry,
exhausted by physical exertion, carrying loads, or traveling on a journey, or likewise when afflicted by the suppression of natural urges. (33–34)

When consumed by one who is excessively emaciated or rough, by one with a distended abdomen, by one who has eaten during indigestion, by one who is weak, or by one afflicted by heat, liquor produces various disorders.
[35] He now explains the disorders arising from liquor.

I shall now describe the symptoms of excessive drinking (pānātyaya), extreme intoxication (paramada), indigestion from alcohol (pānājīrṇa), and the most severe alcohol-induced delirium (pānavibhrama): intense physical suffering, profound confusion, and pain in the heart. (36)
There is constant loss of appetite, thirst, and fever characterized by alternating cold and heat;
a pain arises in the head, sides, bones, and joints as if they were being mangled; and there occurs excessive yawning, twitching, trembling, and exhaustion. (37–38)
Constriction of the chest, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, insomnia,
trembling of the body, diseases of the ears, eyes, and mouth, stiffness in the sacrum (trika), vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha. 39.
Exhaustion, incoherent speech, and the vision of non-existent forms;
being filled with grass, ashes, creepers, leaves, and dust; and being attacked by birds—a man whose mind is deluded perceives these things. (40–41)
One should recognize all these as the symptoms of alcoholism (madātyaya), including the visions of agitated and inauspicious dreams;
likewise, one who is excessively emaciated by grief for a woman, fear, heavy burdens, travel, or physical labor [is also subject to it]. 42.
One who eats food that is dry, scanty, or measured, and drinks wine in excessive quantity— 43—
and who consumes dry, aged wine at night after having destroyed sleep,
that [wine] quickly produces in him an intoxication characterized primarily by wind (vāta). 44.
One should recognize a case of alcoholism (madātyaya) dominated by Vāta by the presence of hiccups, labored breathing, trembling of the head, pain in the flanks, insomnia, and excessive delirium.
This occurs in one who excessively consumes sharp, hot, sour, and strong liquor.
In a man who eats sour, hot, and pungent foods, and who is prone to anger and ignorance,
there arises a severe form of alcoholism (madātyaya) characterized predominantly by pitta,
accompanied by thirst, burning sensations, fever, perspiration, delusion, diarrhea, and vertigo. (46)
One should know that the green-colored variety of alcoholism (madātyaya) is characterized by a predominance of bile (pitta).

This occurs when one consumes food that is sweet, unctuous, and heavy in excess quantity, while being devoted to a lack of physical exercise, sleeping during the day, and indulging in the comforts of beds and seats. (47–48)
That person certainly suffers from alcoholism characterized predominantly by *kapha* (verse 49).

One should recognize as *kapha*-predominant alcoholism in one who is overcome by cold and afflicted with vomiting, anorexia, nausea, drowsiness, a sense of being wrapped in a wet cloth, and heaviness (verse 50).
Madātyaya (alcoholism) arises from all three doṣas and exhibits all their symptoms.

However, experts state that the signs of the final stage of intoxication are the depletion of kapha, heaviness of the limbs, a bad taste in the mouth, retention of feces and urine, drowsiness, and anorexia; furthermore, there is thirst, pain in the head, and a splitting sensation in the joints.

Distension, severe vomiting, or a burning sensation occur when undigested food (ajīrṇa) reaches the stomach during drinking; these signs should be recognized by the physician with certainty as being produced by the provocation of pitta (53).

Furthermore, there are pricking pains in the heart and limbs, salivation of phlegm, a sensation of smoke in the throat, fainting, eructation, intoxication, headache, and a sense of being smeared with oil.
The wise declare that aversion toward various kinds of wine, food, and their derivatives constitutes the delirium of drinking (pānavibhrama) in all its forms.
One should abandon a person struck by drinking who has a sunken upper lip, excessive coldness, intense burning, and a face with the luster of oil;
likewise one whose tongue, lips, and teeth are black, or even blue and yellow, and whose eyes have the appearance of blood.
One should abandon that person who is afflicted by hiccups, fever, vomiting, shivering, pain in the flanks, cough, and vertigo.
Indeed, for diseases arising from alcohol, alcohol itself is the remedy;
just as fire is beneficial for those burned by fire, so is sweating [therapeutic].
The disease that arises from the improper consumption of liquor, whether by excessive or deficient intake, is indeed pacified by drinking liquor in moderation,
combined with citron, tamarind, jujube, and pomegranate. (57)

One should administer wine seasoned with salt, along with *yavānī*, *īṣapuṣā*, *jīraka*, and *śṛṅgavera*, mixed with oily roasted grain flour (*saktu*) and side dishes, for the pacification of chronic disorders arising from *vāta* and *pitta*. (58–59)
Wine mixed with sauvarcala salt, trikaṭu (vyoṣa), and a small amount of water should be given to one who has consumed stale wine; it removes the affliction caused by wind and excessive drinking.
Cavya, sauvarcala salt, asafoetida (hiṅgu), pūrakā, and viśvadīpaka [are also used].
This powder should be drunk with wine to alleviate the disease of alcoholism (pānātyaya). It may also be taken with the juices of the common quail, partridge,
and cock, as well as with the meat of other birds, wild game, fish, and marsh-dwelling animals, along with boiled rice.
Vata-dominant alcoholism (madātyaya) is treated with unctuous, hot, salty, and sour foods, such as veśavāra (minced meat) that is pleasing to the palate, and unctuous wheat-based dishes;
as well as by the merciless embraces of women whose bodies are warm with the heat of youth.
Through the weight of the hips, thighs, and breasts, which provide the comfort of restraint and warmth;
through warm beds and coverings; and through pleasant inner chambers protected from strong winds, alcoholism (madātyaya) is quickly pacified. 64–65.
In cases of excessive alcohol consumption caused by pitta, all cooling treatments should be employed;
one should drink wine mixed with sugar and honey, diluted with half as much water,
or wine combined with the juices of dates, grapes, and *parūṣaka* fruits.
One should give cold pomegranate juice mixed with parched grain flour (śaktu),

or honey-wine (mādhvīka) with sugar, or even another [fermented liquor] combined with plenty of water, at the appropriate time for drinking in cases of alcoholism caused by pitta (pittamadātyaya). 67–68.
One should consume in one's diet śaśānka, piñjala, ena, lāva, and asitapucchaka birds, along with rice and ṣaṣṭika grains seasoned with sweet and sour flavors;
or one may prepare goat meat mixed with paṭola and barley.

One should prepare various kinds of nourishing drinks (*tarpaṇa*), soups (*yūṣa*), and meat broths (*rasa*) mixed with *satīna* beans, or combined with pomegranate and *āmalaka*, as well as with the juices of grapes, *āmalaka*, dates, and *parūṣaka*. (70–71)
Cool foods and drinks, cool beds and seats, the touch of cool breezes and water, and cool groves;
as well as linen, lotuses, blue lilies, jewels, and pearls— 72.
The touches of sandalwood water and the cool rays of the moon are refreshing.
One should feed [the patient] barley and wheat with parched food combined with *yavānī* and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), along with a parched broth. 73–74.
One should cause him to be given barley-food mixed with a profusion of pungent substances, along with the juice of dried horse-gram (kulattha) or radish;
or a dry, sour broth of goat meat, or the broth of wild (jāṅgala) animals.
In cases of alcoholism caused by phlegm (kapha), one should drink a soup of the three pungents (vyoṣa) with a slight sourness.
Alternatively, in cases of alcoholism caused by phlegm, one should eat meat that has been fried in a pot or on a pan until it is dry, seasoned with pungent, sour, and salty flavors.

Scraping with wine mixed with sour gruel (vāma-kadravya) is recommended for alcoholism arising from an excess of phlegm (kapha), as well as fasting according to one's strength; these are the treatments prescribed for vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively. 78.

In cases of poisoning by *sarvaja* [poisons], physicians should employ all of these measures. The juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* with jaggery quickly pacifies intoxication caused by *kodrava*, while milk mixed with sugar, when drunk, quickly pacifies intoxication caused by *dhattūra*. 79–80.
Cold water, when drunk until satiety, immediately pacifies vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, and intoxication caused by betel nut (pūgaphala). Furthermore,
[these conditions may also be cured] by smelling wild cow dung, drinking water, or even consuming salt.
The intoxication arising from betel nut, accompanied by colic, is pacified by a mouthful of sugar;
likewise, its powder, ground and sniffed at that very moment, naturally destroys the intoxication produced by betel leaf alone in men. 82–83.

Pathyā (harītakī) consumed regularly, along with nutmeg and a bath in cold water combined with sugar and curd, quickly destroys the intoxication of jāti; this very same regimen is likewise considered for the purpose of pacifying the intoxication of vibhītaka. 84.

If a person, having drunk liquor, immediately licks sugar mixed with ghee, that liquor—though its potency is well-known—will never intoxicate him even slightly. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on the treatment of alcoholism (madātyaya). 85. 20.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter, on Burning (Dāha).
Burning arises from pitta, just like pitta-fever; its progression is as follows:
the blood, having spread throughout the entire body and become aggravated, certainly causes a burning sensation.
He is fumigated and scorched, copper-colored with copper-red eyes;
his limbs and face smell of iron as if he were being strewn over by fire.
For one whose internal cavities are filled with blood, there is a burning sensation in another part that is most difficult to overcome.

When that heat of the drink reaches the skin, it becomes intensified by pitta and blood and produces a terrible burning sensation; the treatment for this is the same as for pitta disorders. Due to the suppression of thirst, when the water element is depleted, the internal fire (tejas) becomes greatly provoked.
It burns the internal and external body of the person with impaired intellect;
with the throat, palate, and lips completely parched, he extends his tongue and trembles.
This burning sensation, arising from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus), is accompanied by fainting and thirst.
With a feeble voice and devoid of physical activity, he sinks down, severely afflicted.
(6) There is also that which arises from injury to the vital points (*marmābhighātaja*); it is considered the seventh [type] and is incurable.
(7) Furthermore, all [these types] should be rejected in the case of a person whose limbs are cold. (8)
The wise physician should smear the patient with ghee purified a hundred times, or with a paste of barley flour mixed with *kola* and *āmalaka*, or even with fermented grain-wash (*dhānyāmla*);
he should then cover the patient's entire body with a cloth moistened with *āranāla*.

One afflicted by burning heat should anoint oneself with sandalwood paste mixed with lāmajjaka, and sleep upon a bed of lotus leaves and plantain leaves, fanned by palm-leaf fans dripping with drops of sandalwood water.
Cold water is recommended for sprinkling, immersion baths, and the use of fans to alleviate burning sensations and thirst; likewise,
phalinī, lodhra, sevya, ambu, hemapatra, and kuṭannaṭa are beneficial.

An ointment combined with *kālīyaka* resin is recommended for application during a burning sensation. A person afflicted by burning heat should immerse himself in a large tub (*droṇī*) filled with water containing *hrīvera*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, and blue lotuses.
Lotus-bedecked ponds, auspicious water-machines,
and women with limbs anointed with sandalwood paste are considered removers of burning heat and distress.
One should cause [the patient] to drink lotus-water, sugar-water, and milk as well.
One should also prepare milk and sugarcane juice according to the procedure that subdues pitta (15). A preparation made with *patra*, *parpaṭa*, *uśīra*, water-lily,
lotus, *mṛṇāla*, *mudga*, *dhānyaka*, *padmaka*, and *āmalaka* [is likewise effective] (16).
A decoction that is half-remaining, white and cool, mixed with honey,
would remove even the most intense burning sensation in men. One *prastha* of sesame oil should be slowly [boiled] in sixteen times its quantity [of water].
One should boil that [decoction] in sour gruel (kāñjika); it is an excellent remedy for burning sensations and fever. 18. Thus ends the twenty-first chapter on Burning Sensations (udāha).
Now begins the twenty-second chapter on Insanity (unmāda). 22.

Because the defects (doṣas), having resorted to a wrong path, become arrogant and cause intoxication, this mental disease is therefore proclaimed as "unmāda" (insanity). Furthermore, when it has not yet fully developed, it is young and bears the name "mada" (intoxication).
The causes of insanity are: the consumption of incompatible, harmful, or impure foods; the assault of gods, teachers, or the twice-born; mental trauma preceded by fear or joy;
and irregular physical exertion—whether occurring individually or all together through the excessively aggravated *doṣas*.

It is said to be fivefold, including mental suffering, and the sixth arises from poison; for each of these, there is its own appropriate remedy. By these, the impurities of one with little strength become corrupted, vitiating the heart, which is the abode of the intellect.
Occupying the channels that carry the mind, they quickly delude the consciousness of a person.
Confusion of intellect, agitation of the mind, a troubled gaze, lack of fortitude,
incoherent speech, and a vacant heart are the general symptoms of the disease of insanity.

When the Vāyu is excessively aggravated by dry, scanty, or cold food, purgation, depletion of the bodily tissues (dhātus), or fasting, it vitiates the heart already impaired by anxiety and other factors, and swiftly destroys both the intellect and memory. Laughing, smiling, and grinning at inappropriate times; dancing, singing, and speaking incoherently; tossing about the limbs; weeping; roughness of the skin, emaciation, and a reddish complexion; and a sense of strength returning only after digestion—these are the symptoms of the Vāta-type [unmada].
Pitta, accumulated through indigestion, pungent, sour, burning, and cold foods, when its force has become aggravated,
quickly produces extremely fierce insanity in one who lacks self-control, remaining as before in the heart.
It manifests as indignation, agitation, nakedness, threats, running away, heat, and rage.
A desire for shade, cold food, and water, and a yellowish complexion are the signs of [fever] caused by bile (pitta). 10.
Kapha, increased in the vital organ (marman) of one who is lethargic due to over-satiation, destroys intellect and memory; deluding the mind, it produces a disorder. 11.
Slow speech and movement, loss of appetite, a fondness for secluded women, excessive sleep,
vomiting, salivation, weakness after eating, and whiteness of the nails and other parts— these occur when the disease is of the nature of phlegm (kapha).
That which is most terrible, arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), occurs due to all the causes combined.
One should avoid such contradictory medical treatments that assume all forms [of disease].

Furthermore, in one who is terrified by thieves, royal officers, enemies, or others; or whose mind is deeply wounded by the loss of wealth or kinsmen; or who desires to sport with a beloved woman, a most intense mental derangement may arise. (13–14)
He speaks incoherently and follows his own whims; deprived of consciousness, he sings, laughs, and weeps like one utterly deluded.
With bloodshot eyes, his strength and senses destroyed, extremely dejected, and with a dark-complexioned face, he becomes lifeless when struck by poison.
Furthermore, a man whose flesh and strength are wasted may have his face turned downward or upward.
For one who is vigilant and free from doubt does not perish through madness.

One who is sober, whose actions are characterized by valor and heroism, who is endowed with knowledge, discernment, strength, and so forth, and for whom the onset of provocation is fixed, such a mental derangement arises from gods and other [supernatural causes]. 17–18.

Contented, pure, possessing most divine garlands and fragrance, free from drowsiness, speaking truthful and refined speech, radiant, with steady eyes, a bestower of boons, devoted to Brahmanas— such a man becomes beloved by the gods.
(19) One who perspires excessively, speaks of the faults of the twice-born, gurus, and gods, with downcast eyes, devoid of fear, and looking toward wrong paths;
He is contented and does not crave various kinds of food and drink; his mind becomes wicked and he is possessed by the enemies of the gods.

With a joyful soul, frequenting riverbanks and the interior of forests, well-behaved and fond of singing, perfumes, and garlands, the man afflicted by the Gandharva-graha dances and laughs beautifully with very soft sounds.

One with copper-colored eyes, wearing pleasant red garments, deep in voice, moving swiftly, speaking little, patient, radiant, and saying "What shall I give? To whom?"—if such a person is afflicted by the *yakṣa* seizure, he, being tranquil in soul and wearing his garment over the right shoulder, offers rice-balls upon the sacrificial grass for the *pretas*, as well as water. (22)
One who desires meat, yearns for sesame, molasses, and milk-rice (pāyasa), and becomes devoted to those things, is possessed by a paternal spirit (pitṛ-graha).

(23) But he who at times glides on the ground like a serpent, repeatedly licks the corners of his mouth with his tongue, is prone to anger, and longs for ghee, honey, milk, and milk-rice—he should indeed be known as one possessed by a snake-spirit (bhujaṅgama). (24)
One who desires various preparations of meat, blood, and liquor; who is shameless, exceedingly cruel, and overbearing;
who is prone to anger, possesses diverse powers, wanders at night, and hates purity—such a person is seized by Rākṣasas.
He is one who hates gods, Brahmins, and gurus, and reviles the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
One who causes pain to himself, is non-violent toward others, and is frequented by Brahmarākṣasas;

one with disheveled garments, emaciated and harsh, speaking perversely, foul-smelling, extremely impure, and likewise excessively restless; one who eats much, dwells in solitary forest regions, and acts with agitation—trembling and weeping—he is possessed by a Piśāca. (26–27)

One who has large eyes, moves rapidly, vomits foam, suffers from sleepiness, falls down, and trembles excessively, as well as one who has fallen from a mountain, an elephant, or a tree, becomes incurable; likewise, [these symptoms appear] in the thirteenth year. (28) The planetary spirits (*devagraha*) seize children on the full moon day, while the demonic spirits (*asura*) seize them at both twilights.
Gandharvas generally enter on the eighth day, and Yakṣas on the first; the Pitṛs enter during the dark fortnight and also on the fifth day, while Uragas,
Rākṣasas, and Piśācas indeed enter at night on the fourteenth day.
In cases of Vātika epilepsy, the administration of oleation (sneha-pāna) should be performed first; in Pittaja cases, purgation (vireka);

and in Kaphaja cases, emesis (vamana) should be administered, followed by the sequence beginning with enemas (vasti). Furthermore, whatever treatment is prescribed for [other] complications should also be applied in epilepsy.
In cases of insanity (unmāda), that [treatment] should also be administered because the nature of the doshas and the dūṣyas is common [to other diseases].
One should always protect the insane person with great effort from water, fire, trees, mountains, and uneven places, for those can cause immediate loss of life.

The fresh juices of *brāhmī*, *kūṣmāṇḍī* fruit, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*, when used individually, are seen to remove insanity; these same [juices], mixed with *kuṣṭha* and honey, [cure] leprosy.
[Also effective are] *siddhārthaka*, asafoetida, *vacā*, *karañja*, and *devadāru*. (33)
Equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, śvetā, kaṭabhī, bark, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), priyaṅgu, śirīṣa, and the two types of rajanī,
ground with goat's urine— this antidote is used as a drink and as an ointment. (34–35)
Used as a nasal drop, an ointment, for bathing, or as a massage paste, it removes epilepsy, poison, insanity, magical spells, misfortune, and fever;
it destroys fear of malevolent spirits and is highly recommended at the royal court.
Clarified butter prepared with this [mixture] along with cow's urine serves that same purpose.
One should announce the destruction of what is desired and display portents; having smeared a bound person with mustard oil, one should keep them lying face up in the sun. 37–38.
Or else, one should touch him with heated iron, oil, or water, or lash him with whips while he is securely bound in a secluded house;
or one should have him bitten by a snake whose fangs have been extracted, or by lions and elephants. (39)
He should be terrified by enemies and thieves with weapons in their hands;
or else, having led him outside in firm bonds, the king’s men should frighten him with threats of execution, intimidating him by the king’s command.
For when the fear for one's life arises from the body, suffering, or fear,
then his mind, which was agitated in every way, attains tranquility.
[But] the mind of one whose heart is struck by the loss of a beloved object—
Having identified that [condition] through the appearance of similar symptoms, one should bring it to pacification with soothing measures.
(43) Indeed, tri-yūṣaṇa, hiṅgu, salt, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī,
the seeds of śirīṣa and karañja, and white mustard seeds— (44)
A medicinal wick (varti) made from these ingredients ground with cow’s urine is beneficial as an eye-salve (añjana);
it destroys insanity (unmāda), epilepsy (apasmāra), and quartan fever (cāturthika-jvara).
[The drugs are: kuṣṭha, aśvagandhā, the two types of salt, ajamodā, the two types of jīraka, the three pungents (kaṭu), and pāṭhā.
One should powder these auspicious flowers along with *samāṅgī* and *vacā*, and soak the entire powder three times with the juice of *brāhmī*.
Once this powder is dried, a person should lick it in a dose of one *akṣa* with honey and ghee for seven days. 46–47.
This Sarasvata powder was created by Brahmā in ancient times for the benefit of all people who are dull-witted and lacking in discernment.
Through the practice of this, men gain intelligence, wisdom, fortitude, and memory.

Prosperity and the power of poetic composition shall increase further and further. (49) For one who licks at dawn the powder of *viśvā*, *ajamoda*, the two types of *janī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *ugrā*, *yaṣṭyāhva*, *kuṣṭha*, *magadhodbhava*, and *jīraka* mixed with ghee, the Goddess of Speech herself dwells within the mouth. (50)

Having added sixteen times as much water to the pulverized ingredients and boiled them down until one-fourth remains, this is known as the procedure for preparing a decoction (kvātha). [The ingredients are:
Daśamūlī, Rāsnā, Vātāri, Trivṛtā, and Balā.
One should cook two *prasthas* of ghee over a mild fire with decoctions made separately from one *kuḍava* each of *mūrvā* and *śatāvarī*; then,
one should cook it thoroughly again with the paste (*kalka*) of the substances to be mentioned hereafter.
Viśālā, triphalā, kauntī, devadāru, elavāluka, sthirā, anantā, the two types of rajanī, priyaṅgu, the two types of sārivā,
nīlotpala, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, dantī, and the filaments of the pomegranate (dāḍimakesara). 54.
Viḍaṅga, agnipatrī, kuṣṭha, candana, padmaka,
tālīśapatra, bṛhatī, and fresh mālatī flowers—
using these twenty-eight paste ingredients (kalkas), each weighing one karṣa individually.
Having added four times as much water, one should cook ghee with these flour-pastes;
this *mahācaitasanāma* [preparation] removes all disorders of the mind, [and is used] in epilepsy, severe insanity, weak digestion, fever, and cough. (57)
In cases of vātarakta, catarrh, consumption, emaciation, and tertian fever; in dysuria, pain in the waist, and those afflicted by erysipelas;
likewise in anemia, itching, poisoning, urinary disorders, and even in the case of artificial poison.
It is recommended for those whose minds are afflicted by gods and other spirits, for those who stammer, and for those lacking consciousness;
it is auspicious for women and for those who are barren, bestowing longevity and strength. It destroys misfortune and evil demons, and wards off all planetary influences.
It destroys delusion, intoxication, and fainting, while bestowing intelligence, memory, and wisdom.

(61) A physician, remaining pure, should conquer exogenous insanity through worship, offerings, oblations, sacrifices, burnt offerings, mantras, collyrium, and other such means, according to the prescribed rules. (62)
An ointment prepared from black pepper, long pepper, rock salt, honey,
and *gorocanā* is a supreme remedy for driving away madness caused by all gods and other spirits.
Likewise, the hair of bears and jackals, along with *śallakī* and garlic [should be used].
One should administer an inhalation of asafoetida and goat's urine;
by this, even a powerful seizure is quickly pacified.
One should also employ Kalyāṇaka or Mahā-caitasa ghee.
One may administer *Nārāyaṇa-taila* or likewise *Mahānārāyaṇa-taila* against all [spirits] except for the Piśācas; one should not act in opposition toward others,
for if they are provoked to anger, those of great power might kill both the patient and the physician.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter on insanity (unmāda).
Now begins the twenty-third chapter on epilepsy (apasmāra):
When the humors (doṣas) are provoked by anxiety, grief, and other such factors, they become lodged in the channels of the heart.
Having caused the destruction of memory, they produce epilepsy (*apasmāra*).
It is of four types: arising from wind (*vāta*), from bile (*pitta*), from phlegm (*kapha*), and from all the *doṣas* combined.
It consists of entering into darkness, agitation, and the loss of memory due to the aggravation of the *doṣas*.
This disease should be known as apasmāra (epilepsy), for it is indeed most terrible.
Trembling of the heart, a sense of emptiness, perspiration, brooding, fainting, confusion,
and loss of sleep— these occur both during its onset and while it persists.
One afflicted by wind trembles, grinds the teeth, froths at the mouth, and pants; moreover, one sees forms that are reddish-brown on all sides.
One afflicted by bile has yellow foam, limbs, face, and eyes, and perceives blood as yellow.
One with a pitta-type fever sees the world pervaded by a thirst-inducing, hot fire;
one with a kapha-type fever has white foam in the mouth and eyes, cold limbs, horripilation, heaviness, and sees white forms; such a person recovers after a long time.
Apasmāra arising from all three doṣas is to be recognized by all these characteristics;
it is incurable when it occurs in one who is emaciated, as well as in one who is weak and restless,
who trembles frequently, and whose eyebrows are agitated.

And Apasmāra destroys one who is undergoing transformation through the eyes. After a fortnight, or twelve days, or a month, the aggravated *malas* produce Apasmāra with an onset that occurs at some interval.
Garlic should be consumed with oil, and *śatāvarī* with milk;
the juice of *brāhmī* taken with honey is a remedy for all types of epilepsy.
Alternatively, the powder of *siddhārthaka* and other such herbs may be eaten.
Apasmāra (epilepsy) is pacified by an ointment applied to the entire body made from [the drugs] ground with cow’s urine.
An external application of oil cooked with siddhārthaka, śigru, kaṭvaṅga, and kiṇihī, along with four parts of cow’s urine, is beneficial for massage.
Through the application of a nasal medication (*nāvana*) consisting of *nirguṇḍī*, *bhavavandāka*,
and *manaḥśilā*, the great disease of epilepsy (*apasmāra*) is suddenly destroyed.
[14] *Manaḥśilā*, *tārkṣya-viṣṭhā* (the excrement of the *Tārkṣya* bird), and the dung of a pigeon (*pārāvata*)—
From its application as an ointment, it cures epilepsy and especially insanity.
He who eats the powder of *vacā* with honey while subsisting on milk and rice will certainly conquer even most terrible, long-standing epilepsy.
One should drink licorice (*yaṣṭyāhva*) ground with the juice extracted from *kūṣmāṇḍaka* fruit for three days to destroy epilepsy (17). [Likewise,
one should take] ghee boiled with *brāhmī* juice, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
This ancient formulation is supreme for removing epilepsy, insanity, and the influence of seizing spirits.
One should cook ghee with eighteen times its weight of the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* and a paste of *yaṣṭyāhvā*;
drinking that destroys epilepsy.
For one who experiences trembling of the heart, pain in the eyes, perspiration, and coldness of the hands and other limbs,
one should administer the water of Daśamūlī known as Kalyāṇaka.
[This consists of] Pañcakola, Marica, Triphalā, Viḍa salt, and Saindhava salt.

The powder of *kṛṣṇā*, *viḍaṅga*, *pūtīka*, *yavānī*, coriander, and cumin, when drunk with warm water, removes diseases of wind and phlegm; it is also effective in epilepsy, insanity, hemorrhoids, and disorders of the digestive tract. (21)
This auspicious powder is an enkindler of extinguished fire.
Having duly procured two *kīṭameḍhra* insects on a Sunday and wearing them around the neck or on the arm, one shall conquer even the most violent form of epilepsy.
Oil boiled with *śigru*, *kuṣṭha*, water, *ajājī*, garlic, *vyoṣa*, and *hiṅgu* in goat's urine should be used as a nasal drop (*nāvana*) in cases of epilepsy (*apasmṛti*).
Whatever wholesome nasal drops, collyriums, and medicinal remedies have been prescribed for insanity (*unmāda*) [should also be employed].

All of that should also be administered by the best of physicians in cases of epilepsy (apasmāra). Equal parts of mercury, lead, iron, realgar, sulphur, orpiment, and rasāñjana should be ground together with human urine.
One should cook that ball, doubled in size, with fragrant substances in an iron vessel for a moment;
when measured at five *guñjās*, it is an excellent remedy for epilepsy to be consumed along with goat’s ghee and human urine, together with *vyoṣa*, *sauvarcala* salt, and *hiṅgu*.
Afterwards, one should drink one karṣa of this "Bhūtabhairava" [preparation] with water.
(28) Thus ends the twenty-third chapter on epilepsy.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter on wind-diseases.

Due to the consumption of astringent, pungent, bitter, limited, dry, and light food; due to wind, staying awake at night, crossing water, physical injury, and fatigue; due to cold, fasting, sexual intercourse, and the depletion of bodily constituents (dhātus); due to the suppression of natural urges such as excrement; due to passion, grief, anxiety, and fear;

due to excessive bloodletting, emaciation caused by drugs, and excessive vomiting; due to excessive purgation, indigestion, during the rainy season, at dawn and dusk, during the third part of the day, when one has eaten until old age has set in, and even during the season known as Śiśira (late winter). 1–2. [In these conditions, the digestive fire becomes weak.]
The powerful wind, having filled the empty channels of the body, produces various diseases localized in the entire body or in a single limb:
stiffness of the head, emaciation, excessive yawning, and lockjaw.
Stiffness of the tongue, stammering, nasal speech, and muteness; loquacity, incoherent prattle, and lack of perception of tastes;
deafness, ringing in the ears, as well as loss of the sense of touch—these are the afflictions. 4–5.
Stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha) is counted here, as well as wasting of the arms (bāhuśoṣa), apabāhuka,
and viśvācī; upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta) is also mentioned,
along with distension (ādhmāna), counter-distension (pratyādhmāna), vātāṣṭhīlā, and pratiṣṭhīlā.
Distension of the abdomen and its counter-distension, as well as irregularity of the digestive fire (7);
flatulence, pain in the sides, and likewise pain in the sacrum (trika),
frequent urination, suppression of urine, and hardness of the feces (8).
The non-passage of feces, and thereafter sciatica (gṛdhrasī),
as well as the "kalāya-lameness," lameness, and likewise paraplegia;
also croștuśīrṣaka, khallī, and vātakaṇṭaka.
Pādaharṣa (numbness of the feet), pādadāha (burning sensation in the feet), ākṣepa (convulsions) known as daṇḍaka, ākṣepa caused by vāta and pitta, as well as daṇḍāpatānaka (stiffening like a staff),
and ākṣepa caused by trauma— these are recorded as the two types of āyāma (stretching/contraction).
The internal and likewise the external [types], dhanurvāta, kubjaka,
apatantra, apatāna, pakṣāghāta, and khilāṅgaka;
as well as trembling, stiffness, pain, piercing, breaking, and throbbing.
Roughness, emaciation, blackness, coldness, and the bristling of body hair; aching of the limbs, loss of limb function, and contraction of the vessels;
drying up of the limbs, timidity, delusion, and instability of mind. (13–14)
Loss of sleep, loss of perspiration, as well as loss of strength, depletion of semen, loss of menses, miscarriage,
and wandering about— these very eighty diseases arise from the practice of yoga.

These are proclaimed by the sages as the names of the Vātavyādhis (wind-diseases). Sweet, salty, sour, unctuous, hot, sleep-inducing, heavy, sun-exposure, enema, fomentation, nourishing therapy, fire-therapy, water-immersion, drying, oil massage, and rubbing— these bring about the pacification of provoked Vātas.
Now, regarding the symptoms and treatment of specific types of Vata diseases:

when the Vata wind, having taken recourse to the blood, affects the vessels supporting the head, making them rough, painful, and black, that condition known as Shirograha (seizure of the head) becomes incurable. 18.
In cases of headache, however, the treatments for wind (vāta) located in the head should be administered;
an oil massage with oil boiled in a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) and the juice of citron (mātuluṅga), as well as a cranial enema (śirovasti), are indicated. 19
When the wind, having drawn in a single breath, is forcefully exhaled again while accompanied by lassitude and sleepiness, that is called *jṛmbhā* (yawning).
[The remedy is] ginger, long pepper, black pepper, *dīpyaka*, and rock salt— either all together or each separately.
That same substance, either in its natural form or reduced to a fine powder, causes yawning, the onset of stretching, and stiffness; indeed,
when the impulse of yawning has arisen, one should lay a man upon a comfortable bed, and by that means the impulse of yawning will certainly be pacified.
The impulse of yawning subsides through massage with pungent oil,
from eating sweet foods, as well as from chewing betel;
it also ceases through the scraping of the tongue, the consumption of dry food, and from physical injury.
When the Vāyu, aggravated and located at the root of the jaw, causes the jaw to sag,
it produces either an open-mouthed state or a closed-mouthed state;
this is Hanugraha (lockjaw), by which chewing and speaking become difficult.
The physician should raise the chin if it is closed, smooth, and perspiring;
however, if it is open, he should lower it and thus perform the appropriate procedure here. Having repeatedly masticated long pepper and fresh ginger, [he should apply them].
One should spit out [the phlegm] with warm water and cleanse the interior of the mouth.
Having properly peeled and finely minced garlic, a man afflicted by stiffness of the neck (dhanustambha) should eat it with rock salt and sesame oil. 27–28.
Having thoroughly ground garlic pills, black gram, and split pulses, one should cook that paste with rock salt, fresh ginger, and asafoetida;
then, having formed them into balls (vaṭakas), one should fry them slowly in sesame oil.
One should eat those [medicines] like fire; from this, one will become free from lockjaw (hanustambha).
Having anointed [the area] with cooked oil, one should apply mild fomentation (sveda) and maintain a bladder enema (vasti) on the head filled with oil.
The physician should properly crush one hundred palas of Prasāraṇī, including its roots, leaves,
and branches, and boil it in one droṇa of water until the decoction is reduced to one-fourth of the original volume.
Then one should cook that decoction again in a hundred palas of oil;
one should cook it with a hundred palas of whey and an equal amount of sour gruel (kāñjika).
Then one should cook pure cow’s milk, four times the quantity of the oil.
Citraka, pippalīmūla, madhuka, saindhava, vacā,
śatapuṣpā, devadāru, rāsnā, gajapippalī,
the root of prasāraṇī, māṃsī, and red sandalwood. (35)
Likewise, one should prepare all the medicinal pastes with the root of vātāri, the root of balā, and nāgara, using one-eighth part oil;
this is renowned by the name Prasāraṇī-taila and is employed for its therapeutic effects.
When employed in drinks, nasal drops, head-poultices, massage, and likewise in sudation,
it destroys all diseases born of Vāta; specifically, it cures lockjaw,
stiffness of the tongue, and facial paralysis (ādita).
It also cures stammering, viśvācī, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), apabāhuka,
pain in the sacrum (trikaśūla), sciatica (gṛdhrasī), lameness, paraplegia,
kalāyakhañjatā, khallī, rigidity, and contraction. 39–40.
It undoubtedly removes internal and external contractions, as well as daṇḍāpatānaka, dhanurvāta, and hunchbackedness;
it is especially beneficial for those who are emaciated, the elderly, and those whose bodies have been stiffened by vāta. 41.
Because one extends the limbs from that [position], this is called *prasāraṇī*.

(42) The wind (*anila*) situated in the channel of speech (*vāgvāhinī-śirā*) causes the tongue to become stiff; that is *jihvā-stambha* (tongue-stiffness), by which there is an inability to consume food, drink, or speak. (43)

In cases of tongue-stiffness (jihvāstambha), the treatment for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) should be applied according to the specific condition; furthermore, the general therapeutic measures mentioned here are considered beneficial for facial paralysis (ardita) as well.
When the Vāyu, along with Kapha, having become obstructed, enters the sound-carrying channels (dhamanīs), [it causes these symptoms].
It renders men speechless, making them mute, lisping, or stammering. (45) Now follows the treatment for those who are stammering, lisping, or mute:
one *prastha* of ghee [should be cooked] with one *pala* each of *śigru*, *vacā*, salt, *dhātakī*, and *lodhra*.
Today, milk prepared with the *Sapāṭha* [mantras] and known by the name *Sārasvata*, when consumed according to the prescribed rite, instantly overcomes dullness, stammering, and muteness;
it bestows memory, intellect, wisdom, and eloquence, and causes one's speech to become perfectly clear. (46–47)
Turmeric, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, long pepper, ginger,
cumin, *ajamodā*, licorice, and rock salt— these should be taken in equal parts and ground into a fine powder. (48)
A person should lick that powder with clarified butter and consume it every day;
within twenty-one nights, the man will become a retainer of the Vedas, possessing a voice like the rumbling of clouds or a drum, and a tone like that of a cuckoo in rut. 49–50.
When a person utters speech that is disconnected and meaningless due to wind (vāta) provoked by its own causes, that is proclaimed as *pralāpa* (incoherent chatter).
[The following are the fragrant substances: *sattagara*, *varatiktā*, *revata*, *ambhoda*, *tiktā*, *analada*, *turagagandhā*, *bhāratī*, *hāra*, and *hārī*.

Malayaja, daśamūlī, and śaṅkhapuṣpī, when well-ripened, destroy pralāpa (incoherent speech) simply by being drunk, without much delay. When a person eating food does not perceive the sweet and other tastes with his sense of taste, that is called rasa-ajñāna (loss of the sense of taste).
One should rub the dull tongue with *sindhuvāra*, *yūṣaṇa*, and *amlavetasa*.
It is stated that in the absence of *amlavetasa*, *cukra* should be used.
[The ingredients are] *kirātatiktaka*, *kaṭvī*, and the fruit and bark of *kuṭaja*. 54.
Brāhmī fruit, palāśa, sarjikā, black cumin (kṛṣṇajīraka), long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), citraka, ginger (nāgara), and black pepper (ūṣaṇa)—
one should repeatedly rub the tongue with a paste made from these ingredients mixed with the juice of ārdrikā. 55–56.
By that [tongue], one correctly perceives all tastes;
a paste of *kirātatikta* and other herbs removes the emptiness of the tongue. That which is touched by the skin as cold, hot, soft, or rough—
The wise declare that skin disease (tvak) is proclaimed to be empty;
however, in the case of *suptavāta*, the physician should repeatedly perform bloodletting and apply smoke from salt and charcoal mixed with oil. 58–59.
When speaking too loudly, eating hard foods,
laughing, yawning, or from the weight of uneven lying and sitting,
[the wind] enters the joints of the head, nose, lips, chin, forehead, and eyes. (60)
The wind (vāyu) afflicts the face, thereby producing Ardita;
then one half of the face becomes distorted, the neck also turns away, the head shakes, there is an obstruction of speech, and deformity of the eyes and other features occurs. (61–62)

Experts in pathology call that disease *ardita* (facial paralysis), characterized by pain in the neck, chin, and teeth, as well as on that side [of the face]. Briefly stated, it arises from wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), and is thus threefold.

In Ardita caused by Vāta, there occurs salivation, pain, trembling, twitching, lockjaw, and speech impediment; there is swelling and aching of the lips (64–65). In the Pittaja type, the mouth is yellowish, accompanied by fever, thirst, delusion, and a sensation of fuming.
In cases of the kapha-type, there is swelling and stiffness in the cheek, the head, and the nape of the neck (66).
Ardita does not succeed in one who is emaciated, whose eyes do not blink, who speaks incessantly and indistinctly, nor in one who has tremors for three years (67).

Drinking medicated fats, nasal drops, foods that subdue Vāta, poultices, nasal medications, and enemas are recommended for those not afflicted by fever. For a condition characterized by Vāta, milk processed with Bālā or Pañcamūla is beneficial.
Having eaten meat and ghee ground with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) or with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga), he should drink fresh butter;
having consumed milk and meat broth, he should drink the juice of the ten roots.
In the case of Ardita caused by Pitta, one should prescribe cold unctuous substances,
as well as ghee enemas (ghṛtavasti), gargling (praseka), and exclusively milk.
One whose face has become distorted, who is mute, and who suffers from burning sensations, becomes afflicted with Ardita.
One should administer a treatment that destroys wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
When the portion of phlegm (śleṣman) has been reduced, one should treat with nourishing therapies (bṛṃhaṇa).
In the case of facial paralysis (ardita) accompanied by swelling, emesis (vamana) is recommended.

A person afflicted by facial paralysis (ardita) who consumes a paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil will find that paralysis is quickly destroyed, just as a mass of clouds is dispersed by the force of the wind.
[74] [Facial paralysis is also caused by] sleeping during the day, remaining in one posture for too long, and looking upward with distorted vision.
That very same [wind], when obstructed by phlegm, causes torticollis (manyāstambha).
In cases of torticollis, one should employ a decoction prepared from the ten roots (daśamūlī) or the five roots (pañcamūlī), as well as dry sudation and nasal medication (nasya). (75–76)
Then, having anointed the neck with oil or clarified butter (ājya),
and having covered it with arka leaves or castor (eraṇḍa) leaves, the physician should apply fomentation many times with warm chicken egg-shells mixed with rock salt (saindhava) and clarified butter.
By massaging the neck, stiffness of the tendons (manyā-stambha) is pacified.
When the Vāyu is situated in the region of the shoulder, it dries up the shoulder-joint;
from the drying of the shoulder-joint, there occurs a painful wasting of the arm.
In cases of wasting of the arms (bāhuśoṣa), one should drink the great Kalyāṇaka ghee after eating;
likewise, water boiled with the roots of balā mixed with rock salt is recommended for vāta causing arm-wasting and for stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha). 80
Contracting the vessels while situated in the arm, it causes apabāhuka (wrist-drop).
Apabāhuka is the supreme medicine for diseases of the neck, the clavicle, and the supraclavicular region, as well as for stiffness of the neck;
its pacification is achieved by nasal drops (nasya) of cold water, and likewise by *jiṅginī* taken first. 81–82.
One should drink the fresh juice of the root of *balā*, or that of *pāribhadra* and *ātmaguptā*;
or one who applies it as a nasal drop (*nasya*) with the juice of black gram (*māṣa*) will have arms equal to a thunderbolt.
[83] With the waters of black gram, linseed, barley, *kuraṇṭaka*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *gokaṇṭa*, *tuṇṭuka*, the root of *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *kapikacchū*...

This oil known as Māṣa-taila, cooked with a decoction of cotton seeds, hemp seeds, horse gram, jujube, and kola; with the broth of goat meat; and with ginger, Pippalī, Śatapuṣpā, Eraṇḍa root, Punarnavā, Saraṇī, Rāsnā, Balā, Amṛtalatā, and Kaṭuka, indeed cures apabāhuka (sciatica). 84–85.
The tendons (kaṇḍarā) that run from the palms to the fingers and from the back of the arms to the upper arms,
which cause the loss of function in the arms, are called Viśvācī.
[One should administer] a decoction of Daśamūla, Balā, and Māṣa, mixed with oil and clarified butter (86).
Having eaten in the evening, one should drink this as a nasal medication (*nasya*) in cases of *viśvācī* and *apabāhuka*.
Oil prepared with black gram (*māṣa*), rock salt (*sindhuka*), *balā*, *rāsnā*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *vacā*, *śivajaṭā*, and ginger (*nāgara*) [is also used]. (87–88)

When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed below by phlegm (śleṣman) and air (māruta), it may strike upwards after eating and drinking, causing bāhuśoṣa, apabāhuka, viśvācī, uddhatā, as well as pakṣāghāta and ādita. (89)
It causes an abundance of belching; that is called ūrdhvavāta (upward wind).
Take ten parts of viśvā, an equal amount of vṛddhadāraka, three parts of pathyā, and one-fourth part of fried hiṅgu. 90–91.

One part of *saindhava* salt and an equal amount of *citraka* grown with well-developed roots— this powder, when consumed, destroys upward-moving wind (*ūrdhvavāta*), as well as abdominal distension (*āṭopa*), extremely severe pain, and a severely bloated abdomen. (92)
One should recognize that distension (ādhmāna) is a terrible condition born from the obstruction of flatus (vāta).

In cases of distension, fasting should be administered first, followed by digestive stimulants (dīpana) and carminatives (pācana); then one should employ the administration of medicinal suppositories (phalavarti) and purificatory enema therapy (bastikarma). 93–94.

One *karṣa* of black pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) should be taken, along with one *pala* of *trivṛt*, and one *pala* of sugar should also be taken; one should prepare these as a powder in a single mixture. One should lick this powder, measured at one *akṣa*, with honey; it destroys flatulence (*ādhmāna*). 95

One should apply a warm plaster made of *dāru*, *haimavatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, *hiṅgu*, and *saindhava* ground with sour liquids to a case of abdominal enlargement accompanied by colic and flatulence (96).
[The following drugs are used: *abhayā*, *āragvadha*, *dhātrī*, *dantī*, *tikta*, *snuhī*, and *trivṛt*.
Each of these ingredients, including mustā, should be taken in a measure of one pala (97).
Having crushed them all together, one should boil them in two āḍhakas of water until only one-eighth part of the decoction remains in that water (98).
One should slowly cook fresh, huskless seeds of *Jaipāla* weighing one *pala* in that decoction while they are held in a thin cloth,
keeping the fire at a low intensity until the decoction becomes thick. 99.

Then, one should indeed add eight parts of *jaipāla* seeds, three parts of ginger, two parts of black pepper, two parts of mercury, and two parts of sulfur; these should be ground together here for the duration of one *yāma*. (100–101)
This liquid medicine named Nārāca, when consumed in a dose of one *raktikā* with cold water alone, destroys these diseases:
flatulence (*ādhmāna*), colic (*śūla*), abdominal distension (*ānāha*), and likewise secondary flatulence (*pratyādhmāna*). (102)
This [mixture] likewise removes upward-moving wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), and abdominal enlargements (udara).
When the acute symptoms have subsided, one should eat curd mixed with sugar; thereafter, with rock salt, and then a small amount of rice with curd. 103–104.
One should recognize that very condition— arising from the stomach (āmāśaya), with the sides and heart released [from pain]— as *pratyādhmāna*, caused by wind (vāyu) agitated by phlegm (kapha).
When *pratyādhmāna* has arisen, one should administer emetics and fasting.
One should employ treatments such as lamps and the like, as well as enema therapy (basti-karma) as previously described.
If a mass has formed below the navel— whether mobile or immobile—
it appears as a firm, stone-like knot, elongated and protruding upward.
One should recognize *vātāṣṭhīlā* as that which obstructs the external passage.
One should call this very same condition *pratyaṣṭhīlā* when it arises obliquely in the abdomen, accompanied by pain and obstructing flatus, feces, and urine. (108–109)
The treatment for *aṣṭhīlā*, *gulma*, and internal abscess (*antarvidradhi*) should be performed;
furthermore, one should drink the powder of *hiṅgvādi* with warm water.
[The *hiṅgvādi* formula consists of: asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *granthika*, coriander (*dhānya*), cumin (*jīraka*), *vacā*, *cavya*, *agni* (ginger), *pāṭhā*, and *śaṭī*.

Vṛkṣāmla, the three salts (lavaṇatraya), the three pungents (trikaṭuka), the two alkalis (kṣāradvaya), pomegranate (dāḍima), harītakī (pathyā), puṣkaramūla, vetasa, sour citron (amlavetasa), and hapuṣā—these should be combined; the powder made from these should be saturated with the juices of fresh ārdra and the liquid of bījapūra. 111.
That pain which moves downward, arising from the receptacles of feces and urine, as if piercing the anus and the generative organs, is known by the name *tūnī*.
That same [pain], when it arises in the anus and generative organs and spreads in an upward direction (*pratiloma*), is likewise [designated]. 112.
When it moves with force to the colon (pakvāśaya), it is called Pratitūnī. For both Tūnī and Pratitūnī, unctuous enemas (snehavasti) are recommended;
alternatively, one should drink unctuous salt (snehalavaṇa) or the Pippalyādi group of drugs with water.
Asafoetida with alkaline substances, or ghee heated intensely, [is used for this].
The junction between the bones of the buttocks and the bones of the spinal column is considered the *trika* (the sacroiliac region).
The pain there caused by *vāta* is called *trika-śūla*.
One should diligently apply sand-sweating (*vālukāsveda*) for pain in the sacrum (*trika*), or else a person should constantly maintain a fire of dried cow-dung (*karīṣāgni*) beneath [the area].
Ābhā, *aśvagandhā*, *hapuṣā*, *guḍūcī*, *śatāvarī*, *gokṣuraka*, and *rāsnā*— [Note: The text provided appears to be incomplete at the end.]
Having powdered śyāmā, śatāhvā, śaṭī, yavānī, and nāgara in equal parts (117),
one should add guggulu equal to the weight of all these combined, and cast into it clarified butter (ājya) measuring half that portion.
One should consume this in the measure of half a *picu* at the time of dawn, along with milk or vegetable broth (118).
Whether with wine, or lukewarm water, or milk, or even meat broth,
[this treatment is indicated] for wind (vāta) located in the triple-joints, in the knees and hips, in the arms, or in the feet;
and when that [wind] is situated in the joints, in the bones, in the marrow, in the tendons, or in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha).

This removes diseases associated with Vāta and Kapha, as well as those provoked by Vāta, and disorders of the heart, the genitals, and the female reproductive tract (120). Physicians of old have declared this thirteen-ingredient Guggulu to be a great medicine for fractures, bone injuries, lameness, sciatica (gṛdhrasī), and hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta) (121).
When the Vayu (māruta) in the bladder (vasti) is unimpaired, urine flows properly;
indeed, when it is deranged, various disorders arise.
One karṣa of the powder of the bark of Bala and Mūrvā, mixed with sugar, [should be taken].
One should drink a *kuḍava* measure [of this powder] with milk for the repeated cessation of urination (123).
The powder of *pathyā*, *bibhītaka*, and *dhātrī*, along with the powder of iron filings,
when licked together with honey, brings about the repeated cessation of urination (124).
One should regularly consume the powder of barley-alkali mixed with sugar; by this, the suppression of urine will certainly be relieved.
[125] Likewise, the seeds of the pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa) and the seeds of the cucumber (trapuṣa).
One should apply that [medicinal paste] to the bladder; by this, the suppression of urine will be pacified.
(126) One should smear the interior of the bladder with a paste of *āmalakī*;
by this, the suppression of urine is quickly and certainly pacified. (127)
Then, for the suppression of urine, one should slowly insert a wick containing camphor into the opening of the penis, the vagina, or the mouth [of the anus].
[One should massage] the buttocks, thighs, waist, back, knees, calves, and feet in succession.
Gṛdhrasī seizes [the limb] with stiffness, pain, and throbbing, and it twitches repeatedly. Furthermore, it is known to be of two types: from Vāta alone, or from both Vāta and Kapha.
In the type born of Vāta, there is piercing pain (todo) and extreme curvature of the body.
In the type arising from Vāta and Śleṣman, there is throbbing and severe stiffness of the joints of the knees, shanks, and thighs (131), as well as heaviness, dullness of the digestive fire,
drowsiness, salivation, and likewise an aversion to food (132).

Having correctly ascertained through purgation or emesis that the person afflicted by *gṛdhra* is free from *āma* and possesses a stimulated digestive fire, one should treat him with enemas (*vasti*). One should not perform the procedure of enemas at the outset until the upper tract has been purified.
That affection would be useless, like an oblation poured into ashes.
(134) A person should drink castor oil with cow's urine every morning for one month; this practice removes sciatica and stiffness in the thighs. (135)

One should drink oil and ghee with fresh citron juice, along with sour gruel and jaggery; this preparation removes pain in the waist, thighs, back, and sacrum, as well as abdominal tumors, sciatica, and upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
Having extracted the seeds of *eraṇḍa*, one should grind them and boil them in milk.
That decoction is indeed the supreme medicine for sciatica (gṛdhrasī) and pain in the waist (kaṭīśūla). 137.
A decoction of castor root, bilva, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā, when drunk together with yavakṣāra, cures ailments arising from the groins and the bladder.
It removes the pain born of *gṛdhrasī*, even that which has persisted for a long time.
(138) A person should drink the powder of *kṛṣṇā* with cow’s urine and castor oil;
this destroys *gṛdhrasī* arising from phlegm and wind that has been present for a long duration. (139)

He who, suffering from sciatica and loss of movement with numbness, drinks the decoction of *siṃhāsya*, *dantī*, and *kṛtamālaka* mixed with castor oil, shall indeed become swift-moving; what wonder is there in this? (140) The heartwood of the great *nimba* tree, ground with water—
When drunk, it quickly destroys even incurable sciatica (gṛdhrasī).
A decoction made from the leaves of śephālikā, boiled over a gentle fire, will destroy the difficult-to-cure disease of sciatica as soon as it is drunk. 141–142.
One should take one *pala* of *rāsnā* and five *karṣas* of *guggulu*, form them into pills with clarified butter, and consume them; this cures *gṛdhrasī*.
[Likewise, one may use] *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, *āragvadha*, *devadāru*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *eraṇḍa*, and *punarnavā*.
One suffering from pain in the calves, thighs, back, sacrum, or sides should drink this decoction mixed with powdered ginger (144).
One hundred fruits each of *pathyā*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalakī*, increased sequentially by two hundred,
along with one *prastha* of *palankaṣā*, should be kept for one night in one *droṇa* of water (145).

When the decoction has been boiled down until half remains, one should cook it again in an iron vessel. Having removed it from the fire, one should add the following drugs in powdered form, each weighing half a *pala*:
*viḍaṅga*, *dantī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *guḍūcī*, *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper), *trivṛt*, ginger, and black pepper. (146)
For a person who acts according to his desire, the prompt consumption of cold water and foods quickly destroys diseases, including sciatica, fresh lameness, severe splenic enlargement,
digestive fire disorders, abdominal tumors, anemia, itching, vomiting, and gout. (147–148)
This guggulu, beginning with *pathyā*, is renowned on earth by this name and possesses immeasurable power;
it makes a man equal to an elephant in strength and equal to a horse in speed.
It bestows excellence of longevity, as well as strength of vision, acts as a nourisher, and destroys poison. (149)
It heals wounds and is especially recommended by experts for all diseases.
(150) When Vāyu, having taken refuge in the waist, seizes the tendons of the thigh, then the person becomes lame; if both thighs are affected, he becomes a cripple. (151)
One should treat a newly afflicted person who is lame or even a cripple with purgation, non-unctuous enemas, sudation, guggulu, and unctuous enemas.
Such a person trembles at the start of walking and appears as if limping.
One should know that *kalāyakhañja* is characterized by the release of the binding of the joints (153).
The progression of *kalāyakhañja* is said to be like that of the lame and the cripple; in this condition, wise physicians should specifically perform oleation therapy (154).

A swelling arising from vāta and blood (vātaśoṇita) in the middle of the knee, accompanied by great pain, is to be known as kroṣṭukaśīrṣa; it is large and resembles the head of a jackal. For kroṣṭukaśīrṣa, one should take guggulu with a decoction of guḍūcī and triphalā.
One should drink castor oil with milk, or *vṛddhadāraka* with milk;
or, by drinking *guggulu* combined with the juices of partridge meat and by following the treatments for *vātarakta*, one may conquer *jambūka-mastaka*.

For crushing the roots of the feet, calves, thighs, and hands, a paste of *kuṣṭha* and rock salt mixed with sour gruel and oil should be applied while lukewarm during massage; this relieves the pain of *khallī*. (158–159)
When pain arises because the foot is placed on uneven ground or due to fatigue,
and it occurs by means of Vāta localized at the ankle, that they call Vātakaṇṭaka (160). One should perform bloodletting repeatedly in the case of Vātakaṇṭaka.
One should drink castor oil or apply cauterization with needles [to the feet].
When Vāyu, combined with Pitta and blood, causes a burning sensation in the feet—especially during walking—one should diagnose that as Pādadāha (burning of the feet). 161–162.
One should follow the treatment protocol for *vātarakta*, especially in the case of *pādadāha* (burning sensation in the feet).
To alleviate *pādadāha*, one should thoroughly apply a paste made of ground *masūra* and *vidala* pulses with water that has been boiled and then cooled. (163)
If both feet are smeared with fresh butter and thoroughly heated by fire, they are quickly freed from that most dreadful burning sensation. Furthermore,
the feet of one who has become numb will begin to tingle.
That condition should be known as *pādaharṣa* (cramp in the feet), arising from the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*.
In the case of *pādaharṣa*, a therapeutic regimen that pacifies *kapha* and *vāta* should be employed.
However, when the provoked *māruta* (vāyu) attacks all the *dhamanīs* (channels), [it results in *ūrustambha*].
Then, repeatedly and swiftly tossing the body about, the wind—moving restlessly and characterized by frequent convulsions—is known as Ākṣepaka (the "Tossing" wind).
This occurs when the wind is associated with bile and phlegm, or when it is the wind alone. (167)
One should recognize another, the fourth type, as being caused by trauma (abhighāta).
When the Vāyu stiffens the hands, feet, head, back, and hips, causing the limbs to become rigid like a staff, it is called Daṇḍaka; this condition is incurable. 168–169.
When the wind (vāyu), enveloped by phlegm (kapha), remains within the channels (dhamanīs) and causes stiffness like a staff, it is called Daṇḍāpatānaka, which is difficult to treat. [For this,
one should administer] a decoction of balā roots and a decoction of daśamūlī.

Eight parts each of a decoction of barley, jujube, and horse gram, as well as eight parts of milk, and one part of oil— these should be cooked together after adding the sweet group of drugs (madhura-gaṇa) along with rock salt. 171–172.
Likewise, [one should take] aguru, sarjarasa, sarala, and devadāru;
