mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, kuṣṭha, elā, and kālānusārivā (173); māṃsī, śaileyaka, patra, tagara, sārivā, and vacā.
Having properly prepared śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā,
one should place them in a pitcher made of gold, silver, or even clay, and store it well-protected. 174–175.
This Mahābalā oil, when applied without delay,
dispels all wind-related disorders such as ākṣepaka, as well as hiccups, dyspnea, adhimantha, abdominal tumors, and even the most difficult-to-cure cough. (176)
When used for six months, it destroys intestinal hernia (antravṛddhi).

Therefore, one should administer the dose according to the patient's strength to a woman who has recently given birth, as well as to a woman desiring conception and to a man with depleted semen. 177–178.
This is indeed to be employed in every way for one whose wind (vāta) is depleted, one struck in a vital organ (marman), one afflicted by trauma, one with a fracture, and one overcome by exhaustion;
for this must be performed by a king and by those honored by kings.
In those who are always happy, delicate, and wealthy,
the wind (vāyu), possessing great speed, then seizes the network of tendons located in the fingers, the ankles, the abdomen, the heart, the chest, and the throat. 180–181.
With fixed eyes, stiff jaw, and broken sides, vomiting phlegm (182),
when a person bends inward like a bow, then the powerful wind produces internal contraction (abhyantarāyāma). 183.

The powerful wind (vāyu), acting as the primary cause, together with the vessels (sirās), ligaments (snāyus), and tendons (kaṇḍaras) situated in the neck and back, dries up the external [tissues] and causes affliction externally;
where this occurs, the best of physicians call it "external extension" (bahirāyāma).

The wise declare that the breaking of the chest, waist, and thighs is incurable through *tamas*. In both external and internal extension (*prāṇāyāma*), the practice should be performed like [the previous] one. He who bends like a bow is designated as "Dhanuḥ-stambha" (the Bow-posture).
One who is discolored, with a constricted face, drooping limbs, and lost consciousness, perspiring and stiff as a bow, does not live for ten nights.
Or, if the chest or the back becomes elevated sequentially and is accompanied by pain; [he likewise does not survive].
When the wind becomes aggravated, one should designate that condition as *kubja* (hunchback).

In cases of external contraction (*bāhyāyāma*), internal contraction (*antarāyāma*), stiffness of the arms like a bow (*dhanuḥstambha*), and *kubjaka*, *prasāraṇī* oil should be applied; by this, their pacification occurs. (188–189)
All those general treatments previously described for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) should indeed be performed; this oil, however, is especially effective.
When provoked by its own aggravating factors, the Vāyu moves upward from its site.

Afflicting the heart and reaching the head and temples, it causes the limbs to bend like a bow; it likewise causes agitation and delusion. Then, with eyes fixed or closed, one breathes heavily and with great difficulty.
He coos like a pigeon and becomes unconscious; this is apatantraka (192). One should never administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha-vasti) or induce emesis to a patient afflicted by apatantraka (193).
If his breaths are obstructed by phlegm and wind, one should release them with sharp insufflations; once they are released, he regains consciousness.
[The ingredients are] black pepper, drumstick seeds, viḍaṅga, and phaṇijjaka.
One should administer these fine powders for the purpose of head-purgation (śīrṣavirecana).
195–196: Harītakī, vacā, rāsnā, rock salt (saindhava), and sour vetasa (amlavetasa), combined with ghee and fresh ginger (ārdra-ka), destroy apatantraka.
In the absence of *amlavetasa*, it is taught that *cukra* should be given.
Having paralyzed the vision and destroyed consciousness, the man gurgles with his throat;
when the heart is released, he returns to his natural state, but when enveloped by delusion, he falls back into stupor.
Some declare that severe [paralysis] caused by Vāyu is called apatānaka (198). Furthermore,
apatānaka resulting from birth or gestation, from excessive hemorrhaging, or from injury does not succeed in being cured (199).

Now, one should quickly treat a patient afflicted by apatanaka (convulsions), who is unable to bear [pain], is trembling, and cannot even lie upon a bed. For one suffering from apatanaka, water boiled with daśamūlī is recommended.

Rice with meat broth mixed with powdered pippalī that has been digested, as well as massage with oil and strong purgation, are prescribed; subsequently, drinking ghee is considered beneficial for cleansing the channels. (201–202)
Sour curd, when drunk by one who has not eaten, destroys apatānaka;
likewise, a medicated oil enema (sneha-vasti) combined with black pepper may do so.
Furthermore, when the Vāyu seizes half the body and dries up the channels (sirās) and tendons (snāyus), [it causes this condition].
Releasing the joints of one side, it destroys that side; his entire body or half-body becomes incapacitated and unconscious.
Some call this ekāṅgavāta, while others know it as pakṣavadha.
When Vāyu is associated with Pitta, there occur burning sensations, feverish heat, and fainting;
when that same [Vāyu] is enveloped by Kapha, there is coldness, swelling, and heaviness.
They consider a hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta) caused by pure Vāyu to be the most difficult to cure.
A hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta) that is associated with another [disease] is curable, whereas that which is caused by wasting (kṣaya) is incurable.

One should avoid treating it in pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, children, the elderly, or those emaciated, provided they are free from pain when the blood has been depleted. (207–208)
Now, regarding the treatment for hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta):
a decoction of māṣa, ātmaguptā, vātārī, vāṭyālaka, and jaṭā,
combined with hiṅgu and saindhava salt, will destroy hemiplegia.
One māṣa each of asafoetida and rock salt, and one śāṇa each of the drugs beginning with *jaraṇā*.
Oil cooked with a paste of *granthika*, *agnikaṇā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rāsnā*, and *saindhava*, and boiled with a decoction of black gram (*māṣa*), cures hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*). (210–211)
Oil cooked with well-ground *māṣa*, *ātmaguptā*, *ativiṣā*, *urubūka*, *rāsnā*, *śatāhvā*, and salts,
in a fourfold decoction of *māṣa* and *balā*, indeed destroys hemiplegia (*pakṣaghāta*) when the *vāyu* is provoked throughout the entire body, causing trembling and breaking pain in the limbs. (212)
And his joints, overwhelmed by these sensations, seem as if they are bursting;
yet the wind, whether pervading all limbs or affecting only a single limb,
is destroyed by immersion in oil, just as a mountain resists the force of water.
One should identify the remaining [types] by signs corresponding to their names and locations;
in all these cases, one should recognize the association with pitta and the other [humors].
First there is shortness of hair, and then talkativeness as well.
Distension of the abdomen, pain in the flanks, excessive hardness of the stool, as well as non-passage of waste matter, trembling, stiffness, dryness,
emaciation, blackishness, coldness, horripilation, and likewise distress— 216–217.

All [the following] are its symptoms: throbbing of the head, aching of the limbs, dryness of the body, contraction, loss of limb function, delusion, mental instability, loss of sleep, loss of perspiration, loss of strength, and timidity. (218)
The loss of semen, the cessation of the menstrual flow, miscarriage, and exhaustion—219.
The treatment that will be declared for common wind-diseases (vātaroga) should be administered for these as well; by it, they go to complete destruction. 220.
The provoked Vāyu produces such symptoms;
according to the specific cause and location, it becomes the creator of various diseases.
When Udāna is combined with Pitta, there is burning sensation, fainting, vertigo, and exhaustion.

When the *prāṇa* is enveloped by *kapha*, there is absence of perspiration, lack of exhilaration, weak digestion, and coldness; when it is enveloped by *pitta*, vomiting and a burning sensation arise. When [the *prāṇa*] is enveloped by *kapha*, there is debility, lassitude, drowsiness, and a bad taste in the mouth. (222–223)
When the *samāna* vāyu is associated with pitta, there occurs perspiration, a burning sensation, thirst, and fainting;
when it is obstructed by kapha, retention of feces and urine occurs, as well as horripilation of the limbs.
When the *apāna* vāyu is associated with pitta, there is a burning sensation, heat, and blood in the urine.
When Vyāna is enveloped by Kapha, there is heaviness and coldness in the lower body;
when it is enveloped by Pitta, there is a burning sensation, tossing of the limbs, fatigue, stiffness, as well as the Daṇḍaka condition, pain, and swelling. (225–226)
In the case of [fever] with vāta and pitta, one should perform treatments that alleviate vāta and pitta;
in the case of that with kapha, one should perform treatments that alleviate vāta and śleṣman.
When the skin is rough, cracked, numb, emaciated, black, and pruritic;
When the wind has entered the skin, there is stretching and a state of being full of passion;

when it has entered the blood, there are intense pains accompanied by fever, discoloration, emaciation, loss of appetite, and eruptions on the body, as well as a stiffness in what has been eaten. (228–229)
When Vāta has taken refuge in the muscle tissue (māṃsa), the limb feels as if it is being pricked, becomes stiff, and is struck as if by a staff or a fist; it is painful and excessively rigid.
Similarly, when it has taken refuge in the fat (medas), it produces tumors (granthi) and ulcers that are only mildly painful. (230–231)
When Vāta is vitiated and located in the bones, there is cracking of the bones and joints, pain in the articulations, loss of muscle mass and strength, insomnia, and constant aching;
when Vāta has entered the marrow, the pain never subsides.

Vata located in the semen (śukra), when aggravated, may cause it to be discharged quickly or to be retained, or it may even produce a deformity in the semen or the embryo. When Vayu has taken refuge in the skin, one should administer oleation and massage, as well as sudation.
When [the Vāta] resides in the blood, one should apply cooling ointments, administer purgation, and perform bloodletting (234).
When Vāta has reached the muscle and fat tissues, one should employ purgation along with non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa).
When it has reached the bone and marrow, one should apply oleation both externally and internally (235).
Oil cooked with a large quantity of the juice of *ketaka*, *nāgabalā*, and *atibalā*, prepared with a significant amount of rice-wash water (*tuṣodaka*), destroys Vāta located within the bones.
When [Vāta] resides in the semen, sexual vigor, food, and drink that increase strength and semen are beneficial. (236–237)
Now, the specific disorders of vāta according to their particular locations:

when the vāta is vitiated and localized in the gastrointestinal tract (koṣṭha), there occurs suppression of urine and feces, as well as scrotal enlargement (bradhna), cardiac pain, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and pain in the flanks. 238
One should cause the impurities to be digested by means of digestive decoctions, either combined with other substances or otherwise;
in particular, a person whose wind (vāyu) has entered the gastrointestinal tract should drink milk.
[This applies when there is] pain in the heart, sides, abdomen, and navel, as well as thirst, eructation, and choleraic vomiting (visūcikā).
When Vāta is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), cough, dryness of the throat and mouth, and dyspnea occur.
When Vāta resides in the stomach, fasting is recommended first, followed by digestive stimulants (dīpana) and carminatives (pācana);
or emesis, or strong purgation; or old mung beans, barley, and śāli rice.
Decoctions of three types—those made from bhūtīka, pathyā, śaṭī, and puṣkara; those from bilva, amṛtā, dāru, and kanaka; and those from ugrā, viṣā, māgadhikā, and viḍa—destroy phlegm and wind.
(242) Citraka, indrayava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and abhayā [are also used].
This powder, which destroys wind arising from the stomach (āmāśaya), should be drunk with lukewarm water.
In this formulation, six *dharaṇas* each of the six [ingredients] are to be taken separately by the physician over six days; therefore, it is known as "the six *dharaṇas*. (243–244)
When Vāta is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), after the patient has undergone emesis according to the prescribed sequence,
the Ṣaḍdharaṇa formulation should be administered for seven nights with lukewarm water.
When it resides in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), it causes rumbling in the intestines, colic, and flatulence.

When vāyu has entered the colon (pakvāśaya), one should treat the difficulty of passing urine and feces, abdominal distension, and pain in the three regions [of the abdomen] by increasing the digestive fire, performing treatments for upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and administering unctuous purgation (snehavireka). 246–247.
When wind (vāta) has entered the stomach, one should administer digestive stimulants (dīpana) such as alkali and powders;
when it resides in the abdomen, one should give a powder of ginger (śuṇṭhī), kuṭaja seeds, and citraka (agni) with lukewarm water.
This cures the retention of feces, urine, and flatus, as well as colic, flatulence, stones, and gravel.

For one suffering from diseases of the calves, thighs, sacrum, flanks, shoulders, or back, and when wind is vitiated in the anus, the therapeutic procedure known as *udāvartana* (reversal of downward movement) is beneficial. To destroy wind in the heart, *guḍūcī* combined with black pepper [is recommended].
One should diligently drink it in the morning along with warm water; likewise,
one should drink *aśvagandhā* and *bibhītaka* ground with warm water and mixed with jaggery, which diligently destroys heart disease and wind disorders.
One afflicted by pain in the heart due to wind (vāta) shall obtain relief by drinking ground *nāgara* combined with *devadāru*.
When provoked, the wind (samīraṇa) may cause injury to the sense organs, such as the ears and others. 252–253.
When the wind (vāyu) is vitiated in the ears and other sense organs, a regimen that alleviates vāta should be employed,
including oleation, massage, immersion baths, rubbing, and medicinal pastes.
If pain has reached the vessels (sirā), one should perform venesection, contraction, and filling of the vessels.

One should apply external and internal oleation, as well as poultices, massage, ointments, and bloodletting, for wind (vāta) located in the head, as well as for emaciation, hunchbackedness, and spinal deformity. 255–256.
Pain, convulsions, tremors, and stiffness arise from the wind (vāta) located in the tendons (snāyu);
when the wind has entered the tendons and become aggravated, a skilled physician should apply sudation, poultices, cauterization, bandaging, and massage. (257)

When Vāta has entered the joints (sandhi), it destroys the joints and causes pain and swelling. For Vāta located in the joints, one should apply fomentation with unctuous substances (sneha) and poultices (upanāhana). [One may also use] the root of Indravāruṇikā combined with Māgadhī (long pepper) and jaggery.
One should consume a quantity of one karṣa; it dispels sandhivāta (joint-wind). 259.
Jaw-lock, facial paralysis, convulsions, hemiplegia, and apatānaka (tetanus) may or may not be cured with great effort over a long period of time. 260.
One should treat these [conditions] in strong individuals so that they are free from complications.

However, when the flesh and strength are diminished by erysipelas, burning pain, breaking pain, fainting, anorexia, and weak digestion, the Vātas destroy them through hemiplegia (pakṣavadha) and other such afflictions. Thus [it is said]. 261–262.
A person who is swollen, has numb skin, is withered, afflicted by tremors and flatulence,
and suffers from intense pain— such a man will be destroyed by a wind-disease (vātavyādhi).
However, one whose movement is unimpeded and who remains in his natural state, established in his own place, [is not so afflicted].
He shall become possessed of vital breath (vāyu) and, free from disease, live for more than a hundred years.
Now, the general remedies for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi):
one should take half an āḍhaka of black gram (māṣa) and half a tulā of the ten roots (daśamūla).
One should boil thirty palas of goat meat in one droṇa of water;
when reduced to one-fourth, one should remove that decoction and add one prastha of sesame oil and four times as much milk.
The life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, mañjiṣṭhā, cavya, citraka, kaṭphala, the three pungents (vyoṣa), pippalīmūla, rāsnā, āmalaka, gokṣura,
ātmaguptā, eraṇḍa, śatāhvā, and the three salts (lavaṇatraya). 267.
One should cook [the oil] over a gentle fire with a paste (kalka) of these ingredients— Devadāru, Amṛtā, Kuṣṭha, Aśvagandhā, Vacā, and Śaṭī— each measuring one Akṣa;
it is beneficial for men afflicted by hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), facial paralysis (ardita), and lockjaw (hanustambha).
In cases of earache, headache, and cataracts born of the three doṣas;
in the whirling of the hands, feet, head, and neck; in slow walking; in kalāyakhaja, paṅgu, gṛdhrasī, and apabāhuka; [these are the indications for its use]. (270)
This oil is praised for use in drinks, enemas, massages, nasal drops, and filling the ears; it is commended as a remedy for all disorders of Vata.
This was proclaimed by the sages of old as the "Mahāmāṣādi" [oil].
Take seven *pala* each of black gram (*māṣa*), barley (*yava*), linseed (*atasī*), small cucumber (*kṣudrā*), *markaṭī*, *kuraṇṭaka*, *gokaṇṭa*, and *tuṇṭuka*.
Having boiled these with four times the amount of water, one should reduce the decoction until one-fourth remains. 273–274.
One should boil fourteen palas each of cotton seeds, jujube fruit, hemp seeds, and horse gram in four times as much water;
one should take the decoction when it has been reduced to one-fourth.
The wise physician should cook one *prastha* of goat meat in six hundred and forty *palas* of water until only a quarter remains as broth; then,
he should gradually cook all those decoctions with one *prastha* of oil.
One should cook these with the paste of the following ingredients: amṛtā, kuṣṭha, saindhava, rāsnā, punarnavā, eraṇḍa, pippalī, śatapuṣpā, balā, prasāraṇī, māṃsī, and kaṭukā. (278)
One should prepare this oil with these ingredients measured in separate portions over a mild fire. This oil quickly destroys all wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) without exception,
including convulsions (ākṣepaka), hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta), stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), and apabāhuka.
[It cures] trembling of the hands, trembling of the head, as well as viśvācī and ardita.
[The following herbs are used: aśvagandhā, balā, bilva, pāṭalā, the two types of bṛhatī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, atibalā, nimba, śyonāka, and punarnavā. 280–281.
One should take ten palas each of prasāraṇī and agnimantha,
boil them in four droṇas of water until reduced to one-quarter,
and then combine that decoction with one āḍhaka of oil and one āḍhaka of the juice of śatāvarī.
One should add cow’s milk there, four times the quantity of the oil, and then the physician should cook it with the pastes (kalka) of these substances, each weighing one pala:
vacā, candana, kuṣṭha, elā, māṃsī, śaileya, and saindhava. (283–284)
One should prepare this oil with aśvagandhā, balā, rāsnā, śatapuṣpā, indradāru, the four types of parṇī, and tagara; it should be employed for food, massage, drinking, and enema therapy. 285.
Hemiplegia, lockjaw, stiffness of the neck, throat obstruction, 286 hunchbackedness, deafness, lameness, and pain in the waist;
wasting of the limbs, loss of the senses, loss of semen, fever, and consumption— 287.
It removes intestinal hernia, scrotal enlargement, dental disease, stiffness of the head,
pain in the flanks, lameness, loss of intellect, sciatica (gṛdhrasī),
and various other types of vāta disorders located in all parts of the body. (288)
By its power, even a barren woman gives birth to a son;
just as the divine Nārāyaṇa is the destroyer of wicked Daityas,
so too is this supreme oil the destroyer of wind-diseases.
Taking four *āḍhakas* of sesame oil,
one should purify it with a paste of the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*) for the sake of pacifying the humors (*doṣa*).
Therein, one should cook either goat’s milk or cow’s milk in an amount equal to the oil.
The physician should also cook the juice of śatāvarī in an amount equal to the oil. [Then add:
daśamūlī, balā, rāsnā, śigru, utpala, punarnavā, śephālikā, nāgabalā, balā, and prasāraṇī.
Aśvagandhā, sahacara, daśamūla, karañjaka, khadira, candana, lodhra, vacā, asana, palāśa, vakula, eraṇḍa, varuṇa, the two types of śāli, and kaṭambharā. (294)
Śirīṣa, śikhari, vāsā, hiṃsrā, jambu, bibhītaka (295), kāñcanāra, kapittha, pāribhadra, priyālaka,
pāṣāṇabheda, śampāka, dugdhikā, and the fruit of the dāḍima. (296)
Udumbara, saptalā, kanyā, the bark of mālatī, māgadhī, nala-root, barley, kola, and kulattha;
297 ātmaguptā, akarkarī, cotton seeds, vatsādanī, and snuhī.

One should boil ten *pala* portions each of *ketakī*-root, *dhattūra*, *lāṅgalī*, *gardabhāṇḍaka*, *citraka*, *mahānimba*, the five barks (*pañcavalkala*), *muṇḍī*, *ṭaṅkārī*, *muśalī*, *haṃsapādī*, and *viśalyaka* in eight times their quantity of water.
Having strained off the remaining liquid from the decoction, one should cook oil in it again.

[The meat of] the goat, the sheep, the deer, the *eṇa* antelope, the many-horned antelope, the rabbit, the porcupine, the jackal, the monitor lizard, the lion, the tiger, and the bear [should be used]. 300–301.
The wild boar, the rhinoceros, the buffalo, the horse,
as well as the monkey, the brown animal, the cat, the mouse, the urudardura,
the quail, the partridge, the lāva, the khañjarīṭa, and the cakoraka. 302.
The owl, the peacock, and the wild cock; the vulture, Garuḍa, the swan, the cakravāka, and the kāraṇḍava;
the pigeon, the crane, the curlew, the wild bird, and likewise the turtle-dove. (303–304)
The Rohita, the Madgura, the Śilīndhra, and likewise the Śṛṅgaka;
the Illisa, the Gargara, the Varmin, and also the Kāka and the Pika;
the Mahāmatsya, the Kacchapa, the Śiśumāra, and the Sāṅkuci. (305)
The *makara* has the shape of a *ghaṇṭikā*; in its absence, however, one may use *godhikā*. Having obtained these as available, one should cook their decoction with oil.
[The ingredients are: *rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *miśi*, *dāru*, *kuṣṭha*, the four *parṇīs*, *aguru*, and *kesara*.
Sindhūttha, māṃsī, the two types of rajanī, śaileyaka, candana, and puṣkara (308);
elā, yaṣṭī, tagara, abda, patra, bhṛṅga, the aṣṭavarga, vacā, palāśī, sthauṇeya, vṛścīraka, coraka, mūrvā, tvac, kaṭphala, and padmaka (309).
Mṛṇāla, jāti, phala, ketakī, nāgapuṣpa, sarala, murā, jīvantī, uśīra, varā, likewise durālabhā, vānarikā, nakha;
kaivarta, mustā, arjuna, tiktaka, vātāmaka, kharjūraka, and tumburu.
Sadhātaki, granthika, parpaṭa, paṭola, hemāhva, jayantī,
trāyantikā, alambuṣa, śakrabīja, rasāñjana, abhā, trivṛt, aruṇā, drākṣā, kaṇā, droṇa, punarnavā, kauntī, kṛmighna, and hayamāraka. (311–312)

Blue lotus, red lotus, *kāravī*, plantain, *anala*, *gokṣuraka*, *kṣura*, *kaṅkolaka*, *kāleya*, safflower, *turuṣka*, saffron, beeswax, cloves, camphor, *rasālaka*, *kāṇḍa*, musk, *bālaka*, and cloth. 313.
A skilled physician should cook these pastes individually, each measured at two *karṣas*,
under an auspicious constellation, moment, and *lagna*, after having gratified the Brahmins and the best of physicians,
and having worshipped the three-eyed God named Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign of the worlds.
One should indeed preserve it in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
A physician should administer this for massage, collyrium, nasal drops, non-unctuous enemas, immersion baths, and internal drinking, according to the specific disease.
What need is there for much speaking on this matter? When this oil is employed, it will certainly destroy diseases born of Vāta.
Through its regular practice, old age never arises for the person. (317)
Bracelets do not slip from the limbs, and gray hair does not appear (318).
One's eyes become exceedingly radiant, like those of Garuḍa;
there is no loss of high-pitched hearing, nor deafness, nor does any ringing in the ears arise (319).
Trembling of the hands, trembling of the head, and incoherent speech do not arise;
nor does a loss of intellect occur; therefore, there is proficiency in ritual actions, just as the sprouts and other parts of a tree flourish when it is watered with water. 320.
In the same way, the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) of an embodied being increase constantly through this [milk].
It is supremely beneficial for a woman who has miscarried an immature fetus, for one who delivers with painful labor, and for those exhausted by difficult childbirth. (321–322)
A barren woman obtains a son, miscarriages do not occur,
gynecological diseases perish, and menorrhagia is pacified.
There is no other medicine anywhere superior to this oil.
This is a great elixir (rasāyana), strengthening, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were struck down by the Daityas—pierced, with broken and shattered bones, transfixed, and overcome with agony. (324-325)
Having seen this for the benefit of gods and men, the great god Nārāyaṇa spoke these words regarding the oil named Mahānārāyaṇa:
"Nāgara, pippalīmūla, cavya, ūṣaṇa, and citraka. (326)
Fried asafoetida, ajamoda, mustard, the two types of cumin,
reṇuka, indrayava, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, gajapippalī,
kaṭukā, ativiṣā, bhārgī, vacā, mūrvā, and patra; 327–328.
Devadāru, kaṇā, kuṣṭha, rāsnā, mustā, and saindhava;
elā, trikaṇṭaka, pathyā, dhānyaka, and bibhītaka (329);
dhātrī, tvak, uśīra, and yavakṣāra—all these as well.

One should have these made into fine powders in equal proportions (330). As much as there is of these powders, so much guggulu should be added; having kneaded it with clarified butter, one should then thoroughly mix everything together (331).
Having thus prepared that mass, one should keep it in a vessel of ghee;
one should consume eight *ṭaṅkas* of these pills as appropriate.
At first, one should eat a measure of one *śāṇa*, and thereafter, half a *śāṇa*.
Half a *karṣa* at first, and a full *karṣa* thereafter;
this Guggulu is the king of formulations, the most eminent elixir (*rasāyana*).
In its case, no restriction regarding sexual intercourse, food, or drink exists. (333–334)
It cures hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, and abdominal enlargements;
it also treats constipation, weak digestion, dyspnea,
cough, anorexia, urinary disorders (prameha), pain in the navel, worms, wasting diseases, and cardiac oppression.

It destroys all wind-related disorders (vātāmayas), as well as āmavāta, epilepsy (apasmṛti), vātarakta, leprosy (kuṣṭha), and even malignant ulcers (duṣṭavraṇas); it also cures defects of the semen (śukradoṣa), defects of the menses (rajodoṣa), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara). 336–337.
Combined with a decoction of *rāsnā* and other drugs, it removes all diseases caused by *vāta*; *pitta* is removed by a decoction of the *kākolyādi* group; *kapha* by that of the *āragvadhādi* group;
urinary disorders (*meha*) by a decoction of *dārvī*; and jaundice (*pāṇḍu*) by cow's urine. (338)
The increase of fat is [cured] by honey; leprosy (kuṣṭha) by [honey] boiled with neem (nimba);
gout (vātāsra) by a decoction of chinnā; swelling (śotha) by a decoction of radish (mūlaka); and poison originating from rats by [honey] combined with a decoction of pāṭalā. (339–340)
Combined with a decoction of triphalā, it destroys severe eye pain; likewise, a decoction of punarnavā and other herbs cures all types of abdominal enlargements (udararoga).
A decoction prepared from rāsnā, punarnavā, śuṇṭhī, guḍūcī, and eraṇḍa [is also effective].

If the wind (vāta) has spread through the seven tissues (dhātu), accompanied by undigested matter (āmā), and pervades the entire body, a paste of garlic (rasona) mixed with sesame oil and rock salt will remove all diseases of the wind as well as even chronic fevers.
One should eat garlic together with milk, oil, ghee, or meat,

along with *śāli* rice or *ṣaṣṭika* rice, increasing the portion by half a *pala* for seven days; this cures diseases arising from *vāta*, irregular fevers, colic, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and impaired digestion.
It destroys severe splenic enlargement, pain in the arms and flanks, headache, and disorders of the semen.
One should eat garlic when cold, combined with various kinds of food, types of minced meat, wheat preparations, or barley flour, along with milk, oil, or even ghee. (345–346)
Having carefully prepared the meat of *saṃvartaka*, *lāva*, or *kapiñjala* birds, or the flesh of deer, chickens,
boars, *vartīka*, or *hāriṇa* antelopes according to one's digestive strength, one should take pills made from the peeled and dehusked bulbs of garlic that have been cooked. 347.
Having split it open, one should remove the central sprout;
then, having mixed it with curd at night to destroy its fierce odor, one should preserve it.
Thereafter, having washed and dried it, one should grind it on a stone slab.
One should add a fifth part of the powder of these to the paste:
sauvarcala salt, yavānī, fried hiṅgu, saindhava salt, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), and jīraka; these should be ground together in equal proportions. (350)
One should mix sesame oil with a fourth part of the paste therein;

one should consume a karṣa measure in the morning, or according to the requirements of the bodily humors (doṣas) and other factors, taking as a post-drink daily water boiled with vātāri (guḍūcī). 351–352.

It removes wind disorders arising from all parts or a single part of the body, as well as ardita (facial paralysis), apatantraka, epilepsy, insanity, ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), and gṛdhrasī (sciatica);
it also cures pain in the chest, back, waist, sides, and abdomen, and eliminates worms.

One should constantly consume liquor, meat, and sour flavors (354). A man who eats garlic should avoid these things perpetually: physical exertion, exposure to the sun, anger, excessive water, molasses, and women (355).

One suffering from diarrhea, urinary disorders, jaundice, loss of appetite, or pregnancy; one afflicted by fainting, abdominal diseases, bleeding disorders, consumption, or vomiting—these individuals should avoid it. (356)
In the case of pitta, however, one should administer purgation at the conclusion of the treatment while consuming wholesome food;
otherwise, diseases such as skin disorders (kuṣṭha) and anemia (pāṇḍu) arise in him.
One should quickly give breast milk even to infants who are unwilling to take it.
And thus one attains accomplishment through the great heroic mercury (rasa). 359.
Mercury, sulfur, excellent fire (cinnabar), and guggulu are increased in sequence;
therein, mercury shall be one part, and sulfur is prescribed as double that. 360.

Three parts of *triphalā* should be used, four parts of *citraka*, and five parts of *guggulu*; one should rub these with *rubūta* oil. Having added the aforementioned powder to it, one should rub it with that oil.
One should indeed consume a pill weighing one karṣa at the very break of dawn; thereafter,
one should drink a decoction of ginger and castor roots,
and having anointed the back with castor oil, one should apply fomentation.
Upon the completion of the purgation, however, one should feed [the patient] with unctuous and warm food;
for this rasa, known as Vātāri, when consumed regularly for a month by one who abstains from sexual intercourse, removes diseases caused by the wind (vāta). 364
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter on Vātavyādhi (diseases caused by wind).
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter on Ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
[This condition arises] from the consumption of cold, hot, liquid, dry, heavy, and unctuous substances.
Likewise, when there is indigestion or over-exertion, agitation, or from sleep and wakefulness,
the wind (vāta) combined with phlegm (śleṣman) and fat (medas), being excessively accumulated and accompanied by undigested matter (sāma), overcomes the other doshas and enters the thighs.
Filling the interior of the two thigh-bones with stagnant phlegm,
it then stiffens them; thus the thighs become rigid, cold, and insensible,
as heavy as if they belonged to another person, and are accompanied by extreme pain.
Accompanied by the suppression of the limbs of dhyāna, stiffness, drowsiness, vomiting, loss of appetite, and fever,
along with weakness of the legs, difficulty in lifting them, and numbness—
this they call ūrustambha; others, however, call it āḍhyavāta.
Its premonitory symptoms are excessive sleep, poor concentration, lethargy, fever,
horripilation, loss of appetite, vomiting, and weakness in the calves and thighs.
Due to ignorance, those who suspect it to be caused by Vāta may apply oleation therapy, which [further] aggravates it.
There is numbness and sleepiness in the feet, as well as difficulty in lifting them; there is extreme exhaustion of the calves and thighs, and constant burning pain.
The foot feels painful when placed down, and one does not perceive the sensation of cold touch.
He is powerless regarding posture, pressure, movement, and locomotion; indeed, with his thighs and feet shattered, he considers himself led by others.
When a man becomes afflicted by trembling and tormented by the pain of burning and piercing sensations, [he is said to have Vata-vidagdha-jwara].

At that time, one should eliminate ūrustambha; otherwise, it may be cured. However, one should avoid oleation, bloodletting, emesis, enema therapy, and purgation in the case of āḍhyavāta, because those [treatments] provoke that condition.
Therefore, in this condition, one who seeks to protect the *vāta* from the excess of *āma*, fat, and *kapha* should always employ sudation, fasting, and drying therapies;
whatever treatment serves to pacify *kapha* must not provoke the *vāta*.
All of that should always be employed as the remedy for ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
Every drying treatment should be administered there, beginning first with measures that destroy kapha, and subsequently all procedures for the destruction of vāta should be carried out. 13–14.
One should eat old śyāmāka, kodrava, uddāla, and śāli rice, along with meat from wild animals prepared without ghee, and beneficial vegetables that are salt-free.
One should serve vegetables that are salt-free and cooked with water, oil, or clarified butter.

The physician should prescribe aged *śāli* rice combined with salt-free vegetables prepared from *sunīṣaṇṇaka*, *nimba*, *arka*, *vṛntāka*, the sprouts of *āragvadha*, *vāyasī*, *vāstuka*, and other such roots and greens. (16–17)
If the drying therapy causes an aggravation of vāta preceded by insomnia and pain,
then a regimen of oleation and sudation should be employed there to alleviate the vāta disorders.
One should cross a propitious river of cold water by swimming against the current.
Furthermore, one should repeatedly bathe in a lake that is pure, cool, and has still water.
This treatment should be performed while protecting the body's strength and digestive fire, so that when the kapha has dried up, the stiffness of the thighs may reach a state of pacification. 19–20.

In cases of burning sensations (dāha), the physician should apply alkaline urine and sweat, as well as dry massages (utsādana). Furthermore, one should treat with urine and other such substances, or with *karañja* fruits and mustard seeds, or with the roots of *aśvagandhā* or *arka*. (21)
Or,

in the case of ūrustambha accompanied by pain, the physician should perform a firm massage using the roots of picumarda or devadāru, combined with honey, mustard seeds, anthill earth, and clay. (22–23)

A wise person should also consume water boiled with *dantī*, *indravāruṇī*, *vṛṣa*, *surasa*, and *sarṣapa*, as well as *tarkārī*, *surasa*, *śigru*, *vacā*, *vatsaka*, and *nimba*— using their leaves, roots, and fruits— and drink it while warm. (24)
Bhallātaka, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, dāru, pathyā, punarnavā,
combined with the two types of pañcamūlī, destroy ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, and the fruits of bhallātaka [are also used].
By drinking a paste mixed with honey, one is freed from ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
[The following paste consists of: rāsnā, śyāmāka, pathyā, marica, misi, śivā, vella, śaṭī, aśvagandhā, yavāsa, chinnā, ajamodā, sumukha, ativiṣā, vṛddhadāru, and the two types of bṛhatī.
Śuṇṭhī, tiktā, yavānī, sahacara, cavikā, eraṇḍa, dārvī, ājakarṇā,
and ūrustambha quickly destroy avamāta, diseases of kapha and vāta, and daṇḍaka.
One should drink a decoction of granthika, aruṣkara, and kṛṣṇā mixed with honey.
Or one should lick the powder of triphalā combined with kaṭukā and honey;
or a person should drink the powder of ṣaḍdharaṇa with lukewarm water;
or [the powder of] pippalī in increasing doses (pippalī-vardhamāna) with honey or with jaggery.
In cases of ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), they recommend gaṇḍīra and ariṣṭa;
one should drink śilājatu or guggulu, or pippalī and nāgara, with urine or with the decoction of daśamūla. (30–31)

A man suffering from ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) should lick a powder of triphalā, pippalī, musta, cavya, and kaṭukarohiṇī with honey. In cases of ūrustambha where kapha is predominant, one should administer sauraśvara ghee.
One should administer either Śuṇṭhī-ghṛta, or Vaiśvānara-ghṛta, or the beneficial oil beginning with Saindhava; likewise, the guggulu known as Amṛta is also beneficial.
[The following should be used: Kuṣṭha, Śrīveṣṭaka, Udīcya, Sarala, Devadāru, and Keśara.
One should cook mustard oil with ajagandhā, aśvagandhā, and those [other aforementioned] ingredients;
one afflicted by ūrustambha or ardita should drink it in the proper dose along with honey.
[Furthermore, one may take] eight kaṭvaras from two palas each of pippalīmūla and nāgara.
One *prastha* of oil mixed with an equal amount of curd removes the seizing pain in the thighs caused by *gṛdhra-sī*.
Buttermilk produced from curd with added fat is called *kaṭvara*;
for *kaṭvara* made with eight parts [of water], mustard oil is prescribed.
Two palas each of pippalīmūla and śuṇṭhī are prepared; likewise two palas each of the two pañcamūlas, triphalā, citraka, devadāru,
ekāṣṭhīlā, apāmārga, śreyasī, vāyasī, and śubhā.
Balā, bhārgī, pṛthakparṇī, suvahā, madayantikā,
viśālā, uśīra, kāśmarya, the three [types of] agnika, cirabilva, aśoka, kalaśī, and aṃśumatī should likewise be administered. 39.
Payasyā, pīluparṇī, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī—
taking five-pala portions of each of these, the physician should cook one āḍhaka of oil in seven droṇas of water until one-eighth remains. 40–41.
Kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, trikaṭu, citraka, harītakī,
excellent devadāru, aguru, viḍaṅga, and musta; as well as aśvagandhā, śālaparṇī, pāṭhā, mūlī, and śyāmāka.

The physician should prepare this with long pepper (pippalī), ginger (śṛṅgavera), dantī, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and amlavetasa; having boiled it with these as an internal ingredient, once it is cooked, cooled, and strained, he should mix it with honey. 43–44.
Therefore, that same [oil] may be used for nasal administration and drinking; it may also serve as an ointment.
Chronic ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) is pacified by this oil, and it destroys āmavāta, śītavāta, and kṣudravāta. 45–46.
One should cook [the oil] with *sindhuvāra*, *rug*, *viśvājā*, *ugrā*, *bhārgī*, *yaṣṭī*, *sthirā*, and *phala*;
with *dāru*, *viśva*, *śaṭī*, *dhānyaka*, *kṛṣṇā*, *kaṭphala*, and *pauṣkara*; and with *dīpyaka*, *ativiṣā*, *eraṇḍa*, *nīlī*, and blue lotus (*nīlāmbuja*). 47.
Oil mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika), when administered through drinking, massage,

and nasal drops, destroys āmavāta, worms, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, headaches, weak digestion, and diseases such as hemiplegia, joint pain, and stiffness of the limbs. 48–49.
Two palas of rock salt (*saindhava*), five of dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), two each of *granthika* and *citraka*, twenty-two bhallātaka seeds, and two *āḍhakas* of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*);
five *prasthas* of castor oil (*eraṇḍa-taila*). (Verse 50)
It cures the pain of *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica), *ūrugraha* (stiffness of the thighs), and all disorders of *vāta*.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter on *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs).
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter on *āmavāta* (rheumatoid arthritis).
In one who consumes incompatible food and engages in improper activities, whose digestive fire is weak and who remains sedentary;
or in one who performs physical exercise immediately after eating unctuous food— then the undigested matter (āma),
impelled by the bodily wind (vāyu), rushes toward the seat of phlegm (śleṣman).
Because it is excessively undigested,

that food-born rasa reaches the vessels (dhamanīs) and, further vitiated by vāta, pitta, and kapha, becomes multicolored and extremely slimy, causing obstruction (abhiṣyanda) in the channels (srotas).
It produces weakness of the digestive fire and heaviness of the heart;
for this extremely severe condition known as *āma* is indeed the locus of diseases, having arisen from indigestion and the like, and having accumulated gradually in the chest. 4.
One perceives a sensation of rawness, which causes pain in the head and limbs.
When these two [humors] are simultaneously provoked, they enter the junction of the *trika* (the sacroiliac region) and cause the body to become stiff; that is called *āmavāta*.
Aching of the limbs, loss of appetite, thirst, laziness, heaviness, fever,
lack of digestion, and swelling of the body parts are the symptoms of āmavāta (7).
It is the most difficult [to treat] among all diseases when it becomes aggravated.
In the joints of the hands, feet, head, ankles, sacrum, knees, and thighs, it produces painful swelling wherever the *doṣa* reaches;
that region becomes afflicted with pain as if pierced by scorpions. (8–9)
It produces weakness of the digestive fire, excessive salivation, anorexia, heaviness, loss of energy, a bad taste in the mouth, a burning sensation, excessive urination,
hardness in the abdomen, colic, as well as disturbed sleep.
Thirst, vomiting, vertigo, fainting, pain in the heart, hardness of stool, numbness, intestinal rumbling, constipation, and other painful complications arise from [undigested matter];
while that caused by pitta is characterized by burning sensation and redness, and that of the nature of vāta is accompanied by colic.

One should designate that swelling as being afflicted by *kapha* when it is motionless, heavy, and itchy. That which follows a single *doṣa* is curable; that which involves two *doṣas* is said to be palliable;
and that which involves swellings moving through the entire body due to all three *doṣas* is difficult to treat.
Fasting, sudation, bitter, digestive, and pungent substances,
purgation, oleation, and enemas are indicated for *āmavāta*. Furthermore, dry sudation should be administered using vessels filled with sand.
Poultices (upanāhas) should also be applied, though they too must be devoid of oil.
For one overcome by āmavāta and afflicted by thirst, water prepared with pañcakola is said to be beneficial. 15–16.
Either a broth of dried radish, or a broth made from the five basic vegetables, or meat broth,
or sour gruel (kāñjika) sprinkled with powdered ginger;
likewise, fermented grain-water (sauvīra), steamed eggplant, and bitter fruits.
Vāstūka greens, sariṣṭa greens, and punarnavā are beneficial.
So too are paṭola, gokṣura, varuṇa, and kāraveḷla;
as well as barley-based food, koradūṣa grain, and aged śāli and ṣaṣṭika rice.
Likewise, the meat of quails prepared with buttermilk is beneficial; soups of horse-gram (*kulattha*), black gram (*kāla-yaṣṭika*), and chickpeas (*caṇaka*) are also wholesome.
One should provide what is appetizing and suited to the individual's constitution, as well as whatever is beneficial for *āmavāta*.
Śatapuṣpā, vacā, viśvā, gokṣura, the bark of varuṇa,
punarnavā, devadāru, śaṭī, muṇḍitikā, prasāraṇī, tāmalakī, and the fruit of madana— these are equal [in measure]. 21–22.
A plaster made of *śukti*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and flour, applied while lukewarm, is beneficial for anointing.
A poultice (*upanāha*) and an ointment (*pralepana*) should be prepared from *ahiṃsrā*, *kebuka*, the root of *śigru*, and earth from an anthill, ground with urine. (23–24)
One should daily drink Citraka, Kaṭukā, Pāṭhā, Kaliṅga, Ativiṣā, Amṛtā, Devadāru, Vacā, Mustā, Nāgara, Ativiṣā, and Abhayā with warm water as the remedy for Āmavāta. (25)
Śaṭī, śuṇṭhī, abhayā, ugrā, devāhvā, ativiṣā, and amṛtā—this decoction is a digestive (pācana) for āmavāta; it should be taken with a dry diet.
Also, punarnavā, bṛhatī, vardhamāna, and phaṇijjaka [are used].
In the case of undigested āma, the physician should prepare a decoction from mūrvā, śigru, and drumā;
or he may administer a sprinkling for āmavāta with the milk of the castor-oil plant (rubūka). Alternatively, one should lick pathyā together with viśvā, or drink guggulu with urine.
One should eat the paste of viśvā and alambuṣā, or of viśvā and sesame.
A lukewarm decoction of viśvā, pathyā, and amṛtā, combined with honey, when drunk, removes pain in the waist, calves, thighs, and back. (29–30)
This powder, consisting of asafoetida, chavya, viḍa salt, ginger, long pepper, and cumin, each increasing by one part, when drunk, becomes a conqueror of wind-born colic (vātāma).
[31] Long pepper, long pepper root, rock salt, and black cumin—
Cavya, citraka, tālīśapatra, and nāgakeśara—
take two-pala portions of each of these, along with five palas of sauvarcala salt, and one pala each of marica, ajāji, and śuṇṭhī. (32–33)
A skilled physician should crush one kuḍava of pomegranate and two palas of sour vetasa, and mix them all together.
This is known as *pippalyādyam* (the preparation beginning with long pepper), which stimulates a diminished digestive fire.

It destroys hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargement (udara), fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), worms, itching, and loss of appetite— either with wine or with very warm water. There is no medicine superior to this for āmavāta.
One should drink an equal powder of *pathyā*, *viśva*, and *yavānī* with buttermilk, warm water, or even *kāñjika*;
it quickly destroys *āmavāta*, swelling, and weak digestion. (37)

One afflicted by undigested matter (āmadoṣa) should drink a decoction of garlic, ginger, and nirguṇḍī to cure chronic catarrh, cough, heart disease, hoarseness of voice, and loss of appetite. [38–39] One should also take rāsnā, guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, devadāru, and mahauṣadha.
In cases of generalized Vāta associated with Āma, affecting the joints, bones, and marrow, one should drink water boiled with pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara;
this destroys Āmavāta. (40–41)

A person should drink the paste of *śaṭī* and *viśva-oṣadhī* combined with a decoction of *varṣābhū* for seven nights; this destroys *āmavāta*. [Likewise, one may take] *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, *āragvadha*, *devadāru*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *eraṇḍa*, and *punarnavā*.
One suffering from pain in the calves, thighs, sides, the sacrum (trika), or the back should drink a decoction mixed with powdered ginger (43).
In cases of *āmavāta*, one should drink water boiled with the ten roots (*daśamūlī*) combined with long pepper (*kaṇā*), or one should eat *abhayā* and ginger, or *guḍūcī* with ginger (44).
Citraka, yava, pāṭhā, kaṭukā, ativiṣā, and abhayā—
this powder destroys wind arising from the stomach (āmāśaya) and should be drunk with lukewarm water.
Punarnavā, amṛtā, śuṇṭhī, śatāhvā, and vṛddhadāruka [are used for this purpose].
One should administer a powder of *śaṭī* and *muṇḍitikā* with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*).
This powder, which destroys wind arising in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), should be drunk with lukewarm water; it quickly cures *āmavāta* and even severe *gṛdhrasī*.
One should always drink one karṣa of powdered ginger with fermented rice-water (kāñjika); it pacifies āmavāta and is supreme for removing kapha and vāta.
One should likewise drink the powder of the five pungent fruits (pañcakola) with warm water.
It destroys weak digestion, colic, abdominal tumors, worms, phlegm, and loss of appetite (49).
The lion of castor oil swiftly slays the lordly elephant of undigested vata that roams the forest of the body (50).

A person afflicted by the pain of undigested matter (āmavāta) and wind, as well as those suffering from sciatica (gṛdhrasī), hernia (vṛddhi), or similar ailments, should regularly consume harītakī combined with castor oil according to the prescribed method. [51] The leaves of āragvadha should be fried in pungent oil (kaṭutaila).
A person should avoid uncooked foods and meals taken at night.

When the pure Vāyu, accompanied by *sāma*, takes refuge in the waist, it produces pain; that is called *kaṭīgraha* (stiffness of the waist). It is further described as *paṅgu* (lameness) when it causes the destruction of both thighs.
A decoction of *śuṇṭhī* and *gokṣuraka*, consumed every morning, is a digestive aid that destroys pain in cases of *vāta* with *āma* and sciatica;
when combined with *yavakṣāra*, it cures dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). 54.
In cases of pain in the waist, one should drink a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) or water boiled with ginger (nāgara); alternatively, castor oil (eraṇḍa-taila) should be drunk,
or a decoction of long pepper (mahauṣadha) and guduchi (guḍūcī) combined with long pepper.
One suffering from abdominal pain or pain in the pelvic region, especially in cases of sciatica, should drink this.
Having purified castor seeds and ground them, one should cook them in milk; that milk-porridge (pāyasa) is a supreme remedy for sciatica and *gṛdhrasī*.

Ghee, oil, jaggery, fermented gruel, and ginger as the fifth—when this is drunk, it provides immediate nourishment and relieves pain in the waist caused by wind (vāta). Indeed, there is nothing equal to this for wind in the waist when free from undigested matter (āmadoṣa). 58–59.
Cow's urine mixed with the bark of the *surataru* tree should be kept for seven days;
then, combined with *hiṅgu*, *vacā*, *śatapuṣpā*, and rock salt, it should be cooked in a *puṭapāka*. This cures severe pain in the loins of men.
It destroys disorders arising from the increase of *āma* and fat, as well as those born of *vāta*.
A powder made from *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *gokṣura*, *muṇḍitikā*, and *varuṇaka*, when drunk with whey (*mastu*) or sour gruel (*āranāla*), is renowned for curing *sāma-vāta*.
One should drink a powder of *ālambuṣā*, *gokṣuraka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nāgara*, and *amṛtā*—
increased in parts by one for each subsequent drug— with an equal amount of *śyāmā* powder,
using whey, *surā* liquor, buttermilk, *kāñjika*, or warm water. (63)

This destroys āmavāta quickly, as well as swelling and vātaśoṇita (64). The powder beginning with alambuṣā, which resides in the regions of the sacrum, knees, and thighs, destroys fevers, anorexia, and the entire host of diseases (65).
Triphalā is well known as consisting of *harītakī*, *akṣa* (vibhītaka), and *dhātrī* (āmalakī) respectively;
one should employ them either individually or by increasing the quantity of each in successive order.
[Also used are] *alambuṣā*, *gokṣuraka*, and the root of *varuṇaka*.

One should prepare equal parts of *guḍūcī* and *nāgara*; this should be drunk with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) in a dose the size of a cat's paw. This formulation is like nectar for the aggravation of *āmavāta*.
One should prepare fine powders of Alambuṣā, Gokṣuraka, Guḍūcī, Vṛddhadāruka, Pippalī, Trivṛtā, Mustā, Varuṇa, Punarnavā, Triphalā, and Nāgara. (69)
Taken with whey, sour gruel, buttermilk, milk, or meat broth, it quickly destroys *āmavāta* and swelling located in the joints.
Two parts of *maṇimantha* and likewise two parts of *yavānī* [should be used].
Three parts of ajamodā, five parts of nāgara, ten and two parts of harītakī— this auspicious mixture, finely powdered, should be taken with whey,
sour gruel, buttermilk, ghee, or warm water.
When drunk, it conquers āmavāta, diseases of the gulma, heart, and bladder;
splenic disorders, glandular swellings, colic and the like, abdominal distension, hemorrhoids, constipation, and digestive ailments arising from the waist and bladder. (73)
This powder, known as Vaiśvānara, is indeed remembered for its ability to facilitate the downward movement of Vāta.
Equal parts of asītaka, māgadhikā, guḍūcī, śyāmā, varāhī, gajakarṇa, and śuṇṭhī should be held together; one should drink this entire powder with warm water, rice-gruel, or vegetable soup. 74–75.
By means of buttermilk, meat soups, or all types of wines, for one who indulges in food according to his desire,
it cures diseases such as *sabāhuka*, *gṛdhra*, *sikhin*, *vāta*, *viśvācita*, *tūnī*, and *pratitūnī* (76),
as well as ailments of the calves, *āmavāta*, *ardita*, *vātarakta*, stiffness of the waist (*kaṭīgraha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and diseases of the rectum.
One should conquer urustambha (stiffness of the thighs) with its intense onset, accompanied by itching, pallor, and severe swelling,
by cooking one prastha of ghee with six palas of ground ginger and two palas of coriander, adding four times as much water. (77–78)
This destroys diseases of vāta and kapha, is a supreme promoter of the digestive fire, cures hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough, and increases strength, complexion, and appetite.
(79) Ghee mixed with a paste of *nāgara* (ginger), with four times as much *sauvīra* (sour gruel)...
This is established as the most excellent for generating digestive fire and is supreme for removing *āmavāta*.

For the sake of nourishment, it should be prepared with milk; for the retention of feces and urine, with curd; and for the purpose of stimulating digestion, it is proclaimed by the wise to be prepared with whey.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with the decoction and paste of *nāgaraka*, using either four times that amount of the decoction alone or with water alone;
this is supreme for pacifying *vāta* and *kapha* and for stimulating the digestive fire.
This is called Nāgara-ghṛta; it destroys pain in the waist and colic.
Having made one-pala pastes of hiṅgu, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), cavya, and likewise maṇimantha, one should cook them with one prastha of ghee. 83–84.
By administering one *āḍhaka* of fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) with that ghee, it destroys abdominal diseases, colic, constipation, flatulence, *āmavāta*, and stiffness of the waist;
it cures disorders of the *grahaṇī* and is a supreme stimulant for weak digestion. (85-86)

Having ground ginger, barley-alkali, long pepper root, and long pepper, one should cook ghee with four times as much sour gruel (āranāla); this cures colic, constipation, flatulence, āmavāta, and stiffness of the waist. (87)
It destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī* and is a supreme stimulant for the digestive fire (88).
One should drink either Bindughṛta or Dhānvantara-ghṛta,
or even Mahāśuṇṭhī-ghṛta, repeatedly in cases of *āmavāta* (89).

Whatever is a laxative, a digestive stimulant for *sarpis* (clarified butter), or a digestive (*pācana*), all that should be employed in cases of *āmavāta*, as well as *mastu* (whey) with the "six-pala" formulation:
*ajamoda*, black pepper, long pepper, *viḍaṅga*, *suradāru*, *citraka*, and *śatāhvā*.

One *pala* each of rock salt (*saindhava*) and long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*) should constitute nine parts; there should be ten *palas* of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) and as many *palas* (ten) of *vṛddhadāra*;
and five *palas* of *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan). One should prepare a powder by combining all these together.
For one who drinks the powder of equal parts of jaggery, vaṭaka, and *nāda* with warm water,

all diseases born of undigested matter (*āma*) and wind (*anila*), even those most difficult to cure— such as *pratitūnī*, *viśvācī*, and other ailments including the severe *gṛdhrasī*— are destroyed. (93)
Cracking of the waist, back, and anus, as well as intense pain in the calves (94),
swelling in all the joints, and whatever other ailments arise from *āmavāta*—
all these go to destruction like darkness dispelled by the rays of the sun (95).

Through such practice, it produces the awakening of hunger, freedom from disease, stable youth, and the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair; furthermore, it brings about many other qualities in great abundance. (96) [One should take] *citraka*, the root of *pippalī*, *yavānī*, and likewise *kāravī*.
Viḍaṅga, ajamodā, jīraka, and devadāru;
97 cavya, elā, saindhava, kuṣṭha, rāsnā, gokṣura, dhānyaka, triphalā, mustaka, vyoṣa, tvak, uśīra, and yavāgraja. 98

One should have tālīśapatra and patra made into fine powders; then, having thoroughly kneaded an amount of guggulu equal to the total weight of these powders with clarified butter, one should store it in a well-oiled vessel.
Therefore, one should employ it in the proper measure; even for one who eats whatever food they desire, this formulation known as *Yogarāja* is like nectar.
It cures sluggish digestion, *āmavāta*, and other disorders, as well as worms and malignant ulcers. (100)
It destroys spleen disorders, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, flatulence, and hemorrhoids (durnāma).
It makes the digestive fire blazing, increases vitality and strength, and conquers diseases of Vāta even when they have reached the joints and marrow. 101–102.
One *prastha* of jaggery juice is considered to be cooked in a decoction of one *āḍhaka* of *prasāraṇī*; when combined with the powder of the five pungents (*pañcoṣaṇa*), it destroys *āmavāta*.
[In another formulation: eight *palas* of ginger and twenty *palas* of ghee...
One should cook fifty palas of sugar with two prasthas of milk;
then one should add one pala each of powdered vyoṣa and trijātaka, and consume it according to the strength of one's digestive fire. (104–105)

It pacifies *āmavāta*, increases strength and nourishment; it is strengthening, life-prolonging, and vitalizing, and it destroys wrinkles and graying hair. It pacifies *āmavāta* and is the most excellent means for bestowing good fortune. (106–107)
One hundred palas of garlic, one kuḍava of sesame,
as well as asafoetida, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the two alkalis, the five salts,
śatapuṣpā, niśā, kuṣṭha, pippalīmūla, and citraka. (108)
A wise person should have one *pala* each of *ajamodā*, *yavānī*, and *dhānyaka* made into a fine powder;
he should then place it in a sturdy vessel of ghee for sixteen days. (109–110)
Having added one *māna* of oil and half a *prastha* of *kāñjika*, one should consume it in the measure of one *karṣa*; thereafter, one may drink water or wine.
This is for *āmavāta* and *raktavāta* located in the whole body or in a single limb. (111)

Castor oil prepared with the juice of *Prasāraṇī* is recommended for consumption in cases of epilepsy, weak digestion, cough, dyspnea, artificial poisons, insanity, Vata-induced paralysis, and colic in living beings. (112)

It removes all defects and is the supreme remedy for diseases of phlegm (kapha). Oil prepared with the decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūlī), along with their fruits, sour curd, and sour gruel (kāñjika), cures pain in the waist, thighs, and sides, as well as diseases of phlegm, wind (vāta), and seizures.
By the administration of an enema, it destroys [diseases] and produces great strength of the digestive fire (agni).
Saindhava salt, śreyasī, rāsnā, śatapuṣpā, yavānikā, svarjikā, marica, kuṣṭha, śuṇṭhī, sauvarcala, and viḍa [salt]—[these are the ingredients]. 115–116.
One should have vacā, ajamodā, ajagara, pauṣkara, madhuka, and kaṇā—each weighing half a pala—made into a fine powder.
[Add] one prastha of eraṇḍa oil and one prastha of water from śatapuṣpa. 117.
Having added twice as much sour gruel (kāñjika) and likewise twice as much whey (mastu),
one should cook these gathered ingredients slowly over a mild fire. Once prepared, this should be administered as a supreme remedy for curing āmavāta.
When used as a drink, an ointment, or an enema, it greatly increases the strength of the digestive fire;
it is recommended for pain caused by Vāta in the groin, as well as for pain arising in the waist, knees,
and thighs, and likewise for heart and side pain, or when afflicted by an increase of Kapha.
It quickly destroys intestinal hernia (antra-vṛddhi) caused by external pressure, as well as other wind-born diseases of embodied beings;
[one may use] either a small amount of prasāraṇī oil or oil with rock salt and other ingredients. 121.
The administration of an enema with oil prepared from the ten roots (daśamūla) and other ingredients is recommended.
One should take two palas of oil, four palas of sour gruel (kāñjika), and five palas each of the decoction of the ten roots and urine. 122–123.

A wise person should churn together vacā, madana, vāṭyā, śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, saindhava, pippalī, ativiṣā, mustā, rāsnā, kaṭphala, and pauṣkara, each taken in the measure of one akṣa. 124. All of this should be stirred with a churning stick.
Half a *prastha* should be given for the first enema without hesitation;
however, one should exclude two *prasṛtas* for the second and third [enemas] in all disorders of Vāta, in urinary disorders (*meha*), and in diseases of the testicles. 125–126.

In cases of pain in the abdomen, heart, back, or sides; in seizing pains of the knees, shanks, and hips; in constipation, abdominal tumors, and diseases; in afflictions caused by gravel and stones; and in those with fractured or dislocated limbs, or who have been crushed or wounded.

A wise person, free from exertion and possessing great virtues, should avoid this like one suffering from *nirūha* [purgative] therapy: curd, fish, molasses, milk, *potakī*, and flour made of *māṣa* beans; likewise, one afflicted by *āmavāta* should avoid meat derived from marshy animals. 128–129.
Those substances which cause excessive secretions and others that are heavy and slimy should be avoided with great effort by men afflicted by āmavāta (rheumatic disorders). [Rāsnā, eraṇḍa,
śatāvarī, sahacara, duḥsparśā, vāsā, amṛtā...]

A decoction prepared from devadāru, ativiṣā, abhayā, musta, śaṭī, and śuṇṭhī, when drunk along with urubūka oil, is prescribed for vāta associated with āma and pain; it conquers the affliction of āma in the waist, thighs, sacrum, back, abdomen, and chest. (131)
Rāsnā, the root of vātāri, vāsaka, durālabhā, śaṭī, dāru, balā, musta, nāgara, ativiṣā, abhayā,
śvadaṃṣṭrā, vyādhighāta, misi, dhānya, and punarnavā. (132)
Aśvagandhā, amṛtā, kṛṣṇā, vṛddhadāru, śatāvarī,
vacā, sahacara, cavikā, and the two types of bṛhatī— these should be taken in equal parts, with rāsnā added in double that amount. 133–134.
One should administer the decoction prepared by boiling it down until one-eighth remains,
combined with powdered ginger, as well as with ābhādya, along with alambuṣā and others, and combined with ajamodā and others. 135.
The physician should administer the addition [of medicinal substances] according to the specific humor and the specific disease:
in all wind (vāta) disorders, in those affecting the joints and marrow, in all types of constipation (ānāha), and in tremors of the entire body. (136–137)
It is recommended for hunchback, dwarfism, hemiplegia,
facial paralysis, pain in the knees, shanks, and bones, as well as for sciatica,
lockjaw, gout, stiffness of the thighs, and hemorrhoids.
[It is used] for Viśvācī, Gulma, Hṛdroga, Viṣūcī, Kroṣṭuśīrṣaka (139), as well as for Antravṛddhi, Ślīpada, diseases of the female reproductive tract and semen,
diseases of the male organ in men, and the disease of sterility in women (140).
There is nothing superior to this for bestowing pregnancy upon women;
indeed, among all digestive stimulants (*pācana*), this is the most excellent.
This preparation named Mahārāsnādika was fashioned by Prajāpati himself. 141–142.
A decoction made from rāsnā, viśva, viḍaṅga, rubūka, triphalā, daśamūla, and śyāmā separately removes disorders caused by vāta;
it is especially effective in cases of severe hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka), facial paralysis (ardita), and vāta-khañja. 143
It is declared to be auspicious for eye diseases, headaches, fever, epilepsy, and various forms of mental derangement. (144) Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Section on Āmavāta. 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter: The Section on Bile Diseases (Pittavyādhyadhikāra).

[Bile is provoked] by pungent, sour, hot, burning, sharp, and salty substances; by anger, fasting, exposure to the sun, sexual intercourse, thirst, hunger, trauma, physical exercise, wine, and similar factors.
Furthermore, bile produced by food consumed at midday or at noon causes disorders during the middle of the meal, as well as in old age, at night, and in the seasons of summer and autumn;
it also causes premature graying of the hair, redness of the eyes, and blood in the urine.
Likewise, yellowness of the eyes and face, as well as yellowness of the urine,
is declared; there is yellowness of the excrement, yellowness of the limbs,
yellowness of the teeth, and likewise yellowness of the body.
There is also a vision of darkness and a perception of everything as yellow;
sleepiness, lassitude, and so forth, dryness of the mouth, and a metallic taste; 4. as well as bitterness of the mouth and likewise acidity of the face.
The warmth of exhalation, as well as the emission of smoke, delusion, exhaustion, anger, burning sensations accompanied by a sense of splitting,
aversion to light, a desire for cold, lack of satiety, and likewise restlessness— these are the signs.
There is a burning sensation after eating, sharpness of the digestive fire,
discharge of blood, breaking of the stool, and likewise heat of the feces;
as well as heat of the urine, dysuria, scantiness of urine, and thinness of the body-heat.
Furthermore, foul odor of the sweat, as well as the discoloration of the body's covering,
exhaustion of the body, and suppuration of the physique— these forty are considered by the sages to be the diseases of pitta.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter on diseases of bile (pitta).
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter on diseases of phlegm (śleṣman): [caused by] heavy, sweet tastes and the like, unctuousness, and sluggish digestive fire in the stomach.

In the spring season, during the first part of the day immediately after eating, there occurs a phlegm disorder characterized by excessive speech, mental distress, drowsiness, sleep, coldness, and lack of movement; this also occurs during the first part of the night. (1)
First, there is sweetness in the mouth, as well as a coating on the mouth, salivation, and likewise an excess of sleep; furthermore,
there is a gurgling sound in the throat and a craving for pungent, bitter, and hot things.
Dullness of intellect, lack of consciousness, laziness, and satiety;
likewise, sluggish digestion, an excess of impurities, the whiteness of impurities;
an excess of urine, the whiteness of urine, and likewise an excess of semen.
Stiffness, heaviness, and coldness— these twenty, through their association and their established nomenclature, are declared by the sages to be the diseases of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
Dryness, alkalinity, astringency, bitterness, pungency, physical exercise, and spitting [are the causes].

Smoking, fomentation, fire-therapy, cold applications, nasal medication, emesis, sudation, fasting, and so forth; thirst-quenching, travel, wrestling, staying awake at night, water-sports, and sexual intercourse;
as well as specific drinks, foods, activities, and medicines—these remove diseases caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm). 6–7.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter on the disorders of phlegm (śleṣmavyādhi), [chapter] 28. Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter on vātarakta (vātaraktādhikāra), [chapter] 29.
[Caused] by salty, sour, pungent, alkaline, unctuous, hot, and undigested foods;
With moist and dried lotus roots, marshy meat, oil-cakes, and radishes;
with horse-gram, black gram, flat beans, leafy vegetables, minced meat, and sugarcane; and with curd, fermented rice-gruel, *sauvīra* vinegar, *śukta*, buttermilk, wine, and spirituous liquors.

Vāta-śoṇita generally becomes aggravated in those who are delicate, those who indulge in improper diet and lifestyle, the obese, and even those accustomed to comfort, due to incompatible eating, overeating, anger, sleeping during the day, and excessive staying awake at night. (3)

In one who travels by means of elephants, horses, or camels, or who eats food that causes burning, the entire blood is quickly inflamed by the consumption of such burning food. That vitiated blood rapidly accumulates in the feet;
because it is joined with the corrupted wind and due to its predominance, it is called *vātarakta*.
Excessive sweating, or conversely, no sweating at all; blackish discoloration; loss of tactile sensation; pain from wounds;
looseness of the joints; lassitude; exhaustion; the eruption of pustules;
[these occur] in the knees, calves, thighs, hips, shoulders, hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs.
Pricking pain, throbbing, piercing sensation, heaviness, numbness,

itching, and a burning pain in the joints that repeatedly appear and then vanish, along with discoloration and the appearance of circular patches (maṇḍala), are the premonitory symptoms of vātāsṛj (vātarakta).
When Vāta is predominant, there is excessive pain characterized by throbbing and piercing sensations;
the swelling is dry, blackish, or dark-brown, and it fluctuates in size; furthermore, there is contraction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, as well as stiffness of the limbs and intense pain.

In blood (rakta), there is swelling, excessive pain, pricking, a coppery discoloration, and a tingling sensation; it is not relieved by either unctuous or dry treatments and is accompanied by itching and moisture. 10–11. Cold and aversion to cold are the non-therapeutic factors (anupaśaya); stiffness, tremors, and numbness [are the signs].

10. In blood, there is swelling, extreme pain, pricking, a coppery hue, and a tingling sensation; it finds no relief from either unctuous or dry measures and is associated with itching and exudation. 11.
In the case of pitta, there is a burning sensation, confusion, perspiration, fainting, intoxication, thirst,
intolerance to touch, pain with a burning quality, swelling, suppuration, and extreme heat.
In the case of kapha, there is stiffness, heaviness, numbness, unctuousness, and coldness.
In the case of a mixed poison (saṅkara), there is itching, mild pain, and the symptoms of both [poisons] together. Residing at the base of the feet and sometimes even in the hands,
it creeps up the body like the enraged venom of a rat.
Insomnia, anorexia, dyspnea, putrefaction of the flesh, stiffness of the head,
fainting, constant pain, thirst, fever, delusion,
trembling, hiccups, convulsions, erysipelas, suppuration, pricking pain, vertigo, and exhaustion [are the symptoms]. 15.
Curvature of the fingers, cracking, burning sensations, affliction of the vital points (*marmas*), and tumors—these are the complications.
A case free from these complications, as well as one with only delusion, is curable;
a case with incomplete complications is palliable; and one without complications is easily curable.
A case involving a single doṣa is curable; one arising from two doṣas is palliable;

one arising from all three doṣas is incurable, as is that which has complications. Furthermore, a case where the swelling has burst down to the knees, or is cracked, ruptured, or exuding pus, is incurable. (18)

Furthermore, that which is afflicted by secondary complications such as the wasting of vital breath (*prāṇa*) and muscle tissue, or which is *vātarakta*, is incurable; however, if it has arisen for one year, it is palliable.
In a patient suffering from *vātaśoṇita* (gout/vasculitis), one should repeatedly extract blood after first applying oleation (*snigdha*).
One should restrain the wind (vāyu) very gently, according to the specific disorder and the patient's strength.
In cases of severe swelling, burning, and piercing pain, one should extract the blood using leeches;
in cases accompanied by a tingling sensation, itching, pain, and trembling, one should use a horn.
Or one may travel from place to place with the head covered or by means of veins; however,
when the limb is flaccid, blood should not be let, and one must protect against conditions dominated by Vāta, such as deep-seated swelling, stiffness, tremors, and diseases of the veins.
Due to the depletion of blood, the wind (vāyu) may cause lassitude and other disorders arising from wind,
as well as diseases such as lameness and other vāta-related ailments, even up to death without remainder;
therefore, one should extract blood that is unctuous and moist in the proper measure.
Enema therapy (basti-karma) with either rough or mild substances is recommended to be administered repeatedly;
indeed, there is no treatment for vāta-rakta equal to enema therapy.
External treatment should be performed with plasters (ālepana), massages (abhyaṅga), affusions (pariṣeka), and poultices (upanāhana).
One should treat deep-seated [fevers] with purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and the internal administration of fats.
One should avoid sleeping during the day, feverish heat, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, as well as pungent, hot, heavy, obstructive, salty, and sour substances.
Ancient grains such as barley, wheat, wild rice (nīvāra), śāli rice, and ṣaṣṭika rice are suitable for the purpose of food;
for the sake of nourishment, however, birds that scatter their food (viṣkira) and those that peck (pratuda) are beneficial.
So too are āḍhakī, chickpeas, mung beans, lentils, and horse gram.
Soups containing abundant ghee are recommended for vātaśoṇita (gout).
Likewise, the vegetables suniṣaṇṇaka, vetrāgra, kākamācī, śatāvarī, vāstuka, upodikā, and sauvarcala are beneficial. (29–30)

One should give vegetables seasoned with ghee, meat broth, and juices to those accustomed to such food (31). One should treat a condition dominated by Vāta with the internal consumption of ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow; with external massage and enemas; and with comfortably warm poultices.
A plaster of wheat flour soaked in goat’s milk and ghee is likewise [effective];
similarly, fried sesame seeds ground and quenched in milk;
or a plaster of linseed ground with alkali, or with the fruit of *vardhamāna*. (32–33)

One should apply a poultice (pradeha) consisting of both types of *śatāhvā*, *madhuka*, the two kinds of *balā*, *priyālaka*, *kaseruka*, round *vidārī*, and white sugar for blood-associated wind (*pavana-sarakta*).
[34] *Rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *madhuka*, the two kinds of *balā*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and milk [are used for this].
An external application of prepared ghee mixed with the residue of honey will dispel the pain caused by blood and wind (raktānila).
One should drink a decoction of vāsā, guḍūcī, caturaṅgula, and eraṇḍa with castor oil;
this will gradually conquer, without exception, all disorders arising from blood and wind (asṛgvāta) even when they have spread throughout the entire body.
Milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī) immediately relieves colic;
likewise, a lukewarm affusion with clarified butter (sarpiṣ) is beneficial when the condition is dominated by Vāyu.
[Milk] prepared with paṭola, kaṭukā, bhīru, triphalā, and amṛta [is also effective].
Having drunk this decoction, a person shall always conquer vātaśoṇita accompanied by burning sensations (38).
A decoction of trivṛt, vidārī, and ikṣuraka destroys vātarakta;
amṛtā destroys kapha and vāta and dries up kapha and medas (39).
It pacifies vātarakta and destroys itching and erysipelas (visarpa). By consuming the fresh juice, paste, powder, or decoction of guḍūcī for a long period of time, one is liberated from vātaśoṇita.

A digestive decoction prepared with three *karṣas* each of *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, and *dhānyaka* conquers blood-discharged *vāta*, *āmavāta*, and all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). A decoction of *vatsādanyā* drunk mixed with *guggulu* [achieves the same]. 42.
One should destroy blood that is joined with the vital wind (samīraṇa).

Then, having eaten three or five *pathyā* fruits with jaggery (*guḍa*), one should drink a decoction of *chinnaruhā*; this certainly pacifies even that aggravated *vātarakta* which has spread as far as the knees or has even broken out.

One should take pills the size of a jujube fruit (kola), prepared from guggulu, amṛtavallī, abhīru, and āluka, mixed with the juice of emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) or the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Having stirred them with honey, one should eat them; hear now what fruit they produce. 45.
It quickly destroys that most terrible cracking of the feet, the bursting of the entire collection of limbs, and the afflicted person along with their blood.
(46) [One should take] buffalo butter mixed with *bali*.
Having mixed it with cow urine, milk, and salt, one should stir it all together in one place and slowly heat it over a fire;
one should then rub the body with this for the sake of alleviating the cracking of the skin. 47–48.
Thus, this guggulu pill, taken with ghee, pacifies vāta; with jaggery, it pacifies constipation; enriched with sugar and honey, it pacifies pitta and kapha;
mixed with castor oil, it pacifies severe vātarakta; and with ginger, it pacifies āmavāta. (49)

A decoction of *siṃhāsya*, the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), *chinnaruhā*, castor plant (*eraṇḍa*), and *gokṣuraka*, when drunk mixed with castor oil, asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), and powdered rock salt (*saindhava*),
pacifies *vātarakta*, as well as *āmavāta* and pain in the waist (*kaṭīśūla*). (50)

The wise physician should boil the roots of gandharvahasta, vṛṣa, gokṣuraka, amṛtā, bale, and ikṣuraka to treat the obstruction of urine and feces and the highly difficult-to-cure disorders of the *bradhna* (inguinal hernia).
The wise physician should quickly eliminate wind-blood (vātāsṛg) that has been chronic, deep-seated, or ruptured and moving upwards;
it pacifies phlegm and bile and destroys itching and erysipelas (visarpa). 52.
Jaggery and ghee are known to pacify vātarakta and are beneficial for the heart (53). Alternatively, one should consume the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen, or *pathyā* with jaggery (54).
Or, one should drink *kṛṣṇā* (long pepper) according to one's strength in a decoction of *kokilākṣa* and *amṛtā*.
One who eats wholesome food is freed from *vātaśoṇita* (gout/rheumatism) within three weeks.
Oil should be twice the amount of *madhuka*, and goat's milk should be twice the amount of oil;
this should be drunk according to one's digestive strength to alleviate the pain of *vātarakta*.
One should produce buffalo curd using the powder of *agasti* flowers;
with the butter derived from that, one may conquer skin eruptions (*dehaja-sphoṭana*).
A decoction of nine *karṣas* [of the aforementioned ingredients] [is also effective]. 57.
