A decoction made from nine karṣas each of triphalā, nimba, mañjiṣṭhā, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī, vatsādanī, and dāruniśā cures vātarakta, as well as kuṣṭha, pāmā, and raktamaṇḍala. (58)
It removes itching, skin eruptions, and leprosy simply by drinking it;
nine karṣas of the decoction are prepared with one māṣa of five raktikas.
Furthermore, once the decoction has been prepared in this manner, the appropriate dose is administered.
From one *karṣa* up to one *pala*, one should add sixteen parts of water;

from there up to one *kuḍava*, the water is eighteen times [the quantity of the drug]; and from there upwards, until it reaches the measure of a *prastha* and so on, the water is four times [the quantity of the drug].
Purgatives, the drinking of ghee and milk, affusions, enemas,
and an ointment made from the paste of *śālmalī* combined with sheep's milk [are indicated].
For a condition characterized by an excess of blood, milk and ghee [should be used] with the waters of *madhuka* and *uśīra*.
In this case, sprinkling should be performed every moment with fresh milk;
when blood predominates, there should be an excellent application of ghee washed a hundred thousand times,
or of ghee mixed with *sarjarasa* resin, both well-cooled.
One should conquer a predominance of *rakta-pitta* with cooling and pacifying measures;
when there is redness, pain, and burning, one should perform bloodletting and apply an ointment of sesame, *priyāla*, *madhuka*, lotus root, and cane. (65)

A paste made by grinding [the aforementioned ingredients] with ghee and milk is an application that cures diseases characterized by burning sensations (dāha). However, when pitta is predominant, one should apply a very cold decoction prepared from *tugākṣīrī*, *kāśmarya*, *drākṣā*, *āragvadha*, *candana*, *madhuka*, and *kṣīrakākolī*.

A person suffering from vātarakta should drink [milk] mixed with sugar and honey (68). Or, one should drink milk that is warm as it flows from the udder and mixed with urine to facilitate the downward movement of the doṣas;
or, when vāyu is enveloped by pitta and blood, one should drink milk with the powder of trivṛt (69).

A person with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas) should drink castor oil with milk for the purpose of purgation; once it has been digested, he should eat rice with milk. [The decoction consists of] paṭola, triphalā, bhīru, guḍūcī, and kaṭurohiṇī.
A decoction combined with sugar and honey is recommended when pitta is predominant.
Furthermore, the drinking of bitter ghee, frequent purgation, emesis using mild agents, abundant oleation, and fasting are advised. 71–72.
Warm affusions are recommended when there is an excess of *kapha* associated with wind (*vāta*);
affusions with oil, urine, wine, or fermented gruel are always beneficial.
An application (*pradeha*) made from a paste of white mustard seeds is also a remover of pain. (73–74)

In this Siddhayoga, one should not entertain doubt as to whether or not an application of the paste of *savara* and *śigru* with fermented rice-water (*dhānyāmla*) cures afflictions caused by Vāta; it certainly does. For conditions dominated by Kapha, an application of the paste derived from *vājigandhā* and sesame is prescribed.
An ointment made of mustard, nimba, arka, hiṃsrā, alkali, and sesame seeds is beneficial; it is excellent when combined with powdered parched grain, ghee, alkali, and the bark of kapittha.
Likewise, lentils, śigru, and its seeds are beneficial when mixed with fermented rice-gruel (dhānyāmla).
If the coating has formed after a short while, one should sprinkle it with acidic liquids when vāta and kapha predominate.
Water boiled with mustā, āmalaka, and niśā, mixed with honey, should be drunk; by constant use, this conquers blood-bile (raktapitta) accompanied by kapha, even when the disease is chronic.
In cases of vātarakta where kapha is predominant, one should drink a decoction of turmeric and *mṛtaka* sweetened with honey, or a decoction of *triphalā*;
alternatively, one should administer *harītakī* with buttermilk or water. (79)
House-soot, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śatāhvā*, and the two types of *rajanī* constitute a plaster that relieves pain in cases of *vātarakta* where *vāta* and *kapha* predominate.
(80) A paste of *amṛtā*, *kaṭukā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, and *śuṇṭhī*, combined with honey, [is also beneficial]. (81)
Cow’s urine, when drunk, conquers vāta-śoṇita accompanied by kapha;
or one may take a decoction of dhātrī, haridrā, and mustā mixed with honey.
Having carefully extracted the tuber of lāṅgalī, which is equal to amṛta—
One should combine equal parts of the powder of triphalā, iron, and trikaṭu;
or [one may add] guggulu along with amṛtavallī, bhṛṅgarāja, and the juice of āluka.
These should be made into pills the size of a jujube fruit (kola) mixed with the juices of triphalā. 83–84.
One should eat it mixed with honey; hear now what fruit they produce:

whatever [injury] there may be, such as a cracked foot, a badly broken [limb], or that which has reached the knee (85), as well as blood that has emerged from the body, and that which is proclaimed to be incurable.
These [drugs] destroy even severe vāta-śoṇita (blood disorders) in one who is consuming them.
One should grind together balā, atibalā, medā, ātmaguptā, śatāvarī, the two types of kākolī, the two types of kṣīrakākolī, rāsnā, and mṛdvīkā. 86–87.
Ghee prepared with four times its quantity of milk and these [drugs] cures vātarakta (gout/rheumatism), and destroys heart disease, anemia, erysipelas, jaundice, and burning sensations.
Ghee prepared with a paste and decoction of balā, sthirā, nāgabalā, guḍūcī, and śatāvarī [achieves the same].
One should administer oil for anuvasana enemas; it pacifies even aggravated vātarakta.
One should cook ghee with a decoction of trāyantikā, āmalakī, the two types of kākolī, śatāvarī, and kaserukā, along with the pastes of these same ingredients. 89–90.
The juices of both types of *paruṣaka*, *drākṣā*, *kāśmarya*, and *suradruma*, along with various kinds of *vidārī* and four times as much milk—
clarified butter prepared from these is known as *pārūṣaka*.
In cases of vātarakta, chest wounds, emaciation, erysipelas, and bilious fever,
ghee prepared with four times the quantity of śatāvarī juice and an equal amount of milk, containing a paste of śatāvarī as an internal ingredient, destroys vātaśoṇita.
Ghee prepared with equal parts of Ṛṣabhaka, Kṣīrakākolī, Kṣīrikā, and Jīvaka, along with milk, is known as Ārṣabhaka ghee; it cures vātarakta (gout).
Ghee boiled with the decoction and paste of Guḍūcī, together with milk, [is likewise effective].
It destroys Vāta as well as Rakta and conquers even difficult-to-cure Kuṣṭha.

One should administer milk equal in quantity to the oil, and four times the amount of the [other] four [liquids]; one may prepare it with one, two, or three of the liquids, making them four times the quantity of the oil. 95–96.
Ghee prepared with a decoction and a paste of *mahauṣadha* and *amṛtā*, cooked over a gentle fire, is a supreme remedy for *vātarakta*,
as well as for *āmavāta*, *āḍhyavāta*, and other such disorders, including worms, skin diseases, and ulcers. (97)
When administered, it quickly destroys hemorrhoids and abdominal tumors (98).
Ghee cooked with the fresh juice of *amṛtā* and prepared with its paste, when drunk,
removes both superficial and deep-seated vātarakta (99).
One hundred palas of Amṛtā should be boiled in one droṇa of water until one remains;
then, one prastha of ghee should be cooked with eight palas of medicinal paste and four times as much milk. This destroys Vātarakta and Kuṣṭha.
It destroys jaundice and anemia, and removes splenic disorders, cough, and fever.
(101) Amṛtā, madhuka, drākṣā, triphalā, nāgara, balā, vāsā, āragvadha, vṛścīra, devadāru, and trikaṇṭaka— (102)

One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with equal parts of the pastes (*kalka*) of *kaṭukā*, *rohiṇī*, *kṛṣṇā*, the fruits of *kāśmarya*, as well as *rāsnā*, *kṣuraka*, *gandharvā*, *vṛddhadāra*, *ghana*, and *utpala*. (103)
An equal amount of *dhātrī* juice should be given, combined with three parts water (104).
Once it is known to be properly prepared, it is recommended for both food and drink,
as well as for disorders arising from an excess of *doṣas* that have become aggravated along with *vātarakta* (105).

In this most dreadful case of *āmavāta*, the thighs, calves, and knees are both swollen and deep-seated, with the head of the patient resembling that of a jackal and the roots of the limbs greatly enlarged;
for one afflicted by this burning disease, the pain is exceedingly difficult to overcome. (106)
It quickly destroys all these— dysuria, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), urinary disorders (prameha), and irregular fevers— whether they arise from vāta, pitta, or kapha;
by its use at all times, it increases complexion, longevity, and strength.
This most excellent and unsurpassed ghee was prepared by the Aśvins;
it is cooked with the fresh juice of guḍūcī, the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs, and four times as much milk, along with their pastes, and it cures hemorrhaging. 108–109.
Having obtained one hundred parts of *amṛtā*, one should boil them in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth; then,
the wise physician should add a *prastha* of ghee and four times as much milk and cook it together.
And here I shall describe the medicinal paste (kalka) in its proper order:
kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, śatāvarī, payasyā, madhuka, and blue lotus (nīlotpala). 111–112.
One should collect the roots of aśvakanda, or sthirā, kaṭurohiṇī,
ṛddhi, vṛddhi, as well as the two types of medā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, the two types of bṛhatī,
guḍūcī, pippalī, rāsnā, and vāsaka.
One should cook that [mixture] in equal portions over a gentle fire;
it should be administered for drinking, massage,
nasal drops, and as a wash for vātarakta accompanied by wasting, burning sensations, and kroṣṭuśīrṣaka.
When administered, this clarified butter destroys lameness, stiffness of the thighs, wind-disease (vāta), and most severe vātarakta;
it also cures the many types of urinary distress caused by wind, sciatica (gṛdhrasī), and "wind-thorns" (vātakaṇṭaka), according to the word of Dhanvantari. (116–117)

One should prepare each of these oils— of *śatapuṣpā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *madhuka*— with a decoction [of the respective herbs] to alleviate the pain of *vātarakta*. [An oil may also be prepared] with the alkaline water derived from the ashes of *sārivā*, *ariṣṭa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, and *potakī*.
An excellent physician should cook sesame oil with *guḍūcī*, cow’s milk, and the juice of *karmaraṅga*, adding these [other] ingredients:
the two *kākolīs*, *jīvaka*, the two *medās*, *śatāhvā*, and *akṣīriṇī*. 119–120.
With *jiṅgī*, beeswax, *amṛtā*, *anantā*, *sarja*, rock salt, and sandalwood,
one may destroy terrible *vātāsra* (blood disorders caused by wind), as well as cracked and oozing skin conditions, those known as *carmadala*, *pāmā* and other skin diseases, and *vipādikā*. 121

This great Piṇḍataila is renowned for its power to overcome leprosy, hemorrhoids, erysipelas, ulcerative swellings, and fistula-in-ano; there is no disorder of vātarakta that, once aggravated, it cannot swiftly destroy.
Oil cooked with sārivā, sarja, mañjiṣṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and beeswax, combined with milk,
should be applied; or else, oil known as piṇḍataila, prepared with sārivā, sarja, yaṣṭīmadhu, honey, and beeswax, combined with milk, should be used for vātaśoṇita.
Castor oil produced from *Eraṇḍa* seeds is proven to cure the pain of *vātarakta*;

this is achieved through the application of this "lump-oil" (*piṇḍataila*) made from unrefined, churned [castor] oil, combined with the filaments of the lotus, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *phenila*, and the red and blue lotuses. 125.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with equal parts of *sauvīra* (sour gruel) and water, adding five *palas* each of *balā*, *kiṃśuka*, and *candana*.
To this, one should add *lodhra*, *kākolī*, *uśīra*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *keśara*. (126–127)
With leaves of the *madayantī* creeper, lotus filaments, *padmaka*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kālīya*, *medā*, *māṃsī*, and *priyaṅgu*;
with two *karṣas* each of saffron and one *pala* of *mañjiṣṭhā*. (128)

This Mahāpadma oil destroys wind-disorders, hemorrhaging, and fever. It is prepared by boiling a decoction of Padmaka, Uśīra, Yaṣṭyāhva, and Rajanī, along with a paste of Sarja, Mañjiṣṭhā, Vīrā, Kākoli, and Candana.
This is the *Khuḍḍākapadmaka* oil, which cures disorders of wind, blood, and bile.
One should boil one *tulā* of *guḍūcī* in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-quarter;
then, one should slowly cook one *āḍhaka* of oil with those two [decoctions] and one *droṇa* of milk.
The pastes are derived from madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and the group of jīvanīya drugs;
along with kuṣṭha, elā, aguru, mṛdvīkā, māṃsī, vyāghranakha, nakhī, hareṇu, śrāvaṇī, vyoṣa, śatāhvā, śṛṅgī, and sārivā. (133)
Cinnamon bark, cinnamon leaves, aguru, vikrāntā, and likewise sthirā and tāmalakī (134),
along with nata, keśara, hrībera, padmaka, utpala, and candana—
these, prepared in equal parts of one karṣa each, [are used] for drinking, massage, and oil enemas. (135)

It should be used for those afflicted by disorders of wind and blood located within the channels and the constituent elements (dhātus). It is auspicious, promotes virility, grants conception to women, and subdues wind and bile.
It cures sweating, itching, pain, stiffness, tremors of the head, and diseases caused by *ardita* (facial paralysis).
Excellent *guḍūcī* oil destroys the defects caused by wounds.

[One should prepare it with] *guḍūcī*, *madhuka*, the small five roots (*hrasvapañcamūla*), *punarnavā*, *rāsnā*, castor root, and the life-promoting (*jīvanīya*) drugs as they are available. (137–138)
There should be five hundred parts of *balā* for every hundred parts of the other roots;
one *āḍhaka* each of *kola*, *bilva*, barley, *māṣa*, and *kulattha*; and one *droṇa* of dried *kāśmarya* fruits, all to be boiled in one hundred *droṇas* of water. (139)
One should prepare a jarred, purified *droṇa* of oil and set aside four *droṇas* of water;
then one should cook that *droṇa* of oil by adding five times as much milk (*pañcaguṇaṃ payaḥ*), having ground together three *palas* each of sandalwood, *uśīra*, and *keśara*. (140–141)
Patra, elā, aguru, kuṣṭha, tagara, madhuyaṣṭikā, and half a pala of mañjiṣṭhā—this [mixture] when prepared is effective for all [conditions]:
in vātarakta, wounds, emaciation, exhaustion from heavy loads, and diminished semen. (142)

This foremost oil, called Amṛta, destroys trembling, dislocations, fractures, and diseases arising from all parts of the body; it also cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, epilepsy, insanity, and irregular fevers, and acts as a promoter of virility. 143–144.
With lotus stalks, blue lotuses, lotus roots, sārivā, udīcya, and keśara;
with the two types of sandalwood, bhūnimba, lotus seeds, and kaseruka (145); and with paṭola, kaṭukā, anantā, gundrā, parpaṭa, and vāsaka.
Having ground [the herbs] with oil or cooked ghee with the juice of *tṛṇamūla*,
combined with double the amount of milk, this— when employed in enema treatments (*vastikarma*), or through nasal drops, massage, or as a drink— destroys diseases of *pitta*. (146–147)

Oil of sesame seeds boiled according to the prescribed method with the powder of *sarja* resin mixed with flower-salt (*kusumalavaṇa*) in water prepared by boiling gold-peak (*kanakaśikhari*) salt, destroys even the most abundant cases of *indralupta*, *asravāta*, and *vāta*. One should boil one *tulā* of pure *nāgabalā* in a *droṇa* of water until a quarter-remnant decoction is obtained. 148.

Having drained [the ulcer], one should administer one *āḍhaka* of oil mixed with goat's milk; having added five *palas* each of the pastes of *nata* and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, it is cooked. Indeed, when administered as an enema (*vasti*), this pacifies even severe *vātarakta* within seven nights.
This excellent oil, when drunk as prescribed by the Aśvins, makes one free from disease within ten days (verse 150).
Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, the two types of Medā, Ṛṣyaproktā, Śatāvarī, Madhuka, Madhuparṇī, and the two types of Kākolī (verse 151).
One should prepare a paste (kalka) and a decoction (kaṣāya) from mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, daśamūla, punarnavā,
balā, amṛtā, vidārī, aśvagandhā, and aśmabheda;
with these two, one should cook oil or ghee.
Fatty tissue, marrow, and meat from pecking and scratching birds,
prepared with four times the amount of milk, cure vātaśoṇita (gout) and destroy all severe diseases localized throughout the body that are born of vāta. 153–154.

Oil prepared with the decoction and paste of *balā*, with four times the amount of milk, and cooked a hundred times, becomes a remedy for *vātāsṛj* (hemorrhagic disorders) and for *vāta-pitta*. It is auspicious, promotes virility, and increases the semen of men. 155.
This [oil] destroys disorders of the semen and the female reproductive tract, and it cures disorders of Vāta.
One hundred palas of Madhuyaṣṭī, reduced to a quarter in a decoction, should be cooked with one āḍhaka of oil and an equal amount of milk, along with pastes (kalka) measuring one pala each. 156–157.
With śatapuṣpā, varī, mūrvā, payasyā, aguru, and candana;
with sthirā, haṃsapadī, māṃsī, the two types of medā, and madhuparṇī; and with kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, tāmalakī, ṛddhi, and padmaka. (158)
With jīvaka, ṛṣabha, jīvantī, tvak, patra, nakha, and bālaka;
with prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, indu, and vitunnaka—this [decoction] destroys wind-blood disorders, burning sensations, pain, and fever, and it promotes strength and complexion. (159–160)
Having ground one *pala* of *madhuyaṣṭī*, one should cook it with one *prastha* of oil in four times as much milk for one hundred times; that same [oil], when combined with *madhuka*,
should be administered once prepared to cure the three *doṣas*, as well as *vātāsra*, asthma, and cough.
This is auspicious, promotes virility, and destroys diseases such as jaundice and burning sensations.
One should cook oil equal in quantity to milk with the decoction and paste of *balā*;
having processed it a hundred or a thousand times, it cures Vata-blood disorders and Vata diseases.
This is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), clarifying the sense organs,
life-prolonging, nourishing, beneficial for the voice, and a destroyer of defects in the semen and blood.
One should employ one hundred roots of *punarnavā* and likewise purified roots of *ruvūka*.
Having added sixteen palas of ginger and thoroughly crushed it, one should properly cook it in a jar with sixteen hundred and fifty (165) palas of water; then,
when eight hundred palas remain, one should again cook it with one kuḍava of castor oil and five palas of powdered trivṛt.

One *pala* of *nikumbha* powder, two *palas* of *guḍūcī*, and half a *pala* or one *pala* or three *palas* [of other ingredients]; likewise, one *karṣa* each of *yūṣaṇa*, *citraka*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *bhallātaka*, and *viḍaṅga*; as well as one *karṣa* of honey-ore (*mākṣikadhātu*) powder and one *pala* of *punarnavā* powder.
Having administered the powders and allowed them to cool, a person should consume one *karṣa* measure;

this will certainly conquer the seven types of *vātāsṛj* (blood disorders), as well as *vṛddhi*, *gṛdhrasī*, and the ailments arising from the calves, thighs, back, the sacrum (*trika*), and the bladder, and likewise destroys powerful *āmavāta*. 168–169.

Take one karṣa each of yāvaśūka, suradāru, saindhava, mustaka, truṭi, vacā, yavānikā, vyoṣa, dīpyaka, niśā, triphalā, the two types of jīraka, viḍaṅga, and citraka; these should be well-ground, properly mixed, and combined with five palas of honey. (170)
One should grind sugar finely to the consistency of flour and then cast it into hot clarified butter (sarpiḥ).

This [preparation] cures vātarakta, abdominal enlargement (udara), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), splenic disorders, consumption (yakṣma), intermittent fever (viṣamajvara), artificial poison (gara), leucoderma (śvitra), all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), all wounds (vraṇa), and even severe mental disturbances (cittavibhrama). 171–172.

It destroys sciatica, hemorrhoids, and weakness of the digestive fire, as well as great diseases arising in the internal organs, just as a thunderbolt fallen from Indra’s hand swiftly crushes a multitude of excellent hidden mountains.
It is free from the need for dietary restrictions or avoidance of certain foods and drinks, providing happiness at all times and being entirely harmless. (173)

This elixir (*rasāyana*) consisting of pills of *guggulu* prepared by the Aśvins should indeed be consumed. (174) Four *māṣaka*s are prescribed for those with weak constitutions, eight *māṣaka*s for those of middling constitution, and twelve *māṣaka*s for those of superior constitution; one should administer it after having ascertained the patient's digestive capacity (*koṣṭha*). (175)
Due to its tendency to crumble or its heaviness, the method of preparation for guggulu is as follows:
one *prastha* of *guḍūcī*, half a *prastha* of guggulu, and one should specify the same measure for each of the three fruits (*triphalā*). 176.
Having crushed everything together, the physician should boil it in water that is not salty until one-fourth remains; having strained the decoction,
he should cause it to be collected and then cook it again until it reaches a thick consistency.
One should take half a pala each of the powder of dantī, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, guḍūcī, and the bark of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
and one karṣa of trivṛt; all of this should be ground together into a single powder.
Having ascertained that it is well-cooked, the wise person should add it while it is still lukewarm (verse 180).
Then, considering the strength of one's digestive fire, one should consume it in a dose of one karṣa;
this cures vātarakta, leprosy, hemorrhoids, and loss of appetite (verse 181).
It cures malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism (āmavāta), fistula-in-ano, sinus ulcers, excessive flatulence, and swelling— it dispels all of these.
[One should take] three prasthas of amṛtā and one prastha of guggulu.
One *prastha* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and one *prastha* of *varṣābhū* should be gathered together and boiled in non-saline water;
it should be cooked again until reduced to a quarter part and reached a thick consistency.

Half a pala each of the roots of dantī and citraka, kaṇā, viśva, and the three fruits (triphalā), as well as guḍūcī bark and viḍaṅga, are prescribed; one karṣa of trivṛt should be added, and all of this should be powdered together. 185.
Once it has been prepared and has become warm, one should add the supreme *amṛtā-guggulu* to it.
Then, especially one suffering from *amlapitta*, should eat it according to their strength;
it likewise cures *vātarakta*, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids, and the loss of digestive fire.

It destroys malignant ulcers, urinary disorders (prameha), rheumatism (āmavāta), fistula-in-ano, sinus ulcers, excessive flatulence, and edema; likewise, it cures all diseases. This Guggulu, known as Amṛta, was indeed prepared by the two Aśvins. 188–189.
One *prastha* [of mercury] processed with sixteen *palas* each of jaggery, asafoetida, ginger, meat, pumpkin, *guḍūcī*,
and *guggulu* becomes unctuous, resembling gold in luster, and like the fruit of the ripe jambū tree.
That which is fragrant and slimy is declared to be fresh guggulu; however,
that which is dry, foul-smelling, and has undergone a change in color should be known as old, and it must not be given to a patient.
Kṛmiripu, dahanavyoṣa, triphalā, amaradāru, cavya, bhūnimba, the root of māgadhī, musta, śaṭī, vacā, dhātu-mākṣika,
as well as the salts, kṣāra, niśā, yu, kustumburu, gajakaṇā, and ativiṣā— [these are the ingredients]. 193.
One should prepare equal parts of each weighing one *karṣa*; one should add eight *palas* of mineral pitch (*aśmajatu*).
The wise physician should likewise add two *palas* of purified leafless mercury (*pura*) and two *palas* of iron filings.
To this, four *palas* of sugar and one *pala* of *vāṃśī*, combined with *nikumbha*, *kumbha*, and the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), should be added. 194.
One should then add one pala each of the powders; this pill, known as Candraprabhā, should be prepared.

It completely destroys the six types of fever, diarrhea, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and hemorrhoids; it also cures fistula-in-ano, jaundice, anemia, and restores the digestive fire of those with impaired digestion to its brilliance. (195–196)

It destroys diseases arising from pitta, kapha, and vāta; it should be employed in cases of sinus ulcers, wounds in vital spots (marmas), chest injuries with wasting, sciatica, consumption, urinary disorders, and severe elephantiasis (gajaprameha).
It is also used for seminal depletion, urinary stones, dysuria, spermatorrhea, and abdominal diseases.

Having worshipped Śambhu and obtained his grace, the pill praised by Candramas was acquired. (198) There is no restriction regarding food or drink, nor regarding cold, wind, heat, or sexual intercourse;
this medicine should always be administered first, followed by a draught of buttermilk or a drink of whey. (199)
The meat-juice of a goat or the juice of wild animals, followed by a drink of cold water, destroys the eight types of seminal disorders as well as the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha).
Freed from wrinkles and graying hair, even an old man becomes like a youth. (200–201)

Then, having combined girija, guggulu, and lauha, one should repeatedly saturate them with decoctions that alleviate those specific diseases; subsequently, the powder should be mixed with the powders of kṛmighna and other such drugs, and taken with a soup of māṣa and paṭola. 202

Having cast one *prastha* of *guggulu*, whose color resembles the interior of the eye of a noble buffalo, into a mass of water, thirty-two *palas* of *triphalā* should also be added with care according to the prescribed measure.
203. Thirty-two *palas* of *chinnaruhā* should be given with diligence.
Being vigilant, one should stir it with a ladle repeatedly until half the water has been consumed through contact with the fire; then,
having removed it and strained it through a cloth, one should once again prepare it in an iron vessel.
When that [mixture] has become thick, one should add half a pala of triphalā powder, six akṣas of trikaṭu powder,
half a pala of kṛmiripu (viḍaṅga) powder, and one karṣa each of trivṛt and dantī.

Having carefully powdered one *pala* of *guḍūcī* and administered it, one should take as an after-drink (*anupāna*) either vegetable broth, milk, or fragrant water; having consumed this medicine at all times, one may follow one's desires regarding food and lifestyle. (207–208)
Even if it is slight, or if the wind (vāta) and blood (śoṇita) are aggravated one, two, or threefold; even if it has arisen long ago,
or is broken, leaking, dried up, cracked, or split open as far as the knee—
it quickly destroys ulcers, cough, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal tumors (gulma), edema (śvayathu), as well as poisoning, anemia (pāṇḍu), and urinary disorders (meha).

It quickly destroys weak digestion, constipation, and urinary disorders (prameha) as well as carbuncles (piḍakā). When consumed constantly, it overcomes all diseases by the power of time, destroys the defects of old age, and produces a youthful appearance.
One *prastha* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and one *āḍhaka* each of water [should be used];
the cooking of *guggulu* should be performed specifically like that of jaggery (*guḍa*).
[The decoction is prepared] with *triphalā*, *ativiṣā*, *dāru*, *dārvī*, *mustā*, and *aparuṣaka*.
Having prepared a decoction from equal parts of khadirāsana, naktāhva, guḍūcī, nṛpapādapa, bhūnimba, nimba, kaṭukā, kaliṅga,
and kulaka, one should then strain it after it has been boiled in eight times its quantity of water.

Having placed well-prepared powder of *guḍūcī*— half [the quantity]— into water in a brand-new vessel, one should let it sit for seven nights; then, with that pure liquid mixed with *soma*, one should saturate the *kauśika*.
For seven days, the wise physician should mix [the powder] with six jujube fruits and śilājatu; then, having added eight palas of fermented gruel (śukta),
one pala of powdered tāpya, and two palas each of honey and ghee.
Having combined all these together in equal parts, one should lick them with a thin decoction of triphalā, or with mung bean soup, or with the meat broth of wild animals.
When that has been digested—or even while it is still undigested—one should eat old śāli rice or ṣaṣṭika rice. (218–219)
Prepared with juices and soups according to the specific disease and what is wholesome for the patient, this [formula],
when administered for three weeks, swiftly destroys even the most severe vātarakta by its potency, as well as skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and ulcers.
Indeed, the guggulu known as Triphalā heals what is severed and what is split.
Three palas of finely powdered Triphalā decoction, one pala of Saugandhika, and three palas of Kauśika [are to be used]. 221–222.
Taking one *kuḍava* of each of these ingredients along with the *citrataila*,
a physician skilled in the art of cooking should carefully cook it in a sturdy iron vessel. This [oil] destroys wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), lameness, and paraplegia.

It destroys breathlessness that is very difficult to conquer, as well as the five types of cough, skin diseases, vātarakta, gulma, colic, abdominal enlargements, and even rheumatism (āmavāta) that has been neglected by physicians. 225
By its constant use, it destroys old age and graying hair;
one should eat śāli rice and ṣaṣṭika rice combined with ghee, oil, and meat broth.
This is known as Siṃhanāda, which destroys the pride of the elephants of disease.
This [preparation], which bestows brilliance upon people like that of fire, was spoken by Daṇḍapāṇi.

Regarding this, they say that a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā), each weighing three palas, should be used; when a small amount of castor oil (eraṇḍa-sneha) has been added, the cooking is complete, for it becomes hard when too much is used. 227–228.

Having added eight *palas* of *palaṅkaṣā* and one *prastha* each of the three purified fruits (*phalatraya*), the physician should cook [the mixture] in two *droṇas* of water until reduced to one-fourth; then, he should again add *dantī*,
*trivṛt*, *tryūṣaṇa*, *vāruṇī*, *biḍaṅga*, *mustā*, *triphalā*, and *amṛtā*.

One should add half a *pala* measure of well-ground powder of *kaṭu*, *ugragandha*, *āluka*, *māṇaka*, along with *gandhaka* and *pārada*; then, having again cooked it, one should subsequently add the fruits, numbering one thousand, ground into a fine powder. 230–231.

One should eat two heated masha beans; thereafter, water and other liquids should be given as a post-drink (anupāna) for the pacification of undigested matter (āma), wind (vāta) located in the joints, pain in the head, and ailments situated in the knees and waist.
It also cures severe hemorrhoids (arśas), the affliction of irregular fever (viṣamajvara), urinary disorders (prameha), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara). 232.
Thinking "it shall slay the diseases of men," this lion's roar [of Takra] first destroys disorders of fat, blood, and phlegm.
If there is no excessive burning, excessive discharge, or any other great complication caused by it,
then in that case, rice with buttermilk (takrabhakta) is beneficial.

Since Siṃhanāda is wise, he should perform dry massage, bathing with cold water, and likewise lying down; having ascertained the strength of the body, the physician should administer strong purgation, or else not do so at all. (234–235)

The fruit known as *kānaka* is purified by being cooked sequentially in water, sour gruel, and cow’s milk; then, having made it into a powder, one should add a *mānī* of solidified *guggulu* resin to eight *palas* of pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*). 236.

One should boil one *prastha* of each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) in one and a half *droṇas* of water; when reduced to one-fourth and well-strained, it should be placed back on the fire with *trikaṭu*,
*triphalā*, *mustā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *āmalaka*.
One part each of *guḍūcī*, *agni*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *vacā*, *sūraṇa*, and *mānaka*, along with one part each of musk, mercury, and lead, measured at the size of a shell (*śukti*),
and one thousand *kānaka* fruits— these should be powdered and added once the preparation is complete. 239.
Then, having eaten two *māṣa* beans, one should drink hot water or similar liquids;
this quickly produces a digestive fire resembling the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), as well as an increase in intellect, an increase in vitality, and very great strength. (240–241)
It cures rheumatism (āmavāta), headache, nodular arthritis (granthivāta), fistula-in-ano (bhagandara), wind disorders affecting the knees and calves, pain from stiffness in the waist,
urinary stones, dysuria, fractures, cataracts, and abdominal diseases. 242.
It cures acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (prameha), prolapse of the rectum,
the five types of cough, asthma, consumption (kṣaya), irregular fever (viṣamajvara),
splenic enlargement, elephantiasis (ślīpada), abdominal tumors (gulma), and anemia with jaundice (pāṇḍuroga-sakāmala).

This formulation, known as Siṃhanāda and comparable to nectar, destroys swelling, intestinal hernia, colic, and hemorrhoids; it shatters the pride of diseases born of fat, phlegm, and undigested matter. (245)
When a disease is beyond the reach of physicians, Daṇḍapāṇi has prescribed [the following]:
śatāvarī, nāgabalā, vṛddhadāraka, uccaṭā, punarnavā, amṛtā, kṛṣṇā, vājigandhā, and trikaṇṭaka. (246–247)
One should have ten *pala* each of these made into a fine powder;
the wise man should then mix that powder with half as much sugar and knead it together.
He should place it in a very strong vessel, combined with half an *āḍhaka* of honey.
Having stirred it with one *prastha* of clarified butter and three *palas* of the "three aromatics" (*trisugandha*),
a person should eat that along with desired foods and grains according to the strength of their digestive fire;
this cures *vātarakta*, consumption (*kṣaya*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), emaciation, and disorders arising from blood and bile (*pittāsra*).
Having destroyed diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as other ailments caused by them,
it swiftly destroys all maladies and makes a person free from wrinkles and graying hair, adorned with intelligence and memory. (251)
It makes a man fortunate and grants him a lifespan of five hundred years.
This [practice] named *Yogasārāmṛta* increases fortune and fame.
One should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, anger, and tastes that are hot, sour, or salty.
One should avoid daytime sleep, which causes secretions, as well as other heavy foods. 254 Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Section on Vatarakta. 29.
Now begins the Middle Section.
The third part:
Now, the thirtieth chapter on colic (śūla).
Colic is of eight types, arising from the humors (doṣas) individually, collectively, or in pairs.
In all these types of colic (śūla), Vāta is generally the predominant factor [1].

It is provoked by physical exertion, fasting, excessive sexual intercourse, staying awake at night, drinking cold water in excess, eating peas, mung beans, *āḍhakī*, and *kōradūṣaka*, as well as by excessively dry food, overeating, and injury [2].
Due to astringent, bitter, and excessively indigestible foods, incompatible foods, dried meat, and dried vegetables;

due to the suppression of feces, semen, urine, and flatus; and due to grief, fasting, and excessive laughing or talking—the Vāyu (wind), thus aggravated, produces colic (śūla) in the regions of the heart, back, sides, sacrum, and bladder.
In old age, during the onset of night, at the arrival of the rainy season, and in the cold, it becomes intensely aggravated (verse 4).
Its aggravation and subsidence occur repeatedly through the retention and piercing pain of feces and urine;
it finds relief through fomentation, oil massage, rubbing, and the consumption of unctuous and warm foods (verse 5).
But when vāta, obstructed by kapha and pitta and increased by rasa, resides in the heart, it produces a pain that obstructs the breath;
this is known as *hṛcchūla* (heart-pain), arising from the provocation of rasa and vāta. 6.
The wind (vāyu), having suppressed the phlegm (kapha) and piercing as if with needles,
causes pain in the sides accompanied by distension;
because of this, the person breathes through the mouth and has no desire for food.
One cannot even obtain sleep; this is proclaimed as pārśvaśūla (flank pain).
Due to suppression, the aggravated vāyu takes refuge in the bladder and remains there;
consequently, pain arises for him in the channels along the path of the bladder.
The obstruction of feces, urine, and flatus is called *bastiśūla* (bladder pain).
It is caused by alkaline substances, excessively sharp or hot foods, burning oils, *niṣpāva* beans, oil-cakes, and soups of *kulattha* lentils;
as well as by pungent and sour items, fermented grain-liquors (*sauvīra*), various types of wine, anger, fire, physical exertion, and the heat of the sun.

Due to excessive consumption of village (cooked) foods that have been improperly digested, the *pitta* becomes aggravated and then produces colic (*śūla*) at the navel, accompanied by thirst, delusion, burning sensations, pain, perspiration, fainting, giddiness, and emaciation;
it flares up at midday, at midnight, during the summer season, and at the end of the rainy season. 12.
In cold weather, it finds relief through cold things and even through very sweet and cool foods (13).
When *śleṣman* (phlegm) becomes aggravated by marshy water products, *kilāṭa*, milk preparations, meats, sugarcane, flour-based foods, *kṛśarā*, sesame cakes,
and other causes that generate *balāsa*, it produces colic (14).

One should recognize a pain born of two doṣas by these signs of two doṣas: nausea, cough, malaise, anorexia, excessive salivation, heaviness in the stomach, a sense of stagnation in the abdomen, and heaviness of the head; it causes extreme pain whenever food is eaten, and especially at sunrise, during the cold season, and at the arrival of spring. (15-16)

A physician should recognize that colic (*śūla*) occurs in all regions of the body and arises from all [doshas]; indeed, those who know the truth declare this extremely painful condition, which is like poison or a thunderbolt, to be something to be avoided.
It is accompanied by flatulence, nausea, vomiting, heaviness, a sense of being wrapped in wet cloth, abdominal distension, and excessive salivation due to kapha.
They describe colic arising from phlegm as having symptoms identical to those of phlegm itself (18).
They say that when it is of the nature of wind, it is located in the bladder; they also say that when of the nature of bile, it is in the navel;
when associated with phlegm, it is in the heart, the sides, and the abdomen; and when from the combination of all three (sannipāta), it occurs in all regions (19).
That colic located in the buttocks, heart, and flanks is caused by kapha and vāta;
that colic in the abdomen, between the heart and the navel, is caused by kapha and pitta;
and the terrible one that causes burning fever should be known as caused by vāta and pitta. 20.
When food is eaten in excess, the digestive fire becomes weak; the wind, having enveloped that food which has been made stagnant in the stomach, remains there.
When the food has not reached digestion, it causes intense colic pain.

The wise call this colic arising from indigestion (avipāka-ja-śūla), which produces fainting, flatulence, burning sensations, distress in the heart accompanied by nausea, trembling, vomiting, diarrhea, and even delusion. 22–23.

Thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness, loss of appetite, cough, dyspnea, vomiting, and hiccups are known as the secondary complications (upadravas) of colic (śūla). [Verse 24] That caused by a single doṣa is curable; that born from two doṣas is difficult to cure.
Accompanied by all the [dosic] defects, it is terrible, incurable, and characterized by many complications (25). There is pain, excessive thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness, fever (26),
vertigo, loss of appetite, emaciation, and likewise a loss of strength.
These ten are indeed the complications; he in whom they do not exist [is healthy].
When the powerful Vata, aggravated by its own causes and situated nearby, envelops Kapha and Pitta, it becomes the cause of pain (shula).
The pain that occurs when food is being digested is precisely that which arises from the process of transformation (pariṇāmaja).
Its symptoms are also stated here in brief: flatulence, abdominal distension, obstruction of feces and urine, aversion to food, and trembling. (28–29)
The physician should declare that [pain] characterized by oiliness, heat, and predominance of subsidence is of the Vata type;

the wise one should recognize that which is accompanied by thirst, burning, restlessness, sweating, and an excess of pungent, sour, and salty [tastes], and which is primarily relieved by cold, as being of the Pitta type.
Vomiting accompanied by nausea, delusion, slight pain, a long duration, and relief from pungent and bitter tastes should be known as being of the nature of *kapha*.
Having recognized the combined symptoms, one should determine it to be caused by two *doṣas*.
That which arises from the three doṣas is incurable, as is that in one whose muscle, strength, and digestive fire are depleted (33).
Furthermore, that colic which arises when food has been digested or while it is being digested—
whether through the use of wholesome or unwholesome items, or by means of eating or fasting— [is incurable].
If it does not subside through restrictive measures, that condition is described as *annadrava* (liquid-like food).
For the alleviation of colic pain (*śūla*), emesis, fasting, sudation, digestive remedies, fruit-suppositories, alkalis, powders, and pills are recommended. (34–35)
Having diagnosed wind-pain (vāta-śūla), one should treat it with oleation and sudation;
for one afflicted by mild pain, sudation alone is most beneficial.
One should take moist clay that has become thickened through baking and spread it upon a cloth.
Having made that into a poultice (poṭṭala), one suffering from a piercing pain (śūlī) should apply it according to the degree of sweating required.

Or, one may use cotton seeds, horse gram (kulattha), sesame, barley, castor root, linseed (atasī), common sorrel (varṣābhū), and hemp seeds (śaṇabīja), combined with sour gruel (kāñjika), either mixed together or used separately. (37–38)
There may be perspiration, and then pain in the elbows, abdomen, head, buttocks, knees, toes, ankles, shoulders, and waist; this [remedy] conquers all afflictions of wind (vāta) without exception.
(38) Having made a pill with sesame seeds, one should rotate it over the stomach. (39)
By that [application], even a most difficult-to-cross colic (śūla) quickly attains pacification;
one should conquer colic by applying a paste of *madana* mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjikā*).
Having boiled water with *viśva* and the root of *eraṇḍa*, one should drink it. 40.
Combined with asafoetida and sauvarcala salt, this immediately relieves colic (41).
For a man afflicted by colic, sudation alone is most beneficial,
whether performed with milk-porridge, kṛśara-gruel, boluses, or moist piles of meat (42).

A soup of *kulattha* beans combined with oil, rock salt (*saindhava*), and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), along with meat of the common quail (*lāva*), enriched with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), and pomegranate, quickly destroys colic caused by wind (*vātātmaka*).
[43] [This is prepared from] *balā*, *punarnavā*, castor root (*eraṇḍa*), the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *gokṣura*.
Combined with asafoetida and salt, this [preparation] immediately cures diseases caused by Vāta.
(44) One suffering from colic, abdominal tumors, or hiccups should drink Tumburu, Abhayā, asafoetida, Pauṣkara, and the three salts with warm water. (45)
Yavānī, hiṅgu, sindhūttha, kṣāra, sauvarcala, and abhayā should be drunk with the scum of surā; these destroy the pain caused by vāta.
[This is done] with sauvarcala, āmlīkā, jīraka, and marica, each subsequent one being double the quantity of the preceding.
Having ground [the root] with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, a pill is formed that cures wind-pain (*vāta-śūla*).
One should also cause the patient to drink the root of *bījapūraka* together with ghee, in a measure of one *karṣa*; this conquers pain born of wind. 47–48.
Jaggery, śāli rice, yava-kṣāra, drinking ghee, purgatives, and the meat of wild animals are the remedies for those suffering from pitta-type colic (pitta-śūla).
Vessels made of gems, silver, and copper, as well as heavy ones, [are beneficial]. 49.
One should hold vessels filled with water above the trident.
Purgatives that remove bile are recommended, as are the juices of rabbits and quails;
or one may eat *harītakī* combined with jaggery and ghee.
For the sake of pacifying colic, one should lick powdered *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with honey.
One should employ boiled *śāli* rice, meat of wild animals, *ariṣṭa*, pungent broths,
and aged wheat along with honey in cases of colic caused by *kapha*.
The three salts combined with the five spices (pañcakola) and asafoetida,
when drunk with lukewarm water, destroy phlegm-induced colic (kapha-śūla).
In cases of colic caused by undigested matter (āma-śūla), the treatment that destroys phlegm-induced colic should be administered.
When consumed, it removes everything and increases even a weak digestive fire (agni). 54.
The excellent powder of triphalā combined with the powder of tīkṣṇā should be administered with honey and ghee; it is a remedy that wards off all types of colic pain (śūla). 55.
One should apply a lukewarm plaster, ground with sour liquids, consisting of dāru, haimavatī, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, hiṅgu, and saindhava, to the abdomen afflicted with colic.
Likewise, one may use the roots of bailva, eraṇḍa, citraka, and viśvabheṣaja.
Combined with asafoetida and rock salt, this immediately relieves colic.
Having sliced the pumpkin into thin pieces, one should dry them in the heat;
then, placing them all in a pot and covering it with a lid, [one should cook it]. 57–58.
A skillful person, having placed the fire in the crucible, should kindle it in such a way that it does not become ash, but rather becomes a firm charcoal;
then, once it has cooled, one should completely pulverize it. 59.
A man afflicted by severe colic should daily consume two māṣas of this [powder] mixed with powdered dry ginger and water;
even that colic which is incurable is pacified by this.
One should first perform fasting, followed by emesis and purgation for the purpose of pacifying colic in the digestive tract; therein, the procedure for emesis is as follows:
having drunk milk mixed with a decoction of Madana up to the throat.

A wise person afflicted by colic pain of digestion (pakti-śūla) should vomit, according to the prescribed method, the juice of *kāntāraka*, *pauṇḍra*, or *kośakāra* (63), or else a decoction of neem (*nimba*), or the juice of bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*). (64)
Likewise, a purgative administered with trivṛt or dantī, or with castor oil,
immediately relieves the pain of indigestion (pakti-śūla).
[A formulation consisting of] viḍaṅga seeds, taṇḍula, vyoṣa, trivṛt, dantī, and citraka—
Having combined all these together, one should have them made into fine powders (66).
Having prepared boluses with jaggery, one should eat them with warm water; this conquers colic born of the three doṣas and that arising from the transformation of food (pariṇāma-śūla) (67).
If a man should lick a paste made by grinding *nāgara* and sesame seeds with milk,
his severe post-digestive colic (*pariṇati-śūla*) will be destroyed within three nights. (68) Ash produced from a snail, when drunk with warm water, [cures it] instantly.
It surely destroys colic born of digestion (paktija), just as Viṣṇu destroyed the demons.
By licking the powder of iron, harītakī, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī with honey and ghee, one indeed overcomes colic arising from the digestive process (pariṇāmaja). 69–70.
A coconut filled with water and well-saturated with salt,
wrapped in clay, dried, and then baked in a fire of cow-dung,
when eaten with long pepper (pippalī), indeed destroys colic born of the digestive transformation (pariṇāma-śūla).
The colic known as *annadrava*— whether caused by wind (*vātika*), bile (*paittika*), phlegm (*ślaiṣmika*), or a combination of all three (*sānnipātika*)—
does not attain any measure of health until one vomits the liquid food that is pungent, bitter, sour, or acidic. (72–73)
In one who has just experienced the onset of chronic pitta (jaratpitta), it quickly destroys the colic;
having induced emesis to eliminate the pitta and purgation to eliminate the kapha, that which was prescribed for chronic pitta should be performed regarding food and liquids. 74.

That which is prescribed as wholesome for the liquid portion of food is also recommended in the case of chronic bile (jaratpitta), provided the stomachs for undigested matter (āma) and digested matter (pakva) have been purified; then the liquid portion of the food will attain pacification.
[One should take] a well-steamed bean-cake (māṣeṇḍarī), seasoned with salt and cooked in oil.
One afflicted by the suppression of food and wind should eat such [preparations] with clarified butter.
Alternatively, one should lick the powder made from *dhātrī* fruits combined with iron powder, or mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhu* powder, along with honey for that disease. 77–78.
Rice-pudding prepared with *śyāmāka* grains, prepared with *kodrava* grains,
or prepared with *priyaṅgu* grains, is beneficial when taken together;
one may also eat the bulbous roots of the *gauḍika* and *śauraṇa* varieties, as well as the *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
Kernels of peas, barley-meal, or meal made from parched grain;
or wheat-cakes there, combined with ghee and jaggery, along with sugar and cooled milk—these, whether softened, boiled, or stewed, are beneficial. (80–81)
The morbid thirst caused by food is a great disease that is difficult to treat and difficult to diagnose;
therefore, one should exert supreme effort in its pacification. (82) For in the case of morbid thirst caused by old bile, the digestive fire becomes weak.
Therefore, in this matter, one should cause food and drink to be prepared in the proper measure.
(83) Kalāya beans, barley, wheat, śyāmāka, koradūṣaka, rājamāṣa, mung beans, kulattha, kaṅgu, and śāli rice— (84)
Cow’s milk whose essence has been extracted as curd, well-refined cow’s ghee, vāstūka, kāravellī, and karkoṭaka fruits;
peacock, deer, rohita and other fish, and kapiñjala partridges. 85.
In this disease, the Teacher is considered the physician by the sages who act as healers.
(86) One pala each of powdered jaggery, āmalaka, and pathyā, and three palas of iron filings—this entire mixture [should be taken] with honey and ghee. (87)
Having thoroughly mixed it, one should consume it in a quantity of one *akṣa*;
at the beginning, middle, and end of a meal, it destroys the watery nature of food, chronic *pitta*, and most severe *amlapitta*.

One should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, wine, salt, pungent tastes, suppression of natural urges, grief, anger, and pulses, as these may cause colic arising from metabolic transformation (pariṇāma-śūla) that has persisted for a year.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter on colic (*śūla*), or alternatively, the chapter on the transformation of colic, colic from food, and bile disorders (*pitta*). 30. Now begins the thirty-first chapter on upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*) and abdominal distension (*ānāha*). 31. [The causes of *udāvarta* are: wind (*vāta*), feces, urine, yawning, tears, sneezing, belching, vomiting, and the sense organs.
From the suppression of hunger, thirst, respiration, and sleep, the condition known as udāvarta arises.
Just as a whirlpool is formed when wind moves upward, physicians call this disease udāvarta; in this condition, the Vāyu (wind) is the dominant factor.
From the suppression of wind (vāta), there may arise retention of flatus, urine, and feces, distension, exhaustion, pain in the abdomen,
and other diseases born of vāta;
likewise, flatulence, colic, cutting pain, constipation, and upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta).
Or else, feces may come out from the mouth when a person's urge to defecate is suppressed. When there is suppression of urine,
the symptoms are pain in the bladder and penis, difficulty in urination, headache, body curvature,
and a sense of constriction in the groins.
From the suppression of yawning, disorders of the neck, throat, and head arise due to the wind (*pavana*);
likewise, severe diseases of the eyes, nose, and mouth occur, along with ailments of the ears. Furthermore, for one who does not release tears born of joy or grief when they have arisen—
Heaviness of the head and intense pains, along with chronic catarrh (pīnasa), occur; likewise, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), headache, facial paralysis (ardita), hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka),
weakness of the sense organs, and suppression of sneezing result from the forcible retention of a sneeze.

When the force of eructation is suppressed, there occurs a sense of fullness in the throat and mouth, extreme pricking pain, gurgling sounds, or the cessation of the movement of wind; furthermore, disorders born of the wind (vāta) arise in the person.
Itching, urticaria, loss of appetite, freckles, swelling, anemia, and fever also manifest.
Skin diseases, nausea, erysipelas, and disorders arising from the suppression of vomiting;

swelling and pain in the bladder, anus, and scrotum, as well as urinary retention and the formation of seminal stones or their discharge—these various afflictions occur when semen is obstructed. (10–11)
From the suppression of hunger arise lethargy, aching of the limbs, loss of appetite, fatigue, and emaciation of the vision;
from the suppression of thirst arise dryness of the throat and mouth, obstruction of hearing, and pain in the heart.
Furthermore, for one who is exhausted, the suppression of breath may lead to heart disease, fainting, or even abdominal tumors (gulma).
Yawning, aching of the limbs, excessive heaviness of the eyes and head, sleeplessness, or even drowsiness [arise] from the suppression of sleep (15).
Furthermore, the Vāyu, aggravated by dry, astringent, pungent, and bitter foods, and moving through the digestive tract (koṣṭha), immediately causes Udāvarta (16).
It indeed causes the channels that carry flatus, urine, feces, tears, phlegm,
and semen to become obstructed and prevents the passage of feces.
Consequently, the patient suffers from pain in the heart and bladder, and is afflicted by nausea and exhaustion.
A person experiences difficulty in passing flatus, urine, and feces;
[he suffers from] dyspnea, cough, catarrh, burning sensations, delusion, thirst, fever,
vomiting, hiccup, diseases of the head, and disturbances of the mind and hearing.
One should also abandon the wise patient suffering from udāvarta who develops many other disorders born of vāta provocation,
who is afflicted by thirst and vomiting, who is emaciated, tormented by hair-like parasites (śūka),
and who vomits feces.

When undigested food (āma) or feces, having accumulated and become further obstructed by the deranged Vāyu, are discharged not according to their natural course, physicians designate this disorder as Ānāha.
When that Ānāha arises from the presence of Āma, thirst, coryza, and a burning sensation in the head occur.
In the case of [vitiated vāta] arising in the stomach (āmāśaya), there occurs pain, heaviness, stiffness of the heart, and suppression of eructations; 22.

Furthermore, when it arises in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), there is stiffness of the waist, back, feces, and urine, as well as pain, fainting, vomiting of stool, dyspnea, and the symptoms described for alasaka. 23.

In cases of upward movement of wind (udāvarta) arising from the suppression of downward wind (adhovāta), the drinking of unctuous substances (sneha-pāna) is considered beneficial, as well as sudation (sveda); likewise, suppositories (varti) and enemas (vasti) are regarded as beneficial.
However, in cases arising from the obstruction of feces (viḍ-vighāta), the treatment consists of breaking up the stool (viḍ-bhaṅga), dietary measures, and medicinal drugs.
Bathing with oil massage and immersion baths, as well as sudation and enemas, are considered beneficial.
In cases arising from the suppression of urine, one should drink milk mixed with water and *vacā*, or the fresh juice of *duḥsparśā*, or a decoction of *kakubha*. 25–26.

One should drink the seed of the *ervāru* gourd with water, either salted or combined with sugar, sugarcane juice, milk, *drākṣā*, or *yaṣṭīmadhu*; one should employ these in every way according to the procedure for dysuria and urinary calculi. (27)
In cases arising from yawning or physical trauma, one should employ oleation or sudation;
furthermore, one should apply other procedures that pacify the wind (vāyu). In cases arising from the obstruction of tears in the eyes, one should release the water from the eyes.

One should sleep comfortably in his presence and tell him pleasant stories (29). In the case of suppressed sneezing caused by injury, one should induce sneezing through strong odors, nasal drops, or exposure to the sun; furthermore, one should employ oleation and sudation therapies for that which is stuck. (30)
In the case of suppression of eructation, one should employ unctuous fumigation;
when vomiting is suppressed, emesis, fasting, and purgation are beneficial, as is massage with oil. (31)

Milk boiled with four times its quantity of water and prepared with substances that cleanse the bladder should be consumed until the water is entirely evaporated; beloved women should then delight the man who suffers from the upward movement of semen (śukrodāvartin) as he drinks it to his heart's content.
For that [condition], massage, immersion baths, wine, chicken, rice, milk, and sprouts are beneficial, as is sexual intercourse;
likewise, when it arises from the obstruction of hunger, unctuous, warm, and light food is recommended. 34.
One should consume food that is palatable, small in quantity, wholesome, and edible, as well as fragrant flowers that are fit for use.
When thirst has arisen, every cooling procedure is beneficial;
one should drink very little water, cooled with camphor, very slowly.
In cases of exhaustion and labored breathing, rest and rice cooked with milk are recommended (36).
When these arise from the suppression of the urge for sleep, one should drink milk mixed with sugar;
gentle massage, a comfortable bed, sleep, and pleasant stories are beneficial here (37).
One should insert into the anus a suppository made from asafoetida, honey, and rock salt ground together and smeared with ghee; this destroys udāvarta.
[Likewise, one may use] madana, long pepper, kuṣṭha, vacā, and white mustard seeds.
The fruit-candle (phalavarti) described here consists of sugar and milk.
A person should lick one *viḍālapadaka* (cat's paw) measure of the powder of one pala of sugar, one akṣa of trivṛt, and one karṣa of black pepper, mixed with honey, before a meal. 39–40.

This sweet powder known as Nārācaka, containing Savyoṣa, Pippalīmūla, Trivṛt, Dantī, and Citraka, should be administered by the wise in cases of hard stools and upward movement of wind (udāvarta); it is suitable for kings. 41.
Savyoṣapippalīmūla, Trivṛt, Dantī, and Citraka.
One should eat that powder mixed with jaggery upon rising in the morning.
This preparation, known as Guḍāṣṭaka, increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire; it cures upward-moving wind (udāvarta), splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, edema, and anemia.

Having boiled dried and fresh radish, *varṣābhū*, the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and the fruit of *kṛtamāla* in water, one should cook ghee with that decoction; when drunk, it quickly pacifies *udāvarta* entirely. 44
One should employ the therapeutic measures that cure udāvarta for cases of ānāha as well, since their causes and effects are identical; however, a specific distinction is now stated:
*trivṛt*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *harītakī* should be taken in two, four, and five parts respectively.
A pill equal in size to jaggery removes severe constipation.
A wick (varti) made from trikaṭu, rock salt, mustard seeds, soot, kuṣṭha, and madanaphala, cooked in honey or jaggery and fashioned by experts to the thickness of a thumb, [achieves the same]. 46–47.

This suppository, having visible results, when slowly inserted into the rectum after being smeared with ghee, pacifies constipation, abdominal diseases, and likewise gulma in the belly. Thus ends the thirty-first chapter on Udāvarta and Ānāha. 31.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter on Gulma (abdominal tumors/lumps).
When the vitiated *vāta* and other *doṣas* are excessively provoked by improper diet and lifestyle, they produce five types of *gulma*, appearing as knots within the abdominal cavity. (1)
He explains its fivefold nature:
it arises from the humors (doṣas) individually or from all of them combined when they are aggravated;
likewise, it also arises from blood in both men and women. 2.
A gulma may also arise from the menstrual blood (*ārtava*); that occurs in women.
Another type arises from blood (*asṛj*); that occurs in both men and women.
Its five locations are the sides, the heart, the navel, and the bladder.
A knot (granthi) situated between the heart and the navel, whether mobile or immobile,
circular and characterized by growth, is designated as *gulma*. [Its symptoms include] frequent eructation, constipation, a sense of satiety, intolerance [of food], and rumbling in the intestines.
Distension, flatulence, and pain from indigestion are said to be the signs of imminent gulma (abdominal tumors).
One should observe loss of appetite, difficulty in the passage of feces, urine, and flatus, intestinal gurgling,
abdominal distension, and upward movement of wind in all types of gulma.

Dry food and drink, irregular or excessive exertion, suppression of natural urges, affliction by grief, extreme depletion of the tissues, and fasting are the causes of *anila-gulma* (vata-type abdominal tumor).
It manifests as various changes in location, shape, and pain, as well as the retention of feces and flatus, and dryness of the throat and mouth.

A Gulma arising from Vāta produces a dusky-red complexion, cold fever, and pain in the heart, abdomen, flanks, limbs, and head (9). It becomes excessively aggravated when the food is digested and attains mildness after eating; furthermore, it is not relieved by dry, astringent, bitter, or pungent substances (10).
Bitter, sour, pungent, hot, burning, and dry substances; anger, excessive wine, exposure to the sun and fire;
undigested food (āma), injury, and vitiated blood—these are said to be the causes of Pittaja Gulma.
Fever, thirst, lassitude, discoloration of the limbs, severe pain, and a sensation that food is being digested even while eating [are its symptoms].
Perspiration, a burning sensation, and sensitivity to touch like that of an ulcer are the characteristics of a *gulma* arising from *pitta*.

Coldness, heaviness, unctuousness, lack of physical activity, over-satiation, and sleeping during the day are the causes of a *gulma* born of *kapha*; however, all these factors combined when vitiated cause a *gulma* of the *nicaya* (combined) type. 12–13.

Stiffness, cold fever, malaise of the limbs, nausea, cough, loss of appetite, and heaviness— whatever are the symptoms of kapha, these occur when a gulma is born from the provocation of kapha (verse 14).
One should designate the other three types of gulma as having mixed symptoms, for the purpose of determining the pharmaceutical preparation (verse 15).

One should designate as incurable a gulma born of the three doṣas that is characterized by great pain, enveloped in burning heat, hard and elevated like a stone, rapidly suppurating, and dreadful; it robs the strength of the mind, the body, and the digestive fire.
(16) A woman who has recently given birth, one who eats unwholesome food, or one who miscarries an immature fetus during her menses [is at risk].
For the Vāyu, having seized her blood, produces a Gulma that is painful and accompanied by a burning sensation (17).
Its symptoms are identical to those of the Pittaja type; however, learn another distinguishing feature:
it pulsates as a single mass rather than with the limbs, is slow to develop, is accompanied by pain, and possesses all the characteristics of pregnancy.
That blood-born gulma, occurring only in women, is treatable after the tenth month has passed.
When the gulma has gradually accumulated, occupying a vast space, become firmly rooted, bound by vessels, and elevated like a tortoise shell— 19.
Accompanied by weakness, anorexia, nausea, cough, vomiting, restlessness, fever, thirst, drowsiness, and coryza, that [fever] does not succeed in being cured (20).
Having seized [the patient] with fever and dyspnea, and being afflicted by vomiting and diarrhea—
Swelling in the heart, navel, hands, and feet draws away the patient suffering from gulma; moreover, dyspnea, colic, thirst, aversion to food, numbness of the glands,
and weakness arise as signs of death for one with gulma.

Indeed, purgation with castor oil mixed with milk and combined with *pathyā* is highly recommended for sudation and oleation in a gulma caused by the provocation of Vāta; likewise, an alkali derived from *ketaka* flowers combined with *svarjikā* and *kuṣṭha* [is beneficial]. 23.
One should pacify a gulma arising from vāta with oil cooked with turmeric (pīta).
For vāta-gulma, one should employ partridge, peacock, cock, krauñca, and varttaka birds, as well as ghee, śāli rice, and prasannā wine.

In cases of *pitta*-type gulma, one should drink the powder of *trivṛt* with *triphalā* water for purgation; or alternatively, *kampilla* mixed with sugar or honey. A patient suffering from *pitta*-gulma should eat *abhayā* with *drākṣā* or with jaggery (*guḍa*).
One should treat *śleṣmagulma* (kapha-type abdominal tumor) with the same medicinal formulations prescribed for *vātagulma* (vata-type abdominal tumor).

[The following formulation is recommended: asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *granthika*, coriander (*dhānya*), cumin (*jīraka*), *vacā*, *cavya*, *agni* (ginger), *pāṭhā*, *śaṭī*, *vṛkṣāmla*, the three salts (*lavaṇatraya*), the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the two types of alkali (*kṣāradvaya*), and pomegranate (*dāḍima*). (27)

A powder made from *pathyā*, *pauṣkara*, sour *vetasa*, *hapuṣā*, and *ajājī*, processed with the juices of fresh *bījapūra* fruits, cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), flatulence, hemorrhoids, dysentery (*grahaṇī*), upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), recurrent flatulence, abdominal enlargement (*udara*), urinary stones, the two types of *tūnī*, and loss of appetite.
Taken with warm water after being previously drunk, it removes stiffness of the thighs, mental confusion, deafness of the mind, and both *aṣṭhīlikā* and *pratyaṣṭhīlaka*.
It also [removes ailments] in the heart, abdomen, groins, waist, and the interior of the stomach, as well as in the bladder, breasts, shoulder-blades, and the two sides of the body.
This first formulation beginning with *hiṅgu*, as stated in the *Āśvina-saṃhitā*, indeed destroys colic born of *vāta* and *balāsa*.
A wise physician should treat a *gulma* arising from the three *doṣas* after having declared it incurable;
for a *gulma* arisen from *sannipāta*, a regimen that subdues the three *doṣas* is beneficial.
One should consume one *śāṇa* measure each of the powder of *śarapuṅkha* and *pathyā* salt; this powder cures diseases of the abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
There should be one *śāṇa* measure of *svarjikā* and the same amount of jaggery (*guḍa*).
One should eat a pill made from both [of these], which destroys abdominal tumors (gulma).
Palāśa, vajrī, śikhari, ciñcā, akatila, nālaja, yavaja, and svarjikā— these are proclaimed as the eight alkaline substances (kṣāra).
These alkaline preparations cure abdominal tumors (gulma) and act as digestives for indigestion (ajīrṇa).
One should prepare a powder consisting of equal parts of sea salt (sāmudra), rock salt (saindhava), black salt (kāca), barley ash (yavakṣāra), suvarcala salt, borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), and svarjika alkali.
One should impregnate [the substance] for three days with the milky sap of the *vajrī* and the milky sap of the *eraṇḍa* in the sun;
having wrapped it in an *arka* leaf and sealed it in a vessel, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
Afterwards, one should powder that alkali, as well as the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
One should prepare a powder of yavānī, jīraka, and vahnī; one should combine this with an amount of alkali equal to the total weight of the powder, and all of it together.
One should administer two ṭaṅkas of that powder with water.

It is highly beneficial in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, indigestion, edema, all types of abdominal enlargements (udara), weak digestive fire, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and splenic disorders (plīha).
When vāta is predominant, it is beneficial with slightly warm water; when pitta is predominant, it is beneficial with ghee.
When there is an excess of phlegm, it should be taken with cow's urine; when all three humors are involved, with fermented rice water (kāñjika).
Known as Vajrakṣāra, it was proclaimed of old by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū); when consumed, it destroys indigestion as well as the diseases born of indigestion. (40–41)
One *ṭaṅka* of *suvarcikā* and an equal amount of *adrikā*—
one should consume both together for the alleviation of the disease *gulma*.
One should well-enclose a pill of conch-shell powder measuring one *ṭaṅka*.

One suffering from *gulma* disease should lick that [powder] with jaggery in the measure of one *śāṇa*. (43) A patient with *gulma* should swallow the flesh of a young girl, mixed with half a *karṣa* of cow’s ghee and dusted with the fine powder of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *abhayā*, and rock salt. (44)
One suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) should not eat dried meat, radish, fish, dry vegetables, pulses, sweet fruits, or tubers such as the *āluka*.
For one whose body has been lubricated and fomented, an unctuous purgative (snehavirecana) should be administered.
A paste (kalka) derived from śatāhvā, the bark of ācirabilva, dāru, bhārgī,
and kaṇā, when drunk with a decoction of sesame, conquers gulma born of blood.
A decoction of sesame should be combined with jaggery, vyoṣa, ghee, and bhārgī.
Yellow *dhātrī* juice mixed with black pepper cures blood-born *gulma* and the loss of menses in women. Powdered *guṇḍā* and *rocanikā*, combined with sugar and honey, [is likewise effective]. 48.
One should quickly provide for the woman suffering from gulma the means to move about without fatigue.
Furthermore, listen now to another specific remedy for the discharge of blood:
she should drink ghee prepared with the alkaline water of *palāśa*. 49–50.
A woman suffering from *arśas* (hemorrhoids) or abdominal tumors (*gulma*) should drink ghee prepared with alkaline substances and the three pungents (*trikaṭu*).

Furthermore, when in meat broths, milk, water, or other liquids that are being cooked, the production of foam occurs upon boiling, and they take on an appearance similar to spoiled milk; [in such cases, this remedy should be applied].
That alone is the time for its ripening, not any other characteristic.
52 Thus ends the thirty-second chapter on Gulma (abdominal tumors). 32 Now begins the thirty-third chapter on the Spleen and Liver (Plīha-yakṛt). 33
The spleen is born from blood, located to the left and below the heart;
it is declared by the great sages to be the root of the blood-carrying vessels. In a person who consumes burning and obstructive foods, the blood and phlegm become excessively vitiated.
When these two [the spleen and liver] become enlarged, they cause an increase in the spleen; physicians designate that disease as *plīha* (splenic enlargement).

It increases specifically on the left side of the body, and in this condition, the patient suffers from low-grade fever and weak digestion, is afflicted by the symptoms of *kapha* and *pitta*, has diminished strength, and is extremely pale.
Fatigue, vertigo, burning sensation, discoloration,
heaviness of the limbs, delusion, and the appearance of blood in the abdomen are to be known as the symptoms of [jaundice] arising from blood (raktaja).
It is accompanied by fever, thirst, a burning sensation, and is joined with delusion.
An enlarged spleen characterized specifically by yellowish limbs is called *paittika* (bilious).
An enlarged spleen that is mildly painful, bulky, hard, accompanied by a sense of heaviness,
and associated with loss of appetite is called *kaphaja* (phlegmatic).
One whose abdomen is constantly distended, who is perpetually afflicted by upward-moving wind (udāvarta),
and who is overwhelmed by various pains is said to have Vātika-type splenomegaly (plīhā). Even in the incurable form of splenomegaly, the symptoms of all three doshas may be present.
Below and to the right of the heart lies the liver;
it is considered the seat of the pigment-forming bile (*rañjaka-pitta*) and is born from blood.
(9) All the causes and other factors for diseases of the spleen (*plīha*) are the same as those for diseases of the liver (*yakṛt*).
However, their location should be known as being on the left and right sides.
Alkali produced from oyster shells should be drunk with milk according to the proper method;
likewise, long peppers (pippalī) should be drunk with milk for the pacification of the spleen.
Arka leaf, mixed with salt, roasted in a closed crucible (puṭapāka), and finely powdered,
destroys even the most formidable enlargement of the spleen when drunk with whey (mastu).
[12] Asafoetida, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), kuṣṭha, alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), and rock salt—
Combined with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, it becomes a remover of splenic pain.
Long pepper (*pippalī*) saturated with the alkaline water of *palāśa* is considered a pacifier of the pain of splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and a remedy for weak digestion.

The powder of *śaṅkhanābhi* (conch-shell mother-of-pearl) drunk with the juice of a *jambīra* fruit in a dose of one *śāṇa* will certainly and quickly pacify the entire disease of the spleen (*plīhāmaya*), which is as large as a tortoise. The paste of the root of *śarapuṅkha*, stirred with buttermilk and drunk, [achieves the same].

If even a mountain does not remove the enlargement of the spleen, then it floats upon the water. (16) The juice of a well-ripened mango, when drunk together with honey, certainly pacifies the spleen; there is no doubt about this. (17)
A person should eat well-boiled *śālmalī* flowers that have been soaked overnight in water,
combined with powdered *rājikā*, for the alleviation of splenic enlargement (18).
[One should also take] *yavānikā*, *citraka*, *yāvaśūka*, *ṣaḍgranthi*, *dantī*, and *magadhodbhava*.
This powder, when drunk with warm water, or with whey, wine, or fermented liquor (āsava), removes the disease of the spleen (plīhagada).
One should employ all the treatments prescribed for the spleen in cases of liver disease (yakṛdroga),
and bloodletting should be performed on the right arm.

One should drink an alkaline solution extracted from *pūtīka* along with *viḍaṅga* and *kṛṣṇā* in the morning according to one's digestive capacity, for the pacification of liver and spleen disorders. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter on the treatment of spleen and liver disorders. 33.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter, the Section on Heart Disease (Hṛdroga).

Heart disease is declared to be of five types, caused by excessive heat, heavy, sour, astringent, or bitter foods; by physical exertion, injury, overeating, and indulgence; by brooding, and by the suppression of natural urges. (1)
When the humors (doṣas), having become disordered, vitiate the rasa and reach the heart, they cause distress in the heart;
that is designated as hṛdroga (heart disease).
In the type caused by vāta, the heart feels stretched and likewise pierced with pain.
In the Pitta-type heart disease, there is churning, tearing, bursting, or even splitting [of the heart]; there may be burning, parching, and exhaustion from the heat of thirst;
as well as fatigue, a sensation of fuming, fainting, excessive moisture, and dryness of the mouth.
Heaviness, expectoration of phlegm, loss of appetite, stiffness, dullness of the digestive fire,
and a sweet taste in the mouth occur when the heart is pervaded by *balāsa* (phlegm). One should recognize that a cardiac disease arising from all three *doṣas* likewise possesses all these symptoms.
In a patient suffering from heart disease caused by the three doṣas, if that wicked person consumes sesame, milk, jaggery, and similar substances,
a glandular swelling (granthi) arises in a specific part of the vital organ (marman), and the nutrient fluid (rasa) becomes corrupted there.
Due to the putrefaction of this impaired body, worms arise within it.
In the case of worm-induced [disease], there occurs excessive salivation, spitting, pricking pain, colic, nausea, darkness before the eyes, loss of appetite, darkening of the eyes, and emaciation.

Lassitude of the liver (kloma), vertigo, and emaciation are to be known as their complications; however, in the case of that caused by worms, those symptoms which belong to the phlegmatic (kaphaja) types of worms are considered to occur.
Those who drink the powder of the bark of the *kakubha* tree with ghee, milk, or molasses-water [are cured].
Having destroyed heart disease, chronic fever, and internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta), they shall become long-lived.
(11) A powder derived from *harītakī*, *vacā*, *rāsnā*, *pippalī*, ginger (*nāgara*), *śaṭī*, and *puṣkara-mūla* is a destroyer of heart disease. (12)

Having ground the horn of a deer burnt in a closed crucible (puṭapāka), one who drinks it with cow's ghee finds that even the most severe pain in the heart and back is quickly pacified. A powder made from wheat and *pārtha* (arjuna) bark, cooked with oil, ghee, and jaggery, [is likewise effective].
A man who drinks milk alone becomes free from all diseases of the heart.
(14) Wheat and barley flour, cooked with goat’s milk and cow’s ghee and combined with honey and sugar, pacifies severe heart disease in men. (15)
Ghee prepared with the paste and decoction of *pārtha* is recommended for all heart diseases.
Ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of *balā*, *nāgabalā*, and *arjuna*, along with *yaṣṭikā*,
indeed destroys heart disease, as well as vātarakta, wounds, and blood-bile disorders.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter on Heart Disease (Hṛdroga), chapter thirty-five: On Urinary Disorders (Mūtrakṛcchra).
[Caused] by physical exercise, sharp medicinal drugs, dryness, addiction to wine, dancing, and riding on fast-moving vehicles from behind;
