From eating fish from marshy lands in excess, and from indigestion, eight types of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arise in men. When the individual doshas are provoked by their respective etiological factors, or when all of them together reach a state of provocation, they afflict the urinary passage in the bladder; at that time, one voids urine with difficulty in this world.
In the case of Vata, there is intense pain in the groins, bladder, and penis, and one voids urine frequently in small quantities (3).
In the case of Pitta, one voids urine frequently with difficulty, which is yellowish, blood-stained, painful, and burning (4).
In Kaphaja Mutrakricchra, there is heaviness and swelling of the bladder along with the genitals, and the urine is slimy (5).
All forms of [disease] arise from the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), for that is indeed the most difficult affliction. When the urinary channels are injured by a foreign body or struck,
or due to the obstruction of feces, the wind (vāyu) becomes disordered.
It causes flatulence, colic pain from wind, and retention of urine (8).
When the semen is afflicted by the humors and flows back into the urinary tract,
one voids urine with difficulty along with semen, accompanied by pain in the bladder and the penis (9).

The causes of urinary calculi (aśmarī) and the preceding dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) have been described. Urinary calculi and gravel (śarkarā) are identical in their origin and symptoms; now hear from me as I proclaim the specific distinction regarding gravel.
A stone (aśmarī) that is being cooked by bile and dried up by Vāyu,
having lost its cohesive Kapha, is considered to be gravel (śarkarā) as it disintegrates.
There is pain in the heart, trembling, colic in the abdomen, and the digestive fire becomes weak.
Likewise, fainting and severe dysuria may occur.

In cases of vāta-type dysuria, one should administer massage, oleation, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), unctuous enemas (vasti), fomentation (sveda), poultices (upanāha), urethral/suprapubic injections (uttaravasti), and affusions, as well as meat soups prepared with drugs from the sthirādi group that alleviate vāta. 11–12.

One afflicted by diseases of Vāta, suffering from colic, or urinary distress (mūtrakṛcchra), should drink Amṛtā, Nāgara, Dhātrī, Vājigandhā, and Trikaṇṭaka. [Likewise, one may drink a decoction] of Punarnavā, Eraṇḍa, Śatāvarī, Pattūra, Vṛścīra, Balā, and Aśmabhida.
Oil prepared with a decoction of the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), horse gram (kulattha), and barley boiled in water,
along with the paste (kalka) of those same ingredients, ghee, the fat of a boar, and rock salt— when drunk in the proper dose, this cures dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) accompanied by colic caused by Vāta.

Immersion baths, cooling plasters, summer regimens, enemas, and preparations of milk should be employed; likewise, in cases of difficult dysuria caused by pitta, treatments with the juices of *drākṣā*, *vidārī*, and sugarcane, as well as with ghee, should be administered. Kuśa, kāśa, śara, darbha, and ikṣu—these constitute the group derived from grasses.

The Pañcamūla group [of herbs] relieves dysuria caused by pitta and cleanses the bladder. One should drink a well-cooled decoction of śatāvarī, kāśa, kuśa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, vidārī, śālī, ikṣu, and kaseruka, combined with honey and sugar, for dysuria caused by pitta.
In cases of Pitta-type dysuria, one should drink the seeds of *ervāru*, *madhuka*, and *dārvī* with rice-wash water;
likewise, *dārvī* and *āmalakī* juice mixed with honey should be drunk for dysuria caused by Pitta (verse 19).
[One should also take] *harītakī*, *gokṣura*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *pāṣāṇabhida*, and *dhanvayavāsaka*.
One should drink a decoction mixed with honey in cases of dysuria accompanied by burning, pain,
and constipation. Ghee or milk prepared with śatāvarī, kāśa, kuśa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, vidārī, sugarcane, and āmalaka, mixed with sugar, should be administered for dysurias arising from pitta.

Ghee prepared with the fresh juices of *trikaṇṭaka*, castor, *kuśa* grass, and others, along with *abhīru* and *karkāruka*, combined with half a part of jaggery, should be administered for disorders involving painful micturition, urinary stones, and urinary obstruction;
this formulation, moreover, should be specifically employed as the most excellent treatment for all types of urinary stones. 22.

In cases of *kapha*-type dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), one should administer alkaline, hot, and strong medicinal foods and drinks; sudation; a diet of barley; emesis; non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*); buttermilk; and oils prepared with bitter herbs for both massage and internal consumption.
[This may also be done] with urine, wine, or the fresh juice of plantain. 23.
For the destruction of dysuria caused by *kapha*, one should drink a fine powder as a pill with buttermilk (24).
One should drink the seeds of *śitimāraka* combined with buttermilk for the sake of relieving urinary obstruction;
likewise, one should drink coral powder with rice-wash water in cases of *kaphaja* dysuria (25).
A wise person should consume a pill made of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), musta, and guggulu, combined with honey and mixed with a decoction of gokṣura;
this cures urinary disorders (prameha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta). 26.

It undoubtedly destroys urinary calculi (aśmarī) and uterine hemorrhage (pradara). In cases arising from all three doṣas, treatment should be performed after carefully considering the sequence of the locations of the vāyu; when one doṣa is predominant over the other three, emesis should first be administered for kapha, purgation for pitta, and enema for vāta.
Bṛhatī, dhāvanī, pāṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, and liṅgaka constitute the *bṛhatyādi* group, which is digestive and removes urinary disorders (*kṛcchra*) as well as the three humors (*doṣas*).
One should drink milk mixed with jaggery, slightly warm, according to one's desire. (29)
It cures all types of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) and removes gravel (śarkarā) and diseases caused by Vāta. In cases of dysuria arising from trauma, the treatment for Vāta-type dysuria is prescribed.
Alternatively, one should drink wine with sugar and ghee, or boiled milk mixed with half as much sugar.
In cases of dysuria accompanied by blood, one should drink the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) or sugarcane juice mixed with honey.
For dysuria caused by fecal matter (*purīṣaja*), sudation, medicinal powders, massages, and enemas should be employed;
furthermore, a decoction of *gokṣura* seeds combined with *yavakṣāra* (alkali of barley) should be taken regularly.
When drunk, it quickly cures dysuria and the retention of feces (33).
For obstruction of semen, one should lick a preparation of honey with *śilājatu*.
A person should drink milk mixed with *elā*, *hiṅgu*, and clarified butter (34).
For the purification of urinary disorders and the removal of seminal defects,
excellent women should be enjoyed by one whose bodily tissues have been nourished with aphrodisiacs (vṛṣya).
Saptacchada, āragvadha, kevu ka, elā, nimba, karañja, kuṭaja, and guḍūcī [are used for this purpose].
One should cook gruel (yavāgū) in water with that [sādhya] or drink the prepared decoction mixed with honey. 36.
Furthermore, a paste of Ervāru seeds, finely ground and measured at one akṣa, should be drunk with fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) and salts; this destroys dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). 37.
Trikaṇṭaka, āragvadha, darbha, kāśa, durālabhā, parvatabheda,
and pathyā, when drunk with honey, destroy urinary calculi and dysuria even in one whose death has arrived.
One *kuḍava* of the fresh juice of *nidigdhikā* mixed with honey [is likewise effective].

Having drunk this decoction prepared from the roots of atibalā, a man becomes happy, as it removes all urinary disorders (mūtradoṣa). Likewise, the seeds of trapusī, when drunk together with sesame, clarified butter, and milk, conquer all types of painful straining (kṛcchra). 39–40.
One should drink the well-ground paste of triphalā combined with jujube (kola), seasoned with salt and mixed with water, to alleviate urinary pain. [Likewise,
one may drink a preparation] of *yavāru*, castor seeds (*eraṇḍa*), the five grass roots (*tṛṇapañcamūlī*), *pāṣāṇabheda*, and *śatāvarī*.
In cases of *kṛcchra* (urinary distress), a decoction made from *guggulu* mixed with *abhayā* and combined with jaggery is beneficial.
The roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, sugarcane, *śara*,
and *ikṣuvālikā* constitute the "grass-based five-roots" (*tṛṇapañcamūlī*), which is used for urinary obstruction, gravel, and *kṛcchra*.
Jaggery and āmalaka are aphrodisiac, they remove fatigue, provide nourishment, and are pleasing;
they destroy pitta, blood disorders, burning sensations, and colic, and they alleviate dysuria. (44) Yavakṣāra, equal in measure to sugar, is a remedy for all types of dysuria.
A paste of *drākṣā* (grape), sugar, and *sitopalā* (crystallized sugar), combined with whey, destroys urinary distress (*kṛcchra*).
Vidārī, sārivā, chāgaśṛṅgī, vatsādanī, niśā,
and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) from the climbing plants destroy urinary distress caused by pitta and vāta.
Having drunk the powders of cardamom, *aśmabheda*, bitumen, *pīlu*, gourd seeds, the best salt (*saindhava*), and saffron,
stirred in rice-water, even one facing imminent death is restored to life if suffering from dysuria.
Iron powder, finely ground and mixed with honey, [is likewise effective].
It quickly destroys dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) with three linctuses; of this there is no doubt.
(48) One should take one *tulā* of *punarnavā* root, *daśamūla*, *śatāvarī*, *balā*, *turaṅgagandhā*, *tṛṇamūla*, and *trikaṇṭaka*. (49)
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of *vidārīkanda*, *nāgāhva*, *guḍūcī*, and *atibalā* in one *droṇa* of water;
with that decoction reduced to one-fourth, one should cook half an *āḍhaka* of ghee.
Having added two palas each of madhuka, śṛṅgavera, drākṣā, saindhava, and pippalī, as well as one kuḍava of yavānī,
thirty palas of jaggery, and [the same amount] of castor oil; 51–52.
This blameless food is for the sons of lords, for kings, for those equal to kings, and for those who have many wives;
it is also for those suffering from dysuria, those with a sagging waist, and those with constipation. (53)
It is recommended for pain in the penis and groin, as well as for vaginal pain (54).

It is beneficial for the aforementioned types of abdominal tumors (gulma) and for those suffering from vāta-śoṇita; it is strengthening, an elixir (rasāyana), bestowing prosperity, and suitable for the delicate and the young (55).
One *droṇa* of *punarnavā* should be added to a hundred [parts], and another [substance] should also be added.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter on dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter on urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*).
Thirteen types of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta) arise from aggravated doshas;
these include conditions such as vātakuṇḍalika and others, which generally result from the suppression of the urge to urinate.
Due to dryness or the suppression of the urge, urine becomes painful within the bladder.
Entering the urine, it moves about in a distorted, coiled manner;
then the urine is discharged in very small quantities or with pain.
One should recognize this as the severe and most dreadful disease known as Vātakuṇḍalikā.
The wind, having obstructed the bladder and rectum and causing them to distend, produces a painful, mobile, and elevated growth known as *aṣṭhīlā*, which blocks the passages of urine and feces.
This occurs in an unskilled man who suppresses the urge to urinate. (4)
The Vayu located in the bladder obstructs the opening of that organ;
by this, retention of urine occurs, accompanied by pain in the bladder and the abdomen.
This disease is known as Vata-vasti, and it is difficult to treat.
When one suppresses the urge to urinate for a long time, the urine does not flow despite haste; when passing it, it comes out slowly—this is called *mūtrātīta*.
When the flow of urine is obstructed, it is caused by that same upward reversal (*udāvarta*).
When the apāna vāyu becomes aggravated, it fills the abdomen excessively;
it produces distension below the navel accompanied by intense pain.
One should know that as mūtrajaṭhara, born from the obstruction of the lower urinary tract.

In a person whose urine, once it has begun to flow, becomes obstructed in the bladder, the urethra, or the glans penis, or flows out with blood, either slowly, in small quantities, or accompanied by pain— or even without pain— [it is known as Prameha]. 10.
A disease arising from vitiated wind (vāyu) is designated as *mūtrotsaṅga*.

When pitta and vāyu are located in the bladder of a person who is dry and whose body is exhausted, they produce a deficiency of urine accompanied by pain and burning; that condition is known by its own name (*mūtrakṣaya*).

A round, firm, and small nodular growth that appears suddenly at the opening of the bladder, accompanied by pain similar to that of a stone, is called *granthi* (a cyst). [13] When a man who has urinated engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, his semen is expelled by the wind (*vāyu*).
When one urinates after being displaced from a standing position, the urine mixed with semen flows out either before or after the urination;
resembling water mixed with ashes, that is called *mūtraśukra*.
(14) Pitta, provoked by physical exercise, walking, and exposure to the sun, reaches the bladder and is obstructed by Vāyu.

It burns the bladder, the penis, and the anus, and causes the downward discharge of urine that is yellowish, or watery, or even bloody; because it is passed with great difficulty again and again, they call this condition *uṣṇavāta*. 15–16.
If both pitta and kapha are congealed by vāyu, then urine is discharged with difficulty, being yellow, red, white, or thick;
it is accompanied by a burning sensation and has the color of the powder of gorocanā or conch shell. (17)
They call that *mūtrasāda* when the urine is either dry or possesses all [the colors of the stool].
When the feces, mixed with wind, reach the urinary tract of a person who is parched or weak, then [this condition occurs]. (18–19)
One should diagnose *vidghāta* (urinary obstruction caused by feces) when there is difficulty in urinating accompanied by the smell of feces.
Due to rapid travel, leaping, physical exertion, trauma, or compression,
the bladder is displaced from its natural location and remains distended like a pregnancy.
Afflicted by pain, throbbing, and burning, he emits drop after drop; yet when pressed, he may discharge a stream, suffering from stiffness and convulsions.
This terrible condition, resembling a weapon or poison, is called Vastikuṇḍala.
This [fever], generally aggravated by wind (pavana) and difficult for those lacking wisdom to restrain,
when combined with bile (pitta), causes a burning sensation, colic, and discoloration of the urine;
when combined with phlegm (śleṣman), it causes heaviness, swelling, and the urine becomes unctuous, thick, and white.
A bladder whose opening is obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman) and in which pitta is aggravated does not succeed in treatment;

likewise, one whose opening is not displaced is curable, as is one that has become coiled within the bladder—though in the case of a coiled bladder, there is thirst, delusion, and even labored breathing. 25
Regarding the treatment for urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta):
for one who has undergone oleation and sudation, an unctuous purgative is beneficial; in cases of painful urinary obstruction, one should also administer a urethral enema (uttarabasti). 26
For one who drinks in the morning a well-cooled decoction of *nalaka*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, sugarcane, and *balā* mixed with sugar, urinary retention is certainly destroyed; so said Kaca.
One *pala* of the root of the plant named *gojī*, boiled down to [one-quarter] its original volume, when drunk, [cures this condition].
Having added honey and sugar, it dispels the obstruction of urine.
(28) The root of *godhāpadī*, boiled and mixed with ghee, oil, and *gorasa*, when drunk, quickly breaks up a congealed mass of obstructed urine. (29)
One should drink *śilājatu* combined with a decoction prepared from the roots and leaves of *vīrataru*, along with *gokṣura* root, leaf, and fruit;
this, when taken with honey and sugar, removes the pain of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). (30–31)
Having coated a *dhvaja* with the powder of *ghanasāra* and [mixed] goat’s urine or sheep’s urine, and having inserted it, one abandons that obstruction of urine.
[Likewise,] the root of *sadābhadra*, *aśmabhida*, and *śatāvarī*, together with *citraka*—
Rohiṇī, kokilākṣa, vacā, śaila, and trikaṇṭaka— these,
finely ground and drunk with wine, overcome urinary obstruction.
One should drink the root of varhiśikhā with rice-water while subsisting on milk.
One should administer either an enema (basti) or a urethral enema (uttarabasti) to all of them;
or one should drink the fresh juice of Nidigdhikā strained through a cloth;
or a paste of saffron soaked in water with honey overnight.
Having bound and strained the alkaline ash of *pāṭalā* with oil,

or milk prepared with *trikaṇṭaka*, castor, *śatāvarī*, and the five grass roots (*tṛṇapañcamūla*), thickened with jaggery and mixed with ghee— this is recommended for diseases such as dysuria (*kṛcchra*). (36–37)
The root of *vāyasī* and the bulb of *tila*, combined with sugar and white salt, when drunk with the juice of the silkworm cocoon (*kośakāra*), will overcome urinary calculi (*vastikuṇḍala*).
One who eats food with boiled, cooled milk and sandalwood mixed with rice-water [will also be cured].

One should drink this excellent [milk] with sugar when there is hot wind (fever) accompanied by blood. Oil prepared with *śilodbhida*, *eraṇḍa*, *samasthirā*, and *punarnavā* in the juices of *bhīru* should be administered, followed by boiled milk as a post-drink at the appropriate times during conditions such as urinary calculi (*kṛcchra*).

Ghee prepared with the decoction and paste of *dhānyaka* and *gokṣuraka* is beneficial in cases of urinary obstruction (*mūtrāghāta*), painful urination (*mūtrakṛcchra*), and severe disorders of the semen (*śukradoṣa*).
[Likewise,] *pāṣāṇabheda*, *vārāhī*, the root of *śāli* rice, and *śara* grass [are used]. 41.
One should then procure bhallātaka and the root of śirīṣa;
having taken equal parts of all these, the wise physician should boil them and cook one prastha of ghee with the decoction reduced to one-quarter.
Then, the wise one, having added a paste (kalka) of mountain-born ginger (girija), licorice (madhuka),
blue lotus (nīlotpala), kākolī, seeds of trāpuṣa, and likewise kūṣmāṇḍa and ervāru, these should be in equal proportions. 45.
This ghee known as Bhadrāvaha is remembered as a destroyer of hot winds (uṣṇavāta).
Vidārī, vṛṣaka, yūthī, mātuluṅgī, bhūtṛṇa, pāṣāṇabheda, kastūrī, vasuka, vaśira, and anala [are the ingredients]. 46–47.
Punarnavā, vacā, rāsnā, balā, and likewise atibalā;
kaśeru, viṣa, śṛṅgāṭa, tāmalakī, and sthirā; as well as the roots of śara, ikṣu, darbha, kuśa, and kāśa. 48.
Having combined two *palas* [of the herbs], one should cook them in a *droṇa* of water. When the decoction is reduced to one-fourth, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee in that liquid,
along with an equal amount of ghee of the fresh juices of *śatāvarī* and *dhātrī*.
Six palas of sugar and one karṣa each of the following:
liquorice, long pepper, grapes, kāśmarya, and parūṣaka; cardamom, dūrvā, kauntī, saffron, and nāgakeśara.
Having added the eight vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs and twice the amount of milk,
this ghee should be cooked slowly over a mild fire by the wise;
it is indicated for all types of urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta), especially those born of pitta.
It is used for gravel, urinary stones, and pains arising from blood;

for heart disease, pitta-type abdominal tumors (gulma), and disorders born of vāta, blood, and pitta; and for those exhausted by cough, dyspnea, chest injuries, carrying loads, or sexual intercourse. (54)
In cases of thirst, vomiting, trembling, and spitting of blood; likewise in blood disorders, consumption, epilepsy, insanity, and stiffness of the head;
in disorders of the female reproductive tract, menstrual irregularities, seminal defects, and diseases of the voice.
This is a memory-enhancer, aphrodisiac, and the best of virilizers;
it bestows sons and is rich in strength and complexion, especially a destroyer of Vata. It is never obstructed in its action when used in drinks, foods, or nasal medications.
This is called Vidārī-ghṛta, an unsurpassed elixir (rasāyana).
Having ground Akhumala with hot alkaline water (cāranāla), it is applied as a plaster;
it quickly destroys urinary obstruction caused by both [Akhumala] and Karabhī. 58–59.
For one whose blood is depleted due to excessive indulgence with women, sexual abstinence and a nourishing regimen are beneficial; likewise,
the fat of a cock mixed with oil is suitable for use in urethral enemas (uttaravasti).

One should thoroughly churn together equal parts of *svaguptā* fruit, raisins, black sugarcane juice, and powdered sugar, along with half-parts each of milk, honey, and ghee; having licked a dose the size of an *akṣa*, one should drink milk.
It destroys the disorders arising from the depletion of semen and bestows a son upon the barren woman.
(62) One part of honey should be prepared, along with one part each of milk-ghee and powdered sugar; the powder of *drākṣā* (grape) should be equal to that. (63)
One should likewise provide the fruit of *svayamguptā* and similarly of sugarcane juice,
as well as the powder of *pippalī*, in equal proportions; having brought these together into a mortar, one should grind them thoroughly.
One should lick the powder from its palm and then drink milk; by applying this correctly, one is liberated from disorders of the female reproductive tract.
A cloth wick soaked in camphor and resin should be inserted very slowly.
Placed within the urethral passage, it removes urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta).
Whatever medicine has been proclaimed for dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) and stone disease (aśmarī),
one who knows the proper place and time should employ that for various types of urinary obstruction and difficulty in urination.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter on urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta), number 36.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter on urinary calculi (aśmarī), number 37:
three types [of calculi] are considered to arise from vāta, pitta, and kapha, while the fourth is born from semen (śukra).
Generally, all stones (aśmarī) are based on phlegm (śleṣman) and are like Yama [in their destructive power].
When the wind (pavana), along with bile (pitta) or phlegm, dries up the urine located in the bladder together with semen,
then a stone is produced gradually, just as gallstone (rocanā) forms within the bile of a cow.

All [these disorders] have multiple doshas as their basis; now, their premonitory symptoms are distension of the bladder, intense pain all around its vicinity, urine smelling like goat's urine, dysuria, fever, and anorexia. (3)
The general symptom is pain in the navel, the perineum, the bladder, and the head;
the urine flows in broken streams due to the obstruction of the passage.
Upon the removal of that [obstruction], one urinates comfortably with clear urine resembling a *gomedaka* gem.
From its agitation, there occurs a wound with blood due to injury, and excessive pain arises from exhaustion.
Among these, from [aggravated] Vata, the patient is intensely afflicted; he gnashes his teeth, trembles, rubs his penis, and constantly presses upon his navel while moaning.

One who passes feces with wind and urinates drop by drop, and whose stone is dark, rough, and as if covered with thorns—that is a stone formed by the accumulation [of wind] (śyāvā). For its premonitory symptoms, the sequence beginning with oleation (sneha) is prescribed. 7–8.

Having prepared a decoction with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *agnimantha*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), *varuṇa*, *gokṣura*, *kāśmarya*, and the fruits of *āragvadha*, the wise man should add a powder of asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), alkali, and salt, and drink it.
This [decoction] destroys urinary calculi and dysuria, is an excellent digestive stimulant and carminative,
and overcomes Vata located in the abdominal cavity as well as that arising in the waist, thighs, anus, and penis.
(10) [It is prepared with] Elā, Kulyā, Madhuka, Aśmabheda, Kauntī, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Vṛṣaka, and Urubūka.
One should drink well-boiled *aśmajatu* (bitumen) mixed with sugar for urinary calculi and dysuria. Having added the excellent bark of *varuṇa*, ginger, and *gokṣura*,
along with *yavakṣāra* and jaggery, one should boil it and drink it while cold.
It destroys urinary calculi born of Vata that have persisted for a long time.
Pāṣāṇabheda, vasuka, vaśira, aśmantaka, as well as śatāvarī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā—[these are used]. 12–13.
Kapotavaṅkā, ārtagala, kāñcana, uśīra, gundraka, vṛkṣādanī, bhallūka, varuṇa, and the fruit of the śāka plant;
barley, horse gram, jujube fruits, and the nuts of the kataka tree. 14–15.
Ghee boiled in a decoction of these [drugs] with an addition (*pratīvāpa*) of *ūṣaka* and other such substances quickly breaks up a stone (*aśmarī*) produced by Vāta.
Alkaline preparations, gruels (*yavāgū*), thin porridges (*peyā*), decoctions (*kaṣāya*), and milks [should also be used].
One should prepare foods within this group that destroys Vāta (wind):
vīravṛkṣa, agnimantha, kāśa, vṛkṣādanī, kuśa, moraṭa, indīvarī, sūryabhakta, gokṣura, and ṭuṇṭuka. (17–18)
The group beginning with *vīratara*— consisting of *vasuka*, *vaśira*, *darbha*, *śairīya*, *aśmabhedaka*, *gundra*, *nala*, and *kuruṇṭa*—
is considered to alleviate urinary calculi, gravel, dysuria, and afflictions caused by *vāta*. (19)
In cases of excessive wind (vāta), Vīratara is recommended; in its absence, Śara is considered suitable.
When afflicted by pitta, the bladder feels as if it is being burned by heat, as if being cooked;
the stone (aśmarī) is red, yellow, or white, and has the appearance of a Bhallātaka seed kernel. 20–21.
Now, the treatment for pitta-type urinary calculi:
Kuśa, kāśa, śara, gundra, itkaṭa, moraṭā, aśmabhida, darbha, vidārī, vārāhī, the root of śāli rice, and trikaṇṭaka. (22)
Ghee prepared with bhallātaka, pāṭalā, pāṭhā, pattūra, kuruṇṭaka,
punarnavā, and śirīṣa— these being boiled together—
and combined with śilājatu, madhuka, and the seeds of indīvara; 23.
A wholesome preparation sown with the seeds of *trapusa*, *vāruka*, and others,
quickly breaks up a stone (*aśmarī*) born of bile (*pitta*). Furthermore,
alkaline preparations, barley gruels, thin porridges, decoctions, and milks [should be employed].
And one should prepare foods within this group for the destruction of pitta (25).
Madhuka is called *bījaka* because it has been shortened [in name] due to its seeds;
*śilājatu* is known as *śilāhvaya*; and *paṭīra*, *gundra*, and *gundraka* [are synonyms]. (26)
One should add milk and other substances to that decoction as additives (*āvāpaka*), according to availability, grouped into categories; the standard rule (*paribhāṣā*) applies here.
A *basti* (enema) that is cold and heavy feels as if it is being pricked by phlegm (*śleṣman*).
The stones (aśmarī) are large, smooth, honey-colored, or white;
these occur in children, and because their physical support and growth are small, they are easy to grasp and extract. (28-29)

Now, regarding the treatment of phlegm-stone (kaphāśmarī): one should use [the drugs] from the group beginning with Varuṇaka, along with guggulu, elā, hareṇu, kuṣṭha, bhadrāhvā, marica, citraka, and surāhvaya.
Ghee prepared with these [drugs], as well as with the Ushakadi group, quickly breaks up urinary calculi (ashmarī) born of phlegm (kapha). Furthermore,
the Shatyadi group is desired here by the wise, as is the Shyamadi group.
Varuṇa, ārtagala, śigru, tarkārī, naktamālaka,
moraṭā, araṇi, bilva, bimbī, vasuka, citraka,
śairīya, vaśira, akṣīva, ajaśṛṅgī, and śatāvarī. (32)

Darbha, bṛhatikā, and vyāghrī have been proclaimed by the sages as this group beginning with varuṇa; it removes phlegm and fat, destroys headache, and cures abdominal tumors and internal abscesses. (34)
One should prepare alkaline gruels, thin gruels, decoctions, milks, and meals using this group of substances that destroy phlegm (kapha).
However, a large seminal stone (śukrāśmarī) arises from the suppression of semen. 35–36.

Indeed, the wind (anila), having displaced the semen from its place but not yet released it, dries it up and draws it back into the space between the testicles; that semen becomes a stone (śukrāśmarī).
It causes pain in the bladder, difficulty in urination, and swelling of the testicles. (37)
As soon as that [urine] has arisen, the semen enters and dissolves; however, when this space is compressed, it becomes gravel (aśmarī) and sugar-like fragments (śarkarā).
When its form is broken apart by the wind (vāta), it is designated as "gravel" (śarkarā). 38–39.

When that [urine] is broken down into minute particles by the wind moving in its natural direction, it passes out along with the urine; however, when the wind moves in the reverse direction, it becomes obstructed. Having entered the urinary passage, if it remains stuck there, it may produce complications. 40
Weakness, exhaustion, emaciation, abdominal disease, loss of appetite, pallor, hot winds (fever), thirst, cardiac pain, vomiting, protrusion of the navel,
swelling of the scrotum, retention of urine, and suffering from pain— [these are the symptoms]. 41.
This quickly destroys urinary calculi (aśmarī), gravel (śarkarā), and sand-like sediments (sikatā). Regarding seminal calculi (śukrāśmarī), the general procedure for destroying stones applies;
one should take the juice derived from flowers and fruits mixed with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) and jaggery.
One should drink this decoction, which removes urinary obstruction and destroys gravel and stones; it is prepared from sesame, apāmārga, plantain, palāśa, barley, and bilva.
This decoction, when drunk with goat's urine, destroys gravel and stones. (44-45)
Water boiled with the fruits of *kebu*, *aṅkola*, *kataka*, *śāka*, and *indīvara*, when drunk warm with jaggery (*guḍa*), causes sugar (*śarkarā*) to fall downward.
[46] The roots of *pāṣāṇabhid*, *gokṣura*, *uruvūka*, the two types of *kaṇṭakārī*, and that which is called *kṣuraka*—
One should drink this well-ground powder with curd and milk; it serves to break up gravel and urinary stones.
He who properly drinks *rajanī* (turmeric) with jaggery and water from parched grain husks, his long-standing calculus in the penis will quickly pass away.
For one who drinks *kuṭaja* with curd and eats wholesome food,
the gravel in the penis (*meḍhraśarkarā*) will certainly fall out before long.
Alternatively, the seed of the *trāpuṣa* fruit or the flower of the coconut may be drunk with milk.
One becomes comfortable within a few days regarding feces, urine, and gravel.
One should drink a decoction of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *varuṇa*, and *śuṇṭhī* combined with honey;
it destroys gravel, urinary stones, and colic, and is supreme for curing dysuria.
The juice of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* combined with *hiṅgu* and barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), when applied to the bladder and the penis, destroys pain and is an excellent remedy for dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).
(52) *Punarnavā*, iron, *rajanī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *varī*, young bamboo shoots, and *darbha* flowers [are likewise used].
A paste made from milk, mango, wine, and sugarcane juice is beneficial for urinary calculi and gravel (53).
A decoction prepared from the bark of *varuṇa*, *śilājatu*, dry ginger, and *gokṣura*, combined with alkali, even breaks up gravel (54).
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of the five roots known as *pañcamūla*, *tṛṇa*, and *gokṣuraka* in one *droṇa* of water;
this prepared decoction is used for urinary disorders, gravel, and stones.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with a quarter-portion remaining [of the decoction];
one should add a paste (kalka) of jaggery and gokṣuraka seeds therein. Once prepared, this is used for urinary disorders, gravel, and stones.
The finest ghee should be employed for both oleation and as food; likewise,
one should cook oil with a decoction of the bark, leaves, fruits, and roots of *varuṇa* and *trikaṇṭaka*, to be used for non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana-vasti*).
It destroys gravel, urinary stones, and colic, and one is liberated from dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). [The following plants are used:
Kuśa, agnimantha, śairīya, nala, darbha, ikṣu, gokṣura, kapotavaṅkā, avasuka, vaśira, indīvarī, and śara. (58–59)
One should employ oil prepared with the paste (kalka) and decoction (kaṣāya) of dhātakyā, aralu, vandāka, karṇapūra, and aśmabheda, administered through drinking, massage,
enema (vasti), and urethral/vaginal enema (uttara-vasti). 60.

This Kuśādika oil is said to cure diseases caused by gravel and stones, as well as severe dysuria; it likewise cures menorrhagia, vaginal pain, and seminal disorders, and is proclaimed to bestow pregnancy upon barren women.

A decoction made from *nāgara*, *vāruṇa*, *gokṣura*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, and *kapotavaṅkā*, when drunk mixed with jaggery and *yavaśūka*, destroys even severe urinary calculi (63). Powdered seeds of *trikaṇṭaka* combined with honey [are likewise effective].
One should drink [the juice] with cow's milk for seven days to destroy urinary calculi (aśmarī).
One should drink the root of the varuṇa tree as a decoction combined with its paste;
likewise, a slightly warm decoction derived from the root of the śigru tree destroys urinary calculi.

The supernatant liquid of curd (*dadhimanda*), combined with ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), chebulic myrobalan (*pathyā*), and *kālīyaka*, quickly breaks up even severe urinary calculi when drunk.
A decoction made from *pāṣāṇabheda*, *varuṇa*, *gokṣuraka*, and *kapotavaṅkā* [achieves the same].
A superior formulation consisting of *girija* (realgar), sugar-candy (*guḍa*), *karkaṭikā*, and seeds of *trapusa*, when drunk,
certainly breaks even an incurable stone,
just as the hundred-edged thunderbolt released from the hand of Indra splits a mountain peak.
The man who eats the fruit and seeds of *śrīkariṇī* ground with buttermilk,
whether as a vegetable or as a side dish, shall destroy the affliction of urinary stones (*rogāśmarī*). [One should also take] *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, castor seeds, ginger, and the bark of *varuṇa*.

One should drink this excellent decoction in the morning to destroy urinary calculi. In cases arising from blood, one should drink water boiled with dry lotus stalks, *tālaka*, *kāśa*, young sugarcane, sugarcane, and *kuśa* grass, combined with sugar and honey; likewise, one should eat *vidārī*, sugarcane, and *trapusa*.
One should take eight *palas* of the bark of *varuṇa*,
half that amount of *yavaśūka*, and half of that again of jaggery;
having combined and thoroughly ground these, one should consume them in a dose of one *karṣa*.

By drinking hot water, there is certainly the destruction of urinary distress (kṛcchra) and stones (aśmarī). Water filtered through the ashes of *varuṇaka* should be boiled with its powder and *yavaśūka*, continuing until it returns to the state of a fine powder. 73–74.
Combined with jaggery, it destroys that formidable and severe urinary calculus (aśmarī),
as well as splenic enlargement, severe abdominal tumors (gulma), intense pain in the hips and belly,
accumulations of undigested matter (āmācaya), diseases of the bladder, and terrible dysuria (kṛcchra) born of Vāta.

Having cut a Varuṇaka plant—which is grown in a pure place, thick, very young, glossy, and eaten by insects on a day observed as auspicious—one should cause it to be weighed against a stone slab that has been heated in fire, is extremely hard, and is made of stone. 76. One should cause the weight to be taken.
Having quickly collected [the drugs] possessing the four qualities, one should boil them in water until reduced to one-fourth;
then, one should cook that again in a very strong vessel with an equal amount of treacle (guḍa).
Having recognized this thickening once the treacle has transformed, one should take one *pala* of each of these.
One should add the powder of dried ginger, cucumber seeds, gokṣura, kaṇā, pāṣāṇabheda, śītalā, kūṣmāṇḍa, trapusa seeds, kunaṭī, vāstūka, śobhāñjana, drākṣā, elā, girijā, abhayā, and kṛmighna. (78)
A person eating wholesome food should consume this jaggery every day in the prescribed measure;
by eating it, all stones (aśmarī) produced from the various doṣas fall away quickly.
Kulattha, rock salt, the essence of viḍaṅga, sugar, śītali, and barley-alkali [should be used].

One should cook ghee with the seeds of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* and *gokṣura* in the decoction of *varuṇa*. This quickly destroys all stones (*aśmarī*), dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), urinary obstruction (*mūtrābhighāta*), and retention of urine (*mūtrabandha*) from their very roots, just as the fall of a thunderbolt destroys fully grown trees.
Alternatively, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with a decoction of the five roots beginning with *śara* and a paste of *gokṣura*. When prepared, it should be consumed with sugar;
it destroys urinary calculi and dysuria, and removes pain from the seminal passage. (82)
One should boil a crushed *tulā* of *varuṇa* in a *droṇa* of water until one-fourth remains;
having strained it, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with *varuṇa*, *kadala*, *bilva*, *tṛṇaja*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*). (83)
One should add one karṣa each of amṛtā, aśmabheda, the seed of trapusa,
śataparvā, sesame-alkali, palāśa-alkali, and the roots of yūthikā. 84–85.
A person should drink this in the appropriate dose, taking into account factors such as place and time (86).
Once it has been digested, one should first drink molasses and then fermented whey;
this destroys urinary stones, gravel, and dysuria (87).
The oil beginning with rock salt (saindhava) which has been proclaimed by the sages—
that oil should be cooked with double the amount of milk, along with the decoction of vīratarādi and the aforementioned paste, by the best of physicians. (88)
This excellent and superior oil is the best remedy for preventing urinary calculi (aśmarī).
It is highly recommended in all cases of urinary retention (mūtrāghāta), painful urination (mūtrakṛcchra), as well as in cases of being pierced, crushed, fractured, or overcome by exhaustion. 89–90.
Vīra, vṛkṣa, aśmabheda, agnimantha, śyonāka, pāṭalā,
vṛkṣādanī, sahā, eraṇḍa, bhallūka, uśīra, padmaka,
kuśa, kāśa, śara, ikṣu, āsphotā, and kokilākṣa— [these are the ingredients]. 91.
A wise physician should cook oil with the decoctions and pastes of śatāvarī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, setkaṭā, vañjula, kapotavaṅkā, śrīparṇī, and the roots of kāśmarī. 92–93.
In disorders of Vāta and Pitta, the wise physician should administer an enema that destroys pain from gravel and stones and eliminates dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
[This enema consists of] punarnavā, amṛtā, bhīru, along with alkali and the three salts. 94.
With *śaṭī*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *mustā*, *rāsnā*, *kaṭphala*, and *pauṣkara*;
with *yavānī*, *hapuṣā*, *hiṅgu*, *śatāhvā*, and *sājamodaka*; combined with *viḍaṅga*, *ativiṣā*, *yaṣṭī*, and the five spices (*pañcakola*). 95–96.
One should cook one *prastha* of oil with these medicinal pastes (*kalka*) that are equal in measure;
cow’s urine should be added in double the quantity, and likewise, fermented gruel (*kāñjika*) in the same amount.
This oil, beginning with *punarnavā*, should be administered through drinking or by means of an enema (*vasti*).
It destroys gravel, urinary stones, and colic; it provides relief from dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
It cures disorders of the hips, thighs, bladder, penis, abdomen, and groins; it subdues phlegm, wind, and abdominal tumors (āmashūla), and it eradicates inguinal hernia (antravṛddhi). 98–99.

The Saindhava group and others specified in the section on Bradhna (scrotal enlargement) are desired here; however, the Vīratarādi group should always be employed with ghee, cold decoctions, milk, and urethral enemas (uttara-vasti). 100.
If they are strong and do not subside, one should extract them after rejecting [the usual treatment].
When they enter the urinary tract by chance and remain lodged within it, one should remove them by cutting them out with a stream [of water] or else extract them using a hook. 101–102.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter on the disease of urinary calculi (aśmarī).
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter on the pustules of urinary disorders (pramehapiḍikā):
sitting in comfort, the pleasure of sleep, curdled milk (dadhi), the meat-juices of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals, and milks.
Freshly harvested grain, drinks, and preparations of jaggery are all causes of *prameha* and increase *kapha*.

Having vitiated the fat, the flesh, and the moisture produced within the body that has reached the bladder, *kapha* produces these *mehas*; furthermore, when aggravated by hot things, *pitta* also vitiates those very same elements and produces them.
When the [other] doshas have been diminished, the vata draws in the bodily elements (dhātus), corrupts them, and produces the urinary disorders (mehas).

Among these, the ten types arising from kapha are curable; the six from pitta are palliable; and the four from vata are incurable, respectively, because of their similarity of treatment, their dissimilarity of treatment, and their great severity.

Kapha, pitta, and vāta are the doshas; fat, blood, semen, water, muscle-fat, lymph, marrow, flesh, and ojas are the dūṣyas. There are exactly twenty types of prameha in those suffering from urinary disorders.
An abundance of impurities on the teeth and so forth, as well as [excessive sweating] in the hands and feet, constitutes the premonitory symptom (pūrvarūpa).
Burning sensation, sliminess in the body, thirst, and a sweet taste in the mouth arise;

these are the general symptoms, as is the frequent passage of turbid urine. Although there is no difference in the humors (doṣas) or the bodily constituents (dūṣyas), [the specific types] arise from the particularity of their combination.

The differentiation among the types of urinary disorders (meha) is determined by variations in the color and other qualities of the urine. In udakameha, one passes urine that is clear, copious, white, cold, odorless, and resembles water; in slightly turbid and slimy urine, it is known as [piṣṭameha]. 7–8.
One suffering from *ikṣumeha* passes urine that is exceedingly sweet like the juice of sugarcane;
having stood overnight, it becomes thickened, and thus one voids with *sāndrameha*.
One suffering from *surāmeha* passes urine resembling liquor—clear on the surface and thick at the bottom.

With hair standing on end, one who has śukrameha passes urine that is thick and white like flour, or resembles semen, or is mixed with semen; one who has sikatāmeha passes fine, solid particles of impurity in the form of sand. 10–11.
In Śītameha, one passes urine that is very copious, sweet, and extremely cold;
in Śanairmeha, the patient voids urine slowly and gradually; and in Lālāmeha, the urine is slimy and mixed with threads of saliva. 12
By its smell, color, taste, and touch, it is like an alkaline solution with alkali (kṣāra).
In Nīlameha, the urine has a blue luster; in Kālameha, it resembles ink;
in Hāridrameha, it is pungent and burns, resembling turmeric.
In *mañjiṣṭhameha*, the urine is like the water of *mañjiṣṭhā* (red lac) and has a fleshy odor;
in *raktameha*, it is hot, salty, blood-red in appearance, and smells of raw flesh.
In *vasāmeha*, one voids urine frequently that is mixed with fat and resembles fat in appearance.
One who frequently passes urine that resembles marrow or is mixed with marrow has majjameha;
the wise should declare kṣaudrameha to be astringent, sweet, and dry.
One who, like an elephant in rut, constantly voids urine without any sense of urgency has hastimeha.
One suffering from *hastimeha* passes urine that is slimy and bound together.
Indigestion, loss of appetite, vomiting, excessive sleep, cough, and nasal catarrh arise as complications of those urinary disorders born of *kapha*.
Pricking pain in the anus and penis,
tearing of the scrotum, fever, burning sensation, thirst, sour eructation, fainting, and diarrhea are the symptoms of those born from Pitta.
In those born from Vata, there are upward movement of wind (udāvarta), trembling, cardiac oppression, and unsteadiness.
Pain, insomnia, emaciation, dyspnea, and cough arise.
(20) Prameha, when accompanied by the aforementioned complications, excessively discharging, and severely afflicted by carbuncles, destroys the man. (21)

A patient suffering from prameha who is afflicted with complications such as fainting, vomiting, fever, dyspnea, cough, erysipelas, and heaviness is difficult to treat. Since the *rajas* (menstrual blood) flows month after month, one should purify it.
Because women do not excrete all the bodily humors (doṣas) through urine,
one born as a case of prameha or madhumeha is incurable due to the defect of the seed; this also applies to whatever hereditary disorders may exist in the family.
They also declare those [cases] to be incurable.
Indeed, all types of *prameha*, if left untreated over time, develop into *madhumeha* (diabetes mellitus), and at that stage they become incurable.
That [patient] indeed develops honey-like urine (madhumeha), which is of two types:
it arises either when vāyu is provoked by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu-kṣaya), or when its path is obstructed by the doshas.
Being thus obstructed, it manifests the symptoms of the doshas without any apparent cause.
In one moment it is diminished, and in another moment it is full; thus it becomes difficult to cure.
That which is sweet in all its stages and generally flows like honey is called Madhumeha (diabetes mellitus), because of the sweetness of the body [urine] resulting from that condition. 27–28.
Śarāvikā, kacchapikā, jālinī, vinatā, alajī,
masūrikā, sarṣapikā, putriṇī, savidārikā,
and vidradhi— these are the ten types of carbuncles (piḍikā) resulting from the neglect of urinary disorders (prameha).
They arise at the joints, vital points (*marmas*), and in fleshy locations.
*Śarāvikā* is raised in the center, having that same appearance, with a depressed middle;
*Sarṣapī*, however, has the shape and size of a white mustard seed. (30–31)
Kūrmasaṃsthānā, characterized by constant burning, should be known by the wise as Kacchapikā;
Jālinī, however, is intensely burning and covered with a network of flesh, accompanied by deep-seated pain and moisture on the back or even the abdomen. (32)
A large, blue pustule is known by the wise as Vinatā (33). A large pustule with small centers should be known as Putriṇī;
furthermore, one shaped like the leaf of the Masūra bean is to be recognized as Masūrikā (34).
The wise should recognize *alajī* as being red or black and covered with pustules;
*vidārikā* is round and hard like the tuber of the *vidārī* plant (35). It should be known as *vidradhikā* when it possesses the characteristics of an abscess (*vidradhi*) (36).
Those which are known as myehas are composed of that [fat], while these [mūtrakuṇḍalikās] are composed of it [blood].
(37) Even without prameha, these arise from corrupted fat; yet they are not perceived as such until they have occupied their respective sites. (38)

One should avoid treating carbuncles (piḍikā) that have arisen in the anus, heart, head, shoulders, back, or vital points (marmas), especially when accompanied by complications, weakness, or loss of digestive fire (agnisāda).
Thirst, emaciation, contraction of the flesh, delusion, hiccups, intoxication, and fever [are signs of incurability].
Spreading ulcers (visarpa), obstruction of the vital points (marma), and carbuncles (piḍikā) are the complications [of urinary disorders]. 40.
Śyāmāka, kodrava, uddāla, wheat, chickpeas, āḍhakī, and old horse-gram (kulattha) are beneficial for those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin). 41.
For women, bitter vegetables, meat from wild animals, the flesh of deer and birds,
preparations of barley, mung beans, and *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice are recommended.
Sour gruel, wine, buttermilk, oil, milk, ghee, and jaggery [are also beneficial].
One should avoid sour gruel, sugarcane juice, flour-based foods, and the meat of animals from marshy regions (ānūpa).

At the very outset, one should administer oleation to the patient suffering from prameha using any of the oils prepared with the priyaṅgvādi group of drugs, and then induce strong emesis. Following the purgation, one should administer an enema (āsthāpana) using a decoction of the surasādi group mixed with a paste (vāpa) of mahauṣadha, bhadradāru, and mustā, combined with honey and rock salt. Or, for those burning with heat, an enema may be given with a decoction of the nyagrodhādi group, free of oil. In cases where vāta is predominant, the drinking of medicated fats (sneha-pāna) is especially recommended. Furthermore, [decoctions] of pārijāta, jayā, nimba, vahni, and gāyatrī should be used individually.

The eight decoctions— of *pāṭhā*, *sāguru*, yellow *darbha*, white *darbha*, *śārada*, water, sugarcane juice, wine, and sand— taken in sequence with honey, destroy urinary disorders caused by salt and flour, as well as thick urine (*sāndrameha*). (45)
Harītakī, kaṭphala, musta, and lodhra; pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, arjuna, and dhanvana; the two types of haridrā, tagara, viḍaṅga, kanda, viśālā, arjuna, and dīpyaka (46);
dārvī, viḍaṅga, khadira, dhava, surāhva, kuṣṭha, aguru, and candana.
Dārvī, agnimantha, triphalā, vacā, pāṭhā, mūrvā, and likewise śvadaṃṣṭrā (47);
vacā, uśīra, abhayā, guḍūcī, vṛṣa, śivā, citraka, and saptaparṇa—
these ten decoctions, prepared with one-quarter parts and combined with honey, have been prescribed by those who understand kapha-type urinary disorders (48).
Of uśīra, lodhra, arjuna, and candana; of uśīra, mustā, āmalaka, and abhayā; of paṭola, nimba, āmalaka, and amṛtā; of mustā, abhayā, muṣkaka, and vṛkṣaka (49);
of lodhra, āmra, kāsīsa, dhātakī, viśva, arjuna, elā, śirīṣa, and utpala.

In cases of urinary disorders caused by Pitta, these ten decoction formulations—prepared from śirīṣa, dhānya, arjuna, keśara; priyaṅgu, padma, utpala, kiṃśuka; aśvattha, pāṭhā, asana, vetasa; kaṭaṅkaṭerī, utpala, and mustaka—are prescribed to be combined with honey. (50–51)

Ghee prepared with a decoction that cures *kapha*-type urinary disorders is beneficial for *kapha*; ghee prepared with a decoction that destroys *pitta*-type urinary disorders removes *pitta*. [The following are the ingredients:
*kampilla*, *saptacchada*, *śāla*, *bibhītaka*, *rohitaka*, and *kuṭaja*.
One suffering from urinary disorders caused by *kapha* and *pitta* should lick *paṭola*, *kālīya*, *gada*, and *aguru* with honey.
(53) *Dūrvā*, *kaseru*, *pūtīka*, *kumbhīka*, *plava*, and *śaivala*, boiled in water and drunk, are excellent for curing *śukrameha*. (54)

A decoction of triphalā, āragvadha, and drākṣā, when drunk mixed with honey, invariably destroys the phena-type prameha in men. [This applies to] aśvattha, caturaṅgulī, nyagrodha, and the other members of that group, as well as the three myrobalans (phalatraya).
The five decoctions—those called Nīla, Hāridra, Phena, Kṣāra, and Māñjiṣṭhaka—along with red Sāra-mañjiṣṭhā, should be taken with honey;
or alternatively, the powder of Triphalā or that derived from Aśmajatu [should be taken] with honey. 56.
One should lick either a preparation made of iron or one derived from Abhayā for the cessation of urinary disorders (meha).
A decoction prepared with equal parts of Kaṭaṅkaṭerī, Madhuka, Triphalā, and Citraka should be drunk; it is a destroyer of all types of prameha.

Having decocted triphalā, dāruharidrā, viśālā, and mustā, one should drink the decoction mixed with a paste of haridrā (one part) and honey; this is for all types of prameha when they have fully manifested.
[59] One may also consume barley that has been eaten by cows, or even barley alone, after it has been saturated with urine.
One suffering from *prameha* should eat *nimba* with the juice of *mudga* or with *citraka* and *aśvattha*. For one month, he should consume barley flour with water;
these [remedies] destroy fat, bind the urine, and are equal in their efficacy across all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*).
Therefore, barley is especially distinguished as being superior for the treatment of prameha (urinary disorders).
[The following formulation consists of: trikaṭu, triphalā, pāṭhā, the root of śobhāñjana, the seeds of viḍaṅga, hiṅgu, and likewise kaṭukarohiṇī. (61–62)
Bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārī, the two types of haridrā, yavānikā, kebuka, śālaparṇī, as well as ativiṣā and citraka; sauvarcala, jīraka, hapuṣā, and dhānya. (63)
One should have these made into a fine powder in the measure of one *karṣa*. Of barley flour, there should be ninety-two *palas*;
and of ghee, oil, and honey, there should be six *palas* each. 64–65.
The wise person should eat one *modaka* pill, measuring one *karṣa*, every day with these [ingredients]; it will destroy even the most severe and formidable types of *prameha*.
[The ingredients are: *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *śyonāka*, *āragvadha*, and *asan*.
Mango, wood-apple, rose-apple, priyāla, kakubha, dhava (67),
madhūka, madhuka, lodhra, varuṇa, pāribhadraka,
paṭola, meṣaśṛṅgī, dantī, citraka, and māḍhakī (68).
One should prepare fine powders of equal parts of *karañja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *śakra* (indrayava), and the fruits of *bhallātaka*.
This powder, known as *nyagrodhādya*, should be combined with honey.
One should drink the juice of the three fruits followed by urine;
by this practice, the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha) and those conditions of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) are pacified, and pustules (piḍikā) do not arise. (70–71)

One should lick equal parts of powdered iron, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and sugar with honey; this destroys all types of urinary disorders (meha). Alternatively, the fresh juice of guḍūcī may sometimes be drunk. One should also take an equal portion of trikaṭu, triphalā, and guggulu in equal parts.

The wise physician should prepare pills combined with a decoction of *gokṣuraka*; considering the humors, the season, and the strength [of the patient], he should administer this carminative preparation. In this case, there is no need for restrictive dietary rules; one may perform whatever activity one desires.
It quickly destroys urinary disorders (prameha), diseases of the wind (vātaroga), vātaśoṇita, urinary obstruction (mūtrāghāta), defects of the urine (mūtradoṣa), and menorrhagia (pradara).
[The powder of] pomegranate seeds and the grains of kṛmighna [are used].
Rajanī, cavikā, ajājī, nāgara, triphalā, kaṇā,
the fruit of trikaṇṭaka, yavānī, and likewise dhānyaka, combined with vṛkṣāmla, cavikā, lodhra, and sindhūdbhava (rock salt). 76–77.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with these pastes, each weighing one *akṣa*.
It should be administered in appropriate doses during meals or as a drink in all seasons;
it cures the twenty types of *prameha*, as well as urinary obstruction and calculi.
It certainly destroys even the most severe *kṛcchra* (urinary disorders), of this there is no doubt.
This *dāḍimādya-ghṛta*, which cures constipation, abdominal distension, and colic, and destroys jaundice and fever, was proclaimed by the two Aśvins. 79–80.
Śvadaṃṣṭrā with kaṇā, mustā, guḍūcī, the young shoots of phalgu,
sprouts of darbha grass, gaṇḍīra, the leaves of rohiṣa,
kālā, punarnavā, śyāmā, śārivā, and devadāru. 81.
Pippalī, śṛṅgavera, viḍaṅga, and marica; pāṭhā, kampillaka, bhārgī, the two types of haridrā, and nidigdhikā; eraṇḍa root, dantī, citraka, and kaṭurohiṇī. (83)

One should have these made into fine powders in equal proportions; as much of these powders as there is, so much should be iron filings (ayorajas). Then, one should drink a dose the size of a cat's paw with warm water.
Even in the absence of wine, it destroys the twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha), as well as swelling, fever, jaundice, chlorosis,
severe colic pains, and splenic enlargement. 85–86.
The physician should prepare pills from these [drugs] ground with cow’s urine;
they are the foremost remedies for these diseases and increase strength and flesh.
One should collect one hundred [parts] each of *kaṇṭakārī* and *guḍūcī*.
Having crushed [the ingredients] in a mortar, the wise man should boil them in four *droṇas* of water;
when one-fourth remains, he should cook one *prastha* of ghee with *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *rāsnā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *citraka*. 88–89.
One should have the roots of *kāśmarya*, the bark of *pūtīka*, and all parts of the *kaliṅga* plant finely ground into a paste.
A wise person should drink a dose the size of an *akṣa* with milk and *śāli* rice.

This medicated ghee, known by the name Siṃhāmṛta, destroys urinary disorders (prameha), diabetes (madhumeha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara), lethargy, hernia (antravṛddhi), especially skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and consumption (kṣaya). 91–92.
The ten roots (daśamūla), the two types of karañja, devadāru, harītakī,
varṣābhū, varuṇa, dantī, citraka, and punarnavā; 93 sudhā, nīpa, kadamba, bilva, and bhallātaka.
One should boil ten *pala* portions each of *śaṭī*, *puṣkaramūla*, and *pippalīmūla* in one *āḍhaka* of water;
one should also cook one *prastha* each of *yava*, *kola*, and *kulattha*.
With that remaining portion of the decoction, the physician should cook one prastha of ghee,
adding nicula, triphalā, bhārgī, rohiṣa, gajapippalī,
ginger, viḍaṅga, cavya, and kampillaka.
This should be prepared with this [specific] embryo and administered according to the patient's strength.
This is the celebrated and excellent ghee known as Dhānvantara; it cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (prameha), abdominal tumors (gulma), edema (śvayathu), and gout (vātaśoṇita). 97–98.

This ghee cures splenic enlargements, hemorrhoids, abscesses, and those various types of carbuncles; it likewise subdues epilepsy and insanity. Indeed, one should cook one hundred parts each of the medicinal substances separately in water.
When the water has increased by three hundred [units], the ritual discharge (vyutsarga) should occur in due order.
[This is done] with *arjuna*, *paṭola*, and *nimba*, along with *vacā*, *dīpyaka*, *rasā*, *samañjiṣṭhā*, *bhallātaka*, *aguru*, *ghana*, *gadānala*, *candana*, and *uśīra*.

One should cook oil with the paste and decoction of *gokṣuraka*, *somavalka*, fresh *paṭola*, the two types of *haridrā*, *triphalā*, *aśmantaka* and *arjuna*, as well as *dīpyaka* and *lodhra*, along with *mañjiṣṭhā* and *ativiṣā*. 102.
In cases of urinary disorders (meha) arising from phlegm (kapha) and wind (vāta), one should prepare ghee for those caused by bile (pitta).
Having boiled a decoction of the "essence-group" (sāravarga) down until one-fourth remains, one should remove it from the heat, strain it, and then cook it again;
when it is ready, one should add the powders of āmalaka, lodhra, priyaṅgu, dantī, black iron, and copper.

When this has been burnt and turned into a liquid extract (*lehībhūta*), one should pour it out and store it in a well-protected place; then, one should consume it as appropriate. This electuary (*leha*) destroys all types of urinary disorders (*meha*). One should take one hundred *palas* of *gokaṇṭaka*, including its leaves, roots, and fruits, pound them finely, and boil them in water.

Having added fifty *palas* of sugar to water standing at the level of the feet, one should then boil it; when that mixture reaches a thick consistency, one should add two *palas* each of the following powdered ingredients:
ginger, long pepper, black pepper, *nāgadalā*, cinnamon bark, cardamom, jasmine buds, *koṣa*, *kakubha*, and the fruit of *trapusī*. 105–106.
By constantly placing eight pieces of bamboo bark here and licking them daily— pure, like nectar, and weighing one *pala*—
one quickly destroys burning of the urinary tract, constipation, dysuria, urinary calculi, blood in the urine, and diabetes mellitus.
[107] Likewise, *asanā*, *priyāla*, *śāla*, and *khādira*...
Likewise, this Śāla group should be taken by the wise;
with this formulation, an intelligent physician should treat a patient suffering from prameha who has developed madhumeha and has been abandoned by other doctors. (108–109)
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Śukra, when the mountains are heated by the rays of the sun, they indeed exude a resinous substance from their rocks that has the appearance of lac;
this is renowned as *śilājatu*, which wards off great diseases.

Furthermore, among the six metals beginning with trapu (tin), whichever one it may be, that which is known on earth as having six origins should be recognized by its own smell; for from that metal arises śilājatu, which has the luster of lac. 111–112.

Just as that [mercury] possesses the potency or the essence of that iron, so too among tin, lead, iron, and the like, each subsequent one is considered superior; likewise, in their medicinal application, the best are said to possess the best qualities.
All that [pippalī] is bitter and pungent, with an astringent aftertaste, and laxative (sara).
It is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), hot in potency (vīrya), desiccant, and likewise scarifying (chedana).
Among those varieties, that which is light, blackish in appearance, unctuous, and free from grit is the best.

That which smells like cow’s urine or is blue, and which is said to be preeminent for its qualities, should be processed with the groups of essential minerals (sāragaṇas) to remove its impurities; then, from the first day, one should drink it, finely ground with the water of the essence (sārodaka), according to one's strength. 116.
One should eat with meat broth from wild animals, and once that has been digested, take one's meal.
Having consumed one *tulā* of this nectar from its very inception, one conquers the disease known as *madhumeha*, which causes illness. (117–118)
Endowed with a beautiful body, excellent complexion, and strength, one lives for a hundred years free from disease;

by the method of the *bhallātaka* [fruit], it is taught that one gains a hundred [units] on the scale, and ten times that amount for every thousand [fruits]. This is the prescribed rule for the regimen of avoidance.

Shilājatu, when consumed for a period of time, quickly dispels urinary disorders, skin diseases, epilepsy, insanity, elephantiasis, artificial poisons, consumption, swellings, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, jaundice, and irregular fevers.

There is no disease that *śilājatu* cannot overcome; it likewise breaks up gravel and stones that have been present for a long time. Its preparation through soaking and stirring should be performed with beneficial medicinal substances.
Thus, the *mākṣika* mineral, born from the Tāpī river and resembling nectar—
sweet and with the luster of gold, or sour and with the brilliance of silver—
dispels old age, leprosy, urinary disorders, anemia, and consumption. 123–124.
One should avoid kulattha beans and pigeon meat that have been prepared with those [same substances]. For prameha-piḍikās, bloodletting should first be performed;
once they have suppurated, incision is required, and their decoction is recommended for drinking.
A decoction of *vanaspati* (the soap-berry tree), goat’s urine, and a sharp purifying agent;
oil with a paste of the *elādi* group for wound healing;
one should prepare a decoction with the *āragvadhādi* group and apply medicinal rubs (*udvartana*). 127.
One should administer infusions of *śālasāra* and other such substances, as well as food and other items made from chickpeas and similar legumes.
When the urine of a patient suffering from *prameha* becomes free of turbidity, non-viscid, clear, and bitter or pungent, then it is declared that health has been restored. (128–129)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter on the treatment of urinary disorders and carbuncles (pramehapiḍikā).
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter on obesity (sthaulya):
[It occurs] in one who indulges in lack of exercise, sleeping during the day, and foods that increase phlegm (śleṣman).

The sweet taste of food generally increases fat through its oily quality. Because the channels are obstructed by fat, the other bodily tissues do not flourish; consequently, fat accumulates, and one becomes incapable of all activities.
Endowed with labored breathing, thirst, delusion, sleepiness, snoring,
and exhaustion, as well as hunger, perspiration, and foul odor, such a person has little vitality and little sexual desire.
Indeed, fat (medas) is situated within the bellies of all living beings.
For this very reason, an enlargement of the abdomen generally occurs in those who are obese;
because the channels are obstructed by fat, the wind (vāyu) moving particularly within the abdominal cavity kindles the digestive fire and even dries up the food.
Therefore, it quickly digests food, craves nourishment,
and undergoes certain terrible morbid transformations due to the lapse of time;
these two, fire and wind, are particularly the causes of such complications.
For these two burn away the gross [body] like a forest fire and wind;
when fat has become excessively increased, disorders such as wind (anila) and the rest suddenly produce terrible afflictions and swiftly destroy life.
A man whose buttocks, abdomen, and breasts are flabby due to the excessive increase of fat and flesh,
and who lacks the vigor for appropriate exertion, is said to be "excessively obese" (atisthūla).
In such an obese person, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), and fistulas (bhagaṇḍara) are difficult to overcome.
From the sweat and foul odor of fat, minute creatures are born; these afflictions—fever, dysentery, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, elephantiasis, scabies, and jaundice—arise from it.
Old *śāli* rice, mung beans, horse gram, wild millet, and *kodrava* [are recommended].
Purgation and enemas should always be employed by one who is obese.
Likewise, smoking, the avoidance of anger, bloodletting,
and eating only after the previous meal has been digested, as well as a constant diet of barley and wheat, should be observed.
Fasting, sleeping on the ground, nobility of spirit, and the conquest of darkness— through these,

one is gradually liberated from the defects caused by over-nourishment and from obesity. One who is fond of physical exertion, reflection, sexual intercourse, travel, honey, and staying awake [is also freed].
One who subsists on a diet of barley and *śyāmāka* grain inevitably destroys excessive corpulence.
(14) Barley flour mixed with *cavya*, cumin, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), asafoetida, *sauvarcala* salt, and *analā* salt, when drunk with whey, destroys fat and kindles the digestive fire. (15)
The three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (trikaṭuka), along with oil and salt,
when used for six months, destroy phlegm, fat, and wind. Viḍaṅga, ginger, alkali, iron filings, and honey [are also used].
The powder of barley and āmalaka is a formulation that destroys excessive corpulence (17).

Alternatively, the root [of śilājatu] or the powder of triphalā mixed with honey, or the decoction of honey-water, or the application of the five roots beginning with bilva combined with honey [are effective]. (18)
Maṇḍaka, when consumed regularly, is declared to be a certain remover of excessive corpulence.
For one who drinks water boiled with rough leaves, fire, and *śatapuṣpā* mixed with asafoetida, the increase of all types of fat is invariably destroyed. (19–20)

A person should drink an alkaline solution of *vātāri* leaves mixed with *hiṅgu* along with rice and scum (*maṇḍa*) for the destruction of increased fat (*medovṛddhi*). Alternatively, one may take roasted barley flour (*saktu*) made from the ground flour of *gavedhukā* or barley.
A decoction of Triphalā mixed with honey, when drunk, is considered a destroyer of fat (medas).
Likewise, a decoction of Guḍūcī and Triphalā combined with iron filings,
or one should cook Aśmajam or Mahiṣākṣa according to that same procedure.
A castor seed placed inside a *atimuktaka* flower and licked with honey destroys enlargement of the abdomen;
likewise, one who eats wholesome food may take the root of *citraka* with honey.
Or, the root of *eraṇḍa* smeared with honey may be kept for the entire night.
By drinking that water, the enlargement of the abdomen subsides.
Water mixed with honey consumed in the morning destroys obesity;
by drinking hot rice-scum (maṇḍa) with food, one becomes lean of body.

A gruel prepared with a paste of *badarī* leaves and processed with *kāñjika* vinegar destroys obesity; likewise, a decoction of the juice of *agnimantha*, *rasa*, and *śilājatu* [is effective]. Furthermore, [a preparation] with *śaileya*, *kuṣṭha*, *aguru*, *devadāru*, *kauntī*, *mustā*, and the five leaves [is beneficial].

Having thoroughly ground together *śrīvāsa*, *spṛkkā*, *kharapuṣpa*, and *devapuṣpa*, along with all these [other ingredients], a firm massage with the juice of *dhattūra* leaves is prescribed for removing obesity.
[The following formulation consists of: *amṛtā*, *truṭi*, *vella*, *vatsaka*, *kali*, *pathyā*, *āmalakāni*, and *guggulu*.
This [Guggulu], gradually increased in dose and saturated with honey, conquers carbuncles, enlargement of the scrotum, and fistula-in-ano (29).
One who consumes Guggulu in equal parts with Vyosha, Agni, Triphala, Musta,
and Vidanga overcomes all diseases born of fat, phlegm, and undigested matter (Ama) associated with Vata (30).
One who consumes Mahiṣākṣa resin with equal quantities of trikaṭu, agni (citraka), ghanavella, and vacā, along with clarified butter,
quickly destroys disorders arising from phlegm, wind, fat, and other humors, even when they are powerful.
Guggulu, tālamūlī, triphalā, khadira, and vṛṣa— [31]
One should boil ten palas each of trivṛt, alambuṣā, śuṇṭhī, nirguṇḍī, and likewise citraka in five āḍhakas of water;
having reduced it to one-quarter, one should then remove the decoction from the heat.
Twelve palas of well-powdered gold (rukmaloha) should be added;
one prastha of aged ghee combined with eight palas of sugar should be cooked in a copper vessel and then, once well-cooled, opened. 34–35.
Half a *prastha* of honey should be added, along with two *palas* of *śilājatu*,
half a *pala* each of cardamom and cinnamon bark, three *palas* of *viḍaṅga*, and two *palas* each of black pepper, *añjana*, and long pepper, combined with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (36)
Two palas of kāsīsa (green vitriol), finely powdered by the wise, should be mixed with this powder and thoroughly stirred; it should then be placed in a smooth vessel.
Thereafter, one whose body has been purified should consume a dose the size of an akṣa.
One should drink milk as a post-drink (anupāna), or likewise the meat-broth of wild animals;

it is excellent for removing vāta and kapha, and cures skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (meha), abdominal enlargements (udara), jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), edema (śvayathu), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara). 39.
Fainting, delusion, poison, insanity, and toxic drugs are formidable [obstacles]. For those who are corpulent, emaciation is best; for the obese, it is the supreme medicine.
One should excessively emaciate the belly until it resembles the netherworld (pātāla). 40–41.
It is strengthening, an elixir, intellect-promoting, and a supreme aphrodisiac;
it brings prosperity, produces offspring, and destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
One should not eat the root of the plantain, sour gruel, or the *karamardaka* fruit.
One should avoid the *karīra* and *kāravella* vegetables, as they begin with the letter 'ka'.
Then, having strained the decoction of *śālasāra* and other woods reduced to one-fourth its original volume, it should be cooled and sweetened with honey. 43–44.

One should place into a prepared jar that has been saturated with ghee: molasses that has reached the consistency of thick syrup, purified jaggery, and fine powders of the group of drugs beginning with *pippalī*. (45)
When the interior has been smeared with long pepper powder and honey,
the wise and prudent practitioner should repeatedly insert thin, sharp iron plates that have been heated many times in charcoal of the Khadira tree.
Then, having provided a good covering, one should place it in a vessel made of barley husks for three or four months, or until the metal has been completely consumed.
Then, at dawn every day, a person should take the produced juice according to their strength.
One should employ it as appropriate and prepare his diet accordingly.
This [preparation] draws out obesity, awakens the extinguished digestive fire, destroys edema, cures skin diseases and urinary disorders, and removes abdominal tumors and anemia. 49–50.

Lohāriṣṭa is highly efficacious for quickly removing splenic enlargement (plīhodara), destroying irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), and eliminating obstructive secretions (abhiṣyanda). [One should take] the three pungents (vyoṣa), citraka, śigru, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and kaṭurohiṇī.

One should powder two *bṛhatī* plants, the two types of *haridrā*, *pāṭhā*, *ativiṣā*, *sthirā*, asafoetida, the root of *kevuka*, *yavānī*, *dhānya*, *citraka*, *sauvarcala* salt, cumin, and *hapuṣā*. (53)
The portions of powder, oil, ghee, and honey should be equal in measure;
the portion of flour should be sixteen times that amount. One should drink this nourishing preparation (*santarpaṇa*).
By its use, diseases arising from over-nutrition (*santarpaṇa*) are pacified. (54)
Urinary disorders, obstructed flatus, skin diseases,
hemorrhoids, jaundice, splenic enlargement, anemia, edema, dysuria, anorexia, heart disease, pulmonary consumption, cough, asthma, and throat obstruction.
Worms, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī-doṣa), leucoderma, and excessive corpulence [are cured];
furthermore, the digestive fire of men is kindled, and memory and intellect increase.
(57) [This is prepared] with Triphalā, Ativiṣā, Mūrvā, Trivṛt, Citraka, and Vāsaka.
Oil cooked with equal parts of nimba, āragvadha, ṣaḍgranthā, saptaparṇa, the two types of niśā (turmeric),
guḍūcī, indrāsurī, kṛṣṇā, kuṣṭha, sarṣapa, and nāgara, and saturated with the juice of the surasādi group, [is effective]. 58–59.
When applied as a drink, anointment, gargle, nasal drop, or enema,
it overcomes diseases caused by kapha, such as obesity, lassitude, and jaundice.
Sandalwood, saffron, uśīra, priyaṅgu, trutī, and rocanā—
Turushka, aguru, kasturi, karpura, jātipatrikā (61),
the fruits of jātī, kaṅkola, pūga, and lavaṅga, as well as nalikā, nalada, kuṣṭha, hareṇu, tagara, and plava (62).
Navavyāghranakha, spṛkkā, bola, and likewise damanaka;
sthauṇeyaka, coraka, śaileya, and sailavāluka;
sarala, saptaparṇa, lākṣā, and tāmalakī. 63.

One should prepare the oil known as Mahāsugandha by cooking one *prastha* of oil with equal parts of one *śāṇa* each of *lāmajjaka*, *padmaka*, the flowers of *dhātakī*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, and *karcūra*. (64–65)
This is the supreme remedy for removing perspiration, foul odor, itching, and leprosy.
One whose body is anointed with this, even if aged or seventy years old,
becomes youthful, rich in semen, and exceedingly beloved by women.
Fortunate and handsome, he shall go among hundreds of women.
Even a barren woman conceives, and even a eunuch acts as a man.
A sonless man obtains a son and shall live for a hundred autumns.
Thus, this great fragrant oil,
or the juice of *vāsā* leaves combined with conch-shell powder, or even the juice of *bilva* leaves, when applied as an ointment, destroys foul body odor. 69
A powder made from *alambuṣā* drunk with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) quickly destroys foul body odor in men caused by corrupted fat.
An ointment of equal parts *bilva* and *śivā* removes the odor of the armpits.
Furthermore, a ripe *piḍikā* or seed from the *pūtikarañja*,
or the fresh juice of *ciñcā* leaves combined with a paste and other ingredients, or an ointment of burnt turmeric, quickly overcomes long-standing body odor. 71–72.
A rubbing powder (*pragharṣa*) made of *śirīṣa*, *lāmajjaka*, and *hemalodhra* removes skin disorders and excessive perspiration.

An ointment (*pradeha*) consisting of *patra*, *ambu*, *loha*, *abhaya*, and *candana* removes foul body odor. [This ointment] combined with the juice of *hilamocī* and powders derived from sea-foam (*udadhiphena*). (73)

By means of this ointment, one quickly removes the intense foul odor of the body. Having ground a *harītakī* fruit, a person should rub it onto the body and then perform a bath for the sake of pacifying bodily perspiration.

Harītakī, lodhra, leaves of ariṣṭa, mango bark, and pomegranate rind—this is declared to be the cosmetic paste for women; whereas a decoction of jambū is for kings. Ground with cow’s urine and combined with cow’s milk, it destroys leprosy and makes the complexion radiant.
It removes the foul odor of the armpits and other areas; when used with milk by a couple desiring subjugation, it is highly recommended.
(77) One should thoroughly rub the body with the leaves of the *babbūla* tree well-ground with water, followed by well-pounded *harītakī*. (78)
Having performed the rubbing of the body once more, one should afterwards perform the bath;
thus one is quickly freed from perspiration, and therefore one should act in this manner. (79) [Using] the leaves of the bilva, mango, jambu, and pūrakā, mixed with the petals of the kapittha.

Having purified it with *vaca* according to the methods for preparing substances as before, for the sake of excellent fragrance, one should repeatedly fumigate it with *pathyā*, *nakhī*, *candana*, *kuṣṭha*, and *sarja*, along with *aguru* and sugar;
this incense, which captivates the hearts of people, is renowned by the name "Malayānila. (80–81)

In the summer, an unguent made from *caṇḍāṃśuka*, sesame, *lodhra*, *śirīṣa*, *uśīra*, and *kesara* serves to ward off the effects of perspiration. At dawn, one should lick a powder of *abhayā* fruit mixed with wine and honey.

By removing sweat, even a man attains extreme fragrance. (83) An ointment made from jasmine flowers and *karilā* [is effective]; likewise, during the burning heat of *vicarcikā*, a paste of *vica-kila* leaves, *haridrā*, and *parkaṭī* leaves combined with *dūrvā* grass [should be applied]. (84)

By grinding [these ingredients] and applying them as an ointment to the body, *dharmavicarcī* (febrile eruptions) is pacified. 85 When there is discharge from the hands and feet, *guggulu* and the *pañcatiktaka* (five bitter herbs) should be applied;
if one is unable [to apply them], one should untiringly consume the clarified butter known as *pañcatikta*. 86

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Section on Obesity (*Sthaulya-adhikāra*), or alternatively, the Section on Diseases of Fat (*Medas-roga-adhikāra*). Now begins the fortieth chapter, the Section on Emaciation (*Kārśya-adhikāra*):
Vata [is aggravated] by dry foods and drinks, fasting, and eating in measured quantities.
Excessive physical activity, grief, the suppression of natural urges and sleep, constant illness, constant sexual indulgence, over-exertion, eating too little,
fear, and anxiety regarding wealth and other matters are said to be the causes of emaciation.
One who has dry buttocks, abdomen, and neck, with a network of prominent veins,
