whose skin and bones are parched, who is extremely emaciated, and whose facial joints appear large, is considered [to suffer from] splenic disorders,
cough, consumption, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and abdominal enlargements.
Diseases beginning with malabsorption (grahaṇī) run rampant, making one extremely emaciated;
yet, at the time of conception, another person who is exceedingly thin is seen to be very strong,
provided his portion of semen (*śukra*) is predominant.
One whose portion of fat is deficient may be emaciated yet possess great strength;
whereas one whose portion of fat is excessive will have a diminished portion of semen, and thus, even if appearing oily and well-nourished, is seen to be devoid of strength.
However, for one who has become emaciated due to the consumption of dry food and similar causes, one should administer medicine that is nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*),
strength-promoting, aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), and likewise an aphrodisiac tonic (*vājīkarana*).
Ashwagandha, when drunk with milk, ghee, oil, or warm water for half a month, [produces these effects].
It bestows nourishment upon the emaciated body, just as a rain of water does for a young crop.
Oil prepared with the paste of *aśvagandhā* and its decoction, along with milk, grants nourishment to the limbs when used as an oil massage for those who are thin-bodied.

One should employ the horse-ghṛta (aśvagandhā-ghṛta) prescribed for nourishment and for diseases of children; likewise, one should use the horse-ghṛta and other formulations mentioned for aphrodisiac purposes. This applies to one who is excessively emaciated by nature or whose digestive fire is naturally weak.
"And for one who is weak by nature, there is no cure.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter on emaciation (Kārśyādhikāra).
Now begins the forty-first chapter on abdominal enlargements (Udarādhikāra).
All diseases, and especially abdominal disorders, arise when the digestive fire is weak;
they accumulate from the buildup of impurities due to indigestion and unwholesome food. The accumulated doshas obstruct the channels that carry sweat and water.
By vitiating the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they produce abdominal enlargement (udara) in men. [The symptoms include] flatulence,
inability to walk, debility, weak digestion, edema,
lassitude of the limbs, and the obstruction of flatus and feces.
Indeed, burning sensations and lassitude occur in all types of abdominal enlargements (udara).

Eight types of udara arise from the individual doṣas, from all the doṣas combined, and from splenic enlargement (plīha), intestinal obstruction (baddha), perforation (kṣata), and ascites (udaka); hear now their symptoms individually.
In that condition, vātodara (wind-belliedness), there is swelling in the hands, feet, navel, and abdomen;
pain in the sides of the abdomen, the belly, the waist, and the back; splitting pain in the joints; dry cough; aching of the limbs; heaviness; and the retention of waste products.
The abdomen becomes dark-brown or reddish in color, appearing suddenly with fluctuating decrease and increase;
it is accompanied by piercing pain and a sense of being split open, is covered with thin, black veins, and when struck, it produces a sound like that of a distended leather bag.
In this condition, the wind (vāyu) moves everywhere with a painful sound and all-pervasive motion.

In Pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara), there is fever, fainting, burning sensation, thirst, a bitter taste in the mouth, vertigo, diarrhea, and yellowness of the skin and other parts; the abdomen is greenish-yellow.
In *śleṣmodara*, the abdomen is bound with yellowish-brown veins, is perspiring and hot,
feels as if it is burning, emits smoke, is soft to the touch, suppurates quickly, and is intensely painful; furthermore, there is lassitude of the limbs, swelling, and heaviness.
Lassitude, distress, loss of appetite, sleepiness, coughing, and whiteness of the skin and other parts;
a large abdomen that is motionless, unctuous, marked with white streaks,
slow to increase in size, hard, cold to the touch, heavy, and stable— these are the symptoms.

When women of immoral conduct give food and drink mixed with their own nails, hair, urine, feces, or menstrual blood, or when enemies administer poisons, or due to the consumption of contaminated water or toxic substances,
the provoked humors (doṣas) quickly cause a most dreadful abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) characterized by the three symptoms.
In cold winds and especially during heavy rain, it becomes aggravated;
the patient suffers from a burning sensation, faints repeatedly, and becomes pale, emaciated, and parched with thirst.
This is declared to be *dūṣyodara*; now learn of what is called *plīhodara*.
When it increases due to the enlargement of the spleen, one should know that indeed it is *plīhodara* (splenic abdominal enlargement).
It enlarges on the left side of the heart; as for its causes, whatever [cause] there may be, when the spleen has increased, the symptoms which have been described by the best of physicians [occur].

All those [symptoms] are also seen in embodied beings suffering from splenomegaly (plīhodara). Furthermore, when the fat (medas) and liver (yakṛt) are enlarged, that is known as yakṛddālyudara; likewise, when the liver is enlarged on the left side, that very condition is to be understood as yakṛddālyudara. (17–18)
When a man's intestine is properly covered with food that leaves a residue, or with small stones,
and his waste gradually accumulates and becomes obstructed within the channel like a heap of refuse,
his feces emerge from the anus with great difficulty, in very small quantities.

When it increases in the middle of the heart and navel, they call that *udara* "bound anus" (*baddhaguda*). Likewise, when a foreign body or food obstructs the intestine, and the ingested food pierces it—whether arriving naturally or otherwise—a discharge resembling water flows from the pierced intestine and issues forth abundantly from the anus. (20–21)

When the abdomen below the navel increases in size and is excessively pierced with pricking pain as if being split open, this is designated as *parisrāvyudara* (diarrheic abdominal enlargement); now listen as I describe *kṣatodara* (traumatic abdominal enlargement).

One who has been treated with oleation (*sneha*), or an oil enema (*anuvāsana*), or has undergone emesis (*vamana*), purgation (*virecana*), or a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), [and subsequently develops such symptoms...]
If he drinks cold water immediately, the channels that carry it become vitiated. Furthermore, when those channels are smeared with unctuous matter, *dakodara* (ascites) arises as before;
it becomes unctuous, large, with a distended umbilicus, and appears as if filled with water on all sides.

Just as a leather bag swells, trembles, or even makes a sound when filled with water, so too is every abdomen [afflicted] from birth; generally, it is considered most difficult to treat. However, that which is strong, has no fluid accumulation, and has recently arisen can be cured with effort.
Baddhaguda (intestinal obstruction) occurring after a fortnight, as well as all cases of Jātodaka (ascites),
and Chidrāntra (perforated intestine) generally lead to the death of men;
like a leather bag filled with water, they become soft and produce a sound upon agitation.
A large abdomen that is not prominent in its veins, appears empty, and is free from pain; lassitude, a bad taste in the mouth, frequent urination, and rapid defecation;
as well as weak digestion and pallor—these are the signs of one in whom water has accumulated (jātodaka).
One should avoid a patient who has swollen eyes, a deformed perineum, and moist, thin skin; one whose strength, blood, flesh, and digestive fire are depleted;
and one afflicted by side-pain, aversion to food, swelling, and diarrhea. 29.
One should avoid a patient suffering from abdominal dropsy (udari) who has been purged yet continues to swell again.

Castor oil mixed with *daśamūla*, or the juice of *triphalā* combined with cow's urine, destroys wind-type abdominal enlargement (*vātodara*), edema, and colic; likewise, a decoction of *daśamūla* taken with cow's urine achieves the same result. (30–31)
Kuṣṭha, dantī, yavakṣāra, vyoṣa, the three salts (trilavaṇa), vacā,
ajājī, dīpyaka, hiṅgu, svarjikā, cavya, citraka,
and śuṇṭhī— when drunk with warm water, this [mixture] removes the pain of vātodara.
One should boil one *tulā* of garlic in a *droṇa* of water,
along with *trikuṭā*, *triphalā*, *dantī*, *hiṅgu*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *citraka*,
*devadāru*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, honey, *śigru*, and *punarnavā*. (34)

One pala each of sauvarcala salt, viḍaṅga, dīpyaka, and gajapippalī, along with six palas of trivṛt— having ground these together, one should cook the oil over a mild fire with this decoction. (35–36)
Having risen in the morning, one should drink this according to one's digestive strength and in the proper dose;
it destroys all diseases, particularly abdominal ailments, dysuria, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), inguinal hernia, and intestinal worms. (37)
Colic arising in the sides and flanks, colic from undigested matter (āma), loss of appetite, liver disorders, stones, abdominal distension, splenic enlargement, and pain in the limbs—
all these eighty diseases born of vāta perish within a single month. 38–39.
In the case of *pittodara*, however, the physician should first administer a strong purgative to the patient using milk mixed with the paste of *trivṛt* boiled with *eraṇḍa* oil; thereafter,
he should have the patient drink clarified butter cooked with the *pippalyādi* group of drugs.

For the constant cure of *kapha*-type abdominal enlargement, one should give a person who eats wholesome food oil or clarified butter cooked with the paste of ginger and *triphalā*, ground with curd and water;
this should be drunk in all types of abdominal enlargements. 41–42.
A diet of *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, barley, and *nīvāra* millet; as well as *nirūha* enemas and purgatives, are excellent for all types of abdominal enlargements (*jaṭhara*).
[One should avoid] meat from marshy or aquatic animals, leafy vegetables, flour-based foods, and sesame seeds.
One should avoid physical exercise, walking long distances, sleeping during the day, and drinking oily substances (44).
Likewise, one should not eat foods that are pungent, salty, hot, burning, or heavy; furthermore, one should avoid drinking water when the stomach is full (45).
Because the abdomen is rich in impurities, frequent purification is beneficial;
one should repeatedly drink milk with castor oil or with urine.
A patient suffering from Vata-type abdominal enlargement (Vatodara) should drink buttermilk mixed with long pepper and salt.
One suffering from *pittodara* (bilious abdominal enlargement) should drink it sweetened with sugar and black pepper (47).
One suffering from *kaphodara* (phlegmatic abdominal enlargement) should take it combined with *yavānī*, *hapuṣā*, cumin, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
One suffering from *sannipātodara* (abdominal enlargement due to the combination of all three humors) should take it combined with the three pungents, alkali, and rock salt (48).
Yavānī, hapuṣā, dhānyaka, triphalā, upakuñcikā, kāravī, pippalīmūla, ajagandhā, śaṭī, vacā,
śatāhvā, jīraka, vyoṣa, svarṇakṣīrī, and citraka. (49)
Two parts each of the two alkalis (kṣāra), puṣkaramūla, kuṣṭha, and the five salts;
one part each of viḍaṅga and dantī (three parts total for dantī);
trivṛt and viśālā in double the amount [of the other ingredients]; and śātalā should be four times the amount. (50–51)
This powder, named Nārāyaṇa, is a destroyer of hosts of diseases;

having obtained it, diseases retreat just as the Asuras retreated before Viṣṇu. (52) It should be drunk with buttermilk by those suffering from abdominal enlargements, and with the decoction of jujube fruits by those suffering from abdominal tumors.
In cases of wind-disorders caused by obstructed wind, one should drink with wine; in wind-diseases, with *prasannā* wine;
in diarrhea with whey; in hemorrhoids, with pomegranate juice; in cutting pains, with *vṛkṣāmla*; and in indigestion, with warm water. (53–54)
In cases of fistula-in-ano, anemia, cough, dyspnea, throat-obstruction,
heart disease, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), spinal deformity (kubja), weak digestion, and fever;
in cases of venom from fangs, vegetable poisons, snake venom, and artificial poisons— 55.
As it has been said: this purgative should be drunk by one with a soft bowel (snigdhakoṣṭha).

One karṣa each of snuk-milk, dantī, triphalā, viḍaṅga, siṃhī, trivṛt, citraka, and karṣaka [are combined] and cooked with ghee measuring one kuḍava; then, one akṣa or half a karṣa of that [mixture] is taken with water.

Having drunk hot water during purgation, one who knows the proper method should drink gruel or meat broth; the wise declare that this "Nārāca" formulation, when administered with skill, is a remedy for abdominal diseases.
(58) One should take one *karṣa* of the paste of *vajrāṇḍī*, wrapped in curd and the like.
For the constant pacification of abdominal diseases, one should swallow [the medicine] with water. 59.

A decoction prepared according to the prescribed method by those skilled in the rules, using *punarnavā*, *dāruniśā*, *satiktā*, *paṭola*, *pathyā*, *picumanda*, *mustā*, *nāgara*, and *acchinnaruhā*—all these together—[is effective]. 60.

Taken in the morning with cow’s urine and combined with guggulu, this [medicine] certainly destroys for men all types of edema, abdominal diseases, cough, colic, dyspnea, and the affliction of jaundice. 61.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, on the treatment of abdominal diseases. 41.

Now begins the forty-second chapter on swelling (śotha). Swelling occurs in those who are undergoing purification, those afflicted by mental delusion, and those emaciated by fasting or weakness, due to the excessive consumption of alkaline, sour, pungent, hot, and heavy substances, as well as from the intake of curd, uncooked food, clay, vegetables, incompatible foods, flour-based preparations, *garu* poison, and food mixed with anger. 1.

Hemorrhoids, physical inactivity, impurity of the body, injury to the vital points (marmans), difficult labor, and improper administration of therapeutic measures are declared to be the causes of endogenous swelling (nija-śvayathu). Furthermore,
the vitiated Vāyu, along with blood, Pitta, and Kapha, leads the corrupted humors outward through the vessels.

For when their movement is obstructed by these [factors], they take refuge in the skin and flesh and produce a raised, compact swelling; because it is a collection [of humors], they call that "nicaya" (accumulation).
It would be heavy, unstable, elevated, hot, and characterized by thinness of the veins.

Loss of body hair, horripilation, and discoloration are declared to be the general signs of swelling (śvayathu). A swelling caused by Vāyu is mobile, characterized by thin, rough, reddish, or dark skin; it is accompanied by numbness, horripilation, and pain; it subsides without apparent cause and rises again when pressed; it is more pronounced during the day, and this is the swelling arising from wind.

That which is soft, malodorous, colored with black and yellow tints, accompanied by giddiness, fever, perspiration, thirst, and intoxication, which becomes painful to the touch and causes redness of the eyes, and is characterized by intense burning and suppuration, is Pittaja swelling (pitta-śotha). That which is heavy, stable, pale, associated with anorexia, salivation, drowsiness, vomiting, and suppression of the digestive fire [is Kaphaja swelling].

One who has suppressed a swelling caused by a single [dosha] through fasting and other means will not recover; such a swelling caused by kapha, characterized by three folds [on the abdomen], may even rise up again.
A swelling born from the combination of two doshas should be understood through the conjunction of their respective etiology and clinical features.
A swelling arising from the derangement of all three doshas (sannipāta) exhibits all possible forms and possesses mixed characteristics.
Due to trauma from weapons and the like, such as cutting, piercing, or wounding;
or through contact with frost, wind, ocean spray, or the sap and bristles of the *bhallātaka* and *pikacchu* plants, an edematous swelling accompanied by spreading (visarpa) may occur.
The fever characterized by bile (pitta) is generally very hot and has a reddish appearance.
That caused by poison arises from the crawling over or urination by venomous creatures,
as well as from the bites of teeth, tusks, or claws— even of creatures that are not poisonous.
Due to contact with substances defiled by feces, urine, semen, or impure objects;

from the touch of the wind carrying poisonous trees; or from being dusted with artificial poisons (*gara-yoga*), [the poison] becomes mild, mobile, adhesive, rapid in action, and causes burning sensations and pain. (13)

The doshas, when situated in the stomach (āmāśaya), produce swelling in the upper part of the body; when situated in the seat of bile (pittāśaya), they produce it in the middle; and when located in the seat of feces (varcaḥsthāna), they produce it in the lower part. However, having pervaded the entire body, they likewise produce generalized edema (sarvasara). 14
Vomiting, dyspnea, anorexia, thirst, fever, diarrhea,
and debility— these seven are the complications of edema.
(15) Dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, debility, and fever [are also its signs].
One should avoid a patient suffering from swelling who has no appetite for food.
Swelling in the central part of the body, that which spreads to all limbs, that which occurs in half the body as a fatal sign (ariṣṭa), and that which creeps upwards— these are difficult to cure.
An edema caused by no other affliction that has arisen on the feet kills a man; however, one arising on the face kills a woman, and one arising from the bladder kills both.
Water boiled with ginger, *punarnavā*, castor root, and the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) [is beneficial].
In swelling caused by Vāta, a decoction of paṭola, triphalā, ariṣṭa, and dārvī, taken with guggulu, is recommended for both drink and food;
likewise, it destroys swelling produced by Pitta as well as that arising from Śleṣman. 19–20.
In cases of combined causes, one should employ a combined treatment; indeed, in all types, one should drink the strained juice of *bilva* leaves mixed with pungent spices.
In swelling caused by external factors (*āgantuja*), one should apply cooling measures such as affusions and plasters.
Black earth mixed with sesame seeds removes swelling when combined with *bhallātaka*.
When smeared with sesame seeds ground with buffalo milk and mixed with fresh butter (*navanīta*), swelling arising from *bhallātaka* is pacified.
An ointment made of yaṣṭīmadhu, milk, and sesame seeds combined with fresh butter, along with the powder of śāla leaves, destroys swelling caused by the *āruṣkara* plant;
or alternatively, the fresh butter of a buffalo mixed with milk and sesame seeds, when applied as an ointment, achieves the same result. (24–25)
A decoction of *pathyā*, *haridrā*, *bhārgī*, *amṛtā*, *citraka*, *dārvī*, *punarnavā*, *dāru*,

and *mahauṣadha* forcibly destroys swelling located in the abdomen, hands, feet, and face before long. A decoction derived from the three fruits (*phalatrika*), prepared with cow's urine, [should be used].

It destroys swelling arising from vāta and kapha located in the testicles. Alternatively, milk that has been well-boiled according to the prescribed method with vṛścīra, devadruma, and nāgara, or with dantī, trivṛt, tryūṣaṇa, and citraka, when drunk, is praised by physicians as a supreme remedy for swelling.
Likewise, one should perform a soothing sprinkling with a decoction of *seka*, *arkavarṣābhū*, and *nimba* to remove swelling,
or even with lukewarm cow’s urine.
Furthermore, [one may use] *punarnavā*, *dāru*, *śuṇṭhī*, *śigru*, and *siddhārthaka*.
This plaster, ground with sour gruel and applied lukewarm, removes all types of swelling.

Alternatively, a person should consume one *karṣa* (approximately 12g) of jaggery with fresh ginger, or jaggery with dry ginger, or jaggery with *abhayā*, or jaggery with long pepper, gradually increasing the dose by one *karṣa* until it reaches three *palas* (approximately 180g), and continue this for either a fortnight or a month.

When Viśva is practiced in equal measure with jaggery, followed by an after-drink of Bṛścīra juice, it destroys edema, catarrh, diseases of the throat and mouth, along with asthma, cough, anorexia, chronic rhinitis, and the like; it likewise cures chronic fever, hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), and other diseases of kapha and vāta. (32)
It destroys all swelling, just as a fierce wind disperses a dense mass of clouds.
(33) A powder made of pippalī and ginger, taken with jaggery, is a destroyer of swelling;
it pacifies indigestion caused by undigested matter (āmājīrṇa), relieves colic, and cleanses the bladder. (34)

Three palas of jaggery should be taken, along with three palas of ginger; black pepper equal to the ginger, and one pala each of iron filings and sesame seeds—this powder is prescribed as the destroyer of all types of swelling (śvayathu). 35.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the decoction and paste of *māṇaka*; this cures swelling caused by a single *doṣa*, by two *doṣas*, or by all three *doṣas*.
[36] [Ghee may also be cooked] with dried radish, *varṣābhū*, *dāru*, *rāsnā*, and *mahauṣadha*.
Matured oil used as an ointment removes swelling accompanied by pain.
(37) Thus ends the forty-second chapter on Swelling (Śotha).
Now begins the forty-third chapter on Enlargement of the Scrotum (Vṛddhi) and Hernia (Bradhna). (43)
This disease, Vṛddhi, is of seven types according to whether it arises from the humors (doṣas), blood, fat, urine, or the intestines;

however, even those arising from urine and the intestines have the wind (vāyu) as their sole cause, though with specific distinctions. It produces an enlargement by carrying [the humors] toward the scrotum and the testicles.
The wind, its movement obstructed, blocks the vessels leading to the scrotum;
it feels like a leather bag filled with air, is rough, and causes pain without an apparent cause due to vāta.
Due to pitta, it resembles a ripe udumbara fruit and is characterized by burning, heat, and suppuration.
That caused by *kapha* is cold, heavy, unctuous, itchy, hard, and slightly painful (5).
That born from blood is covered with black vesicles and exhibits the symptoms of increased *pitta* (6).
The increase of fat (*medas*) is like that of *kapha*, being soft and resembling the fruit of the palmyra palm (7).

In one who habitually suppresses the urge to urinate, that [urine] becomes turbid as he moves, like a leather bag filled with water; it causes a mild urinary obstruction accompanied by pain, along with a trembling of the scrotum and the perineal region. (8)
When the small intestine is agitated by foods that provoke the wind (vāta), by immersion in cold water,
by the retention [of breath], by battle, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, by uneven movements of the limbs,
and by other such disturbances;
When the Vāyu becomes deranged, it may draw [the contents] down from its own location;
then, situated at the groin joint, it produces a swelling resembling a knot.
If neglected, that same Vāyu causes enlargement of the scrotum (muṣkavṛddhi), accompanied by distension, pain, and stiffness.
When compressed, it moves with an internal sound; when released, it returns, distending as it goes.

When there is an adhesion of the intestinal parts to the scrotum due to a collection of wind (vāta), this is *antravṛddhi* (intestinal hernia), which is incurable and resembles *vātavṛddhi* (flatus-induced scrotal enlargement) in appearance. 11
Due to the consumption of excessively unctuous, heavy, dry, or putrid meat,

the bodily humors (doṣas) produce a swelling resembling a glandular tumor at the inguinal joints; characterized by fever, pain, and a sense of exhaustion in the limbs, one should designate this condition as *bradhna*.
One should avoid overeating, traveling on foot, fasting, heavy foods, suppressing natural urges, riding on the back of an animal, physical exercise, and sexual intercourse.
(13) In the case of an increase of Vāta, one should drink unctuous purgatives as they are indicated.
One should drink castor oil mixed with milk for one month;
or a person should drink guggulu along with castor oil and cow’s urine,
which quickly overcomes even long-standing vātavṛddhi.
One should treat the increase of pitta following the procedure for *pittagranthi*;
when there is an increase arising from pitta, one should remove the blood with leeches.
[The remedies are: sandalwood, licorice, lotus, *uśīra*, and blue water-lily.
An ointment made from [the powder] ground with milk removes burning, swelling, and pain.
One should drink a decoction of the three pungents (trikaṭu) and the three myrobalans (triphalā), along with alkali and salt;
this is an excellent purgative that destroys the increase of phlegm (kapha). 17–18.
In this [condition], plasters that are pungent, sharp, and hot, as well as sudation, dry [applications], affusions, poultices, and everything else that is hot, are desired;
one should repeatedly remove blood from a blood-born [ulcer] by means of leeches.
One should drink a purgative combined with sugar and honey;
likewise, a cold external application is recommended, as it alleviates all types of Pitta.
One should follow the regimen for the increase of Pitta in cases of blood-born (rakta-ja) fever, whether the associated Āma is unripened or ripened.
One should apply a warm paste of *surasā* and other head-purgative (*śirovirecana*) substances mixed with urine to the suppurated fat that has arisen;
The wise physician should pierce [the swelling] below the suture on the side with a *brīhimukha* instrument, provided it has not reached the scrotum; in cases of *mantravṛddhi*,
one should apply the procedure for *vātavṛddhi* and employ fomentation with heat there as is beneficial.
Having drunk castor oil prepared with *balā* in the appropriate manner,
a person conquers enlargement of the abdomen (*antravṛddhi*) accompanied by flatulence and colic.
[One may also use] *rāsnā*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *amṛtā*, *eraṇḍa*, *balā*, *āragvadha*, and *gokṣura*.
A decoction prepared according to the prescribed method with *paṭola* and *vṛṣa*,
combined with *ruvū* oil, removes the increase of *antra*. A decoction prepared with *gandharvahasta* oil and milk [achieves the same].
Powder derived from the roots of *viśālā* undoubtedly destroys *vṛddhi*.
An ointment made from the paste of *vacā* and mustard seeds destroys swelling;
an ointment made from the bark of *śigru* and mustard seeds removes swelling caused by *kapha* and *vāta*.
One should employ purified mercury, as well as sulphur, and these [metals] in their killed state:
iron, tin, copper, and then bell-metal, all duly purified; likewise, realgar, blue vitriol, conch-shell, and cowrie-shells.
The three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), cavya, viḍaṅga, vṛddhadāraka, karcūra, the root of māgadhī, pāṭhā, along with yavakṣāra, vacā,
the seeds of elā, devadāru, as well as the five salts (lavaṇapañcaka). 30–31.

One should then grind these ingredients in equal parts and prepare pills (vaṭikā) weighing one ṭaṅka each with a decoction of harītakī; whoever swallows one such pill along with water, [attains the desired result].
Even an enlargement of the scrotum that is considered incurable truly perishes quickly;
likewise, a well-prepared paste made from *abhayā* fried in castor oil and combined with *kṛṣṇā* and rock salt is the supreme remedy for *bradhna* (inguinal hernia).
Cumin, *havuṣā*, costus, *gomeda* stone, and jujube fruit, ground together with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), form a supreme ointment for conquering inguinal hernia (*bradhna*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, on the treatment of inguinal hernia (*vṛddhi-bradhna*). 43.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter, on goiter (galagaṇḍa), scrofula (gaṇḍamālā), tumors (granthi), and swellings (arbuda):
When a swelling is bound [to the neck] and hangs down from the throat like a testicle, it is called a goiter.
Whether it be large or small, one should designate that as *galagaṇḍa*.

When Vāta and Kapha become vitiated in the throat and likewise take refuge in the *manya* muscles and the fat (*medas*), they produce a swelling; because it is characterized by its own specific symptoms appearing gradually, they call it *galagaṇḍa*.
Accompanied by throbbing, with black veins visible on the surface, and being dark-red in color, the swelling caused by Vāyu (wind) is rough to the touch;
it increases slowly and may only occasionally reach suppuration.
Furthermore, that person experiences a bad taste in the mouth, as well as dryness of the palate and throat.
The kaphaja type is stable, similar in color to the skin, heavy, characterized by intense itching, cold, and large;

it increases slowly over time or takes a long time to suppurate, being sometimes accompanied by mild pain (4). Furthermore, the person suffers from a sweet taste in the mouth as well as a coating on the palate and throat (5).
Oily, soft, pale, with an unpleasant odor, accompanied by fat, associated with itching and painless,
it hangs down like a gourd, has a small base, undergoes increase and decrease corresponding to the body's state,
causes the mouth of the person to become oily, and constantly produces a subtle sound in the throat.

A physician should not treat a man who breathes with difficulty, whose entire body is flaccid, who has been ill for over a year, who suffers from loss of appetite, who is emaciated, who has a goiter, or whose voice is broken. [One should also avoid treating those with swellings] the size of a *karkandhu*, *kola*, or *āmalaka* fruit located in the armpits, shoulders, neck, or groins.
Due to fat and phlegm, there may be a "garland of swellings" (gaṇḍamālā) characterized by many lumps that mature slowly over a long period;
some of these lumps undergo suppuration and discharge, while others disappear and new ones arise.
Because it persists for a long time, some authorities call this condition "apacī."
It is considered curable when accompanied by rhinitis, pain in the flanks, cough, fever, and vomiting; however, it is incurable when these symptoms are present.

Vāta and the other [doshas], having vitiated the muscle and blood, and likewise the fat and the vessels, produce a swelling that is round, elevated, and knotted; therefore, it is designated as a *granthi* (glandular swelling).
It is stretched, cut, and pricked; it falls away, is churned, and is split open.
Like a black, soft bladder that has been distended and burst, the wind-born [disease] discharges clear blood.
It is intensely burning, smoking, sucking, cooking, and as if it were on fire.
Due to the provocation of pitta, the swelling becomes red or even yellow; when it bursts, it discharges blood that is excessively vitiated.

Due to the provocation of kapha, the swelling is cold, discolored, slightly painful, and characterized by excessive itching; it is as hard as a stone, grows slowly over a long period, and when it bursts, it discharges thick white pus.
The swelling and subsiding of the body correspond to the increase and decrease [of the fat]; it is unctuous, large, accompanied by itching, and painless.

When incised, the fat produced here flows out like oil from oil-cakes; such is the fat. In a weak person, the Vayu, having been provoked by various forms of physical exertion, seizes the network of the vessels.
By contracting, compressing, and even drying it up, it quickly forms a raised, circular knot (granthi).
That is a vein-knot (śirāja-granthi); it is difficult to cure if it is painful and mobile.
However, one that is painless, immobile, large, or arising from a vital spot (marman) should be rejected as incurable.

When the *doṣas* become concentrated in a certain region of the body and vitiate the flesh and blood, they produce a raised mass that is round, firm, slightly painful, large, deeply rooted, slow to grow, and does not suppurate; those learned in the scriptures call this a deep-seated elevation of flesh an *arbuda*. 18.

It is produced by vāta, pitta, kapha, blood, muscle, and fat; its symptoms are always identical to those of a *granthi* (cyst). When the *doṣa* is vitiated, it contracts and compresses the blood vessels, and consequently, it remains non-suppurating (*apāka*).

This fleshy mass, covered with sprouts of flesh, swells up while discharging pus; it quickly grows and constantly secretes corrupted blood. This blood-natured tumor is incurable; moreover, one afflicted by this arbuda becomes pale due to being tormented by the complications of blood depletion.
When a limb is afflicted by blows from fists and the like, the vitiated flesh develops a swelling that is painless, glossy, without change of color, non-suppurating, stone-like, and immovable;
this occurs severely in a man whose flesh is corrupted and who is excessively devoted to meat. (22-23)
That which arises subsequently upon a previously formed growth is known as *adhyarbuda* by those who know arbudas;
and that which arises from two [pre-existing] pairs, either simultaneously or sequentially, is called *dvirarbuda*, and that is incurable.
They say this fleshy arbuda (*māṃsārbuda*) is incurable, and among those that are curable, one should likewise avoid these [specific types].

That which has flowed out from the vital points (marmas), or that which is born within the channels, or that which is immovable—these do not undergo suppuration due to the predominance of phlegm (kapha) and especially due to the abundance of fat (medas). Furthermore, because of the stability of the humors (doṣas) and their knotted nature, all tumors (arbuda) are by their very nature [non-suppurating]. 25–26.
One should grind mustard seeds, *śigru* seeds, hemp seeds, flax seeds, barley,
and radish seeds with sour buttermilk; this cures goiters,
cervical lymphadenitis (*gaṇḍamālā*), and even severe glandular swellings.
By this very application, they are destroyed and quickly go to dissolution.
An ointment made from the ashes of *jalakumbhīka* mixed with *rakṣoghna* oil is recommended for a goiter, even one that has been long-standing. (28–29)

A person of restricted diet should grind the root of white Aparājitā in the morning and drink it with clarified butter for the pacification of goiter (galagaṇḍa). Water that has been kept for seven days in a ripe bitter bottle-gourd (tiktālābu) [is also used].

For those who consume wholesome food, this oil, when drunk, immediately destroys goiter (galagaṇḍa). Or, for the constant benefit of one suffering from the disease of goiter, one should drink oil prepared with amṛtavallī, nimba, hiṃsrā, abhayā, vṛkṣaka, pippalī, the two types of balā, and devadāru. (31–32)
In cases of goiter (galagaṇḍa), one should employ the consumption of pungent and dry foods such as barley, mung beans, and patola, as well as emesis and bloodletting; furthermore,
one should apply scarifications where goiters or gopālikās arise.
This medicinal paste has been experienced in many ways by many people.
One should regularly consume salt, a water-pitcher [of water], and a powder of long pepper every morning for the pacification of goiter (galagaṇḍa). 34–35.
A decoction of *kāñcanāra* bark combined with powdered ginger and copious honey,
or a decoction made from the roots of *varuṇa*, when drunk even once,
quickly destroys even long-standing *gaṇḍamālā*. (36–37)
Having ground one *pala* and half a *pala* of the bark of *kāñcanāra* with rice-water and drinking it, one dispels *gaṇḍamālā*.
One should take five *palas* of the bark of *kāñcanāra*.
One *pala* each of *nāgara*, *kaṇā*, and *marica*;
half a *pala* each of *pathyā*, *bibhītaka*, and *dhātrī*; and one *akṣa* each of *varuṇa*, *patra*, *kailā*, and *tvac*. (39–40)
Taking one *ṭaṅka* at a time, one should grind all of them together into a powder;
for as much as this entire powder there is, there should be an equal amount of *guggulu*. Having crushed everything together into a single mass, one should form it into a pill and preserve it.
Having made pills the size of a *śāṇa*, a person should consume them at dawn;
they conquer severe goiter, scrofula, tumors, swellings, glandular knots, ulcers, abdominal lumps, leprosy, and fistula-in-ano. 42–43.
A decoction made from *muṇḍitikā* should be given as a post-drink (*anupāna*),
as should a decoction of the heartwood of *khadira*, or a lukewarm decoction of *abhayā*. One should cook [the medicine] with one *pala* of the paste of *cakramarda* root.
Having added one-fourth part of oil extracted from saffron filaments with a pungent substance over a gentle fire, one should add vermilion and set it aside;
this oil quickly destroys even the most dreadful glandular swelling (gaṇḍamālā). 45–46.
Oil cooked with the roots and fruits of *guñjā* and two parts water, when applied as an ointment or used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), removes even the most severe *gaṇḍamālā*.
[47] Sandalwood, *abhayā*, lac, *vacā*, and *kaṭukarohiṇī*— [Note: The verse continues with the preparation of another medicinal oil.]
Having drunk this oil prepared with these [herbs], one may eliminate apacī along with its root.
(48) Oil boiled with vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, madhuka, saindhava, and devadāru, when used as a nasal drop (nasya), shall remove even difficult apacī. (49)

An ointment prepared from the alkali of *svarjikā* root combined with powdered conch shell destroys glandular swellings (*granthi*) as well as tumors (*abuda*). If a glandular swelling does not disappear through medicinal treatment, it should be extracted by a surgeon using an instrument.
The physician should treat it with ghee processed with the [five] products of the cow and other substances, as well as for other types of wounds.
Having extracted even a glandular swelling (granthi), one should follow the procedure prescribed for wounds;
however, excepting a vascular knot (śirā-granthi), the surgical instrument is applied to the remaining types. 51–52.
Since there is no distinction between *granthi* (knots) and *arbuda* (tumors) with respect to their location, cause, shape, humor involved, or the bodily tissue affected,
the physician who knows the prescribed methods should treat tumors according to the treatment for knots.
(53) Haridrā, Lodhra, Patra, Aṅga, Gṛhadhūma, and Manaḥśilā—
This plaster, thickened with honey, is an excellent remover of fat and edema (54).
An alkali prepared from radish, combined with turmeric and conch-shell powder, is a proven plaster that destroys edema (55).

An abscess (arbuda), even a large one, will be pacified after seven nights if it is smeared with the milk of a banyan tree, kuṣṭha, and romaka, and bound with a banyan leaf. (56) The seeds of śigru and mūlaka, as well as surasā and yava, are destroyers of demons (rakṣoghna).
Having ground *aśvaripu* with buttermilk (*takra*), one should apply it for the pacification of *arbuda*.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter on goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), scrofula (*gaṇḍamālā*), nodules (*granthi*), and tumors (*arbuda*).
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter on elephantiasis (*ślīpada*).
In regions where there is an abundance of stagnant water and which remain cool throughout all seasons, elephantiasis (ślīpada) occurs especially frequently.
When a swelling arising in the groin accompanied by fever and intense pain gradually spreads to the feet of men, it is known as elephantiasis.
That ślīpada may also occur on the hands, ears, eyes, penis, lips, and nose; so some say.
That caused by vāta is black and dry, cracked, intensely painful, characterized by frequent pain without apparent cause, and accompanied by fever.
That born of pitta resembles yellow in appearance and is accompanied by intense burning and fever;
that born of kapha, however, is unctuous, white, pale, heavy, and stable.
One should recognize all three of these types of ślīpada as arising from the predominance of kapha.
Since heaviness and largeness do not exist without phlegm,
that which grows like an anthill with thorns and reaches a great size after a year must be especially avoided.

That which arises from a diet and lifestyle characterized by phlegm (ślaiṣmika), as well as that produced in a man of abundant phlegm (kapha)— which is accompanied by discharge, has all its symptoms highly elevated, and is also itchy— should be avoided;
[it should be treated] with fasting, ointments, sudation, purgation, and bloodletting.
One should generally treat elephantiasis (ślīpada) with warm remedies that alleviate phlegm (śleṣman).
One should apply a plaster made of white mustard, *śobhāñjana*, *devadāru*, and *viśvauṣadha* mixed with urine;
or alternatively, a paste of *punarnavā*, *nāgara*, and mustard seeds mixed with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*).
An ointment made from *dhattūra*, castor root, *nirguṇḍī*, *varṣābhū*, drumstick plant, and mustard seeds destroys elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), even that which is long-standing and severe;
even elephantiasis born of long duration, though considered incurable, comes to an end.
By applying a plaster made from the root of *sahadevā* mixed with *tāla*, [the disease is cured].
(11) A paste of seven *tāmbūla* leaves, combined with hot water and salt, when consumed, removes *ślīpada*. (12)
One should drink a decoction of *śākhoṭa* bark mixed with cow’s urine for the destruction of elephantiasis (*ślīpada*) and the removal of disorders of the fat (*medas*).
A person should drink turmeric combined with jaggery along with cow’s urine.
One should lick a powder of *varṣābhū* and *triphalā* combined with *pippalī* and honey to overcome chronic *ślīpada*;
one should also daily drink *harītakī* prepared with *gandharva-taila* along with cow's urine.
He becomes free from the constriction of elephantiasis within seven nights.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter on elephantiasis (ślīpada).
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter on abscesses (vidradhi).
The doshas, having vitiated the skin, blood, flesh, and fat, and taking refuge in the bone,
gradually produce a severe swelling that is highly elevated;
it has deep roots, is painful, and may be circular or elongated.
That is known as Vidradhi (abscess), and it should be understood as being of six types.
He explains the sixfold nature of Vidradhi:
[it arises] separately from each of the Doshas, from all of them combined, from injury, and likewise from blood.
Now, the characteristics of all six of these are being described:
A wound that is black or reddish, uneven, extremely painful, slow to suppurate, and slow to heal is a carbuncle (vidradhi) caused by Vāta. 4.
A swelling resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, or dark-brown, accompanied by fever and a burning sensation,
arising quickly and suppurating rapidly, is a vidradhi (abscess) born of pitta. One shaped like a shallow bowl, pale, cold, unctuous, and with little pain [is born of kapha].
The Vidradhi (abscess) arising from Kapha is characterized by slow suppuration and delayed maturation;
their discharges are respectively considered thin, yellow, and white.
The Ghata-loha type is large, uneven, and characterized by various colors, pains, and discharges.
Alternatively, a sannipātika abscess may ripen irregularly.
When those who indulge in unwholesome practices are struck by various factors or suffer a wound, the heat from the injury spreads through the wind (vāyu), which then impels the blood and pitta.
Fever, thirst, and a burning sensation arise in that embodied being;
for this is an exogenous abscess (āgantuvīdradhi), characterized by the symptoms of a pitta-type abscess.
It is covered with black vesicles, is dark-brown in color, and is accompanied by intense burning pain, aching, and fever.

The blood abscess (raktavidradhi) is said to have the symptoms of a bile abscess (pittavidradhi). Beyond these internal abscesses, they further describe [the following]: through the consumption of heavy, unwholesome, incompatible foods, dried vegetables, and sour foods, [abscesses arise]. (10–11)
The doshas, aggravated either individually or collectively by excessive sexual indulgence, physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, and burning foods,
produce an internal abscess (vidradhi) that resembles an anthill in its elevation.
One should recognize the symptoms of these [internal abscesses] occurring in the rectum, the opening of the bladder, the navel,
the abdomen, the groins, as well as the kidneys, spleen, liver, heart, or the kloman,
by means of the characteristics of external abscesses.

When the abscess arises in the anus, there is obstruction of flatus; in the bladder, painful and scanty urination; in the umbilical region, hiccups and yawning; and in the abdomen, provocation of the wind (māruta).
When the abscess arises in the groin, there is intense stiffness of the waist and back. (15)
In the kidneys, there is contraction of the flanks; in the spleen, obstruction of the breath; 16.
a severe gripping pain in all the limbs and cough arise in the heart; in the liver, labored breathing; and in the kloman, one repeatedly drinks water. 17.
Those wounds above the navel that have suppurated go upward; others, however, go downward.
One may live if they discharge downward, but one does not live if they discharge upward. Among those located outside the heart, navel, and bladder, if they are ruptured, [the patient] lives.
A person might perhaps survive among the other types [of abscesses], but never among the others;
the five types caused by the *vidradhi* [doshas] are curable, while the one caused by the combination of all three (*sānnipātika*) must be avoided.
Their stages of being unripened (*āma*), ripened (*pakva*), and suppurated (*vidagdha*) should be understood in the same manner as those of swelling (*śotha*).

The application of leeches is recommended for every type of abscess; however, mild purgation, fasting, and fomentation are advised, except when pitta is predominant. For an unripened (suppurating) abscess, one should employ medicinal treatments as prescribed for wound-swelling.
In a case of Vātavidradhi, a thick, lukewarm plaster composed of the paste of Vātaghna roots mixed with muscle fat (vasā), oil, and ghee should be applied;
alternatively, one should apply a plaster of ground barley, wheat, and mung beans mixed with clarified butter (ājya).
Indeed, an unripened abscess dissolves in an instant;
a physician should apply a plaster of payasyā, uśīra, madhuka, and candana, ground with milk and mixed with ghee, to a paittika abscess.
One should apply a paste made from the five barks mixed with ghee,
or one should drink a decoction of triphalā combined with one akṣa of the paste of trivṛt. [Alternatively, one may use] brick, sand, iron dross, and cow dung together.
One should apply a fomentation to a phlegmatic abscess (śleṣmavidradhi) using a lukewarm plaster of urine.
Or, one should sprinkle a painful swelling or ulcer with a lukewarm decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī), or with meat broth mixed with oil.

An expert physician should perform all the therapeutic measures for the two types of abscesses— those caused by blood and those caused by external factors— in their entirety, exactly as prescribed for a pitta-type abscess (pittavidradhi).
[29] With red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, niśā, madhuka, and gairika...
An application of milk is for a boil caused by blood or external factors (30).
Indeed, these [drugs] when drunk quickly destroy a deep-seated abscess (koṣṭha-sambhava):
long pepper, cumin, great-flowered leadwort, and the fruit of Dhamargava (31).
The root of śvetavarṣābhū, or the root of varuṇa boiled with water and drunk, is the supreme destroyer of internal abscesses (antarvidradhi).
Gāyatrī, triphalā, nimba, kaṭukā, and madhuka taken in equal parts [are also effective].

One should take four parts each of Trivṛt and Paṭola root, and add dehusked Masūra; this decoction heals ulcers and removes abdominal tumors (gulma), abscesses (vidradhi), erysipelas (visarpa), burning sensations, delusion, and fever. (33-34)
Thirst, fainting, vomiting, heart disease, hemorrhagic disorders, skin diseases, and jaundice—
by washing the root of the *śigru* tree with water, grinding it, and straining the juice through a cloth, a person drinking that liquid with honey destroys internal abscesses. (35)

A decoction of *śobhāñjanaka* combined with asafoetida and rock salt quickly destroys internal abscesses, especially when taken every morning. Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter on abscesses (vidradhi). 46.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter on the swelling of ulcers (vraṇaśotha).

There are six types of ulcerous swellings arising from the individual or combined doshas, as well as those born of blood and those caused by external organisms; all these possess the characteristics of swelling. 1.
An ulcer caused by Vāta ripens unevenly; one arising from Pitta ripens either quickly or slowly; and one born of Kapha ripens like that of Pitta.
Swellings originating from blood or external causes are similar to those of Pitta.
There is mild heat, slight swelling, hardness, and a color identical to that of the surrounding skin.
Dullness of sensation is also a characteristic of an undigested swelling (āmadoṣa). It burns as if by fire, it suppurates as if by caustic,
it is stung as if by a swarm of ants, and likewise it feels as if it were being cut.
It is indeed pierced by a weapon and beaten as if by a staff;
it is tormented within as if by hands and pricked as if by needles.
It becomes parched, burning, and discolored, as if being squeezed by a finger.
Whether sitting, lying down, or standing, one does not find peace, as if pierced by a scorpion (verse 6). When the swelling becomes extended, it resembles an overdistended bladder;
fever, thirst, and loss of appetite—these are the symptoms of the ulceration process (verse 7).

The subsiding of pain, slight redness without swelling, the appearance of wrinkles, a pricking sensation, and frequent itching; the alleviation of complications, depression, and the bursting of the skin—these are the signs. 8.
If the swelling subsides when pressed with the fingers, it is like the movement of water in a vessel; if pus flows out from one side when the end is pressed,
and there is a desire to eat, these are the signs of a suppurated wound.
Without wind (vāyu) there is no pain, nor is there suppuration without bile (pitta), and without phlegm (kapha) there is no pus;

therefore, at the time of full maturation, all swellings are cooked by these three very doshas. After some time, however, the bile that has arisen forcibly brings the wind and phlegm under its control.
Therefore, this wise man considers the second type of suppuration among others to be that which cooks the blood.
Furthermore, in swellings born of phlegm (kapha), the blood undergoes deep-seated suppuration; consequently, the signs of suppuration become clearly manifest through the coldness of the swelling.
There is discoloration of the skin, slight pain, and a hardness like that of stone;
just as fire driven by the wind violently consumes dry undergrowth upon reaching it, so too does pus, if not drained, devour the flesh, vessels, and sinews here in this body.
The physician who knows how to recognize what is raw, what is being scorched, and what is properly cooked—he alone is a true doctor; all others are merely those who live like thieves.
He who cuts open a raw [ulcer] out of ignorance, and he who neglects one that is cooked, [is no better than a thief].
Those two who act without certainty should be known as being like outcaste dog-cookers (śvapaca).

First, an application of a swelling-removing plaster (lepa), then irrigation (pariṣecana), then softening (vimlāpana), bloodletting (asṛṅmokṣa), and thereafter a poultice (upanāhana) should be applied.
Maturation, incision, subsequent compression, purification, healing, and restoration of color— these are remembered as the successive stages for a wound (vraṇa).
Just as one would sprinkle water upon a house that is already ablaze, [so must these treatments be applied].
Just as this quickly pacifies fire, so does this ointment alleviate pain.
An ointment consisting of the root of *bījapūra*, *hiṃsrā*, *devadāru*, *mahauṣadha*,
*rāsnā*, and *agnimantha* is a destroyer of swelling caused by *vāta*.

A paste made by grinding together liquorice, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, the root of *nala*, *padmaka* wood, *keśara*, *uśīra*, *bālaka*, and lotus, mixed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), is unctuous and destroys swelling caused by pitta. 21.
A poultice made from the pastes of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa*,
combined with ghee, should be applied to swelling arising from pitta; this application is highly recommended for swellings of traumatic origin and those born of blood.
Ajagandhā, ajaśṛṅgī, mañjiṣṭhā, sarala,
ekaiṣikā, and aśvagandhā— this ointment destroys swelling caused by phlegm (kapha). Kṛṣṇā, purāṇapiṇyāka, śigrutvak, sikatā, and śivā [are also used].
This plaster, ground with urine and applied lukewarm, destroys swelling caused by phlegm (kapha). One should not apply a plaster at night, nor one that has fallen off,
nor one that is stale, nor should one keep it while it is drying.
The intense heat, shrouded by darkness, emerges from the openings of the pores of the skin;
it flows out even without an ointment at night. Therefore, one should not apply an ointment during the night.
However, even at night, an ointment must be applied by the wise.
In cases of deep-seated suppuration arising from blood and bile (raktapitta),
just as a fire is extinguished when doused with water, so too is the fire of the humors (doṣāgni) suddenly pacified by irrigation (pariṣeka). 28–29.
One should sprinkle a swelling caused by Vāta with warm decoctions of Vāta-alleviating herbs, oils, meat broths, ghees, and sour gruel (kāñjika).
One should sprinkle a swelling arising from Pitta, blood, or injury with very cold liquids.
One should sprinkle [the area] with milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and sugarcane juice boiled with pitta-alleviating drugs;
for swelling arising from phlegm (kapha), one should sprinkle it with decoctions of phlegm-destroying herbs that have been cooled, as well as with oil, alkaline water, and urine.
Once this hardened [fetus] has been born, its gradual softening is the task;
having anointed and fomented it, the physician should very slowly and gently massage it with a bamboo tube, or with the palm of the hand, or with the thumb.

For the purpose of pacifying pain as well as for the subsiding of inflammation, one should perform bloodletting when the swelling has recently arisen; for all other treatments are on one side, while bloodletting is on the other. (35)
For redness is the root of sensation; if that is absent, there is no pain.
A wound that is discolored, hard, dark-brown, and has little sensation—especially one caused by horns, leeches, or even footprints [is not a true ulcer]. 36–37.
Fomentation (svedana) should be applied to painful, severe, and hard swellings, as well as to ulcers of a similar nature;
one should also apply poultices (upanāha) to both unripened (āma) and ripened (vidagdha) swellings.
That which is undigested (avidagdha) becomes pacified, while that which is digested (vidagdha) reaches the state of being fully processed (pakvatām vrajet).
One should place the roots of daśamūlī, balā, rāsnā, vājigandhā, prasāriṇī, and vātaripu (musta) into a jar filled with water and sea salt. 39–40.
Śobhāñjana, kaṇā, saindhava, viśvabheṣaja,
the seeds of śaṇa and kārpāsa, atasī, kulatthikā, 41 tila, yava, siddhārtha, kuṭhera, mūlaka, and misi.
With these available substances combined with sour liquids, made into a paste and warmed comfortably, one should perform fomentation (sveda) slowly according to the prescribed method;
by this, swelling caused by Vata is undoubtedly pacified. 42–43.
Punarnavā, dāru, śuṇṭhī, śigru, and siddhārtha,
ground with sour gruel and applied as a lukewarm paste, destroy all types of swelling (44).
That swelling which does not subside through the application of such pastes and other measures—
One should apply digestive (pācanīya) substances for that poultice (upanāhana):
the fruits of hemp, radish, and drumstick; sesame, mustard, linseed, flour, yeast, and hot substances are digestive. 45–46.
Incision is employed for diseases that are internal, located in non-oral cavities, situated in the axillae (utsaṅga), or mobile;
in a disease curable by excision, this should be performed according to the specific location and the proper measurement.
Having applied the instrument, one should drain the morbid humors (doṣas) according to what has been prescribed.

For children, the elderly, the weak, the emaciated, the timid, and women, as well as for ulcers located on vital points (marmans), incision is not performed; instead, there should be the application of medicinal substances as a paste.
Cirabilva, agnika, dantī, citraka, and hayamāraka cause a breakage [of obstructions] through an application of the excrement of pigeons, crows, and vultures (50).
Likewise, an alkaline substance and alkali are proclaimed to be "cleavers" (dāraṇa).
Elephant tusk ground in water and applied as a mere drop of ointment is said to be the supreme means for breaking up even extremely hard swellings (śotha).
Regarding slimy substances, however, there is excessive pressure on the skin and the roots [of the hair].

One should briefly apply a paste of the powders of barley, wheat, and beans; one should wait while the paste dries for the purpose of pressing, and one must not smear it on the face, as otherwise the morbid humors (doṣas) would be discharged.
For a purified wound, a decoction arising from *paṭola* and *nimba* leaves is the supreme purifier and is employed in all cases;
however, in a wind-type (*vātika*) wound, one should use that of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), and in a bile-type (*paittika*) wound, that of the milky trees (*kṣīrin*). 54.
A decoction of the *āragvadha* group is beneficial for purification in cases born of *kapha*. A decoction prepared from *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*,
and *vetasa* is traditionally known to destroy swelling and venereal sores when used for washing wounds.

A paste made from sesame, rock salt, liquorice, neem leaves, the two types of turmeric, and trivṛt, ground together with ghee, purifies wounds. Alternatively, the root of single-sārivā alone is a purifier for all wounds. 57–58.
Nimba leaves, sesame, dantī, trivṛt, rock salt,
and honey constitute a paste that pacifies malignant ulcers and acts as a purifier and hair-restorer (59).
A paste made from nimba leaves applied as a plaster purifies and heals ulcers.
By eating it, one removes vomiting, weak digestion, pitta, kapha, and worms;
by using it as a suppository (varti), it purifies even minute ulcers located in the joints and vital points (marmas). [60] With abhayā, trivṛt, dantī, lāṅgalī, honey, and rock salt... [61]

A wick made from neem leaves, ghee, honey, and dārvī and madhuka, or a paste of sesame seeds, shall cleanse and heal a wound that has had its putrid flesh removed, where the flesh remains, and which is not healing.
62. For those wounds where the necrotic flesh has been cleared away, but the remaining flesh does not grow back.
A paste made from sesame seeds mixed with honey should be applied for healing. 63.
Aśvagandhā, ruhā, lodhra, kaṭphala, madhuyaṣṭikā, samaṅgā, and dhātakī flowers are excellent for healing wounds. 64.
Wine mixed with honey is said to promote the healing of wounds in men.
An ointment made from the leaves of *suṣavī*, *dhattūra*, *balā*, *moṭā*, and *kuṭheraka*—each used separately—effects the healing of deep wounds. (65)
Wounds dusted with the powdered bark of *kakubha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *jambu*, *kaphala*, and *lodhra* will certainly heal quickly.
These should be finely ground into powder for healing through dusting.
One should apply a lukewarm paste of barley flour, madhuka, oil, and ghee to alleviate burning sensations and pain. (67–68)
An ointment made of karañja, ariṣṭa, and nirguṇḍī destroys worms in ulcers;
likewise, an ointment of garlic, or one made of asafoetida and nimba, [achieves the same].
[Alternatively, an ointment] with nimba leaves, vacā, asafoetida, ghee, salt, and mustard seeds [is effective]. 69.
Fumigation with guggulu is beneficial for wounds; it removes dryness, worms, itching, and pain.

Those wounds that are characterized by discharge, suppuration, and foul odor, as well as those that have been long-standing or chronic swellings, attain relief when drunk with a decoction of triphalā mixed with guggulu.

One desiring the pacification of erysipelas (visarpa), eruptive boils (visphoṭa), and malignant ulcers (duṣṭavraṇa) should drink, at dawn, a decoction of paṭola, nimba, asana-sāra, dhātrī, pathyā, and akṣa, combined with guggulu.
[72] Manahśilā, mañjiṣṭhā, lākṣā, and the two types of haridrā (rajanīdvaya)...
An ointment consisting of ghee and honey is prescribed for restoring the natural color of the skin.
One who eats aged *śāli* rice— unctuous, in small quantities, warm, and accompanied by other liquids and the meat of wild animals— quickly heals a wound.
With *taṇḍulīyaka*, *jīvantī*, *vāstūka*, and *suniṣaṇṇaka*;
with young radish, eggplant, *paṭola*, and *kāravellaka*;
together with pomegranate and *āmalaka*, fried in ghee and seasoned with rock salt. (75)
One should also avoid other substances with similar qualities, or the broth of mung beans and the like;
furthermore, one should strictly avoid sour items, curd, leafy vegetables, meat from marshy or aquatic animals, milk, and heavy foods when there is a wound.
Swelling in a wound arises from exertion, and redness from staying awake; both of these, as well as pain, result from sleeping during the day, while death results from sexual intercourse.
In the case of an inflamed fresh wound, one should perform purification by means of upward and downward therapies.
Cooling therapy should be administered to destroy the heat of rakta-pitta (blood-bile). Having assessed the patient's strength, one should employ fasting, dietetic measures, and bloodletting;
this protocol is especially recommended for cases where the bone is rubbed or fractured.
When [the vessels] are cut, split, pierced, or injured, blood flows excessively;
due to that loss of blood, the Vāyu (wind) causes intense pain there.
In such cases, one should apply affusion, administer internal oleation, and employ medicinal pastes and poultices.
They administer an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) and various pain-relieving medicines separately.
For one whose limbs have been severed by a sword or similar weapon, a wound filled at that very moment with the juice of the roots of *Gāṅgerūkī* will immediately become free from pain.

One should employ all astringent, sweet, and cooling treatments for fresh wounds; after seven days, one should proceed according to what was previously stated. If the blood is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), the person should administer emesis.
When it is located in the colon (pakvāśaya), one should administer purgation.
A decoction prepared from bamboo bark, castor root, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and pāṣāṇabheda,
combined with asafoetida and rock salt, will cause the blood situated in the abdominal cavity to flow out.

One should eat food with the unsalted broth of barley, jujube, and horse-gram, or drink gruel mixed with rock salt (saindhava). [The decoction consists of] jasmine, neem, patola leaves, kaṭukā, daruharidrā, and sārivā. 87–88a.
Ghee prepared with equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, abhayā, siktha, tuttha, madhuka, and the seeds of naktāhvā,
when applied, causes wounds that are narrow-mouthed, located in vital spots (marman), exuding, deep-seated, painful, and sinus-like to become purified and heal. 88

Following the instruction of elder physicians and through traditional oral transmission, the wise should add beeswax that has been thoroughly processed with *jātī* and *vṛta*. [The leaves of] *jātī*, *nimba*, *paṭola*, and *naktamāla* [are used]. 89.
Beeswax, madhuka, kuṣṭha, the two types of niśā, kaṭurohiṇī,
mañjiṣṭhā, padmaka, pathyā, the bark of lodhra, blue utpala,
sārivā, tutthaka, and likewise the fruit of naktamāla.
Having carefully ground these ingredients into a paste in equal proportions, a physician skilled in the art of cooking should properly prepare sesame oil for use in cases of poisonous ulcers,
eruptive boils, and skin diseases such as leprosy.
In cases of ringworm and erysipelas, in all instances of insect bites,
and indeed in wounds from immediate weapon injuries or burns,
as well as for the excision of malignant flesh from the body wounded by nails or teeth; 93–94.
This oil, beneficial when used as an ointment, is both purifying and healing;

it is well-known by the names of its ingredients such as *jātī* and others, and is esteemed by physicians. (95) [It is prepared] with *citraka*, garlic, *rāmaṭha*, *śarapuṅkha*, *alāṅgalī*, and *sindūra*.
Likewise, mustard oil well-cooked with poisonous substances and kuṣṭha is known as *viparītamalla* oil;
it eradicates malignant ulcers, sinus tracks that are incurable despite many medicines, and those caused by one who eats unwholesome food. (96–97)

Take equal parts of the powders of *amṛtā*, *paṭolamūla*, *triphalā*, *trikaṭuka*, and *kṛmighna*; the portion of *guggulu* should be equal to the total weight of these. One should consume one pill of this daily; this is the dosage for this case as well.
It conquers wounds, disorders of wind (vāta), blood (asṛj), abdominal tumors (gulma), abdominal enlargement (udara), edema (śotha), and diseases caused by wind.
For one who has been scorched by fires, heating and warm medicinal treatment should be administered;
when the body has been properly fomented, it becomes beautiful through that fomentation.
By its very nature, water is cold and it excessively coagulates the blood;
therefore, heat indeed provides relief, whereas cold never does.
(101) In the case of a severe burn, one should then apply treatments that are both cold and hot.
One should apply only cool ointments and plasters of ghee to him.
When it has been properly cauterized, the physician should apply a plaster consisting of tugākṣīrī, plakṣa, candana, and gairika, combined with amṛta and ghee.
One should apply a paste made from the flesh of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals mixed with flour over this [burn].
Once it is excessively burnt and the flesh has become shattered, one should remove the necrotic tissue and subsequently perform cooling treatments using the husks of shali rice.
Or one should apply a plaster of *tinduka* decoctions mixed with clarified butter;
this is the best remedy for all types of burns caused by fire.
A plaster made from beeswax, clay, cumin, honey, and *pathyā*, combined with all [the aforementioned ingredients], [is effective] when applied.
Cow's ghee, when prepared with the decoction and paste of *paṭolī*, quickly cures ulcers born of [unwholesome] digestion;
it destroys pain, discharge, burning sensations, and eruptions in burned wounds. (106–107)
When vitiated blood mixed with vāta flows out from a wound that is swollen and knotted, causing burning, itching, and other symptoms, it is known as *vraṇagranthi* (a knotted ulcer).
[One should apply] *kampillaka*, *viḍaṅga*, and the bark of *dārvī*. 108.
Having ground these, one should cook oil; that is the supreme remedy for removing ulcers and glandular swellings (109).
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter on the swelling of ulcers, or rather, the section on exogenous ulcers and burns from fire, [Chapter] 47.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter on Fractures (Bhagna).
O Agni, fracture is briefly of two types: that occurring in the shaft (kāṇḍa) and that occurring at the joint (sandhi). Among these, the fractures at the joint are:
crushed (utpiṣṭa), dislocated (viśliṣṭa), displaced (vivartita), oblique (tiryaggata), dislodged (kṣipta), and depressed (adhaḥ). 1.
Painful extension, contraction, and movement, along with an aversion to touch—these are said to be the general signs of a dislocated joint. Furthermore, there is swelling all around;
specifically, pain occurring at night and constant pain are the signs of a separated joint.
When the joint is twisted, there is pain in the sides; when it moves obliquely, intense pains arise;
when it is excessively displaced, there is extreme agony and the cessation of pain upon its being reduced; when it is displaced downward, there is looseness of the leg at the joint.
A fracture, however, occurs in many ways within the shaft [of the bone] and is specifically classified by names corresponding to those [types of displacement].
In the section on shafts (kāṇḍa), however, there are the karkaṭaka and aśvakarṇa types; those that are pulverized, crushed, or have their bones shattered;

those broken in the shafts, or excessively displaced; those that have reached the marrow, burst open, or are crooked—(5) those cut in two or even in twelve ways in the shaft; indeed, its general characteristic at the front is as follows: (6)
Sagging of the limbs, excessive swelling and pain, as well as a constant and extreme increase in distress; when pressed, a sound is produced here, intolerance to touch, throbbing, piercing pain,
and no relief whatsoever in any state— this indeed is the sign of a fractured limb.
In a person who eats little, lacks self-control, is dominated by vāta, or is afflicted by complications, a fracture heals with great difficulty.
Furthermore, a fractured pelvic bone that is dislocated from its joint or displaced likewise [heals with difficulty].
The physician should avoid treating one whose hips are crushed; likewise,
he should avoid one whose skull bones are not joined together, or who has a crushed forehead, as well as fractures of the breast, anus, back, temples, or head.
One should also avoid that bone which, despite being properly joined, undergoes distortion due to improper placement, faulty binding, or even from agitation;
young bones may be bent, whereas cartilages (nalaka) are broken.
The skull-caps were split apart and the neck-ornaments burst asunder;
the bones in the hands, the pair of flanks, the back, the breasts, the belly, the anus, and even in the feet, spoke out like bracelets. 12–13.
Having recognized that a fracture has occurred at the outset, one should sprinkle it with cold water;
an ointment of mud should be applied, and a bandage provided with *kuśa* grass should be fastened.
One should elevate what is depressed and press down what is protruding.
One should turn upwards that which has been smeared, cast down, or gone below.

(15) One should collect the bark of the *madhūka*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *kadamba*, and *nicula* trees, as well as that of the *vaṃśa*, *sarja*, and *arjuna* trees, for the purpose of *kuśa*-grass. (16)
One should bind it over the cloth, neither too tightly nor too loosely;
one should release it every three days during cold weather and every two days during heat, or at the end of a month, or after five days, depending on the nature of the broken humors. 17.
For the purpose of anointment, a paste of mañjiṣṭhā and madhūka ground with water, mixed with ghee washed a hundred times and flour of śāli rice, should be applied as an ointment;
by this, exogenous swellings produced by immediate trauma are pacified. (18)
By applying a paste of flour and salt, or by means of the juices of *amlīkā* fruits;
(19) [one should take] the root of *āmrātaka*, *amlīkā* fruit, and leaves of *śigru*;
(20) as well as the root of *paunarnava* and *vardhamāna*, and also that of *kembuka*.
Having crushed everything together with buttermilk and likewise with sour gruel (kāñjika),
one should cook it and administer this excellent remedy; by it, the pain is destroyed,
and the swelling and the bone certainly and quickly undergo healing.
A decoction of *nyagrodha* and other such trees, well-cooled, should be used for sprinkling;
in cases of pain, one should administer a decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūlī*) mixed with milk. Alternatively, the wise physician should apply *cakrataila* while it is comfortably warm.
One should treat him with non-burning foods and flour-based preparations;
for his exhaustion, which causes the loosening of the joints, has been overcome.
Meat, meat broth, milk, clarified butter, and soup made from satīna beans [are recommended].
One who understands [the treatment] should provide nourishing food and drink for the one with a fracture.

In the morning, a person with a fracture should drink cow's milk from a calf that has calved once, mixed with clarified butter, prepared with sweet medicinal herbs, cooled, and combined with lac. 25–26.
In cases of dislocation, fracture, or bone injury, one should drink a paste of *asthisaṃhāra*, lac, wheat, and *arjuna* mixed with ghee, or alternatively, with milk. Furthermore,
for those consuming a paste of garlic, honey, lac, ghee, and sugar, [the bones will heal].
The joining of bones that are severed, shattered, or fallen away will occur before long.
By combining this powder with honey, ghee, arjuna, and lac, a fracture is joined when it is licked while consuming milk and ghee. (28–29)
Having powdered the root of *śṛgālavinnā* and drunk it with meat broth,
one heals a fractured bone within three weeks.
One who has a fractured bone should drink *ābhā* powder mixed with honey for three days.
When applied yellow, the bone becomes perfectly firm, resembling the essence of a diamond (vajrasāra).

Oil mixed with the paste of *amlīkā* fruit and *sauvīra* (sour gruel), along with sweat-inducing treatments that destroy pain from fractures and injuries, or oil prepared with medicinal herbs, [is used] for swelling (*śvayathu*). 31–32.

Equal parts of *ābhā*, the three fruits (*phala-trika*), and the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), combined with an amount of *guggulu* equal to the total of these, should be administered to heal fractures and dislocations.
(33) *Lākṣā*, *asthi-saṃhṛt*, *kakubha*, *aśvagandhā*, *nāgabalā*, and *pura* should be reduced to powder.
It destroys pain that has become broken, released, or unstable, and makes the limbs as firm as a thunderbolt.
One should soak black sesame seeds in stagnant water night after night,
dry them day by day, and then saturate them with cow’s milk.
For the third week, one should cultivate [the plant] with honey-water;
then, having drunk the milk, one should powder the dried and finely cut [roots].
[One should also take] the Kākolyādi group, along with Yaṣṭyāhvā and Mañjiṣṭhā, as well as Sārivā. (36–37)
Having powdered kuṣṭha, sarjarasa, māṃsī, suradāru, candana,
and śatapuṣpā, one should mix them with sesame powder.
For the purpose of pressing, milk boiled with all these fragrant substances (sarvagandha) should be prepared.
One should cook that oil again with four times its quantity of milk,
along with yaṣṭī, maṃśumatī, patra, jīvantī, turaga,
rodhra, prapauṇḍarīka, and kālānusārivā.
Having ground together śaileyaka, kṣīraśuklā, anantā, madhūlikā, and śṛṅgāṭaka, as well as the previously mentioned medicinal herbs,
one who is learned in the scriptures should cook that oil with these over a gentle fire.
This oil is always beneficial for those with fractures in all types of treatments; it is likewise used in cases of convulsions, hemiplegia, dryness of the palate,
as well as in facial paralysis, stiffness of the neck, diseases of the head, earache, and lockjaw.
For deafness, blindness, and those whose vital essence has wasted away in women,
this is wholesome for drinking, as well as for massage, nasal drops, enemas, and food;
by this very means, the growth of the neck, shoulders, and chest is produced.

And the face, resembling a lotus with its fragrant breath—this [treatment] worthy of a king should be performed by physicians for kings alone. In that case, a powder mixed with an amount equal to sesame flour is desired. 45–46.

Indeed, a fracture occurring in early life may be declared easily curable for a person with few complications, provided it is treated during a season that is neither too hot nor too cold. In such a case during the first stage of life, the joint shall become stable within one month.
In the middle stage [of healing], it takes twice the time, and likewise in the final stage, three times. One should protect it with great effort so that it does not become broken;
for when the flesh, vessels, and ligaments have matured [with suppuration], it is cured only with great difficulty. (48–49)
If a fracture remains intact despite falling or a blow, causing swelling and pain,

the physician should apply cold affusions and medicinal plasters. However, in the case of a fractured bone accompanied by an ulcer, the physician should treat the ulcer with ghee and honey as the primary ingredients.
Having removed [the foreign body] with decoctions, one should treat the remainder as in the case of a fracture;
one should also apply the oleaginous substances (snehas) prescribed for wind-diseases (vātavyādhi) there as well.
One should avoid salt, pungent substances, alkaline matter, sour things, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse.

One should avoid physical exercise, as well as broken food and dry food (52). When a fracture has been properly set— so that the joint is not dislocated, the limbs are not deficient, the protrusion is not prominent, and there is no interference with the performance of auspicious activities— it should be declared healed (53).
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the section on the broken [limbs], in the middle section of the *Bhāvaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Miśra Bhāva, son of the illustrious Miśra Laṭakananata;
it also concludes the third part.
The Fourth Section:
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter, on the Treatment of Sinus Ulcers (Nāḍī-vraṇa).
That ignorant person who neglects an ulcer while it is still in the stage of swelling, or who, being of improper conduct, neglects an ulcer when it is full of pus; [he brings about his own ruin].

It enters within, piercing through its previously established locations; then, because that pus flows excessively, it is considered a "channel" (*nāḍī*) since it carries [the discharge], and it is thus regarded as a *nāḍī*. (1) It arises from the three *doṣas* either individually, separately, or combined together, and another type arises from the cause of a foreign body (*śalya*). (2)
Among these, that caused by Vāyu has rough, narrow openings, is accompanied by pain, and discharges a large amount of frothy fluid at night; 3.
that caused by Pitta produces thirst and fever, is associated with burning sensations, and discharges a large amount of yellow, hot fluid during the day; 4.
that caused by Kapha should be known as having thick, white, slimy discharge, being stiff, itchy, and painful, with the symptoms increasing at night. 5.

One should designate that [condition] as a "ghora-gati" (dreadful course), which arises from the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm, and is characterized by burning fever, labored breathing, fainting, and dryness of the mouth; it is like the Night of Doom that robs one of life.
When the minute channels are somehow cleared, the foreign body, once introduced into the aforementioned sites, quickly produces its course.
