It causes a sudden discharge of frothy, churned, warm blood mixed with pus, accompanied by constant pain. (7) A sinus ulcer arising from the three doṣas is incurable; indeed, the last four types are curable only with great effort. (8) Now follows the treatment for sinus ulcers (*nāḍīvraṇa*).
In that case, having first applied a poultice to a fistula caused by Vāta and having completely incised the sinus tract,
one should fill it with well-ground sesame seeds and fruits of Apāmārga mixed with Saindhava salt and then bandage it;
or, for the constant washing of the ulcer, one should employ the great Pañcamūla.
Having collected hiṃsrā, haridrā, kaṭukā, balā, gojihvikā, and the root of bilva,
one should cook oil for the purpose of purifying, filling, and healing a wound.
First, the wise physician should apply poultices (utkārikā) containing milk and ghee to a wound of pitta-nature.
Having removed the foreign body with a surgical instrument, one should fill the wound with a paste of sesame, *nāgadantī*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*.

For washing as well, a skillful physician should always employ *niśā* (turmeric) along with *soma* and *nimba*. [The oil should be prepared] with *śyāmā*, *tribhaṇḍī*, *triphalā*, and *haridrā*, well-boiled together with *tilvaka* wood.

Ghee mixed with milk, by nourishing the wound, destroys even that sinus track which has reached the internal cavities (koṣṭha). Having first applied a poultice to a sinus arising from phlegm (kapha) using horse-gram, white mustard, barley-flour, and husks, and having softened it, one should recognize the path of the probe and then apply the surgical instrument to completely eliminate it.
One should apply neem, sesame, agni, dantī, and surāṣṭrajā, combined with rock salt, to the ulcer;

furthermore, for washing, the expressed juices of karañja, neem, jāti, arka, and pīlu should be employed. (14) Svarjikā, rock salt, dantī, agni, yūthikā, and jalanīlikā— The final line appears to be a fragment of a list of medicinal substances used in the treatment of ulcers. A complete translation of that specific line would require the full verse context. Based on the provided text, the translation is as follows: Svarjikā, rock salt, dantī, agni, yūthikā, and jalanīlikā.

Oil extracted from the seeds of *kharamañjarī* and processed with cow’s urine pacifies malignant ulcers and removes sinus ulcers caused by *kapha*. Oil prepared with *saindhava*, *arka*, black pepper (*marica*), the substance called *jvalana*, *mārkava*, and the two types of *rajanī* likewise accomplishes these effects. (15)
This oil will soon destroy even a deep-seated sinus caused by phlegm and wind.
However, having incised a sinus originating from a foreign body, extracted the foreign body, and purified the channel,
one should bandage the wound with sesame seeds saturated with honey and ghee, and thereafter perform its healing.
Having prepared a decoction from the category of unripe fruits of the *kumbhīka*, *kharjūra*, *kapittha*, *bilva*, and forest trees, one should cook oil therein, adding *musta*, *saralā*, *priyaṅgu*,
*saugandhika*, *mocarasa*, *ahipuṣpa*, the various types of *lodhra*, and indeed *dhātakī*.
By this means, a sinus or ulcer arising from a splinter will heal easily and quickly.
Thus ends the *kumbhīkādyataila* (oil for kumbhīkā and other conditions).
One should prepare a wick from the milky sap of *snuhī*, *arka*, and *dārvī*, and fill [the cavity] with it.

This king of formulations destroys the channels located throughout the entire body. (20) A wick made from the powder of *āragvadha*, *niśā*, and *kālā*, combined with clarified butter and honey, should be applied to a wound; it is a purifier that eliminates the [abnormal] course [of the disease]. (21)
A wick (varti) made from these, combined with honey, or the "best salt" (saindhava) said to destroy sinus tracts,
or the oil prescribed for malignant ulcers— when used, it quickly destroys the [sinus] track.
[This oil is prepared] with *jāti*, *arka*, *sampāka*, *karañja*, *dantī*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), and *yāvaśūka*.
A wick made from *snuhī* milk ground with *citraka* quickly destroys the sinus tract (23).
A mixture of *bibhītaka*, the stone of the mango, *vaṭa* sprouts, *hareṇukā*, and the seeds of *śaṅkhinī*,
combined with boar dung and fine soot, should be applied to the sinuses after mixing them with oil (24).
Castor oil boiled with the wool of a ram and black dūrvā grass,
when applied by means of a cotton wick, overcomes even long-standing sinus ulcers (nāḍī-vraṇa). One should likewise cook castor oil with the fresh juice of karcūra.

Oil prepared with the paste of sindūra and the juice of karcūra destroys sinus tracts, malignant ulcers, and erysipelas (visarpa). It cures scabies, malignant ulcers, and sinus tracts, acting as a destroyer of all types of wounds. (26–27)

Oil prepared with *bhallātaka*, *arka*, black pepper, the best salt (*saindhava*), *viḍaṅga*, the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric), *citraka*, and the juice of *mārkava* destroys sinus tracts caused by *kapha* and *vāta*, as well as scrofula (*apacī*) and ulcers.
(28) [Also, oil prepared with] *svarjikā*, *saindhava*, *dantī*, the root of *nīlī*, and its fruit...
Oil prepared with four times the quantity of urine cures sinus ulcers;
the entire regimen for treating ulcers, beginning with purification and healing, should be applied.
Guggulu, triphalā, and vyoṣa, taken in equal parts and combined with clarified butter, [are also effective].
One should eat a single pill, the size of a seed of the Akṣa fruit, without weariness;
it destroys sinus, malignant ulcers, pain, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids, just as the king of birds destroys serpents. (30–31)
The physician should apply those same wicks prescribed for the treatment of two types of wounds to all sinus tracts (nāḍīs),
even those located near vital points (marmas) in the case of those who are emaciated, weak, or timid. 32.
One should cut it with an alkaline thread and never with a surgical instrument.
Having sought out its course with a probe following the path of the alkaline thread,
one should insert the needle at the end of that course, lift it up quickly, and then extract it.

Having brought the thread to the end, the wise physician should perform a firm ligation; then, observing the strength of the caustic, he should insert another thread soaked in caustic until the sinus is cut through. 35.

This procedure should be performed by a knowledgeable physician in cases of fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara). In cases of tumors (arbuda) and similar conditions, one should lift [the growth] and apply a thread at its base,
or it may be covered all around with needles having the shape of barley grains.
One should bind the base with a thread, and when it has been cut, one should treat the wound.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter on sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa).
Now begins the fiftieth chapter on fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara).
Pricking pain, burning, itching, and various types of pain in the waist and skull are the premonitory symptoms that will occur when bhagaṃdara (fistula-in-ano) is about to manifest.
A boil that causes distress arises on either side within a two-aṅgula area of the anus.
Bhagandara (fistula-in-ano) is to be known as a distinct disease, and it is of five types.
Bhoja provides the etymological derivation of the term *bhagandara*: "It [is so called] because it spreads from the *bhaga* (the anus) all around toward the rectum and likewise the bladder."
Because it is caused by the Lord (Bhagavat), this is called *bhagaṃdara*.

When the Vāyu, excessively aggravated by astringent and parching substances, produces a carbuncle (*piḍakā*) in the region of the anus, it undergoes a severe suppuration due to neglect; once burst, it discharges reddish froth accompanied by pain.

In that case, when urine, feces, and semen enter through numerous wounds, one should call it *śataponaka*. When pitta, excessively provoked by its aggravating factors, produces a red pustule located in the anus,
which then quickly suppurates and discharges cold, putrid matter, one should call that *bhagandara* "camel-neck" (*uṣṭraśirodhara*).
The kapha-born fistula (bhagandara) is characterized by itching, thick discharge, hardness, mild pain, a whitish appearance, and constant oozing.
A carbuncle (piḍakā) resembling a cow's udder is marked by multicolored pain and discharge.

The *śambūkāvartaka* type is considered to have a course resembling the spiral of a snail shell (7). The *kṣatagati* type has its course in the anus; it increases through neglect, and worms arise which, having torn [the tissue], create various paths with their mouths and ulcers—one should call that *unmārgin* hemorrhoid *bhagaṇḍara*. (8)
All types of fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) are difficult to cure and are formidable; among them, those arising from all three doṣas and especially those born of injury (kṣataja) are incurable.
Furthermore, flatus, urine, feces, semen, and even worms may be discharged through them.
If they discharge from a fistula-in-ano, they destroy that patient. Therefore, one should treat the carbuncle itself with great care through purification,
bloodletting, irrigation, and other means, so that it does not undergo suppuration.
A well-ground paste of *vaṭapatra*, brick-dust, *śuṇṭhī*, *guḍūcī*,
and *punarnavā* is recommended as an ointment for *bhagaṃdara* when it is in the stage of a carbuncle (*piḍakā*).
For carbuncles that have not yet suppurated, fasting (*apatarpaṇa*) should be administered first.
One should perform treatment until the purgation is complete; for those with perforated ulcers, the procedure will now be described.

Having applied the sequence of treatments such as probing with an eṣaṇī probe, incision, caustic application, and thermal cauterization, one should manage it like a common wound according to the specific doṣa and in the proper order.
This [application] made with milk, flour, sesame, *ariṣṭa*, and *madhuka*, well-cooled,
is recommended for fistula-in-ano accompanied by blood and pain.
[The paste consists of] *sumanā*, banyan leaves, *guḍūcī*, and *viśvabheṣaja*.
An ointment made from *saindhava* salt ground with buttermilk destroys fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇdara*). 16.
*Trivṛt*, sesame, *nāgadantī*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*, combined with clarified butter, rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey, shall serve as an elevating agent (*utsādana*). 17.
Having consumed the water from a *khadira* tree, one should drink a decoction of the three fruits (*triphalā*);
[this, along with] *mahiṣākṣa* and *viḍaṅga*, is a destroyer of fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇdara*).
One should eat the meat of a snail prepared in various ways, such as with side dishes and the like.
One who avoids indigestion for a month is indeed freed from fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara).
The Nyagrodhādi group of drugs, which is beneficial for cleansing and healing, when cooked into oil or ghee, destroys fistula-in-ano. 19–20.

Sesame, *jyotiṣmatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *lāṅgalī*, *girikarṇikā*, *śatāhvā*, *trivṛt*, and *dantī* are purificatory [drugs] for anal fistula (21). Sesame, *abhayā*, *lodhra*, the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, the two types of *niśā*, *balā*, *lodhra*, and soot (*agāradhūma*)— The following is the English translation of the provided Sanskrit verses: Sesame, *jyotiṣmatī*, *kuṣṭha*, *lāṅgalī*, *girikarṇikā*, *śatāhvā*, *trivṛt*, and *dantī* are purificatory [drugs] for anal fistula (21). Sesame, *abhayā*, *lodhra*, the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, the two types of *niśā*, *balā*, *lodhra*, and soot (*agāradhūma*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion given.]
For the cleansing and healing of fistula-in-ano and ulcers born of venereal disease (upadaṃśa),
the wise physician, having ascertained the course of the fistula, should diligently fill it with a wick made from the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, along with *dārvī*. 22–23.
This application of cat bone, combined with the juice of *triphalā*, undoubtedly destroys the channel situated within the entire body;
it quickly cures fistula-in-ano and is supreme for removing malignant ulcers. (24)
A paste of trivṛt, tejovatī, and dantī cures sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa).
Jyotiṣmatī, lāṅgalakī, śyāmā, dantī, trivṛt, tilā, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, golomī, tilvaka, and girikarṇikā [are used for this purpose]. 25–26.

The group consisting of *kāsīsa*, gold, and *kṣīrī* is prescribed for purification. (27) Viḍaṅga essence, triphalā, māgadhikā, and kaṇā, when licked together with honey and oil, become healers of worms, skin diseases, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, consumption, and sinus ulcers. (28)
Having collected *citraka*, *arka*, *trivṛt*, *pāṭhā*, *malayūha*, *yamāraka*,
*sudhā*, *vacā*, *lāṅgalakī*, *haritāla*, *suvarcikā*,
and *jyotiṣmatī*, the wise man should cook [them] in oil.
This oil, named Viṣyandana, should be administered for fistula-in-ano;
it acts as a purifier, a healer, and likewise restores the natural skin color.
[It is prepared] with niśā, akṣīra, saindhava salt, purā, aśva, hara, and vatsaka.
This accomplished oil for anointing is supreme for curing fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara).
One should cook oil with karavīra, niśā, dantī, lāṅgalī, salt, agni, mātuluṅga, and vatsāhva for the treatment of fistula-in-ano.

A pill composed of three parts each of Triphalā, Pura, and Kṛṣṇā is beneficial for those suffering from swelling, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano. Furthermore, in cases of *śataponaka*, the physician should create incisions along the channels.

Then, once they have descended [into the vessel], the physician who understands [the procedure] should treat the remaining vessels; in that case, if the disease involves many openings, either an "ardhalāṅgalaka" incision or a "lāṅgalaka" incision should be made. 34–35.
Either the *sarvatobhadra* or the *gotīrthaka* should be constructed. When there is a cut on two equal sides, it is considered the *lāṅgalaka*;
when one side is shorter, it is known as the *ardhalāṅgalaka*.

Experts in excision say that when the anus is incised in four ways while avoiding the raphe, it is called the *sarvatobhadra* excision; an excision made with a blade applied from the side is considered the *gotīrthaka*. 38.
The physician should cauterize all the channels of discharge with fire;

then, having incised with the camel-necked or ewe-eared instrument, he should apply alkali. In the case of a fistula-in-ano, the wise physician, having excised the channel of discharge, [should proceed as follows].
One should cauterize the path of the discharge with an alkaline solution or with fire;
having sought out the path, one should cut it with a blade like a date-palm leaf.
[The instruments are] the *candrārddha*, the *ardhacandra*, the *cakra*, the *sūcīmukha*, and the *avāṅmukha*.
Having incised [the area], one should properly cauterize it with fire or, alternatively, with alkali (kṣāra). However,
wherever pain arises from the falling of the surgical instrument upon these [wounds], an irrigation with warm *aṇu-taila* is recommended.
In the case of an exogenous [abscess], the physician, having carefully incised the vein with a surgical instrument,
should— being wise and well-composed— cauterize that wound as prescribed, using either a Jambū-fruit-shaped probe heated to the color of fire or a heated metal rod. 44–45.
A man whose ulcer has healed should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, combat, riding on the back of animals, and heavy burdens for one year.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, on Fistula-in-Anus. 50.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter: On Upadaṃśa (Gonorrhea).

Due to blows from the hand, injury from nails or teeth, lack of cleansing, excessive sexual indulgence, or disorders of the female reproductive tract, as well as through various improper conducts, five types of *upadaṃśa* arise in the penis. (1)
One should diagnose a case caused by Vāta by means of eruptions that are accompanied by piercing pain, bursting, and throbbing, and are blackish;
by those caused by Pitta, which are yellow, associated with excessive discharge and burning;
and by those caused by blood, which resemble flesh in appearance, are reddish-black, and ooze blood, possessing symptoms identical to those of Pitta.

One afflicted by *trimalopadaṃśa*— characterized by itching, swelling, large white and dense patches accompanied by discharge due to *kapha*, and various types of discharges and pains— is said to be incurable (verse 3).
That in which the flesh is shattered and devoured by worms, leaving only the scrotum remaining, should be abandoned as incurable (verse 4).
The fool who, as soon as [the disease] has arisen, does not perform the treatment because he is attached to sensual objects,
dies from it when his penis is destroyed by swelling, worms, burning, and suppuration over time.
(5) In cases of venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*) that are curable, for the person whose body has been lubricated and fomented—

One should pierce a vein in the middle of the penis or apply leeches; one should also remove the excessively aggravated humors from both sides. When the humors have been promptly extracted, pain and swelling subside.
Alternatively, if the patient is weak or has not undergone purgation,
one should remove his excessively aggravated doshas by means of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha);
however, one must take great care to protect the digestive fire, for it brings about the wasting away of the penis.
For vātika [conditions], ointments and affusions should be prepared with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *yaṣṭyāhva* (liquorice), *sarala*, *aguru*, and *dāru*; likewise with *rāsnā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *pṛthvīkā*.
[Also included are] *nicula*, castor seeds, barley, wheat, and parched grain flour (*saktu*).

One should apply a lubricating, pleasantly warm plaster composed of these [substances] for a condition arising from Vata (vātaja). For a condition arising from Pitta (paittika), one should apply a lubricating plaster made of red ochre, gold, mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, uśīra, padmaka, sandalwood, and blue lotus.
One should apply a plaster for the pitta-type [fever] using lotus, water-lily, lotus-stalks, arjuna, and vetasa, along with ghee, madhuka, and substances that are unctuous;
one should also sprinkle it with ghee, milk, sugar, sugarcane juice, honey, and water.
Alternatively, one should apply a very cold decoction of the *vaṭa* tree and others; or,
for a swelling arising from *kapha*, one should apply a warm plaster made from the barks of *śāla*, *ajakarṇa*, *aśvakarṇa*, and *dhava*, ground with wine and mixed with oil.
One should cause a sprinkling with a decoction of *āragvadha* and other such herbs to be administered (15). Furthermore,

for upadaṃśa arising from pitta and blood, one should prepare a powder made from *nimba*, *arjuna*, *aśvattha*, *kadamba*, *śāla*, *jambū*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *vetasa*, and apply it as a wash and an ointment (16).

One should apply a plaster for upadaṃśa made from these ingredients ground in equal parts: the bark of *dāruharidrā*, *śaṅkhanābhi*, *rasāñjana*, lac, cow-dung exudate, oil, honey, ghee, and milk. (17)

By this, the ulcers, as well as the swelling and the burning sensation, are pacified. In both types of upadaṃśa (syphilis), one should perform the treatment after declaring the prognosis, having considered the strength and weakness of the doṣas and what is appropriate for each of those two.
If it should ever reach suppuration, one should quickly incise it with a surgical instrument;
having removed that [pus], one should apply a plaster of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and honey.
For a plaster, the tender shoots of the *vaṭa* tree, *arjuna*, *jambu*, *pathyā*, *lodhra*, and *haridrā* are beneficial. (20)
Likewise, for the purpose of causing the discharge of pus from venereal sores (upadaṃśa), a powder should be prepared with pure collyrium (vimalāñjana).
For the pacification of upadaṃśa, the washing of the ulcer should be performed with a decoction of triphalā or with the juice of bhṛṅgarāja.

One should employ a wash or a decoction made from the leaves of *jayā*, *ajapā*, *aśvamāra*, *arka*, and *śampāka* respectively for the treatment of inflammation of the penis (*meḍhrapāka*). Alternatively, one should drink a decoction of *śampāka*, *nimba*, *triphalā*, and *kirāta*, along with *khadira* and *āsana*.

The application of guggulu combined with triphalā is a practice that removes all types of secondary infections (upadaṃśa). For secondary infections, a powder made of blue lotuses, white water lilies, red lotuses, and fragrant lotuses is recommended as an external application (pradeha). 24–25.

Dusting the testicles with the powder of *bandhūka* or *kadalī*, or with the hair of a pomegranate twig, or with an application of betel nut (*pūgaphala*), is recommended. [Likewise,] *saurāṣṭrī*, red ochre (*gairika*), blue vitriol (*tuttha*), *puṣpakāsīsa*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) [are used]. 26.
One should collect lodhra, rasāñjana, haritāla, manaḥśilā, hareṇukā, and elā in equal parts and grind them into a powder; this powder,
combined with honey, is highly esteemed for use in upadaṃśa (venereal sores).
Ash produced by burning [the herb] in a sealed crucible (puṭa), along with orpiment and realgar,
is the supreme remedy for destroying secondary infections and erysipelas.
One should burn the three myrobalans (triphalā) in a frying pan, reduce them to a fine powder (masī), and combine it with honey and rock salt.

This ointment for *upadaṃśa* heals the ulcer immediately. (30) An application made from *tirīṭa*, *añjana*, *vajrākṣa*, *kovidāra*, and *ibhakeśara*, ground with water, is recommended for the disease of men (*puruṣavyādhi*). (31)

Rasāñjana combined with śirīṣa or pathyā, applied as an ointment with honey, should be employed to remove diseases affecting the entire body. Bhārgī, śikharija, mūla, bhadra, and śrī, well-ground together—
Real red arsenic (manaḥśilā) mixed with honey indeed pacifies upadaṃśa in a short time.
By carefully applying a powder of *śatadhauta* [ghee] and iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*) powder to the penis, a man shall obtain relief from the disease.
Even an incurable pain arising in the penis comes to an end through the application of a plaster made from the root of *karavīra* ground with water. [Likewise,
it is cured] by means of *varā*, *nimba*, *arjuna*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *āsana*, and *vāsaka*.
Boluses (vaṭakas) the size of an akṣa fruit should be prepared from these powders mixed with guggulu; they quickly destroy all diseases arising in the penis,
including venereal sores (upadaṃśa), blood disorders, and even malignant ulcers.

Ghee prepared with a paste (kalka) and decoction (kaṣāya) of karañja, nimba, arjuna, śāla, jambu, vaṭa, and other such trees, destroys the disorder of upadaṃśa (venereal disease), even when accompanied by burning, suppuration, discharge, and redness.
[38] [Likewise, ghee prepared with] bhūnimba, nimba, triphalā, paṭola, karañja, dhātrī, khadira, asana, and others...
Ghee cooked quickly with the pastes of these [herbs] along with water is declared to be a remover of all types of *upadaṃśa*.
The ghees that I shall describe for use in skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), sinus ulcers (*nāḍī-vraṇa*), and wounds (*vraṇa*) should also be employed for *upadaṃśa* through irrigation, massage, and as food.

One should cook oil with these three—smoke from a house, *rajani*, and the dregs of wine—in increasing proportions; this removes itching, swelling, and pain, and is indeed a supreme cleanser, healer, and cure for venereal sores (*upadaṃśa*). 41

This oil, combined with gojihvā, viḍaṅga, yaṣṭīmadhu, and all the aromatic substances (sarvagandha), is desired as a healing agent for all types of secondary ulcerations (upadaṃśa). [42] Likewise, the leaves of jambū, vetasa, and dhātrī [are used].
Likewise, the leaves of the *naktamāla*, as well as *padma* and *utpala* [leaves]; 43.
*elā*, *ativiṣā*, the stone of the *āmra* fruit, *madhuka*, *priyaṅgu*, lac, *kālīyaka*, *lodhra*, sandalwood, and that which is called *trivṛtā*; 44.
One should grind these very substances together with goat's urine and cook one *prastha* of oil with these ingredients, each measuring one *akṣa*.
This prepared oil is undoubtedly a healer of all wounds. 45.
This is proclaimed by the sages as the best remedy for *upadaṃśa* (venereal disease).
For one whose penis flesh is wasting away until only the scrotum remains, seeds of bitter *kośātakī* and *alābu* prepared with *nāgara* [ginger] [should be used]. 46–47.
Oil destroys various types of malignant ulcers without exception. One should constantly consume barley-based food and only well-water;
furthermore, one should employ the therapeutic measures for hemorrhoids that have been excised or cauterized.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, on Upadaṃśa (venereal sores).
Now begins the fifty-second chapter, on Liṅgārśas (piles of the penis).
[The condition] characterized by growths appearing like sprouts, situated one above the other...
Gradually, a wick-like growth arises resembling the crest of a cock;
located within the cavity of the anus, at its junction, or even at the junction of the anal folds,
it is known as *liṅgavarti*, while others call it *liṅgārśas*.
A discharge that is slimy and difficult to treat arises from the three *doṣas*.

Having completely excised the *liṅga-varti* with an alkali, one should cauterize it; then, one should properly manage the wound like any other ulcer, applying a balanced powder and treating the complications.
A powder made from equal parts of svarjikā, tuttha, śaileya, añjana, rasāñjana, manaḥśilā, and alaktaka removes fleshy protuberances (māṃsāṅkura).
By wrapping it with the leaves of ghṛtakumārī, one removes carmakīla and other specific types of knots in the third stage.
Just as adverse fate renders even the most significant forms of human effort—though they have gained a firm footing during the day—ineffective, so too [this remedy acts].
However, one should grind the root of the *cāraṭī* plant with bull’s urine;
applied as a plaster, it quickly destroys splinters produced by weapons.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter on the treatment of hemorrhoids of the penis (liṅgārśas).
Now begins the fifty-third chapter on the defects of the glans (śūkadoṣa): The fool-minded man who desires the enlargement of the penis through improper means—
Eighteen diseases born of *śūka* arise in him;
these eighteen defects of *śūka* are shaped like white mustard seeds and are caused by the impurity of the *śūka*.
A pimple caused by phlegm (śleṣman) and wind (vāta) should be known as *sarṣapikā*;

it is hard, uneven, and curved due to the wind, and is called *aṣṭhīlikā*. That which is constantly filled with hair-like bristles (*śūka*) and knotted together is called *grathita*, arising from phlegm.
Kumbhikā arises from blood and bile (raktapitta); it is red, resembling the fruit of the Jambu tree, or white.
Alajī is likewise described by the wise as being similar to the pustules of prameha, red and black, and covered with eruptions.
That which is crushed or pressed, or inflamed due to the provocation of Vāta,
becomes a *saṃmūḍha-piḍakā* when it is intensely rubbed with both hands.
Those many long pustules which burst in the middle are likewise [known as such].
Sovamantha, arising from kapha and blood, causes pain and horripilation (9). A swelling covered with pustules, produced by pitta and blood,
and shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, should be known as Puṣkarikā (10).
However, blood vitiated by *śūka* causes a loss of sensation;
that which is red, resembling mung beans or black gram, and arising from *raktapitta*, is the piḍakā known as *uttamā*, produced by the undigested state of *śūka*. 11–12.
That disease which is produced by wind and blood, characterized by numerous small openings on all sides of the penis that persist for a long time, is to be known as śataponaka (13).
That which is caused by wind and bile, producing fever and burning sensations, is to be known as tvakpāka (14).

When the penis is afflicted with black vesicles and blood-stained pustules, accompanied by severe pain like that of a rat-bite, it should be known as *śoṇitārbuda* (blood-tumor). One should recognize that an *arbuda* arising from flesh is caused by the corruption of the flesh. 15–16.

The physician should recognize that condition as *māṃsapāka* (flesh-ripening), caused by all three doṣas, wherein the flesh wastes away and all sensations [of pain] are present; one should designate this as a *vidradhi* (abscess) arising from the combination of all three doṣas, as previously described. 17–18.
Whether black, variegated, or white, poisonous insects that have fallen quickly cook the penis entirely; once the flesh has turned black, it withers away from that embodied being. 18.
One should recognize those tilakālakas as arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).

Among them, the fleshy tumor (māṃsārbuda), that which is known as the suppuration of the flesh (māṃsapāka), the abscess (vidradhi), and those tilakālakas that appear— these do not succeed in being cured.
In all cases of the disorders caused by *śūka*, one should administer anti-venomous treatments;
one should extract the blood with leeches, administer mild purgatives,
and also cause *guggulu* to be processed in combination with a decoction of *triphalā*.
One should indeed perform ointments and sprinklings with cold milk alone.
Oil cooked with *dārvī*, *surasā*, *yaṣṭyāhvā*, house-soot, and *niśā* destroys diseases of the penis when used for massage. 21–22.

Rasāñjana alone, by mere application as an ointment, brings to pacification every disease of the eyes, including those accompanied by putrid pus, ulcers, swelling, itching, and pain. (23) Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, on the disorders caused by insect stings. 53.
Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter on the medical treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
For those who consume incompatible foods and drinks that are liquid, unctuous, and heavy, and who suppress vomiting as it arises along with other natural urges, [skin diseases occur]. (1)
For those who engage in excessive physical exercise and exposure to fire even after overeating;
for those who consume cold and hot things, fasting, and food out of sequence;
and for those afflicted by heat, fatigue, or fear who suddenly partake of cold water—(these are the causes of fever).

Also for those who eat when their food is undigested or overeat, those who practice the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarma) improperly, those who indulge in new grain, curd, fish, salt, and sour things,
and those who consume black gram, radish, flour-based foods, sesame, milk, and molasses.
For those who indulge in sexual intercourse when food is undigested, those who sleep during the day,
those who insult Brahmins and their gurus, and those who perform sinful deeds,
the three humors— wind and the others— as well as the skin, blood, flesh, and fluids [become corrupted].
These seven groups of substances corrupt [the skin],
and from them arise the seven and eleven types of *kuṣṭha* (skin diseases):
first the triad, then *sidhma*, and likewise *kākaṇaka*.
Puṇḍarīka, Ṛkṣajihvaka, and the seven great kuṣṭhas;
Ekakuṣṭha is recorded first, then Gajacarma is recorded; thereafter Carmadala is proclaimed, and then Vicarcikā as well. 8.
That very same [condition] is called vipādikā; beyond that are pāmā, kacchū,
and then dadru, visphoṭaka, kiṭibha, alasaka, and veṣṭita—
these are declared by the best of physicians to be the minor types of kuṣṭha.

Leucoderma (kuṣṭha) is of seven types according to the humors (doṣas): by each individually, by combinations of two, and by their combined presence; although all involve the three humors, they are designated by whichever is predominant.
(11) It may be excessively smooth or rough to the touch, and it is characterized by sweating or lack of sweating and discoloration.
Burning sensation, itching, numbness of the skin, pricking pain, elevation of eruptions (koṭha), exhaustion,
excessive pain in ulcers, rapid onset, long duration,
dryness even of healed wounds, and provocation [of the disease] by even slight causes.
Horripilation, blackness of the blood, and the primary symptoms of leprosy (kuṣṭha) arise;
the humors (doṣas), having vitiated and loosened the skin, cause it to shift here and there due to its lack of stability and produce discoloration— this they declare to be leprosy.

From wind (vāta) arises the *kāpāla* leprosy; from bile (pitta), the *audumbara*; from phlegm (kapha), that called *maṇḍala*, as well as *vicarcī* and the one called *ṛkṣa* arising from wind and bile;
and *carma*, *ekakuṣṭha*, *kiṭibha*, *sidhma*, *alasaka*, and *vipādikā*.
Dadru and śatāruṣī arise from vāta and śleṣman; puṇḍarīka, along with visphoṭa, pāmā, and carmadala, arise from pitta and kapha;
while the wise say that kākaṇaka arises when all the doṣas are aggravated.
That leprosy which has the appearance of a blackish-red skull, is rough, thin, characterized by intense pricking pain, and is irregular in its manifestation, is known as Kāpāla-kuṣṭha.
One should declare that leprosy which resembles the fruit of the Udumbara tree to be Audumbara-kuṣṭha.
Surrounded by pain, burning, redness, and itching, with bristling hair,
white or reddish in color, stable, thick, unctuous, and elevated in its circular patches,
with difficulty in separating when patches are joined to one another— this is called Maṇḍala-kuṣṭha.

That which is white-coppery, thin, and generally sheds dust when rubbed on the chest, resembling the flower of the alābu, is sidhma (vitiligo). That which has the color of kākaṇantikā, is unripe [in appearance], and is intensely painful—
That *kākaṇa* leprosy, which exhibits the symptoms of all three *doṣas*, is never cured.
That which is white with red margins, resembling the petal of a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), and characterized by redness and swelling, is *puṇḍarīka*, dominated by *kapha*. 22–23.
That which is rough, with red margins, dark-brown within, painful, and shaped like a bear’s tongue is called ṛkṣajihva (bear-tongue).
That which is painless, has a large area, and resembles a piece of fish is [called] matsyaśakala (fish-scale). 24.1–24.2ab.
That single type of kuṣṭha is called carma; it is thick like an elephant's hide (25).
It is red, accompanied by pain and itching, and is covered with eruptions; it even causes the skin to peel away, and that which cannot endure touch is known as carmadala (26).
An itchy, dark-brown eruption with abundant discharge is called *vicarcikā* (eczema).

27. Cracking of the hands and feet accompanied by intense pain is known as *vaipādikā*. 28. Numerous small pustules that exude fluid and cause a burning sensation are called *pāmā* (ringworm), characterized by itching. 29.
That very same [condition], when accompanied by intense burning, is known as *sphoṭa* (boils), occurring in the hands and the buttocks with severe itching.
30. *Dadru* is a raised circular patch characterized by itching, redness, and pustules.
31. *Visphoṭa* consists of eruptions that are dark-brown or reddish in appearance and have thin skin. 32.
A dark, rough-to-the-touch, and coarse eruption is known as *kiṭibha*.
*Alasaka* is characterized by being covered with itchy, reddish swellings (*gaṇḍa*). *Śatāru* is reddish-brown, accompanied by burning pain and distress, and consists of many ulcers (*bahuvraṇa*).
When Kuṣṭha is located in the skin (tvak), discoloration and roughness arise in the limbs;
there is numbness of the skin, horripilation, excessive perspiration, itching, and suppuration when Kuṣṭha is produced in the blood (śoṇita). 36–37.
Excessiveness, dryness of the mouth, roughness, the eruption of pustules, pricking pain, vesicles, and firmness occur when Kuṣṭha has taken refuge in the muscle tissue (māṃsa).
(38) Lameness, loss of movement, splitting pain in the limbs, and the spreading of ulcers occur [when it has reached the bone].

When [the disease] has reached the fat (medas), the symptoms are exactly as previously described; furthermore, there occurs the collapse of the nose, redness of the eyes, the appearance of worms in wounds,
impairment of the voice, and pain when the kuṣṭha has reached the bone and marrow.

When offspring is born from a husband and wife who both suffer from an abundance of leprosy (kuṣṭha) and whose blood and semen are corrupted, that child also should be known as afflicted with leprosy.
(41) Vāta-type leprosy is rough, dark-brown or reddish, dry, and accompanied by pain.
That which arises from pitta is considered to be putrefied, accompanied by burning, redness, and discharge;
that arising from kapha is thick, unctuous, and characterized by itching, coldness, and heaviness;
a kuṣṭha born from two doṣas exhibits the signs of both, while that born from all three doṣas (sānnipātika) exhibits all three sets of symptoms. 42
That which is located in the skin, blood, or flesh, and is characterized by a predominance of vāta and śleṣman, is curable;
that which has reached the fat (medas) or is born from two doṣas is palliable; that which is situated in the marrow or bone should be rejected.
That which produces worms, is accompanied by burning sensations and weak digestion, and arises from all three doṣas, is incurable. (43)

It destroys leprosy in this world, overcoming the patient who suffers from cracked and oozing limbs, bloodshot eyes, and a hoarse voice, and which has transcended the five therapeutic measures (pañcakarma).
From leprosy alone arises vitiligo (śvitra), as well as kilāsa and aruṇa.

It has been described as non-exuding, arising from and dependent upon the three *dhātus*: from *vāta* it is rough, reddish, and copper-colored like a lotus petal, accompanied by burning and loss of body hair; from *kapha* it is white, thick, and heavy. (45)
One should recognize that [the disease] accompanied by itching occurs successively in the blood, flesh, and fat;
both types are characterized by their color alone, and each subsequent one is more difficult to treat.
[The disease is considered new] when the hair is not white, is thick, and is not matted together.
A case of vitiligo (*śvitra*) that is not caused by fire-burns is curable; otherwise, it should be avoided.
Even if it is recent, vitiligo occurring on the genitals, the palms of the hands, or the lips must be especially rejected by one who desires success. 47–48.
Through incidental physical contact, exhalation, eating together,
sharing a bed or seat, and even through the use of the same clothes, garlands, and ointments,
[diseases such as] itching, leprosy, venereal sores, possession by spirits, insanity, wounds, and fever are transmitted.
And contagious diseases spread from person to person.
If one dies of leprosy (kuṣṭha), that same disease shall afflict one who is born again;
therefore, this loathsome disease is proclaimed as the most grievous leprosy. 49–50.
In cases of kuṣṭha where vāta is predominant, ghee is the best treatment; where kapha is predominant, emesis;
and where pitta is predominant, external application, affusion, and bloodletting are most excellent. (51) [One may also use] harītakī, karañja, siddhārtha, niśā, avalguja, and saindhava.
An ointment made from these ingredients ground together with *viḍaṅga* and cow's urine cures skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). This powder derived from *somarājī*, combined with *śṛṅgavera*,
used as a rubbing paste (*udvartana*), destroys even severe skin diseases that have taken firm root.
I shall proclaim the elixir (rasāyana) as it was declared by Brahmā and employed by the great seers, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others;
[one should take] flowers during the flowering season and fruits during the fruiting season.
Having collected the bark, roots, and leaves of *picumarda*, one should take two parts each and prepare them as single portions.
[Then add] *triphalā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), *brāhmī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *aruṣkara*, and *agni*. (55–56)
Equal parts of the essence of *viḍaṅga*, *vārāhī*, iron powder, and *amṛtā*, along with the two types of *niśā*, *avalguja*, and *vyādhighāta*, combined with sugar;
and a powder consisting of *kuṣṭha*, *indrāyava*, and *pāṭhā*—these, when mixed together, [are effective]. 57.
One should saturate the *pañcanimba* seven times with a thick decoction of *khadira*, *āsana*, and *nimba*, and then with the juice of *mārkava*.
Once the wise practitioner has become unctuous and his body purified, he should administer it on an auspicious day. (58)
It may be taken with honey, or with bitter clarified butter (tiktahavis), or with a decoction of khadira and asana;

or it may be made into a linctus with warm water. The dose should be increased by one pala according to the passage of time. Once that has been digested, one should eat food that is unctuous, light, and wholesome. 59

Eczema, fig-like eruptions, lotus-like sores, scabies, ringworm, kiṭibha, alasa, and others; the hundred-fold diseases, carbuncles, erysipelas, and chains of pustules; the three types of leucoderma arising from the provocation of phlegm (kapha); fistula-in-ano, elephantiasis, gout, stiffness, blindness, sinus ulcers, and diseases of the head.

It destroys all types of prameha, all forms of pradara, and the poison of fangs as well as root-poison. Through the consumption of honey, one who has a large belly becomes one with a waist as slender as a lion's; its joints become well-knit. Furthermore, even those such as serpents that bite will quickly meet their destruction through constant use of it.
May he live long, free from disease and old age, devoted to auspiciousness, and possessing a splendor equal to the moon.
(63) Take five palas of Śaśilekhā, ten palas of Guggulu belonging to Girija, three palas of Tāpya, and two palas each of Loha and Srāvaṇīka. (64)

One should swallow in the morning a pill prepared from these— triphalā, the sprouts of karañja, khadira, guḍūcī, trivṛt, dantī, mustā, viḍaṅga, rajanī, kuṭaja bark, nimba, vahi, and saṃpāka— mixed with honey.
This self-originated formulation, known by the name Svāyambhuva, removes leprosy, blood disorders, and wind disorders in a short time through cow urine;
it destroys vitiligo, anemia, irregular abdominal ailments, urinary disorders, and tumors,
as well as wrinkles and graying hair.
Citraka, triphalā, vyoṣa, ajājī, kāravī, vacā,
saindhava, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, cavya, elā, yavāsaka,
viḍaṅga, ajamodā, mustā, and amaradāru. (68)
The physician should crush all these ingredients together with an equal quantity of guggulu and, mixing them with clarified butter, form them into pills;
these should be consumed at the time of breakfast in the morning, according to one's digestive strength.
It destroys the eighteen types of skin diseases, as well as worms, foul ulcers, disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, diseases of the mouth, throat obstructions, sciatica,
fractures, and abdominal tumors.
It conquers even diseases located within the internal organs, just as Viṣṇu conquers the asuras.
This supreme medicine, named Kaiśoraka, which was previously mentioned in the section on vātarakta, is the best remedy for destroying skin diseases and vātarakta. 72–73.
Having cut two *prastha*s of *bhallātaka* fruit, one should throw them into water measuring one *droṇa*;
then, having crushed two *prastha*s of *guḍūcī*, one should throw that into the water;
when reduced to a fourth part, one should remove the decoction from the heat.
When the decoction has been strained through a cloth, one should add what is to be described hereafter:
one *śarāva* measure of ghee, one *āḍhaka* of milk, one *prastha* of white sugar, and half a *prastha* of honey should be added. (75–76)
One should cook all [the ingredients] together in a single vessel over a mild fire slowly;
when all the liquid has become thickened, one should remove it from the fire.
We shall now state the powders to be added therein: bilva, viṣa, and amṛtā.
Vākucī, then Dadra-ghnu, Picumarda, Harītakī (78),
Akṣa, Dhātrī, Mañjiṣṭhā, Marica, Nāgara, Kaṇā,
Yavānī, Saindhava, Musta, Tvak, Elā, and Nāgakeśara (79).
One should add here the powder of these, measured at half a pala each: parpaṭa, patra, young uśīra, candana, the seeds of gokṣura, karcūra, and red sandalwood (raktacandana). 80.
One should consume exactly one *pala* of this with water in the morning;
this electuary destroys [diseases] for one who eats wholesome food.
When used regularly, it cures all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), gout (*vātarakta*), and hemorrhoids (*arśas*). 81–82.

A person who has consumed *bhallātaka* should avoid physical exercise, exposure to the sun, fire, sour substances, meat, curd, women, oil massage, as well as travel on foot. (83) [The following herbs are:
*nimba*, *gopāruṇā*, *kaṭvī*, *trāyantī*, *triphalā*, and *ghana*.
Parpaṭa, avalguja, anantā, vacā, khadira, candana;
(84) pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, śaṭī, bhārgī, vāsā, bhūnimba, vatsaka; śyāmā, indravāruṇī, mūrvā, viḍaṅga, indrayava, anala. (85)
Hastikarṇa, amṛtā, ādraka, kapaṭola, the two types of rajanī, kaṇā, āragvadha, saptāhvā, trivṛt, vetra, uccaṭā-phala (86),
mañjiṣṭhā, lāṅgalī, rāsnā, naktamāla, and punarnavā.
One should take two palas each of the essence of *dantībījaka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kuraṇṭaka*,
*aṅkoṭaka*, and *śākhoṭa*; having taken all of these individually, one should cook them slowly in one *droṇa* of water.
When one-eighth of the decoction remains, one should remove it from the fire; having strained it through a cloth, one should place it in a sturdy vessel.
(89) Then, having cut a thousand *bhallātaka* fruits with a sharp knife, [one should boil them] in water.
When eight parts remain, one should remove that decoction from the fire (90).
Having strained it through a cloth, one should mix the two decoctions together; then, adding one hundred palas of jaggery, one should cook it slowly like a linctus (91).

One *pala* each of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *musta*, *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), sandalwood (*candana*), *kuṣṭha*, and *dīpyaka* should be added; for the sake of fragrance, one *pala* each of the four aromatics (*cāturjāta*) should also be thrown therein. (92)
Indeed, this great bhallātaka has been proclaimed by Mahādeva;
when employed with the desire for the welfare of living beings, it swiftly overcomes vitiligo, audumbara, ringworm, ṛkṣajihva, and kākaṇa. 93.
It cures puṇḍarīka, the disease known as sacarma, visphoṭa, raktamaṇḍala (94), itching, kapālakuṣṭha, pāmā, vipādikā,
vātarakta, the six types of hemorrhoids, anemia, ulcers, and worms (95).

Through constant practice, one may overcome hemorrhagic fever, upward-moving wind, cough, asthma, fistula-in-ano, premature graying of hair, and even the most difficult to cure rheumatism (āmavāta). Indeed, it is said that in matters of recreation, diet, and sexual intercourse, there should be no restriction.
It produces supreme luster and kindles the digestive fire.
As a post-drink (anupāna), either water boiled with *chinnā* or milk should be administered;
however, hot food and sour substances should always be avoided during meals, especially the latter.
A decoction prepared from mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, tiktā, vacā, dāruniśā, āmalaka, and nimba destroys all types of kuṣṭha,
as well as vātarakta, itching, scabies, and raktamaṇḍala. (99)

One should destroy ringworm (dadrū), erysipelas (visarpa), and boils (visphoṭa) by the regular practice of drinking [this]. 100 Mañjiṣṭhā, vākucī, cakramarda, picumardaka, harītakī, haridrā, dhātrī, vāsā, and śatāvarī. 101
Balā, nāgabalā, yaṣṭīmadhuka, kṣuraka, the creeper of paṭola, uśīra, guḍūcī, and raktacandana—
this decoction beginning with mañjiṣṭhā is the supreme destroyer of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 102.
This [formula] is the destroyer of vātarakta (gout/rheumatism), and it eliminates itching and skin eruptions (maṇḍala).
It consists of mañjiṣṭhā, kuṭaja, amṛtā, ghana, vacā, muṇḍī, the two types of haridrā, kṣudrā, iṣṭa, paṭola, tiktaka, kaṭukā, bhārgī, viḍaṅga, and agnika. 103.
Mūrvā, dāru, kaliṅga, bhṛṅgarāja, agnimantha, āyāntī, pāṭhā, varī, gāyatrī, triphalā, kirātaka, mahānimba, asana, and āragvadha;

(104) śyāmā, valguja, candana, varuṇaka, dantī, śākhoṭaka, vāsā, sarpaṭa, sārivā, prativiṣā, anantā, viśālā, jala, and mañjiṣṭhā—this is the first decoction (kaṣāya). Whoever consumes it, his skin disorders will dissolve away after a long time, as will the eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha). (105)
Vātarakta is destroyed, all blood-related diseases vanish, erysipelas,
skin vacuity, and eye diseases are pacified.
(106) [The formulation consists of] marica, trivṛtā, musta, haritāla, and manaḥśilā.
Devadāru, the two types of haridrā, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and candana; viśālā, karavīra, milk from the arka plant, and the juice of cow dung—one karṣa of each should be prepared. 107–108.
One should take half a pala of viṣa and one prastha of oil,
and cook them with four times as much water and twice as much cow's urine;
this Maricādya oil destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) when used for massage.
Through massage with this [oil], vitiligo becomes discolored at that very moment.
This oil conquers itching, scabies, sidhma, and eczema, as well as puṇḍarīka and ringworm; furthermore, it removes the sense of emptiness in those who use it constantly.
Black pepper, trivṛt, dantī, milk of the arka plant, cow dung and its juice, devadāru, the two types of haridrā, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, sandalwood,
viśālā, karavīra, yellow orpiment, and realgar. (112)
Citraka, lāṅgalī, musta, viḍaṅga, cakramardaka,
śirīṣa, kuṭaja, nimba, saptaparṇa, amṛtā, snuhī, śyāmāka, naktamāla, khadira, vākucī, and vacā. (113–114)
One pala each of jyotiṣmatī and palikā, two palas of poison,
one āḍhaka of mustard oil, and four times that amount of cow urine should be cooked slowly over a mild fire in an earthen or iron vessel. 115.
This oil, beginning with long pepper (marica), has been proclaimed by the great sages.
With this oil, the physician should anoint ulcers of the abdominal cavity, as well as ringworm (pāmā), eczema (vicarcikā), tinea corporis (dadru), itching, and eruptive boils (visphoṭaka). 116–117.
Wrinkles, graying hair, discoloration, dark spots, and likewise blemishes are eliminated by this massage, and a state of youthful delicacy is produced;
this is for those women in their first youth to whom this nasal therapy (nasya) is administered. 118.
Even when they have reached old age, their breasts would not sag;
whether it be an ox, a horse, or an elephant afflicted by wind, its wind-related ailment would be cured by these three ointments. 119–120.

Take borax, realgar, sulphur, and ṭaṅkaṇa, combined with rock salt; add sulphur twice the amount of mercury and conch-shell powder equal to that. Having ground these for one day with the juice of *jambīra* fruit, one should add poison amounting to a thirtieth part [of the total].
One should eat two *māṣas* of this combined with buffalo ghee (122).
Thereafter, one should lick one *karṣa* of *vākucī* seeds with honey and clarified butter.
This elixir named Tālakeśvara removes all types of leprosy (123).
Rasa, vālī, copper, pure fire (cinnabar), śilājatu, viṣatinduka,

and varā— these should be taken in equal parts along with gaganam (mica) and all four types of karañja seeds. Having thoroughly ground everything together with honey and ghee, it should be carefully placed in a vessel of ghee.
One should consume one *karṣa* of this daily as wholesome food, along with *śāli* rice, milk, and the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar).
Even one whose ears, fingers, and nose are shattered may, by means of this, become equal in form to the God of Love (*Smara*).
In this case, the abandonment of sexual intercourse is prescribed; when the root [of the plant] is established, one should eat rice with water.
Kuṣṭha, radish seeds, priyaṅgu, mustard seeds, turmeric, and keśara—this group of six destroys long-standing sidhma when applied as a paste ground with the juice of śikhari. 127.
Radish seeds ground with the juice of śikhari, when used as a plaster, [cure] sidhma.
Or one destroys [the stain] with the alkali of the plantain mixed with turmeric. 128.
One karṣa each of the seeds of dārvīmūlaka, realgar, deodar, and betel leaf—each of these individually—[should be used]. 129.

One *śāṇa* of conch powder should be taken; all these together with water form a plaster that is the best for destroying *sidhma*. A paste of mango pulp mixed with a little rock salt [should be applied] in water.
Rubbed in a copper vessel, it removes skin spots through its application.
Furthermore, by rubbing dried *dhātrī* fruits with water using both hands, a person afflicted with skin spots attains comfort. 131–132.
One pala of cumin ground with half a pala of vermilion— having cooked these two with mustard oil, it is the supreme remedy for all scabies (pāmā).
[With] mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, lac, lāṅgalī, turmeric, and gandhaka...
Oil cooked with these powders under the sun is a supreme remedy for scabies (pāmā).
Likewise, rock salt, *cakramarda*, mustard seeds, and long pepper,
ground together with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), are excellent for removing scabies and itching.

Sesame oil cooked in the juice of *arka* leaves and combined with a paste of turmeric destroys scabies, itching, and eczema. Realgar, alum, ferrous sulfate, sulfur, and rock salt— [these are used for the same purpose].
The physician [should take] one karṣa each of svarṇakṣīrī, śilābhedī, śuṇṭhī, kuṣṭha, māgadhī,
lāṅgalī, karavīra, dadrughna, kṛmihā, anala,
dantī, and nimba leaves. 137–138.
Having made [the ingredients] into a paste, one should cook two *prastha*s of pungent oil with the milk of *arka* and *sehuṇḍa*, each measuring one *pala*,
and also with one *āḍhaka* of cow’s urine, cooking it slowly over a mild fire. 139.
Through massage, this [oil] removes even the incurability of scabies (kacchū), as well as ringworm (pāmā), itching, skin diseases, and blood disorders;
this oil, called Kaṇḍūrākṣasa, was spoken by Hārīta. 140–141.
The leaves of *kṛtamāla*, the petals of *naktamāla*,
the foliage of *droṇapuṣpī* and *palāśa*, mustard seeds, black mustard, turmeric (142),
*kuṭaja*, *madhuka*, *musta*, ginger, and red sandalwood.
This paste, prepared from dhātrī, yavānikā, and dāru,
when combined with kaṭutaila and used for rubbing the body (udvartana), certainly removes scabies (kacchū), ringworm (pāmā), and diseases such as śītapitta. (143–144)
Kuṣṭha, kṛmighna, dadrughna, niśā, saindhava, and sarṣapa,
ground with sour liquid and applied as a paste, destroy dadru and kuṣṭha.
(145) Dūrvā, abhayā, saindhava, cakramarda, and kuṭheraka, ground with kāñjika and buttermilk [are likewise effective].
Even with three applications of these ointments, they destroy ringworm (*dadrū*) and leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), even when deeply rooted. 146.
The grass known as *gaṇḍalikā*, white mustard (*siddhārthaka*), and the leaf of *snuhī*—these three should be in equal parts, while the *dadrūghna* [drug] should be twice the amount of them. 147.
One should mix those aforementioned ingredients with eight parts of buttermilk;
after three days have passed,
one should thoroughly grind them with a wild stone and apply that paste to the *dadru* (ringworm).

This ointment destroys ringworm (dadrū) within seven days. 149 The seeds of *avalguja* drunk with a decoction of the bark of *bibhītaka* and the roots of *malayū*, combined with jaggery, removes even difficult cases of leucoderma (*śvitra*) and *puṇḍarīka*. 150
One *kuḍava* of *avalguṇa* seeds mixed with a fourth part of yellow orpiment (151),
along with half a *tolaka* of realgar, *guñjā* fruit, and the root of *agni*,
ground with cow’s urine, produces a restoration of natural skin color in cases of vitiligo (152).

White leprosy (śveta-kuṣṭha) comes to an end within half a fortnight or slightly more when anointed with the root of black *girikarṇī*; likewise, a decoction of *dhātrī* and the heartwood of *khadira*, combined with the powder of *vākucī*, [achieves the same]. 153.
One who regularly consumes [the powder] as white as a conch, the moon, or a jasmine flower will remove vitiligo (śvitra).
One should drink the powder with churning-water (mathita); anointed with oil and exposed to the heat of the sun while subsisting on buttermilk, one becomes a remover of vitiligo. 154–155.
Four palas of *somarājī*, one pala of *khadira*, and one karṣa each of the paste ingredients— *paṭola* root, *triphalā*, *trāyamāṇā*, *durālabhā*, and *kaṭukā*— should be finely ground. 156.
One should administer two palas of pure *kauśika* here;
this prepared ghee destroys leucoderma (*śvitra*) as water extinguishes fire, and it is the supreme medicine for the eighteen types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). (157–158)
The medicated ghee known as Somarājī-ghṛta was prepared by Brahmā in ancient times for the benefit of people suffering from vitiligo, leprosy, and other such diseases.
(159) Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter on leprosy. 54.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter: On Cold-Pitta, Udarda, Koṭha, and Utkoṭha.
(1) When Kapha and Vāta are aggravated by contact with cold winds, they combine with Pitta and spread both externally and internally.
Thirst, loss of appetite, nausea, exhaustion of the body, heaviness of the limbs,
and redness of the eyes are the symptoms of its premonitory stage (pūrvarūpa). An external swelling arises, shaped like a wasp sting.
The physician should recognize this as *śītapitta*, characterized by excessive itching and tearing, vomiting, fever, and a burning sensation, with a predominance of *vāta*.
It is further marked by circular patches (*maṇḍala*) that are elevated, reddish, and itchy.
The cold season (śaiśira) is characterized by an abundance of phlegm (śleṣman) and is known as the time for urticaria (udarda).
Due to improper emesis, the aggravation of pitta and phlegm, and the suppression of natural urges, many circular patches appear, accompanied by itching and redness.
When that [condition] is accompanied by complications, it is called *utkoṭha* by the wise.
In cases of *śītapitta*, emesis with *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vāsaka* is recommended,
as is purgation with *triphalā* and warm *pūrakāṣṭha*.
One should perform an oil massage with mustard oil and a sprinkling with warm water;
then, one should consume nine karṣas of the three myrobalans (triphalā) combined with honey.
[This formulation consists of] three, five, and one parts of triphalā, puru (long pepper), and kṛṣṇā (black pepper) respectively.
This pill is beneficial for those suffering from cold-pitta (śītapitta), hemorrhoids (arśas), and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara). Thus ends the "Nine-Kārṣika" formulation.
[One should take] sugar combined with the three pungents (trikaṭu), along with jaggery and āmalaka fruits.
One should also eat yavānī (Trachyspermum ammi) combined with vyōṣa (the three pungents) and kṣāra (alkali).
The juice of fresh ginger, mixed with old jaggery, should be drunk;
it is excellent for removing śītapitta and destroys weak digestion.
This rubbing paste, consisting of a paste of *siddhārtha* and *rajanī*, along with *prapunnāṭa* and sesame seeds, mixed with mustard oil, is beneficial.
Furthermore, the man who eats *dīpyaka* with good molasses while consuming wholesome food [will be cured]. 12.

Within seven days, his urticaria arising throughout the entire body will vanish. Having drunk *mahātikta* ghee, one should likewise let blood; then, for one who has been lubricated and fomented, one should first perform purification (*saṃśuddhi*) of the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*).
For one whose body has been purified by emesis, one should administer treatments that destroy leprosy (kuṣṭha).
A person should always consume nimba leaves mixed with āmalakī and ghee;
this destroys eruptive boils, itching, worms, śītapitta, urtikā, koṭha, and kapha. 14–15.
One *prastha* of fresh ginger, two *kuḍavas* of cow’s ghee,
two *prasthas* of cow’s milk, and half of that [milk]— namely one *prastha*— is considered the quantity for sugar.
[Then add] long pepper, the root of long pepper, black pepper, and ginger.

Take one pala each of citraka, viḍaṅga, mustaka, nāgakeśara, tvak, elā, patra, and karcūra; having prepared this according to the prescribed method, one should consume it in a dose of one pala. 17–18.

Indeed, this fresh piece of *khaṇḍa* (sugar-candy), when consumed in the morning, dispels cold-pitta (*śītapitta*), urticaria (*udarda*), *koṭha*, *utkoṭha*, consumption (*yakṣman*), internal hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*), cough, dyspnea, and anorexia.
It cures wind-tumors (vātagulma), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), swelling, itching, and even worms;
it kindles the digestive fire in the stomach and increases strength and virility.
It brings about nourishment of the body; therefore, this should always be used.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter on Śītapitta, Udarda, Koṭha, and Utkoṭha.
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter on Visarpa (Erysipelas).
Due to the provocation of the doṣas caused by the consumption of salty, sour, pungent, and hot substances, etc., [Visarpa arises].
Visarpa is to be known as sevenfold because it spreads in every direction.
He explains the sevenfold nature of visarpa: that which is caused by vāta, by pitta, by kapha, and by the combination of all three (sānnipātika).
These four types of visarpa will be described; three are born from the combination of two humors (dvandvaja).
That which arises from vāta and pitta is called āgneya; that which is produced by kapha and vāta is named granthi; and that terrible one known as kardamaka originates from pitta and kapha.
Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (dūṣyas), while the three humors (doṣas) are the impurities;
these seven constituents serve as the causes for the arising of the spreading diseases (visarpas).
Among them, the Vata-type spreading disease has symptoms identical to those of Vata-fever.
Accompanied by swelling, throbbing, pricking pain, piercing, aching, distress, and horripilation;
from pitta, it moves rapidly, possesses the symptoms of pitta-fever, and is very red;
from kapha, it is characterized by itching, is unctuous, and has a pain similar to that of kapha-fever.
That arising from the combination [of all three humors] is endowed with all symptoms: fever, vomiting, fainting, diarrhea, thirst, giddiness,
breaking pain in the bones, loss of digestive fire, darkness before the eyes, and anorexia.

It causes all parts of the body to appear as if strewn with glowing embers; whatever region the Visarpa spreads to, that very place becomes like cold embers— appearing black, blue, or red— and quickly swells up.

Like a blister burnt by fire, it spreads rapidly; due to its swift movement, that Visarpa follows the vital points (marmas). When the Vata is exceedingly powerful, it causes pain in the limbs, takes away consciousness and sleep, and excites labored breathing.
And having fallen into such a state of hiccupping, he finds no relief anywhere,
being seized by the agony of itching while moving about on the ground, beds, seats, and so forth;
thus afflicted, he suffers from distress arising from both mind and body.
One who is difficult to awaken from sleep suffers from what is called agnivisarpa (fire-like erysipelas).

When the wind (vāyu), obstructed by phlegm (kapha), breaks through that phlegm in many ways, it reaches the skin, vessels, ligaments, and flesh— either the phlegm itself or the blood in one whose blood has increased.
Having vitiated the long, thick, and rough-natured channels, it produces a garland of red nodules accompanied by intense pain and fever,
along with dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, consumption, hiccup, vomiting, and vertigo. (15)
Accompanied by delusion, discoloration, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of digestive fire—
this is Granthivisarpa, born from the provocation of Vāta and Kapha.
From Kapha and Pitta arise fever, stiffness, drowsiness, lethargy, and headache.
Lassitude of the limbs, restlessness, a coating sensation, anorexia, vertigo, fainting, loss of digestive fire, aching of the bones, thirst, heaviness of the sense organs,
the presence of *sāma* (undigested matter), and obstruction of the channels— this [kapha] spreads throughout the body. 17–18.
Generally, it affects the stomach region, is not excessively painful, and is not covered with pustules; it is very yellowish-red and pale,
unctuous, blackish-blue in luster, dirty-looking, swollen, and heavy.
Deep-seated in its maturation, intensely hot, and becoming moist upon contact, it breaks open;
with skin like mud, flesh that has fallen away, and clearly visible networks of tendons and veins,
smelling like a corpse— this spreading inflammation (vīsarpa) they call Kardama.
But that which arises from the combination [of all three humors] is endowed with all symptoms (verse 22).
Provoked by an external cause such as a wound, the wind (vāyu), inciting the bile along with blood, produces visarpa (erysipelas),
which is covered with eruptions resembling horse-gram (kulattha) beans.
Sphota (vesicular eruptions) is characterized by swelling, fever, pain, burning sensations, and dark-red blood.
Fever, diarrhea, vomiting, tearing of the skin and flesh, exhaustion, loss of appetite, and indigestion are the complications of visarpa (erysipelas).
Visarpas caused by vāta, kapha, and pitta are curable, as is that which arises from all three combined (sarvātmaka) and that caused by injury (kṣatakṛta).

However, the type consisting of pitta alone, as well as that which has the appearance of añjana (añjanavapuḥ), are incurable; indeed, all types occurring in vital spots (marma) are difficult to treat.
[These conditions are managed] through purgation, emesis, ointments, affusions, and bloodletting.
One should treat the various types of visarpa according to their specific doshas with non-burning (avidāhin) remedies.
An ointment consisting of rāsnā, blue lotus (nīlotpala), devadāru, sandalwood, madhuka, and balā,
combined with ghee and milk, destroys vāta-visarpa.

A very cold plaster consisting of *kaśeru*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, lotus, *uśīra*, along with *śaivala*, blue lotuses, and lotus-mud, mixed with ghee and applied between layers of cloth, should be administered for a *visarpa* caused by pitta. (28) [Also:
*triphalā*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *samaṅgā*, and *karavīraka*.
A plaster of *nalada* root and *anantā* is beneficial for *śleṣmavisarpa*.
For *agnivisarpa*, which involves the pacification of *vāta* and *pitta*, it is beneficial;
for *granthivisarpa*, actions that remove *vāta* and *śleṣman* are beneficial. (29–30)
That which pacifies *pitta* and *kapha* is beneficial for the type known as Kardama-visarpa; for that born from the three *doṣas*, one should perform a treatment that removes all three.
[One should use] *śirīṣa*, *yaṣṭī*, *nata*, *candana*, *elā*, *māṃsī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *bāla*.

An ointment consisting of ten ingredients mixed with ghee should be applied; it removes erysipelas, skin diseases, fever, and swelling. (32) For erysipelas, affusions and plasters made from the five barks, or from padmaka, uśīra, madhuka, and candana, are recommended. (33)
A decoction prepared with bhūnimba, vāsā, kaṭukā, paṭolī, the three fruits (triphalā), candana, and nimba cures erysipelas,
burning sensations, fever, swelling, itching, eruptions, thirst, vomiting, and heart disease.
[34] Regarding the medicated ghees for skin diseases and various types of wounds:
These [substances] should be employed for erysipelas (visarpa) through affusions, ointments, and food.
Oil cooked with karañja, saptacchada, lāṅgalī, snuhī, arka, milk, anala, bhṛṅgarāja, turmeric, urine, and poisons destroys erysipelas, eruptive boils (visphoṭa), and scabies (vicarcikā).

By means of the treatments prescribed for leprosy (kuṣṭha), skin eruptions (sphoṭa), and smallpox (masūrikā), the wise physician should also quickly eliminate all types of erysipelas (visarpa). Having purified those that have suppurated, one should treat them according to the prescribed sequence for ulcers. Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter on Erysipelas. 56.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter, on diseases of the ligaments (snāyuroga).
The dosha, aggravated in the extremities, produces swelling like erysipelas;
having burst through that [skin], it dries up the flesh along with its heat at the site of the wound.
One should make a thread resembling a fiber from those lumps made of buttermilk and barley flour;
by cutting it very slowly, the wound heals, but if it is cut quickly, it brings about irritation. From its falling away, there is relief from swelling, though it may recur in another location.
That is known as *snāyu* (sinew); the treatment prescribed here is like that for *visarpa* (erysipelas).
If it is accidentally severed in the arms or even in the shanks, it certainly causes contraction and lameness.
One should perform treatments such as oleation, sudation, and external applications as appropriate.
Asafoetida (rāmaṭha), when drunk with cold water, cures diseases of the tendons (snāyuka).
A frog prepared with fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika) and applied through sudation cures even the most severe snāyuka.
In the same way, *babbūla* seed ground into a paste destroys [the disease] when applied as an ointment.
Having drunk cow's ghee for three days, one should drink the fresh juice of *nirguṇḍī* for three days;
this certainly destroys even the most fierce *snāyukama*, of this there is no doubt.

The root of *suṣavī* ground with Himalayan water, when drunk, quickly brings peace to this fierce disease of the cords (*tantuka-roga*) even in men with ulcers; likewise, by drinking *gandharvagandha* with ghee. [8] Ati-viṣā, mustaka, bhargī, viśvauṣadha, pippalī, and bibhītaka—these [are used].
This powder, when drunk with warm water, destroys the cords [of the body] in men.
An application made from the ground roots and leaves of the *śigru* tree, mixed with rock salt and sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
is considered the supreme remedy for the disease of the sinews (*snāyuka*).

By carefully applying a plaster made from the root-paste of *ahiṃsraka* ground with water, the tendon will not come out; of this there is no doubt. (11) Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, on the treatment of diseases of the tendons. 57.

Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter: On Eruptions (Visphoṭaka). The humors—wind and the others—are provoked by pungent, sour, sharp, hot, burning, dry, and alkaline substances; by indigestion, overeating, and exposure to the sun; and likewise by the adverse influence of the seasons. (1)
Residing in the skin and vitiating the blood, flesh, and bones,
they produce all kinds of terrible eruptions preceded by fever;
these eruptions, born of blood and bile, are like those burnt by fire and are accompanied by fever.
These are known as *visphoṭas*, occurring either in some parts or throughout the body.
Headache, intense piercing pain, fever, thirst, breaking pain in the joints, and a blackish discoloration— these are the characteristics of *vāta-visphoṭa*.
Accompanied by fever, burning sensations, pain, suppuration, discharge, and thirst,
it is yellowish or reddish in color and characterized by eruptions caused by pitta (5). Vomiting, loss of appetite, stupor, itching, hardness, and pallor [are also present].
That in which there is no redness and the suppuration occurs slowly is a *visphoṭa* caused by *kapha*.
With itching, burning, fever, and vomiting, it is caused by *kapha* and *pitta*.
That which is produced by *vāta* and *pitta* is characterized by intense pain.
One should recognize a kapha-vata type [of swelling] by itching, numbness, and heaviness (9).
Furthermore, it is depressed in the center, elevated at the edges, hard, and undergoes little suppuration;
it is accompanied by burning sensations, redness, thirst, delusion, vomiting, fainting, pain, and fever.
Delirium, trembling, and drowsiness— this [fever] born from the three doṣas is incurable (10).
It should be known that those caused by blood and by pitta are red like the fruit of the guñjā plant, accompanied by bleeding, and characterized by a burning sensation.
They do not attain success even through hundreds of perfected yogas.
These eight types are external, but there is also an internal one;
in that [internal state], an intense internal agony accompanied by fever arises. 11–12.
If a person finds no relief when [the blood] has gone outside, or if it does not flow out at all, the wise physician should perform the treatment for *vātaja* eruptions (*visphoṭaka*) there.
Thirst, dyspnea, putrefaction of the flesh, burning sensation, hiccup, fainting, and fever [are the symptoms].
The complications of those [visarpa] cases are said to be the obstruction of the vital points (marmas) and the spreading of the disease (visarpa).
Hiccups, dyspnea, anorexia, thirst, body ache, pain in the heart, fever, nausea, and eruptions are the complications of visarpa. (14–15)
A fever caused by a single doṣa is curable; one born from two doṣas is difficult to cure;
but one accompanied by all symptoms, which is terrible and has many complications, is indeed incurable.
(16) In the case of eruptive boils (visphoṭa), fasting should be performed, followed by emesis and a wholesome diet.

Having observed the strength of the doshas, purgation has been appropriately described [as follows]: (17) The sages have declared that aged śāli rice, barley, mung beans, masūra lentils, and likewise āḍhakī—these foods are beneficial in the case of visphoṭa. (18)
A person should drink the decoction of two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), rāsnā, dāruharidrā, uśīra, durālabhā, guḍūcī, dhānyaka, and musta;
this quickly destroys eruptions caused by vāta. 19
In the case of Pitta-type fever, [the decoction] of Drākṣā, Kāśmarya, Kharjūra, Paṭola, Ariṣṭa, Vāsaka,
Kaṭukā, Alāja, and Duḥsparśā, combined with sugar, should be administered. [Likewise, one may use] Bhūnimba, Saptaparṇa, Vāsā, Triphalā, Indravāruṇī, and Vatsaka.
In cases arising from Kapha, [a decoction] of *picumarda* and *paṭola* boiled with honey is used; likewise,
[a decoction] of *kirātatiktaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *ambuda*, and *vāsaka*, combined with *paṭola*, *parpaṭa*, *uśīra*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), and *kauṭaja*.
A decoction of the twelve parts [of the plant] destroys all eruptive boils (visphoṭaka).
To destroy the disease of eruptive boils, an intelligent person should apply a plaster made from the seeds of the *kuṭaja* tree ground with rice-water.
A decoction made from *chinnā*, *paṭola*, *bhūnimba*, *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *parpaṭa*, along with *khadira* and *mustā*, destroys eruptive fever (*visphoṭaka-jvara*).
[24] Sandalwood, *nāgapuṣpa*, *sārivā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*—
An application of *śirīṣa* bark and *jātī* [flowers] serves to destroy burning sensations.
(25) An ointment made of blue lotus (*utpala*), sandalwood (*candana*), *lodhra*, *uśīra*, and the two types of *sārivā*, ground with water, destroys eruptions, burning, and pain. (26)
Having ground the marrow of *putrajīva* in water, one should apply it as an ointment;

it instantly destroys *kālasphoṭa*, *visphoṭa*, and painful eruptions, and it eliminates glandular swellings of the armpit (*kakṣagranthi*), the throat (*galagranthi*), and the ear (*karṇagranthi*). 27.
Copper kills [the disease], and *putrajīva* destroys the *sphoṭaka*.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter on *visphoṭaka*.
Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter on the diseases of the Franks (*phiraṅgaroga*).
Because it occurs predominantly in the country known as Phiraṅga, this disease is called "Phiraṅga" by those expert in pathology.
This Gandharoga, known as Phiraṅga, certainly arises in embodied beings.

This disease is indeed an exogenous (āgantuja) one arising from contact with a foreigner or through association with a foreign woman; here, there is a transmission of the humors (doṣas). An excellent physician should recognize it by observing their specific symptoms.
Syphilis (phiraṅga) is known to be of three types: external, internal, and both external and internal; I shall now describe their symptoms.
Among these, the external syphilis resembles a vesicle or pustule and is accompanied by slight pain.
That which is felt like a cracked wound is considered easily curable (sukhasādhya). That which occurs internally within the joints, producing pain and swelling like *āmavāta*,
is considered difficult to cure (kaṣṭasādhya) by the wise.
Emaciation, loss of strength, collapse of the nose, dullness of the digestive fire, wasting of the bones, and deformity of the bones— these are the complications of syphilis (phiraṅga).
That which is external, recent, and free from complications is curable.

This internal disease is difficult to cure; sages of old have said that a disease which has spread both internally and externally, is chronic, occurs in one who is emaciated, is accompanied by complications, and is pervasive, is incurable.
Now, regarding the treatment of the disease known as *phiraṅga*: "The elixir known as camphor will certainly destroy this disease called *phiraṅga*"; so said the physicians of old. 10.
The supreme procedure for consuming *rasakarpūra* is now written:
by means of this procedure, one should eat it, and swelling in the mouth will not be found.
(11) Having kneaded wheat flour, one should fashion a small cup.
Into the middle of that, the physician should place mercury measuring four *guñjās*.
Then, he should form it into a pill so that it is not visible on the outside;
he should dust that bolus with the fine powder of cloves.
One should swallow that betel leaf with water in such a way that it does not touch the teeth; thereafter, one should eat [the areca nut] and avoid vegetables, sour things, and salt.
One should also avoid fatigue, heat, travel, and especially sexual intercourse. 14.
Mercury should be measured at eight *ṭaṅkas*, equal to eight *ṭaṅkas* of *khadira* [wood], and the *ākārakarabha* should also be taken measured at two *ṭaṅkas*.
Honey measured at three *ṭaṅkas* should be placed entirely into the mortar (*khalva*). 15.
Having thoroughly ground all of that, the physician should prepare seven pills (vaṭīs).
The patient should consume one pill with water every morning;
he must avoid sour and salty foods, and his syphilis (phiraṅga) will perish.
One *karṣa* of mercury should be taken, along with exactly the same amount of sulfur; rice grains should be one *akṣa* in measure, and from these one should prepare a collyrium (*kajjalī*).
One should make seven pills from that and employ them as smoke.

By that, the end of the Phiraṅgas shall come within seven days; of this there is no doubt. (19) One should rub with both hands the mercury measured by one iṣṭaṅka, along with the juice of yellow flowers, balā, and leaves, until the mercury is no longer visible. (20)
Then, one should wash the hands in this manner for seven days;
by abandoning salt and sour [foods], the syphilis (phiraṅga) will perish. One should grind neem leaves with Pathyā, the latter being one-eighth the quantity of the former.
The *dhātrī* (myrobalan) should be of that same quantity, with one-sixteenth part of *nimba*.
This powder, measured by the *śāṇa*, should be consumed with water; it certainly destroys syphilis (*phiraṅga*), both external and internal. (22–23)

One should consume a powder made from *copacīnī* in the measure of one *śāṇa*, mixed with honey, for the destruction of the disease of syphilis; one should avoid salt. (24) If, however, a person is unable to give up salt, [the following should be done].
He should indeed consume rock salt, which is supremely beneficial and sweet.
One karṣa of mercury, one karṣa of sulphur, and one karṣa of khadira—of these, he should prepare a collyrium (kajjalī). 25–26.
