One should take half a karṣa each of turmeric, saffron, the two types of *truṭi*, the two types of *jīra*, *yavānikā*, the two types of sandalwood, black pepper, bamboo manna, *māṃsī*, and cinnamon leaf; having ground all these together, one should add them [to the preparation].
One should grind all of that with two palas each of honey and ghee separately; then a person should consume half a karṣa of it,
and the ulcer arising from the disease of syphilis will certainly be destroyed.
Even a long-standing, great ulcer is pacified;
for one who consumes this, swelling does not arise within the mouth.
One should avoid salt here for twenty-one days.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, on the diseases of the Phirangas (syphilis).
Now begins the sixtieth chapter, on Masūrikā (smallpox) and Śītalā (measles).
[Caused] by the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, and alkaline foods, incompatible foods, and eating before the previous meal has been digested.
Through the consumption of spoiled grains, beans, vegetables, and the like, as well as through corrupted air and water,
and even by the gaze of malevolent planets, the provoked humors (doṣas) arise in this body and, becoming conjoined with vitiated blood, produce disease.
Eruptions shaped like lentils (masūra) are called masūrikā.
Prior to these, there occurs fever, itching, breaking pain in the limbs, restlessness, giddiness,
swelling of the skin accompanied by discoloration, and likewise redness of the eyes.

Eruptions caused by Vāta are blackish-red, rough, accompanied by intense pain, hard, and slow to suppurate. There is also a splitting sensation in the joints, bones, and limbs, as well as cough, tremors, restlessness, and vertigo.
There is dryness of the palate, lips, and tongue, accompanied by thirst and loss of appetite (5).
Red, yellow, or white eruptions (sphoṭa) arise from the provocation of pitta; they are characterized by burning sensations, intense pain, and suppurate quickly (6).
Diarrhea, body ache, burning sensation, thirst, and likewise loss of appetite;
inflammation of the mouth and inflammation of the eyes, as well as a sharp and most dreadful fever—these Pitta-characterized disorders occur in those born from blood (raktaja). 7–8.
Excessive salivation, stiffness, headache, heaviness of the limbs, nausea accompanied by loss of appetite, excessive sleep, drowsiness, and lassitude;
[the ulcers] are white, unctuous, very large, itchy, and characterized by mild pain. (9)
Masūrikā eruptions are proclaimed to arise from kapha and to take a long time to suppurate (10). Those that are blue, flattened and wide, depressed in the center, very painful,
discharging putrid matter, slow to suppurate, and abundant, are born from all three doṣas (11).
Now, the specific characteristics of the smallpox (*masūrikā*) affecting the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are as follows:
when the smallpox reaches the skin, they arise with minimal morbidity, resembling water bubbles; once burst, they exude fluid. (12)
Those located in the blood are red in appearance, suppurate quickly, have thin skin, are curable, are not excessively vitiated, and when burst, they discharge blood.
Those located in the flesh are hard, unctuous, take a long time to suppurate, have thick skin, [are curable, and are not excessively vitiated].

Those born from fat (medas) are circular in shape, soft, slightly elevated, accompanied by severe fever, large, glossy, and painful. They are further characterized by body aches, thirst, itching, fever, and aversion to food. 14.
Confusion, aversion, and fever may arise from these; someone might even emerge from them. 15.
Those arising from the marrow are small, body-like, rough, flattened, and slightly elevated;
they cause extreme confusion and are accompanied by pain and aversion. 16.
Like being stung by bees, they cause the bones to ache on all sides;
they cut through the vital points (*marmadhāma*) and swiftly carry away the life-breaths (*prāṇa*).
These boils appear as if ripe, are unctuous and smooth, yet are accompanied by extreme pain. 17.
In Masūrikā born from Śukra (semen), there are indeed symptoms accompanied by numbness, aversion, delusion, burning sensations, and insanity;
however, only the signs have been specified, and no means of survival is seen. 18–19.
These seven types of carbuncles (piḍakās), when mixed with the [three] doshas, should be recognized by the symptoms of those doshas.
Accompanied by throat obstruction, loss of appetite, stiffness, delirium,
and aversion to food, these carbuncles known as carmakas are declared to be difficult to treat.

Those arising from phlegm and bile (kapha-pitta) are characterized by the elevation of the hair follicles, are accompanied by cough and loss of appetite, have hairs at their tips, and are preceded by fever;
those located in the skin and those located in the blood are likewise born of bile and phlegm. 22.
Measles caused by phlegm and bile are easily curable;
these subside in embodied beings even without medical treatment.
Those arising from wind, those produced by wind and bile, and those caused by wind and phlegm— [these require treatment]. 23.
Therefore, one should treat these with great effort, for they are most difficult to cure.
Those arising from *sannipāta* are incurable; I shall now describe their symptoms:
some are like coral, while others resemble the fruit of the *jambu* tree.
Some are like a net of iron, others resemble the seeds of the flax plant; their various colors arise from the different types of humors (doṣas).
Cough, hiccup, urinary disorder, and a sharp, most dreadful fever [arise].
There is delirious speech, restlessness, and fainting; thirst, a burning sensation, and extreme dizziness (27).
Blood may flow from the mouth, as well as from the nose and the eyes; making a gurgling sound in the throat, one breathes with great and terrible difficulty (28).
If these symptoms are observed in one afflicted by *masūrikā* (smallpox), medicine should not be administered by the best of physicians.
One afflicted by *masūrikā* who breathes heavily through the nose [is incurable].
Afflicted by thirst and corrupted by wind, he violently gives up his life-breaths.
At the end of Masūrikā, there may be swelling in the elbow, the wrist, or even on the shoulder-blade; it is difficult to treat and extremely severe.
Some cases of smallpox (masūrikā) are seen to be cured quickly even without effort;
some are observed to be extremely difficult; some may or may not be cured; and some, whose fatal course has ripened, do not recover at all despite diligent treatment. (32-33)
In cases of *masūrikā* (smallpox) and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), the application of ointments and similar treatments is beneficial;
furthermore, the treatment prescribed for *pitta-śleṣma-visarpa* (erysipelas caused by pitta and phlegm) is recommended here as well.
[One should apply] a paste of white sandalwood and the liquid extract derived from *hilamocī*.
At the onset of masūrikā, one should drink either [the decoction] or simply the juice alone (verse 35).
The two types of pañcamūla, rāsnā, dhātrī, uśīra, durālabhā,
amṛtā, dhānyaka, and musta conquer vāta-type masūrikā (verse 36).
A paste made from the barks of *mañjiṣṭhā*, *bahupāda* (nyagrodha), *plakṣa*, *śirīṣa*, and *udumbara* is beneficial as an external application for all types of *masūrikā* caused by Vāta.
[Likewise, a paste of] *guḍūcī*, *madhuka*, *drākṣā*, *moraṭa*, and *dāḍima* [is also beneficial]. 37.
At the time of suppuration, medicine mixed with jaggery (guḍa) should be administered;
by this, the vāyu is not provoked and the masūrikās reach full maturation.
During the stage of masūrikā, one should eat śāli rice along with mudga and masūra lentils. 38–39.

At the very onset of a Pitta-born Masūrikā, one should first consume only sweet-tasting food along with a small quantity of Saindhava salt, as well as a decoction of Paṭola root or the fresh juice of Moraṭa. 40
Nimba, parpaṭaka, pāṭhā, paṭola, the two types of candana,
uśīra, kaṭukā, dhātrī, as well as vāsā and durālabhā— this decoction of these [drugs], when boiled and cooled, is excellent when mixed with sugar. 41–42.
A wise physician should employ [this treatment] in cases of *masūrikā* born of *pitta*,
as well as in burning sensations, fever, erysipelas (*visarpa*), and ulcers where *pitta* predominates.
(43) *Masūrikā* born of blood are destroyed by the letting of blood.
Having decocted vāsā, mustaka, bhūnimba, triphalā, indrayava, yavāsaka, paṭola, and ariṣṭaka, one should drink it with honey;
by this, smallpoxes arising from kapha are pacified. 44–45.
For masūrikā eruptions arising from kapha and those arising from pitta, an ointment should be applied made from the bark of śirīṣa and udumbara, and from the leaves of khadira and ariṣṭa (46).
[Also beneficial are] nimba, parpaṭaka, pāṭhā, paṭola, and kaṭurohiṇī.
The two types of *candana*, *uśīra*, *dhātrī*, *vāsā*, and *durālabhā*— this decoction, beginning with *nimba*, when drunk mixed with sugar,
destroys *masūrī* of all origins, even when accompanied by erysipelas and fever. (47–48)
One who has risen [from the ordeal] and enters [the water] should be led back outside again;
[this is done with] a decoction of the bark of *kāñcana* and *ārā*, sprinkled with the powder of *tāpya*.
Alternatively, there is a decoction of *dhātrī* fruit and *madhuka* mixed with honey. 49.
When sores have developed in the mouth or the throat, gargling is recommended;
for the eyes, they praise irrigation with a decoction of *gavedhu*, *madhuka*, and water.
[The ingredients are: *madhuka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *mūrvā*, the bark of *dārvī*, and blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*).
Uśīra, lodhra, and mañjiṣṭhā are beneficial as ointments and for eye-drops (51).
By this, visual defects arising from [excessive] exposure to the sun are destroyed and do not recur; one should apply an ointment to the eyes made from the bark of the *bahuvāra* tree (52).
One should rub the moistened [vagina] with the powder of the five barks (*pañcavalkala*);
some authorities desire it to be done with ashes, while others with the dust of cow dung (53).
[One should also apply] the exudation of *suṣavī* leaves combined with the powder of turmeric.
One should drink [this] for the pacification of horripilation, fever, erysipelas, and ulcers. (54) Thus ends the section on Masūrikā.
Now begins the section on Śītalā, a variety of Masūrikā.
Afflicted by the goddess Śītalā, one indeed becomes like a case of masūrikā; and she causes fever just as an irregular fever (viṣamajvara) presided over by a spirit does.
She is said to be of seven kinds, and we shall now describe their varieties.

Preceded by fever, the *bṛhatī* smallpox (*śītalā*) consists of large pustules; it emerges after seven days and reaches its full development after seven days. Then, in the third week, it dries up and falls away of its own accord.
When one among them has ripened and bursts open and exudes [fluid],
one should perform the dusting (*avadhūlana*) there with the ashes of wild cow dung (58).
One should drive away the flies with the leaves and branches of the *nimba* tree.
One should provide cool water even during fever, but one must not heat it. One should place the [deceased] on pure, beautiful, secluded, and cool ground;
no impure person should touch him, nor should anyone approach his vicinity.
Indeed, many physicians here do not prescribe medicine;
some, however, certainly do. Therefore, I shall now state their opinion:
those who drink turmeric ground well with cool water together with the seeds of *nimbākṣa* [are cured].
For them, there shall never arise in this body afflictions caused by the cold season in this world.

(62) Those who first drink white sandalwood mixed with the juice of the *moca* plant, along with *madhuka* and the juice of *vāsā*, blended with the essence of *sumanas* flowers, do not suffer from disorders of the cold season on earth. (63)
Cooling remedies should be administered along with the protection against Śītalā;
one should tie nimba leaves all around the interior of the house. At no time whatsoever should anyone enter while impure from food remnants.
Even for eruptions (sphoṭa) accompanied by burning sensations, a heap of protective powder (rakṣā-reṇu) is beneficial;
by this, they undergo drying and do not reach suppuration.
Sandalwood, vāsaka, musta, guḍūcī, along with drākṣā— [these are used]. 66.

A cold decoction of these [herbs] destroys fever accompanied by chills. One should bring those fevers to subsidence through recitation, fire-offerings, oblations, gifts, rites for well-being, worship, and the honoring of Brahmins, cows, Śambhu, and Gaurī.

A Brāhmaṇa endowed with faith should recite this hymn of praise to the goddess Śītalā in the presence of one afflicted by Śītalā; by that, the Śītalās are pacified. (68) Of this Śrī Śītalā Stotra, Mahādeva is the seer and Anuṣṭubh is the meter.
The application [of this mantra] is for the purpose of recitation to pacify the afflictions caused by the deity Śītalā. 69.
Skanda said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, [please grant me] the auspicious hymn of praise (stava) to Śītalā.
"You ought to explain in its entirety that which removes the fear of boils.
Īśvara said:
"I bow to the goddess Śītalā, who is mounted upon a donkey and is naked."

Having reached the *yāma* (watch) called Śītala, one may turn back from the great fear of eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*). For one afflicted by burning heat who utters "Śītale, Śītale," the terrible fear of eruptive boils will quickly perish.

The man who meditates upon you while in the midst of water and worships you shall not experience the terrible fear of eruptive boils within his family. [73] O Śītalā, for one consumed by fever and filled with a foul odor...
They call you the life-restoring medicine for a man whose sight has been lost.
I bow to the goddess Śītalā, who is mounted upon a donkey, naked,
equipped with a broom and a water-pot, and whose head is adorned with a winnowing basket.
O Śītalā, you remove the difficult-to-overcome bodily diseases of men; for those whose bodies are ravaged by eruptive boils, you alone are a showerer of nectar.
(76) As for goiters, seizures, and whatever other dreadful diseases afflict men—
"O Śītalā, by the mere thought of you, those [ailments] go to their destruction.
There exists neither mantra nor any medicine for the disease of sin; you alone, O Śītalā, are the sustainer—no other deity do I see. (77–78)

O Goddess, death does not occur for that person who meditates upon you as situated between the navel and the heart, resembling a lotus fiber. That man who always recites this octet of the goddess Śītalā—
The terrible fear of erupting boils does not arise in his family.
This should be heard and recited by men endowed with devotion; it is a supreme and great means of securing well-being for the destruction of calamities. 80–81.
This Śītalāṣṭaka should certainly not be given to just anyone;
rather, it should be bestowed upon one who is endowed with devotion and faith. 82.
Thus ends the Śītalāṣṭaka Stotra in the glorious Kāśī Khaṇḍa.
Now, regarding the varieties of Śītalā:
that which arises from Vāta and Kapha is Kodravā, having the appearance of Kodrava grain; some call it Pakvā, but it does not undergo suppuration. 83
Like a water-leech, it pierces the limbs especially;
after seven or twelve days, it subsides even without medicine. Or, one may administer a remedy prepared from the eight-fold khadira wood.
One should indeed apply a decoction of *kodrava* grain at that time for its pacification.
That which arises from heat, characterized by heat, accompanied by itching, and pleasant to the touch, is known by the name *pāṇisahā*; it withers away of its own accord within seven days.
The fourth [type] is shaped like a mustard seed and has the color of a yellow mustard seed;
it should be known by the name *sarṣapikā*, and one should avoid applying oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) here.
The fifth arises from a slight cause of heat and has the appearance of a black mustard seed (*rājikā*).

This [disease] occurs in children; it dries up easily and spontaneously. The sixth day, marked by a raised red circle like a *koṭha* eruption, is characterized by pain preceded by fever; the fever may persist for three days.
Due to the merging of *sphoṭas*, this [vein] is seen to consist of many *sphoṭas* (89);
it should be understood as having a single *sphoṭa* and being black, and is designated as "born of skin" (90).
All seven of these should be understood as presided over by the goddess Śītalā and her retinue.
One should perform the conduct appropriate for the cool season during all these [periods].
Some cool-natured [practices] succeed easily even without effort;
some are seen to be more difficult, while others may or may not succeed.
However, some do not succeed at all, even when treated with great effort.
(92) Thus ends the sixtieth chapter on Śītalā and Masūrikā.
Now begins the sixty-first chapter on Minor Diseases (Kṣudraroga). (61)
The bodily heat produced by anger, grief, and fatigue, having reached the head, together with the *pitta*, cooks the hair; by that, graying (*palita*) is produced.
One *karṣa* of iron powder and five *karṣas* of mango pulp [should be used].
Having ground two *pala* of *dhātrī*, two *pathyā*, and one *bibhītaka*, one should place them in an iron vessel and let them sit overnight;
this ointment destroys gray hair before long—of this there is no doubt. (2–3)

One should cook oil with these ingredients: first the root of *kāśmarya*, then the flower of *sahacara*, the root of *ketaka*, iron powder along with *bhṛṅgarāja*, and a portion of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
having prepared this in an iron vessel, one should bury it in the ground for one month.
Even hair that is as white as kāśa grass becomes like honey through this yoga.
Triphalā, nīlikā leaves, bhṛṅgarāja, and iron filings,
ground together with goat's urine and applied as an ointment, are supremely effective for turning the hair black.
The pitta, following the hair follicles and combined with vāta,
causes the hairs to fall out; thereafter, the kapha along with blood obstructs the hair follicles, and consequently, no further growth occurs.
O Indra, one should contemplate that baldness is cured by *ruhyā*.
Having rubbed [the head] with the fresh juice of bitter *paṭolī* leaves, even long-standing baldness is certainly pacified within three days by *ruhyā*. 7–8.
Gokṣura and sesame flowers, with equal parts of honey and clarified butter—
when applied as a paste to the head, the hair grows thick by means of this. Having prepared the soot of elephant tusks, goat’s milk, and rasāñjana—
By applying this as an ointment, even on the palms of the hands, hair grows.
Through applications of liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), blue water-lily (*indīvara*), grapes (*mṛdvīkā*), oil, clarified butter (*ājya*), and milk,
hair loss (*indralupta*) is pacified, and the hair becomes thick and firm.
Oil cooked with *jātī*, *karañja*, *varuṇa*, *karavīra*, and *agni* destroys *indralupta* (alopecia) through massage; of this there is no doubt.
[Likewise,] the milk of *snuhī*, the milk of *akā*, *lāṅgalī*, *mārka*, and *viṣa* [are effective].
Goat’s urine, cow’s urine, *raktikā*, *indravāruṇī*, white mustard,
and *tīkṣṇagandhā*— oil properly cooked with these ingredients will, by rule, destroy the disease of baldness.
When the scalp becomes harsh, itchy,
and rough due to the provocation of Vāta and Kapha, one should recognize that as Dāruṇaka; in this condition, an ointment mixed with honey should be applied to the head.
Priyāla seed, madhuka, kuṣṭha, and māṣa, along with rock salt (16),
as well as mango seed and two parts of harītakī in equal proportions,
ground with milk— this ointment destroys even the most terrible [disease].
By applying a plaster of *khākhasa* seeds with milk, one removes severe [skin diseases].
Oil boiled with *guñjā* fruits and the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* destroys itching, severe [diseases], heart disease, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and the *kāpāla* affliction. 17–18.
One should recognize as *aruṃṣikā* those eruptions on the head that have many openings, are excessively moist, and are caused by the provocation of phlegm, blood, and parasites.
(19) The filaments of the blue lotus combined with the fruit of the *dhātrī* [are used for its treatment].
And a plaster combined with yaṣṭīmadhuka destroys aruṣikā when applied.
Oil cooked with triphalā, iron filings, yaṣṭī, mārkava, utpala, sārivā, and rock salt (saindhava) shall destroy aruṣikā.

One should recognize as irivellikā a circular swelling located on the head, accompanied by severe pain and fever, which possesses all [dosic] natures and all symptoms. The treatment for paittika visarpa that has been proclaimed [is also applicable here].
The physician should treat these as if they were irivellikā;
one should recognize that firm, intensely painful pustule arising within the ear as panasi, which is originated by vāta and kapha. 23–24.

The physician should first apply fomentation to a panasiṅkā and then apply an ointment made from the pastes of manaḥśilā, kuṣṭha, niśā, tālaka, and dāru. Once he recognizes that it has suppurated, he should incise it and treat it like an ulcer.
A swelling arising from vāta and kapha at the joint of the jaw,
which is firm, slightly painful, and unctuous, should be known as pāṣāṇagardabha (stone-ass).
A skilled physician should first apply sudation to the pāṣāṇagardabha.
Then, one should apply warm pastes (kalka) prescribed by Panasika;
one should also apply other pastes that destroy swelling caused by phlegm (kapha).
Once it has reached suppuration, one should incise it and treat it like an ulcer (vraṇa).
When the blood has been extracted by leeches, it subsides even without medicine;
this has been observed in many instances where [the swelling] was first scarified.
These [tumors], arising from phlegm, wind, and blood, resemble the thorns of the *śālmalī* tree. (30)
Pustules that arise in young people are to be known as *mukhadūṣikā*. (31) Now, regarding the treatment of *mukhadūṣikā*:
a fourth part of a finger's breadth [of paste] is prescribed as a facial application.
The medium [dose] should be one-third [of that], while the superior [dose] should be half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula). Its duration of action is said to last as long as the paste has not dried;
once dried, it becomes devoid of its qualities and likewise irritates the skin.
An ointment of *lodhra*, *dhānyaka*, and *vacā* removes pimples of youth;
likewise, black pepper combined with ox-gall applied to the face has the same effect.
An ointment made of white mustard, *vacā*, *lodhra*, and rock salt [is also effective].
Emetics also quickly destroy the pustules that arise during youth.
(35) The sharp thorns of the *śālmali* tree, ground with milk alone and applied as a paste for three days, will make the face resemble a lotus. (36)

When the vāyu, provoked by anger and exertion and joined with pitta, suddenly reaches the face and spreads out a circular patch, one should designate that as a *vyaṅga* (freckle) on the face— painless, thin, and dusky-brown. 37
They know that such blackness on the face or body is *nīlikā*.
One should treat *vyaṅga*, *nīlikā*, *nyaccha*, and *tilakālaka* with head-piercing [procedures], medicinal pastes, and likewise with massages. (38–39)
An ointment made from *vaṭa* sprouts and lentils destroys facial freckles (*vyaṅga*).
For freckles, an ointment of *mañjiṣṭhā* mixed with honey is recommended; alternatively, an ointment of rabbit blood is also praised. (40)
A paste of vyaṅgahṛt, varuṇa, and tvak, ground with goat’s urine,
or a plaster of jātīphala, removes freckles and dark spots; likewise, by rubbing with the milk of *arka* and *haridrā* and applying it as a plaster.

The blackness of the face that has developed over a long period will certainly subside; by smearing the mouth with lentils ground with milk and mixed with ghee for seven nights, it will truly become like the petal of a white lotus.
One should apply a plaster made of these— banyan leaves, *mālatī*, red sandalwood, *kuṣṭha*, *kālīyaka*, and *lodhra*—
for the destruction of youthful pimples and facial freckles.
By this, even the face may be freed from dark spots and the like.
Saffron, sandalwood, *lodhra*, *pataṅga*, red sandalwood, *kālīyaka*, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā*—[these are the ingredients]. 45–46.
Patraka, padmaka, padma, kuṣṭha, gorocanā, niśā,
lākṣā, dāruharidrā, gairika, nāgakeśara,
palāśa flowers, priyaṅgu, and banyan sprouts. 47.

The physician should cook two *prasthas* of oil over a gentle fire with *mālatī*, beeswax, mustard, fragrant *vacā*, and milk four times the quantity of the oil, each of these ingredients ground separately in the measure of one *akṣa*. 48–49.
By applying this as a facial ointment, it destroys freckles along with dark spots, moles,
lentigoes, and dark patches, and removes impurities from the face; it likewise removes the *padminī-kaṇṭaka* and the *jatumaṇi*.

One should fashion the face, beautiful as the orb of the full moon. (51) A glandular swelling (*granthi*) formed by the three *doṣas* alone—whether in the region of the neck, shoulders, armpits, hands, feet, joints, or throat—resembles an anthill; it arises through inaction and gradually attains growth. (52)

Physicians call this disorder *valmīka* (anthrax/ant-hill), which spreads like erysipelas with many openings that cause a pricking pain; it rises with elevated tips, is incurable, and especially chronic.
Furthermore, when the hands and feet are covered with many holes from above, [it is known as] *pādadārī*.
A *valmīka* (anthrax-like growth) that is accompanied by swelling should be avoided by one who knows [the truth].
Having excised the *valmīka* with a surgical instrument, one should treat it with alkaline caustic (*kṣāra*) and fire (*agni*),
following the procedure prescribed for *arbuda*, and after purifying it, one should heal it.
If a *valmīka* (ant-hill-like swelling) has formed that is not excessively large and does not arise from a vital organ (*marman*),
the physician, having performed purification (*saṃśodhana*) there, should let out the blood using the roots of *kulattha* beans, *guḍūcī*, and salt. 56.
With the roots of ārevata and likewise the roots of dantī,
along with the roots of śyāmā mixed with meat-mince and parched grain flour, the physician should apply a plaster and perform a poultice that is very unctuous and pleasantly warm. (57–58)

Then one should recognize it as healed; having understood all the stages in their proper order and having severed the [path of] the disease, the wise physician should apply a caustic after thoroughly cleansing the corrupted flesh. 59.
One should rub the area with a caustic after purifying the vitiated tissues.

Once the wise physician has ascertained that the ulcer is purified, he should apply healing measures. He should cook nimba oil with realgar, orpiment, bhallātaka, small cardamom, aguru, sandalwood, jasmine leaves, and sour gruel.
Indeed, that which destroys an anthill, characterized by many openings and many ulcers, should be known as *kakṣā*.
One should designate it as *kakṣā* when black vesicles with pain arise in the armpits, shoulders, and sides, produced by the provocation of pitta. (62–63)
Having seen such a single eruption, resembling a pustule,
arising on the skin due to the provocation of bile, they call it the garland named *gandhanī*. A physician should treat both the armpit eruption and the garland named *gandhanī*.
By the previously mentioned treatment for Pittaja Visarpa,
eruptions arise in the armpits that tear the flesh, produce internal burning and fever, and resemble a blazing fire. (65-66)
One should know that *agnirohiṇī*, which kills a person within seven days, ten days, or a fortnight, is incurable as it arises from the derangement of all three humors (*sānnipātika*).
One should treat *agnirohiṇī* according to the procedure prescribed for *pittavīsarpa*.
Under Rohiṇī, one should perform fasting, bloodletting, and drying treatments, as well as the purification of the body; however, one should abandon that [growth] if it is enlarged.
It is round like the root-tuber of the Vidārī plant and occurs at the joints of the armpits and groins.
One should recognize the red *vidārikā* as being caused by all [three doshas] and possessing all their symptoms (69).
In the case of *vidārikā*, bloodletting with leeches is beneficial at the initial stage;
once it has suppurated, incision is performed, after which the standard regimen for wound management is prescribed (70).
When Vāta and Pitta, taking hold of the flesh of the nail in embodied beings, cause burning and suppuration, one should designate that disease as Cippa (nail-fungus).
When a nail is afflicted by trauma, it becomes rough, white, and harsh.
One should recognize that [disease] as *kunakha* or by the name *kulīra*.
One should treat *cippa* with bloodletting and cleansing;
furthermore, once its heat has subsided, one should sprinkle it with warm water.
Then, having excised [the growth] appropriately even with a surgical instrument, the wise physician should drain it and subsequently heal it according to the procedure prescribed for ulcers (74).
Having placed turmeric and *abhayā* in an iron vessel, one should prepare their fresh juice.
Having ground that [substance], one should repeatedly apply the resulting paste to the earlobe.
When wrapped with seven tender leaves of the *kāśmarya* tree,
the swelling of men's fingers will certainly and quickly subside.
One should treat *kunakha* (whitlow) according to the procedure for *śleṣmavidradhi* (phlegmatic abscess).
If *kunakha* is not pacified by applying borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) to the tip of the nail,
then even a stone will float upon water.
When the wind, moving everywhere, affects the skin of the penis due to massage, pressure, or likewise due to trauma,
then that skin, afflicted by the wind, turns inside out.
It is accompanied by pain and burning, and in some cases it undergoes suppuration.
Beneath the jewel, a swelling in the form of a knot hangs down; one should know that painful condition arising from wind to be *parivartikā*.
That same [type of swelling], when accompanied by itching and hardness, and associated with phlegm (śleṣman), should be treated as follows:

one should apply a poultice (upanāha) made of substances that alleviate Vāta, such as Śālvaṇa and others, after it has been well-fomented and anointed with ghee; this should be done for either three nights or five nights. (81–82)
Then, having lubricated it, one should slowly split the skin and press upon the *maṇi*.
Once the skin has entered over the *maṇi*, one should apply fomentations (*upanāhana*) and administer Vāta-alleviating enemas (*vasti*), while feeding the patient unctuous foods. (83–84)
When a man, out of passion, forcibly approaches a woman who has very little sexual desire,
or due to a blow from the hand, or by forceful rubbing on a leather surface, or through massage, pressure, or the obstruction of the flow of semen (85), [the following occurs].
One should recognize that condition in which the skin is torn open as *avapāṭikā*.
Due to Vāta, it is rough, dry, thin, black, and accompanied by pain;
due to Pitta, it is yellow or red and accompanied by burning sensations and thirst.
Hardened by phlegm, unctuous, itchy, and slightly painful— 87—
the physician should treat this avapāṭikā with oleation and sudation therapies.
88 However, when the penis is afflicted by vāta, the skin retracts over the glans.
When the glans penis is constricted by a leather thong, it obstructs the urinary stream;
while that [urethral opening] remains thus blocked, the urine flows out with a weak stream and without pain for the person, yet the glans does not open up. 90
One should recognize that obstruction of light accompanied by pain arises from Vāta (91).
When there is obstruction of light, one should insert a tube— made of iron, wood, or horn— that is open at both ends and smeared with ghee (92).
One should sprinkle it with the fat and marrow of a porpoise and a boar,
and likewise add wheel-oil combined with wind-alleviating substances.
After three days, one should properly insert a considerably thicker tube into the passage.
One should thus increase the flow of the channels and administer unctuous food;
or, having incised [the fistula] while avoiding the *sevanī*, one should treat it like an acute wound (94).
Due to the suppression of natural urges, the Vāyu becomes obstructed and localized in the rectum.
It obstructs the great channel and makes the opening narrow;
because of the narrowness of the passage, his feces pass with difficulty.
One should recognize this disease as "obstructed anus" (sanniruddhaguda), which is very difficult to overcome. 95–96.

For one whose anus is constricted, an irrigation with oils that alleviate Vata is beneficial; likewise, the procedure for treating a constricted foreskin (niruddhaprakaśa) has also been described. Furthermore, in one who neglects bathing and body-massage, impurity may accumulate in the scrotum.
When it becomes moistened by sweat, it then produces itching (98).
From that scratching, pustules and discharge quickly arise; they call this vṛṣaṇakacchū, born from the provocation of phlegm and blood (99).
A formulation prepared with *sarjāhvā*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), white mustard (*sitāsiddhārtha*), and [clarified butter] certainly pacifies itching of the testicles through massage. 100.
The physician, however, should treat scrotal eczema (*vṛṣaṇakacchū*) like [the disease] *pāmā*.
One should also remove it by means of the treatment prescribed for *ahipūtana*.
Itching arising from blood and phlegm occurs in an infant when the anus is not washed while being smeared with feces and urine, or when it is perspiring yet not bathed. (101–102)
From scratching that area, pustules and discharge quickly arise; one should recognize that terrible condition, where these have coalesced into a single lesion, as *ahipūtana*.
In that case, one should first purify the mother’s breast milk through cleansing treatments.
Washing wounds with decoctions of triphalā and khadira is beneficial;
a plaster composed of conch-shell, sauvīra, and yaṣṭyāhvā should be applied in the case of ahipūtana.
Due to dysentery and diarrhea, the anus protrudes outward.

One should diagnose prolapse of the rectum in a person whose body is dry and weak. (105) In the case of rectal prolapse, one should foment the rectum, anoint it with unctuous substances, and once it has re-entered, one should carefully secure it with a porous cow-hide. (106)

If one should eat the tender leaf of a lotus plant mixed with sugar, having ascertained this [remedy], it has been prescribed that there shall be no prolapse of the rectum for him. Alternatively, in the case of rectal prolapse, an ointment made from the fats of mice may be applied.
One should foment the anus with well-cooked rat meat;
or, one suffering from prolapse of the rectum (pāyubhraṃśa) should habitually consume vṛkṣāmla, anala, caṅgerī, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavāgraja with buttermilk to stimulate the digestive fire. 108–109.
One should take equal parts of musk-rat and the ten roots; with the decoction and paste of these two, one should cook oil according to the prescribed method.
By the application of massage with that oil, prolapse of the rectum is cured.
In this manner it is destroyed; likewise, *gudaśūla* (rectal pain) and *bhagaṇḍara* (fistula-in-ano) are cured.
That which is accompanied by burning, has red margins, is non-suppurating, intensely painful, itchy, and causes fever, is known as *śūkaradaṃṣṭraka* (pig-toothed). 111–112.

A powder made from the root of *bhṛṅgarāja* combined with *rajanī*, when applied as a paste immediately, destroys the teeth of a boar. A paste of the root of *rājīva* drunk with cow’s ghee in the morning [achieves the same].
It pacifies the terrible fever arising from the tusks of a boar. (114) The root of *mārkava*, ground with cold water at night, destroys the disease called *vīsarpa* when applied as an ointment. (115)

One should recognize that which is deep-seated, with little swelling, similar in color to the surrounding skin, situated on the surface, and characterized by a lingering tendency toward suppuration as *antahprapākinī* (internally suppurating).
The physician should treat the *anuśayī* type according to the therapeutic measures prescribed for *śleṣmavidradhi* (phlegmatic abscess). 116–117.

One should recognize that condition as *alasa* (elephantiasis) when the feet have moistened spaces between the toes and are accompanied by itching and burning, resulting from contact with contaminated mud.
Sprinkling the feet with sour gruel (*āranāla*) and applying an ointment is beneficial for *alasa*.
One should apply a plaster made of *paṭola*, *kunaṭī*, *nimba*, *rocanā*, black pepper, and sesame seeds,
prepared with the fresh juice of *kṣudrā* and *kaṭutaila*.
Then, one should dust it with a powder of *kāsīsa*, *kunaṭī*, and sesame flour.
A paste composed of karañja seeds, turmeric, ferrous sulfate (kāsīsa), padmaka, honey, yellow pigment (rocanā), and arsenic (haritāla) is beneficial for those suffering from alasa.
For one who habitually walks about, the wind [is beneficial] when the two [extremities] are excessively dry.
It causes a painful fissure in the feet that is located on the soles;
a wise physician should treat this *pādadārī* by releasing the vessels and cleansing the soles. Furthermore, having applied oleation and sudation, one should repeatedly anoint the feet.
Beeswax, fat, marrow, and ghee mixed with alkali,
along with the powder of *sarja* (resin) and rock salt (*saindhava*) saturated with ghee and honey—
having churned these together and smeared them with pungent oil— is beneficial for wiping the feet. (123–124)
A proven medicinal paste prepared with honey, beeswax, red ochre, clarified butter, jaggery, *mahiṣākṣa*, and the resin of *śāla*—
combined with red ochre— removes suppuration and cracking [of the skin].
[This is prepared] with the seeds of *unmattaka* and the alkaline water of *mānaka*.
Ripe castor oil undoubtedly destroys dāri.
When the foot is crushed by gravel or wounded by thorns and the like, a knotty swelling as large as a jujube fruit arises; that is called kadara. 126–127.

One should cauterize a *kadara* [fungus] by excising it and applying either oil or fire. Those [spots] which are black, the size of sesame seeds, painless, and dark, arising from an excess of wind, bile, and phlegm, one should know as *tilakālaka*.
That which appears on the body as painless, firm,

black like a bean, elevated, and resembling a mosquito-bite should be designated as *maśaka* (a skin eruption) caused by Vāta. Small, thin pustules with fine tips and darkish bases are also [caused by Vāta].
Those caused by Kapha and Pitta perish quickly.
A circular patch (maṇḍala) arising from Kapha and blood is uniform, elevated, and painless;
it is congenital (sahaja), and for some, it is characterized as a mole (lakṣma), while others identify it as a birthmark (jatumaṇi). 131–132.
The *jatumaṇi* should be known as black and glossy, arising from the three [doṣas] with an excess of *śleṣman*.
Other excellent physicians, however, call a painless red growth *lakṣma*.
One should treat *carmakīla*, *jatumaṇi*, *maśaka*, and *tilakālaka* [according to their respective natures].
Having excised it with a surgical instrument, one should cauterize it completely with alkali or fire.
Whether large or small, dark-brown or black, a painless circular patch on the body is designated as *nyaccha*. (134–135)
One should treat it with venesection, medicinal plasters, and likewise with massages;

one should smear Nyaccha with milk, the milks of trees, and pastes derived from milk-yielding trees, as well as with the leaves and roots of Tribhuvanavijayā, and the Śiṃśapā of old growth. 136. With these [one should treat it].
The application of an ointment (udvartana) prepared with these is proven to remove *nyaccha* and *vyaṅga*.
A circular, itchy, pale patch covered with thorns resembling the spikes of a lotus plant is called *padminī-kaṇṭaka*; it is born from *kapha* and *vāta*. 137–138.
In the disease known as *padminīkaṇṭaka*, one should induce vomiting with neem water;
one should also cause the patient to drink ghee prepared with that same [neem] water along with honey.
Alternatively, frequent rubbing with a paste of neem and *āragvadha* is beneficial. (139–140)

One should cook cow’s ghee with four times as much decoction of neem leaves; then, once it has been prepared, one should cook it again with the pastes made from the leaves of *nimba* and *kṛtamāla*. When it is fully processed, one should drink it in a dose of one pala.
One is liberated from the thorn of the lotus-pond [padminīkaṇṭaka] only in this way, and not otherwise.
(142) Smooth, matching the color of the skin, knotted, painless, and resembling a mung bean—this is known as ajagallikā, arising from phlegm and wind, occurring in children. (143)
In that regard, one should treat Ajagallikā with leeches when it is suppurated;
one should repeatedly apply a paste of oyster shell, Saurāṣṭra clay, and alkali.
When Ajagallikā becomes hardened, one should liquefy it by means of an application of alkali. 144
A pustule that is shaped like a barley grain, prominent, knotted, and embedded in the flesh, caused by phlegm and wind, is called *yavaprakhyā* (barley-like).
A pustule that is thick, straight, elevated, and circular— [is called *utsedha*]. 145.146ab.
One should know that Antrālajī, characterized by little pus, arises from Kapha and Vāta (146).
In the case of Antrālajī, which resembles a barley grain, one should first treat it with fomentations and then apply a plaster made from the pastes of realgar, devadāru, and kuṣṭha.
One should treat a suppurated [abscess] according to the procedures for ulcers as previously described.
One should recognize that which has an open mouth, great burning, resembles a ripe udumbara fruit, is wide-open, and is circular as being caused by pitta. 147, 188.
The physician should recognize that which resembles the pericarp of a lotus in its center, covered with pustules, and pierced by many openings, as arising from Vāta and Pitta; likewise,
a circular, elevated, reddish area covered with pustules [is known as Maṇḍalaka].
One should know that *gardabhikā* is painful and arises from *vāta* and *pitta*.
That swelling which spreads like *visarpa*, being thin and non-suppurating, causing burning sensations and fever due to *pitta*, is to be known as *jālagardabha*. 151

The physician should treat the open, ulcerated *gardabhī* and *jālagardabha* types of erysipelas (*visarpa*) caused by bile with the appropriate therapeutic measures; however, once suppuration has occurred, he should promote healing with clarified butter processed with sweet medicinal herbs. 152
When five or six hard pustules, elevated like a tortoise shell, are clustered together due to the provocation of kapha and vāta, that condition is known by the wise as *kacchapī*.
One should first apply fomentation (*sveda*) to *kacchapī*, and thereafter apply an ointment (*pralepa*). 153–154.
The physician should quickly treat that ulcer with the medical management for wounds, using a paste made from turmeric, kuṣṭha, white arsenic, orpiment, and devadāru.
Once it has reached the muscle, vessels, ligaments, fat, phlegm, and likewise the wind (vāyu), [the treatment must be applied].

This [disease] forms a knot; once it is ruptured, it exudes an excessive discharge resembling honey, ghee, or fat. Therein, the increased Vāyu dries up the flesh and consequently produces a knotted growth known as Śarkarā.

Then, from the vessels, blood flows suddenly—foul-smelling, excessively moist, and of various colors; one should know that to be Sharkarābuda. One should treat Sharkarābuda according to the procedure prescribed for Medobuda. 158–159.
Lack of enthusiasm in one who is capable is called laziness regarding action;
excessive unease due to anxiety is described by the wise as discontent. When food, having been stirred up, does not pass through, it is called salivation or spitting.
If his heart is oppressed, one should diagnose that as *utkleśa* (nausea/distress).
Sweetness in the mouth, drowsiness, a twisting sensation in the heart, giddiness,
and a lack of appetite for food— these symptoms indicate *glāni* (exhaustion/depression).
It arises from exhaustion, loss of vitality, suffering, indigestion, and fatigue (162).
That upward movement of the wind which occurs due to the provocation of the *udāna* and because food is not properly settled is called eructation (*udgāra*) (163).
Āṭopa is defined as a rumbling sound arising from the stomach;
that knowledge which belongs to one situated in darkness is called *tamas* by the wise.
(164) Thus ends the sixty-first chapter on minor diseases. 61.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter: On Diseases of the Head (Śiro-roga).
Diseases of the head arise from the three [humors]—vāta, pitta, and kapha—as well as from their combination (sannipāta), blood, wasting (kṣaya), and parasites (kṛmi). 1.
Sūryāvarta, Anantavāta, Śaṅkhaka, and Ardhabhedaka—
these are declared to be the characteristics of this eleven-fold [headache].
When intense headaches occur without apparent cause, and especially excessively at night;
When there is relief from binding and fomentation, that headache is caused by Vāta (3). That headache in which the head feels as if covered with hot coals, where the eyes and nose burn,
and where exhaustion occurs at night due to cold applications, is caused by the provocation of Pitta (4).
If the head is smeared with phlegm (kapha), feels heavy, and is stiff and cold,
and if the eyes, nose, and face are swollen, that is headache caused by the provocation of phlegm.
When all three [humors] are involved in the headache, all the symptoms arise together.
The blood-type [headache] has symptoms identical to those of pitta, and there is an inability to tolerate touch of the head.

Due to the extreme depletion of fat, phlegm, and blood products located in the head, a headache arising from *kṣaya* (depletion) occurs; it is a painful affliction of the head that becomes exceedingly severe and intensely agonizing.
It increases further through fomentation, emesis, fumigation, nasal medication, and bloodletting.
In the case of a wasting-type head disease (śiroroga), the limbs whirl and throb, the head aches, the eyes are disoriented, there is fainting, and exhaustion of the body occurs.
When one's head is excessively pierced as if being devoured, throbbing within,
and blood mixed with pus flows from the nose, that terrible affliction is known as *kṛmi-śirobhitāpa* (head-fever caused by worms).
When, at sunrise, a dull ache gradually comes upon the eyes and eyebrows with great intensity, [it is the onset of fever].
It increases together with the sun and ceases when the sun turns away;
sometimes a living being finds relief through cold or attains comfort through heat.
They call that most grievous disorder, which affects the entire body, "the turning away of the sun" (sūryāpavarta). 11–12.

When the three doshas are indeed vitiated, they severely compress the carotid region (manyā), producing extremely intense pain; they quickly take up residence specifically in the eyes, the eyebrows, and the temple region (śaṅkhadeśa), and moreover,
they cause trembling of the jaw and disorders arising from the eyes.
They describe that as Anantavāta, a disorder of the head arising from the three doṣas.
When pitta, rakta, and vāyu become vitiated and concentrated in the region of the temples, they indeed produce a severe swelling accompanied by intense pain, burning, and redness. 14–15.

Obstructing the head and likewise the throat with the force of poison, that which is known by the name Śaṅkhaka destroys life within three nights; it survives for three days, and one should administer medicine to it while rejecting [other] treatments. 16.

The powerful Vāyu (wind), aggravated by the consumption of dry food, overeating, exposure to the morning wind, excessive sexual intercourse, suppression of natural urges, physical exertion, and strenuous exercise—
whether acting alone or combined with Kapha— seizes the head.

It causes intense pain, resembling a blow from a weapon or a thunderbolt, in the neck, the eyebrows, the temples, the ears, the eyes, and half of the forehead; such a condition is called *ardhāvabhedaka*.
When it becomes excessively aggravated, it may even destroy the eye or the ear.
In cases of head diseases born of Vāta, one should administer oleation, sudation, rubbing,
as well as drinks, food, and poultices that remove Vāta disorders.
Kuṣṭha, the root of Eraṇḍa, and Nāgara, ground with buttermilk, [should be applied].
Slightly warm, it removes pain in the head through application as an ointment on the forehead.
This juice, which is an axe to asthma, especially when used as a nasal drop (nasya), certainly removes headache; there is no doubt that it should be employed in this manner. 21–22.

A skin, sixteen finger-breadths in height and extending over the head, should be wrapped around the head; below that, one should smear it with a paste of māṣa beans. While the patient is seated and motionless, one should fill [the cavity] with lukewarm oils.
One who suffers from pain should retain it for a full watch (three hours), or even for half a watch.
This head-enema (śirovasti) removes diseases of the head caused by Vāta, as well as pain in the jaw, neck, eyes, and ears, facial paralysis (ardita), and trembling of the head.
This head-pouch (śirovasti) is applied even without food for five or seven days, or even longer as desired; thereafter,
once the oil has been removed, one should release the binding of the pouch.
One should massage the head, forehead, face, neck, shoulders, and so forth;
having washed the body with pleasantly warm water, one should eat whatever is wholesome—namely, meat from wild animals which is beneficial, as well as *śāli* rice and other such grains. (27–28)
Or one may eat green gram, black gram, and horse gram at night alone, seasoned with pungent spices and ghee; likewise, one should drink warm milk.
In cases of head disease caused by pitta, [one should apply] cool substances with sandalwood water.
The touch of white, blue, and red lotuses, as well as pleasant breezes, are beneficial; holding on the head ghee that has been washed a hundred times is also wholesome.
A small amount of camphor and fresh saffron serve as a "axe" for asthma.
One should grind all these with goat’s milk and sandalwood;
the physician should administer this as a nasal drop (nasya) for headache born of Pitta, though this is considered beneficial for all types of head pain. 32
An errhine (nasya) consisting of a paste of jaggery and ginger removes headache.

In cases arising from blood (raktaja), all treatments—diet, external applications, and affusions—should be like those for pitta; however, the specific distinction is the application of both cold and heat, along with bloodletting.

In cases born of kapha, fasting and sudation with dry, hot, and fiery substances are indicated; in that arising from the combination of all three (sannipāta), treatment that alleviates sannipāta should be performed, for they specifically prescribe the drinking of aged ghee. 35
Castor root, tagara, śatāhvā, jīvantikā, rāsnā, rock salt,
bhṛṅga, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā, and ginger, along with black sesame oil (36),
mixed with goat’s milk and oil, and cooked four times the quantity in bhṛṅga juice.
Six drops should be administered through the nose; they destroy all disorders of the head (37).

They cause fallen hair and gray hairs to regrow, make teeth that have become loose at their roots very firm, make the eyes resemble those of Suparṇa or a vulture, and provide extraordinary strength to the arms (38).
In the case of wasting (kṣayaja), a nourishing regimen should be adopted to destroy the wasting;
ghee processed with Vāta-alleviating and sweet drugs should be used for drinking and as nasal drops (nasya).
In the case of that caused by worms (kṛmija), nasal drops should be administered using the three pungents (vyoṣa), naktāhva, and the seeds of śigru.
A nasal medication (nasya) combined with goat's urine should be administered as a supreme remedy for worms.
In the case of *sūryāvarta*, medicinal treatments such as nasal therapy should be prescribed.
Likewise, one *prastha* of the fresh juice of *kumārī* and the juice of *dhattūra* [should be used].
One should cook one *prastha* of oil in two *prasthas* of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* combined with four *prasthas* of milk,
using the pastes of *madhuka*, *hrīvera*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *bhadramusta*.
With nakha, karpūra, bhṛṅga, elā, jīvantī, padma, kuṣṭhaka, mārkava, āsaka, tālīsa, sarjaniryāsa, patrakā, viḍaṅga,
śatapuṣpā, aśvagandhā, and gandharvahastaka— 44.

Having cooked [the ingredients] with one karṣa each of *śothahṛt* and coconut, the physician should remove it from the fire, strain it through a cloth, and place it in a clean vessel well-perfumed with incense;
then, he should keep it securely hidden for three nights according to the prescribed rite. (45–46)
Then, one should employ oil for massage and as an errhine (nasya) applied to the head; it thoroughly pacifies facial paralysis (ardita), stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), diseases of the head,
dryness of the palate, nose, and eyes, fainting, and halīmaka.

In cases of pain from jaw disorders, griping colic, deafness, or earache, one should administer ghee mixed with jaggery; one should eat *ghṛtapūra* cakes, apply nasal drops (*nāvana*) of milk and ghee, and drink milk and ghee. 48–49.
Fomentation with sesame seeds ground with milk and with the drugs of the *jīvanīya* group is recommended.
The juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* mixed with an equal amount of goat’s milk and heated over a low fire, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), is a supreme remedy that quickly destroys *sūryāvarta*. 50.
In cases of hemiplegia (ardhāvabhedaka), oleation and sudation are indeed the primary remedies;
furthermore, purgation, cleansing of the body, medicated smoking, and unctuous, warm food should be administered.
One should apply a paste made by grinding equal parts of viḍaṅga and black sesame seeds.
Therefore, one should also administer nasal therapy (nasya), which dispels the splitting pain in the head;
one should drink milk with sugar, or coconut water, or very cold water, or ghee as a nasal application for those two [conditions]. 52–53.

In the case of *anantavāta*, the procedure beneficial for *sūryāvarta* should be performed; venesection must also be carried out for the pacification of *anantavāta*. Furthermore, a diet that destroys *vāta* and *pitta* should be administered.
A *saṃyāva* cake with honey on top, and especially a *ghṛtapūpa* (ghee-cake), are beneficial.

A decoction made from *pathyā*, *akṣa*, *dhātrī*, *rajanī*, *guḍūcī*, *bhūnimba*, and *nimba*, taken with jaggery, destroys pain in the eyebrows, temples, ears, eyes, and head when placed in the nose for a moment. (55–56)
One should apply this ointment— consisting of dārvī, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, nimba, uśīra, and padmaka— for the pacification of śaṅkhaka;
furthermore, one should perform ablutions with cold water and consume cool milk.
A paste made from the milky sap of trees is beneficial as an ointment for the temple of the head (śaṅkhaka).
Equal parts of liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka) and black gram (māṣa) should be used, with poison constituting one-fourth part of that;
their powder should be very fine, and of that powder, a dose the size of a mustard seed [should be applied]. 58–59.

Placed inside the nostrils, this removes all headache; this yoga, whose efficacy has been witnessed, is honored by those who have experienced its results. 60. Now begins the sixty-third chapter on diseases of the eyes (63).
The physician should know that the circle of the eye is two finger-breadths in thickness, measured by the belly of one's own thumb,
and two and a half finger-breadths in circumference on all sides;
this applies to the circles of the eyelashes, the eyelids, the white part, the black part, and the pupil.
Their middles are gradual, while the four at the end increase progressively.
Twelve diseases are seen there, as well as two other ailments;
four are on the black path, while eleven arise from the white portion.
One [disease] is proclaimed to be in the eyelid, two in the eyelashes, and nine in the joints; thus, seventeen diseases are said to be in the entire eye.
In this way, there are seventy-eight diseases in total in the eye. 4.

Ten [eye diseases] arise from wind (vāta), likewise eleven from bile (pitta), thirteen from phlegm (kapha), sixteen are to be known as arising from blood (rakta), and twenty-five are born from all [three humors combined].
Furthermore, there are two external [diseases] of the eyes; thus, seventy-six eye diseases are recorded.

From entering water when tormented by heat, from gazing at distant objects, from the reversal of dreams, from perspiration, from exposure to dust and smoke, from the suppression of vomiting, from excessive emesis, from sour gruel,
fermented rice-water, raw mangoes, horse-gram, and black gram, and from the suppression of the passage of feces, urine, and flatus.
The humors produce disorders in the eyes due to excessive weeping, grief, and distress; from injury to the head; from traveling too rapidly;
likewise, from the inversion of the seasons, affliction by suffering, excessive sexual indulgence, suppression of tears, and from gazing at minute objects. (8–9)
When the humors (doṣas), having become disordered, ascend and take refuge in the vessels (śirās) that follow them, extremely severe diseases arise in the regions of the eyes.
[One should know] the [tear] drop, which is the size of a lentil leaf and is produced from the essence of the five elements.

Those who contemplate the eyes say that the vision of men is like a glowworm or a spark, perfected by imperishable energies; it is covered by an external membrane of the eye shaped like a cavity, and they describe this sight as being naturally adapted to cold.
The external [tejas] is dependent on water; among those [layers], another is dependent on flesh;
the third layer is dependent on fat; and yet another is dependent on the bone.
It is held that the abundance of these [elements] for the purpose of vision is equal to a fifth part. 13.
When a disorder of the vision is established in the first layer [of the eye],
one sometimes perceives forms indistinctly;
when it has reached the second layer, the vision becomes severely impaired.
He sees flies, mosquitoes, and hair as if they were gnats; he sees circles, banners, rays, and earrings, as well as various shimmering forms, rain, clouds, and darkness. 15–16.
Due to a distortion in the range of vision, one perceives forms that are distant as being near, and those that are near as being at a distance;
and even though exerting extreme effort, one does not see the hole of a needle. (17–18)
When the [vayu] has entered the third plexus, one sees upwards but not downwards;
And one would perceive according to the defect; when the defect is powerful, vision [perceives] it.

When the defect is situated below, one does not see what is nearby or what is far away; when the defect is situated above, one does not see what is nearby; and when the defect is situated at the side, one does not see things situated at the side. (20–21)
When a defect is situated all around, one sees things as if crowded together;
when a defect is situated in the middle of the vision, one sees what is large as small. When a defect is situated obliquely in the vision, one perceives a single object as two.
One should see [the object] as twofold when it is situated at two locations, and as manifold when it is not fixed in one place.
That defect known as *timira*, having reached the fourth layer (*paṭala*), obstructs vision on all sides; in some cases, this is called *liṅganāśa*.
Even in this state, which is shrouded in darkness and where the great disease has not yet fully ascended,
one perceives the moon and the sun along with the stars, lightning in the atmosphere, and pure, radiant splendors as if they were shining.
That very same loss of vision (liṅganāśa) is designated as *nīlikā* and *kāca*.

There are six diseases based on the visual faculty, for there are indeed six types of liṅganāśa; among them, those caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha, all three combined, and the sixth is called *parimlāyin*, which arises from blood. 26–27.

Likewise, a person whose vision is impaired by pitta, or another by kapha, or one who sees smoke, as well as those with short-sightedness, the condition known as "blindness like a mongoose," and similarly the condition known as "deep-seated" (gambhīra)— in these cases,
due to vāta, one indeed perceives forms as if they were spinning.
Due to bile (pitta), a person perceives everything as turbid, reddish, and as if distorted;
they see the sun, fireflies, Indra’s bow, and flashes of lightning, as well as dancing peacocks and all things as blue. 29–30.

One may see extremely subtle forms as white as a cow’s tail-whisk or like white clouds, and even when there are no clouds, one may see a vast expanse of clouds; through phlegm, one sees forms that are glossy and white.
Like a person seeing lattices submerged in water,
one perceives all variegated objects as overwhelmed by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), appearing multiplied in many ways or even split in two on every side.
Furthermore, a person may see celestial bodies with missing or extra limbs;
he may see them as red or blood-colored, as various kinds of darkness, or as green, black, and yellow. (33–34)
One should treat pitta that has become faint due to blood as if it were parimlāyin (fading).
By that [treatment], one would see the quarters of the sky as yellow, as if seeing the rising sun,
and indeed see trees as if they were being scattered with fireflies by their very splendors.
Liṅganāśa is also said to be of six types according to the colors produced by vāta and the other [doṣas]. As for the color produced by vāta and so forth:
a reddish hue is prescribed as being born of māruta (vāta), while a faded and bluish hue arises likewise from pitta. (37)
That caused by phlegm (kapha) is white; that born from blood is reddish; and that arising from all the humors (doṣas) together is variegated.
A circular patch (maṇḍala) caused by wind (vāta) is reddish, unstable, and rough;
whereas a patch caused by bile (pitta) is blue, or has the luster of bell-metal, or is yellowish.
Due to phlegm (śleṣman), it is thick, unctuous, and as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon;
like a white drop of water resting on a trembling lotus petal, that circular patch spreads when the eye is being rubbed. 40–41.
The circular patch (maṇḍala) may be variegated when the loss of vision (liṅganāśa) is caused by the three doṣas;
the blood-born maṇḍala has the luster of coral or a lotus petal.
A blood-born maṇḍala on the pupil has the reddish glow of a thick glass lens.
When a disease is fading away, it may appear withered or even bluish; however, due to the depletion of the *doṣas*, its manifestation may sometimes occur spontaneously.
Indeed, the specific symptoms of each *doṣa* manifest in all cases according to their respective nature. (43–44)

When the vitiated *pitta* reaches the eye, the vision of that man becomes yellow; he sees all forms as yellow, for that man’s sight is indeed scorched by *pitta*. When the disorder reaches the third layer (*paṭala*), he does not see by day, but perceives at night.

At night, that person whose vision is assisted by cold and in whom bile (pitta) is diminished sees all things clearly; likewise, a man whose vision is corrupted by phlegm (śleṣman) perceives those very same objects as white. When the morbid humor (doṣa) is situated in all three layers [of the eye] to a slight degree, it forcibly brings about night-blindness (naktāndhya).
By day, his vision being aided by the sun, he perceives forms due to the diminished state of the phlegm (kapha).
(47) The man whose vision is struck by grief, fever, exhaustion, or afflictions of the head, and who perceives all things as smoke, is designated as one with "smoky vision" (dhūmadarśin). (48)
He who sees forms with great difficulty during the day, or perceives even large objects as small,
yet sees things clearly at night, is declared by the sages to be of the short-statured (hrasva) class. Furthermore,
that man whose vision flashes like that of a mongoose when afflicted by the humors is likewise described.
If one sees variegated forms even during the day, that indeed is the disorder known as *nakulāndhya*.
When the vision is distorted and afflicted by wind (*śvasana*), it undergoes contraction from within; when accompanied by deep-seated pain, the wise call that eye disease *gambhīrikā*. 50–51.
Furthermore, two external types are prescribed here: that caused by a specific cause (*nimitta*) and that which is causeless (*animitta*).

Among these, the one caused by a cause should be known as arising from a headache characterized by the symptoms of *abhiṣyanda* (excessive secretions), as well as from the sight of celestial sages (*surarṣi*), *gandharvas*, great serpents (*mahoraga*), and even the sun.
The vision of that man is destroyed; this is known as *liṅganāśa* (loss of the visual axis) caused by no apparent external cause.
In that condition, the eye appears quite distinct and the vision is clear and the color of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).
However, when struck by trauma, the vision of men tears, sinks, or fails. 53–54.
Thus end the diseases of the visual axis;
now follow the diseases arising from the black circle (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala): those with ulcers and those without ulcers, as well as pākātyaya and ajakājāta.
These four types of eye diseases are invariably located in the black portion (kṛṣṇapradeśa).

When the form appears as if submerged in the black portion, or when it seems as if pierced by a needle, and there is an excessive flow of very hot discharge, that is declared to be the ulcerated white [sclera] (savraṇa-śukla). 55–56.

That which is not near the vision, nor deeply seated, nor exuding, nor painless, nor characterized by a double whiteness—such a case rarely attains success. However, a white discharge located in the black part [of the eye], flowing in nature and appearing like a conch, the moon, or a jasmine flower, [is curable]. 57.
They say that which is transparent like a cloud in the sky, thin, and without ulcers is most easily curable (58).
That which is deep-seated, thick, white, and long-standing is said to be difficult to treat (59).
Furthermore, that which has a gap in the middle, is covered by flesh, is mobile, arises from the vessels, and causes loss of vision [is also difficult].
Blood appearing on two layers at the edge, as well as that which has been present for a long time, should be avoided.

(60) Some declare that case incurable where there is a fall of warm tears and pustules on the black portion, and the white portion resembles a mung bean; others, however, say it is like the wing of a partridge. (61)

When a white film spreads from all sides over a black pupil due to a disorder, they say that this condition— known as *akṣipākātyaya* or *akṣikopa*, involving all [the humors]— must be rejected as incurable. (62) A painful condition resembling goat dung, which is reddish and characterized by red, slimy tears, [is also incurable].
When a collection [of symptoms] arises after attacking the black portion (*kṛṣṇa*), one should determine that it is *ajakājāta*. (63) Thus end the diseases arising from the black circle (*maṇḍala*).
Now follow the diseases arising from the white portion of the eye (*śuklabhāga*).
Indeed, there are five diseases known as *prastāri*, *śukla*, *kṣataja*, *adhimāṃsa*, and *snāyu*;

furthermore, *śuktikā*, *arjuna*, *piṣṭaka*, *śirājāla*, and the various *piḍakās* (pustules), along with *balāsagrathita*—these are indeed the eleven diseases of the white part (*śuklabhāga*) of the eye. 64.
Prastāryarma is thin, spread out, dark-brown, resembling blood, or white;
it is very pale, soft, and grows slowly over a long period in the white portion [of the eye].
Raktārma is soft and has the luster of a lotus; it is a fleshy growth that accumulates on the white portion.
The fifth type of *arman* is the thick, stable, and spreading *snāyv-arman*, which is rich in flesh and resembles the liver;
it is dark-brown (*śyāva*), has spots resembling flesh, and is covered with a thick layer of soft flesh. (68–69)
That which is white in appearance, covered with white [spots], is known as *śukti*. 70.
That single drop which has the luster of rabbit's blood and appears upon the white [part] is called *arjuna*. 71.
Due to the provocation of phlegm and wind (*śleṣma-māruta*), the flesh on the white part becomes elevated.
Know that *piṣṭaka* is like ground flour, resembling a mirror smeared with impurities.
A network-like appearance, hard, reddish at the head, and consisting of a spreading of vessels, is known as *sirājāla*. 72–73.
Those white pustules covered with veins that arise near the black portion [of the eye] should be known as *śirājā*.
That which has the luster of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), is not soft, and resembles drops of water on the white of the eye should be recognized as *balāsa*.
Thus end the diseases arising in the white portion [of the eye].
Now, the diseases arising from the eyelids (vartma) are:
utsaṅginī, kumbhīkā, pothakī, vartmaśarkarā, asovartma, śuṣkārśas, and likewise añjananāmikā and dūṣikā. (76)
Inward-facing, copper-colored, and situated along the outer edge of the eyelid, accompanied by pustules on its ridges, it is born from all [doshas], characterized by thick scaling and itching;
at the edge of the lid, these pustules become swollen, burst, and discharge [pus]. (77)
Pustules resembling the seeds of the *kumbhīkā* plant, arising from the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*),
which are exuding, itchy, heavy, similar in appearance to red mustard seeds, and painful, are known as *pothakī*. (78–79)
Covered with very fine and dense pustules,
a pustule that is rough and large, located on the eyelid, is *vartma-śarkarā* (80).
Pustules resembling the seeds of the *ervāru* gourd, which cause mild pain, [are called *vartma-kaṇḍū*].
Smooth or rough growths situated on the eyelid are designated as *vartmārśas*.
A long, sharp, rigid, and hard growth arising from within is well known by the name of the disease *śuṣkārśas* (dry hemorrhoid).
A copper-colored, soft, small pustule arising on the eyelid, accompanied by burning and pricking sensations and mild pain, is known as *añjanan-dūṣikā*.
When the eyelid is covered all over with pustules, it is [known as *vartma-saṃplava*]. 83.
One should recognize *bahalavartman* by its being of the same color as the skin, firm, and thickened.
When a person cannot close their eye evenly due to itching, slight pain, and swelling of the eyelid, that condition is called *vartmabandhaka*.
When the eyelid is copper-colored, slightly painful, and even,
yet suddenly becomes red, the wise know that as *kliṣṭavartman*.
Furthermore, when blood combined with pitta causes a burning sensation, it is known as *kliṣṭa*.
When that [discharge] has become moistened, it is called *vartmakardama* (87).
When the eyelid is dark-brown both externally and internally, swollen, painful, itchy, and exuding moisture, it is known as *śyāvavartman* (88).
One should recognize that condition as *praklinnavartma* in a person whose eyelid is painless yet swollen on the outside, while being excessively moistened within;
it is a case where the eyelids, though washed, become closed again and again. 89.
One should know that when the eyelids are not fully ripened, it is *aklinnavartman* (90).
When the eyelid is detached from its joints, motionless, and does not close, one should know this as *vātahatavartman*, whether it is painful or painless (91).
One should diagnose as arbuda a growth situated at the edge of the eyelid that is uneven,
knotty, painless, reddish, and hanging; furthermore, when Vāyu enters the blinking vessels located within the eyelid, [it causes] nimeṣinī.
It moves the eyelids and does not heal.
That which arises on the eyelid, red, soft, and sprout-like, is blood-born;
it is a hemorrhoidal growth (śoṇitārśas) that increases even after being excised. 93–94.
A painless, itchy, slimy growth the size of a jujube fruit (kola), which is external, hard, thick, and arises from the eyelid margin, is known as lagaṇa.
The three doṣas may produce an external swelling with perforations on both eyelids.
When the humors, such as wind (vāta) and others, cause the contraction of the eyelid margins, the internal moisture flows out like the sap from a lotus stalk;
this condition is known by the experts as *kuñcana*. (96–97)
Thus end the diseases of the eyelids; now, the diseases of the eyelashes:
*pakṣmakopa* and *pakṣmaśāta* are two diseases localized in the eyelashes. 98.
Indeed, eyelashes stirred by the wind enter the eye;
rubbing against it repeatedly, they produce irritation, and they even fall from their sockets onto both the dark and white portions of the eye.

That extremely severe disease should be known as *pakṣmakopa*. When, after the eyelashes have fallen out, [inflammation] arises at the edge of the eyelids and causes rubbing between the black and white parts of the eye, it is called *pakṣmakopa*. 99–100.

Pitta located in the eyelids and the follicles of the lashes causes the falling out of the lashes and produces itching and burning; this condition should be designated as Pakṣma-śāta (falling of the lashes).
Thus end the two diseases of the lashes.

Now, regarding diseases arising from the junctions: there is that which occurs at the junction of the eyelashes and the eyelid (*pakṣma-vartma-sandhi*), another at the junction of the eyelid and the white of the eye (*vartma-śukla*),
another at the junction of the white and the black of the eye (*śukla-kṛṣṇa*), and yet another at the junction of the black of the eye and the pupil (*kṛṣṇa-dṛṣṭi*).
Mataḥ (inflammation of the eyelid), Kanīnaka-gataḥ (inflammation of the inner corner of the eye), and Ṣaṣṭha-cāpāṅga-saṃśritaḥ (inflammation extending to the outer corner)—these three;
Pūyālasa, Sopanāha, and the four types of Srāvas (discharges); Parvaṇikā, Alajī, and Jantugranthi—these are the nine diseases occurring at the joints (sandhi). 102–103.
A suppurated swelling arising from the joints that discharges thick, foul-smelling pus is called *pūyālasa*.
A small, non-suppurating glandular swelling at the junction of the eye, characterized by itching and being painless, is known as *upanāha*.
When the humors (*doṣas*) reach the joints via the tear ducts, they produce discharges (*srāvas*) endowed with their respective symptoms.
Indeed, some call that discharge *netranāḍī*; I shall describe its symptoms in four ways.
(106) A yellowish, pale, hot, or watery discharge flowing from the middle of the joint is known as *pitta-srāva* (bile-discharge).
(107) That which flows white, thick, and slimy is declared to be the disorder *śleṣma-srāva* (phlegm-discharge). (108)
A swelling at a joint that suppurates and discharges pus is considered to be caused by all three doshas (sarvaja).
109. A discharge of blood is a disorder arising from blood and other factors; in that condition, the blood flows hot and in abundance.
110. A copper-colored, thin, circular swelling accompanied by burning and suppuration should be known as *parvaṇī*, arising from blood.

An alajī occurs at the junction of the black and white parts [of the eye]; when it is provoked in that very location, it manifests with the aforementioned symptoms. (111) Worms born at the junction of the eyelid and the lashes cause itching;
these worms, appearing in various forms at the junction of the eyelid and the white part, move internally, corrupting the eye. (112)
Thus are the diseases arising from the junctions (sandhi).
Now, regarding the diseases arising from the entire eye:
four types of *syanda* (ophthalmia) are prescribed here, as well as four types of *adhimantha* (ocular inflammation).

Pāka (inflammation) accompanied by swelling, that same condition without swelling, Hatādhimantha, and Anilaparyaya; 113. Śuṣkākṣipāka as described here, as well as Vāta arising from another cause, and Amlādhyuṣitā, Śirāharṣa, and Śirāpāta—all these occur in the entire eye. 114.
Thus, there are seventeen diseases of the entire eye;
I shall now describe their individual characteristics here as they truly are.
Abhiṣyanda is fourfold, arising from vāta, pitta, kapha, and blood.
Generally, a terrible disease arises that produces afflictions of all the eyes (116). Pricking pain, stiffness, horripilation, friction, roughness, headache,
a sense of dryness, and cold lacrimation occur when the eye is afflicted by Vāta (117).
Burning sensation, suppuration, longing for cold things, smoking sensation, and the emergence of tears; hot lacrimation and yellowness of the eyes—these occur when the eyes are afflicted by pitta.
Longing for warmth, heaviness, swelling of the eyes, itching, coating, and extreme coldness [are the signs of kapha].
When the eyes are afflicted by *kapha*, there is frequent discharge that is slimy;
when afflicted by blood (*rakta*), the eyes become copper-colored, tearful, red-eyed, and covered with excessively red streaks all around—these are the same symptoms as those of *pitta*. 119–120.
From these aforementioned morbid humors (abhiṣyandas), when left untreated, there arise in men as many types of Adhimantha, characterized by intense pain in the eye;
it feels as if the eye is being excessively torn out and likewise churned.
One should recognize that condition as Adhimantha by its specific symptoms when it occupies half of the head.

A Kapha-born Adhimantha destroys vision after seven nights, one born of blood after five nights, and a Vata-born one after six nights; however, a Pitta-born Adhimantha destroys it immediately through improper conduct. (122–123)
Accompanied by itching, exudation, and tearing, resembling a ripe udumbara fruit, and characterized by inflammation and suppuration along with swelling—this is *netrapāka* (inflammation of the eye).
In the case of *netrapāka* without swelling (*aśothaja*), the symptoms are present but devoid of swelling. (124)

When the Vata-dominant Adhimantha, due to neglect, forcibly dries up the eye with violent pains, it becomes incurable; indeed, this disease is known as Hatadhimantha. Furthermore, the Vata moves repeatedly over the eyebrows and the eyes.
When there are various intense pains, that should be known as *vātaparyaya*.

That eye which is contracted, has harsh and dry eyelids, feels as if it is being burned, has blurred vision, is extremely painful, and is afflicted by dryness upon waking—that eye is struck by *śuṣkākṣipāka*. 126–127.
If the Vāyu located in the temples, ears, head, jaw, or the nape of the neck, or elsewhere, causes excessive pain in the eyebrows and eyes, they call that condition Anyatovāta (pains on both sides).
The entire eye becomes dark-brown with red margins and undergoes suppuration.

Accompanied by constant burning, swelling, discharge, and aggravated by sour substances due to their acidity; whether painless or painful, when the blood-vessels of the eye become copper-colored and repeatedly fade away on all sides, this condition is designated as *śirotpāta*. (129–130)
