If the piercing pain in the head arising from delusion is neglected, it becomes the disease known as *śirāpraharṣa*; it causes the eyes to turn copper-colored, produces excessive discharge, and likewise renders one unable to look upon anything.
The eye is characterized by intense pain, accompanied by redness and swelling. (131)
They know the eye affected by *āma* (undigested morbid matter) to be characterized by rubbing, pricking pain, aching, lacrimation, and swelling.
132 Mild pain, itching, absence of redness or inflammation, diminished lacrimation, and a clear coloration of the eyes are the characteristics of a healthy eye (*nirāma*). 133

Thus, all eye diseases arise from the feet; for those two [feet] are situated broadly in the middle of the body and extend upward to the head, and since they reach the eyes in many ways, [therapies] such as sprinkling, rubbing, and ointments applied to the feet lead to the improvement of the eyes. 134
The wicked corrupt the eyes through contact with dust, heat, friction, pressure, and the like;
therefore, one should always employ shoes, ointments, and washing that are beneficial for vision.
Śāli rice, mung beans, barley, and the meat of wild animals are wholesome for the eyes.
Especially the flesh of birds, vāstūka, and taṇḍulīyaka;
the fruits of paṭola, karkoṭaka, and kāravella cooked with ghee,
as well as fresh eggplant— whether sweet or bitter— are beneficial for the eyes.
Bitter, sour, heavy, sharp, and hot foods; black gram (*māṣa*), flat beans (*niṣpāva*), sexual intercourse, wine, dried meat, oil-cake, fish, leafy vegetables, sprouted grains,
and burning foods— these are unwholesome for one suffering from eye disease.

One should treat the eye with these medicinal pastes by means of *sekam* (sprinkling), *āścyotanam* (dropping), *piṇḍī* (pulp), *viḍāla* (cat-like application), *tarpaṇam* (satiation), as well as *puṭapāka* (steaming) and *añjanam* (collyrium).
Among these, *sekam* is beneficial for the entire eye when administered as fine streams.
For a mortal person with closed eyes, a [collyrium] four finger-breadths wide should be applied.

That too is emollient in cases of wind (vāta), while it is healing (ropaṇa) in cases of bile (pitta) and blood (rakta); however, in cases of phlegm (kapha), it should be scraping (lekhanīya). Its dosage is now described. 137–138.
Six hundred applications of these [drops] should be used for lubrication, four hundred for healing,
and three hundred for irrigation to clarify the eyes.
Alternatively, the blinking and opening of the eyes by men may be counted by a finger snap.
The utterance of long syllables is considered by the wise to be mere speech.
However, sprinkling [with medicated water] should be performed during the day; in the case of an extremely severe disease, it may be done at night.
Goat's milk boiled with the leaves, roots, and bark of *eraṇḍa* is beneficial.
Warm lukewarm water poured into the eyes destroys *vātābhiṣyanda*.
Having made a small sachet with a fine cloth using a paste of *pathyā*, *akṣa*, *āmalaka*, and the bark of *khāsa*, one should combine it with the liquid extracted from *ahi-phenā*. 141–142.
If one places [this] upon the eyes, all eye-disorders will be quickly destroyed;
this is the yoga taught by compassionate sages for the benefit of the world.
(143) If, after eating, one rubs the palms of the hands together and applies [the resulting substance] to the eyes...
That water very quickly dispels darkness;
bathing with black sesame seeds is beneficial for the eyes and removes wind disorders.
Bathing constantly with *āmalaka* fruits brings about supreme strength of vision. (144–145)
The decoction of triphalā, when used for washing, conquers eye diseases;
as a gargle, it destroys mouth diseases; and when drunk, it removes jaundice (kāmalā).
[146] Regarding the pouring down of drops of decoction, milk, juice, or oil:
When the eyes are opened with a gap of two finger-breadths, that is said to be *āścyotana*.
For scraping, eight drops are prescribed; for healing, ten drops;
and for oleation, twelve drops are prescribed; these should be lukewarm when applied in cold weather. (147–148)
In cases of heat, [the eye drops] should be cold in nature; this is the certainty for all instances.
In cases of Vāta, they should be bitter and unctuous; in Pitta, sweet and cold; and in Kapha, bitter, hot, and dry. Thus, eye-drops (āścyotana) are beneficial according to these respective sequences.
The dose for all types of eye-drops (āścyotana) should be one hundred and fifty drops (mātrās).
A lukewarm decoction made from the five roots beginning with bilva, along with bṛhatī, eraṇḍa, and śigru, used as an eye-drop destroys vāta-type ophthalmia and visual obstructions.

An eye-drop (āścyotana) made from triphalā destroys all types of ophthalmia (abhiṣyanda). A bolus (piṇḍī) the size of a jujube fruit (kola), prepared from the paste of the aforementioned medicinal herbs and bound with a piece of cloth, destroys ophthalmia and corneal ulcers (vraṇa). 152–153.

A bolus that is unctuous and warm is prescribed for Vāta; it is considered cooling for Pitta and dry and warm for Kapha. This procedure has been declared by the wise. (154) A bolus made from castor leaf, root, and bark destroys Vāta.

A bolus prepared with *dhātrī* (myrobalan) is for [excess] *pitta*; one made with *śigru* leaves is for *kapha*. A bolus made even with *nimba* leaves will alleviate both *pitta* and *śleṣman* (phlegm).
A bolus made of *śuṇṭhī* and *nimba* leaves, slightly warm and containing a little rock salt, [is likewise beneficial].

A bolus of Triphalā applied to the eyes removes swelling, itching, and pain caused by Vāta and Kapha; it also alleviates Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha disorders of the eyes. A paste made from Pathyā, Akṣa, Āmalaka, Khākhāsa, and the bark of Snuhi, combined with Ahiphena and water, [is likewise beneficial].
The medicinal paste (*piṇḍī*) prepared from that [substance] pacifies all morbid humidities. 158.
*Viḍālaka* is an external ointment for the eyes, excluding the eyelashes; its dosage should be understood as being like that prescribed for facial applications. 159.
The lowest application for smearing the face is one-fourth of a finger's breadth;
the middling is three parts; and the best shall be half a finger.
Its duration is said to last even during the period of staying [in the world] as long as the paste has not dried.
But if it is dry, it is devoid of its qualities and likewise vitiates the skin.
(161) A paste made from equal parts of yaṣṭi, gairika, sindhūttha, dārvī, and tārkṣya, ground with water and applied externally, removes all eye diseases. (162)
Alternatively, an ointment may be applied using *rasāñjana*, or with the leaves of *pathyā* and *bilva*, or with *vacā*, *haridrā*, and *viśva*, or likewise with *nāgara* and *gerika*.
[This should be done] while the patient lies on his back in a room protected from wind, sunlight, and dust. (163)

The two sockets of the eyes should be made circular, even, firm, and without gaps using moistened bean flour (māṣacūrṇa). One should fill them with melted clarified butter scum (ghṛtamaṇḍa) and lukewarm water. 164–165.

One should fill the eyes with ghee washed a hundred times or with ghee produced from milk, while the eyelashes remain submerged; one should keep them filled for as long as they remain so, then, once the eyes are closed, one should slowly open them.
This nourishing procedure was described by physicians in the Purāṇas for a condition where the eye is parched,
completely dried up, distorted, and turbid, accompanied by decayed eyelashes, growths on the eyelids, and painful opening of the eyes. (167–168)

An expert in eye diseases should properly perform *tarpaṇa* (eye saturation) for that eye which is afflicted by *timira*, *arjuna*, *śukra*, and other such conditions, as well as by *abhiṣyanda*, *adhimantha*, dry ophthalmia (*śuṣkākṣipāka*), swelling (*śotha*), and various disorders caused by *vāta*. 169
In diseases of the eyelids, the wise physician should maintain the saturation for one hundred recitations;
in a healthy state, or in diseases of the joints caused by *kapha*, for five hundred recitations;
in *kapha*-related black discoloration of the eyes, for six hundred; and indeed, for seven hundred in *kapha*-related diseases.

Eight hundred [drops] for disorders of vision, one thousand for eye-pain (adhimantha), and one thousand for wind-related diseases; thus indeed is the satiation [to be administered]. Then, having caused the oil to flow from the outer corner of the eye, one should cleanse the eye.
Then, having applied steamed barley flour stimulated by the potency of fats,
one should purge his *kapha* with appropriate medicinal smoking (*dhūmapāna*).
Alternatively, one should provide nourishment (*tarpaṇa*) for one day, three days, or even five days.
In the case of satiation (tarpaṇa), one should observe these signs of satisfaction regarding the eye:
waking up feeling as if one has slept comfortably, clarity, acuity of vision, contentment, alleviation of disease, and lightness of function. (175–176)

One should designate as *atitarpita* (over-satiated) an eye that is turbid with heavy secretions, excessively unctuous, accompanied by tearing, itching, and exudation, characterized by friction and pain,
and filled with discharge, swelling, and disease, rendering it incapable of perceiving forms. (177)
The eye that is turbid, harsh, and dry is under-nourished (dhīnatarpita).

Due to the abundance of these two defects, it must be treated with great effort; the remedy for these two consists of the applications of drying (rukṣa) and unctuous (snigdha) therapies respectively. 178–179.
Tarpaṇa (eye-satiation) is not recommended for the eyes during cloudy days, extreme heat or cold, when there is mental anxiety, agitation, or when complications have not yet subsided.
Two bilva fruits of fatty meat are considered the maximum dose of one pala of medicinal substance.
One should grind all the ingredients measured by one *kuḍava* together into a single mass; having thoroughly kneaded them together and wrapped them well with leaves,
the wise physician should cook them according to the procedure for *puṭapāka* and extract that juice.

One should apply it correctly according to the procedure prescribed for the *tarpaṇa* rite; it should be poured daily into the eyes of one lying on their back, [protecting them] from heat, wind, space, sunlight, and the sun itself. 183.
One who has had their eyes satiated with medicinal drops, or one who has undergone *puṭapāka* therapy, should not look [at bright light].
(184) Now, for one whose humors have been fully ripened, one should apply collyrium (*añjana*) as indicated;
that substance by which collyrium is prepared is considered "collyrium" (*añjana*). (185)

One should indeed prepare three types of medicinal powders—pills, pastes, and powders—and three types of collyriums; these should be applied with a probe or a finger, each succeeding one being inferior to the preceding.
These are distinctively threefold: emollient (snehana), healing (ropaṇa), and scraping (lekhanā).
An ointment that is sweet and rich in unctuousness (sneha) is considered emollient (snehana).
An ointment endowed with astringent and bitter tastes along with unctuousness is known as healing (ropaṇa).
An ointment prepared with alkaline, bitter, and sour tastes is called scarifying (lekhana). (187–188)
The physician should prepare pills the size of a mustard seed for sharp collyrium;
for medium strength, the measure should be one and a half times that, and for mild strength, it should be double.
However, *rasakriyā* (extracted resin) is considered the best and is regarded as being the size of a *trivṛt* fruit.

The medium-sized [probe] consists of two *viḍaṅga* seeds; the inferior one consists of a single *viḍaṅga*. They say there should be four probes for lubrication (*snehana*), powder (*cūrṇa*), and collyrium (*añjana*); three of these are for healing (*ropaṇa*). Both of those [the last two types] are considered to be for scraping (*lekhanīya*). 190–191.

A smooth probe, eight finger-breadths in length, made of stone or metal, shaped like a pea in its circular cross-section, and curved at both ends, is prescribed for the application of unguents. It may also be fashioned from gold or silver. 192.
A probe made from intense iron or stone is intended for scraping, while a finger is said by the wise to be used for healing due to its softness.
[193] It should be purified with the juices of triphalā, bhṛṅga, and ginger, and with clarified butter. [194]
An ointment-stick heated over a serpent that has been sprinkled with cow urine, honey, ghee,
and milk certainly removes all diseases born of the eyes;
one should apply this collyrium below the black portion [of the eye] as far as the eye itself.
In the winter and the cool season, collyrium is desired at midday;
in summer and autumn, it is desired either in the forenoon or in the afternoon; during the rainy season, when there are no clouds and it is not excessively hot, and indeed always in spring. (196–197)
One should apply it in the morning or in the evening; however, one should never do so at all times.
Collyrium is not recommended when one is exhausted, weeping, frightened, intoxicated by liquor, suffering from acute fever, experiencing indigestion, or when the natural urges have been suppressed.

Having ground together one, two, and three parts respectively of Pathyā, Akṣa, and Dhātrī seeds, one should prepare pills with water; this collyrium, containing two parts of hareṇukā, quickly removes ocular discharge as well as the pain of vātarakta. (200)

Rasāñjana, the two types of haridrā, and the tender leaves of mālatī and nimba, combined with cow dung juice, form a pill that destroys night-blindness; for its application as an ointment, the prescribed measure is one part of this together with half a part of hareṇukā. (201)
Equal parts of conch-shell navel, the marrow of the bibhītaka fruit, harītakī, realgar, long pepper, black pepper, kuṣṭha,
and vacā should be ground with goat’s milk and made into pills the size of a barley grain.
Having ground it to the size of a mustard seed, one should apply it as a collyrium with water.

It conquers timira, fleshy growths (māṃsavṛddhi), cataract (kāca), film over the eye (paṭala), arbuda, night-blindness, and the flower-like growths of the rainy season; [this] pill is like the rising moon. 203–204.

Karañja seeds, repeatedly saturated with the fresh juices of palāśa flowers, form a wick that destroys cataracts (puṣpa) of the eye. Having ground the fruit of the kataka tree, one should apply it as an ointment to the eyes with honey.
That [collyrium], combined with a small amount of camphor, serves to clarify the eyes.
(206) Rasāñjana, resin of the *sarja* tree, jasmine flowers, realgar, sea-foam, salt, red ochre, and likewise black pepper; (207)
These ingredients, ground with honey in equal proportions, form an ointment for use when the eyelids are moistened; it destroys moisture and itching and promotes the growth of eyelashes.
It cures itching with milk, eye discharge with honey, and [other ailments] with clarified butter.
Timira (blindness) is removed by *puṣpataila*, and night-blindness (*niśāndhatā*) by *kāñjika*;
likewise, *punarnavā* quickly removes it, just as the sun dispels darkness.
A decoction of *babbūla* leaves, once reduced to a linctus, acts as an ointment for this purpose.
Eye discharge will undoubtedly reach dryness through the use of food mixed with honey (verse 211). Furthermore,
the powder derived from the finest camphor combined with the milky sap of the banyan tree quickly destroys two-month-old *kusuma* [cataract] when applied as a collyrium (verse 212).
One should apply collyrium to the eyes using black pepper rubbed with honey and dog's saliva;
excessive sleep will then subside, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
Indeed, one should pour heated *sauvīra* (antimony) into the juice of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Likewise, having been sprinkled seven times with the breast milk of women and ground into powder,
one should apply it as an ointment to the eyes every day; this is beneficial for the eyes and will undoubtedly destroy all eye disorders.
Having ground the *rasaka* on a stone slab and thoroughly saturated it with water,
one should take all that liquid and discard the powder that has settled at the bottom.
When that water has completely dried, it becomes like a thin wafer (*parpaṭī*).
Having powdered it, one should thoroughly saturate it three times with the juices of triphalā.
One should then add camphor powder equal to one-tenth part of that; by applying this as an ointment to the eyes, all diseases of the eyes are destroyed.

An ointment made from the powdered skin of a hen’s egg, stone, glass, conch-shell, sandalwood, and rock salt is said to destroy flowers and the like. [219] Pearl, camphor, glass, agallochum, black pepper, long pepper, rock salt, and *elavāluka*— The provided text contains two Sanskrit verses (numbered 219). Here is the translation of the first verse: "An ointment made from the powders of the shell of a hen's egg, stone, glass, conch-shell, sandalwood, and rock salt is declared to be the destroyer of flowers and other such things. (Note: The second line of the second verse fragment provided—"muktākarpūrakācāgurumaricakaṇāsaindhavaṃ sailavālam"—is incomplete, as it lacks the verb or predicate to complete the sentence.)

Dry ginger, kakkola, bell-metal, tin, copper, iron, stone, conch-shell, navel-shell, mica, blue vitriol, the skin of a right-side hen’s egg, along with lac, blood, harītakī, liquorice, royal cobalt, jasmine flower, fresh tulasī flower, and likewise bījaka; 220.

One *māṣaka* each of *pūtīka*, *nimba*, *arjuna*, *bhadramusta*, *tāmrasāra*, and *rasagarbha* should be carefully ground with honey until very fine; by this, those diseases residing in the eyes that have become excessively aggravated are cured. (221)
Peace must certainly be established by this great group of people, beginning with Muktā and the rest:
Kaṇā, salt, pungent [ginger], Rasāñjana, Sāñjana, the phlegm of the ocean (guggulu), sugar, and white Punarnavā. 222.
One should grind together rajani, aruṇacandana, madhuka, tuttha, pathyā, śilā,
ariṣṭadalasāvara, sphaṭika, śaṅkhanābhi, and indra;
these should be purified by rubbing them with a thick cloth.
Likewise, one should grind iron with honey and pieces of copper;

this collyrium, called Nayanashona, has been proclaimed by the sages to forcibly effect the destruction of cataracts (timira), the removal of film (paṭala), and the eradication of ocular tumors (puṣpa). 224
Take harītakī, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and black pepper,
along with the marrow of bibhītaka, conch-shell navel,
and realgar; having made all these equal in measure, one should grind them with cow’s milk.
It destroys cataracts, itching, films, and tumors;
it eliminates even three-year-old white [cataracts] in a single month, as well as excess fleshy growths and night-blindness. (226–227)
Rajanī, nimba leaves, pippalī,
marica, viḍaṅga, bhadramusta, and abhayā as the seventh—
having ground these together with goat's urine, one should dry them in the shade to form a pill (vaṭī). 228.
It destroys darkness with water, but with cow's urine it destroys [the disease] *piṣṭaka*;
it destroys *paṭala* with honey and *puṣpaka* with women’s milk.
This *candraprabhā* wick was fashioned by Rudra himself. (229–230)
Having cooked *kaṇā* (long pepper) in the midst of goat's liver and then ground it with its own juice, it quickly destroys night-blindness; likewise, *mūṣaṇa* taken with honey has the same effect.
One *prastha* of the juice of *triphalā* and one *prastha* of *bhṛṅgarāja* [should be prepared].

One *prastha* of the juice of *vṛṣa* and an equal amount of the juice of *śatāvarī*, one *prastha* each of the juices of *guḍūcī* and *āmalakī*, as well as goat's milk— one *prastha* of each— having collected all these together, one should cook ghee with them. (232–233)
A paste (kalka) consisting of long pepper (kaṇā), sugar (sitā), grapes (drākṣā), the three myrobalans (triphalā), blue water-lily (nīlotpala),
licorice (madhuka), milk-creeper (kṣīrakākolī), honey-leafed plant (madhuparṇī), and sowthistle (nidigdhikā)—
once this has been properly prepared, one should recognize it as ready and store it in a clean vessel.

Drinking [the medicine] from above, from below, or in the middle is recommended. It removes as many eye diseases as there may be; likewise, it is beneficial when blood is mixed with [the humor], when the blood is vitiated, or when the blood has been drained. 235–236.
In night-blindness, timira, kāca, nīlikā, paṭala,
arbuda, abhiṣyanda, adhimantha, and even in the most severe pakṣmakoṣa, as well as in all eye diseases produced by the three doṣas; 237.
This great ghee, beginning with Triphalā, is declared to be supremely beneficial.

(238) One hundred *harītakī* fruits, twice that amount of *bibhītaka*, and four times that amount of *āmalaka* should be taken; [the quantity] of *vṛṣa* and *ārkava* should be equal [to the *āmalaka*]. (239)
Having added four parts of water, one should cook it slowly over a mild fire;
having preserved one-fourth part, one should remove that decoction from the heat.
[Then add] sugar, madhuka, drākṣā, madhuyaṣṭī, and nidigdhikā.

One should slowly cook one *prastha* of ghee with an equal amount of milk and a paste (*kalka*) consisting of *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nāgakeśara*, *pippalī*, *nandana*, *musta*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *utpala*. (241–242)
It destroys cataracts (satimira), pterygium (kāca), night-blindness (naktāndhya), and white opacities (śukla), as well as discharge, itching, swelling, astringency,
turbidity of the eye, and the membranes of the eyelid (bindvarma-paṭala). 243.
What need is there for much speaking here? This [remedy] removes all eye diseases.
For one whose vision is impaired by looking at the sun or fire, this has been declared by the sages to be the supreme and most beneficial medicine. (244-245)

Just as a mirror, when polished, attains supreme clarity, so too does the eye attain clarity by drinking this [mixture]. Furthermore, two droṇas of water are added here along with one *tulā* each of *vṛṣa* and *mārkava*. (246)
A decoction made from vāsā, viśvā, amṛtā, dārvī, raktacandana, citraka,
bhūnimba, nimba, kaṭukā, paṭola, triphalā, ambuda,
niśā, kaliṅga, and kuṭaja destroys all eye diseases. (247)
It certainly destroys hoarseness, chronic catarrh, dyspnea, and cough. 247.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter on eye diseases.
Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter on ear diseases. 64.
Earache, ringing in the ear, deafness, and a whistling sound;
ear discharge, itching of the ear, and likewise earwax;
pratināha, jantukarṇa, and the two types of abscesses (vidradhi).
Ear-inflammation (karṇapāka), putrid ear (pūtikarṇa), and likewise the four types of hemorrhoids (arśas);
similarly, the seven types of tumors (arbuda) and the four types of swellings (śopha)—
these twenty-eight diseases located in the ear have been described.

When the vital air (samīraṇa) enters the ear and moves abnormally in all directions, being obstructed by the respective humors (doṣas), it causes extreme pain in the ears; this is described as Karṇaśūla, which is difficult to treat. Furthermore, fainting, burning sensations, fever, cough, dyspnea, and vomiting [may also occur].
These complications arise in earache for one who is about to die.
When wind is located in the ear-cavity, one hears various sounds such as those of kettledrums, clay drums, and conch shells; that is called "ringing in the ears" (karṇanāda).
When the wind, carrying sound, remains obstructing the channel—
whether pure or associated with phlegm— hearing loss (bādhirya) arises because of it.
One should avoid treating hearing loss that has arisen in the very young or the very old, as well as that which has been present for a long time.
When the bodily air (vāyu), combined with bile (pitta) and other humors, produces a sound in the ears similar to the whistling of bamboo,
it is called *karṇakṣveḍa* (whistling in the ears).
This occurs due to a blow to the head, or from submerging in water, or even from a fall or a wound.
When the ear, afflicted by wind (anila), discharges pus, it is proclaimed as *karṇasaṃsrāva* (ear-drip).
Wind combined with phlegm (kapha) indeed causes itching in the ear.
Phlegm, dried by the heat of bile (pitta), produces earwax (*karṇagūthaka*).
When that earwax becomes liquefied and flows, reaching the nostrils and the mouth,

then it becomes a disorder known as *karṇapratināha*, which causes a splitting pain in the head. Furthermore, when insects or flies become trapped there, or even when they lay their eggs, [the same occurs].

Because it is smeared with collyrium during the act of hearing, this disease is designated by the ancient physicians as *krimikarṇaka* (ear-worm). Indeed, insects and centipedes, having entered the ear canal,
cause intense restlessness, agitation, and excruciating pain.
The ear is pricked as if by needles and experiences a throbbing sensation; when the insect moves, there is intense pain, but when it is motionless, the pain is mild.
Furthermore, an abscess may arise from injury or trauma, or it may be caused by the bodily humors (doṣas).

It discharges blood that is red, yellow, or reddish-brown, accompanied by pricking pain, fuming, burning, and sucking sensations. Ear- suppuration (karṇapāka), however, caused by pitta, results in putrefaction and moistening.
This occurs through the ripening of an ear abscess (karṇavidradhi) or from filling the ear with water.
That which flows with putrid pus should be known as *pūtikarṇaka*.
One should recognize ear-swelling (*karṇaśotha*), tumors (*arbuda*), and polyps (*arśas*) by their previously described characteristics.
From Vāta, there is ringing, intense pain, swelling of the ear-wax, thin discharge, and loss of hearing.
From pitta arise swelling with redness, cracking, a burning sensation, and the discharge of putrid, yellow fluid (21).
From kapha arise deafness, itching, firm swelling, and a white, unctuous discharge with little pain (22).
From the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) arise all these symptoms together, and the discharge there has the color of the predominant humor (23).
Now, regarding diseases of the earlobe (*karṇapālī*):
due to its extreme delicacy, if the earlobe— which had been neglected for a long time— is suddenly subjected to excessive stretching, a painful swelling accompanied by cracking occurs on the lobe.
Resembling blackish-red in color and rigid, that condition caused by wind is known as *paripoṭaka*. Due to contact with heavy ornaments, or even from beating and friction,
a dark swelling occurs at the margin (*pālī*), accompanied by burning, suppuration, and pain.
An eruption arising from blood or from blood and bile (raktapitta) is known as sagada.
When one forcibly stretches the ear, the Vayu becomes aggravated in the lobe (pālī);
seizing the Kapha, it produces a swelling that is stiff and painless.
Unmanthaka is a disorder arising from phlegm and wind (kapha-vāta) characterized by itching (sakandūka).

When a wound is improperly incised and allowed to grow, there occurs a swelling accompanied by itching, burning, and pain, which suppurates; this three-humored (tridoṣa) condition increases suffering. (26–27)
When phlegm, blood, and parasites are provoked, they become the size of mustard seeds and spread about, producing a pustule on the margin accompanied by itching and burning;
born from phlegm, blood, and parasites, it spreads here and there.

One who licks a preparation containing śaṣkuli and other ingredients is known as a *parilehī*. This is considered the general remedy for all four diseases: earache, ringing in the ears, deafness, and tinnitus.
Fresh ginger, honey, rock salt, and oil—these, when applied lukewarm to the ears, shall alleviate pain. [Likewise, the juice] of garlic, fresh ginger, śigru, vāruṇī, and radish [should be used]. 29.
The fresh juice of the plantain is best when used lukewarm as an ear-drop (30).
One should place sprouts of the arka plant, ground with sour liquid and mixed with oil and salt, inside a hollowed-out stem of the sudhā plant that has been covered with clay (31).
One should squeeze the [herbs] that have been steamed by the process of *puṭapāka* until the juice emerges; one should then instill that lukewarm juice into the ear for the alleviation of pain.
(32) A leaf of the *arka* plant, yellowed by ripening and smeared with clarified butter, heated over a fire of peacock feathers—
Indeed, water that has been heated until it is comfortably warm and poured into the ear after being squeezed [of impurities] removes the pain.
For an ear afflicted with intense pain, accompanied by ringing sounds and discharges,
they recommend goat's urine, slightly warmed and mixed with rock salt.
Oil prepared according to the prescribed method over a mild fire with the root of white Arka (Calotropis gigantea) quickly removes earache arising from the three doṣas when used as a filling.
Oil derived from mustard seeds, combined with asafoetida, rock salt, and dry ginger, [achieves the same].
Filling [the ear] with this necessarily removes matured pain in the ear (karṇaśūla).
In cases of earache, tinnitus, deafness, and ringing in the ears, filling [the ear] with pungent oil (kaṭutaila) containing Vata-alleviating medicinal herbs is beneficial. (36–37)
Oil prepared with the juice of *śikharī* and *kṣāra*, processed with a paste made from those same ingredients,
removes ringing in the ears (*karṇanāda*) and deafness (*bādhirya*) when used as an ear-drop (verse 38).
One should cook oil by grinding *bilva* fruits with the urine of cows.
That [oil] containing both water and milk is the supreme remedy for deafness;
thus is the Bilva oil used for ear discharge, putrid ears, and likewise for worms in the ear.
One should perform the general rites as well as the specific yogic practices.
By adding the juice of *bījapūra* mixed with the powder of *svarjikā*, ear-discharge, pain, and burning sensations will undoubtedly be destroyed. 40–41.
Oil prepared with the tender sprouts of the mango, the rose-apple, the licorice, and the banyan tree removes the disease of putrid ear (pūtikarṇa).
Oil cooked with the juice of *jātī* leaves likewise conquers putrid ear.

Pounded *rasāñjana* mixed with honey and a woman’s milk is recommended for chronic, discharging *pūtikarṇaka*. [One should also use] *kuṣṭha*, *hiṅgu*, *vacā*, *dāru*, *śatāhvā*, *viśva*, and *saindhava*.
Oil prepared with goat's urine removes putrid ear-disease (pūtikarṇa).
One should cook mustard oil with the flesh of a snail;
by the mere filling of it [into the ear], ear-canal disease (karṇanāḍī) is pacified. 44–45.

One should cook eight *pala* of mustard oil with one *muṣṭi* (a handful) of the powder made from sulfur, realgar, and turmeric, along with an equal amount of the juice of *dhattūra* leaves; this, when applied, conquers even long-standing sinus infections (*nāḍī*) occurring in the ear.
To destroy worms in the ear, one should perform an anthelmintic treatment (*kṛmighnī kriyā*).

The smoke of eggplant and mustard oil are also beneficial; filling [the ear] with yellow orpiment mixed with cow’s urine is likewise advised. For foul odor in the ear, guggulu is said to be the best remedy for fumigation.

The physician should treat ear swellings as well as ear polyps (karṇārśas) and ear tumors (karṇārbuda) according to the procedures prescribed for swellings, polyps, and tumors. In cases of atrophy of the earlobe (pālīsaṃśoṣaṇa), one should employ the treatments for Vata-type ear pain.
One should diligently apply fomentation to her, and once she has been sweated, one should cause her to grow with sesame seeds (verse 50).
Oil cooked with śatāvarī, vājigandhā, milk, and eraṇḍa seeds, along with additional milk, when applied, will easily cause the growth of the breasts (verse 51).
One should cook oil with the paste of *jīvanīya* and milk;
one should treat *paripoṭaka*, after blood has been removed, with that oil.
One should treat *utpāta* with cold applications and leeches.
Oil cooked with *halinī* and *surasā*, combined with the fat of a monitor lizard (*godhā*) and a heron (*kaṅka*), when applied as an ointment, will certainly destroy *unmantha*.
Having sprinkled it with a decoction made from the leaves of *jambu*, mango, and *bilva*, it will increase the pain [of the disease]. (53–54)

One should thoroughly lubricate it with decoctions and oil, and dust it repeatedly with those powders; having fomented it with heated cow-dung cakes and rubbed it smooth, one should smear it with camphor pastes ground into a paste with goat's urine. 55
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter on diseases of the ear.
Now begins the sixty-fifth chapter on diseases of the nose:
first, rhinitis (pīnasa) is described, and after that, putrid rhinitis (pūtinasya).
Nasal suppuration (nāsāpāka) is also counted here, as well as purulent blood (pūyaśoṇita).
Sneezing (kṣavathu), discharge (bhraṃśathu), inflammation (dīpti), nasal obstruction (pratīnāha), and discharge from the nose (parisrava);
nasal dryness (nāsāśoṣa), the five types of catarrh (pratiśyāya), and seven types of tumors (arbuda).
There are four types of hemorrhoids, four types of swellings, and four types of blood-bile disorders; these thirty-four diseases are recorded as affecting the nose.
One whose nose becomes constricted, withers, becomes excessively moist, or emits a foul odor [is afflicted].
The creature who does not perceive smells and tastes, and who is afflicted here by *pīnasa*,
one should declare that disorder to be born of wind and phlegm, possessing symptoms identical to those of catarrh (*pratiśyāya*).
When the wind is corrupted at the root of the throat and palate by the aggravated humors (*doṣa*), [it causes this condition].
When putrid matter flows out from both the mouth and the nostrils, they call that disease *pūtinasya*.
When pitta localized in the nose produces painless ulcers in a disorder where suppuration is powerful,
one should diagnose it as *nāsikāpāka* (nasal suppuration), or likewise when there is discharge and sloughing.

When the vital points (marmans) of the nose are afflicted by various aggravated humors (doṣas), the nose of the person discharges pus mixed with blood; this disease they call Pūyarakta. When the wind (vāyu), being severely vitiated, resides in the vital point located in the nose, it exits through the nostrils.

Experts in disease call that condition *kṣavathu* (sneezing), which follows from an excess of *kapha* and is characterized by frequent and loud sounds. Alternatively, due to the consumption of sharp substances, smelling pungent things excessively, or gazing at the sun,
or when the fresh bones and vital points (*marman*) are rubbed by urine and the like, another type of *kṣavathu* is expelled.
When thick, burnt, and salty phlegm, previously accumulated in the head, falls from the nose due to being heated by pitta, they call that disease *bhraṃśathu*.
When the nose is intensely inflamed with burning, the wind (air) issues forth as if it were smoke.

When the nose of a person feels as if it were on fire, they declare that disease to be *dīpti* (burning). When phlegm along with wind obstructs the passage of exhalation, one should declare that condition *pratīnāha* (nasal obstruction). When a thick, yellow, white, or thin discharge flows from the nose due to the humors (*doṣa*), one should declare that condition *srāva* (nasal discharge).

When the phlegm residing in the nose is intensely dried up by vāyu and pitta, a person breathes with great difficulty both upward and downward; this condition is called *nāsāpariśoṣa* (nasal dryness). [15] Due to suppression [of natural urges], indigestion, excessive speaking, anger, seasonal irregularities, and heat in the head—

When the head suffers from the defect of congestion due to staying awake, excessive sleep, cold water, frost, or the sprinkling of sexual emissions and tears, the aggravated *vāyu* gives rise to catarrh (*pratiśyāya*).
Likewise, when *vāyu* and the other [humors] have accumulated individually or collectively in the head, as does the blood, they produce the same condition.
When provoked by various aggravating factors, they indeed give rise to catarrh (pratiśyāya).
The onset of sneezing, a sense of fullness in the head, stiffness, body ache, horripilation,
and other diverse complications are known to precede catarrh in human beings.
The nostrils are obstructed and covered, with a thin discharge trickling out;
there is dryness of the throat, palate, and lips, as well as piercing pain in the temples, excessive sneezing, and a bad taste in the mouth.
In the case of a vāta-type pratiśyāya, there may be impairment of the voice.
In the pitta-type, a warm, yellowish discharge flows from the nose;
the patient becomes emaciated, excessively pale, feverish, and oppressed by heat.
From the nose, in a case caused by phlegm, white, cold, and copious phlegm flows;
the person has a whitish complexion, swollen eyes, and feels heaviness in the head, being greatly afflicted by itching in the throat, palate, lips, and head. (21–22)
That catarrh which, having occurred repeatedly, suddenly subsides—
whether it has reached maturity or not— is known as *sarvabhava*.
The nose becomes moist again and again, and then dries up once more.
Furthermore, it may contract again or likewise dilate again;
or the breath may be foul-smelling and the person does not perceive odors. One should recognize such a corrupted catarrh as being difficult to cure.
In the case of a hemorrhagic coryza (*raktaja-pratiśyāya*), however, bleeding occurs, and it is accompanied by the symptoms produced by pitta-type coryza;
furthermore, the person’s eyes become copper-colored and he suffers from oppression in the chest. (26)
His breath becomes foul-smelling and he no longer perceives odors;
all types of catarrhs in a person who fails to seek treatment eventually become malignant and then incurable. (27–28)
Furthermore, white, glossy, and minute worms emerge there;
therefore, its symptoms are identical to those caused by worm-induced diseases of the head, including deafness, blindness, loss of smell, and terrible eye diseases. (29)
Advanced cases of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa) cause emaciation, weak digestion, and cough.

Tumors (arbuda) are of seven types, swellings (śotha) are of four types, and hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta) are of four types; those who know the tradition understand that these same categories apply to the nose as well.
Heaviness of the head, loss of appetite, nasal discharge, a thin and feeble voice,
and frequent spitting— these are the symptoms of *āmapīnasa* (undigested mucus-nasal disease).
Thick phlegm, accompanied by the signs of undigested matter (*āma*), sinks into the channels.
Purity of voice and complexion are the signs of a mature case of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa).
In all types of chronic rhinitis at all times, as soon as they arise, a person should eat black pepper with jaggery and curd; thus he attains comfort. 33–34.
One should administer the powder or the decoction of kaṭphala, pauṣkara, śṛṅgī, vyoṣa, yāsa, and kāravī, along with the juices of fresh ginger, in cases of coryza,
hoarseness of voice, asthma, and chlorosis. (35)
This is recommended for the combination of humors (sannipāta), as well as for phlegm disorders, cough, fever, and dyspnea.
An avapīḍa (nasal drop) prepared with kaliṅga, hiṅgu, marica, lākṣā, surasa, kaṭphala, kuṣṭha, ugrā, śigru, and jantughna is highly praised.

This powder, beginning with *vyoṣa* (the three pungents), consisting of equal parts of *citraka*, *tālīsa*, *tintiḍīka*, *amlavetasa*, *cavya*, and *ajājī*, with one-quarter part each of *elā*, *tvak*, and *patra*,
should be mixed with old jaggery. (38)
It destroys chronic rhinitis, dyspnea, and cough, and is supreme for providing relish and improving the voice.
(39) Oil prepared with *vyāghrī*, *dantī*, *vacā*, *śigru*, *surasa*, *vyoṣa*, and rock salt, when instilled into the nose, removes the affliction of putrid rhinitis. (40)
Oil prepared with the seeds of *śigru*, *siṃhī*, and *nikumbha*, along with *vyoṣa* and rock salt (*saindhava*), and the juice of *bilva* leaves, cures foul-smelling nasal discharges (*pūtinasya*).
[One should also use] beeswax mixed with ghee and *guggulu*, applied with care.
One should prescribe smoke therapy as a remedy for diseases of sneezing and for the condition of *bhraṃśathu*.
Oil or clarified butter cooked with the paste and decoction of ginger, kuṣṭha, pippalī, bilva, and drākṣā, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), destroys *kṣavathu*. 42–43.
Nasal medication (nasya) made from the juice of *nimba* and *añjana* is beneficial; when there is inflammation, mild fomentation of the head is advised.

After the nasal medication has been administered, one should inhale vapors of milk and water, and eat with mung bean soup. In cases of nasal discharge (*nāsāsrāva*), the powder mentioned for the nostrils should be administered through a tube, as well as those *avapīḍa* applications which are wholesome.
Strong fumigations made from *devadāru* and *agnika*, as well as goat meat, are prescribed here as wholesome;
in all types of catarrh (*pratiśyāya*), staying in a room free from drafts and wrapping the head with a heavy cloth is beneficial. 45–46.
Viḍaṅga, rock salt (saindhava), asafoetida (hiṅgu), guggulu, realgar (manaḥśilā),
and vacā— this powder, when inhaled, destroys coryza (pratiśyāya).
A person should drink the smoke of parched grain flour (śaktu-dhūma) combined with clarified butter and oil.
This medicated smoke, when smoked, is excellent for removing coryza, cough, and hiccups. In cases of coryza, one should inhale smoke prepared with all types of aromatic substances,
or snuff powdered *cāturjātaka*, or black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*).

Jayā leaves cooked in a closed vessel (puṭapāka), combined with oil and rock salt, when habitually used, are the supreme medicine for all types of catarrh (pratiśyāya). Pippalī, śigru seeds, viḍaṅga, and black pepper [are likewise beneficial].
This expressed juice (avapīḍa) is praised for the prevention of catarrh (pratiśyāya).
One should treat those [conditions] respectively with head-anointing, sudation, nasal drops, lukewarm foods, emetics, and the drinking of ghee. 51–52.
The wise physician should apply those anti-worm formulations that have been described in sequence against worms, as well as anti-worm nasal drops and medicinal drugs.
[He should also treat] hemorrhages, swellings, and likewise tumors of the mouth.
These [diseases] occur in the nose; one should apply the respective treatment for each.
Oil prepared with house-soot, long pepper, wood-ash, *naktamāla*, rock salt, and *śigru* seeds is beneficial for diseases of the nose and ears. (54–55)
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter on diseases of the nose.
Now begins the sixty-sixth chapter on diseases of the mouth:
the lips, the roots of the teeth, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate.
The throat, mouth, and so forth constitute the entire sevenfold division, which is called the "mouth.
There are eight [channels] at the lips, ten at the roots of the teeth, six likewise in the teeth,
eight in the tongue, and nine in the palate.
Eighteen types are said to occur in the throat, and three are recorded as occurring in all [the aforementioned sites].
Thus, all diseases of the mouth are considered by the wise to be sixty-seven in number.
[They arise] from the consumption of marshy meat, alkaline substances, curd, black gram, and the like.
The humors, when aggravated and dominated by phlegm, produce diseases of the lips within the mouth.
Thus, there are eight diseases of the lips: those caused by each of the humors individually, by all three combined, by blood, by flesh, by fat, and that arising from injury.

Due to the provocation of the wind (māruta), the lips become rough, harsh, and stiff, afflicted by the pain of wind; they are cracked and split apart. Furthermore, they are covered all over with painful pustules.
From *pitta*, [the swelling] is characterized by burning, suppuration, and pustules, and has a yellowish appearance (7).
From *kapha*, it is covered with pustules of the same color as the skin, is painless, itchy, white, slimy, cold, and heavy (8).
Those [two] which are once black, once yellow, and likewise once white,
should be known as arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) and are accompanied by numerous pustules;
they are further afflicted by pustules having the color of the date fruit (kharjūra).
When afflicted by blood, the eyes flow with blood and have a reddish luster;
when corrupted by flesh, they are heavy, swollen, and protrude like a mass of flesh, and living beings swarm there from both sides of the man's face.
Resembling the surface of clarified butter, itching and soft due to fatty tissue,
they discharge a copious secretion resembling clear crystal;
appearing like blood, they crack and are aggravated by trauma.
The two lips are said to be "churned" (mathita) when they are accompanied by itching.
Diseases characterized predominantly by phlegm and blood occur in the gums, the roots of the teeth, and the lips;
therefore, one should repeatedly apply warm bloodletting to these areas.
In cases of Vata-type [diseases], the wise physician should administer anointment with the four types of fats combined with beeswax, as well as tube-sudation (nāḍī-sveda). Furthermore,
one should perform venesection, emesis, purgation, the drinking of bitter decoctions, and a diet consisting of meat broth.
One should apply cold plasters and cold affusions to the lower parts when they are afflicted by pitta (16). When blood has been extracted, head-purgation, medicinal smoking, sudation,
and gargling should be employed in cases of lip disease caused by kapha.

When the disease born of fat (medas) has been purified and fomented, a gargle is beneficial; likewise, *priyaṅgu*, *triphalā*, and *āragvadha*, mixed with honey, are used as a rubbing powder (*pratisāraṇa*) for the teeth, tongue, and mouth. Furthermore, powders, pastes, and electuaries [prepared from these] are likewise applied. (18)
Gently rubbing with a finger is called *pratisāraṇa*.
Having observed the specific *doṣa* involved, one should treat all diseases of the lips accordingly;
once they have developed into ulcers, one should treat them like ulcers.
Śītāda was mentioned previously, as were dantapuppuṭaka, dantaveṣṭa, sauṣira, and mahāsauṣira; after that, paridara was declared, and upakuśa is remembered [next]. 21.21–22ab.
Then Vaidarbha is mentioned, as well as Khallīvardhana;
likewise Adhimāṃsaka, Dantanāḍī, and five types of Dantavidradhi—these sixteen [diseases] occur in the gums (dantaveṣṭa). 22–23.

When blood suddenly flows from the gums, and the gingival tissues become foul-smelling, blackish, moist, and soft, and the teeth begin to decay and the tissues eat away at one another; 24. [This is the condition known as Danta-pupputaka.]
That disease arising from phlegm and blood is called Śītāda (cold-sore).
In this condition, a great swelling develops on two or even three teeth; that disease born of phlegm and blood is named Dantapuppuṭaka (gum-boil). 25–26.
When pus and blood flow and the teeth become loose, with the gums becoming spongy, that condition is to be known as arising from vitiated blood (duṣṭa-śoṇita-sambhava).
A swelling at the roots of the teeth accompanied by pain, born of kapha and vāta, [is called danta-puppuṭaka].
Saliva flows and there is itching; that disease should be known as *sauṣira*.
The teeth waver from their sockets, the palate is torn apart, the gums suppurate, and the mouth becomes inflamed.
That disease in which that "all-born" (sarvaja) disorder known as mahāsauṣira occurs,
wherein the gums wither away and one spits out blood—
that disease born of pitta, blood, and kapha is to be known as paridara. 29–30.

In the *veṣṭa* type, there is burning and suppuration; due to these two, the teeth become loose and, when struck, they bleed with mild pain. When the blood does not flow out, the gums swell and the mouth becomes foul-smelling.

That condition in which there is an eruption arising from pitta and blood at the roots of the teeth is Upakuśa (32). That in which great swelling occurs when the roots of the teeth are rubbed and the teeth become loose is Vaidarbha, caused by injury (33).
When the wisdom tooth (mārutan) erupts, it becomes aggravated by wind and gives rise to intense pain;
this condition is known as khallīvardhana, and once it has emerged, the pain subsides.
When the lower back wisdom tooth erupts, there is great swelling and great pain.
That which causes salivation and is produced by *kapha* should be known as *adhimāṃsaka*.
(35) Five types of sinus tracts (*nāḍī*) located at the roots of the teeth are to be understood as previously described.
(36) Due to the impurities of the gums and blood, a great swelling occurs both externally and internally.
If it bursts open, pus and blood constantly flow from it; this is *danta-vidradhi* (tooth abscess).
In *śītāda*, once the blood has been removed, one should prepare a decoction of *nāgara*, mustard seeds, and *triphalā* in water, and perform gargling with it.
The powder of kāsīsa, lodhra, kṛṣṇā, manaḥśilā, priyaṅgu, and tejohvā,
mixed with honey, removes putrid flesh in cases of śītāda (gangrene).
Oil or ghee that alleviates vāta is highly recommended for śītāda.
In the case of *dantapuppuṭaka* (swelling of the gums), bloodletting should be performed while the condition is still acute;
then, a rubbing (*pratisāraṇa*) with the five salts, alkali, and honey is beneficial, as is head-purgation (*śirovireka*), unctuous nasal therapy (*nasya*), and a fatty diet. 40–41.
Once the gums have been drained,
one should rub the wound with a powder of *lodhra*, *pattaṅga*, *madhuka*, and *lākṣā*, saturated with honey.
For gargles, milky trees should be used along with honey, ghee, and sugar.
One should perform the chewing of *bakula* flowers to stabilize loose teeth.
(43) One should prepare pills from *bhadramusta*, *abhayā*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *viḍaṅga*, and the sprouts of *ariṣṭa*, ground with cow’s urine and dried in the shade. (44)
A man suffering from loose teeth should place that [mixture] in his mouth and sleep;
there is no remedy for loose teeth superior to this.
One should properly boil blue *sahācara* and *tulā-vṛta* with a *droṇa* of water.
Then, one should slowly cook oil with a decoction measuring four parts, along with paste (kalka) of Anantā, Khadira, Eranda, Jambu, Āmra, Yaṣṭīmadhuka, and Utpala, each weighing half a pala.
This oil, when combined with clarified butter (ghṛta), immediately bestows stability upon the teeth when applied to the mouth.

In a case of *sauṣira* where the blood has been removed, an application of *lodhra*, *mustā*, and *rasāñjana* mixed with honey is recommended; for gargling, the milky trees (*kṣīrin*) are beneficial. A wise physician should employ the treatment prescribed for *śītāda* in the case of *paridara*.
In cases of *upakuśa*, one should likewise cleanse both [the tongue and the palate] and the head;
the physician should drain the ulcer with the leaves of *kāṣṭhodumbarikā* and rub it with salts mixed with honey and *vyoṣa*. 49–50.
Having extracted [the supernumerary tooth] according to the treatise, one should cleanse the roots of the teeth in the Vaidarbha manner; thereafter, one should apply milk and all cooling treatments.
Having extracted the supernumerary tooth, one should then apply fire [cauterization].
In this case, the wise physician should follow the procedure as in the treatment for *kṛmidanta* (worm-infested teeth).
Having excised the excess flesh, one should treat it with these powders mixed with honey:
*vacā*, *tejovatī*, *pāṭhā*, *svarjikā*, and *yāvaśūka*. (52–53)
In this case, long peppers (pippalī) with honey are prescribed for gargling,
and a decoction of paṭola, nimba, and triphalā is recommended for rinsing the mouth.
One should perform the treatment for sinus ulcers on the teeth as prescribed for sinus ulcers in general.
If a tooth-nerve (nāḍī) should arise within a tooth, one should extract that tooth after cutting away the flesh with a surgical instrument, provided it is not an upper tooth; having extracted it,
one should also cauterize it with either alkali or fire.
If it is neglected, the tooth will certainly break and penetrate into the jawbone;
therefore, one should extract the broken tooth along with its root.
However, when an upper tooth is extracted, blood flows excessively.

Indeed, from the blood-ablution (rakta-abhiṣeka) previously mentioned, terrible diseases arise; the person becomes one-eyed, and a throbbing pain arises in his upper tooth. Therefore, the physician must not extract it.
Rinsing [the mouth] should be done with decoctions (kaṣāya) made from *jāti*, *madana*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, and *khadira* (59), or with *jāti*, *madana*, *kaṇṭakī*, and *svādukaṇṭaka* (60),
or likewise with those prepared from *mañjiṣṭhā*, *lodhra*, *khadira*, and *yaṣṭyāhva*.
The oil that has been prepared should destroy the disease located in the teeth (dantagatā gati). One should apply the procedure prescribed for abscesses (vidradhi) in the case of a dental abscess;
however, a skilled person should not perform surgical intervention there.
Dālana was mentioned previously, as was Kṛmidantaka;
Bhañjanaka, Dantaharṣa, and Dantaśarkarā have been described here, as well as Kapālikā and Śyāvadantaka. (63)
Karāla is the name of the eighth; thus eight diseases of the teeth have been proclaimed.
That disease in which pain arises in the teeth as if they were being split apart is called Dālana, caused by the movement of Sadāgati (Vāyu). 64–65.

That which has black cavities, is unstable, exudes discharge, is accompanied by inflammation and great pain, and suffers pain without apparent cause, should be known as *kṛmidantaka* (worm-infested tooth). Where the mouth becomes crooked and the breaking off of teeth occurs, [that is *dālana*].

The disease caused by kapha and vāta is known as bhañjanaka (67). O twice-born ones, when the teeth cannot endure cold, dry, strong winds, or sour sensations, that condition arising from vāta and pitta is proclaimed as dantaharṣa (trembling of the teeth) (68).

The impurity that has settled on the teeth, which is phlegm dried by wind and is rough to the touch like sugar, is to be known as *danta-śarkarā* (tooth-tartar). When the teeth, being covered with this impurity, crack as if they were earthen shards, [it is called *kapālikā*]. 69.69–70.1a.
That which is characterized by cavities between the teeth is known as *kapālikā*, while *dantaśarkarā* consists of tartar on the teeth.
When a tooth is completely scorched by bile mixed with blood, and has become either dark brown or blue, it is called *śyāvadantaka*.
Where the wind residing in the teeth gradually produces teeth that are jagged and misshapen, that condition is called Karāla; it does not succeed [in treatment]. 72.
Now follows the medical treatment for diseases of the teeth.
One should cook one *prastha* each of oil, lac-juice, and alkali,
along with these drugs measured at one *pala* each, and four times as much of their decoctions:
*lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, saffron from the lotus, and *padmaka*.
That oil, when held in the mouth with sandalwood, blue lotus, and licorice (yaṣṭyāhva), cures toothache,
loosening of the teeth, falling out of teeth, tartar (kapālikā), sitala fever, putrid breath, loss of appetite, and a bad taste in the mouth. (74–75)

This oil, beginning with lac (*lākṣā*), quickly destroys these diseases and makes the teeth firm; it is highly esteemed for dental ailments. One should conquer the fixed carious tooth (*kṛmidantaka*) by means of sweating and bloodletting.
Likewise, *avapīḍa* [expressions] destroy wind disorders through the holding of oil-filled gargles (77).
By means of ointments of *bhadradāru* and other drugs along with *varṣābhū*, by unctuous foods, and by mild *hiṅgu* placed between the teeth, caries is destroyed. (78)
A gargle consisting of a decoction of *bṛhatī*, *bhūmika-dambā*, *pañcāṅgula*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*,
mixed with oil, alleviates the pain of worms in the teeth. (79) [Likewise,] each of the following— *nīlī*, *vāyasajaṅghā*, and the root of *kaṭutumbī*— [is similarly effective].
Having ground it while held between the teeth, they say it destroys dental caries (80).
Lukewarm gargles of oils, of ghee, and of the three-fold mixture (traivṛta),
as well as decoctions of wind-subduing herbs, destroy the throbbing of the teeth (81).

In this condition, unctuous smoke and unctuous nasal drops (nasya) are beneficial; likewise, thin gruels (peyā), meat soups, barley gruels (yavāgū), the cream of milk (kṣīrasantānikā), and ghee are recommended.
A head-poultice (śirovasti) is also beneficial, as is any therapeutic regimen that subdues vāta.
The physician should extract the calculus after removing the roots of the teeth,
and then he should rub the area with powdered lac mixed with honey;
furthermore, one should perform the treatments for *dantaharṣa* (tooth sensitivity) here without exception.
A toothache is most difficult to endure; even in that case, this regimen is prescribed:
one suffering from dental disease should not eat sour fruits, cold water, dry food, tooth-cleansing sticks, or anything that is excessively hard. 84–85.
Five diseases of the tongue are proclaimed: those born of Vāta, those born of Pitta, those born of Kapha, the one known as Alāsa, and Upajihvikā.
When afflicted by Vāta, the tongue becomes cracked, numb, and resembles the leaf of a Śāka plant.
From pitta, it is characterized by constant burning and is covered with long, blood-stained thorns (88).
From kapha, it is heavy, thick, and covered with elevations of flesh resembling the thorns of the silk-cotton tree (śālmalika) (89).
A deep swelling on the underside of the tongue, consisting of kapha and blood, is known as alāsa.

When it has increased, it paralyzes the tongue, and the base of the tongue undergoes severe inflammation (90). A swelling in the shape of the tip of the tongue that arises on the underside of the tongue, originating from phlegm and blood,
and accompanied by salivation, itching, and a burning sensation, is called *upajihvikā* (91).
For disorders located in the tongue, bloodletting is recommended;
a gargle (kavala) consisting of guḍūcī, pippalī, and nimba, along with pungent substances, is beneficial.
As for the treatment prescribed previously for lip disorders caused by vāta: [it should be applied here as well].
Indeed, when thorns have arisen from wind (vāta), that [treatment] should be performed by the physician.

However, in the case of a [wound] born of bile (pitta) that has been rubbed and from which vitiated blood has flowed out, sweet applications for rubbing, gargling, and nasal drops are beneficial. 92–93.
When the thorns arising from phlegm have been scraped away and the blood has subsided, a paste of the *pippalyādi* group mixed with honey should be applied as a rubbing agent (*pratisāraṇa*).
Having scraped the *upajihvā*, one should rub it with an alkaline solution (*kṣāra*).

One should treat this condition with head-purgatives (śirovireka), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), and medicated smokes (dhūma). This powder consisting of trikaṭu, alkali, harītakī, and citraka should be used for rubbing (pragharṣaṇa) to pacify upajihvā; one should also cook oil with these same ingredients.
Galaśuṇṭhī, Tuṇḍikerī, Abhrūṣa, Kacchapa,
Tālvarbuda, Māṃsasaṅghāta, Tālu-puppuṭa, and likewise Tālu-śoṣa are described. 97.

Tālu-pāka (inflammation of the palate) is also mentioned; thus, these nine diseases of the palate [are described]. A long swelling arising from the root of the palate due to phlegm and blood, resembling an inflated bladder and causing thirst, cough, and dyspnea, physicians call this disease by the name Kaṇṭha-śuṇḍī. 98–99.

A swelling that is thick, characterized by pricking pain, burning, and suppuration, arising from phlegm (kapha) and blood, is called Tuṇḍikerī (100). A stiff, red swelling arising from blood, accompanied by fever and intense pain, should be known as Abhrūṣa (101). A disease arising from phlegm that is elevated like a tortoise shell, painless, and slow to develop, should be known as Kacchapa (102).

One should know that a swelling in the center of the palate, shaped like a lotus and characterized by redness, is an *arbuda* arising from pitta (103). A painless mass of corrupted flesh and phlegm located within the palate is called *māṃsasaṃghāta* (104).
A painless, stationary growth the size of a jujube fruit (*kola*) at the site of the palate, resulting from phlegm combined with fat, is *puppuṭa* (105).

Excessive dryness or even cracking of the palate occurs, along with severe labored breathing; this dryness of the palate caused by Vāta is described as *tāluśoṣa* (palatal dryness). Pitta produces an extremely terrible suppuration in the palate itself; this they call *tālpāka* (suppuration of the palate).
[One should treat it] with Kuṣṭha, Uṣaṇa, Vacā, Saindhava, Kaṇā, Pāṭhā, and Plava.
The physician should perform a rubbing treatment for *galashuṇḍī* with honey.
Having pulled out the *galashuṇḍikā* using the thumb and fingers as a pincer, he should cut it with a round-tipped blade (*maṇḍalāgra*) if it is situated on the upper surface of the tongue. (108–109)
From excessive cutting, blood flows profusely and the man consequently dies;
from insufficient cutting, swelling occurs, as well as salivation, discharge, and vertigo.
Therefore, a physician who is skilled and experienced in practice should proceed with great care.
Having cut away the uvula, one should follow this prescribed procedure:
then, one should rub it with a mixture of long pepper, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, vacā, black pepper, and ginger, combined with honey and salt.
Having decocted vacā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, rāsnā, kaṭurohiṇī, and picumarda, one should employ this as a gargle for cases of tuṇḍikerī, abhuṣa,
kūrma, saṅghāta, and tālupuppuṭa.
This same procedure should be performed, with the specific distinction being surgical intervention (110).
In the case of inflammation of the palate (tālupāka), a treatment that destroys pitta should be applied;
in the case of dryness of the palate (tāluśoṣa), oleation and sudation should be used, along with a regimen that subdues vāta (111).
Rohiṇī is said to be fivefold: kaṇṭhaśālūka, adhijihva, valaya, balāsa, and ekavṛndaka;
then vṛnda, śataghnī, gilāyu, and kaṇṭhavidradhi. (112)
Galaugha, svaraghna, and likewise māṃsatāna,
as well as vidārī in the region of the throat— these eighteen diseases are recorded.
In the throat, vāta, pitta, and kapha, having become aggravated and combined, vitiate the flesh and likewise the blood.

This disease Rohiṇī destroys life by means of sprouts that obstruct the gullet; there are fleshy sprouts with intense pain all around the tongue that cause obstruction of the throat. That Rohiṇī is declared to be caused by Vāta, being afflicted by severe complications of a Vāta-nature. 115–116.

That which arises from Pitta is characterized by rapid onset, rapid burning, and rapid suppuration, and is accompanied by intense fever (117). That which originates from Kapha obstructs the channels, is slow to suppurate, heavy, and stable (118). That which arises from all three Doshas possesses deep-seated suppuration, irresistible potency, and exhibits the symptoms of all three Doshas (119).
That which is covered with eruptions (sphoṭa) and has symptoms identical to those of pitta is declared curable; however, that which is of the nature of blood is incurable.
That born from all three doṣas kills in three days, that arising from kapha in five days, that produced by pitta in seven days, and that originated from vāta in ten days. 120–121.

A swelling arising from phlegm (kapha) that occurs on the neck, shaped like the kernel of a jujube fruit, having the appearance of a thorn or a spikelet, and being rough and firm, is called *kaṇṭhaśālūka*; it is curable by the application of a surgical instrument.
A swelling resembling the tip of the tongue, occurring above the tongue due to phlegm mixed with blood, [is known as adhijihva].
One should know that *adhijihva* is indeed a disease; one should avoid it once suppuration has set in (123).
*Balāsa* causes a swelling that has arrived and become elevated, obstructing the passage of food;
since it is entirely impossible to ward off, they call it *valaya*, which must be avoided by all means (124).
When Kapha and Vata are aggravated, they produce swelling in the throat accompanied by the affliction of dyspnea;
physicians call this difficult-to-cure disease that pierces the vital organs (marma) by the name Balāsa.
A circular, elevated swelling at the base, accompanied by burning, itching, non-suppurating, soft, and heavy, [is known as Galaśuṇḍikā].
This disease, produced by both *balāsa* (phlegm) and *kṣataja* (blood), is proclaimed by the name *vṛnda*.

They describe *vṛnda* as being elevated, circular, characterized by intense burning, and accompanied by severe fever; one should know that it arises from the provocation of *pitta* and *kṣataja*, while that which is of the nature of *vāta* is accompanied by piercing pain (*todana*). 126–127.
A thick, wick-like growth that obstructs the throat, covered excessively with fleshy excrescences,
causing manifold pains and life-threatening, and resembling a *śataghnī* weapon due to its origin from the three *doṣas*, is known as *śataghnī*.
A hard, slightly painful knot in the throat, the size of an *āmalaka* stone, formed from phlegm and blood, is [known as] *granthi*.
That which appears as if stuck and consumed is known as *gilāyu*, and it is to be treated with surgical instruments (129).

That swelling which arises having pervaded the entire throat and wherein all types of pain are present is *galavidradhi*; it is indeed identical to the *sarvaja* [type of abscess] caused by all three doṣas (130).
When there is a great swelling obstructing the throat, accompanied by high fever and the cessation of the movement of breath,
born from phlegm combined with blood in the throat— that is proclaimed as Galaugha (throat-obstruction).
He who, being exhausted, breathes incessantly, with a broken voice and a parched, loosened throat— [is afflicted by this].

When the channels of the vital air (anila) are corrupted by phlegm (kapha), that disease should be known as svaraghna (voice-destroyer), characterized by labored breathing. That which is a spreading swelling (śvayathu) that is extremely difficult to treat and gradually causes obstruction of the throat is called māṃsatāna; it is a life-threatening disorder caused by all [three humors] and is characterized by hanging down. 132–133.

One should recognize Vidārī as a swelling in the inner throat caused by Pitta, accompanied by constant burning and piercing pain, copper-colored, with putrid and sloughing flesh; it is especially located on the side upon which the patient lies. For the curable types of Rohiṇī, bloodletting is beneficial.
Emesis, inhalation of medicated smoke, gargling,
and nasal therapy should be employed; once the blood has been removed from a disorder born of Vata, one should rub the area with salts and repeatedly hold lukewarm oil-gargles.
Having drained out [the discharge] from a condition arising from pitta, one should rub [the area] with sugar, honey, and priyaṅgu;
a gargle prepared with decoctions of drākṣā and paruṣaka is beneficial.
One should rub away [the discharge] from a kapha-born [condition] using soot (āgāradhūma) and pungent substances. 135
Oil prepared with white *viḍaṅga*, *dantī*,
and rock salt (*saindhava*) should be administered as nasal drops (*nasya*) and as a gargle (*kavala*) in cases of an excess of *kapha*.
The physician should treat *rohiṇī* arising from blood in the same manner as that arising from *pitta*.
After draining the *kaṇṭhaśālūka*, one should treat it like a *tuṇḍikerī*;
one should eat a small amount of unctuous barley-food once a day. One should also treat *adhijihvaka* in the same manner as *upajihvaka*. 137–138.
Having drained a single cluster [of pus], one should perform the purificatory procedure;
generally, one should treat a cluster as if it were a single cluster.
Furthermore, that disease known as *gilāyu* should be treated with a surgical instrument.
One should excise a galavidradhi (throat abscess) when it is located away from vital spots and has fully ripened.
In diseases of the throat, a skilled physician should perform treatment here through bloodletting and sharp procedures such as nasal administration (nasya). 140–141.
One should administer a decoction made from the bark of *dārvī*, *nimba*, *tārkṣya*, and *kaliṅga*;
or a decoction of *harītakī* mixed with honey is beneficial. [The following drugs are also used:
*kaṭukā*, *ativiṣā*, *dāru*, *pāṭhā*, *musta*, and *kaliṅga*.
Cow’s urine boiled and drunk destroys diseases of the throat.
(143) Mṛdvīkā, kaṭukā, vyoṣa, dārvītvak, triphalā, ghana, pāṭhā, rasāñjana, dūrvā, and tejohvā—these well-ground into a fine powder [are used for the same purpose]. (144)
This great medicine, combined with honey, should be administered for diseases of the throat;
these three formulations are said to remove disorders of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha.
[One should take] Yavāgraja, Tejovatī, Pāṭhā, Rasāñjana, Darunishā, and Kṛṣṇā.
One should prepare a pill with honey and hold it in the mouth for all diseases of the throat (146).

Three types of diseases arising in the mouth are recognized according to the individual *doṣas*, while those arising from all [the *doṣas*] combined are known as *sarvamukha-ja* (147). That condition in which the face is covered on all sides with pricking pustules is *sarvasara* caused by *vāta* (148).
That which is covered with red, burning, and yellowish pustules due to the provocation of pitta;
that which is covered with painless, itchy, and bleeding [pustules] due to kapha;
and those arising from flesh, blood, or all three doṣas are to be rejected when the lips are afflicted.

In the gums, however, those with three roots, displacement, and cavities are to be rejected (151). Furthermore, among diseases of the teeth, blackening, splitting, and breaking do not succeed in being cured. Likewise, among diseases of the tongue, *alāsa* is incurable, as is *arbuda* among those arising in the palate.
Svaraghna, valaya, vṛnda, balāsa— which is indeed dreadful— vidārikā,
galaugha, māṃsatāna, śataghnī, and rohiṇī in the throat;
these eleven diseases are declared to be incurable.
In those cases as well, the physician, having declared the prognosis hopeless, may proceed with treatment:
one should rub a sarvasara ulcer caused by vāta with powders of salts;
oil prepared with vāta-alleviating drugs is beneficial for gargling and nasal administration.

In the case of a person whose entire body is affected by a pitta-type sarvasara, once the body has been purified, every pitta-alleviating regimen that is sweet and cooling should be administered; furthermore, applications such as rubbing (pratisāraṇa), gargles (gaṇḍūṣa), medicated smoking (dhūma), and purification therapies (saṃśodhana) should be employed. 154.

In cases of generalized vitiation by *kapha*, one should employ a therapeutic regimen that alleviates *kapha*. In the case of stomatitis (*mukhapāka*), one should perform venesection and administer head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*).
Furthermore, gargles (*kavalagraha*) should be prepared with honey, urine, ghee, milk, and cooling substances. (155–156)
A decoction made from *jātī* leaves, *amṛtā*, *drākṣā*, *yāsa*, *dārvī*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*),
mixed with honey and used as a cold gargle, cures inflammation of the mouth (157). Furthermore,
one should constantly chew *jātī* leaves in many ways.
Within three days from chewing black cumin, costus, and indrayava, mouth ulcers, wounds, discharge, and foul odor are pacified.
[This is achieved] with the fresh sprouts of *paṭola*, *nimba*, *jambu*, mango, and *mālatī*. 158–159.
An excellent decoction made from the five sprouts (pañcapallava) is used for cleansing the mouth;
alternatively, a decoction derived from the five barks (pañcavalkala) or from triphalā should be employed for mouth-rinsing with honey when there is inflammation of the mouth (mukhapāka). (160)

The juice of *dārvī* boiled down until it becomes a thick extract (*rasakriyā*), when mixed with honey, cures diseases of the mouth, blood disorders, sinus ulcers, and fistulas. [Likewise, a preparation made from] *saptacchada*, *uśīra*, *paṭola*, *musta*, *harītakī*, and *tiktakarohiṇī* [is similarly effective]. 161.

One should drink a decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu, rājadruma, and candana to alleviate inflammation of the mouth. For one whose face has been burnt, a gargle consisting of sesame seeds, blue lotus, ghee, sugar, milk, and honey is a cure for oral inflammation.

Even tasted but once, the rind of the citron fruit removes all foul odor from the mouth; it wards off the unwholesome wind. Turmeric, neem leaves, licorice, and blue lotus [are likewise beneficial]. 164.
Oil should be cooked with these; it is supreme for removing inflammation of the mouth.
One pala of yaṣṭīmadhu, thirty palas of nīlotpala, and one prastha of oil—cooked according to the rule with twice as much milk—should be used as a nasal drop (nasya). 165–166.

Anointing (abhyaṅga) necessarily removes the discharge from the face at night, the accumulation of humors (doṣa) in the body, and the roughness of the hair for living beings as they progress [in age]. 167.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter on diseases of the mouth. 66.
Now begins the sixty-seventh chapter, on Poisons (Viṣādhikāra).
Poison is said to be of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama). The first has ten bases, while the second has sixteen substrates.
Root, leaf, fruit, flower, bark, milky sap, resin, exudate, mineral, and bulb— these are the ten substrates of stationary beings (plants).
[2] Sight, breath, fangs, nails, roots, and impurities [are the substrates of mobile beings].
Semen, saliva, blood, touch, and the bite; crushed [venom], the anus, bones, and bile—these ten and six are the sources of mobile (jaṅgama) poisons.
Now, the general effects of stationary (sthāvara) poisons:
Unwinding [of the limbs], delusion, and likewise delirium;
yawning, trembling, and labored breathing—these occur in men from leaf-poisons (patraviṣa).
Swelling of the scrotum, burning sensation, and aversion to food occur from fruit-poisons (phalaviṣa).
From poisons derived from flowers, there may arise vomiting, flatulence, and likewise fainting (7).
Indeed, when poisons derived from bark, sap, or resin are consumed, foul breath, roughness of the skin, headache, and the discharge of phlegm occur (8).
Foaming at the mouth, diarrhea caused by milk-poison, and a heavy tongue (9);
pain in the heart, fainting, and a burning sensation in the palate caused by mineral poisons—these types of poison should generally be declared fatal. (10)
The thirteen types of potent poisons originating from bulbs that have been mentioned—
all these should be understood by the skilled as possessing ten qualities.
Whether the poison be stationary, mobile, or even artificial, [it is characterized by these ten qualities].
It immediately destroys all that [dosha], being endowed with ten qualities:
dry (rūkṣa), hot (uṣṇa), sharp (tīkṣṇa), subtle (sūkṣma), fast-acting (āśu), pervasive (vyavāyi), expansive (vikāśi), clear (viśada), and light in digestion (laghupāki); these are the ten. 12–13.
Because it is dry, it aggravates the wind (vāyu); because of its heat, it provokes the bile (pitta) along with the blood;
because of its sharpness, it confuses the intellect; and indeed, because of its subtlety, it severs the vital attachments (marmabandha), enters the limbs of the body, and causes disfigurement.
Because of its swiftness, it is said to act quickly; because of its penetrating nature, it removes the *prakṛti* (the fundamental constitution).
Because of its expansive quality, it diminishes the *doṣas*, the *dhātus*, and even the *malas*. It excels due to its clarity, and it is difficult to treat because of its lightness.

Because it is difficult to digest and does not undergo proper transformation, it causes long-term affliction. (15) Furthermore, if the flesh of a living being at the site of a wound suppurates immediately, or if blood flows and continues to suppurate repeatedly,
or if it becomes blackened, moist, excessively putrid, or if the flesh sloughs away from the wound— (16)
One should determine that a man whose thirst and fever, as well as burning and fainting, have been caused by him has been struck with a poisoned arrow;
these very symptoms would also occur if a venomous substance were applied to his wound by enemies.
One who understands the gestures of men can discern their intentions through changes in speech, physical movements, and facial expressions.
A wise man should recognize the giver of poison by these signs:
when questioned, he does not give an answer; though wishing to speak, he falls into confusion; and he speaks much that is meaningless and incoherent, like a fool. (18–19)
He may snap his fingers, scratch the earth, laugh, or even tremble;
he becomes terrified and gazes about alone;
his face turns pale and sallow, and he scratches himself slightly with his nails. (20)
The distressed man repeatedly touches his hair with his hand;
wishing to depart, he looks again and again toward the side doors; and the unconscious giver of poison behaves in a contrary manner. (22)
Mobile poison (jaṅgamaviṣa) causes sleep, lethargy, exhaustion, burning sensation, indigestion, horripilation, swelling, and diarrhea.
The snakes known as Bhogin, Maṇḍalin, and Rājila consist of the nature of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha respectively.
These have been described in their proper order as having the form of pairs with an interval between them.
They are to be known as the hooded serpents (*phaṇinaḥ*) and the coiled serpents (*bhoginaḥ*); they are numbered here as twenty.
Variegated by various circles (*maṇḍalas*), they are broad and slow-moving.
Six of those are known as *maṇḍalinaḥ* and are remembered as having the nature of fire, the sun, and poison (26).
Those which appear variegated with glossy, multi-colored stripes running horizontally and vertically are indeed the *rājilas*; they too are six in number (27).
A bite by a *bhogin* (ringed cobra) is black and causes all types of wind disorders (*vāta-vikāra*);
a bite by a *maṇḍalin* (hooded cobra) is yellow, characterized by swelling and softness, and involves disorders of bile (*pitta*).
A bite by a *rājila* (king-cobra) results in a stable swelling that is slimy (*picchila*).
A bite that is pale, glossy, and characterized by very thick blood indicates a disorder of all the *kapha* humors.

(29) Men bitten under the constellation Aśvinī, at a temple of a deity, a cremation ground, an anthill, during the two twilights, at crossroads, in the southern direction, or in the region of the ancestors (*pitr-loka*), as well as those bitten in their vital organs (*marman*), should be avoided. (30)

The venom of the *darvīkara* snakes kills quickly; it becomes doubled in potency during the heat of the monsoon winds. (31) Those bearing the marks of a chariot wheel, a plow, an umbrella, a svastika, and a goad should be known as *darvīkara* snakes—hooded serpents that move swiftly. (32)
