In those afflicted by indigestion, pitta, or heat; in children, the elderly, and the hungry;
in those who are emaciated, wounded, suffering from urinary disorders, or afflicted with leprosy; in the dry, the weak, and likewise in pregnant women;
and in one who has suffered a surgical wound where no blood is present and no streaks or lines appear—[in these cases, one should avoid purgation].

One should avoid that person who, despite cold water, has no horripilation; whose face is distorted, whose hair falls out, whose nose collapses, and who suffers from a broken voice; and one should also avoid him if there is black or red swelling at the site of the bite, or if the jawbones become rigid. 34.
He from whose mouth thick vomit issues forth, he from whom blood flows both upwards and downwards,
and he who sees the four fangs [of the serpent]— he too is to be abandoned by physicians.
(35) One who is excessively deranged, afflicted, has a feeble voice, or is discolored;
One should abandon a person whose fatal signs (ariṣṭa) are extreme and whose symptoms progress with excessive velocity; in such a case, one should not perform any medical treatment.

Poison that has become old, or been neutralized by anti-poisonous herbs, or dried up by forest fires, wind, or heat, or which has naturally lost its potency, indeed attains the state of *dūṣīviṣa* (latent or chronic poison).

Due to a deficiency of vigor, one should not suppress it when it is associated with phlegm; for that [condition] persists for many years, and one afflicted by it experiences loose stools, foul odor, a bad taste in the mouth, thirst, fainting, vertigo, stammering speech, vomiting, restlessness, or even finds a lack of interest in activities. (38)
If located in the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes diseases of phlegm and wind; if located in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), it causes diseases of wind and bile.
With its head and limbs trembling, the patient becomes like a bird whose wings have been plucked.
Furthermore, when situated within the rasa and other tissues, it produces the aforementioned disorders arising from those constituent elements (dhātus). 39–40.
Now listen first to the symptoms of that [fever] which quickly subsides during cold winds and cloudy days (41):

drowsiness, heaviness, yawning, or else a sense of detachment, joy, or bodily aching (42); thereafter, it causes indigestion, lack of appetite for food, and the appearance of circular rashes and eruptions.
At the end of a month, it causes swelling of the hands and feet, fainting, vomiting, and diarrhea;

it produces chronic poisoning (dūṣīviṣa), as well as dyspnea, thirst, and fever, and brings about the enlargement of the abdomen. One [variety] generates insanity, another causes constipation, and yet another destroys the semen.

It causes stammering, leprosy, and various other types of disorders. Because it repeatedly pollutes the bodily tissues (dhātus) by vitiating the location, time, food, and daytime sleep, it is known as *dūṣīviṣa* (latent poison). 44–45.

For a self-controlled person, [dūṣīviṣa] that has arisen recently is curable, while that which has persisted for a year is palliable; however, it becomes incurable in one who is emaciated and indulges in unwholesome things.
For the sake of enhancing a woman's beauty, [one may apply] sweat, menstrual blood, and various impurities from the body.
And enemies administer *gara* poisons mixed with food.

By these, one becomes pale, emaciated, and has diminished digestive fire; furthermore, due to the *gara*, there occurs the aggravation of the vital points (*marman*), flatulence, and the onset of swelling in the hands. (47–48)
Abdominal enlargement, disorders of the digestive tract, consumption, abdominal tumors, wasting, fever,
and the symptoms of other such diseases were manifested;
for from the sage’s perspiration-drops, as soon as they reached the grass, it was cut down.
From them were born sixteen known as the *lūtās*.
Once, it is said, Viśvāmitra, the best of kings, went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent of sages, and provoked him to anger.
From the forehead of that enraged sage, drops of sweat fell down with intense radiance at the mere sight [of the king],
even though the grass had been cut and gathered for the sake of the cow. 52.
From her were born these terrible [serpents] of various forms and great venom;
among them, eight are difficult to treat and must be avoided, as are another eight.
When bitten by them, there is swelling at the site of the bite and the flow of blood.
Fever, burning sensations, diarrhea, and diseases born of the three doshas may occur; likewise, pustules of various shapes, large circular patches,
and swellings that are extensive, soft, red, dusky, and shifting may arise.
This is the general characteristic of the bite of all spiders (lūtā):
that which is black or dark-brown in the center of the bite, covered with a web-like membrane, resembling a burnt area, and accompanied by intense suppuration, discharge, swelling, and fever. (56)
One should identify that as being bitten by *lūtā* spiders possessing *dūṣīviṣa* poison.
There occurs swelling, white, pale, red, or yellow pustules, fever, and life-threatening conditions such as burning sensations, hiccups, and stiffness of the head. (57–58)
In one afflicted by the poison of a rat (ākhu-dūṣī-viṣa), there occurs pale blood at the site of the bite, circular patches, fever, loss of appetite, horripilation, and a burning sensation.
Furthermore, fainting, swelling of the limbs, discoloration, suppuration, dullness of hearing, and fever manifest. (59)
Heaviness of the head, salivation, and vomiting of blood are incurable when caused by a rat; furthermore, blackness or various colors of the swelling,
as well as delusion and diarrhea, occur in one bitten by chameleons.
The venom of a scorpion first burns like fire, then quickly pierces upward; afterwards it spreads, yet finally it remains localized at the site of the sting.
A person bitten by those [scorpions] that are incurable has their heart, nose, and tongue afflicted.
When the flesh falls away excessively, one seized by intense pain gives up their life-breaths (63).
Swelling, spreading inflammation, piercing pain, fever, or even vomiting are the symptoms when bitten by a *kaṇabha*; furthermore, the bite site itself disintegrates (64).
One bitten by the *kṛṣṇaloma-ucciṭiṅga* has a stiff penis and experiences intense pain;
he feels as if his limbs have been sprinkled with cold water. One bitten by the *ekadaṃṣṭrā* is swollen, painful, yellowish, and suffers from thirst.
One bitten by poisonous frogs becomes drowsy and suffers from vomiting.
Poisonous fish, moreover, cause burning, swelling, and pain.
Poisonous leeches, however, cause itching, swelling, fever, and fainting.
Burning sensation, swelling, pricking pain, and perspiration [occur]; house-lizards [cause these at the site].
(69) The venom of the centipede produces perspiration, pain, and burning at the site of the bite.
(70) A bite by a mosquito is characterized by itching, slight swelling, and mild pain. (71)

A bite by a *kīṭa* (insect) is incurable and resembles [the bite of] a mosquito; a wound from a mosquito is characterized by immediate exudation, a dark discoloration, and is accompanied by burning sensations, fainting, and fever.
Among the various types of fly bites, the *sthagikā* is the most fatal.

Whatever is caused by four-footed or two-footed creatures through their claws or teeth results in swelling, suppuration, discharge, and even fever. When the humors (doṣas) have become clear, the bodily tissues (dhātus) have returned to their natural state, there is a desire for food, and the urine and feces are normal, [the patient is considered recovered]. 74.
A physician should recognize that a person whose complexion, senses, mind, and movements are clear and serene is not afflicted by poison (verse 75).
One should diligently induce emesis in a man suffering from immobile (sthāvara) poison,
for there is no treatment for it equal to emesis.
Since poison is said to be excessively hot, sharp,
and piercing, therefore, for all types of poisoning, a cold affusion is prescribed; for heat and sharpness especially aggravate the bile (pitta), which in turn aggravates the poison.
One should sprinkle the vomited matter with cold water and quickly administer anti-venomous medicine mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One should give sour juice to drink and rub the patient with black pepper.

Whichever dosha one perceives to have numerous symptoms, one should apply treatment with medicines possessing qualities opposite to those [symptoms]. (77) Śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, koradūṣa, and priyaṅgu—
For those afflicted by poison, purification through emesis and purgation is for the purpose of eliminating the food [ingested]. 78.
The root, bark, leaves, flowers, and seeds of the *śirīṣa* tree, when ground with cow’s urine and applied as a paste, are a supreme antidote to poison. 79.

For one afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* (slow-acting poison), after having administered a very unctuous enema, one should cause them to undergo purification through both the upper and lower routes and administer this preeminent anti-toxin (*agada*) which destroys *dūṣīviṣa*:
long pepper (*pippalī*), *dhyāmaka*, spikenard (*māṃsī*), lodh tree bark (*lodhra*), cardamom (*elā*), and *suvarcikā*. (80)
A decoction of black pepper, *bālaka*, *elā*, as well as *kanaka* and *gairika*, when combined with honey, removes *dūṣīviṣa*.
[Likewise,] *abhayā*, *rocanā*, *kuṣṭha*, *arka* leaves, and *utpala* [are used].
The roots of *nalavetasa*, *garala*, and *surasā* (82), along with *kaliṅga*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *anantā*, and *śatāvarī*,
as well as *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *samaṅgā*, and the filaments of the lotus (83).
Having made a paste [of the drugs], one should cook the ghee, adding four times as much milk; when it is properly cooked, removed from the heat, and cooled,
the physician should add honey equal in quantity to the ghee, and after performing the protective rite (rakṣā), store it away.
It destroys poisons, difficult terrains, and the harmful effects of administered poisons (85).
By mere touch, it destroys all poison, as well as skin damaged by poisons, asthma caused by yoga-poisoning, itching, flesh-eating worms, and loss of consciousness (86).
When applied as collyrium, anointment, a drink, or an enema, it destroys poison; it is the supreme destroyer of venom for those bitten by snakes, insects, rats, spiders, and the like.
The root of *dhattūra* should be drunk after being ground with milk.
Also, the *aṅkoṭa* plant born of the bamboo lineage is a diligent destroyer of dog venom (88).
An ointment made from the two types of *rajanī*, *pattaṅga*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *nāgakeśara*, ground with cold water, will instantly destroy spider venom (89).
A paste made from cumin mixed with ghee and rock salt,
applied lukewarm with honey as an ointment, removes the poison of a scorpion.
Furthermore, smelling the fragrance of a crushed *sūryāvarta* leaf [is also beneficial].
A man bitten by a scorpion becomes free from poison in an instant.
(91) Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter on poisons. Now begins the sixty-eighth chapter on women's diseases.
Due to incompatible foods, wine, overeating, indigestion, miscarriage, excessive sexual intercourse, travel, grief, extreme emaciation, injury from heavy loads, and sleeping during the day—
these are said to be the four types of pradara (uterine discharge) caused by the derangement of phlegm, bile, wind, and their combination.
In all cases of asṛgdara (menorrhagia), there is body ache and pain;
when caused by kapha, it is undigested, resembling slimy mucus, pale, and like the water in which boiled rice has been rinsed.
When caused by pitta, it is hot, accompanied by distress, and flows with great force, appearing yellow, blue, black, or red.
That which is rough, reddish, frothy, scanty, and scanty, accompanied by a pricking sensation, and resembling meat-washings, arises from Vāta.
That which resembles honey, clarified butter, or the color of yellow orpiment, or has the appearance of marrow, and is putrid, arises from all three Doṣas.
Experts declare that to be incurable; therefore, a physician should not undertake its treatment.
Upon its excessive discharge, there occurs weakness, fatigue, fainting, intoxication, thirst,
burning sensations, delirium, pallor, drowsiness, and diseases born of Vata.
[One should treat] her who constantly discharges a flow accompanied by thirst, burning sensations, and fever.
One should avoid a woman who is weak, whose blood is diminished, or who is afflicted by tamas, as she is incurable.
Menstrual flow that is free from sliminess and burning pain for one month, or persists for five nights,
and is neither excessive nor too scanty, should be declared pure.

A woman should drink sour gruel (dadhi) mixed with sauvarcala salt, cumin, madhuka, and blue lotus (nīlotpala), combined with honey, for the pacification of vāta-ārsas (menorrhagia or metrorrhagia). [Verse 11] One karṣa of madhuka and likewise one karṣa of white sugar—
One should drink *balā* ground with rice-water in the event of menorrhagia;
or one should eat the well-powdered root of the plant called *kaṅkatikā*,
combined with sugar and honey, in the case of menorrhagia.
If the root of the *vyāghranakhī* plant, which grows toward the north, is brought from a pure place under the asterism of Uttaraphalgunī and tied around the waist, it will cause blood to flow.
(12) *Rasāñjana*, the root of *taṇḍulaka*, and honey, when drunk with rice-water, [cures hemorrhage].
Bhārgī, together with ginger, destroys menorrhagia of all origins and asthma.
(13) One should drink milk boiled with a decoction of the bark of Aśoka, well-cooled, in the morning according to one's strength; this is a destroyer of severe menorrhagia. (14)
Having uprooted the root of *kuśa* grass, one should grind it with rice-water;
by drinking this for three days, a woman is completely freed from *pradara*.
One should drink the juice of the fruit of the *udumbara* tree mixed with honey.
To destroy excessive menstrual bleeding (*asṛgdara*), one should eat food with milk and sugar (16).
Having made a bolus (*modaka*) from the powder of *alābu* fruit mixed with sugar and honey, one should consume it for the pacification of *pradara* (vaginal discharge) (17).

A decoction prepared from dārvī, rasāñjana, kirāta, vṛṣa, abda, bilva, honey, sandalwood, and the flowers of the sun (lotus), when drunk according to the prescribed method mixed with honey, destroys painful menorrhagia characterized by red or white discharge; it also cures raktapitta, and pieces of kūṣmāṇḍa fruit are beneficial as mentioned in the section on raktapitta. 18.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter on *pradara* (leucorrhea).
Now begins the sixty-ninth chapter on *somaroga* (menorrhagia):
[It arises] from excessive sexual indulgence in women, as well as from grief and even from physical exhaustion.
Furthermore, through the application of malevolent spells (*ābhicārika-yoga*) or likewise through the application of poisons (*gara-yoga*),
the waters situated within the entire body become agitated and overflow;
having fallen from their place, they indeed pass out through the urinary tract.
Clear, stainless, cool, odorless, painless, and white,
those [discharges] flow in excess; being weak, she is unable to restrain their force and finds no comfort anywhere.
His head becomes loose, and his mouth and palate dry up;
there is fainting, yawning, and delirium, and his skin becomes excessively rough.
He never finds satisfaction with foods, edibles, or drinks.
Because they sustain the body, those waters are designated as "soma";
therefore, due to the depletion of soma, women are said to suffer from the disease known as "soma. [One should consume] the ripe fruit of the plantain, the juice of the myrobalan fruit, and honey.
One should eat it together with sugar; this is the supreme retention of Soma.
(7) One should cause [the patient] to drink powdered black gram (*māṣa*) with licorice (*madhuka*), *vidārī*, and honey-sugar with milk in the morning; this is the supreme retention of Soma. (8)
If that same Soma, being diseased, flows repeatedly with urine, one should have the patient drink Vāruṇī liquor mixed with the powder of cardamom leaves (9),
or a paste of Āmalakī seeds with honey and sugar, taken with water.

By drinking [this] for just three days, there is the destruction of white leucorrhea (śvetapradara). 10. One who delights in a diet of buttermilk and rice should drink nāgakeśara ground with buttermilk for three days for the pacification of white leucorrhea. 11.
When urine flows excessively for a long time due to a chronic somaroga, they call that condition mūtrātisāra, which is extremely destructive to one's strength.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter on somaroga. 69.
Now begins the seventieth chapter, on Gynecological Diseases (Yoniroga).

Verses 1: Due to improper diet and lifestyle, when the humors (doṣas) become vitiated, diseases may arise in the female genital tract (bhaga) from the menstrual blood, from the seed, or even through the influence of fate.
Udāvartā, vandhyā, viplutā, pariplutā, and vātalā—these five types of gynecological diseases arise from the disorder of vāta.
Similarly, there are five types arising from the disorder of pitta; among them, the first is lohitakṣarā.
Prasraṃsinī, Vāmanī, Putraghnī, Pittalā (3), Atyānandā, Karṇinī, Caraṇānandapūrvikā,
and also Atipūrvā— these are to be known as Śleṣmalā and Kaphādimā (4).
The *ṣaṇḍhī*, the *aṇḍinī*, the *mahatī*, the *sūcīvaktrā*, and the *tridoṣiṇī*—
these five are declared to be [abnormal] uteri due to the provocation of all three *doṣas*.
In the *udāvartā* type, the woman discharges frothy menstrual blood with great difficulty.
A woman who is sterile (bandhyā) should be known as one who has ceased menstruating; one who is "overflowing" (viplutā) suffers from constant pain.
In the case of the "flooded" (pariplutā) type, there is intense suffering from the afflictions of sexual intercourse;
she is characterized by a predominance of wind (vāta), being rough, stiff, and afflicted by piercing and pricking pains.
In all four of these [types] as well, there are pains caused by wind (vāta).
That [type] which always discharges blood with burning is called *lohitakṣarā*.
That which hangs down and drops when shaken is *prasraṃsinī*. That which gives birth with difficulty is *duṣprajāyinī*.
A *vāmanī* womb, ejecting seed accompanied by *rajas*, causes the embryo to fall once it has been established;
a *putraghnī* womb [causes death] due to the discharge of blood. A *pittalā* womb is excessively characterized by burning, suppuration, and fever.
In all four of these initial types as well, there is an increase in symptoms of bile (pitta). Atyānandā finds no satisfaction through sexual intercourse.
In Karṇinī, a fleshy growth (karṇikā) arises in the vagina due to phlegm (śleṣman) and blood.
In sexual intercourse, the woman with excessive discharge (*aticaraṇā*) surpasses the man many times; in those two cases, the seed does not remain.
The womb of one who is phlegmatic (*śleṣmalā*) is slimy, itchy, and excessively cold.
In all four of these [types of vaginal prolapse], there is an increase in the symptoms of *śleṣman* (phlegm).

A girl who has not reached puberty, whose breasts do not develop, who is sterile, and whose vagina feels rough during intercourse, becomes *aṇḍinī* (one with testicles) due to being seized by *mahāmeḍhra*.
The *ativivṛtā* has an excessively wide opening, while the *atisaṃvṛtā* has a needle-like mouth.
Both arise from all the *liṅga*s (genital swellings) and are born from the provocation of all the *doṣa*s.
Furthermore, in all four of these [types], the symptoms of all [the *liṅga*s] are observed. 15–16.
In this world, five types of births arising from all the [three] doṣas are incurable (17).
Due to sleeping during the day, excessive anger, over-exertion, excessive sexual intercourse,
and injury from nails, teeth, and so forth, the vāta and other doṣas become provoked as follows (18).

When [the fetus] is produced in the womb resembling pus and blood and having the shape of a *lakuca* fruit, it is called "born from a bulb" (*kanda-yoni*). One should diagnose that as being caused by wind (*vātika*) when it is dry, discolored, or cracked.

One should know that which is accompanied by burning, redness, and fever to be of the nature of pitta (20). That which resembles the flower of the sesame plant and is characterized by itching is of the nature of kapha.
One should declare that which is endowed with all the symptoms to be of the nature of sannipāta (21).
Upon the appearance of her menses, a woman should constantly consume fish,
sour gruel (*kāñjika*), sesame, black gram, *udaśvit*, and likewise curd.
[She should also take] *ikṣvāku* seeds, *dantī*, *capalā*, jaggery, *madana*, *kiṇva*, and barley awns.
A wick made from *sasnuk* milk and inserted into the vagina produces menstruation. If the leaves of *jyotiṣmatī* are drunk for three days with *svarjikā* salt and *ugrāsana*,
ground with cold milk, it will certainly produce menstrual flow.
Balā, sitā, sātibalā, madhūka, the sprout of a banyan tree, and gajakeśara—
when this is drunk with honey, milk, and ghee, a barren woman will certainly give birth to a virtuous son.
Milk prepared with a decoction of aśvagandhā and mixed with ghee [is likewise effective].

Indeed, a woman who has bathed after her menses, having drunk [this] in the morning, conceives a child. (26) A girl who has bathed after her menses, having drunk the root of the *lakṣmaṇā* plant uprooted during the Puṣya asterism ground with milk, will conceive; of this there is no doubt. (27)

The root of *kuraṇṭa*, the flowers of *dhātakī*, sprouts of *vaṭa*, and blue lotus—this mixture taken with milk certainly bestows pregnancy. Furthermore, that woman who, eating wholesome food, drinks *pārśvapippala* along with cumin, [attains the same result]. 28.
She gives birth to a son here who is endowed with a white arrow-feather; it is not otherwise.
Having ground a single leaf of the *palāśa* tree with milk and drunk it, a pregnant woman obtains a powerful son; of this there is no doubt. (29–30)

Having drunk the root of *śūkaraśimbī* or the pulp of *dadhiphala* with milk, or likewise the seed of *bhavaliṅgī*, a woman does not give birth to a daughter. [31] The root of *putrakamañjarī* combined with *viṣṇukrāntā* and *liṅginī* [achieves the same].
Having drunk this for eight days while pregnant, a woman will by no means give birth to a daughter.
(32) She who drinks an equal powder of *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* with milk at the time of her menses will never conceive a fetus anywhere. (33)
A woman who for three days eats hibiscus flowers ground with *āranāla* and consumes a handful of aged molasses will not conceive a fetus;
in those [lunar] days, the sequence beginning with oil is prescribed.
Enema, massage, affusion, ointment, and the application of a medicinal wick (picu) should be administered.
One should cook sesame oil with nata, vārttākinī, kuṣṭha, rock salt, and amaradāru; a woman should then apply this oil as a medicinal wick.

When the womb is constantly disordered, pain is relieved by that [treatment]. Furthermore, one should treat a wind-disordered (vātalā), rough, stiff, or insensitive womb with *kumbhī-sveda* (pot-fumigation) in a closed inner room.
Or she should always apply a tampon soaked in sesame oil into the vagina (37).

For vaginal disorders characterized by pitta, cooling treatments— such as irrigation, massage, and the application of tampons— that alleviate pitta should be employed, as well as ghee for the purpose of oleation (38).
One should insert a prolapsed organ that has been smeared with ghee and steamed in milk;
having covered it with minced meat (veśavāra), one should then apply a bandage.
[This is done] with ginger, black pepper, long pepper, coriander, cumin, and pomegranate.
Veśavāra prepared with the root of *pippalī* is prescribed by the wise. For burning of the vagina (*yonidāha*), one should always drink the juice of *dhātrī* mixed with sugar;
or one may drink the root of *sūryakāntā* with rice-water.
In the case of a vagina that discharges pus, filling it with boluses made from cleansing substances mixed with cow's urine and salt is beneficial.
For one that is foul-smelling or slimy, however, powder derived from the five astringent decoctions (pañcakaṣāya) should be used.
One should fill or retain [the enema] with water boiled from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree and other such plants.

A suppository made of long pepper (*pippalī*), black pepper (*marica*), black gram (*māṣa*), *śatāhvā*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), and rock salt (*saindhava*), equal in size to the index finger, is a purifier of the womb when inserted into the vagina. 43–44.
In the case of *karṇinī*, wicks made from purifying substances should be inserted.
One should wash the vagina with a stream of water boiled with *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *dantī*; by this, the itching therein is pacified.

Having finely powdered mudga-gram soup along with khadira, pathyā, jātīphala, nimba, and pūga, one should strain it through a cloth and insert it into the vagina; thereby the womb becomes contracted and water will no longer leak from it. 47.

The physician should boil the root of *kapikacchū* according to the prescribed method; by washing with this decoction, the vagina becomes contracted. [Also used are] the two types of cumin (*jīraka*), black salt (*kṛṣṇa*), *suṣavī*, *surabhi*, and *vacā*.

Vāsaka, rock salt (saindhava), alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), and yavānikā—having fried a powder of these slightly in ghee and made a sweetmeat (modaka) with sugar, one should eat it according to one's digestive fire; thus one is freed from diseases of the female reproductive tract. 49–50.

A tampon (picu) prepared with sesame oil cooked in a decoction of rat (*mūṣaka*) destroys those diseases of the female reproductive tract when retained in the vagina; of this there is no doubt. [One should take] triphalā, two types of *sahacara*, *guḍūcī*, and *punarnavā*.
Having made a paste of śukanāsā, the two types of haridrā, rāsnā, medā, and śatāvarī,
one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk; once prepared, this should be administered to a woman for the alleviation of gynecological disorders.
Mañjiṣṭhā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, triphalā, sugar, balā,
the two types of medā, payasyā, the two types of kākoli, and the root of aśvagandha;
(54) ajamodā, the two types of haridrā, priyaṅgu, and kaṭurohiṇī.
One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *karṣa* each of blue lotus (*utpala*), white water lily (*kumuda*), raisins (*drākṣā*), the two *kākolī*s, and the two types of sandalwood (*candana*).
Four times the amount of ghee—namely, the juice of *śatāvarī* and milk—should be added. (55–56)
Having drunk this clarified butter, a man always acts like a bull among women;
he procreates heroic sons who are rich in intelligence and pleasing to behold. Furthermore, for one whose fetus is unstable, or who gives birth to a dead child—
It may cause one to give birth to a short-lived child or a daughter; it is recommended for vaginal diseases, menstrual disorders, and leukorrhea;
it increases progeny, promotes longevity, and wards off all malevolent planets. (58–59)
This is indeed proclaimed by the Aśvins as "Phalaghṛta";
physicians add the unmentioned root of *lakṣmaṇā* to it.
In that case, ghee from a cow whose calf is still living and which is of a uniform color is employed.

A flame of fire is offered using only cow-dung from the forest. One should fill the womb with the powders of red ochre, mango seeds, *jantughna*, *rajanī*, collyrium, and *kaṭphala*, combined with honey.
One should irrigate [the vagina] with a decoction of triphalā mixed with honey; thus, a woman is completely freed from the disease known as yonikanda.
In that regard, for the stabilization of a displaced fetus, there is the decoction of hrīvera and other ingredients.
Water boiled with *hrīvera*, *ativiṣā*, *musta*, *moca*, and *śakra* should be administered when the fetus is displaced, in cases of menorrhagia, or even when there is pain in the abdomen.
[64] [Likewise, water boiled with] *madhuka*, *candana*, *uśīra*, *sārivā*, and lotus petals [is beneficial].
A decoction combined with sugar and honey [is used] for fever in a pregnant woman (65).
Having prepared a decoction of sandalwood, sārivā, lodhra, and raisins, mixed with sugar, one should administer it for the pacification of fever in a pregnant woman.
Taken with goat's milk, it destroys chronic intermittent fever (viṣamajvara).
One should lick parched rice flour (lāja-śaktu) with decoctions of the barks of mango and jambu;
by merely licking this, a pregnant woman shall conquer dysentery (grahaṇī).
A pregnant woman should drink a decoction of *hrībera*, *aralu*, red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), *balā*, *dhānyāka*, *vatsādanī*, *mustā*, *uśīra*, *yavāsa*, *parpaṭa*,
and *viṣā* in cases of various diseases, pain, diarrhea, hemorrhage, or fever.
This yoga, which was proclaimed by the sages of old as supreme even for the purpose of childbirth, [is ruined] by the afflictions of fatigue from traveling on the path of worldly passions,
by fever, fasting, jumping, blows, indigestion, and running. (68–69)
From emesis and purgation, from suppression [of natural urges], from causing miscarriage, from the habitual use of sharp, alkaline, hot, pungent, bitter, and dry substances;
from the suppression of natural urges, from injury, from irregular sitting and lying postures, and from fear. (70)
When the embryo falls, there is a painful discharge of blood. From the fourth month onwards, there is a flow of the fetal matter;
thereafter, for those with a firm body, the fall occurs in the fifth or sixth month.

Due to trauma, sitting in an uneven posture, or being oppressed by pressure, the fetus falls in an instant like a ripe fruit from a tree. (73) If blood should flow repeatedly from the womb of a pregnant woman, [it is a sign of danger].
To suppress that [discharge], she should drink milk boiled with blue lotus and the like.
Blue lotus, reddish lotus, kahlāra, kumuda, white lotus, and madhuka—this is the group known as the utpalādi (blue-lotus group). 74–75.
When consumed regularly, it indeed removes burning sensations, thirst, heart disease,
hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), fainting, as well as vomiting and loss of appetite.
When the fetus descends, there may be a burning sensation and pain in the sides.
Backache, dysentery, flatulence, and urinary retention arise;
furthermore, as it moves from one location to another, agitation occurs in the stomach, the large intestine, and other sites, while the previously mentioned complications also manifest. (77–78)
In those cases of burning sensation and other symptoms, one should employ unctuous and cooling treatments;
milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *urubūka*, and *gokṣuraka*,
combined with sugar, is excellent for removing the colic of a pregnant woman.
A pregnant woman should drink milk prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *madhuka*, *kṣudrā*, and *amlāna*, combined with sugar and honey; this removes her pain.
A fresh *mallikā* flower grown in a house or a storehouse made of clay [is also beneficial].
One should powder together samaṅgā, dhātakī flowers, red ochre (gairika), rasāñjana, and likewise sarjarasa, according to their availability;
one should lick that powder with honey for the purpose of pacifying miscarriage. 81–82.
Or she should drink the paste of *kaśeru*, blue lotus, and *śṛṅgāṭaka* with milk;
or, for abdominal distension (*ānāha*), she should drink milk boiled with *vacā*, garlic, asafoetida, and *sauvarcala* salt, and the pregnant woman will become comfortable. (83)
One should boil milk with a paste made from the roots of the five grasses (*tṛṇapañcaka*).
A pregnant woman, having drunk that milk, is released from urinary obstruction. (84) The "five grasses" consist of *śālī*, *ikṣu*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *śara*.
Their root removes thirst, burning sensations, pitta, blood disorders, and retention of urine (85).
Madhuka, śākabīja, payasyā, suradāru, aśmantaka, black sesame, tāmravallī, and śatāvarī [are also used]. (86)
Vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, priyaṅgu, utpala, sārivā,
anantā, sārivā, rāsnā, padmā, madhuka,
the two types of bṛhatī, kāśmarī, the sprouts of milk-exuding trees, their bark, and ghee. 87.
Pṛśniparṇī, vacā, śigru, śvadaṃṣṭrā, madhuparṇikā, śṛṅgāṭaka, and viṣa; drākṣā, kaśeru, madhuka, and sugar—O child, these are the seven formulations completed by half-verses. 88–89.
These should be administered in their respective order with milk in cases of miscarriage;
thus the fetus does not fall and the pain of labor is pacified.
(90) Kapittha, bṛhatī, bilva, paṭola, ikṣu, and digdhikā—
In the eighth month, the physician should administer roots boiled in milk.
In the ninth month, one should drink milk prepared with madhuka, anantā, payasyā, and sārivā.
In the tenth month, milk prepared with śuṇṭhī and payasyā is beneficial.

In the eleventh month, for the alleviation of the pregnant woman's colic, she should drink a beneficial decoction of ginger, madhuka, and devadāru with milk; or she should drink kṣīrikā, utpala, milk, samaṅgā, mūlaka, and śivā. (93–94)
In the twelfth month, a pregnant woman should drink this colic-alleviating medicine consisting of sitā, vidārī, kākolī, kṣīrī, and mṛṇālikā;
thus the fetus is nourished and severe pain subsides. 95–96.
If the embryo, dried up by the wind (vāta), does not fill the womb,
she should drink milk and meat broth prepared with nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya) substances.
[97] When the menstrual blood is dried up and the limbs have not formed, it is afflicted by the wind and becomes completely parched.

Because that [element] has been abandoned by the *jīva*, it remains hard. (98) If the wind (*vāyu*) associated with semen, blood, or old age should occasionally cause abdominal distension, then that distension subsides of its own accord. (99)
At that time, this embryo was carried away by Naigameya, who resounds through the world;
if it remains light due to minimal activity, the woman gives birth to the fetus in the ninth or tenth month. 100.
In the eleventh or twelfth month, or otherwise due to a morbid transformation (vikāra),
listen now to the treatment for that woman who, because of the contraction of the fetus by the wind (vāta), does not give birth even at the time of delivery. (102–103)
She should pound this [mixture] with a pestle in a mortar; then, desiring childbirth, she should sit upon an uneven seat or use an uneven vehicle.
If there is a delay in delivery, one should fumigate the vulva on all sides.
One should bind the root of *lāṅgalī* with a thread made from the slough of a black cobra or from *piṇḍītaka*;
or one should wear *suvarcalā* or *viśalyā*, and she will give birth quickly. 105–106.

The head of a cow that has become a skeleton, when placed above the maternity chamber, causes a woman to give birth with ease at that very moment. [107] And by means of a paste made from the root of *potakā* mixed with sesame oil, [the same result is achieved].
Having smeared the interior of the birth canal with this, a woman gives birth easily (108).
Furthermore, black *vacā* ground with water and mixed with castor oil, when applied as an ointment to the navel,
indeed brings about easy delivery for women who have been oppressed by many complications (109).
Having drunk the root of the *mātuluṅga* combined with *madhuka* and mixed with ghee, a woman gives birth easily.
(110) Having tied the northern root of the sugarcane with a thread equal in length to her own body, [she should drink it].
In the region of the waist, a pregnant woman gives birth easily and without delay.
By binding the root of a palmyra tree at its base with a thread of its own length around the waist, a woman will certainly give birth with ease. 111–112.
The wind (vāyu), indeed, becomes obstructed and causes the pain of a malpresented fetus (mūḍhagarbha) in the vagina, the abdomen, and other regions, as well as the retention of urine.
Then, due to that vitiated wind, the fetus, exceeding its normal proportions, enters the birth canal in various ways:

as a *saṃkīlaka* (stuck like a peg), a *pratikhura* (with feet turned back), a *parigha* (like a crossbar), or a *bīja* (seed-like). Among these, it may enter with arms and feet upwards, or with the head [downwards].

And he who becomes stuck like a stake is indeed a "stake" (kīla) because his hooves are visible; for he is one whose body is stuck. 114 Some block the door with their heads and bellies, while others have their bodies bent by twisting them around.

One enters with one [limb], another with both arms; some go crosswise, another face downwards, and yet another enters by turning sideways—thus the eightfold manner of entering the womb occurs at birth. Furthermore, she whose head is cast down, whose limbs are cold, and who is shameless [is also mentioned].
When the veins protrude dark blue, she destroys the fetus, and the fetus likewise destroys her.
When the fetus is dead, there is a lack of fetal movement, loss of the *āvīna* pains, a dark-yellowish pallor, foulness of breath, and internal colic. (116–117)

The embryo perishes in the womb when it is afflicted by mental or external afflictions of the mother, or when it is oppressed by diseases; furthermore, there is obstruction by the birth canal, attachment, and even the presence of makkalla (foul matter) within the womb. 118.
The woman might die from a difficult labor, as well as from the complications already described.
However, those women who have successfully delivered many children even during times of distress and have thereby rightly acquired renown—those women should perform this procedure. (119–120)
If the fetus is alive but unconscious, she should carefully extract it from the womb with her hand, which has been smeared with clarified butter and inserted into the birth canal. However,
if the fetus is dead, she should insert a surgical instrument into the pregnant woman's womb.
She was skilled in the meaning of both weapons and treatises, light-handed, and free from fear.
However, she should never pierce a living being with a weapon;
for one who is being pierced might kill both his mother and himself.
A wise physician should not neglect a dead fetus for even a moment;
for it quickly kills the mother, just as an animal killed by excessive food.
Indeed, whichever part of the fetus is attached within the womb, that [the physician] must [extract].
Having extracted [the fetus] correctly by cutting it away, one should protect the woman with great effort. (125) Once the fetus has been thus removed, one should sprinkle her with warm water;
then, once her body has been anointed, one should apply an unctuous substance to the birth canal. (126)
In this way, the womb becomes soft and that pain is pacified.
(127) One should grind equal parts of *tumbī* leaf and *lodhra*; an application of this paste should be made to the vulva, and the womb will quickly become uninjured. (128)

The fruit of the *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees, combined with sesame oil and smeared with honey upon the vagina, is an excellent means for tightening it. A woman who has recently given birth should drink this mixture to reduce the enlargement of her abdomen.
If, after seven times three weeks (twenty-one days), the *kaṇājaṭā* mixed with morning-churned [curd] has not fallen from the womb of a woman who has given birth,
then it causes colic, flatulence, and dullness of the digestive fire.

One should rub her throat with a finger wrapped in hair; and with mustard seeds bound in a snake-skin, a bitter gourd, or a bottle-gourd, one should fumigate the vulva on all sides with these powdered and smeared with pungent oil. 132.
Indeed, one should smear the palms and soles of the hands with a paste of *lāṅgalī* root; for this ensures that the woman who has given birth does not miscarry again.
One should then slowly insert a hand with trimmed nails and lubricated into the birth canal of the woman who has recently delivered.

With that same hand, one should extract the other [membrane]; once the fetus has been delivered of its placenta, one should sprinkle it with warm water, and then, after her body has been anointed, one should apply an unguent into the birth canal. 135
In a woman who has recently given birth, the Vata, aggravated by dryness,
obstructs the blood that has been dried up by sharp and hot qualities, and indeed produces a cyst (granthi) below the navel,
in the flanks, in the bladder, or even at the top of the bladder. (136)
Then, pain occurs in the navel, the bladder, and likewise in the abdomen;
there is distension of the colon and retention of urine arises—
this is declared by physicians to be the symptomatology of the disease known as makkalla.
A woman should drink finely powdered yavakṣāra with warm water or with clarified butter for the cessation of makkalla (colic).
[She should also take] pippalī, pippalīmūla, marica, and gajapippalī. 139.
Nāgara, citraka, cavya, reṇuka, elā, ajamodā, 140 sarṣapa, hiṅgu, bhārgī, pāṭhā, indrayava, jīraka,
mahānimba, mūrvā, viṣā, tiktā, and viḍaṅga. 141
This group of drugs beginning with *pippalī* indeed destroys phlegm and wind;
a woman should drink a decoction of these combined with salt, which removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), colic, and fever, stimulates digestion, and ripens undigested matter (*āma*). (142)

One should daily eat old jaggery mixed with the powder of the three pungents (tri-kaṭuka), the four aromatics (cātur-jātaka), and coriander (kustumburu) to destroy colic (makkalla), as it is supreme for alleviating phlegm and wind and for curing abdominal tumors (śūla) and gulma. 143–144.
A woman who has given birth should consume appropriate food and engage in suitable activities;
she should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, and exposure to cold.
Whatever disease arises in a woman after childbirth due to improper conduct [must be treated].
That [disease] may be difficult to cure or incurable; therefore, one should follow the prescribed regimen.
Those diseases which arise in a woman who has recently given birth are indeed severe, resulting from improper treatment, excessive distress, or irregular eating and indigestion. 146–147.
Body ache, fever, cough, thirst, heaviness of the limbs, swelling,
colic, and diarrhea are the symptoms of puerperal diseases (sūtikā-roga). Fever, diarrhea, swelling, colic, abdominal distension, and loss of strength [are also present].

Drowsiness, anorexia, salivation, and other such conditions arising from vāta and śleṣman are indeed diseases difficult to cure when they are based on depleted muscle tissue and strength; all these, along with their complications, are designated by the name "sūtikā" (puerperal disorders). 159–160.
For the purpose of pacifying the diseases of puerperal fever, one should perform treatments that alleviate vāta;
one should administer a lukewarm decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) mixed with ghee. [One should also give] amṛtā, nāgara, sahacara, bhadrotkaṭa, pañcamūlaka, and jalada.
Boiled and cooled, and mixed with honey, this quickly pacifies the affliction of puerperal fever (sūtikātaṅka).
Devadāru, vacā, kuṣṭha, pippalī, viśvabheṣaja, bhūnimba, kaṭphala, musta, tiktā, dhānya, and harītakī—[these constitute the formulation]. 152–153.
Gajakṛṣṇā, duḥsparśā, gokṣura, dhanvayāsaka,
bṛhatī, ativiṣā, chinnā, karkaṭa, and kṛṣṇajīraka—
these taken in equal parts and combined with sindhu (rock salt) and rāmaṭha (asafetida). 154.
One should have the woman who has recently given birth drink the decoction reduced to one-eighth;
this is for those afflicted by colic, cough, fever, dyspnea, fainting, tremors, headache, delirium, thirst, burning sensations, drowsiness, diarrhea, and vomiting. (155–156)
The decoction of the *devadārvādi* group is the supreme medicine for a woman who has recently given birth; it destroys the diseases of childbirth arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*.
Likewise, [the group includes] *jīraka*, *sthūlajīra*, and the two types of *śatapuṣpā*.
Yavānī, ajamodā, dhānyaka, and methikā; śuṇṭhī, kṛṣṇā, kaṇāmūla, citraka, and hapuṣā;
badarī, gajacūrṇa, kuṣṭha, and likewise kampillaka. (158–159)

These [herbs] should be taken in a measure of one *pala* each; it is considered that there should be one hundred *palas* of jaggery (*guḍa*), two *prasthas* of milk, and likewise one *kuḍava* of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
This "Five Cumin" preparation (*pañcajīrakapāka*) is for the pacification of women who have recently given birth.
It is appropriate for diseases of childbirth, diseases of the womb, fever, consumption,
cough, asthma, jaundice, emaciation, and disorders of wind (vāta).
In this preparation, there should be two palas of clarified butter, two prasthas of milk, and [two palas] of sugar.

Then, fifty palas of this powder are added along with ginger; having cooked it according to the prescribed method like jaggery, half a *prastha* [of liquid] is used, mixed with three handfuls of coriander, five palas of *kṛmighna* (black pepper), one pala each of cumin and cumin-seed. 163.
One pala each of vyoṣa (the three pungents), ambhoda (musta), dala (patra), uragendra (elā), sumanas (jātī), tvak, drākṣā, and viḍaṅga,
cooked with sugar candy, is known as *nāgarakhaṇḍa*; it removes diseases of the puerperal state and pacifies thirst, vomiting, fever, burning sensations, emaciation, dyspnea, and cough.

It destroys diseases of the spleen, removes worms, and stimulates a sluggish digestive fire. (164) She should remain completely purified, eat unctuous, wholesome, and moderate food, and constantly devote herself to sudation and massage for one month without weariness. (165)
Whether the breasts contain milk or are without it, when the bodily humors (doṣas) reach a woman's breasts and vitiate the blood and flesh, they lead to breast diseases;
for the vessels situated in the breasts of virgins have their openings closed.
Because the morbid humors (doṣas) do not spread within them, those women do not suffer from diseases of the breasts.
Furthermore, in those who have given birth or are pregnant, these [breasts] become naturally distended and consequently leak. 169–170.
Of these five types, however, excluding the blood-born abscess (śoṇitavidradhi),

their symptoms are identical to the symptoms of the Brahma-abscess (brāhmavidradhi). Upon observing a swelling arising on the breast, the physician should apply the various treatments prescribed for abscesses.

In cases of undigested milk (āma) or when it causes burning, as well as during its digestion, one should constantly apply cold substances that subdue pitta to her breasts due to their suppression. 172. One should employ cooling substances here that destroy pitta.
One should remove the blood with leeches, but one should not apply poultices to the breasts.
An ointment made from the root of *viśālā* destroys the pain arising in the breasts;
an ointment made from the pastes of *niśā* and *kanaka* is said to alleviate breast affliction.
An ointment made from *vandhyākarkoṭikā* quickly destroys the root [of the disease]. 175.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter on gynecological diseases (70).
Thus ends the section on the diseases of women.
Now begins the seventy-first chapter, on the diseases of children (Bālaroga).
Since the child-seizing spirits (bālagraha) afflict the infant due to improper conduct, one should therefore protect the child from their calamities with great effort. 1.
First is Skandagraha, and also Skandāpasmāra;
then Śakunī, Revatī, Pūtanā, Andhapūtanā,
Śītapūtanā, and likewise Mukhamaṇḍikā.
And the ninth is Naigameya; these are declared to be the Bālagrahas (seizers of children).
These nine, beginning with Skanda, who are the seizers of children, are said to be glorious, possessing divine bodies, and having both female and male forms.
These were created by Kṛttikā, Umā, Agni, and Śūlin for the protection of Skanda while he was staying in the Forest of Reeds and guarded by his own splendor;
Skanda was thus created by the Blessed Lord, the enemy of Tripura.
That planet also bears another name, Kumāra; he who is known as Skandāpasmāra is equal in luster to Agni. He is called Skandasakha and is also named Viśākha.
These planets are proclaimed to have female forms and various shapes;
they are portions of Gaṅgā, Umā, and Kṛttikā, characterized by the qualities of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa).
Furthermore, the planet Naigameya, with the face of a ram, was created by Pārvatī.
Indeed, Kumāradhārī was truly like a second self to the divine Guha.
Then, when Skanda had been appointed as the general of the celestial army by the Blessed One, these grahas approached Guha, who wielded a blazing spear.
With palms joined in reverence, they said to him, "Let a boon be granted to us.
For their sake, Skanda then urged the god Śiva.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, spoke to those Grahas.
The threefold world— consisting of the animal realm, the human realm, and the divine realm—
exists and is sustained through mutual assistance. Thus,
the gods gratify both humans and those of the animal realm.
By means of heat, rain, snow, and winds occurring at their proper times,
as well as through sacrifices, reverential salutations with joined palms, recitations, and burnt offerings correctly performed, men likewise please the deities.

And since nothing remains of the portion allotted by inheritance, your auspicious livelihood shall depend entirely upon children— in those families where neither the gods nor the ancestors are worshipped. (15–16)
Even if they are Brahmins, virtuous people, teachers, or guests,

[one should not give] to those who have ceased their purificatory practices and conduct, nor to those of despicable livelihood, nor to those who have stopped offering alms and oblations, nor to those whose houses contain broken brass vessels.
"Indeed, those various grahas will harm children unexpectedly;
therein shall be your abundant livelihood and your worship.
Thus have the grahas arisen, and for this reason they harm children. (19)
Children afflicted by planets are therefore most difficult to treat.
In one moment the child becomes agitated, in another he trembles and weeps;
he tears at his nurse with his nails and teeth, and even injures himself.
He gazes upward, gnashes his teeth, groans, yawns,
twitches his eyebrows, bites his lips, and repeatedly vomits foam;
he is excessively emaciated, keeps awake at night, has swollen limbs, and his stool and voice are altered.
He smells of fish and blood, and does not eat as he did before;
he becomes weak, with soiled limbs and lost consciousness—this is declared to be the characteristic of one possessed by an ordinary graha. 23–24.

With drooping limbs, smelling of blood, vomiting from his mouth, with a distorted face and one eyelid and eye motionless as if struck, he is agitated; his eyes appear watery, he weeps feebly, and being afflicted by Skanda, his stool becomes hard and he clenches his fists tightly.
He loses consciousness and regains it again; stiffened, he seems to dance with his hands and feet.
One who, while yawning, voids feces and urine with difficulty or emits froth, and is possessed by its companion [the *śakunī*], should be recognized as a child afflicted by the *śakunī*.

Such a child has drooping limbs, is terrified with fear, smells like a bird, is tormented by weeping and wounds, and his body is covered on all sides with eruptions accompanied by burning and suppuration. (26–27)

With a red face, greenish excrement, and an extremely pale or dark body, the child—afflicted by burning pain in the mouth and hands, with a distressed frame, and severely tormented by Revatī—seizes the ears and nose;
he passes stool that is mixed with feces, sleeps neither by day nor by night, and emits excrement with a smell like that of a crow. (28)
The prince seized by Pūtanā suffers from vomiting, horripilation, and thirst (29).

The physician should declare that a child who clings to the breast while being afflicted by diarrhea, cough, hiccup, vomiting, and fever; who is of poor complexion, constantly emits the smell of blood, and is possessed by Andhapūtanā, is likewise afflicted (30).
Crying out in terror, trembling violently, he becomes huddled up, accompanied by pain and gurgling in the intestines;
with drooping limbs, he is excessively chilled by cold—the physician should then declare him seized by Śītapūtanā.
(31) He whose limbs are withered, whose hands, feet, and face are bloody, who eats much, and whose belly is clouded and covered with prominent veins—[he is seized by Śakunī].
If a child becomes agitated and has a smell like urine, he should be known as one seized by Vaktramandika (32).
He who vomits froth, bends at the waist, laughs while agitated, looks upward, makes continuous moaning sounds, has a smell like fat, and loses consciousness, is possessed by Naigamesha (33).

Bathing with a decoction of *sahā*, *muṇḍitikā*, and northern plants (*udīcyaka*) removes the influence of the planets (34). Anointing with *saptacchada*, *āmalaka*, *niśā*, and *candana* [is also beneficial]. Snake-skin, garlic, *mūrvā*, mustard seeds, and the sprouts of *ariṣṭa* [are used for fumigation] (35).
This incense made of cat hair, *viḍa* grass, wool, *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and *vacā*, mixed with honey, destroys all fevers in children and eliminates all planetary influences (*graha*).
For the pacification of the planets, rites for the propitiation of children (*bālaśāntīṣṭakarma*) should be performed. (36)
Vacā, kuṣṭha, as well as brāhmī, siddhārthaka,
sārivā, saindhava, and pippalī— with ghee as the eighth ingredient—
this prepared ghee, which promotes intelligence, should be drunk every day at dawn.
The boy shall possess firm mindfulness, quick intelligence, and become wise.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rakṣasas, nor Bhūtas, nor Mātṛs shall have power over boys who drink this Aṣṭamaṅgala.

The treatment for a child afflicted by the Viśiṣṭagraha spirit consists of sprinkling with a decoction of leaves from wind-alleviating trees for the pacification of a boy seized by the Skandagraha spirit. 39.
One should cause him to drink clarified butter prepared with *devadāru*, *rāsnā*, and the groups of sweet (*madhura*) drugs, along with milk (verse 40).
[Also,] mustard seeds, sloughed snake skin, *vacā*, *kākādanī*, and clarified butter.
The hair of camels, goats, sheep, and cows may also be used as incense.
One should wear the roots of the *somavallī*, *indravṛkṣa*, *vandāka*, *bilva*, *śamī*, and *mṛgādanī* tied together as an amulet. 41–42.
Having offered red garlands, banners, red perfumes, various kinds of food, and a bell as a sacrificial oblation to the God, one should place a cock at the temple of Skanda for one's welfare;
then, for three nights, one should perform a bath at night in the courtyards with fresh rice and barley. 43. Aṃ.
Then the wise man should kindle the fire with water purified by the Gāyatrī and with oblations. 44.
Hereafter I shall proclaim the protection that destroys the sins of children, which must be performed day after day by physicians who are free from sloth. 45.

May that imperishable god Skanda, who is the treasury of austerities, of splendors, of glories, and of forms, be gracious to you. May the lord of the army, the omnipresent god of the divine hosts, be propitious.
May the Lord Guha, the destroyer of the enemy Devāsena, protect you.
May he who is the son of the Great God of gods and of Pāvaka, and the son of Gaṅgā, Umā, and the Kṛttikās, grant you well-being. 47–48.
May the God who destroyed Krauñca— wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with red sandalwood, and possessing a divine red body— protect you.
[49] There is the group of plants beginning with bilva, śirīṣa, golomī, and surasā.
It should be employed as a sprinkling for the pacification of Skanda and epilepsy (50).
Surasā, śvetasurasā, pāṭhā, phañjī, phaṇijjaka,
saugandhika, bhūstṛṇaka, rājikā, and śvetabarbarī (51).
Kaṭphala, kharapuṣpā, kāsamarda, śallakī,
viḍaṅga, then nirguṇḍī, karṇikāra, udumbara, 52 balā, kākamācī, and likewise viṣamuṣṭikā.
This group beginning with *surasā* is renowned for removing phlegm and worms (53).
Oil cooked with the eight types of urine is beneficial for massage (54)— namely,
that of the cow, goat, sheep, buffalo, horse, donkey, camel, and elephant.
This is known as the "Eightfold Urine" (mūtrāṣṭaka), which is approved in all medical treatises.
Subsequently, ghee should be cooked with a decoction of milk-tree barks and the kākolyādi group of drugs, and then administered along with milk.
Kākoli, kṣīrakākoli, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, as well as ṛddhi, vṛddhi, medā, mahāmedā, guḍūcī,
mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, padmaka, and vaṃśalocanā. 57.
Śṛṅgī, prapauṇḍarīka, jīvantī, madhuyaṣṭikā,
and drākṣā constitute the group known as the Kākolyādi;
it increases breast milk, is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and removes pitta, blood disorders, and impurities.
The application of *vacā* and *hiṅgu* is prescribed here for cleansing;
furthermore, the excrement of vultures and owls, hair, elephant nails, clarified butter,
and the hair of a bull should always be employed in fumigation (*uddhūpana*).
One should offer an endless number of *kukkuṭī*, *bimbī*, and *markaṭī* fruits;
likewise, one should present cooked and uncooked meats, clear liquor, blood, milk, and rice with mung beans to Skanda and Apasmāra at a *vaṭa* tree. 61–62.
Then, one should cause a ritual bath to be performed at a crossroads and recite this:
"May he who is known as Skandāpasmāra, the beloved friend of Skanda, Viśākha of auspicious countenance, be for the welfare of this child. (63–64)
For one afflicted by the seizure of a bird (śakunigraha), a knowledgeable physician should perform a sprinkling with a decoction of cane (vetasa), mango (āmra), and wood-apple (kapittha);
[and likewise] with hrīvera, madhuka, uśīra, sārivā, utpala, and padmaka.
One should smear the child with lodhra, priyaṅgu, mañjiṣṭhā, and gairika.
Indeed, the incenses prescribed for Skanda-graha are beneficial here as well;
furthermore, the clarified butter (ghṛta) that pacifies Skanda-apasmāra is highly esteemed in this case too.
One should also carry śatāvarī, mṛgairvāru, nāgadantī, nidigdhikā, lakṣmaṇā, sahadevī, and bṛhatī;
as well as a garland made of sesame seeds and rice, yellow orpiment, and realgar.
This Bali offering should be presented at a Karañja tree by one who is self-restrained;
and his bath should be performed according to the rules in a bower,
using white Āśirīṣa, Gandhāśman, Dhava, Guggulu, and mustard seeds.
Oil for anointing that has been proven effective should be applied first;
furthermore, for the sake of pacifying the influence of Śakuni, one should apply a beneficial medicinal plaster (pradeha).
One should also perform various kinds of worship of Śakuni with auspicious flowers.
Then, one should bathe him according to the rite spoken by Nikumbha and recite:
"May the goddess who moves through the atmosphere, adorned with all ornaments, facing downwards with a slender beak—the bird—be gracious unto you. (72-73)
May she who is difficult to behold, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), with tawny limbs, a terrifying voice,
a protruding belly, and spike-like ears— the Bird (Śakunī)— be gracious to you.
[74] Also Aśvagandhā, Ajaśṛṅgī, Sārivā, and Punarnavā.
Indeed, a sprinkling with a decoction of these along with *vidārī* [should be performed];
likewise, oil should be used for anointing in cases of *kuṣṭha*, as well as with *sarjarasa*, *palaṅkaṣā*, *nalada*, and *gaurakadambaka*. (75–76)
The child should drink ghee prepared with dhava, aśvakarṇa, kakubha, śallakī, tinduka, as well as the drugs of the kākolyādi group.
A plaster consisting of kulattha, powdered conch-shell, and aśvagandhā should also be applied.
Vulture and owl excrement, barley, *yavaphala*, and clarified butter—
this should be used as an incense for the child during both twilights.
White flowers, parched grain, milk, boiled rice of the *śāli* variety, and curd [should also be offered].
At Gotīrtha, Bali should be offered to Revatī by one who is self-restrained (79).
The physician should cause a bath to be performed at the confluence for Dhātrī and Kumārā; there the Goddess appears bearing various weapons, adorned with variegated garlands and ointments (80).
May Cṛlatkuṇḍalinī, Śyāmā, and Revatī be gracious to you—those goddesses adorned with various ornaments who constantly worship her;
as do Lambā, Karālā, Vinatā, and likewise Bahuputrikā. 81.
May the goddess Revatī and Śuṣkanāsā be gracious to you.
82 Kapotavaṅkā, śyonāka, varuṇa, pāribhadraka, and āsphotā—these indeed should be employed for the ritual sprinkling of children. 83
Fresh curd-whey (payasyā), golomī, yellow orpiment,
realgar, kuṣṭha, and resin of sarja are prescribed as a paste for the preparation of oil. Ghee prepared with tugākṣīrī and madhuka is also beneficial.
Kuṣṭha, tālīsa, khadira, spandana, and arjuna (85),
as well as the pith of panasa, kakubha, and badara, along with cock bones, ghee, and mustard seeds— this constitutes the fumigation. 86.
One should wear *kākādanī*, *citraphalā*, *bimbī*, and *guñjā*.
The physician should place fish-rice, *kṛśarā*, and minced meat within a hollowed-out pair of earthen bowls as an offering in that person's empty house. 87–88.
The bathing of the consecrated infant with discarded food is prescribed;
[using] kuṣṭha, tālīsa, khadira, as well as candana and spandana (89),
along with devadāru, vacā, hiṅgu, kuṣṭha, and girikadambaka.
Cardamom and hareṇu seeds should also always be employed for fumigation.
(90) Clad in soiled garments, with dirty and coarse hair, the goddess Pūtanā, dwelling in an empty house, may protect the child. (91)
A decoction made from the leaves of bitter trees should be used for sprinkling.
Nimba, paṭola, kṣudrā, guḍūcī, and likewise vāsaka—
this group known as the "five bitter ones" (pañcatiktaka) is renowned for curing erysipelas and skin diseases.
One should collect long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), leadwort (citraka), liquorice (madhuka), honey, śāliparṇī, and the two types of bṛhatī for the purpose of preparing ghee;
furthermore, one should apply a paste of all the fragrant substances (sarvagandha) to the body and the eyes with cooling applications. 94
One should prepare for fumigation chicken excrement, hair, snake-skin, and worn-out clothing, using them repeatedly.
One should also wear the kukkuṭī, markaṭī, bimbī, and anantā plants.
Raw meat, as well as cooked meat and blood, should be offered at a crossroads; furthermore,
for the sake of the child's protection, one should offer them inside the house and perform an auspicious ritual bathing of the child with waters scented with all kinds of perfumes.
O Karālā, Piṅgalā, and Muṇḍā, clothed in saffron-colored garments—
O Goddess Gandhapūtane, being pleased, protect this child!
(97) [Take] cow urine, horse urine, mustā, and amaradāru.
One should take kuṣṭha and all the fragrant substances for the purpose of preparing the oil.
Having boiled the barks of rohiṇī, nimba, khadira, palāśa, and kakubha, one should cook ghee in that decoction along with milk. 98–99.
One should collect vulture and owl droppings, the skin of a goat smelling like a goat, and nimba leaves for the purpose of fumigation;
one should also wear guñjā, balā, and kākādanī.

One should also propitiate Śītapūtanā with offerings of mung-bean rice at a river; furthermore, the ritual bathing of the child is prescribed at the edge of a body of water. An offering should be presented to the goddess, consisting of wine and blood.
May Śītapūtanā— the goddess who eats boiled mudga beans, who drinks wine and blood, and who always delights in reservoirs of water— protect you! (103) Kapittha,
bilva, tarkārī, vāsā, and gandharvahastaka...
And *kuberākṣī* should be employed for the sprinkling of children.
Likewise, having combined the juices of *bhṛṅga* and trees with *hayagandhā*, one should cook oil and fat to prepare an ointment for the infant. 104–105.
Bakuchi, resin of the Sarja tree, Kuṣṭha, and clarified butter are beneficial for fumigation.
One should likewise bring colorants, powders, garlands, collyrium, mercury, and realgar;
then, one should offer a sacrificial oblation in the middle of the cow-pen. 106–107.
One should bring milk-rice together with sacrificial cakes for the purpose of the offering;
and it is beneficial to perform a ceremonial bath right there with waters purified by mantras.
[She should be] adorned, full of desire, fortunate, and able to assume any form at will.
May Mukhamaṇḍikā, who dwells in the midst of the cow-pen, protect you.
(109) A sprinkling [of water] should be performed with bilva, agnimantha, and pūtīka; likewise with priyaṅgu, sarala, anantā, śatapuṣpā, and kuṭannaṭa. (110)
One should cook oil with cow urine, curd-whey, and sour *kāñjika*;
one should also apply *vacā*, *vayasyā*, *jaṭilā*, and *golomī*.
In this case, an ointment (*utsādana*) is beneficial for destroying Skanda-epilepsy.
One who desires the welfare of the child should, while the people are asleep, apply fumigation with the excrement of monkeys, owls, and vultures; likewise,
one should offer sesame and rice, garlands, and various kinds of edible foods.
In the science of pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), one should offer [the oblation] to Meṣa at the root of a Plakṣa tree;
bathing beneath a milk-tree is also prescribed.
He is the knower of all, with moving eyes and brows, able to assume any form at will, and possessed of great glory.
May the god Naigameya, the protector of children, guard [them].
O Dhātrī! When the humors (doṣas) in the body become aggravated by heavy foods, poisons, or those that are harmful, then the breast milk becomes vitiated. 115–116.
In a woman who indulges in improper diet and lifestyle, the three doshas—Vata and the others—become vitiated and corrupt the breast milk; consequently, diseases arise in the infant.
When drinking milk corrupted by Vata, the child suffers from Vata-related ailments.

Drinking milk vitiated by pitta, the infant becomes weak-voiced and emaciated in limb, with suppressed feces, urine, and flatus; he is perspiring, has loose stools, suffers from jaundice and bile-related diseases, is prone to thirst, and his entire body feels hot. (118–119)

A child who drinks milk corrupted by phlegm becomes salivating, afflicted with diseases of phlegm, drowsy, dull-witted, swollen, red-eyed, and prone to vomiting. In cases arising from two humors (dvi-doṣaja), the symptoms of both are present; in cases arising from all three (sarva-doṣaja), all symptoms appear. 120–121.
All diseases such as fever and others that were previously mentioned for adults should likewise be understood by the best of physicians to occur in children as well;
however, those diseases which occur only in children and not in adults [are to be distinguished]. 122.
Understand with diligence those [diseases] of which tālukaṇṭaka is the foremost. 123.
When phlegm (kapha) becomes aggravated in the flesh of the palate, it produces tālukaṇṭaka; by this, a depression of the palatal region occurs at its apex. 124.
Falling of the palate, aversion to the breast, drinking with difficulty, vomiting of feces, thirst, pain in the eyes, throat, and mouth, weakness of the neck, and vomiting— these,
along with erysipelas arising from the head or the bladder, are fatal for an infant. 125.
Padmavarṇa and Mahāpadmaroga arise from the three humors (doṣas); [the former] proceeds from the two temples to the heart, and from the heart it goes to the anus.
Kukūṇaka occurs in the eyelids of infants due to defects in breast milk.
The eye becomes painful, itchy, and discharges profusely.
The child rubs his forehead, the orbital ridge, and the tip of the nose;
he is unable to look at the light of the sun and is incapable of opening his eyes. (127–128)
When the umbilical region is distended by wind and accompanied by pain, it is called *tuṇḍi*;
a disease known as *gudapāka* (rectal inflammation) arises in an infant due to *pitta*.
When the anus of a child is not washed and becomes contaminated with feces and urine, [this condition occurs]. (129)
In one who has been sweated or is undergoing sudation, an itching arises from the provocation of blood and phlegm (rakta-kapha).
From scratching that, pustules and discharge quickly appear;
one should recognize that formidable, consolidated ulcer as *ahipūtana*.
Smooth, matching the color of the skin, knotted, painless, and resembling a mung bean— this is known as *ajagallikā*, arising from phlegm and wind, occurring in children.
(132) A child, while generally drinking the breast milk of his pregnant mother, [develops this].

Accompanied by cough, weak digestion, vomiting, drowsiness, emaciation, loss of appetite, and vertigo, as well as enlargement of the abdominal cavity, they call that disease *pārigarbhika* or *paribhava*; in that condition, one should administer digestive stimulants (*dīpana*). 133–134.

The eruption of teeth in an infant is considered the cause of all diseases, particularly of fever, diarrhea, cough, vomiting, and headache; it also gives rise to ophthalmia, scabies, and erysipelas. 135–136.

The same medicine previously prescribed for the fevers and other ailments of adults should be administered to children as well; however, it should be given without [administering] treatments for burning sensations and the like.
Those very same humors (*doṣas*), bodily constituents (*dūṣyas*), and diseases such as fever are present in both cases.

Therefore, that very same medicine is prescribed there, but in a smaller dose. Viśvāmitra states that for a newborn infant, the dose should be as small as a *viḍaṅga* fruit. 138. He describes the smallest dose for a child: "The medicine for one just born is indeed the size of a *viḍaṅga* fruit."
By this very measure, one should increase the dose month by month.
In the first month, a single *raktikā* of medicine should be given to the child; it should be made into a linctus with honey, milk, sugar, and clarified butter. 139–140.
One should increase it by one [māṣa] each year until it becomes a full year;
thereafter, the interest shall be one māṣa per month until sixteen years have passed.
After that, it shall remain fixed for as long as seventy years.
Then, like a child, she should be made to sit up gradually by her mother.
This dose is proclaimed for powders, pastes, and electuaries; however, for decoctions, that same dose should be understood as four times greater.

Medicine for an infant who drinks milk should be given with milk and ghee; however, O nurse, for those diseases for which specific formulations that act as healers will be described, [the medicine] should be given alone, neither with milk nor with ghee. (144)
One should have that child suckle from breasts smeared with those [medicines].
Whenever pain arises in his limbs or minor members, he repeatedly touches that spot; being touched there, he cries out. (145–146)
One should not hold [the breath] with the eyes closed when there is disease in the head;
nor when there is disease in the bladder, for one suffering from retention of urine will experience hunger and thirst.
Due to the obstruction or dysfunction of feces and urine, there may arise vomiting, flatulence, and rumbling in the intestines.
One should recognize diseases located in the abdomen by [abdominal signs] and those situated throughout the body by [the child's] crying.
In a child, everything may be restricted except for breast milk; one should cause the wet-nurse to fast according to the proper measure, for this constitutes fasting for the infant. (148–149)
A lukewarm decoction prepared from bhadramustā, abhayā, nimba, paṭola, and madhuka destroys all fevers in a child.
A powder of vanakṛṣṇā, aruṇā, and śṛṅgī, combined with honey, [is likewise effective].
It destroys fever and diarrhea in children, and removes cough, dyspnea, and vomiting.
(151) Bilva, dhātakī flowers, water with lodhra, and gajapippalī— these,
prepared as a decoction and an electuary mixed with honey, should be administered to children suffering from diarrhea.
Water boiled with *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*,
and *sārivā* should be given with honey even to a child suffering from severe diarrhea.
[153] *Viḍaṅga*, *ajamodā*, and the seeds of *pippalī*...
Having mixed their powders together, the physician should have the child drink them with comfortably warm water when diarrhea has set in during the stage of *āma*. [The ingredients are:
the juice of *mocā*, *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, and the filaments of the lotus (*padmakeśara*). (154)
A gruel made from these ground ingredients destroys bloody diarrhea (raktātīsāra).
One should have the child drink a decoction prepared with ginger, ativiṣā, musta, bālaka, indrayava, and yava in the morning; it destroys all types of diarrhea.
Parched grain, liquorice, licorice, sugar, and honey,
combined with rice-water, quickly destroy dysentery.
(157) Turmeric, pine resin, deodar, bṛhatī, and elephant pepper—
Pṛśniparṇī and Śatāhvā, when licked with honey and ghee, stimulate the digestive fire, cure malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and alleviate pain from Vāta along with jaundice;
they destroy fever, dysentery, and anemia, and remove all diseases of children. (158–159)
One should lick the juice of mustaka, ativiṣā, vāsā, kaṇā, and śṛṅgī with honey; thus the child is freed from the five types of cough that have arisen.
A linctus made of vyāghrī, sumanas, jātī, and keśara [is also effective].
Honey removes coughs that have been long-standing in an infant.
Rice mixed with sugar and combined with rice-water—this drink should be given to the infant to cure cough and dyspnea. 161–162.

The powder of drākṣā, vāsā, abhayā, and kṛṣṇā, licked with honey and ghee, quickly destroys dyspnea, cough, and likewise tamaka-pāṇḍuroga. One should also administer the powder of kaṭukarohiṇī together with honey.
It quickly pacifies hiccups as well as vomiting that has persisted for a long time.
(164) The combination of mango stone, parched grain (lāja), and rock salt, taken with honey, will cure vomiting.
(165) In cases of vomiting, the medicinal preparation known as Medhya, drunk with breast milk, honey, and ghee, is effective.
One should have the patient lick the juice of two vārtākī fruits along with pañcakola (166). Or, one may lick a powder of pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara,
rock salt, viśva, elā, hiṅgu, and bhārgī mixed with ghee (167).
Cold water destroys constipation and Vata-type colic (śūla).
A linctus prepared with long pepper, black pepper, sugar, honey, fine cardamom, and rock salt is an excellent remedy for children suffering from urinary retention.
But when the child is weak, even while suffering from internal fire (fever), he should be made to eat powdered vidārī-kanda, wheat, and barley soaked in ghee;
immediately thereafter, he should drink boiled milk mixed with honey and sugar. 170
Musta, seeds of kūṣmāṇḍa, bhadradāru, and kaliṅgaka—
having ground these and smeared them with water, this plaster removes swelling in a child.
One should drink a decoction of paṭola, triphalā, ariṣṭa, and haridrā.
For the pacification of wounds, erysipelas, eruptions, and fever,
a decoction of *sārivā*, sesame, *lodhra*, and *madhuka* is always recommended for the child to rinse a mouth that is discharging fluid. (172–173)
In cases of inflammation of the mouth (mukhapāka), an application of *aśvattha* bark, leaves, and honey should be made.
To a child who cries, one should give for his comfort the powder of *pippalī* and *triphalā* saturated with ghee and honey to be licked. 174–175.
Having drunk a paste of *harītakī*, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha* combined with honey along with breast milk, a child is freed from *tālukaṇṭaka*.
[176] [The paste consists of] the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *lodhra*, *punarnavā*, ginger, and the two types of *bṛhatī*.
They prescribe a lukewarm ointment that subdues *śleṣman* (phlegm) to be applied in cases of *kukūṇaka*.
One should foment the protruding umbilical swelling with a lump of clay heated by fire, sprinkled with milk, and still warm; by this, the swelling is pacified.
For inflammation of the umbilicus (nābhipāka), oil boiled with niśā, lodhra, priyaṅgu, and madhuka is recommended for massage; these same drugs may also be used as a dusting powder.
For inflammation of the umbilicus, the burnt ashes of goat dung should be used as a dusting powder.
One may also prepare [a remedy] with the powders of milky trees or with the dust of sandalwood (180).
In the case of anal inflammation (gudapāka) in children, one should administer Pitta-alleviating treatments;
Rasanjana is especially beneficial for both internal consumption and topical application.

A powder made from conch shell, *yaṣṭī*, and collyrium removes anal inflammation in children. (181) An ointment consisting of conch shell, *sauvīra* salt, and *yaṣṭī* should be applied for *ahipūtana*. (182) In the case of *pārigarbhika* disease, however, digestive stimulants (*vahnidīpana*) are employed. (183)
One should rub the area around the teeth with honey and powder, or with *dhātakī* flowers and *pippalī*, using the juice of *dhātrī* fruit;
thus, diseases arising from the eruption of teeth will not afflict the child. (184)

For when the teeth have grown, diseases caused by them are indeed pacified. (185) Gold-dust well-prepared, kuṣṭha, honey, ghee, vacā, matsyākṣaka, śaṅkhapuṣpī, honey, ghee, and gold— The result of this is that the child becomes free from disease and lives for a hundred years. (186) One should give it to the child on the sixth day, or on the eighth, or on the twelfth; or else, having performed the rite of tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa), one should give it on the auspicious day. (187) By this, the child becomes endowed with long life, strength, and splendor, and is freed from all diseases. (188) One should give it to the child while reciting the mantra "tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam" or the mantra "gaurīrmimāya salilāni takṣatī. (189) Having thus given the medicine, one should perform the rite of protection (rakṣā) for the child. One should also recite the mantra "namo bhagavate āryāvalokiteśvarāya" over it. (190) This is the supreme secret of the Bodhisattva, which brings about the welfare of children. It should be kept hidden and not revealed to anyone. (191) Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of childhood diseases in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*. (Note: The numbering provided follows the original verse sequence.)

Arkapuṣpī with honey and ghee; powdered gold with vacā and gold powder; kaiṭarya; and white dūrvā grass with ghee and honey—these four medicinal potions (prāśas) have been declared, each concluded by half a verse.
These are known to promote the physical form, intelligence, strength, and nourishment of children.
(187) One should prepare an oil with an equal quantity of lac juice and four times as much curd-whey (*mastu*), combined with *rāsnā*, *candana*, *kuṣṭha*, *āhvā*, *vājigandhā*, and *niśā*. (188)
A preparation of śatāhvā, dāru, yaṣṭyāhva, mūrvā, tiktā, and hareṇu,
when properly prepared, destroys fever and demons and promotes strength and complexion in an infant.
Chapter on Diseases of Infants is completed.
This Middle Section is completed.
Now begins the Uttarakhanda (Latter Section) in the chapter on therapeutics;
herein begins the seventy-second chapter: Vājīkaraṇa (Aphrodisiacs).
