That substance which makes a man capable of sexual intercourse like a stallion is called *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac) by the sages, the best among physicians. One who is incapable of sexual intercourse is a *klība*; the state of being such is called *klaibya* (impotence).
That [cause] is said to be of seven kinds, and its etiology is now described:
when the mind of a man desiring sexual union is wounded by various unpleasant objects, the penis falls limp, and from this, impotence arises.
Impotence arising from sexual union with a woman who is disliked is known as mental impotence (3).
From the excessive consumption of pungent, sour, hot, and salty substances, a depletion of semen due to pitta is observed; from that, impotence is produced (4).
He who is habitually addicted to excessive sexual intercourse and does not engage in aphrodisiac practices suffers from the loss of virility caused by the depletion of semen;
From the cutting of the veins that carry semen, there occurs a lack of erection (mehana-anunnati).

Due to the suppression of the sixth [fluid] by one who is strong and has an agitated mind through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya), that is known as impotence caused by the obstruction of semen.

That which is innate impotence from birth is indeed the seventh [type]. Innate impotence and that which arises from the cutting of a vital point (marmacheda) are incurable. For those types of impotence that are curable in this world, one should apply the opposite of their cause.

Since the primary medical treatment is the avoidance of the causes [of disease], a man who has been properly purified and is free from illness may employ aphrodisiac formulations from the age of sixteen until the end of the seventies. 10–11.
A man desiring long life should not engage in sexual union with women before the age of sixteen, nor after seventy;
for diseases such as wasting, swellings, and venereal sores are exceedingly difficult to overcome.
Otherwise, there may be untimely death for one who indulges in women.
For men who are playful, wealthy, endowed with beauty and youth, and who have many wives, aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa) is beneficial. 13–14.
For the elderly who desire sexual pleasure, for those seeking the favor of women,
for those exhausted by excessive indulgence with women, for the impotent, and for those of scanty semen— these beneficial aphrodisiac formulations provide gratification and bestow strength. (15)
These too are to be enjoyed by those with nourished bodies, depending on the time and other factors:
various foods, diverse drinks, song, words pleasing to the ear, and likewise the pleasure of touch. (16-17)
The night adorned with the moon as its tilaka, the passionate woman in the bloom of youth,
song pleasing to the ear, betel, wine, garlands,
fragrant scents, diverse forms, and pleasure groves— 18.
The absence of mental obstruction makes a man virile.

One afflicted by disease, even if eighty years old, should lick a mixture of honey-ore, honey, mercury, iron powder, harītakī, śilājatu, viḍaṅga, and ghee for twenty-one days with one-pointed concentration; thus he shall enjoy women like a youth. 19–20.
Satva, guḍūcī, gaganam, along with lodhra, elā, sitā, and māgadhikā— this mixture,
when licked with honey, makes even a eunuch serve a hundred women.
Pāyasa prepared in the milk of cows that have recently calved [is likewise effective].

Having eaten wheat flour mixed with sugar, honey, and ghee, even one who is old becomes exhilarated and may even approach ten wives. [One should take] half an āḍhaka of curd, slightly sour and sweet, along with candied sugar of lunar brilliance.
One *prastha* of honey, one *pala* each of clarified butter and ginger, eight *māṣas* of black pepper,
likewise four *māṣas* of long pepper, and one *karṣa* of cloves—
having placed these on a white cloth, one should slowly lift them with the palm of the hand and strain the liquid. 23.
In an earthen vessel rubbed with musk and sandalwood paste and perfumed with the smoke of aguru,
one should mix all of that together with camphor and set it aside for one's own use;
for this Rasālā was indeed prepared by Makareśvara himself.
Like a beloved wife who is always dear to her husband, she kindles passion and brings pleasure to the enjoyer.
(24) The formulations for increasing sexual vigor consist of gokṣura, ikṣuraka seeds, vājigandhā, and śatāvarī.

Mushali, vanaribija, yashti, nagabala, and bala—(25) the powder of these, prepared with milk and fried in cow's ghee, should be made into a bolus (modaka) with sugar; when consumed, it is a supreme aphrodisiac. (26)
Milk should be eight times the amount of the powder, and ghee is considered equal to the powder;
one should consume twice as much sugar as all these combined, according to the strength of one's digestive fire (agni).
Since this has been prepared by collecting many aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) ingredients, [it is highly effective]. 27.

Therefore, among many yogas, this yoga is considered the most excellent. (28) Four parts of space, followed by two parts, then mercury, one part, the seed-syllable of Śambhu, and likewise three parts of the "dead" [metal]— this is the perfected root-essence.

Take two parts each of the four ingredients—nutmeg (*jātīphala*), black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), and ginger (*nāgara*)—along with two parts of cloves (*devapuṣpa*) and two parts of cinnamon leaves (*jātīpatra*); all these should be ground together as one powder.
Two parts of this entire mixture should be sugar, which, combined with ghee and honey, should be made into boluses (*modaka*). 29.
Having observed the fire, one should boldly consume it for the sake of increasing fresh bliss;

this yoga, known as *vājīkaraṇa*, is here proclaimed by the name Bhairavānanda, the destroyer of all diseases, which crushes the pride of Kāmadeva through the loosening of the bonds of many women. 30.

One should eat the testicles of a goat or a tortoise prepared with long pepper and salt and cooked in ghee; this is a powerful aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa). One should have ten palas of betel nut from the Deccan region finely ground.
That [substance], having been steamed by contact with water, becomes very soft; it should be compressed and ground into a powder.

That powder, purified through a cloth, should be cooked in eight times its quantity of pure cow’s milk mixed with one añjali of clarified butter and a thick consistency; one should add half a tulā of sugar to it. (32)
Once it is cooked by that fire, one should bring it toward the earth and then cast back into it whatever [substances] there may be;
those I shall now describe in detail, having observed them with respect from the *Saṃhitās*:
cardamom, *nāgabalā*, *balā*, along with *capalā*, nutmeg, and *liṅgaka*.
It is provided with *jātī* leaves, excellent leaves, and *patraka*, and is combined with bark. [Also included are:
*viśvā*, *vīraṇa*, *vārivārida-varā*, *vāṃśī*, *varī*, *vānarī*, *drākṣā*, *ikṣu*, *gokṣura*, then *mahatī*, *kharjūrikā*, and *kṣīrikā*.
Dhānyāka, kaśeruka, madhuka, śṛṅgāṭaka, jīraka,
pṛthvīkā, yavānikā, varaṭikā, māṃsī, misī, methikā,
and among the tubers here, vidārikā, muśalī, and gandharvagandhā. 34.
Karcūra, karikeśara, black pepper, fresh seeds of cucumber,
seeds produced from the śālmalī tree, seeds of karikaṇā, and white lotus-born [seeds], along with white sandalwood and red sandalwood, together with flowers known as śrī; 35.

Having separately pulverized all these ingredients, each weighing one *pala*, one should add to them mercury, tin, lead, iron, and mica, which have been processed according to one's preference; furthermore, one should add as much musk and camphor powder as is available.
Afterwards, one should prepare for him *modaka* pills the size of *bilva* fruits (36).
Having eaten those, he should always eat according to the strength of his digestive fire (*agni*).
Once the previously consumed food has reached its state of digestion, he should consume sour taste before the next meal.
One should regularly consume this betel-nut preparation known as *strīrativallabha*;
he shall have increased virility and intensified passion, becoming like a stallion capable in sexual union.
He will always possess a blazing digestive fire, be strong, free from wrinkles, joyful, and well-nourished.
Even he who is old is as charming as a youth, as beautiful as the full moon.
If, moreover, in this beloved of Rati, there were a perfect *khurāśāṇikā*,
the seed of the *dhattūra*, the sun’s ray, a *potha*, and likewise the drying up of the ocean— 38.
One should add half a part each of *sanmājūphalaka*, *khasaphala*, bark, and *kārṣikā*, along with *vijayā*; this indeed becomes the Kāmeśvara modaka.
(39) The great Khaṇḍakūṣmāṇḍaka, as described in the section on *raktapitta*, [is also effective].
It is known as a destroyer of diseases such as *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) and a great aphrodisiac. 40.
One should add one *droṇa* of the juice of ripe mangoes, one *āḍhaka* measure of sugar, one *prastha* measure of ghee, and eight *palas* of ginger. 41.
One *kuḍava* measure of black pepper (*marica*) and two *pala* measures of long pepper (*pippalī*),
having added one *āḍhaka* of water, should all be combined together;
one should cook this in an earthen vessel, stirring it with a wooden ladle.
When it has thickened and has been removed from the heat, one should add the powders of these:
coriander, cumin, harītakī, citraka, mustaka, cinnamon, large cumin, pippalīmūla, and nāgakeśara. (43–44)
One should take cardamom seeds and cloves separately in the measure of one *palapalaka*; once prepared, when cooled, one should add two *kuḍavas* of honey.
A person should consume this, measuring one *pala*, prior to a meal.
Alternatively, one should eat this in a fixed measure according to one's digestive capacity;
by its use, a man becomes as capable in sexual intercourse as a horse, and he shall always be strong, nourished, and free from disease. (46-47)

This powder of *gokṣura*, prepared with goat’s milk and taken with honey, destroys malabsorption (*grahaṇī*), consumption (*kṣaya*), asthma (*śvāsa*), anorexia (*arocaka*), acid gastritis (*amlapitta*), severe dyspnea (*mahāśvāsa*), hemoptysis (*raktapitta*), and jaundice (*pāṇḍutā*). (48)
That which is produced by improper application destroys the virility of one who has consumed it. 49.
As for substances such as sandalwood and the like, [the primary ones are] sandalwood, red sandalwood, pattaṅga, kālīya, agaru, and black agaru. 50.
Devadruma, sarala, padmaka, and tūṇika; camphor, musk, the fragrant vine, and kastūrikā; silhika, fresh saffron, and likewise nutmeg (jātīphalaka). 51.
Clove leaf, cloves, small cardamom, and large cardamom; 52.
kankola fruit, cinnamon bark, cinnamon leaves, nagakesara, vetiver, likewise spikenard, and either costus or white sandalwood; 53.
Murā, karpūraka, śaileya, bhadramustaka, reṇukā, priyaṅgu, śrīvāsa, guggulu,
as well as lākṣā, nakha, rāla, and dhātakī flowers. (54)

Having ground granthiparṇa, mañjiṣṭhā, tagara, and likewise beeswax—each in the measure of one śāṇa—one should slowly cook a prastha-measure of oil; this should be properly poured into an auspicious vessel. 55–56.
One whose body is anointed with this, even if aged and eighty years old,
becomes young again, rich in semen, and exceedingly beloved by women. Even a barren woman conceives, and even an old man becomes like a youth.

A sonless man obtains a son and may live for a hundred autumns. This great oil, beginning with sandalwood, destroys hemorrhaging, consumption, fever, burning sensations, excessive perspiration, foul odor, leprosy, and itching.
Daśamūla, kaṇā, vahni, kapittha, vibhītaka, kaṭphala, marica, viśvamūla, pippalī, saindhava,
raktarohītaka, dantī, drākṣā, jīraka, and the two types of niśā.
Dhātrī, jantughna, śikhari, śṛṅgī, dāru, and punarnavā; 61 dhānyāka, devakusuma, rājavṛkṣa, trikaṇṭaka, vṛddhadāru, kuberākṣī, and the root of vīraṇikā. 62

One should boil one *āḍhaka* each of these pairs of medicinal substances and one *āḍhaka* of *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) in five *āḍhakas* of water. Once the *pathyā* has become thoroughly cooked, honey should then be added.
Then, following the instructions of the guru according to the prescribed rite for three days,
one should further add five days and likewise ten days;
thereafter, once the Abhayā is fully perfected, one should place it in a vessel of ghee.
Afterwards, one who is devoted to wisdom should carefully place the previously mentioned stalks into a pure, very firm vessel filled with honey.
This auspicious Harītakī was prepared by Dhanvantari.
The man who consumes this regularly finds all diseases destroyed in every way:
asthma, cough, consumption, jaundice, hiccups, vomiting, vertigo, diseases of the mouth, as well as thirst, loss of appetite, and weak digestion. (67–68)
It cures enlargement of the liver and spleen, as well as extremely severe vātarakta, pain in the head, eyes, and ears, as well as intestinal obstruction (baddhaguda-udara),
malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and other difficult disorders arising from the three doṣas.
Known as Madhupakva, it destroys numerous diseases. One should gently heat one *kuḍava* measure of the seeds of *kapikacchu* in a *prastha* of cow's milk until it becomes thick. 70–71.
Having taken these [ingredients] and made them into a paste, one should grind them finely;
having formed small pills from this paste, one should cook them in cow's clarified butter (gavya-ājya),
and once well-cooked, those pills should be coated with double the amount of sugar.
All the pills should be placed in honey so that they may be easily swallowed;
one should consume five *ṭaṅkas* of them both in the morning and in the evening.
By this, even he who is slow to ejaculate and he who has a drooping penis shall become swift in his flow.
He too attains great capacity for sexual union like a stallion;
there is no other supreme aphrodisiac substance equal to this.
[The ingredients are: Ākārakarabha, ginger, cloves, saffron, and long pepper.
One karṣa each of nutmeg, jasmine flowers, and sandalwood should be ground separately; one pala of *ahiphena* (opium) should be added to that.
Having combined everything, one should consume a dose of one māṣa with honey.
This [remedy] causes the retention of semen in men and produces bliss;
a lover should employ it at night to arouse the passion of women.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter on aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa). 72.
Now begins the seventy-third chapter, on Rasāyana (Rejuvenation Therapy).
That medicine which destroys old age and disease, and likewise promotes the stabilization of youth, is beneficial for the eyes, nourishing, and aphrodisiac—that is Rasāyana. (1)
Through the practice of *rasāyana*, a person may obtain long life, memory, intelligence, health, youthfulness, strength of body and senses, and luster.
However, the procedure for *rasāyana* is not effective for one whose body is impure.
It does not shine when applied to soiled clothing, like a dye-mixture applied to it.
Cold water, milk, honey, and ghee— each one individually,
or all three combined, when drunk beforehand, will preserve one's youth.

The fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī* should be used; likewise, the powder of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* with milk, the juice of *guḍūcī* along with its roots and flowers, and indeed the paste of *śaṅkhapuṣpī* should be employed. These bestow longevity, destroy diseases, and increase strength, digestive fire, complexion, and the voice.
These are purifying elixirs (*rasāyana*), and *śaṅkhapuṣpī* is especially purifying.
Tugākṣīrī combined with honey, *pippalī* with salt,
or *triphalā* with sugar, constitutes a perfected elixir.

One who desires the qualities of a rejuvenative tonic (rasāyana) should consume Abhayā in succession with rock salt, sugar, dry ginger, Pippalī, honey, and jaggery during the rainy season and the other seasons respectively.
Furthermore, one should drink half a pala of freshly ground Punarnavā with milk for half a month.
Whether for three months, three times that, or for an equal period, even one who has grown old shall become young again.
Those who drink the fresh juice extracted from *bhṛṅgarāja* every day for one month, subsisting on milk alone, become endowed with strength and virility and attain a lifespan of a hundred years. (10)
Having prepared śatāvarī, muṇḍitikā, guḍūcī, sahastikarṇā,
and sahatālamūlī in equal proportions, one should lick them with clarified butter or honey.
Thereby, a man shall have a body free from old age, disease, and death, and be endowed with virility, strength, and other virtues.
Resembling a god, he shines eternally, composed of light and endowed with abundant growth.
(12) Having drunk Ashvagandha for half a month with milk, ghee, oil, or warm water, it bestows nourishment upon virility and the body, just as rain does for a young tree. (13)

One *pala* of iron, one *pala* of *guggulu*, three *palas* of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), five *palas* [of the three pungents], eight *palas* of powdered *triphalā*, and one *karṣa* [of other ingredients] should be added here; by licking this, one attains immortality itself.
Not only does he who duly practices this elixir (*rasāyana*) enjoy a long life in this world, [but also attains the aforementioned state].
He attains that auspicious state frequented by the celestial sages, as well as the imperishable Brahman.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the Section on Elixirs (Rasāyana). [Followed by] the author’s benediction.
As long as the orbs of the sun and the moon shine in the sky;
as long as the seven oceans and the mountains remain upon the back of the earth;
and as long as the circle of the world rests upon the circle of the hoods of the Lord of Serpents; [so long may this work endure].
Let virtuous physicians everywhere study this auspicious Bhāvaprakāśa;
and may there always be long life and happiness for those teachers of this work and those who show it respect among men, through the grace of the venerable Brahmin Someśāditya.
This Uttara-khaṇḍa is completed;
and this work is finished.
